title.en: Makite and the Lone-Dweller's Candles
title.zh: 馬基特與獨居者的蠟燭

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Makite', eBook #28932

summary.en: A unsuccessful hunter abandons his seal-rich in-laws to live alone in the hills, sleeps in a lone-dweller's house hung with reindeer and fox skins, and learns by threat where the candle-like treasures grow — on the farther of two blue hills in the south. Surviving his host's midnight bow, he kills the pursuer with a backward-thrust harpoon, witnesses the dwarfs' wave-war with the inland-dwellers, and returns home to hang the candle-things from the high hill in his own house.
summary.zh: 獵運不濟的馬基特拋下多豹的妻族，獨自入山居住。他借宿獨居者之屋——牆掛馴鹿狐皮，屋內有如蠟燭之物——逼問得其所來：在南天兩座藍山中較遠的山頂。夜半避過主人的弓，又反手一叉殺了追兵；其後目擊矮人與內陸人鬥水成浪之戰，歸家後取回山頂蠟燭之物，懸掛屋中直至終老。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s; lone-dweller (tornit/inlander) narratives are a major cycle of Greenlandic oral literature.

passages.text: Makite took to wife the sister of many brothers, but he never managed to catch a seal in his kayak while his wife's brothers caught them in great numbers. Hearing that his wife would leave him because he never caught anything, he resolved in his grief to go up into the hills and live there all alone. When darkness fell he set off; his wife's father saw him go and cried to the house, 'Go after him' — but Makite made his steps longer and longer until the brothers gave up the pursuit. At dawn he came to a house with hangings of nothing but reindeer and foxes' skins, and went in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Makite'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬基特娶了有許多兄弟的女子為妻，但他始終沒能在皮划艇裡捕到一隻海豹，而他妻子的兄弟們卻捕到許多。他聽說妻子因為他什麼也捕不到而要離開他，便在悲痛中決意上山，獨自住在那裡。天黑時他動身出發；他妻子的父親見他離去，便朝屋裡喊道：「去追他」——但馬基特把步子邁得越來越大，直到那些兄弟放棄了追趕。黎明時他來到一座屋子，屋裡掛的全是馴鹿皮和狐狸皮，他便走了進去。

passages.text: The door hinge creaked and the house shook; the lone-dweller, its master, came in and offered food, but Makite would eat nothing until he learned what those candle-like things in front of the window were. 'That is no concern of one who is not himself a lone-dweller,' came the answer — until Makite threatened to kill him. Then the lone-dweller told: on the nearer of the two great blue hills away south you will find nothing, but he who climbs the farther hill and reaches the top will find such things there; but this cannot be done by one who is not a lone-dweller. During the night Makite caught the host quietly stringing his bow to kill him in his sleep, feigned waking, and at dawn slipped out; pursued, he ran three times round a big rock and thrust his harpoon out behind him without turning, striking the pursuer in the side and killing him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Makite'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 門軸吱嘎作響，屋子也震動起來；獨居者，也就是這屋的主人，走了進來，奉上食物，但馬基特什麼也不肯吃，除非弄明白窗前那些像蠟燭的東西究竟是什麼。「這不關一個自己不是獨居者的人的事，」對方答道——直到馬基特威脅要殺了他。於是獨居者說道：在南邊兩座藍色大山中較近的那座上，你什麼也找不到；但誰若爬上較遠的那座山並到達山頂，就會在那裡找到這樣的東西；然而這不是一個自己不是獨居者的人所能做到的。夜裡，馬基特察覺主人悄悄拉開弓，想趁他睡夢中殺他，便假裝醒來，黎明時溜了出去；被追趕時，他繞著一塊大石跑了三圈，頭也不回地把魚叉向身後刺出，刺中追趕者的肋側，將他殺死。

passages.text: Wandering at hazard he came to a great plain with something like a house in the middle: the house of a dwarf, crowded with folk streaming in and out, too small even to put his foot in the passage until told to heave up the passage way with his back. The old creature warned him as he went out: look towards the west, the inland-dwellers are coming. The dwarfs went out to fight, posting themselves on the plain in two silent lines; when the inlanders' dog gave a great bark, a mighty wave rolled up to the dwarfs — and shrank to nothing close by them. Then the dwarfs' dog barked, their own wave rose and washed right over the inland folk, drowning all but a few. Makite built himself a house, fetched some of the candle-like things from the high hill, hung them up in his house, and lived there until he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Makite'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他漫無目的地遊蕩，來到一片大平原，平原中央有個像屋子的東西：那是一個矮人的屋子，裡面擠滿了人，進進出出，川流不息，那通道小得他連腳都伸不進去，直到有人叫他用自己的背把通道撐起來。那老東西在他出去時警告他：朝西看，內陸的居民來了。矮人們出去迎戰，在平原上排成兩列沉默的隊伍；當內陸人的狗發出一聲響亮的吠叫，一道巨浪朝矮人們湧來——卻在他們近旁縮小得無影無蹤。接著矮人的狗吠叫起來，他們自己的浪湧起，直直漫過內陸人，除了少數幾個，全都淹死了。馬基特給自己蓋了一座屋子，從高山上取來一些像蠟燭的東西，掛在屋裡，便住在那裡，直到死去。

title.en: Asaloq: The Strength Trial and the Magic Songs
title.zh: 阿薩洛克：角力試煉與咒歌

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Asaloq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Searching for his vanished foster-brother in a three-layered umiak, Asaloq passes a black ripple of sea-lice that eats one skin layer and a ripple of sea-serpents that eats another, to land among strangers whose squint talebearer-boy betrays his presence. Summoned before their strong man, he eats until the food falls out of his stomach and pulls arms until the skin is worn from his own — leaving strongest of all — then hides on an island and sings magic songs until the pursuing umiaks give up and row home.
summary.zh: 阿薩洛克乘三層皮大舟尋找失蹤的結拜兄弟，途經海虱黑浪（蝕去一層皮）與海蛇黑浪（再蝕一層），抵達異鄉；斜眼傳話童洩其蹤。彼族力士召他比武——他大吃至腹中之物盡吐，又拉臂拉到自身皮開肉綻，終以最強者離場。北來大舟搜捕之際，他立於山頂高唱咒歌，直到追兵放棄返航。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Sea-lice and sea-serpent passages are cosmological hazards of the Greenlandic kayak world.

passages.text: Asaloq had a foster-brother who disappeared one day while he was out in his kayak. Finding him nowhere, Asaloq built a big umiak covered with three layers of skins and rowed south with his wife. A black ripple appeared on the sea ahead: the sea-lice, which ate away the outermost layer of skins before they got through. Another black ripple: the sea-serpents, which cost them a second layer. With one layer left they rowed in fear, rounded a point, and came in sight of a place with many houses, where the strangers caught hold of their boat and hauled it up for them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Asaloq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿薩洛克有一個義兄弟，有一天他乘皮划艇外出時失蹤了。阿薩洛克到處都找不到他，便造了一艘蒙著三層皮的大划艇，帶著妻子向南划去。前方海面上出現一道黑色的漣漪：那是海蝨，在他們穿過之前就啃掉了最外面的一層皮。又一道黑色漣漪：那是海蛇，使他們又損失了一層皮。只剩一層皮時，他們滿懷恐懼地划著，繞過一個岬角，望見一個有許多屋子的地方，那裡的外鄉人抓住他們的船，替他們把船拖了上去。

passages.text: The place had a strong man in its midst, and a squinting talebearer boy who, in spite of being set up behind the lamp, slipped out and ran to tell. Faces filled the window: 'We are sent to bid the stranger come.' In the crowded house the strong man called from the far end of the bench, 'Let us have a wrestling match'; a skin was spread on the floor and food brought in — Asaloq ate till there was no more left, and when he rose, all he had eaten fell out of his stomach. Then the pulling of arms: he pulled at the arms of all the men until the skin was worn from his own arm, the flesh almost bare. Straightening out every arm in the house, he went out strongest of all and rowed south with his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Asaloq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個地方有個力大無窮的人，還有一個瞇著眼的搬弄是非的男孩；這男孩雖然被安置在燈後，卻仍溜了出去，跑去報信。窗口擠滿了臉孔：「我們奉命來請那位陌生人過來。」在擁擠的屋裡，那壯漢從長凳的遠端喊道：「我們來比一場角力吧。」地上鋪開一張獸皮，食物也端了進來——阿薩洛克一直吃到再沒有東西剩下；當他起身時，他吃下的一切都從胃裡掉了出來。接著是較量臂力：他與所有男人較臂力，直到他自己手臂上的皮都磨掉了，肉幾乎裸露。他把屋裡每個人的手臂都扳直之後，以最強者的身分走了出去，帶著妻子向南划去。

passages.text: On a little island they pitched their tent on the sunny side; from the hilltop Asaloq saw many umiaks coming from the northward, which camped on the shady side, searching carefully about — 'He can hardly be on such a little island.' Asaloq sang magic songs over them from the top of the hill until he heard them say, 'We may as well go home again.' Not until they were out of sight did he row on south, and at last they reached Aluk, where their bones still rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Asaloq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一座小島上，他們把帳篷搭在向陽的一側；阿薩洛克從山頂望見許多烏米亞克（umiak，大型皮艇）從北方駛來，那些人把營地紮在背陰的一側，仔細四處搜尋——「他不可能在這麼小的一座島上。」阿薩洛克從山頂對他們唱起魔法之歌，直到他聽見他們說：「我們還是回家去吧。」直到他們消失不見，他才繼續向南划去，最後他們抵達阿盧克，他們的遺骨至今仍安息在那裡。

title.en: Ukaleq: Killed by the Magic Bear, Raised by His Mother
title.zh: 烏卡萊克：魔熊之殺與母親之復生

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Ukaleq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Ukaleq, who never failed to kill whatever game he chased, dies at last to a Magic Bear whose teeth whisper his killing to the comrades who find him. His mother, keeping the dress he wore as a little child, hushes it in her carrying bag through five days without food or drink until it begins to crawl — and as it springs out the dead man begins to breathe and sit up, restored. At a great spirit calling, an old wifeless man's question shames the woman who owned the Magic Bear so that she dies on the spot; Ukaleq goes home and never hunts bears again.
summary.zh: 從不失手的獵手烏卡萊克終為魔熊所殺——熊齒低語向同伴揭露真相。其母藏著他幼時舊衣，將之抱於行囊中如哄嬰兒，絕食絕飲五日，直到囊中之物蠕動欲出；舊衣一躍而出，屋搖震動，死者開始呼吸、坐起，復活如初。大降靈會上，無妻老人一句質問，令養魔熊的老嫗羞死當場；烏卡萊克從此再不獵熊。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Magic Bear (a tupilak-like created bear) and child's-dress resurrection beliefs documented as told in the source.

passages.text: Ukaleq was a strong man who had only to go out after whatever game was heard of, even a great bear, to kill it. One winter, hunting on the new ice, he found the bear not easily brought down; it sighted him and turned to pursue, and though he wounded it now and again as he fled, he was killed himself at last — at the same moment the bear fell dead. When his comrades came to look at it, its teeth began to whisper, and then they knew Ukaleq had been killed by a Magic Bear. They took the dead man home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ukaleq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏卡萊克是個強壯的人，只要聽說有什麼獵物，哪怕是一頭大熊，他只需出去便能將牠殺死。有一年冬天，他在新結的冰上打獵，發現那頭熊不容易被擊倒；熊看見了他，便轉身追來，他一面逃一面不時將牠刺傷，最後自己卻被殺死了——就在同一刻，那頭熊也倒地而死。當他的同伴前來察看那頭熊時，牠的牙齒開始低聲細語，他們這才明白烏卡萊克是被一頭魔法熊殺死的。他們把死者帶回了家。

passages.text: His mother had kept the dress he wore as a little child. She had him laid in the middle of the floor on a skin, put the dress in her carrying bag, went out to the cooking place in the passage, and said: 'For five days I will neither eat nor drink.' Then she began hushing the dress in the bag as if it were a child, hushing on and on until it began to move — and just then someone came out saying Ukaleq was beginning to quiver. She hushed still harder; the thing in the bag tried to crawl out as someone called that Ukaleq had begun to breathe and was sitting up. The bag's occupant sprang out and made the whole house shake. They made up a bed on the side bench; after five days without eating or drinking he came to himself, and commenced to go out hunting once more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ukaleq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的母親一直保存著他小時候穿的那件衣服。她讓人把他放在地板中央的一張獸皮上，把那件衣服放進她的背袋裡，走到通道裡的炊煮處，說道：「五天之内，我既不吃也不喝。」然後她開始在袋中像哄孩子一樣哄著那件衣服，哄了又哄，直到它開始動了起來——就在那時，有人出來說烏卡萊克開始顫動了。她哄得更用力了；袋裡的東西試圖爬出來，同時有人喊道烏卡萊克已經開始呼吸，並且坐了起來。袋中之物跳了出來，震得整座屋子都搖晃。他們在側邊的長凳上鋪了一張床；五天不吃不喝之後，他恢復了神智，又開始外出打獵了。

passages.text: Next winter, when the ice had formed, the villages held their spirit callings and visited one another. Ukaleq went with his family to a big calling in a house with three windows, crowded with folk. Midway, an old woman sitting cross-legged on the bench turned and said: 'We heard last autumn that Ukaleq had been killed by a Magic Bear.' An old wifeless man turned to her at once: 'Was it by any chance your Magic Bear that killed him?' She answered, 'Mine? Now where could I have kept such a thing?' — but after saying that she did not move; she even forgot to breathe, for shame at having been discovered, and died on the spot. Ukaleq went home and never went out hunting bears again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ukaleq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二年冬天，冰結成之後，各村舉行了招魂聚會，彼此往來拜訪。烏卡萊克帶著家人去參加一場在一座有三扇窗戶的屋裡舉行的大型聚會，屋裡擠滿了人。聚會進行到一半，一個盤腿坐在長凳上的老婦人轉過身來說：「我們去年秋天聽說烏卡萊克被一頭魔法熊殺死了。」一個沒有妻子的老人立刻轉向她：「殺死他的，該不會正好是妳的魔法熊吧？」她回答：「我的？唉，我能把那種東西藏在哪裡呢？」——但說完這話之後，她一動也不動；她甚至忘了呼吸，因為被人識破而羞愧，當場就死了。烏卡萊克回了家，此後再也不出去獵熊了。

title.en: Raja Suran Descends to the Sea-Kingdom in a Glass Chest
title.zh: 蘇蘭王乘玻璃櫃潛入海底王國

region.en: Southern Java Sea (symbolic pin — the open sea crossed between Kling and Tamsak)
region.zh: 爪哇南部海域（象徵性定位：克林與淡馬錫之間的公海）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (Raja Suran's descent), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Wishing to see the wonders of God's creation, Raja Suran seals himself in a locked glass chest lowered by a golden chain into the sea. He lands in the submarine realm of Zeya, marries the sea-king's daughter Putri Mahtab-al-Bahri, fathers three sons, and escapes upward on a flying, swimming sea-horse named Sambrani — the Malay Annals' charter myth of the dynasty's descent from the world under the water.
summary.zh: 蘇蘭王欲一睹上帝造化之奇，乃自封於玻璃櫃中，繫以金鏈沉入海底。抵水下之境澤亞，娶海王之女瑪赫塔布，生三子；後騎能飛能泳之海馬桑布拉尼上歸人世——《馬來紀年》以此為王族出自水下世界之憲章神話。

sensitivity.note: Literary dynastic chronicle (Sejarah Melayu); Malaysian and Indonesian Malay communities hold the heritage; the text itself is public domain. Cross-cluster: descent to the otherworld parallels Inanna/Ishtar and Izanagi.

passages.text: Raja Suran, considering that he had now become acquainted with the contents of the land, wished to acquire information concerning the nature of the sea. For this purpose he ordered a chest of glass, with a lock in the inside, and fixed it to a chain of gold. Then, shutting himself up in this chest, he caused himself to be let down into the sea, to see the wonders of God Almighty's creation. At last the chest reached a land, denominated Zeya, when Raja Suran came forth from the chest and walked about to see the wonders of the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇蘭王（Raja Suran）心想自己如今已熟知陸地上的種種事物，便希望獲知關於海洋性質的種種情報。為此，他命人打造一隻玻璃箱，內側裝有鎖，並把它繫在一條金鏈上。然後，他把自己關在這隻箱子裡，命人將他縋入海中，以便觀看全能真主所造萬物的奇觀。最後，箱子抵達了一片名為澤亞（Zeya）的陸地，蘇蘭王便從箱中出來，四處走動，觀看這地方的奇觀。

passages.text: In Zeya he found a people so numerous that God alone could know their numbers, and their king, Aktab-al-Arz, seated him upon his own throne and gave him his daughter, Putri Mahtab-al-Bahri, in marriage; by her he had three sons. At length Suran reflected what advantage it was to stay so long below the earth, and how he might carry his sons' line upward, for it would be a great disadvantage to cut off the line of Secander Zulkarneini.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在澤亞，他發現一個人口眾多到唯有真主才能知其數目的民族；他們的國王阿克塔布-阿爾-阿爾茲讓他坐上自己的王座，並將自己的女兒普特麗·馬赫塔布-阿爾-巴赫里許配給他為妻；他與她生了三個兒子。後來，蘇蘭思忖，長久留在地下究竟有何益處，又該如何將子孫的血脈向上延續，因為斷絕塞坎德·祖爾卡爾奈尼的血脈將是極大的不利。

passages.text: His father-in-law furnished him with a sea-horse named Sambrani, which could fly through the air as well as swim in the water. Suran mounted amid the lamentations of his spouse; the steed quickly cleared the nether atmosphere and rapidly traversed the upper ocean, where his followers perceived him, and by presenting a mare on the shore they lured Sambrani to land and recovered their king. Suran then commanded that the account of his descent be inscribed on a stone monument for posterity, to be found by one of his descendants who should reduce all the rajas under the wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的岳父為他備了一匹名為桑布拉尼的海馬，此馬既能飛越空中，亦能游於水中。蘇蘭在妻子的哀泣聲中跨上馬背；這匹駿馬迅速穿出下層的大氣，疾速橫越上方的海洋，他的追隨者在那裡望見了他，並在岸上牽出一匹母馬，將桑布拉尼誘上岸來，從而尋回了他們的國王。蘇蘭隨後下令，將他下海的經過銘刻於石碑之上，以傳後世，留待他的一位後裔——那位將使所有羅闍皆屈從於風之下者——發現。

title.en: The Rusty Needles: China Cheats the Conqueror
title.zh: 生鏽的鐵針：中國以計退敵

region.en: Tamsak (Singapore), Malay Annals geography
region.zh: 淡馬錫（今新加坡一帶，《馬來紀年》地理）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (the ruse of the mantri of China), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When Raja Suran's immeasurable host threatens China, a sagacious mantri loads a prow with old, toothless sailors, seeds of bidara trees, and iron bars thick as an arm, all rusted over, and sends it to Tamsak. The 'traders' explain that they left China as children and have grown old on the voyage — so vast is the distance. Believing the world's measure, Suran turns back without a battle.
summary.zh: 蘇蘭王大軍將犯中國，中國一賢臣獻計：以滿載老邁無齒水手、巴旦樹種與粗如臂之鐵條（皆已鏽蝕）之船駛至淡馬錫，訛稱自幼離華、行旅經年、樹已結實、鐵已鏽細——蘇蘭王信路途無涯，遂罷兵而返。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle fiction; an episode of ruse-warfare in the Malay Annals' Alexander-derived prehistory.

passages.text: It was reported in the land of China that Raja Suran was advancing with an innumerable army and had arrived at Tamsak. The raja of China was alarmed and said to his mantris and chieftains: 'If the Kling raja approach, the country will be inevitably ruined; what method do you advise to prevent his approach?' Then a sagacious mantri said: 'Lord of the world, your slave will fall on a device.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 中國之地有傳聞說，羅闍·蘇蘭正率領無數大軍推進，已抵達塔姆薩克。中國的羅闍大為驚恐，對他的曼特里斯與首領們說道：『倘若克林羅闍逼近，此國必將毀於一旦；你們有何計策可阻止他前來？』於是，一位睿智的曼特里斯說道：『世界之主啊，您的奴僕將獻上一計。』

passages.text: He ordered a prow filled full of fine needles but covered with rust, planted with seeds of the casamak and bidara trees, and selected a party of old and toothless people to sail to Tamsak. When Suran's men asked how far it was to China, the Chinese replied: 'When we set sail we were all young, about twelve years of age, and we planted these seeds; now we have grown old and lost our teeth, and the seeds we planted have become trees which bore fruit before our arrival here.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他命人備好一艘船，船中裝滿上好的針，卻覆以鐵鏽，並種上卡薩馬克樹與比達拉樹的種子，又挑選了一隊年老無牙之人，揚帆駛往塔姆薩克。當蘇蘭的人問起此地距中國尚有多遠時，那些中國人答道：『我們啟航之時，皆尚年少，約十二歲，並種下這些種子；如今我們已年老，牙齒盡落，而我們所種的種子已長成大樹，且在我們抵達此地之前便已結果。』

passages.text: They took out some of the rusty needles and showed them, saying: 'When we left China these bars of iron were thick as your arm; now they have grown thus small by the corrosion of rust.' If the account were true, said Suran, the land of China must be at an immense distance — when should they ever arrive? All the champions assented, and Raja Suran turned back his host without a battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們取出一些生鏽的針展示出來，說道：『我們離開中國時，這些鐵條粗如你們的手臂；如今因鏽蝕而變得這般細小。』蘇蘭說道，倘若此言屬實，則中國之地必定遙遠至極——他們何時才能抵達？所有勇士皆表贊同，羅闍·蘇蘭便未經一戰即率軍折返。

title.en: The Fall of Gangga Nagara: Suran and Ganggi Shah Juana
title.zh: 剛迦王國之陷落：蘇蘭對剛吉沙朱阿納

region.en: Gangga Nagara on the river Dinding, Perak (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 霹靂州丁丁河畔剛迦城（象徵性定位）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (conquest of Gangga Nagara and Glang Kiu), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: On his march, Raja Suran breaks the steeps of Gangga Nagara with his chacra and duels its raja on elephant-back: Ganggi Shah Juana's arrow fells Suran's huge elephant, but Suran springs up and cuts off the defender's head. He marries the dead king's sister and rides on to destroy Glang Kiu and its raja Chulan in a mêlée of amokas — the Annals' grand old-war set piece.
summary.zh: 蘇蘭王征途之中，以查克羅擊碎剛迦陡城之門，與守王於象背決鬥：剛吉沙朱阿納一箭射倒蘇蘭巨象，蘇蘭躍起拔劍斬其首。娶其妹剛迦公主，續而破翡翠之地格蘭基烏，陣斬朱蘭王——此乃《紀年》古戰史之壯闊段落。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle battle-legend; Perak (Malaysia) place-myth recorded within the shared Malay chronicle tradition.

passages.text: Raja Suran mounted his huge elephant and approached the gate of the fortress, notwithstanding the showers of spears and arrows with which he was assailed; he smote the gate with his chacra, and it immediately tumbled down, while the raja entered the fort with all his champions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 羅闍·蘇蘭騎上他那頭巨象，逼近堡壘的城門，儘管矛與箭如雨般向他襲來；他以恰克拉擊打城門，城門當即倒塌，而這位羅闍便率領他所有的勇士進入堡壘。

passages.text: Raja Ganggi Shah Juana seized his bow and smote the elephant of Raja Suran on the forehead, which instantly fell down. Raja Suran quickly sprang up and drew his sword, and smote off the head of Raja Ganggi Shah Juana; after the raja's death all his subjects submitted, and Suran married Putri Gangga, the beautiful sister of the slain king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 岡吉沙胡阿納王抓起他的弓，射中蘇蘭王那頭大象的前額，大象當即倒地。蘇蘭王迅速躍起，拔出劍來，砍下岡吉沙胡阿納王的頭；這位羅闍死後，他所有的臣民都歸順了，蘇蘭便娶了被殺國王那位美麗的妹妹普特麗岡加為妻。

passages.text: At Glang Kiu the place of the emerald, raja Chulan met him with a host like the sea rough with waves; elephants rushed against elephants, horses bit horses, and the dust ascended to the heavens till the day was darkened like an eclipse. Suran and Chulan charged each other on their elephants roaring like thunder; Chulan's spear pierced Suran's elephant from side to side, and Suran's arrow struck Chulan on the breast and pierced him to the back, and Chulan fell dead on his elephant. Suran took to wife his daughter, Putri Onang-kiu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在翡翠之地格朗基烏，朱蘭羅闍率領著如波濤洶湧的大海般的軍隊與他相遇；象衝向象，馬咬著馬，塵土升上天空，直到白晝昏暗如日蝕。蘇蘭與朱蘭騎著象彼此衝殺，咆哮如雷；朱蘭的長矛將蘇蘭的象從一側刺穿到另一側，蘇蘭的箭射中朱蘭的胸膛，穿透到背後，朱蘭便死在他的象上。蘇蘭娶了他的女兒普特麗奧南基烏為妻。

title.en: Bichitram Shah Abandons His Kingdom for the Sea
title.zh: 比奇特蘭沙棄國出海

region.en: The sea of Silbou (symbolic pin, western Malay world)
region.zh: 西爾布之海（象徵性定位，馬來世界西部）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. I (Bichitram Shah's fleet), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Angry that his father Raja Suran gave him only a small territory while his brothers received kingdoms, Bichitram Shah embarks with twenty war-vessels to conquer the maritime lands. After taking scores of countries he reaches the sea of Silbou, where a hurricane scatters his fleet: half returns to Chandukani, the fate of the other half is unknown — the Annals' template of the sea-faring prince from whom the Palembang line will later descend.
summary.zh: 父王蘇蘭僅予小邑，比奇特蘭沙憤而率二十艘戰船出海，征服海上諸邦；至西爾布海遇風暴，船隊四散——半數歸于昌杜卡尼，半數下落不明。《紀年》以此為海上王侯漂泊之母題，日後巴鄰旁王系即出其後。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle legend; fine as a comparative 'hero on the sea' motif record.

passages.text: On his eldest son Bichitram Shah, Raja Suran only conferred a territory of small extent; and the young prince being displeased at this measure, resolved to abandon his country. He embarked with twenty vessels fitted out with all the apparatus of war, determining to conquer all the maritime districts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇蘭王只把一小片領地封給他的長子比奇特拉姆沙；這位年輕的王子對此心懷不滿，決意離開自己的國家。他帶著二十艘配備齊全戰具的船隻出海，決心征服所有沿海地區。

passages.text: After conquering several scores of countries, he at last reached the sea denominated Silbou, where, being caught in a dreadful hurricane, his fleet was dispersed, and the half of them returned to the country of Chandukani, but the fate of the other half is unknown. The adventures of this prince were very numerous, but they are only alluded to briefly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. I (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在征服了幾十個國家之後，他終於到達了名為西爾布的海洋；在那裡，他遭遇了一場可怕的颶風，艦隊被吹散，其中半數返回了昌杜卡尼國，而另一半的命運則無人知曉。這位王子的冒險經歷極為繁多，但此處僅簡略提及。

title.en: The Rice That Turned to Gold on the Mountain of Belidung
title.zh: 勿里洞山上化金之稻

region.en: Mount Sagantang Maha Miru, near Palembang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 巴鄰旁附近薩甘當摩訶米魯山（象徵性定位）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (Wan Ampu and Wan Malin), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Two rice-cultivating women of Belidung, Wan Ampu and Wan Malin, see their fields gleam like fire in the night. At dawn the grain has become gold, the leaves silver, the stalks brass — and on the golden ground stand three young men: Bichitram Shah's heir as Sang Sapurba on a white steer, with Nila Pahlawan and Karana Pandita holding sword and lance. The Annals' founding apparition of the Palembang dynasty, and the origin of the Awang and Dara castes.
summary.zh: 勿里洞二女萬阿木普與萬馬林耕稻於薩甘當山上，夜見田如火光；晨起視之，穀化金、葉化銀、稈化銅——金土之上立三少年：白牛背上的王儲（後稱三保爺·三蘇爾巴），持劍執矛二侍從立於兩側。此即巴鄰旁王系之顯聖神話，亦阿旺、達拉二姓之由來。

sensitivity.note: Dynasty-foundation apparition; Palembang and Minangkabau communities hold the heritage; public-domain source.

passages.text: There were two young women of Belidung, Wan Ampu and Wan Malin, employed in cultivating rice on this mountain, where they had large and productive rice-grounds. One night they beheld their rice-fields gleaming and glittering like fire; 'It is some great snake or naga,' said Malin, and they lay quiet for fear. When it was daylight they went to see what it was, and found the grain of the rice converted into gold, the leaves into silver, and the stalks into brass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伯利東有兩個年輕女子，萬安普與萬馬林，在這座山上種稻，她們在那裡有大片而豐產的稻田。一天夜裡，她們看見自己的稻田閃爍發光，如同火焰一般；「準是某條大蛇或那伽，」馬林說道，她們便因害怕而靜靜躺著。天亮時她們前去查看究竟是什麼，發現稻穀變成了金子，葉子變成了銀子，稻稈變成了黃銅。

passages.text: On the ground which had assumed this golden colour they saw three young and handsome men: one in the dress of a raja mounted on a bull white as silver, the others holding a sword and a spear. Asked whether they were Jins or Peris, the centre one answered that they were of the race of men, descendants of Raja Secander Zulkarneini and offspring of Raja Suran, whose crown was the evidence of their descent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那片染上這金色的大地上，她們看見三個年輕英俊的男子：一個身穿羅闍的服飾，騎著一頭白如銀子的公牛，其餘兩人手持劍與矛。問他們是精靈還是仙人，中間那人回答說他們屬於人類，是塞坎德爾祖爾卡內尼羅闍的後裔、蘇蘭羅闍的子孫，他們的王冠便是其出身的明證。

passages.text: The girls invited them home and cut the paddy for their food; the prince's name was changed to Sang Sapurba. The bull vomited foam, from which emerged a man named Bat'h, with an immense turban, who began to recite the prince's praises in the Sanscrit language, giving him the title Sang Sapurba Trimarti Tribhuvena. From Bat'h descend the original reciters of the cheritras; Nila Pahlawan and Karana Pandita married the two women, and their male offspring were called Baginda Awang and the female offspring Baginda Dara — hence the origin of all the Awangs and Daras.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那些女子邀請他們回家，並割下稻穀作為他們的食物；王子的名字被改為桑·薩普爾巴。那頭公牛吐出泡沫，從泡沫中出現了一個名叫巴特的人，頭戴巨大的頭巾，開始用梵語歌頌王子的功德，賜予他桑·薩普爾巴·特里馬爾蒂·特里布韋納的稱號。巴特是切里特拉諸吟誦者的始祖；尼拉·帕拉萬與卡拉納·潘迪塔娶了那兩名女子，他們所生的男性後裔被稱為巴金達·阿旺，女性後裔被稱為巴金達·達拉——所有阿旺與達拉的起源便由此而來。

title.en: The Thirty-Nine Leprous Brides of Sang Sapurba
title.zh: 三蘇爾巴王的三十九位痲瘋新娘

region.en: Mount Sagantang Maha Miru, Palembang (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩甘當山，巴鄰旁（象徵性定位）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the leprosy of the low-born brides), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When the heaven-descended prince Sang Sapurba wishes to marry, local rajas bring their daughters — but thirty-nine brides of unsuitable rank are stricken with leprosy 'as with a plague sent as a curse' the moment they join him. Only Wan Sundaria, daughter of the Palembang raja Damang Lebar Dawn, of sufficiently noble blood, escapes untouched — the Annals' mythic warning that kingship of divine descent must be matched with royal blood.
summary.zh: 天降王子三蘇爾巴欲娶親，諸邦獻女——然門第不配者，一與王合即患痲瘋，凡三十九人，如遭天譴。惟巴鄰旁王女萬蘇達莉亞出身高貴，獨免於災——《紀年》以此警示：神裔之王必配王族之血。

sensitivity.note: Royal-hypogamy taboo in the Annals; flagged as interpretive — the leprosy curse encodes caste/royal endogamy rules.

passages.text: It was soon noised over the whole country that a descendant of Raja Secander Zulkarneini had descended on the mountain Sagantang Maha Miru, and all the rajas of the neighbouring countries came with rich presents to pay their respects to him. As he wanted to marry, they all brought him their daughters; but as they were not of proper rank for such a noble prince, as soon as they associated with him they were stricken with a leprosy, as with a plague sent as a curse, to the number of thirty-nine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，全國上下便傳聞拉惹·塞坎德·祖爾卡爾內尼的後裔降臨於薩甘唐·馬哈·米魯山上，鄰近各國的拉惹們都帶著豐厚的禮物前來向他致敬。由於他想要成婚，他們都把自己的女兒帶來獻給他；但因為她們的門第不足以匹配如此高貴的王子，所以一旦與他結合，便染上了痲瘋病，如同上天降下詛咒的瘟疫一般，人數多達三十九人。

passages.text: The raja of Palembang had a daughter of extreme beauty, Wan Sundaria. Sang Sapurba sent to ask her in marriage; her father excused himself, alledging that she would probably be struck with sickness, and would only resign her on certain conditions. After the marriage it was found that she had escaped the curse of leprosy which had afflicted his former wives, to the raja's great satisfaction, and Damang Lebar Dawn came in great haste, rejoiced to find her in excellent health.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴鄰旁（Palembang）的拉惹有一個容貌極美的女兒，名叫萬·孫達里亞。桑·薩普爾巴派人前去求婚；她的父親婉言推辭，聲稱她很可能也會染上疾病，並表示只有在某些條件下才願將她許配。婚後發現她並未染上困擾他前幾位妻子的痲瘋詛咒，拉惹大為滿意，達芒·勒巴爾·道恩也急忙趕來，欣喜地發現她身體極為健康。

title.en: The Covenant of Damang Lebar Dawn: Why a Malay Raja May Not Shame His People
title.zh: 達萬·勒巴爾道恩之盟約：馬來王何以不可羞辱其民

region.en: Palembang, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘巴鄰旁

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the marriage conditions), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Before giving his daughter to Sang Sapurba, Damang Lebar Dawn imposes conditions binding both lines forever: his descendants shall serve the raja's line, but shall never be bound, shamed, or reviled — great faults punished only by death under law; while the raja's line shall never suffer treason from his people's descendants, on pain of heaven 'turning their authority upside down.' The Annals presents this mythic oath as the constitutional origin of Malay kingship and its corresponding loyalty.
summary.zh: 達萬·勒巴爾道恩嫁女之前與三蘇爾巴立盟：其後裔世奉王室，然永不受縛、不受辱、不受詈——重罪唯依法處死；而王系永不受其民後裔之叛，違者天罰顛覆其權。《紀年》以此神話之誓為馬來君權與臣忠之憲政起源。

sensitivity.note: Charter-myth of Malay constitutional custom (adat); the Annals states this oath as the origin of the no-shaming rule.

passages.text: The conditions were that on Sangsapurba marrying his daughter, all the family of Damang Lebar Dawn should submit themselves to him; but that Sangsapurba should engage, both for himself and his posterity, that they should receive a liberal treatment — that when they committed faults they should never be exposed to shame nor opprobrious language, but if their faults were great, that they should be put to death according to the law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 條件是：桑薩普爾巴娶其女兒之後，達芒·勒巴爾·道恩的全族應歸順於他；但桑薩普爾巴須為自己及其後代承諾，他們應受到寬厚的對待——當他們犯下過錯時，絕不應使他們蒙受羞辱或遭受辱罵之言，但若他們的過錯重大，則應依法處死。

passages.text: Sangsapurba requested in his turn that the descendants of Damang Lebar Dawn should never move treasonable practices against his descendants, even though they should become tyrannical. 'Very well,' said Damang Lebar Dawn, 'but if your descendants break your agreements, probably mine will do the same.' These conditions were mutually agreed to, and the parties swore to perform them, imprecating the divine vengeance to turn their authority upside down who should infringe these agreements.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 桑薩普爾巴則反過來要求，達芒·勒巴爾·道恩的後代絕不應對他的後代圖謀叛亂，即使他們變得暴虐無道亦然。『很好，』達芒·勒巴爾·道恩說道，『但若你的後代違背你們的約定，我的後代大概也會如此。』這些條件經雙方相互同意，各方並發誓履行，並祈求神明降罰，使違背這些約定者權位傾覆。

passages.text: From this condition it is that none of the Malay rajas ever expose their Malay subjects to disgrace or shame; they never bind them, nor hang them, nor give them opprobrious language; for whenever a raja exposes his subjects to disgrace, it is the certain token of the destruction of his country: hence also it is that none of the Malay race ever engage in rebellion, or turn their faces from their own rajas, even though their conduct be bad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正因這一條件，馬來諸拉惹從不使其馬來臣民蒙受恥辱或羞辱；他們從不捆綁他們，從不吊死他們，也從不對他們說辱罵之言；因為每當一位拉惹使其臣民蒙受羞辱，那便是其國家滅亡的確定徵兆：因此，馬來族人也從不參與叛亂，或背棄自己的拉惹，即使他們的行為不端亦然。

title.en: The Bathing-House of Seven Stories: Installation of Sang Sapurba
title.zh: 七層浴殿：三蘇爾巴的即位大典

region.en: Palembang, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘巴鄰旁

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the royal bath), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: To celebrate the marriage that escaped the leprosy curse, Damang Lebar Dawn builds the seven-storied bathing-house Pancha Presadha, and for forty days and nights the country feasts until 'the heaps of half-burnt rice lay like hillocks' and buffalo heads float in seas of rice-broth like islands. The royal couple then circles the bath seven times, bathes on its highest story, and ascends the golden throne — the Annals' fullest picture of royal installation ritual.
summary.zh: 為慶婚姻之成，達萬·勒巴爾道恩建七層浴殿『五重寶』；四十晝夜大宴，燒半之米堆積如丘，牛首浮於米湯如島。王與后繞殿七匝，登最高層共浴，後易禮服登金座鳴鼓即位——此為《紀年》所載最詳之王室即位儀注。

sensitivity.note: Royal installation ritual narrative; the bath rite (bersalin) persisted in Malay courts.

passages.text: After his return to Palembang, Damang Lebar Dawn ordered a splendid bathing-house to be constructed, and the architect was the aforesaid Bat'h. This bathing house was named Pancha Presadha, and it had seven stories, and terminated in five towers on the roof. A public festival was then made for the space of forty days and forty nights, attended by all the inferior rajas, mantris, eunuchs, bantaras, champions, and commons in general.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達曼·勒巴爾·道恩返回巴鄰旁後，下令建造一座華美的浴場，建築師即為前述之巴特。此浴場名為潘查·普雷薩達，共有七層，屋頂以五座塔樓作結。隨後舉行為期四十晝夜的公眾慶典，所有下級拉者、曼特里、宦官、班塔拉、勇士及一般平民皆出席參與。

passages.text: The heaps of half-burnt rice rejected lay like hillocks, and the skimming of the foam of the rice-broth stood in little seas, in which floated the heads of buffaloes and goats like so many islands. After the completion of the forty days and nights, the bathing water was introduced with all kinds of music and an immense concourse of people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 棄置的半焦米飯堆積如小丘，米湯浮沫撇出後積成小海，其中漂浮著水牛與山羊的頭顱，宛如眾多島嶼。四十晝夜屆滿後，沐浴之水在各種音樂與龐大人群的簇擁下被引入。

passages.text: The husband and wife, with a great multitude, seven times encircled the bathing-house, and afterwards bathed in the highest story, Bat'h officiating at the bath. After bathing they changed their garments — Sangsapurba arraying himself in the derapata deremani and the queen in the burudaimani — then mounted the golden throne of authority, and the state drums were beat; Bat'h inserted the Panchawa Panchara on the temples of the royal pair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夫婦二人偕同大批人眾，繞行浴場七圈，隨後於最高層沐浴，由巴特主持沐浴之禮。沐浴之後，二人更換衣袍——桑薩普爾巴著德拉帕塔·德雷馬尼，王后著布魯達伊馬尼——繼而登上黃金權座，邦國鼓聲響起；巴特將潘查瓦·潘查拉飾於王室夫婦的鬢角。

title.en: Putri Tunjong Bui, the Princess Born of a Foam-Bell
title.zh: 泡沫之鐘公主：敦戎布伊

region.en: River of Palembang, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘巴鄰旁河

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (Putri Tunjong-bui), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: One day the river of Palembang brings down a foam-bell of uncommon size, and within it appears a young girl of extreme beauty. Sang Sapurba adopts her as his daughter and names her Putri Tunjong Bui, the Princess Foam-Bell — the river-born daughter who will be given in marriage to the young Chinese noble left at court, linking the Palembang line to China.
summary.zh: 一日巴鄰旁河漂下一泡沫巨鐘，鐘中現一絕美少女。三蘇爾巴收為養女，名曰『泡沫之鐘公主』敦戎布伊——此河生之女後嫁留朝之中華貴胄，將巴鄰旁世系與中國相連。

sensitivity.note: Foundling-from-river motif in the dynastic chronicle.

passages.text: It happened on a certain day that the river of Palembang brought down a foam-bell of uncommon size, in which appeared a young girl of extreme beauty. The raja being informed of the circumstance ordered her to be brought to him; this was done, and the raja adopted her as his daughter. She was named Putri Tunjong-bui, or the Princess Foam-bell, and the prince was extremely fond of her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某日，巴鄰旁河上漂來一具異常巨大的泡沫鐘，其中現出一名絕美少女。拉者聞知此事，下令將其帶來；此事遂行，拉者收養她為女兒。她名為普特里·通宗布伊，即泡沫鐘公主，王子對她極為寵愛。

passages.text: The young Chinese of noble birth who had remained at Palembang became greatly attached to the raja, and the raja to him; he wished to settle him in marriage with the Putri Tunjong-bui. The present rajas of Palembang, according to the chronicle, are all descended of this family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那位留在巴鄰旁的貴族出身中國青年與拉者極為親近，拉者亦親近於他；拉者欲安排他與普特里·通宗布伊成婚。據編年史所載，巴鄰旁現今的諸位拉者皆出自此家族。

title.en: The Signet Sent to China: A Marriage Alliance Across the Sea
title.zh: 送印之中國使節：跨海聯姻

region.en: Palembang, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘巴鄰旁

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (marriage of Putri Sri Devi), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The raja of China, hearing that a heaven-descended raja reigns in Palembang, sends ten prows bearing three bahars of gold to ask for his daughter. The warriors counsel compliance 'to promote the friendship between the Malay and the Chinese rajas,' and the elder princess Sri Devi is sent north with a letter stamped with the signet Kampen — declaring that only letters bearing its counterpart may ever be trusted from the Malay line.
summary.zh: 中國王聞天裔之王在巴鄰旁，遣十船載三巴哈爾之金求娶公主。群臣議從，以敦馬中之誼；乃以長公主斯里提毗許嫁，附蓋『甘般』印信之國書——明示：惟印文相符者方可信為馬來王系之書。

sensitivity.note: Diplomatic myth in the Annals; part of the Chinese alliance cycle.

passages.text: It was now noised all over the world that the descendant of Raja Secander Zulkarneini was now in the land of Palembang, even so far as the land of China. Then the raja of China sent to Palembang ten prows to ask his daughter in marriage, bringing as presents three bahars of gold and a great quantity of articles of China, with male and female slaves to convey the raja's letter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時消息傳遍天下，謂拉者·塞坎德·祖爾卡內尼的後裔如今身在巴鄰旁之地，甚至遠及中國之地。於是中國拉者派遣十艘船前往巴鄰旁，為其女求婚，並帶來三巴哈爾黃金及大量中國器物作為禮物，另有男女奴僕護送拉者之書信。

passages.text: The warriors were of opinion that if the request were not complied with the safety of the country would be endangered; besides, said they, there is no greater prince than the raja of China. Then Sangsapurba granted the request to promote the friendship between the Malay and the Chinese rajas, and the elder princess, Sri Devi, was delivered to the Chinese ambassador, together with a letter stamped with the signet Kampen, desiring that when a paper signed with a similar stamp should arrive in China, they might depend on its being sent by the Malay rajas, but not to credit any other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾武士認為，若不應允此請求，國家安危將受威脅；他們又說，世上沒有比中國拉者更偉大的君主。於是桑沙普爾巴應允所請，以促進馬來與中國拉者之間的友好，並將長公主斯里·德維交給中國使臣，另附一封蓋有坎彭印璽的書信，言明日後若有蓋著同樣印璽的文書送抵中國，便可確信是馬來拉者所遣，但其他文書則不可採信。

passages.text: The raja of China was highly gratified with the daughter of the raja from the mountain Sagantang, and treated her with the dignity due to her rank; she in due time produced a son, from whom are descended the royal race who reign in China at the present time, says the chronicle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 中國拉者對來自薩甘唐山之拉者的女兒極為滿意，以與其身份相稱的尊榮待之；她後來生下一子，據編年史所載，當今統治中國的王族即出自其後裔。

title.en: Fresh Water Within the Rotan Rings on the River of Cuantan
title.zh: 瓜南河藤環內之淡水

region.en: Mouth of the river Cuantan, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘瓜南河口

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the fresh water of Cuantan), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Sailing in search of a new country, Sang Sapurba's exhausted fleet finds the river of Cuantan all salt water, with no fresh supply. The raja bids his crew tie rotans into circles and cast them on the water; descending into a small boat, he sets his feet inside the rings, and 'by the power of God Almighty and the virtue of a descendant of Raja Secander Zulkarneini' the water within the circles turns fresh. The Annals explains that to this day fresh and salt water mingle at that place.
summary.zh: 三蘇爾巴船隊溯瓜南河，淡水告罄。王命以藤結環投於水面，自乘小舟以足入環之內；『憑上帝之大能與亞歷山德羅王裔之德』，環內之水化為甘泉，全船得以汲飲。《紀年》云：至今其處淡鹹交錯。

sensitivity.note: Etiological place-myth of the chronicle, tied to the Minangkabau founding.

passages.text: Raja Sangsapurba arrived at the point of Balang, where he observed a river's mouth of very great extent: the river of Cuantan, whose country was extremely populous. It was represented to him that all the fresh water was exhausted, and that there was no place to obtain more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 桑沙普爾巴拉者抵達巴朗岬，見一河口極為寬闊，即寬坦河，其地人煙極盛。有人向他稟報，所有淡水皆已枯竭，再無他處可取水。

passages.text: Then Raja Sangsapurba directed them to bring rotans and tie them in circles and throw them into the water; then having himself descended into a small boat, he inserted his feet into the water within the circles of bamboo, and by the power of God Almighty and the virtue of a descendant of Raja Secander Zulkarneini, the water within these circles became fresh, and all the crews supplied themselves with it, and unto this day the fresh water is mixed with the salt at this place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是桑沙普爾巴拉者命人取來藤條，編成圓圈投入水中；隨後他親自下到小舟之中，將雙腳伸入竹圈之內的水中，憑藉全能真主之力與拉者塞坎德·祖爾卡內尼後裔之德，圈內之水遂變為淡水，全體船員皆取以飲用；至今此地淡水仍與鹹水相混。

title.en: Sacatimuna the Serpent of Menangcabow and the Sword of One Hundred and Ninety Notches
title.zh: 米南加保之蛇薩卡蒂穆納與一百九十缺口的寶劍

region.en: Menangcabow (Minangkabau), Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘米南加保

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. II (the killing of Sacatimuna), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The chiefs of Menangcabow, having no raja, will crown Sang Sapurba on one condition: that he destroy Sacatimuna, the immense serpent that no blade has ever stunned or wounded, which destroys their cultivation. His champion Peramas Cumambang advances with the sword Chora Samanda Kian; the serpent unfolds coils like a hillock and the champion cuts it in three — but the sword carries away one hundred and ninety notches, and the Pagaroyung dynasty is founded on the victory.
summary.zh: 米南加保諸酋無王，允立三蘇爾巴，惟一條件：誅其地巨蛇薩卡蒂穆納——凡刃不能傷、糟害田禾之蛇。王遣勇士珀拉馬斯執劍『卓拉·薩曼達基安』往討；蛇身盤曲如丘，勇士一劍斷為三截——然劍上留一百九十缺口。巴加爾容王朝即以此勝開基。

sensitivity.note: Dragon-slayer charter of Minangkabau kingship as told in the Annals; note the notched-sword detail (the monster's hide tests the hero's weapon).

passages.text: All the chief men of Menangcabow consulted about appointing him their raja, since they had none. Then the ancient chiefs desired them first to enquire if he would engage to kill the snake Sacatimuna which destroys all our cultivation; it had resisted all their efforts either to cut or pierce without either being stunned or wounded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 梅南查博的全體首領因無人為君，便商議立他為拉者。眾老首領希望他們先探問他是否願意承諾殺死那條毀壞我們所有田地的薩卡蒂穆納巨蛇；此蛇曾抵禦他們的一切努力，無論砍削或刺擊，皆未能將其擊昏或使之受傷。

passages.text: A champion named Peramas Cumambang was sent with his famous sword Chora Samanda Kian to perform this service. As soon as he approached the place, the snake, smelling a man, unfolded his coils; the champion saw it lying with huge coils like a hillock, and as the snake put itself in motion he smote it with the sword and cut it into three parts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位名為佩拉馬斯·庫曼邦的勇士，帶著他的名劍喬拉·薩曼達·基安，奉命前去完成此事。他一接近該地，巨蛇便嗅到人氣，展開盤繞的身軀；勇士見牠盤臥如小丘，當巨蛇開始蠕動時，他揮劍砍去，將其斬為三段。

passages.text: In this combat, however, the sword Chora Samanda Kian received one hundred and ninety notches. Then all the people of Cuantan appointed Sangsapurba their raja, and he was established raja of Menangcabow, and of him are descended all the generations of the rajas of Pagaroyung unto this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. II (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而在这场战斗中，乔拉·萨曼达·基安这把剑留下了一百九十道缺口。随后，宽坦的所有人推举桑萨普尔巴为他们的罗阇，他被立为美南加保的罗阇，帕加罗永历代罗阇的世系皆出自他，直至今日。

title.en: The Storm That Would Not Cease Till the Crown Went Overboard
title.zh: 不擲王冠風浪不止

region.en: Straits between Bentan and Tamasak
region.zh: 民丹與淡馬錫之間的海峽

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. III (the crossing to Tamasak), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Crossing from Bentan toward the white sands of Tamasak, Sang Nila Utama's galley is caught in a storm; the crew jettisons the baggage, then everything, yet the sea still rises until the master warns that only the diadem can save them. The crown goes over the side and the storm instantly ceases — the omen that the prince must land unadorned and win his kingdom by new means, the prelude to the founding of Singhapura.
summary.zh: 三尼拉·烏他馬自民丹渡海往淡馬錫白灘，途中風暴驟起；拋盡行李衣物，浪仍不息——直至舟師言：『非棄王冠不能救。』王冠一擲，風浪立平——此乃異兆：王子必須卸卻榮飾、以新法贏得國土，《獅城建立》之序曲。

sensitivity.note: Sea-omen episode in the Singapore founding narrative.

passages.text: As they were passing over, they were caught in a severe storm, and the vessels began to leak, and the crews were unable, after repeated exertions, to throw out the water. They were compelled to throw overboard the greater part of the baggage; the water nevertheless continued to gain ground, and every thing was thrown overboard till nothing now remained but the diadem.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. III (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他们航行途中遭遇猛烈风暴，船只开始漏水，船员们虽一再奋力排水，仍无法将水舀出。他们被迫将大部分行李抛入海中；然而水势仍不断上涨，于是一切都被抛入海中，直到最后只剩下那顶王冠。

passages.text: Then the master addressed the Prince Sang Nila Utama, stating that the vessel could not support the weight of the diadem, and that if it was not thrown overboard the vessel could not be relieved. The prince ordered the diadem to be thrown overboard, when the storm ceased and the vessel rose in the water, and the rowers pulled her ashore, and Sang Nila Utama landed on the sands of Tamasak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. III (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 于是船长向桑·尼拉·乌塔玛王子禀告，说船只无法承受王冠的重量，若不将王冠抛入海中，船便无法脱险。王子下令将王冠抛入海中，风暴随即平息，船身浮起，桨手们将船划向岸边，桑·尼拉·乌塔玛便登上了塔玛萨克的沙滩。

title.en: The Beast on the Sands: How Singhapura Got Its Name
title.zh: 沙灘上的異獸：獅子城命名之由

region.en: Tamasak (Singapore)
region.zh: 淡馬錫（新加坡）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. III (the lion of Tamasak), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Hunting on the plain near the river of Tamasak after the storm, Sang Nila Utama sees a swift, beautiful beast — red-bodied, black-headed, white-breasted, larger than a he-goat — that vanishes inland at the sight of people. No one can name it until the aged Damang Lebar Dawn declares it the singha, the lion of the ancient histories: 'this is a fine place, that contains so fierce and powerful an animal.' The prince settles there and names the country Singhapura, the Lion City.
summary.zh: 風暴之後，三尼拉·烏他馬在淡馬錫河畔平原行獵，見一異獸：身紅、首黑、胸白，捷美勝山羊，見人即遁入內陸。無人能名之，至老臣達萬·勒巴爾道恩言：『此即古史所載之辛哈（獅）。此地能容如此猛獸，必為吉壤。』王子遂居其地，名之曰辛哈補羅——獅子城。

sensitivity.note: The best-known Malay foundation myth (Singapore's name); recorded within the Annals' Palembang-Singapura-Malacca cycle.

passages.text: There they saw an animal extremely swift and beautiful, its body of a red colour, its head black and its breast white, extremely agile, and of great strength, and its size a little larger than a he-goat. When it saw a great many people, it went towards the inland and disappeared. Sang Nila Utama enquired what animal was this, but none could tell him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. III (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他们在那里看见一只极为迅捷而美丽的动物，身躯呈红色，头部黑色，胸部白色，极其灵巧，力大无穷，体型比公山羊略大一些。它一见众多的人，便朝内陆方向而去，消失不见了。桑·尼拉·乌塔玛询问这是什么动物，却无人能告诉他。

passages.text: Till he enquired of Damang Lebar Dawn, who informed him that in the histories of ancient time the singha or lion was described in the same manner as this animal appeared. 'This is a fine place which contains so fierce and powerful an animal.' Then Sang Nila Utama directed that he should not return; the queen sent people, elephants and horses, and thus Sang Nila Utama settled the country of Tamasak, named it Singhapura, and reigned over it, panegyrized by Bat'h with the name of Sri Tri-buana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. III (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 直到他询问达芒·勒巴尔·道恩，后者告诉他，在古代的史书中，singha 即狮子的描述，正与此动物所显现的模样相同。‘这是一处好地方，竟有如此凶猛而强大的动物。’于是桑·尼拉·乌塔玛下令不再返回；王后遣人送来大象与马匹，桑·尼拉·乌塔玛就此定都于塔玛萨克之地，将其命名为僧伽补罗，并统治其地，巴特以斯里·特里·布瓦纳之名为他颂扬。

title.en: Ikardlituarssuk and the Weeping Mother of Seals
title.zh: 伊卡利圖亞舒克與泣涕的海豹之母

region.en: South Greenland (Cape Farewell district)
region.zh: 南格陵蘭（費爾韋爾角一帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition (South Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Ikardlituarssuk', eBook #28932

summary.en: When famine freezes the sea solid, the village promises a new kayak paddle to whoever can magic it away. Ikardlituarssuk calls his helping spirits, creeps through a crack between land and ice, and walks the sea bottom — past sharks lying in the weed — to the lamp-lit house of Tornarssuk's mother, a weeping woman from behind whose ears fall strange things while birds dive in her lamp and seals bob about the house. Tickled out of her tears, she frees the birds and sends the seals swimming out, asking only a young seal's hide for breeches — and the next day the sea is dark with open water.
summary.zh: 海冰封港、大饑之年，村人懸新槳為賞。伊卡利圖亞舒克召喚靈助，自陸冰之隙潛入，徒步海床——過伏於海藻間的鯊群——至燈下啜泣的托那舒克之母家中。她耳後落出奇物，燈內群鳥潛游，屋中海豹浮沉。少年竭力搔癢逗她破涕，她便放出群鳥、遣出海豹，只求一幼豹之皮做褲。翌日海色轉暗，堅冰盡去。

sensitivity.note: South Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Tornarssuk (the great bear spirit of the inland) is a major figure of Greenlandic shamanism.

passages.text: One autumn the sea froze right out from the coast without a speck of open water, and famine came; the fellow-villagers offered a new kayak paddle as reward to whoever could magic it away, but there was no wizard in the village. Then Ikardlituarssuk's little brother began to coax him — how very nice it would be to win that new paddle — and it was revealed that Ikardlituarssuk had once sat on the knee of a wizard while helping spirits were called. One evening he called up his helping spirits, went down to the water's edge, crept in through a crack between the land and the ice, and started off walking along the bottom of the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ikardlituarssuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一年秋天，海水一直冻到离岸很远的地方，不见一片开阔的水面，饥荒随之而来；同村的乡亲们悬赏一支新的皮划艇桨，谁能用巫术把冰驱散便归谁，可村里并没有巫师。于是伊卡尔德利图阿尔苏克的小弟弟开始央求他——赢得那支新桨该有多好啊——而这也透露出，伊卡尔德利图阿尔苏克曾坐在一位巫师的膝上，那时正召唤着助灵。一天傍晚，他召来自己的助灵，走到水边，从陆地与冰层之间的裂缝中钻了进去，沿着海底走了起来。

passages.text: Walking along, he saw what seemed dogs lying among the seaweed — they were sharks. Then he saw a little house, its entrance narrow as the edge of a woman's knife, and got in that way. Inside sat the mother of Tornarssuk, the spirit who lived down there, weeping by her lamp. Picking behind her ears, she threw down many strange things; inside her lamp many birds dived down, and inside the house many seals bobbed up. The visitor began tickling the weeping woman as hard as he could to encourage her, and at last she was encouraged: she freed a number of the birds and made a sign for many of the seals to swim out of the house. One fjord seal she liked so much that she plucked a few hairs from its back, to have it for breeches when it was caught, and went home to rest without a word.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ikardlituarssuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他一路走去，看見海草間似乎躺著幾隻狗——那些其實是鯊魚。接著他看見一間小屋，屋子的入口窄得像女人用的小刀的刀刃，他便從那裡鑽了進去。屋裡坐著托納爾蘇克的母親，也就是住在那下方的精靈，正伏在燈旁哭泣。她從耳後抓了抓，扔下許多奇怪的東西；在她的燈裡，許多鳥兒潛了下去，而在屋裡，許多海豹冒了出來。訪客開始使勁地搔那哭泣女人的癢，想逗她開心，最後她終於被逗樂了：她放走了好些鳥兒，又打了個手勢，讓許多海豹從屋裡游出去。有一隻峽灣海豹她非常喜歡，便從牠背上拔下幾根毛，打算等牠被捕到時拿來做褲子，然後她一言不發地回家休息去了。

passages.text: Next morning the sea ahead was quite dark and all the ice had gone. The woman warned the villagers: 'Do not kill more than one; if any of you should kill two, he will never kill again.' And: 'If any of you should catch a young fjord seal with a bare patch on its back, you must give it to me to make breeches.' Each hunter made a catch that day; only one had caught two — and that man never caught a seal again for the rest of his life, while all the others always made their catch, some several at a time. Thus Ikardlituarssuk, with his little brother cheering him on, won the new paddle as the reward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ikardlituarssuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早晨，前方的海面一片漆黑，所有的冰都不見了。那女人警告村裡的人：『不要殺超過一隻；你們之中若有誰殺了兩隻，他就再也捕不到獵物了。』她又說：『你們之中若有誰捕到一隻背上有一塊光禿處的小峽灣海豹，必須把牠交給我做褲子。』那天每個獵人都捕到了獵物；只有一個人捕到了兩隻——而那個人在餘生中再也沒捕到過海豹，其他所有人則總能有所收穫，有些人一次還能捕到好幾隻。就這樣，伊卡爾德利圖阿爾蘇克在他小弟弟的加油打氣下，贏得了那支新槳作為獎賞。

title.en: The Raven Who Wanted a Wife
title.zh: 求婚的渡鴉

region.en: Upernivik, North Greenland
region.zh: 北格陵蘭烏珀納維克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Upernivik, North Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Raven who wanted a wife', eBook #28932

summary.en: A mourning sparrow rejects the raven's boastful suit — his fine forehead, long beard, big beak, and offal dinners — so the lovesick raven flies off to court the wild geese. They warn that no one can fly with them who cannot rest on water, but the raven vows to sail through the air. Weary and sleepless, he cries for something to rest on; his two goose wives sit side by side for him, then drop the sleeping suitor into the sea. Drowned, he breaks into little pieces, and his soul becomes the little sea ravens.
summary.zh: 麻雀泣亡夫，渡鴉自誇額闊鬚長、巨喙威風，許以穢物為食，求婚遭拒。痴情的渡鴉改向雁群求愛，雁群警告：不能浮水者勿同行；渡鴉自詡可以翱翔不歇。疲憊難眠之際，他喊要歇腳處——兩位雁妻並肩落水相讓，卻趁他入睡將他棄於海中。渡鴉溺斃碎裂，魂化為小海鴉。

sensitivity.note: Upernivik (North Greenland) bird tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Raven as comic braggart is a standard figure of Greenlandic animal tales.

passages.text: A little sparrow was mourning her lost husband, who used to catch worms for her. As she wept, a raven came up and asked why. 'It is not fitting for one to weep who can hop over high blades of grass,' he told her, and proposed himself: 'Take me for a husband; I have a fine high forehead, broad temples, a long beard and a big beak; you shall sleep under my wings, and I will give you lovely offal to eat.' The sparrow refused: 'You have a high forehead, broad temples, a long beard and a big beak, and will give me offal to eat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Raven who wanted a wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一隻小麻雀正為失去的丈夫哀悼，他從前總為她捉蟲子。她哭泣時，一隻渡鴉走過來問她為什麼哭。『能跳過高高的草葉的人，是不該哭泣的，』他對她說，然後向自己求婚：『娶我做丈夫吧；我有漂亮的高額頭、寬闊的太陽穴、長長的鬍鬚和一個大喙；你將睡在我的翅膀下，我會給你美味的內臟吃。』麻雀拒絕了：『你有高額頭、寬闊的太陽穴、長長的鬍鬚和一個大喙，還會給我內臟吃。』

passages.text: So the raven flew away to seek a wife among the wild geese, so lovesick he could not sleep. The geese were just preparing to fly away to other lands. 'Seeing that a miserable sparrow has refused me, I will have you,' he told two of them; they warned him that none could go with them who could not swim or rest upon the surface of the water, for there were no icebergs along the way — but he vowed he would sail through the air. The geese flew, the raven with them, and very soon he felt himself sinking from weariness and lack of sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Raven who wanted a wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是渡鴉飛走了，到野雁中去尋找妻子，他相思得睡不著覺。雁群正準備飛往別的地方。『既然一隻可憐的麻雀都拒絕了我，我就要你們，』他對其中兩隻說；她們警告他，凡是不會游泳、不能在水面上歇息的人，都不能跟她們同行，因為沿途沒有冰山——但他發誓說他能在空中航行。雁群飛了起來，渡鴉跟著她們，很快他就因疲憊和缺乏睡眠而覺得自己在下沉。

passages.text: 'Something to rest on!' gasped the raven. 'Sit you down side by side' — and his two wives sat down together on the water while their comrades flew on. The raven sat on them and fell asleep; but when the geese saw the others flying farther and farther away, they dropped the raven into the sea and flew off after their flock. 'Something to rest on!' he gasped as he fell, and at last went to the bottom and was drowned. After a while he broke up into little pieces, and his soul was turned into little sea ravens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Raven who wanted a wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『給個能歇腳的地方！』渡鴉喘著氣說。『你們兩個並排坐下』——於是他的兩個妻子一起坐在水面上，而她們的同伴繼續往前飛。渡鴉坐在她們身上睡著了；但當雁群看見其他同伴越飛越遠時，她們就把渡鴉丟進海裡，飛去追趕雁群。『給個能歇腳的地方！』他墜落時喘著氣說，最後沉到海底淹死了。過了一會兒，他碎裂成小塊，他的靈魂變成了小海鴉。

title.en: The Man Who Took a Vixen to Wife
title.zh: 娶母狐為妻者

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The man who took a Vixen to wife', eBook #28932

summary.en: Wanting a wife unlike all others, a man marries a vixen who sheds her skin into a beautiful woman with a tail-turned top-knot. After wife-swapping, the borrower scorns her foxy smell; enraged, she knocks out the lamp with her tail and flees to the hills to live with a worm in human form — the soul of a worm the man once burned, its burn marks still in its face. The man masters the worm at arm-pulling, then wanders to the tiny shore-dwellers, dwarfs who call the eider duck walrus, and shares a 'mighty walrus' fore-flipper that is only an eider's wing.
summary.zh: 欲娶奇妻的男子捕捉母狐成婚；狐婦脫去皮毛，化作頂結如尾的美人。換妻之俗中，借宿者嫌她狐騷難聞；她怒極，以尾擊熄油燈，遁入山中和一條化為人形的蠕蟲同住——那正是男子昔年燒死的蟲魂，臉上燒痕猶在。男子角力勝蟲，遠行至岸邊小人族——他們稱絨鴨為海象——共享『巨大海象』的肩肉，其實不過是絨鴨一翼。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Wife-exchange described as the source community's custom of its era; recorded without endorsement.

passages.text: There was once a man who wished to have a wife unlike all other wives, and so he caught a little fox, a vixen, and took it home to his tent. Returning one day from hunting, he found his little fox-wife become a real woman, a lovely top-knot made of what had been her tail, the furry skin taken off — very beautiful indeed. She longed to see other people, and they settled at a place where one of the men had taken a little hare to wife; the two men thought it a pleasant thing to change wives, and did so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who took a Vixen to wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個人，想要一個與所有其他妻子都不同的妻子，於是他就捉了一隻小狐狸，一隻雌狐，帶回他的帳篷裡。有一天他打獵回來，發現他的小狐妻變成了一個真正的女人，用她原來的尾巴做成了一個可愛的髮髻，毛皮被取了下來——真是非常美麗。她渴望見到其他人，於是他們就在一個地方定居下來，那裡有一個男人娶了一隻小野兔為妻；這兩個男人覺得交換妻子是件愉快的事，便這麼做了。

passages.text: The borrower began to feel scorn of her after living with her a little while: she had a foxy smell, and did not taste nice. Noticing this, the little vixen was very angry, for it was her great desire to be well thought of by the men. She knocked out the lamp with her tail, dashed out of the house, and fled far up into the hills, where she met a worm and stayed with him. Her fond husband searched long and found her at last, living with the worm in human form — and it was revealed that this worm was the man's old enemy: the soul of a worm he had once burned, the marks of burning still in its face. The worm challenged him to pull arms; the man found him easy to master and won, then went out no longer caring for his wife at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who took a Vixen to wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那借宿的男子與她同住不久，便開始嫌棄她：她身上有股狐狸的氣味，滋味也不好。那小母狐察覺此事，十分惱怒，因為她極盼受男人們看重。她用尾巴打滅了燈，衝出屋外，遠遠逃入山中，在那裡遇見一條蟲，便與牠同住。她那痴心的丈夫尋了許久，終於找到她，見她與一條化作人形的蟲同住——這才顯露出來，這條蟲原是那男子的舊仇：是他曾燒死的一條蟲的魂魄，臉上還留著焚燒的痕跡。那蟲向他挑戰比臂力；男子發覺輕易便能制伏牠，贏了，此後便出去，再也不把妻子放在心上。

passages.text: He wandered far and came to the shore-dwellers, whose houses stood on the shore just by high-water mark: small houses, dwarf people who called the eider duck walrus, looking just like men and not at all dangerous — folk our forefathers knew, the teller says, though we never see such now. To enter the stone-roofed house the great wizard made himself quite small, and they set before him the whole fore-flipper of a mighty walrus, which was really nothing more than the wing of an eider duck; they fell to upon it and ate, but did not eat it all up. After staying some time he went back to his house, and there is no more to tell of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who took a Vixen to wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他遠遊而去，來到海濱居民那裡，他們的屋子就立在海濱高潮線旁：屋子矮小，居民是些矮人，把絨鴨叫作海象，模樣與人無異，全然無害——講述者說，這是我們祖先所識的族類，雖然我們如今從未見過這等人物。為進那石頂的屋子，那大巫師把自己變得十分矮小，他們便在他面前擺上一頭巨海象的整隻前鰭，其實那不過是一隻絨鴨的翅膀；他們動手吃了起來，卻沒有吃光。他待了些時，便回自己的屋子去了，關於他再沒有別的可說。

title.en: The Great Bear and the Barking-Dog Stars
title.zh: 大熊與犬吠之星

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The great bear', eBook #28932

summary.en: A grieving mother, running from her dead child, shelters with bears in human form and is fed by a big bear-hunter who begs her never to speak of them to men, for fear for his two cubs. Homesick, she blurts out 'I have seen bears,' sledges drive out, and the father bear bites his own cubs to death so they will not fall into men's hands, then tears the betrayer to death. As he breaks out, the dogs that close upon him become wonderfully bright and rise up as stars — the Qilugtussat, the barking dogs about a bear — and men learn to beware of bears, for they hear what men say.
summary.zh: 喪子而逃的婦人借宿於人形的熊家，大熊日日出獵養家，並求她回去後切勿向人言及，免兩隻小熊遭害。思鄉的她終究忍不住說出『我見過熊』——雪橇出動，公熊不忍幼子落入人手，親自咬死二子，再撲殺洩密的婦人；破屋而出時，群犬圍攻，卻忽然亮起升天化星——那便是環繞大熊的犬吠之星。從此人方知：熊能聽懂人言。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo (Inughuit) star-lore recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Qilugtussat is identified with stars about the Great Bear in the source.

passages.text: A woman ran away from her home because her child had died, and on her way came to a house with bearskins lying in the passage way; she went in, and the people who lived there were bears in human form. Yet for all that she stayed with them. One big bear used to go out hunting to find food for the household, putting on its skin and staying away long, always returning with some catch. One day the runaway woman grew homesick and greatly desired to see her kin, and the bear spoke to her: 'Do not speak of us when you return to men' — for it was afraid lest its two cubs should be killed by the men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The great bear'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個女人因孩子死了而離家出走，途中來到一座屋子，過道裡鋪著熊皮；她走了進去，住在那裡的人原是化作人形的熊。儘管如此，她仍與他們同住。一頭大熊常出去打獵，為這一家子覓食，披上熊皮，久久在外，總帶著獵物回來。一天，那出走的女人起了鄉思，極想見親人，那熊便對她說：「你回到人間時，不要提起我們」——因為牠怕自己的兩隻幼崽被人殺害。

passages.text: Home again, she felt a great desire to tell what she had seen, and one day, sitting with her husband in the house, said: 'I have seen bears.' Many sledges drove out, and when the bear saw them coming towards its house it felt so sorry for its cubs that it bit them to death, that they might not fall into the hands of men; then dashed out to find the woman who had betrayed it, broke into her house, and bit her to death. When it came out, the dogs closed round it and fell upon it — and suddenly all of them became wonderfully bright and rose up to the sky in the form of stars. These are the Qilugtussat, the stars which look like barking dogs about a bear. Since then men have learned to beware of bears, for they hear what men say.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The great bear'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 回到家中，她極想說出自己所見，一天與丈夫坐在屋裡，說道：「我見過熊。」許多雪橇馳騁而出，那熊見他們朝自己的屋子而來，為幼崽傷心至極，便咬死牠們，免得落入人手；隨後衝出去找那出賣牠的女人，闖進她的屋子，把她咬死。牠出來時，群狗圍攏上來撲向牠——忽然牠們全都變得奇異明亮，化作星辰升上天空。這便是奇盧克圖薩特（Qilugtussat），那些看上去像圍著一頭熊吠叫的狗一般的星辰。自此以後，人們便學會提防熊，因為牠們聽得見人所說的話。

title.en: The Man Who Became a Star: Nalaussartoq
title.zh: 化星者：佇聽之星

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The man who became a star', eBook #28932

summary.en: Children playing in a ravine time after time frighten away an old man's seal; at last he cries 'Close up, Ravine!' and the hillside shuts them in. Trapped, they lick water poured down a crack and die of hunger, and the neighbours who fall upon the sorcerer chase him — until he becomes bright and rises to heaven as a great star. It is Nalaussartoq, 'he who stands and listens,' low in the western sky when the lights return after the great darkness.
summary.zh: 谷中嬉戲的孩子屢屢驚走老人的海豹；老人怒喊『合上吧，山谷！』山坡應聲閉合。孩童受困谷中，僅能舔食石縫滴下的水，終餓死。鄰人起而追討術者，他逃竄之際忽然發光，升天化為大星——即『佇聽之星』納勞薩托克，於長夜初盡時低懸西天，永不高升。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo (Inughuit) star-lore recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Source note identifies the star as Venus.

passages.text: An old man stood out on the ice waiting for seal to come up to their breathing holes, while on the shore opposite a crowd of children played in a ravine, time after time frightening away a seal just as he was about to harpoon it. At last he grew angry at the spoiled catch and cried out: 'Close up, Ravine, over those who are spoiling my hunting' — and at once the hillside closed over the children at play. One of them, carrying a little brother, had her fur coat torn in the closing. Trapped inside, they fell to screaming; none could bring them food, only water poured down a crack, which they licked from the sides, and at last they all died of hunger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who became a star'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個老人站在冰上，等候海豹浮到牠們的呼吸孔來，而對岸一群孩子在山溝裡玩耍，一次又一次地把他正要叉住的海豹嚇跑。最後他對這被攪壞的獵獲發了怒，喊道：「合攏吧，山溝，蓋住那些壞我打獵的人」——那山坡立刻合攏，蓋住了玩耍的孩子。其中一個背著小弟弟的女孩，毛皮大衣在合攏時被扯破了。他們被困在裡面，放聲尖叫；無人能送食物給他們，只有水從一道裂縫流下，他們便從兩側舔飲，最後全都餓死了。

passages.text: The neighbours fell upon the old man who had shut the children up by magic in the hill, and he took to flight with the others running after him. But all at once he became bright and rose up to heaven as a great star — visible now in the west when the lights begin to return after the great darkness, low down, never climbing high in the sky. We call it Nalaussartoq, the teller says: he who stands and listens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who became a star'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鄰人們撲向那用巫術把孩子們關進山裡的老人，他拔腿逃走，眾人在後追趕。但他忽然變得明亮，化為一顆大星升上天去——如今在大黑暗之後光明初復之時，可見於西方，位置低垂，從不升上高空。講述者說，我們稱它為納勞薩爾托克（Nalaussartoq）：即那站立傾聽者。

title.en: The Woman with the Iron Tail
title.zh: 鐵尾婦人

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The woman with the iron tail', eBook #28932

summary.en: An iron-tailed man-eater waits for her guests to fall asleep, then leaps into the air to fall upon them, piercing them through with her tail. One visitor only feigns sleep, sidesteps, and lets her break the tail on a stone; fleeing to his kayak, he out-magics her with words alone — 'Oh, if only I could send my harpoon through her' — and such is the power of spoken wishes that she falls dead on the spot, her killing days over.
summary.zh: 鐵尾食人婦專候客睡熟，騰空躍起以尾刺穿而食。一名訪客佯睡側身，讓她砸斷鐵尾於石上；逃至皮艇時，他以言語為咒——『願我的魚叉穿她而過』——話音之力竟令她當場斃命。鐵尾既折，她自此再不能殺人。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo (Inughuit) tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Word-power (the efficacy of spoken formulae) is a core belief of Inuit narrative practice.

passages.text: There was once a woman who had an iron tail, and more than this, she was an eater of men. When a stranger came to visit her, she would wait until her guest had fallen asleep, then jump up in the air and fall down upon the sleeping one, piercing him through with her tail. Once a man came to her house and lay down to sleep; when she thought him asleep she jumped up and dropped down upon him — but he was not asleep at all and moved aside, so that she fell on a stone and broke her tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The woman with the iron tail'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個女人，她長著一條鐵尾巴，不僅如此，她還是個吃男人的傢伙。每當有陌生人來訪，她總會等到客人睡著，然後縱身躍起，朝那熟睡的人落下，用尾巴把他刺穿。有一次，一個男人來到她家躺下睡覺；她以為他睡著了，便縱身躍起，朝他落下——但他根本沒睡，閃到了一旁，於是她跌在石頭上，摔斷了自己的尾巴。

passages.text: The man fled out to his kayak with the woman running after. When she reached him she cried: 'Oh, if I could only thrust my knife into him' — and even her words had power, nearly upsetting the man. 'Oh, if only I could send my harpoon through her,' the man cried in return, and so great was the power of his words that she fell down on the spot. The man rowed away, and the woman never killed anyone after that, for her tail was broken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The woman with the iron tail'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那男人逃向他的獨木舟，女人在後面追趕。她追到他跟前時喊道：『唉，要是我能把刀刺進他身體就好了』——就連她的話也有力量，幾乎把那男人掀翻。『唉，要是我能把魚叉擲穿她就好了，』那男人回喊道，他的話力量之大，竟使她當場倒地。男人划船離去，那女人此後再沒殺過任何人，因為她的尾巴斷了。

title.en: How the Fog Came
title.zh: 霧的由來

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'How the fog came', eBook #28932

summary.en: A Mountain Spirit steals corpses from graves to eat at home; a man seeking to see the thief lets himself be buried alive with a flat stone under his coat. Carried off, he clutches willow twigs to make himself heavy, then kills the Spirit and its children and flees, pursued by the Spirit's wife: he raises hills before her, calls a stream over its banks, tricks her into drinking it up, and — 'Look at the tail of your tunic' — makes her bend until her belly bursts. The steam that rises out of her turns to fog, which still floats among the hills to this day.
summary.zh: 山魔盜墓食屍；一人欲窺其形，活埋自身、懷藏平石以防刺殺。魔攜『屍』歸家，倦極而眠；人醒轉，殺魔與其子，倉皇而逃。魔妻追趕，他喊『山嶺升起』、『溪水上岸』，又誘她飲水。臨別一句『你的衣尾垂在腿間』，教她彎身自視，肚腹爆裂——蒸氣沖天化霧，至今縈繞山間。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo (Inughuit) origin-legend recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Grave-robbing Mountain Spirit is a standard figure of the inland; tale presented as told.

passages.text: A Mountain Spirit stole corpses from their graves and ate them when it came home. A man wishing to see who did this thing let himself be buried alive, having stuck a flat stone under his coat in case the Spirit should try to stab him. The Spirit came, saw the new grave, dug up the body and carried it off; on the way the man caught hold of all the willow twigs they passed, making himself as heavy as he could so that the Spirit was forced to put forth all its strength. At last the Spirit reached its house, flung the body down on the floor, and lay down to sleep while its wife went out to gather wood for cooking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'How the fog came'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個山靈從墳墓裡偷走屍體，回家後便把它們吃掉。一個男人想看看究竟是誰幹的這種事，便讓自己活著被埋葬，並在衣服底下墊了一塊扁石，以防那山靈試圖刺他。山靈來了，看見新墳，挖出屍體便把它帶走；一路上那男人抓住他們經過的所有柳枝，盡可能讓自己變沉，逼得山靈不得不使出全身力氣。最後山靈到了自己的家，把屍體扔在地上，躺下睡覺，而它的妻子則出去拾柴做飯。

passages.text: 'Father, father, he is opening his eyes,' cried the children. 'Nonsense, children, it is a dead body which I have dropped many times among the twigs on the way,' said the father. But the man rose up, killed the Mountain Spirit and its children, and fled as fast as he could. The Spirit's wife saw him and mistook him for her husband, crying 'Where are you going?' and ran after him. Running over level ground, the man cried 'Rise up, hills!' and many hills rose at once, so that the woman lagged behind. He sprang across a little stream and called 'Flow over your banks!' — and it was impossible for her to get across.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'How the fog came'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『父親，父親，他睜開眼睛了，』孩子們喊道。『胡說，孩子們，這是我一路上在柳枝間扔了好多次的一具死屍，』父親說。但那男人站起身來，殺死了山靈和它的孩子們，然後拼命逃走。山靈的妻子看見了他，把他誤認作自己的丈夫，喊道『你要去哪兒？』便追了上去。那男人跑過平地時喊道『山丘們，升起來！』許多山丘立刻升起，那女人便落在了後面。他躍過一條小溪，喊道『漫過你們的河岸吧！』——她便再也無法過去了。

passages.text: 'How did you get across?' cried the woman. 'I drank up the water. Do you likewise' — and she began gulping it down. Then the man turned and said: 'Look at the tail of your tunic; it is hanging down between your legs.' When she bent down to look, her belly burst; and as she burst, a steam rose up out of her and turned to fog, which still floats about to this day among the hills.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'How the fog came'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『你是怎麼過來的？』那女人喊道。『我把水喝乾了。你也照做吧』——她便開始大口吞水。這時那男人轉過身說：『看看你外衣的尾巴；它垂在你兩腿之間。』當她彎下腰去看時，她的肚子爆裂了；就在她爆裂之時，一團蒸氣從她體內升起，化作了霧，這霧至今仍在山間飄蕩。

title.en: The Man Who Avenged the Widows
title.zh: 為寡婦復仇者

region.en: Kangarssuk, West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭康加舒克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The man who avenged the widows', eBook #28932

summary.en: Envious of Angusinanguaq's beautiful wife, his fellow-hunters strand him on a lonely island, towing his kayak away so he can never leave. But he was a great wizard: winding his body in hide strips and bending into a curve, he gathers magic power and flies home through the air, arriving before his would-be murderers. None plans against him again. Later he rows out to the fierce island-folk who call down fogs on kayakers, takes them by surprise, kills many, and piles their heads on the side bench — and the widows come one by one to his hut to thank him.
summary.zh: 獵手們嫉妒安古西南瓜克的美妻，乘獵鴨之機將他遺棄孤島，拖走他的皮艇。豈知他是大巫：以皮條纏身、屈身成弓，聚靈力飛行，竟搶先歸家。從此無人再敢謀其妻。其後他獨駕皮艇突襲那些召霧害人的島民，殺其眾男，頭顱堆於長凳，得勝而歸——眾寡婦逐一入其帳中道謝。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Includes lethal revenge raid as told in the source; presented as archival narrative.

passages.text: In the old days, when men were yet skilful rowers in kayaks — before a great sickness carried off all the older men and the young forgot how to build kayaks — there lived at Kangarssuk a man named Angusinanguaq, who had a very beautiful wife, wherefore all men envied him. One day, when they set out to hunt eider duck on the far islands, the other men agreed to leave him behind on a little lonely island; they caught their ducks, gathered eggs, and pushed out from the land without waiting for him, taking his kayak in tow so that he might never more be able to leave the island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who avenged the widows'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在古時候，男人們還擅長划獨木舟——那是在一場大病把所有年長的男人都帶走、年輕人忘了如何造獨木舟之前——康加爾蘇克住著一個名叫安古西納古阿克的男人，他有一個非常美麗的妻子，因此所有男人都羨慕他。有一天，當他們出發去遠方的島上獵絨鴨時，其他男人商量好把他丟在一座孤零零的小島上；他們捕了鴨子，撿了蛋，沒等他便離了岸，還把他的獨木舟拖在後面，使他再也無法離開那座島。

passages.text: When the umiaks came in sight of the tents they saw a man going from one tent to another, visiting the women left behind — and the old man steering shaded his eyes and said: 'The man is Angusinanguaq.' It was revealed that he was a great wizard: when the boats had left and he could not find his kayak, he wound his body about with strips of hide, bending it into a curve, and gathered magic power wherewith to move through the air, as is the way of wizards, coming back to the place long before those who had sought his death. From that day none ever planned again to take his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who avenged the widows'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當那些皮艇（umiak）駛近帳篷時，他們看見一個男人從一頂帳篷走到另一頂帳篷，探訪那些被留下來的婦女——掌舵的老人用手遮住眼睛說：「那人是安古西納瓜克（Angusinanguaq）。」後來才顯明他是一個了不起的巫師：當船隻離去、他找不到自己的獨木舟時，他用獸皮條纏繞自己的身體，把它彎成弧形，並聚集魔力，藉以在空中穿行，正如巫師的作風，遠在那些圖謀害他性命的人之前就回到了此地。從那天起，再也沒有人打算奪走他的妻子。

passages.text: In those times there were people on the islands too — a fierce folk whom none might come near; when a kayak from the mainland neared their village they called down a fog upon it, so that the paddler could not see and perished. One day Angusinanguaq planned to avenge his fellow-villagers: he rowed out to the unapproachable ones and, being a great wizard, took them by surprise, killed many of the men, cut off their heads, and piled them up on the side bench before rowing away. There was great joy among the widows of all those dead hunters when they learned he had avenged their husbands, and they went into his hut one by one and thanked him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who avenged the widows'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在那個時代，島上也住著人——那是一群兇猛的人，誰也無法靠近；當來自大陸的獨木舟接近他們的村落時，他們便召來一陣濃霧籠罩其上，使划槳的人看不見而喪命。有一天，安古西納瓜克計畫為他的同村人報仇：他划船出去，前往那些不可接近的人那裡，由於他是個了不起的巫師，便出其不意地襲擊他們，殺了許多男人，砍下他們的頭，堆在側邊的長凳上，然後划船離去。當那些死去的獵人的寡婦們得知他已為她們的丈夫報了仇，都歡喜不已，她們一個接一個地走進他的小屋向他道謝。

title.en: The Bride with Forty Champions: Nila Panchadi Comes to Singhapura
title.zh: 四十勇士護嫁的妮拉潘佳蒂

region.en: Singhapura (Singapore)
region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. IV (marriage of Raja Kichil Besar), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The raja of Bijanagar in the land of Kling refuses all suitors for his peerless daughter Nila Panchadi, 'as not being of her own race' — until word of the Singhapura dynasty, descended from Raja Suran, reaches him. He sends her north with forty champions in a vessel of five hundred rowers; three months of festivities precede the wedding, and Singhapura's line is joined to the kings of the land of Kling.
