summary.zh: 克林國比賈那伽王拒絕一切求婚者——『非同族者不嫁』絕世之女妮拉潘佳蒂；獨聞獅城王系亦出蘇蘭王之裔，乃遣五百槳巨舟、四十勇士護女北上。歡宴三月，公主下嫁獅城王子——兩王世系自此相連。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle alliance episode; the 'same race' clause mirrors Sang Sapurba's endogamy myth (batch-217).

passages.text: There was a raja of the land of Kling, Adi Bernilam Raja Mudeliar, descended of Raja Suran, who had a daughter named Nila Panchadi, of celebrated beauty and most excellent qualities. How many were the rajas who preferred their suit to her, but her father refused to give her in marriage to them, as not being of her own race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. IV (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 克林（Kling）之地有一位羅闍（raja），名叫阿迪·伯尼拉姆·羅闍·穆德利亞爾（Adi Bernilam Raja Mudeliar），是羅闍·蘇蘭（Raja Suran）的後裔，他有一個女兒名叫妮拉·潘查迪（Nila Panchadi），以美貌和極佳的品德聞名。有多少羅闍向她求婚，但她的父親拒絕把她嫁給他們，因為他們不是她同族的人。

passages.text: At last the fame of her beauty reached Singhapura, and Sri Tri-buana sent ambassadors to solicit her hand for his son Raja Kichil Besar. The raja of Bijanagar rejoiced at the letter, desiring that the prince should not take the trouble of coming, but that he would send his daughter to Singhapura. The next monsoon she sailed attended by forty champions in a vessel equipped with five hundred rowers, and after three months of festivities the prince was united to the Kling princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. IV (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後，她美貌的名聲傳到了辛伽普拉（Singhapura），斯里·特里布阿納（Sri Tri-buana）派遣使者為他的兒子羅闍·基奇爾·貝薩爾（Raja Kichil Besar）求娶她。比賈納加爾（Bijanagar）的羅闍對這封信感到欣喜，希望王子不必勞煩前來，而由他將女兒送往辛伽普拉。次年季風時節，她乘船出航，隨行有四十名勇士，所乘船隻配備五百名槳手；經過三個月的慶典之後，王子便與這位克林公主成婚。

title.en: The Wood-Shaving Ring: Java's Letter of Contempt and the Hatchet Answer
title.zh: 刨花之環：爪哇的辱信與斧頭的回敬

region.en: Singhapura (Singapore)
region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. V (the shaving of wood), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The bitara of Majapahit sends Singhapura a letter enclosing a wood-shaving seven fathoms long, hewn fine as paper and rolled up like a ring: 'Younger brother, observe the skill of the artificers of Java; have you any such in Singhapura?' The raja answers with a greater wonder — his artificer Pawang Bentan shaves the head of a forty-day-old boy with a hatchet, unharmed, amid the rolling of the child's head. The insulted bitara reads the point: 'he threatens to shave our head like the boy's' — and sends a hundred junks to war.
summary.zh: 馬卓帕希特王致獅城一函，內附刨花一條，長七尋，薄如紙、捲之成環：『賢弟且觀爪哇工匠之技；獅城可有此等人物？』獅城王答以更奇之技——工匠帕旺·本丹以斧為四十日嬰兒剃頭，嬰啼哭轉首而毫髮無傷。馬卓王讀其意：『彼欲如剃嬰般剃我首級』——遂發百艘戰船而來。

sensitivity.note: Famous insult-and-answer challenge episode; a classic 'boast contest' (jurus) motif in Malay-Javan court legend.

passages.text: The bitara of Majapahit sent an ambassador to Singhapura with a letter enclosing a shaving of wood, seven fathoms in length, formed with the hatchet, fine as paper, and nowhere cut or broken; it was rolled up and its circumference like a ring. The letter read: 'Younger brother, observe the skill of the artificers of Java; have you any such in Singhapura?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. V (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 滿者伯夷（Majapahit）的比塔拉（bitara）派遣使者前往辛伽普拉，帶著一封信，信中附有一片木刨花，長七噚，是用斧頭削成的，薄如紙，處處沒有割斷或破裂；它被捲起來，周長如一枚戒指。信中寫道：「弟弟，請見識爪哇工匠的技藝；你們辛伽普拉可有這樣的人？」

passages.text: Sri Paduca Vicrama Vira ordered the artificer Pawang Bentan to hew off the hair from the head of a boy of forty days old with a hatchet in the presence of the ambassador of Java. The artificer executed his commission without delay, notwithstanding the exertions of the boy and the constant rolling motion of his head, to the great astonishment of the Javanese ambassador. 'To shave a boy's head with a hatchet is somewhat more difficult than to pare off your shaving,' said the raja; 'carry this axe to Majapahit with our compliments.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. V (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯里·帕杜卡·維克拉馬·維拉（Sri Paduca Vicrama Vira）命令工匠帕旺·本坦（Pawang Bentan）在爪哇使者面前用斧頭剃下一個四十天大的男嬰頭上的頭髮。那工匠毫不遲延地執行了任務，儘管那男孩不斷掙扎、頭不停地滾動，仍令爪哇使者大為驚嘆。「用斧頭剃男孩的頭，比削下你們那片刨花要難一些，」羅闍說，「把這把斧頭帶回滿者伯夷，並致上我們的問候。」

passages.text: The Sri Bitara was highly enraged at the narrative. 'I understand the raja's meaning; he threatens to shave our head like the boy's, if we should proceed to Singhapura.' Without delay he ordered his warriors to proceed in a hundred junks to Singhapura and attack it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. V (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯里·比塔拉聽聞此言，勃然大怒。「我明白拉者（raja）的意思；他是在威脅我們，倘若我們繼續前往辛加布拉，就要像對待那男孩一樣剃光我們的頭。」他毫不遲延，下令麾下戰士乘百艘戎克船前往辛加布拉，向其進攻。

title.en: The Hundred Junks of Majapahit Break Against Singhapura
title.zh: 百艦來犯：馬卓帕希特兵敗獅城

region.en: Singhapura (Singapore)
region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. V (the Javanese attack), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: A hundred junks under the champion Damang Viraja land Javanese warriors on Singhapura: 'there was clattering of arms on armour, and the earth shook with the stamping of warriors, and loud rose the hubbub of contending hosts.' Blood streams on the ground till evening, when the Javans fall back to their prows; Singhapura is not worsted, and the hosts return to Majapahit.
summary.zh: 馬卓王遣百艘大船，載名將達萬·維拉查之爪哇兵登岸攻獅城：『甲葉相擊聲不絕，戰士踏地地為震，兩軍喧囂聲蓋天。』血染大地直至日暮，爪哇兵退回船中；獅城未敗，敵軍歸國。

sensitivity.note: Chronicle battle set-piece; Singhapura's repulse of Majapahit.

passages.text: The fleet which the bitara sent under the command of the famous champion Damang Viraja arrived at Singhapura, and the Javan warriors immediately rushed ashore and commenced the war with the people of Singhapura. Thick waxed the press of war, there was clattering of arms on armour, and the earth shook with the stamping of warriors, and loud rose the hubbub of contending hosts, so that no other noise could be heard. Many were the slain on both sides, and the blood streamed on the ground till evening, when the Javans fell back to their prows. Singhapura, however, was not worsted; the Javan hosts returned to Majapahit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. V (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 比塔拉派遣、由著名勇士達芒·維拉惹（Damang Viraja）統率的艦隊抵達辛加布拉，爪哇戰士立即衝上岸，與辛加布拉的百姓開戰。戰事愈演愈烈，兵器鏗鏘地撞擊鎧甲，大地因戰士的踏步而震動，交戰雙方喧囂震天，以致其他聲響皆不可聞。雙方死傷眾多，鮮血直流至地面，直到傍晚爪哇人才退回船首。然而辛加布拉並未落敗；爪哇大軍返回滿者伯夷。

title.en: Badang Swallows the Spectre's Vomit
title.zh: 巴當吞下鬼魅之嘔物

region.en: Sungey Basisi, Sayang country near Singhapura (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 獅城附近斯揚之地之鱗河（象徵性定位）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (the champion Badang), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The slave Badang's fish-snare is emptied night after night, leaving only scales and bones. Watching among the reeds he seizes the glutton — a hantu with eyes red as fire and beard hanging to its navel — and bargains: not riches, which would belong to his master, but strength 'to rend up by the roots trees of one or two fathoms girt.' The spectre's price is terrible: Badang must lick up its vomit. He swallows it while gripping the beard, shivers the forest with a wave of his hand, and earns his freedom.
summary.zh: 奴隸巴當的魚梁夜夜被吃空，只餘鱗骨。他藏身蘆葦之中，擒住那食魚之魅——雙目如火、鬚垂至臍的鬼。鬼願獻禮求生：巴當不取財富（歸主人所有），而求『徒手連根拔起一兩尋粗之樹』之力。鬼言：須先食其嘔物。巴當緊握鬼鬚吞之，從此揮手之間森林盡倒，並以此換得自由身。

sensitivity.note: Strength-through-monster bargain; the Badang cycle is one of the Annals' folk-epic insets.

passages.text: Badang had set in the river a snare for fish; on going next morning to examine it he found no fish, but the scales and bones of them. The same occurred for several days, when he concealed himself one night among the reeds, and saw a hantu, or spectre, with eyes red as fire, hair coarse and matted as a basket, and beard hanging down to his navel, come to eat the fish that were caught. He made his heart strong and rushed to seize it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴當在河裡設下捕魚的陷阱；翌晨前去查看時，卻不見魚，只見魚鱗與魚骨。如此數日皆然，於是他在某夜藏身於蘆葦叢中，看見一個漢圖（hantu，即幽靈），雙眼紅如火焰，頭髮粗硬糾結如籃筐，鬍鬚垂至肚臍，前來吃捕獲的魚。他鼓起勇氣，衝上前去抓住它。

passages.text: 'If I should desire riches,' thought Badang, 'they would all belong to my master; but if I ask for strength to perform my master's business, that would be of some advantage. Give me strength, so that I may rend up with one hand by the roots trees of one or two fathoms girt.' The hantu consented on a condition: 'provided you can agree to lick up my vomit.' Badang vomited it up and swallowed it, holding the spectre by the beard, and then tried his hand on the largest trees, shivering them to pieces with the greatest facility.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「倘若我求取財富，」巴當心想，「那全都會歸我主人所有；但若我求取力氣以辦理主人的事務，那倒有些好處。請賜我力氣，讓我單手便能將一兩噚粗的樹木連根拔起。」漢圖應允，但附有一個條件：「只要你肯舔食我的嘔吐物。」巴當嘔出嘔吐物並將其吞下，同時抓住幽靈的鬍鬚，隨後便以最大的樹木試手，輕而易舉地將它們震得粉碎。

passages.text: He returned to his master's dwelling, shivering all the trees before him and clearing away the brushwood with the waving of his hand, till he had cleared away the deep forest almost like a plain. When his master inquired what faculty he had for the purpose, Badang related the whole affair, and thereupon received his freedom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他回到主人的住所，沿途將所有樹木震碎，揮手便清除灌木叢，幾乎把幽深的森林清成了一片平原。當主人問起他有何本領辦成此事時，巴當將整件事的經過一一敘述，於是獲得了自由。

title.en: Batu Blah: The Stone Split by Badang's Falling Head
title.zh: 裂石：巴當之頭劈開巨石

region.en: Cowala Sayang, Johor coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柔佛海岸瓜拉斯揚（象徵性定位）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (the split stone), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Summoned to fetch the kuras leaf of Cowala Sayang for his raja, Badang rows a prow of eight fathoms alone, using a campas-tree trunk a fathom in girth for an oar. Climbing for the leaf, the branch breaks and he falls head-first onto a huge stone, splitting it in two — 'but not his skull.' The split stone, Batu Blah, and even his prodigious oar, are pointed out to travellers for generations after.
summary.zh: 王欲食瓜拉斯揚之古拉斯葉，巴當獨自划八尋長舟前往，以一尋粗之坎帕斯樹幹作槳。攀樹摘葉，枝折墜地——頭撞巨石，石裂為二，『而顱骨無恙』。裂石（巴都布拉）與其巨槳，世代為旅人指認之古蹟。

sensitivity.note: Place-etiology inside the Badang cycle.

passages.text: The raja of Singhapura wished to eat of the kuras leaf, which grows at Cowala Sayang, and Badang departed alone in a prow eight fathoms in length, with a trunk of the campas tree for an oar, which was a fathom in girt. When he reached Cowala Sayang he ascended the kuras tree; but the branch broke with him, and he fell down with his head on a huge stone, which stone was split in two, but not his skull.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 辛加布拉的拉者想品嚐生長於科瓦拉·沙揚（Cowala Sayang）的庫拉斯（kuras）葉，巴當便獨自乘一艘八噚長的船首出發，以一根一噚粗的坎帕斯（campas）樹幹為槳。他抵達科瓦拉·沙揚後，攀上庫拉斯樹；然而樹枝與他一同折斷，他頭朝下墜落在一塊巨石上，那塊石頭裂成兩半，他的頭骨卻沒有裂開。

passages.text: This stone is still to be seen at Cowala Sayang, and is named Batu Blah, or the split stone; and the said prow, with the trunk of the tree which he used for an oar, are still to be seen at Cowala Sayang. Badang returned to Singhapura the next day, bringing with him a cargo of plantains and sugar-canes for his food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這塊石頭至今仍可在 Cowala Sayang 見到，名為 Batu Blah，意即裂石；而前述的船首，連同他用作槳的樹幹，至今也仍可在 Cowala Sayang 見到。Badang 次日返回 Singhapura，帶回一船的大蕉與甘蔗作為食糧。

title.en: Badang Launches the Fifteen-Fathom Prow with One Hand
title.zh: 巴當獨力推動十五尋巨舟

region.en: Singhapura (Singapore)
region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (the launching of the pilang), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The raja builds a great pilang prow of fifteen fathoms and orders it launched. Fifty men fail; two or three hundred fail; two or three thousand fail. Then the raja calls Badang, who launches it with such force that it flies straight across to the opposite shore — and the king appoints him a hulubalang, a champion, whose fame reaches even the land of Kling.
summary.zh: 王造十五尋巨舟命人下水：五十人不動，二三百人不動，二三千人不動。王乃召巴當——他一推之下，巨舟飛越水面直達對岸。王遂封之為呼魯巴蘭（戰將），其名遠播克林之地。

sensitivity.note: Feat-of-strength episode in the Badang cycle.

passages.text: The raja of Singhapura constructed a prow of the kind named Pilang, fifteen fathoms in length, at the raja's residence. When it was finished he ordered fifty men to launch it, but they were unable; it was then essayed by two or three hundred, and afterwards by two or three thousand, all of whom were unable to succeed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Singhapura 的 raja 在 raja 的居所建造了一艘名為 Pilang 的船首，長十五噚。船首建成後，他命令五十人將它推下水，但他們無法做到；接著由二三百人嘗試，之後又由二三千人嘗試，全都無法成功。

passages.text: Then the raja ordered Badang to attempt it alone, and he launched it with such force that it flew directly to the opposite shore. After this exploit the king appointed him a champion, or hulubalang, and his fame extended even to the land of Kling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是 raja 命令 Badang 獨自一試，他奮力一推，船首便直飛到對岸。經此壯舉之後，國王任命他為勇士，即 hulubalang，他的名聲甚至遠播至 Kling 之地。

title.en: The Stone Hurl of Badang: Seven Ships Staked and Lost
title.zh: 巴當舉石定輸贏：七船為注

region.en: Point of Singhapura (Tanjon Singhapura)
region.zh: 獅城岬（今新加坡南端）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (Badang and the Kling champion), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The Kling champion Nadi Vijaya Vicrama arrives to wrestle Badang, staking seven loaded ships on the outcome. Evenly matched at play, they turn to the huge stone before the raja's hall: the Kling champion can barely raise it to his knee, but Badang poises it easily several times and hurls it into the mouth of the river — 'that is the rock which is at this day visible at the point of Singhapura.' The challenger surrenders his seven ships in shame.
summary.zh: 克林勇士納迪·維賈亞渡海來摔跤，以七艘滿載之船為注。二人相持不下，遂約舉王殿前巨石分高下：克林勇士僅能舉至膝而放；巴當卻輕鬆拋舉數次，擲石入河口——『即今日獅城岬外所見之礁石』。挑戰者羞愧獻上七船而歸。

sensitivity.note: Wrestling-and-stone feat; the Annals ties the rock at Singapore point to Badang's throw.

passages.text: There was in the land of Kling a champion of such amazing force that nobody could venture to contend with him, named Nadi Vijaya Vicrama. Hearing of the prowess of Badang, the raja of Kling sent him to Singhapura to contend in wrestling, staking seven ships with their loading on the issue of the contest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Kling 之地有一位力大無窮的勇士，無人敢與他較量，名叫 Nadi Vijaya Vicrama。Kling 的 raja 聽聞 Badang 的勇武，便派他到 Singhapura 比試角力，並以七艘滿載貨物的船作為比試的賭注。

passages.text: There was a huge stone lying before the raja's hall, and the Kling champion said to Badang: 'Let us come to a serious exertion of strength, and lift up this stone; let him be reckoned worsted who shall be unable to lift it.' The Kling champion exerted all his strength and lifted it up to his knee and let it fall. Badang took up the stone, poised it easily several times, and threw it out into the mouth of the river — that is the rock which is at this day visible at the point of Singhapura. Then the Kling champion delivered up to Badang the seven ships which had been staked with their contents, and owned that he was conquered. He returned with great sorrow and shame to the land of Kling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: raja 的廳堂前橫著一塊巨石，Kling 的勇士對 Badang 說：「讓我們來一場真正的較量，把這塊石頭舉起來；舉不起的人便算輸。」Kling 的勇士使盡全力，把石頭舉到膝蓋，然後放下。Badang 拿起石頭，輕鬆地拋接數次，然後把它扔進河口——那就是今日在 Singhapura 岬角仍可見到的岩石。於是 Kling 的勇士把作為賭注的七艘船連同船上貨物交給 Badang，並承認自己敗了。他滿懷悲傷與羞愧返回 Kling 之地。

title.en: The Knee at the Feast: Badang Unmanned the Champion Bandrang
title.zh: 宴席上的膝蓋：巴當暗中壓服班德朗

region.en: Singhapura (Singapore)
region.zh: 獅子城辛哈補羅（新加坡）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (Bandrang of Perlac), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Bandrang, the redoubtable champion of Perlac, comes to stake a storehouse against Badang. Warned by his raja not to despair, Badang asks that the challenger be invited to a feast first: seated together, Bandrang presses his knee down on Badang's — and Badang, quick as thought, presses down his, so secretly that no one sees. A silent hour of locked knees breaks the champion: next morning the ambassador begs to cancel the contest, and Badang is instead set to fixing a great iron chain across the strait.
summary.zh: 珀拉克勇士班德朗前來，以一倉貨物為注挑戰巴當。巴當請王先設宴款客；席間二人並坐，班德朗以膝下壓——巴當閃電般回壓其膝，隱秘無人察覺。對坐一時，勇士之膝已被鎖死。翌晨使臣請求罷賽；巴當未戰而勝，改被派去橫鎖海峽之鐵鏈。

sensitivity.note: Silent contest-of-strength at table — a celebrated Malay narrative device.

passages.text: Badang represented that Bandrang was the most powerful champion of the time, and that no one was reckoned equal to him; 'if therefore I should be conquered, do not be disconcerted: it may be best for you to invite him this evening to an entertainment, when I shall endeavour to discover if I can contend with him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Badang 稟報說，Bandrang 是當世最強悍的勇士，無人被認為能與他匹敵；「因此，倘若我敗了，請不要驚慌：您最好今晚邀他赴宴，我當設法探明自己能否與他較量。」

passages.text: Bandrang and Badang were seated together. Bandrang immediately pressed his knee down upon that of Badang, but Badang quickly extricated himself, and having raised his own knee pressed down that of Bandrang, who could not, with all his efforts, raise his knee: this was done so secretly that none observed it except themselves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 班德朗與巴當同坐一處。班德朗立刻把自己的膝蓋壓在巴當的膝蓋上，但巴當迅速脫身，並抬起自己的膝蓋壓住班德朗的膝蓋，班德朗使盡全力也無法抬起膝蓋：此事做得極為隱密，除了他們二人之外無人察覺。

passages.text: Next morning the ambassador asked that the contest be put off altogether, as it might possibly excite dissatisfaction between the two rajas; Bandrang had requested him to find some method of breaking off the contest, for he perceived his strength to be inferior. The raja smiled and assented, and instead set Badang to fix a large and heavy iron chain behind the strait of Sri Kama to prevent the passing of vessels.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日清晨，使者請求將比試完全取消，因為此事恐會引起兩位拉者之間的不滿；班德朗曾請求他設法中止比試，因為他自覺力量不如對方。拉者微笑應允，改派巴當在斯里卡馬海峽後方固定一條巨大沉重的鐵鍊，以阻止船隻通行。

title.en: Two Stone Pillars from Kling over Badang's Grave
title.zh: 克林王送石柱於巴當之墓

region.en: Point of the straits of Singhapura
region.zh: 獅城海峽之岬

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (Badang's death), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When Badang dies he is buried at the point of the straits of Singhapura. Tidings reach the land of Kling, whose raja sends two stone pillars to be raised over the grave as a monument — 'these are the pillars which are still at the point of the bay.' Even in death, the Annals insists, the strongman's fame draws honours from across the sea.
summary.zh: 巴當死，葬於獅城海峽之岬。訊至克林，其王遣二石柱豎於墓上為紀念——『即今灣岬之石柱』。壯士雖死，其名跨海受祭。

sensitivity.note: Grave-monument etiology closing the Badang cycle.

passages.text: After a long time, Badang also died, and was buried at the point of the straits of Singhapura, and when the tidings of his death reached the land of Kling, the raja sent two stone pillars, to be raised over his grave as a monument, and these are the pillars which are still at the point of the bay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了許久，巴當也去世了，葬於辛伽普拉海峽的尖端；他死去的消息傳到克林之地後，拉者送來兩根石柱，要立在他的墳上作為紀念碑，這兩根石柱至今仍立於海灣的尖端。

title.en: The Barnacles Turned to Gold: Marah Silu of Pasangan
title.zh: 藤壺化金：帕桑甘的馬拉·西魯

region.en: Pasangan, Samudra coast, north Sumatra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘三摩陀海岸帕桑甘（象徵性定位）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (Marah Silu's gold), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The fish-weir keeper Marah Silu keeps finding kalang-kalang (barnacles) in his traps and casting them back — until, enraged, he boils them: the barnacles turn to gold and the foam of the boiling water to silver. His brother Marah Chaka, told that Silu 'eats barnacles,' seeks to kill him; Silu flees to the forest of Jaran and wins followers by giving away gold — the obscure fisherman fated to become the first sultan of Samudra.
summary.zh: 設魚梁的馬拉·西魯屢屢在梁中拾得藤壺，丟回海中又復出現；怒而煮之——藤壺化金、煮水之沫化銀。兄長馬拉·查卡聞『弟食藤壺』欲殺之；西魯逃入查蘭森林，散金收眾——賤業漁人注定成為三摩陀首位蘇丹。

sensitivity.note: Low-born founder tested by rumour (the 'barnacle-eater' slander) before exaltation.

passages.text: Marah Silu gained his livelihood by keeping fish-weirs on the shore of the sea, and he repeatedly found in them kalang-kalang, or biche de Mar, which he rejected into the sea; no sooner had he adjusted his weirs, but he found they had returned. He got angry and boiled them, when the kalang-kalang were converted into gold, while the foam of the water in which they had been boiled was converted into silver.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬拉希魯以在海邊設置魚樑為生，他屢次在魚樑中發現卡拉卡拉朗，即藤壺，便將其丟回海中；可是他才剛安置好魚樑，就發現牠們又回來了。他發怒將牠們煮沸，卡拉卡拉朗便化為黃金，而煮牠們的水所生的泡沫則化為白銀。

passages.text: At last Marah Chaka was informed that his brother Marah Silu was in the habit of eating kalang-kalang, and was enraged and wanted to kill him. When Marah Silu heard of this intention he fled to the forest of Jaran, where he lived a long time and gave liberally of the gold he had acquired to all the people in his vicinity, and they all became obedient to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後馬拉查卡得知他的兄弟馬拉希魯有吃卡拉卡拉朗的習慣，勃然大怒，想要殺他。馬拉希魯聽說這個意圖後，便逃往查蘭森林，在那裡住了很久，並把他所得的黃金慷慨分送給附近所有的人，眾人於是都順從他。

title.en: The Ant as Big as a Cat: The Naming of Samatra
title.zh: 大如貓的螞蟻：三摩陀之名

region.en: Hill of Semadra, north Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘瑟馬德拉丘

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (the great ant), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Hunting from his forest refuge, Marah Silu's dog Sipasei gives tongue on an eminence; ascending, Silu finds a huge ant as large as a cat — and eats it. He makes the hill his residence and names it Semadra, 'the great ant' (semut raya): the name from which, the Annals says, comes Samatra (Sumatra), the island promised in a hadis as a land that would one day 'produce many Wali-alah.'
summary.zh: 馬拉·西魯行獵，犬西帕塞於丘上吠叫；登丘見一巨蟻，大如貓——遂食之。即以該丘為居，名之『瑟馬德拉』，意即『大螞蟻』（semut raya）——《紀年》云：蘇門答臘之名即由此而來，並引聖訓言此地將出眾多聖徒。

sensitivity.note: Name-etiology for Sumatra; entomophagy as royal omen.

passages.text: On a certain day Marah Silu went a hunting, and his dog Sipasei gave tongue on an elevated piece of ground. When Marah Silu had ascended the eminence, he observed a huge ant which was as large as a cat; he took this ant and ate it, and this eminence he made his residence, and named it Semadra, which signifies the great ant (semut raya).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某日，馬拉希魯外出打獵，他的狗西帕塞在一處高地上吠叫起來。馬拉希魯登上高地後，看見一隻巨大的螞蟻，大小如貓；他捉住這隻螞蟻並吃了牠，又把這處高地作為自己的居所，命名為塞馬德拉，意即大螞蟻（semut raya）。

passages.text: It is related in the hadis of the prophet Muhammed that he said to his companions: 'In the latter times men shall hear of an island under the wind, named Samadra; as soon as this shall happen, go and convert it to Islamism, for the island shall produce many Wali-alah, or persons of gifted piety.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 先知穆罕默德的聖訓中記載，他曾對同伴們說：「在後世，人們將會聽聞一座位於風下之地的島嶼，名叫薩瑪德拉；此事一旦發生，你們便去，使它皈依伊斯蘭教，因為這座島將產生許多瓦利阿拉，即蒙受天賦虔誠之人。」

title.en: The Fakir's Test: Only Samadra Could Read the Koran
title.zh: 苦行僧之試：惟三摩陀能誦古蘭

region.en: Samudra, north Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘三摩陀

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (the conversion of Marah Silu), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Fulfilling the hadis, the sharif of Mecca sends a vessel with a fakir disguised in it — Sultan Muhammed of Matabar, descended from Abubacar. Sailing from Pasuri through Lambri and Haru, he offers the Koran at every land and none can read it, until at Samadra the fisherman Marah Silu, after the prophet spat into his mouth in a dream, reads it aloud. The hidden sultan installs him as Sultan Malac al Salih — the Annals' conversion miracle of Sumatra's first Islamic sultanate.
summary.zh: 應聖訓，麥加謝里夫遣船，船中偽裝之苦行僧乃馬塔巴爾蘇丹穆罕默德（出自阿布·巴克爾之裔）。沿途經帕蘇里、蘭布里、哈魯，出示古蘭，皆無人能誦；至三摩陀，漁人馬拉·西魯——夢中先知唾其口——朗誦經文。隱姓之王遂冊立之，號『馬立克·薩利赫』——此即蘇門答臘首個伊斯蘭蘇丹國之皈依神蹟。

sensitivity.note: Conversion legend of the Annals; respectful treatment of an Islamic hagiographic episode.

passages.text: Then the sheref of Mecca sent a vessel properly fitted out, and ordered the mariners to proceed to the land of Samadra. They reached the land of Matabar, where a raja named Sultan Muhammed, descended from Abubacar, appointed his eldest son to the government and embarked in the guise of a fakir, desiring them to convey him to the land of Samadra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是麥加的謝里夫派遣了一艘裝備妥當的船，命水手們前往薩瑪德拉之地。他們抵達馬塔巴爾之地，當地一位名叫蘇丹穆罕默德的拉者，乃阿布巴卡爾的後裔，任命其長子治理政事，自己則裝扮成一名法基爾登船，請他們將他載往薩瑪德拉之地。

passages.text: After a long voyage they arrived at the land of Pasuri, the whole of the inhabitants of which embraced Islamism; the fakir went ashore carrying the Koran and presented it to the people to read, but not one of them could read it. The same happened at Lambri and at Haru. When Marah Silu went to sleep he dreamed that he was face to face with the holy prophet, who desired him to open his mouth, on which the prophet spat into it, and he immediately awaked, when his body had the odour of Narawastu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 經過漫長的航行，他們抵達帕蘇里之地，當地全體居民都皈依了伊斯蘭教；那名法基爾帶著《古蘭經》上岸，將其呈給眾人誦讀，但他們之中無一人能讀。在蘭布里和哈魯也是如此。當馬拉希魯入睡時，他夢見自己與聖先知面對面，先知要他張開嘴，隨即向其中吐唾沫，他立刻醒來，身上散發著納拉瓦斯圖的香氣。

passages.text: When the morning came the fakir landed and ordered Marah Silu to read the Koran, and he read it. Then the fakir said to Sheikh Ismail, the nakhoda: 'This is the land of Samadra, mentioned by the holy prophet.' Sheikh Ismail landed all the royal accoutrements he had brought, and installed Marah Silu as raja, under the title of Sultan Malec al Salih.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了早晨，那名法基爾登岸，命馬拉希魯誦讀《古蘭經》，他便讀了出來。於是法基爾對船長謝赫伊斯邁爾說：「這裡便是聖先知所提及的薩瑪德拉之地。」謝赫伊斯邁爾將他帶來的全部王室服飾器物卸上岸，並以蘇丹馬利克·薩利赫的稱號，立馬拉希魯為拉者。

title.en: Putri Ganggang Seated Highest: The Envoy Who Chose the Concubine's Daughter
title.zh: 最高處的邦邦公主：使者選中庶女

region.en: Perlac, Aceh, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘亞齊珀拉克

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (the embassy for a bride), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Sultan Malac al Salih sends Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din to Perlac to ask a raja's daughter in marriage. The raja seats his two legitimate daughters undermost and the concubine's daughter, Putri Ganggang, above them, rosy in water-jambu colours, ordering her to open betel for her sisters. Asked which lady he seeks, the envoy unknowingly answers 'the one who sits uppermost' — and the laughing raja grants her: her black-sheep elevation becomes a marriage into the Samudra throne.
summary.zh: 馬立克·薩利赫遣使赴珀拉克求親。珀拉克王使二嫡女坐於下，庶出之女邦邦公主獨坐高處，身著玫瑰色衣，命為二妹剖檳榔。使者不知內情，言：『我求坐在最高處之小姐』——王大笑允嫁。庶女之『僭位』反成三摩陀王室聯姻。

sensitivity.note: Seating-test betrothal episode (the low-born bride raised to honor).

passages.text: The raja of Perlac had three daughters, two of whom were legitimate, and one by a concubine, named Putri Ganggang; he showed all three to Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din, seating the two legitimate daughters undermost, and the natural daughter above them in a more elevated place, and ordered her to open betelnut for her sisters. She was dressed in rosy-coloured clothes, with a vest of the colour of the water jambu, with earrings like the young palm leaf, and looked extremely handsome.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 佩拉克的拉者有三個女兒，其中兩個是嫡出，一個是妾室所生，名叫普特里·岡岡；他將三人都帶到西迪·阿里·蓋亞斯·艾德丁面前，讓兩個嫡出的女兒坐在最下首，而將庶出的女兒安置在她們上方更尊貴的位置，並命她為姊妹們剖開檳榔。她身穿玫瑰色的衣裳，外罩一件水蒲桃色的背心，耳環狀如幼嫩的棕櫚葉，容貌極為秀美。

passages.text: Then said Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din, 'I ask the young lady who sits uppermost;' but he did not know that she was the natural daughter of the raja. Then loud laughed the raja, saying, 'Whichever of them you please, you are welcome to her.' He ordered a hundred prows to be prepared and sent Putri Ganggang to the land of Samadra, where the marriage was consummated after several days of splendid entertainments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是西迪·阿里·蓋亞斯·艾德丁說道：「我請求娶坐在最上首的那位小姐；」但他並不知道她是拉者的庶出女兒。拉者聽罷大笑，說道：「她們之中你中意哪一個，便娶哪一個。」他命人備妥一百艘船，將普特里·岡岡送往薩瑪德拉之地，在那裡經過數日盛大的宴慶之後，婚事便告完成。

title.en: The Dog Sipasei Finds Pasai
title.zh: 獵犬西帕塞尋得巴賽

region.en: Pasai (Pasei), north Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘巴賽

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (the founding of Pasei), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When Perlac is conquered and refugees flee to Samudra, Sultan Malac al Salih resolves to found a settlement for his two sons. Crossing the river on his elephant Parmadewan, his dog Sipasei gives tongue; he finds a piece of elevated ground 'as if it had been levelled,' clears it, builds a town — and names it Pasei after the dog. His eldest son is made its raja and the royal possessions are divided between the brothers, founding the Pasai line.
summary.zh: 珀拉克陷落，難民逃至三摩陀；蘇丹決為二子另建邦邑。乘象帕爾瑪提萬渡河，獵犬西帕塞吠叫示地——得一高丘，平整如人工鋪就；闢之建城，以犬之名『巴賽』名之。長子封為其王，王室象馬兵眾分而二之——巴賽王朝由此開基。

sensitivity.note: City-naming by hunting-dog; classic Southeast Asian foundation device.

passages.text: At this time the country of Perlac was conquered by its enemies, and the inhabitants took refuge in Samadra. Then Sultan Malec al Salih determined to found another settlement for his sons. Having mounted his elephant Parmadewan he crossed the river; his dog Sipasei gave tongue, and the Sultan quickly found an elevated ground of nearly the size of a palace and its appurtenances, very fine and smooth, as if it had been levelled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時，Perlac 之國為敵人所征服，居民避難於 Samadra。蘇丹 Malec al Salih 遂決意為其諸子另闢居地。他騎上大象 Parmadewan 渡河；其犬 Sipasei 出聲吠叫，蘇丹旋即發現一處高地，大小約與一座宮殿及其附屬建築相當，極為平整光滑，宛如曾經剷平一般。

passages.text: He ordered this place to be cleared out and a negri or town founded there, a palace erected, and the whole to be named Pasei, after the prince's dog. He ordered his eldest son Malec al Zaher to be raja; and having divided his people, elephants, horses and royal accoutrements into two parts, he divided them between his sons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他下令清理此地，於此建立 negri（城鎮），興建宮殿，並以王子之犬命名，全稱為 Pasei。他命長子 Malec al Zaher 為 raja（王）；又將其人民、大象、馬匹及王室裝備分為兩份，分賜諸子。

title.en: The Man Who Went Out to Search for His Son
title.zh: 尋子記

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The man who went out to search for his son', eBook #28932

summary.en: Searching the coasts for a son lost in his kayak, a wizard-father outfaces a giant whose drum-skin is human belly, killer-whale helping spirits, a ravine man-eater he turns on his own legs, a moss-stopped seal bone that asks a favour, a mussel luring him to the bottom, and a boot-drying ogress felled by word-magic. The last stranger shows him his son's kayak skin, stretched out — the boy has been eaten — and the father tramples the man-eater's bones to nothing.
summary.zh: 父親沿海尋找失蹤之子：先後挫敗欲吞他的鼓皮巨人（殺人鯨靈助破屋救主）、誘他入深谷的食人巨漢（反将其摔落）、求他拔出孔中青苔的海豹骨、誘他下海的蚌精、以及靴子掛高的老嫗（一句咒語使其斃命）。最後一名生人展示晾曬的皮——正是兒子的皮艇皮——孩子已被吞食；父親將食人者踐踏至骨碎。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Cannibalism motifs presented as told in the archival source.

passages.text: In the days of the forefathers, a man went out along the coasts searching for his son, who had gone out in his kayak and not returned. One day he saw a giant beside a great glacier and rowed up to him; entering the giant's house, he was shown a beautiful drum with a skin taken from the belly of a man — and the giant trembled all over with the desire to eat him. Great salmon began dropping down through a hole in the roof, and the frightened guest could not get out of the place; but being a great wizard he called upon his helping spirits: 'Killer whales, killer whales — come forth, my helping spirits and show yourselves, for here is one who desires to eat me up.' They came forth, the house was crushed, the giant killed, and the man rowed on in search of his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who went out to search for his son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在先祖的時代，有一人沿著海岸外出尋找他的兒子，其子乘獨木舟出海後未歸。一日，他見一巨人立於大冰川旁，便划船靠近；進入巨人之屋後，巨人向他展示一面美麗的鼓，鼓面取自人腹之皮——而那巨人因想吃掉他而渾身顫抖。大鮭魚開始從屋頂的洞中落下，這驚恐的客人無法離開此地；但他身為大巫師，便召喚其助靈：『虎鯨，虎鯨——現身吧，我的助靈，顯現吧，因為這裡有一個想吃掉我的人。』牠們現身了，屋子被壓毀，巨人被殺，那人便繼續划船尋找自己的兒子。

passages.text: He met a second big man who did nothing but eat men and threw their kayaks down a great ravine. 'Come here and look,' said the man-eater, leading him to the deep ravine and trying to thrust him backwards into it — but the man caught the giant's legs and cast him down instead. Rowing on, he heard the bone of a seal calling to him: 'Take away the moss which has stopped up the hole that goes through me,' and did so. A mussel at the bottom of the sea cried for him to row his kayak straight down through the water to visit it — but that mussel wanted to eat him, and he did not heed it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who went out to search for his son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他遇見第二個大漢，此人只吃人，並將他們的獨木舟扔下大深谷。『過來看看，』那食人者說道，領他至深谷邊，試圖將他往後推入谷中——但那人抓住巨人的雙腿，反將他推了下去。繼續划行時，他聽見一塊海豹骨呼喚他：『把堵住貫穿我身上那個洞的苔蘚拿開，』他便照做了。海底的一隻貽貝呼喚他，要他把獨木舟筆直划入水中去拜訪牠——但那隻貽貝是想吃他，他並未理會。

passages.text: One day he saw an old woman and rowed up to her. 'Let me dry your boots,' she said — and hung them up so high he could not reach them, so that he could not sleep for fear. It was revealed she was a man-eater; he got hold of his boots and fled to his kayak with her running behind: 'If only I could catch him, and cut him up' — and the kayak nearly upset, so strong were her words. 'If only I could send a bird dart through her,' said the man, and as he spoke the woman fell down on her back and broke her knife. He rowed on and met a stranger who said, 'See what a skin I have stretched out here' — and he knew at once it was his son's kayak: the stranger had eaten his son. The man went up on land and trampled the man-eater to death, so that all his bones were crushed, and went home again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who went out to search for his son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一日，他見一老婦，便划船靠近。『讓我替你烘乾靴子吧，』她說道——並將靴子掛得極高，他搆不著，以致他因恐懼而無法入睡。後來顯露她乃是食人者；他抓住自己的靴子，逃向獨木舟，她在後面追趕：『但願我能抓住他，把他剁碎』——獨木舟幾乎翻覆，她的話語竟如此有力。『但願我能射一支鳥鏢穿過她，』那人說道，話音剛落，那婦人便仰面倒下，折斷了她的刀。他繼續划行，遇見一個陌生人說道：『看看我在這裡撐開的這張皮』——他立刻認出那是他兒子的獨木舟：那陌生人吃掉了他的兒子。那人上岸，將食人者踩死，使其骨骼盡碎，然後返回家園。

title.en: Atungait, Who Went A-Wandering
title.zh: 浪遊者阿通蓋特

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Atungait, who went a-wandering', eBook #28932

summary.en: The great Atungait picks the strongest woman at the football ground — a small player who alone can knead his double-thick ribbon-seal skin — and drives off with her through strange lands: up a sheer rock he bores his own footholds, past the all-left-handed, the man-eaters who eat one another, and the lame, copper-ajangat-playing people whose stolen plaything he rescues by trailing sole-leather that swallows their pursuing rock-ridges. Flying home, he finds his wife rubbing noses with a stranger, kills her for lying, spares the honest stranger, and marries the strong woman.
summary.zh: 阿通蓋特在足球場上挑中力氣最大的女子——小個子卻能揉軟他特製的雙厚環斑海豹皮——一同駕犬出遊。途中他徒手在絕壁上鑿階登頂，犬隊循跡而上；歷經全用左手的部落、互相吞食的食人族、以及賴銅環戲的跛足者——搶走銅環戲後，以拖地的皮底誘使追來的岩脊沉入冰中。他飛回家中，見妻子與陌生人磨鼻，因她撒謊而殺之，饒了誠實的陌生人，轉而娶了那位強女。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Killing of the lying wife presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Atungait, that great man, had a fancy to go on a sledge trip with a strong woman. He had a ribbon seal flayed, forbidding his wife to scrape the meat side clean so that the skin might be as thick as possible, and dried it. In winter he visited a tribe well known for its football, marked the one strongest among the players — a woman small of stature who always contrived to snatch the ball from the others — and gave her the great thick skin to knead soft, which no other woman could have done. He took her on his sledge and drove off wandering through the lands around.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atungait, who went a-wandering'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那偉人 Atungait 突發奇想，要與一名強壯的女子一同乘雪橇出遊。他剝下一張帶紋海豹皮，禁止妻子將肉面刮淨，以使皮盡可能厚實，然後將其晾乾。冬季，他拜訪了一個以足球聞名的部族，選中玩者中最強壯的一人——一名身材矮小的女子，她總能從他人腳下奪得球——並將那張厚實的大皮交給她揉軟，這是其他女子都做不到的。他帶她坐上雪橇，驅車漫遊於周圍各地。

passages.text: They came to a high steep rock rising from open water; Atungait sprang up on it and began running up, so strong that at every step he bored his feet far down into the rock. He called to his dogs, and one by one they followed by the way of his footsteps — all save one, which died. Then he hoisted up his sledge and his wife and drove on. They passed a place of people who were all left-handed; then man-eaters who ate one another, having no other food, but could do him no harm; then people who had one leg shorter than the other from birth, lying on the ground all day playing ajangat, with a fine plaything made of copper. Atungait stayed some time, and when he set out, stole their plaything and destroyed all their sledges; the lame ones, unable to pursue, dealt magically with rocky ridges, which rushed over the ice towards the travellers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atungait, who went a-wandering'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們來到一塊從開闊水面上聳立而起的高峻岩石前；阿通蓋特一躍而上，開始往上奔跑，力氣大得每踏一步，雙腳都深深陷進岩石裡。他呼喚他的狗，牠們便一隻接一隻循著他的腳印跟來——只除了一隻，那隻死了。接著他拉起雪橇、帶上妻子，繼續前行。他們經過一個全是左撇子的人的地方；又經過食人族，那些人彼此相食，因為沒有別的食物，卻傷不了他；再經過一些天生一條腿比另一條短的人，他們整日躺在地上玩阿姜加特，玩著一件精美的銅製玩物。阿通蓋特逗留了一陣，臨出發時偷走了他們的玩物，並毀壞了他們所有的雪橇；那些瘸腿的人追不上，便施法於岩脊，岩脊便衝過冰面，朝旅人奔來。

passages.text: Hearing something like the rushing of a river, Atungait turned and perceived rocks rolling towards him. 'Have you a piece of sole-leather?' he asked his wife, and she tied it to a string to drag behind the sledge; when the stones reached it they stopped suddenly and sank down through the ice, while the lame ones cried behind: 'Bring back our plaything, and give us our copper thing again.' Longing for home and not knowing where they were, Atungait flew off through the air — for he was a great wizard — found his house, looked in at the window, and saw his wife rubbing noses with a strange man. 'Huh! You are not afraid of wearing away your nose, it seems.' She rushed out; 'You have grown clever at kissing,' he said; 'No, I have not kissed any one,' she cried — and Atungait grasped her roughly and killed her, because she had lied. The stranger came out and admitted the truth, and Atungait let him live because he spoke it. After that he flew back to the strong woman and made her his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atungait, who went a-wandering'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿通蓋特聽見像是河水奔流的聲響，回頭一看，只見岩石正朝他滾來。「你有一塊鞋底皮嗎？」他問妻子，她便把皮子繫在繩上，拖在雪橇後頭；石頭一碰到它，便猛然停住，沉入冰下，而那些瘸腿的人在後頭喊道：「把我們的玩物還回來，再把你們的銅玩意兒還給我們。」阿通蓋特渴望回家，卻不知身在何處，便從空中飛去——因為他是個了不起的巫師——找到了自己的屋子，從窗戶往裡看，看見妻子正和一個陌生男子互碰鼻子。「哼！看來你不怕把鼻子磨掉啊。」她衝了出來；「你倒學會了親嘴，」他說；「不，我沒親過任何人，」她喊道——阿通蓋特便粗暴地抓住她，把她殺了，因為她說了謊。那陌生人走了出來，承認了實情，阿通蓋特因他說了真話，便饒他一命。之後他飛回那強壯的女人那裡，娶她為妻。

title.en: Kumagdlak and the Living Arrows
title.zh: 庫馬格拉克與活箭

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Kumagdlak and the living arrows', eBook #28932

summary.en: Ill with a bad leg in his lonely tent, Kumagdlak sees enemies land from umiak and kayak. His arrows tremble of themselves, for their points are men's shinbones and their master is uneasy; as a great wizard he can breathe life into them so they fly and kill alone, and his mother's child-carrying pouch thong turns every enemy arrow wide. The taunt about tasting the water of the dead is answered: his first arrow flies over the boats, the second cuts the old leader's bowstring and pierces him, and the living arrows win the battle before a conjured storm drowns the rest.
summary.zh: 瘸腿獨居的庫馬格拉克見敵舟登岸。他的箭簇由人脛骨所製，因主人不安而自行顫動；身為大巫，他呵氣即可賦箭生命，使其自飛殺敵；幼時母親攜兒袋的皮帶一揮，敵箭盡皆偏飛。老者譏他將『飲地下亡者之水』，他以活箭回敬——首箭越船而過，次箭截斷老人弓弦、穿其身而歿；群敵潰逃，他再喚風暴，令殘敵盡葬海底。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Arrows of men's shinbones and the breath-given life of weapons are documented wizard-lore.

passages.text: Kumagdlak lived apart from his fellows, with his wife the only living being beside himself. One day, looking for stones to build a fireplace, she saw many enemies approaching over the sea: 'An umiak and kayaks,' she cried. Her husband lay in the house with a bad leg, ill at ease. 'My arrows — bring my arrows!' he cried, and his wife saw all his arrows lying there trembling, because their points were made of the shinbones of men, and they trembled because their master was ill at ease. Kumagdlak, feathering them with birds' feathers, was a great wizard: by breathing with his own breath upon those arrows he could give them life, causing them to fly towards his enemies and kill them; and when he stood unprotected, he grasped the thong of the pouch in which his mother had carried him as a child and struck out with it, and then all arrows aimed at him flew wide of their mark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kumagdlak and the living arrows'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫馬格德拉克與同伴分開居住，除了妻子之外，身邊再無別的活物。有一天，他妻子去找石頭砌火塘，看見許多敵人從海上逼近：「一艘烏米亞克大船和幾隻皮划艇，」她喊道。她丈夫因腿傷躺在屋裡，心神不寧。「我的箭——把我的箭拿來！」他喊道，妻子便看見他所有的箭都躺在那裡顫抖，因為箭頭是用人的脛骨做的，它們顫抖，是因為主人心神不寧。庫馬格德拉克給箭裝上鳥羽，是個了不起的巫師：他只要對那些箭吹出自己的氣息，就能賦予它們生命，讓它們飛向敵人，把他們殺死；而當他毫無遮擋地站著時，他抓住母親在他小時候背他的那個袋子的皮帶，揮舞起來，於是所有瞄準他的箭都偏離了目標。

passages.text: The enemies hauled up on shore, and the eldest among them cried out: 'Kumagdlak! It is time for you to go out and taste the water in the land of the dead under the earth — or perhaps you will go up into the sky?' 'That fate is more likely to be yours,' answered Kumagdlak. Standing at the entrance of his tent he knew that if but the first arrow could be sent whirling over the boats, none of them would be able to harm him. The arrow flew over the boats; the next cut through the string of the old speaker's bow and pierced the old man himself. Then, his wife handing him the arrows as he shot, he began shooting down the others; the men from the boats shot at him, but all their arrows flew wide, and his enemies, growing fewer and fewer, at last fled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kumagdlak and the living arrows'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 敵人把船拖上岸，其中年紀最大的喊道：「庫馬格德拉克！該是你出來，嘗嘗地下死者之地的水了——或許你會上天去吧？」「那樣的命運更可能落在你身上，」庫馬格德拉克答道。他站在帳篷入口，知道只要能把第一支箭旋飛過那些船，他們就誰也傷不了他。那支箭飛過了船；下一支射斷了那位老說話者弓上的弦，並刺穿了老人本人。接著，妻子在他射擊時把箭遞給他，他便開始射倒其餘的人；船上的人朝他射箭，但他們的箭全都偏飛，他的敵人越來越少，最後逃走了。

passages.text: Kumagdlak took all the bodies down by the shore and plundered them, taking their knives; and when the boats had got well out to sea, he called up a great storm, so that all the others perished. The waves washed the bodies this way and that along the coast until the clothes were worn off them. Here ends the story of the man who, lame in his own house, was yet beyond the reach of the weapons of the living.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kumagdlak and the living arrows'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫馬格德拉克把所有屍體拖到岸邊，劫掠了他們，取走他們的刀；等那些船駛到遠海，他喚來一場大風暴，其餘的人便全都喪命。海浪把屍體沿岸沖來沖去，直到衣服都磨掉了。那個在自己屋裡瘸了腿、卻仍舊在活人武器所及之外的人的故事，到此結束。

title.en: The Giant Dog of the Hills
title.zh: 山間巨犬

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Giant Dog', eBook #28932

summary.en: A childless man owns a dog big enough to haul whales and narwhal ashore, hooking the narwhal on its side teeth; thongs through holes in its jaws steer it, and the amulet meant for his son — a knot of hard wood — makes it hard for death to come at it. It crushes three bear-sized dogs, then takes to hunting the inland-dwellers and dragging home their legs, hairy-booted, in its jaws — and from that giant dog, the teller says, the inland folk got their great fear of all dogs.
summary.zh: 無子的男人養著能拖鯨上岸的巨犬——一角鯨咬在它的側齒上，頜穿孔中的皮繩可供操縱；本該給兒子的護身符（硬木結）令它難以死去。巨犬咬碎三隻熊般大的敵犬，又慣於獵殺內陸人、拖回毛靴之腿獻給主人——內陸人見犬便懼的天性，正是從這隻巨犬而來。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The inland-dwellers (tornit) are the legendary giant folk of Greenlandic tradition.

passages.text: There was once a man who had a giant dog: it could swim in the sea, and was so big it could haul whale and narwhal to shore, hooking the narwhal on to its side teeth and swimming with them hanging there. The owner had cut holes in its jaws and let in thongs, so that he could make it turn either way by pulling at them; when he and his wife wished to journey anywhere they had only to mount on its back. He had long wished for a son, and as none was born, he gave the great dog the amulet his son should have had — a knot of hard wood — and the dog was thus made hard to resist the coming of death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Giant Dog'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個人，養著一隻巨犬：牠能在海裡游泳，體型大得能把鯨魚和獨角鯨拖上岸，用側牙鉤住獨角鯨，就這麼拖著牠們游。主人在牠的顎上鑿了孔，穿進皮帶，這樣一拉皮帶就能叫牠轉向任何一邊；他和妻子想到哪裡去，只需騎上牠的背。他早就盼著有個兒子，既然沒有兒子出生，他便把兒子本該有的護身符——一個硬木結——給了那隻巨犬，巨犬因此變得堅硬，足以抵禦死亡的到來。

passages.text: Once the dog ate a man, and its owner had to leave the place and settle elsewhere, hiding it in the hills and keeping it busy with a great bone whenever a stranger's kayak came in. Its size and fierceness made him many enemies: once a stranger drove in with a sledge drawn by three dogs as big as bears, to kill the giant dog; it pretended to be afraid at first, but when the stranger's dogs set upon it, it turned and crushed the skulls of all three in its teeth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Giant Dog'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，那隻狗吃掉了一個人，牠的主人只得離開此地，遷居他處，把牠藏進山裡，每逢有陌生人的獨木舟靠岸，便丟一根大骨頭給牠，讓牠忙著啃咬。牠的體型與凶猛為主人招來許多仇敵：有一次，一個陌生人乘著由三隻熊一般大的狗所拉的雪橇前來，要殺死那隻巨犬；巨犬起初裝作害怕，但當陌生人的狗撲向牠時，牠便轉身，用牙齒咬碎了那三隻狗的頭骨。

passages.text: In time the man noticed his dog going off on long journeys into the hills and sometimes returning with the leg of an inland-dweller — he could tell by the hairy boots — and understood the dog had made it a custom to attack the inland folk and bring back their legs. From this giant dog, the teller says, the inland-dwellers got their great fear of all dogs: it would appear suddenly at the window and drag them out. But it was a good thing something frightened the inland-dwellers, for they had themselves an evil custom of carrying off lonely folk, especially women, who had lost their way in the fog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Giant Dog'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 日子一久，那人注意到他的狗會長途跋涉進入山中，有時回來時帶著一個內陸居民的腿——他從那毛茸茸的靴子便認得出來——於是明白這狗已養成襲擊內陸人、並帶回他們腿的習慣。講述者說，內陸居民對所有狗的極度恐懼，正是源自這隻巨犬：牠會突然出現在窗前，把他們拖出去。不過，有東西令內陸居民害怕倒是件好事，因為他們自己有個邪惡的習俗，就是擄走落單的人，尤其是那些在霧中迷了路的女人。

title.en: The Inland-Dwellers of Etah
title.zh: 伊塔的內陸人

region.en: Etah, Smith Sound, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭伊塔（史密斯海峽）

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Inland-dwellers of Etah', eBook #28932

summary.en: A dog-team scents out an inland-dweller's house by the great lake east of Etah; the terrified tornit thrust out an old woman, who dies of fright at the dogs. The visitor apologizes; they answer that her skin was already wrinkled and it does not matter — then flee far up country, never to be seen, their house remains yielding only a single narwhal tusk. The inland-dwellers are not really dangerous, only shy and dog-fearing: one coast woman's tornit husband bled from the eyes at sight of dogs, and their runners' swiftness is trained inside a worm-filled ribbon-seal skin that sucks their blood and lightens their feet.
summary.zh: 犬隊循跡至伊塔以東大湖畔的內陸人之屋；驚恐的托尼特人推出一名老婦，老婦見犬嚇死。來人致歉，答曰『她的皮本已皺了，無妨』——隨即舉族遠遁深山，自此絕跡；屋基中只掘出一支獨角鯨牙。內陸人本無危險，只是怯懦怕犬：海濱女子蘇瓦克的內陸丈夫，一見犬便雙目滲血；其飛毛腿訓法，是將人縛入填滿蠕蟲的環斑海豹皮中，吸盡血液，使腳下輕快。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Tornit (inland-dwellers) ethnogenesis material; note also documents death of the old woman as told.

passages.text: A sledge drove round to the east of Etah, up into the land near the great lake; suddenly the dogs scented something and dashed off over a great plain, then checked and sniffed at the ground — the entrance to an inland-dweller's house. The inland-dwellers screamed aloud with fear when they saw the dogs, thrust out an old woman, and hurried in to hide; the old woman died of fright at the sight of the dogs. The man went in, very ill at ease because he had caused the death of the old one: 'It is a sad thing that I should have caused you to lose that old one.' 'It is nothing,' answered the inland-dwellers, 'her skin was already wrinkled; it does not matter at all.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Inland-dwellers of Etah'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一輛雪橇繞行到埃塔的東邊，向上進入大湖附近的地帶；忽然，狗群嗅到了什麼氣味，便飛奔過一片廣闊的平原，隨後停住，嗅著地面——那是一個內陸居民屋子的入口。內陸居民一看見狗，便嚇得放聲尖叫，推出一個老婦人，自己則急忙躲進去藏身；那老婦人一見狗便嚇死了。那人走了進去，心裡十分不安，因為他害死了那個老婦人：「我竟害你們失去了那位老婦人，真是件令人難過的事。」「這沒什麼，」內陸居民回答，「她的皮早就皺了；一點也不打緊。」

passages.text: The sledges drove home, but the inland-dwellers were so terrified that they fled far up into the country and have never been seen since; the remains of their houses were all that could be found, and when men dug there for more, nothing came up but a single narwhal tusk. The inland-dwellers are not really dangerous, the teller explains — only shy, and very greatly afraid of dogs: there was a woman of the coast-folk, Suagaq, who took a husband from among the inland folk, and when that husband came to visit her brothers, the blood sprang from his eyes at sight of their dogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Inland-dwellers of Etah'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雪橇駛回家去了，但內陸居民驚恐萬分，逃到內陸極深處，此後便再也沒有人見過他們；能找到的只有他們屋子的殘跡，而當人們在那裡再往下挖時，除了單單一根獨角鯨的長牙之外，什麼也沒挖出來。講述者解釋說，內陸居民其實並不危險——只是膽怯，而且非常怕狗：海岸居民中有個女人蘇阿加克，從內陸人當中招了個丈夫，而當那丈夫來探望她的兄弟時，一看見他們的狗，血便從他眼中迸了出來。

passages.text: The tornit train themselves to become swift runners so that they may catch foxes. When an inland-dweller is to become a swift runner, they stuff him into the skin of a ribbon seal filled with worms, leaving only his head free; the worms suck all his blood, and this, they say, makes him very light on his feet. There are still some inland-dwellers left, but they are now gone very far up inland.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Inland-dwellers of Etah'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 托爾尼特人訓練自己成為迅捷的跑者，好能追上狐狸。當一個內陸居民要成為迅捷的跑者時，他們便把他塞進一張裝滿蟲子的帶紋海豹皮裡，只讓他的頭露在外面；那些蟲子吸盡他所有的血，他們說，這使他腳下變得非常輕盈。如今仍有一些內陸居民留存，但他們現在已遷到內陸極深處去了。

title.en: Neruvkaq, Who Stabbed His Wife in the Leg
title.zh: 刺妻者內魯瓦克

region.en: Natsivilik, Smith Sound, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭納齊維利克（史密斯海峽）

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The man who stabbed his wife in the leg', eBook #28932

summary.en: Neruvkaq torments his inland-dweller wife Navarana, stabbing her leg with an awl, until she flees to her many brothers. They storm his roof, losing one leg at the joint; he decks himself in a child's tunic sewn all over with walrus tusk that no one can kill, puts his sealskin coat on the dog as a decoy, leaps to the great meat-stone — footprints still on it — and shoots his enemies down while his mother strengthens him by magic. But the frightened Navarana will not come out from under the bench, and chews the walrus meat he thrusts in to her until she dies there — 'the old sneak!'
summary.zh: 內魯瓦克以錐刺妻子納瓦拉納的小腿取樂，她終投奔內陸的眾兄弟。兄弟們踏其屋頂，一足被切於膝；他穿上縫滿海象牙的幼時舊衣——著之者無人能殺——以犬著皮外套誘敵，縱身躍上分肉巨石（足印至今猶存），其母以巫術助力，亂箭退敵。然而嚇破膽的納瓦拉納再不肯出長凳之下，啃著丈夫塞入的海象肉，最後死於其處——『那老膽小鬼！』

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Domestic violence presented as told in the source; the closing taunt is the teller's own.

passages.text: Neruvkaq's wife Navarana was of the tunerssuit, the inland-dwellers, their only sister with many brothers, and they lived at Natsivilik, the place with a great stone where men lay out meat. Neruvkaq was cruel to his wife: he would stab her in the leg with an awl, and when the point reached her shinbone she would snivel with pain. 'Do not touch me; I have many brothers,' she said, but as he did not cease ill-treating her she ran away to those brothers at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who stabbed his wife in the leg'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 內魯夫卡克的妻子娜瓦拉娜出身於圖內爾蘇伊特人，也就是內陸居民，是眾多兄弟唯一的姊妹，他們住在納齊維利克，那是有塊供人攤放肉類的大石頭的地方。內魯夫卡克對妻子很殘忍：他會用錐子刺她的腿，當錐尖刺到她的脛骨時，她便痛得抽抽噎噎。「別碰我；我有很多兄弟，」她說，但由於他並未停止虐待她，她最後便逃到那些兄弟那裡去了。

passages.text: All the many brothers moved down to Natsivilik, sprang upon the roof of Neruvkaq's house, and began to trample it; one thrust his foot through, and Neruvkaq's brother cut it off at the joint — 'He has cut off my leg' — and the brother-in-law hopped about on one leg until the blood was gone from him and he died. Neruvkaq hastened to put on a tunic worn as a little child, made larger from time to time and covered all about with pieces of walrus tusk: none could kill him as long as he wore that. He put the sealskin coat on his dog and thrust it out as a decoy — the brothers outside stabbed the dog to death, taking it for him — and jumped to the great meat-stone, so strongly that his footmarks are seen on the stone to this day; there he took his arrows all barbed with walrus tusk and began shooting his enemies down, his mother giving him strength by magic means.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who stabbed his wife in the leg'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾多兄弟一同下到納齊維利克，跳上內魯夫卡克的屋頂，開始踩踏；其中一人把腳踩穿屋頂，內魯夫卡克的兄弟便齊關節砍斷了那隻腳——「他砍斷了我的腿」——那姻親便單腳跳著，直到血流盡而死。內魯夫卡克急忙穿上他幼時所穿、後來不時加大、周身綴滿海象牙碎片的長袍：只要穿著它，誰也殺不了他。他把海豹皮外套套在狗身上，將狗推出去當誘餌——外面的兄弟們以為是他，便把狗刺死了——他隨即跳向那塊巨大的肉石，力道之大，至今石上仍可見他的腳印；他在那裡取出全數裝著海象牙倒鉤的箭，開始射殺敵人，他的母親則以巫術助他力量。

passages.text: Soon but few enemies were left, and they fled away southward, fleeing and fleeing without stopping until they had gone a great way. Navarana, now afraid of her husband, crept in under the bench and hid; she would not come out again, so her husband thrust in a great piece of walrus meat, and she chewed and gnawed at it to her heart's content. 'Come out, come out, for I will never hurt you any more,' he said — but she had grown so afraid of him that she never came out any more, and so she died where she was at last: the old sneak, the teller calls her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The man who stabbed his wife in the leg'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久敵人只剩寥寥數人，他們便向南逃去，逃了又逃，一刻不停，直到走了很遠。納瓦拉娜此時懼怕丈夫，便爬進長凳底下躲藏；她再也不肯出來，於是丈夫塞進一大塊海豹肉，她便盡情咀嚼啃食。「出來吧，出來吧，我再也不會傷害妳了，」他說——但她已變得如此怕他，再也不肯出來，最後就死在那裡：那個老鬼祟，講述者這樣稱她。

title.en: Avovang: The Soul That Lived in the Bodies of All Beasts
title.zh: 阿沃萬格：寓於百獸之魂

region.en: Kangerdlugssuaq, East Greenland
region.zh: 東格陵蘭康格盧克蘇瓦克峽

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts', eBook #28932

summary.en: Avovang, whom nothing could wound — enemies stab at him standing on his child-wrapping dog-neck skin, and drag him to a cliff he refuses to fall from — is finally shoved through a seal breathing-hole by men who covet his southern wife. His soul, wanting to know the manner of every beast's life, becomes seal, fox, dog, reindeer, wolf, walrus, and raven in turn, learning each creature's gait and food, and avenges itself on its murderers as a seal that drowns them and a fox that wrecks their sledges — until a nail-less toe fells it at last, and the soul creeps into a woman's body to be born again as a man.
summary.zh: 刀槍不入的阿沃萬格——敵人屢刺不傷，拖上懸崖也摔他不死——終被覬覦其南地妻子的同伴自海豹呼吸孔推入海中。其魂為遍歷百獸之生態：先化海豹、狐狸復仇，淹死撞毀仇人；再為偷食之犬、逐群之鹿（『後腿向天邊踢出』）、追獵之狼、潛底之海象、腳寒之鴉；末了重為海豹，卻栽在一個剪去大趾甲的獵人手裡。魂自手套鑽入婦人之身，轉世重為男子。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Soul-migration through animal bodies is core Inuit cosmology; the tale doubles as natural-history teaching.

passages.text: There was a man named Avovang, of whom it is said that nothing could wound him; he lived at Kangerdlugssuaq. One nearing-summer day, when his brother stood by a seal's breathing hole, a sledge dashed up with the warning that many sledges would come to kill his brother; the brother hid away up a steep rocky slope. The sledges drove up before the house, and Avovang went out to meet them carrying the skin of a dog's neck that had wrapped him as a child; standing on that piece of skin, he could not be wounded though the men stabbed again and again. Mockingly he told them his body was now like a piece of knotty wood with the scars of their wounds. Dragged to the top of a high cliff to be cast down, he changed himself each time into another man who was not their enemy, until they were forced to drive away without having done what they wished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有個名叫阿沃旺的人，據說沒有什麼能傷得了他；他住在康格爾德盧格蘇阿克。臨近夏天的一天，他的兄弟守在海豹的呼吸孔旁，一輛雪橇疾馳而來，警告說將有許多雪橇前來殺他兄弟；兄弟便躲上陡峭的岩坡。雪橇駛到屋前，阿沃旺帶著一條狗頸皮出去迎他們，那皮是他幼時裹身之物；他站在那塊皮上，任憑眾人一再刺戳，也傷不了他。他嘲弄地告訴他們，他的身體如今就像一塊多節的木头，滿是他們所刺傷痕。他被拖上高崖之頂，要將他拋下，他卻每次都變作另一個不是他們仇敵的人，直到他們不得不一無所獲地離去。

passages.text: He desired once to travel south to buy wood, as men were wont in the old days, and took a wife from among the people of the south on that journey. While the men stood looking for seal breathing-holes they all felt a great desire to possess Avovang's wife, and tried to kill him: Qautaq stabbed him in the eyes, and the others sent him sliding down through a breathing hole into the sea. His widowed wife, so angry she broke all the wood they had brought from the south into small pieces, went home. Then a great seal rose in the sledges' path, and many fell through the thin ice and were drowned; then a fox lured them up a mountain of screw-ice and dashed them down, so that only two escaped. It was the soul of Avovang that had changed first into a seal and then into a fox, bringing about the death of his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次他想南下去換木頭，正如古時人們慣常所為，那趟旅程中他從南方人中娶了一個妻子。當男人們站著尋找海豹呼吸孔時，他們都強烈地想要佔有阿沃旺的妻子，便設法殺他：考塔克刺他的眼睛，其餘的人把他從呼吸孔推落海中。他守寡的妻子氣得把他們從南方帶回的木頭全折成小塊，然後回家去了。接著一頭巨大的海豹在雪橇行進的路上浮起，許多人從薄冰上跌落溺死；然後一隻狐狸把他們誘上螺旋冰堆成的山，再使他們摔下，只有兩人逃脫。那正是阿沃旺的靈魂，先化為海豹，再化為狐狸，促成了他仇敵的死亡。

passages.text: Afterwards he made up his mind to let himself be born in the shape of every beast on earth, that he might one day tell his fellow-men the manner of their life. He was a dog, eating what men threw away and tired at last of the many beatings; a reindeer, taught to kick out towards the farthest edge of the sky at the gallop and to eat moss and lichen, growing fat with suet; a wolf, taught 'Kick up towards the sky' so he could overtake the reindeer and get food; a walrus, taught to swing his hindquarters up to the sky to dive, and fed on mussels and little white stones; and a raven — 'The ravens never lack food, but they often feel cold about the feet.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來他下定決心，讓自己以世上每一種野獸的形貌重生，好有朝一日向同胞講述牠們生活的方式。他曾是狗，吃人丟棄之物，終於厭倦了無數次的挨打；曾是馴鹿，學會奔馳時朝天空最遠處踢腿，吃苔蘚與地衣，長得肥厚多脂；曾是狼，學會「朝天空踢」，好追上馴鹿、取得食物；曾是海象，學會把後身朝天擺起以便下潛，以貽貝和小白石為食；也曾是渡鴉——「渡鴉從不缺食，但腳上常覺寒冷。」

passages.text: At last he became a seal again and lay under the ice watching the men who came to catch him; being a great wizard he could hide himself under the nail of a man's big toe. But one day a hunter who had cut off the nail of his big toe harpooned him; hauled up on the ice and cut up in the house, Avovang went with the mittens the man cast to his wife and crept into the body of the woman — and after a time he was born again, and became once more a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The soul that lived in the bodies of all beasts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後他又變成一頭海豹，躺在冰下觀望前來捕他的人；由於他是個大巫師，他能藏身於人腳大趾的指甲之下。但有一天，一個曾剪去自己大趾甲的人用魚叉刺中了他；他被拖上冰面，在屋裡被切割，阿沃旺隨著那人扔給妻子的手套而去，鑽進那女人的身體——過了一段時日，他再度出生，又變回了一個人。

title.en: The Eldest Magician: Earth of a Tray, Heaven of an Umbrella
title.zh: 太初魔法師：盤大之地，傘大之天

region.en: Selangor, Malay Peninsula (collected from charm-books and magicians)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（採自符咒書與巫師）

period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I 'Nature', the cosmogonic excerpts from Malay charm-books

summary.en: A Malay charm-book opens creation with the Eldest Magician: before the spheres existed, the Creator pre-existed by Himself and made the Earth 'of the width of a tray and the Heavens of the width of an umbrella.' In a second charm the word Kun ('Be!') is spoken by God and echoed by Muhammad; the seed becomes a root, the root a tree, the tree brings forth leaves, and heaven and earth take shape around it.
summary.zh: 馬來符咒書以『太初魔法師』開篇：混沌未分，造物主獨存，先造『盤大之地』與『傘大之天』。另一咒云：神言『昆』（Kun，即是！），穆罕默德應之；種子生根、根成樹、樹生葉，天地遂成。

sensitivity.note: Malay Islamic-folk cosmogony recorded from magicians' charm-books; a syncretism of Qur'anic 'Kun' with older Malay imagery, noted by Skeat himself.

passages.text: Before the spheres, or of Space and Void, the Creator of the entire Universe pre-existed by Himself, and He was the Eldest Magician. He created the Earth of the width of a tray and the Heavens of the width of an umbrella, which are the universe of the Magician. From before the beginning of time existed that Magician — that is, God — and He made Himself manifest with the brightness of the moon and the sun, which is the token of the True Magician.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在諸天界或空間與虛空之前，整個宇宙的創造者已獨自先存，祂就是最年長的魔法師。祂創造了托盤般寬廣的大地與傘蓋般寬廣的諸天，那便是魔法師的宇宙。在時間開始之前，那位魔法師——也就是神——就已存在，祂以日月的光輝顯現自身，那是真魔法師的印記。

passages.text: In another charm, 'Kun' said God, 'Payah kun' said Muhammad, and a seed was created. The seed became a root, the root a tree, and the tree brought forth leaves. Then Heaven and Earth were created — Earth of the width of a tray, Heaven of the width of an umbrella.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在另一道咒語中，「Kun」神說，「Payah kun」穆罕默德說，於是一粒種子被創造出來。種子變成根，根變成樹，樹長出葉子。然後天地被創造出來——托盤般寬廣的大地，傘蓋般寬廣的諸天。

title.en: The Navel of the Earth: A Tree of Four Branches
title.zh: 大地之臍：四枝之樹

region.en: Selangor, Malay Peninsula (charm-book cosmology)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（符咒書宇宙觀）

period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I, the pillar of the Ka'bah as Navel of the Earth

summary.en: God 'created the pillar of the Ka'bah, which is the Navel of the Earth, whose growth is comparable to a Tree, whose branches are four in number' — Sajeratul Mentahar, Taubi, Khaldi, and Nasrun 'Alam — extending north, south, east and west, 'where they are called the Four Corners of the World.' A Malay charm-book thus fuses the world-axis and the world-tree under the navel-stone of Mecca.
summary.zh: 神『造克爾白之柱，即大地之臍，其生長如樹，樹有四枝』——薩傑拉圖勒·門塔哈爾、陶比、哈爾迪、納斯倫·阿拉姆——分向東西南北延伸，『是為世界四隅』。馬來符咒書以麥加之臍石統合世界軸與世界樹。

sensitivity.note: Syncretic world-tree; treated respectfully as recorded folk cosmology.

passages.text: The account proceeds to describe how God 'created the pillar of the Ka'bah, which is the Navel of the Earth, whose growth is comparable to a Tree, whose branches are four in number, and are called, the first Sajeratul Mentahar, and the second Taubi, and the third Khaldi, and the fourth Nasrun 'Alam, which extend unto the north, south, east, and west, where they are called the Four Corners of the World.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這段敘述接著描述神如何「創造了克爾白的柱子，也就是大地的肚臍，其生長可比於一棵樹，其枝共有四條，第一條名為Sajeratul Mentahar，第二條名為Taubi，第三條名為Khaldi，第四條名為Nasrun 'Alam，它們延伸至北、南、東、西，在那裡被稱為世界的四角。」

title.en: The Serpent Broken in Two: How Sakatimuna's Body Made the World
title.zh: 巨蛇斷為兩截：薩卡蒂穆納之軀化成世界

region.en: Menangcabow, Sumatra (origin of the serpent myth), recorded in Selangor charm-books
region.zh: 蘇門答臘米南加保（蛇神話之源），雪蘭莪符咒書採錄

period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I, Gabriel kills the serpent Sakatimuna

summary.en: God's word comes in secret to Gabriel: 'Take me down the iron staff of the Creed which dangles at the gate of heaven, and kill me this serpent Sakatimuna.' Gabriel does so; the serpent breaks asunder, its head shooting above the heavens, its tail penetrating beneath the earth — and its body becomes the world: the rainbow from its sword, grass from the hair of its body, trees from the hair of its head, rain from its tears, dew from its sweat, and genii of every kind from its remains.
summary.zh: 神諭密告迦伯列：『取下懸於天門之鐵杖，為我誅殺巨蛇薩卡蒂穆納。』迦伯列從命；蛇身斷裂——首部直上諸天，尾部下穿大地——其軀化成萬象：虹霓出自其劍，草出自身毛，樹出自頭髮，雨出自其淚，露出自其汗，精怪自其餘軀而生。

sensitivity.note: Dismembered-primordial-being cluster (compare Purusha, Ymir, Pangu, Tiamat); Skeat notes the anthropomorphic serpent as likely an Indian Naga reminiscence — flagged as interpretive. Cross-cluster: the same serpent-name Sakatimuna appears slain by Sang Sapurba in the Malay Annals.

canonical_translation: Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), English

narrative.en:
Among the cosmogonic excerpts that Skeat collected from Malay charm-books and magicians in Selangor, the most dramatic is the killing of the primordial serpent Sakatimuna — a serpent remembered (Skeat notes, citing Newbold and Leyden) as having ravaged the country of Menangkabau in Sumatra about the twelfth century, and the same monster-name that the Malay Annals gives as slain by Sang Sapurba's champion.

BEGINNING: THE COMMISSION. God's word comes in secret to Gabriel: 'Take me down the iron staff of the 'Creed' which dangles at the gate of heaven, and kill me this serpent Sakatimuna.' The weapon is itself sacred — a staff inscribed with the confession of faith, hanging at heaven's gate; the snake must be killed from above.

MIDDLE: THE BREAKING. Gabriel does as commanded, and the serpent 'brake asunder, the head and forepart shooting up above the heavens, and the tail part penetrating downwards beneath the earth.' The world is thus split open at the moment of the serpent's death: a being who spanned both heaven and earth is cut at the middle, and its two halves become the bounds of the upper and lower worlds.

END: THE ANATOMY OF THE WORLD. The rest of the charm describes the transformation of the serpent's parts into the things of the world — 'the rainbow from the serpent's sword with its hilt and cross-piece, grass from the hair of its body, trees from the hair of its head, rain from its tears, and dew from its sweat,' while most of its anatomy turns into the good and evil genii that crowd Malay popular belief. Skeat draws out the remarkable anthropomorphism: this is 'a serpent in little more than name,' likely a reminiscence of the Indian Naga — and he compares the seated human figure with folded arms on every Malay kris hilt.

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) explains natural phenomena (rain, dew, grass, trees, the rainbow) from a slain primordial body; (2) fixes the vertical axis of the Malay cosmos (head above heaven, tail below earth); (3) peoples the spirit-world (genii from the serpent's remains); and (4) links the Malay folk cosmology to the historical dragon-slayer tradition of Menangcabow (Sang Sapurba in the Annals, with the sword of one hundred and ninety notches in the Sultan of Pagaruyung's title-list) — the same monster, slain twice: once at creation, once at the founding of kingship. The charm's geography deserves a final note: because the serpent's head shoots above the heavens and its tail below the earth, the Malay world inherits a vertical ladder along which prayer, smoke and spirit-travel all move — the same axis the Kayan tree-ladder and the Ka'bah-as-navel-tree express in their own idioms. The serpent's notional death also explains why the genii born from its remains are ambivalent: they are the leftovers of a primordial killing, neither wholly good nor wholly bad, and the charm-books' invocations address them as kin rather than strangers. The Menangcabow connection closes the loop in time as well as space: a serpent that ravaged the highlands in the twelfth century, was slain by a champion whose sword still shows the notches, and was killed once more at the beginning of the world in the charm-books' memory — the same monster met twice, once by kings and once by creation.
narrative.zh: 斯凱特在雪蘭莪所採之馬來符咒書宇宙論中，最戲劇者為誅殺原初巨蛇薩卡蒂穆納——此蛇名亦見於《馬來紀年》（蘇門答臘米南加保十二世紀之害獸；三蘇爾巴勇士所誅者同名）。神諭密告迦伯列執天門之鐵杖（刻有信仰箴言）誅蛇；蛇斷為兩截——首上諸天，尾下穿地——世界於蛇死之刻被劈開。蛇軀化成萬象：虹出自劍、草出身毛、樹出頭髮、雨出淚、露出汗；其餘遺骸化為善惡精怪。斯凱特指出其強烈擬人特徵，謂近似印度那伽。功能：釋自然現象、立宇宙縱軸、生精怪世界、並與米南加保屠龍王權傳統（紀年中三蘇爾巴誅蛇、巴加爾容王列劍一百九十缺口）相銜——同一怪物，死於創世，又死於王權之始。

functions: Explains rain, dew, grass, trees and the rainbow as transformations of a slain primordial serpent
Fixes the vertical axis of the Malay cosmos: serpent head above heaven, tail beneath the earth
Peoples the Malay spirit-world: good and evil genii born from the serpent's remains
Links folk cosmology to the Minangkabau dragon-slayer kingship tradition (Sacatimuna of the Malay Annals)

variants.name: Sakatimuna/Icktimani slain by Sang Sapurba's champion (Malay Annals)
variants.summary: The same serpent-name as the Menangcabow ravager, cut in three by the sword Chora Samanda Kian, which carries away 190 notches; the foundation of the Pagaruyung line.

variants.name: Comparative dismembered-primordial-being myths
variants.summary: World formed from a slain primordial body; the Malay version uniquely makes the body's tears and sweat into weather.
