passages.text: The word of God Almighty came in secret to Gabriel, saying, 'Take me down the iron staff of the Creed which dangles at the gate of heaven, and kill me this serpent Sakatimuna.' Gabriel did so, and the serpent brake asunder, the head and forepart shooting up above the heavens, and the tail part penetrating downwards beneath the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 全能神的言語秘密地臨到加百列，說：「取信條的鐵杖——那懸在天門處的——把我放下，替我殺死這條蛇Sakatimuna。」加百列照做了，蛇被劈成兩半，頭部與前半身向上射到諸天之上，尾部則向下穿透到大地之下。

passages.text: The rest of the account describes the transformation of all the parts of the serpent's anatomy, which are represented as turning, with a few exceptions, into good and evil genii. The rainbow is described as originating from the serpent's sword with its hilt and cross-piece, grass from the hair of its body, trees from the hair of its head, rain from its tears, and dew from its sweat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這段敘述其餘部分描述了蛇身各部位的轉化，除了少數例外，它們被描述為變成善靈與惡靈。彩虹被描述為源自蛇的劍及其劍柄與護手，草源自牠身上的毛，樹木源自牠頭上的毛，雨源自牠的淚，露源自牠的汗。

title.en: The Earth on the Buffalo's Horns
title.zh: 牛角載地

region.en: Selangor, Malay Peninsula (collected cosmology)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（採錄宇宙觀）

period: Recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I, shape of the earth

summary.en: The earth is carried by a colossal buffalo standing on an island in the nether ocean. When one horn begins to tire, the buffalo tosses the world up and catches it on the other horn — and that is an earthquake. Around everything girts an immense serpent or dragon, the Ular Naga, which feeds upon its own tail.
summary.zh: 大地由巨牛負於牛角之尖，立於下界大洋中之島上。一角疲倦時，巨牛便將世界拋起、接於另一角尖——此即地震。宇宙外環巨蛇（烏拉·那伽），自噬其尾。

sensitivity.note: World-buffalo cosmology; Skeat compares the Indian elephant variant (Ramayana, Vishnu's boar).

passages.text: A further development of the Malay theory of the earth declares it to be carried by a colossal buffalo upon the tip of its horns. When one horn begins to tire the buffalo tosses it up and catches it upon the tip of the other, thus causing periodical earthquakes. This world-buffalo stands upon an island in the midst of the nether ocean. The universe is girt round by an immense serpent or dragon (Ular Naga), which feeds upon its own tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬來大地理論的進一步發展宣稱，大地由一頭巨大的水牛以牛角尖端托著。當一隻角開始疲倦時，水牛便將它拋起並用另一隻角的尖端接住，如此便造成了週期性的地震。這頭世界水牛站在下界海洋中央的一座島上。宇宙被一條巨大的蛇或龍（Ular Naga）環繞，牠以自己的尾巴為食。

title.en: The Pauh Janggi: The Tree in Mid-Ocean That Swallows the Tides
title.zh: 寶塢江宜：吞潮之海中神樹

region.en: Middle of the great ocean (symbolic pin, Malay cosmology)
region.zh: 大洋之中（象徵性定位，馬來宇宙觀）

period: Recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I, the theory of the tides

summary.en: In the middle of the great ocean grows the immense tree Pauh Janggi, at whose root a monstrous crab alternately opens and shuts the door of the sea-passage: when it opens, the waters pour out (ebb-tide); when it shuts, they back up (flood-tide). Skeat identifies the tree with the legendary palm of the coco-de-mer, whose twin nuts Malay sailors washed ashore on Sumatran coasts from a palm growing below the sea.
summary.zh: 大洋之中生巨樹『寶塢江宜』；樹根處巨蟹開合海底通道之門：門開水瀉（退潮），門閉水壅（漲潮）。斯凱特指其即雙椰子傳說之海底棕櫚——馬來水手偶於蘇門答臘海濱拾得沖上之雙椰。

sensitivity.note: Tide-myth; the tree-of-the-ocean motif parallels Indian and Oceanic world-trees.

passages.text: In the middle of the great ocean grows an immense tree, called Pauh Jangi, at the root of which a monstrous crab opens and shuts the door of the sea-passage, letting out and holding in the waters — the Malay explanation of the tides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在浩瀚大洋的中央，生长着一棵巨树，名为「泡姜吉」（Pauh Jangi）。在其根部，有一只巨大的螃蟹开合着海道的门户，放水流出，又将水拦住——这便是马来人对潮汐的解释。

passages.text: The tree appears to be a tradition of the Cocos Maldiva: the old belief was that the fruit was produced on a palm growing below the sea, whose fronds, according to Malay seamen, were sometimes seen in quiet bights on the Sumatran coast, and whose curious twin nuts were cast up on the shores of the Indian Ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. I (with Skeat's note on the coco-de-mer); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此树似乎是科科斯与马尔代夫一带的传统：古老的信仰认为，其果实结于生长在海底的一株棕榈之上；据马来水手所言，这株棕榈的叶状枝有时可在苏门答腊海岸静谧的海湾中见到，而其奇特的双生果核则被冲上印度洋的岸边。

title.en: The Heart of the Earth: Azrael and the Making of Adam
title.zh: 大地之心：亞茲拉爾取土造亞當

region.en: Selangor, Malay Peninsula (charm-book myth)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（符咒書神話）

period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II 'Creation of Man', the Heart of the Earth

summary.en: God sends Gabriel, then Israfel, then Michael to fetch 'the Heart of the Earth' — and the Earth refuses each in turn: 'if you take away my Heart I shall assuredly die.' Only Azrael wrests it, seizing the Earth's middle finger (which stretches and becomes the jari bantu, the Devil's Finger). Gabriel mixes the white heart-clay with water — too soft; with fire — too hard; strikes out the image of Adam, and craves life for it from God.
summary.zh: 神先遣迦伯列、伊斯拉斐爾、米迦勒取『大地之心』——地神逐一拒之：『若取我心，我必死。』唯亞茲拉爾奪得，緊握地神中指（手指拉長，即『魔鬼指』）。迦伯列以白心之土和黏：加水則軟，加火則硬——終打成亞當之像，向神求其生命。

sensitivity.note: Malay modification of Arabic Adam-creation lore, as Skeat notes; treated as folk theology with care.

canonical_translation: Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), English

narrative.en:
Skeat's chapter on the creation of man records, from a Selangor charm-book dictated by a Malay magician, the fullest Malay folk version of the moulding of Adam — a local transformation of Arabic lore that keeps the Earth herself as a speaking character.

BEGINNING: THE REFUSALS. God Almighty spake unto Gabriel, 'Be not disobedient, O Gabriel, but go and get me the Heart of the Earth.' Gabriel cannot get it: 'I will not give it,' said the Earth. The Prophet Israfel goes and cannot get it; Michael goes and cannot get it. In the fuller parallel account, Azrael first salutes the Earth in orthodox fashion and is met with the same point-blank refusal, 'forasmuch as I was so created by God Almighty, and if you take away my Heart I shall assuredly die.'

MIDDLE: THE WRESTLING. Azrael loses his temper, gives the Earth a push with his right hand and his left, grasps at the Heart of the Earth and carries it back to the presence of God. The magician who dictated the account added that when Azrael stretched forth his hand, the Earth-spirit caught hold of his middle finger, which yielded to the strain, became longer than the rest, and received its Malay name of the 'Devil's Finger' (jari bantu) — an etiology of the longest finger carried inside a creation myth.

END: THE MOULDING. Gabriel takes the lump of earth which was the Earth's Heart and mixes it first with water to soften it — too soft; then with fire to harden it; and when the image is made, obtains life from God to put into it. The image of Adam is struck out, life is craved and given — and the sequel (recorded in the companion record) tells of the first image's breaking, the steel spine of Khorassan, and the descent of our Lady Eve at dawn.

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) grounds the creation-of-man motif in a living Earth that must be despoiled — a price-of-life theology; (2) etiologizes the human hand (the Devil's Finger); (3) registers Malay syncretism: Qur'anic angels and Arabic traditions retold in the idiom of the Malay Earth-spirit; and (4) supplies the Malay comparative analogue to the world's clay-humans cluster (Nüwa, Enki and Ninhursag, the Maya failures, Obatala). The charm's casting of the Earth as a speaking, refusing, grieving person is its most distinctive feature and deserves emphasis: where most clay-human myths simply take the mud, the Malay magician's Earth negotiates, objects on the ground that she was made by God and will die if her heart is removed, and leaves a mark on the thief's hand. The result is a theology in which the material of human life is acknowledged to be stolen — an ethic of apology built into the first page of the human story. The second account's detail that the Heart of the Earth was white carries its own symbolism, for white is the royal colour of the Malay world; the first man is moulded, in effect, of royal clay. The charm ends in marriage and in twins: Eve descends while Adam prays, is caught, lost, and caught again, and the first children are born in pairs — handsome with handsome, plain with plain — the charm-book's quiet answer to the question of how difference entered the world.
narrative.zh: 斯凱特自雪蘭莪巫師口授之符咒書中錄得最完整的馬來造亞當傳說：神遣天使取『大地之心』，地神連拒三位天使，並言：『若取我心，我必死』；唯亞茲拉爾強奪，地神反握其手，致中指拉長成『魔鬼指』。迦伯列以心土和黏塑亞當——加水則軟、加火則硬——終成其像而求神賦生。功能：以活的地神受剝為生命之代價、釋人手指之由來、登錄馬來宗教融合、並成泥人造人跨文化母題之馬來版本（可比女媧、恩基、馬雅失敗泥人、約魯巴奧巴塔拉）。

functions: Price-of-life theology: man is moulded from the living Earth's stolen heart
Etiology of the jari bantu (the elongated middle finger) inside the creation narrative
Register of Malay-Islamic syncretism: Qur'anic angels in an animist Earth-spirit idiom
Malay analogue in the world-wide clay-humans motif cluster

variants.text_tradition: Parallel charm-book account in Skeat 1900, ch. II
variants.summary: Adds that the Heart of the Earth was white, and the fuller exchange between Azrael and the refusing Earth, ending with the push of both hands.

variants.name: Comparative clay-humans myths
variants.text_tradition: Qur'an (Adam of clay); Chinese (Nüwa); Sumerian (Enki/Ninhursag); Maya Popol Vuh
variants.summary: Humans moulded from earth; the Malay version is distinctive in making the Earth a refusing, speaking victim.

passages.text: God Almighty spake unto Gabriel, saying, 'Be not disobedient, O Gabriel, but go and get me the Heart of the Earth.' But he could not get the Heart of the Earth: 'I will not give it,' said the Earth. Then went the Prophet Israfel to get it, but he could not; then went Michael, but he could not; then went Azrael, and at last he got the Heart of the Earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 全能的神对加百列说：「加百列啊，不要违命，去把地之心取来给我。」但他取不到地之心：大地说：「我不给。」于是先知伊斯拉菲勒前去取它，却也取不到；接着米迦勒前去，也取不到；随后阿兹拉伊勒前去，终于取得了地之心。

passages.text: In the parallel account the Earth refuses 'forasmuch as I was so created by God Almighty, and if you take away my Heart I shall assuredly die.' Azrael gave the Earth a push with his right hand and his left, and grasping at the Heart of the Earth got hold of it and carried it back to the presence of God; when he stretched forth his hand the Earth-spirit caught hold of his middle finger, which yielded to the strain and became longer than the rest — the 'Devil's Finger' (jari bantu).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在与之平行的记述中，大地拒绝道：「因为我本是全能的神如此所造，你若取走我的心，我必定死去。」阿兹拉伊勒用右手和左手推了大地一把，抓住地之心，将它取到手，带回到神的面前；当他伸出手时，大地之灵抓住了他的中指，那中指因这拉扯而变长，比其余各指都长——即「魔鬼之指」（jari bantu）。

passages.text: Gabriel took the lump of earth which was the Earth's Heart and mixed it first with water to soften it — it was too soft; then with fire to harden it; and when the image was made, obtained life from God to put into it, striking out the image of Adam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 加百列取来那块作为地之心的泥土，先与水混合使之柔软——它太软了；再与火混合使之坚硬；待形像造成之后，又向神求得生命注入其中，塑成了亚当的形像。

title.en: The Broken Image and the Steel Spine of Khorassan
title.zh: 碎像與呼羅珊鋼骨

region.en: Selangor, Malay Peninsula (charm-book myth)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（符咒書神話）

period: Recorded 1890s in Selangor; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II, the making and breaking of Adam's image

summary.en: When the image of Adam is raised and life craved for it, God gives life — 'Then sneezed God Almighty, and the image of Adam brake in pieces.' Azrael returns to remake it, and this time God commands that steel of Khorassan be driven down the first man's back, becoming his thirty-three bones, harder at the top, softer below — 'the harder steel shot up skywards, and the softer steel penetrated earthwards.' Thus Adam lives, in a body half mineral, half divine.
summary.zh: 亞當之像既立，求神賦生；神施生——『忽聞神打噴嚏，亞當之像碎裂』。亞茲拉爾重塑之，神命以呼羅珊之鋼打入其背，化為三十三骨——上硬下軟：『硬鋼上指諸天，軟鋼下貫大地』。亞當遂活，其身半屬礦物、半屬神造。

sensitivity.note: Sequel of the Adam-moulding charm; a Malay folk anatomy of the spine.

passages.text: Then he raised up the image of Adam, and craved Life for it from Almighty God, and God Almighty gave it Life. Then sneezed God Almighty, and the image of Adam brake in pieces, and he (Azrael) returned to remake the image of Adam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 随后他立起亚当的形像，向全能的神求取生命，全能的神便赐予它生命。接着全能的神打了个喷嚏，亚当的形像便碎裂了，于是他（阿兹拉伊勒）又回去重新塑造亚当的形像。

passages.text: Then God Almighty commanded to take steel of Khorassan, and drive it down his back, so that it became the thirty-three bones, the harder steel at the top, the softer below it. The harder steel shot up skywards, and the softer steel penetrated earthwards. Thus the image of Adam had life, and dwelt in Paradise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是全能的神命令取來呼羅珊的鋼鐵，將其打入他的背中，使之成為三十三根骨頭，上方為較硬的鋼，下方為較軟的鋼。較硬的鋼向上射向天際，較軟的鋼則向下穿入地中。亞當的形象遂有了生命，並居住在樂園之中。

title.en: Tan Puteh, the Daughter of the River
title.zh: 河之女：譚普特

region.en: Palembang river-mouth tradition (Malay legend recorded in Skeat)
region.zh: 巴鄰旁河口傳說（斯凱特採錄馬來傳說）

period: Legend recorded 1890s (J.R.A.S., S.B., No. 9); published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II, the legend of the foam island (Teh Purba)

summary.en: Volumes of foam collect in the river 'the size of an elephant'; a childless couple — the wife of white Semang blood — go to bathe, push aside the froth-island, and find a female infant sitting in its midst enveloped in cloud-like foam. They adopt her as 'the daughter of the river' and name her Tan Puteh (Teh Purba); as she grows, their wealth increases and the village becomes an important place — the white royal blood of the river-born child blessing the town.
summary.zh: 河面聚起大象般之泡沫堆；無子的白膚塞芒血統夫婦沐浴時推開泡沫之島，見泡沫雲團中坐一女嬰。二人收為養女，昭告鄉里，稱之『河之女』，名譚普特（德·普爾巴）；自此家道日隆，村邑漸成重鎮——河生兒之王室白血為地方賜福。

sensitivity.note: Parallel to the Annals' Putri Tunjong Bui (foam-bell princess of Palembang) — Skeat notes the kinship; flagged as a shared Malay river-foundling motif.

passages.text: Volumes of foam collected in a mass the size of an elephant. Nakhodah Kasim's wife went to bathe, and finding this island of froth in her way she attempted to move it away with a stick; she removed the upper portion of it and disclosed a female infant sitting in the midst of it enveloped all round with cloud-like foam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 成堆的泡沫聚集成一團，大小如同一頭大象。納霍達·卡辛的妻子前去沐浴，發現這座泡沫之島擋住了去路，便試圖用棍子將其撥開；她撥去了上層的部分，露出一個女嬰坐在其中，四周被雲朵般的泡沫團團包裹。

passages.text: The couple adopted the child willingly, for they had no children, and treated her thenceforward as their own. They assembled the villagers and gave them a feast, solemnly announcing their adoption of the daughter of the river. The child was called Tan Puteh, but her father gave her the name of Teh Purba; as she grew up the wealth of her foster-parents increased, and the village gradually became an important place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這對夫婦欣然收養了這個孩子，因為他們沒有子女，自此便待她如親生。他們召集村民，設宴款待，鄭重宣布收養這個河之女。這孩子名叫丹·普特，但她的父親給她取名為德·普爾巴；隨著她漸漸長大，養父母的財富日益增加，村莊也逐漸成為一個重要的地方。

title.en: The Regalia Born of Themselves at the Burning Mountain
title.zh: 烈火山中自生之王器

region.en: Between the two peaks of Gunung Merapi, Menangkabau, Sumatra (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 蘇門答臘米南加保瑪拉皮雙峰之間（象徵性定位）

period: Informant statement recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic, 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II, magic powers of the regalia

summary.en: Skeat's Selangor informant declared that the royal regalia 'came into existence of themselves (terjadi sendiri), at a spot between the two peaks of a burning mountain (gunong merapi) in the country of Menangkabau in Sumatra'; that 'rain could not rot them nor sun blister them'; that any one who brushed past them would fall to the ground — and that no fewer than seven buffaloes must be slaughtered before the 'Moving Mountains' (two peaked state pillows) can be replaced when worn out.
summary.zh: 斯凱特之雪蘭莪消息人言：王室重器『自生』（terjadi sendiri）於蘇門答臘米南加保瑪拉皮烈火雙峰之間；『雨不能朽之，日不能灼之』；凡人掠其身而過者立仆；若『移山』（一對尖形王枕）用舊需換，須先宰水牛七頭。

sensitivity.note: Regalia-sanctity belief; living royal-institution lore, paraphrased respectfully.

passages.text: My informant declared that these objects came into existence of themselves (terjadi sendiri), at a spot between the two peaks of a burning mountain (gunong merapi) in the country of Menangkabau in Sumatra. He also averred that 'rain could not rot them nor sun blister them,' and that any one who brushed past them would fall to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 向我提供消息的人宣稱，這些物件是自行生成的（terjadi sendiri），生成於蘇門答臘米南加保地區一座燃燒之山（gunong merapi）的兩座山峰之間的一處地方。他還斷言，「雨水不能使之腐爛，烈日不能使之起泡」，任何擦身而過的人都會跌倒在地。

passages.text: No fewer than seven buffaloes have to be slaughtered before the 'moving mountains' (when worn out) can be replaced — the peaked state pillows of the royal couch, among the least conspicuous but most carefully hedged objects of the regalia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在「移動之山」（磨損之後）得以更換之前，必須宰殺多達七頭水牛——那是御榻上尖頂狀的靠枕，屬於王權象徵物中最不顯眼卻最受嚴密守護的物件之一。

title.en: The Sultan Whose One Eye Is the Sun: The Title-List of Menangcabow
title.zh: 一目如日之蘇丹：米南加保王號全錄

region.en: Pagaruyung, Menangcabow, Sumatra
region.zh: 蘇門答臘米南加保巴加爾容

period: Recorded by Marsden 1784 (History of Sumatra, p. 270); reproduced in Skeat 1900

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. II, reproducing Marsden's enumeration of the Sultan of Menangcabow's titles

summary.en: Marsden recorded the full pretensions of the Sultan of Menangcabow: son of Raja Iscunder-sulcarnainny; master of the sword Chooree-se-mendong-geree with its hundred and ninety gaps 'made in the conflict with the arch-devil Se Cattee-moono, whom it slew'; master of fresh water in the ocean to the extent of a day's sailing; of the cock Sengonannee, unconquered; of the buffalo Se Binnooang Satiee whose horns are ten feet asunder; of the gun brought from heaven; 'who may slay at pleasure without being guilty of a crime'; and of whom 'one of whose eyes is as the sun and the other as the moon.'
summary.zh: 馬爾斯登錄得米南加保蘇丹全銜：亞歷山德羅之裔；佩劍『珠里色門東』上有百九十缺口——『誅滅大魔西卡提穆納』之戰所留；掌大洋一日航程內之淡水；畜不敗之雄雞森戈南尼；畜水牛西賓努安薩蒂，雙角相距十尺；有天降之銃；『可任意殺人而不為罪』；『一目如日、一目如月』。

sensitivity.note: Royal title-catalogue; the 190-notch sword directly cross-links to the Sacatimuna serpent slain in the Annals and the serpent killed by Gabriel in Skeat's charm-books.

passages.text: The Sultan of Menangcabow, whose residence is at Pagarooyoong, who is king of kings, son of Raja Iscunder-sulcarnainny — possessed of the sword named Chooree-se-mendong-geree, which has an hundred and ninety gaps, made in the conflict with the arch-devil Se Cattee-moono, whom it slew; who is master of fresh water in the ocean, to the extent of a day's sailing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784), p. 270, reproduced in Skeat (1900); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 米南加保的蘇丹，居於帕加魯永，乃王中之王，伊斯坎德爾-蘇爾卡奈尼（亞歷山大）之子——持有名為「Chooree-se-mendong-geree」的寶劍，劍上有十九道缺口，乃與大惡魔 Se Cattee-moono 交戰時所留，該惡魔已被此劍誅殺；他還是海洋中淡水的掌管者，其範圍達一日航程之遠。

passages.text: He is possessed of the buffalo named Se Binnooang Satiee, whose horns are ten feet asunder; of the unconquered cock Sengonannee; of a gun brought from heaven; who may slay at pleasure without being guilty of a crime; who, when he goes to sleep, wakes not till the gandang nobat sounds; one of whose eyes is as the sun and the other as the moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Marsden, History of Sumatra (1784), p. 270, reproduced in Skeat (1900); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他擁有一頭名為 Se Binnooang Satiee 的水牛，其雙角相距十尺；擁有一隻未嘗敗績的公雞 Sengonannee；擁有一桿自天而降的槍；他能隨心所欲地殺人而不算犯罪；他入睡之後，若非 gandang nobat 之聲響起便不會醒來；他的一隻眼如太陽，另一隻眼如月亮。

title.en: Papik, Who Killed His Wife's Brother
title.zh: 殺內兄者帕皮克

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Papik, who killed his wife's brother', eBook #28932

summary.en: Envious because his wife's brother Ailaq always harpoons the seals, Papik kills him silently; Ailaq's old mother vows to eat him alive and, preparing to die, lets the tide cover her on the shore. As a ghost in her bearskin coverlet she comes over the ice as a monster no dog will bark at, spreads fog and terror — a fatherless boy marked with blood nearly dies as food for the monster — until an old woman's taunt, 'There is your cousin — bark at him!', looses the dogs. Under the coverlet: human bones. Papik is found hacked in every part, and the fathers' tale teaches that murder is punished by fear itself.
summary.zh: 因內兄阿拉克每獵必中，帕皮克妒而生恨，無聲殺之。阿拉克老母立誓要生吞他，伏坐岸邊任潮水淹沒。其魂裹著熊皮罩毯化為怪物，踏冰而來，群犬噤聲、濃霧迷漫——無父男孩染血幾成怪物之食——直至老嫗一句『那是你表親，叫吧！』解開犬的咒縛。熊皮之下，竟是人骨。帕皮克被尋獲時遍體殘破，五官盡失——老嫗為子報仇。族中故老相傳：無故殺人者，必為畏懼本身所誅。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s; graphic vengeance detail recorded as told in the source.

passages.text: Papik's custom was to go hunting with his wife's brother Ailaq; but whenever the two went out together, it was always Ailaq who came home with seal in tow while Papik returned empty-handed, and day by day his envy grew. Then one day Ailaq did not return at all, and Papik was silent at his home-coming. Late that evening Ailaq's old mother spoke: 'You have killed Ailaq.' 'No, I did not kill him.' Then the old woman rose and cried: 'You killed him, and said no word. The day shall yet come when I will eat you alive, for you killed Ailaq, you and no other.' She made ready to die — for as a ghost she meant to avenge her son — took her bearskin coverlet, went down to the shore close by the water, and let the tide come up and cover her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Papik, who killed his wife's brother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帕皮克的習慣是與他妻子的兄弟艾拉克一同外出打獵；然而每當兩人一同出門，總是艾拉克帶著海豹歸來，而帕皮克空手而回，他的嫉妒便日復一日地增長。後來有一天，艾拉克根本沒有回來，帕皮克回家時一言不發。那天傍晚，艾拉克的老母親開口說道：「你殺了艾拉克。」「不，我沒有殺他。」於是老婦人站起身來喊道：「你殺了他，卻一句話也不說。總有一天我會把你活活吃掉，因為是你殺了艾拉克，是你，不是別人。」她準備赴死——因為她打算化作鬼魂為兒子復仇——她拿起自己的熊皮被褥，走到近水的岸邊，任潮水漲起將她淹沒。

passages.text: For a long time Papik did not dare go out hunting; at last he began again. One day two men stood out on the ice by the breathing holes and heard the snow creaking with the sound of a cry, moving towards Papik, who stood a little apart; a fog came down over the ice, and then fury-shouting and fear-screaming — the monster had fallen upon Papik to devour him. Fleeing in to land they met sledges of hunters setting out and urged them back lest they be slain by fear too. At the village all crowded into one house, struggling so hard that a fatherless boy was thrust into a tub of blood, and wherever he went the snow was marked with blood: 'Now we are already made food for that monster, since that wretched boy marks out the way with a trail of blood.' Someone said let us kill him; but the others took pity and let him live.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Papik, who killed his wife's brother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很長一段時間，帕皮克不敢外出打獵；最後他又重新開始了。有一天，兩個男人站在冰上呼吸孔旁，聽見積雪發出吱嘎之聲，伴著一聲呼喊，朝稍稍站開的帕皮克移動而去；一陣霧降臨冰面，接著是狂怒的吼叫與恐懼的尖叫——那怪物已撲向帕皮克要吞噬他。他們逃回陸地，遇見正要出發的獵人雪橇隊，便催促他們折返，以免也被恐懼所殺。在村裡，眾人全擠進一間屋子，推擠得如此猛烈，以致一個無父的男孩被擠進一桶血裡，他所到之處雪上都留下血跡：「如今我們已經成了那怪物的食物，因為那可憐的男孩用血跡標出了路。」有人說把他殺了吧；但其他人心生憐憫，讓他活了下來。

passages.text: The evil spirit came in sight out on the ice, the tips of its ears showing over the hummocks as it crept along; when it came up to the houses, not a dog barked, and none dared surround it, for it was not a real bear. At last an old woman cried to the dogs: 'See, there is your cousin — bark at him!' The dogs were loosed from the magic that bound them, the men dashed forward and harpooned the thing — and cutting it up, they knew its skin for the old woman's coverlet, and its bones were human bones. The sledges that drove out to the abandoned gear found everything torn to pieces, and Papik cut about in every part: eyes, nose, mouth, and ears hacked away, the scalp torn from his head. Thus the old woman took vengeance for her son Ailaq. So the fathers used to tell: when any man killed his fellow without good cause, a monster would come and strike him dead with fear, and leave no part whole in all his body. The people of old times thought it an ill thing for men to kill each other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Papik, who killed his wife's brother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那惡靈在冰上現身，牠爬行時耳尖在雪堆之上隱約可見；當牠來到屋舍前，沒有一隻狗吠叫，也沒有人敢圍住牠，因為牠不是真正的熊。最後一位老婦人對狗喊道：「看哪，那是你們的表親——對牠吠叫吧！」狗兒們從束縛牠們的魔法中解脫，男人們衝上前去用魚叉刺那東西——將牠切開後，他們認出牠的皮正是老婦人的被褥，而牠的骨頭是人的骨頭。駕雪橇趕往被棄置的器具處的人發現一切都被撕成碎片，帕皮克全身各處都被砍割：眼睛、鼻子、嘴和耳朵都被削去，頭皮從他頭上被撕下。老婦人便這樣為她的兒子艾拉克復了仇。所以父輩們常說：若有任何人無正當理由殺害同胞，便會有怪物前來，以恐懼將他擊死，使他全身上下沒有一處完好。古時的人們認為人與人相殺是一件惡事。

title.en: Patussorssuaq, Who Killed His Uncle
title.zh: 殺叔者帕圖舒亞克

region.en: Kugkat / Natsivilik, Smith Sound, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭庫卡特與納齊維利克（史密斯海峽）

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Patussorssuaq, who killed his uncle', eBook #28932

summary.en: Fonder of his uncle's beautiful wife than of his own, Patussorssuaq kills the uncle at the ice edge rather than see the couple depart, then takes the widow. His own wife flees barefoot over the hills, hood-loose inland folk running past her on the way. Little joy follows: the widow dies soon, and at Natsivilik a fox — the soul of dead Alataq, whose amulet was a fox — snaps playfully at his coat-fringe before the ghost comes as a bear and bites him limb from limb, calling down forgetfulness on the daughter who tried to tell.
summary.zh: 帕圖舒亞克愛叔父的美妻勝過己妻；叔父攜妻遠行獵途中，他在冰邊將叔父殺害，占其寡婦。己妻光腳翻山逃回娘家，途中見內陸人披髮奔逃。得手的美妻不久病死；夏日集會時，一隻狐狸——亡叔阿拉克的魂魄（其護身符本是狐）——戲咬他的衣邊，隨後化作熊影將他啃噬得四分五裂；想報信的女兒被咒術奪去記憶，想起來時已太遲。殺人者必遭報。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s; killing and ghost-vengeance presented as told in the source.

passages.text: At Kugkat lived a very beautiful woman whose husband was Alataq; at the same place lived Patussorssuaq, Alataq's nephew, who had a wife of his own but was yet fonder of his uncle's wife. One spring day Alataq made up to go out on a long hunting journey, taking his wife with him. Standing at the edge of the ice, ready to start, they were joined by Patussorssuaq — 'Are you going away?' 'Yes, both of us' — and at these words he fell upon his uncle and killed him at once, for he could not bear to see the woman go away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Patussorssuaq, who killed his uncle'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在庫格卡特住著一位非常美麗的女子，她的丈夫是阿拉塔克；同一地方還住著帕圖索爾蘇阿克，他是阿拉塔克的姪子，自己雖有妻子，卻更喜愛他叔父的妻子。某個春日，阿拉塔克準備出門作一趟長途狩獵，帶著他的妻子同行。他們站在冰緣，正待出發，帕圖索爾蘇阿克也來了——「你們要走了嗎？」「是的，我們兩個都走」——話音剛落，他便撲向他的叔父，當場將他殺死，因為他無法忍受看著那女子離去。

passages.text: Patussorssuaq's wife snatched up her needle and sewing ring and fled, following the shadow of the tent over the hills to her parents, without even time for her skin stockings, her feet growing sore on the ground; on her way she saw people running with their hoods loose on their heads, as the inland folk do, but they fled away from her. The murderer went back to his own tent meaning to kill his own wife, already weary of her, but she was gone; the terrified boy inside lied that he had seen nothing. Patussorssuaq then took Alataq's widow and lived with her — but after a little time she died, and thus he had but little joy of the woman he had won by misdeed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Patussorssuaq, who killed his uncle'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帕圖索爾蘇阿克的妻子抓起她的針和頂針便逃，循著帳篷的影子翻山越嶺逃往她父母家，甚至來不及穿上她的皮襪，雙腳在地上走得疼痛；途中她看見人們頭上鬆鬆地披著風帽奔跑，如同內陸之人那樣，但他們卻從她身邊逃開。兇手回到自己的帳篷，打算殺死自己的妻子，他早已厭倦了她，但她已經走了；裡面那個驚恐的男孩謊稱自己什麼也沒看見。帕圖索爾蘇阿克於是娶了阿拉塔克的遺孀，與她同住——但過了不久她便死了，因此他從這個以惡行奪來的女子身上，得到的歡樂寥寥無幾。

passages.text: At the beginning of summer, many people were gathered at Natsivilik, Patussorssuaq among them. Out hunting, he was snapped at by a fox that caught the fringe of his coat; striking at it and missing, he thought it a common fox — but it was the soul of dead Alataq, playing with him a little before killing him outright, for Alataq's amulet was a fox. A little after, he was bitten to death by the ghost of Alataq coming upon him in the shape of a bear. His daughter heard the cries and hurried in to tell — but just as she came into the house she had quite forgotten all she wished to say, the vengeful spirit having called down forgetfulness upon her by magic means; when she remembered, it was too late. They found Patussorssuaq torn limb from limb; he had defended himself with great pieces of ice, as they could see, but all in vain. Thus punishment falls upon the man who kills.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Patussorssuaq, who killed his uncle'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 初夏時節，許多人聚集在納齊維利克，帕圖索爾蘇瓦克也在其中。他外出打獵時，一隻狐狸咬住了他外套的邊緣；他揮手去打卻沒打中，還以為那只是一隻普通的狐狸——但那其實是死去的阿拉塔克的靈魂，在徹底殺死他之前先戲弄他一番，因為阿拉塔克的護身符正是一隻狐狸。不久之後，他被化為熊形的阿拉塔克鬼魂撲上，咬死了。他的女兒聽見叫喊聲，急忙趕去報信——可是她剛一進屋，就把想說的話全忘得一乾二淨，因為那復仇的鬼魂施法使她忘卻；等她記起來時，已經太遲了。他們發現帕圖索爾蘇瓦克被撕得肢體四散；看得出來他曾用大塊的冰自衛，但全然徒勞。殺人者所受的懲罰便是如此。

title.en: The Men Who Changed Wives
title.zh: 換妻者之禍

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The men who changed wives', eBook #28932

summary.en: Talilarssuaq the mischief-maker frightens the wife he has borrowed by stabbing a knife through the bench-skins; her husband Navssarssuaq dresses in his best, drags the jester out, and stabs him — 'You might at least have waited till I had dressed' — casting him on the rubbish heap. To his own wife, running to meet him, he says no, he will not murder her too, for their youngest boy is not yet grown big enough to be without her. But an avenging spirit begins to catch at him, and when sickness later kills him, it is thus spared the tearing of the ghost.
summary.zh: 頑童塔利拉舒亞克借得他人之妻，竟以刀穿凳皮嚇人；其夫納瓦舒亞克一言不發，盛裝執刃而來，拖他下凳刺死——『你好歹等我穿好衣裳』——屍棄垃圾堆。歸途遇己妻問是否也殺她，他低聲道：不，幼子保盧納還小，離不開你。此後有復仇之靈時時抓住他；待瘟疫奪其性命，那靈便無從撕裂他。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Wife-exchange described as the source community's custom of its era.

passages.text: There were once two men, Talilarssuaq and Navssarssuaq, and they changed wives. Talilarssuaq was a mischievous fellow, given to frightening people. One evening, sitting in the house with the other's wife, whom he had borrowed, he thrust his knife suddenly through the skins of the bench; the woman ran to her husband: 'Go in and kill Talilarssuaq; he is playing very dangerous tricks.' Navssarssuaq rose without a word, put on his best clothes, took his knife, went straight up to Talilarssuaq — now lying on the bench talking to himself — pulled him out on the floor and stabbed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The men who changed wives'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有兩個人，塔利拉爾蘇瓦克和納夫薩爾蘇瓦克，他們交換了妻子。塔利拉爾蘇瓦克是個愛惡作劇的傢伙，動不動就嚇唬人。一天晚上，他與借來的別人的妻子同坐在屋裡，忽然把刀刺穿坐榻的皮墊；那女人跑到她丈夫那裡說：「進去把塔利拉爾蘇瓦克殺了吧；他玩的把戲太危險了。」納夫薩爾蘇瓦克一言不發地站起身，穿上他最好的衣服，拿起刀，徑直走到塔利拉爾蘇瓦克面前——他正躺在坐榻上自言自語——把他拖到地上，刺死了他。

passages.text: 'You might at least have waited till I had dressed,' said Talilarssuaq; but Navssarssuaq hauled him out through the passage way, cast him on the rubbish heap, and went his way saying nothing. On the way he met his wife, who asked: 'Are you not going to murder me, too?' 'No,' he answered in a deep voice, 'for Pualuna is not yet grown big enough to be without you' — Pualuna being their youngest son. Some time after that deed he began to perceive that he was haunted: 'There is some invisible thing which now and again catches hold of me,' he told his comrades. It was the avenging spirit, watching him. About that time many in the place fell sick, and among them Navssarssuaq; the sickness killed him, and thus the avenging spirit was not able to tear him in pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The men who changed wives'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你至少也該等我穿好衣服吧。」塔利拉爾蘇瓦克說；但納夫薩爾蘇瓦克把他從過道裡拖了出去，扔在垃圾堆上，一言不發地走了。路上他遇見自己的妻子，她問道：「你是不是也要殺我？」「不，」他用低沉的聲音回答，「因為普阿盧納還沒長大到離得開你」——普阿盧納是他們最小的兒子。那件事之後過了些時候，他開始察覺自己被鬼纏上了：「有個看不見的東西不時抓住我。」他對同伴們說。那是復仇的鬼魂，正窺伺著他。大約就在那時，村裡許多人病倒了，納夫薩爾蘇瓦克也在其中；那場病要了他的命，因此那復仇的鬼魂終究沒能把他撕成碎片。

title.en: Artuk, Who Did All Forbidden Things
title.zh: 犯盡禁忌者阿爾圖克

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Artuk, who did all things forbidden', eBook #28932

summary.en: Having buried his wife, Artuk refuses to observe the mourning taboos — he hacks frozen meat with a stone axe, shakes out his inner coat on the ice, drinks sun-melted water on an iceberg — declaring it all lies, in scorn of his fellows' beliefs. Fear comes upon him the day he drives out; he binds his unwilling son to the sledge uprights and never returns alive. That evening his daughter hears two spirits laughing mockingly in the air; the sledges find Artuk torn to pieces far out on the ice, the untouched son dead of fright beside him.
summary.zh: 妻子下葬後，阿爾圖克拒守喪禁——以石斧砍凍肉、在冰上抖內衣、登冰山飲日融之水——斥舊俗為謊，蔑視族人信仰。一日驅犬出行，恐懼襲來，他將不肯同行的兒子縛上雪橇立柱，竟一去不返。當晚女兒聽見空中兩靈竊笑——那是父親遭報的信號。次日雪橇四出，在遠冰上尋見他：已被撕為碎片，如歷來冒犯祖俗者一般；縛在橇上的兒子分毫未傷，卻活活嚇死。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Mourning taboos are core Inuit ritual law; the tale is the tradition's own enforcement narrative.

passages.text: A man whose name was Artuk had buried his wife, but refused to remain aloof from the doings which those who have been busied with the dead are forbidden to share, saying he did not hold by such old customs. Some fellow-villagers were cutting up frozen meat for food; after watching them work at the meat with their knives for a while, he took a stone axe and hacked at it, saying 'That is the way to cut up meat' — and this although it was forbidden. The same day he went out on the ice and took off his inner coat to shake it, though that was forbidden; and he went up on to an iceberg and drank water the sun had melted there, knowing well this too was forbidden. All these things he did in scorn of what his fellows believed, for he said it was all lies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Artuk, who did all things forbidden'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個名叫阿爾圖克的人埋葬了妻子，卻不肯避開那些接觸過死者的人所禁忌參與的事情，說他不信奉這些老規矩。幾個同村的人正在切凍肉作食物；他看他們用刀切了一會兒肉，便拿起一把石斧砍起肉來，說「切肉就該這樣」——儘管這是被禁止的。當天他走到冰上，脫下內衣抖了抖，儘管這也是被禁止的；他又登上一座冰山，喝了太陽在那裡融化的水，明知這同樣是被禁止的。他做這些事，都是為了蔑視同伴們所信奉的東西，因為他說那全是謊言。

passages.text: But one day, starting out with his sledge, fear came upon him and he dared not go alone; his son would not go with him willingly, so he took him and bound him to the uprights of the sledge, and carried him so. He never returned alive. Late in the evening his daughter heard in the air the mocking laughter of two spirits, and knew at once they laughed so that she might know how her father had been punished for his ill-doing. Next day many sledges went out to search, and found Artuk far out on the ice, torn to pieces, as is the way with those whom the spirits have punished for refusing to observe the customs of their forefathers. The son, bound to the sledge, had not been touched — but he had died of fright.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Artuk, who did all things forbidden'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 可是有一天，他駕著雪橇出發時，恐懼襲上心頭，不敢獨自前往；他的兒子不願跟他去，他便把兒子抓來綁在雪橇的立柱上，就這樣載著他走。他再也沒有活著回來。那天深夜，他的女兒在空中聽見兩個鬼魂嘲弄的笑聲，立刻明白它們這樣笑，是要讓她知道她父親因作惡而受到了怎樣的懲罰。第二天，許多雪橇出去搜尋，在冰上很遠的地方找到了阿爾圖克，他被撕成了碎片，凡因拒絕遵守祖先習俗而受鬼魂懲罰的人，下場都是如此。綁在雪橇上的兒子並未被碰過——但他是被嚇死的。

title.en: The Thunder Spirits: Two Sisters of the Mountain
title.zh: 雷霆雙靈：山中二姊妹

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The thunder spirits', eBook #28932

summary.en: Scolded once too often for their noise, two sisters run away with only a dogskin, a piece of boot skin, and a fire stone, and build a house on a high mountain, refusing ever to return. When they must die of hunger they turn into evil spirits and become thunder: shaking the dried boot skin raises the south-westerly gales, striking the fire stone lights great fire in the heavens, and their tears pour down as rain. Returning to frighten men to death — sparing only a child-back-carrying woman to tell of it — they fear one thing alone: the blood of a cut red dog, led dripping round the house.
summary.zh: 兩姊妹厭父親斥責，攜犬皮、靴皮與火石上山築屋，拒不歸家。饑餓將死之際化為惡靈，成為雷霆：抖動乾靴皮則西南狂風驟起，擊打火石則天際烈焰，落淚則大雨傾盆。她們重返人間嚇死多人，獨留一名背孩子的婦人傳述其可怖。雷霆唯懼一物——割耳放血的黑狗，血繞屋滴灑，屋便不著火。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Thunder etiology and the red-dog protective rite are documented as living practice in the source.

passages.text: Two sisters were playing together, and their father, who had but few children and was not wont to hear any kind of noise, could not bear the sound; at last he began to scold them, telling them to take their playing farther away. When the girls grew up and began to understand things, they desired to run away on account of the scolding, and set out taking with them only a little dogskin, a piece of boot skin, and a fire stone, going up into a high mountain to build themselves a house. Their father and mother searched for them in vain, for the girls kept hiding themselves; they had grown to be true mountain dwellers, keeping far from the places of men. Only the reindeer hunters saw them now and again, and the girls always refused to go back to their kin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The thunder spirits'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩姐妹在一起玩耍，她們的父親兒女不多，素來聽不得任何聲響，受不了那聲音；最後他開始責罵她們，叫她們到遠一點的地方去玩。女孩們長大、開始懂事之後，因為受不了責罵，便想逃走，於是只帶了一小塊狗皮、一片靴皮和一塊火石，上山去給自己蓋房子。她們的父母找來找去也找不到，因為女孩們總是躲著；她們已成了真正住在山裡的人，遠離人煙。只有獵馴鹿的人偶爾見到她們，而女孩們始終不肯回到親族那裡去。

passages.text: When at last the time came that they must die of hunger, they turned into evil spirits and became thunder. When they shake their dried boot skin, the gales come up, the south-westerly gales; great fire is seen in the heavens whenever they strike their fire stone, and the rain pours down whenever they shed tears. Their father held many spirit callings hoping to make them return, and ceased only when he found they were dead. But after the girls had become spirits, they came back to the places of men, frightening many to death — first of all their own father and mother, because of the trouble they had made. The only one they did not kill was a woman bearing a child on her back, and her they let live, that she might tell how terrible they were.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The thunder spirits'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當她們終於到了必須餓死的時刻，便化為惡靈，成了雷。她們抖動曬乾的靴皮時，狂風便起，是西南狂風；每當她們敲擊火石，天上便見大火，每當她們落淚，大雨便傾盆而下。她們的父親懷著許多靈的職分，盼望能使她們歸來，直到發現她們已死，方才作罷。但女孩們化為靈之後，又回到人間之地，嚇死了許多人——首先是他們自己的父親和母親，因為他們所惹的禍。她們唯一沒有殺的，是一個背著孩子的女人，這女人她們讓她活著，好叫她述說她們是多麼可怕。

passages.text: When the thunder spirits come, even the earth itself is stricken with terror: stones which lie on level ground, not on any slope at all, roll in fear towards men. The thunder comes with the south-westerly gales; there is a noise and crackling in the air as of dry skins shaken, the sky glows from time to time with fire from their firestone, and great rocks and everything which stands up high in the air begin to glow. When this happens, men take out a red dog and cut its ear until the blood comes, then lead the beast round about the house, letting the blood drip everywhere, for then the house will not take fire. A red dog was the only thing those girls who were turned to thunder feared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The thunder spirits'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雷靈來時，連大地本身也為之驚恐：平地上、全然不在斜坡上的石頭，也因恐懼而朝人滾來。雷隨著西南狂風而來；空中發出聲響與噼啪之聲，如同抖動乾皮一般，天空不時因她們火石的火而發亮，巨石以及一切高聳於空中的東西都開始發光。每逢此事發生，人們便牽出一隻紅狗，割其耳朵直到流血，然後牽著這牲口繞屋而行，讓血滴得到處都是，因為這樣屋子便不會著火。紅狗是那些化為雷的女孩唯一畏懼之物。

title.en: Nerrivik, Ruler of the Sea Creatures
title.zh: 涅里維克：海洋眾獸之主

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Nerrivik', eBook #28932

summary.en: A bird-man courts and marries a woman, catching fish he calls seal; when he loses his walrus-tusk spectacles she sees his bad eyes and weeps at his ugliness, and her visiting brothers carry her home. The bird-husband raises a storm with his wings to reclaim her, and the frightened crew, judging her the storm's cause, throw her into the sea — her grandfather cutting off the hand that grasped the boat. Drowned, she becomes Nerrivik, ruler over all the creatures of the sea; with but one hand she cannot comb her hair, and when men catch no seal the wizards go down to comb it, and she sends seal and other creatures forth by way of thanks.
summary.zh: 鳥人假扮男子娶得妻子，捕魚而稱之為海豹；丟了海象牙眼鏡後，妻子看清他的醜眼而泣。探望的兄弟們將她帶回。鳥夫以巨翅搧起風暴索妻，驚惶的舟人把災因推向她，將她拋入海中——抓住船舷的手被祖父一劍砍斷。溺斃的她沉入海底，成為統御海中眾獸的涅里維克：獨手難梳長髮，漁獲不至時，巫師下海為她梳髮，她便遣出海豹群獸以為回報。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo sea-ruler myth recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Nerrivik is the Smith Sound name of the sea-mother, cognate with Sedna of the Central Eskimo; cross-ref sedna-sea-mother.

passages.text: A bird once wished to marry a woman: he got himself a fine sealskin coat, and having weak eyes made spectacles out of a walrus tusk, greatly set upon looking as nice as possible. Then he set off in the shape of a man, came to a village, took a wife, and brought her home, going out thereafter to catch fish, which he called seal, and brought to her. Once he lost his spectacles, and his wife, seeing his bad eyes, burst out weeping because he was so ugly — but her husband only laughed: 'Oho, so you saw my eyes? Hahaha!' And he put on his spectacles again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Nerrivik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一隻鳥想要娶一個女人：他給自己弄了一件上好的海豹皮外套，又因眼睛不好，用海象牙做了一副眼鏡，極力想顯得盡可能好看。隨後他化作人形出發，來到一個村落，娶了一個妻子，把她帶回家，此後便出去捕魚，他稱之為海豹，帶回來給她。有一次他丟了眼鏡，他的妻子見他眼睛不好，便放聲大哭，因為他實在太醜了——但她的丈夫只是笑：「哦呵，原來你看見我的眼睛了？哈哈哈！」於是他又戴上了眼鏡。

passages.text: Her brothers, longing for their sister, came out one day to visit her, and while her husband was out hunting they took her away with them. The husband, coming home to find her gone, set out in pursuit — swinging his wings with mighty force and raising a violent storm, for he was a great wizard. The boat began to take in water, the wind grew fiercer as he doubled the beating of his wings, the waves rose white with foam, and when those in the boat began to suspect that the woman was the cause of the storm, they took her up and cast her into the sea. She tried to grasp the side of the boat, and her grandfather sprang up and cut off her hand — and so she was drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Nerrivik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她的兄弟們思念姊妹，有一天便出來探望她，趁她丈夫外出打獵時，把她帶走了。丈夫回家發現她不見了，便動身追趕——奮力鼓動雙翼，掀起猛烈的風暴，因為他是一個了不起的巫師。船開始進水，他加倍鼓翼，風便越發猛烈，波濤翻湧起白沫；船上的人開始疑心那女人是風暴的起因，便把她抓起，拋入海中。她試圖抓住船舷，她的祖父跳起來砍斷了她的手——於是她便溺死了。

passages.text: At the bottom of the sea she became Nerrivik, ruler over all the creatures in the sea. When men catch no seal, the wizards go down to Nerrivik: having but one hand, she cannot comb her hair, and this they do for her, and she, by way of thanks, sends seal and other creatures forth to men. Men call her Nerrivik because she gives them food. That is the story of the ruler of the sea — the Smith Sound telling of the one-handed sea-mother, sister-tale to the Sedna of the Central Eskimo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Nerrivik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在海的深處，她成了涅里維克，統轄海中一切生靈。當人們捕不到海豹時，巫師們便下到涅里維克那裡：她只有一隻手，無法梳理頭髮，這便由他們替她梳理，而她為表感謝，便把海豹和其他生靈送給人們。人們稱她涅里維克，因為她賜給他們食物。這就是海之統轄者的故事——這是史密斯灣所講述的那位獨手海母，與中部愛斯基摩人的塞德娜互為姊妹篇的故事。

title.en: The Wife Who Lied
title.zh: 撒謊之妻

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The wife who lied', eBook #28932

summary.en: Navaranapaluk, a man-eater's daughter married into a peaceful tribe, goes visiting in midwinter wearing mittens on her feet to fake mistreatment; her pitying kinsfolk make war, slay the village's women while the men are away, and hoist the bodies on poles. The three escaped women plait arrow-sinew until the naked bone shows on their fingers; the avengers hide among rocks behind the enemies' houses, betrayed — and destroyed — by one barking dog on the roof. The widows are carried off; Navaranapaluk, seized by two men together, has both arms cut through, and dies for having lied.
summary.zh: 食人族之女嫁入和平部落，訪親途中以襪代靴，偽稱受虐；族人憐憫興兵，趁男獵女守之際屠戮全村婦女，屍懸長杆。三名倖存女子捻製箭弦，捻至指骨外露；復仇者伏於敵屋後岩間，卻因屋頂一犬吠聲而敗露——敵眾盡歿，寡婦被擄。撒謊的納瓦拉納帕盧克被兩名男子同時拖走，雙臂被刀切斷，血盡而亡——此乃她撒謊的報應。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Graphic massacre and mutilation presented as told in the archival source.

passages.text: Navaranapaluk came of a tribe of man-eaters, but when she grew up she was taken to wife by one of a tribe that did not eat men. Once, going off on a visit to her own people, she put mittens on her feet instead of boots, to make it appear that her husband's people had dealt ill by her. It was midwinter, and her kinsfolk pitied her greatly when they saw her come thus, and agreed to make war against the tribe her husband belonged to. They set out and came to that village at a time when all the men were away and only the women at home; these they took and slew, and only three escaped — one covered with the skin she was dressing, one hidden in the box for dog's meat, and one crept into a store shed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The wife who lied'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 納瓦拉納帕盧克出身於一個食人的部族，但她長大後，被一個不食人的部族的人娶為妻子。有一次，她動身去探望自己的族人，把連指手套套在腳上充當靴子，好讓人以為她丈夫的族人待她不好。當時正是隆冬，她的親族見她這般前來，大為憐憫，便商定向她丈夫所屬的部族開戰。他們出發，來到那個村落時，男人們都外出了，只有女人在家；他們把她們捉住殺掉，只有三人逃脫——一人蒙著她正在鞣製的獸皮，一人藏在裝狗肉的箱子裡，一人鑽進了儲藏棚。

passages.text: When the men came home they found all their womenfolk killed, the more angered that the slayers had hoisted the bodies on long poles with the points stuck through them, and thought at once of Navaranapaluk, who had fled. They fell to making ready for war, preparing arrows in great numbers; the three women who were left alive plaited sinew thread to fix the points, working so eagerly that at last no more flesh was left on their fingers, and the naked bone showed through. Coming up behind the enemies' houses, they hid themselves among great rocks. The slayers, who had kept watch since their return, believing the avengers would not fail to come, took turns watching; then one old woman among them dreamed that two creatures were fighting above her head, and the household gathered to ask counsel of the spirits — when suddenly a dog on the roof of the house began to bark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The wife who lied'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男人們回家時，發現所有婦女都被殺害，更為憤怒的是，兇手將屍體吊在長桿上，桿尖穿透其身，他們立刻想到已逃走的納瓦拉納帕盧克。他們著手備戰，大量製作箭矢；三名倖存的婦女編織筋線以固定箭頭，工作得極為急切，最後手指上的肉盡皆磨去，露出赤裸的骨頭。他們繞到敵人的屋後，藏身於巨石之間。兇手們自歸來後便一直守望，相信復仇者必會前來，於是輪流警戒；隨後，他們當中一名老婦夢見兩隻生物在她頭頂上方爭鬥，全家人便聚集起來向神靈請示——就在此時，屋頂上的一隻狗忽然開始吠叫。

passages.text: The men dashed out, but their enemies had already surrounded the house, and shot down every man with arrows until there were no more left; then they chose themselves wives from among the widows and bore them off. But two of them took Navaranapaluk and hurried off with her, and she — thinking both wished to have her to wife — cried out, 'Which is it to be? Which is it to be?' The men laughed and made no answer, but ran on with her; then suddenly they cut through both her arms with their knives. Soon she fell, the blood went from her, and she died. This fate they meted out to her because she lied.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The wife who lied'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男人們衝了出去，但敵人早已包圍了屋子，用箭射殺了每一個男人，直到一個不剩；隨後他們從寡婦中挑選妻子，將她們擄走。但有兩人帶走了納瓦拉納帕盧克，匆匆離去，而她——以為兩人都想娶她為妻——喊道：『究竟是哪一個？究竟是哪一個？』男人們笑了，沒有回答，只是帶著她繼續奔跑；接著他們忽然用刀砍斷了她的雙臂。不久她便倒下，血流盡而亡。他們如此處置她，只因她說了謊。

title.en: The First Javans: Exiles from the Red Sea
title.zh: 最早的爪哇人：自紅海而來的流亡者

region.en: Java (Javanese origin tradition, recorded by Raffles)
region.zh: 爪哇（爪哇族源傳說，拉弗爾斯採錄）

period: Javanese origin traditions recorded in Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, opening traditions

summary.en: Javanese tradition held that the island's first inhabitants came in vessels from the Red Sea (Laout Mira), coasting along Hindustan — then an unbroken continent with the Indian Archipelago, later split into islands by convulsions of nature. Banished from Egypt, they carried their several worships with them: some adored the sun, others the moon, others fire, water, or the trees of the forest, living in hordes under the eldest man's rule.
summary.zh: 爪哇古傳：最初居民乘舟自紅海（勞特·米拉）而來，沿印度斯坦海岸航行——彼時印度斯坦與群島尚為連陸，後經天變裂為諸島。流亡者出埃及，各攜其祀：或拜日、或拜月、或拜水火、或拜林中之樹，成群而居，以族中最長者為酋。

sensitivity.note: Eighteenth-century Javanese etiological tradition on the peopling of the island; noted as tradition, not history.

passages.text: Amongst the various traditions regarding the manner in which Java and the Eastern Islands were originally peopled, it has been related that the first inhabitants came in vessels from the Red Sea, and that in their passage they coasted along the shores of Hindustan — that peninsula then forming an unbroken continent with the land in the Indian Archipelago, which has since been divided into so many distinct islands by convulsions of nature.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於爪哇與東方群島最初如何有人居住的種種傳說中，有一說謂最早的居民乘船自紅海而來，途中沿著印度斯坦的海岸航行——該半島當時與印度群島的土地連成一片不間斷的大陸，後來因自然的劇變而被分割成如今這許多各自獨立的島嶼。

passages.text: These people are supposed to have been banished from Egypt, and to have carried with them their different modes of worship: some adored the sun, others the moon, others the elements of fire or water, and others the trees of the forest. They lived in hordes without fixed habitations or established law; respect for age was the only substitute for civil obedience, and the oldest man of the horde was considered its chief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據信這些人被逐出埃及，並隨身帶著各自不同的崇拜方式：有人崇拜太陽，有人崇拜月亮，有人崇拜火或水等元素，還有人崇拜森林之樹。他們成群而居，沒有固定的住所，也沒有成文的律法；對年長者的尊敬是唯一取代公民服從的東西，而群體中最年長的男子被視為首領。

title.en: The Bird of Departure: How the First Javan Hordes Knew When to Move
title.zh: 啟行之鳥：爪哇先民何以知遷徙之時

region.en: Java (early-migration omen rite)
region.zh: 爪哇（早期遷徙占兆之儀）

period: Javanese tradition recorded in Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the libunggaga omen

summary.en: When the crop was gathered, the eldest of the horde appointed the mode and time of moving on. They left the remains of their feast in an open plain to attract the bird libunggaga (a crow or raven), while young men shook the angklung and imitated its cry. If the bird did not eat, or flew contrary to the intended route, the departure was deferred; but if it ate and flew ahead, they slew and burnt a lamb in gratitude, and danced away behind the bird's flight.
summary.zh: 穀既收，族長定遷徙之時。眾置宴餘於曠野以引『利邦嘎嘎』之鳥（鴉或鵲），少年搖安克隆（angklung）竹琴、學鳥鳴。鳥不食或逆行則留；食而先行則宰羊焚之謝神，眾隨鳥飛之向，舞而遷焉。

sensitivity.note: Omen-bird migration rite; Raffles himself compares the Dayak kite-divination of Borneo in a footnote.

passages.text: The horde, after offering their sacrifices and feasting in an open plain, left the remains of their repast to attract the bird called libunggaga, and the young men shook the angklung and set up a shout in imitation of its cry. If the bird did not eat of the meal offered to it, or took a course opposite to that which the horde wished to pursue, their departure was deferred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這群人獻上祭品，在開闊的平原上宴飲之後，留下吃剩的食物以吸引一種名叫利本加加（libunggaga）的鳥，年輕男子則搖動昂克隆（angklung），並模仿牠的叫聲高聲呼喊。倘若那鳥不食所獻的食物，或飛往與這群人欲行之路相反的方向，他們的啟程便延後。

passages.text: But when the bird, having eaten of its meal, flew in the direction of their intended journey, the ceremony was concluded by slaying and burning a lamb as an offering of gratitude to the Deity, and the whole party danced and sprang to the music of the angklung, moving on behind the omen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但當那鳥食畢其餐，朝他們預定旅程的方向飛去，儀式便以宰殺並焚燒一隻羔羊作為對神明的感恩獻祭而告終，全體人員隨著昂克隆的樂聲起舞跳躍，跟在那預兆之後前行。

title.en: Aji Saka Lands on Java: 'Nothing but Dust, and Man'
title.zh: 阿吉·薩卡登爪哇：『惟塵土與人而已』

region.en: Java (first year of the Javan era)
region.zh: 爪哇（爪哇紀元元年）

period: Javanese tradition ascribed to Javan era year 1 (Aji Saka tradition), recorded in Raffles 1817

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the arrival of Aji Saka

summary.en: In the first year of the Javan era the minister of Prabu Jaya Baya of Astina landed on Java, then the abode of a race of Rakshasas named Nusa Kendang. The date was fixed in chronograms as nir dhu tampo jalar — 'nothing, dust, not anything (but) man.' He discovered the grain jawawut, the principal subsistence of the inhabitants, and in consequence changed the island's name from Nusa Kendang to Nusa Jawa — the culture-hero who founds Java itself.
summary.zh: 爪哇紀元元年，阿斯提那王普拉布·查亞巴亞之首相登陸爪哇——其時島為羅剎所居，名『努薩·根當』。紀年以編年詩紀之：nir dhu tampo jalar——『空、塵、無物（惟人）』。他發現島民賴以為生之稷（jawawut），因改島名為『努薩·爪哇』——文化英雄親手為爪哇命名。

sensitivity.note: Aji Saka charter myth; the chronogram-pun etymology is typical of Javanese date-lore.

passages.text: Prabu Jaya Baya was a great and powerful prince of Astina; his Peng'gawa, or chief minister, a man of great enterprise and ability, was sent to visit and civilize foreign countries. In the course of his travels he landed on Java, then the abode of a race of Rakshasas, and known by the name of Nusa Kendang.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 普拉布·查亞·巴亞是阿斯蒂納一位偉大而強大的王子；他的彭加瓦，即首席大臣，是一位極具進取心與才幹的人，被派去訪問並開化外國。在他的旅行途中，他登上了爪哇，當時那裡是羅剎族的居所，以努沙·肯當之名為人所知。

passages.text: This happened in the first year of the Javan era, and is distinguished in the chronogram Sang'kala by the words nir dhu tampo jalar, meaning literally 'nothing, dust, not anything (but) man,' and metaphorically the figures 0001. He here discovered the grain called jawawut, at that time the principal subsistence of the inhabitants; and in consequence of this discovery he changed the name of the country from Nusa Kendang to Nusa Jawa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此事發生於爪哇紀元的第一年，並在年代記號「桑卡拉」中以「nir dhu tampo jalar」一詞標明，字面意為「無、塵、非任何物（惟）人」，隱喻則為數字0001。他在此發現了一種名為「爪哇烏特」的穀物，當時是居民的主要食糧；由於這一發現，他將該國之名由努沙·肯當改為努沙·爪哇。

title.en: Two Dead Rakshasas and the Javan Alphabet of Twenty Letters
title.zh: 兩具羅剎遺骸與爪哇二十字母

region.en: Java (Aji Saka cycle)
region.zh: 爪哇（阿吉·薩卡傳說圈）

period: Javanese Aji Saka tradition, recorded in Raffles 1817

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the invention of letters

summary.en: Journeying through the island, Aji Saka met the dead bodies of two Rakshasas, each holding a leaf with an inscription on it — one in purwa (ancient) characters, the other in Siamese. He united the two inscriptions and thus formed the Javan alphabet of twenty letters. He then fought several combats with the Rakshasas, particularly one Demata Chingkar, before returning to Astina with a written account of all he had seen and done.
summary.zh: 阿吉·薩卡行遍島中，遇羅剎屍骸二具，各持一葉，葉上各有銘文——一為古字（purwa），一為暹羅字。他合二銘而創爪哇二十字母。其後數與羅剎戰——尤與『德瑪塔·欽卡爾』激鬥——然後歸阿斯提那復命。

sensitivity.note: Alphabet-origin myth; the demon's script becoming human letters is a distinctive Javanese etiology.

passages.text: In his progress through the island he met with the dead bodies of two Rakshasas, each holding a leaf with an inscription on it, one in purwa (ancient), the other in Siamese characters: these he united, and thus formed the Javan alphabet of twenty letters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在島上遊歷期間，遇到了兩具羅剎的屍體，各持一片寫有銘文的葉子，一片為普爾瓦文（古文字），另一片為暹羅文字：他將二者合併，於是構成了由二十個字母組成的爪哇字母表。

passages.text: He had several combats with the Rakshasas, particularly with one Demata Chingkar; and after fixing the date of his different discoveries and leaving mementos of his visit wherever he went, he finally returned to Astina and delivered to his sovereign a written account of all he had seen and done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他與羅剎多次交戰，尤其是與一個名叫德馬塔·欽卡爾的羅剎；在確定了他各項發現的日期，並在所到之處留下他來訪的紀念物之後，他最終返回阿斯蒂納，向他君主呈交了一份關於他所見所為的書面記述。

title.en: The Code of Sun and Moon, Reformed by Aji Saka
title.zh: 日月法典與阿吉·薩卡之改革

region.en: Java (early legal tradition)
region.zh: 爪哇（早期法統傳說）

period: Javanese tradition of pre-Saka law, recorded in Raffles 1817

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the judicial code of sun and moon

summary.en: Before Aji Saka, Java's only trace of civilization was a judicial code titled 'sun and moon,' with mild punishments: a thief restored the stolen property and paid a fine in cattle or produce, becoming the injured party's slave if the theft was great — but transferable to no other master; murder was not punished by death but by a heavy fine and perpetual servitude in the deceased's family. Aji Saka reformed the code, and his abstract of ordinances was believed in use as late as Janggala (A.D. 900) and Majapahit (A.D. 1300).
summary.zh: 阿吉·薩卡之前，爪哇唯一法典曰『日月』，刑罰寬和：竊者還贓、納牛粟之罰；重竊則為被害者（或其親）之奴，不得轉賣他人；殺人不死，處重罰並終身服役於死者之家。薩卡改革法典，其刑典摘要行用至章格拉（900年）與馬卓帕希特（1300年）之世。

sensitivity.note: Legal-mythical charter; the 'sun and moon' code is presented as pre-Indian Javan law.

passages.text: The only trace of anterior civilization was a tradition that before his time there existed a judicial code, under the title of sun and moon, the punishments of which appear not to have been severe: a thief was bound to make restitution of the property stolen, and to pay in addition a fine in cattle or produce; and if the theft was considerable, he became the slave of the injured party or his relations, without, however, being transferable to another master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 先前文明的唯一痕跡，是一個傳說：在他之前存在一部名為「日與月」的司法法典，其刑罰似乎並不嚴厲：竊賊須歸還所竊財物，並另付以牲畜或農產品計的罰金；若盜竊數額重大，他便成為受害方或其親屬的奴隸，然而不得轉讓給另一主人。

passages.text: Murder was not punished by death, but by a heavy fine, and perpetual servitude in the family of the deceased. Aji Saka is represented to have reformed this code; and an abstract collection of ordinances, said to have been made from his instructions, is believed to have been in use as late as the time of Janggala (A.D. 900), and even of Majapahit (A.D. 1300).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 殺人並不處以死刑，而是處以重罰，並在死者家中終身為奴。據說阿吉·薩卡曾改革此法典；據信，一部據稱依其指示編成的法令摘要彙編，一直沿用至姜加拉時代（公元900年），甚至至滿者伯夷時代（公元1300年）。

title.en: Sang Yang Kalamerta: The Dewata's Son Who Guards the Harvest
title.zh: 桑·揚·卡拉默爾塔：護穀懲惡之神子

region.en: Majapahit country, East Java (temple inscription)
region.zh: 東爪哇馬卓帕希特之地（廟碑）

period: Javanese inscription, year 1216 Saka (c. 1294 CE), translated in Raffles 1817 (Appendix)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), Appendix, translation of a Javan inscription naming Sang Yang Kalamerta

summary.en: A Javan temple inscription teaches the cultivator that 'he who superintends the implements of tillage is the son of a Dewata, named Sang Yang Kalamerta; he is very good, for he protects all the cultivation in the country' — and that Sang Yang Kalamerta has been empowered by Batara Guru to destroy first all vicious persons, secondly evil speakers, and thirdly liars. The god of the plough is the enforcer of the three vices.
summary.zh: 爪哇廟碑訓誡耕者：『掌農具者乃神（Dewata）之子，名曰桑·揚·卡拉默爾塔；其神至善，護佑國中一切耕穫。』且巴塔拉·古魯授權於此神：先誅惡人、次誅惡言者、再誅說謊者。掌犁之神亦懲三惡之判官。

sensitivity.note: Inscriptional deity-lore tying agriculture to moral order; translation via Raffles' appendix.

passages.text: But be it known to the cultivator, that he who superintends the implements of tillage is the son of a Dewata, named Sang Yang Kalamerta; he is very good, for he protects all the cultivation in the country. It is that Sang Yang Kalamerta who, from the first, has caused terror to all such subjects as do not obey the commands of Batara Guru: because Sang Yang Kalamerta has been empowered by Batara Guru to destroy first all vicious persons, secondly evil speakers, and thirdly liars. These three vices do you reject, and ask forgiveness of the Batara, so that you may avoid the fury of Sang Yang Kalamerta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the inscription translation in Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但務農者當知，掌管耕具者乃一位提婆之子，名為桑·揚·卡拉梅爾塔；他極為善良，因為他保護國中一切耕作。正是這位桑·揚·卡拉梅爾塔，自始便使所有不遵從巴塔拉·古魯命令的臣民感到恐懼：因為桑·揚·卡拉梅爾塔已受巴塔拉·古魯授權，首先毀滅一切邪惡之人，其次毀滅口出惡言之人，第三毀滅說謊之人。此三種惡習，你們當棄絕，並向巴塔拉祈求寬恕，好使你們得以避開桑·揚·卡拉梅爾塔的盛怒。

title.en: The Kris of Hornets and the Fall of Majapahit
title.zh: 黃蜂之克利斯與馬卓帕希特之亡

region.en: Majapahit, East Java
region.zh: 東爪哇馬卓帕希特

period: Fall of Majapahit in Javan year 1400 (c. 1478 CE); tradition recorded in Raffles 1817

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the supernatural weapons of the Demak confederates

summary.en: The overthrow of ancient Majapahit 'was not to be effected by human means alone.' The confederates sent magical gifts to the field: Sunan Ngampel Denta a chain-jacket (baju rantai) that would loose thousands of rats at the height of battle; Sunan Giri the sacred kris from which a swarm of hornets was to issue; Sunan Bintang a magic wand able to produce allies on all sides. Thus armed, Pangiran Kudus drove the enemy before him, and the city 'so long celebrated for the splendour of its court and the glory of its arms' became a wilderness — 'Lost and gone is the pride of the land.'
summary.zh: 馬卓帕希特古國之亡『非人力所能獨成』。同盟諸王遣神物助戰：蘇丹·安佩爾贈鎖子甲——戰酣時甲中湧出千鼠；蘇丹·吉里贈神克利斯——揮之則黃蜂群出；蘇丹·賓塘贈魔杖——危急時四方召來盟軍勇士。邦義蘭·庫杜斯持之破敵，聖城遂荒——『舉國之榮，盡付東流』。

sensitivity.note: Muslim-Javan conquest legend with thaumaturgic weapons; the kraton pusaka tradition.

passages.text: The overthrow of the ancient kingdom, if we are to believe the Javans, was not to be effected by human means alone, and supernatural expedients were resorted to. Sunan Ngampel Denta sent a baju rantai, or chain jacket, with an injunction not to open it until the engagement was at its height, when thousands of rats would issue from it and assist in putting an end to the struggle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 若我們相信爪哇人所言，這個古國的傾覆並非僅憑人力所能達成，他們還訴諸了超自然的手段。蘇南·恩甘佩爾·登塔送來一件巴朱·蘭泰，即鎖子甲衣，並附囑咐云：在戰事達到最激烈之時方可開啟，屆時將有數千隻老鼠從中湧出，協助終結這場爭鬥。

passages.text: Sunan Giri contributed, with the same instructions, the sacred kris, from which a swarm of hornets was to issue; and Sunan Bintang sent a magical wand or cane, which in cases of extremity possessed the power of producing allies and warriors on all sides. Thus provided, the Mahometan army took the field under Pangiran Kudus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇南·吉里同樣附以相同的指示，貢獻了那柄神聖的克里斯短劍，將有一群大黃蜂從中湧出；蘇南·賓唐則送來一根魔法杖或手杖，此杖在危急關頭具有從四方招來盟友與戰士的力量。如此配備齊全之後，伊斯蘭軍隊在龐吉蘭·庫杜斯率領下開赴戰場。

passages.text: In this protracted engagement the faithful were at first worsted; but the commander, availing himself of the enchanted box and miraculous weapons, at last succeeded in driving the enemy before him, and the city of Majapahit, surrounded on all sides, submitted to the hostile forces. Thus did the sacred city, so long celebrated for the splendour of its court and the glory of its arms, become a wilderness — 'Lost and gone is the pride of the land.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這場曠日持久的交戰中，信士們起初受挫；但統帥善用那魔法寶盒與奇蹟般的武器，最終成功將敵人驅逐於前，而滿者伯夷城四面被圍，遂向敵軍投降。這座神聖之城，長久以來以其朝廷的輝煌與武力的榮耀著稱，就這樣化為荒野——「這片土地的驕傲已失落消逝。」

title.en: Chandra Kirana Given to Malacca: The Batara's Daughter and Hang Tuah
title.zh: 月公主許嫁滿剌加：巴塔拉之女與漢都亞

region.en: Majapahit, East Java
region.zh: 東爪哇馬卓帕希特

period: Malay Annals tradition (quoted by Raffles 1817); Majapahit-Malacca alliance legend

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X (quoting the Malay Annals on the marriage of Chandra Kirana)

summary.en: The Batara of Majapahit had a daughter, Raden Galuh Chandra Kirana, celebrated far and wide, whom many rajas sought. Her fame reached Malacca, and Sultan Mansur, enamoured by description, fitted out five hundred great prahus; forty nobles and forty noble virgins attended him, and among the chieftains came the celebrated Hang Tuah the Laksamana, 'who was highly admired and exhibited wonderful feats.' The Batara gave his daughter to the Raja of Malacca, seated his son-in-law beside himself on a seat of equal honour — and bestowed Siantan on Laksamana, 'from which time the rulers of Siantan are descendants of Laksamana.'
summary.zh: 馬卓帕希特巴塔拉有女查德拉·基拉娜，艷名遠播，列王爭聘。名聲傳至滿剌加，蘇丹滿速沙聞名傾心，備五百大船、貴胄四十、名媛四十親往；扈從之中有名將漢都亞（海軍統帥），技藝驚人。巴塔拉以女妻滿剌加王，令婿與己並坐同尊——又以錫亞丹封漢都亞，『自此錫亞丹之主皆統帥之後』。

sensitivity.note: Majapahit-Malacca alliance legend shared by the Malay Annals; the Panji-cycle princess Chandra Kirana transferred to dynastic marriage.

passages.text: The Batara had a daughter named Raden Galuh Chandra Kirana, whose beauty was celebrated far and wide, and many rajas sought her in marriage. Her fame reached Malacca, and Sultan Mansur became enamoured of her by description. He ordered Paduka Raja, the bandahara, to fit out a fleet of five hundred large prahus with innumerable small ones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Malay Annals passage quoted in Raffles, History of Java (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴塔拉有一女，名為拉登·加盧·錢德拉·基拉娜，其美貌遠近聞名，許多羅闍都前來向她求婚。她的聲名傳至馬六甲，蘇丹·曼蘇爾聞其描述而傾心愛慕。他命令盤陀訶羅帕杜卡·羅闍裝備一支由五百艘大船與無數小船組成的艦隊。

passages.text: Among the chieftains who accompanied the Raja of Malacca was the celebrated Hang Tuah or Laksamana, who was highly admired and exhibited wonderful feats. The Batara gave his daughter Chandra Kirana in marriage to the Raja of Malacca; and the Batara, delighted with his son-in-law, caused him to be placed on a seat of equal honour with himself, both on public occasions and at meals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Malay Annals passage quoted in Raffles, History of Java (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨馬六甲羅闍同行的首領之中，有著名的漢·圖亞，即拉克薩馬納，他深受讚賞，並展現了奇妙的技藝。巴塔拉將其女錢德拉·基拉娜嫁與馬六甲羅闍；巴塔拉對這位女婿甚為喜愛，無論在公開場合或進膳之時，都命他坐在與自己同等尊榮的座位上。

passages.text: Then, being about to depart, the Raja requested to be presented with the kingdom of Indra-giri, which was accordingly given to him. He then bestowed Siantan on Laksamana, from which time the rulers of Siantan are descendants of Laksamana. By the princess he had a son, named Raden Galang, who was killed one day by a man running amok.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Malay Annals passage quoted in Raffles, History of Java (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後，拉者即將啟程離去，請求將因陀羅耆利王國贈予他，於是便給了他。他接著將西安坦賜予拉克薩馬納，自此西安坦的統治者皆為拉克薩馬納的後裔。他與公主育有一子，名為拉登·加朗，某日被一名發狂奔跑之人殺害。

title.en: The Invulnerable Prince of Janggala and the Arrow of Jepara Iron
title.zh: 章格拉不敗王子與哲帕拉鐵箭

region.en: Janggala, East Java
region.zh: 東爪哇章格拉

period: Madura-tradition legend of Janggala, recorded in Raffles 1817

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the death of the prince of Janggala

summary.en: The accounts of the succession of Paji to his father's throne are discordant, but in the Madura tradition Prabu Jaya Sangara, chief of Madura (then called Nusa Antara), was jealous of the power of Janggala, landed there, and in a desperate action killed Paji with an arrow from his own bow — in fulfilment of a prophecy which foretold that the prince would be invulnerable except to the iron (tisi) of Jepara, from which the prince of Nusa Antara had manufactured his arrow. The one hole in an invulnerable man is always the one his enemy happens to own.
summary.zh: 帕吉繼位之事傳說紛紜；馬都拉傳說云：馬都拉（時稱努薩·安塔拉）之王普拉布·查亞·桑卡拉忌章格拉之勢，登陸決戰，以帕吉自用之弓一箭斃之——應了那則預言：王刀槍不入，唯懼哲帕拉之鐵；而努薩·安塔拉王子之箭，恰以哲帕拉鐵鍛成。刀槍不入者，必有其一破綻，而破綻恰在仇人手中。

sensitivity.note: Invulnerability-prophecy motif (Achilles-type) in Javanese court legend.

passages.text: In some accounts Paji is represented as having succeeded on his father's death; in others, as dying prematurely: Prabu Jaya Sangara, chief of Madura (then called Nusa Antara), jealous of the power of Janggala, is said to have landed, and in a desperate action killed Paji with an arrow from his own bow. This was in fulfilment of a prophecy which foretold that he would be invulnerable, except to the iron tisi of Jepara, from which this prince had manufactured his arrow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在某些記載中，帕吉被描述為於父親死後繼位；在另一些記載中，則被描述為早逝：據說馬都拉（當時稱為努沙安塔拉）的首領帕拉布·查亞·桑加拉嫉妒姜加拉的勢力，登陸後在一場殊死戰鬥中，以自己弓上射出的箭殺死了帕吉。這應驗了一則預言，該預言說他將刀槍不入，唯有傑帕拉的鐵蒂西能傷他，而這位王子正是用此鐵製造了他的箭。

title.en: Kagssagssuk, the Homeless Boy Who Became a Strong Man
title.zh: 流浪孤兒卡格薩克舒克

region.en: Smith Sound, Polar Eskimo country, Northwest Greenland
region.zh: 西北格陵蘭史密斯海峽極地因紐特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition (Polar Eskimo, Smith Sound); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man', eBook #28932

summary.en: The Great Fire, whip of live ribbon seal, frizzles a whole house of noisy children — only homeless Kagssagssuk survives on the drying frame, and the village punishes him for the truth. Ground down by Umerdlugtoq, who hauls him by the nostrils, and by a beating grandmother, he trains by stone-twirling with a pitying giant until stones sing 'leu-leu-leu' in the air, then hauls an umiak from the ice, kills three bears with his fists, casts the wicked grandmother on her own fire, and holds Umerdlugtoq out over a precipice by the nostrils — 'Do not fear; for you never used to kill me.' Later his pride turns him to crushing children, and his fellows harpoon him.
summary.zh: 『大火』以活環斑海豹為鞭，將喧嘩的孩童們燒成焦炭——流浪兒卡格薩克舒克因藏於晾架而倖存，村民卻罵他撒謊。他受大人物烏默德盧格托克提鼻羞辱、惡祖母毒打；與悲憫的巨人推石練力，石在空中『嚕嚕』作響；拖出冰封大舟、赤手殺三熊、將惡祖母擲入火中，再把烏默德盧格托克提鼻懸於懸崖——『別怕；你從前從未殺過我。』後來他得勢驕橫，竟捏碎孩童，終被同伴魚叉所殺。

sensitivity.note: Polar Eskimo tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The killing of the wicked grandmother and of children in the coda is presented as told in the source.

passages.text: When the men and women had gone to a spirit calling, the children left behind played in one big house, and homeless Kagssagssuk, alone outside, warned them: 'You must not make so much noise, or the Great Fire will come.' They would not believe him — and the Great Fire appeared: he had a great live ribbon seal for a whip, with long claws, and he began dragging the children out through the passage, each one frizzled up as it was drawn. Little Kagssagssuk had cried to be lifted to the drying frame under the roof for his gloves, and so escaped; the Great Fire, going away, touched a hanging skin with his finger. None of the gathered villagers believed the boy — 'You have killed them yourself' — so he dared them to make a noise like the children did, and the Great Fire came again; but this time the people poured boiling oil over its living whip, and it went away. From that time the village was unkind to the boy who had told the truth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當男人和女人們前去召喚神靈時，被留下的孩子們在一座大屋裡玩耍，而無家可歸的卡格薩格蘇克獨自在外，警告他們說：「你們不可發出這麼大的聲響，否則大火就要來了。」他們不肯相信他——於是那大火出現了：他以一條巨大的活帶紋海豹作鞭子，長著長長的爪子，開始把孩子們從通道裡拖出去，每一個被拖出時都被烤得焦捲。小卡格薩格蘇克曾哭喊著要人把他舉到屋頂下的晾架上去取他的手套，因而逃過一劫；那大火離去時，用手指碰了碰一張懸掛著的獸皮。聚集的村民中沒有人相信這男孩——「是你自己把他們殺死的」——於是他激他們發出像孩子們那樣的聲音，那大火又來了；但這一次，人們把滾油澆在它那活鞭子上，它便離去了。從那時起，村裡的人對這個說了實話的男孩便很不友善。

passages.text: He had lived in the house of Umerdlugtoq, a great man, but now he was forced to stay outside; if he stepped in only to dry his boots, Umerdlugtoq lifted him up by the nostrils and cast him over the high threshold. One grandmother beat him whenever she could; the other, his mother's mother, took pity and dried his clothes. They fed him on tough walrus hide, and he gnawed it with the help of a little stone he kept in his breeches; he slept among the dogs and warmed himself on the roof in the warm air of the smoke hole, to be hauled down by the nostrils again. Wandering one spring day, he met a giant cutting up his catch; his cry for meat was too small to hear until the giant said 'Bring me luck' and threw down a little piece, thinking it one of the dead who asked. Kagssagssuk, already having helping spirits, made the piece a big one and ate his fill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他原本住在一個大人物烏梅爾德盧格托克的屋裡，但如今他被迫待在外面；倘若他僅是為了烘乾靴子而踏進屋內，烏梅爾德盧格托克便揪住他的鼻孔把他舉起，扔過那高高的門檻。有一位祖母一有機會就打他；另一位祖母，即他母親的母親，心生憐憫，替他烘乾衣服。他們拿堅韌的海象皮給他吃，他則靠著藏在褲子裡的一塊小石頭啃咬它；他睡在狗群中間，在屋頂上藉著煙洞冒出的暖氣取暖，卻又被人揪住鼻孔拽了下來。某個春日他外出遊蕩，遇見一個巨人正在切割他的獵獲物；他討肉的喊聲太小，無人聽得見，直到那巨人說「給我帶來好運吧」，便扔下一小塊，還以為是哪個死者在討要。卡格薩格蘇克此時已有助靈，便把那小塊變成了大塊，飽餐了一頓。

passages.text: When his hidden meat turned out stolen by the giant himself, the giant, feeling kindly, proposed they play together: pushing stones until they twirled. At first Kagssagssuk fell backwards; then he ceased falling and could move the stones, each larger than the last, until he could make even the biggest twirl in the air, the stone saying 'leu-leu-leu-leu' as it flew. Seeing them equal in strength, the giant said: 'Now you have become a strong man. But since it was by my fault that you lost that piece of meat, I will by magic means cause three bears to come right down to your village.' Kagssagssuk went home, hauled an umiak free of the ice in the night to show his strength, and was mocked for it by Umerdlugtoq.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他藏起來的肉原來是被那巨人自己偷走時，那巨人心生善意，提議他們一起玩耍：推石頭，直到石頭旋轉起來。起初卡格薩格蘇克向後跌倒；後來他不再跌倒，能夠推動石頭，一塊比一塊大，直到他能讓最大的那塊也在空中旋轉，那石頭飛起時發出「勒—勒—勒—勒」的聲音。見二人力量相當，巨人說：「如今你已成了一個強壯的人。但既然你丟失那塊肉是我的過錯，我便要用魔法之術引三頭熊徑直來到你的村莊。」卡格薩格蘇克回到家中，夜裡把一艘烏米亞克皮艇從冰中拖出，以顯示他的力氣，卻因此遭到烏梅爾德盧格托克的嘲笑。

passages.text: When three bears appeared exactly as the giant had said, Kagssagssuk borrowed his grandmother's boots and went out, treading so hard the footprints seemed made in soft snow. He grasped the biggest bear — a mother with two half-grown cubs — with his naked fists and wrung its neck; then hammered the cubs' skulls together. Carrying the bear over his shoulders and a cub under each arm as if they were no more than hares, he skinned them and cooked the meat on a big flat stone for his kind grandmother — and cast the wicked grandmother on the fire, where all burned up but her stomach. Umerdlugtoq fled with his wives to a tent on a precipice edge; up came Kagssagssuk, caught him by the nostrils and held him out over the edge, shaking him until they burst: 'Do not fear; I am not going to kill you. For you never used to kill me.' Then he called out from inside the tent, 'I am in here with your wives!' — took vengeance on all who had ill-treated him, went south, and lived there. But being so strong he grew filled with the desire to be feared and began catching hold of children and crushing them; therefore his fellow-villagers harpooned him one day when he was out in his kayak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kagssagssuk, the homeless boy who became a strong man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當三頭熊正如巨人所說的那樣出現時，卡格薩格蘇克借來他祖母的靴子走了出去，踩得那麼用力，腳印彷彿是印在鬆軟的雪上。他赤手空拳抓住最大的那頭熊——一頭帶著兩隻半大幼崽的母熊——扭斷了它的脖子；接著又把兩隻幼崽的頭骨互相撞擊。他把那頭熊扛在肩上，兩腋下各夾一隻幼崽，彷彿它們不過是野兔一般，剝了它們的皮，把肉放在一塊大平石上為他善良的祖母烹煮——又把那惡毒的祖母扔到火上，燒得只剩她的胃。烏梅爾德盧格托克帶著他的妻子們逃到懸崖邊的一座帳篷裡；卡格薩格蘇克走上來，揪住他的鼻孔，把他懸在崖邊，搖晃他直到鼻孔爆裂：「別怕；我不會殺你。因為你從前也從不曾殺我。」接著他從帳篷裡喊道：「我和你的妻子們在裡面呢！」——他向所有曾虐待過他的人報了仇，然後南下，住在那裡。但由於他如此強壯，心中漸漸充滿了令人畏懼的渴望，開始抓住孩子們把他們捏碎；因此有一天，當他划著獨木舟外出時，他的同村人用魚叉刺死了他。

title.en: Qasiagssaq, the Great Liar
title.zh: 大話家瓜西亞克舒克

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar', eBook #28932

summary.en: Sleepless, seal-less Qasiagssaq resolves to live by lies: he steals a fellow-hunter's black seal and shows off its narwhal-tusk tow-line; hammers his own knee-caps and kayaks to pieces and piles iceberg fragments on himself to fake an iceberg calving; ties his bladder floats to a stone to counterfeit a struck walrus; whistles at a speckled seal rather than pierce its skin with harpoon holes, losing it; fakes a dead daughter's name to beg beads, a cooking pot, and loads of food; and lures his starving in-laws with tales of seals daily thrown away.
