At last he announces a dead whale that is never there, ness after ness, and the exasperated villagers kill him.
summary.zh: 失眠無獵的瓜西亞克舒克決定靠謊言過活：竊取同伴的黑海豹、炫耀獨角鯨牙拖繩；自錘膝蓋、砸爛皮艇、懷揣冰塊，偽稱冰山崩塌；將浮囊繫石假冒中鯨海象；為保全妻子褲料皮而對海豹吹哨，反使其逃逸；假冒亡女之名騙取珠串、炊鍋與食糧；又以『村中海豹日日棄置』誘饑餓的岳母來投。最後他謊稱發現鯨屍，引眾船一岬又一岬地空跑，眾人終於將他殺死。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The name-stealingmourning episode is a documented but sensitive social custom; presented as told.

passages.text: Qasiagssaq was a great liar who could never sleep well at night and always woke his fellow-villagers for the morning hunt — but never brought home anything himself. 'It is no use my trying to be a hunter; I may as well make up some lie or other,' he said, and that very day, seeing a fellow-villager towing a big black seal to an island to land it, he rowed round behind the man, stole it, and towed it home. His wife shaded her eyes and watched his kayak come in with its catch; the villagers cried 'Here is Qasiagssaq has made a catch' and admired the deep black markings and the tow-line thick with trappings of the finest narwhal tusk — 'I have had it a long time,' he said. The last kayak in told the truth: he had landed that seal on the island and found it gone. That evening a voice asked at the window for the tow-line back, and Qasiagssaq sprang up with it — while his wife said, as she would say again and again, 'When Qasiagssaq does such things, one cannot but feel shame for him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡西亞格薩克是個大騙子，夜裡從不能安睡，總是把同村的村民叫醒去晨獵——自己卻從不帶回任何獵物。「我當獵人是沒用的；倒不如編些謊話什麼的。」他說道。就在那一天，他看見一個同村的人正把一頭大黑海豹拖到一座島上登陸，便划船繞到那人背後，把它偷走，拖回了家。他的妻子手搭涼棚，望著他的獨木舟載著獵物歸來；村民們喊道：「這不是卡西亞格薩克打到了獵物嗎！」又讚嘆那深黑的斑紋，以及那條綴滿最上等獨角鯨牙飾物的拖繩——「這東西我早就有了。」他說。最後一艘歸來的獨木舟道出了實情：是他把那頭海豹拖上島的，回來卻發現不見了。那天傍晚，有個聲音在窗外討要那條拖繩，卡西亞格薩克便帶著它一躍而起——而他的妻子則說道（這話她往後還會一遍又一遍地說）：「卡西亞格薩克做出這種事，叫人怎能不替他害臊。」

passages.text: Rowing home empty-handed another day, he laid one knee across a stone and hammered both knee-caps to pieces with another stone, then battered his kayak's woodwork to bits, piled fragments of iceberg upon it and even inside his raven-skin clothes, and rowed home: 'An iceberg calved.' Two women had watched the whole performance from the shore and told it all; his wife only said her usual 'shame,' and he frightened her with 'Hrrrr!' Later he laid a long stone on his kayak, rowed out among waiting kayakers, tied his two small bladder floats to the stone, and rowed away as fast as he could — announcing on coming in that he had struck a great walrus which had gone down with his floats. But the kayaker still out brought back the floats themselves: 'They had been tied to a stone, and the knot had worked loose.' 'When Qasiagssaq does such things, one cannot but feel shame for him.' 'Hrrrr!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一天，他空手划船回家，把一條腿的膝蓋橫擱在一塊石頭上，用另一塊石頭把自己的兩塊膝蓋骨砸得粉碎，接著又把獨木舟的木結構砸成碎片，在上面堆滿冰山的碎塊，甚至塞進他那件渡鴉皮衣服裡，然後划船回家：「一座冰山崩解了。」兩個女人從岸上目睹了這整場把戲，把事情全說了出來；他的妻子只說了那句慣常的「害臊」，他便用「哼——！」嚇唬她。後來，他把一塊長石頭擱在獨木舟上，划到等候著的獨木舟手們中間，把兩個小浮囊繫在石頭上，然後拼命划走——回來時宣稱自己擊中了一頭大walrus（海象），那海象帶著他的浮囊沉了下去。可是仍在外面的獨木舟手把浮囊本身帶了回來：「它們是繫在一塊石頭上的，繩結鬆脫了。」「卡西亞格薩克做出這種事，叫人怎能不替他害臊。」「哼——！」

passages.text: Once, coming on a speckled seal crawled up on the ice, he lifted his harpoon to throw — then looked at the point and laid it down again: 'Would it not be a pity, now, for that skin, which is to be used to make breeches for my wife, to be pierced with holes by the point of a harpoon?' He began whistling to the seal, to take hold of it, and the seal went down; up again, whistled at again, down again — and did not come up any more. Hearing that an old couple in another village had lost their little daughter, he visited them and, clearing his throat, said loudly: 'To-day my little daughter Nipisartangivaq is doubtless crying at her mother's side as usual.' The mourners, grateful, gave him beads, a cooking pot, and great quantities of food for 'his little girl' — and more came with meat until the villagers said plainly: 'Qasiagssaq and his wife have no children.' The strangers would not even land: 'Then tell them to give us back the beads and the cooking pot.' 'Now you have lied again... one cannot but feel shame for you.' 'Hrrrr!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，他遇見一頭爬上冰面的斑海豹，舉起魚叉要擲——卻又看了看叉尖，把它放了下來：「這張皮是要給我妻子做褲子的，如今卻要讓叉尖戳出窟窿，豈不可惜？」他開始對海豹吹口哨，想讓它靠過來，海豹卻沉了下去；又浮上來，他又吹口哨，它又沉下去——從此再沒浮上來。他聽說另一個村子裡有一對老夫婦失去了他們的小女兒，便去拜訪他們，清了清嗓子，大聲說道：「今天我那小女兒妮皮薩爾坦吉瓦克想必又像往常一樣，在她母親身邊哭著呢。」那對哀悼的夫婦心懷感激，送給他珠子、一口煮鍋，還有大量食物，說是給「他的小女兒」的——接著又有人送來肉，直到村民們直截了當地說：「卡西亞格薩克和他妻子根本沒有孩子。」那些外村人連岸都不肯上：「那就叫他們把珠子和煮鍋還給我們。」「如今你又撒謊了……叫人怎能不替你害臊。」「哼——！」

passages.text: Visiting his wife's mother, whose lamp was out of blubber and whose child cried for hunger, he lamented his own foolishness — 'Over in our village, seals are daily thrown away. You must come back with me to our place' — then hurried ahead and let her find nothing on his rubbish heap but carrion of ravens, one of which he 'caught in his snare' to cook on shoulder-blade lamp and pot. In time he came home crying: 'I have found a dead whale; to-morrow we must all go out in the umiak and cut it up.' Many umiaks and kayaks rowed east with him — 'Where is it?' 'Over there, beyond that little ness' — ness after ness, nothing to be seen. 'Qasiagssaq is lying as usual. Let us kill him.' 'Wait a little; let us first make sure that it is a lie, and if you do not see it, you may kill me' — and at last they did as they had said, and killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Qasiagssaq, the great liar'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他去探望妻子的母親，見她燈裡沒了鯨脂，孩子餓得直哭，便哀嘆自己的愚笨——「在我們村裡，海豹天天都扔掉。你得跟我回我們那兒去」——然後搶先趕回去，讓她在他的垃圾堆上只找到些渡鴉的腐肉，其中一隻是他「用陷阱捉住」的，放在肩胛骨做的燈和鍋上煮。過了些時候，他哭著回家：「我發現了一頭死鯨；明天我們大家得乘大艇出去把它切開。」許多大艇和獨木舟跟著他往東划去——「在哪兒呢？」「在那邊，過了那個小岬角」——一個岬角又一個岬角，什麼也看不見。「卡西亞格薩克又像往常一樣撒謊。我們殺了他吧。」「等一等；我們先弄清楚這是不是謊話，要是你們看不見它，你們盡可以殺我」——最後他們果真照自己說的做了，把他殺了。

title.en: Rama Banished: The Old Javanese Ramayana Opens in the Forest
title.zh: 羅摩流放：古爪哇《羅摩衍那》開篇於林中

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE; reliefs carved c. 9th century (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919), Prambanan and Panataran relief narrative; Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: The oldest surviving major work of Javanese literature retells Rama's story in courtly kakawin verse: exiled through his father's old promise, Rama leaves Ayodya with his wife Sinta and his brother Leksmana for the Dandaka forest, refusing royal comforts for the fourteen years of exile — the episode carved at the head of the Prambanan relief cycle.
summary.zh: 爪哇文學最古之偉構以典雅頌詩重述羅摩故事：因父王舊諾而遭放逐，羅摩攜妻悉多、弟勒什曼那入檀陀迦林，十四年放逐甘捨王宮之樂——此段即普蘭巴南浮雕長卷之首章。

sensitivity.note: Javanese Ramayana tradition (kakawin); a shared Hindu-Javanese heritage; passages are condensed paraphrases of the kakawin narrative as it is read in the relief commentary.

passages.text: Bound by the old promise made to a junior queen, King Dasa Rata of Ayodya must send his heir Rama into exile. Rama accepts without protest, and Sinta and his brother Leksmana insist on sharing the forest life; the three leave the palace, and the court of Ayodya follows them with laments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin (c. 9th c.), opening cantos, as read in Kats' relief commentary (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 由於昔日對一位次妃許下的舊諾言所約束，阿約迪亞的達薩·拉塔國王不得不把他的繼承人羅摩送去流放。羅摩毫無怨言地接受了，辛塔和他的弟弟雷克斯馬納堅持要一同分擔森林生活；三人離開王宮，阿約迪亞的宮廷伴隨著哀嘆之聲為他們送行。

passages.text: In the Dandaka forest the exiles take up the ascetic life: Rama in bark garments, Sinta learning forest fare, Leksmana building their leaf-hut. The Kakawin dwells on the beauty of the forest exile as much as the hardship, for the poem was composed for a Javanese court that read the story as its own sacred genealogy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在丹達卡森林中，流放者們過起了苦修生活：羅摩身穿樹皮衣，辛塔學著吃森林裡的食物，雷克斯馬納為他們搭建樹葉小屋。這部《卡卡溫》既著力描寫森林流放的美，也同樣著力描寫其艱辛，因為這首詩是為一個爪哇宮廷而作的，那個宮廷把這個故事讀作自身神聖的譜系。

title.en: The Golden Deer and the Abduction of Sinta
title.zh: 金鹿與悉多被劫

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin Marica episode

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: The demon Marica transforms into a golden deer that grazes before Sinta's hut; while Rama pursues it and Leksmana draws the protective circle, the rakshasa king Rawana approaches disguised as an old beggar, seizes Sinta, and carries her through the air toward Alengka as the mountain birds scatter.
summary.zh: 羅剎摩里遮化作金鹿，現於悉多茅舍之前；羅摩追鹿、勒什曼那畫護圈之際，十首魔王拉瓦那假扮老乞婆近前，一把抱起悉多，乘空而遁，群鳥驚散。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via the relief commentary; the abduction episode heads the Prambanan narrative frieze.

passages.text: A wondrous deer of gold appears grazing before the hermitage. Sinta, charmed, begs Rama to catch it; the deer is the demon Marica transformed, and as Rama's arrow finds it the dying demon imitates Rama's own voice crying for help.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, Marica episode (Kats 1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一頭神奇的金鹿出現在隱修院前吃草。辛塔為之著迷，懇求羅摩去捕捉牠；這頭鹿實為妖魔馬里查所化，當羅摩的箭射中牠時，垂死的妖魔模仿羅摩自己的聲音呼救。

passages.text: Believing his brother's cry, Leksmana leaves the protective circle he had drawn; in that instant Rawana approaches Sinta in the guise of an old ascetic, gains her confidence, then seizes her. As Rawana carries her skyward toward Alengka, the birds of the forest scatter before him and Sinta drops her ornaments for anyone who may follow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 萊克薩馬納相信了兄弟的呼救聲，離開了他所畫的保護圈；就在那一刻，拉瓦納化身為一名老苦行者接近辛塔，取得她的信任，隨即將她擄走。當拉瓦納帶著她騰空飛往阿冷卡時，林中的鳥兒在他面前四散，辛塔則將自己的飾物拋下，留給任何可能追來的人。

title.en: Jatayu Falls: The Old Eagle Who Fought the Ten-Faced King
title.zh: 神鳥賈塔尤之歿

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin Jatayu episode

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: The great eagle Jatayu, old friend of Rama's house, attacks Rawana in mid-air to stop the abduction; his wings are cut, and he falls dying to the rocks, his claws still fixed in the demon king. Rama later finds him, and from the dying eagle learns for the first time where his wife has been carried.
summary.zh: 巨鷹賈塔尤——羅摩家門之故交——凌空攔截拉瓦那；其翼被斬，抱著魔王墜岩而死。羅摩後至，自垂死神鳥之口始知愛妻去向。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via relief commentary; bird-hero motif.

passages.text: Hearing Sinta's cries, the ancient eagle Jatayu rises against Rawana's flying chariot and grapples with the ten-faced king in the sky, tearing at his chariot and armor; but Rawana severs his wings with his sword, and the old bird falls dying on the mountain rocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, Jatayu episode (Kats 1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 聽到辛塔的哭喊，古老的巨鷹賈塔尤起身迎向拉瓦納的飛車，在空中與這十面之王搏鬥，撕扯他的戰車與鎧甲；但拉瓦納以劍斬斷牠的雙翼，這隻老鳥便奄奄一息地墜落於山岩之上。

passages.text: Rama and Leksmana, searching, find the broken Jatayu and hear from him the tale of the abduction — that Sinta lives and is carried to Alengka. The eagle dies in Rama's arms, and the brothers perform his funeral rites before turning toward the south in grief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 羅摩與萊克薩馬納四處搜尋，發現了傷殘的賈塔尤，從牠口中得知擄掠的經過——辛塔尚在人世，正被帶往阿冷卡。巨鷹在羅摩懷中死去，兄弟二人為牠舉行了葬禮，隨後滿懷悲傷轉向南方。

title.en: Subali and Sugriwa: The Monkey Brothers' Feud
title.zh: 蘇巴利與蘇格里瓦：猴族兄弟之爭

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin Subali-Sugriwa episode

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: In the Kakawin's telling, the monkey-king Subali has seized his brother Sugriwa's throne and wife; Rama's arrow pierces Subali as the brothers duel, and the dying Subali rebukes Rama for killing from hiding. Sugriwa is restored and pledges his monkey host to the search for Sinta.
summary.zh: 猴王蘇巴利奪弟蘇格里瓦之王位與妻室；兄弟相搏之際，羅摩一箭穿蘇巴利之身。垂死猴王責羅摩藏於暗處殺人。蘇格里瓦復位，傾其猴兵以助羅摩尋妻。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via relief commentary; note the moral ambiguity of Rama's arrow, which the Javanese poem sharpens.

passages.text: The mighty Subali, invulnerable to his enemies, has driven his brother Sugriwa from the throne of the monkeys and taken his wife. Sugriwa, hunted through the forest, meets Rama and pledges his service if Rama will slay his brother. As the two monkey-brothers close in battle, indistinguishable in their fury, Rama from cover pierces Subali with an arrow. The dying Subali confronts Rama: is it hero's work, to kill unseen the mightiest of monkeys? Rama answers that justice against the wrong done to a brother is the law of kings; Sugriwa is enthroned and gathers his host for Rama.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, Subali episode (Kats 1919); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 強大的蘇巴利刀槍不入，將弟弟蘇格里瓦逐出猴國王座，並奪走他的妻子。蘇格里瓦在林中遭追獵，遇見羅摩，並立誓若羅摩肯殺其兄，他便為羅摩效命。當這兩位猴兄弟在戰鬥中逼近，狂怒之下難分彼此，羅摩從暗處以一箭射穿蘇巴利。垂死的蘇巴利質問羅摩：暗中殺死最強大的猴子，這可是英雄所為？羅摩回答，為兄弟所受的冤屈伸張正義，乃是君王之法；蘇格里瓦登基為王，並為羅摩召集大軍。

title.en: Hanuman's Embassy: The Tail Set Alight in Rawana's Court
title.zh: 哈奴曼使團：宮中燃尾

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin Hanuman embassy episode

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: Sent across the sea as Rama's envoy, Hanuman finds Sinta in the Asoka garden and delivers his message; seized and brought before Rawana, he mocks the ten-faced king to his face. Ordered to be burned, he wraps his tail in oil-soaked cloth — and with the burning tail leaps free, setting the golden city of Alengka itself on fire.
summary.zh: 哈奴曼奉羅摩之命渡海為使，於如意林中覓見悉多、傳遞口信；被擒押至拉瓦那殿前，仍当面譏誚十首王。王命焚其尾——他以油布裹尾；尾一著火，他便掙脫而起，反將金色之城阿楞迦付之一炬。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via relief commentary; the burning of Alengka is among the most carved Prambanan panels.

passages.text: Hanuman leaps the ocean and, shrinking to monkey size, searches the Asoka garden until he finds Sinta under guard; kneeling, he gives her Rama's token and message and carries back her answer. Provoked by the rakshasa women, he is seized and dragged before Rawana's throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, Hanuman embassy (Kats 1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈奴曼躍過大海，縮小成猴子的身形，搜遍阿育王園，終於在守衛之下找到辛塔；他跪下，呈上羅摩的信物與口信，並帶回她的答覆。他遭羅剎女挑釁，被抓住並拖到拉瓦納的王座之前。

passages.text: Before the ten-faced king the monkey-envoy will not kneel; Rawana orders his tail wrapped in cloth and set on fire. Hanuman slips his bonds, leaps free trailing flame, and runs the ramparts and gates of Alengka, leaving the golden city burning behind him before returning over the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在十面王面前，猴使不肯下跪；羅瓦那下令用布裹住他的尾巴並點火焚燒。哈奴曼掙脫束縛，帶著火焰縱身躍出，奔過阿楞卡的城牆與城門，任那座金色之城在他身後燃燒，隨後越海而歸。

title.en: The Leap Across the Ocean
title.zh: 飛渡大洋

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin leap episode

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: Chosen for the reconnaissance across the water, Hanuman grows to the size of a mountain, pauses on the mount of spring (Mahendra) to gather himself, and takes the leap: over fish and sea-demons who rise to test him, over the island-city of the rakshasas — the Kakawin lingers on his flight as the poem's showpiece of heroic transformation.
summary.zh: 哈奴曼受選渡海偵察，身長如山；立於摩亨陀山巔蓄勢一躍——海中魚怪躍起相試，被他一一越過；直抵羅剎島城。爪哇頌詩以此飛躍為英雄變身之絕筆。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via relief commentary.

passages.text: The monkeys seek one able to cross the sea unaided, and Hanuman is chosen: he grows vast as a mountain and takes his stand on the mount of spring, then leaps — the sky fills with his passage and the sea rises in waves beneath him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, leap episode (Kats 1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 群猴尋覓一位能獨力渡海者，哈奴曼被選中：他身形漲大如一座山，立於泉之山上，繼而縱身一躍——天空滿是他掠過的蹤跡，大海在他腳下翻湧起層層波濤。

passages.text: Mid-ocean, sea-demons and fish rise to seize the flying monkey by his shadow; he mocks them, dips a paw, and passes on until the towers of Alengka rise on the horizon and he lands, small again, among the rakshasa city's trees.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 行至海中，海妖與魚群浮起，循著飛猴的影子要將他擒住；他嘲弄牠們，伸爪一探，便繼續前行，直到阿楞卡的塔樓浮現於天際，他才降落下來，身形復歸渺小，落在那羅剎之城的樹林之間。

title.en: Trijata's Dream: Sinta Comforted in the Asoka Garden
title.zh: 特里賈塔之夢：如意林中的慰藉

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin Trijata episode

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: Held in the Asoka garden, Sinta refuses Rawana's suit under threat of death; the rakshasa princess Trijata — who has dreamed Alengka burning and Rawana dragged by monkeys — takes Sinta's side, warns the garden's guards, and comforts her: the omen says the ten-faced king's power is already breaking.
summary.zh: 悉多被囚如意林，拒拉瓦那之求而遭死脅；羅剎公主特里賈塔夜夢阿楞迦烈火焚城、十首王為群猴所曳——遂站到悉多一邊，告誡園中看守，並慰其心：異兆已示十首王氣數將盡。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via relief commentary; the female ally within the enemy city.

passages.text: In the garden of Asoka trees Sinta, guarded by rakshasa women, refuses Rawana's suit even under the threat of the sword. The rakshasa princess Trijata, Rawana's kin but his conscience, has seen in dream the city burning and the ten-faced king dragged headlong by monkeys.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, Trijata episode (Kats 1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在阿輸迦樹園中，辛塔由羅剎女們看守，縱然刀劍相脅，她仍拒絕羅瓦那的求愛。羅剎公主特利賈塔雖為羅瓦那的親族，卻是他良知的化身，她曾在夢中見到城池焚燒、十面王被群猴拖曳而去。

passages.text: She tells Sinta the dream and gives her protection against the garden's tormentors; Sinta, half despondent, half comforted, waits in the garden — the omen has named the outcome of the war before the monkey host has crossed the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她將此夢告訴辛塔，並護她免受園中看守者的欺凌；辛塔半是沮喪、半是安慰，在園中等待——猴軍尚未渡海，這徵兆已預示了戰爭的結局。

title.en: Wibhisana Defects: The Righteous Brother of the Ten-Faced King
title.zh: 維比薩那來歸：十首王之義弟

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin Wibhisana episode

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: Rawana's younger brother Wibhisana, alone at court, counsels returning Sinta and saving Alengka; Rawana denounces him before the assembly, and Wibhisana crosses to Rama's camp, where the monkeys suspect a spy until Rama accepts him as a brother — the Kakawin's figure of the divided family of the rakshasas.
summary.zh: 十首王之弟維比薩那於殿上力諫：還妻以救阿楞迦。拉瓦那當眾斥之；維比薩那遂投羅摩大營——群猴疑其為細作，羅摩以兄弟相待，納之。爪哇詩中，羅剎王族之裂由此始。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via relief commentary.

passages.text: When the war-omen darkens, Wibhisana stands in Rawana's council as the single voice for surrendering Sinta; Rawana publicly reviles him as a traitor before the rakshasa chiefs, and Wibhisana departs over the water to the monkeys' camp. Sugriwa's counselors cry spy, but Rama receives the rakshasa prince, takes his counsel, and accepts him as a brother — the Kakawin lets the defection stand as proof that righteousness, not race, is the measure of kinship in the war for Sinta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, Wibhisana episode (Kats 1919); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當戰爭的凶兆轉暗，維比沙納在羅瓦那的議會中獨持一議，主張交還辛塔；羅瓦那當著羅剎首領們的面公然斥他為叛徒，維比沙納遂渡水前往猴軍之營。蘇格里瓦的謀士們高呼他是間諜，羅摩卻接納了這位羅剎王子，聽取他的諫言，並以兄弟之禮待他——這部《卡卡文》讓這場叛離成為明證：在為辛塔而戰的戰爭中，衡量親疏的尺規是正義，而非族類。

title.en: Kumbakarna Roused: The Sleeper Who Fights His Own King's War
title.zh: 醒來的昆巴卡那：為君而戰的沉睡者

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin Kumbakarna episode

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: When Alengka's armies break, the giants rouse Kumbakarna, the vast brother who sleeps half the year. He first rails at Rawana for bringing ruin on the house by stealing another's wife — then, because he is Rawana's brother, takes up his club for the doomed city and dies fighting the monkeys, ground at last by Rama's arrows.
summary.zh: 阿楞迦軍潰之際，羅剎們喚醒半年沉睡之巨靈昆巴卡那。他先痛斥拉瓦那：劫他人之妻而傾家國！——然身為其弟，終提杵為將亡之城而戰，力戰群猴，卒亡於羅摩箭雨之下。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via relief commentary; the Javanese Kumbakarna is more moralizing than his Indian counterpart, a favourite of wayang.

passages.text: The sleeping giant Kumbakarna must be roused with drums and slaughter as his appetite wakes; told of the war he rebukes Rawana to his face — the abduction of Sinta, he says, will destroy the rakshasa house — yet when the king calls on his loyalty as a brother, the giant takes up his club for Alengka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, Kumbakarna episode (Kats 1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 沉睡的巨人昆巴卡纳须以鼓声与杀戮将他唤醒，因他的食欲随之苏醒；听闻战事，他当面斥责拉瓦纳——他说，掳走辛塔必将毁灭罗刹一族——然而当国王以兄弟之情召唤他的忠诚时，巨人仍为阿楞卡举起他的巨棒。

passages.text: He crashes through the monkey host, devouring and dashing, until Rama's arrows find him; the giant falls denouncing the war he could not refuse. The Kakawin grants him the dignity of the man who tells the truth and then dies for the kinship he is bound by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他冲入猴军之中，吞噬践踏，直至罗摩的箭矢寻到他；巨人倒下，痛斥这场他无法拒绝的战争。《卡卡温》赋予他尊严，使他成为说出真话、而后为血缘羁绊赴死之人。

title.en: The Bridge of Stone Across the Sea
title.zh: 跨海石橋

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin bridge episode

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: The monkey host builds the causeway to Alengka: monkeys, bears and spirits hurl boulders into the strait until a bridge of stone runs across the sea, and Rama's army pours over it — the Kakawin and the Prambanan sculptors alike relish the spectacle of an army of monkeys as engineers.
summary.zh: 猴兵築堤跨海：猿、熊、神魔向海峽擲石，石橋乃成；羅摩大軍踏橋而渡。爪哇頌詩與普蘭巴南石刻同樣沉迷於群猴為工程師之奇觀。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via relief commentary.

passages.text: On the advice of the sea, the army resolves to bridge the strait: monkeys tear up mountains, bears carry boulders, and the stones, thrown into the water, bind together into a causeway that runs to the walls of Alengka. Rama's host crosses the stone bridge in column, the sea churning under the weight of the monkeys, and the rakshasa sentries bring the news to Rawana that the son of Dasa Rata has brought the forest itself against the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, bridge episode (Kats 1919); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 听从大海的建言，大军决意在海峡上架桥：猴子掀翻山岭，熊搬运巨石，石块投入水中，彼此联结成一条直通阿楞卡城墙的堤道。罗摩的大军成列走过石桥，海水在群猴的重压下翻腾，罗刹哨兵将消息报与拉瓦纳：达萨拉塔之子竟将整座森林带到了城前。

title.en: The Ten-Faced King Falls
title.zh: 十首王之死

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕群）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, c. 9th century CE (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); kakawin final battle

license: Public domain (1919); kakawin story content public domain

summary.en: At the last, Rama and Rawana meet on the field: each arrow cut off is answered by a new head or new arms, until Rama's great arrow flies at the one mortal spot. The ten-faced king of Alengka falls, the city mourns its king, and Wibhisana is installed in his place — the kakawin closes its war with the funeral of a magnificent enemy.
summary.zh: 決戰之場，羅摩對拉瓦那：斬一首則生一首，斬一臂則生一臂；直至羅摩神箭射中那唯一之致命處。十首王殞命，滿城舉哀；維比薩那受立為王——爪哇頌詩以一位壯麗敵人之葬禮收束全詩之戰。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase via relief commentary.

passages.text: In the last duel every head and arm Rawana loses grows again, and the battle seems endless; Rama, instructed by the gods' favour and Wibhisana's word, draws the great arrow and aims not at the heads but at the mortal centre of the ten-faced king. Rawana falls, and even the monkeys stand silent at the fall of so great an enemy. Wibhisana performs the funeral and is enthroned in Alengka; Rama, Sinta restored, prepares the return toward Ayodya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, final battle (Kats 1919); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Old Javanese Ramayana kakawin, as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在最后的决斗中，拉瓦纳每失去一头一臂便重新长出，战斗似无止境；罗摩蒙众神眷顾与维比沙纳之言指点，拉开巨弓，不瞄准那些头颅，而瞄准这十面之王的致命要害。拉瓦纳倒下，纵是群猴也在如此强敌的陨落前默然肃立。维比沙纳主持葬礼，并于阿楞卡登位；罗摩迎回辛塔，准备踏上归往阿约迪亚的归途。

title.en: Sinta Through the Fire
title.zh: 悉多歷火

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java (relief cycle and later Javanese wayang versions)
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南（浮雕及爪哇哇揚戲後世版本）

period: Old Javanese Ramayana tradition and Javanese wayang retellings (Kats 1919)

source.work: J. Kats, Het Ramayana op Javaansche tempel reliefs (1919); Javanese Ramayana tradition, fire-ordeal episode

license: Public domain (1919); story content public domain

summary.en: Rescued but publicly doubted, Sinta ascends the pyre herself and calls on Agni to speak her truth: the fire does not burn her, and the god rises with her in his arms to declare her pure. The Javanese tradition gives the ordeal to Sinta's own initiative — the trial that proves her is one she demands.
summary.zh: 悉多雖獲救而遭眾疑，遂自登火堆，呼火神阿耆尼為證：烈焰不傷其身，火神抱之而出，向眾宣告其貞潔。爪哇傳統中，此歷火之判乃悉多自請——證明她的考驗，由她自己發起。

sensitivity.note: Fire-ordeal episode; flagged interpretive on gender — the Javanese versions vary in how the ordeal is framed.

passages.text: Doubt falls on Sinta's year in captivity, and rather than endure it she commands the pyre to be built: ascending the flames herself she calls on Agni, god of fire, as witness of her truth. The pyre burns and leaves her untouched; Agni rises bearing her and proclaims to the host that fire has found nothing to consume. The Kakawin and the wayang alike close the episode on the public vindication of Sinta before the monkey host and the rakshasa captives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Ramayana tradition (fire ordeal), as read in Kats (1919); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Javanese Ramayana tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 辛塔被囚一年的清白蒙上疑云，她不愿忍受此疑，遂命人筑起火葬堆：她亲自登上火焰，呼唤火神阿耆尼为她贞洁作证。火葬堆燃烧，却未伤她分毫；阿耆尼升起，将她托起，向大军宣告火焰一无所获、无可吞噬。《卡卡温》与哇扬戏皆以辛塔在猴军与罗刹俘虏面前公开昭雪而结束此段。

title.en: The Eagle and the Whale
title.zh: 鷹與鯨

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale', eBook #28932

summary.en: Taunted with 'an eagle you shall have' and 'a whale you shall have,' two refusing sisters are each carried off by exactly that husband — the eagle to a high cliff ledge, the whale to a rock. Both plait sinew lines to escape; the brothers kill the eagle with crossbows (the smallest homeless boy's arrow strikes first), and rescue the whale's wife by sea: she ties her restraining string to a stone, and as the pursuing whale closes on their umiak she throws out hairband, mittens, lining, frock, and coat, each swallowed in a burst of foam — the last thing, her breeches, buys them the shore, and the whale is cast up as a sun-bleached bone.
summary.zh: 兄弟戲言『那就讓鷹娶你』『那就讓鯨娶你』，兩位拒婚的姊妹果真被鷹與鯨各自擄走。二人皆編筋索謀逃；兄弟們以弩射殺鷹夫——最小孤兒一箭先中。鯨妻則將拴她的繩繫於石上逃歸；鯨追大舟時，她依次擲出髮帶、手套、手套內襯、外衣、內衣，鯨逐件撲吞，泡沫翻騰；最後一件褲子為船贏得海岸，鯨擱淺為一副日曬白骨。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Animal-husband (bird/whale) type tale; cross-tradition parallel to star-husband and animal-bridegroom tales.

passages.text: In a certain village many brothers had two sisters, both of an age to marry, whom they often urged to take husbands, but the sisters would not. At last one of the men said: 'What sort of a husband do you want, then? An eagle, perhaps? Very well, an eagle you shall have' — and to the other: 'And you perhaps would like a whale? Well, a whale you shall have.' Suddenly a great eagle swooped down on the one girl and flew off with her to a high ledge of rock, and a whale came and carried off the other sister likewise. The eagle and his wife lived on a ledge far up a steep cliff; he flew out over the sea to hunt, sometimes appearing with a walrus in one claw and a narwhal in the other, while his wife plaited sinews for a line wherewith to lower herself down the rock — and one day, trying the line, found it too short, and plaited more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某村中有许多兄弟，他们有两个姊妹，皆已到了婚嫁之年，兄弟们常劝她们择夫出嫁，姊妹俩却不肯。最后其中一名男子说道：『那么，你们想要什么样的丈夫？也许是一只鹰？好吧，就让你们嫁给鹰。』又对另一人说：『你也许想要一头鲸？好吧，就让你们嫁给鲸。』忽然一只巨鹰俯冲而下，抓住其中一个姑娘，带她飞往高处的岩台；一头鲸也游来，同样带走了另一个姊妹。鹰与他的妻子住在陡崖高处的一座岩台上；他飞出海上狩猎，有时一爪抓着海象、一爪抓着独角鲸归来，而他的妻子则搓编筋线，好借此从岩石上垂降而下——有一天她试了试那线，发觉太短，便又搓编了更多。

passages.text: The brothers, longing for their sister, set to work making crossbows, and among them a little homeless boy so small he had not strength to draw a bow, but must get another to draw it for him every time he wanted to shoot. When all was ready they called to her from the foot of the cliff, and as soon as her husband had gone hunting she lowered herself down. Towards evening the eagle appeared out at sea with a walrus in each claw, dropped one down to the brothers, found his wife gone, threw his catch away, and came gliding on widespread wings — but whenever he tried to fly down to the house they shot at him, and none could hit, until the little homeless boy cried 'Let me try too!'; another bent his bow for him, the arrow struck, and as the eagle fluttered down the others shot so many arrows into it that it could not quite touch the ground. Thus they killed their sister's husband, who was a mighty hunter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兄弟們思念姊妹，便動手製作弩弓；其中有一個無家可歸的小男孩，個子小得連拉弓的力氣都沒有，每次想射箭都得叫別人替他拉弓。一切準備妥當後，他們在崖腳下呼喚她，她的丈夫一出門去打獵，她便攀下崖來。到了傍晚，鷹從海上出現，兩爪各抓著一頭海象，扔了一頭給兄弟們，發現妻子不見了，便丟下獵物，展開雙翼滑翔而來——可是每當牠想飛下屋子，他們就朝牠射箭，卻誰也射不中，直到那個無家可歸的小男孩喊道：「讓我也試試！」另一人替他拉開弓，箭射中了，正當鷹撲騰著往下墜時，其餘的人朝牠射了那麼多箭，使牠幾乎碰不到地面。他們就這樣殺死了姊妹的丈夫，那是一個了不起的獵手。

passages.text: The other sister and the whale lived together likewise, the whale so fond of her he would hardly let her out of his sight; she too grew homesick and plaited her sinew line, and her brothers, testing their new-built umiak against a flying guillemot, took the too-slow boat to pieces and built a swift one that beat the bird. When the girl said 'I must go outside a little,' the whale pulled the string tied to her; 'I am only just outside the passage,' she cried — and tied the string to a stone, running down the hill while the whale hauled at the stone thinking it his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另一個姊妹也同樣與鯨同住，那鯨如此喜愛她，幾乎不讓她離開自己的視線；她也想家了，便編起自己的筋線，而她的兄弟們用一隻飛翔的海鳩來試他們新造的烏米亞克皮艇，把那隻太慢的船拆了，另造了一隻快船，賽過了那隻鳥。當姑娘說「我得出去一會兒」時，鯨便拉扯繫在她身上的繩子；「我只是剛到過道外面，」她喊道——隨即把繩子拴在一塊石頭上，奔下山去，而鯨還拉著那塊石頭，以為那就是他的妻子。

passages.text: The brothers fled with her in the umiak, and the whale rolled out into the sea and overhauled them, seeming to make the boat stand still. 'Throw out your hairband' — the sea foamed up and the whale stopped; 'Throw out one of your mittens,' then the mitten's lining, her outer frock, her inner coat — each pounced on in a burst of foam, the boat closer and closer to land — 'Throw out your breeches!' The sea lashed into foam, the umiak reached the land, and the whale, trying to follow, was cast up on the shore as a white and sun-bleached bone of a whale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Eagle and the Whale'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兄弟們帶著她乘烏米亞克皮艇逃走，鯨滾入海中追上了他們，似乎使船停住不動。「把你的髮帶扔出去」——海水翻騰起來，鯨停了下來；「把你的一隻手套扔出去」，接著是手套的襯裡、她的外袍、她的內衣——每一件都被牠在陣陣浪花中撲住，船離陸地越來越近——「把你的褲子扔出去！」海水激成一片泡沫，烏米亞克皮艇靠了岸，而那鯨想要跟來，卻被衝上灘頭，成了一具被陽光曬得發白的鯨骨。

title.en: The Two Little Outcasts and the House That Vanished
title.zh: 兩名棄兒與消失的小屋

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The two little Outcasts', eBook #28932

summary.en: Two orphan boys, whose ptarmigan catches are always taken from them, find in a ravine a fox-skin-covered little house where a lone boy plays kayak-man with a cutting-board; his giant mother returns with a load on her back, feeds them marvelously, and buys one of their arrow-sets with meat enough to carry. Warned — 'Do not let any others come selling arrows' — the villagers go anyway the next day, and the house in the ravine is gone: not a stone, not a shed, no trace of the woman; and that was the last time the boys went out hunting ptarmigan.
summary.zh: 兩名父母雙亡的男孩天天獵雷鳥，獵物卻總被村人奪走。某日他們在峽谷底發現一所覆著藍白狐皮的小屋，屋中獨童以切肉板為皮艇、木棍為槳玩耍；其巨婦之母負重而歸，款待他們，並以滿背肉食購下他們一副箭。臨別告誡：『別讓別人也來賣箭。』村民不聽，次日全都背箭前往——谷中那屋已消失無蹤：不見片瓦、不見棚屋、不見婦人。從此男孩們再也不去獵雷鳥。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The non-human household is a standard Greenlandic otherworld encounter.

passages.text: There were two little boys who had no father and no mother, and went out every day hunting ptarmigan with no weapons save a bow — and the men of the place were always eager to take their catch. One day, finding no ptarmigan, they came to wild difficult cliffs and looked down into a ravine at something that looked like a stone: a little house. Climbing on the roof and looking down through the air hole, they saw a little boy on the floor with a cutting-board for a kayak and a stick for a paddle, playing at being a man in a kayak; twice they called to him before he ran to hide, and they found him inside, sobbing a little, pressing himself close against the wall. 'Do you live here all alone?' 'No, my mother went out early this morning, and she is out now, as usual.' 'We have come to be here with you because you are all alone,' they said, and he ventured out from the wall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The two little Outcasts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有兩個小男孩，沒有父親也沒有母親，每天出去獵雷鳥，除了弓以外別無武器——而當地的人們總是急著要拿走他們的獵物。有一天，他們找不到雷鳥，來到險峻的荒野崖邊，俯視一道深谷，看見一個像石頭的東西：一座小屋。他們爬上屋頂，從天窗往下看，只見屋裡地上有個小男孩，拿一塊砧板當皮艇、一根棍子當槳，玩著扮作乘皮艇的人；他們喚了他兩次，他才跑去躲起來，他們在屋裡找到他，他正微微抽泣，緊緊貼著牆。「你一個人住在這裡嗎？」「不，我母親今天一早就出去了，她現在還在外面，跟平常一樣。」「我們來這裡陪你，因為你孤零零的一個人，」他們說，他便從牆邊壯著膽子走了出來。

passages.text: Toward evening the boy said, 'Now I can see her, away to the south' — and they saw a mighty big figure with something on her back coming quickly nearer, throwing down her burden with a great noise. She came in hot and tired: 'Thanks, kind little boys. I had to leave him alone in the house, as usual, and now you have stayed with him while I was fearing for him on my way.' She brought dried flesh of fox and reindeer and a big piece of suet, and the fox meat proved wonderfully good to eat. The little boy whispered in her ear — he had a great desire for one of their sets of arrows — and they gave it. When the outcasts set off home, she paid them with as much meat as they could carry and warned them: 'Be sure you do not let any others come selling arrows.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The two little Outcasts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了傍晚，那男孩說：「現在我能看見她了，在南邊遠處」——他們看見一個高大的身影背著什麼東西，正迅速走近，把背上的重物砰然放下。她氣喘吁吁、疲憊不堪地走進來：「謝謝你們，好心的小男孩們。我不得不像平常一樣把他一個人留在家裡，如今你們在我一路為他擔心的時候陪著他。」她帶來狐狸和馴鹿的乾肉，還有一大塊板油，那狐狸肉吃起來竟出奇地美味。小男孩在她耳邊低聲說了幾句——他非常想要他們的一套箭——他們便給了他。當這兩個棄兒動身回家時，她用他們拿得動的那麼多肉酬謝他們，並告誡道：「千萬別讓任何別的人來賣箭。」

passages.text: The village received the returning boys with astonishment at their load; the food was wonderfully good to eat. 'That we were given in payment for one set of arrows,' they said. 'We must certainly go out and sell arrows, too,' said the others, and although the two told them the warning — 'Do not let any others come selling arrows' — all fell to making arrows at once and set out the next day, the little outcasts going in despite of their desire, because the others ordered them. When they came to the ravine, the house was no longer there: not a stone of it, not the two sheds, nothing; and no one could tell where that woman had gone. And that was the last time they went out hunting ptarmigan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The two little Outcasts'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 村裡的人見兩個男孩歸來，對他們帶回的東西大為驚訝；那食物吃起來出奇地美味。「這是一套箭換來的，是人家給我們的，」他們說。「我們也一定得出去賣箭，」其他人說，儘管那兩人把告誡告訴了他們——「千萬別讓任何別的人來賣箭」——大家還是立刻動手做箭，第二天就出發了，那兩個小棄兒雖然不情願，也只得跟著去，因為別人命令他們。當他們來到那道深谷時，屋子已經不在了：連一塊石頭都沒有，那兩間棚屋也沒有，什麼都沒有；誰也說不出那女人去了哪裡。而那便是他們最後一次出去獵雷鳥。

title.en: Atdlarneq, the Great Glutton
title.zh: 大胃王阿德勒涅克

region.en: West Greenland coast
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸

period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Atdlarneq, the great glutton', eBook #28932

summary.en: The strongman Atdlarneq, who never failed to catch a seal, loiters south instead and finds a house where three yellow-seamed women come out one by one — and their master, whose cheeks are made of copper, smells him the moment he hides. Forced to eat a sack of fish, half a black seal's blubber, the frozen half, and a whole seal, drinking the water bucket to the last drop, he survives thanks to a swallowed grass stalk that made room — and never goes southward again.
summary.zh: 從不失手的力士阿德勒涅克這天卻沿岸南游，撞見一戶人家——三名黃色滾邊的婦人一一出屋，她們的銅腮主人一下便嗅出躲藏的他，逼他吃光一袋魚、半扇黑海豹油脂、凍肉半扇、整隻海豹，喝乾水桶。幸而他開吃前吞了一根草莖騰出胃袋，才沒被撐死。自此他再也不敢南行。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Copper-cheeks (Qerreripag) is a bogey figure of Greenlandic folklore, per the source's note.

passages.text: Atdlarneq was a strong man: if he rowed but a little way out in his kayak he caught a seal, and was never content with only one. But one day, instead of hunting seal, he paddled close along the shore making south, and sighted a little house on the sunny side of a cape. A woman came out — a yellow band round her hair, yellow seams to all her clothes — and he waited for another; another came out, the same; then a third, quite like the others, bearing a dish in her hand. Then at last he went on shore, and they received him very kindly, bringing great quantities of food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atdlarneq, the great glutton'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿特德拉爾內克是個強壯的人：他只要划著皮艇出去不遠，就能捕到一隻海豹，而且從不滿足於只捕一隻。可是有一天，他沒有去獵海豹，卻沿著海岸向南划行，看見一座海角向陽的一面有一間小屋。一個女人走了出來——她頭髮上繞著一條黃帶，所有衣服的縫線也都是黃的——他等著另一個出來；又出來一個，打扮一模一樣；接著第三個也出來了，和其餘的完全一樣，手裡端著一隻盤子。最後他終於上了岸，她們非常親切地接待他，拿來大量的食物。

passages.text: In the evening the three women began going outside again and again, and when he asked why, all answered at once: 'It is because we now expect our dear master home.' Afraid, Atdlarneq hid behind the skin hangings — and the master came, his cheeks made of copper, sniffing: 'Hum! There is a smell of people here.' Crawling out, he was received eagerly: 'Has he had nothing to eat yet? Then bring food at once.' A sack full of fish and a big piece of blubber from the half of a black seal, and a violent command: 'You are to eat this all up, and if you do not eat it all up, I will thrash you with my copper cheeks!' He chewed and chewed, ate it all up, drank the water bucket to the last drop, then ate the frozen half-seal, then a whole black seal, until there was no more left, and again emptied the bucket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atdlarneq, the great glutton'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了晚上，那三個女人一次又一次地往外走，他問為什麼，她們異口同聲地回答：「因為我們現在正等著我們親愛的主人回家。」阿特德拉爾內克害怕起來，躲到皮帳簾後面——主人回來了，他的雙頰是銅做的，抽著鼻子聞：「哼！這裡有人的氣味。」他爬了出來，受到熱切的接待：「他還沒吃過東西嗎？那就立刻把食物拿來。」一整袋魚，一大塊取自半隻黑海豹的鯨脂，還有一道嚴厲的命令：「你要把這些全吃光，要是你不全吃光，我就用我的銅頰揍你！」他嚼了又嚼，全吃光了，把水桶喝到最後一滴，接著吃了那半隻凍海豹，又吃了一整隻黑海豹，直到一點不剩，然後又喝空了水桶。

passages.text: After all that he felt very well indeed, and seemed hardly to have eaten until now — because he had swallowed a little stalk of grass before he began, which made room in him. So Atdlarneq slept, and next morning went back home; but after having thus nearly gorged himself to death, he never went southward again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atdlarneq, the great glutton'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吃過這一切之後，他覺得非常舒服，彷彿直到此刻才真正吃過東西——因為他在開始之前先吞下了一小根草莖，這在他肚裡騰出了地方。於是阿特德拉爾內克睡下了，第二天早晨回家去了；但自從這樣幾乎把自己撐死之後，他就再也不往南去了。

title.en: Angangujuk, Lost to the Inland Folk
title.zh: 安甘古茹克被內陸人抱走

region.en: Godthaab (Nuuk), West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭努克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Angangujuk', eBook #28932

summary.en: Playing kayak-man in the passage, little Angangujuk vanishes from his mother's callings. His furious father blames her, hunts down wizards, and at last finds a spirit-finder who sends word: the child is up between two great cliffs, in the care of two old inland folk. Journeying east, they come on smoking houses where the tornit quarrel over who shall keep the boy; a magic sleep is called down sleeper by sleeper until the last yawns, the child is snatched (his clothes poked down with poles from the high drying frame), and the umiak rows for the farthest islands while the inlanders beat their own house down in fury.
summary.zh: 小安甘古茹克在甬道裡扮演皮艇手，忽然應聲消失。父親遷怒母親，遍訪巫師，終得通靈者指路：孩子就在兩座巨崖之間，由兩名內陸老人照看。一行東行至炊煙裊裊的屋群——托尼特人正為誰撫養孩子爭執不休。巫師逐一施下沉睡咒，連最後一人也打呵欠倒下；父親奪回赤身的兒子，晾架太高，須用長杆把衣裳捅下來。大舟疾駛遠島，內陸人怒而拆屋。自此他們再不住大陸。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. The inland-folk child-stealing motif is presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Angangujuk's father was very strong, and the three of them lived alone without other neighbours. One day the mother, scraping meat from a skin, let the child play at kayak outside in the passage, near the entrance, calling to him now and again: 'Angangujuk!' — and the child answered from outside. Once there came no answer; she left the skin and searched about, but could not find the child, and began to feel greatly afraid, dreading her husband's return. When he came out from behind a rock dragging a seal, he asked where their little son was, and on her answer — that he had vanished while playing kayak-man in the passage — he answered: 'It is you, wicked old hag, who have killed him. And now I will kill you.' She begged him to wait and first seek out one who could ask counsel of the spirits; he brought home wizards, and let them go without so much as a bite of meat when they could not find the child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Angangujuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安岡古尤克的父親非常強壯，他們三人獨自住著，沒有別的鄰居。有一天，母親正從一張皮子上刮肉，讓孩子在門外通道裡、靠近入口的地方玩皮艇的遊戲，不時朝他喊：「安岡古尤克！」——孩子就在外面應聲。有一次卻沒有回應；她放下皮子四處尋找，卻找不到孩子，開始非常害怕，生怕丈夫回來。當他從一塊岩石後面拖著一隻海豹出來，問他們的小兒子在哪裡，聽了她的回答——說他在通道裡玩皮艇人的遊戲時不見了——他便答道：「是你這個惡毒的老婆子殺了他。現在我要殺了你。」她求他等一等，先去找一個能向神靈請教的人；他帶回了巫師們，當他們找不到孩子時，他連一口肉都沒讓他們吃就把他們打發走了。

passages.text: At last he found a very clever finder of hidden things, fastened a stick to his face, and made him lie on the bedplace working until the spirit came. The spirit finder declared: 'It would seem that spirits have here found a difficult task. He is up in a place between two great cliffs, and two old inland folk are looking after him.' They wandered away towards the east until they sighted many houses with smoke coming out of all the smoke holes; through the window the father saw they were quarrelling about his child, who was crying, each one eager to have him. Asked what he would like to eat, the child refused everything; asked if he wanted to go home very much, Angangujuk answered quickly: 'Yes.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Angangujuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後他找到一個非常擅長尋找隱藏之物的能手，把一根棍子綁在他臉上，讓他躺在床鋪上施法，直到神靈降臨。那尋靈者宣稱：「看來神靈們在此遇到了一件難事。他在兩座巨崖之間的一處地方，有兩個內陸的老人在照看他。」他們往東走了很久，直到望見許多房屋，所有的煙孔都冒著煙；父親透過窗戶看見他們正為他的孩子爭吵，孩子哭著，每個人都爭著要他。問他想吃什麼，孩子什麼都不要；問他是不是很想回家，安岡古尤克立刻回答：「想。」

passages.text: 'Try now to magic them to sleep,' said the father, and the wizard began calling down a magic sleep upon those in the hut, one by one sinking to sleep and snoring, until only two remained awake; then one yawned and rolled over, and at last the great finder of hidden things called down sleep with all his might over the last one, who also rolled over. Angangujuk's father went in quickly and caught up his son — naked; his clothes hung on a drying frame so high they had to poke them down with poles. They came out, walked far, cut the moorings of the umiak, and rowed out to the farthest islands; the inland folk, seeing them gone, went up to the house and beat down roof and walls and all there was of it. After that time Angangujuk's parents never again took up their dwelling on the mainland.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Angangujuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「現在試著施法讓他們睡著，」父親說，於是巫師開始向屋裡那些人降下催眠的魔法，他們一個接一個沉入睡眠、打起鼾來，直到只剩兩個還醒著；接著一個打了個哈欠翻過身去，最後那位偉大的尋隱者竭盡全力向最後一個降下睡眠，那一個也翻了過去。安岡古尤克的父親迅速走進去，抱起他的兒子——光著身子；他的衣服掛在晾衣架上，高得他們不得不用竿子把它戳下來。他們出來，走了很遠，割斷了烏米亞克大船的纜繩，划到最遠的島嶼去；那些內陸人見他們走了，便走到那屋子前，把屋頂、牆壁以及所有的一切都打塌了。自那以後，安岡古尤克的父母再也不在大陸上居住了。

title.en: Atarssuaq's Son, the Seal-Skinned Swimmer
title.zh: 阿塔舒亞克之子：海豹皮泳者

region.en: Godthaab (Nuuk), West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭努克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Atarssuaq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Unable to be killed by his many enemies, Atarssuaq trains his newborn son by daily dunkings, then in a fjord-seal skin dried like a bladder; the boy becomes so clever a diver his father weeps for fear of sharks. When the enemies kill Atarssuaq and many kayaks come north to finish the family, the boy lures them out to sea by surfacing and vanishing, climbs a grounded iceberg, topples each wave of climbers with a great piece of ice, drowns the kayaks, and spares the last — a weeping man armed with only a fish-killing stick — with a warning never to come again.
summary.zh: 仇人殺不死阿塔舒亞克，他便把新生兒日日拋水練泳，再讓他穿上如膀胱般晾乾的海豹皮；少年潛水之巧，令父親一度哭怕鯊魚。父親被害後，北方大隊皮艇來襲，少年時隱時現誘其出海，攀上擱淺冰山，以巨冰逐一砸落攀爬者，又拽翻皮艇、按人入水。最後一名——只持殺魚棍、泣不成聲的男子——被他放回，並留下警告：再來者無一生還。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Killing raid presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Atarssuaq had many enemies who tried in vain to hurt him, for they could not kill him. When his wife bore him a son, he bore the child down to the water and threw him in, waited until he kicked out violently, and took him up again — doing so every day for long after while the child grew, so that the boy became a very clever swimmer. Atarssuaq once caught a fjord seal, took off the skin all in one piece, dried it like a bladder, and made his son put it on when he went swimming. To see how clever the boy had become, he followed him out to sea in his kayak, the boy swimming more and more under water, disappearing each time the father raised his throwing stick; sent to keep under water as much as he could for a long way, the boy stayed down so long that the father, afraid, had just begun to cry — 'If only the sharks have not found him!' — when his son came up again, and they went in to land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atarssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿塔爾蘇阿克有許多敵人，他們千方百計想傷害他，卻都徒勞無功，因為他們殺不了他。他的妻子為他生下一個兒子後，他便把孩子抱到水邊，扔進水裡，等他猛烈地蹬踢起來，才又把他抱起來——此後很長一段時間裡，孩子日漸長大，他每天都這樣做，於是這男孩成了非常靈巧的游泳好手。有一次，阿塔爾蘇阿克捕到一頭峽灣海豹，把皮整張剝下來，像膀胱一樣吹乾，讓兒子去游泳時把它套在身上。為了看看兒子究竟變得多麼靈巧，他划著皮艇跟隨兒子出海；男孩越來越往水下潛，每次父親舉起投擲棒，他便消失不見；他被吩咐盡可能長久地潛在水下，游出很遠一段路，男孩在水下待得太久，父親害怕起來，剛要哭喊——「但願鯊魚沒有找到他！」——他的兒子便又浮了上來，於是他們一起划回岸上。

passages.text: One day his father did not come back from hunting, because his enemies had killed him. Evening came, and next morning a kayak from the north put in: 'To-morrow the many brothers will come to kill you all' — and turned at once and went back. In the morning many kayaks appeared from the northward, and the boy, told by his mother to put on his swimming dress, went down to the shore, close to the water; the kayaks rowed towards him saying he had fallen in, searched about for him, and he came up just in front of the bone shoeing on the nose of one kayak, dived down again, and so led all those kayaks out to the open sea. There he sighted a grounded iceberg, climbed it by sticking his hands into the ice, heard them propose to cut steps up to him, and waited until the head of the foremost came over the edge before letting fall a great piece of ice that sent them all down; again they crawled up, again the ice fell, and all who had climbed on were killed, lured on by him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atarssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他的父親打獵沒有回來，因為敵人把他殺死了。傍晚來臨，第二天早晨，一隻皮艇從北方靠岸：「明天，那眾多兄弟要來把你們全都殺死」——說完立刻掉頭回去了。早晨，許多皮艇從北方出現，男孩聽母親的話穿上泳裝，走到岸邊，緊挨著水；那些皮艇朝他划來，說他掉進水裡了，四處搜尋他，他卻正好在一隻皮艇船首骨製包皮的前面浮上來，又潛了下去，就這樣把那些皮艇全都引向外海。他在那裡望見一座擱淺的冰山，把手插進冰裡爬了上去，聽見他們打算鑿出台階爬上他這裡，便一直等到最前面那人的頭探過冰緣，才扔下一大塊冰，把他們全都打落下去；他們又爬上來，冰塊又落下，凡是爬上來的人都被他引誘著送了命。

passages.text: The others turned back, saying he would kill them all if they did not go; the boy jumped down, swam to the kayaks, and began tugging at their paddles till they turned over, the men righting themselves with their throwing sticks, until he was forced to hold them down himself under water till they drowned. Of all those many kayaks only one was left, a man with no weapon but a stick for killing fish, who rowed weeping in towards land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atarssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其餘的人掉頭回去，說若不走，他會把他們全都殺死；男孩跳下水，游到皮艇邊，開始拉扯他們的槳，直到皮艇翻覆，那些人用投擲棒把自己扶正，最後他只好親自把他們按在水下，直到他們溺死。那許多皮艇中只剩下一隻，划艇的人除了一根殺魚的棍子外別無武器，他哭著向陸地划去。

passages.text: The boy pulled the paddle away from him, and the man began paddling with his hands; the boy gripped his hands from below until he dared no longer put them in the water at all, weeping greatly: 'It is ill for me that ever I came out on this errand, for it is plain that I am to be killed.' The boy looked at him a little, and said: 'You I will not kill. You may go home again' — giving back his paddle and calling after him: 'Tell those of your place never to come out again thinking to kill us. For if they do not one of them will return alive.' None ever came against them after that time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Atarssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男孩把槳從他手裡奪走，那人便用手划起來；男孩從下面抓住他的雙手，直到他再也不敢把手伸進水裡，放聲大哭：「我出來辦這趟差事，真是倒楣，因為看來我分明是要被殺死的。」男孩看了他一會兒，說道：「你，我不殺。你可以回家去了」——把槳還給他，又在他身後喊道：「告訴你們那裡的人，再也不要出來，妄想殺我們。因為他們若來，沒有一個能活著回去。」此後再沒有人來與他們為敵。

title.en: Puagssuaq and the Whistling Visitor
title.zh: 普瓦克舒克與吹哨訪客

region.en: Godthaab (Nuuk), West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭努克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Puagssuaq', eBook #28932

summary.en: A wifeless ptarmigan-hunter finds in a rocky valley a house like a stone where an old couple sits alone. He whistles twice; the husband nudges his wife — 'You, Puagssuaq, you can talk with the spirits' — then, at the third whistle, decides the sound is 'the voice of a shore-dweller; one who catches miserable fish.' The wife lets down her hair to call the spirits, and the passage way begins closing around the unseen visitor; it opens of itself, he slips out, and runs the whole hillside home without ever being pursued.
summary.zh: 以獵雷鳥為生的無妻者誤入巖谷中一所石屋般的小屋，屋內一對老夫婦獨坐。他吹了兩聲口哨，老翁推了推老伴：『普瓦克舒克，你能通靈，快去問問。』第三聲哨響，老翁凝神道：『聽！倒像是海濱人的聲音——一個只會捕可憐小魚的傢伙。』老嫗披髮欲召靈，甬道已無聲收攏，將合未合之際忽然自開，他趁隙溜出，一路狂奔上山——竟無人追來。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Whistling as spirit-call is a documented Greenlandic practice.

passages.text: There was once a wifeless man who always went out hunting ptarmigan, every day. One day, from a place whence he could see out over a rocky valley that looked good to go into, he went down; before he had come to the bottom he caught sight of something that looked like a stone — and when he could see quite clearly it was not a stone at all, he walked up to it. Looking in, he saw an old couple sitting alone inside; he crawled very silently in through the passage way, looked at them a long time, and gave a little whistle. Nothing happened, so he whistled a second time, and now they heard it: the man nudged his wife and said, 'You, Puagssuaq, you can talk with the spirits. Take counsel with them now.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Puagssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個沒有妻子的人，天天出去打雷鳥。有一天，他從一個能望見一片岩石山谷的地方走下去，那山谷看上去很值得一探；還沒走到谷底，他就瞥見一樣東西，看上去像塊石頭——等他看得清清楚楚，那根本不是石頭，便朝它走去。往裡一看，他看見一對老夫婦獨自坐在裡面；他悄無聲息地從通道爬進去，看了他們很久，輕輕吹了一聲口哨。沒有動靜，於是他又吹了第二聲，這回他們聽見了：老頭碰了碰妻子，說道：「你呀，普阿格蘇阿克，你能和神靈說話。現在就向他們請教吧。」

passages.text: At the third whistle the old man looked at his wife again and said earnestly: 'Listen! It sounds as if that might be the voice of a shore-dweller; one who catches miserable fish.' The wifeless man saw the old woman letting down her hair, because she was about to ask counsel of the spirits — and then saw the passage way about him beginning to close up, already nearly closed. But then it opened again of itself; thinking only of coming out from that place, he slipped out when it opened, and began running as fast as he could. For a long time he ran on, with the thought that someone would surely come after him — but he came up the hillside without having been pursued at all, went home, and told what had happened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Puagssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 吹到第三聲口哨時，老頭又看了看妻子，懇切地說：「聽！聽起來那也許是住在岸邊的人的聲音；一個專捕可憐魚兒的人。」那沒有妻子的人看見老婦人把頭髮放下來，因為她正要向神靈請教——接著又看見他周圍的通道開始合攏，已經幾乎合上了。可隨後它又自行張開；他一心只想著離開那個地方，趁它張開時溜了出去，拔腿拼命奔跑。他跑了很久，心想必定有人追來——可他一路跑上山坡，竟全然無人追趕，回到家裡，把發生的事講述了一遍。

title.en: Tungujuluk and Saunikoq: The Bear and the Walrus
title.zh: 通古茹盧克與薩烏尼洛克：熊與海象

region.en: Godthaab (Nuuk), West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭努克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Tungujuluk and Saunikoq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Two village wizards, one turning bear at spirit-callings and the other walrus. Childless Saunikoq, jealous of Tungujuluk's kayaking son, stalks the boy in bearskin — and laughs away the father's knife just in time. Tungujuluk waits many days, then takes walrus shape himself, lets Saunikoq harpoon him, folds the bladder float under his arm, and rows home to hold a meat feast where he lays the recovered bladder and line beside the dish: 'Aha, at last I have paid you for the time when you came in the shape of a bear, and mocked us.' Saunikoq rows north in his umiak and is never seen again, so great was his shame.
summary.zh: 同村兩巫師：降靈時一化熊、一化海象。膝下無子的薩烏尼洛克妒忌通古茹盧克會划艇的兒子，披熊皮暗伏欲殺——父親舉刀之際，熊開口大笑，他才認出是鄰人，強自收刀。多日後，通古茹盧克自化海象，任其叉中，挾浮囊而泳歸，設宴將浮囊繩線擺在肉盤旁：『啊哈，你扮熊來嘲弄我們的帳，今日總算還清。』滿座大笑；薩烏尼洛克羞愧難當，次日清早駕大舟北去，從此無人再見。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Wizard shape-shifting (bear/walrus skins) is documented angakok practice.

passages.text: Tungujuluk and Saunikoq were men from one village, and both were wizards: when they heard a spirit calling, one would change into a bear, and the other into a walrus. Tungujuluk had a son, but Saunikoq had no children; and as soon as the boy was old enough, Tungujuluk taught him to paddle a kayak, at which Saunikoq grew jealous and began planning evil. One morning he went out hunting seal as usual, went up to an island, called for his bearskin, got into it, and moved off towards Tungujuluk's house, landing a little way off and stealing up to kill the son — not knowing the father had already come home and was sitting busily at work on the kayak he was making for his boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Tungujuluk and Saunikoq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 通古尤盧克與紹尼科克是同一個村莊的人，兩人都是巫師：當他們聽見精靈呼喚時，一個會變成熊，另一個會變成海象。通古尤盧克有一個兒子，但紹尼科克沒有子女；男孩一到了夠大的年紀，通古尤盧克便教他划獨木舟，紹尼科克因此心生嫉妒，開始謀劃惡事。有一天早晨，他如往常一樣出海獵海豹，登上了一座島，呼喚他的熊皮，鑽進皮中，朝通古尤盧克的家而去，在稍遠處上岸，悄悄潛近，要殺死那個兒子——卻不知道父親早已回家，正坐著忙於製作要給兒子用的獨木舟。

passages.text: Just as the big bear came close, the boy went weeping home to his father, who looked round, took a knife, and ran towards it, about to stab — when it began to laugh. Tungujuluk remembered that his neighbour Saunikoq was able to take the shape of a bear, and was now so angry that he had nearly stabbed him in spite of all, holding back his knife only with difficulty. But he did not forget. Many days later he went out in his kayak, went up on an island, called his other shape to him, crawled into it, and became a walrus; then he went where it was the custom for kayaks to hunt seal, rose to the surface quite near Saunikoq, made himself small, and crept over to one side of the skin so the stroke could not fail. Struck, he floundered but not too violently lest he break the line, swam away under water with the bladder float, folded it up under his arm, took out the air, and swam in to land near where his kayak lay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Tungujuluk and Saunikoq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正當那頭大熊走近時，男孩哭著跑回家找父親，父親回頭一看，拿起一把刀，朝牠奔去，正要刺下——牠卻開始笑了起來。通古尤盧克想起鄰居紹尼科克能化為熊的形貌，此刻氣得幾乎不顧一切要刺他，好不容易才收住了刀。但他並沒有忘記。許多天之後，他划著獨木舟出海，登上了一座島，呼喚他的另一形貌前來，爬進其中，變成一頭海象；接著他前往獨木舟慣常獵海豹的地方，在離紹尼科克很近處浮出水面，把自己縮小，悄悄爬到皮筏的一側，好讓這一擊萬無一失。被擊中後，他翻騰掙扎，卻不敢太過猛烈，以免扯斷繩索，帶著浮囊潛水游開，把浮囊摺疊夾在腋下，放出空氣，然後游向岸邊，在他獨木舟停泊處附近登陸。

passages.text: He took the harpoon point out, went out hunting, struck a black seal, rowed home at once, and made his wife cook the breast piece; when the other kayaks came home he made a meat feast, and Saunikoq, thinking nothing of any matter, came in with the others. They ate and were satisfied, and each man told of his day's hunting, until Saunikoq said: 'To-day, when I struck a walrus, I did not think at all that it should cause me to lose my bladder float. Where that came up again is a thing we do not know. That bladder float of mine was lost.' Then Tungujuluk took the bladder and line from his kayak, laid them beside the meat dish, and said: 'Whose can this bladder be, now, I wonder? Aha, at last I have paid you for the time when you came in the shape of a bear, and mocked us.' The many who sat there laughed greatly; Saunikoq got up and went away, and next morning very early set out and rowed northward in his umiak, and since then he has not been seen — so great a shame did he feel.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Tungujuluk and Saunikoq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他取下魚叉尖，出海打獵，擊中一頭黑海豹，立刻划船回家，叫妻子煮那塊胸肉；當其他獨木舟歸來時，他擺了一場肉宴，紹尼科克不疑有他，隨眾人一同進來。他們吃飽喝足，每個人都講述自己當天打獵的經過，直到紹尼科克說：「今天我擊中一頭海象時，壓根沒想到那會害我丟了浮囊。那浮囊後來在哪裡浮上來，我們並不知道。我那個浮囊丟了。」於是通古尤盧克從他的獨木舟上取下浮囊和繩索，擺在肉盤旁邊，說道：「我倒想知道，這浮囊現在會是誰的呢？啊哈，我終於報復了你化作熊形前來嘲弄我們的那一次。」在座的許多人哄堂大笑；紹尼科克起身離去，第二天一早便出發，划著他的大皮船向北而去，此後再沒有人見過他——他感到的羞恥竟如此之深。

title.en: Anarteq, Who Became a Salmon and Came Back
title.zh: 化鮭復歸的阿納特克

region.en: Godthaab (Nuuk), West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭努克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Anarteq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Drowned playing with a reindeer calf he had struck in the lake, Anarteq wakes as a salmon; his old father, left to hunt like a young man, returns years later to the abandoned fjord and weeps for his son. The salmon coming up from the sea takes hold of the father's steering paddle — twice, the second time so the slow raising of the paddle draws the son up with it — and Anarteq becomes a man again, hunting many years to feed his kin.
summary.zh: 阿納特克在湖中戲弄被自己擊中的馴鹿幼崽，反被踢翻皮艇溺斃，醒來已化身鮭魚。老父失去獨子，只得像年輕人般親自出獵，多年後重返故地，峽灣深處垂淚思子。海中隨群而上遊的鮭魚游近大舟，銜住父親的舵槳——第一次嚇得父親收槳，第二次他緩緩上提，竟連兒子一併提出水面——阿納特克復為人身，此後多年捕獵養家。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Human-salmon transformation is part of West Greenland reincarnation belief.

passages.text: There was once an old man who had only one son, called Anarteq, and many daughters, all fond of going out reindeer hunting to the eastward in a fjord. At the base of the fjord Anarteq let his sisters drive the reindeer up the hillside so that the beasts came out into a big lake, where he could row out in his kayak and kill them all; in a few days they had their umiak filled with meat. One day, the reindeer having swum out and Anarteq striking them down, he saw a calf, caught hold of it by the tail and began to play with it — but suddenly the reindeer heaved up its body above the surface of the water and kicked at the kayak so that it turned over. He could not get up, because the kayak was full of water; at last he crawled out of it, and the women on shore could not get out to help him. 'Now the salmon are beginning to eat my belly,' they heard him say, and very slowly he went to the bottom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Anarteq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個老人，只有一個兒子，名叫阿納爾特克，還有許多女兒，她們都喜歡到東邊一處峽灣去獵馴鹿。在峽灣底部，阿納爾特克讓姊妹們把馴鹿趕上山坡，使鹿群跑進一個大湖裡，他便可划著獨木舟出去把牠們全部殺死；幾天之內，他們的大皮船就裝滿了肉。有一天，馴鹿游了出去，阿納爾特克正將牠們一一刺倒，他看見一頭小鹿，便抓住牠的尾巴玩弄起來——不料那馴鹿突然把身子抬出水面，朝獨木舟踢去，把船踢翻了。他爬不起來，因為獨木舟裡灌滿了水；最後他從船裡爬了出來，岸上的女人們卻無法出去救他。她們聽見他說：「現在鮭魚開始吃我的肚子了。」他便極其緩慢地沉到了水底。

passages.text: When Anarteq woke again to his senses he had become a salmon. His father was obliged to go back alone, and from that time, having no son, he had to go out hunting as if he had been a young man, never again rowing up to those reindeer grounds. Anarteq, now a salmon, went with the others in the spring, when the rivers break up, out into the sea to grow fat. But his father, greatly wishing to go once more to their old hunting grounds, went there again as chief of a party after many years had passed, his daughters rowing for him; and when they came near the base of the fjord he thought of his son and began to weep. His son, coming up from the sea with the other salmon, saw the umiak and his father in it weeping, swam to it, and caught hold of the paddle with which his father steered — and the father, greatly frightened, drew the paddle out of the water, saying: 'Anarteq had nearly pulled the paddle from my hand that time.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Anarteq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當阿納爾特克再度恢復知覺時，他已變成了一條鮭魚。他的父親只得獨自回去，從那時起，因為沒有了兒子，他得像年輕人一樣出海打獵，再也不曾划船到那些馴鹿獵場去。阿納爾特克如今是條鮭魚，春天河流解凍時，便與其他鮭魚一同游入海中長肥。但他的父親非常想再去一次他們舊日的獵場，於是許多年過去後，他又率領一隊人前往，由女兒們為他划船；當他們接近峽灣底部時，他想起兒子，便哭了起來。他的兒子與其他鮭魚從海中游上來，看見大皮船和船中哭泣的父親，便游過去，抓住父親用來掌舵的槳——父親大為驚恐，把槳從水中抽起，說道：「這一回阿納爾特克差點把槳從我手裡拉走了。」

passages.text: For a long while he did not venture to put his paddle in the water again; when he did at last, he saw that all his daughters were weeping, and a second time Anarteq swam quickly up to the umiak. Again the father tried to draw in his paddle when the son took hold of it, but this time he could not move it — then at last he drew it quite slowly to the surface, in such a way that he drew his son up with it. And then Anarteq became a man again, and hunted for many years to feed his kin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Anarteq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有好長一段時間，他不敢再把槳放入水中；等他終於放下去時，看見所有的女兒都在哭泣，阿納爾特克第二次迅速游向大皮船。兒子抓住槳時，父親又想把它抽回來，但這一次他怎麼也拉不動——最後他才極其緩慢地把槳提到水面，就這樣把兒子也一起拉了上來。於是阿納爾特克又變回了人，此後許多年間打獵供養他的親族。

title.en: The Guillemot That Could Talk
title.zh: 會說話的海鳩

region.en: Godthaab (Nuuk), West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭努克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Guillemot that could talk', eBook #28932

summary.en: A wifeless man rows north from the south to hear the talking guillemot of the bird cliffs. At the foot of a mightily big cliff his guide points out the nest; the bird comes out, stretches itself very long, stares down at the kayaks, and says quite clearly: 'This, I think, must be that southern man, who has come far from a place in the south to hear a guillemot.' The southerner falls forward on his face, dead of fright. Buried below the nest, he has no grave-marker but the bird's; and his widowless crew winter there, fed by him — his soul, the teller hints, still catching fish for the umiak's women until they keep him south as a husband.
summary.zh: 無妻男子自南方北行，只為一聽傳說中會說話的海鳩。巨大鳥崖之下，嚮導指向鳥巢；海鳩出巢，伸長身子俯瞰皮艇，清楚說道：『想必這就是那位南方人，不遠千里來聽海鳩說話。』南方人撲面倒地，活活嚇死。他被葬於鳥巢之下；其大舟上的婦人們在此過冬，靠『他』捕魚為生——次年南歸時，眾人不肯放他北返，無妻的他遂在南方娶妻成家。

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Talking-bird motif; the teller's joke about the dead man procuring food marks the tale's comic-macabre register.

passages.text: A man from the south heard one day of a guillemot that could talk, to be found somewhere in the north, and set off northward, toiling along in an umiak. At a village he asked the way — 'Three days' journey away you will find it' — stayed only the night, went on, and at the next village one of the men offered to be his guide. They rowed until they came in sight of a mightily big bird cliff, and at its foot the guide said: 'Here, here is the nest of that guillemot bird.' The man prepared to be very careful when the bird came out; it came out, went to the side of the cliff, stared down at the kayaks, stretching its body to make it very long, and sitting up there said quite clearly: 'This, I think, must be that southern man, who has come far from a place in the south to hear a guillemot.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Guillemot that could talk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 南方有一個人，有一天聽說北方某處有一隻會說話的海鳩，便動身往北去，划著一艘烏米亞克船（umiak，一種大型皮船）一路辛勞前行。到了某個村落，他問路——「再走三天的路程你就會找到牠」——他只過了一夜便繼續上路；到了下一個村落，其中一個男人願意替他帶路。他們划著船，直到望見一座極其巨大的鳥崖，帶路的人在崖腳下說：「這裡，這裡就是那隻海鳩鳥的巢。」那人準備好，等鳥出來時要萬分小心；鳥出來了，走到崖邊，俯視著下方的獨木舟（kayak），把身子伸得極長，端坐在那裡清清楚楚地說：「這想必就是那個南方人吧，他從南方某處遠道而來，只為聽一隻海鳩說話。」

passages.text: The bird had hardly spoken when the guide saw that the man from the south had fallen forward on his face, dead — having died of fright at hearing the bird speak. There being no other thing to be done, he covered up the body at the foot of the cliff below the guillemot's nest, went home, and told the others of his place; and the umiak and its crew of women stayed there and wintered in that place. Next summer, when they were making ready to go southward again, they had no man to go with them — but on the way that wifeless man procured food for them by catching fish, and when he had caught enough to fill a pot, he rowed in with his catch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Guillemot that could talk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那鳥話音剛落，帶路的人就看見那個南方人已面朝下撲倒在地，死了——他是因聽見鳥說話而驚嚇致死。事已至此，別無他法，他便把屍體掩埋在崖腳下、海鳩巢的下方，然後回家，把自己那地方的事告訴了其他人；而那艘烏米亞克船和船上的一群婦人便留在那裡，在那地方過了冬。次年夏天，當她們準備再次南行時，卻沒有男人與她們同行——但在途中，那個沒有妻子的男人為她們捕魚供食，等他捕到的魚夠裝滿一鍋時，他便帶著漁獲划船回來。

passages.text: In this way he led them southward. When they came to their own country, they had grown so fond of him that they would not let him go northward again — and so that wifeless man took a wife from among those women, because they would not let him go away to the north. It is said that the skeleton of that wifeless man lies there in the south to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Guillemot that could talk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他就這樣領著她們往南去。當她們回到自己的家鄉時，她們已變得十分喜愛他，不肯再讓他往北去——於是那個沒有妻子的男人便從那些婦人當中娶了一個妻子，因為她們不肯讓他離開到北方去。據說那個沒有妻子的男人的骸骨至今仍躺在南方那裡。

title.en: Kanagssuaq, Who Shared His Catch with Kiliteraq
title.zh: 卡納克舒克與基利特拉克的雪中義氣

region.en: Godthaab (Nuuk), West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭努克

period: Inuit oral tradition (Godthaab, West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Kanagssuaq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Icebound and starving on a little island, Kanagssuaq carries his kayak on his head across the floes through snow and heavy sea, and from that day never comes home without a catch. Out in blinding weather he meets Kiliteraq, the only other hunter to venture out, gives him the whole belly skin and blubber to chew, makes his tow-line fast for him through breaking waves, and rows off into the thickly falling snow. When spring comes and the guillemots are driven together, Kiliteraq comes south to find him and pays the debt with a beaded walrus-hide tow-line and a worked bearskin seat — 'Here is that which shall thank you for that service.'
summary.zh: 海冰封島、糧盡之際，卡納克舒克頂著皮艇踏冰出海，頂風冒雪獵豹而歸，此後再無空手之日。暴風雪中他遇上唯一敢出門的獵手基利特拉克，割下整片豹腹皮請他咀嚼油脂，又在碎浪中為他繫好拖繩，然後駛入大雪消失。春至群獵海鳩時，基利特拉克南來尋他，以串珠海象皮拖繩與熊皮座墊相贈——『這些是為謝你那次相助。』

sensitivity.note: Godthaab district tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Hunter's reciprocity ethic presented as told in the source.

passages.text: Kanagssuaq went out from his own place to live on a little island, and took to wife the only sister of many brothers. Once the cold became so great that the sea between the islands was icebound, and they could no longer go out hunting; at last they had used up their store of food, and all remained lying down from hunger and weakness. Once, when there was open water to the south where they often caught seal, Kanagssuaq took his kayak on his head and went out hunting, rowing out in a northerly wind with snow falling and a heavy sea; he came upon a number of black seal but struck only a little fjord seal, which came up between him and the others — easier to cut up, he said. When he had got this seal he took his kayak on his head again and went home across the ice, his house-fellows shouting for joy at the little creature he sent sliding in; next day he caught two black seal, and after that never went out without bringing home something.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kanagssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡納格蘇阿克（Kanagssuaq）離開自己的住處，到一座小島上生活，並娶了許多兄弟唯一的姊妹為妻。有一次，嚴寒來得如此之烈，島與島之間的海面都結了冰，他們再也無法外出打獵；最後他們吃光了儲存的食物，全都因饑餓和虛弱而躺著不動。有一次，南邊有一片開闊的水面，他們常在那裡捕海豹，卡納格蘇阿克便把獨木舟頂在頭上出去打獵，在落雪、海面洶湧的北風中划了出去；他遇到一群黑海豹，卻只擊中了一隻小峽灣海豹，那隻海豹浮現在他與其他海豹之間——他說，這隻比較好切。他捕到這隻海豹後，又把獨木舟頂在頭上，越過冰面回家，家裡的人見他把那隻小獵物滑送進來，都歡呼起來；第二天他捕到兩隻黑海豹，此後每次外出，沒有一次不帶回些東西。

passages.text: The north wind and the snow and the cold continued, and when he lay out waiting for seal he often wished he might meet Kiliteraq, the great hunter from another place, the only one who would venture out in such weather. Great dearth of food had come also to Kiliteraq's place, and he took his kayak on his head and went out across the ice; coming some way, he sighted Kanagssuaq, who had already made his catch and was getting his tow-line out. As soon as he came up, Kanagssuaq cut away the whole of the belly skin and gave it to him, and Kiliteraq, desiring blubber greatly, took good big pieces to chew. When black seal came up, Kanagssuaq bade him row in to where they were; Kiliteraq harpooned one and killed it on the spot — but as he wound up the harpoon line, a breaking wave rolled down and hid the kayak utterly; the bladder showed behind it, then the kayak with paddles held in balancing position. A second wave washed over him as he tried the tow-line again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kanagssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 北風、落雪與嚴寒持續不斷，當他伏臥著等候海豹時，常希望自己能遇上基利特拉格（Kiliteraq），那是另一個地方的了不起的獵人，也是唯一敢在這種天氣裡外出的人。基利特拉格的地方也發生了嚴重的食物匱乏，他便把獨木舟頂在頭上，越過冰面出去；走了一段路，他望見了卡納格蘇阿克，後者已經捕到了獵物，正把拖繩取出來。他一走近，卡納格蘇阿克便割下整塊腹部的皮給了他，基利特拉格極想得到鯨脂，便拿了大塊大塊的好肉嚼起來。黑海豹浮上來時，卡納格蘇阿克叫他划到海豹所在之處；基利特拉格用魚叉刺中一隻，當場將牠殺死——但當他收捲魚叉繩時，一道破碎的浪頭滾下來，把獨木舟完全吞沒了；浮囊在浪後顯露出來，接著是獨木舟，槳仍握在保持平衡的姿勢中。當他再次試著拉拖繩時，第二道浪又從他身上沖過。

passages.text: Coming up, he said: 'I am now so far out that I cannot make my tow-line fast. Will you do this for me?' Kanagssuaq made his tow-line fast, and as soon as the seal was in tow, Kiliteraq rowed away in the thickly falling snow and was soon lost to sight; when he came home, his many comrades were filled with great thankfulness towards him. A few days later the snow was falling only far away on the horizon, the weather became fine, and in spring they hunted guillemots, driving them together in flocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kanagssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他浮上來後說：「我現在離得太遠，無法把拖繩繫牢。你能替我繫嗎？」卡納格蘇阿克替他把拖繩繫牢，海豹一被拖上，基利特拉格便在密密落下的雪中划走了，很快就消失不見；當他回到家中，他眾多的同伴對他充滿了極大的感激。幾天之後，雪只在遠方地平線上落下，天氣轉好，到了春天，他們便獵捕海鳩，把牠們成群地驅趕到一起。

passages.text: One day, amid the killing and loading, a kayak came in sight on the sunny side — Kiliteraq — who thrust his way through the kayaks to Kanagssuaq, stuck his paddle in between the thongs, drew out from behind his kayak opening a splendid tow-line of walrus hide beautifully worked with many beads of walrus tooth, and a second time a piece of bearskin fashioned to the seat of a kayak. These he gave to Kanagssuaq, saying: 'Once in the spring, when I could not make my tow-line fast to a seal, you helped me, and made it fast. Here is that which shall thank you for that service.' And then he rowed away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Kanagssuaq'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，在宰殺與裝載之際，一具獨木舟在向陽的一側映入眼簾——那是基利特拉格——他奮力穿過眾多獨木舟，來到卡納格蘇阿克面前，將槳插進皮索之間，從獨木舟艙口後方抽出一條華美的海象皮拖繩，繩上精巧地串著許多海象牙製的珠子，接著又第二次抽出一塊做成獨木舟座位的熊皮。他把這些送給卡納格蘇阿克，說道：「有一年春天，我無法把拖繩繫牢在一隻海豹上，是你幫了我，把它繫牢了。這便是報答你那番相助之物。」說罷，他便划槳離去。

title.en: Kemush Creates the World and the Dry Bones of the Dead
title.zh: 克穆什造世與枯骨成人

region.en: Klamath Lake country, southern Oregon (symbolic pin at Klamath Falls)
region.zh: 克拉斯湖故地，俄勒岡南部（象徵定位於克拉馬斯福爾斯）

period: Collected from Klamath narrators; retold 1910 (Judson)

source.work: Katharine Berry Judson (ed.), Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, A.C. McClurg, 1910 — 'How Kemush Created the World' (Klamath)

summary.en: Kemush, Old Man of the Ancients, springs from the ashes of the northern lights at Morning Star's call and makes the flat earth, planting roots, pines, waterfowl and game. Then he and his daughter Evening Sky dance five nights with the spirits of the dark, gather their abandoned dry bones, and scatter them two by two across the land, where they become the first peoples, the chipmunk people and the Klamath.
summary.zh: 克穆什（古人老者）應晨星之呼自北極光灰燼中躍出，造平坦大地，植百草松杉、放水鳥野獸。後與女兒暮空於冥界舞火五夜，收攏鬼魂遺下的枯骨，兩兩撒於山川之間，骨化為原初諸族、花栗鼠人與克拉斯人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a published Klamath folk-narrative in Judson 1910; not verbatim. Collector's preface notes ceremonial and coarse content was excluded; no restricted ceremonial knowledge is reproduced. Category 'myth': sacred cosmogony preserved as folktale. Pin is symbolic, at Klamath Falls.

passages.text: In the time that was, Kemush, Old Man of the Ancients, slept in Yamsi, the Lodge of the North Wind. He had sprung quickly from the ashes of the northern lights and made the world at the call of Morning Star. At first Kaila, the earth, was flat and bare; then Kemush planted grass and camas roots in the valleys, set the pines and juniper on the steeps, and put the mallard and white goose on river and lake, the deer and foxes in the forest, the mountain sheep and grizzly among the rocks. All the earth was new except Shapashkeni, the rock, where was built the lodge of Sun and Moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 25 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在往昔之時，遠古之老者凱穆什睡在亞姆西，即北風之屋。他自北極光的灰燼中迅速躍出，應晨星之召而造了世界。起初，大地凱拉平坦而光禿；後來，凱穆什在山谷中種下青草與卡馬斯百合的根，在陡坡上植下松樹與杜松，把綠頭鴨與白雁放上河流與湖泊，把鹿與狐放進森林，把山地綿羊與灰熊安置在岩石之間。整個大地都是新的，唯有沙帕什凱尼，那塊岩石，例外——日與月之屋便建於其上。

passages.text: The sun halo Wanaka called Kemush from the lodge door, and together they followed the trail of Shel, the sun, to the edge of the dark; but the Indian, Maidu, was not yet created. Kemush and his daughter Evening Sky went down to the Place of the Dark, to the lodges of the spirits, and for five nights in a great circle about a vast fire they danced with the ghosts. The spirits were without number, like leaves on the trees; but when the sun called to the world, they became dry bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths and Legends of the Pacific Northwest, pp. 25-26 (Judson 1910); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 日暈瓦納卡從屋門口呼喚凱穆什，他們一同循著太陽謝爾的蹤跡，走到黑暗的邊緣；然而那印第安人，邁杜，尚未被造出。凱穆什與他的女兒暮空下到黑暗之地，來到眾神靈的屋舍，連續五個夜晚，他們圍著一堆巨大的篝火，在大圓圈中與鬼魂共舞。神靈多得不可勝數，如同樹上的葉子；但當太陽向世界呼喚時，他們便化為枯骨。

passages.text: On the fifth day, when the sun was new, Kemush rose and put the dry bones into a sack, and as he followed the sun's trail to the edge of the world he threw the bones away two by two — to the place of steepness, to the crawfish trail, to the snow-ridge, to the mountain of the great blue heron. The bones became Maidu the Indian, Aikspala the chipmunk people, and last of all Maklaks, the Klamath Indian.
