summary.en: Born of Bima and the giantess Arimbi, the infant Gatotkaca is so strong that his grandfather rages at the omen and hurls the baby into the sky; the child falls to earth from the clouds and the ground does not break under him — an established wayang icon. Trained in the sky, he becomes the flying warrior with the iron pancreas (maja pait) and the wired bones (wisnu janma? the kitang antaka) — the Pandawa's air force.
summary.zh: 五子怖軍與巨人族雅林比所生之嬰戈陀卡查，天生神力；其外祖父怒此異兆，將嬰孩擲向天空——嬰兒自雲霄墜地而大地不裂（哇揚戲定式）。後於天界受訓，成為『苦楝入骨』『 wired bones』之飛行戰士——般度軍之空軍。

sensitivity.note: Javanese wayang innovation: Gatotkaca's sky-birth and sky-training are distinctively Javanese, not in the Indian epic.

passages.text: The infant son of Bima and the giantess Arimbi shows strength beyond mortal measure; in fury and wonder the giant kindred hurl him toward the sky, and he falls back from the clouds to the earth without breaking the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition (wayang purwa); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 毗摩與女巨人阿林比所生的幼子，展現出超越凡人的力量；巨人族在憤怒與驚異之中將他拋向天空，他從雲端墜回大地，卻未擊破地面。

passages.text: Taken up and trained in the heavens, he returns as the flying knight Gatotkaca — invulnerable to all weapons of earth by the iron bone within him — and becomes the terror of the Kurawa's chariots when he takes the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他被帶往天界受訓，歸來時成為飛行的騎士加托卡查——因體內有鐵骨，凡間一切武器皆傷他不得——當他騰空而起，便成了俱盧族戰車的夢魘。

title.en: The Fall of Gatotkaca
title.zh: 戈陀卡查之殞

region.en: Kurushetra plain (Bharatayuddha)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（婆羅多之戰）

period: Bharatayuddha kakawin, composed c. 1157 CE at Kediri (Sedah and Suralaya)

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE), the death of Gatotkaca; Javanese war narrative

summary.en: Karna has but one arrow that can kill a flying god-ward: the Kuntawijayadanu, held in reserve by Krishna's counsel against the day it is aimed at Arjuna. Gatotkaca's night assault on the Kurawa camp forces Karna's hand — the arrow flies, the flying knight falls, and the Pandawa lose the terror of the skies while Karna loses the shot that was kept for Arjuna.
summary.zh: 迦爾納只有一支能殺飛行之神的箭——『恭塔維賈亞』；依克裏希那之策，此箭本為射阿周那而留。戈陀卡查夜襲俱盧大營，逼得迦爾納不得不放箭——飛騎殞落，般度軍失去空中之威；而迦爾納失去那支本為阿周那而留之箭。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin war episode; the strategic sacrifice is read in Java as Kresna's chess.

passages.text: Karna holds in reserve the one weapon that can bring down the invulnerable flying warrior; Kresna has warned the Pandawa that the arrow is aimed at Arjuna. On the night the Kurawa camp is broken, Gatotkaca's assault forces Karna to spend the shot on him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157) narrative; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 迦爾納保留著唯一能擊落這名刀槍不入的飛行戰士的武器；黑天曾警告般度族，那支箭本是瞄準阿周那的。俱盧族軍營被攻破的那一夜，加托卡查的猛攻迫使迦爾納將這一箭用在他身上。

passages.text: The arrow flies, the iron-boned knight falls from the sky, and the Pandawa mourn their air-lord while counting the exchange a victory: Karna has fired his certain death, and the bowman who might have killed Arjuna has spent it on the giant's son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin narrative; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 箭飛出，鐵骨騎士自天而降，般度族哀悼他們的空中之主，同時將這場交換算作勝利：迦爾納已射出他那必殺的一箭，而本可能殺死阿周那的弓箭手，卻把它用在了巨人之子身上。

title.en: The Bharatayuddha of Kediri: Kurushetra on Javanese Soil
title.zh: 諫義里《婆羅多之戰》：爪哇大地上的俱盧之野

region.en: Kediri, East Java (court of composition)
region.zh: 東爪哇諫義里（創作宮廷）

period: Composed c. 1157 CE (kakawin by Mpu Sedah and Mpu Suralaya) for the court of Kediri

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE), court epic of Kediri

summary.en: Java's greatest war-poem retells the Mahabharata's climactic war in courtly kakawin verse, composed by two rival court poets (Mpu Sedah and Mpu Suralaya) for King Jayabaya of Kediri — in Javanese tradition, a king famed for prophecy. The poem's eighteen-day war is read as an allegory for the politics of its own century, and as the charter of the wayang war-plays.
summary.zh: 爪哇最偉大之戰詩以宮廷頌詩重述《摩訶婆羅多》決戰，由諫義里王查亞巴雅（爪哇傳統中的預言之王）之兩位御用詩人賽達與蘇拉拉雅合著。詩中十八日大戰被讀作其世紀政治之寓言，亦為哇揚戰戲之憲章。

sensitivity.note: Court epic; the Jayabaya prophecy-legend attaches to this poem's royal patron.

passages.text: The court poets of Kediri compose the war of the Pandawa and Kurawa in kakawin verse — the rival masters Sedah and Suralaya dividing the cantos — for a king whose court read the Indian war as the mirror of its own politics.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157) and its composition-legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 諫義里的宮廷詩人以卡卡文詩體譜寫般度族與俱盧族之戰——相互競爭的大師塞達與蘇拉亞分寫各章——為的是一位國王，其宮廷將這場印度之戰視為自身政治的鏡像。

passages.text: In the poem the eighteen days of Kurushetra are fought in Javanese terms — Kresna as the charioteer-god, Gatotkaca in the sky, Bima's mace, Karna's arrow — and the great lines of the Javanese war-poetry descend from it into the wayang repertoire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin's reception; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 詩中，俱盧之野的十八日之戰以爪哇的方式進行——黑天為御者之神，加托卡查在空中，怖軍的狼牙棒，迦爾納的箭——爪哇戰爭詩的宏偉詩行由此而下，流入哇揚戲的劇目之中。

title.en: Bima Breaks the Thigh of Duryodana
title.zh: 怖軍擊碎難敵之股

region.en: Kurushetra plain (Bharatayuddha)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（婆羅多之戰）

period: Bharatayuddha kakawin, composed c. 1157 CE

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE); final mace-duel episode

summary.en: The war closes with the mace-duel of Bima and Duryodana. Forbidden by the rules of combat to strike below the navel, Bima waits until Kresna — drumming his own thigh as a signal — reminds him of the insult to Drupadi; the mace comes down on the thigh, the usurper's pride is broken with his bone, and the eighteen days end.
summary.zh: 大戰終結於怖軍與難敵之鐵杵決鬥。鬥規禁止擊腰以下；克裏希那拍擊己股示意——怖軍憶起德羅帕迪之辱，鐵杵落下，股骨碎裂，篡位者之傲與其骨同碎；十八日之戰遂終。

sensitivity.note: Breaking the combat taboo to end the war — flagged as interpretive in the Javanese retellings, where Kresna's signal is explicit.

passages.text: In the last duel the maces of Bima and Duryodana break against each other while the hosts stand down; the rules of the fight forbid a blow below the navel, and Bima's fury is checked by the law. Kresna drums his hand upon his own thigh; Bima, reading the signal and remembering Drupadi, swings the mace down upon the thigh of Duryodana. The bone of the usurper breaks with his pride, and the war of the eighteen days is over.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在最後的決鬥中，怖軍與難敵的狼牙棒相互擊碎，而兩軍按兵不動；決鬥的規則禁止擊打肚臍以下，怖軍的怒火為法則所遏。黑天以手叩擊自己的大腿；怖軍領會這信號，憶起木柱王之女，揮狼牙棒向下擊中難敵的大腿。篡位者的骨頭隨其驕傲一同折斷，十八日之戰就此結束。

title.en: Abhimanyu in the Enclosure of Death
title.zh: 激昂被困死陣

region.en: Kurushetra plain (Bharatayuddha)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（婆羅多之戰）

period: Bharatayuddha kakawin, composed c. 1157 CE

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE); chakravyuha episode

summary.en: Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, learned the breaking of the discus-formation in his mother's womb — but only the way in. At Kurushetra he pierces the wheel-array alone, fights through its concentric traps, and is killed inside it by a conspiracy of six; the wayang lakon of Abimanyu's death is the Javanese school of the young hero destroyed by knowledge half-given.
summary.zh: 阿周那之子激昂於母腹中習得破『轉輪陣』之法——惟知入而不知出。俱盧戰場上，他隻身突入輪陣，力破層層羅網，終為六人之合謀困殺於陣中。哇揚戲『激昂之死』即爪哇之堂課：僅授一半知識，足以毀掉年輕英雄。

sensitivity.note: Half-knowledge motif; the Javanese lakon stresses the mother's tale overheard in the womb.

passages.text: Abhimanyu learned the art of entering the discus-array while still unborn, listening as Kresna explained the formation to Subhadra; the explanation stopped at the way in, and the boy in the womb never heard the way out. At Kurushetra the wheel-array closes around the young prince; he fights inward through the rings of the trap, but having no key to the exit he falls inside it, cut down by six champions together — the death that shames the war's law and hardens the Pandawa's heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157) narrative; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿毗曼紐尚在母胎中時便學會了進入輪陣之法，他聽著黑天向蘇跋陀羅講解陣形；講解止於入陣之法，胎中的男孩從未聽到出陣之法。在俱盧之野，輪陣合攏圍住這位年輕王子；他向內穿過陷阱的重重環圈而戰，卻因沒有出口的鑰匙而陷落其中，被六位勇士合力誅殺——這死亡令戰爭的法則蒙羞，也使般度族的心腸變硬。

title.en: Kresna the Charioteer: The God Who Drives the War
title.zh: 禦者克裏希那：駕馭戰爭之神

region.en: Kurushetra plain (Bharatayuddha)
region.zh: 俱盧之野（婆羅多之戰）

period: Bharatayuddha kakawin, composed c. 1157 CE

source.work: Kakawin Bharata Yuddha (c. 1157 CE); Kresna's counsel and chariot

summary.en: In the Javanese war, the god Batara Kresna refuses armies and offers instead to drive Arjuna's chariot; from the box-seat between the two hosts he steers the whole battle — counselling, withholding and revealing weapons, arranging that Gatotkaca draws Karna's reserved arrow — the wayang's charioteer is the intelligence of the war wearing a mortal's seat.
summary.zh: 爪哇戰事之中，巴塔拉·克裏希那拒受兵馬，只求為阿周那禦車；於兩軍之間的車轅上，他駕馭全局——進策、藏箭、示箭，安排戈陀卡查誘出迦爾納之留箭。哇揚戲之禦者，乃坐在凡人座位上的戰爭智囊。

sensitivity.note: Kresna's warcraft; paraphrase of the kakawin's divine strategist.

passages.text: Asked to choose between the hosts, Kresna offers his person unarmed and his chariot without armies; the Pandawa take the god as charioteer, and the Kurawa take his troops. From the driver's seat the god steers the eighteen days: he signals the thigh to Bima, holds Arjuna's bow steady at the moment of doubt, and disposes the death of Gatotkaca so that Karna's reserved arrow is spent — the war is won in the seat of the driver.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin (c. 1157); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Bharatayuddha kakawin; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當被要求在兩軍之間作出選擇時，黑天獻出他本人——不持武器——以及他的戰車，但不帶軍隊；般度族接受這位神為御者，俱盧族則接受他的軍隊。這位神從御者之座駕馭這十八日：他向怖軍示意大腿，在阿周那心生疑慮之際穩住他的弓，並安排加托卡查之死，使迦爾納那支留存的箭被耗盡——這場戰爭是在御者之座上贏得的。

title.en: Semar Sent Down to the Pandawa
title.zh: 塞馬爾下凡隨般度五子

region.en: Wayang purwa cycle, Central Java
region.zh: 哇揚戲班（中爪哇）

period: Wayang purwa tradition (Javanese innovation; Worsfold 1893 records the Punakawan)

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893), the Punakawan servants of the wayang; Javanese wayang purwa tradition

summary.en: A purely Javanese invention: the gods send down Semar — pot-bellied, ironical, servile in speech — to serve the heroes as Punakawan clown-servant, with his sons Gareng, Petruk and Bagong. In the dalang's theology Semar outranks every god on the stage: the clown who carries the truth of the play, the deity who hides as a servant.
summary.zh: 純爪哇之創造：諸神遣塞馬爾——大腹便便、言語譏誚、口稱卑賤——攜三子加楞、佩特魯克、巴貢下凡，充當英雄之僕（普納卡萬丑角）。在達朗（戲偶師）的神學裏，塞馬爾位在臺上諸神之上：丑角承載戲之真理，神明隱於僕身。

sensitivity.note: Living wayang tradition; the Punakawan are a Javanese (not Indian) layer of the Mahabharata on Java.

passages.text: To keep the heroes of the plays human, the Javanese wayang adds what the Indian epic does not have: the Punakawan, clown-servants led by Semar, who fetch, advise, mock and out-think their masters between the battles. Court theology makes the joke serious: the pot-bellied servant Semar is the oldest of the gods in disguise, granted to the Pandawa as companion and conscience. When the heroes listen to Semar they are listening, the dalang says, to the one voice on the stage above the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the wayang purwa tradition as described in Worsfold (1893); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the wayang purwa tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 為了讓劇中的英雄保持人性，爪哇的哇揚戲加上了印度史詩所沒有的東西：由塞瑪爾率領的小丑僕從「普納卡萬」，他們在戰鬥之間為主人奔走、獻策、嘲弄，並以智謀勝過主人。宮廷神學讓這玩笑變得嚴肅：大腹便便的僕從塞瑪爾，是眾神中最年長者所喬裝，被賜予般度族作為伴侶與良知。達朗（操偶師）說，當英雄們聽從塞瑪爾時，他們所聽的，是舞台上凌駕於眾神之上的那一個聲音。

title.en: The Pandawa Walk Away: The Great Renunciation
title.zh: 般度五子棄世行

region.en: Himalayan ascent (wayang purwa ending)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅登天之路（哇揚戲結局）

period: Wayang purwa tradition; Javanese Mahabharata adaptations

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893); Javanese Mahabharata tradition

summary.en: The Mahabharata's Javanese finale: the Pandawa crown their heir, set aside their weapons, and walk toward the mountain of the gods in wedding garments — one by one they fall on the way as their secret failings are named, until Puntadewa alone, and the faithful dog, reaches the summit.
summary.zh: 爪哇版《摩訶婆羅多》之終章：般度五子立嗣君，卸下武器，著婚衣向諸神之山而行——旅途中他們的隱秘罪愆被逐一點名，逐一倒下；最後唯堅戰與那忠犬抵達山巔。

sensitivity.note: Renunciation-and-ascent finale; cross-cluster with Arda Viraf and other ascent narratives.

passages.text: After the war the Pandawa set their heir on the throne and begin the walk to heaven in royal garments; on the climb each falls in turn as the weight of an old failure is spoken aloud — the teller of lies, the glutton of pride, the keeper of a favour half-earned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition (wayang purwa); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大戰之後，般度族扶立其繼承人登上王位，便身著王袍開始走向天國；在攀登途中，眾人隨著一樁樁舊日過失被高聲道出而依次倒下——說謊者、驕矜貪婪者、受了半份恩惠而念念不忘者。

passages.text: Puntadewa alone goes on, refusing at the gate of heaven to enter without the dog that has followed him; the dog is his own honour in disguise, and both are admitted — the wayang closes the epic on the reward of one flawless virtue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Mahabharata tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 唯有堅戰繼續前行，在天國之門前拒絕拋下跟隨他的那條狗而獨自進入；那條狗正是他自己榮譽的化身，於是兩者一同被接納——哇揚戲以一種無瑕美德的獎賞，為這部史詩作結。

title.en: Kagsagsuk: The Persecuted Orphan and the Amarok
title.zh: 卡格薩克舒克：受虐孤兒與狼靈

region.en: West Greenland (Greenlandic and Labrador copies)
region.zh: 西格陵蘭（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from nine copies (Greenland and Labrador), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Persecuted by the whole settlement — lifted by the nostrils, teeth pulled, rolled in snow — the orphan Kagsagsuk calls 'Lord of strength' between two mountains, and the amarok wolf-spirit shakes seal-bones out of his body five times until he cannot be thrown. Trained daily in secret, he carries a driftwood spar on his shoulders by night, then splits, swings, and hurls three bears in front of the crowd; the same people who mocked him offer boots and seats, and he crushes them one by one, sparing only the kind, and roams the coast leaving marks of his great deeds.
summary.zh: 孤兒卡格薩克舒克受全村凌虐——被提鼻懸舉、拔牙禁刀、雪中翻滾——他在兩山之間呼喚『力之主』，狼靈阿馬洛克五次摔他，震出體內海豹小骨，直至他再也摔不倒。他夜半肩扛浮木示力，冰上連破三熊——拋擲如玩具——昔日施虐者爭相奉衣讓座，他逐一捏碎，獨饒善者；沿海岸炫耀神力，遺蹟至今猶存。

sensitivity.note: Rink collates nine copies; same tale-type as Rasmussen's Kagssagssuk (cross-ref inuit-kagssagssuk-homeless-boy). Graphic vengeance recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: There was once a poor orphan boy who lived among uncharitable men; his name was Kagsagsuk, and his foster-mother a miserable old woman. Their wretched shed adjoined the house-passage, and they were not allowed into the main room; Kagsagsuk did not even venture into the shed, but lay in the passage warming himself among the dogs, crying 'Na-ah! Na-ah!' mocking himself in imitation of them. The men lifted him above the threshold only by putting their fingers into his nostrils — these accordingly enlarged, but otherwise he did not grow at all. They gave him frozen meat without a knife, saying his teeth might do instead, and sometimes pulled out a couple of teeth, complaining of his eating too much; the boys rolled him in the snow filling his clothes with it, and the girls covered him all over with filth. At length he ventured out among the mountains by himself, choosing solitary places and meditating how to get strength, as his foster-mother had taught him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個可憐的孤兒，住在不仁慈的人們中間；他名叫卡格薩克蘇克，他的養母是個悲慘的老婦人。他們那破爛的棚屋緊挨著屋子的過道，他們不被允許進入正屋；卡格薩克蘇克甚至不敢走進棚屋，只躺在過道裡，在狗群之間取暖，哭喊著「吶——啊！吶——啊！」模仿牠們來嘲弄自己。男人們只有把手指伸進他的鼻孔，才能把他提過門檻——他的鼻孔因此被撐大了，但除此之外他一點也沒長高。他們不給刀子就丟給他凍肉，說他的牙齒可以代勞，有時還拔掉他幾顆牙，抱怨他吃得太多了；男孩們把他滾進雪裡，讓雪塞滿他的衣服，女孩們則用穢物把他全身塗遍。終於，他獨自壯著膽子走進群山之間，選擇僻靜之處，思索著如何獲得力量，正如他養母所教導他的。

passages.text: Standing between two high mountains, he called out: 'Lord of strength, come forth! Lord of strength, come to me!' A large animal appeared in the shape of an amarok (a fabulous animal, originally a wolf); terrified, Kagsagsuk tried to run, but the beast overtook him and, twisting its tail round his body, threw him down — and a rustling sound followed as small seal-bones, like toys, fell from his own body. 'It is because of these bones that thy growth has been stopped,' said the amarok, and repeated the process: again bones fell, fewer each time, until the fifth throw he did not fall at all but jumped along the ground. 'If it be thy wish to become strong and vigorous, thou mayst come every day to me,' said the beast, adding that human beings would not be able to conquer him any more, but he had better stick to his old habits; when winter came and the sea was frozen, three great bears would appear, and they should be killed by his hand. He met the amarok every day, feeling stronger each time, kicking the very rocks on his way home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他站在兩座高山之間，高聲呼喊：「力量之主啊，出來吧！力量之主啊，到我這裡來！」一隻形似阿瑪洛克（一種傳說中的動物，原為狼）的巨大野獸出現了；卡格薩克蘇克驚恐萬分，想要逃跑，但那野獸追上了他，用尾巴纏住他的身體，把他摔倒在地——接著傳來一陣窸窣之聲，一些像玩具般的小海豹骨頭從他體內掉落出來。「正是因為這些骨頭，你的生長才被阻斷了，」阿瑪洛克說道，並重複了這個過程：骨頭再次掉落，每次都比前一次少，直到第五次摔擲時，他根本沒有倒下，而是沿著地面跳躍。「如果你希望變得強壯有力，你可以每天來找我，」那野獸說道，還說人類再也無法征服他了，但他最好還是保持舊有的習慣；當冬天來臨、海面結冰時，會出現三隻大熊，牠們應當由他的手來殺死。他每天都與阿瑪洛克相會，每次都感到更加強壯，回家的路上甚至能踢動岩石。

passages.text: At nightfall he asked for his mother's boots, slipped out, loosened the moorings of a great piece of driftwood the kayakers had been unable to carry up, flung the spar on his shoulders, and buried it behind the house; in the morning the whole settlement cried that there must be a man of extraordinary strength among them, the young men each giving themselves great airs — the impostors. Kagsagsuk stuck to his old habits until the sea froze. Then the men came running in to report three bears climbing an iceberg, and nobody dared attack them: now was his time. With his foster-mother's boots he ran through the crowd as if they had been a shoal of small fish, heels almost touching his neck, the snow sparkling in rainbow colours about him. Ascending the iceberg, he made himself hard — invulnerable by charm — and seizing the largest bear by the fore-paws flung it against the iceberg, the haunches severed from the body: 'This was my first catch; now, flense away and divide!' The second he threw down the same way; the third he swung above his head and hurled at the bystanders — 'This fellow behaved shamefully towards me!' — until they all fled before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜幕降臨時，他向母親要來靴子，悄悄溜了出去，解開一塊皮划艇手們無法搬上岸的巨大浮木的纜繩，把那根木樑甩上肩頭，埋在屋後；到了早晨，整個定居點都驚呼，他們之中必定有一個力大非凡的人，年輕男子們個個自命不凡——那些冒牌貨。卡格薩克蘇克保持著舊有的習慣，直到海面結冰。然後男人們跑進來報告，說有三隻熊正在攀爬一座冰山，卻沒有人敢攻擊牠們：現在正是他的時機。他穿著養母的靴子，穿過人群，彷彿他們只是一群小魚，腳跟幾乎碰到後頸，周圍的積雪閃爍著彩虹般的色彩。他登上冰山，讓自己變得堅硬——以咒術變得刀槍不入——抓住最大的那隻熊的前爪，把牠摔向冰山，牠的後腿與身體分離：「這是我的第一個獵物；現在，剝皮分割吧！」第二隻他也以同樣的方式摔下；第三隻他舉過頭頂，朝旁觀者擲去——「這傢伙對我行為可恥！」——直到他們全都從他面前逃走。

passages.text: He brought the two bear-skins to his foster-mother — 'There is one for thy couch, and another for thy coverlet!' — ordered the flesh cooked, and was requested to enter the main room; peeping above the threshold as was his wont, 'I really can't get across, unless some one will lift me up by the nostrils' — and nobody else venturing, his old foster-mother came and lifted him as he desired. All the men now became very civil: 'Step forward,' 'Come and sit down, friend,' 'Here is a nice seat for Kagsagsuk,' and the girls rivalled each other in offering to make clothes for him. But at supper he squeezed the girl who fetched his water so hard the blood rushed from her mouth — 'Why, I think she is burst!' — while the parents meekly rejoined she was good for nothing but fetching water. The boys he called great future seal-hunters and crushed to death; others he killed by tearing their limbs asunder, and the parents only said, 'It does not signify — he was a good-for-nothing.' Thus he went on until the whole household had perished by his hand, sparing only the poor people who had been kind to him; taking the best kayak left, he roamed all over the country in the pride of his heart, and even nowadays marks of his great deeds are shown along the coast — which is why the history of Kagsagsuk is supposed to be true.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 1 'Kagsagsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他把那两张熊皮帶給他的養母——「一張給你的臥榻，另一張給你的被褥！」——吩咐把肉煮了，又被請進正屋；他照例從門檻上方探出頭來，「我實在過不去，除非有人抓住我的鼻孔把我提起來」——旁人都不敢上前，於是他那年老的養母走過來，照他的意思把他提了過去。這時所有男人都變得十分客氣：「往前走啊」，「來坐下吧，朋友」，「這兒有個好位子給卡格薩克蘇克」，姑娘們也爭相要替他做衣服。可是吃晚飯時，他把替他打水的姑娘捏得太緊，血從她嘴裡湧了出來——「哎呀，我看她是被捏爆了！」——而她的父母卻溫順地答道，她除了打水一無用處。他把男孩們稱作未來了不起的捕海豹好手，卻把他們捏死；其餘的人他則扯斷四肢弄死，而他們的父母只說：「不要緊——他本來就是個沒用的東西。」他就這樣一直下去，直到那一家人全死在他手裡，只饒過了那些待他好的窮苦人；他挑了一隻剩下的最好的皮划艇，滿心得意地漫遊了整個地方，甚至到今天，沿海一帶還展示著他那些豐功偉績的痕跡——正因如此，卡格薩克蘇克的故事才被認為是真實的。

title.en: The Blind Man Who Used His Mother for a Hunting-Bladder
title.zh: 以母為浮囊的盲人

region.en: West Greenland (Greenlandic and Labrador copies)
region.zh: 西格陵蘭（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from eight copies (Greenland and Labrador), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Witchcraft on a thong-seal skin blinds a son who wants it for hunting-lines; starved and cheated of his own bear-meat by his mother, he is cured by wild-geese droppings on his eyes at the lake. Feigning blindness, he tests her with three dreams, then makes her serve as his hunting-bladder at the white-whale hunt and pushes her into the sea — 'My ullo! It was I who nursed thee!' Her spreading hair turns to the narwhal's long teeth; brother and sister flee the deed into the interior, grow immensely old, and the man returns once to denounce himself in the moonlight before vanishing forever.
summary.zh: 母親在長鬚海豹皮上施咒，令取皮製獵繩的兒子雙目失明；她又私藏熊肉、以貝類餓他。湖畔雁糞落眼復明。他佯盲三次試母，繼而在白鯨獵中令母親充當浮囊，把她推入海中——『我的烏羅刀！是我養大你的！』其散髮化為一角鯨長牙。兄妹懼罪遁入內陸，壽至極高；男子最後一次現身月光下自陳其罪，從此絕跡。

sensitivity.note: Rink collates eight copies (two Labrador). Matricide and narwhal etiology recorded as told in the 1875 source; the angakok denunciation scene is a documented Greenlandic confession custom.

passages.text: A widow had a son and a daughter; the son grew up useful in different ways and commenced seal-hunting, and one day in early winter caught a thong-seal. His mother wanted the skin for a ledge-cover, but he insisted on having it for hunting-lines; angry, she prepared the skin, removing the hairs with witchcraft, saying: 'When he cuts thee into thongs, when he cuts thee asunder, then thou shalt snap and smite his face' — and rejoiced in the thought that it would hit him. When he cut out the first thong and scraped it with a shell, a small blister burst, hitting both his eyes and blinding him. The winter coming on destitute, they lived entirely on mussels, and the blind boy took his place on the ledge, unable to hunt. A great bear appeared eating away their window-pane and thrust its head into the room; the mother and sister fled in terror, but the blind man asked his sister for his bow and her right aim for him, shot, and the bear fell. The mother said, 'Thou hitst the window instead of the beast'; his sister whispered, 'Thou hast killed a bear.' Yet the mother never gave him any of the boiled bear-flesh, only shell-fish, concealing her having any flesh, to starve him; his sister gave him his portion in her absence, which he swallowed in haste.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個寡婦，有一兒一女；兒子長大後在各方面都派得上用場，開始捕海豹，初冬的一天捕到一隻皮帶海豹。他母親想要那張皮來做窗臺的罩子，他卻堅持要拿來做捕獵用的繩索；母親一氣之下，把皮處理了，用巫術把毛去掉，說道：「當他把你割成皮條，當他把你割開，那時你就要崩斷，打在他的臉上」——還滿心歡喜地想著它會打中他。當他割出第一根皮條，用貝殼刮它時，一個小水泡爆開，打中了他的雙眼，把他弄瞎了。冬天來臨，家道貧困，他們全靠貽貝過活，瞎眼的男孩只能坐在窗臺上，無法打獵。一隻大熊出現，啃掉了他們的窗玻璃，把頭探進屋裡；母親和妹妹嚇得逃走了，但盲人向妹妹要來他的弓，要她替他瞄準，一箭射去，熊倒了下來。母親說：「你打中的是窗子，不是那隻野獸」；他妹妹卻悄聲說：「你殺死了一隻熊。」然而母親從不給他一點煮熟的熊肉，只給貝殼類，還隱瞞自己有肉的事，想把他餓死；他妹妹趁她不在時把自己的那份給了他，他匆匆吞了下去。

passages.text: In spring the sister reminded him how delightful it was when he could see and go hunting, and at daybreak they went out together, he holding her garments. At a large plain beside a lake he lay down while she went for fuel; wild geese flew overhead and one cried, 'Look at the poor young man down there; he is blind: would we could make him see.' Something warm fell on his eyes — the goose's excrement — and a voice said: 'Keep thy eyes shut till the sound of our wings has altogether passed away, then thou mayst try to open them.' The goose swept its wings across his face repeating 'Mind thou dost not open thy eyes.' When the noise had passed he opened his eyes wide and had his sight restored. His sister would not believe until she looked into his reopened eyes; they agreed not to let their mother know.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 春天裡，妹妹提醒他，從前他能看見、能去打獵的時候是多麼快活，於是天亮時他們一同出去，他抓著她的衣服。在湖邊一大片平原上，他躺了下來，她則去撿柴；野雁從頭頂飛過，其中一隻叫道：「看看下面那個可憐的年輕人；他瞎了：但願我們能讓他看見。」有什麼溫熱的東西落在他眼睛上——是雁的糞便——接著有個聲音說：「閉著眼睛，等我們翅膀的聲音完全過去了，你再試著睜開。」那隻雁用翅膀掃過他的臉，反覆說：「當心，別睜開眼睛。」聲音過去後，他把眼睛睜得大大的，視力恢復了。他妹妹不肯相信，直到望進他重新睜開的眼睛；他們說好不讓母親知道。

passages.text: Approaching the house he caught sight of his bear-skin drying and its bones and paws; shutting his eyes, he took his place on the ledge, feigned sleep, and 'dreamed' three times — of the skin behind the house, the bones at the entrance, and two bear's paws under the couch — the mother repeating 'Thou must surely have been thinking about somebody who happened to hurt thee some time ago.' At the third dream, suddenly opening his eyes: 'Mother, I mean these' — and she knew he had regained his sight, exclaiming 'Eat them, just eat them!' He resumed seal-hunting, but the idea of revenge grew on him. At the white-whale season he hunted with his sister fastened as his hunting-bladder; and one day asked her if she liked their old mother — 'I am more fond of thee than of her; thou art the only one I do love.' 'Well, then, to-morrow she shall serve us for a bladder. I'll pay her off for having made me blind.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 快到家時，他瞥見他那張熊皮正在晾著，還有它的骨頭和爪子；他閉上眼睛，坐到窗臺上，裝睡，還「夢」了三次——夢見屋後的皮、門口的骨頭，以及臥榻下的兩隻熊掌——母親反覆說：「你一定是想起了某個碰巧從前傷過你的人吧。」第三次做夢時，他突然睜開眼睛：「母親，我說的就是這些」——於是她知道他恢復了視力，驚叫道：「吃吧，儘管吃吧！」他重新開始捕海豹，但復仇的念頭在他心裡越長越大。到了捕白鯨的季節，他帶著妹妹去打獵，把她當作捕獵用的浮囊繫著；有一天他問她喜不喜歡他們的老母親——「我喜歡你勝過喜歡她；你是我唯一真正愛的人。」「那麼，明天就讓她給我們當浮囊吧。她把我弄瞎，我要跟她算這筆帳。」

passages.text: The mother declared herself willing and went down to the open sea with them next morning. When the white whales appeared she said, 'Take one of the smallest, and not the large ones,' crying out at the very little fish, 'Look out and try for one of these' — 'They are still too big,' he answered, and harpooned one of the very largest, letting go his hold of the line. When the animal had drawn his mother close to the water he cried, 'Dost thou remember the time thou madest me blind?' and pushed her on: 'That fellow will give me my revenge.' Close to the edge of the water she cried, 'My ullo! It was I who nursed thee' — and was plunged into the sea; still she reappeared crying 'My ullo, my ullo; I nursed thee!' then disappeared forever. It is said she was afterwards transformed into a fish, her spreading hair turning into long horny teeth, from which the narwhals are said to have their origin. Brother and sister, terrified at their deed, fled eastward to the large continent, he refusing at first to kill a bird for pity at their gift of sight, until he killed one swan for his sister — the only bird he caught for the rest of his life. They grew immensely old without friends; at last he went to an angakok's spirit-calling and denounced himself — 'I am that very man... do come out and see what I am like' — standing in the bright moonlight with hair snowy white as a hood of white hare-skins, face black, clothes of reindeer-skins. His sister could no longer move from old age; their house-fellows were terrible beings with heads like seals. 'After this, I will not show myself any more to human creatures; those to whom I wanted to denounce myself I have done it to.' He turned away and has never been seen afterwards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 2 'The Blind Man who recovered his Sight'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 母親表示願意，第二天早晨便和他們一起下到外海。白鯨出現時，她說：「挑一條最小的，別挑那些大的」，又對著那條很小的魚喊道：「當心，試著抓一條這樣的」——「它們還是太大了，」他答道，卻叉中了一條最大的，鬆開了手中的繩子。那隻動物把他的母親拖近水邊時，他喊道：「你還記得你把我弄瞎的那一回嗎？」說著把她往前一推：「這傢伙會替我報仇的。」到了水邊，她喊道：「我的烏洛啊！是我把你養大的」——隨即被拖入海中；她仍舊浮現出來喊道：「我的烏洛，我的烏洛；是我把你養大的！」然後就永遠消失了。據說她後來變成了一條魚，她那散開的頭髮變成了長長的角質牙齒，據說獨角鯨的角便由此而來。兄妹二人被自己的所作所為嚇壞了，向東逃往那片大陸，他起初因念及他們得見光明的恩情，不忍殺鳥，直到為妹妹殺了一隻天鵝——那是他餘生所捕的唯一一隻鳥。他們沒有朋友，活到極老；最後他去參加一位巫師的召靈會，當眾揭露了自己——「我就是那個人……請出來看看我現在是什麼樣子」——他站在明亮的月光下，頭髮雪白如白兔皮做的風帽，臉是黑的，身穿馴鹿皮的衣服。他妹妹年老得再也動彈不得；與他們同住的是些可怕的生物，頭像海豹。「從今以後，我不再向人類顯現了；那些我想向之揭露自己的人，我已經向他們揭露了。」他轉身離去，此後再沒有人見過他。

title.en: Igimarasugsuk, the Wife-Eater, and the Magic Driftwood
title.zh: 食妻者伊基馬拉舒克與魔木

region.en: West Greenland (Greenlandic and Labrador copies)
region.zh: 西格陵蘭（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

period: Inuit oral tradition; well known to every child in Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Secretly killing and eating his wives and children, Igimarasugsuk murders his wife's little brother and forces her to share the meal. Fattened on reindeer-tallow till she cannot move, she rolls to a muddy pool, drinks herself lighter, stuffs her jacket as a decoy for his lance, and sings herself inside a great driftwood log that opens at her spell. Traced to the log, the fox-hole, and the bushes, he laments at every dead end — 'Oh what a pity I put off eating her so long!' — until she reaches berry-gatherers and safety.
summary.zh: 伊基馬拉舒克暗殺並吞食歷任妻子與子女；他殺害妻弟逼妻子同食。他以馴鹿脂油將妻子餵至不能動彈；她滾至泥塘飲水瘦身，以絮衣假人誘其長矛，再唱咒使巨木開合藏身。蹤跡屢斷於巨木、狐穴、灌木叢——他每到一處便哀嘆『可惜當初不早些吃掉她！』——直至她抵達採莓人群而脫身。

sensitivity.note: Rink notes this tale is known to every child in Greenland. Same tale-type as Rasmussen's Imarasugssuaq (cross-ref inuit-imarasugssuaq-wife-eater). Cannibalism recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: It was said of Igimarasugsuk that he always lost his wives in a very short time, and always as quickly married again; but nobody knew that he always killed and ate his wives, as well as his little children. At last he married a girl who had a younger brother and many relatives besides. Returning from a reindeer-hunt, he one day sent his brother-in-law to fetch his axe from underneath the boat-pillars — and followed him; on hearing her brother's shrieks, the wife peeped out and beheld him pursuing the boy, striking him on the head so that he fell dead on the spot. He then ordered his wife to dress and boil parts of her brother's body, and commenced eating, offering her a piece of an arm and insisting she eat with him; she only feigned to do so, concealing her portion under the ashes of the fire. 'I actually think thou art crying!' exclaimed the husband. 'No,' she said, 'I am only a little shy.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說伊吉馬拉蘇格蘇克總是在很短的時間內就失去妻子，又總是同樣快地再娶；但沒有人知道，他總是把妻子殺死吃掉，連自己的小孩也不例外。最後他娶了一個姑娘，她有個年幼的弟弟，還有許多親戚。有一天，他打馴鹿回來，打發他的小舅子到船柱底下去取他的斧頭——自己卻跟了上去；妻子聽到弟弟的尖叫聲，探頭一看，見他正追著那男孩，打他的頭，男孩當場倒地而死。接著他吩咐妻子把弟弟的屍體收拾好、煮了，便開始吃起來，遞給她一塊手臂上的肉，非要她和他一起吃；她只是假裝吃，把自己的那份藏在火灰底下。「我瞧你準是在哭！」丈夫嚷道。「沒有，」她說，「我只是有點兒害羞。」

passages.text: After devouring his brother-in-law he began to fatten his wife, ordering her to eat nothing but reindeer-tallow and drink only what a small shell would hold, until she grew so fat she could not move about at all. One day he went away, having securely shut the entrance to the summer-tent and fastened it with strong cords. When he had been gone a considerable time she took her knife, let herself fall from the bench, and rolled herself as far as the entry; by great efforts she crossed the threshold, cut the strings fastening the outer curtain, rolled down to a muddy pool and drank a great deal of water, after which she felt less heavy and was able to get up and walk back. She re-entered the tent, stuffed out her jacket, put it on the bench with its back turned outward, fastened the entrance well, and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他吞食了妻舅之後，便開始把妻子養肥，命令她只准吃馴鹿油脂，只准喝一個小貝殼所能盛下的水，直到她胖得完全無法行動。有一天，他外出離去，先把夏季帳篷的入口牢牢關閉，並用粗繩繫緊。他離去許久之後，她取出刀子，從長凳上讓自己跌落下來，一路滾到入口處；她費盡力氣越過門檻，割斷繫住外層簾幕的繩索，滾到一處泥濘的水窪邊，喝下大量的水，之後便覺得身子不那麼沉重，能夠起身走回去。她重新進入帳篷，把她的外衣塞得鼓脹，背朝外放在長凳上，把入口牢牢繫好，然後離去。

passages.text: Convinced her husband would pursue her, she went down to a very large piece of drift-wood hauled ashore and worked a spell upon it, singing: 'KissugssuaK pingerssuaK, ia-ha-ha, arape, Kupe, sipe, sipe sisaria' — and forthwith the timber opened midways and she entered it, again singing, and it closed around her in darkness. She heard her husband coming: he had entered the tent and thrust his lance into the stuffed jacket, and discovering what it really was, ran out, following her footprints all the way to the timber, where she plainly heard him say: 'Oh what a pity I waited so long in killing her! oh poor miserable me!' Every trace ending at the timber, he went away; she sang the timber open, crept out, and ran on, hiding herself in a fox-hole — where every trace again ended, and she heard him digging the very earth with his hands before tiring and going away, returning and bemoaning himself in the same manner.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她深信丈夫會追趕她，便走到一塊被拖上岸的極大浮木旁，對它施了法術，唱道：「KissugssuaK pingerssuaK，ia-ha-ha，arape，Kupe，sipe，sipe sisaria」——那木頭隨即從中裂開，她走了進去，又唱了一遍，木頭便在她四周合攏，將她圍在黑暗之中。她聽見丈夫走來：他已進入帳篷，把長矛刺進那件塞鼓的外衣，發現那究竟是什麼之後，便跑出去，一路循著她的足跡追到那塊木頭處，她在裡面清楚聽見他說：「唉，我真後悔拖了這麼久才殺她！唉，我這可憐的苦命人！」所有足跡都止於那塊木頭，他便離去了；她唱著讓木頭裂開，爬了出來，繼續奔逃，躲進一個狐狸洞裡——那裡的足跡又再度斷絕，她聽見他用手刨挖泥土，直到疲倦才離去，之後又返回，以同樣的方式哀嘆自己。

passages.text: Taking refuge behind some bushes, she again heard the old lament — 'What a pity I put off eating her so long!' — 'Here every trace of her ends.' At length she caught sight of people gathering berries; on perceiving her they were about to take fright, when she cried out, 'I am the wife of Igimarasugsuk,' and they approached her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 3 'Igimarasugsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她躲在一些灌木叢後面避難，又聽見那熟悉的哀嘆——「我真後悔拖了這麼久才吃她！」——「她的所有足跡到此為止。」最後她瞥見一群人正在採集漿果；他們一察覺到她，正要受驚，她便喊道：「我是Igimarasugsuk的妻子」，他們便向她走近。

title.en: The Origin of Death: Raven Outvotes Coyote
title.zh: 死亡之起源：渡鴉否決郊狼

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (1) The Origin of Death' (Thompson, collected by Teit)

summary.en: Coyote the traveller finds Raven, a selfish chief who wants long winters, all the game, and mortal men. Coyote pleads that death brings sorrow and proposes death like sleep with return; Raven and his followers — Crow, Fly, Maggot — demand final death so they may feed on corpses. Coyote concedes that people shall die when their time comes, but only until the world changes again. Soon Raven's own daughter sickens and dies, the first death, and her desperate father begs to undo the decree; Coyote answers that it is settled and cannot be altered.
summary.zh: 郊狼行旅，遇自私酋長渡鴉；彼欲嚴冬、獨佔獵物，且不欲人長生。郊狼陳說死亡之苦，倡『死如眠、可復返』；渡鴉與其黨羽——鴉、蠅、蛆——卻要人永死，以便食屍。郊狼終允：人屆期而亡，然至世界再變之時將不再死。未幾渡鴉之女病死，是為首亡；渡鴉哀求更改，郊狼答：事已定，不可易。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson (Nlaka'pamux) narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only; no restricted ceremonial knowledge. Category 'myth'. Messenger-debate variant of the origin-of-death cluster.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to Raven, a bad, selfish chief, who wanted to make everything difficult for other people and easy for himself. He wanted the game for himself, wanted long winters, and did not want man to be immortal. Coyote questioned him why he wanted people to die; Raven said, 'If people were immortal, there would be too many. Let them become sick and die.' Coyote said death would introduce sorrow into the world: 'Let them be sick, but not die.' But Raven's people supported their chief, and Crow, Fly, Maggot and many others clamored for people to die, so that they might feed on corpses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 1 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在旅行，來到渡鴉那裡，渡鴉是個邪惡又自私的酋長，他想讓別人的一切都很艱難，而讓自己的一切都很容易。他想把獵物據為己有，想要漫長的冬天，並且不願人類永生不死。郊狼問他為何要人死去；渡鴉說：「如果人永生不死，就會太多了。讓他們生病死去。」郊狼說死亡會給世界帶來悲傷：「讓他們生病，但不要死去。」但渡鴉的族人支持他們的酋長，烏鴉、蒼蠅、蛆蟲以及許多其他者都喧嚷著要人死去，好讓他們能以屍體為食。

passages.text: Coyote proposed, 'Let people die for a while, and then come to life again. Let death be like sleep.' Raven answered, 'No; if they die, let them die for good, and let their bodies rot.' At last Coyote agreed: 'Well, it is ordained that people shall die when their time has come. Their bodies shall be buried, and their souls shall go to the spirit-land; but this will only be until the world changes again, when they will die no more.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 1 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼提議：「讓人死去一段時間，然後再復活。讓死亡像睡眠一樣。」渡鴉回答：「不；如果他們死了，就讓他們永遠死去，讓他們的屍體腐爛。」最後郊狼同意了：「好吧，就註定人到了時候便要死去。他們的屍體將被埋葬，他們的靈魂將前往精靈之地；但這只會持續到世界再次改變之時，那時他們就不再死去了。」

passages.text: Shortly after that, Raven's daughter became sick and died — she was the first to die. Raven tried to restore her to life, but failed, and wept. He went to Coyote and said, 'Let us change what we said before. Do not let people die and remain dead forever!' Coyote answered, 'No, it is settled now, and cannot be altered.' Thus it happens that people die and are buried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 1 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久之後，渡鴉的女兒病了並死去——她是第一個死去的人。渡鴉試圖使她復活，卻失敗了，便哭泣起來。他走到郊狼那裡說：「讓我們改變先前所說的吧。不要讓人死去並永遠保持死亡！」郊狼回答：「不，如今已成定局，無法更改。」於是事情便是這樣：人會死去並被埋葬。

title.en: Coyote Steals Fire: The Dancing Head-Dress and the Burning Country
title.zh: 郊狼盜火：燃燒之國

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (2) Coyote Steals Fire' (Thompson, collected by Teit)

summary.en: From a mountain top Coyote sees a light far to the south, learns from his own excrements that it is fire, and sets out with Fox, Wolf, Antelope and all the good runners. They dance with the Fire people, Coyote in a head-dress of pitchy pine shavings with long cedar-bark fringes; when the fire blazes high, his fringes catch, he runs out swinging them through the flames, and the fire is carried in relays by the runners while the Fire people kill them one by one. Coyote gives the fire to a tree, hides as dung, and escapes through smoke; the spreading fire burns many people until Coyote brings rain and flood to quench it. Since then fire is in wood: cedar-bark carries fire, pitch-wood kindles, and smoke always signs fire.
summary.zh: 郊狼自山頂見南方遠光，問於己糞，知其為火，遂與狐、狼、羚羊等善跑者同行盜火。眾與火族共舞，郊狼戴松脂刨花冠、垂雪松皮長纓；火旺時冠纓著火，他揮纓掠火而逃，眾接力傳火，火族逐一誅之。郊狼以火授樹，化糞藏身，冒煙得脫；火燎原，焚斃多人，郊狼召雨洪滅火。自此火藏於木：雪松皮可攜火，松脂易燃，煙常為火之兆。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'. Fire-theft cluster parallel.

passages.text: From the top of a mountain Coyote saw a light far away to the south. He did not know what it was; he defecated and questioned his excrements, and they said, 'That is fire.' He made up his mind to go and get it, and many people accompanied him — Fox, Wolf, Antelope, and all the good runners. When they reached the house of the Fire people, they told them, 'We have come to visit you, to dance, to play, and to gamble.' The Fire people danced first, with the fire very low; then Coyote's people danced in a circle around it, complaining that they could not see, until the fire blazed up high.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 2 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼從一座山頂上望見南方遠處有一點火光。他不知道那是什麼；他排了便，並詢問自己的排泄物，它們說：「那是火。」他下定決心去取火，許多人伴隨他同行——狐狸、狼、羚羊，以及所有善跑者。當他們來到火之民的家時，他們對火之民說：「我們來拜訪你們，來跳舞、嬉戲、賭博。」火之民先跳舞，火燒得很低；接著郊狼的人們圍著火跳舞，抱怨說他們看不見，直到火熊熊燃起、燒得老高。

passages.text: Coyote's people pretended to be very hot and went out to cool themselves, taking up positions for running; only Coyote remained, dancing about wildly until his head-dress of pitchy yellow-pine shavings with its long fringes of dry cedar-bark took fire. He pretended to be afraid and asked the Fire people to put it out; when near the door he swung the burning fringes across the fire and ran out. The Fire people pursued; he gave the head-band to Antelope, and the fire was carried in relays, the pursuers killing the runners one by one until only Coyote was left. He ran behind a tree and gave the fire to it, then changed himself into dung; the Fire people found nothing, and wind-driven sparks set the grass ablaze.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 2 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼的人們假裝熱得難受，便出去納涼，各自佔好奔跑的位置；只有郊狼留下來，狂亂地舞個不停，直到他那頂以富脂黃松木鉋花製成、垂著乾雪松樹皮長流蘇的頭飾著了火。他假裝害怕，請火之民把火撲滅；當他靠近門口時，他把燃燒的流蘇掃過火堆，然後跑了出去。火之民追趕；他把頭帶交給羚羊，火便由眾人接力傳遞，追趕者一個接一個地殺死奔跑者，直到只剩下郊狼。他跑到一棵樹後，把火交給那棵樹，然後把自己變成糞便；火之民什麼也沒找到，而隨風飛揚的火星把草地點燃了。

passages.text: The fire spread all over the country and burned up many people. Coyote caused a heavy rainfall and a flood, which put it out. After this the fire was in the trees, and grass and trees could be used for making fire: dry cedar-bark carries fire and serves for slow-matches, pitch-wood ignites easily for starting fires, and since then smoke and fire have been inseparable in the world — smoke is always a sign of fire, and wind makes fire blaze, which is why people blow on fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 2 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 火蔓延到整個地方，燒死了許多人。郊狼引發了一場大雨和洪水，把火撲滅了。此後火便存在於樹木之中，草和樹木可以用來取火：乾雪松樹皮能帶火，可作慢燃的火引；富脂木容易點燃，可用來生火；從那時起，煙與火在世間便密不可分——煙始終是火的徵兆，而風使火熊熊燃燒，這就是人們要對火吹氣的原因。

title.en: Coyote Tames the Elk: Teaching the People to Hunt
title.zh: 郊狼馴鹿：教民狩獵

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (3) Coyote and Elk' (Thompson, collected by Teit)

summary.en: After introducing the salmon, Coyote comes to a country whose people cannot hunt: they kill only with clubs and stones, the game fears them not at all, and some animals hunt and eat people. Refugees flee from Elk, who hunts men as they hunt deer. Coyote meets Bull Elk 'hunting for my wives,' asks if he kills people, and transforms him into a common elk — 'Henceforth people shall hunt and kill you.' Then he teaches the people to make bows and arrows, to hunt, cut up and cure meat, and to dress skins.
summary.zh: 郊狼既授鮭，行至獵術未開之國：其民唯以棍石擊獸，獸不畏人，甚者反獵食人。民逃避麋鹿。郊狼遇公麋自稱『獵吾妻』，問其食人否，答『間或為之』，遂化之為凡獸：『自此人獵汝而殺汝。』復教民製弓矢、獵獸、剖肉、治皮、乾藏。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: After Coyote had introduced the salmon, made fishing-utensils, and shown the people how to fish, prepare, and cure salmon, he went to another country. The people there did not know how to hunt: they used clubs and stones, and obtained very little game, for the animals were not afraid of them — often the game chased the people, and some kinds of game even hunted and ate people. One day Coyote met some people running, and they said, 'Elk is hunting us. He will kill and eat us.' Coyote asked why they did not kill him, and they answered, 'We are afraid. He is more powerful than we are.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 3 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼引進了鮭魚、製作了漁具，並教人們如何捕魚、處理和醃製鮭魚之後，便前往另一個地方。那裡的人不會打獵：他們用棍棒和石頭，獵獲的獵物極少，因為動物不怕他們——獵物常常追逐人，有些種類的獵物甚至獵食人。有一天，郊狼遇見一些人在奔跑，他們說：「麋鹿在獵我們。他會殺死並吃掉我們。」郊狼問他們為什麼不殺死他，他們回答：「我們害怕。他比我們強大。」

passages.text: Coyote went on and soon met a Bull Elk, and asked him where he was going. 'I am hunting for my wives,' said the elk. 'Do you kill people?' asked Coyote, and he answered, 'Yes, sometimes.' Coyote transformed him into a common elk, saying, 'Henceforth people shall hunt and kill you.' Then he taught the people how to make bows and arrows, how to hunt, cut up, and cure meat, and how to dress skins; after this they hunted deer and other game.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 3 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼繼續前行，不久遇見一頭公麋鹿，便問他要到哪裡去。「我在尋找我的妻子們，」麋鹿說。「你殺人嗎？」郊狼問，他回答：「是的，有時殺。」郊狼把他變成一頭普通的麋鹿，說：「從今以後，人們將獵殺你。」然後他教人們如何製作弓箭，如何打獵、切割和醃製肉，以及如何鞣製獸皮；此後他們便獵取鹿和其他獵物。

title.en: Coyote, Fox, and the Sun People's Bag
title.zh: 郊狼、狐狸與太陽族的袋子

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (5) Coyote, Fox, and the Sun People' (Thompson, collected by Teit)

summary.en: Travelling near the Sun's house, Coyote and Fox find a bag hanging from a pole and cannot tell what is inside. Fox's pipe answers 'Sun-rays,' Coyote's excrements answer 'hot wind.' Fox shoots a large-pointed arrow and bursts the bag: sun-rays and hot wind pour out with a great noise, and the two flee with the Sun people chasing them — until they turn, threaten to shoot, and the frightened Sun people run home.
summary.zh: 郊狼與狐近太陽之屋而行，見竿頭懸囊，不知何物。狐抽煙問卜，答『日光』；郊狼問糞，答『熱風』。狐以大鏃箭射爆其囊，日光熱風轟然而出，二人奔逃，太陽族人追之；二人回首威嚇欲射，追逐者懼而返家。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox were travelling and went near the Sun's house. There they saw a bag hanging from the end of a pole, and neither could tell what was in it. Fox smoked his pipe and questioned it, and the pipe answered, 'Sun-rays.' Coyote defecated and questioned his excrements, and they answered, 'Hot wind.' The two disputed as to who was right. Fox told Coyote to pull down the bag; Coyote tried in vain to reach it, tried to push over the pole, and finally pierced it at the bottom with his arrow-flaker, making a small hole through which something bright came out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 4 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼和狐狸正在旅行，來到了太陽的家附近。他們在那裡看見一個袋子掛在竿子的末端，兩人都說不出裡面裝的是什麼。狐狸抽了他的煙斗並向它發問，煙斗回答：「太陽光線。」郊狼排了便，並詢問自己的排泄物，它們回答：「熱風。」兩人爭論誰對誰錯。狐狸叫郊狼把袋子拉下來；郊狼試著去搆卻搆不到，又試著推倒竿子，最後用他的箭桿整形器在袋子底部刺穿，弄出一個小洞，有某種明亮的東西從中流了出來。

passages.text: Fox said, 'That must be a sun-ray; pull it down!' Coyote took hold of it and burned his hand, so Fox hit the bag with a large-pointed arrow and burst it. Then the hot wind and the sun-rays came out with a great noise, and Coyote and Fox ran away, pursued by the people of the lodge. When they were nearly overtaken, they turned around and threatened to shoot the Sun people, who at once became afraid and ran back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 4 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 狐狸說：「那一定是太陽光線；把它拉下來！」郊狼抓住它，手卻被燒傷了，於是狐狸用一支大尖頭箭射中那袋子，把它射破了。接著，熱風和太陽光線隨著巨大的聲響湧出，郊狼和狐狸便逃走了，被小屋裡的人們追趕。當他們幾乎被追上時，他們轉過身來，威脅要射殺太陽族的人，那些人立刻害怕起來，跑了回去。

title.en: Coyote Teaches People to Mate
title.zh: 郊狼教民婚配

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (6) Coyote teaches People to mate' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Coyote comes to a country where men and women know not how to propagate, and shows them how to mate; the women will not let him go until he is thoroughly fatigued, and when he runs away they chase him. After that the women of that country bear children.
summary.zh: 郊狼行至男女不識生育之國，示以婚配之道；眾女不放其行，直待他力竭方止；他遁走，眾女追之。此後該國婦女始能誕育子女。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Brief culture-hero episode on the origin of procreation, paraphrased plainly. Published folk-narrative only; no ceremonial content. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to a country where lived men and women who knew not how to propagate. He showed them how to mate. The women would not let him go until he was thoroughly fatigued; then he ran away, and they chased him. After that the women of that country bore children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 4 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在旅行，來到一個住著不知如何繁衍的男女的地方。他教他們如何交配。女人們不肯放他走，直到他疲憊不堪；然後他逃走了，她們追趕他。此後，那個地方的女人們便生下了孩子。

title.en: Coyote and the Marmots of the Clashing Rocks
title.zh: 郊狼與夾石間的旱獺

region.en: Mountain pass, Upper Salmon River, Thompson country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 上薩爾蒙河山隘，湯普森人故地（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (7) Coyote and the Marmots' (Thompson)

summary.en: Two marmots guard a mountain pass from behind rocks, clashing them together on every traveller until nothing can pass through but the wind. Coyote enters the pass; as the rocks begin to close he wedges his antler arrow-flaker across, holds the gap, transforms the marmots into animals and the moving rocks into stationary cliffs — the narrow passage between two cliffs through which the trail runs to this day.
summary.zh: 兩隻旱獺匿石後守山隘，凡有行者，即合石擊斃，唯風可過。郊狼入隘；當石欲合時，以鹿角整箭器橫撐其間，石不得合；遂化旱獺為獸、化活動之石為屹立巖崖——今小道所經兩崖間之窄徑即其遺。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote came to a pass in the mountains — some say on Upper Salmon River — inhabited by two Marmots, who sat one on each side behind rocks. When people passed through, they clashed the rocks together and killed them; nothing could pass through except the wind. Coyote heard of them and determined to pass through. When he was in the middle, the rocks began to shut; but he placed his antler arrow-flaker across, and they could not shut. He transformed the Marmots into animals, and the rocks into stationary cliffs. There is a narrow passage between two cliffs, through which the trail passes now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 4 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼來到山中的一處隘口——有人說是在上薩蒙河——那裡住著兩隻旱獺，牠們分別坐在岩石後面的兩側。當人們經過時，牠們便把岩石相撞，將人殺死；除了風以外，什麼也無法通過。郊狼聽說了牠們的事，決心要通過。當他走到中間時，岩石開始合攏；但他把他的鹿角箭羽器橫放過去，岩石便無法合攏。他把旱獺變成了動物，把岩石變成了固定的懸崖。兩座懸崖之間有一條狹窄的通道，如今小徑就從那裡穿過。

title.en: Coyote Attacked by Comb and Awl: The Tools Enslaved
title.zh: 梳與錐襲郊狼：器物淪為奴

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (8) Coyote is attacked by Comb and Awl' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Entering a tidy underground lodge where no one is visible, Coyote covets its fine things: the comb combs him violently, the awl pierces him, the smoothing-stones jump and scratch off his skin, and the stone hammer stuns him with a blow to the head. Beaten, he runs away crying the decree that turns them into mere tools: 'Henceforth you shall be mere tools and slaves of people.'
summary.zh: 郊狼入一整潔之地下屋，屋中無人而物什井然。他貪取美梳，梳即狂梳其身；取錐，錐即刺之；取磨箭石，石跳動抓剝其皮；取石錘，錘重擊其首，昏厥而逃。逃時怒下咒令：『自此爾等不得為人、不得傷人，只為凡器、為人之奴。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote came to an underground lodge, which he entered. He saw no one inside; but everything looked in order, as if people lived there — bows and arrows, quivers, war-clubs, baskets, and bags. He picked up a nice comb and examined it, and thought he would take it. As he turned to go away he heard people murmuring; looking around, he saw nothing. As he started to climb the ladder, the comb scratched and combed him violently. 'Stop! I will put you back,' he said. Then he thought he would take an awl: again the murmuring, and as he started to run away, the awl pierced him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 4-5 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼來到一間地下的屋子，走了進去。他在裡面沒看見任何人；但一切看起來都井然有序，彷彿有人住在那裡——弓和箭、箭袋、戰棍、籃子和袋子。他撿起一把漂亮的梳子端詳，心想把它拿走。當他轉身要走時，他聽見有人低聲抱怨；環顧四周，卻什麼也沒看見。當他開始爬上梯子時，那把梳子猛烈地抓撓並梳理他。「停下！我把你放回去，」他說。然後他想拿走一把錐子：又傳來低聲抱怨，當他開始逃跑時，那把錐子刺穿了他。

passages.text: He took a pair of fine stones for smoothing arrows, and they attacked him, jumping up and down and scratching off his skin. Lastly he took a stone hammer, and it hit him so hard on the head that he was stunned, and ran away. Angry, he cried out: 'You shall no longer be people and have power to attack: henceforth you shall be mere tools and slaves of people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 5 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他拿了一對用來磨箭的漂亮石頭，它們便攻擊他，上下跳動，刮掉他的皮。最後他拿了一把石錘，它重重地打在他的頭上，把他打暈了，他便逃走了。他憤怒地喊道：「你們不再是人，也不再有力氣攻擊：從今以後，你們只是工具，是人們的奴隸。」

title.en: Coyote and the Geese: Carried Up by the Flock
title.zh: 郊狼與雁：被雁群捲上半空

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (9) Coyote and the Geese' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Coyote cuts a club and whistles a flock of geese out of the sky, claps his hands, and they all fall down; but when he clubs them among the cackling, flapping birds, the wings raise such a wind that he is lifted off his feet and carried away, missing first the swamp-grass, then the willows, then the tree-tops, until he drops head-first into the middle of a swamp. Mosquitoes and flies bite him and crawl into him, and at last Fox comes along and pulls him out.
summary.zh: 郊狼削棍吹哨，群雁盤旋而降；拍掌一響，盡落於地。他執棍亂擊，雁聲撲翼釀成大風，竟將他掀上半空，先抓沼草不得、再抓柳梢不得、復抓樹梢不得，終倒栽於沼心泥中不得自拔。蚊蠅噬之，鑽入其身。後狐狸至，方拔之出。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling through a country of lakes and swamps. He saw a large flock of geese flying overhead and wished he could kill and eat them. He cut a club of wood, and whistled; they halted, and circled around. He clapped his hands, and they all fell down. He ran among them and clubbed them; but they merely cackled, laughed, and flapped their wings, and in the noise and confusion he could not see where he was hitting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 5 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在穿越一片遍布湖泊和沼澤的地方。他看見一大群鵝從頭頂飛過，希望能殺幾隻來吃。他砍了一根木棒，吹了聲口哨；牠們停了下來，盤旋起來。他拍了拍手，牠們全都掉了下來。他跑到牠們中間，用棒子打牠們；但牠們只是嘎嘎叫、笑著、拍打翅膀，在喧鬧和混亂中，他看不清自己打在哪裡。

passages.text: The wings caused a strong wind, and as they rose Coyote was taken off his feet and carried along by them. He caught at the swamp-grass tops, then at the willow-bush tops, then at the tree tops, but could not hold on. He was carried to a point above the middle of a near-by swamp, where he dropped head first into the mud and could not extricate himself. The mosquitoes, flies, and insects bit his legs and his backside and crawled into him. At last Fox came along and pulled him out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 5 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翅膀激起一陣強風，當牠們升空時，郊狼被帶離地面，隨著牠們一同飛去。他先抓住沼澤草的頂端，接著抓住柳叢的頂端，然後抓住樹梢，卻都抓不住。他被帶到附近一片沼澤中央的上方，在那裡頭朝下栽進泥裡，無法脫身。蚊子、蒼蠅和各種昆蟲叮咬他的腿和臀部，還爬進他的身體裡。最後狐狸走來，把他拉了出來。

title.en: Coyote, Fox, and the Egg-Gatherers
title.zh: 郊狼、狐狸與拾蛋女

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (10) Coyote, Fox, and the Egg-Gatherers' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: While Coyote and Fox sleep off a fat meal, mischievous women tickle them with feathers and exchange their noses. When they wake each laughs at the other's face — and it is only at the lake, seeing their reflections, that they realize their own faces were changed too; they quarrel, each blaming the other, until they hear people laughing and know a trick was played. Following the tracks, they find the women gathering ducks' eggs in a swamp.
summary.zh: 郊狼與狐食肥酣睡，戲弄之婦以羽搔癢，並互換二獸之鼻。二人醒後互笑對方之臉，及至湖邊照影，方知己顏亦遭改換；遂互相指責爭吵，直至聞人笑聲，始知被戲。循足跡而去，見婦人正於沼中拾鴨蛋。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox had cooked some fat meat, and, after eating, fell sound asleep. Some women who found them asleep thought they would have some fun with them. They tickled them with feathers, but the two slept on; then they changed their noses. When the two awoke, they laughed at each other, but neither thought his own face had also been changed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 5-6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼和狐狸煮了一些肥肉，吃過之後便沉沉入睡。幾個女人發現他們睡著了，心想不妨捉弄他們一番。她們用羽毛搔他們，但兩人仍舊沉睡；於是她们換掉了他們的鼻子。兩人醒來後互相取笑，卻誰也沒想到自己的臉也被換過了。

passages.text: Thirsty because they had eaten so much fat, they went down to a lake to drink; and when they saw by their reflections how ugly they had become, they quarrelled, each blaming the other for being the cause of his changed appearance. They heard people laughing, and then knew that a trick had been played on them. They followed the tracks of the women, and saw them busy gathering ducks' eggs in a swamp.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因為吃了太多肥肉而口渴，他們下到一座湖邊喝水；當他們從倒影中看見自己變得如此醜陋時，便爭吵起來，各自責怪對方是自己容貌改變的緣由。他們聽見有人在大笑，這才明白自己被人捉弄了。他們循著那些女人的足跡追去，看見她們正忙著在沼澤裡撿拾鴨蛋。

title.en: Coyote and his Guest: The Broken Beak
title.zh: 郊狼與客：折喙記

region.en: Spences Bridge, Thompson River, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斯賓塞斯布里奇，湯普森河，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (11) Coyote and his Guests' (Thompson, from Spences Bridge)

summary.en: Coyote feasts at Kingfisher's lodge, where his host dives through a hole in the ice with a withe and brings up fish four times. On returning the visit, Coyote fits a pitch-wood beak to his nose, climbs a tree over a shallow waterhole, gives the kingfisher's cry — and breaks his nose and his head in the hole. Kingfisher laughs at the bungling guest, then catches fish for him so they may eat.
summary.zh: 郊狼赴翠鳥之宴，見主人持藤條自冰洞潛水，四度銜魚而歸，飽食而去。回請之日，郊狼黏松脂木為喙於鼻，攀樹臨淺水窟，學翠鳥啼而俯衝——鼻首俱碎。翠鳥笑其拙，仍捕魚相饗。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Bungling-host episode. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once upon a time Coyote visited Kingfisher. Since Kingfisher had no food, he went out carrying a withe, climbed a tree, uttered the Kingfisher's cry, and dived through a hole in the ice; soon he emerged carrying a fish, and repeated this four times. He strung the fish on the withe, returned to the lodge, and cooked them for Coyote, who ate until he was satiated. On leaving, Coyote invited Kingfisher to visit him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，郊狼去拜訪翠鳥。翠鳥因為沒有食物，便帶著一根柳條出門，爬上樹，發出翠鳥的鳴叫，從冰上的洞裡潛了下去；不久他浮上來，帶著一條魚，如此重複了四次。他把魚串在柳條上，回到屋裡，把魚煮給郊狼吃，郊狼一直吃到飽足。臨走時，郊狼邀請翠鳥來拜訪他。

passages.text: When Kingfisher entered Coyote's house, he saw nothing to eat. Coyote went out, cut a willow withe to carry the fish, fitted to his nose a long piece of pitch-wood to serve as a beak, and climbed a tree overhanging a shallow hole from which he used to draw water. He uttered the Kingfisher's cry and dived down into the hole, where he broke his nose and his head. Kingfisher laughed at the bungling Coyote, then caught some fish for him so that they might eat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翠鳥走進郊狼的家時，看不到任何可吃的東西。郊狼走出去，砍了一根柳條用來串魚，在鼻子上裝了一塊長長的松脂木當作鳥喙，然後爬上一棵懸在淺水坑上方的樹——那水坑是他平日取水的地方。他發出翠鳥的鳴叫，朝水坑潛了下去，結果撞傷了鼻子和頭。翠鳥嘲笑這笨手笨腳的郊狼，隨後替他抓了些魚，好讓兩人有東西吃。

title.en: Coyote and his Elk Wife
title.zh: 郊狼與麋妻

region.en: Nicola country, Thompson land, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉之地，湯普森人鄉土，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (12) Coyote and his Elk Wife' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Elk chief gives Coyote one of his daughters to wife, with a rule: she may be bitten on the rump for meat, the wound healing each time, but not before four nights, and never more than once a day. Coyote, hungry on the road north, breaks the rule; his wife runs away and becomes an elk living in the Nicola country, and ever since elks have been numerous there.
summary.zh: 麋酋以女妻郊狼，且立規：餓時可齧其妻臀部為食，創口自癒；惟四夜之前不得咬，此後每日不得逾一次。郊狼北行飢甚，破戒而咬；妻奔逃，化為麋居尼古拉之地。自此該地麋群繁盛。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote had been travelling somewhere to the south, where he met Elk chief, who gave him one of his daughters to wife, telling him: 'If you are hungry, you may take a bite of meat from your wife's rump, which will heal over each time. However, you must not bite her before four nights have passed, and after that not more than once a day.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼曾往南方某處旅行，在那裡遇見麋鹿酋長，酋長把一個女兒嫁給他為妻，對他說：「你若餓了，可以從你妻子臀部咬一塊肉來吃，每次都會癒合。不過，在四夜過去之前，你不可咬她；在那之後，一天也不可超過一次。」

passages.text: Travelling north, Coyote had reached the Nicola country; he hunted on the way, but could get no game, and was hungry. 'Why should I have an Elk wife and not eat her?' he said. 'Why should I wait when I am hungry?' He snapped at his wife, but she ran away; he followed and coaxed her back. In the evening, when they camped, he jumped at his wife and bit her. She ran away and became an elk that lived in the Nicola country. Coyote went on alone and came to the Thompson River; ever since that time elks have been numerous in the Nicola country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 6 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼向北行進，來到了尼古拉地區；他一路上打獵，卻一無所獲，飢腸轆轆。「我既然有了一頭麋鹿妻子，為什麼不吃掉她呢？」他說。「我餓著肚子，為什麼還要等呢？」他朝妻子撲咬過去，她卻逃走了；他追上去，好言哄勸，把她帶了回來。傍晚他們紮營時，他又撲向妻子，咬了她。她逃走了，變成了一頭麋鹿，住在尼古拉地區。郊狼獨自繼續前行，來到了湯普森河；自那時起，麋鹿便在尼古拉地區繁衍眾多。

title.en: Coyote Digs Roots in the Sky Country
title.zh: 郊狼在天國掘根

region.en: Sky country above the Thompson lands (symbolic pin at Nicola Valley)
region.zh: 湯普森人故地上空之天國（象徵定位於尼古拉谷）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (14) Coyote digs Roots' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Hungry and seeing no lodges or people, Coyote cuts a root-digger and digs a large tatu'En root; wind rushes up through the hole, and he can see people walking far below. He puts the plant back and digs another with the same result — for he must have been in the sky country, and those roots were stars.
summary.zh: 郊狼飢而四顧無人煙，削枝為掘根杖，掘得大株 tatu'En 根；風自穴中上衝，他俯視竟見極下方行人往來。復土掩之，再掘一株，其象依然——蓋其所處乃天國，而其所掘之『根』實為星辰。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Sky-world episode; the pin is symbolic. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to a country where many tatu'En roots grew. He was hungry, and could find no game, nor could he see any lodges or people. He cut a stick to serve as a root-digger, and said, 'I will dig some roots and eat them.' He saw a large one and dug it out; wind rushed up through the hole, and he could see people walking way down below. He put the plant back again. He dug another one, and the same thing happened. He must have been in the sky country, and these roots were stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 7 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼四處遊歷，來到一個長著許多 tatu'En 根的地方。他餓了，卻找不到獵物，也看不見任何屋舍或人。他削了一根木棍當作挖根的工具，說道：「我要挖些根來吃。」他看見一根大的，便把它挖了出來；風從洞裡呼嘯而上，他竟能看見人們在下方深處行走。他把那株植物放了回去。他又挖了一根，同樣的事又發生了。他必定是身處天空之國，而這些根便是星辰。

title.en: Fox Steals Coyote's Food: The Rock that Held Him
title.zh: 狐竊郊狼之食：困人之石

region.en: Lower Nicola Valley, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 下尼古拉谷，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (15) Fox steals Coyote's Food' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Waiting for his ground-squirrels to bake, Coyote sits on a rock, leans back and falls asleep; the rock holds him fast while Fox eats every squirrel. Released at last, Coyote finds Fox asleep in tall grass and fires the grass — but Fox escapes through the smoke, his skin scorched: since then the fox is reddish. The hollowed stone with Coyote's seat-marks still lies in the Lower Nicola Valley.
summary.zh: 郊狼烤松鼠以待熟，坐石倚之而眠；石困其身，狐竟食盡松鼠。久之方脫，尋狐於高草間縱火焚之；狐自煙中遁，皮已烙赤——狐之赤色由此。下尼古拉谷今猶存中空之石，上有郊狼坐痕與立痕。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote killed some young ground-squirrels and made a hole in which to bake them. He stood waiting for them to be done; then, feeling tired, he sat down on a rock near by, leaned back, and fell asleep. When he woke up, he saw Fox eating the squirrels. He tried to get up, but the rock held him. 'Leave some for me, Brother Fox!' — but Fox ate all the squirrels and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 7 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼殺了幾隻年幼的地松鼠，挖了一個坑用來烘烤牠們。他站著等牠們烤熟；後來覺得累了，便坐到附近的一塊岩石上，向後一靠，睡著了。他醒來時，看見狐狸正在吃那些松鼠。他想站起來，岩石卻把他困住了。「給我留一些吧，狐狸兄弟！」——可是狐狸把松鼠全吃光了，逕自離去。

passages.text: After a long time Coyote was released, and gave chase to Fox, finding him asleep in some tall grass. He set fire to the grass and thought he had killed him, but Fox escaped in the smoke, his skin scorched; since then the fox has been of a reddish color. The stone on which Coyote lay may still be seen in the Lower Nicola Valley, hollowed in the middle, with the mark of Coyote's seat on a stone near by and the marks of his feet on another. It is not known who released Coyote: some say Fox made the stone seize him and afterwards let him go; some say the stone never seized him, but that Fox caused him to stick to it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 7-8 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了很久，郊狼才脫身，隨即追趕狐狸，發現他睡在一些高高的草叢中。他放火燒草，自以為燒死了他，但狐狸從煙中逃走了，皮毛被燒焦；自那時起，狐狸便帶上了赤紅的顏色。郊狼躺過的那塊石頭，至今仍可在下尼古拉谷見到，石頭中央凹陷，附近一塊石上有郊狼坐過的痕跡，另一塊上則有他腳印的痕跡。究竟是誰放開了郊狼，並不清楚：有人說是狐狸讓石頭抓住他，之後又放了他；有人說石頭從未抓住他，而是狐狸使他黏在了上面。

title.en: Fox Steals Coyote's Food: The Tree that Fell
title.zh: 狐竊食其二：倒木之計

region.en: Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (16) Fox steals Coyote's Food' (Thompson)

summary.en: Half-brothers who play tricks on each other: Coyote cooks a carcass in a pit and naps under a branchy tree; Fox comes along and makes the tree fall on him, trapping him while the meat is eaten to the last morsel before Coyote can work free.
summary.zh: 郊狼與狐為異父兄弟（或表親），慣相捉弄。郊狼烹獸於坑，臥枝繁樹下小憩；狐至，令樹倒壓之。郊狼被困之際，狐將肉食盡，待其掙脫，片甲無存。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox were half-brothers (or cousins). They often played tricks on each other. Once Coyote had found a carcass (or had killed some game), which he began to cook in a pit; while he was waiting under a branchy tree for the meat to be done, he fell asleep. Fox came along and caused the tree to fall on Coyote, who could not get away for a time. While he was imprisoned, he saw Fox eating the meat, and begged him to leave some; but Fox ate it all before Coyote could get away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 8 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼和狐狸是同父異母的兄弟（或表兄弟）。他們常常互相捉弄。有一次，郊狼找到了一具獸屍（或獵到了一些獵物），便開始在坑裡烹煮；他在一棵枝葉繁茂的樹下等候肉煮熟時，睡著了。狐狸走過來，使那棵樹倒在了郊狼身上，郊狼一時無法脫身。他被困住的時候，看見狐狸在吃肉，便求他留一些；可是還沒等郊狼脫身，狐狸就把肉全吃光了。

title.en: Coyote Wears Fox's Rattle
title.zh: 郊狼戴狐之鈴

region.en: Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (17) Coyote wears Fox's Rattle' (Thompson)

summary.en: Fox fastens a rattle to his tail, warns Coyote it is dangerous and that only he can wear it — and Coyote insists. Fox ties it on with a warning not to go through brush, knowing Coyote will do exactly that; the rattle snags in the bushes and pulls out his entrails. Fox returns, takes the rattle, puts the entrails back, kicks Coyote awake — and Coyote believes he has been asleep.
summary.zh: 狐縛鈴於尾，告誡郊狼此物危險，唯彼能戴；郊狼固請。狐為其繫上，並囑勿穿叢莽——明知其必犯。郊狼穿林，鈴為枝椏所鉤，竟拽出其腸。狐至，取鈴、納腸、踢其醒；郊狼醒後猶自以為方才熟睡。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Another time Fox fastened a rattle to his tail, and Coyote wanted to get it. Fox told him it was dangerous, and that only he himself could wear it; but Coyote persisted, so Fox fastened it to Coyote's tail and warned him not to go through any brush — knowing that Coyote would try to go through brush in order to learn why this had been forbidden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 8 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又有一次，狐狸把一個搖響器繫在自己的尾巴上，郊狼想要得到它。狐狸告訴他這很危險，只有他自己才能佩戴；但郊狼執意要，於是狐狸把搖響器繫在郊狼的尾巴上，並警告他不要穿過任何灌木叢——他心裡清楚，郊狼為了弄清楚這禁令的緣由，一定會設法穿過灌木叢。

passages.text: Coyote walked through bushes and stripped the rattle from his tail. He felt something pulling at his backside, and discovered that the rattle had caught in the bushes and was pulling out his entrails. He did not know what to do, and fainted. Fox came along, took away the rattle, and put back Coyote's entrails. Then he kicked Coyote, who awoke and believed that he had been asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 8 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼穿過灌木叢，尾巴上的響環被扯了下來。他感覺有什麼東西在拉扯他的臀部，這才發現響環卡在灌木叢裡，正把他的內臟往外拽。他不知該怎麼辦，便昏了過去。狐狸走了過來，取走響環，把郊狼的內臟放了回去。接著他踢了郊狼一腳，郊狼醒來，還以為自己剛才睡著了。

title.en: Coyote and the Woodpeckers
title.zh: 郊狼與啄木鳥

region.en: Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (18) Coyote and the Woodpeckers' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Trapped in a cave (some say a hollow tree), Coyote calls all the animals and birds to his aid; all fail, until the woodpeckers take over — one cracks the rock, a second widens the crack, a third widens it further, and the Red-Headed Woodpecker splits it open so Coyote escapes. Some tellers add that the birds pulled him out by the tail.
summary.zh: 郊狼困於穴中（或云空心樹），呼百獸百鳥相救，皆無功；最後啄木鳥上陣：其一啄裂巖石，二鳥繼之擴裂，三鳥再擴，紅頭啄木鳥終劈石而開，郊狼得脫。或云眾鳥銜尾拽之而出。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was caught in a cave, and called on all animals and birds for aid. They tried to release him, but failed. Finally he called on the Woodpeckers: one of them struck the rock and cracked it; the second widened the crack; the third one widened it still more; and finally the Red-Headed Woodpecker split it open, so that Coyote was able to get out. Some people say Coyote was caught in a hollow tree, and that the Woodpeckers pecked a hole and took him out; some add that they pulled him out by the tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 8-9 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼被困在一個洞穴裡，向所有走獸與飛鳥求救。他們試著救他出來，卻都失敗了。最後他向啄木鳥求救：其中一隻啄擊岩石，把石頭啄裂；第二隻把裂縫啄得更寬；第三隻又把裂縫啄得更寬；最後紅頭啄木鳥把岩石劈開，郊狼這才得以脫身。有人說郊狼是困在一棵中空的樹裡，啄木鳥啄出一個洞，把他弄了出來；還有人補充說，他們是拽著他的尾巴把他拉出來的。

title.en: The Giant Mosquitoes Tamed
title.zh: 巨蚊之馴

region.en: Swamp edge, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 沼邊，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (19) The Mosquitoes' (Thompson)

summary.en: Formerly mosquitoes were large, fierce, and ate people. Mosquito and his wife lived at the edge of the timber near a swamp, hunting human prey — he took only women, his wife only men, and they preferred the blood from the privates. Coyote (or some other transformer) turned them into the small insects of today, decreeing that they should frequent swamps and woods, suck only a little blood, and never again have power to kill people.
summary.zh: 古時蚊體巨大、兇殘食人。蚊夫婦居林緣沼畔，獵人吮血——夫專獵女子，妻專獵男子，尤嗜下體之血。郊狼（或其他變形者）化之為今日之小蚊，且令：『自此爾等往來沼林，僅能吮微血，不得再殺人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Formerly mosquitoes were very large, fierce, and ate people. Mosquito and his wife lived in a house at the edge of the timber, near a swamp. They hunted people and killed them by sucking their blood; Mosquito hunted only women, and his wife hunted only men. Coyote (or some other transformer) turned them into mosquitoes, saying: 'Henceforth you shall be small insects, and shall frequent swamps and woods. You shall be able to suck a little blood only. You shall not have power to kill people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 9 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前蚊子非常巨大、兇猛，還會吃人。蚊子與妻子住在林邊近沼澤的一間屋子裡。他們獵捕人類，吸人的血把人殺死；蚊子只獵女人，他的妻子只獵男人。郊狼（或某位別的變形者）把他們變成蚊子，說道：「從今以後，你們要成為小小的昆蟲，出沒於沼澤與樹林。你們只能吸一點點血。你們不會再有殺人的能力。」

title.en: The Cannibal Who Used an Elk as a Decoy
title.zh: 以假麋為餌的食人魔

region.en: Lakeshore flat, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湖岸平地，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (20) The Cannibal who used an Elk as a Decoy' (Thompson)

summary.en: A cannibal lives in a large hollow tree beside a lake, keeping a stuffed elk-skin within arrow range on the open flat; when a hunter stalks the decoy, the cannibal shoots and eats him, and many bones and skulls lie around the tree's base. Coyote defecates and makes his excrements whistle; when the cannibal looks out of the tree-top to see who is there, Coyote slips in and shoots him from behind.
summary.zh: 食人魔居湖畔大空心樹，於箭程之內曠地置填草麥皮麋為餌；獵人窺麋，即遭其射殺吞食，樹下白骨纍纍。郊狼便溺並令己糞作哨聲；魔自樹頂探首張望之際，郊狼潛入樹中，自後一箭斃之。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote (or some other transformer) was travelling, and came to a place where a cannibal lived in a large hollow tree. He used as a decoy a stuffed elk-skin, kept within arrow range on an open flat near a lake-shore. When a hunter stalked the elk, the cannibal shot and ate him; many bones and skulls were around the base of the tree. Coyote defecated, and made his excrements whistle. When the cannibal looked out of the top of the tree, thinking some one was there, Coyote entered the tree and shot the cannibal, hitting him from behind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 9 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼（或某位別的變形者）正在旅行，來到一個地方，那裡有個食人者在巨大的空心樹裡居住。他用一張填塞好的麋鹿皮作誘餌，把它放在湖岸附近一片開闊平地上、弓箭射程之內。當獵人悄悄接近那隻麋鹿時，食人者便開槍射殺他，把他吃掉；樹根周圍散落著許多骨頭與頭骨。郊狼拉了屎，讓自己的糞便發出哨聲。當食人者從樹頂探頭張望，以為那裡有人時，郊狼進了樹，從背後開槍擊中食人者。

title.en: Coyote Steals the Sweat-House-Man's Blanket
title.zh: 郊狼竊汗屋人之毯

region.en: Creek-side sweat house, Thompson country (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 溪畔汗屋，湯普森人故地（象徵定位於利頓）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (21) Coyote steals Sweat-House-Man's Blanket' (Thompson)
