summary.en: Finding a fine blanket covering an apparently empty sweat house, Coyote carries it off — but something invisible follows, strikes his legs, knocks him down, blinds him and rolls him about until he loses consciousness: it is Sweat-House-Man, or the Wind, come to punish him. He wakes in the middle of a swamp, bruised, bleeding, stung by mosquitoes, sand-flies infesting mouth, nose, ears and hair, and can barely crawl out; the blanket returns to its owner.
summary.zh: 郊狼見汗屋覆以美毯，內似無人，遂攜毯而逃。行不多遠，無形者自後追擊：擊其腿、倒其身、蔽其目、翻滾其體至不省人事——乃汗屋之人（或即風神）前來懲罰。醒時已在沼心，遍體鱗傷，蚊噬蟲鑽，口鼻耳髮皆為沙蠅所據，掙扎良久方出泥沼；毯則物歸原主。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to a creek, where he saw a sweat-house covered with a nice blanket. He listened, but heard nothing except the noise sometimes made by hot stones. He lifted up a corner of the blanket, looked in, saw no one, thought, 'I will take this blanket,' and went off with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 9 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在旅行，來到一條小溪邊，看見一座汗屋，上面蓋著一條漂亮的毯子。他側耳傾聽，除了熱石頭偶爾發出的聲響外，什麼也沒聽見。他掀起毯子的一角，往裡看，沒看見任何人，心想：「我要把這條毯子拿走。」便帶著它走了。

passages.text: When he had gone some distance, he heard a noise behind; he looked and saw nothing, but the noise came nearer until it became so terrible that Coyote started to run. Something knocked him down, picked him up again, struck his head and blinded him; he seemed to be torn to pieces and was rolled about until he lost consciousness. It was Sweat-House-Man, or the Wind, come to punish Coyote. When he woke, he found himself in the middle of a swamp, bruised and bleeding, stung by mosquitoes, his eyes and body swollen; sand-flies had crawled into his mouth, nose, ears, and hair. He extricated himself with difficulty and after tiresome travelling in the mud came out of the swamp; the blanket went back to Sweat-House-Man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 9-10 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他走了好一段路，聽見身後有聲響；他回頭看，什麼也沒看見，可那聲響越來越近，直到變得可怕至極，郊狼便開始奔跑。有什麼東西把他撞倒，又把他拎起來，擊打他的頭，使他雙目失明；他彷彿被撕成碎片，被翻來滾去，直到失去知覺。原來是汗屋之人，也就是風，前來懲罰郊狼。他醒來時，發現自己身處沼澤中央，遍體鱗傷、流著血，被蚊子叮咬，眼睛和身體都腫了起來；沙蠅爬進了他的嘴、鼻子、耳朵和頭髮裡。他好不容易才脫身，在泥濘中艱難跋涉之後走出了沼澤；那條毯子則回到了汗屋之人那裡。

title.en: Coyote and the Rolling Bowlder
title.zh: 郊狼與滾石

region.en: Upper Uta'mqt (Lillooet) and Nicola Valley country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 上利盧埃特與尼古拉谷故地（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (23) Coyote and the Rolling Bowlder' (Thompson)

summary.en: In the Upper Uta'mqt country a bowlder at the foot of a cliff kills people by rolling on them, and Coyote learns which one it is by questioning his excrements. Standing below it, he hears it coming, drives his double-headed arrow-flaker into the ground with one end pointing uphill, and the bowlder shatters on the point — the patch of sharp white rock fragments that lies there now. Henceforth bowlders shall not kill people by rolling downhill: people shall be able to get out of their way.
summary.zh: 上利盧埃特之地，崖下巨石滾落殺人；郊狼問糞而知其為何石。立於石下，聞其滾近，將雙頭整箭器直插土中、一端朝上；巨石撞於鋒端，碎為粉末——今該處白色碎石一片即其遺。郊狼令：『自此滾石不得殺人，人皆得避之。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. A special form of the rolling-rock motif (cf. record coyote-rolling-rock). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling somewhere in the Upper Uta'mqt country, and came to a side-hill where there were bowlders at the foot of a cliff. Below, the side-hill was smooth. A bowlder lived here that killed people by rolling on them. Coyote did not know which one it was, and questioned his excrements; they told him, and it was a long distance above him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 10 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在上烏塔姆克特（Upper Uta'mqt）一帶某處旅行，來到一處山坡，崖腳下有一些巨石。下方山坡很平滑。這裡住著一塊會滾到人身上把人壓死的巨石。郊狼不知道是哪一塊，便詢問自己的糞便；糞便告訴了他，而那塊巨石在他上方很遠的地方。

passages.text: When he was below it, he heard a noise and saw it coming. He stuck his double-headed arrow-flaker into the ground with one end pointing uphill, and when the bowlder hit the point, it broke into fragments — the patch of sharp fragments of white rock that is there now. He said: 'Henceforth bowlders shall not kill people by rolling downhill. People shall be able to get out of their way.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 10 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他來到那塊巨石下方時，他聽到一陣聲響，看見它正滾下來。他把自己的雙頭箭石剝片器插進地面，一端朝上坡方向，當巨石撞上尖端時，它碎成了碎片——就是如今仍在那裡的那片白色岩石銳利碎片。他說：『從今以後，巨石不得再滾下山坡壓死人。人們應當能夠避開它們。』

title.en: The Coyote People
title.zh: 郊狼子孫

region.en: Interior Salish country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 內陸薩利什故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (26) The Coyote People' (Thompson)

summary.en: Coyote married a woman and had many children by her, and from these children descend the Salish tribes — the Thompson from one, the Shuswap from another, the Okanagon and Lillooet from others — which is why their languages are related. The Chilcotin, Carriers, Lower Fraser and Coast peoples are of different parentage, and for this reason the Thompson and Shuswap are often called 'Coyote people' in stories.
summary.zh: 郊狼娶妻生子甚多，內陸薩利什諸族皆其後裔：湯普森出自其一，舒什瓦普出自其二，奧卡諾根與利盧埃特又出自其他——故其語言同源。奇爾科廷、卡里埃、下弗雷澤與海岸諸族則另有始祖。因此故事中常稱湯普森人與舒什瓦普人為『郊狼子孫』。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Ethnogony; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote married a woman, and had many children by her. From these children are descended the Salish tribes: the Thompson are the descendants of one; the Shuswap, of another; Okanagon and Lillooet, of others. Therefore the languages of these tribes are related. The Chilcotin and Carriers must be of different parentage — some say they are the descendants of Deer or Bird people — and the Lower Fraser and Coast people are also different. On account of this story the Thompson and Shuswap are often called 'Coyote people' in stories.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 12 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼娶了一個女人，與她生了許多孩子。薩利什（Salish）諸部落就是這些孩子的後裔：湯普森人（Thompson）是其中一個孩子的後裔；舒斯瓦普人（Shuswap）是另一個的後裔；奧卡納干人（Okanagon）和利盧埃特人（Lillooet）又是其他孩子的後裔。因此這些部落的語言彼此相關。奇爾科廷人（Chilcotin）和卡里爾人（Carriers）必定出自不同的父母——有人說他們是鹿人或鳥人的後裔——下弗雷澤人（Lower Fraser）和沿海居民也與眾不同。由於這個故事，湯普森人和舒斯瓦普人在故事中常被稱為『郊狼之民』。

title.en: Old-Coyote and the Separation of Languages
title.zh: 老郊狼與語言之分

region.en: Nicola Valley, Thompson country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尼古拉谷，湯普森人故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (27) Old-Coyote and the Coyote People' (Thompson, from Nicola Valley)

summary.en: Old-Coyote, ancestor of all the Indians, had many wives, and from them descend the Thompson, Okanagon, Shuswap — and, as he travelled the world, the Salish, Kalispel, Nez Perce, Yakima, Blackfeet and all the interior tribes. Once all his descendants spoke one language like Shuswap; then Old-One separated the good from the bad, transformed the bad into coyotes, led the good forth, and settled them wide apart — so that when they met again they spoke different languages. Coyotes abound in the region of Old-Coyote's descendants and his travels, but nowhere else.
summary.zh: 老郊狼為印第安人之祖，多妻而子孫遍佈——湯普森、奧卡諾根、舒什瓦普，乃至薩利什、卡利斯佩爾、內茲珀斯、亞基馬、黑腳與內陸諸族皆其苗裔。其子孫初本同語（近舒什瓦普語）；後老者（Old-One）分善惡，化惡者為郊狼，率善者散居遠地，故重逢時言語已異。郊狼之多，唯見於老郊狼子孫之地與其遊蹤之處。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Language-separation ethnogony; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Old-Coyote (called 'Uncle Coyote' by some) was the ancestor of all the Indians. He had many wives; from some are descended the Thompson, from others the Okanagon, from still others the Shuswap. One of his sons had two wives, Lu'la and Tce'xa, varieties of ducks, and the latter had a simple-minded sister, the Frog, who followed her as her servant. Many of his sons had magical powers, and as Coyote travelled over a large part of the world he left children in many places: the Salish, Kalispel, Nez Perces, Yakima, and Blackfeet, and all the interior tribes, have sprung from Coyote's children. Because these tribes sprang from Coyote, they are called 'Coyote people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 12-13 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老郊狼（有些人稱他為『郊狼叔叔』）是所有印第安人的祖先。他有許多妻子；湯普森人出自其中一些妻子，奧卡納干人出自另一些，舒斯瓦普人又出自另一些。他的一個兒子有兩個妻子，即盧拉（Lu'la）和采哈（Tce'xa），她們是不同種類的鴨子，後者有一個頭腦簡單的妹妹青蛙，跟隨她充當她的僕人。他的許多兒子都有法力，而當郊狼走遍世界大部分地方時，他在許多地方留下了子女：薩利什人、卡利斯佩爾人（Kalispel）、內茲珀斯人（Nez Perces）、亞基馬人（Yakima）和黑腳人（Blackfeet），以及所有內陸部落，都源自郊狼的子女。因為這些部落源自郊狼，所以他們被稱為『郊狼之民』。

passages.text: The descendants of Coyote spread over the country and occupied many parts that were not formerly inhabited. At one time they all spoke the same language, like Shuswap; some of them were bad people, but most were good. At a later date Old-One separated the good people from the bad: he transformed all the bad ones into coyotes, led the good ones forth, and made them settle at different places, widely apart. Afterwards, when the people met, they spoke different languages. For this reason coyotes abound in the region inhabited by Old-Coyote's descendants and in the country over which he travelled, but nowhere else.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 13 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼的後裔遍布各地，佔據了許多從前無人居住的地方。有一個時期，他們全都說同一種語言，像舒斯瓦普語一樣；他們當中有些是壞人，但大多數是好人。後來，老一（Old-One）把好人與壞人分開：他把所有壞人都變成郊狼，把好人領出來，讓他們分別定居在彼此相距遙遠的不同地方。後來，當人們相遇時，他們說的已是不同的語言。因此，郊狼大量出沒於老郊狼後裔所居住的地區以及他曾走過的地方，而在別處則沒有。

title.en: Coyote and the Flood: The Stone Canoe on Zoke'ski
title.zh: 郊狼與洪水：佐克斯基山上的石舟

region.en: Thompson River, Zoke'ski mountain, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湯普森河佐克斯基山，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote Tales, (28) Coyote and the Flood' (Thompson)

summary.en: A flood covers the whole country but the tops of the highest mountains — some say sent to put out a great world-fire, others to clean the earth. People and animals drown; some flee to peaks, some drift on logs, for no one knows how to make canoes. Only Coyote makes a canoe of horse-tails or grass, and with his friends drifts many days until they strike Zoke'ski mountain on the south side of the Thompson River, where the flood recedes. Leaving the canoe, he transforms it into stone — the thirty-foot stone canoe with three figures in it that stands near the mountain top — and the water-marks on the mountains, the mountain lakes and fish, and the tribes settled at Lytton and Nicola all descend from that voyage.
summary.zh: 洪水滔天，唯最高山尖未沒——或云為滅世界大火，或云為洗滌大地。人獸多溺斃；逃山頂者、抱木漂流者皆有，唯無人會造舟。獨郊狼以馬尾或草製舟，攜友漂流多日，撞上湯普森河南岸之佐克斯基山，水退。棄舟時化之為石——山頂附近今存三十尺石舟，內有三個人形，有的已消失。山中水痕、高湖之魚、利頓與尼古拉之移民，皆源於此舟。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Flood cluster parallel. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was living somewhere in the interior. He was a chief and father of the people; no one knows whence he came. For some reason a flood came, and covered the whole country except the tops of the highest mountains. Some say the flood came to put out a great fire which raged in the world; others say it was made to clean the earth. Many people and animals were drowned. Some fled to the high mountains, but the flood rose so rapidly that they were overtaken; some reached the tops and were saved. Some drifted about on logs, for no one knew how to make canoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 13 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼住在內陸某處。他是一位首領，也是眾人之父；沒有人知道他來自何方。由於某種原因，一場洪水來了，淹沒了整個地方，只有最高山峰的頂端除外。有人說洪水是為了撲滅一場肆虐世間的大火；也有人說它是為了清洗大地。許多人和動物都被淹死了。有些人逃往高山，但洪水漲得太快，把他們追上了；有些人到達山頂，得以倖存。有些人在木頭上漂流，因為沒有人知道如何造獨木舟。

passages.text: Only Coyote made a canoe of horse-tails or grass, and he and some of his friends embarked in it. They drifted for many days, and at last struck a mountain on the south side of the Thompson River called Zoke'ski, where the flood receded rapidly. Coyote descended to the Thompson River and for a time took up his abode there; on leaving his canoe he transformed it into stone. It may still be seen near the top of the mountain: about thirty feet long, with figures of three persons in it, some of which have now disappeared. The water-marks of this flood may be seen on parts of the mountains; owing to the flood, water and fish are now found all over the mountains, which before were dry, with no lakes above the level of the low valleys. The survivors of the flood are the ancestors of the various tribes; some of the people from Coyote's canoe settled here and there — at Lytton, at Nicola, and other places.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 13 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 只有郊狼用木賊或草編成一艘獨木舟，他和幾位朋友登上了船。他們漂流了許多天，最後撞上位於湯普森河南側、名為佐克斯基的一座山，洪水在那裡迅速退去。郊狼下到湯普森河，在那裡住了一段時日；離開獨木舟時，他把它變成了石頭。至今仍可在山頂附近看見它：約三十英尺長，裡面有三個人的形貌，其中一些如今已經消失。這場洪水的痕跡可以在部分山嶺上看到；由於這場洪水，如今山上到處都有水和魚，而從前那裡是乾燥的，沒有高於低窪谷地水準的湖泊。洪水的倖存者就是各部落的祖先；郊狼獨木舟上的一些人分別定居在各處——在利頓、在尼古拉，以及其他地方。

title.en: Sesulia'n and Seku'lia: The Two Transformers
title.zh: 雙變形者：塞蘇利安與塞庫利亞

region.en: Fraser River from Shuswap country to the Thompson, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 弗雷澤河，自舒什瓦普至湯普森故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sesulia'n and Seku'lia' (Thompson, from Spences Bridge)

summary.en: Two good Transformers come down the Fraser from the Shuswap country, teaching the people arts and turning the proud to stone while helping the grateful. At Styne Creek a man mocks them and is petrified with his lodge and household; their footprints remain in the rock near Styne. They carry patterns of every tool drawn on hide, and teach fire-drills, cooking, stone-working, arrow-flaking, knives and harpoons; at Spuzzum they watch a man lower his son by a bark rope to snatch salmon bare-handed, and reveal to him, pattern by pattern, bark twine, the bag-net, the hoop and the dip-net — how to catch, cook and cure salmon. They disappear travelling east, and will return with Coyote when the world changes, when everything evil will be destroyed.
summary.zh: 兩位善之變形者自舒什瓦普順弗雷澤河而下，教民百藝：傲慢者化石，受教者受助。於斯泰因溪，一男子嘲之，遂與屋中人眾俱化石；溪畔林中今猶存二人足印。彼等攜繪於獸皮之百器圖樣，教鑽木取火、烹飪、治石、鑿鏃、刀叉魚叉諸術。至斯普澤姆，見一父以樹皮繩縋子徒手捉鮭而不得，遂一一示以圖樣：樹皮繩、網袋、網圈、抄網——教其捕鮭、烹鮭、藏鮭。二人東行而隱，將與郊狼同返；屆時世有大變，凡惡皆滅。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Transformer/culture-hero cycle with eschatological return; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Two Transformers, Sesulia'n and Seku'lia, came down the Fraser River from the Shuswap country. They were good men, and taught the people many arts: they transformed those who were proud, while they helped those who were grateful for advice and instruction. They reached Styne Creek at dusk. A number of people were living in an underground lodge just north of the creek, and their dogs began to howl when the Transformers approached. A man went out to see who was coming, and when he saw the Transformers he made fun of them; therefore they transformed him, the house, and the people into stone. When leaving this place, Sesulia'n left the mark of his right foot on a stone, and a little farther down the river Seku'lia left the mark of his left foot; both impressions of human feet may still be seen in the woods near Styne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 13-14 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩位變形者，塞蘇利亞恩與塞庫利亞，從舒斯瓦普地區順著弗雷澤河而下。他們是好人，教給人們許多技藝：他們懲罰那些驕傲的人，卻幫助那些對勸告與教誨心懷感激的人。他們在黃昏時抵達斯泰恩溪。有一群人住在溪流正北方的一座地下屋裡，當變形者走近時，他們的狗開始嚎叫。一名男子出去看是誰來了，當他看到變形者時，便嘲弄他們；因此他們把他、那座房屋以及那些人全都變成了石頭。離開這個地方時，塞蘇利亞恩在一塊石頭上留下了右腳的印記，再往下游不遠處，塞庫利亞留下了左腳的印記；在斯泰恩附近的樹林裡，至今仍可看見這兩個人類腳印的痕跡。

passages.text: The Transformers taught people how to make tools and implements: they carried patterns drawn on hide of every object that people use, and taught how to make fire-drills, how to cook, how to work stone, flake arrow-heads and spears, how to make knives and harpoons. When they reached the Fraser Canyon near Spuzzum, they saw the river full of salmon, and across it a man lowering a boy by a cedar-bark rope to try to catch salmon with his hands — in vain. When the man wished that somebody would teach them how to catch the fish, the Transformers held up their hands above their heads, palms turned toward him, and he saw and understood them at once: first a pattern of bark twine, then a bag-net, then the hoop for a dip-net, and finally how to catch, cook, and cure salmon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 14 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 變形者教人們如何製作工具和器具：他們帶著畫在獸皮上的圖樣，涵蓋人們所使用的每一樣物件，並教人如何製作鑽火器、如何烹煮、如何加工石頭、如何打製箭頭和矛頭、如何製作刀子和魚叉。當他們抵達斯普祖姆附近的弗雷澤峽谷時，他們看見河裡滿是鮭魚，而對岸有一個人用雪松樹皮繩把一個男孩垂下去，想用手抓鮭魚——卻是徒勞。當那人希望有人能教他們如何捕魚時，變形者把手舉過頭頂，掌心朝向他，他立刻看見並明白了他們的意思：先是樹皮繩的圖樣，然後是袋網，接著是撈網的圓框，最後是如何捕捉、烹煮和醃製鮭魚。

passages.text: The Transformers went on to the boundary of the Lower Fraser tribe, and returned up the river to the Thompson tribe. Later on they left the country and disappeared; it is said they travelled through other countries to the east, teaching the people their arts. It is believed they will accompany Coyote when he returns: then there will be great changes on the earth, and many people will die — everything that is evil will be destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 14-15 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 變形者繼續前行，到了下弗雷澤部落的邊界，然後溯河而上，回到湯普森部落。後來他們離開這片土地消失了；據說他們穿越其他地區向東而去，把他們的技藝教給人們。人們相信，當郊狼歸來時，他們會伴隨他一同前來：那時大地上將發生巨大的變化，許多人將會死去——一切邪惡之物都將被毀滅。

title.en: Arjuna on Mount Indrakila: The Ascetic Warrior
title.zh: 阿周那苦修於因陀羅吉拉山

region.en: Mount Indrakila (symbolic pin, East Javanese court geography)
region.zh: 因陀羅吉拉山（象徵性定位，東爪哇宮廷地理）

period: Kakawin Arjunawiwaha composed by Mpu Kanwa, c. 1030 CE, court of Airlangga

source.work: Kakawin Arjuna Wiwaha (c. 1030 CE), cantos 1-3 (the tapa)

summary.en: The Arjunawiwaha ('Arjuna's Wedding'), the first great Javanese court epic, opens with the gods in terror: the demon-king Niwatakawaca cannot be conquered until a mortal ascetic's power is ripened. Arjuna, resting between wars, is sent to Mount Indrakila to perform tapa — standing on one leg, taking only wind for food — until the fire of his asceticism endangers the world itself and the gods must send messengers to cool him.
summary.zh: 《阿周那婚禮》——爪哇首部偉大宮廷史詩——開篇即諸神惶恐：魔王尼瓦塔卡瓦查不可克，除非一位凡人苦修者之力臻於圓熟。阿周那於戰暇奉命赴因陀羅吉拉山行『塔帕』苦修——獨腿而立、僅以風為食——直至其苦修之火危及世界，諸神不得不遣使為其降溫。

sensitivity.note: Court kakawin (c. 1030 CE); composed for King Airlangga, read as his mirror. Paraphrase of the kakawin narrative.

canonical_translation: Based on the kakawin narrative as summarized in standard editions; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Arjunawiwaha, composed by Mpu Kanwa around 1030 CE for the court of King Airlangga, is the earliest fully surviving Javanese court kakawin, and it opens not with a battle but with a theology of power.

BEGINNING: THE GODS' TERROR. The demon-king Niwatakawaca of Mount Mamertha has accumulated such tapa-power that no god can harm him; the gods' counselor (Indra) perceives that only a human ascetic, ripened by austerity, can match him — and only one mortal is worthy: Arjuna, the Pandawa archer, who has retired between wars. A divine mission descends to ask Arjuna to become, for the moment, a hermit.

MIDDLE: THE TAPA. On Mount Indrakila Arjuna performs the full ascetic discipline: hair matted, body smeared, standing on the tips of his toes, eating nothing but wind, until his radiance scorches the worlds. The gods, alarmed that their own instrument may burn the cosmos, send first the apsaras to tempt him back into flesh and then Indra himself to test his resolve with a hunting-deity disguise and an assault of illusions; Arjuna, unmoved in both temptations, is recognized as a genuine master of desire.

END: THE MISSION ASSIGNED. Pleased, the gods grant Arjuna boons of weapons, and Indra assigns him the conquest of Niwatakawaca — with the crucial counsel that the demon's single vulnerability (his heart hidden beneath his false magic) can be learned only from within the demon's palace, by a woman planted at his side. The war of the kakawin is thus won before it is fought: the hero's ascetic power is to be spent through seduction and information rather than arrows.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative (1) teaches that royal power in Java is founded on tapa (ascetic heat), the same force demons use, held under discipline; (2) models the courtier-king (Airlangga) as Arjuna — powerful, controlled, victorious through wisdom and alliance rather than raw force; (3) supplies the comparative tapa-motif (heat versus heaven) parallel to the Indian sources it adapts; and (4) anchors the whole Javanese tradition of reading epic as statecraft. The choice of Arjuna for the role is itself the kakawin's argument: the archer who has already renounced the rewards of victory in the Indian epic is here sent back into asceticism at the height of his powers, so that the poem can insist that discipline is not the refuge of the weak but the completion of strength. The Indrakila episode also fixes the kakawin's characteristic balance of Sanskrit inheritance and Javanese courtliness: the demon-king plot, the nymphs' temptation and the boons of weapons are recognizably Indian, but the temper of the telling — the emphasis on ceremony, self-command and intelligence as the marks of the victor — is the court of Airlangga looking into the epic as into a mirror. Read this way, the tapa is the poem's training manual for kings: the sovereign who cannot burn the world with his own heat has not yet earned the right to aim it at an enemy.
narrative.zh: 《阿周那婚禮》由坎瓦於約1030年為艾爾朗加之朝所作，為現存最早爪哇宮廷頌詩。其開篇乃權力神學：魔王尼瓦塔卡瓦查苦修之力無神能敵；唯凡人苦修之熱方可相抗——而唯一配得上者，即戰暇退隱之神射手阿周那。他奉神命赴因陀羅吉拉山行塔帕：立於足尖、以風為食，其光芒竟灼燒世界；諸神先遣天女誘惑、後由因陀羅親試幻象，阿周那不動如山，遂被認可為欲望之真主。神乃賜其神兵，授以討魔之命，並授密策：魔王唯一弱點唯有潛入其宮、由枕邊女子探得。功能：立『王室之力源於苦修』之爪哇神學、以艾爾朗加為阿周那之鏡像、提供跨文化之苦修母題、並奠定爪哇『史詩即政術』之解經傳統。

functions: Teaches that royal and demonic power alike flow from tapa (ascetic heat) held under discipline
Models the courtier-king Airlangga as Arjuna: controlled, wise, victorious through alliance
Supplies the Javanese tapa-versus-heaven motif parallel to its Indian sources
Anchors the Javanese tradition of reading epic as statecraft

variants.name: Indian Mahabharata parallel (Kairata episode)
variants.summary: Arjuna's tapa and the contest with Shiva; the Javanese kakawin redirects the power toward the demon-king plot and the heavenly bride.

variants.name: Later wayang lakon of Arjuna's tapa
variants.summary: The tapa becomes a standard wayang play in which Semar and the Punakawan accompany the ascetic, adding comic counterpoint.

primary_sources.citation: Composed c. 1030 CE at the court of Airlangga, Kahuripan, East Java; surviving in Old Javanese MSS (e.g. Leiden cod. or.); narrative paraphrased.

secondary_sources.work: P. J. Zoetmulder, Kalangwan: A Survey of Old Javanese Literature
secondary_sources.citation: Zoetmulder 1974, The Hague: Nijhoff — the standard survey of the kakawin and its court context.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of a Kakawin Arjuna Wiwaha manuscript/text collection

passages.text: The gods are in terror: Niwatakawaca's accumulated austerity makes him invulnerable to every divine weapon, and only the perfected tapa of a mortal can balance him. The divine mission descends to Arjuna, the archer resting between wars, and asks him to become a hermit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (c. 1030), opening cantos; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾神陷入恐懼：尼瓦塔卡瓦查累積的苦行使他對一切神兵利器都刀槍不入，唯有凡人修成的圓滿苦行才能與他抗衡。神聖的使命降臨到阿周那——那位在戰爭之間歇息的弓箭手——身上，要求他成為一名隱修者。

passages.text: On Mount Indrakila Arjuna stands on the tips of his toes, eats only wind, and lets his radiance scorch the worlds; when the apsaras fail to move him and Indra's disguises fail to break him, the gods recognize a true master of desire and grant him the mission and the boons of weapons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在因陀羅吉拉山上，阿周那踮著腳尖站立，只以風為食，任憑自己的光芒灼燒諸界；當天女們無法動搖他、因陀羅的種種化身也無法使他屈服時，眾神認出了一位真正駕馭欲望的大師，便賜予他使命與武器的恩惠。

title.en: The Heavenly Nymphs Failing at the Hermit's Stone
title.zh: 天女惑於不動之修士

region.en: Mount Indrakila (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 因陀羅吉拉山（象徵性定位）

period: Kakawin Arjunawiwaha, c. 1030 CE (Mpu Kanwa)

source.work: Kakawin Arjuna Wiwaha (c. 1030 CE), the temptation cantos

summary.en: The most erotic cantos of Old Javanese poetry are sent as a weapon: Indra dispatches the apsara-host — Supraba among them — to melt the hermit's discipline with dance, scent and art. The nymphs tire, dawn finds them defeated, and Arjuna stands 'like a stone' — the kakawin's celebrated paradox that desire fails where it is most beautifully deployed.
summary.zh: 古爪哇詩最香艷的段落被用作武器：因陀羅遣天女之群——蘇普拉巴在其中——以舞、香與藝融解修士之戒律。天女力竭，黎明見其敗退；阿周那立如頑石——爪哇頌詩最著名的悖論：慾望以最美的方式發動，卻在不動者面前失敗。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase; court-erotic imagery treated as literary theology.

passages.text: Indra sends the apsaras of heaven to the hermitage, Supraba first among them; for a night they dance, play, and pour out every art of attraction at the stone-still ascetic. At dawn the nymphs withdraw defeated, and the gods' counselor marvels: the warrior unmoved by the host of heaven's beauty is ripe to be heaven's own weapon. Arjuna is awarded the mission the temptation was meant to disqualify him from.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (c. 1030), temptation cantos; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 因陀羅派遣天界的飛天仙女前往隱修處，蘇帕芭為其首；她們徹夜舞蹈、嬉戲，向那靜如磐石的苦行者傾盡一切魅惑之術。黎明時分，眾仙女敗退而去，諸神的謀士驚嘆道：這位不為天界眾美所動的武士，已成熟為堪當天界自身之武器者。阿周那獲授的使命，正是那場誘惑本欲使他失去資格者。

title.en: Arjuna's Wedding: Supraba Given to the Victor
title.zh: 阿周那婚禮：天女蘇普拉巴歸於勝者

region.en: Heaven and Mount Mamertha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 天堂與瑪默爾塔山（象徵性定位）

period: Kakawin Arjunawiwaha, c. 1030 CE (Mpu Kanwa)

source.work: Kakawin Arjuna Wiwaha (c. 1030 CE), the wedding cantos

summary.en: The kakawin closes with its title-scene: Arjuna, having destroyed Niwatakawaca with Supraba's intelligence, is received in heaven and married to the apsara who was first his enemy's companion and then his co-conspirator — the 'wedding' (iwaha) that seals the alliance of mortal discipline and divine grace.
summary.zh: 頌詩以其題名之場收束：阿周那依蘇普拉巴之智誅滅尼瓦塔卡瓦查，天界迎之，娶那位曾為敵之伴、後為其同謀的天女——這場『婚禮』封印了凡人苦修與神恩的聯盟。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase; read at court as the union of king and divine power.

passages.text: With the demon-king destroyed, Arjuna is welcomed into heaven; Supraba, who had entered the enemy's palace to learn his secret and gave it to the hero, is now given to him as bride. The Arjunawiwaha ends in festival: the marriage of the disciplined mortal and the apsara of heaven, celebrated in the poem's most courtly verse, sealing the theology that the king's power is married, not stolen, from the divine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (c. 1030), wedding cantos; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魔王既滅，阿周那受迎入天界；蘇帕芭曾潛入敵宮探得其秘密並告知這位英雄，如今被許配與他為妻。《阿周那的婚禮》以慶典作結：受戒的凡人與天界飛天仙女的婚姻，以詩中最為典雅之詩句頌揚，印證了這樣的神學——國王的力量是與神聖聯姻而得，而非竊取而來。

title.en: Niwatakawaca's Secret: The Demon-King Undone from Within
title.zh: 尼瓦塔卡瓦查之秘：自內而潰的魔王

region.en: Mount Mamertha (symbolic pin, Old Javanese epic geography)
region.zh: 瑪默爾塔山（象徵性定位，古爪哇史詩地理）

period: Kakawin Arjunawiwaha, c. 1030 CE (Mpu Kanwa)

source.work: Kakawin Arjuna Wiwaha (c. 1030 CE), Niwatakawaca cantos

summary.en: The demon-king Niwatakawaca's invulnerability hides a single mortal secret. Supraba, sent as a bride into his palace, learns it from him and passes it to Arjuna; the hidden heart is struck, and the tapa-armoured tyrant falls — the Javanese epic's doctrine that no citadel of power lacks an inside.
summary.zh: 魔王尼瓦塔卡瓦查刀槍不入，唯藏一致命之秘。蘇普拉巴以新娘之身入其宮，探得其秘而傳於阿周那；隱藏之心被擊中，以苦修為甲的暴君隨之倒下——爪哇史詩之教義：任何權力堡壘皆有內隙。

sensitivity.note: Kakawin paraphrase; intelligence-war motif.

passages.text: Niwatakawaca, the tapa-powered tyrant of the demons, is armoured against every weapon of the gods; his single vulnerability is hidden where no assault can reach — inside his own palace, in his own confidence. Supraba, sent into the palace as a bride, learns the secret at its source and passes it to Arjuna; the hidden centre is struck and the invulnerable king falls. The epic concludes that power is conquered by knowledge carried in trust, not by force alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Arjunawiwaha (c. 1030); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 尼瓦塔卡瓦查，這藉苦行之力而稱霸的群魔暴君，披有抵禦諸神一切武器的鎧甲；他唯一的弱點藏於任何攻擊皆不能及之處——在他自己的宮殿之內，在他自己的自信之中。蘇帕芭以新娘之身被送入宮中，於其源頭探得秘密並傳與阿周那；那隱藏的核心遭擊中，刀槍不入的國王就此倒下。史詩歸結道：力量乃憑藉受託而承載的知識所征服，而非僅憑武力。

title.en: The Burning of Smara: The Love-God's Ashes
title.zh: 愛神焚身：蘇瑪羅之灰

region.en: Kediri, East Java (court of composition)
region.zh: 東爪哇諫義里（創作宮廷）

period: Kakawin Smaradahana composed by Mpu Dharmaja, c. 12th century CE, for King Kamesvara of Kediri

source.work: Kakawin Smaradahana (c. 12th c. CE), the burning of Kama

summary.en: Old Javanese poetry's most poignant catastrophe: to break Shiva's meditation, the love-god Smara (Kama) fires his flower-arrow; the angered god opens his third eye and burns Smara to ash, and desire itself dies from the world. In the poem's frame the loss is not permanent — Smara lives on bodiless in every loving heart, and the tale is read at Kediri as the story of King Kamesvara ('Love's Slayer') himself.
summary.zh: 古爪哇詩中最哀傷的災變：為破濕婆之禪定，愛神蘇瑪羅（迦摩）射出花箭；震怒之神開第三眼，將其焚為灰燼，慾望自世界中死去。然詩之框架言其不滅——蘇瑪羅無形而存於每一顆相愛之心；諫義里宮廷將此篇讀作國王格梅斯瓦羅（『毀愛者』）自身之傳。

sensitivity.note: Court kakawin; the king's name-pun (Kamesvara) is the poem's hidden subject.

passages.text: To wake the meditating Shiva, the love-god Smara draws his bow of flowers and strikes the god with desire; Shiva's third eye opens and burns Smara where he stands, reducing the archer of hearts to ash. With Smara burned, desire dies from the world: couples grow cold, birds forget song, and heaven itself pines. The poem's consolation is bodiless survival — Smara lives in every heart that loves, invisible, and the burnt god's story is told at Kediri as the king's own name in disguise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kakawin Smaradahana (c. 12th c.); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kakawin Smaradahana; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 為喚醒正在冥想的濕婆，愛神斯瑪拉張開他的花弓，以慾念射中這位神祇；濕婆的第三隻眼睜開，當場將斯瑪拉焚燒，把這心之射手化為灰燼。斯瑪拉既焚，慾念便從世間死去：伴侶漸生冷淡，鳥兒忘卻歌唱，連天界本身也為之憔悴。此詩的慰藉在於無形的存續——斯瑪拉活在每一顆愛著的心中，隱而不見；這焚身之神的故事，在諫義里被講述，實為國王自身名號的化名。

title.en: Calon Arang, the Widow of Girah
title.zh: 格拉之寡婦加隆·阿朗

region.en: Girah, East Java (Airlangga's kingdom)
region.zh: 東爪哇格拉鎮（艾爾朗加王國）

period: Legend embedded in the Pararaton (Book of Kings); events set in the reign of Airlangga, c. 11th century CE

source.work: Pararaton (Book of Kings), the Calon Arang episode; Rangga Lawe and related Javanese MSS tradition

summary.en: The most feared witch of Javanese legend: the widow Calon Arang of Girah, who learned leyak magic and sickened the whole country with plague when no man would marry her daughter Ratna Manggali. King Airlangga, unable to defeat her by arms, sends the ascetic Mpu Barada in disguise; the widow is killed in her own ritual, and Girah is burnt to the ground.
summary.zh: 爪哇傳說中最令人畏懼的女巫：格拉鎮寡婦加隆·阿朗，習得黎雅克邪術；因無人肯娶其女拉特娜·芒加利，憤而以瘟疫荼毒全國。艾爾朗加王以兵不能克，乃遣苦修者姆普·巴拉達偽裝入鄉；寡婦死於自家祭儀，格拉全鎮付之一炬。

sensitivity.note: Pararaton episode; the leyak-witch figure remains part of living Balinese-Javanese folklore — treated as literature, not as accusation against living persons.

canonical_translation: Based on the Pararaton's Calon Arang episode; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Pararaton, the 'Book of Kings' of the Javanese tradition, embeds one of Java's great dark legends in the reign of King Airlangga (c. 1000-1040s CE): the tale of Calon Arang, the widow of Girah.

BEGINNING: THE WIDOW'S GRUDGE. In the village of Girah lives the widow Calon Arang, keeper of the black arts of the leyak — the headless flying witches of Javanese-Balinese fear. Her daughter Ratna Manggali is beautiful and good, but no man will marry into the witch's house; the stigma of the mother's magic blights the daughter's marriage prospects, and the widow's humiliation hardens into fury.

MIDDLE: THE PLAGUE OF GIRAH. To punish the country that spurned her daughter, Calon Arang unleashes her art: sickness spreads from Girah through the land of Airlangga's kingdom, people die in heaps, and the court's armies and prayers cannot stop the invisible attack. The king learns that the source is a woman and her grudge, not an enemy state.

END: THE COUNTER-WITCH. Unable to meet the widow by force, Airlangga turns to the ascetic Mpu Barada (with his disciple Mpu Bahula, given as a bridegroom to Ratna Manggali in some tellings, whose marriage opens the widow's house to the spy). Barada learns her arts under the guise of a pupil, then — at the climactic leyak ritual, when the widow and her followers begin their dance and transformation — he strikes her down, and the disease dies with her. Girah is burned to the ground so that nothing of the witch's town remains.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) polices the line between ritual power and witchcraft: the same arts that serve community become plague when privately held; (2) encodes gendered scapegoating, for the widow's rage begins in her daughter's blocked marriage — the court narrative sides with the state against the woman it cannot integrate; (3) provides the leyak cycle's charter (headless fliers, graveyards, night dances) as living folklore to this day; and (4) historicizes Airlangga's reign with a supernatural enemy worthy of the king who commissioned the Arjunawiwaha. The episode's afterlife is as significant as its plot. In Bali the widow's figure hardened into Rangda, the mask-queen of the leyak, and the Barong-Rangda drama re-enacts the plague and the counter-force in every village that keeps both masks; in Java the tale remained a literary episode of the Pararaton and its prose descendants, told as part of Airlangga's reign rather than as cult. The gendered logic of the story has drawn sustained scholarly attention: the court's counter-plot begins with a marriage — Mpu Bahula wed to Ratna Manggali — so that the daughter's blocked marriage, the cause of the plague, becomes the instrument of its ending. The witch's power is thus answered not by force but by the restoration of the alliance her grudge was protesting; the legend's own structure acknowledges what the widow wanted before it destroys her for wanting it.
narrative.zh: 《列王志》（Pararaton）在艾爾朗加王朝（約1000-1040年代）嵌入爪哇著名黑暗傳說：格拉鎮寡婦加隆·阿朗。她精通黎雅克邪術（無首飛行之巫）；其女拉特娜·芒加利美善而無人敢娶——母親之辱化為怨怒，乃以瘟疫荼毒全國，宮廷兵馬禱告俱不能止。王知病源乃一婦人之怨，遂遣苦修者姆普·巴拉達（一說其徒巴拉休拉詐娶其女以開其門）偽裝入鄉習其術；於最高潮之黎雅克祭舞之際擊殺之，瘟疫隨之而止；格拉全鎮焚燬以絕其跡。功能：劃分儀式之力與巫術之界、映照國家對無法整合之女性的替罪機制、為今日活態黎雅克傳說立憲章、並為艾爾朗加之治增一超自然之敵。

functions: Policing the boundary between licensed ritual power and illegitimate witchcraft (leyak)
Gendered scapegoat narrative: the widow's rage born from her daughter's blocked marriage
Charter of the leyak cycle (headless night fliers, graveyard dances) in living folklore
Supernatural enemy matched to Airlangga, the king of the Arjunawiwaha

variants.name: Pararaton main text
variants.summary: The compact chronicle-embedded version: the widow's plague and the ascetic's counter-plot.

variants.name: Balinese Rangda identification
variants.text_tradition: Balinese Calonarang ritual drama (Barong dance cycle)
variants.summary: Balinese tradition reads the widow into the Barong-Rangda drama; Rangda the widow-witch battles Barong nightly as village purification.

variants.name: Later Javanese babad retellings
variants.text_tradition: Middle Javanese prose versions (Calon Arang as herstory)
variants.summary: Expanded tellings add the daughter's marriage, the disciple's infiltration, and Girah's burning in detail.

primary_sources.work: Pararaton (Book of Kings), Calon Arang episode
primary_sources.citation: Javanese chronicle MS tradition (Leiden cod. or. 4692 and kin); episode set in Airlangga's reign, c. 11th century CE; narrative paraphrased.

secondary_sources.work: P. J. Zoetmulder, Kalangwan
secondary_sources.citation: Zoetmulder 1974, The Hague: Nijhoff — on the literary context of the Pararaton's legend material.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of a Pararaton text edition

sensitivity_guidance: Witch-legend of a living folklore sphere; keep strictly literary, avoid applications to living persons or communities.

passages.text: In Girah lives the widow Calon Arang, keeper of the leyak arts; her daughter Ratna Manggali is beautiful, but no man dares marry into the witch's house, and the widow's humiliation hardens into a grudge against the whole country. Sickness pours out of Girah into the land of King Airlangga; people die beyond the reach of arms and prayer, until the court understands that the plague is a woman's art turned loose.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pararaton's Calon Arang episode; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Pararaton episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在吉拉，住著寡婦卡隆阿朗，她是蕾雅克巫術的守持者；她的女兒拉特娜·芒加利容貌美麗，卻無人敢娶入這女巫之家，寡婦的屈辱遂硬化為對整個國度的怨恨。疫病自吉拉湧出，蔓延至國王艾爾朗加之境；人們死於刀兵與祈禱皆不能及之處，直到宮廷明白，這場瘟疫乃是一名女子的巫術被放縱所致。

passages.text: The king sends the ascetic Mpu Barada in disguise to learn the widow's art; at the height of her ritual dance he strikes her down, the sickness dies with her, and Girah is burnt to the ground so that nothing of the witch's village remains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pararaton episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王派遣苦行者姆普·巴拉達喬裝前往，探學寡婦的巫術；在她儀式之舞達到極盛之際，他將其擊倒，疫病隨她而死，吉拉被焚為平地，使這女巫之村不復留下任何痕跡。

title.en: Ken Arok Usurps Tumapel: The Murderer Who Founded a Dynasty
title.zh: 肯·阿洛克奪取杜馬佩爾：刺客立國

region.en: Tumapel (Singhasari), East Java
region.zh: 東爪哇杜馬佩爾（信訶沙里）

period: Pararaton tradition; events c. 1222 CE

source.work: Pararaton (Book of Kings), the Ken Angrok narrative

summary.en: The Pararaton opens its dynastic history with regicide: the peasant-bandit Ken Arok murders the ruler of Tumapel (Tunggul Ametung) with the cursed kris Kyai Tanting Kembang, made by a smith whose wife he first dishonoured, marries the ruler's wife Ken Dedes — already pregnant and fated by prophecy to bear kings — and founds the Singhasari line from which Majapahit will descend. The chronicle does not disguise the crime; it makes the crime the price of the dynasty.
summary.zh: 《列王志》以弒君開其王朝史：草莽之徒肯·阿洛克以被咒之克利斯『丹婷·格孟』（先辱鑄師之妻而得）刺殺杜馬佩爾之主棟古爾·阿默通，娶其妻肯·德德絲——此女已孕，且預言注定誕下諸王——遂開信訶沙里王朝，日後馬卓帕希特即出其後。編年史不掩其罪；而以罪為王朝之代價。

sensitivity.note: Pararaton narrative; violence in the founding myth treated as literature.

passages.text: Ken Arok, a restless man of the village, serves the ruler of Tumapel while plotting his rise; the cursed kris Kyai Tanting Kembang, forged in blood and grudge, is set to kill for him until it finds its final victim in Tunggul Ametung, the ruler himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pararaton's Ken Angrok narrative; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 肯·阿羅克，一個不安分的村中之人，侍奉著圖馬佩爾的統治者，同時暗中謀劃自己的崛起；那把受詛咒的克里斯短劍「基亞伊·坦廷·肯邦」，以鮮血與怨恨鍛造而成，注定要為他殺人，直到它找到最終的犧牲者——統治者通古爾·阿梅通本人。

passages.text: Ken Arok takes the widow Ken Dedes as his wife — already with child by the murdered ruler, and already marked by the prophecy that whoever possesses her bears kings. From that marriage the Singhasari dynasty is founded, and the chronicle's history of Java begins in a murder it never hides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pararaton narrative; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 肯·阿羅克娶了寡婦肯·德德斯為妻——她已懷有被謀殺的統治者的孩子，且早已被那則預言所標記：凡擁有她者，皆將孕育君王。這段婚姻奠定了辛哈沙里王朝，而編年史中爪哇的歷史，便始於一樁它從不隱瞞的謀殺。

title.en: The Panji Cycle: The Lost Prince and Princess of Janggala
title.zh: 潘基傳說：章格拉失散的王儲與公主

region.en: Janggala and Kediri, East Java
region.zh: 東爪哇章格拉與諫義里

period: Panji romance tradition, c. 13th-15th centuries; retold across the Malay world

source.archive: Javanese and Malay manuscript tradition (Panji cycle)
source.work: The Panji romances (Hikayat Panji tradition); East Javanese court romance

summary.en: Java's great romance: Panji, hero of Janggala, and his betrothed Sekar Taji (Chandra Kirana) of Daha are separated at the wedding by war and disguise; she wanders from court to court as a cooking-maid, a dancer, a queen under false names, while he searches under a string of aliases — until a ring, a dance, or a sleep-word reveals them to each other. The cycle's hundreds of tellings spread from Java into Malay, Thai, Burmese and Khmer court literature.
summary.zh: 爪哇之偉大傳奇：章格拉英雄潘基與達哈未婚妻瑟卡爾·達吉（查德拉·基拉娜）於婚禮之日因戰亂而失散；公主以假名流浪諸宮——或為庖娘、或為舞者、或為他國之王后；王子則以化名四處尋訪——直至一枚戒指、一支舞、或一句夢語令二人相認。此傳說百餘異本自爪哇遠播馬來、暹羅、緬甸與柬埔寨宮廷文學。

sensitivity.note: Court romance cycle; Southeast Asia's most widespread indigenous literary export.

passages.text: The wedding of the prince of Janggala and the princess of Daha is broken by war on the wedding morning itself; both vanish into exile under false names, she into servitude and queenship in foreign courts, he into a wandering of disguises that carries his fame from land to land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Panji romance tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 姜加拉王子與達哈公主的婚禮，就在婚禮當天早晨被戰爭所破壞；兩人皆以假名流亡，她淪為異邦宮廷中的奴僕與王后，他則在層層偽裝中漂泊，使他的名聲從一地傳至另一地。

passages.text: Recognition comes by tokens rather than faces: the ring dropped in the bath, the dance learned in childhood, the sleep-talk that betrays a name. The cycle's countless versions end in the reunion of the two courts through the marriage of the two wanderers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Panji romance tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 相認憑藉的是信物而非面容：遺落在浴池中的戒指、幼時學會的舞蹈、洩露姓名的夢囈。這一故事循環的無數版本，皆以兩位漂泊者成婚、兩座宮廷重歸於好作結。

title.en: Roro Jonggrang and the Thousand Temples in One Night
title.zh: 拉羅·鍾格朗與一夜千廟

region.en: Prambanan, Central Java
region.zh: 中爪哇普蘭巴南

period: Javanese legend attached to the Prambanan temple (temple name recorded by Worsfold 1893); older oral tradition

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893), ch. V, the temple of Loro-Jonggrang at Brambanan; Javanese oral legend

summary.en: To win the princess Roro Jonggrang, the ogre-prince Bandung Bondowoso must build a thousand temples in one night; the demons work at supernatural speed until the princess, fearing the dawn, orders her maids to pound rice and kindle fires — the cocks crow a false morning, the last temple lacks its idol, and the cheated prince turns the deceiver herself into stone: the Durga image in the northern cell of the temple still called Loro Jonggrang, 'the maiden of beautiful form.'
summary.zh: 為娶公主拉羅·鍾格朗，羅剎王子萬丹·邦多沃索須一夜建成千座神廟；群魔以妖速施工，公主懼黎明將至，密令宮女舂米生火——雄雞誤鳴而假晨至，最後一廟無像，被欺的王子將欺人者化為石：今日廟北殿中那尊杜爾迦像，仍名『拉羅·鍾格朗』——『美體之女』。

sensitivity.note: Best-known Central Javanese foundation legend; paraphrase of the oral cycle with the temple-name etymology from Worsfold.

canonical_translation: Based on the Javanese oral legend and the temple-name note in Worsfold (1893); paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The legend of Roro Jonggrang is Central Java's most famous etiological myth, fixed to the great Saivite temple of Prambanan — whose name, as Worsfold records, 'is simply the native name given to the particular Durga represented in the shrine, and means literally the Maiden with beautiful hips.'

BEGINNING: THE WAR AND THE WOOING. In the wars between the kingdoms of Pengging and Boko, the ogre-prince Bandung Bondowoso overthrows Pengging and demands the hand of Roro Jonggrang, daughter of the defeated king, as the price of peace. She cannot refuse and cannot accept; she sets an impossible bride-price: a thousand temples to be built in a single night.

MIDDLE: THE DEMONS BUILD. The prince commands his legions of ogres and spirits, and they work at supernatural speed — quarries open, walls rise, temples multiply through the dark hours toward the thousandth. As dawn approaches and the count nears its end, the princess acts: she orders the village women to pound rice in mortars and to kindle cooking fires on the eastern heights, so that the cocks, deceived by light and noise, crow before their time.

END: THE STONE MAIDEN. The demons scatter in terror at the false dawn; the work stops at nine hundred and ninety-nine temples, and the last one is left with no idol in its cell. Bandung Bondowoso, cheated, names the deception and curses his deceiver: Roro Jonggrang is turned to stone, seated forever in the shrine of the great temple — the image of Durga that the temple's own name commemorates. The thousandth temple, the people say, is the princess herself.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) explains the skyline of Prambanan and the Durga image's name; (2) encodes the cock-crow false-dawn motif (parallel to European rooster tales) as female resistance to a forced marriage; (3) fixes the moral ambiguity at the legend's heart — the princess lies, the prince curses, and both are caught in stone and story; and (4) binds modern Javanese identity to the monuments of the Hindu past through a story told in every school and wayang performance. The legend's geography is exact: the temple whose northern cell holds the stone Durga is the great Saivite complex at Prambanan, whose central temple still carries the name Loro Jonggrang, and the bandung of the ogre-prince's name is remembered in the plain to the west. Schoolchildren and dalangs alike tell the tale with the same beats — the impossible bride-price, the supernatural work-crew, the pounding mortars and fires on the eastern hills, the cock's false crow, the curse — and the wayang stages it as a standard lakon with the ogre-legions as shadow spectacle. The story's moral balance is deliberately uncomfortable: the princess lies to save her freedom, the prince curses her for a deception his own wager invited, and both are fixed forever in the landscape — one as stone, one as the name of the ruin where the stone sits. Javanese tellers rarely resolve the discomfort; the legend keeps it, as the temple keeps the image.
narrative.zh: 拉羅·鍾格朗傳說為中爪哇最著名釋源神話，附於普蘭巴南濕婆大神廟——沃斯福德記其廟名『即殿中所祀杜爾迦之土名，意為美體之女』。傳說：萬丹·邦多沃索王子破彭金國，索敗王之女拉羅·鍾格朗為妻；公主既不能拒又不能許，乃定天價彩禮：一夜建成千座神廟。王子驅群魔以妖速築廟，黎明將至、大功將成之際，公主密令村婦舂米、東嶺生火，雄雞受欺而提前報曉；群魔驚散，工程止於九百九十九廟，末廟無像。王子受騙，怒而將公主化為石，永坐大神廟北殿——即廟名所紀之杜爾迦像。村人云：第一千座廟，就是公主自己。功能：釋普蘭巴南廟群與杜爾迦像之名、以『假晨雞鳴』母題（可比歐洲雄雞傳說）寫女性對逼婚之抵抗、刻畫傳說核心的道德曖昧（公主設詐、王子施咒、二者皆困於石與故事）、並經由課堂與哇揚戲將爪哇認同繫於印度教古蹟。

functions: Etiology of the Prambanan skyline and the Durga image's name Loro Jonggrang
False-dawn cock-crow motif as female resistance to a forced marriage
Moral ambiguity: the lie that saves and the curse that punishes, both fixed in stone
Bridge between living Javanese identity and the Hindu monument past

variants.name: Borobudur bride-rejection telling (Scidmore 1897)
variants.text_tradition: Central Javanese temple legend recorded by Eliza Scidmore
variants.summary: The same pattern at Borobudur: a suitor builds the temple by night for the princess of Mendoet, who rejects the finished work as 'dead images' and leaves him to eternal meditation.

variants.name: Wayang lakon of Bandung Bondowoso
variants.summary: The legend is staged as a standard play, with the ogre-legions and the false dawn rendered in shadow.

primary_sources.work: Loro Jonggrang legend (Central Javanese oral tradition)
primary_sources.citation: Oral legend of Prambanan; temple-name etymology recorded in Worsfold, A Visit to Java, London 1893, ch. V.

secondary_sources.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java
secondary_sources.citation: Worsfold 1893, London: Cassell — ch. V on the temple of Loro-Jonggrang and the Durga image's name.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive full text of Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893)

passages.text: Bandung Bondowoso, prince of the ogres, demands the defeated king's daughter as the price of peace; Roro Jonggrang sets a bride-price meant to be impossible: a thousand temples built in one night. The ogre-legions build at supernatural speed through the dark hours; as the count nears a thousand, the princess orders the village women to pound rice and kindle fires on the eastern hills, and the cocks, deceived, crow before the true dawn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese oral legend of Roro Jonggrang; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Javanese oral legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 食人魔王子班東·邦多沃索，要求以戰敗國王的女兒作為和平的代價；羅羅·瓊格朗則提出一項註定不可能的聘禮：一夜之間建造一千座神廟。食人魔軍團以超自然的速度在黑夜中建造；當數目接近一千時，公主下令村中婦女在東邊山丘上舂米並點燃火堆，受騙的公雞便在真正的黎明到來之前啼叫。

passages.text: The demons scatter at the false morning; the work stops short, the last temple lacks its idol, and the cheated prince turns the deceiver to stone — the Durga image in the shrine that bears her name, Loro Jonggrang, 'the maiden of beautiful form.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese oral legend, with the temple-name note from Worsfold (1893); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾妖魔在虛假的清晨中四散而去；工程戛然而止，最後一座神廟缺少神像，受騙的王子便將那欺騙者化為石頭——即那座以她之名「羅羅·瓊格朗」命名的神龕中的杜爾迦神像，意為「形貌美麗的少女」。

title.en: Jaka Tarub and the Seven Bidadari: The Peeped Rice-Pot
title.zh: 加卡·塔魯布與七位天女：被偷看之飯鍋

region.en: Central Java (Mataram region, lake of the bidadari)
region.zh: 中爪哇（馬打藍地區，天女之湖）

period: Javanese folk legend (oral tradition); recorded in 19th-20th century collections

source.work: The legend of Jaka Tarub and Nawang Wulan (Javanese folktale cycle)

summary.en: The youth Jaka Tarub steals the shawl of the youngest of seven bathing bidadari and keeps her as his wife, Nawang Wulan — who cooks rice for the household from a single grain and forbids him ever to look into the pot. Of course he peeks: the rice turns to husks and chaff, the sky-robe is found, and Nawang Wulan rises back to heaven, leaving only her child — whom she may visit on a moonbeam, but never return to.
summary.zh: 青年加卡·塔魯布竊走七位浴水天女中最幼者之披肩，娶之為妻，名娜萬·吳蘭——她以一粒米為全家煮飯，並立禁令：永不可窺視飯鍋。他终究偷看：米化為糠殼，天衣被發現；娜萬·吳蘭復歸天上，只留下一個孩子——她可以沿月光下凡探望，卻永不能重返人間。

sensitivity.note: Celestial-wife cycle (star-wife type); the rice-pot taboo ties heaven to the harvest.

passages.text: Seven bidadari descend to bathe in the lake, hanging their shawls on the trees; Jaka Tarub takes the youngest's shawl, and the sky-maiden, grounded, accepts his house and his name for her — Nawang Wulan. She cooks with heaven's thrift — one grain fills the pot — and lays one prohibition: never look inside. Driven by doubt and slander, he peeks: the grain turns to husks, the hidden shawl is found, and Nawang Wulan, clothed again in light, rises to heaven, leaving the child below. Mother and child meet on the moonbeam she lowers at nights, but the marriage is over: the taboo broken is a marriage broken, and the boy grows up half of the sky, half of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese legend of Jaka Tarub; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Javanese legend; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Javanese legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 七位仙女下凡到湖中沐浴，將披巾掛在樹上；賈卡·塔魯布取走了最年幼仙女的披巾，這位天女滯留人間，接受了他的家，也接受了他為她取的名字——娜旺·烏蘭。她以天上的節儉方式烹煮——一粒米便能裝滿一鍋——並立下一條禁令：絕不可窺看鍋內。在疑心與讒言的驅使下，他偷看了：米粒化為糠殼，藏起的披巾被尋獲，娜旺·烏蘭重新披上光輝，升返天界，將孩子留在人間。母子於她每夜垂下的月光上相會，但婚姻已然結束：禁忌被打破，便是婚姻被打破，而男孩長大成人，一半屬於天空，一半屬於大地。

title.en: Timun Mas, the Golden Cucumber Girl
title.zh: 金瓜少女蒂蒙·瑪斯

region.en: Central Java (village of Mbok Sirni)
region.zh: 中爪哇（西爾尼大娘之村）

period: Javanese folk legend (oral tradition)

source.work: The legend of Timun Mas (Javanese folktale cycle)

summary.en: The childless widow Mbok Sirni bargains with the green ogre Buto Ijo for a child and is given a cucumber seed: from the golden cucumber crawls the girl Timun Mas, with a payment falling due on her seventeenth birthday. Armed by a hermit with four packets — cucumber seeds, needles, salt and shrimp-paste — the girl flees the ogre, casting each gift behind her: a cucumber field to devour, a bamboo forest of needles, an ocean of salt, and a boiling sea of paste that swallows the giant whole.
summary.zh: 無子的西爾尼大娘與綠羅剎『布托·伊佐』訂約得子，得黃瓜一粒種——金瓜中爬出少女蒂蒙·瑪斯，而十七歲生日的贖金亦到期。隱士授她四包法物——黃瓜籽、鐵針、鹽、蝦醬——少女棄家而逃，邊逃邊擲：瓜田令巨魔飽食、針竹成林刺其足、鹽化大洋阻其路、蝦醬沸海將巨魔整個吞沒。

sensitivity.note: Giant-evader folktale; the four-throw escape is the Javanese analogue of magic-flight.

passages.text: Mbok Sirni's bargain brings a golden cucumber from whose rind crawls the girl Timun Mas — but the ogre Buto Ijo keeps the contract, and on her seventeenth birthday comes to collect the child for his meal. The hermit gives her four packets to throw as she flees: the seeds become a cucumber field the ogre must stop and devour; the needles a bamboo thorn-forest that stings his feet; the salt an ocean; and the shrimp-paste a boiling mud-sea in which the giant sinks and is swallowed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese legend of Timun Mas; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Javanese legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 姆博克·西爾妮的契約換來一條金黃色的黃瓜，從瓜皮中爬出了女孩蒂蒙·瑪斯——但食人魔布托·伊卓堅守契約，在她十七歲生日那天前來收取這孩子作為他的餐食。隱士給了她四個包裹，讓她在逃亡時拋擲：種子化作一片黃瓜田，食人魔必須停下腳步將其吞食殆盡；針化作一片竹刺林，刺痛他的雙腳；鹽化作一片汪洋；蝦醬則化作一片沸騰的泥海，巨人沉陷其中，被吞沒。

title.en: Keong Emas: The Princess in the Golden Snail
title.zh: 金螺中的公主

region.en: Daha and Kediri, East Java (Panji-cycle setting)
region.zh: 東爪哇達哈與諫義里（潘基傳說背景）

period: Javanese folk romance (oral tradition, Panji cycle offshoot)

source.work: The legend of Keong Emas (Javanese folktale, Panji-cycle offshoot)

summary.en: The rejected suitor king of AntanginJagar, cursed and transformed, pays out his rage in magic: Princess Sekar Taji, lost on the wedding morning, is turned into a golden snail and cast into a river; a fisher-widow nets the snail and keeps it as a treasure, for the snail secretly cooks and cleans her hut. When the widow spies on the gift, the woman inside is caught — and the long recognition begins that will carry the princess back to her name, her ring, and her waiting Panji.
summary.zh: 安坦金賈加爾的被拒求婚者懷怨弄法：婚晨走失的瑟卡爾·達吉公主被化為金螺、拋入河中；漁婦撒網得螺，視為寶物收藏——螺竟暗自為她煮飯掃屋。漁婦窺破其秘，螺中人現形——漫長的相認之旅由此開始，公主終將尋回自己的名字、戒指，以及等待她的潘基。

sensitivity.note: Panji-cycle offshoot; the animal-bride motif attached to Java's great romance.

passages.text: Denied at the wedding morning, the rejected king works his grudge into magic: Sekar Taji is transformed into a golden snail and thrown into the river, her name lost with her shape. A fisher-widow nets the shining snail and keeps it caged as treasure; unknown to her, the woman inside slips out by night to cook and sweep the hut. Discovered at last, the princess tells her name and story, and the recognition sets the whole Panji cycle's search back on its road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese Keong Emas legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在婚禮之晨遭到拒絕，被拒的國王將怨恨煉成魔法：塞卡爾·塔吉被變成一隻金蝸牛，投入河中，她的名字隨著她的形貌一同失落。一位漁婦寡母網住了這隻閃亮的蝸牛，將牠當作珍寶關在籠中；她並不知道，裡面的女子每夜悄悄溜出，烹煮打掃小屋。終於被發現後，公主說出了自己的名字與來歷，而這番相認，使整個潘吉傳奇循環的尋覓重新踏上了路途。

title.en: The Hill of Tidar: The Nail That Fastens Java to the Earth
title.zh: 蒂達爾丘：把爪哇釘在大地上的釘子

region.en: Hill of Tidar, Magelang, Central Java
region.zh: 中爪哇馬格朗蒂達爾丘

period: Javanese sacred-geography tradition, recorded in Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897)

source.work: Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), the hill of Tidar

summary.en: At the base of Java's central volcano trio, Soembung — 'the very centre of Java' — native legends cling to the little hill of Tidar: it is the 'spike of the universe,' the nail which fastens the lovely island to the face of the earth. A whole island's stability hangs on one small green hill.
summary.zh: 爪哇中央三峰環峙之處，松邦峰——『爪哇之正中』——山腳的小丘蒂達爾承載著本地傳說：它是『宇宙之釘』，將這可愛的島嶼釘牢在大地之上。整座島的安穩，繫於一座小小的青山。

sensitivity.note: Sacred-geography note; Tidar hill is also a modern military academy site.

passages.text: Soembung is the very center of Java, and native legends cling to the little hill of Tidar at its base — the 'spike of the universe,' the nail which fastens the lovely island to the face of the earth. At the base of Java's central volcano trio, Soembung — 'the very centre of Java' — native legends cling to the little hill of Tidar: it is the 'spike of the universe,' the nail which fastens the lovely island to the face of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 松邦是爪哇的正中心，當地的傳說依附於其山腳下的小丘蒂達爾——「宇宙之釘」，將這座美麗島嶼釘牢在地球表面的釘子。在爪哇中央三座火山之麓，松邦——「爪哇的正中心」——當地的傳說依附於小丘蒂達爾：它是「宇宙之釘」，將這座美麗島嶼釘牢在地球表面的釘子。

title.en: Papandayan the Forge: The Chained Giants in the Mountain
title.zh: 帕潘達揚『鍛爐』：山中的鎖鏈巨人

region.en: Papandayan volcano, Garut, West Java
region.zh: 西爪哇加魯特帕潘達揚火山

period: Sundanese mountain legend recorded in Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897)

source.work: Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), Garoet and Papandayang

summary.en: Inside the Papandayan crater the pools of sulphur boil like vats of molten gold, scattering golden drops, and steam jets roar from the quaking solfatara; the natives named the mountain 'The Forge,' and their legends hear chained giants groaning inside the mountain — the underworld's prisoners heard in the rumblings of the volcano.
summary.zh: 帕潘達揚火山口內，硫磺池如熔金之釜沸騰四濺；地汽嘶吼、大地顫動。土人名此山為『鍛爐』，傳說中聽見鎖鏈之巨人在山中呻吟——那是冥界囚徒在火山轟鳴裏的聲音。

sensitivity.note: Volcano-legend; the forge metaphor is recorded traveller ethnography.

passages.text: The kawa, or crater, is a bowl deep sunk in rocky walls, with pools of liquid sulphur boiling like vats of purest molten gold; from the rumblings and strange underground noises one can understand the native legends of chained giants groaning inside of the mountain, and their name for Papandayang, 'The Forge.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡瓦，即火山口，是一個深陷於岩壁之中的碗狀窪地，液態硫磺的池子如純淨熔金的巨缸般沸騰；從隆隆聲響與奇異的地下聲息中，人可以理解當地關於被鎖鏈縛住的巨人於山腹中呻吟的傳說，以及他們對帕潘達揚的稱呼——「鍛爐」。

title.en: The Prince of Mendoet: A Temple Built in Ten Days, a Family in Stone
title.zh: 門多特王儲：十日建廟，闔家化石

region.en: Mendoet temple, near Borobudur, Central Java
region.zh: 中爪哇婆羅浮屠附近門多特廟

period: Central Javanese temple legend recorded in Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897)

source.work: Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), Boro Boedor and Mendoet

summary.en: The two-year-old daughter of Prince Dewa Kosoumi is stolen by a revengeful courtier; twelve years later the broken-hearted prince meets and marries the most beautiful girl he has ever seen — his own child. When the truth is told, the priests rule that no forgiveness is possible unless he builds a great temple in ten days; the kingdom's artists finish Borobudur-like marvel within the term, but one statue is missing. The gods turn the prince, the mother, and the child to stone: they sit in the cell at Mendoet as proof of the tale for all time.
summary.zh: 德瓦·科蘇米王儲兩歲之女被復仇的廷臣偷走；十二年後，心碎的王儲遇見並娶了平生所見最美的少女——竟是自己的女兒。真相揭穿，祭司裁定：唯有十日之內建成大神廟方可赦免；全國工匠瘋狂趕工如期而成——卻恰好缺一尊像。神遂將王儲、其妻、其子化為石：三人永坐門多特廟中之室，為此故事作萬世之證。

sensitivity.note: Temple legend; incest-expiation narrative treated as recorded folklore.

passages.text: The little daughter of the great Prince Dewa Kosoumi is stolen by a revengeful courtier; twelve years later the prince, wandering the country in search of her, meets and marries the most beautiful young girl he has ever seen. The revengeful courtier of years before tells the prince that his beautiful wife is his own daughter; the priests assure the prince that no forgiveness is possible, and that his only expiation lies in a walled cell and prayer — unless within ten days he can construct a Boro Boedor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), Boro Boedor and Mendoet; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Scidmore (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 偉大的德瓦·科蘇米親王的小女兒被一名心懷報復的朝臣擄走；十二年後，親王為尋她而漫遊鄉間，遇見並娶了他平生所見最美麗的年輕女子。多年前那名心懷報復的朝臣告訴親王，他美麗的妻子正是他自己的女兒；祭司們向親王保證，不可能獲得寬恕，他唯一的贖罪之道在於一間有牆的密室與祈禱——除非他能在十日之內建造一座婆羅浮屠。

passages.text: All the artists and workmen of the kingdom, working with zeal and frenzy to save their ruler, complete the temple within the fixed time — but the pile lacks just one statue of the full number required. Prayers and appeals are useless: the gods turn the prince, the mother, and the child to stone, and they sit in the cell at Mendoet as proof of the tale for all time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 王國中所有的藝術家和工匠，懷著熱忱與狂熱搶救他們的統治者，在規定的時限內完成了這座神廟——但這座建築群還差一尊雕像，才湊足所需的總數。祈禱與懇求都無濟於事：眾神將王子、母親與孩子化為石頭，他們就坐在門杜特的密室裡，成為這段傳說永恆的明證。

title.en: 'These Images Are Dead': The Princess Who Rejected Borobudur
title.zh: 『這些像都是死的』：拒絕婆羅浮屠的公主

region.en: Borobudur, Central Java
region.zh: 中爪哇婆羅浮屠

period: Central Javanese temple legend recorded in Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897)

source.work: Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897), Boro Boedor and Mendoet

summary.en: In the hypnotic hours at Borobudur one can best believe the tradition that the temple rose in a night at miraculous bidding, built by the son of the Prince of Borobudur as the condition of marrying the daughter of the Prince of Mendoet. Every detail rigidly prescribed, the work is finished; the princess inspects the miles of carvings and hundreds of statues and says coldly: 'Without doubt these images are beautiful, but they are dead. I can no more love you than they can love you' — and leaves her lover to brood in eternal meditation on the temple walls.
summary.zh: 在婆羅浮屠催眠般的午後，人們最易相信那傳統：此廟乃一夜之間奉神諭而起，由婆羅浮屠王子所建，以此為迎娶門多特公主之條件。工程如期而成，公主巡視綿延的浮雕與成百的雕像，冷然道：『無疑這些像很美，但它們是死的。我愛不上你，正如它們愛不上你。』——她轉身離去，留下她的追求者在廟牆上永恆地冥想。

sensitivity.note: Bride-rejection temple legend; the Javanese analogue of the Roro Jonggrang cycle applied to Borobudur.

passages.text: The tradition says the temple rose in a night at miraculous bidding, built by the son of the Prince of Boro Boedor as a condition to his receiving the daughter of the Prince of Mendoet for a wife; the suitor was to build it within a given time, and every detail was rigidly prescribed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說這座神廟在奇蹟般的號令下一夜之間拔地而起，由婆羅浮屠王子的兒子所建，作為他迎娶門杜特王子之女的條件；這位求婚者須在規定的時限內建成此廟，且每一處細節都有嚴格的規定。

passages.text: The princess came with her father to inspect the great work — miles of bas-reliefs, hundreds of statues fresh from the chisel. 'Without doubt these images are beautiful,' she said coldly, 'but they are dead. I can no more love you than they can love you'; and she turned and left her lover to brood in eternal sorrow and meditation upon that puzzle of all the centuries — the Eternal Feminine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Scidmore (1897); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 公主隨父親前來視察這項宏偉的工程——綿延數里的淺浮雕、數百尊剛出鑿的雕像。「這些雕像無疑很美，」她冷冷地說，「但它們是死的。我能愛你，正如它們能愛你一般不可能」；說罷她轉身離去，留下她的愛人獨自沉思，在永恆的悲傷與冥想中思索那困擾所有世紀的謎題——永恆的女性。

title.en: Kumagdlat and Asalok: The Raid on the Erkileks
title.zh: 庫馬格拉克與阿薩洛克：襲擊厄基萊克族

region.en: Inland plain by a lake (legendary American-continent setting)
region.zh: 湖畔內陸平原（傳說中的美洲大陸故地）

period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from five Greenland copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Three devoted cousins are split by a resentful old hag's lie, and Kumagdlat steals away with his boat, passing the settlements as a diving spotted seal by a seal-skull amulet — betrayed only by a clairvoyant fool. Reunited by chance under the setting sun, the cousins leap a stone's-throw to a refuge island, shoot the pregnant erkilek woman through the body, survive an arrow-storm (Merak's throat healed by Kumagdlat's life-restoring spell), destroy the tribe at their waterfall hiding-place, and carry home beautiful knives from copper-pot furnished tents — thanking the old bachelor who had kept Kumagdlat's family from starving.
summary.zh: 三位至親的表兄弟被老嫗的謊言離間；庫馬格拉克載家私夜遁，以海豹頭骨護符將船假作潛水斑豹，唯有先知般的愚者識破。日落時分兄弟重逢於高原，齊躍一石之遙登避難小島；夜襲厄基萊克帳——一箭射穿孕婦——箭雨中梅拉克喉傷，賴庫馬格拉克復生咒語而癒。瀑布藏匿處他以飛石盡殲其族，攜美柄寶刀而歸，並設宴致謝救其家人免於饑餓的老鰥夫。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads this tale as a memory of primeval Eskimo-Indian conflicts on the American continent and of earliest tool-culture (shells, stone, metal). Graphic violence recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Three cousins named Kumagdlat, Asalok, and Merak were very fond of one another; Kumagdlat kept a house and boat by himself, the other two in partnership, and they all assisted each other early and late, exercising and exhibiting their mutual strength. Kumagdlat had an old crone living with him, very cross-tempered; he warned her he would put her to death some day, and she behaved quietly until one day she exclaimed: 'It is not without reason that I am so quiet and low-spirited; from the first day thou beganst to maintain and support me I have been very sorry for thee... Is it not that thy cousins love thee so very dearly? Nevertheless they now intend to put an end to thy life.' She had invented this lie, being so ill-natured she could not even sleep at night — but from that time Kumagdlat began to fear his cousins, and began to shun them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有三個表兄弟，名叫庫馬格德拉特、阿薩洛克和梅拉克，彼此非常友愛；庫馬格德拉特獨自擁有一間屋子和一艘船，另外兩人合夥共用，他們從早到晚互相幫助，鍛鍊並展示彼此的力量。庫馬格德拉特身邊住著一個性情非常暴躁的老太婆；他警告她總有一天會殺了她，她於是安分守己，直到有一天她喊道：「我如此安靜、如此消沉並非沒有緣由；從你開始供養、扶助我的第一天起，我就一直為你感到非常難過……還不是因為你的表兄弟們如此深愛著你嗎？然而他們現在卻打算結束你的性命。」這謊言是她編造的，她天性如此惡劣，甚至夜裡都睡不著——但從那時起，庫馬格德拉特開始畏懼他的表兄弟，並開始迴避他們。

passages.text: Excusing himself twice that his kayak must dry, he loaded his boat and pushed off, telling the people on shore to tell his cousins to follow him out to their usual reserves. They returned, followed next morning — and found no marks or traces of him. Kumagdlat had the skull of a seal for an amulet: passing inhabited places he fixed it on the prow of his boat so the people would think it nothing but a spotted seal diving up and down; in one settlement a fool — fools being considered clairvoyants — cried 'A boat! a boat!' while the others could see only a diving seal, and from this news Asalok's party knew Kumagdlat must have passed. Travelling night and day, he stopped at a well-peopled place where a very old man was busily making a boat, his hair white as the side of an iceberg, a bearded young man beside him: 'Before this young man here was born I commenced building that boat, and by this time I have only just finished the hull' — his only tools being heaps of shells piled right and left. 'Here we have not got so much as a single knife; but yonder, in the interior of the country, live people who have knives in abundance... Farther inland numerous erkileks have their abodes, and they are immensely rich. However, when any of the coast people go there they never return.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他兩次推託說他的皮划艇必須晾乾，裝好船後便推船離岸，囑咐岸上的人轉告他的表兄弟，要他們跟隨他到他們慣常的獵場去。他們回來了，次日早晨跟隨而去——卻找不到他的任何蹤跡或痕跡。庫馬格德拉特以一枚海豹頭骨為護身符：經過有人居住的地方時，他便把它固定在船頭，好讓人們以為那不過是一隻斑海豹在上下浮沉；在一個聚落裡，一個傻子——傻子被視為有千里眼——喊道「一艘船！一艘船！」而其他人只看見一隻潛水的海豹，阿薩洛克一行人由此得知庫馬格德拉特必定已經經過。他日夜兼程，在一個人口稠密的地方停了下來，那裡有一位非常年邁的老人正忙著造船，他的頭髮白得像冰山的側面，身旁還有一個蓄著鬍鬚的年輕人：「在這個年輕人出生之前，我就開始造那艘船了，到如今我才剛剛造好船身」——他僅有的工具是左右堆積成堆的貝殼。「我們這裡連一把刀都沒有；可是那邊，在內陸腹地，住著刀多得用不完的人……再往內地，眾多埃爾基萊克人居住於此，他們極其富有。然而，沿海的人一旦去那裡，就再也回不來了。」

passages.text: Kumagdlat made himself a small bow and arrows, a quiver of seal-skin, and started for the erkileks all by himself; meanwhile the brothers Asalok and Merak, wandering long, discovered an extensive plain where the erkileks lived in many tents with only a lake for their sea. Hiding till nightfall, they espied under the setting sun a very tall man carrying a burden on his back — 'Why, is not that man like Kumagdlat?' — and the three, happily reunited, resolved that since they had met, one of the hateful erkileks should fall. Kumagdlat told his cousins how the old hag had calumniated them. In the dark they chose a small island right opposite the tents, a stone's-throw off, as a place of refuge; Kumagdlat, with the burden on his back, leaped first and gained the island, Asalok too, and Merak — though not without touching the water. Depositing all but two arrows each, they returned to the mainland, entered the largest tent, and through the skin curtain beheld an old married couple: the man, howling like a dog, licking the pregnant woman's belly as she handed him reindeer-tallow. 'Next time he begins to lick her, I'll take aim and shoot her' — and Kumagdlat shot her right through the body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫馬格德拉特為自己做了一把小弓和幾支箭、一個海豹皮箭袋，便獨自出發前往埃爾基萊克人的地方；與此同時，阿薩洛克和梅拉克兩兄弟長途漫遊，發現了一片廣闊的平原，埃爾基萊克人在那裡支起許多帳篷居住，只有一個湖充當他們的海洋。他們躲藏到夜幕降臨，在落日下瞥見一個非常高大的男人背著重物——「咦，那個人不就是庫馬格德拉特嗎？」——三人欣喜地重聚，並決定既然他們已經相遇，就該有一個可惡的埃爾基萊克人倒下。庫馬格德拉特告訴表兄弟們那個老巫婆是如何誹謗他們的。黑暗中，他們選定正對帳篷、僅一石之遙的一座小島作為避難之所；庫馬格德拉特背著重物率先躍起，登上了小島，阿薩洛克也是，梅拉克也是——雖然不免沾到了水。他們每人只留下兩支箭，其餘的都放下，然後回到大陸，走進最大的帳篷，透過皮簾看見一對老夫婦：那男人像狗一樣嚎叫，舔著孕婦的肚子，而她把馴鹿油脂遞給他。「下次他再開始舔她，我就瞄準射她」——庫馬格德拉特一箭射穿了她的身體。

passages.text: A fearful yell rose, and the cousins hurried across to the island, lying in a row, Kumagdlat in front, Merak hindmost. The erkileks armed and discharged arrows — the women pulling them from above discharged them much quicker than the men — and one whistling through the air struck Merak dangerously in the throat because he ventured to raise his head. 'Dost not thou know any spell for restoring life?' asked Asalok; Kumagdlat murmured words until the arrow had gone half-way out of Merak's throat, and at the third speaking Merak was alive and unhurt. When the erkileks had used up all their arrows, Kumagdlat had only the skin of his temple grazed; the cousins arose to pay them back with their bows, shot a great number, pursued the rest along a river to a waterfall hiding-place, and Kumagdlat killed them all by throwing stones as they issued forth one by one. The children who had remained immovable, feigning death, were caught and pierced through the ears and killed — only one boy and a girl left alive. The furniture of the erkileks held pots of copper with copper handles, and boxes whose covers unlocked of themselves with the quantity of clothes they contained; other boxes held knives with beautiful handles, of which they took as many as they could possibly carry, and made their way to the coast. There Kumagdlat's wife, mocked by neighbours crying that those who went to the erkileks never brought back beautiful knives, was believed a widow and kept from hunger by an old bachelor. Kumagdlat came descending the hill with great loads of hafted knives, thanked him — 'Having such great cause to be thankful towards him, I must have him come in' — and made him sit down and accept two of the knives. The cousins afterwards returned to their old home and grew very renowned for vigour and dexterity, killing bears as well as kilivfaks, the fabulous beasts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 4 'Kumagdlat and Asalok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一聲驚恐的喊叫響起，表兄弟倆急忙奔向那座島，排成一列，庫馬格德拉特在前，梅拉克在最後。erkileks 們武裝起來並射出箭矢——女人們從上方拔箭再射出，比男人們快得多——其中一支箭呼嘯著劃過空中，危險地射中梅拉克的喉嚨，因為他竟敢抬起頭來。「你難道不懂得任何起死回生的咒語嗎？」阿薩洛克問道；庫馬格德拉特低聲念誦詞句，直到那支箭從梅拉克的喉嚨裡退出一半，念到第三遍時，梅拉克便活了過來，安然無恙。當 erkileks 們用盡了所有的箭，庫馬格德拉特只擦傷了太陽穴的皮；表兄弟倆起身用弓箭回敬他們，射死了許多，又沿著一條河追擊其餘的，追到一處瀑布的藏身之所，庫馬格德拉特趁他們一個接一個出來時投擲石塊，把他們全部殺死。那些一動不動、裝死留在原地的孩子們被抓住，耳朵被刺穿而死——只留下一個男孩和一個女孩活著。erkileks 們的家具中有帶銅柄的銅鍋，還有一些箱子，其箱蓋會因所裝衣物的數量而自行開啟；另一些箱子裡裝著刀柄精美的刀子，他們盡其所能地拿了許多，然後前往海岸。在那裡，庫馬格德拉特的妻子被鄰居們嘲笑，他們喊著說那些去找 erkileks 的人從沒帶回過精美的刀子，她被認定為寡婦，靠一位老單身漢的接濟才免於飢餓。庫馬格德拉特帶著大量裝了柄的刀子下山而來，向他道謝——「既然有如此重大的理由要感謝他，我非得請他進來不可」——並讓他坐下，接受其中兩把刀子。表兄弟倆後來回到舊日的家園，因精力充沛和身手矯捷而聲名大噪，既能殺熊，也能殺基利夫法克這種傳說中的野獸。

title.en: Akigsiak: Son of the Coast and the Interior
title.zh: 阿基克夏克：海濱與內陸之子

region.en: Fiord head and inland country (legendary contact zone)
region.zh: 峽灣深處與內陸（傳說中的接觸地帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition; six copies collated, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 5 'Akigsiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Carried off by an inlander as a bride, a coast woman bears Akigsiak, feared for strength among the inland folk though smaller of growth. In four reports to the coast people he tells of escaping the monstrous fat-bodied reptile of the north that he had earlier fled in a snowstorm; of luring a whale up the river by an old coast man's magic lay and sharing it with all; of a salmon-shaped giant fish hauled back across the river by a head-over-heels leap; of the pot-bearer igalilik he crushed down a precipice — and of the inorusek giant whose stone-throwing dare made him kill a passing kayaker, a deed of repentance after which he never ventured among the coast people again.
summary.zh: 海濱女子被內陸人擄為妻，生子阿基克夏克；他身量雖小，卻為內陸族所畏。他先後四次向海濱人自述：雪暴中誤遇北方巨蟒，几番跳越反擊，昏倒逃生，族人循跡剖其脂肉過冬；依老海濱人之咒歌引鯨入河、遍分其肉；又於窄河處翻躍對岸，從敵手奪回鮭形巨魚；以及他推下懸崖的負鍋巨人、與受石擲慫恿誤殺過路皮艇客的悔恨——自此他再不敢涉足海濱。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads this tale as referring to historical Eskimo-Indian contact. Killing of the kayaker recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: In days of yore some people went far into a firth to fish for salmon, and one of the women was carried off by an inlander to a very remote place; belonging to the coast people, she afterwards married her captor, and they begat a son named Akigsiak. In boyhood two of his father's nephews were his constant playfellows, but Akigsiak soon outdid them completely, even in swiftness; as his mother was of the coast people while his father was from the interior, he was smaller of growth, yet respected and feared by the other inlanders, with a great reputation for strength and ability in hunting. He sought intercourse with the coast people to gain information about his mother's relatives, and at such a meeting once told them: 'When my father grew older he was incapable of providing for us. One winter we had a great famine, and every day I went out in search of provisions; meanwhile my father watched me from the tops of the highest mountains, taking note of any change in the weather, and as soon as the sky darkened he made me a signal I could hear far and wide, after which I took my way homewards.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 5 'Akigsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 往昔有些人遠赴一處峽灣捕撈鮭魚，其中一名婦女被一個內陸人擄到極偏遠的地方；她本屬海岸民族，後來嫁給了擄走她的人，生下一個兒子，名叫阿基格西亞克。童年時，他父親的兩個姪子是他形影不離的玩伴，但阿基格西亞克很快就在各方面完全勝過他們，甚至在速度上也是如此；由於他母親是海岸民族而父親來自內陸，他身材較為矮小，卻受到其他內陸人的敬重與畏懼，在狩獵的力量與本領方面享有盛名。他設法與海岸民族往來，以打聽母親親屬的消息，在一次這樣的會面中曾對他們說：「我父親年歲漸長後，就無力供養我們了。有一個冬天我們遭遇大饑荒，我每天外出尋找食物；與此同時，我父親從最高的山頂上注視著我，留意天氣的任何變化，一旦天色暗下來，他就向我發出一個我能遠遠聽見的信號，之後我便踏上回家的路。」

passages.text: His father warned him he might go anywhere except to the north, because of a monstrous reptile reported to ravage those parts. One day the signal came before he had killed any game, and he did not obey it; the storm overtook him, and wandering blind in wind and snow-drift he discovered what appeared to be two large windows of a house, then that the other parts were like a hill — and finally that this was the terrible reptile his father had warned him against. He took to flight; the reptile had seen him and pursued, but whenever it came up he leapt across it, striking it with his lance. At last, it quite close upon him, he cried aloud with fatigue, fell to the ground, and lost his senses — to be awakened by a cool touch upon his face: the reptile lay close to his feet, unmoving. With his eyes constantly fixed on it he crept cautiously away, rose, and walked on, not reaching home until the fourth day, having been given up for lost. His father said their housemates had nothing to help him with, but he told how he had barely escaped the reptile, apparently leaving it dead — 'The body of the reptile is said to consist of nothing but fat,' said his father, adding that the house-fellows were almost starving. They went out in search of the monster; many died on the road before reaching the spot, but those who arrived flensed away at him and found him principally fat mixed with a little lean flesh, and had it for food the whole winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 5 'Akigsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他父親告誡他，除了北方之外哪裡都可以去，因為據說有一隻巨大的爬蟲類怪物在那裡肆虐。有一天，他還沒獵到任何獵物，信號就來了，他沒有遵從；暴風雪襲擊了他，他在狂風與飛雪中盲目遊蕩，發現了看似一棟房屋的兩扇大窗，接著又發現其餘部分像一座山——最後才明白這就是父親告誡他提防的那隻可怕爬蟲。他拔腿就逃；那爬蟲已看見他並追了上來，但每當它逼近，他就躍過它，用長矛擊打它。最後，它緊逼到他身邊，他因疲憊而大聲喊叫，倒在地上，失去了知覺——卻被臉上的一陣清涼觸感喚醒：那爬蟲躺在他腳邊，一動不動。他雙眼緊盯著它，小心翼翼地爬開，站起身來繼續走，直到第四天才回到家，期間眾人已認定他失蹤了。他父親說同屋的人沒有什麼能幫他的，但他講述了自己如何勉強逃脫那爬蟲，似乎已把它弄死了——「據說那爬蟲的身體除了脂肪別無他物，」他父親說，並補充說同屋的人幾乎快餓死了。他們外出尋找那怪物；許多人在到達那地點之前就死在路上，但到達的人剝開它的皮，發現它主要是脂肪，混有少許瘦肉，整個冬天都拿它當食物。

passages.text: The next time he told how, on an excursion with his father, they observed a whale close outside the sea-shore with a number of coast people standing on the beach; by his father's orders he ran down and made an old man teach him a magic lay for luring the whale up the river. As soon as the whale had entered the river a crowd of inlanders appeared, and before they could penetrate the whale's skin with their harpoons, Akigsiak ran home to fetch his weapons — rounding three large bays on the way — and returned in good time to despatch the whale, giving everybody his share, not forgetting the old coast man, whom he protected against the inlanders. At the third meeting he told how, hearing that other inlanders had caught an immense fish shaped like a salmon, he hurried to the river-side and threw his harpoon into it too, but his companions being too few, the inlanders on the opposite side hauled it from them; he hastened to where the river was narrower, and in jumping across hurled himself round, head over heels, alighting on his feet on the opposite shore — where he frightened away the other inlanders, took his share of the fish, threw it across to his own people, and jumped back the same way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 5 'Akigsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 下一次他講述道，有一次他與父親外出，他們看見一頭鯨魚就在海岸外不遠處，海灘上站著許多海岸民族的人；他奉父親之命跑下去，讓一位老人教他一首引誘鯨魚溯河而上的咒歌。鯨魚一進入河中，一大群內陸人就出現了，在他們能用魚叉刺穿鯨魚的皮之前，阿基格西亞克跑回家去取他的武器——途中繞過了三個大海灣——並及時趕回結果了那頭鯨魚，分給每個人自己的一份，也沒忘記那位海岸老人，還保護他免受內陸人的侵害。在第三次會面時，他講述道，他聽說其他內陸人捕到一條形似鮭魚的巨魚，便急忙趕到河邊，也把自己的魚叉投了進去，但他的同伴太少，對岸的內陸人把它從他們手中拖走了；他趕到河面較窄的地方，在跳躍過河時整個人翻了個筋斗，頭下腳上，最後雙腳落地落在對岸——在那裡他嚇跑了其他內陸人，取了自己那份魚，把它扔給自己人，又用同樣的方式跳了回來。

passages.text: At the fourth meeting he told of a quarrel with an igalilik — a pot-bearer, one of the fabulous inlanders who carry boiling pots on their shoulders — whom he pushed down a precipice, crushing him to death against the rocks. At last Akigsiak met an inorusek, another kind of gigantic inlander, on the high banks of a river; amusing themselves throwing stones, the inorusek persuaded him to try to hit a kayaker passing below, whom he did not fail to kill on the spot.
