From her flesh Old-One rolled balls of mud and transformed them into the beings of the ancient world, people and yet animals, each powerful in some ways and helpless in others, many of them cannibals who could not tell people from deer; his last balls, shaped like Indians, he blew upon, and they became alive — the most helpless of all created things, whom the monsters preyed upon. When evil still prevailed, the Chief sent Coyote to earth to destroy the monsters, make life easier, and teach the people the best way to do things.
summary.zh: 老者（即主神）以一女子之身造大地，並言其為萬民之母。大地至今有靈：土壤為其肉，草木為其髮，巖石為其骨，風為其息。寒則顫慄收縮，熱則舒展汗出；其動則地震生。老者取其肉搓為泥丸，化為上古生靈——亦人亦獸，各有其能亦各有其弱，多為食人者，人獸不分。最後所搓者形似印第安人，吹氣而活——乃受造物中最弱者，遂為怪物所噬。世間仍多惡，主神乃遣郊狼下凡，誅怪獸、濟眾生、授民以術。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The informant also told a Garden-of-Eden/Jesus episode under missionary influence, noted here as collection context but not treated as a separate Plateau record. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Old-One, or Chief, made the earth out of a woman, and said she would be the mother of all the people. Thus the earth was once a human being, and she is alive yet; but she has been transformed, and we cannot see her in the same way we can see a person. Nevertheless she has legs, arms, head, heart, flesh, bones, and blood: the soil is her flesh; the trees and vegetation are her hair; the rocks, her bones; and the wind is her breath. She lies spread out, and we live on her. She shivers and contracts when cold, and expands and perspires when hot. When she moves, we have an earthquake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 80 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「老者」或稱「酋長」，用一個女人造出了大地，並說她將成為所有人的母親。因此，大地曾經是一個人，而她至今仍然活著；只是她已被轉化，我們無法像看見人那樣看見她。然而她有腿、有臂、有頭、有心、有肉、有骨、有血：泥土是她的肉；樹木與草木是她的頭髮；岩石是她的骨；風是她的氣息。她舒展躺臥，我們便活在她身上。寒冷時她顫抖收縮，炎熱時她舒展出汗。當她移動時，我們便有了地震。

passages.text: Old-One, after transforming her, took some of her flesh and rolled it into balls, as people do with mud or clay, and transformed them into the beings of the ancient world, who were people, and yet at the same time animals. Some could fly like birds and others swim like fishes; all had greater powers and were more cunning than either animals or people — but not well balanced: each was exceedingly wise in some things and exceedingly foolish in others. As a rule they were selfish, there was much trouble among them, and some were cannibals who lived by eating one another: they knew they had to live by hunting, but did not know which beings were people and which deer, and thought people were deer and preyed on them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 80-81 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老者將她轉化之後，取了她的一些肉，搓成球，如同人們搓泥或黏土一般，並將它們轉化為遠古世界的生靈；他們是人，卻同時也是動物。有些能像鳥一樣飛，有些能像魚一樣游；他們全都擁有比動物或人更大的力量，也更為狡黠——但並不均衡：每一個都在某些事上極其聰慧，在另一些事上卻極其愚笨。一般而言，他們自私自利，彼此之間紛爭不斷，其中有些是食人者，靠互相吞食為生：他們知道自己必須靠狩獵過活，卻分不清哪些生靈是人、哪些是鹿，竟以為人是鹿而捕食他們。

passages.text: Old-One made each ball of mud a little different from the others, and rolled them over and over, shaping them and making them alive. The last balls he made were almost all alike and different from any of the preceding ones: they were formed like Indians, and he called them men. He blew on them, and they became alive. They were Indians, but were ignorant and knew no arts — the most helpless of all things created, and the cannibals and other monsters preyed on them particularly. The people and animals were made male and female so that they might breed; thus everything living sprang from the earth, and when we look around we see everywhere parts of our mother. The Chief then sent Coyote to earth to destroy all the monsters and evil beings, to make life easier and better for the people, and to teach them the best way to do things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 81-82 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老者使每一個泥球都與其餘的略有不同，將它們反覆搓揉，塑造成形，並使它們活了起來。他最後造的幾個球幾乎全都一樣，且與先前任何一個都不同：它們的形狀像印第安人，他便稱他們為人。他向他們吹氣，他們便活了過來。他們是印第安人，卻無知無識，不懂任何技藝——是一切受造之物中最無助的，食人者與其他怪物尤其捕食他們。人與動物都被造成雌雄兩性，以便繁衍；於是萬物生靈皆從大地而生，我們環顧四周，便處處看見我們母親的肢體。酋長隨後派遣郊狼到大地去毀滅所有怪物與邪惡生靈，使人們的生活更安適、更美好，並教導他們做事的最佳方法。

title.en: Coyote Sent to Set the World in Order
title.zh: 郊狼受命整飭世界

region.en: Okanagon and Sanpoil country, Washington (symbolic pin at Okanogan River)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根與桑普瓦故地，華盛頓州（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

period: Told by Red-Arm (Nespelim/Lower Okanagon); collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 1. Coyote' (Okanagon, told by Red-Arm)

summary.en: Chief saw that the people were having a hard time, preyed upon by many evil beings and about to be killed off; not wanting them exterminated, he sent Coyote to help them — endowing him with great magical power to surmount all obstacles, with power to transform evil beings, and with wisdom and cunning, and giving even Coyote's excrements power to be his friends and advisers. He told him to travel all over the world and set it right, adding that when Coyote's work was finished, he would meet him, see his work, and then give him a rest.
summary.zh: 主神見民困苦，備受諸惡所噬，行將滅絕；不欲其亡，乃遣郊狼相助：授以大神力可越一切險阻，賜其變形諸惡之權，并賜智慧狡計；甚至其糞便亦得言語，為其友與謀士。命其周行天下，整飭其間；並許諾功成之日，將親見其業，而後許其休息。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was sent by Chief to set the world in order. Chief saw that the people were having a hard time and were preyed upon by many evil beings; they were about to be killed off. Chief did not want the people to be exterminated, so he sent Coyote to help them. He endowed him with great magical power, so that he could surmount all obstacles; he gave him power to transform evil beings, and he gave him wisdom and cunning. He also gave to Coyote's excrements the power to be his friends and advisers. He told him to travel all over the world and to set it right. Coyote had to travel much and to work hard. Chief said that when Coyote's work was finished, he would meet him, see his work, and then give him a rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 65 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼受酋長派遣，去整頓世界。酋長見人們處境艱難，受許多邪惡生靈捕食；他們即將被趕盡殺絕。酋長不願人們被消滅，於是派遣郊狼去幫助他們。他賜予他強大的法力，使他能克服一切障礙；他賜予他轉化邪惡生靈的力量，又賜予他智慧與狡黠。他也賜予郊狼的排泄物成為他朋友與謀士的力量。他吩咐他走遍世界，將其導正。郊狼必須遠行，必須辛勤工作。酋長說，當郊狼的工作完成時，他會與他相見，察看他的成果，然後賜他安息。

title.en: Origin of the Columbia River: Coyote and the Dripping Water
title.zh: 哥倫比亞河之起源：郊狼與滴水

region.en: Dry coulee that became the Columbia River, Washington (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 乾涸峽谷，後成哥倫比亞河，華盛頓州（象徵定位）

period: Told by Red-Arm (Nespelim/Lower Okanagon); collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (2a) Origin of the Columbia River' (Okanagon, told by Red-Arm)

summary.en: Hearing water drip, Coyote mimics it four times — 'Hox-hox-hox-hox!' — and, angered that the noise never ceases, kicks the dripping place and laughs that no more water shall drip. But the water follows him, growing in volume as it flows; on the dry plateau he grows thirsty, and each time he descends to drink the creek has become a larger stream behind him. Driven to walk, then wade, then swim with his mouth close to the water, he drinks so much that he loses consciousness — and thus, from a few drops, the Columbia River originated.
summary.zh: 郊狼聞滴水聲，四度模仿『霍霍霍霍』而不得其靜，怒而踢水滴之處，笑曰：『吾已勝汝，水不得復滴作響。』然水銜尾而至，愈流愈盛；於乾燥高地上，郊狼屢渴屢下飲，每次下望，溪已成河。最後涉水而泳，口貼水面暢飲，竟致不省人事——區區滴水，遂成哥倫比亞大河。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Landscape etiology for the Columbia; the pin marks the dry coulee of the tale. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and heard water dropping. He said, 'I will go and beat it.' He sat down near it and cried, 'Hox-hox-hox-hox!' in imitation of water dripping. He tried four times, but the noise never ceased. He became angry, arose, and kicked the place where the water dropped; the noise ceased. He thought he had beaten it, and laughed, saying, 'I beat you. No more shall water drip thus and make a noise.' Shortly after he had gone, the water began to drip as before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 65-66 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在旅行，聽見水滴落的聲音。他說：「我要去把它打敗。」他在那聲音附近坐下，模仿水滴落的聲音喊道：「霍克斯—霍克斯—霍克斯—霍克斯！」他試了四次，但那聲音從未停止。他發怒了，起身踢向水滴落之處；聲音便停止了。他以為自己打敗了它，便笑著說：「我打敗你了。你再也不能這樣滴水作聲了。」他離去後不久，水又像先前一樣開始滴落。

passages.text: He became angry: 'Did I not say water shall not run and make a noise?' The water was coming after him, and increased in volume as it flowed. He kept on running, still hearing the noise of water, and travelled along the edge of a plateau where there was no water nor trees, and everywhere below the coulee was dry. It was warm, and he became very thirsty; looking down into the coulee he saw a small creek, went down, and drank his fill — but had barely reached the top again when he was thirsty once more, and the creek below had grown. The more he drank, the sooner he became thirsty again; the fourth time the water had risen to a good-sized river close by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 66 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他發怒了：「我不是說過水不得奔流作聲嗎？」那水正跟在他身後，邊流邊增大水量。他繼續奔跑，仍聽見水的聲響，沿著一處高原的邊緣前行，那裡既無水也無樹，下方各處的乾谷都是乾的。天氣炎熱，他口渴難耐；他向乾谷下方望去，看見一條小溪，便走下去喝了個飽——但他才剛回到上面，便又渴了，而下方的小溪已經變大了。他越喝，渴得越快；到了第四次，水已漲成一條相當大的河流，就在近旁。

passages.text: 'What may be the matter? I am always thirsty now. There is no use of my going away. I will walk along the edge of the water' — and still thirsty, 'I will walk in the water.' It reached up to his knees; he walked deeper, to the waist, then to the arms. Then he said, 'I will swim, so that my mouth will be close to the water, and I can drink all the time.' Finally he had drunk so much that he lost consciousness. Thus the water got even with Coyote for kicking it; and thus from a few drops of water originated the Columbia River.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 66 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「這究竟是怎麼回事？我現在總是口渴。我離開也沒有用。我要沿著水邊走」——他仍然口渴，「我要走進水裡。」水淹到他的膝蓋；他走得更深，到了腰部，然後到了手臂。接著他說：「我要游泳，這樣我的嘴就能靠近水面，我就能一直喝個不停。」最後他喝得太多，失去了知覺。水就這樣報復了踢它的郊狼；哥倫比亞河就這樣由幾滴水發源而成。

title.en: Coyote and the Rain: Wishing a River
title.zh: 郊狼求雨：許願成河

region.en: South of the Columbia River, dry coulee country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河以南，乾谷之地（象徵定位）

period: Collected on the Okanagon River; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (2b) Coyote and the Water or Rain' (Okanagon)

summary.en: Travelling hot and dry down a waterless coulee, Coyote tries resting in the shade of a rock and a tree, but both crack and lean over him and he flees. He wishes for a cloud — one comes; for many clouds — the sky overcasts; for rain — a little falls; for much rain — it pours; for a creek to cool his feet — one runs; then for a river to drink easily — and the river rises to his chin and carries him away to a distant country, where he floats ashore exhausted, and the ravens, crows, magpies and buzzards come to feed on him, thinking he is dead, until he gets up and chases them away.
summary.zh: 郊狼行於無水乾谷，燥熱難當。先於巖蔭歇腳，巖裂傾之，逃；再憩樹蔭，樹鳴壓頂，又逃。乃許願求雲——雲至；求多雲——天陰；求雨——微雨；求大雨——傾盆；求溪潤足——溪成；求河暢飲——河水齊頸，竟將其捲往異鄉。飄至岸邊，力竭而臥；渡鴉、烏鴉、喜鵲、兀鷹誤以為其已死，群集啄之，他起身驅散之。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once Coyote was travelling somewhere south of the Columbia River. He was going down a coulee in which there was no water; the weather was very hot, and he felt very hot and dry. He saw a large rock and said, 'I will rest in its shade'; but the rock began to crack and lean over, and Coyote became afraid and ran away. After a while he saw a tree and thought he would rest in its shade; but it began to creak and lean over, so he ran away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 66 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，郊狼正在哥倫比亞河以南的某個地方旅行。他正沿著一條沒有水的乾谷往下走；天氣非常炎熱，他感到又熱又乾。他看見一塊大石頭，便說：「我要在它的陰影下休息」；但那塊石頭開始裂開並傾斜過來，郊狼害怕起來，便跑開了。過了一會兒，他看見一棵樹，心想可以在它的陰影下休息；但那棵樹開始嘎吱作響並傾斜過來，於是他就跑開了。

passages.text: He looked at the sky, but saw no clouds, and said, 'I wish a cloud would come!' Soon a cloud came up and shaded him. 'That is not enough. I want many clouds.' Soon the sky became overcast, but it was still hot; then he wished for rain, and a little came. 'I want much rain.' It began to pour down. 'I want a creek, so that my feet may be cool' — a creek ran and he walked in it. 'That is not enough. I want a river, so that I may be cool and drink easily.' A river ran then, reached to his chin, and carried him away to a distant country, where he floated ashore quite exhausted and lay on the bank. The ravens, crows, magpies, and buzzards came to feed on him, thinking he was dead; he got up and chased them away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 66-67 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他仰望天空，卻看不到雲，便說：「我希望有一朵雲來！」不久一朵雲升了上來，為他遮陰。「那還不夠。我要很多雲。」不久天空陰雲密佈，但天氣仍然炎熱；於是他祈求下雨，下了一點點。「我要很多雨。」大雨開始傾盆而下。「我要一條小溪，好讓我的腳涼快」——一條小溪流淌起來，他走進溪中。「那還不夠。我要一條河，好讓我涼快，也容易喝水。」於是有一條河流淌起來，水深及他的下巴，把他沖到一個遙遠的地方，他在那裡筋疲力盡地漂上岸，躺在河岸上。渡鴉、烏鴉、喜鵲和禿鷲前來啄食他，以為他死了；他站起身來把牠們趕走了。

title.en: Coyote Introduces the Salmon
title.zh: 郊狼引鮭記

region.en: Columbia River from its falls to Spokane (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河自瀑布至斯波坎（象徵定位）

period: Told by Red-Arm (Nespelim/Lower Okanagon); collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (3a) Introduction of Salmon' (Okanagon, told by Red-Arm)

summary.en: Flushed down his own wished-for river, Coyote drifts as a canoe to the weir of the two We'lwel sisters, who own all the salmon below the falls while the interior knows nothing of them. Taken up as a dish, filled with boiled salmon, the dish is discovered emptied; when the younger sister tries to smash it on a rock it becomes a crying baby, and they rear 'our younger brother' — who eats their stores, then breaks their weir under a horn-spoon helmet while they beat him in vain. The salmon run upstream to the Coyote people, the sisters are transformed into sandpipers, and up every river Coyote goes the salmon follow: he makes fishing-places for the people who treat him well and barriers for those who refuse him, leaving Spokane Falls half-dug because the people above would not give him a wife.
summary.zh: 郊狼為己所願之河沖走，化舟漂至 We'lwel 二姊妹之魚梁；彼等獨佔瀑布以下之鮭，內陸之人尚不識鮭味。姊妹取舟為盤盛熟鮭，鮭卻失蹤；妹怒欲碎盤於石，盤忽化啼嬰，遂收養為『小弟』——他偷食其存糧，並戴羊角勺盔頂拆魚梁，棒擊無效。鮭遂上溯至郊狼子孫之地；二姊化為鷸鳥。此後郊狼行至何處，鮭隨至何處：善待其者得漁場，拒婚者得石障；斯波坎瀑布即因上方之人不許婚而半途停工之坑。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Salmon-liberation culture-hero cycle; the Similkameen variant (3b) with franker content was not separately cut. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a large river, and Coyote floated along in it. After drifting a long time he regained consciousness, and when he discovered himself in the middle of a large, swift-running river he became afraid and changed himself into a small canoe. Away down below, somewhere above the place where Portland is now, where there is a fall in the river, there lived the two We'lwel sisters, who owned a weir that extended across the stream. Below the weir the river was full of salmon, while above it, in the interior, there were none: the Indians there knew nothing of salmon at that time, and lived on game, roots, and berries. Coyote, still in the form of a canoe bottom up, struck the weir and remained there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 67 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一條大河，郊狼在其中漂流。漂流了很久之後，他恢復了知覺，當他發現自己身處一條又大又湍急的河流中央時，他害怕起來，把自己變成了一隻小獨木舟。在下方某處，大約在今日波特蘭所在之地的上游，河中有個瀑布，那裡住著兩位韋爾韋爾（We'lwel）姊妹，她們擁有一道橫跨河流的魚梁。魚梁下方，河裡滿是鮭魚；而魚梁上方，在內陸，卻一條也沒有：當時那裡的印第安人對鮭魚一無所知，靠獵物、根莖和漿果為生。郊狼仍保持著獨木舟底朝上的形態，撞上了魚梁，便留在那裡。

passages.text: In the morning the sisters came out to clean the weir of driftwood, and saw the small canoe bottom up. The younger said, 'We must save it. It will make a fine dish to hold our salmon in'; the elder said, 'Do not touch it. It has been made by some one. Possibly it is Coyote.' The younger took it home and put boiled salmon into it, and when they returned from root-digging the salmon in the dish had disappeared, and also some of the fish they had been drying. The younger sister became angry and tried to break the dish on a rock; as she was about to do so, the dish assumed the shape of a baby and began to cry, and she took pity: 'Oh, he will make a nice younger brother for us!' Coyote grew fast; tied up when they went root-digging, he unfastened himself and ate their roots and dried salmon, tying himself up again before they returned. 'How good our younger brother is!' the women would say.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 67 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 早晨，姊妹們出來清理魚梁上的漂流木，看見那隻底朝上的小獨木舟。妹妹說：「我們得把它留下。它可以做成一個好盤子，用來盛我們的鮭魚」；姊姊說：「別碰它。它是某個人做出來的。說不定是郊狼。」妹妹把它帶回家，把煮熟的鮭魚放進去，當她們挖完根莖回來時，盤子裡的鮭魚不見了，她們正在曬的一些魚也不見了。妹妹生氣了，想把盤子在石頭上砸碎；正當她要砸的時候，那盤子變成了一個嬰兒的形狀，開始哭了起來，她心生憐憫：「哦，他會成為我們的好弟弟！」郊狼長得很快；她們去挖根莖時把他綁起來，他卻自己解開，吃掉她們的根莖和乾鮭魚，又在她們回來之前把自己綁好。「我們的弟弟多好啊！」女人們會這麼說。

passages.text: Coyote planned to break the women's weir and let the salmon pass up river. The fourth day, when the elder sister's root-digger broke and something felt wrong, they hastened home — meanwhile Coyote had put a sheep's-horn spoon on his head and was breaking the weir. They rushed at him and beat him over the head with sticks, but he kept on working faster than ever, the horn spoon protecting him. When the weir was broken, he ran up the opposite bank, and the king-salmon were ascending the river in great numbers. The sisters sat down on the bank and wept: 'You have stolen our salmon for your Coyote people! You are all Coyote people! You are bad people!' He answered, 'You thought you had a little boy, a little brother. You thought he knew nothing, but he was greater than you!' Then he transformed them into birds — sandpipers — saying, 'Henceforth you shall run by the water's edge. You shall no longer have control over salmon. Salmon shall henceforth run up the river.' The place where the weir was is now a fall in the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 67-68 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼計劃破壞女人們的魚梁，讓鮭魚往上游去。第四天，當姊姊的挖根棒折斷，她們感到有些不對勁時，便急忙趕回家——與此同時，郊狼把一隻羊角匙放在頭上，正在破壞魚梁。她們朝他衝過去，用棍子打他的頭，但他卻越幹越快，羊角匙保護著他。魚梁被破壞後，他跑上對岸，而王鮭正大批地往上游去。姊妹們坐在岸上哭泣：「你把我們的鮭魚偷去給你的郊狼族人！你們全是郊狼族人！你們是壞人！」他回答說：「你們以為你們有一個小男孩，一個小弟弟。你們以為他什麼都不懂，但他比你們更偉大！」然後他把她們變成鳥——磯鷸——說道：「從今以後，你們要沿著水邊奔跑。你們不再能控制鮭魚。從今以後，鮭魚要往上游去。」魚梁所在的地方，如今成了河中的一道瀑布。

passages.text: Coyote walked along the river-bank, and the salmon followed him. Hungry, he wished the king-salmon to jump ashore; on rocky and clayey banks the slimy fish slipped back, but the fourth time it jumped on a sandy shore and he caught it. He cooked and ate his fill, then carried the rest on his back, asking a girl at every camp to marry him — all refused. At the mouth of the Similkameen he left the salmon and went up alone; the people there refused him because he was ugly, so he said, 'You shall have plenty of sheep, but salmon you shall not have. You will have to travel long distances to obtain your salmon,' and made a barrier so no salmon ascend the Similkameen. Above the Okanagon falls the people did not want him, and he made a rock barrier there. At Kali'tcamen the old people wanted to marry their daughters to him; he made a fine salmon-fishing place there, contracting the river and smoothing the rocks so children could play on them, and made a salmon-weir — then learned the girls would not have him, and kicked the weir to pieces. But he thought, 'The girl alone is bad; it is not the old people's fault. They were good to me,' and left the place as he had made it, where people have always been able to capture salmon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 68-69 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼沿著河岸行走，鮭魚跟隨著他。他餓了，便希望那條王鮭跳上岸來；在岩石與黏土質的岸邊，那滑溜的魚又滑了回去，但第四次牠跳上了沙岸，他便捉住了牠。他將魚煮熟吃飽，然後把剩下的背在背上，每到一處營地便向一個女孩求婚——全都被拒絕了。在西米爾卡米恩（Similkameen）河口，他留下鮭魚獨自上行；那裡的人因為他醜陋而拒絕他，於是他说：『你們將會有許多羊，但鮭魚你們不會有。你們將得遠行才能取得你們的鮭魚。』並造了一道屏障，使鮭魚無法上溯西米爾卡米恩河。在奧卡納岡（Okanagon）瀑布上游，人們不要他，他便在那裡造了一道岩石屏障。在卡利特卡門（Kali'tcamen），老人們想把女兒嫁給他；他在那裡造了一處良好的捕鮭之地，使河流收窄、岩石磨平，讓孩子們能在上面玩耍，又造了一道捕鮭堰——隨後得知女孩們不願要他，便將那堰踢得粉碎。但他心想：『壞的只是那女孩；這不是老人們的過錯。他們待我很好。』於是他讓那地方保持他所造的樣子離去，那裡的人們一直都能捕到鮭魚。

passages.text: At Nespe'lim Creek and at Hi'tcox near Spoke'in the same happened: the people accepted him, the girl refused him, and he had pity on the old people — 'There shall always be some salmon here,' he said. At Snuxami'na he threw half a cooked salmon into the river, where it became a rock like the side of a king-salmon. At Ski'tco, where the town of Spokane now is, he found a barrier across the stream and began to dig it away; but when he thought, 'Perhaps the people above are bad and will not give me a wife. Why should I favor them?' he went and saw the people who refused him, and left the hole the way it was: it forms now Spokane Falls, and not many salmon go up there, therefore the Coeur d'Alene have no salmon. At Tqemi'p the leavings of a cooked salmon became rocks forming an eddy, where, he said, some salmon of the first run will always die. At Colville the Wolverene people had ordered two of their daughters to marry him for the sake of fine food, and he filled their weir with king-salmon every morning; near there he made a dam and showed the people the methods of fishing with dip-nets and spears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 69-70 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在內斯佩利姆溪（Nespe'lim Creek）與斯波坎（Spoke'in）附近的希特科克斯（Hi'tcox），同樣的事也發生了：人們接納了他，女孩拒絕了他，而他憐憫那些老人——『這裡將永遠有些鮭魚，』他說。在斯努克薩米納（Snuxami'na），他將半條煮熟的鮭魚扔進河裡，那半條魚化作一塊狀如王鮭側身的岩石。在斯基特科（Ski'tco），即今斯波坎市所在之處，他發現溪流中有一道屏障，便動手挖掘；但當他心想：『也許上游的人不好，不會給我妻子。我為何要偏袒他們？』他便前去見那些拒絕他的人，讓那洞保持原樣：它如今形成了斯波坎瀑布，沒有多少鮭魚上溯到那裡，因此科達倫（Coeur d'Alene）人沒有鮭魚。在特克米普（Tqemi'p），一條煮熟鮭魚的殘餘化作岩石，形成一處漩渦，他在那裡說，第一波洄游的鮭魚總會有些死在那裡。在科爾維爾（Colville），狼獾族人為了得到好食物，命他們的兩個女兒嫁給他，而他每天早晨都用王鮭裝滿他們的魚堰；在那附近他造了一道壩，並向人們示範用撈網與魚叉捕魚的方法。

title.en: Coyote and the Steelhead-Salmon Sisters
title.zh: 郊狼與鋼頭鱒姊妹

region.en: Winter ice of the Columbia, great fishing-station (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 冬季哥倫比亞河冰面，大漁場（象徵定位）

period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (3c) Coyote and the Steelhead-Salmon' (Okanagon)

summary.en: Walking the winter ice, Coyote doubles back to meet the two Steelhead sisters and proposes a wrestle, intending to throw the elder; instead she hurls him on the ice so hard that it kills him. He lies drying to bones and skin until Fox hears of his death and jumps over his bones — Coyote comes to life, sits up, yawns, and says he only lay down for a nap. Ever since, that stretch of the river has been a good place for steelhead, where the Indians catch numbers in springtime; it became one of the great fishing-stations of the Columbia, for Coyote is said to have turned back from there, and not many salmon go above it.
summary.zh: 郊狼冬日行於冰面，折返欲戲鋼頭鱒二姊妹，假意摔跤以圖不軌；孰料姊姊將其重摔於冰上，竟斃命。屍身日久風乾，僅餘皮骨；狐聞其死訊，躍過其骨，郊狼遂活，坐起哈欠道：『吾不過臥此小憩。』自此該段河道多鋼頭鱒，春日漁獲甚豐，成哥倫比亞大漁場之一——相傳郊狼至此折返，故其上鮭魚不多。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling along the ice of the river. It was wintertime. He saw the two Steelhead sisters on the ice, and said, 'I will go back, meet them, and fool them.' When they met, the elder sister recognized him, and said, 'Halloo, Coyote! Where are you going? What do you want?' He answered, 'Oh, I am just travelling along on the ice! Yes, I want something. I wish to wrestle with you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 71-72 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正沿著河上的冰面行走。時值冬季。他看見那兩位鋼頭鱒姊妹在冰上，便說：『我要折回去，與她們相遇，捉弄她們一番。』當他們相遇時，姊姊認出了他，說道：『喂，郊狼！你要去哪裡？你想要什麼？』他答道：『哦，我只是在冰上走走罷了！是的，我想要點東西。我想和妳們角力。』

passages.text: They wrestled, and the woman threw him upon the ice so hard that it killed him. He lay there a long time, and dried up, until only his bones and skin remained. Fox heard of his death, and jumped over his bones; Coyote came to life, sat up, and yawned. He said, 'I just lay down here and had a nap.' Fox said, 'You were dead a long time, and I have brought you to life.' Ever since that time this part of the river has been a good place for steelhead-fish, and the Indians catch numbers there in the springtime. This place became one of the great fishing-stations on the Columbia; not many salmon go above it, for Coyote is said to have turned back from there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 72 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們角力，那女人把他摔在冰上，摔得那麼重，竟把他摔死了。他躺在那裡很久，乾枯下去，直到只剩下骨頭和皮。狐狸聽聞他的死訊，便從他的骨頭上跳過；郊狼活了過來，坐起身，打了個呵欠。他說：『我只是在這裡躺下打了個盹。』狐狸說：『你死了很久，是我使你復活的。』自那時起，這一段河流便成了捕鋼頭鱒的好地方，印第安人在春天在那裡捕獲許多。這地方成了哥倫比亞河上偉大的捕魚站之一；沒有多少鮭魚上溯到那裡，因為據說郊狼從那裡折返了。

title.en: Coyote and the Ice People
title.zh: 郊狼與冰族

region.en: House of ice in the snowy north (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北地冰雪之屋（象徵定位）

period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (5) Coyote and the Ice People' (Okanagon)

summary.en: The three Ice or Cold people kill Indians with cold weather, cold winds and ice, and love the cold; many have died at their hands. Coyote consults his excrements, who teach him their secret names and a plan: his three droppings become fresh service-berries (a gift), the heat of the sun to melt their house, and dead pine-needles (ka'ma). Addressed as a relative, admitted as one of the Ice people, he complains of the heat while the ice house melts and drips; outside, he fires the pine-needles he left at the door and burns the house down, killing Cold and his wife. The daughter escapes — had Coyote caught her too, there would be no cold or ice in the world now — and he transforms her: 'Henceforth you shall be known as Cold, but you shall not be able to kill people, excepting once in a while an exhausted hunter.'
summary.zh: 冰族三口以嚴寒冰雪殺人，且酷愛寒冷；斃命其手者眾。郊狼問計於己糞，得其所授密名與計策：三次所遺糞便分別化為鮮 service-莓（禮物）、融冰之陽光、以及易燃之枯松針（ka'ma）。他以親戚之名入其冰屋，被視為同族；他佯稱屋內酷熱，冰屋漸融滴漏。出屋後點燃入門時所留松針，四面縱火，冰屋焚燬，寒夫婦斃命，唯女逃逸——若郊狼亦擒之，世間將再無冰雪——遂化之為寒：『自此汝名為寒，然不得殺人，唯偶爾奪疲憊獵人之命。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Cold-monster-slaying culture-hero episode. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came near to where the Ice people lived. They killed Indians by means of cold weather, cold winds, and ice; they loved the cold, and many people had been killed by them. Coyote determined to kill them, but did not know how; he defecated and asked his excrements what he should do. They told him, 'The three Ice or Cold people are very powerful. When you reach their house, you must address them as relatives. Call the man brother-in-law; when you address them, call the husband xwexwens-takain, the wife xwixwemkellks, and the daughter le'luaken.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 74 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在旅行，來到冰族人居住之處附近。他們藉寒冷的天氣、寒風與冰來殺害印第安人；他們喜愛寒冷，許多人已被他們殺害。郊狼決心殺死他們，卻不知如何下手；他排了便，問他的糞便該怎麼辦。它們告訴他：『那三個冰族或寒冷之人非常強大。當你到達他們的屋子時，你必須以親屬之稱稱呼他們。稱那男人為姊夫；當你稱呼他們時，稱丈夫為 xwexwens-takain，稱妻子為 xwixwemkellks，稱女兒為 le'luaken。』

passages.text: There was much snow on the ground, and the weather was very cold. Coyote defecated three times, and asked each piece of dung what it would be. The first said, 'I shall be fresh service-berries; the Ice people give berries to their daughter.' The second said, 'I shall be heat of the sun, which will soon melt the ice; when it begins to drip, say your house is very hot, then open your shirt and blow on your body.' The last said, 'I shall be ka'ma' — dead yellow pine-needles. When Coyote reached the house of these people he was nearly frozen; he went in and acted as directed. The Ice people said, 'This man must be a relative. He knows our names and all we do. Besides, nobody ever came in here without dying. He must be one of the Ice people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 74 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 地上積雪甚多，天氣非常寒冷。郊狼排了三次便，問每一塊糞便它將變成什麼。第一塊說：『我將變成新鮮的唐棣果；冰族人把漿果給他們的女兒。』第二塊說：『我將變成太陽的熱力，很快就會融化冰；當冰開始滴水時，你就說你的屋子很熱，然後敞開襯衫，向自己的身體吹氣。』最後一塊說：『我將變成 ka'ma'——枯黃的松針。』當郊狼到達這些人的屋子時，他幾乎凍僵了；他走進去，照著指示行事。冰族人說：『這人必定是親戚。他知道我們的名字和我們所做的一切。況且，從來沒有人進到這裡而不死的。他必定是冰族的一員。』

passages.text: Coyote surprised them by complaining of the heat. Before long the ice of the house began to melt and drip; Coyote opened his shirt and blew on his body, saying, 'What a hot house you have!' The Ice people danced and sang and blew to make it colder, but the house continued to melt. 'I cannot stand the heat,' he said, went outside, set fire to the dead yellow pine-needles he had left at the door, and threw the burning needles all over the outside of the house while the heat of the sun melted it from within. Soon it was burned, and Cold and his wife were killed by the heat; their daughter rushed out and escaped. Had Coyote succeeded in catching her too, there would have been no cold or ice in the world now. Coyote transformed her, saying, 'Henceforth you shall be known as Cold, but you shall not be able to kill people, excepting once in a while an exhausted hunter.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 74 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼抱怨天氣太熱，令他們大感意外。不久，屋子的冰開始融化滴落；郊狼敞開襯衫，朝自己的身體吹氣，說道：「你們這屋子可真熱啊！」冰人又跳舞又唱歌又吹氣，想讓屋子更冷，但屋子仍舊繼續融化。「我受不了這股熱氣。」他說，走到屋外，點燃他留在門口的枯黃松針，趁著太陽的熱氣從屋內融化屋子時，把燃燒的松針扔滿屋子外頭。不久屋子便燒了起來，寒冷與他的妻子被熱氣燒死；他們的女兒衝了出去，逃走了。倘若郊狼也把她捉住，如今世上便不會有寒冷與冰了。郊狼將她變形，說道：「從今以後，你將被稱為寒冷，但你不能再殺人，只偶爾能殺死一個筋疲力盡的獵人。」

title.en: Coyote Visits the Blackfeet
title.zh: 郊狼訪黑腳族

region.en: Eastern foot-hills of the Rocky Mountains, Blackfoot country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 落基山東麓，黑腳族故地（象徵定位）

period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (6) Coyote and the Blackfeet' (Okanagon)

summary.en: Coyote, who has no relatives to mourn him, goes east to see the fighting people; ashamed to arrive alone, he asks his excrements — threatening to dry them up — until they turn three droppings into twenty horses, fine clothes and a fine head of hair. The Blackfeet receive the 'great chief' and keep his gift-horses; but when his wife, angry at his scolding, strikes his pinto with a stone, it turns to excrement, he falls into the filth, and the people strike camp, leaving the gift horses at their stakes to become dung where they stand.
summary.zh: 郊狼自知死後無親可泣，遂東行往觀好戰之民。恥於孤身赴會，乃問計於己糞，並以乾死相脅；三枚糞塊遂化為駿馬二十、華服一套、美髯一束。黑腳族人奉為『大酋長』，厚待三日，並留其所贈之馬。第三日，其妻怒其惡言，以石擊其花馬——馬化為糞，郊狼墜入穢中；族人拔營而去，所贈之馬盡留樁旁，原地化糞。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote's wife was the Short-Tailed Mouse. He said to her, 'Wife, I have no relatives to cry and feel sorry if I die. I am going to see the people on the Plains, who do much fighting.' He went to the Blackfoot country, and when he reached the eastern foot-hills of the Rocky Mountains, he saw from the edge of a hill great numbers of people with horses pitching tents. He said to his wife, 'I am ashamed to go among these people alone.' He defecated three times and asked his excrements what to do; they said, 'You are bothering us again.' Coyote spat in the air and said, 'If you do not answer me quickly, you will dry up and die' — and his excrements became afraid and answered at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 75-76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼的妻子是短尾鼠。他對她說：「妻子，我沒有親人會在我死後為我哭喪、為我哀悼。我要去見平原上的人，他們常打仗。」他前往黑腳人的地方，當他抵達落磯山脈東麓時，從一座山丘的邊緣望見大批帶著馬匹的人正在搭帳篷。他對妻子說：「我不好意思獨自一人到那些人當中去。」他拉了三次屎，問他的糞便該怎麼辦；它們說：「你又來煩我們了。」郊狼朝空中吐了口唾沫，說道：「你們若不趕快回答我，就會乾掉死掉。」他的糞便害怕了，立刻回答。

passages.text: The first piece said, 'I shall be a band of twenty horses'; the second, 'I shall be fine clothes'; the last, 'I shall be a fine head of hair.' Coyote put on the fine clothes and fine hair, and mounted his wife on a large pinto horse. The Blackfeet saw him coming and said, 'Here is a great chief coming to visit us.' He gave most of his horses as presents to the chiefs, stopped three days, and was well entertained. On the third day he told his wife, 'Be very careful not to throw any stones at our horses'; but that day his wife became angry at his talking nastily to her, and struck his horse with a stone — immediately it turned into excrement, and he fell down in the midst of it, stuck there up to his waist. Now the people found him out: 'It is Coyote.' They struck camp and left him still cleaning himself of the filth, leaving at their stakes the horses he had given them — and there they became excrement.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第一塊說：「我要變成二十匹馬的一群。」第二塊說：「我要變成華美的衣服。」最後一塊說：「我要變成一頭漂亮的頭髮。」郊狼穿上華美的衣服、戴上漂亮的頭髮，讓妻子騎上一匹大花馬。黑腳人見他前來，說道：「有位大酋長來拜訪我們了。」他把大部分的馬匹當作禮物送給酋長們，停留了三天，受到盛情款待。第三天，他對妻子說：「千萬小心，別朝我們的馬扔石頭。」但那天他妻子因他對她說些下流話而生氣，便拿石頭打他的馬——那馬立刻變成糞便，他跌倒在糞堆中央，陷到腰部。這時人們認出了他：「是郊狼。」他們拔營離去，留下他仍在清理身上的污穢，並把牠們送給他們的馬留在他們的樁柱旁——那些馬也變成了糞便。

title.en: Coyote, Fox, and Panther: The Bride Who Howled
title.zh: 郊狼、狐狸與山君：夜半狼嚎的新娘

region.en: Okanagon Lake villages, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根湖村落，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected at Okanagon Lake; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (7) Coyote, Fox, and Panther' (Okanagon, from Okanagon Lake)

summary.en: Fox's luck fails and the friends starve; urged three days to break the spell, Coyote at last washes, dresses his hair and paints his face like a woman, and goes to Panther's village as a bride sent by her parents. Panther agrees to wait; Coyote carries three packs of food home to his starving brother Fox. Wise Prairie-Chicken tells the people their chief's bride is Coyote, and as the sweat-house gathering is about to reveal it, Coyote runs above, howls like a coyote, and shouts the taunt — 'You will never have a good wife, Panther, you bad warrior, you bad man of the warpath!' — and Panther is too ashamed to speak.
summary.zh: 狐運蹇獵空，二友斷糧；三日催促郊狼破咒無果，郊狼忽洗浴梳妝敷粉如女子，投山君（Panther）部落，自稱父母許嫁而來。山君守禮待之；郊狼則三日三擔食物送回家中餵狐。智鳥草原雞識破，告眾：『酋長新婦非女子，乃郊狼也！』眾人正欲於汗屋中道破，郊狼繞屋嚎叫如狼，揚聲嘲罵：『山君惡徒！戰陣懦夫！汝永不會得好妻！』山君羞愧無言。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox were living together. They were friends, and always had plenty to eat, for Fox was a good hunter. Once upon a time he had bad luck, and could not get any game — perhaps he had been bewitched — and the friends began to starve. Fox said to Coyote, 'You are powerful and gifted. Try to break our spell of bad luck, so that we may procure game.' Coyote did not answer; for three days Fox repeated his request, thinking, 'Coyote will do something foolish.' The fourth night Fox spoke again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 75-76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼與狐狸住在一起。他們是朋友，總有充足的東西吃，因為狐狸是個好獵手。有一次他運氣不好，打不到任何獵物——也許他是中了邪——這對朋友便開始挨餓。狐狸對郊狼說：「你法力高強、天賦異稟。試著破除我們這倒楣的咒詛，好讓我們能獵到獵物。」郊狼沒有回答；一連三天，狐狸反覆提出請求，心想：「郊狼會做出什麼蠢事來。」第四天夜裡，狐狸又開口了。

passages.text: Early the following morning Coyote arose, went to wash himself at a spring near by, returned to the lodge, and drew from under his pillow his comb and paint-pouch. Without speaking, he dressed his hair and painted his face after the manner of women, then dressed himself and left the house. He travelled about aimlessly until he came to the houses of many people, whose chief was Panther, and sat down alongside of him. 'I do not come here for nothing, chief. My father and mother sent me here to marry you.' Panther answered, 'I do not desire to act contrary to the pleasure of your parents. I will not decline their offer, if they have chosen me as their son-in-law.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天一早，郊狼起身，到附近的泉水邊洗漱，回到帳篷，從枕頭底下取出他的梳子和顏料袋。他一言不發，照女人的樣式梳理頭髮、塗抹臉龐，然後穿戴整齊，離開屋子。他漫無目的地四處遊蕩，直到來到許多人的住處，那些人的酋長是黑豹，他便在酋長身旁坐下。「酋長，我來這裡不是無緣無故的。我的父母派我來這裡嫁給你。」黑豹回答：「我不願違背你父母的心意。既然他們選我作女婿，我就不會拒絕他們的提議。」

passages.text: Night came, and Panther asked Coyote to go to bed with him; but Coyote drew away, saying, 'I am a maiden and have never known man. I am afraid and ashamed. I am also thinking of my parents. If you will give me a pack of food to take to my parents three successive days, I will be yours.' Panther agreed, and on the following morning Coyote carried a pack of food to his starving younger brother. Prairie-Chicken, who was a wise person, said to the others, 'Our chief is a great man, but he has made a grave mistake. His wife is not a woman, she is Coyote.' Now Prairie-Chicken and others made a sweat-house and invited Panther to sweat with them, intending to tell him who his wife really was and to purify him. When Panther was inside, Coyote ran about above the sweat-house and howled like a coyote, shouting, 'You will never have a good wife. Panther, you bad warrior, you bad man of the warpath!' Panther was ashamed, and said nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜幕降臨，黑豹邀郊狼與他同床；但郊狼退開，說道：「我是個少女，從未識得男人。我又害怕又羞愧。我也惦記著我的父母。你若肯連續三天給我一份食物帶給我的父母，我便屬於你。」黑豹同意了，第二天早晨，郊狼便帶著一份食物去給他挨餓的弟弟。草原松雞是個有智慧的人，對其他人說：「我們的酋長是個了不起的人，但他犯了大錯。他的妻子不是女人，是郊狼。」於是草原松雞和其他人搭了一座汗屋，邀黑豹與他們一同出汗，打算告訴他他的妻子究竟是誰，並為他淨身。黑豹在裡面時，郊狼在汗屋上方跑來跑去，像郊狼一樣嚎叫，喊道：「你永遠不會有好妻子。黑豹，你這糟糕的戰士，你這戰道上的壞男人！」黑豹羞愧難當，一言不發。

title.en: Lutung Kasarung: The Langur Monkey Who Was a God
title.zh: 魯通·卡薩魯恩：原為神明的葉猴

region.en: Wangun and Pakuan Pajajaran, West Java (Sundanese country)
region.zh: 西爪哇旺恩與帕庫安·巴查查蘭（巽他之地）

period: Sundanese chronicle tradition (Raffles 1817, vol. II ch. X, quoting the Sunda annals)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X (the Lutung Kasarung narrative of the Sunda traditions)

summary.en: Kuwu Mangkubumi sends a pellet-shooter to fell what he takes for a large black monkey on the pandi tree — and the 'monkey' speaks: 'Don't shoot at me; go home and tell your master to come here himself.' Prabu Lutung Kasarung comes down, is offered to two elder daughters who refuse him, and is accepted gladly by the youngest, Niai Purba Sari — at whose wedding he lays aside the black monkey's skin and resumes his former beautiful appearance, establishing the line of Pakuan Pajajaran.
summary.zh: 庫烏·芒庫布米遣獵手射擊潘迪樹上的『大黑猴』——『猴』竟開口：『莫射我；回家告你主人親自前來。』普拉布·魯通·卡薩魯恩下樹相見；兩位長女皆拒嫁之，唯幼女妮艾·普爾巴·沙莉欣然接納——婚禮之上，他褪去黑猴之皮，恢復本來俊美容貌，帕庫安·巴查查蘭王朝由此而立。

sensitivity.note: Sundanese founding legend (Carita Parahyangan tradition as recorded by Raffles); animal-husband motif with divine identity.

canonical_translation: Raffles, History of Java (1817), English; paraphrase

narrative.en:
The Sunda traditions that Raffles recorded in 1817 preserve West Java's founding myth in a form the lowland Javanese chronicles never tell: the god who comes as a monkey.

BEGINNING: THE SPEAKING MONKEY. Kuwu Mangkubumi establishes his youngest daughter, Purba Sari, in the interior near the gadug tree, and sets a pellet-shooter to work the district. One day the shooter sees on the great pandi tree what looks like a large black monkey, and takes aim; the creature speaks: 'Don't shoot at me; you had better go home and tell your master to come here to me himself.' The shooter returns aghast, and his master comes to the tree, where Prabu Lutung Kasarung descends and talks with him — a being of such extraordinary accomplishment that the Kuwu takes him home delighted.

MIDDLE: THE CHOICE OF DAUGHTERS. Wishing to attach so wondrous a creature to his house, the Kuwu offers him first to the eldest daughter, who refuses; then to a younger, who refuses likewise. Only the youngest of all, Niai Purba Sari, accepts him with great pleasure — the marriage goes to the daughter humble enough to take the suitor as he appears.

END: THE SKIN LAID ASIDE. When Niai Purba Sari becomes his wife, he lays aside the black monkey's skin and resumes his former, beautiful appearance; he receives the name of Niang Galarang, establishes himself at Pakuan Pajajaran — where the inscribed stone stands — and governs there. His wife becomes pregnant; he leaves the government to his ministers and withdraws to Bukit Padang as a Pattala; and their son, Silawangi, will grow into the great king of the Sundanese chronicles.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) grounds Pakuan Pajajaran, the Sundanese royal capital, in a divine-visitor marriage; (2) makes the acceptance of the humble appearance the test of rightful bride (the youngest-daughter motif); (3) ties kingship to the withdrawal of the god-founder into ascetic retreat; and (4) supplies the Sundanese counterpart to Java's Janggala-Kediri genealogies. The episode's social geometry repays attention: the Kuwu's household tests the suitor's appearance twice and both elder daughters decline, so that the divine visitor is accepted only by the youngest — the standard folktale marker of the daughter undervalued by her family, whose acceptance is rewarded with the god's true form and, through her son Silawangi, with the kingship of Pajajaran itself. The narrative also fixes two toponyms of the Sundanese landscape, the kampung Wangun and the kampung Tagur founded by the couple, and ends with the founder's characteristic withdrawal: as soon as the succession is secure, Niang Galarang leaves the seat of government to his ministers and removes to Bukit Padang as a Pattala, the ascetic retreat that later Sundanese tradition reads as the model of royal completion. In the full pantun tellings the monkey shape is the punishment of a heavenly exile, and the marriage that restores his form is the last condition of his return — the West Javanese version of the exiled-god theme that the Arjunawiwaha states in courtly verse.
narrative.zh: 拉弗爾斯1817年所錄巽他編年傳說保存了西爪哇開基神話：神以猴身而來。庫烏·芒庫布米置幼女普爾巴·沙莉於內地加都古樹旁；獵手見潘迪樹上『黑猴』而瞄準，猴竟人言。魯通·卡薩魯恩下樹，才華驚人，庫烏攜歸。庫烏欲以女妻之：長女拒、次女拒，唯幼女妮艾·普爾巴·沙莉欣然接受。婚後神褪猴皮復其真容，得名尼揚·加拉朗，建都帕庫安·巴查查蘭（即今碑石之地）；妻有孕後，他將國政委於大臣，退隱布基特·巴當為隱者；其子西拉萬吉將成巽他編年史之偉王。功能：以神婚立帕庫安王都、以『接納平凡外表』為擇婿考驗（幼女母題）、以神主退隱繫王權於苦修、並成爪哇章格拉-諫義里譜系之巽他對應。

functions: Grounds Pakuan Pajajaran, capital of the Sundanese kingdom, in a divine-visitor marriage
Youngest-daughter test: the rightful bride accepts the suitor as a monkey
The god-founder's withdrawal into ascetic retreat as the pattern of Sundanese kingship
Sundanese counterpart to the Javanese dynastic genealogies

variants.name: Later Sundanese pantun epic (Lutung Kasarung)
variants.summary: The expanded telling makes Lutung Kasarung the exiled son of Guru Batara Sunan Ambu, sent to earth and monkey-shaped until his mission of restoring justice is done.

variants.name: Bible-animal-husband parallels
variants.summary: Beast-suitor whose monstrous skin hides divinity; compare the Javanese Keong Emas snail-bride in reverse.

primary_sources.citation: Quoted in Raffles, The History of Java, London 1817, vol. II ch. X, from the Sunda traditions of Pakuan Pajajaran.

secondary_sources.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java
secondary_sources.citation: Raffles 1817, London: Black, Parbury and Allen — vol. II ch. X, the Sunda tradition block.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Raffles, History of Java, vol. II (1817)

sensitivity_guidance: Founding legend of the Sundanese royal tradition; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: The pellet-shooter came to the large pandi tree, and observing on it what he supposed to be a large black monkey, wished to shoot it; whereupon Prabu Lutung Kasarong, whom he mistook for the monkey, thus addressed him: 'Don't shoot at me; you had better go home and tell your master to come here to me himself.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那射彈丸的人來到大榕樹前，見樹上有一隻他以為是黑色大猴子的東西，便想射牠；於是，被他誤認為猴子的普拉布·魯通·卡薩隆這樣對他說：「別射我；你最好回家去，叫你的主人親自到這裡來見我。」

passages.text: The Kuwu took him home highly delighted; in course of time he wished to present him to his eldest daughter, and on her refusing to accept of him he offered him to a younger one, but neither would receive Prabu Lutung Kasarong. He then gave him to the youngest of all, named Niai Purba Sari, who accepted of him with great pleasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫武興高采烈地把他帶回家；過了些時日，他想把他獻給自己的長女，長女拒絕接受他，他便把他獻給另一個較年幼的女兒，但兩人都不要普拉布·魯通·卡薩隆。於是他把他交給最年幼的女兒，名叫尼艾·普爾巴·薩里，她十分樂意地接受了他。

passages.text: When Niai Purba Sari became his wife, he laid aside the black monkey's skin with which he was clothed, and immediately resumed his former and usual beautiful appearance. He afterwards received the name of Niang Galarang, and established himself at Pakuan Pajajaran, where the Balutulis (inscribed stone) now is, and which was the seat of government of the Maha Raja.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當尼艾·普爾巴·薩里成為他的妻子後，他脫下身上所披的黑猴皮，立刻恢復了他從前慣有的俊美外貌。他後來得到尼昂·加拉朗之名，並在今日巴魯圖利斯（刻石）所在之處、即摩訶羅闍的治所帕庫安·帕查查蘭定居下來。

title.en: Prabu Silawangi and the Hall of Eight Hundred Pillars
title.zh: 西拉萬吉王與八百柱大殿

region.en: Pakuan Pajajaran, West Java
region.zh: 西爪哇帕庫安·巴查查蘭

period: Sundanese chronicle tradition (Raffles 1817, vol. II ch. X)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X (Silawangi narrative)

summary.en: Silawangi, the beautiful son born to Niai Purba Sari, removes to Sumedang Larang, marries many wives, and returns to Pakuan Pajajaran by way of the south coast, embarking at Nusa Kambangan. Established as Raja amid great rejoicings, all the princes from the river Chi Pamali to Java Head submit to him; he builds the pentebanj audience-hall 'Sangaka Domas' of eight hundred pillars, and the interior hall 'Rarasmi Kanchana' of golden flowers — and the tradition gives him one hundred and fifty wives and one hundred and fifty sons-in-law made great officers.
summary.zh: 妮艾·普爾巴·沙莉所生之美貌王子西拉萬吉，先移居蘇梅當·拉朗，廣娶眾妻；後經南海岸、自努薩·坎班甘登舟還都帕庫安·巴查查蘭。即位慶典連宵，西自芝帕馬利河至爪哇角諸王皆服；乃建八百柱大殿『桑嘎卡·多馬斯』、內殿『金花殿』——傳說並言其有一百五十妻、一百五十婿皆為高官。

sensitivity.note: Sundanese royal charter legend; the 800-pillar hall is Pajajaran's remembered splendour.

passages.text: When the time was come, Niai Purba Sari brought forth a son of the most exquisitely beautiful features, to whom she gave the name Silawang'i. When Silawangi grew up, he removed from Pakuan Pajajaran to Sumedang Larang, where he was soon afterwards married, first to one raja's daughter and then to the daughter of the Peng'gawa of that place, so that he had many wives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 時候到了，尼艾·普爾巴·薩里生下一名容貌極其俊美的兒子，為他取名西拉旺吉。西拉旺吉長大後，從帕庫安·帕查查蘭遷往蘇美當·拉朗，不久便在那裡成婚，先娶一位羅闍的女兒，後又娶當地彭加瓦的女兒，因此他有許多妻子。

passages.text: On his arrival at Pakuan Pajajaran, Prabu Silawangi established himself as Raja; all the princes from the river Chi Pamali beyond Java Head submitted to him. He then built without the kraton a hall of audience, called Sangaka Domas, or the hall of eight hundred pillars; and in the interior of the kraton another, called Rarasmi Kanchana, or that of golden flowers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 普拉布·西拉旺吉抵達帕庫安·帕查查蘭後，自立為羅闍；從爪哇角以外奇·帕馬利河一帶的所有諸侯都歸順於他。他隨後在克拉通之外建了一座覲見廳，名為桑加卡·多馬斯，即八百柱之廳；又在克拉通內部建了另一座，名為拉拉拉斯米·坎查納，即金花之廳。

passages.text: The tradition goes on to relate that Prabu Silawangi had one hundred and fifty wives, and that his sons-in-law, of whom there were also one hundred and fifty, were made great public officers — the Sundanese memory of Pajajaran's widest power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說接著敘述，普拉布·西拉旺吉有一百五十個妻子，而他的一百五十個女婿都被任命為顯要的公職——這是巽他人記憶中帕查查蘭國勢最盛的時代。

title.en: Sangkuriang and Dayang Sumbi: The Boat That Became a Mountain
title.zh: 桑古里揚與達揚·松比：化為山巒的小舟

region.en: Tangkuban Perahu, near Bandung, West Java
region.zh: 西爪哇萬隆附近覆舟山（唐庫邦·珀拉胡）

period: Sundanese oral legend; recorded in 19th-20th century collections

source.work: The legend of Sangkuriang and Dayang Sumbi (Sundanese oral tradition, Tangkuban Perahu etiology)

summary.en: The princess Dayang Sumbi, exiled for breaking a vow, is courted by the dog Tumang who is really a god; her son Sangkuriang, sent hunting, kills the dog without knowing it is his father, and serves its liver to his mother, who strikes his head and drives him into the world. Years later the marked wanderer returns and woos his own mother; she recognizes the wound, sets him the impossible task of damming the Citarum and building a great boat in one night, and cheats the finishing dawn — and the kicked, half-finished boat lies overturned on the plain as the mountain Tangkuban Perahu.
summary.zh: 因違誓而遭放逐的公主達揚·松比，被化身為犬的神明托芒求愛；其子桑古里揚奉命出獵，不知那犬正是生父而殺之，以其肝烹於母親——母親擊其首，將其逐入世界。多年後，帶傷的流浪者歸來向親母求婚；母親認出傷痕，令其一夜之間築壩截芝塔龍江並造巨舟，又設計騙過完工的黎明——被踢翻的半成之舟倒扣於平原之上，是為覆舟山。

sensitivity.note: Oedipal-type West Javanese foundation legend; treated as literature, cited carefully.

canonical_translation: Based on the Sundanese oral legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
Sangkuriang is West Java's great etiological legend — the mountain Tangkuban Perahu ('the overturned boat') above Bandung is the story's fossil.

BEGINNING: THE VOW AND THE DOG-HUSBAND. The beautiful Dayang Sumbi has vowed to marry whoever returns her discarded shuttle; the dog Tumang fetches it, and she must keep the vow — in the fuller tellings Tumang is a god in dog-form. She bears a son, Sangkuriang, and the dog remains as the household's hunter.

MIDDLE: THE LIVER DISH. Sent hunting, the boy returns empty-handed; on his mother's chiding, he shoots the dog Tumang, not knowing it is his father, and cooks its liver for her meal. When the truth is told, Dayang Sumbi strikes him on the head with the rice-ladle, leaving the mark by which he will one day be known, and the boy wanders off into the world.

END: THE BOAT AND THE FALSE DAWN. Years later a powerful young stranger courts the still-beautiful Dayang Sumbi; she recognizes the scar and understands that this is her son. To delay the incest she sets a task fitted to his giant's strength: in a single night he must dam the Citarum river and finish a great boat to carry the lake away. Supernatural helpers raise the dam and shape the boat; fearing his success as dawn comes, she spreads a red cloth (in some tellings lights the eastern sky) so that the cocks crow early — the spirits flee, the work stops short, and Sangkuriang, cheated, kicks the boat over. It lies overturned on the plain as the mountain; the dammed valley remains as the Bandung basin, and the mother retreats to the hill-top to wait for the day the boat rises again.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) etiologizes Tangkuban Perahu and the Bandung plain; (2) polices the incest boundary through the riddle of the unrecognizable son (the wound-mark motif); (3) dramatizes the false-dawn trick as female resistance; and (4) grounds Sundanese identity in a landscape-story told at every school and tourist site in West Java. The landscape completes the argument. Tangkuban Perahu's distinctive profile — a tilted ridge that does look like an overturned hull — is the story's standing exhibit, and the Bandung basin below is the lake the dam would have made; local tellings add that Dayang Sumbi waits on the summit for the day the boat is righted and the flood returns. The false-dawn device links the legend across the island to the Roro Jonggrang cycle, in which the same trick of pounded rice and kindled fires defeats a supernatural suitor's deadline; in both, the woman's wit beats the ogre's or the giant's labour, and the punishment lands on the deceiver in a form that fixes her in the landscape. The Sangkuriang telling is the darker of the two because the suitor is also the son: the wound-mark that lets the mother recognize him is the same mark her ladle made, so that the legend binds its incest horror to the memory of a punishment already given — the mother has struck the boy once, and the blow returns wearing courtship's clothes.
narrative.zh: 桑古里揚乃西爪哇第一大釋源傳說——萬隆上方之覆舟山即其化石。開篇：達揚·松比誓嫁拾回梭子者；神化犬形之托芒拾之，遂成婚生子桑古里揚。中段：少年出獵空手而歸，受母嗔責，射殺家犬托芒——不知即其父——以其肝烹食；真相既明，母以飯杓擊其首（留下他日相認之疤），逐之於世。結尾：多年後偉岸青年向仍美豔之母求婚；母認疤而知為己子，遂設巨力方能完成之難題：一夜之內築壩截芝塔龍江、造巨舟以載湖而走。妖眾助其築壩造舟；黎明將成之際，母展紅布（或燃東天）令雞早鳴——妖眾驚散、工程中止，桑古里揚受欺而踢翻其舟；舟覆於平原是為覆舟山，築壩之谷留為萬隆盆地，母親退居山頂，等待小舟再起之日。功能：釋覆舟山與萬隆平原之由來、以『不可辨之子』維護亂倫禁忌、以假晨之詐寫女性抵抗、並以山水故事奠定西爪哇認同。

functions: Etiology of Tangkuban Perahu ('the overturned boat') and the Bandung basin
Policing the incest boundary through the unrecognizable-son wound-mark motif
False-dawn trick as female resistance within the suitor's test
Landscape-story anchoring West Javanese identity

variants.name: Sundanese pantun telling (Bujang Nitik and kin)
variants.text_tradition: Sundanese oral epic and folk drama
variants.summary: Expanded tellings name the god-husband as Sunan Ambu's son and detail the boat-building with the punk of spirits.

variants.name: Comparative false-dawn escape motifs
variants.text_tradition: Roro Jonggrang legend; European cock-crow tales
variants.summary: The deceived dawn as resistance device; compare the Central Javanese temple-builder legend.

primary_sources.work: Sangkuriang and Dayang Sumbi (Sundanese oral legend)
primary_sources.citation: Oral legend of West Java; recorded in modern Sundanese and Indonesian collections; paraphrased.

secondary_sources.work: Eliza R. Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East
secondary_sources.citation: Scidmore 1897, New York — West Javanese regional setting and Garut/Bandung highland context.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Scidmore, Java, the Garden of the East (1897) — West Javanese regional context

sensitivity_guidance: Living legend of West Java; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: Dayang Sumbi, exiled for breaking her vow, is courted by the dog Tumang, who is a god in dog-form; her son Sangkuriang grows up in the household of his unknowing father. Sent hunting, the boy shoots the dog and serves its liver to his mother; when the truth is told she strikes him on the head with the rice-ladle — the mark by which he will later be known — and he wanders off into the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend of Sangkuriang; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達揚·松比因違背誓言而被放逐，化為犬形的神祇圖芒前來向她求愛；她的兒子桑庫里昂在他不知情的父親家中長大。男孩被派去狩獵，射殺了那隻狗，並將牠的肝端給母親；真相揭曉後，她以飯勺擊打他的頭——那正是日後辨認他的印記——他於是流浪遠走，踏入世間。

passages.text: Years later the marked wanderer courts his own mother; she sets the giant's task of damming the Citarum and finishing a great boat in one night, then cheats the finishing dawn with a spread cloth so that the cocks crow early. The spirits flee, the boat lies half-finished, and Sangkuriang's kick turns it over on the plain — the mountain Tangkuban Perahu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 多年後，這位帶著印記的流浪者向自己的母親求愛；她給他出了一項巨人的任務：在一夜之間築壩攔截芝塔倫河，並造好一艘大船，隨後又鋪開布匹，使公雞提早啼叫，以此騙過完工的黎明。眾精靈逃散，船隻半成而止，桑庫里昂一腳將它踢翻在平原上——那便是覆舟山（坦庫班·佩拉胡）。

title.en: Situ Bagendit: The Lake That Swallowed the Miser's Village
title.zh: 巴根迪湖：吞沒吝嗇婦之村

region.en: Situ Bagendit, Garut, West Java
region.zh: 西爪哇加魯特巴根迪湖

period: Sundanese oral legend

source.work: The legend of Situ Bagendit (Sundanese oral tradition)

summary.en: The rich widow of the village refuses every beggar; one day an old woman asks only for water and is mocked, and warns that the village's wealth will not save it. That night the springs burst: the rice-fields, the barns, the widow seated on her treasure, and the whole village sink under a new lake — Situ Bagendit, the 'lake of the widow,' where fishers say the drowned rice-bins still lie.
summary.zh: 村中富婦拒絕一切乞者；一日老嫗只討一瓢水而遭譏，乃警告：財富救不了此村。當夜泉眼迸裂：稻田、糧倉、坐在財寶上的寡婦乃至全村，盡沉於新湖之下——是為巴根迪湖（『寡婦之湖』），漁人言湖底猶有沉沒的糧倉。

sensitivity.note: Sinking-village flood legend; hospitality-test type in the Sundanese highlands.

passages.text: The widow of the village turns away every beggar; to the old woman who asks only for water she answers with mockery, and receives a warning that her wealth will not save the place. That night the springs burst open: the rice-fields, the granaries, the widow on her treasure and the whole village sink beneath a new lake — Situ Bagendit, the widow's lake — where the drowned barns, fishers say, are still to be found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend of Situ Bagendit; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 村中的寡婦對每個乞丐都予以驅趕；面對只求一口水的老婦，她以嘲弄相答，於是得到警告：她的財富救不了這個地方。當夜泉眼迸裂：稻田、糧倉、坐在財寶上的寡婦以及整個村莊，都沉入一座新湖之下——巴根迪特湖，即寡婦之湖——漁人說，那些淹沒的穀倉至今仍可尋見。

title.en: Prabu Siliwangi: The Vanished King of Pajajaran
title.zh: 普拉布·西利萬吉：消失的巴查查蘭之王

region.en: Pakuan Pajajaran and the West Javanese mountains
region.zh: 帕庫安·巴查查蘭與西爪哇群山

period: Sundanese dynastic legend (Pajajaran line); medieval and early modern tradition

source.work: The legend of Prabu Siliwangi (Sundanese dynastic tradition, Pakuan Pajajaran line)

summary.en: In Sundanese memory the last great king of Pakuan Pajajaran, Prabu Siliwangi, becomes more legend than history: the archetype of the just ruler of the Parahyangan, credited in tradition with retreating from the fallen capital into the mountains rather than submit, and henceforth present in the highlands as a hidden presence — the name invoked by every later West Javanese court and shrine that claimed his authority.
summary.zh: 在巽他人記憶中，帕庫安·巴查查蘭末代偉王普拉布·西利萬吉漸成傳說：巴查查蘭（Parahyangan，『眾神之地』）公正之王的原型；相傳都城傾覆之際，他不肯臣服而隱入群山，此後便以隱形之力存於高地——日後西爪哇每一宮廷與聖所凡欲承其權威者，皆呼其名。

sensitivity.note: Dynastic memory-legend; kept at the level of attested tradition, avoiding invented specifics.

passages.text: In Sundanese tradition the last great king of Pakuan Pajajaran, Prabu Siliwangi, is remembered as the archetype of the just ruler of the Parahyangan — the 'land of the gods' — his name the standard by which later West Javanese courts claimed authority.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sundanese dynastic tradition as preserved in the chronicle material recorded by Raffles (1817) and later collections; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在巽他傳統中，巴庫安·巴查查蘭最後一位偉大的國王普拉布·西利旺吉，被銘記為帕拉希揚——「眾神之地」——公正統治者的典範，他的名字成為後世西爪哇各宮廷宣稱權威的標準。

passages.text: Tradition credits him with refusing submission when the kingdom fell, withdrawing from the capital into the mountains, and remaining thereafter a hidden presence in the highlands — the vanished king who legitimizes every shrine and court that invokes his name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sundanese dynastic tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳統認為，當王國覆滅時，他拒絕臣服，從都城退入群山，此後便一直是高地中的隱秘存在——那位消失的國王，凡以他之名者，無論神龕或宮廷，皆因他而獲得正統。

title.en: The Shuttle and the Vow: Dayang Sumbi's First Promise
title.zh: 梭子與誓言：達揚·松比的初諾

region.en: West Javanese highlands (Sundanese country)
region.zh: 西爪哇高地（巽他之地）

period: Sundanese oral legend (prelude of the Sangkuriang cycle)

source.work: The shuttle-vow prelude of the Sangkuriang cycle (Sundanese oral tradition)

summary.en: Weaving at her loom, the princess Dayang Sumbi drops her shuttle through the floor-hole and vows that whoever brings it back — man, animal, or god in any shape — shall be her husband. A dog brings it up the stair; the vow is kept, the dog-god Tumang becomes her husband, and the union that scandalizes her father sends her into exile — where she will bear the boy whose own vow, years later, will shake the mountains.
summary.zh: 公主達揚·松比織機之上梭子墜落，遂發誓：無論何人（人或獸、或神之任何形體）拾還此梭，即嫁之為夫。拾梭而來者是一隻狗；誓言必守，犬神托芒遂為其夫；此樁醜事觸怒其父，她被逐出家門——在那裏她將誕下那個多年後以誓言撼動群山的男孩。

sensitivity.note: Vow-kept-literally motif; prelude of the Sangkuriang cycle.

passages.text: Weaving at her loom, Dayang Sumbi drops the shuttle and vows that whoever returns it — man, animal, or god in any shape — shall be her husband; a dog brings it up the stair, and the vow is kept to the letter. The dog-god Tumang becomes her husband, the union scandalizes her father's house, and she is exiled — bearing in time the son Sangkuriang, whose own promise, years later, will shake the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend (shuttle-vow prelude); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Sundanese legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達揚·松比在織機前織布時，梭子掉落，她立誓：無論是誰將它送回——男人、動物，或以任何形貌出現的神祇——都將成為她的丈夫；一隻狗將梭子銜上階梯，誓言便按字面履行了。犬神圖芒成為她的丈夫，這樁結合令她父親的家門蒙羞，她因此被放逐——日後生下了兒子桑庫里昂，而多年之後，他自己的承諾將震動群山。

title.en: A Tale About Two Girls: Eagle and Whale Husbands
title.zh: 兩女故事：鷹夫與鯨夫

region.en: Coast and bird cliff, Greenland-Labrador copies
region.zh: 海岸與鳥崖（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

period: Inuit oral tradition; constructed from two manuscripts (Labrador and Greenland, before 1828), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 8 'A Tale about Two Girls', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Playing with eagle-bones and whale-bones, two girls boast — 'I will have an eagle for my husband' and 'I will have a whale for mine' — and are instantly taken, one to a cliff top, one to the sealed bottom of the sea. The eagle's bride knots a sinew string down to sea level and is rescued by a passing kayaker, the eagle shot when tricked into spreading his wings; the whale's bride, kept picking whale-lice and roped to a stone, is fetched by brothers who built a gull-beating umiak, throwing jackets into the pursuer's jaws until the shore is reached and the whale turns to a piece of whalebone.
summary.zh: 兩個小女孩在灘上玩鷹骨與鯨骨，各自誇口：『我要嫁鷹』『我要嫁鯨』——話音未落，一個被鷹掠上崖頂，一個被鯨拖入封閉的海底。鷹妻編鳥筋繩垂至海面，由過路皮艇客救出；鷹受騙展翅而被射殺。鯨妻被繩繫石上、日日揀鯨蝨；其兄以快過海鷗的大舟來救，她解繩繫石而逃，將外衣內衣逐一擲入鯨口拖延，抵岸之際鯨化為一片鯨骨。

sensitivity.note: Animal-husband type; variant of the same tale as Rasmussen's 'The Eagle and the Whale' (cross-ref inuit-eagle-and-whale) and Rink tale 12.

passages.text: Two little girls were playing with small bones on the beach, the one with eagle-bones, the other with whale-bones. Suddenly an eagle came soaring above them, and one of the girls said, 'I will have an eagle for my husband'; the other replied, 'Thou mayst rejoice that thou hast already got a husband; I will have a whale for mine.' Instantly a whale was seen to spout out at sea. The eagle took one girl up and flew away with her, and the whale took the other down to the bottom of the sea, having first made her eyes and ears impenetrable so that the water could not enter. The eagle carried his bride to the top of a steep cliff and brought her different sorts of little birds for food; but she gathered all the sinews of the birds' wings, knotted them together to make a string, and one day, when the eagle was away, found that it reached down to the level of the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 8 'A Tale about Two Girls'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩個小女孩在海灘上玩著小骨頭，一個拿著鷹骨，另一個拿著鯨骨。忽然一隻鷹在她們上方盤旋而下，其中一個女孩說：「我要以鷹為夫。」另一個回答：「你已有了丈夫，大可歡喜；我要以鯨為夫。」頃刻間，只見一頭鯨在海面噴出水柱。鷹把一個女孩抓起，帶著她飛走了；鯨則把另一個女孩帶到海底，先使她的眼睛和耳朵堅不可入，讓海水無法滲進。鷹把新娘帶到一座陡峭懸崖的頂上，給她銜來各種小鳥作食物；但她把鳥翅上的筋腱全都收集起來，一一打結連成一條繩索，有一天趁鷹外出時，發現這繩索垂到了與海面相齊之處。

passages.text: Another day she saw a kayaker rowing along the shore and called out to him to send a boat to rescue her; soon afterwards the boat appeared, and she went sliding down by her string of sinews and got back to her parents. The eagle, missing his mate, soared above the houses beating his wings, and one of the inhabitants cried out to him, 'If thou wantest to show thou hast been married into our family, spread out thy wings' — and when the eagle did so they shot him through the body. The other girl, secured to the bottom of the sea by a rope, had nothing to do but sit picking the lice from off the whale's body. Her two brothers set about building a boat of immense swiftness to deliver their sister; when finished, it could not match a bird in speed and was broken to pieces, another begun — that one matched a flying bird but was discarded, and a third outdid even the gull.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 8 'A Tale about Two Girls'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一天，她看見一個划著獨木舟的人沿岸而行，便向他呼喊，請他派一艘船來救她；不久之後船出現了，她便順著那條筋腱繩索滑下，回到了父母身邊。鷹失去了伴侶，在屋舍上方鼓著翅膀盤旋，其中一個居民對牠喊道：「你若想表明你已與我們家結親，就把翅膀張開。」鷹照做了，他們便射穿了牠的身子。另一個女孩被一條繩索繫在海底，無事可做，只能坐著從鯨身上捉蝨子。她的兩個兄弟著手建造一艘極其迅捷的船去救妹妹；船造好後，卻連一隻鳥的速度都比不上，被拆成了碎片；又開始造第二艘——那一艘能與飛鳥並駕齊驅，卻也被棄置不用；第三艘甚至勝過了海鷗。

passages.text: They started from home to fetch back their sister. Becoming aware of their approach, she loosened the cord that held her, twisted it round the stone, and left with the boat. When the whale on his return drew the cord and discovered she was gone, he hurried after her; coming quite close to the boat, she threw her outer jacket into the water. Having snapped at it he let it go and pursued again; quite close up with them, she flung her inner jacket, which again detained the whale — but he reached them a third time. Then she threw her long jacket, and before he could overtake them they had landed; when the whale reached the shore he was transformed into a piece of whalebone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 8 'A Tale about Two Girls'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們從家中出發，去接回妹妹。她察覺他們逼近，便鬆開繫住自己的繩索，把它纏繞在石頭上，隨船離去。鯨回來時拉動繩索，發現她已不在，便急忙追趕；追到離船極近時，她把外層的短外套扔進水裡。鯨一口咬住又放開，再次追來；追到極近時，她又扔出內層的衣服，再次拖住了鯨——但牠第三次追了上來。於是她扔出那件長外套，還沒等牠追上，他們已經登了岸；鯨抵達岸邊時，化作了一塊鯨鬚。

title.en: The Brothers Visit Their Cannibal Sister
title.zh: 兄弟探訪食人姐姐

region.en: South Greenland (winter station beyond the high mountains)
region.zh: 南格陵蘭（高山以南的越冬地）

period: Inuit oral tradition; very popular in Greenland, literal translation from a single South Greenland manuscript, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Told late that they have a sister beyond the southern mountains — white-haired on one side and living among cannibals — two brothers travel by night to her house of three windows. A tub of berries mixed with blubber holds a shrunk human hand clutching the berries; she has turned cannibal because, she says, 'this nasty fellow has made me one.' The brother-in-law warns of sledge-lashings cut by his children, gives the shout that turns the settlement out black with people, then kills the lone pursuing sledge-driver and returns home freighted with human limbs — while the brothers escape and never see their sister again.
summary.zh: 兩兄弟成人後才得知：高山以南有位單側白髮的姐姐，嫁入食人族。他們趁夜抵達其三窗之屋；漿果拌脂油的大木桶底，竟見一隻枯縮斷腕抓握著莓果——姐姐承認自己已食人：『是這可憎的傢伙把我變成這樣。』姐夫早命孩子割斷鄰人雪橇繩索，送客出門一聲大喊，全村黑壓壓湧出——雪橇盡數散架，唯獨一輛追來，被他殺死車主、滿載人肢而歸。兄弟們逃出生天，從此再未見過姐姐。

sensitivity.note: Rink translated a single South Greenland manuscript nearly literally. Cannibalism recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: A man had three children, the eldest a daughter, who married a man from a far-away place in the south while her brothers were still little; in their boyhood they did not know they had a sister, their father purposely never mentioning it, and even grown and catching seals they had never heard of her until one day the mother said, 'I think ye don't even know that ye have got a sister!' Asked where she lived, she answered: 'Look there; do you see the high mountains yonder to the south of us? Beyond these is the winter station of your sister, whose hair, strange to say, is quite white on one side. However, ye must not think of going there, for the people she is living among are all cannibals.' The eldest brother gave up the idea; the younger longed as much as ever, and despite the parents' warning — if ye reach the country in the day-time, wait the fall of night and go near only when they are all asleep, lest ye be murdered — the brothers set out, and the parents gave them up for lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個男人有三個孩子，最大的是個女兒，她在兩個弟弟還小的時候，嫁給了一個來自南方遠方之地的男人；兄弟倆年幼時並不知道自己有個姊姊，父親刻意從不提起，甚至長大後外出捕海豹，也從未聽聞過她，直到有一天母親說：「我看你們甚至不知道自己有個姊姊呢！」問她住在哪裡，她答道：「看那邊；你們看見我們南邊那些高山了嗎？高山之外便是你們姊姊過冬的居所，說來奇怪，她的頭髮有一邊是全白的。不過，你們千萬別想去找她，因為與她同住的人全是食人者。」大哥打消了念頭；弟弟卻一如既往地渴望前去，不顧父母的警告——「你們若在白天到達那地方，要等到夜幕降臨，等他們全都睡熟了才靠近，免得被殺害」——兄弟倆還是出發了，父母只得當他們已經喪命。

passages.text: Reaching the high mountains in the south they examined the land below for houses — 'When people are found to be living at the foot of the mountains, the ravens will be sure to be soaring in the air above' — until above a craggy hill a great number of ravens were flying. They secured their sledges and waited the fall of night; quite dark, they drew near many houses, the first with three windows, mounted the roof cautiously, and looked down the vent-hole: a nasty-looking man sat in front of the lamp beside his wife, who seemed to be picking lice off him and appeared quite white on one side of her head. 'Were we not told that our sister was to be white-haired on one side of her head? Do come and see!' The younger bade him spit down through the hole before the lamp; the moment he did, the woman pushed the man: 'Somebody must have come from afar to see us; do make haste and get up!' He rose, took his bow ready bent, and went outside — to be accosted before he had set eyes on them: 'We have come here to visit our sister, and have been told that she is quite white on one side of her head.' Whispering 'Your sister is within; please go in,' he at once played the part of a brother-in-law and ordered a meal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們抵達南方的高山，察看下方的陸地有無屋舍——「凡是有人住在山腳下，渡鴉必定在空中盤旋」——直到看見一座崎嶇的山丘上方有大批渡鴉飛翔。他們繫好雪橇，等待夜幕降臨；天色全黑後，他們靠近了許多屋舍，第一座有三扇窗，他們小心翼翼地爬上屋頂，從通風口往下看：一個面目可憎的男人坐在燈前，身旁是他的妻子，她似乎正在替他捉蝨子，頭的一邊看上去全白。「不是有人告訴我們，我們的姊姊頭的一邊是白髮嗎？快來看哪！」弟弟叫哥哥先從洞口朝燈前吐口水；他剛一吐，那女人便推了推男人：「一定有人從遠方來看我們了；快點起來！」他起身，拿起已上好弦的弓，走到外面——還沒等他看清他們，就聽人說道：「我們是來探望姊姊的，聽說她頭的一邊全白。」他低聲說：「你們的姊姊在裡面；請進。」隨即擺出姊夫的身分，吩咐備飯。

passages.text: The guests understood the only housemates of their sister were her children, the boot-drying beams hung with boots and skin-stockings of all sizes. A large tub of berries mingled with blubber was set before them, and the brothers, almost beginning to feel at ease, caught sight in the bottom of the tub of a human hand cut off at the wrist, clutching the berries, very much shrunk. 'We don't eat such food as this' — but she only drew the tub closer and began to eat along with the children; taking hold of the hand and biting the thumb, the children all cried, 'Mother, do let us have some too!' The eldest brother went close beside her: 'Hast thou also turned cannibal?' — and giving her husband a pull, she answered, 'This nasty fellow has made me one.' The brother-in-law ordered something separate cooked on the lamp, cautioning them not to let it burn too high lest the neighbours detect and make a row about it, and told how, when their people caught a whale last winter, a man happened to have a fall and was cut up with it. Before the meal he whispered to his children, 'Go out and cut asunder all the lashings of our neighbours' sledges, but beware of making a noise' — all done, though one was forgotten.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 客人們明白，與姊姊同住的只有她的孩子，烘靴子的橫樑上掛滿了各種尺寸的靴子和毛皮襪。他們面前擺上一大盆拌了鯨脂的漿果，兄弟倆幾乎開始感到自在，卻在盆底瞥見一隻從手腕處砍下的人手，緊緊抓著漿果，已十分乾癟。「我們不吃這樣的食物」——但她只是把盆拉得更近，和孩子們一同吃了起來；她抓起那隻手咬下拇指，孩子們都嚷道：「母親，也讓我們吃一點！」大哥湊到她身旁：「你也變成食人者了嗎？」——她拉了拉丈夫，答道：「是這個討厭的傢伙把我變成這樣的。」姊夫吩咐在燈上另煮些東西，告誡他們別讓火燒得太旺，免得鄰居察覺而鬧起來，又說起去年冬天他們的人捕到一頭鯨時，恰好有一個人摔了一跤，便和那鯨一同被切分了。開飯前，他低聲對孩子們說：「出去把鄰居雪橇上所有的綁繩都割斷，但要小心別弄出聲響」——全都辦妥了，只漏掉了一處。

passages.text: The host said that as soon as they finished he would accompany them a little way off, and that when they had left the mainland he would give a shout: 'Ye'll just see what will happen.' Seeing them off in their sledges, he cried out aloud as they turned onto the ice, 'The visitors are setting off — the visitors are going to leave!' — and when the brothers looked around, the place was black with people crowding the doorways and windows, some having just caught hold of their clothes, others quite naked, hastening off to their sledges; but when they were about to start, the sledges all broke down. The travellers took fright and urged on their dogs; one sledge, however, was following and apparently gaining, and the brother-in-law, hastening to pursue it, killed the driver besides a number of the other people, and afterwards filled his sledge with human limbs — thus freighted returning to his house. The brothers reached home late at night and reported how their sister had turned a cannibal and how they had barely escaped death through the aid of their brother-in-law; but they never saw their sister again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 9 'The Brothers visit their Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 主人說，他們一吃完，他就會陪他們走一小段路；等他們離開大陸，他就會喊一聲：「你們就瞧著會出什麼事吧。」他送他們上雪橇，趁他們轉上冰面時大聲喊道：「客人們動身了——客人們要走了！」——兄弟倆回頭一看，只見那地方黑壓壓一片，人們擠滿了門口和窗口，有的剛抓住他們的衣服，有的赤身裸體，正匆匆趕向自己的雪橇；可就在他們要出發時，所有雪橇都壞了。旅人們嚇壞了，催趕著狗；然而有一架雪橇跟在後面，顯然越追越近，他們的姐夫急忙追上去，殺了那趕雪橇的人，還殺了不少別的人，隨後用人的肢體裝滿了自己的雪橇——就這樣載著這些東西回到家中。兄弟倆深夜到家，講述了他們的姐姐如何變成食人者，以及他們如何靠姐夫的幫助才勉強逃脫一死；但他們再也沒見過姐姐。

title.en: Kunuk the Orphan Boy: Brothers, Giants, and the Great Plain
title.zh: 孤兒庫努克：兄弟、巨人與大平原

region.en: Fiord entrance and southern giant-land (legendary migration route)
region.zh: 峽灣口與南方巨人之地（傳說遷徙路線）

period: Inuit oral tradition; constructed from three copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two obliging orphan boys see an armed host advancing in the water-drawing moonlight, hide their little sister in wood-chips, and climb the rafters — seven raiders slaughter the household and spear the hidden girl. Carrying her corpse until they bury it in a cave, they train into stone-throwing, bear-crushing champions, marry the daughters of a wronged old man, harden their bodies against the chief's walrus-skin whip, kill him with his own trick, free the village — 'In future ye shall have no masters' — then sail south to destroy the giant Ungilagtake and his lame-legged champion, though the younger brother dies of grief at his sister's grave on the way.
summary.zh: 兩名殷勤的孤兒在月光汲水時預見武裝大軍襲來；他們把幼妹藏入木屑堆、自己攀上椽木——七名來襲者屠戮全家，長矛更刺穿木屑下的幼妹。兄妹三人扶屍南逃，葬妹於巖洞，自此練成擲石碎熊之勇；投奔被「強者」害子的老人，娶其二女，以硬身術破強者的海象皮鞭，反以其道殺之，解放全村——『從此你們再無主子』——繼而南征巨人翁吉拉格塔克與其三舟而行的跛腿冠軍；然而弟弟因在妹妹墳前悲泣致病，未至目的地而亡。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads the tale as referring to Eskimo-Indian struggles and intertribal wars and migrations. Graphic violence recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Several men had their permanent winter-quarters near the entrance to a fiord, and with them lived two boys, very officious and obliging: in the morning they helped turn and rub the men's gloves, arranged the kayak implements and tools, fetched the water for their morning drink, exercised in archery all day, and carried their things from the beach at return. One evening in winter, by moonlight, drawing water, the youngest said, 'I think I see a lot of faces down in the water' — 'Is it not the reflection of the moon?' 'No, come and look for thyself' — and Kunuk, looking, saw by way of clairvoyance a host of armed men advancing towards them. They ran to tell the people at home, but were only told it must have been the moon that deceived them; seeing the armed men the third time, they deliberated what to do with their little sister, put her down in a heap of chips close to the window and covered her well up, then climbed the rafters beneath the roof of the house-passage, lying at full length, faces downwards, holding one beam with their hands and their feet against the next.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有幾個人在一處峽灣入口附近有固定的過冬居所，和他們住在一起的還有兩個男孩，非常殷勤、樂於助人：早晨他們幫忙翻轉、揉搓男人們的手套，整理皮划艇的器具和工具，打來早晨喝的水，整天練習射箭，回來時還把東西從海灘上搬回來。冬天的一個傍晚，趁著月光打水時，最小的那個說：「我覺得水裡好像有好多張臉。」——「那不是月亮的倒影嗎？」——「不是，你自己過來看看。」——庫努克一看，憑藉洞察力看見一大群武裝的人正朝他們逼近。他們跑去告訴家裡的人，卻只被告知那一定是月亮騙了他們；第三次看見那些武裝的人時，他們商量該拿小妹妹怎麼辦，把她放在窗邊一堆木屑裡，好好蓋住，然後爬上屋廊屋頂下的椽子，全身平趴著，臉朝下，雙手抓住一根橫樑，雙腳抵住另一根。

passages.text: Presently a large man with a spear made his way through the entrance, then another; they counted seven, who came rushing into the house — and a fearful cry was heard from those who were put to death. While the raiders lingered inside, Kunuk's brother was losing strength; the aggressors came storming out, fighting right and left, flinging their spears everywhere, and likewise into the heap of chips where their little sister lay. When the last had disappeared the younger boy fell to the ground, Kunuk after him. They found their sister struck right through the body with a lance, entrails protruding; the house floor was all covered with blood, every one of the inmates killed, besides one of the assailants. Alone in the dreary house, they left the place that very night, carrying their wounded sister by turns and taking care the entrails did not come out of their proper place; they wandered on until, at a firth quite frozen over, past a steep promontory, their little sister died, and they buried her in a cave among the rocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不一會兒，一個手持長矛的大個子從入口擠了進來，接著又是一個；他們數到七個，全都衝進屋裡——隨即傳來被殺者可怕的叫喊聲。襲擊者在屋裡逗留時，庫努克的哥哥漸漸支撐不住；那些人又衝了出來，左右砍殺，把長矛往各處亂擲，也擲向他們小妹妹躺著的那堆木屑。等最後一個消失後，年幼的男孩跌落在地，庫努克也跟著落下。他們發現妹妹被長矛刺穿了身體，腸子都露了出來；屋裡的地面滿是鮮血，所有屋裡的人都被殺死，襲擊者中也死了一個。他們孤零零地待在這淒涼的屋裡，當夜就離開了那地方，輪流抬著受傷的妹妹，小心不讓腸子從原位掉出來；他們一路流浪，直到在一處完全凍結的峽灣、一座陡峭的海角那邊，小妹妹死了，他們把她葬在岩石間的一個洞穴裡。

passages.text: From the beginning of their flight they exercised themselves in boxing and lifting large stones to strengthen their limbs, and grew into strong and vigorous men ere they met other people again. A man on the ice beside a huge piece of hunting-wood adopted them as his sons, and their foster-parents encouraged them never to forget their enemies.
