They caught ptarmigan and foxes without any weapons by throwing large stones; practised boxing and wrestling, making a point never to fall but roll together along the ground; and at last grew so dexterous they could kill a bear without any weapon — giving him a blow, and when he turned upon them taking no more notice than if he had been a hare, merely taking hold of him by the legs and smashing him to pieces. They took a northerly direction and came at last to a great inlet where kayakers hunted seal — but only one of them, their chief or 'strong man,' was provided with weapons: the others had only to chase and frighten the animals, and anyone daring to wound them was punished by the chief in person. The brothers were too modest to go down at once, and meanwhile witnessed the cutting-up of a walrus, each person getting a huge piece excepting an old man in the poorest tent, who got nothing but the entrails, carried home from the beach by his two daughters. Taking pity on his patience, the brothers went to him in the dark; the old man offered them his daughters in marriage, Kunuk choosing the youngest, his brother the eldest — and thus they got married.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從逃亡之初，他們就練習拳擊、舉大石頭來強健四肢，在再次遇到別人之前，已長成強壯有力的男子。一個站在冰上、身旁有一大塊獵用木料的人收他們為養子，養父母鼓勵他們永遠不要忘記仇人。他們不用任何武器，只靠扔大石頭就捉到雷鳥和狐狸；練習拳擊和摔跤，特意做到從不摔倒，而是扭在一起在地上打滾；最後變得如此靈巧，不用任何武器就能殺死一頭熊——給牠一拳，當牠撲向他們時，他們毫不在意，只當牠是隻野兔，只抓住牠的腿把牠摔得粉碎。他們朝北走，最後來到一個大海灣，那裡有划皮划艇的人獵海豹——但只有一個人，即他們的首領或「大力士」，配備了武器：其他人只能追趕、驚嚇獵物，誰敢刺傷獵物，首領就親自懲罰誰。兄弟倆太謙遜，沒有立刻下去，同時目睹了一頭海象被分割，每人分到一大塊，只有最破爛帳篷裡的一個老人什麼也沒分到，只得到腸子，由他的兩個女兒從海灘搬回家。兄弟倆憐憫他的忍耐，天黑時去找他；老人提出把女兒們嫁給他們，庫努克選了最小的，他哥哥選了最大的——他們就這樣成了親。

passages.text: Going down to the place they had examined the boats closely, and had taken the 'strong man's' javelin away with the intention of hiding it, sticking it so deep into hard dry turf by a spring that only what could be seized with two fingers was to be seen. An old gossip — mother to the 'strong man' — spied the strangers, and a multitude gathered at the tent entrance; in the morning the chief cried out that it was a fine day for a walrus-hunt, then fell silent: 'My javelin has been taken away.' All rushed to the rock leading to the spring to pull it out of the earth, but nobody succeeded, having pulled and bitten it until the end was quite wasted; Kunuk just took it between his two fingers and disengaged it as if it were a very small matter. Their father-in-law told them that under the great boat lay the perfectly fitted-up kayaks of his dead son, murdered by the 'strong man' who envied his still greater strength, making the old man the enemy of his own daughters. Then came the cry: 'Let the strangers come on for a boxing and fighting match on the great plain up yonder!' A pole was set up, beside it the leader with a whip of walrus-skin with a knot on the end, and a stuffed white hare — whoever set foot on it was quickly lashed. Kunuk was first; at the very moment the 'strong man' lifted his whip, Kunuk stooped and hardened his limbs by charm, so the whip gave a loud crack and Kunuk came away unhurt while the chief believed he had killed him. Then the chief proposed the younger brother take the whip for a change, went himself and put his foot on the hare — and Kunuk's brother, crying 'Look out and harden thy body!' smote him at the same time, so that he fell down dead on the spot. All his inferiors rejoiced greatly: 'Henceforth ye shall be our leaders!' — but the brothers rejoined, 'In future ye shall have no masters, but hunt at liberty and at your own will.' They practised all manner of kayaking feats with bladder-arrows of one entire blown-up seal-skin, and once lanced a very large she-walrus at greater distance than usual, the arrow going right through to the very vent-holes of the bladder. Hearing of the giant Ungilagtake, with his huge sword, from whom nobody was ever known to escape, they supposed him to have been among the armed men who attacked their housemates, and determined to find him out. But on the voyage south, Kunuk's brother, recognising the burial-place of their little sister on the land, sobbed bent over the helm, took ill from that very day, and died before they reached their destination, so that Kunuk came alone to Ungilagtake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們下到那地方，仔細察看了那些船，把「大力士」的標槍拿走，打算藏起來，把它深深地插進泉邊堅硬乾燥的草皮裡，只露出能用兩根手指捏住的一點。一個愛嚼舌根的老婦——「大力士」的母親——窺見了這些陌生人，一大群人便聚集在帳篷門口；早晨首領喊道，今天是獵海象的好天氣，隨後又沉默下來：「我的標槍被人拿走了。」所有人都衝到通往泉邊的岩石那裡，想把標槍從土裡拔出來，卻沒人成功，他們又拉又咬，把槍尾都弄壞了；庫努克只用兩根手指捏住它，就把它拔了出來，彷彿是件微不足道的小事。他們的岳父告訴他們，那條大船底下放著他死去的兒子完好配備的皮划艇，那兒子是被「大力士」殺害的，因為「大力士」嫉妒他更強的力量，這使老人成了自己女兒們的敵人。接著傳來喊聲：「讓陌生人到上面那片大平原來比拳擊和格鬥吧！」立起了一根杆子，旁邊站著首領，手持一根末端打結的海象皮鞭，還有一隻填塞的白兔——誰踩上去，就會立刻挨鞭子。庫努克先上；就在「大力士」舉起鞭子的那一刻，庫努克彎下身子，用咒法使身體堅硬，於是鞭子啪的一聲巨響，庫努克卻毫髮無傷地走開，而首領還以為自己把他打死了。接著首領提議換弟弟來挨鞭子，自己走過去把腳踩在白兔上——庫努克的弟弟喊著「當心，把身體繃硬！」同時給了他一擊，他就當場倒地死了。他所有的下屬都大喜：「從今以後，你們就是我們的首領！」——但兄弟倆回答：「今後你們不會再有主人，可以自由自在地按自己的意願去打獵。」他們用一整張吹脹的海豹皮做的浮囊箭練習各種皮划艇技藝，有一次在比平常更遠的距離刺中一頭很大的母海象，箭一直穿透到浮囊的排氣孔。聽說有個巨人溫吉拉格塔克，帶著一把巨劍，從沒聽說有人能從他手下逃脫，他們猜想他就在襲擊他們同屋人的那些武裝者之中，便決定去找出他。但在南行的航程中，庫努克的哥哥認出了陸上他們小妹妹的墓地，伏在舵上抽泣，從那天起就病倒了，還沒到達目的地就死了，於是庫努克獨自來到溫吉拉格塔克那裡。

passages.text: In the depth of winter they were met by many people on the ice, and a somewhat biggish man — himself an enemy of Ungilagtake — showed them how the giant used to behave to strangers: lifting an entire seal-skin stuffed with sand by a strap with his third finger, and challenging the guest to do the same (Kunuk lifted the thing with his little finger, unbent arm, and put it down without being fatigued), and throwing a lance at the stranger amid a song of 'Bend thee down, stranger!' — at which Kunuk bent so low nothing but his chin was visible, and the host lost his aim. Warned to make a bold entrance, Kunuk and his wife came up to a large house with three windows occupied by Ungilagtake's numerous stolen wives; refreshments were served, and when they had finished eating, Ungilagtake ordered Kunuk to seat himself opposite, drew out a huge spear from beneath the bench, struck the drum, and the whole joined in a song: 'Bend thee down, stranger that has come among us; the great Ungilagtake, who never missed his aim, is going to thrust his spear at thee.' He bent down, only his chin appearing — and whilst Ungilagtake took aim, Kunuk nimbly jumped and caught hold of one of the roof-beams, the spear going far below him; flung at a second time, he quickly jumped down and the spear came flying above him amid great cheers. Taking aim the third time, Kunuk seized the spear, saying he too would like to have a try at killing with it; they exchanged places, Kunuk struck up a song for Ungilagtake, and the very moment the giant prepared to bend his back, Kunuk had already taken aim — the spear hit him in the throat, and he fell dead on the spot. Everybody rushed out of the house, and Kunuk, following, found himself seized from behind by Tajangiarsuk, the giant's companion with a double back, immensely strong; on a plain of ice covered with projecting stones chosen on purpose to dash adversaries against, the wrestling-match began. Kunuk flung him down so the blood gushed out of his mouth; a still stronger and larger champion got Kunuk down, knee already on his heart, when Kunuk suddenly grasped his shoulders from beneath and pressed the lungs out of him; then came 'the last of the lot, him with the lame legs,' of such immense size that he had to lie across three boats to get along, creeping to the combat-field on his elbows. Kunuk whirled him round by the waist until his feet turned right outwards, letting him fall so that his skull was crushed. The people rejoiced and cried, 'Thanks to thee! now we shall have no masters!' — and those who had been robbed of their wives got them back again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 10 'Kunuk the Orphan Boy'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隆冬時節，許多人在冰上迎接他們，一個身材相當高大的人——他本人也是溫吉拉格塔克的仇敵——向他們演示那巨人往常如何對待陌生人：用第三根手指提著一條帶子，舉起一整張填滿沙子的海豹皮，並挑戰客人照做（庫努克用小指、伸直手臂提起那東西，放下時毫不疲倦），還在一首歌中向陌生人擲標槍，歌裡唱著「彎下腰吧，陌生人！」——庫努克彎得極低，只露出下巴，主人便失了準頭。有人提醒他要大膽進門，庫努克和妻子來到一座有三扇窗的大房子，裡面住著溫吉拉格塔克眾多擄來的妻子；茶點端了上來，吃完後，溫吉拉格塔克命令庫努克坐到對面，從長凳下抽出一支巨大的長矛，敲響鼓，所有人一起唱道：「彎下腰吧，來到我們中間的陌生人；從不失手的偉大溫吉拉格塔克，要向你刺出他的長矛了。」他彎下腰，只露出下巴——就在溫吉拉格塔克瞄準時，庫努克敏捷地一跳，抓住一根屋樑，長矛從他身下遠遠飛過；第二次擲來時，他迅速跳下，長矛在眾人的歡呼聲中從他上方飛過。第三次瞄準時，庫努克抓住長矛，說他也想試試用它殺人；他們交換了位置，庫努克為溫吉拉格塔克唱起歌，就在巨人準備彎下腰的那一刻，庫努克已經瞄準——長矛擊中他的喉嚨，他當場倒地而死。所有人都衝出屋子，庫努克跟在後面，發現自己被從背後抓住，那是巨人的同伴塔揚吉亞爾蘇克，他長著雙重脊背，力大無窮；在一塊特意選來把對手摔上去的、佈滿突出石塊的冰原上，摔跤開始了。庫努克把他摔得口吐鮮血；一個更強更大的勇士把庫努克摔倒，膝蓋已壓在他胸口，庫努克突然從下面抓住他的雙肩，把他的肺都擠了出來；接著來的是「最後一個，那個腿瘸的」，身材巨大，得橫躺在三條船上才能行動，用胳膊肘爬到格鬥場。庫努克抓住他的腰把他掄轉，直到他的腳完全朝外，再把他摔下，砸碎了他的頭骨。人們歡呼道：「多謝你！如今我們不會再有主人了！」——那些被奪走妻子的人也重新得回了妻子。

title.en: Malin Kundang: The Shipwrecked Son Who Cursed His Mother
title.zh: 馬林·昆當：詛咒母親而遭石化之子

region.en: Air Manis beach, Padang, West Sumatra
region.zh: 西蘇門答臘巴東·愛之水海灘

period: Minangkabau oral legend; recorded in 19th-20th century collections

source.work: The legend of Malin Kundang (Minangkabau oral tradition)

summary.en: A poor widow's son sails away from the Minangkabau coast and returns years later a rich captain, wed to a princess; passing his village, he denies his ragged, kneeling mother before his wife and crew — she curses him, and the storm that answers turns his golden ship to stone. The wreck-shape on the reef of Air Manis is still shown to travellers, with the footprint beside it.
summary.zh: 貧寡婦之子自米南加保海岸出海，多年後以富商船長之身歸來，且娶得公主；行經故村，竟當妻室水手之面否認跪地襤褸的老母——母親咒之，應咒的風暴將其金船化為石。愛之水海灘礁上之沉船形岩，至今為旅人指認，石旁猶有其足印。

sensitivity.note: The best-known Minangkabau moral legend (the ungrateful son); pilgrimage-site etiology.

canonical_translation: Based on the Minangkabau oral legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
Malin Kundang is the Minangkabau world's great morality tale, told wherever a merantau people explains what leaving home owes to the mother who stayed.

BEGINNING: THE POOR HOUSE. In a fishing village on the Minangkabau coast a widow struggles to raise her only son, Malin Kundang. The boy, restless and ambitious, begs leave to go merantau — to seek his fortune abroad, as Minangkabau men must. He takes ship and is gone for years; his mother keeps his memory and her poverty, walking to the shore to watch for sails.

MIDDLE: THE DENIAL. Malin Kundang returns a rich captain in a golden ship, married to a princess, with a crew in livery. Ashamed of his origins before his new world, he passes his village without stopping; his mother, recognizing the son she begged heaven for, kneels before him and asks only to be acknowledged. Before wife, crew and passengers he denies her: he does not know this old woman, he says, ordering her pushed aside.

END: THE STORM AND THE STONE. The mother rises from the dust and curses her son: may he become a rock. As the ship puts out to sea, a black storm rises out of a clear sky; the golden ship is wrecked and turned to stone on the reef, the crew scattered, the captain flung onto the beach and frozen mid-crawl as stone. The rock on the shore of Air Manis is pointed out to this day as the ship-wreck shape, with the kneeling son beside it — and beside that, the legend insists, a hollow like a footprint.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) polices the merantau ethic: leaving is commanded by custom, but the umbilical debt cannot be defaulted; (2) makes matrilineal authority visible — the mother's curse, not the father's law, is the operative power; (3) etiologizes the reef-shapes of Air Manis beach as pilgrimage evidence; and (4) supplies the Malay world's best-known parallel to the filial-impiety petrification tales (Si Tanggang of the Peninsula). The tellings vary in detail but not in structure. In some versions the mother strikes the ship's rail with her hand, in others she kneels in the road; the curse may name the ship, the son, or both; and the petrification may catch the vessel at sea or the son crawling ashore. The Padang coast has consolidated the geography: the reef-shapes at Air Manis beach are pointed out as ship and kneeling man, and a hollow nearby serves the legend as the footprint of the son or of the mother who watched for his sails. The Minangkabau use of the tale is pedagogical: it is told to children preparing to merantau as the negative half of the custom's charter, the tale that explains why every departure must keep its line back to the mother's house. The Peninsula's Si Tanggang telling carries the same structure under another name, and the two traditions clearly descend from a shared Malay-world legend of the rich son who comes home too proud to kneel.
narrative.zh: 馬林·昆當乃米南加保世界之道德大傳——凡論『走他鄉』之民對留鄉之母負何債者皆述之。開篇：海濱漁村貧婦獨力撫養獨子馬林·昆當；少年懷志求去他鄉（merantau），乘船遠行多年，母親守貧守望，日日到岸邊看帆。中段：他以富船長之身歸來，金船、公主妻、華服水手；因恥於寒微，過家門而不入。母親認出跪求相認的兒子，在妻室水手面前遭他否認：『我不認識這老婦。』結尾：母親起身咒其為石；晴空裏風暴驟起，金船觸礁化石，船長被拋上海灘，爬行姿態凝固為石。愛之水海灘礁石至今被指為沉船之形、跪子之岩，石旁更有足印之凹。功能：規訓走他鄉之倫理——離鄉合俗，臍債不可賴；使母系權威可見——母咒而非父法為有效之力；釋愛之水海灘礁形為朝聖之證；並為馬來世界之『不孝石化』傳說（馬來半島之西·當當）供給最著名之平行文本。

functions: Policing the merantau ethic: the emigrant's umbilical debt to the mother cannot be defaulted
Matrilineal authority made visible — the mother's curse as operative power
Etiology of the reef-shapes of Air Manis beach, Padang
Malay-world parallel to the Si Tanggang petrification tale

passages.text: A poor widow's only son, Malin Kundang, takes ship from the Minangkabau coast to seek his fortune abroad; his mother keeps her poverty and her watch at the shore, waiting for his sails. He returns a rich captain in a golden ship with a princess wife; passing his village he denies the kneeling mother who begs only to be acknowledged, ordering her pushed aside before his crew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau legend of Malin Kundang; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Minangkabau legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位貧窮寡婦的獨子馬林·昆當（Malin Kundang）從米南加保海岸乘船出海，遠赴異鄉尋求財富；他的母親守著貧困，在岸邊守望，等待他的船帆歸來。他歸來時已成富有的船長，乘著金色船隻，帶著一位公主妻子；途經自己的村莊時，他否認了跪地哀求、只求被認下的母親，下令船員將她推到一旁。

passages.text: The mother curses him: may he become a rock. A storm out of a clear sky wrecks the golden ship and turns it to stone on the reef of Air Manis, with the captain flung ashore and frozen mid-crawl — the shapes still pointed out to travellers, with a hollow beside them like a footprint.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 母親詛咒他：願他化為岩石。晴空驟起的風暴擊毀了金色船隻，將它變成礁石上的石頭，位於亞伊爾·馬尼斯（Air Manis）的暗礁上，船長被拋上岸，僵止在爬行途中——這些形狀至今仍被指給旅人看，旁邊有一處凹陷，宛如腳印。

title.en: The Buffalo That Won the War: How Minangkabau Got Its Name
title.zh: 贏得戰爭的水牛：米南加保之名由來

region.en: Minangkabau heartland, West Sumatra (Pagaruyung)
region.zh: 西蘇門答臘米南加保腹地（巴加爾容）

period: Minangkabau oral legend; recorded in early European accounts and local tradition

source.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784), the Menangkabau country; Minangkabau oral name-legend

summary.en: Invaded by a mighty Javanese army, the Minangkabau, too few to fight in the open, propose a single combat of buffaloes — and produce a starving calf with knives honed and bound to its tiny horns. The calf, seeking milk, gores the enemy's great fighting bull to death; the Javanese withdraw, and the land is named Minangkabau, 'the buffalo that won' (menang kerbau) — the origin myth of a people who call cleverness mightier than numbers.
summary.zh: 強大的爪哇軍入侵，米南加保人寡不敵眾，遂提議以水牛單挑定勝負——並牽出一頭挨餓的小牛，銳刃縛於其幼角。小牛尋乳本能，一觸即以角刃剖開敵方巨牛之腹；爪哇軍撤退，其地遂名『米南加保』——『得勝之牛』（menang kerbau）——一個以智勝於眾的民族的自敘神話。

sensitivity.note: Name-etiology legend of the Minangkabau; the matrilineal people's self-image as clever underdogs.

canonical_translation: Based on the Minangkabau oral name-legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The name-legend of Minangkabau is the charter story of the matrilineal highland people of West Sumatra, told with the buffalo that appears on their palace roofs — the bagonjong with its sweeping horn-like gables.

BEGINNING: THE INVASION. A great army out of Java under a mighty raja descends on the Minangkabau country; the highlanders, outnumbered past any hope in open battle, ask for terms — and the invader offers single combat of champions, in the form of a buffalo fight: his great bull against any beast the Minangkabau can produce.

MIDDLE: THE STARVING CALF. The Minangkabau produce a mere calf, starved for days and separated from its mother, with small sharp knives honed and lashed to its horns. On the field the enemy bull paws and bellows; the calf, a baby still, is let go — and runs straight at the great beast, nosing for milk.

END: THE NAME. The calf's bound blades rip the bull open in the first charge, and the fighting beast falls; the invader keeps the wager and withdraws his army. The land is named for its victory — Minangkabau, 'the buffalo that won' (menang kerbau) — and the people's houses are roofed with horns in memory of the calf that beat a bull.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) explains the name of the people and the horn-roofed architecture of their rumah gadang; (2) states the Minangkabau ethic that cleverness, preparation and mother-ties outweigh force; (3) encodes the memory of Javanese pressure on the highlands; and (4) links the matrilineal social order (mother-calf) to the land's safety. The legend's staging deserves its details: the wager of a single buffalo-fight replaces a war of annihilation, the calf's horns are armed in secret with small knives honed and lashed in place, and the animal's milk-seeking charge turns its hunger into the weapon. The story is told against the architecture as much as against the invader: the rumah gadang's sweeping horn-gables are read as the trophy of the calf's victory, so that every village skyline repeats the founding ruse. The historical layer beneath the legend is the memory of Javanese military pressure on the Sumatran highlands, which the Minangkabau chronicle traditions attach to Majapahit and to the line of Pagaruyung recorded in the Malay Annals; the buffalo contest is thus both name-charter and memory of survival — a people outnumbered, who won by preparing a weapon their opponent's strength could not anticipate.
narrative.zh: 米南加保之名源傳說是西蘇門答臘母系高原民族的憲章故事——其王宮屋頂之牛角形山牆即其象徵。開篇：爪哇大軍壓境；高原人力寡難戰，乃求和，侵略者提議以水牛單挑定輸贏。中段：米南加保人牽出一頭挨餓多日、與母分離的小牛，幼角上縛著磨利的尖刃。場上敵牛刨地吼叫；小牛被放開，逕直朝巨牛奔去——尋奶。結尾：小牛縛刃一觸即剖開巨牛之腹，戰牛倒地；侵略者守約撤軍。此地遂以『得勝之牛』（menang kerbau）為名，人民的房屋以牛角形屋頂紀念那頭戰勝公牛的小牛。功能：釋民族之名與大屋（rumah gadang）牛角頂之由來、立『智與備與母系勝於力』之倫理、銘記爪哇壓力之歷史記憶、並將母系秩序（母子相連）繫於土地之安。

functions: Explains the name Minangkabau ('the buffalo that won') and the horn-gabled rumah gadang roofs
States the ethic that cleverness and preparation outweigh force
Encodes the historical memory of Javanese military pressure on the highlands
Links the matrilineal social order to the land's safety

variants.name: Majapahit-invasion framing
variants.summary: Later tellings name the invader as Majapahit and the victor's line as the Pagaruyung dynasty of the Malay Annals' Sang Sapurba.

primary_sources.citation: Oral legend of the Minangkabau highlands; recorded in local tradition and early European accounts; paraphrased.

secondary_sources.work: William Marsden, The History of Sumatra
secondary_sources.citation: Marsden 1784, London — the Menangkabau country, its people and Pagaruyung tradition.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Marsden, The History of Sumatra (1784)

passages.text: A mighty Javanese army invades the Minangkabau highlands; too few for open battle, the highlanders ask for terms, and the invader offers to settle the war by a single combat of buffaloes. The Minangkabau produce a starving calf with small knives honed and bound to its horns; set loose on the field, the calf runs straight at the great fighting bull nosing for milk, and its bound blades rip the beast open in the first charge. The invader keeps the wager and withdraws his army; the land is named Minangkabau — 'the buffalo that won' — and the people roof their houses with horn-shaped gables in memory of the calf that beat a bull.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau name-legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一支強大的爪哇軍隊入侵米南加保高地；高地人兵力太少，無法正面交戰，便請求議和，入侵者提出以一場水牛單鬥來解決戰爭。米南加保人牽出一頭飢餓的小牛，將小刀磨利綁在牠的角上；小牛被放到場上，直奔那頭正嗅尋乳汁的巨型鬥牛，牠角上綁著的刀刃在第一次衝撞中便將那巨獸剖開。入侵者遵守賭約，撤回了軍隊；這片土地被命名為米南加保——「獲勝的水牛」——而人們以角形的山牆為房屋加頂，以紀念那頭擊敗公牛的小牛。

title.en: Sabai nan Aluih: The Daughter Who Took Up the Gun
title.zh: 莎拜·南·阿魯伊：舉槍的女兒

region.en: Padang Tarab, Minangkabau highlands, West Sumatra
region.zh: 西蘇門答臘米南加保高原巴當·塔拉卜

period: Minangkabau kaba (oral romance) tradition

source.work: The kaba of Sabai nan Aluih (Minangkabau oral tradition)

summary.en: The famous beauty Sabai nan Aluih works the rice-fields with her aged father, the mild Mupo Rajo Nan Saludo; the quarrelsome great chief Rajo Babanding of Sungai Pagu demands her for a wife, and when the father resists the chief kills him. Sabai takes up her father's gun at the head of the young men of the valley, shoots the chief dead from a distance, refuses all marriage, and becomes the kaba's heroine of the daughter who ends the feud herself.
summary.zh: 著名美人莎拜·南·阿魯伊隨老父（溫和的穆波·拉佐·南·薩魯多）耕於田間；性暴的大酋長拉佐·巴班丁（蘇埃·帕古）索她為妻；老父抗拒，酋長竟殺之。莎拜於谷中青年之首拿起父親的獵槍，遠距一槍斃酋長；拒絕一切婚約，成為kaba傳說中親手了結仇怨的女兒。

sensitivity.note: Minangkabau heroine-romance; vengeance narrative treated as literature.

passages.text: Sabai nan Aluih works the rice-fields beside her aged father, Mupo Rajo Nan Saludo of Padang Tarab; the powerful chief Rajo Babanding demands her in marriage, and when the mild old father refuses him, the chief kills him at the field's edge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba of Sabai nan Aluih; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩拜·南·阿盧伊（Sabai nan Aluih）與年邁的父親——巴東·塔拉布（Padang Tarab）的穆波·拉惹·南·薩盧多（Mupo Rajo Nan Saludo）——一同在稻田裡勞作；有權勢的首領拉惹·巴班丁（Rajo Babanding）要求娶她為妻，當溫和的老父拒絕他時，首領在田邊殺死了他。

passages.text: The daughter takes up her father's gun and leads the young men of the valley against Sungai Pagu; from long range she shoots Rajo Babanding dead, ends the feud with her own hand, and refuses every offer of marriage — the kaba's figure of the daughter who becomes her father's avenger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女兒拿起父親的槍，率領谷中的青年對抗雙溪·帕古（Sungai Pagu）；她從遠處射殺了拉惹·巴班丁，親手了結了這場世仇，並拒絕了一切求婚——她是卡巴（kaba）中那位成為父親復仇者的女兒形象。

title.en: Anggun nan Tongga: The Kaba of the Mother and the Drifting Son
title.zh: 安貢·南·東加：母與漂泊之子之歌

region.en: Minangkabau highlands, West Sumatra
region.zh: 西蘇門答臘米南加保高原

period: Minangkabau kaba (oral romance) tradition

source.work: The kaba of Anggun nan Tongga (Minangkabau oral tradition)

summary.en: The noblewoman Anggun nan Tongga bears a son alone, sets him adrift on the river in a casket with royal tokens, and years later unknowingly takes the grown stranger as a husband — the Minangkabau kaba's great tragedy of separated kin, in which the recognition comes too late and the punishment falls on the house; the tale is told as a warning that a mother's secrecy can become a house's doom.
summary.zh: 貴婦安貢·南·東加獨自誕下一子，將其置於帶王家信物之木匣漂流於河；多年後，竟在不知情中嫁與這位成年的陌生人——米南加保kaba的大悲劇：至親離散、相認已遲、懲罰降於全家；故事警語曰：母親的隱瞞可成全家之禍。

sensitivity.note: Tragic kaba with an incest-recognition core; treated as literature, summarized without explicit detail.

passages.text: Anggun nan Tongga bears a son alone and hides the birth, setting the infant adrift in a casket bearing the tokens of his birth; the child is raised far away, knowing nothing of his mother. Years later the grown stranger arrives at her house and is taken as a husband without recognition; when the tokens at last reveal the truth, the recognition has come too late, and the punishment of the hidden birth falls on the whole house — the kaba told as a warning against a mother's secrecy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba of Anggun nan Tongga; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安貢·南·通加（Anggun nan Tongga）獨自生下一子，並隱瞞了這樁生育，將嬰兒放入一隻載有他出生信物的匣子裡漂流而去；這孩子在遠方長大，對自己的母親一無所知。多年後，長大成人的陌生人來到她家，在彼此不相識的情況下被招為丈夫；當信物終於揭示真相時，相認已來得太遲，隱瞞生育的懲罰降臨到整個家族——這則卡巴被講述為對母親隱瞞之事的警示。

title.en: Cindua Mato: The Journey to the Sky-Kingdom
title.zh: 金杜阿·馬托：上天國之旅

region.en: Minangkabau highlands and the sky-kingdom of the kaba
region.zh: 米南加保高原與kaba中之天國

period: Minangkabau kaba (oral epic) tradition

source.work: The kaba of Cindua Mato (Minangkabau oral tradition)

summary.en: The greatest Minangkabau kaba: the youth Cindua Mato ('ray of the sun'), sent up the sky-tree by the king to fetch the magical remedies of the sky-kingdom, climbs into heaven, wins the friendship of the sky-princesses, and carries down the cures that save his king — but the sky-world does not let its guests go freely, and the return costs the hero what heaven's princess loves in him. The kaba ends with the exchange fixed forever: Minangkabau's kings may have heaven's help, but heaven keeps its price.
summary.zh: 米南加保最偉大之kaba：青年金杜阿·馬托（『日光』）奉王命沿天樹而上，往取天國之仙藥；他攀入天界，贏得天國公主之誼，攜救王之藥而返——然天國不肯輕放其客，此行令英雄付出天國公主所愛之代價。kaba終章之約定永不改變：米南加保之王可得天之助，而天必收其價。

sensitivity.note: Sky-voyage kaba; the Minangkabau ascent narrative par excellence.

passages.text: Sent by his king to fetch the remedies that only the sky-kingdom keeps, the youth Cindua Mato climbs the sky-tree into heaven, where he wins the friendship of the sky-princesses and learns the cures of the upper world. The king is saved, but heaven does not release its guests freely: the kaba closes on the price heaven keeps from the hero, and on the standing bargain that Minangkabau's kings may call on the sky — if the sky may take its due.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba of Cindua Mato; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Minangkabau kaba; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 青年金杜阿·马托奉国王之命，前去取回唯有天界才有的灵药；他攀上天树，登上天庭，在那里赢得了众位天女的友谊，并习得上界的疗法。国王得救了，但天界并不会无偿放走它的客人：这部卡巴故事止于天界向这位英雄索取的代价，以及米南加保诸王可以求助于天界的那项长期约定——倘若天界也可取其应得之物。

title.en: The Faithless Wife and the Fox-Woman
title.zh: 不貞之妻與狐婦

region.en: Lake and hill country, Greenland-Labrador copies
region.zh: 湖泊與山地（格陵蘭及拉布拉多流本）

period: Inuit oral tradition; five manuscripts (one Labrador), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Tracking his wife to a lake, a husband sees her strip and go out to a masculine being risen from the water, and kills her by stuffing vermin into her. Alone after, he finds his supper cooked and boots dried daily — until he spies the little woman with a huge hair-tuft: a fox in woman's shape, whose rank smell betrays her. His jealous cousin cries 'Whence comes this nasty smell?'; she grows a tail, quenches the lamp with it, cries 'Ka, ka, ka!' and flees as a fox to a cave, sending out beetle, spider, and caterpillar before he heaps fuel at the entrance and burns her alive — then, quite alone again, kills himself in a fit of madness.
summary.zh: 丈夫跟蹤妻子至湖邊，見她褪衣入水與水中顯形的男子相會，遂以蟲豸塞入其身將她害死。此後獨居的他日日發現飯已煮好、靴已烘乾——跟蹤之下，發現梳著巨髻的小婦人竟是化形的狐狸，異味洩底。嫉妒的表親一句『這惡臭從何而來？』令她生出尾巴、以尾熄燈、狐叫三聲奪門而逃；他追至巖洞，洞中先後擲出甲蟲、蜘蛛、毛蟲，他便在洞口堆柴把她活活燒死——而後孤身一人，於瘋狂中自戕。

sensitivity.note: Rink notes this and tale 12 intermix with an omitted 'dog's offspring' tale across five manuscripts. Graphic killing recorded as told in the 1875 source; animal-wife motif parallels Rink tale 12 and Rasmussen's vixen tale.

passages.text: A man living alone with his wife noticed that she often left the place without his knowing where she went, seldom being at home on his return from day-work. Suspicious, he one morning feigned going far away, paddled only to the nearest point, and hid behind rocks; his wife emerged from the tent in her best attire, and he stole up behind her, following till she reached a lake — where he observed her throw off something into the water, upon which a masculine being appeared, and she, undressing, went out to him in the water. At this sight the husband got into a great rage, gathered all kinds of vermin, and one day when he was quite alone with his wife stuffed them into her, and in this manner killed her. From that time he was all alone, but did not wish to go out in his kayak minding his usual business.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一个与妻子独居的男子发觉，她常常外出，却不知她去了何处；他干完一天的活回家时，她很少在家。他心生疑虑，一天早晨假装远行，只把独木舟划到最近的一处，便躲在岩石后面；他的妻子穿着最漂亮的衣裳从帐篷里出来，他悄悄跟在她身后，一路尾随她来到一个湖边——他看见她往水里扔了什么东西，随即出现了一个男性，她便脱下衣服，下水向他走去。丈夫见此情景勃然大怒，收集了各种虫豸，有一天趁与妻子独处时把它们塞进她体内，就这样杀死了她。从那以后他便孤身一人，却不愿再划着皮艇外出做他惯常的营生。

passages.text: Returning to his lonely tent one day he was very much surprised to find his supper cooked and the smoking meat served up; the next day the same happened again — meat smoking hot on his dish, boots dried and ready to put on — and all this was repeated every day. One day he paddled only a little way off the coast, went on shore, and hid where he could keep a look-out on his tent; he soon observed a little woman, with her hair dressed up in a very large tuft, come down the hill and enter his tent. Quickly paddling home and creeping up, he lifted the door-curtain softly, noticed a strong unpleasant smell, and saw the little woman busily trimming his lamp: she was really a fox transformed into the shape of a woman, which accounted for the smell. Nevertheless, he took her for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天他回到孤零零的帐篷，十分惊讶地发现晚饭已经煮好，热腾腾的肉已盛在盘中；第二天又是如此——盘中肉热气腾腾，靴子已烘干、随时可穿——而且天天如此。一天，他只把独木舟划到离岸不远的地方，便上岸躲在一处能望见自己帐篷的地方；不久他就看见一个小妇人，头发高高挽成一大髻，从山上下来，走进他的帐篷。他急忙划船回家，悄悄走近，轻轻掀起门帘，闻到一股刺鼻的怪味，看见那小妇人正忙着修剪他的灯芯：她其实是一只化作女人形状的狐狸，那股气味便由此而来。尽管如此，他还是娶她为妻。

passages.text: One day he met his cousin out at sea, told him about his new wife, praising her loveliness, and asked him to come and see her — 'But if thou shouldst happen to notice a rank smell about her, be sure not to make any remarks about it.' The cousin followed him at once, and having landed together they both entered the tent; but when the visitor observed how nice and pleasant the wife of his cousin was, he grew quite jealous, and to make mischief exclaimed, 'Whence comes this nasty smell?' Instantly the little woman rose to her feet: she had now got a tail, wherewith she extinguished the lamp, and like a fox cried, 'Ka, ka, ka!' and ran out of the tent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天他在海上遇见自己的表兄弟，向他谈起自己的新妻，称赞她的美貌，并请他来家中看看她——『不过，倘若你碰巧闻到她身上有股难闻的气味，千万别说出来。』表兄弟立刻跟着他来了，两人一同上岸，走进帐篷；可是这位来客一见表兄弟的妻子如此姣好可人，便十分嫉妒，存心捣乱地嚷道：『这股难闻的气味是从哪儿来的？』那小妇人立刻站起身来：她此时已长出一条尾巴，用尾巴扑灭了灯，像狐狸一样叫道：『咔，咔，咔！』随即跑出了帐篷。

passages.text: The husband followed her quickly; when he again caught sight of her she was transformed into a fox, running up hill as fast as possible, and at last vanished into a cave. While he stood outside calling for her, she first sent him a beetle, then a spider, and at last a caterpillar; he grew quite enraged, heaped fuel together at the entrance, and burned her alive — and once more he was quite alone, and at last killed himself in a fit of madness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 11 'The Faithless Wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 丈夫急忙追了出去；当他再次看见她时，她已化作一只狐狸，拼命往山上跑，最后消失在一个洞穴里。他站在洞外呼唤她时，她先派出一只甲虫，又派出一只蜘蛛，最后派出一条毛虫；他怒不可遏，在洞口堆起柴薪，把她活活烧死——于是他又一次孤身一人，最终在一阵疯狂中自尽了。

title.en: The Man Who Mated Himself with a Sea-Fowl
title.zh: 與海鳥結親者

region.en: Sand-hill and gulls-hill, Greenland coast
region.zh: 格陵蘭海岸沙丘與鷗丘

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A lonely bachelor plays father to seal skulls, then steals the prettiest bather's clothes at a lake; her flock fly off as birds, and she stays as his wife once he promises to let her keep them — until the day she fastens bird wings on their two sons, then on herself, and the whole family flies away as sea-fowl. Following the water-road down a salmon's back, he finds his bird-wife courted by a pug-nosed man in a house of women, pursues her in vain, and sees house and household turn to gulls and a gulls-hill.
summary.zh: 孤獨的老鰥夫以海豹頭骨扮作兒女取樂；後在湖畔偷走最美浴女的衣裳，使其留在岸邊為妻。妻子起初不敢飛走，但終有一日替兩個兒子縛上鳥翼，自己隨後——一家化為海鳥飛去。老漢順著鮭魚尾下的水路尋去，見妻子正被一個塌鼻男子在女人成群之屋中求婚；追之不及，回頭一看，屋已化作鷗丘，眾女皆化為鷗。

sensitivity.note: Animal-wife type; parallels Rasmussen's vixen tale and Rink tale 8's bird-husbands reversed. Swan-maiden motif.

passages.text: An old bachelor used to amuse himself by playing with skulls of seals, feigning them to be his children: going out kayaking he put them down on the beach, saying, 'Now mind ye be good children, and go straight up to the house!' — and finding them in the same place on his return, cried out, 'Ye seem to be all deaf and dumb; did not I tell ye to keep off from the water before I set off?' Then taking hold of one of the heads he threw it into the sea, 'Look, there's your little brother fallen into the water!' Another time, feeling himself very sad and lonely, he ran far away into the country and fell in with a great many women bathing in a lake. An idea seized him; noiselessly he stole away to where they had put their clothes, securing those belonging to the one he thought the prettiest, and stepped boldly forward. The women hastened back to their clothes, and having put them on immediately changed into birds and flew away; only she who had been robbed of her clothes remained behind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一个老单身汉常拿海豹的头骨玩耍取乐，把它们当作自己的孩子：他划着皮艇出门时，把它们放在海滩上，说道：『你们这些孩子要乖乖的，径直回家去！』——回来时见它们仍在原处，便嚷道：『你们好像又聋又哑；我不是吩咐过你们，在我出发之前别靠近水边吗？』随后他抓起其中一个头骨扔进海里，说：『瞧，你们的小兄弟掉进水里了！』又有一次，他感到十分悲伤孤独，便远远跑到乡野里去，遇见许多女人在一个湖里沐浴。他心生一计，悄悄溜到她们放衣服的地方，把自认为最漂亮的那个女人的衣服藏了起来，然后大胆地走上前去。那些女人急忙奔回自己的衣服旁，穿上衣服立刻变成鸟飞走了；只有那个被夺去衣服的女人留了下来。

passages.text: The bachelor went straight up to her, asking whether she would like to be his wife, and in return she said, 'Yes, thou mayst take me if thou likest, only give me my clothes.' She got them, but he kept hold of her lest she too should fly; dressed, he took her home and married her. Next morning he did not venture out in his kayak for fear she might take flight, giving up kayaking altogether until one day she declared, 'Now thou mayst leave me without fear, for I do really love thee, and thou mayst depend upon me' — and then he again began to go out seal-hunting. She begat a son, then another, and afterwards no more children. Walking with them, she would admonish them to gather bird wings and feathers, saying, 'Children, ye are akin to birds.' On a certain day she fastened a pair of these wings upon one of the boys, who was at once changed into a sea-fowl and flew away; she did the same to his brother, and last of all put on wings herself and followed them in the shape of a sea-fowl. When the old husband came home he found neither wife nor children, at which he grew very sad; he did not cease going out in his kayak, although he no more chased seals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那名單身漢逕直走到她面前，問她是否願意做他的妻子，她回答說：「好，你若喜歡，盡可娶我，只是把我的衣裳還給我。」她拿回了衣裳，但他仍緊緊抓住她，唯恐她也飛走；待她穿戴整齊，他便帶她回家，娶了她。翌日清晨，他不敢划著皮艇出海，唯恐她會飛走，索性完全放棄了划皮艇，直到有一天她宣稱：「如今你盡可放心離開我，因為我真心愛你，你盡可信任我。」——此後他才又開始出海獵捕海豹。她為他生下一個兒子，接著又生了一個，之後便再無子女。與孩子們一同散步時，她總會叮囑他們去撿拾鳥的翅膀與羽毛，說道：「孩子們，你們與鳥類同宗。」某一天，她將這樣一對翅膀縛在其中一個男孩身上，那男孩立刻化作一隻海鳥飛走了；她對他的兄弟也如法炮製，最後自己也裝上翅膀，化作海鳥的模樣跟隨他們而去。那年邁的丈夫回到家中，發現妻子與孩子都不見了，為此十分悲傷；他並未停止划皮艇出海，儘管他再也不追捕海豹了。

passages.text: One day he put in close to a sand-hill, left his kayak on the beach, crossed the hill, and went a good way into the country, where he saw a man with his back turned towards him working at a piece of timber with his axe, the lower parts of his body visibly trembling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他將皮艇靠攏一座沙丘，把皮艇留在灘上，翻過沙丘，深入內陸走了好一段路，在那裡他看見一個男人背對著他，正用斧頭砍削一塊木料，那人的下半身明顯地顫抖著。

passages.text: 'From what side art thou drawing nigh?' 'I am coming against thee.' 'If thou hadst come from behind, I should have killed thee on the spot.' The old man offered his new kayak, then his new axe, for news of three persons; the woodworker bade him: 'Go and sit down on the tail of a salmon in yonder river; but when thou hearest the voices of children, mind thou don't open thine eyes!' Carried along by a rapid current with eyes shut, he heard children crying 'Alas, our father is nigh!' and the mother answering, 'Lo, we left your father without any means of conveying him hither' — but the children repeated, 'Our father is coming.' On shore he went to a house with fine windows, its inmates all women, his wife sitting close to the back wall and opposite her a man with a pug-nose constantly repeating, 'Wilt thou not marry me?' — 'No, I have already got another husband.' When the pug-nosed fellow had left also, the old man made an attempt to take his wife back; but she quickly followed the other out, and while he pursued her she was transformed into a gull, as were also the rest of the women; the pug-nosed man was changed into a wild-duck — and when the discarded husband turned round, he saw that the house had been transformed into a gulls-hill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 12 'The Man who mated himself with a Sea-fowl'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「你是從哪一邊靠近的？」「我是迎面朝你而來的。」「你若從背後而來，我當場就把你殺了。」老人先後拿出他的新皮艇、又拿出他的新斧頭，只為換取三個人的消息；那木匠吩咐他道：「去，坐到那邊河裡一尾鮭魚的尾巴上；但當你聽見孩子們的聲音時，切記不可睜開眼睛！」他被湍急的水流帶著前行，閉著雙眼，聽見孩子們喊著：「哎呀，我們的父親就在附近了！」而母親回答說：「瞧，我們撇下你們的父親，沒給他留下任何前來此地的法子。」——但孩子們一再重複：「我們的父親來了。」上岸後，他來到一棟窗戶精美的屋子，屋裡盡是女人，他的妻子緊靠後牆坐著，她對面是一個塌鼻子的男人，那男人不斷重複著：「你難道不願嫁給我嗎？」——「不，我已經有另一個丈夫了。」待那塌鼻子的傢伙也離去後，老人試圖把妻子帶回去；但她迅速跟著另一個男人出去了，他追趕她時，她化作了一隻海鷗，其餘的女人也同樣化作海鷗；那塌鼻子的男人則化作了一隻野鴨——而當那被拋棄的丈夫轉過身來，他看見那棟屋子已化作一座海鷗丘。

title.en: The Barren Wife and Kujavarsuk the Ten-Seal Hunter
title.zh: 不孕之婦與十豹獵手庫亞瓦舒克

region.en: West Greenland coast and birds-cliff
region.zh: 西格陵蘭沿岸與鳥崖

period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from three copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A magician-fisherman's prescription — a bird from the birds-cliff for an amulet, an unsunned black hollow stone, and his grandmother's collar-bone from the grave — wins the childless couple a son, Kujavarsuk, destined always to take ten seals a day. When the sea closes to one lead, the beads-tempted angakok-woman Igdlutsialik's daughter descends three days to conciliate the old Arnarkuagssak of the sea-bottom and the ice breaks up; but the mother's brother, cheated of his brisket, fashions a many-shaped tupilak against the boy — which, beaten by the amulet-bird, turns on its maker and devours him in his kayak, leaving Kujavarsuk to die at a very old age.
summary.zh: 漁巫開出藥方：鳥崖取鳥為護身符、取未見日光的黑色空心石、再取祖母墓中鎖骨——不孕夫婦遂得子庫亞瓦舒克，命中註定日得十豹。海冰封死之際，貪珠串的巫女沉海三日，馴服海底老嫗阿納庫阿克薩克，堅冰乃解。然而被剋扣胸肉的舅舅懷恨，以百獸之骨捏成百變圖皮拉克加害外甥；怪物被護身鳥啄傷羞怒，反噬其主，把他連人帶艇翻入海中吞食——庫亞瓦舒克自此安享天年。

sensitivity.note: Arnarkuagssak is the Greenlandic sea-mother (Sedna-figure); cross-ref sedna-sea-mother and inuit-nerrivik-sea-ruler. Rink appends a Kujavarsuk whale-fishery variant (namesake competition, whale close to shore) not cut separately.

passages.text: A man had a wife who begat him no children; envious of all the people who had children, he one day told her to make herself trim and nice and walk to the fishing-place of an old man who had given up seal-hunting — an old man who was a great magician. Afraid of her husband, he would not approach her, and she returned; the husband himself then promised him half his catch if he could think of some means to get children. From that day the husband always put by half the seals he caught for the old man; noticing his wife was enceinte, he asked the old man to take up his abode in their house, and he rejoined: 'Thy wife will bear thee a son. To-morrow when thou goest out kayaking thou must row to the birds-cliff and get hold of a bird, which he shall use for an amulet' — then a hollow black stone on which the sun had never shone, and finally his grandmother's collar-bone from her grave. When all these things had been gathered, the wife brought forth a son, named Kujavarsuk by the old man, the stone put close to his feet and the bird stuck up above the window.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個男人娶了一個妻子，卻未能為他生下子女；他嫉妒所有有子女的人，有一天便叫妻子打扮得整齊漂亮，走到一個已放棄獵捕海豹的老人那兒去——那老人是個法力高強的大巫師。他畏懼她的丈夫，不敢靠近她，她便回去了；此後丈夫親自向那老人許諾，若能想出法子讓他得子，便將自己漁獲的一半分給他。從那天起，丈夫總是把他捕到的海豹留下一半分給那老人；他察覺妻子有了身孕，便請那老人住到他們家中，老人回答說：「你的妻子將為你生下一個兒子。明日你划皮艇出海時，須划到鳥崖那兒，抓住一隻鳥，他將以此作為護身符。」——接著是一塊太陽從未照過的黑色空心石，最後是他祖母墳中取出的鎖骨。待這些東西都齊備之後，妻子生下了一個兒子，老人為他取名庫亞瓦爾蘇克（Kujavarsuk），那塊石頭被放在他腳邊，那隻鳥則被豎立在窗戶上方。

passages.text: The old man told the father to provide a kayak fitted up with all requisites for the hunt as soon as the boy could use it; even before the covering skins had dried it was put in the water and the boy shoved off the beach. 'The very first time he goes out, one of the quiet seals will rise to the surface, and he shall not return home till he has captured ten of them; and in future he will always get ten seals whenever he goes out kayaking.' The old man and father followed him closely, and a seal popped its head above the water; he paddled on and harpooned it, the old man quite transported, and from that time the boy began to hunt. Grown up, he took two wives and became of great use to his house-fellows and neighbours — in times of need their only provider. One winter the sea froze very early, leaving only one opening right in front of their dwelling-place, out of which he got his ten seals every day; later the cleft narrowed until his kayak touched the edge with both ends, and at last it altogether closed up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 老人吩咐那父親，一等男孩能使喚皮艇，便備好一艘配齊一切狩獵所需之物的皮艇；甚至連蒙皮的皮子都還沒乾，皮艇就被放入水中，男孩被推離了灘岸。「他頭一回出海，便會有一隻安靜的海豹浮上水面，他不捕到十隻便不得回家；今後他每次划皮艇出海，總能捕到十隻海豹。」老人與父親緊隨其後，一隻海豹把頭探出水面；他繼續划槳，以魚叉刺中了牠，老人欣喜若狂，從那時起男孩便開始狩獵。長大成人後，他娶了兩個妻子，對同屋之人與鄰里大有助益——在困厄之時，他們唯一的供養者便是他。某年冬天，海面很早就結了冰，只留下一處正好在他們住所前方的開口，他每日便從那兒捕得他的十隻海豹；後來那裂口越縮越窄，直到他的皮艇兩端都抵住了邊緣，最後終於完全封合。

passages.text: Great perplexity came over the people, who deliberated whether it would not be necessary to call in an angakok: someone mentioned that in the summer he had seen the widow Igdlutsialik's daughter practising the angakok art in a lake. Kujavarsuk sent a messenger to offer her a large seal-skin if she would make the ice break up; she declined, refusing clothes and lamps too, until someone brought her a handful of beads that took her fancy. Putting on her summer dress, she walked down to the water-side and disappeared among the loose ice-blocks; she remained in the depths of the ocean for three days, and at the bottom of the sea had a struggle with the old woman — the arnarkuagssak of Eskimo mythology — to make her let loose the animals of the sea, which she purposely detained and kept swimming about underneath her lamp. Having managed to conciliate her, she returned to the earth on the evening of the third day, letting the people know she wanted every other seal caught — those with the most beautiful skin as well as the common fiord seals — for herself. On the following morning at dawn the ice broke up and an opening appeared near the houses; each man soon caught two seals, but Kujavarsuk as usual got ten, which made the others very jealous.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾人陷入了極大的困惑，商議著是否非得請一位巫師（angakok）前來不可：有人提到，他在夏天曾看見寡婦伊格德盧齊亞利克（Igdlutsialik）的女兒在一個湖裡演練巫術。庫亞瓦爾蘇克派了一名使者前去，許以一大張海豹皮，請她設法讓冰層裂開；她拒絕了，連衣裳與燈也一併推辭，直到有人送來一把合她心意的珠子。她換上夏裝，走到水邊，消失在浮冰之間；她在海洋深處待了三天，在海底與那老婦人——愛斯基摩神話中的阿爾納夸格薩克（arnarkuagssak）——搏鬥，要她放出海中的生靈，那老婦人故意扣留牠們，讓牠們在她的燈下不停游動。設法安撫了她之後，她在第三日傍晚回到地面，讓眾人知道她想要每隔一隻捕獲的海豹——那些皮毛最美的，以及普通的峽灣海豹——都歸她所有。翌日破曉時分，冰層裂開，屋舍附近出現了一處開口；每個人很快都捕到了兩隻海豹，但庫亞瓦爾蘇克一如往常捕得了十隻，這讓其他人十分嫉妒。

passages.text: One day his wives had only put by a piece of the back instead of the briskets for his mother's brother, expected home later in the evening; offended at the want of consideration, he resolved to make, by help of sorcery, a tupilak for Kujavarsuk. Gathering bones of all sorts of animals, he fashioned it so it could take the shape of different animals, birds as well as seals, and having stirred them into life, let it loose with orders to persecute Kujavarsuk. Diving into the sea it appeared in the shape of a seal, but he was already on his way home drawing his kayak on the shore — the same on the second and third day. It then determined to pursue him to his house and frighten him to death: transforming itself into a toogdlik (the great northern diver), it commenced shrieking outside the house; Kujavarsuk went out but could not be brought to look at it, so the charm would not work. Going underground to pop up into the room, it succeeded no better; rising at the back of the house, just as it was about to climb up the roof it met his own amulet-bird, which at once set about picking and scratching its face. Turning desperate — 'Why did this miserable fool of a man ever make me!' — in the height of its wrath it turned against its maker: diving into the water near his fishing-place, it emerged right beneath his kayak, fairly upsetting it, and devoured him on the spot, then fled far away out on the roaring ocean. Kujavarsuk afterwards remained unmolested and died at a very old age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 13 'The Barren Wife'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他的妻子們只留下一塊背部的肉，而沒有為他母親的兄弟留下胸肉，那人本預計當晚稍晚回家；他因這份欠缺體貼而心生不滿，決意藉助巫術，為庫亞瓦爾蘇克造一個圖皮拉克。他收集各種動物的骨頭，將其塑造成能化為不同動物——鳥類與海豹皆可——的形貌，並使之活轉過來，然後放它出去，命它去迫害庫亞瓦爾蘇克。它潛入海中，化為海豹之形出現，但他早已在歸家途中，正把皮划艇拖上岸——第二日、第三日亦然。它於是決意追到他家中，將他嚇死：它變身為圖格德利克（大北方潛鳥），開始在屋外尖聲啼叫；庫亞瓦爾蘇克走了出去，卻怎麼也不肯看它一眼，因此咒術無法生效。它鑽入地下，想從屋內冒出，也未能得逞；它從屋後升起，正當它要爬上屋頂時，遇上了他自己的護身鳥，那鳥立刻啄抓它的臉。它走投無路——「這可憐的蠢人為何要造出我來！」——在盛怒之下，它轉而對付造它的人：它潛入他捕魚處附近的水中，正好從他的皮划艇底下冒出，將艇徹底掀翻，當場把他吞食，然後遠遁到咆哮的大洋之上。庫亞瓦爾蘇克此後再未受侵擾，活到極老才去世。

title.en: The Two Brothers and the Supernatural Boat
title.zh: 兩兄弟與幽靈之舟

region.en: Fiord mouth, sunny and shady shores, West Greenland
region.zh: 西格陵蘭峽灣口的陽岸與陰岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; compiled from four manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A servant-girl, frozen speechless by the sight, watches an umiariak — a supernatural boat manned with fabulous beings — land glittering-sworded people who spear a tent through from all sides and leave all its inmates dead; the seals move out to sea with the water foaming. The surviving brother suspects her until he sees the pierced tent, then has an angakok spy the enemies far inland; guided by a one-eyed inlander whose shouts conjure three bears and then a multitude of archers, he hides behind his protector until the arrows abate, overtakes and kills the whole enemy party, and is repaid with renowned white-streaked reindeer skins carried home faster than he can follow.
summary.zh: 僕女目睹幽靈之舟——奇異生物駕駛、閃刀者登岸——將帳篷四面戳穿、殺盡居民，海豹隨泡沫奔海。倖存的弟弟起初疑心僕女行兇，見了洞穿的帳篷才釋疑；遂請巫師遙望，敵蹤遠在內陸。獨眼內陸人引路，一聲呼喚召出三熊、再呼喚召出弓箭大軍；弟弟藏於其身後，箭雨漸歇，二人追殺敵眾至一個不留。獨眼人看中他的魚叉，以斑紋白鹿皮相易；小婦人負皮疾奔，先他而抵，把鹿皮置於屋頂——他從此心安。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note: the umiariak is the avenging boat of seals overkilled; the inlanders may echo the Loucheux ('squint-eyes') Indians, described as arrow-proof by a movement of the eyes. Killed household recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Two brothers lived in the mouth of a fiord, the elder on the sunny side of the inlet, the other on the shady side. One night the servant of the younger brother, going behind the house, suddenly perceived something bright glittering out on the sea, and detected a boat that seemed to grow in size as it approached — an umiariak, a supernatural boat manned with fabulous beings. She wanted to run but was not able to stir; she tried to call out but could not utter a sound, and so must needs keep quiet. She saw a number of people land, all carrying glittering swords, walk straight up to the tent, and stick their spears through it from all sides; loud cries were heard from within, and the foreigners rushed down to their boat. She saw the water foaming and a multitude of seals moving out seawards, and was not able to rise till they were quite out of sight. Then she went to the tent, where she found all the inmates killed, and the earth covered with blood; though it was still dark she could not wait, but set off at once and wandered ever so far round the whole bay to reach the opposite shore where the other brother lived, and told him all her housemates had been put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩兄弟住在一個峽灣的灣口，兄長住在水灣向陽的一側，弟弟住在背陰的一側。一天夜裡，弟弟的僕人走到屋後，忽然看見海面上有東西閃閃發亮，並發現一隻船隨著靠近似乎越變越大——那是一艘烏米亞利亞克，一艘載著神話生靈的超自然之船。她想跑，卻動彈不得；她想呼喊，卻發不出半點聲音，只得默不作聲。她看見一群人上了岸，個個手持閃亮的刀劍，徑直走向帳篷，從四面把長矛刺進帳中；裡面傳出響亮的叫喊，那些外來者便衝回他們的船上。她看見海水翻騰，一大群海豹向海外游去，直到它們完全消失不見，她才得以起身。隨後她走到帳篷，發現裡面的人全被殺死，地上滿是血跡；雖然天還黑著，她卻等不下去，立刻動身，繞著整個海灣走了極遠的路，才到達對岸另一兄弟居住的地方，告訴他所有同屋的人都被殺害了。

passages.text: Somehow he got suspicious, believing she herself had killed them; seeing this, she merely said, 'First go and look for thyself, and afterward thou mayst kill me if thou likest.' He went across to his brother's station, and when he had seen the tent pierced from all sides he was reassured with regard to the servant, and only thought of finding out the enemies. He bespoke an angakok to come and point them out to him: at night, lamps extinguished, the angakok spoke, 'Look there; far away in the interior of the land, I espy them.' The next day the surviving brother paddled to the fiord head, left his kayak, and walked inland armed only with his spear until he discovered a house; stealing to the window he beheld a man with only one eye busily carving some implement out of wood, who caught sight of the stranger and invited him in — motioning him off a little, 'Don't sit quite so close to me; I might happen to cut thee.' A loud peal of laughter followed, and from beneath the ledge emerged a lot of narrajut (big-bellied), the only womankind of his household, returning with great quantities of meat, chiefly reindeer flesh and tallow. 'To-morrow I will go with thee and help thee to find out thy enemies, but now thou must lie down to rest here; thou hast nothing to fear.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不知怎的，他起了疑心，認為是她自己殺了那些人；見此情形，她只說道：「你先自己去看看吧，之後你若願意，盡可殺我。」他渡過水灣到兄弟的住處，當他看到帳篷四面被刺穿，便對那僕人放了心，只想著要找出那些敵人。他請來一位安加科克，請他為自己指出敵人的所在：夜裡，燈火熄滅，那安加科克說道：「看那邊；在陸地深處很遠的地方，我瞧見了他們。」第二天，那倖存的兄弟划槳到峽灣盡頭，留下皮划艇，只帶著長矛徒步深入內陸，直到發現一座房屋；他悄悄走到窗邊，看見一個只有一隻眼睛的人正忙著用木頭雕刻某件器具，那人瞧見了這陌生人，便邀他進屋——同時稍稍示意他退開些，「別坐得離我這麼近；我可能會不小心割到你。」接著響起一陣大笑，從壁架下鑽出一大群納拉尤特（大肚者），那是他家中僅有的女眷，帶著大量肉食歸來，主要是馴鹿肉和油脂。「明天我跟你一起去，幫你找出你的敵人，但現在你得在這裡躺下歇息；你沒什麼好怕的。」

passages.text: Next day the one-eyed man followed him, taking a large bunch of arrows fitted up in a skin cover, walking so quickly his companion could hardly keep up. Stopping, he put his arrows on the ground and said, 'Turn thy face towards the interior and give a shout'; the brother cried out aloud without knowing why, and three large bears instantly appeared — the one-eyed man aimed his bow and killed them all. 'Turn round and call as before!' — and a multitude of people appeared, armed with bows and arrows. Dreadfully frightened, he was told, 'Go and hide behind me; but mind, as soon as thou puttest forth thy head they'll shoot thee,' and sheltering behind his protector, trembling all the while, he saw the arrows flying right and left, decreasing in number, and finally abating altogether — the enemies having discharged all their arrows had taken flight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，那獨眼人跟隨他同行，帶著一大捆裝在皮套裡的箭，走得極快，他的同伴幾乎跟不上。他停下來，把箭放在地上說道：「把臉轉向內陸，大喊一聲」；那兄弟不知為何便放聲大喊，三隻大熊立刻出現——獨眼人瞄準他的弓，把它們全都射死。「轉過身去，像剛才那樣呼喊！」——於是一大群人出現了，個個手持弓箭。他嚇得要命，卻被告知：「去躲到我身後；但記住，你一探出頭，他們就會射你。」他躲在他的保護者身後，一直渾身發抖，看著箭矢左右飛射，數目漸減，最後完全止息——那些敵人射光了所有的箭，便逃走了。

passages.text: The one-eyed man took up his bow, the still revengeful brother his spear, and both set off in pursuit, overtaking and killing the whole of them. On the way home the inlander noticed his companion's weapon, questioned him, never having seen the like before, and told him he would like very much to purchase it — and because of his handsome behaviour he had his wish. On their return they went together to his storehouse, and he was repaid with the renowned sea-hare skin (white reindeer skins with black streaks), one of the little women called to take them down: she put the bundle on her stomach and ran so fast with it that the visitor could not keep pace with her. Reaching home, he found them put on the roof of his house, and from that time his mind was at rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 14 'The Two Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獨眼人拿起他的弓，那仍懷復仇之心的兄弟拿起他的長矛，兩人一同出發追擊，追上並殺光了他們所有人。歸途中，那內陸人注意到同伴的武器，便問起他，因為他從未見過這樣的東西，並告訴他自己非常想買下它——由於他為人慷慨得體，他如願以償。他們回來後，一同前往他的儲藏屋，他以著名的海兔皮（帶黑色條紋的白色馴鹿皮）作為回報，其中一個小婦人被喚來把這些皮取下來：她把那捆皮放在肚子上，跑得飛快，那訪客怎麼也跟不上她。回到家中，他發現那些皮已被放到他屋頂上，從那時起，他的心便安定了下來。

title.en: Mula Jadi Na Bolon: The Batak Creation and the Naga Padoha Beneath
title.zh: 穆拉·賈迪·納·波隆：巴塔克創世與地下那伽

region.en: Toba Batak country and Mount Pusuk Buhit, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘多巴巴塔克之地與普素·布希山

period: Batak cosmogonic tradition recorded by H. N. van der Tuuk (J.R.A.S., N.S. vol. XIII, 1860s) and later ethnography

source.work: Batak cosmogonic tradition (Mula Jadi Na Bolon; Batara Guru's raft; Naga Padoha), as recorded in van der Tuuk's Batak studies

summary.en: In the beginning was Mula Jadi Na Bolon, 'the origin of becoming,' alone in the void; he creates the three levels of the world and three sons to rule them. The middle world is spread as dry land over the primeval waters — supported, the Toba Batak say, on the raft Batara Guru made at the creation, and held upon the back of the underworld serpent Naga Padoha, whose stirrings are the earthquakes.
summary.zh: 太初有『形成之源』穆拉·賈迪·納·波隆，獨存於虛空；他造世界三層，並生三子以分掌之。中界乃鋪於原水之上之乾土——多巴巴塔克人說：大地枕於巴塔拉·古魯創世時所造之筏上，臥於地下巨蛇那伽·帕多哈之背；蛇之一動，即為地震。

sensitivity.note: Batak cosmogony; the raft detail is cited by Skeat (1900) from the J.R.A.S. Batak material; paraphrase of the standard telling.

canonical_translation: Based on the standard Batak cosmogonic account (van der Tuuk tradition); paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Batak cosmogony recorded in the great Batak studies of the nineteenth century tells how the world rests on agreements made in the deep past — and on a serpent who never agreed to them.

BEGINNING: THE ALONE ONE. Before everything was Mula Jadi Na Bolon, 'the origin of becoming,' alone in space, without companion or material. From his own substance he brings forth the framework of the cosmos in three levels — the upper world of the gods, the middle world of men, and the underworld of the dead and the powers below — and then three sons, to whom he allots these levels: Batara Guru in the highest, Sori Deak in the middle, and Mangalabulan below.

MIDDLE: THE RAFT AND THE SERPENT. The middle world is made habitable by spreading dry earth over the primeval waters; the earth rests, in the standard telling, on a raft which Batara Guru made for its support at the creation (the detail Skeat quotes from the J.R.A.S. Batak material). Beneath everything lies Naga Padoha, the great serpent of the underworld, on whose back the world-raft rides; when the serpent stirs — cramped, offended, or simply tired — the earth shakes, and the Batak offerings must remind him of his charge.

END: THE GRANDDAUGHTER'S DESCENT. To people the middle world, the line of the high god descends: Batara Guru's daughter (in the standard account the granddaughter of Mula Jadi Na Bolon) is sent down to the middle world and becomes the ancestress of mankind there; her descendants people the Toba highlands around the great lake, and the first of them, Si Raja Batak, is born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit. The three-level cosmos thus becomes a genealogy: the Batak live between the gods above and the serpent below, related to both.

FUNCTIONS. The cosmogony (1) explains the vertical order of the Batak universe and the places of ritual speech; (2) etiologizes earthquakes as the serpent's movement beneath the raft; (3) grounds the clans (marga) in a divine descent tied to Pusuk Buhit; and (4) supplies the world-serpent cluster's Sumatran highland form. The serpent's office is the cosmology's hinge: Naga Padoha is not a rebel to be defeated but a bearer to be maintained, and the Batak ritual address to him is contractual — offerings remind the serpent of the charge accepted at the creation, and earthquakes are read as arrears. The raft, likewise, is not merely a platform but a covenant-object: the world sits on something made, and made things can be renegotiated. To people the middle world, Batara Guru's daughter descends, and the genealogy that follows is the Batak system in miniature: the clans of the Toba country trace their marga to Si Raja Batak, born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit beside the lake, so that the cosmology's vertical levels — gods above, serpent below — are connected by a family tree running through the mountain's slopes. The story is told at both weddings and funerals, where the two directions of the vertical axis are invoked in turn.
narrative.zh: 十九世紀巴塔克研究記錄之創世論講述世界如何依遠古之約而安——以及一條從未應約之蛇。開篇：先有『形成之源』穆拉·賈迪·納·波隆，獨存無伴無材；自其本質生出三層宇宙（神之上界、人之中界、亡者與下方之力之下界），並生三子分掌：巴塔拉·古魯居最高，梭裏·迪亞克居中，芒加拉布蘭居下。中段：以乾土鋪於原水而使中界宜居；標準敘述云：地枕於巴塔拉·古魯創世時所造之筏（斯凱特引自J.R.A.S.巴塔克材料）；而萬物之下，臥著下界巨蛇那伽·帕多哈，世界之筏騎於其背；蛇一動（或拘、或怒、或倦），大地便震，巴塔克之祭品須提醒它記其職守。結尾：神裔降中界生民：巴塔拉·古魯之女（標準敘述中為穆拉之孫女）受遣下凡，成為人類之祖；其後裔繁於大湖周圍之多巴高地，其首者西·拉賈·巴塔克生於聖山普素·布希。三層宇宙於是成為譜系：巴塔克人上承諸神、下繫巨蛇，與兩界皆有血緣。功能：釋宇宙縱序與儀式語言之位、釋地震為筏下之蛇之動、以神裔繫氏族於聖山、並為世界蛇母題供給蘇門答臘高地之形態。

functions: Explains the three-level vertical cosmos of Batak ritual speech
Etiologizes earthquakes as the stirring of Naga Padoha beneath the world-raft
Grounds the Batak clans (marga) in divine descent tied to Mount Pusuk Buhit
Sumatran highland form of the world-serpent motif cluster

passages.zh: 起初，唯有穆拉·賈迪·納·博隆，即「生成之源」，獨處於虛空之中；他從自身的實體中生出世界的三個層次和三個兒子——上界的巴塔拉·古魯、中界的索里·德阿克、下界的曼加拉布蘭。

passages.text: The middle world is spread as dry earth over the primeval waters, resting on the raft which Batara Guru made for its support at the creation; beneath all lies the underworld serpent Naga Padoha, on whose back the raft rides, and whose stirrings are the earthquakes that offerings must soothe. The daughter of Batara Guru descends to people the middle world, and her line culminates in Si Raja Batak, born on the holy mountain Pusuk Buhit — the Batak living related to the gods above and the serpent below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the standard Batak account (raft detail as cited in Skeat 1900 from the J.R.A.S. Batak material); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the standard Batak account; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 中間世界如乾燥的陸地般鋪展於原初之水上方，安放在巴塔拉·古魯於創世時為支撐它所造的筏上；一切之下伏著冥界巨蛇納迦·帕多哈，筏便行於其背上，而牠的翻動即是地震，必須以獻祭安撫。巴塔拉·古魯之女降臨以繁衍中間世界，其血脈終結於聖山普蘇克·布希特上所生的西·拉賈·巴塔克——巴塔克人因此與上方的諸神及下方的巨蛇皆有親緣。

title.en: The Origin of Lake Toba: The Fisherman Who Broke the Taboo
title.zh: 多巴湖之由來：破禁的漁夫

region.en: Lake Toba and Samosir island, North Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘多巴湖與沙摩西島

period: Toba Batak oral legend; recorded in 19th-20th century collections

source.archive: Indonesian oral tradition (Toba Batak legend cycle)
source.work: The legend of the origin of Lake Toba (Toba Batak oral tradition)

summary.en: The fisherman who casts his hook into the Toba valley catches a golden fish that becomes a woman; he marries her on one condition — that he never tell anyone she was once a fish. Years later, in anger at his son, he breaks the promise; that night the sky darkens, the rains fall without end, the valley sinks, and the wife returns to the water: the drowned valley is Lake Toba, and the island where she set down her son in the flood is Samosir.
summary.zh: 漁夫在多巴谷地垂釣，釣上一尾化為女子之金魚；他娶之，唯一條件：永不可對人言其曾為魚。多年後，他怒於其子而破誓；當夜天昏雨瀉不止，谷地下陷，妻子歸水——被淹之谷是多巴湖，而她在洪水中放下兒子之處，便是沙摩西島。

sensitivity.note: Best-known Toba Batak legend; taboo-broken-flood cluster.

canonical_translation: Based on the Toba Batak oral legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The origin legend of Lake Toba is the Toba Batak's great taboo-broken catastrophe story, told to explain the largest volcanic lake on earth and the island in its middle.

BEGINNING: THE GOLDEN FISH. A fisherman works the small rivers of the Toba valley and one day hooks a fish of golden shine; it speaks, and becomes a woman of great beauty. He marries her on her one condition: that he never tell anyone where she came from — that she was a fish of the water. They live well, and she bears a son.

MIDDLE: THE BROKEN SECRET. The boy grows hungry and greedy at meals, and one day the father, exhausted and furious, shouts the secret at him: 'You eat like the child of a fish — for your mother was a fish!' The word is out; the fish-wife hears it and grieves, for the promise that kept the world ordered is broken.

END: THE FLOODING OF THE VALLEY. That night the sky closes; rain falls without pause, and the waters rise from the earth as well as the sky. The wife returns to the water that made her, taking to safety the son she sets on the high ground that will become the island of Samosir; the father's valley floods entire. What had been fields and villages becomes Lake Toba, and the headland opposite Samosir keeps the father's name in the local tellings — the taboo's price still visible in the landscape.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) etiologizes Lake Toba and Samosir island; (2) polices the marriage-tell-no-origin taboo that governs many Batak affinity relationships; (3) supplies the Malay-world flood cluster with its highland Sumatran form; and (4) ties the landscape's topography to a moral memory told on every school trip to the lake. The legend's landscape is precise and checkable: Lake Toba fills a vast volcanic caldera, and Samosir is the island in its middle; the tellings align the boy's refuge with Samosir's high ground and keep the father's memory in the headland opposite. The moral architecture is equally exact: the fish-wife's single condition is the classic affinity taboo of the Batak world, in which a marriage partner's origin must not be named, and the father's breach is not mere anger but the public unmaking of the marriage's fiction — the word spoken aloud costs the world its surface. Village tellings distribute the blame variously: in some the son provokes the outburst, in others neighbours demand the secret, in others the father boasts; the flood follows the word, not the speaker. As comparative material, the legend belongs to the taboo-broken-flood cluster — Deucalion's flood, the sinking-village tales of Sundanese Situ Bagendit — with the distinctive feature that the survivor is the child of the taboo-breaker and the flood the return of the tabooed parent to her element.
narrative.zh: 多巴湖由來傳說乃多巴巴塔克最大之破禁災變故事，用以解釋世上最大火山湖及其中央之島。開篇：漁夫於多巴谷小河垂釣，一日釣得金光之魚；魚能言，化為美貌女子。他娶她，但只有一個條件：永不說出她的來歷——她本是水中之魚。二人生活美滿，得一子。中段：兒子進餐貪饞；一日父親疲憊憤怒，衝口而出：『你吃得像魚之子——因你母親本是魚！』誓言既破，魚妻聞言而悲——維持世界秩序的承諾已斷。結尾：當夜天閉，雨瀉不止，水自地中亦湧；妻子歸於其所從來之水，攜子置於高地——即日後之沙摩西島；父親的谷地盡沒。昔日田舍化為多巴湖，沙摩西對岸之岬在當地敘述中仍保留父親之名——禁忌之價，至今顯於山水。功能：釋多巴湖與沙摩西島、規訓巴塔克姻親之『勿言來歷』禁忌、為馬來世界洪水母題群供給蘇門答臘高地之形態、並將地貌與道德記憶繫於湖畔之講述。

Policing the tell-no-origin taboo that governs Batak affinity marriages

Topography as moral memory in the landscape of the lake
