sensitivity_guidance: Colonial-era collection (1912); Bornean Dayak communities hold the heritage — paraphrase only, no verbatim ritual text.

passages.text: In the beginning there was a barren rock. On this the rains fell and gave rise to moss, and the worms, aided by the dung-beetles, made soil by their castings. Then a sword-handle came down from the sun and became a large tree. From the moon came a creeper, which hanging from the tree became mated with it through the action of the wind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kayan creation myth in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初只有一塊光禿的岩石。雨水落在其上，生出了苔蘚，而蠕蟲在蜣螂的幫助下，以其排泄物造出了土壤。接著，一個劍柄從太陽降下，變成了一棵大樹。從月亮來了一條藤蔓，它懸掛在樹上，藉著風的作用與樹交合。

passages.text: From this union were born Kaluban Gai and Kalubi Angai, the first human beings, male and female; these were incomplete, lacking the legs and lower half of their trunks, so that their entrails hung loose and exposed. Leaves falling from the tree became the various species of birds and winged insects, and from the fallen fruits sprang the four-footed beasts; resin oozing from the trunk gave rise to the domestic pig and fowl, distinguished by their understanding of matters hidden from all others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kayan creation myth; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 由這結合生出了卡魯班·蓋與卡魯比·安蓋，即最初的人類，一男一女；他們並不完整，缺少雙腿和軀幹的下半部，以致內臟鬆垂外露。從樹上落下的葉子變成了各種鳥類和有翅昆蟲，從落下的果實中生出了四足野獸；從樹幹滲出的樹脂生出了家豬和家禽，牠們因通曉其他一切生物所不知的隱秘之事而與眾不同。

passages.text: The incomplete first humans produced Pengok Ngai and Katira Murei; Katira Murei bore Batang Uta Tatai, who married Ajai Avai and begot the five progenitors of the existing peoples — the Kayans, Kenyahs and some Klemantans claiming Oding Lahang, the Sebops and Punans claiming Tokong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kayan creation myth; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那不完整的最初人類生出了彭戈克·蓋與卡蒂拉·穆雷；卡蒂拉·穆雷生了巴唐·烏塔·塔泰，他娶了阿賈伊·阿瓦伊，生出了現存各民族的五位始祖——卡揚人、肯雅人和一些克萊曼坦人自稱出自奧丁·拉杭，塞博普人和普南人則自稱出自托孔。

title.en: The Frog's Advice: Tokong and the Charter of Head-Hunting
title.zh: 青蛙之諫：托貢與獵首之憲章

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

period: Kayan/Klemantan myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the Tokong story

summary.en: Preparing to attack a village, Tokong is hailed by a frog crying 'cut through the neck.' The people, who had taken only their enemies' hair to adorn their shields, scoff — until the frog decapitates a small frog to demonstrate, and promises prosperity of every kind. Tokong carries away the heads of his enemies, and as the party returns home the padi grows from knee-high to full ears; head-hunting is adopted from that day as the rite that makes the crops and the household prosper.
summary.zh: 托貢正欲攻村，一蛙呼曰：『斬其頸！』眾人素來只取敵髮飾盾，皆嘲笑之——直至青蛙斬一小蛙以示範，並許諸般繁榮。托貢遂取敵首而歸；歸途經過田中，稻穀自膝高驟長至穗滿。自此獵首成為使莊稼興旺、家宅昌盛之禮。

sensitivity.note: Historical headhunting charter-myth, recorded 1912; presented as ethnographic record of a discontinued practice, framed with care.

passages.text: Once upon a time, when Tokong and his people were preparing to attack a village, he was addressed by the frog, who called out words meaning in the Sebop language 'cut through the neck.' At first the people, who hitherto had taken only the hair of their enemies to adorn their shields, scoffed at this advice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tokong story in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，當托孔（Tokong）與他的族人正準備攻打一座村莊時，青蛙向他開口說話，在塞博普語（Sebop）中喊出意為「砍穿脖子」的話語。起初，族人向來只取敵人的頭髮來裝飾盾牌，對這番建議嗤之以鼻。

passages.text: But the frog assured them that the taking of heads would bring prosperity of every kind, and demonstrated the procedure by decapitating a small frog. Tokong carried away the heads of his enemies, and this was followed immediately by increased prosperity: as the party passed through their fields the padi grew very rapidly, from knee-high to full ears before they had passed through. The words of the frog thus came true, and Tokong and his people continued the new practice, and from them it was learned by others — the charter of the head-hunting rite and its promise of the harvest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Tokong story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但青蛙向他們保證，獵取人頭會帶來各式各樣的興旺，並以小青蛙為例，示範了斬首的過程。托孔帶走了敵人的頭顱，隨即而來的便是日益興旺：當一行人穿過他們的田地時，稻禾生長得極快，在他們尚未走出田地之前，便已從及膝之高長成飽滿的稻穗。青蛙的話於是應驗了，托孔與他的族人繼續奉行這項新習俗，其他人又從他們那裡學得此舉——這便是獵頭儀式的起源，以及它對豐收的許諾。

title.en: Lafaang in the Sky: The Bridegroom Who Lost His Arm
title.zh: 拉方上天：失臂的姐夫

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

period: Long Kiput (Klemantan) star myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the story of Lafaang (Orion)

summary.en: The daughter of Palai (the constellation Pegasus) loves the Long Kiput youth Lafaang and brings him to the sky. Sky custom defeats him at every turn: food taken with fingers instead of a needle, trees that fall when the axe is merely laid at their feet — until a tree felled carelessly cuts off Lafaang's left arm, the very arm missing in the constellation Orion. Disgusted and homesick, he is let down to earth by a creeper with sugar-cane tops and banana roots, hears his newborn child cry as he descends, and plants the gifts in soil instead of throwing them — which is why, the myth says, cane and banana remain inferior wherever they grow, and why Orion still moves overhead, one-armed.
summary.zh: 帕拉伊（飛馬座）之女愛上隆基普青年拉方，引他上天。天界之俗處處敗他：以指代針取食、斧置樹腳樹即自倒——直到一棵粗心砍伐之樹墜落，斬斷拉方左臂——正是獵戶座所缺之臂。他厭倦思鄉，由藤蔓縋回地面，懷中帶著甘蔗梢與香蕉根；下降之際聽見新生兒啼哭而求回頭被拒。他將贈物種入土中而非擲地——神話言：故甘蔗香蕉至今低劣；而獵戶座仍缺臂巡天。

sensitivity.note: Star-myth with bride-taken-to-sky structure; Orion's missing arm fixed etiologically.

passages.text: The daughter of Palai fell in love with a Long Kiput youth, Lafaang, and invited him to ascend to the heavens, warning him that the customs of her celestial home were very different from those of earth. He found it difficult to conform: he put food into his mouth with his fingers instead of using a needle, and felled trees by chopping, when he was merely to lay the axe at their feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lafaang story in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帕萊（Palai）的女兒愛上了一位隆基普特（Long Kiput）青年拉法昂（Lafaang），並邀他升上天界，同時警告他，她天界家鄉的習俗與人間大不相同。他發現自己難以遵從：他用手把食物送進嘴裡，而不用針；他砍伐樹木，而按規矩他只須把斧頭放在樹腳下即可。

passages.text: This breach of custom was punished by the fall of a tree that cut off Lafaang's left arm — the arm wanting in the constellation. Disgusted by these incidents, he made up his mind to return to his own people; his wife let him down to earth by a long creeper, giving him sugar-cane tops and banana roots previously unknown to men, and he heard the cry of his new-born child as he descended but was not allowed to return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lafaang story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這違反習俗之舉招致了懲罰：一棵樹倒下，砍斷了拉法昂的左臂——那正是星座中所缺的那條手臂。他對這些遭遇深感厭惡，決心回到自己的族人那裡；他的妻子用一條長藤把他放回人間，給了他人類前所未見的甘蔗梢與香蕉根，他在下降途中聽見自己新生兒的哭聲，卻不被允許回去。

passages.text: Told to throw the gifts on the ground, he planted them carefully in soil instead; the plants grew up inferior, and such they have remained wherever they have spread. Lafaang died among his own people on earth, but the bright constellation that bears his name and shape still moves across the heavens, reminding men of his journey to the world above the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Lafaang story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他被告知要把這些禮物扔在地上，他卻仔細地將它們栽入土中；這些植物長得低劣，此後無論傳播到何處，它們都一直如此。拉法昂死於人間自己的族人之中，但那以他的名字與形貌命名的明亮星座，仍舊運行於天際，提醒著人們他曾踏上前往天外世界的旅程。

title.en: Usaï the Giant: Why the Sky Is Far Away
title.zh: 巨人烏賽：天何以高遠

region.en: Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河流域（象徵性定位）

period: Klemantan myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the story of Usaï

summary.en: At one time the sky was close to the earth; but one day Usaï, a giant working sago with a wooden mallet, accidentally struck his mallet against the sky, and since then the sky has been far out of man's reach. The rest of the myth follows the giant's grief down the Baram: the dammed river that drowns his wife, the weeping stations that name every rapid, his cut-down death at Miri with 'my brains are sago, my liver is tobacco,' and the mosquitoes of his day, big as fowls, hewn small by the people.
summary.zh: 昔天低近地；一日巨人烏賽舂西谷米，木杵誤擊於天——自此天高而人不可及。神話續敘巨人順巴蘭江而下之悲：築壩引水而妻溺亡；沿江哭泣之處各成灘名；至米里被伐如樹而亡——遺言曰『吾腦為西谷、吾肝為菸草』；其世之蚊大如雞，為眾人斬小。

sensitivity.note: Sky-lifting motif (cf. Maui, Reushi); landscape etiology of the Baram rapids.

passages.text: At one time the sky was close to the earth, but one day Usaï, a giant, when working sago with a wooden mallet accidentally struck his mallet against the sky; since which time the sky has been far up out of the reach of man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Usaï story in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曾經有一段時期，天空離大地很近，但有一天，巨人烏賽（Usaï）在用木槌製作西米時，不慎將木槌撞到了天空；自那時起，天空便高高在上，遠非人力所能觸及。

passages.text: Building a dam to catch a prawn for his wife, Usaï saw the dam give way and his wife drowned in the rush of water; he waded weeping down the Baram, and his stations of grief gave the river its named rapids — weeping anew at every bend where he found her coat, her waist-cloth, or nothing at all, until the sea was only knee-deep to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Usaï story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏賽為了替妻子捕捉一隻蝦而築了一道堰，卻見堰潰決，妻子溺斃於奔湧的水流之中；他泣著涉水順巴南河而下，他每一處哀悼駐足之地，便使這條河有了那些以之為名的急灘——他在每一個河灣重新痛哭，那裡他尋見她的外衣、她的腰布，或什麼也尋不著，直到海水於他只及膝深。

passages.text: At Miri the people took him for a great tree and hewed him down; blood poured from his foot, and he spoke: 'I am about to die. My brains are sago, my liver is tobacco. Where my head falls there the people will have much knowledge, where my feet lie will be the ignorant ones.' He fell with a mighty crash, head toward the sea; a thousand Miris were killed by the fall, and the mosquitoes of his day, big as fowls, were hewn into small pieces — so that now they are the smallest of animals, but their bite is still painful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Usaï story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在美里，人們把他當作一株大樹，將他砍倒；血從他的腳湧出，他說道：「我將要死了。我的腦髓是西米，我的肝是菸草。我的頭落下之處，那裡的人們將擁有許多知識；我的腳躺臥之處，將是那些無知的人。」他隨著一聲巨響倒下，頭朝向大海；千人因這一倒而喪命，而他那一日如家禽般巨大的蚊子，被砍成了小塊——所以如今牠們是最微小的動物，但牠們的叮咬依然疼痛。

title.en: Simpang Impang and the Wind-Spirit: The Flood, the Half-Man, the Compensation
title.zh: 半身人與風靈：洪水、半人與賠償

region.en: Batang Lupar country, Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲巴唐盧帕爾流域（象徵性定位）

period: Iban (Sea Dayak) myth recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the Iban story of Simpang Impang

summary.en: Men who cut up a python for cooking bring on a deluge; all the land is covered and only the peak of Tiang Laju stands above the flood, with one woman, a dog, a rat and a few small animals. The woman, taking a hint from a creeper warmed by friction, produces fire by rubbing wood; lacking a husband she takes the creeper as mate and bears a son who is only half a human being — one arm, one leg, one eye: Simpang Impang. When the wind-spirit scatters the rat's padi the half-boy demands compensation at the house of the wind, outlasts the spirit's ordeal contests with the help of fish, swift and ant, burns the wind-house with his father the fire-drill, and wins the price: 'I'll make you a whole man with two arms and two legs and two eyes.'
summary.zh: 人們誤斬巨蟒而炊，招致大洪水；大地盡沒，唯蒂昂·拉尤峰出於水面，一婦人攜犬、鼠及小獸登峰。婦人見藤蔓摩擦生暖而悟，鑽木取火；無夫，遂以藤為伴，產下半身之子——一臂一腿一目：半身人辛邦·因邦。風靈吹散鼠之稻穀，半身人前往風之居所索償；得魚、雨燕、螞蟻之助連勝神判，再以生父鑽火器焚風屋——風靈終允賠償：『我讓你成為完人，兩臂兩腿兩目。』

sensitivity.note: Iban composite myth (flood + quest + fable); Hose notes its heterogeneous, fun-loving character.

passages.text: Some people came upon a huge python in the jungle and, taking it for a log, sat on it and wounded it; heavy rain fell for days and days, till all the land was covered with water and only the top of Tiang Laju stood out above the flood, with one woman, a dog, a rat and a few small animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iban story of Simpang Impang in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有些人於叢林中遇見一條巨蟒，誤以為是一段木頭，便坐在其上，並將牠弄傷；大雨連日連夜落下，直到整片土地都被水淹沒，唯有蒂昂拉朱的頂端露出洪水之上，還有一名女子、一隻狗、一隻鼠和幾隻小動物。

passages.text: The woman, taking the hint from a creeper warmed by friction against a tree, rubbed the creeper hard on a piece of wood and so for the first time produced fire; having no husband she took the creeper for her mate, and gave birth to a son who was but one-half of a human being — one arm, one leg, one eye — Simpang Impang.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iban story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那女子從一條因與樹摩擦而發熱的藤蔓得到啟示，將藤蔓在一塊木頭上用力摩擦，於是第一次生出了火；她沒有丈夫，便以那藤蔓為配偶，生下一個兒子，而這兒子只是人的一半——一臂、一腿、一目——即辛龐英龐。

passages.text: When the wind-spirit scattered the padi grain in dispute with the rat, Simpang Impang demanded his corn back at the house of the wind; helped by the fish, the swift and the ant through the spirit's contests of diving, jumping and blow-pipe, and armed at last with his father the fire-drill, he burned the wind-spirit's house, and the spirit paid compensation — 'I'll make you a whole man with two arms and two legs and two eyes' — and did as asked for the tree and the lake that had sent messages with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Iban story; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當風靈因與鼠爭執而吹散了稻穀，辛龐英龐便在風的屋中索回他的穀物；他藉著魚、迅捷者與螞蟻之助，通過了風靈的潛水、跳躍與吹箭種種較量，最後以他的父親火鑽為武器，燒了風靈的屋子，風靈便付出補償——「我要使你成為一個完整的人，有兩臂、兩腿和兩目」——並照所求的，為那曾隨他傳訊的樹與湖而行。

title.en: The Mouse-Deer and the Tortoise: 'Please Throw Me in the River'
title.zh: 鼠鹿與水龜：『請把我丟進河裏』

region.en: Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河流域（象徵性定位）

period: Kenyah fable recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the Kenyah fable of the mouse-deer and the tortoise

summary.en: The mouse-deer Plandok gives the tortoise Kelap a leg up the fruit-tree and abandons him; caught by the household as the thief, Kelap begs for each punishment — fire ('last time they left one side untouched'), the cane-press ('last time they squeezed only one side') — and weeps only at the river. Thrown in, he surfaces: 'That's alright, this is my home.' The villagers try to poison the water with tuba, but one man uses the tortoise's back for a stone, and Kelap sinks his back little by little until they think the river is rising and give up.
summary.zh: 鼠鹿普蘭多克扶水龜柯拉普上果樹而棄之；柯拉普被屋中人當賊擒獲，對各種刑罰皆討饒求之——火刑（『上次只燒了一面』）、蔗壓（『上次只壓了一面』）——唯獨怕被丟入河中而啼哭。眾人將其拋入河中，他浮出水面：『沒錯，這就是我的家。』村民欲以毒藤毒水，一人竟以其背為砧杵搗毒藤；柯拉普讓背慢慢下沉，眾人以為河水漲了，只好作罷。

sensitivity.note: Classic trickster fable (punishment-inversion type); also performed as social parable among the Kenyahs.

passages.text: Plandok the mouse-deer gives Kelap the tortoise a leg up the laden fruit-tree; Kelap throws down all the fruit, cannot get down, and is caught by the people of the house as the thief. Brought to punishment, Kelap begs for every fate but the river: 'please put me in the fire; last time they only half did the thing and left one side untouched'; 'please squeeze me in the press; last time they squeezed only one side of me.' So they throw him into the river, and he surfaces calling that this is his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kenyah fable in Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Kenyah fable; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鼠鹿普蘭多克托了烏龜克拉普一把，助牠爬上結滿果實的果樹；克拉普把果實全都扔了下來，卻下不了樹，被那屋裡的人當作賊捉住。被帶去受罰時，克拉普懇求除了河以外的每一種命運：「請把我放進火裡吧；上次他們只做了一半，留下一邊沒碰」；「請把我壓在壓榨器裡吧；上次他們只壓了我的一邊。」於是他們把他扔進河裡，他浮出水面，喊著說這裡才是他的家。

passages.text: The people resolve to poison the water with tuba; one man, taking Kelap's back for a stone, beats his tuba upon it, and Kelap sinks his back lower and lower till the water covers it — 'the water's rising, it's no good trying to poison the river' — and the people go home defeated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Kenyah fable; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾人決意以魚藤毒水；一人誤將克拉普的背當作石頭，把魚藤往他背上捶打，克拉普便將背越沉越低，直到水淹沒了它——「水漲起來了，想毒這條河是沒用的」——眾人只得敗興而歸。

title.en: Laki Tenangan: The Fatherly God Above All Departments
title.zh: 拉基·特南安：超越諸職司的慈父之神

region.en: Kayan country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸加揚之地（象徵性定位）

period: Kayan religious tradition recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the gods of the Kayans

summary.en: Above the Kayan departmental gods stands Laki Tenangan, 'more powerful than all the rest, to whom are assigned no special functions' — a beneficent, fatherly god who protects mankind, whose identity the Kayan freely admits with the supreme gods of the Klemantans and Kenyahs. Prayers are carried to him by the souls of slaughtered pigs and fowls, with fire and ascending smoke; an old woman praying for her sick child says: 'Make my child live that I may bring him up with me in my occupations... If I put you above my head, all men look up to me as to a high cliff.'
summary.zh: 加揚諸職司神之上，立著拉基·特南安——『權能勝過其餘眾神，而不司任何特定職務』——仁慈如父、護佑人類之神；加揚人坦然承認他與克勒曼丹人、肯雅人之至上神同為一體。禱詞由被宰豬雞之魂傳達，並輔以火與升煙；老嫗為病兒禱曰：『讓我的孩子活下來，好讓我帶著他一起勞作……若我將您置於我頭頂之上，萬人都會仰望我，如仰望高崖。』

sensitivity.note: Supreme-god theology recorded 1912; Hose & McDougall compare its 'catholicity' across tribes.

passages.text: Beside or above all the departmental gods is Laki Tenangan, a god more powerful than all the rest, to whom are assigned no special functions; he seems to preside over the company of lesser gods much as Zeus ruled the lesser gods of the Greeks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912), the Kayan gods; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在諸位部門神之旁或之上，是拉基·特南岸，一位比其餘眾神都更有力量的神，卻未獲指派任何專門職能；他似乎統領著眾小神的群體，正如宙斯統治希臘人的眾小神一般。

passages.text: Laki Tenangan is conceived as beneficent and fatherly; the Kayan admits his identity with Pa Silong and Bali Penylong, the supreme gods of the Klemantans and Kenyahs — a catholicity which, the recorders note, gives the Kayan religion a claim to rank very high among religious systems.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉基·特南岸被設想為仁慈而如父一般；卡揚人承認他與帕·西隆及巴利·佩尼隆——克萊曼坦人與肯雅人的至高神——實為同一，此種兼容並蓄，據記錄者所言，使卡揚人的宗教在諸宗教體系中享有極高的地位。

passages.text: Prayers are transmitted to him by the souls of domestic pigs or fowls, one of which is always killed and charged to carry the prayer, while fire and ascending smoke establish the communication. The supplicant cries: 'Make my child live that I may bring him up with me in my occupations. You are above all men. Protect us from whatever sickness is abroad. If I put you above my head, all men look up to me as to a high cliff.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912), the recorded prayer; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 祈禱經由家豬或家禽的靈魂傳達於他，每次必宰殺其中一隻，命其攜帶祈禱，同時以火與升起的煙建立溝通。祈求者喊道：「讓我的孩子活下去，好讓我能在自己的勞作中將他撫養長大。你凌駕於所有人之上。護佑我們免受一切流行疫病之害。若我將你置於我頭上，眾人便都如仰望高崖一般仰望我。」

title.en: The Trusty Messengers: Omen Birds and the Sacrifice of Beads
title.zh: 忠實的信使：占卜鳥與斷珠之祭

region.en: Kayan and Kenyah country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸加揚與肯雅之地（象徵性定位）

period: Religious practice recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the omen birds and sacrificial rites

summary.en: The Kayans seek to read in the behaviour of the omen birds and in the entrails of slaughtered pigs and fowls the way the gods respond to prayer: 'they regard the true omen birds as the trusty messengers of the gods.' Bad omens are retried with fresh victims until satisfactory ones come; and the sacrifice is real deprivation — the pigs stuck upon stakes before the altar-post are left to rot, a woman whose child's recovery stays unanswered will break a bead of great value, or cut off her hair.
summary.zh: 加揚人在占卜鳥之行止與被宰豬雞之腸中，讀取諸神對禱告的回應——『他們視真正的占卜鳥為諸神忠實的信使』。凶兆則以新的犧牲重占，直至得吉；而犧牲是真實的剝奪——釘於祭柱前木樁上的豬任其腐爛；若病兒痊癒之禱未蒙應允，婦人會折斷貴重之珠，或剪下自己的頭髮。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic record of living religious practice (1912); paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: The Kayans seek to read in the behaviour of the omen birds and in the entrails of the slaughtered pigs and fowls indications of the way in which the gods respond to their prayers; for they regard the true omen birds as the trusty messengers of the gods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡揚人試圖從預兆鳥的行為以及所宰殺豬禽的內臟中，解讀諸神如何回應其祈禱的徵象；因為他們視真正的預兆鳥為諸神忠實的信使。

passages.text: If the omens first obtained are bad, more fowls and pigs are usually killed and omens again observed; in an important matter, as the illness of a beloved child, the process may be repeated many times until satisfactory omens are forthcoming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 若最初所得的預兆為凶，通常會再宰殺更多家禽與豬隻，並再次觀察預兆；在重要之事上，例如愛子患病，此過程可能重複多次，直到出現令人滿意的預兆為止。

passages.text: The slaughtering is regarded as sacrifice in the ordinary sense — an offering of some valued possession: the pigs stuck upon stakes before the altar-post are left to rot; a woman will break a bead of great value when her prayers for the restoration of her child's health remain unanswered, or on such an occasion may cut off her hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 宰殺之舉被視為一般意義上的獻祭——即獻上某種珍貴的所有物：被釘在祭壇柱前木樁上的豬任其腐爛；當一名婦女為孩子康復所作的祈禱未獲回應時，她會打碎一顆價值不菲的珠子，或在這樣的場合剪去自己的頭髮。

title.en: The Kayan Pantheon: Gods of War, Life, Madness and the Ferry of Souls
title.zh: 加揚神譜：戰神、生命之神、瘋神與渡魂者

region.en: Kayan country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸加揚之地（象徵性定位）

period: Religious tradition recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the gods of the Kayans

summary.en: The Kayans recognise gods presiding over the great departments of life: the god of war, Toh Bulu; three gods of life, Laki Ju Urip, Laki Makatan Urip and Laki Kalisai Urip; the god of thunder and storms, Laki Balari, with his wife Obeng Doh; the god of fire, Laki Pesong; the harvest gods Anyi Lawang and Laki Ivong; the god of lakes and rivers, Urai Uka; Balanan the god of madness; Toh Kiho the god of fear; and Laki Katira Murei and Laki Jup Urip, who conduct the souls of the dead to Hades — the minor gods, Hose suggests, perhaps deified ancestors, their names the names of Kayan grandfathers.
summary.zh: 加揚人奉眾神分掌人生諸大事：戰神托赫·布盧；三位生命之神（拉基·朱·烏里普、拉基·瑪卡丹·烏里普、拉基·卡利賽·烏里普）；雷暴之神拉基·巴拉里及其妻奧本·多赫；火神拉基·珀松；穀神安宜·拉旺與拉基·伊旺；湖河之神烏萊·烏卡；瘋神巴拉南；懼神托赫·基霍；以及引亡魂至冥府的拉基·卡蒂拉·穆雷與拉基·朱普·烏里普——小神或為受尊崇之祖先，其名即加揚祖父之名。

sensitivity.note: Pantheon record; the ancestor-deification hypothesis is the recorders' interpretation.

passages.text: The Kayans recognise a number of gods that preside over great departments of their lives and interests: the god of war, Toh Bulu; three gods of life; the god of thunder and storms, Laki Balari, and his wife Obeng Doh; the god of fire, Laki Pesong; gods of the harvest; a god of the lakes and rivers; Balanan, the god of madness; Toh Kiho, the god of fear; and two gods who conduct the souls of the dead to Hades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912), the Kayan pantheon; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡揚人承認若干掌管其生活與利益之重大領域的神祇：戰神托布魯（Toh Bulu）；三位生命之神；雷電與風暴之神拉基巴拉里（Laki Balari）及其妻奧本多（Obeng Doh）；火神拉基佩松（Laki Pesong）；收穫諸神；湖泊與河流之神；瘋狂之神巴拉南（Balanan）；恐懼之神托基霍（Toh Kiho）；以及兩位引領亡者靈魂前往冥界的女神。

passages.text: Some of these gods are distinctly friendly, others — the gods of madness and fear — terrible and malevolent; while the god of thunder and the conductors of souls are neither. The names of many minor deities are proper personal names in common use, and the title Laki is the respectful title of grandfathers — suggesting that these minor gods may be deified ancestors of great chiefs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些神祇中有些明顯是友善的，另一些——瘋狂之神與恐懼之神——則可怕而懷有惡意；至於雷神與引領靈魂者則兩者皆非。許多小神的名字都是日常通用的專有人名，而「拉基」（Laki）這一稱號是對祖父的敬稱——這暗示這些小神可能是偉大首領被神化的祖先。

title.en: Measuring the Stars with a Bamboo of Water: Dayak Sky-Lore
title.zh: 以竹筒量星：達雅克星空之學

region.en: Upper Baram river country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸巴蘭河上游之地（象徵性定位）

period: Astronomical tradition recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the constellations of the Borneans

summary.en: Most Borneans are familiar with the principal constellations and name them from resemblances to men, animals and objects. The Long Kiputs call the great square of Pegasus 'Palai,' the padi storehouse; the Pleiades they call a well; the constellation of Aldebaran, a pig's jaw. They measure a star's altitude by filling a tall bamboo vessel with water, inclining it until it points to the star, then measuring the water-line — an indigenous astrolabe of bamboo and water.
summary.zh: 婆羅洲人多識主要星座，依其似人似獸似物而命名。隆基普人稱飛馬座大方形為『帕拉伊』——稻倉；稱昴星團為井；稱畢宿座為豬顎。他們以高竹筒盛水，傾筒對星，再直立量水面之高——此即以竹與水製成的本土星儀。

sensitivity.note: Ethnoastronomy record; the sowing season is set by these observations.

passages.text: Most of the Borneans are familiar with the principal constellations, and name them in accordance with the resemblances they discover to men, animals, and other objects; some of the tribes determine the arrival of the season for sowing padi by the observation of the stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912), the constellations; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大多數婆羅洲人熟悉主要的星座，並依照他們所發現的與人、動物及其他物體的相似之處為其命名；有些部族藉由觀察星辰來判定播種稻米的季節何時到來。

passages.text: The Long Kiputs name the great square of Pegasus Palai, the padi storehouse; the Pleiades they call a well; and the constellation of which Aldebaran is a member they call a pig's jaw. They measure the altitude of a star by filling a tall bamboo vessel with water, inclining it until it points directly to the star, and then setting it upright again, and measuring the height at which the surface of the water remaining stands above its floor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隆基普特人（Long Kiputs）將飛馬座的大四邊形命名為帕萊（Palai），即稻米倉庫；他們稱昴星團為一口井；而畢宿五所屬的星座，他們稱之為豬顎。他們測量星辰高度的方法是：將一個高大的竹製容器注滿水，傾斜它直至正指向該星，然後再將其直立，並測量所餘水面高出容器底部的高度。

title.en: Malaise, Who Travelled to Akilinek
title.zh: 馬萊塞遠航阿基利內克

region.en: Akilinek, the fabulous country beyond the seas
region.zh: 海外幻境阿基利內克

period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from two copies (one East Greenland verbal narration), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 17 'Malaise — The Man who travelled to Akilinek', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Drifted east on the breaking ice with gull amulets, two sisters land on the rich other-country of Akilinek, marry two kayakers who race ashore for them, and escape home over the ice with their babies when one husband threatens death for a daughter — leaving the infants frozen on the snow. Jeered at home for telling nothing, they finally boast of the hunting 'in Akilinek,' and Malaise rows out to it under a threefold-covered boat, laughing his timid wife's tears down. Meeting their escaped husbands, he fills a drinking-tub with water dusted with hairs from dead men's reindeer-skin stockings — each suitor who drinks turns into a reindeer and is shot into the sea, one 'miserable specimen' spared to live on.
summary.zh: 兩姊妹隨碎裂的浮冰東漂，憑海鷗護身符登陸豐饒的阿基利內克，嫁給爭先上岸的兩名皮艇客；因丈夫揚言『再生女兒便殺你』，她們攜嬰越冰而逃，嬰兒凍斃雪中。歸家後，她們起初守口如瓶，飽受譏誚，終於誇口『阿基利內克才是獵人的天堂』。馬萊塞遂以三層皮的艘船西航尋地，途中以亡者馴鹿皮襪之毛混水設壺於敵必經之石——每名前夫喝水即化馴鹿，被他射落海中，獨留一個『可憐的標本』活命傳種。

sensitivity.note: Akilinek is the fabulous country beyond the seas in Greenlandic tradition. Infant deaths and sorcerous killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Malaise was a jolly, fearless fellow who lived in prosperity with his two sisters, both younger than himself, wintering at the mouth of a fiord; when he went out kayaking, his sisters followed him on foot along the beach, returning as soon as they saw him put back. One day, the sea all covered with ice, the sisters went to the outermost islets to gather roots; suddenly an eastern gale overtook them, the ice broke up, and they were taken far out to sea in very bad weather. When the sky cleared they came in sight of high land, drifted to it, and landed safely, almost starving — the ice-floe they had floated on turned to foam behind them. Each had part of a gull for an amulet. Wandering across the country, they came to a little bay into which a river emptied: 'There will be salmon yonder, I warrant, or there would not be so many gulls about.' The river abounded in salmon; catching one they made a fire by rubbing wood, fried the fish on a slab, and were quite satisfied with half the tail-piece. At low tide the beach turned quite dry, covered with spotted seals and various other kinds, of which they killed as many as they required with big stones, and took up their abode there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 17 'Malaise'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬萊斯（Malaise）是個快活無畏的漢子，與兩個比他年幼的妹妹富裕地同住，在一處峽灣口過冬；當他划著皮艇出海時，妹妹們便沿著海灘徒步跟隨，一見他折返便即刻回家。某日，海面盡覆冰層，姊妹倆前往最外側的小島採集根莖；忽然一陣東風襲來，冰層破裂，她們在極惡劣的天氣中被帶往遠海。待天空放晴，她們望見高聳的陸地，漂流而至，平安登岸，幾乎餓斃——她們所乘的浮冰在她們身後化為泡沫。兩人各持一片海鷗的殘片作為護符。她們漫遊鄉間，來到一處有河流注入的小海灣：「那兒必定有鮭魚，我敢說，否則不會有這麼多海鷗。」河中盛產鮭魚；她們捉得一條，以摩擦木頭生起火來，在石板上煎魚，半截尾肉便令她們十分滿足。退潮時海灘乾透，滿是斑海豹及各種其他海豹，她們用大石頭擊殺所需之數，便在此定居下來。

passages.text: One day two kayakers hunting spotted seals, seeing the girls, were heard to exclaim, 'Well, he who gets ashore first shall marry the prettiest of the two'; both took to their paddles, he who first reached the shore touching the elder sister, the other taking the younger — and quite forgetting their hunt, they hastened home to fetch a boat, returning with a good crew and bringing the girls to their house, where they lived as happy as could be for some time. After a while each had a daughter; but the eldest noticed her sister had quite lost her spirits, and asked why she was always sobbing and crying: her husband had told her he would kill her if she next time bore him a daughter. 'We'll pack up our clothes, and as soon as the ice forms, we'll return to our old home; but don't let them suspect anything.' They made themselves new clothes and put them by in bags concealed beneath the boat outside; the seal-hunting ceased, the men went out visiting and dancing at a large house close by, and the sisters waited a convenient opportunity. One dance-night, when nobody was to be seen outside, they walked up and down lulling their children to sleep in short breeches only; the little girls who used to nurse the children ran out after them, but were drawn in by a funny song — and the sisters hastened to the boat, put the babies into their amowts, and started.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 17 'Malaise'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，兩個划著獨木舟獵捕斑海豹的人看見了那兩個女孩，只聽他們喊道：「這樣吧，誰先上岸，誰就娶兩人中較美的那一個。」兩人都奮力划槳，先上岸的碰上了姐姐，另一個則娶了妹妹——他們完全忘了打獵的事，急忙趕回家去取船，帶著一隊好手回來，把兩個女孩帶回他們的屋裡，此後有一段時日，他們過得再快活不過。過了些時候，兩人各得了一個女兒；但姐姐發覺妹妹精神全無，便問她為何總是抽抽噎噎、哭個不停：原來她丈夫告訴她，若她下一胎再生女兒，他就要殺了她。「我們把衣服收拾好，等冰一結，就回我們的老家去；可別讓他們起疑。」她們給自己做了新衣服，裝進袋子裡，藏在外面船底下；獵海豹的事停了，男人們出門到附近一間大屋裡做客跳舞，姊妹倆便等著合適的時機。有一晚跳舞時，外頭一個人也看不見，她們只穿著短褲，來回走動哄孩子入睡；平日裡照看孩子的小女孩們跟著跑了出來，卻被一支古怪的歌聲引了回去——姊妹倆便急忙奔向船，把嬰兒放進她們的皮舟裡，出發了。

passages.text: Keeping on shore at first, then out on the ice, they wandered all night long, hiding behind blocks of ice at daybreak when they heard the sound of sledges following their traces. Where their footprints were lost, their pursuers halted and called out, 'Your poor little children are crying for you'; they did not leave their retreat until evening, then set forth and continued their journey — but on the way they suffered their babies to freeze to death, and having put them down on the snow, left them there. Reaching land, they recognised the place of their former winter-station, and behold, their own little house just as they had left it. Malaise was very much astonished to see his sisters entering, and questioned them about Akilinek and the hunting in those parts, but he could not make them tell anything. After their return he displayed great energy in fishing and hunting, until the days began to lengthen, when the sisters turned to him: 'Though almost nothing is to be got in this poor country, it cannot be denied that Malaise strives hard enough to provide for us; but, to be sure, in Akilinek there is something for a hunter.' Then they told him all he wished; even in fine weather Malaise did not stir out, and when they had told him of the many seals found on the dry beach he could not forbear: 'I really must try Akilinek — in spring when the saddleback-seals appear. I will give my women's boat a threefold covering.' His wife began crying, being of a very timid disposition; but Malaise only laughed at her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 17 'Malaise'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她們起初沿著岸走，後來上了冰面，整整一夜都在趕路，天亮時聽見雪橇循著她們的足跡追來的聲響，便躲在冰塊後面。追兵到了足跡消失的地方，停下來喊道：「你們那可憐的小娃娃在哭著找你們呢。」她們直到傍晚才離開藏身之處，然後動身繼續趕路——可是途中她們任憑嬰兒凍死，把他們放在雪地上，就丟下不管了。到了陸地，她們認出從前過冬的地方，瞧，她們自己的小屋還跟她們離開時一模一樣。馬萊斯見兩個姊妹走進來，大為驚訝，便問她們阿基利內克的事和那一帶的狩獵情形，卻怎麼也問不出個所以然來。她們回來之後，他打起魚、獵起獸來幹勁十足，直到白晝開始變長，姊妹倆才對他說：「雖說這窮地方幾乎什麼也弄不到，但不能不承認，馬萊斯為了養活我們，著實賣力；不過嘛，阿基利內克那兒，獵人總歸是有收穫的。」於是她們把他想知道的一切都告訴了他；此後即便天氣晴好，馬萊斯也不肯出門，而當她們告訴他乾灘上有許多海豹時，他再也按捺不住：「我非得去阿基利內克試一試不可——就等春天鞍背海豹出現的時候。我要給我的婦人船蒙上三層皮。」他妻子生性極為膽小，哭了起來；馬萊斯卻只是笑她。

passages.text: As soon as the saddleback-seals appeared he caught as many as they wanted for boat-covers, got the three coverings, and waited a favourable opportunity. One windless morning: 'The day is fine and it is quite calm now; let us be off for Akilinek' — his wife again crying, laughed down. Pushing off westward, the sisters rowed all by themselves while their sister-in-law cried in the bottom of the boat; to tease her further Malaise rose and looked aft, observing, 'I think we are going to have a gale, it is getting quite black out there!' — and she cried in good earnest, to his very great diversion. Having lost sight of their own country, he found they went too slow and cut the outer covering away because it had grown too wet; before sighting any land he likewise cut off the second cover, then suddenly sprang to his feet: 'I see the loom of the land yonder!' His wife got up and stuck to the oars bravely. Coming close to the land, the sisters recognised the bay where they had first landed, and observed their former husbands coming on to attack them. Before their departure Malaise had been out to the grave of some relative in search of a pair of reindeer-skin stockings, brought away with him; he now took a drinking-vessel, filled it with water, poured in some dust mingled with the hairs of the stockings, and put the tub down on an adjacent rock their adversaries were obliged to pass. When the eldest came up he took a drink — and was at once transformed into a reindeer, shot by Malaise and rolled into the sea; the other had no better luck. In this manner Malaise killed all their companions excepting one, to whom he said, 'I will spare thee that thou mayst live on, a miserable specimen of thy countrymen.' Some time afterwards he again gave his boat three separate coverings, filled it with narwhal-horns, matak, salmon, and many other valuables, and reached his former home, where he stayed content until his death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 17 'Malaise'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鞍背海豹一出現，他就捕了足夠蒙船用的數量，備好了三層船皮，等著合適的時機。一個無風的早晨：「天氣好，現在風平浪靜，我們動身去阿基利內克吧」——他妻子又哭了起來，被他一笑置之。船向西划去，姊妹倆自己划著槳，她們的嫂子卻在船底哭泣；馬萊斯為了再逗她，站起身來往船尾看，說道：「我看我們要遇上大風了，那邊天都黑下來了！」——她便當真大哭起來，叫他樂得不行。看不見自己的家鄉之後，他嫌她們划得太慢，就把外層船皮割掉，因為它已經太濕了；還沒望見任何陸地，他又照樣割掉了第二層船皮，然後忽然跳起身來：「我看見那邊陸地的影子了！」他妻子站起來，奮力划槳。船靠近陸地時，姊妹倆認出她們當初上岸的那個海灣，又看見她們從前的丈夫正上前來攻擊她們。動身之前，馬萊斯曾到某個親戚的墳上找一雙馴鹿皮襪子，帶了回來；這時他取來一隻飲水用的器皿，裝滿水，撒進一些混著襪子毛的灰塵，把這盆子放在對手必經的一塊岩石上。姐姐走上前來喝了一口——立刻變成一頭馴鹿，被馬萊斯射殺，滾進海裡；另一個的運氣也好不到哪裡去。馬萊斯就這樣殺光了他們所有的同伴，只留下一個，對他說：「我饒你一命，讓你活下去，做你同鄉裡一個可憐的樣本。」又過了些時候，他再次給他的船蒙上三層船皮，裝滿獨角鯨的角、瑪塔克、鮭魚和許多別的值錢東西，回到了他從前的家，在那裡心滿意足地住到死。

title.en: Navaranak or Javraganak: The Go-Between Who Made Enemies Friends
title.zh: 納瓦拉納克：挑撥兩族的通譯女

region.en: Interior and coast boundary, North Greenland / Okak, Labrador
region.zh: 北格陵蘭內陸與海岸交界／拉布拉多奧卡克島

period: Inuit oral tradition; two separate narratives (North Greenland; Labrador, Okak island), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 18 'Navaranak or Javraganak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The servant-maid Navaranak, tired of ferrying matak and tallow between inlanders and coast-people, tells each side the other is preparing invasion — until the inlanders fall on the coast villages while the men are out hunting, mothers killing their own children in fright, a pregnant woman bribing her way free beneath the ledge. Dragged to death behind a rope when she is caught, Navaranak's murder is avenged on her whole people in a lake-surrounded arrow-battle. In the Labrador variant the Indian servant Javraganak brings her 'many brothers' on a night the murmuring outside is mistaken for hares on the house-tops, and she is dragged to death by an angakok-made road through a mountain.
summary.zh: 通譯女納瓦拉納克厭倦了在內陸人與海濱人之間往返運送鯨皮與鹿脂，便向雙方謊稱對方將入侵——內陸人終於趁男獵女守之際血洗海濱村落，母親們惶恐中親手殺死自己的孩子；一名孕婦以全部家產換得免死。她被繩索拖拽至死，族人隨即遠征湖畔內陸營地，箭戰全殲其族。拉布拉多流本中，印第安僕女雅夫拉加納克於野兔奔騰之夜引來族人屠村，最後亦被拖曳致死。

sensitivity.note: Rink's variants localize the same events: North Greenland inlanders, Labrador Indians, and a South Greenland version identifying the inlanders with the ancient Scandinavian settlers. Graphic massacre recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: The inlanders and the coast-people in the beginning were friends. A servant-maid called Navaranak used to be sent out by the inlanders to the coast-people to fetch back matak (edible whale-skin), and in exchange brought them reindeer-tallow; but after a time she grew weary of this work, and resolved to free herself by making them enemies. For this purpose she told the inlanders that the coast-people were going to attack them, and to the coasters she asserted that the inlanders were making ready to invade them. At length she provoked the inlanders to such a degree that they resolved upon attacking the coast-people, choosing a time when they were well aware the men had all gone out hunting; accompanied by Navaranak, they fell upon the helpless women and children. In their fright some of the mothers killed their own children, but one woman who was pregnant fled down beneath the ledge; and when Navaranak was sent back by the inlanders to find her out, she promised her all she possessed not to betray her. Some also escaped by hiding among the rocks, but all the rest were killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 18 'Navaranak or Javraganak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 起初，內陸人和海岸人是朋友。內陸人常派一個名叫納瓦拉納克的女僕到海岸人那裡去取瑪塔克（可食用的鯨皮），再拿馴鹿油脂跟他們交換；可是過了些時候，她厭倦了這差事，便決心挑撥他們成仇，好讓自己脫身。為此，她對內陸人說海岸人要來攻打他們，又對海岸人聲稱內陸人正準備入侵。最後她把內陸人挑唆到這般地步，使他們決意攻打海岸人，還特意挑了一個他們明知男人們全都外出打獵的時機；他們在納瓦拉納克的帶領下，撲向那些無助的婦孺。驚慌之中，有些母親親手殺了自己的孩子，但有一個懷孕的婦人逃到岩壁下面；內陸人派納瓦拉納克回去找她，她答應把所有的東西都給納瓦拉納克，求她不要告發。也有一些人躲在岩石間逃過一劫，其餘的全被殺害了。

passages.text: When the men returned, those left alive ran down and told them what had happened; coming up from the beach and beholding all their dead, the men were almost desperate. When the time came for flensing and cutting up the whale, Navaranak did not arrive as usual — she seemed to have disappeared altogether. When summer had come round, the men prepared a great many arrows and set out for the interior to take revenge on the inlanders. On their way they called out, as was their wont, 'Navaranak, come on; we have got matak for thee!' but no one appeared; again they went on a good distance, then repeatedly called out — and this time she answered the summons and went up to them. Noticing their arrows, she was about to take flight; reassuring her, they told her she had no need to do that. When she had ventured quite close, they asked where her countrymen were to be found — 'Further away in the interior of the country!' — but now they made her fast to a rope and dragged her along with them until she perished. They arrived at a very large lake where the tents of the inlanders were pitched all around, waited till all had entered the tents, and made their attack: arrows came flying from both sides, but those of the inlanders soon grew fewer, and the coast-people remained all unwounded. When they had done with the men they went inside, killing women and children; and having thus satisfied their revenge, returned to their homes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 18 'Navaranak or Javraganak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男人們回來時，倖存的人跑下去把發生的事告訴了他們；他們從海灘上來，看見親人全都死了，幾乎悲痛欲絕。到了剝鯨皮、切鯨肉的時候，納瓦拉納克卻沒有像往常那樣出現——她似乎整個人都消失了。夏天一到，男人們準備了許多箭，動身前往內陸，要向內陸人報仇。路上他們照慣例喊道：「納瓦拉納克，來呀；我們給你帶瑪塔克來了！」卻沒有人出現；他們又往前走了一大段路，再連聲呼喊——這回她應了召喚，走到他們跟前。她瞧見他們的箭，正要逃走；他們安慰她，說她不必如此。等她大著膽子走近了，他們便問她的同鄉在哪裡——「在內陸更深處！」——可是這回他們把她綁在繩子上，一路拖著她走，直到她死去。他們來到一個很大的湖邊，內陸人的帳篷在四周搭了一圈，他們等到所有人都進了帳篷，才發動攻擊：箭從兩邊飛來，但內陸人的箭很快就少了，海岸人卻毫髮無傷。他們收拾完男人，又進到裡面，殺死婦孺；這樣報了仇，便回家去了。

passages.text: On the island of Okak, in Labrador, this tale is told as follows: At Kivalek, on the island of Okak, there once lived a great many people, among whom was an Indian woman named Javraganak. From her childhood she had lived with the coast-people as their servant, but had always remained a stranger among them. One day when she was hungry and longed for one of her Indian dishes, she said, 'At Pangma my countrymen have plenty of tongues' — an old man sneeringly replied, 'I daresay thou hast many brothers and relatives away there; thou hadst better make them come over here,' and at night she wandered away to give them warning. In those times hares were very abundant, and sometimes you might even hear them run about on the house-tops. One night Javraganak came with a great number of her countrymen; those within heard a murmuring sound outside, and the old man said, 'Well, if that is not the hares again!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 18 'Navaranak or Javraganak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在拉布拉多的奧卡克島上，這個故事是這樣講的：奧卡克島上的基瓦萊克，從前住著許多人，其中有一個名叫賈夫拉加納克的印第安女人。她從小就住在海岸人家裡當僕人，卻始終是個外人。有一天她餓了，饞起家鄉的一道菜，便說：「在龐馬，我的同鄉有好多舌頭。」一個老人譏諷地回答：「我看你在那邊準有許多兄弟親戚；你不如叫他們過來這裡。」當夜她就溜出去給他們報信。那時候野兔非常多，有時甚至能聽見牠們在屋頂上跑來跑去。一天夜裡，賈夫拉加納克帶著一大群同鄉來了；屋裡的人聽見外頭有窸窸窣窣的聲響，那老人說：「唉，這要不是那些野兔才怪！」

passages.text: They are very lively, it seems.' Besides him there was not a man at home, all being out hunting — and so it happened that all the inhabitants were put to death by Javraganak's Indian countrymen, many seeking refuge in a cave, where some were suffocated and others murdered. On their return the men found their wives and children all killed, but shortly afterwards set out to kill the murderers. Among these men was an angakok who made a road for them right through a mountain, and the countrymen of Javraganak were all destroyed. She, however, was not to be found, having gone to hide herself; but the men had great trust in their angakok. At last a man happened to call out, 'How I wish that Javraganak would serve me again!' — upon which she immediately appeared, looking very comfortable. They all fell upon her, wound a cord around her body, and dragged her along the ground till she died; and in this way she was paid back for what she had done to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 18 'Navaranak or Javraganak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們似乎非常活潑。除了他之外，家裡沒有別的男人，全都出去打獵了——於是事情就這麼發生了：所有居民都被賈夫拉加納克（Javraganak）的印第安同胞殺死，許多人躲進一個洞穴避難，有些人在洞中窒息而死，另一些人則被殺害。男人們回來時，發現他們的妻子兒女全都被殺，但不久之後便出發去殺那些兇手。這些人當中有一位安加科克（angakok，巫師），他為他們開出一條直穿山嶺的道路，賈夫拉加納克的同胞全都被消滅。然而她卻遍尋不著，因為她已躲藏起來；但男人們對他們的安加科克深具信心。最後，有一個人恰好喊道：『我多麼希望賈夫拉加納克再來服侍我啊！』——她立刻現身，看上去十分安適自在。他們一齊撲向她，在她身上繞了一根繩索，把她在地上拖行直到死去；她就這樣為她對他們所做的一切付出了代價。

title.en: Avarunguak or Agdlerut: Wintering Among Bears in Human Shape
title.zh: 阿瓦龍瓦克：與人形之熊同冬

region.en: Southern auk-coast and the country behind the mountains
region.zh: 南方海鳩海岸與群山彼端

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Court-hunted from his pinching village, Avarunguak steers for the forbidden huge tent and winter with a family of five-windowed giants who eat his walruses, feed him from their own stores, and exam every whelp's joints — the seventh alone 'perfect.' He proves himself by licking out all the lamp-oil, joins their raid on their enemies, slips away at the prescribed moment, and sees his hosts turn to bears pursuing — until his salmon amulet makes him too slippery to catch. Leaving in spring, he learns the truth: they had been wintering among bears in human shape, and the people who later killed a bear sealed the family's doom.
summary.zh: 因村中捏人取樂之風被眾人追逐的阿瓦龍瓦克，反而駕舟投宿被禁的五窗巨宅，與五口之家過冬——巨人家族吃掉他的海象、以自家存糧養他，逐只檢視狗崽關節，唯第七只『四肢俱全』。他以舔盡全屋燈油證明自己，隨其出征仇敵；在指定時刻藉口出屋逃走，回頭只見主人一家化熊緊追——幸而他以鮭魚為護身符，滑溜難捉。翌春辭別時，他們囑咐：『無論去哪裡，告訴人們見熊不可殺。』——原來這一家人本就是人形之熊；南方殺熊的消息傳來，他們的命運便已註定。

sensitivity.note: Bears-in-human-shape motif (compare Rink tale 6/30 note on the great bear). The bear-taboo injunction is a core Greenlandic hunting ethic.

passages.text: At a well-peopled place the trick of pinching was a favourite amusement with the inhabitants. One night a girl, an only sister with a number of brothers, came running in crying, 'I wonder who it can possibly be who is always running after me and paying court to me?' — they told her to bring him into the house next time. When she brought him in, it was a man totally unknown to all of them: Avarunguak had grown up in solitary places, and when he came among people he married this girl, learned to manage a kayak, and grew an excellent hunter. Once they had visitors from the south, and an old woman of the party accosted him: 'If Avarunguak were to hear of the nice hunt, and the many auks we have down in the south, I am sure he would be wanting to go there!' He could not sleep for the desire to go at once, and the next morning ordered his housemates to make ready for the voyage south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一個人口稠密的地方，捏人這把戲是居民們喜愛的消遣。一天夜裡，一個女孩——她是眾多兄弟唯一的姊妹——哭著跑進屋裡說：『我真想知道，那個老是追著我、向我獻殷勤的究竟會是誰？』——他們叫她下次把他帶進屋裡來。當她把他帶進來時，那是一個他們全都不認識的男人：阿瓦倫瓜克（Avarunguak）在荒僻之地長大，當他來到人群之中，便娶了這個女孩，學會了操縱獨木舟（kayak），並成長為一名出色的獵人。有一次，有南方來的訪客，其中一位老婦人對他說：『要是阿瓦倫瓜克聽說南方有那麼好的獵場、有那麼多海雀，我敢說他一定會想去那兒的！』他因渴望立刻前往而無法入睡，第二天早晨便吩咐同屋的人準備南航。

passages.text: On the way out, the people they encountered all made answer that the place was not very nigh yet; at a resting-place they were told: 'When ye leave here, and have doubled the cape, ye will come in sight of a very large tent — this ye must shun; but soon afterwards ye will perceive a little white point, and having also passed this, ye will fall in with a great many people. To those ye shall go up.' Avarunguak steered his boat towards the large tent, unheeding the advice of his companions; a huge man came out receiving them very civilly: 'It is really a matter of difficulty to get any one to keep company with here; pray stay and live with me' — and they prepared for wintering there. Every morning Avarunguak awoke early, but somehow his housemate was always out and off before him; when the auks came screaming across the country the huge man bade him shut the curtain closely so only one bird could get in at a time, and not begin to catch any of them until the tent was quite full. Avarunguak began catching them too soon, the birds instantly left, and he heard the man scolding — 'Didst thou not mind my telling thee that thou wert not to catch them till the tent was quite full, lest I should be in want of food?' — still, he had got a great many birds, quite sufficient to live upon for a good length of time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在出發途中，他們遇到的人全都回答說那地方還不很近；在一處歇腳的地方，他們被告知：『你們離開這裡，繞過那海角之後，就會看見一頂非常大的帳篷——這頂帳篷你們必須避開；但不久之後你們會看到一個小小的白點，也經過了這個之後，你們就會遇到許多人。你們就走到那些人那裡去。』阿瓦倫瓜克不顧同伴們的勸告，把船駛向那頂大帳篷；一個巨人走了出來，非常客氣地接待他們：『在這裡要找個人作伴還真是件難事；請留下來和我一起住吧』——於是他們便準備在那裡過冬。每天早晨阿瓦倫瓜克都起得很早，但不知怎的，他的同屋總是比他先出去、先離開；當海雀尖叫著飛越這片地方時，那巨人吩咐他把簾子緊緊拉上，好讓一次只能進來一隻鳥，並且在帳篷完全裝滿之前不要開始捕捉。阿瓦倫瓜克太早開始捕捉，鳥兒立刻離去，他聽見那人在責罵——『我不是告訴過你，在帳篷裝滿之前不要捉，免得我缺食物嗎？』——不過，他已經捉到很多鳥，足夠吃上好長一段時間了。

passages.text: When the walrus time came, the big man warned he did not pursue them — 'the red walrus is a very ferocious beast, and at that time I do not venture out at all' — but Avarunguak grew very excited and lanced his first walrus; his big companion came down to the beach, took half of the walrus, dragged it along with only one hand past Avarunguak's tent, and carried it off to his own, where he sat eating it all by himself while his wife and daughter only looked on. Next time the big man's wife carried off his prize, and after her their three daughters did the same by turns; not until they had all got their walrus did they desist. In the beginning of winter Avarunguak always caught plenty, but the big man, having no kayak of his own, never went out; the sea froze up and all hunting ceased. 'Here we are all badly off; but I know that behind our country there is good hunting enough, and thither we intend to go to-morrow.' Asked how swift he might be — 'I think I can run a race with any of the quadrupeds' — he was taken along only after much beseeching, all carrying cords of sealskin round their necks. Crossing the mountains they beheld a bare land, and the big man spoke: 'Dost thou see yonder lofty mountains far away? Behind, there is a sea where the white whale in abundance are found; but when we get so far, thou must only aim at the small ones, because thou wilt not be expert enough to carry home one of the larger ones.' The daughters had to take hold of Avarunguak by his arms to help him along; at the appointed place each watched at a cleft in the ice — no sooner did Avarunguak see a huge white whale rise than he aimed at and killed it, while the others each brought up two fish. Scolded for disobeying, he was to have his fish tied to theirs and be dragged home sitting on top of it — 'Since I commenced hunting I have never let my game be carried home by any one but myself, nor shall I do so now. I have caught the fish myself, and will take care to bring it home' — and they let him have his own way, disappearing from his sight as if blown away. It was evening and again beginning to dawn before he could see his home, meeting the others coming back to fish anew; not till the fourth day did he get home, having been obliged to eat all the matak of his dolphin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海象的季節到來時，那巨人警告說他並不追捕牠們——『紅海象是非常兇猛的野獸，那時候我根本不敢外出』——但阿瓦倫瓜克變得非常興奮，用魚叉刺中了他的第一頭海象；他那高大的同伴走到海灘上，取走海象的一半，只用一隻手就把它拖過阿瓦倫瓜克的帳篷，帶回自己的帳篷，獨自坐著把它全吃掉，而他的妻子和女兒只能在一旁看著。下一次，那巨人的妻子取走了他的獵物，之後他們的三個女兒輪流照樣做；直到她們全都分到了海象，才肯罷休。初冬時節，阿瓦倫瓜克總是捕到很多，但那巨人沒有自己的獨木舟，從不外出；海面結冰，一切打獵都停止了。『我們在這裡都很困苦；但我知道我們這地方背後有足夠的好獵場，我們打算明天到那裡去。』有人問他跑得有多快——『我想我能和任何四足獸賽跑』——他是在眾人再三懇求之後才被帶上的，大家都把海豹皮繩掛在脖子上。翻過山嶺，他們看見一片荒蕪的土地，那巨人說道：『你看見遠處那些高聳的山嗎？山後有一片海，那裡有大量的白鯨；但當我們到了那裡，你只能瞄準小的，因為你身手不夠好，帶不回一頭大的。』女兒們必須抓住阿瓦倫瓜克的雙臂幫他前進；到了約定的地方，各人守在一處冰縫旁——阿瓦倫瓜克一看見一頭巨大的白鯨浮起，便瞄準並殺死了牠，而其他人各帶回了兩條魚。他因不聽話而被責罵，他的魚要被綁在他們的魚上，讓他坐在上面被拖回家——『自從我開始打獵以來，我從沒讓任何人替我搬運獵物回家，現在也不會這樣做。魚是我自己捕的，我會負責把它帶回家』——於是他們就讓他照自己的意思做，而他們則像被風吹走一般從他眼前消失了。直到傍晚、又開始破曉，他才看得見自己的家，途中遇見其他人正回來重新捕魚；直到第四天他才回到家，因為他不得不把他那頭海豚的瑪塔克（matak，鯨皮）全都吃掉。

passages.text: About this time Avarunguak's people had a dog that happened to whelp. When the first whelp appeared, the huge man whispered something to his wife, on which she brought it him, and he took hold of it and examined all its joints; each new-born whelp was brought to him to be examined in the same way, but when they had handled the seventh — the last — they were heard saying, 'This one is perfect; there is not a limb wanting.' From that time they seemed despondent; Avarunguak, beginning to fear their intentions, one day said to them, 'If you would like to have a dog, you are welcome to take the one you like best' — they chose the last born and became so fond of it that they let it stop on the ledge and sleep beside them at night, and from this time Avarunguak himself became a great favourite. While the winter lasted the big man spoke as follows: 'We intend soon to go and visit our enemies.' Avarunguak was very desirous to join, but was told, 'No, friend; thou wouldst too soon be worn out: for, in the first place, thou canst not eat blubber and flesh enough; and secondly, because of thy clumsiness and want of speed' — 'As to the blubber and flesh, methinks I do well enough as regards both of them' — 'Well, then, try to lick out the oil of all the lamps here, beginning with the outermost.' Avarunguak succeeded, and a few days after was told he might accompany them. The instructions: when they have entered and begin licking the oil, he must help; they will each be presented with one large white fish, and he must thrust his knife into it, turn it round, put the cut piece into his mouth, and suddenly exclaim, 'I must go outside, but I will be back in a moment, and go on eating; I enjoy it very much' — but when outside take to his heels and run for home as fast as possible, and before he has been off long, they shall empty the lamps and soon overtake him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大約在這時候，阿瓦倫瓜克家的人有一隻狗恰好產崽。當第一隻幼崽出現時，那巨人對他的妻子低聲說了幾句，她便把幼崽帶給他，他抓住牠，檢查牠所有的關節；每一隻新生的幼崽都被帶到他面前，以同樣的方式檢查，但當他們處理完第七隻——也就是最後一隻——時，只聽他們說：『這一隻完美無缺；一點肢體都不缺。』從那時起，他們似乎很沮喪；阿瓦倫瓜克開始害怕他們的意圖，有一天對他們說：『如果你們想要一隻狗，歡迎你們挑最喜歡的一隻帶走』——他們選了最後出生的那一隻，並且非常喜愛牠，讓牠待在壁架上、夜裡睡在他們身旁，從這時起，阿瓦倫瓜克本人也變得非常受寵。整個冬天，那巨人這樣說道：『我們打算不久就去拜訪我們的敵人。』阿瓦倫瓜克非常想加入，卻被告知：『不行，朋友；你太早就會累垮的：因為第一，你吃不了那麼多鯨脂和肉；第二，因為你笨手笨腳、又不夠快』——『至於鯨脂和肉，我想我兩方面都還行』——『那麼好吧，試著把這裡所有燈裡的油都舔出來，從最外面那盞開始。』阿瓦倫瓜克成功了，幾天之後他被告知可以隨他們同行。指示是：當他們進去並開始舔油時，他必須幫忙；他們每人會被送上一條大白魚，他必須把刀刺進魚裡，轉一圈，把切下的那塊放進嘴裡，然後突然喊道：『我得出去一下，但我馬上就回來，繼續吃；我非常喜歡吃』——但一到外面就拔腿就跑，盡可能快地跑回家，而他離開沒多久，他們就會把燈裡的油喝光，很快追上他。

passages.text: Some time after, they carried out their intention of visiting their enemies in their place of abode, setting about licking the oil of the lamps, Avarunguak joining them to the best of his ability. When the hosts saw a stranger among their visitors they regarded him keenly, so the huge man interposed, 'That is a new housemate of ours; he is living with us at present, and assists us every way' — praising and flattering him very much, making a great deal of his dexterity and strength, adding he was more than a match for them every way, anything but the truth, but they dared not do otherwise for fear of their enemies. 'Bring in the meal for the visitors' — large white fish were brought in, the guests soon fell to; but Avarunguak forgot he had been advised to leave off in good time, never remembering till he was quite satisfied, then quickly pronouncing the words he had been told, took himself off and commenced running as fast as possible. Coming near their own house he turned round and saw that the creatures he had been visiting were transformed into bears, pursuing him closely; his own housemates soon overtook him, the daughters again taking him by the arms to speed him on. When they had almost reached the house the enemies seemed at their very heels, and Avarunguak was deserted by his protectors, who gave him a blow so that he fell, and the bears instantly gathered round him — but he chanced to have a salmon for his amulet, and this did him good service in making him too slippery to be caught hold of, and thus he escaped. When spring came round, Avarunguak took a fancy to remove to another place; on departing, his huge companion said to him, 'I hope thou wilt soon return and stay with us; but wherever thou goest, mind to tell the people never to kill a bear when one appears.' Thus they departed — but on turning round they now saw that their housemates too had been transformed into bears: they had been wintering among bears in human shape. Later on they heard that some people in the south had killed a bear, and still later Avarunguak and his wife died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了些時候，他們付諸行動，到敵人的居所去拜訪他們，著手舔燈裡的油，阿瓦倫瓜克也盡其所能地加入他們。當主人們看到訪客中有一個陌生人時，便銳利地打量他，於是那巨人插話道：『那是我們的新同屋；他目前和我們住在一起，各方面都幫助我們』——極力讚美奉承他，大肆誇獎他的靈巧和力氣，還說他在各方面都勝過他們，這與事實完全相反，但他們因懼怕敵人而不敢不如此。『把給訪客的飯菜端進來』——大白魚被端了進來，客人們很快便吃了起來；但阿瓦倫瓜克忘了有人曾勸他及時停手，直到吃得心滿意足才想起來，於是趕快說出別人教他的那句話，抽身離去，開始盡可能快地奔跑。快到自己家時，他回頭一看，看見他剛才拜訪的那些生物已變成熊，緊緊追著他；他自己的同屋很快追上了他，女兒們又抓住他的雙臂幫他加速。當他們幾乎到家時，敵人似乎就在他們腳後跟，阿瓦倫瓜克卻被他的保護者拋棄了，他們給了他一拳使他跌倒，熊立刻圍了上來——但他恰好有一條鮭魚作護身符，這幫了他大忙，使他滑溜得抓不住，就這樣逃脫了。春天到來時，阿瓦倫瓜克起了念頭要搬到別處去；臨別時，他那高大的同伴對他說：『我希望你很快回來和我們同住；但不論你到哪裡，記得告訴人們，當一頭熊出現時，千萬不要殺牠。』他們就這樣離去了——但回頭一看，他們這才發現他們的同屋也變成了熊：他們原來是和一隻隻人形的熊一起過冬。後來他們聽說南方有些人殺了一頭熊，再後來阿瓦倫瓜克和他的妻子都死了。

title.en: The Girl Who Married an Atliarusek
title.zh: 嫁給岩中小人的少女

region.en: Outermost islet and rock-dwelling of the atliarusek, Greenland fiord
region.zh: 格陵蘭峽灣最外島與岩中人居所

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Scorned by the suitors who nearly killed him for refusing to give up his daughter, a selfish old man winters on an outermost islet — where his daughter is secretly wed to an atliarusek, an elf of the sea-shore rocks, who keeps out of sight, then brings home hunting-lines and beach-loads of seals. Joining his people, the couple's boats dive beneath the waves past the inhabited places, load up with reindeer; and when the old man fetches his former mockers to a feast, he quotes their own taunts back to them: 'Your words were these: Thou wilt surely never get a clever husband for thy daughter. But you see I have, for all that. Now help yourself, if ye please, and eat as much as ever ye like.'
summary.zh: 因不肯交出女兒而被求婚者毒打的老人遭全村嘲笑，攜家遷居最外小島過冬——女兒卻已秘密嫁給岩中人阿特利亞烏塞克。他先是隱形，繼而懸起獵繩、沙灘上滿是海豹；春日同行，舟隊竟能潛入波下穿過有人居住之地，滿載馴鹿而歸。老人隨後將昔日嘲笑他的人全數接來設宴，把當年的話擲回他們面前：『你們說：你這女兒休想嫁個好獵手。可你看，我偏偏找到了。現在請隨意吃喝吧。』

sensitivity.note: Atliarusek (probably = ingnersuak) are elves or gnomes with abodes in rocks along the sea-shore, per Rink's note. Boat-diving motif parallels the inland-dweller corpus.

passages.text: An aged couple had a daughter who had a great many suitors; but the old people were very selfish and wanted to keep her at home. Meanwhile a man came who was very anxious to get the daughter; at last he fought them, and had nearly killed them — the old man escaped into his boat. The other men of the place despised and scorned him, but he got the boat loaded and left, the others shouting contemptuously, 'It won't be easy for thee to get a husband for thy daughter! The poor old thing, who is quite unable to hunt — he to dare reject any one! Only let him come to be in want of necessaries, and then look out if there be any one to help him!' He set off without deigning to answer, and landed at one of the outermost islets, where they built their house and put up for the winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一對年老的夫婦，他們有個女兒，求婚者眾多；但老夫婦非常自私，想把她留在家中。這時來了一個男子，極想娶這女兒；最後他與老夫婦打了起來，幾乎把他們打死——老人逃進了自己的船裡。當地其他男人都鄙視、嘲笑他，但他把船裝滿了東西便離開了，其他人輕蔑地喊道：『你要給你女兒找個丈夫可不容易啊！這可憐的老東西，連打獵都完全不行——他竟敢拒絕任何人！只等他缺東少西、需要人幫忙的時候，看看還有沒有人肯幫他！』他懶得回答，便動身離去，在一座最外圍的小島登陸，他們在那裡蓋了房子，住了下來過冬。

passages.text: One morning the old man awoke saying, 'I wonder what I have just been seeing? Methinks I saw a man gliding through the doorway'; he questioned his daughter, but she kept silence, and he got suspicious. Next morning he saw a real man slip out of the doorway, and on being closely questioned the daughter confessed that she was married to an atliarusek — 'For fear thou wouldst not like him, he keeps out of sight; but if thou dost not mind, he will come and live with us.' The father said it was all right, and he might come at once; towards evening the daughter several times left the room, returning at last with a hunting-line hung up on a nail to dry — he had returned and brought home the produce of his hunt, but must take some part of it to his relatives. Outside they saw many seals on the beach, and rejoiced very much at their sudden prosperity. The following morning the old man beheld the stranger reposing beside his daughter; the son-in-law had already taken himself off whenever the old man stirred. 'Why do you not make him come and stay with us? We like him very well indeed' — and in the evening when he again returned with his catch, he went inside and made himself at home, the parents very civil to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天早晨，老人醒來說道：『不知我剛才看見的是什麼？我好像看見一個男子從門口溜了出去』；他問女兒，女兒卻默不作聲，他便起了疑心。第二天早晨，他看見一個真正的男子從門口溜出去，經再三追問，女兒才承認自己嫁給了一個atliarusek——『因為怕你不喜歡他，他一直避不見面；但如果你不介意，他就會來和我們同住。』父親說這沒問題，他可以馬上就來；傍晚時分，女兒好幾次離開屋子，最後回來時，掛了一條獵線在釘子上晾乾——他已經回來了，帶回了打獵的收穫，但必須拿一部分去給他的親屬。他們在外面看見海灘上有許多海豹，對這突如其來的好運非常歡喜。第二天早晨，老人看見那陌生人躺在女兒身旁；原來老人一有動靜，女婿便早已溜走了。『你為什麼不叫他來和我們一起住呢？我們真的很喜歡他』——到了晚上，他又帶著獵物回來，便走進屋裡，自在得像在自己家一樣，老夫婦對他非常客氣。

passages.text: In spring he wanted to go further inland along the fiord-side, as was generally his custom, but told them he was obliged to join his parents, being their only son, and as such ought not to let his sisters be without protection. When they again met, he told them they were now ready for starting; the father-in-law likewise put his boat into the water, and as they were going to set off, another boat appeared coming straight out of the beach — both went along together and made the land at the same time in the evening. Next morning they started again; approaching an inhabited place, the head-man of the atliaruseks told them always to keep close in their wake, and all of a sudden they saw his boat sink beneath the surface and totally disappear. The old man got rather frightened; but on arriving at the spot their boat dived down in the same manner, without any damage to the crew, catching sight of their companions' boat right ahead — they continued their course beneath the waves of the sea. Having safely passed the inhabited places, they once more rose to the surface and continued their voyage without further peril; arriving at their place of destination, they went reindeer-hunting and got their boats fully laden. Wintering again, the son-in-law provided amply for them, and they prospered and were well off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 春天，他想沿著峽灣岸邊往內陸更遠處去，這向來是他的習慣，但他告訴他們，他必須去和自己的父母會合，因為他是獨子，理當如此，不該讓姊妹們無人保護。他們再次相見時，他告訴他們現在可以出發了；岳父也把船放下水，正當他們要動身時，又有一條船從海灘那邊直駛出來——兩條船並行前進，傍晚同時靠岸。第二天早晨他們又出發了；接近一個有人居住的地方時，atliaruseks的首領叫他們始終緊跟在他們船後的航跡裡，忽然他們看見他的船沉入水面，完全消失了。老人有些害怕；但到了那地點，他們的船也以同樣的方式潛了下去，船上的人卻毫髮無傷，只見同伴的船就在正前方——他們繼續在海浪之下前行。安全通過那些有人居住的地方後，他們又浮上水面，繼續航行，不再有危險；到達目的地後，他們去打馴鹿，把船裝得滿滿的。又過了一個冬天，女婿充分供養他們，他們日子興旺，過得很好。

passages.text: About this time intelligence reached them that the men who had once scorned and abused them were living in great want, and the old man determined to help them: he loaded his kayak with matak and brought it to them. They asked whence he had got it — whether it was not taken from the carcass of a whale driven on shore accidentally; he left without deigning an answer, and talking the matter over at home the son-in-law exclaimed, 'I should really like to have a look at these people' — so the old man went back to fetch all the men who had formerly been his daughter's suitors, returning with a large train of kayaks following him. They landed and were very hospitably received and regaled with reindeer-meat and seal-flesh; when they had satisfied their appetite, the old man accosted them: 'I wonder if ye can still remember what ye were telling me a long time ago when ye had nearly killed me, wanting by main force my daughter for your wife? Your words were these: Thou wilt surely never get a clever husband for thy daughter. But you see I have, for all that. Likewise ye said that ye would deny me your assistance if ever I came in want: now help yourself, if ye please, and eat as much as ever ye like.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大約在這時，他們得到消息說，從前輕蔑、辱罵過他們的那些人如今生活非常困苦，老人便決定去幫助他們：他把獨木舟裝滿了matak，給他們送去。他們問他這是從哪裡得來的——是不是從偶然擱淺的鯨魚屍體上取下來的；他懶得回答便走了，回家後說起這件事，女婿說道：『我倒真想看看這些人』——於是老人回去把從前向他女兒求婚的那些男人全都找來，回來時身後跟著一大隊獨木舟。他們上岸後受到非常殷勤的款待，飽餐了馴鹿肉和海豹肉；等他們吃飽了，老人對他們說道：『不知你們還記不記得，很久以前你們幾乎把我打死、硬要逼我女兒做你們妻子時，對我說過的話？你們的話是這樣的：你女兒肯定永遠找不到一個能幹的丈夫。可是你們看，我到底還是找到了。你們還說過，要是我哪天有了困難，你們絕不會幫我：現在你們請自便吧，想吃多少就吃多少。』

title.en: The Twelve Sacred Krisses of Lombok: One Needle for Every Head
title.zh: 龍目島十二聖克利斯：每人一針

region.en: Mataram, Lombok (Sasak country)
region.zh: 龍目島馬塔蘭（薩薩克之地）

period: Sasak tradition as narrated by A. R. Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), the Lombok chapters

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. I, the Lombok chapters (the twelve sacred krisses)

summary.en: Wallace's great myth-narrative of Sasak Lombok: climbing the sacred mountain, the Rajah falls into a trance and is shown the coming plague by 'the great spirit, with a face like burnished gold.' The escape is institutional: every village must send one needle for every head of its people; twelve krisses are forged from the counted needles in sight of all men; and when sickness appears, the kris cures only if the count was exact — the myth of a census that carries both salvation and the tax-gatherer's power.
summary.zh: 華萊士所述薩薩克龍目之偉大神話：拉賈登聖山入恍惚之境，『面如磨金之偉靈』示以將臨之瘟疫。救贖乃制度性的：每村須按人口繳針一根；以清點之針，於眾目睽睽之下鍛成十二把克利斯；疾病若至，唯針數無誤之村方能得克利斯之效——此乃『戶籍即救恩亦即稅吏之權』的神話。

sensitivity.note: Wallace's narrative reconstruction of Lombok tradition (1869); read as a literary rendering of a ritual myth, flagged for its colonial narrating position.

canonical_translation: Wallace 1869 (English); paraphrase of the narrative

narrative.en:
Wallace's Lombok chapters open with the fullest English telling of a Sasak ritual myth — the pilgrimage of the Rajah of Lombok and the forging of the twelve sacred krisses.

BEGINNING: THE SUMMONS AND THE PILGRIMAGE. A great spirit bids the Rajah undertake the journey up the mountain; the whole island prepares — cattle killed and meat salted, peppers and sweet potatoes gathered, betel nuts climbed for, sirih-leaf bundled, tobacco pouches and lime boxes filled for the journey. On the eve of the start the chiefs encamp at Mataram under the tall waringin-trees, and with blazing fires fright away 'the ghouls and evil spirits that nightly haunt the gloomy avenues.' In the morning a great procession of princes on black horses with tails sweeping the ground conducts the Rajah toward the mountain.

MIDDLE: THE TRANCE AND THE COMMAND. On the mountain-top the Rajah falls into a trance: the great spirit appears with a face like burnished gold and warns that plague, sickness and fevers are coming upon all the earth — men, horses and cattle — but that the people of Lombok, having obeyed by coming up to the great mountain, may learn the escape. The command is precise and strange: twelve sacred krisses are to be made, and to make them every village and every district must send a bundle of needles — a needle for every head in the village.

END: THE FORGE AND THE VIRTUE. Every village hastens to collect needles exactly, fearing that one needle wanting would ruin the whole village; the head men bring their bundles to Mataram, and the Rajah stores them with his own hands in a camphor-wood chest with silver hinges, each bundle marked with the village and district of its coming. When every village has sent its bundle, the needles are divided into twelve equal parts, and the best steelworker of Mataram brings forge, bellows and hammers to the palace and forges the twelve krisses under the Rajah's eye and in the sight of all men. Wrapped in new silk, they are put away until wanted. And their virtue is conditional: when sickness appears in a village one of the krisses is sent, and 'sometimes the sickness went away, and then the sacred kris was taken back again with great honour' — but when the sickness would not go, 'everybody was convinced that there had been a mistake in the number of needles sent from that village,' and the kris is taken back with heavy hearts, for was not the fault their own? Wallace lets the tale close with its political edge: the needle-count is the census, and the census is the tax — 'the Rajah became very rich, and increased the number of his soldiers, and none of the Rajahs or Sultans among the Malays were so great or powerful as the Rajah of Lombok.'

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) explains the sacred krisses of Lombok as ritual instruments of plague-control contingent on communal exactness; (2) encodes the theology of counting — the head counted is the head protected and the head taxed; (3) charters the mountain as the seat of the great spirit's speech; and (4) demonstrates, in a single narrative, how ritual, administration and state power braid together in the Sasak kingdom. Wallace's framing matters as much as the tale: he tells the story in quasi-scriptural cadence — 'And when it was quite certain that every village had sent in its bundle...' — and closes it with the census's economic teeth, the tribute compared needle to needle and the under-reporting villages sent back to recount. The needle-count is thus a double charter: a plague-ritual that requires exact communal enumeration, and a fiscal instrument that teaches every village what the ruler knows about its own heads. Read as myth, the krisses give Lombok's Sasak kingdom a theology of precision: the sacred works only when the count is true, and falsehood anywhere in the chain — one needle short, one head unreported — voids the cure for the whole village. Wallace heard the tale as local tradition on the island in the 1850s; its afterlife in print made it the best-known single legend of Lombok in the English-reading world.
narrative.zh: 華萊士龍目章以最完整的英文敘述了薩薩克儀式神話——龍目拉賈的登山與十二聖克利斯的鍛造。開篇：偉靈命拉賈登山；全島備辦——宰牛醃肉、採椒集薯、攀樹取蔞葉、檳榔煙盒皆滿；啟程前夜，酋長宿於馬塔蘭大榕樹下，燃大火以驚走『夜夜出沒於幽暗林道之食屍鬼與惡靈』。晨起大行列：黑鬃曳地之王馬引拉賈登山。中段：山巔拉賈入恍惚，偉靈現——面如磨金——預言瘟疫將臨人畜；然因龍目人遵命登山，得授救法：須鍛聖克利斯十二把，而鍛之之法，乃每村每區按人頭繳針一根。結尾：諸村急急收針、唯恐缺一；頭人親送至馬塔蘭，拉賈親手貯於銀扣樟木箱，各束記村名；針足之日，分為十二份，馬塔蘭最佳鐵匠攜爐、風箱與錘入宮，於眾目下鍛成十二器，裹以新絲待用。其效有條件：村中有疫，遣一器往——『疫或立止，則以大禮迎歸』；若疫不止，『眾人皆信乃針數有誤』，頭人懷沉重之心迎回——豈非己過？華萊士讓故事收束於政治之鋒：點針即點頭，點頭即徵稅——『拉賈因此大富，增兵置馬，馬來諸蘇丹無出其右』。功能：以『社區精確』為條件釋聖克利斯為疫控儀器；立『點數神學』——被點之頭即受護之頭、亦即被稅之頭；以聖山為偉靈發言之座；並於一個敘事中演示儀式、行政與王權在薩薩克王國中如何編織為一。

functions: Explains the sacred krisses of Lombok as plague-controlling instruments contingent on communal exactness
Encodes a theology of counting: the head counted is the head protected and the head taxed
Charters the mountain as the seat of the great spirit's speech
Demonstrates how ritual, census and royal power braid together

variants.name: Wallace's frame narrative
variants.summary: Wallace presents the tale as local Lombok tradition retold in quasi-scriptural style, with his own ironic coda on the tax.

secondary_sources.citation: Wallace 1869, London: Macmillan — vol. I, Lombok: Mataram, the mountain pilgrimage and the krisses.
