sensitivity_guidance: Living Sasak royal-ritual memory; paraphrase respectfully, note the colonial narrating frame.

passages.text: On the top of the mountain the Rajah fell into a trance, and the great spirit appeared to him with a face like burnished gold, and said: 'Oh Rajah! much plague and sickness and fevers are coming upon all the earth, upon men and upon horses and upon cattle; but as you and your people have obeyed me and have come up to my great mountain, I will teach you how you and all the people of Lombock may escape this plague.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), the Lombok kris narrative; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在山頂上，拉者陷入了恍惚之中，偉大的神靈出現在他面前，面容如打磨過的金子一般，說道：『哦，拉者！大瘟疫、疾病和熱病即將降臨整個大地，降臨到人、馬和牛身上；但既然你和你的子民聽從了我，登上了我的大山，我就要教你和龍目島全體人民如何逃過這場瘟疫。』

passages.text: The great spirit commanded that twelve sacred krisses should be made, and that to make them every village and every district must send a bundle of needles — a needle for every head in the village. When any grievous disease appeared in any village, one of the sacred krisses should be sent there; and if every house had sent the right number of needles, the disease would immediately cease; but if the number had not been exact, the kris would have no virtue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 偉大的神靈吩咐要打造十二把神聖的克里斯短劍，而為了打造它們，每個村莊、每個地區都必須送來一捆針——村裡每個人頭一根針。哪個村莊出現任何嚴重的疾病，就應把其中一把神聖的克里斯送到那裡；如果每戶人家都送來了正確數量的針，疾病就會立刻停止；但如果數量不準確，那把克里斯就不會有任何效力。

passages.text: All made haste to collect the needles with the greatest accuracy, fearing that if one were wanting the whole village would suffer; the bundles were marked with the names of their villages and kept by the Rajah in a camphor-wood chest, and the best steelworker of Mataram forged the twelve krisses at the palace in the sight of all men. And when any sickness appeared, sometimes it went away and the kris was taken back with great honour — and sometimes it did not, and then everybody was convinced there had been a mistake in the number of needles sent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾人都急忙以最精確的方式收集針，唯恐若少了一根，整個村莊都要遭殃；這些針束都標明所屬村莊之名，由拉者保管於一只樟木箱中，而馬塔蘭最優秀的鐵匠當著眾人的面，在王宮裡鍛造了這十二把克里斯劍。而每當有疾病出現，有時它會自行消退，那把克里斯劍便以極大的敬意被送回——有時則不然，於是所有人都深信，送來的針數必定出了差錯。

title.en: The Pilgrimage of the Rajah: Fires Against the Ghouls of the Avenues
title.zh: 拉賈朝山：以火驅逐林道之鬼

region.en: Mataram and the sacred mountain, Lombok
region.zh: 龍目島馬塔蘭與聖山

period: Sasak tradition as narrated by Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. I, the pilgrimage of the Rajah of Lombok

summary.en: The eve-of-departure scene of the Lombok pilgrimage: the chiefs encamp under the waringin-trees of Mataram, and with blazing fires fright away the ghouls and evil spirits that nightly haunt the gloomy avenues — the whole island provisioning the king's ascent of the sacred mountain, where the great spirit waits to speak.
summary.zh: 龍目朝山啟程前夜之景：酋長宿營於馬塔蘭大榕樹下，燃烈火以驚走『夜夜出沒於幽暗林道之食屍鬼與惡靈』——全島為王者登聖山備辦糧秣，偉靈正候於山巔待發言。

sensitivity.note: Pilgrimage scene in Wallace's narrative; part of the kris-myth cycle.

passages.text: On the day before that appointed for starting, all the chiefs, both great and small, came to Mataram, the abode of the king, with their horses and their servants, and the bearers of their sirih boxes, and their sleeping-mats, and their provisions; and they encamped under the tall waringin-trees that border all the roads about Mataram, and with blazing fires frightened away the ghouls and evil spirits that nightly haunt the gloomy avenues.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在預定出發日的前一天，所有首領，無論大小，都帶著他們的馬匹、僕從、捧檳榔盒的人、睡墊與糧食，來到馬塔蘭——國王的居所；他們在環繞馬塔蘭各條道路的高大榕樹下紮營，並以熊熊烈火驅趕每夜出沒於幽暗林蔭道上的食屍鬼與惡靈。

passages.text: In the morning a great procession was formed to conduct the Rajah to the mountain: the royal princes mounted their black horses whose tails swept the ground, and all, even the Rajah, were bare-legged to above the knee, everyone attended by servants bearing his sirih and betel boxes — the king ascending to do honour to the great spirit who had bid him undertake the journey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日清晨，一支盛大的隊伍排成行列，護送拉者前往山中：王族諸親王子騎著尾巴掃及地面的黑馬，所有人，甚至連拉者本人，都赤著腿直至膝上，人人皆有僕從隨侍，捧著他的檳榔與蒟醬盒——國王登山，以向那位命他踏上此程的偉大精靈致敬。

title.en: The Lost Chief of Wanumbai: The People Taken Across the Sea
title.zh: 萬努拜失去的酋長：被帶越大海的人們

region.en: Wanumbai, Aru Islands, Maluku
region.zh: 馬魯古群島阿魯萬努拜

period: Aru tradition told to Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. II, the Aru chapters (Wanumbai tradition)

summary.en: Long ago strangers came to Wanumbai; the chief resisted, there was fighting, and the chief and his people were carried away — or, some say, escaped in his boat and was lost at sea. All believe they still live in some foreign country; the evidence is a hundred fathoms of cloth sent back once by fishermen who met them at sea, and children of the lost people, kept shut in a large box by a Bugis trader at Dobbo. The villagers ask the passing naturalist, who must know, where their chief is now.
summary.zh: 久遠之前，異邦人來到萬努拜；酋長抵抗，因而交戰，酋長與其族人被擄走——另一說：他乘舟遁入大海，一去不返。眾人皆信其仍活在某海外之邦；證據為昔年漁夫海上相遇時託帶之百庹布匹，以及在多波被布吉商人閉於大箱中收藏的『失落者之子』。村人央求過路博物學家——你必無所不知——告知其酋長如今何在。

sensitivity.note: Recorded tradition with trauma at its core (raiding and taking of captives); treated as oral-history myth with care.

passages.text: A long time ago, they said, some strangers came to Aru, and came here to Wanumbai, and the chief of the Wanumbai people did not like them, and wanted them to go away, but they would not go, and so it came to fighting, and many Aru men were killed, and some, along with the chief, were taken prisoners and carried away by the strangers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), the Wanumbai tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說，很久以前，有些陌生人來到阿魯，又來到萬努拜，萬努拜人的首領不喜歡他們，想趕他們走，但他們不肯離去，於是便起了爭鬥，許多阿魯人被殺，有些人連同首領一起被俘，遭陌生人擄走。

passages.text: They all believe that the chief and the people that went with him still live in some foreign country; and if they could but find out where, they would send for them to come back again. As proof of it they tell of the Wokan fishermen who met these lost people in the sea and were given a hundred fathoms of cloth to bring to Wanumbai — which the thieving Wokan men kept and denied — and of the Bugis trader at Dobbo who kept the children of the lost people shut up in a large box and would not let them be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們全都相信，那位首領和隨他而去的人至今仍住在某個異國；只要他們能查出是在何處，便會派人去接他們回來。為證明此事，他們講述了沃坎的漁夫曾在海上遇見這些失散之人，並獲贈一百噚布匹要帶回萬努拜——那些手腳不乾淨的沃坎人卻將布私吞並矢口否認——還有多博的布吉商人把失散之人的孩子關在一只大箱子裡，不許人見。

passages.text: They had sought for their people everywhere — on the land and in the sea, in the forest and on the mountains, in the air and in the sky — and could not find them; therefore they must be in the white man's country, and they begged the visitor, in an imploring tone, to tell them if he knew where their chief and their people now were.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們曾四處尋找自己的族人——在陸上與海中，在森林與山間，在空中與天上——卻都找不到；因此他們必定是在白人的國度裡，於是他們以懇求的語氣央求這位訪客，若他知道他們的首領與族人如今何在，務必告訴他們。

title.en: The Strangers Who Raised the Drowned: Wounds Healed by Spitting
title.zh: 起死回生的異邦人：唾而癒傷

region.en: Wanumbai, Aru Islands, Maluku
region.zh: 馬魯古群島阿魯萬努拜

period: Aru tradition told to Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. II, the Aru chapters (the superhuman strangers)

summary.en: The Aru telling of the strangers who took their people makes them more than men: 'they were wonderfully strong, and each one could kill a great many Aru men; and when they were wounded, however badly, they spit upon the place, and it immediately became well. And they made a great net of rattans, and entangled their prisoners in it, and sunk them in the water; and the next day, when they pulled the net up on shore, they made the drowned men come to life again, and carried them away.'
summary.zh: 阿魯人敘述擄走族人的異邦人非同凡人：『其力大無比，一人可殺阿魯壯士多人；縱受重傷，一唾即癒。彼等結巨藤網，網羅被俘者沉於水中；翌日收網上岸，令溺者復生，攜之而去。』

sensitivity.note: Resurrection cluster parallel; the strangers are remembered through their miracles, as defeated peoples remember conquerors.

passages.text: They said the strangers were wonderfully strong, and each one could kill a great many Aru men; and when they were wounded, however badly, they spit upon the place, and it immediately became well. They made a great net of rattans, and entangled their prisoners in it, and sunk them in the water; and the next day, when they pulled the net up on shore, they made the drowned men come to life again, and carried them away — the drowned-raising that fixes the strangers beyond the boundary of the human.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), the Aru tradition; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Wallace (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們說那些陌生人強壯得不可思議，每一個都能殺死許多阿魯人；而當他們受傷時，無論傷得多重，只要朝傷處吐口水，傷口便立刻痊癒。他們用藤條編成一張大網，把俘虜纏在網中，沉入水裡；到了第二天，當他們把網拉上岸時，又讓那些溺死的人復活過來，把他們帶走——這使死者復生之舉，使這些陌生人被置於人類的界限之外。

title.en: The Making of a Demigod: Wallace Among the Alfuros
title.zh: 半神之鑄造：阿爾弗人中的華萊士

region.en: Wanumbai, Aru Islands, Maluku
region.zh: 馬魯古群島阿魯萬努拜

period: Observed by Wallace himself, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. II, the Aru chapters (Wallace on his own myth-making)

summary.en: A myth observed in the making, by its own future subject: the Aru villagers believe the preserved animals in Wallace's boxes will come to life again; a spell of fine weather at his arrival convinces them he can control the seasons; his walking alone in the forest is a wonder, and every confession of ignorance is taken for a blind — 'you know everything; you make the fine weather for your men to shoot.' Wallace predicts that to the next generation he will have been transformed into a magician, a worker of miracles, and of supernatural knowledge.
summary.zh: 一次由『未來神話主角』親眼記錄的神話鑄造：阿魯村民相信華萊士箱中製成的標本將復活；他抵達時恰逢連日好天，眾人遂信其能掌四季；他獨行於森林一事本身即是奇觀；凡他自承無知，皆被視為掩飾——『你必無所不知；是你為射獵的同伴造了好天氣』。華萊士預言：至下一代，他將被改寫為行奇蹟、具超凡智慧之法師或半神。

sensitivity.note: A reflexive record: the mechanics of myth-making documented by the subject himself.

passages.text: I have no doubt that to the next generation, or even before, I myself shall be transformed into a magician or a demigod, a worker of miracles, and a being of supernatural knowledge. They already believe that all the animals I preserve will come to life again; and to their children it will be related that they actually did so. An unusual spell of fine weather setting in just at my arrival has made them believe I can control the seasons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我毫不懷疑，到了下一代，甚至更早，我自己就會被轉化為一名巫師或半神，一位行奇蹟者，一個擁有超自然知識的存在。他們已經相信，我所保存的所有動物都會重新活過來；而對他們的孩子，將會講述這些動物確實如此復活了。恰在我抵達時出現的一段不尋常的晴朗天氣，使他們相信我能控制季節。

passages.text: The simple circumstance of my always walking alone in the forest is a wonder and a mystery to them, as well as my asking about birds and animals I have not yet seen; every confession of ignorance is thought to be a blind. 'You must know,' say they; 'you know everything: you make the fine weather for your men to shoot, and you know all about our birds and our animals as well as we do.' My very writing materials and books are to them weird things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我總是獨自在森林中行走這一簡單的情況，對他們而言是奇蹟與謎團，我詢問那些我尚未見過的鳥類和動物也是如此；每一次承認無知都被認為是掩飾。他們說：『你一定知道；你什麼都知道：你為你的人製造晴朗天氣好讓他們射獵，而且你對我們的鳥和我們的動物，了解得和我們一樣多。』就連我的書寫用具和書籍，對他們來說也是怪異之物。

title.en: The Offering on the Leaf: A Morsel for the Deity of the Spot
title.zh: 葉上之供：獻給此地之神

region.en: Forest near Macassar, South Sulawesi
region.zh: 南蘇拉威西望加錫近郊森林

period: Custom observed by Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. I, the Macassar chapters (forest offering)

summary.en: At the midday rest in the forest Wallace's Macassar boys would put a minute fragment of rice and meat or fish on a leaf, and lay it on a stone or stump as an offering to the deity of the spot — 'for though nominal Mahometans, the Macassar people retain many pagan superstitions, and are but lax in their religious observances.'
summary.zh: 林中午歇時，華萊士的望加錫僕童會取米與肉或魚之一小片，置於葉上，安放在石頭或樹樁上，作為獻給『此地之神』的供品——『望加錫人雖名義上是穆斯林，卻保留許多異教迷信，宗教儀行亦頗鬆懈』。

sensitivity.note: Everyday syncretic practice recorded 1869; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: At such times my Macassar boys would put a minute fragment of rice and meat or fish on a leaf, and lay it on a stone or stump as an offering to the deity of the spot; for though nominal Mahometans, the Macassar people retain many pagan superstitions, and are but lax in their religious observances.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在這種時候，我的望加錫男孩會把一小粒米和一點肉或魚放在一片葉子上，擱在一塊石頭或樹樁上，作為獻給該地神靈的供品；因為望加錫人雖名義上是穆罕默德信徒，卻保留了許多異教迷信，對宗教儀式也相當鬆懈。

title.en: The Tiger of Modjo-agong: The Hunt Ring and the Teeth as Charms
title.zh: 摩佐阿貢之虎：圍獵之環與護身之齒

region.en: Modjo-agong, near Wonosalem, East Java
region.zh: 東爪哇溫諾薩蘭附近摩佐阿貢

period: Incident and custom observed by Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. I, the Wonosalem chapters (the tiger hunt)

summary.en: A boy riding home at dusk is carried off and devoured by a tiger half a mile from Modjo-agong; the Waidono gathers seven hundred men, and the ring-hunt closes on the animal — 'they surround a large tract of country, and draw gradually together until the animal is enclosed in a compact ring of armed men; when he sees there is no escape he generally makes a spring, and is received on a dozen spears.' The skin is worthless, but the skull is hacked to pieces — 'to divide the teeth, which are worn as charms.'
summary.zh: 一名少年黃昏騎牛車歸家，於距摩佐阿貢村半里處被虎銜入叢林吞食；瓦伊多諾集七百人圍獵——『圍一大片土地，漸漸收攏，直至猛獸被逼入武裝人群之密環；虎見無路可逃，通常縱身一躍，撞上十數支矛尖，瞬間斃命』。皮毫無價值，而顱骨被砍碎——『為分其齒，齒可佩為護符』。

sensitivity.note: Man-eater and protective-charm custom; presented as historical ethnography.

passages.text: A boy had been killed and eaten by a tiger close to Modjo-agong: he was riding on a cart drawn by bullocks, and was coming home about dusk on the main road, when not half a mile from the village a tiger sprang upon him, carried him off into the jungle close by, and devoured him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個男孩在莫佐阿貢附近被一隻老虎咬死並吃掉：他當時乘坐一輛由公牛拉的車，在黃昏時分沿大路回家，就在離村子不到半英里處，一隻老虎撲向他，把他拖進附近的叢林，將他吞噬。

passages.text: The Waidono got together about seven hundred men in chase of the animal, which they found and killed: they surround a large tract of country and draw gradually together until the animal is enclosed in a compact ring of armed men; when he sees there is no escape he generally makes a spring, and is received on a dozen spears. The skin of an animal thus killed is worthless, and the skull was hacked to pieces to divide the teeth, which are worn as charms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦伊多諾人聚集了約七百人追捕那隻野獸，他們找到了牠並將牠殺死：他們包圍一大片地區，逐漸收攏，直到那隻野獸被圍在一個由武裝人員構成的緊密圓圈之中；當牠看出無路可逃時，通常會縱身一躍，隨即被十幾支長矛迎上。這樣殺死的野獸，其皮毛毫無價值，而頭骨則被砍成碎片，以便分取牙齒，這些牙齒被當作護身符佩戴。

title.en: The Turks, a Race of Giants: Rumour-Made Myths in Matabello
title.zh: 土耳其人乃巨人族：瑪塔貝洛的謠言神話

region.en: Matabello Islands, Maluku
region.zh: 馬魯古群島瑪塔貝洛群島

period: Beliefs recorded by Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. II, the Goram and Matabello chapters (strange ideas)

summary.en: The Matabello and Goram islanders held that the Russians were not only beaten but wholly converted to Islam, and that 'the Turks are the largest and strongest people in the world — in fact a race of giants; that they eat enormous quantities of meat, and are a most ferocious and irresistible nation.' Wallace guesses the source: Arab priests or hadjis returned from Mecca, echoing the ancient prowess of Turkish armies — a case-study of how news becomes myth in the far islands.
summary.zh: 瑪塔貝洛與戈蘭島民相信：俄人不僅敗於土耳其，且已全數皈依伊斯蘭；又謂『土耳其人是世上最高大最強壯之民族——實為巨人族；食肉無算，兇猛不可抵擋』。華萊士推想其源：阿拉伯教長或自麥加歸來之朝聖者，追述土耳其古軍之威——此為遠島之上『新聞如何化為神話』之標本。

sensitivity.note: Recorded belief-lore about distant peoples; kept as an example of rumour-myth formation, with no endorsement of its claims.

passages.text: The people of Matabello amused me much by their strange ideas concerning the Russian war: they believe that the Russians were not only most thoroughly beaten by the Turks, but were absolutely conquered, and all converted to Islamism; and they can hardly be convinced that such is not the case.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬塔貝洛人對於俄羅斯戰爭的種種奇思異想，令我覺得十分有趣：他們相信俄羅斯人不僅被土耳其人徹底擊敗，而且完全被征服，全都改信了伊斯蘭教；旁人幾乎無法使他們相信事實並非如此。

passages.text: Another of their notions is, that the Turks are the largest and strongest people in the world — in fact a race of giants; that they eat enormous quantities of meat, and are a most ferocious and irresistible nation. Whence such strangely incorrect opinions could have arisen it is difficult to understand, unless they are derived from Arab priests, or hadjis returned from Mecca.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace (1869); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們的另一種想法是：土耳其人是世上最高大、最強壯的民族——實際上是一族巨人；他們食量驚人，嗜食肉類，是極其兇猛、不可抵擋的民族。這種離譜至極的看法究竟從何而來，實難理解，除非是得自阿拉伯祭司，或自麥加朝聖歸來的哈吉之口。

title.en: The Lost Daughter and the Reptile Husband
title.zh: 失蹤的女兒與蟒形丈夫

region.en: Large inland valley, Greenland
region.zh: 格陵蘭內陸大谷

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 21 'The Lost Daughter', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Gone for good one day, the daughter of two hunter-brothers returns hooded and 'married to one not of human race,' nursing a biting, blood-lipped reptile in her amowt. Her brothers storm the great house in the valley, tear her offspring to pieces, and spear the house-sized husband as it comes in twined about her body — then warn her off her bad habits. But a black-streaked worm grows daily in her hand until she disappears again, the mother dying on the search, one brother's leg broken, and the family giving up all hope.
summary.zh: 兩獵手的妹妹某日一去不返；再現時兜帽之下竟孕育著會咬唇吮血的蟲怪，並自陳『嫁的丈夫非人類』。兄弟們攻入谷中大屋，撕碎其後代，又以弓矛射殺如屋牆般巨大、盤繞其身的丈夫，並誡她勿再犯舊習。然而她掌中一條黑紋小蟲日漸長大，最後她再度消失；母親死於尋女途中，一個兄弟折了腿——全家從此放棄希望。

sensitivity.note: Animal-husband and monstrous-offspring motifs; graphic violence recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: An old woman lived with her three children, two sons and a daughter. The sons were good hunters and loved their sister exceedingly; as time passed on the mother observed a change in her daughter's manners, and one day the daughter went out by herself and stayed away for good. The brothers sought her far and wide, gave it up at last, and again took to kayaking and hunting, living alone with their mother. One day, when she was all by herself, lying on the ledge beneath the skin coverlet, she remarked a thing like a shadow gliding across the doorway, and turning that way beheld her long-lost daughter; perceiving the amowt (hood) she wore, she asked her to come and sit beside her, admiring her beautiful clothes, the amowt particularly, made of soft and thin reindeer-skin. When a low cry was heard from within it, the mother asked her to take out the little one she was carrying to let her see it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 21 'The Lost Daughter'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個老婦人與她的三個孩子同住，兩個兒子、一個女兒。兒子們是好獵手，極疼愛妹妹；日子過去，母親察覺女兒的舉止有了變化，有一天女兒獨自外出，從此一去不返。兄弟倆四處遍尋，終於放棄，重又划著皮艇打獵，與母親相依為命。有一天，母親獨自一人躺在獸皮被褥下的床板上，忽見一團影子似的東西掠過門口，轉頭望去，竟見到了失散已久的女兒；她瞧見女兒戴著的兜帽（amowt），便喚她過來坐在身旁，讚賞她美麗的衣裳，尤其是那頂兜帽，是用柔軟而薄薄的馴鹿皮製成的。忽聽得兜帽裡傳出一聲低低的啼哭，母親便叫她抱出所帶的小東西讓她看看。

passages.text: The daughter answered her, 'What I carry on my back is no human being. Thou hadst better hide thyself beneath thy skin coverlet.' The mother did so, but peeping through a small opening, was dreadfully alarmed at seeing her daughter produce a large reptile, which she allowed to bite her lips so as to make them bleed; having caressed it in a motherly way, she let it suck at her breast, then replaced it in her amowt and asked her mother to look up again. 'Where is thy dwelling-place, child?' 'My house lies far from here, in a very large valley; but my husband is not of human race: so none of you must ever think of coming to see me,' she added, and left. In the evening, when the sons returned, the mother told them what had happened: 'I have seen your sister, but in a very low and contemptible state. Only think! she carried a vile reptile in her amowt, and was also married to such a one!' The brothers got into a great rage, prepared their bows and arrows to attack the vermin, and starting together soon found the great house in the valley.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 21 'The Lost Daughter'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女兒答道：「我背上的不是人。你還是躲到獸皮被褥底下吧。」母親照做了，卻從一個小縫裡偷看，驚恐地見到女兒取出一隻巨大的爬蟲，任牠咬自己的嘴唇，咬得流血；她像母親般撫愛牠一番，讓牠吮吸自己的乳房，然後把牠放回兜帽裡，又叫母親再抬頭看。「孩子，你住在何處？」「我的家在很遠的地方，在一座極大的山谷裡；但我丈夫不是人類，所以你們誰也別想來看我。」她說完便走了。傍晚兒子們回來，母親把發生的事告訴他們：「我見到你們的妹妹了，可她淪落到極卑賤可鄙的地步。你想想！她兜帽裡竟帶著一隻醜惡的爬蟲，還嫁給了這樣的東西！」兄弟倆勃然大怒，備好弓箭要去誅殺那毒物，一同出發，不久便在山谷中找到了那座大屋。

passages.text: After a careful inspection of all the mountains they ventured to peep through the window, and saw their sister comfortably seated in a snug and well-furnished room. They entered at once, killed her offspring, and having torn it to pieces, threw it outside. They did not leave their sorrowing sister during the day-time; but towards evening they saw her dreadful husband approaching from some remote part of the country — its size like the wall of a house, in its mouth a large reindeer. When it came nearer the brothers went out to hide at the back of the house, whence they saw the reptile drop the reindeer on the ground and afterwards enter the house; peeping again, they saw the creature twining itself closely round the body of their sister, so that only the tuft of her hair was visible.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 21 'The Lost Daughter'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們仔細察看過所有山嶺之後，才壯著膽子從窗戶窺探，只見妹妹舒舒服服地坐在一間溫暖而陳設齊整的屋裡。他們立刻進去，殺了她的孽種，把牠撕成碎片，扔到屋外。白天他們一直陪著悲傷的妹妹；到了傍晚，他們看見她那可怕的丈夫從國土某處偏遠之地歸來——身軀大如屋牆，口中銜著一頭大馴鹿。待牠走近，兄弟倆便出去躲在屋後，從那裡看見那爬蟲把馴鹿丟在地上，隨後進了屋；他們再一窺看，只見那東西緊緊纏繞在妹妹身上，只露出她的一綹頭髮。

passages.text: They tightened the strings of their bows, keeping them ready bent, then made a little noise to alarm the beast: the instant it emerged from the house it was aimed at from both sides, and when all their arrows had been spent, finished off and killed with their spears. They made for home bringing their sister along, as well as all her things and some dried reindeer; and the sister was once more with her parents, who warned her to leave off her former bad habits. After a little her manner towards them again suddenly changed; they perceived she was always carrying something about in her hand — a small worm or reptile with black streaks round its body. Every day it grew in size, so that before long both sides appeared out of her hand; and now she disappeared a second time. The brothers again went in search of her, this time taking their mother along; but she soon died on her way, one brother had his leg broken, and henceforth they gave up all hope of ever finding their sister.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 21 'The Lost Daughter'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們繃緊弓弦，讓弓保持張開待發，然後弄出一點聲響驚動那野獸：牠一出屋，兩邊便同時瞄準射擊，待箭都射盡，再用長矛結果了牠的性命。他們帶著妹妹回家，也帶上她所有的東西和一些乾馴鹿肉；妹妹重又回到父母身邊，父母告誡她改掉以往的惡習。過了不久，她對他們的態度又驟然改變；他們發覺她手裡總是拿著什麼東西——一條身上有黑色條紋的小蟲或小爬蟲。牠一天天長大，不久兩端都從她手中露了出來；這回她又失蹤了。兄弟倆再次出去尋找，這回帶上了母親；但母親不久便死在途中，一個兄弟折斷了腿，從此他們便斷了再找到妹妹的一切希望。

title.en: Angutisugsuk: The Bewitched Wall and the Brother's Spear
title.zh: 安古提舒克：被咒的牆與兄弟之矛

region.en: Winter quarters at the fiord, Greenland
region.zh: 格陵蘭峽灣越冬地

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two offended old men bewitch the empty house-wall to sow discord in the family of three hunter-brothers. The charm works: a wooden plate and spoon promised for mending a jacket sets wife against wife, brother against brother, until Angutisugsuk lames his own brother and flees with the unloved wife, returning again and again to kill him. Ambushed at last through an old man's hand-omen spell, he is hamstrung, speared in the shoulder, and dies on the beach — and the mournful cry goes up, 'Alas! we have killed him who did well towards us,' the wronged second wife put to death in his place.
summary.zh: 兩名懷恨的老人對空屋的牆壁施咒，播下猜忌。咒術應驗：一隻木盤木勺引發兩妻相爭、兄弟相殘——安古提舒克打瘸親弟，攜不受寵的次妻出走，又屢屢返回謀殺胞弟。老人以手背朝下之兆施咒設伏，他終被縛住腳筋、肩上連中數矛，倒斃海灘——眾人哀嘆『唉！我們殺了待我們那麼好的人』；肇事的次妻亦被處死陪葬。

sensitivity.note: Sorcery-by-proxy (bewitching a house) is a documented Greenlandic belief. Killing of the wife recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: There were three brothers, the eldest called Angutisugsuk, who had never lived apart, all clever hunters, especially Angutisugsuk. One winter the weather was dreadfully severe and all the neighbours in great want; only the three brothers had enough to spare, and the others claimed their assistance. Two old men came to them with that intention, and during their visit the wife of Angutisugsuk remonstrated that they were having rather too many visitors, at which the old men quickly took offence. In spring, when Angutisugsuk's family left their winter-quarters on a long excursion, they visited the place in their kayaks, entered the empty house, and practised all manner of sorcery and witchcraft upon the wall adjoining the ledge occupied by Angutisugsuk's wife, in order to produce discord among the family when they came back from their travels.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有三兄弟，長兄名叫安古提蘇克蘇克，他們從未分開居住，個個都是靈巧的獵人，尤其是安古提蘇克蘇克。有一年冬天，天氣酷烈異常，所有鄰居都極度匱乏；唯有這三兄弟尚有餘裕，其他人便向他們求助。有兩個老人懷著這個打算前來，在他們作客期間，安古提蘇克蘇克的妻子抱怨說訪客未免太多了些，兩個老人聞言立刻動怒。到了春天，安古提蘇克蘇克一家離開冬居，外出作長途遠行時，他們划著皮艇來到那地方，進入空屋，對著安古提蘇克蘇克妻子所臥的床榻旁那面牆，施行種種巫術與魔法，好讓這家人遠行歸來後彼此不和。

passages.text: In autumn they all returned to the old house as usual. One day Angutisugsuk stayed home to make a wooden plate and spoon; he had got two wives, both clever at needle-work, and offered to give her who would mend his fur jacket the plate and spoon. The first wife answered before the second could put in a word — 'I want to have them — I will mend the jacket' — and worked very quickly; but the second wife, the best beloved, became envious and got into a passion. Perceiving this, the husband struck her, because of her having borne him no children; at this his youngest son began crying, and seeing it, the child's uncle fell upon the father, who was still ill-treating his second wife. In this fight Angutisugsuk thrust his brother against the door-sill with such force that his thigh-bone was bruised, and would have followed up his advantage but for the younger brother and some others who interfered. Thus it came to pass as the old men had planned when they went and bewitched the empty house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了秋天，他們都像往常一樣回到老屋。有一天，安古提蘇克蘇克留在家中做木盤和木匙；他有兩個妻子，都擅長針線，他提出誰替他縫補毛皮外套，就把木盤和木匙給誰。第一個妻子搶在第二個妻子開口之前答道——「我要那些東西——我來補外套」——而且手腳極快；但第二個妻子，也就是他最寵愛的那個，心生嫉妒，發起脾氣來。丈夫見狀便打了她，因為她沒替他生下孩子；他最小的兒子見了便哭起來，孩子的叔父看見，就撲向那仍在虐待第二個妻子的父親。在這場爭鬥中，安古提蘇克蘇克把弟弟猛力推撞到門檻上，撞傷了他的大腿骨，若不是弟弟和另外幾個人攔阻，他還要繼續進逼。於是事情正如兩個老人所謀劃的那樣發生了——他們當初就是去對那空屋施了巫術。

passages.text: Having lamed his brother, Angutisugsuk next day loaded his boat and went off, taking a small roofless house a little north of his former station, making a shift with his tent-poles for roof-beams; his proper wife he left behind, taking only the second one. Seeing his brother was now able to stir, he resolved to kill him, and repeatedly returned to despatch him, but always found his younger brother or his nephew by his side — these two watching the sick man by turns, only one at a time going out in his kayak. Encountering his nephew at sea he resolved to pursue him, but as soon as they came within sight of the house on shore he left off and turned back. The invalid bade his son ask the neighbours to assist in getting Angutisugsuk out of the way, 'because he has gone raving mad; but two or three men will not suffice, for he is immensely strong himself.' The son brought a considerable party of kayakers, who hid their kayaks behind the house for the night; early in the morning they saw Angutisugsuk emerging from behind a rocky point, and an old man among the strangers drew his hood closer and pronounced a magic spell, adding that if it were likely to succeed, Angutisugsuk as a sure sign would turn the backs of his hands downwards instead of using the palms in ascending the beach. Watching him closely, they noticed he did as foretold, and no longer had any doubt of their success.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安古提蘇克蘇克把弟弟弄瘸之後，第二天便裝載好船離去，在舊居稍北處找了一間沒有屋頂的小屋，拿帳篷桿權充屋樑；他把正妻留下，只帶了第二個妻子。他見弟弟如今已能動彈，便決意殺他，屢次回去要結果他性命，卻總見弟弟或外甥守在他身旁——這兩人輪流看護病人，一次只出去一人划皮艇。他在海上遇見外甥，便決意追趕，但他們一望見岸上的屋子，他就作罷折返。病人吩咐兒子去請鄰居幫忙除掉安古提蘇克蘇克，「因為他已經瘋得發狂了；但兩三個人不夠，他本人力大無窮。」兒子帶來了一大群划皮艇的人，他們把皮艇藏在屋後過夜；清早他們看見安古提蘇克蘇克從一處岩石岬角後走出來，陌生人中有一個老人把風帽拉得更緊，念了一道咒語，又說若這咒語有望成功，安古提蘇克蘇克必會以手背朝下、而非用手掌上岸，作為確鑿的徵兆。他們密切注視他，果然見他如預言那般做了，於是對成功再無懷疑。

passages.text: He drew his kayak only half-way out of the water, went straight up to the house as if to enter at once, then bethinking himself of something turned back to the large boat for a flensing-knife and proceeded to the entry. The men reclined on the side-ledge couches except two posted at the inner entrance ready to seize him. Seeing his brother on the main ledge, he addressed him: 'Here is a brave man for thee! I'll show thee the way to fight! Didst thou really believe I did not intend to kill thee?' — and advancing a step or two was soon seized by the two men and quickly disarmed. Conducted outside, all the rest fell upon him, but nobody could manage to overthrow him; at last, hamstrung, he fell, and they held a council as to which of them should first stab him. The invalid brother was carried out to finish him off, put down close beside him, had his spear fetched from under the boat, and lanced his brother several times in the shoulder: 'Now let go your hold; if he boasts himself a man, he will be sure to rise.' He did get up and went towards his kayak on the beach, but fell down dead before he reached it. Then the surviving brother exclaimed, 'Alas! we have killed him who did well towards us. In the short, dark days, when we were almost starving, he did not mind toiling away for us. I am sorry indeed: now do kill me also!' He asked his brother, his son, and all the other men; finding nobody would do it, he said, 'Well, then, go and fetch his second wife, and kill her at any rate; it was she who began it all.' They did so; the person who slew her admonished the bystanders to put together all her things, all her clothes, jackets of reindeer-skin, breeches and boots of seal-skin, carry them along with her, close up the burial-place well, and heap plenty of stones on top of it. Later on, when the invalid recovered, he felt great remorse for his act of violence; but the old magician was quite satisfied that Angutisugsuk should have been killed by his brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 22 'Angutisugsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他只把皮艇拖出水面一半，便逕直朝屋子走去，彷彿要立刻進門，隨後想起什麼，又折回大船去取一把割鯨刀，然後走向入口。眾人斜倚在側邊的坐榻上，只有兩人守在內門處，準備擒住他。他看見弟弟躺在正中的坐榻上，便對他說：「這兒有個勇士給你！我來教你怎麼打架！你真以為我無意殺你嗎？」——他向前邁了一兩步，隨即被那兩人擒住，迅速繳了械。他被帶到屋外，其餘眾人一齊撲上，卻誰也制伏不了他；最後他的腿筋被割斷，倒了下來，眾人便商議該由誰先刺他。那殘廢的弟弟被抬出來結果他，被放在他身旁，叫人從船下取出他的長矛，朝哥哥的肩頭刺了好幾下：「現在放開他吧；他若自誇是條漢子，必定會站起來。」他果然起身，朝灘上的皮艇走去，卻還沒走到就倒地死了。這時那活下來的弟弟驚呼道：「唉！我們殺了他，可他待我們一向很好。在那短暫昏暗的日子裡，我們幾乎餓死，他卻不辭辛勞為我們奔波。我實在懊悔：現在把我也殺了吧！」他求弟弟、求兒子，又求所有其他人；見無人肯動手，便說：「那麼，去把他第二個妻子帶來，至少把她殺了；這一切都是她起的頭。」他們照辦了；殺她的人告誡旁觀者把她所有的東西、所有衣物、馴鹿皮外套、海豹皮褲和靴子都收攏起來，連她一同帶去，把墓穴封好，在上面堆上大量石頭。後來，那殘廢的弟弟康復之後，對自己的暴行深感悔恨；但那老巫師卻十分滿意，認為安古提蘇克蘇克理應被他弟弟殺死。

title.en: Sitliamat: The Bear That Pushed Them Home
title.zh: 西特利阿馬特：推冰送歸的熊

region.en: Drift-ice and the unknown other shore
region.zh: 浮冰海與未知的彼岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; abridged text, resembling tales 16 and 19, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Storm-driven onto an unknown shore, three brothers and their companion shelter with an old couple whose pale, weaponless son recovers among them. At parting the old man dives into the sea as a bear: gull-amulet men glide on the waves' surface, the raven-amulet companion sinks and is left behind, and the bear shoulders their iceberg home with the warning to shut their eyes — landing them south of their old habitation, where boys play who were named in memory of them. Their lost wives remarried are restored, and in winter a bald-headed bear is feasted with entire seals at the entrance and vanishes forever into the sea.
summary.zh: 風暴把三兄弟拋上異鄉海岸；一對老夫婦收留他們，其慘白的無器之子也漸漸康復。臨別時老人躍海化熊：護身符為海鷗者踏浪滑行，渡鴉護符的同伴沉底被留，熊以肩推冰山送他們閉眼歸鄉——上岸處男孩們正以他們的名字玩耍。被再嫁的妻子們歸還原夫；冬日一頭白首之熊登岸受整豹之宴，飽食後循跡入海，從此絕跡。

sensitivity.note: Amulet-bird (gull vs raven) as homecoming fate; bald-headed bear gratitude motif. Parallel transformation endings to tale 16 (Tiggak).

passages.text: There were three brothers, the eldest named Sitliarnat, who one day all went out hunting on the frozen sea, accompanied by a person in no way related to them. All of a sudden a south-east storm arose, the ice creaked and gave way beneath their feet, and nothing remained but to mount an iceberg; having got there, they drifted far away out on the great ocean, nearly starving with hunger when they at length touched upon an unknown shore and landed. Roaming about in search of people, they passed an isthmus on which they observed a little hut with only one window. Sitliarnat spoke: 'Let them make me their first prize' — and crossed the threshold in front of his companions. Inside they found only an old couple, the sole inhabitants; the four strangers seated themselves on the ledge, and nobody spoke until the old man, eyeing them more closely and breathing upon them, asked, 'Whence do you come?' 'Some time ago we set off from the land on the other side of the ocean, and went out on the ice to catch seals; but a gale from the south-east came on, breaking up the ice and drifting us across to your country. So here we are; three of us are brothers, and the fourth is a companion of ours.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有三兄弟，長兄名叫西特利亞爾納特，有一天他們一同到冰封的海上打獵，隨行的還有一個與他們毫無親屬關係的人。忽然颳起一陣東南風暴，冰面嘎吱作響，在他們腳下裂開，除了爬上一座冰山別無他法；上了冰山之後，他們便漂流到遼闊的大洋上，遠離陸地，等到終於靠上一處陌生的海岸登陸時，幾乎餓死了。他們四處遊走尋找人家，經過一道地峽，看見那裡有一間只有一扇窗戶的小屋。西特利亞爾納特說：「讓他們把我當作頭一份獵物吧」——說著便搶在同伴之前跨過門檻。屋裡只有一對老夫婦，是僅有的居民；四個陌生人坐到坐榻上，誰也不開口，直到那老人把他們細細打量一番，朝他們吹了口氣，問道：「你們從哪兒來？」「不久前我們從大洋對岸的陸地出發，到冰上去捕海豹；不料東南方向起了大風，把冰吹裂，把我們一路漂到你們這地方來。所以就這樣到了這裡；我們三個是兄弟，第四個是我們的同伴。」

passages.text: 'After travelling so far people are apt to get hungry,' the old man observed to his wife, adding words the people did not understand; she fetched some blubber in a pan, boiled it, and served it in a wooden dish — though almost fainting with hunger, they only tasted a very little of it, and soon after a proper meal was set before them. 'Our only provider is staying away a long time; we have been expecting him back this last month. He left us to go out hunting, and has not yet returned; we are much afraid he may have encountered some wicked people and have come to grief.' The visitors began to think, 'What sort of people may these be?' — but stayed on, the old man providing food for some time. One morning they heard a voice calling from without, 'I want to get in; do let me get in!' — the old man returned holding his son by the hand, very pale and haggard, who lay on the side ledge for several days until one morning he rose up very early, recovered in health, strength, appetite, and aspect, and took up his task as provider — strange to say, never seen to carry any weapons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「走了這麼遠的路，人難免會餓的，」老人對妻子說，又補了幾句旁人聽不懂的話；她去取來一鍋鯨脂，煮了，盛在木盤裡端上——他們雖然餓得幾乎昏過去，卻只稍稍嘗了一點，不久之後，一頓像樣的飯菜便擺在他們面前。「我們唯一的供養者出門很久了；這一個月來我們一直盼他回來。他出去打獵，至今未歸；我們很擔心他遇上了壞人，遭了不測。」來客們心裡開始琢磨：「這會是什麼樣的人呢？」——但還是留了下來，老人一連好些天供他們吃喝。有一天早晨，他們聽見外面有人喊：「我要進去；讓我進去呀！」——老人牽著兒子的手回來，那兒子面色蒼白、形容枯槁，在側邊坐榻上躺了好幾天，直到有一天早晨他很早起身，健康、力氣、胃口和氣色都恢復了，又擔起供養者的職責——說來奇怪，從沒見他帶過任何武器。

passages.text: The visitors prolonged their stay for several years. One evening the old man questioned the eldest brother, 'What did they give thee for thy amulet when thou wert born?' 'In my infancy I got a carrion-gull, one of those that always seek the carrion farthest out to sea.' 'So thou mayst be sure of returning to thy own country at some time or other.' All the brothers had the same bird; but the companion's was a raven, a bird that always seeks his prey landward — 'I doubt if thou wilt ever see thy country again, if it is so.' The old man used to rise the earliest of them all, seen on some mountain-top marking the state of the air and the weather, and one day entered with the remark, 'When the wind goes down and the weather gets settled, I shall take you across' — they wondered, there being no ice, neither boats nor kayaks, and they did not even know in what direction their country was situated. One morning while they were still fast asleep he cried, 'It is no time for sleeping now. Make haste and get up, if ye really long for your homes; I shall see you along myself' — and following him down to the steep shore where they had landed years ago: 'Now watch me!' Taking a run he leapt into the sea, dived down, and reappeared in the shape of a bear: 'If Sitliarnat really has a gull for his amulet, it will soon appear to him. Do as I have done, and throw thyself into the water.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這些訪客延長了他們的停留，一住便是數年。某天傍晚，老人問那長兄：「你出生時，他們給你什麼作護身符？」「我幼年時得的是一隻海鷗，就是那種總是往最遠的外海去尋覓腐肉的海鷗。」「那麼你或可確信，總有一天你會回到自己的故鄉。」眾兄弟得的都是同一種鳥；但同伴得的卻是一隻渡鴉，一種總是往陸地尋覓獵物的鳥——「若果真如此，我懷疑你還能再見到你的故鄉。」老人向來是眾人中起得最早的，有人見他在某座山頂上察看空氣與天氣的狀況；有一天他走進屋裡說道：「等風停了、天氣穩定下來，我就送你們過去」——他們心中疑惑，因為既沒有冰，也沒有船或皮划艇，他們甚至不知道自己的故鄉位於哪個方向。某天清晨，他們仍熟睡未醒，他喊道：「現在可不是睡覺的時候。快起來，如果你們真的渴望回家；我會親自送你們一程」——於是他們跟著他下到多年前登岸的那陡峭的海岸邊：「現在看著我！」他助跑幾步，縱身躍入海中，潛了下去，再現身時已是一頭熊的模樣：「如果 Sitliarnat 真的以海鷗為護身符，牠很快就會出現在他面前。照我做的去做，把自己投入水中。」

passages.text: Sitliarnat still lingered a little, but the bear went on, 'If thou dost not follow me into the ocean, thou wilt never get home.' He ran on and took the leap; as soon as he had plunged down he again rose, merely touching the surface with his feet, gliding along as if on solid ice instead of on the waves of the sea — and the gull also made its appearance, a large iceberg seen which he climbed, both his brothers following. The old man turned to the fourth: 'Thou, too, wouldst like to return, I know; now try thy wings!' He plunged into the sea trying to fly, but went right down, and would have lost breath but for the bear, who put him on shore: 'No, thou wilt never get home, because thou hast got a raven for thy amulet; thou canst return to my house as before.' The bear spoke to the three: 'Shut your eyes and sit close together. If ye open your eyes, ye will never get home. I shall now put my shoulder to the iceberg, and push you away.' Their place of refuge began to shake beneath them, and they had started on their journey, moving onwards until they felt a quake as if touching something hard. 'Open your eyes' — they beheld a country spreading before them and recognised it as their own, landed just a little south of their former habitation. They asked the bear to enter, that they might recompense him in some way; but he said, 'No, I don't care for being paid — I merely intended to do you a good turn; but when in winter-time ye should happen to see a bear with a bald head, and your companions prepare to hunt him down, then try to make them desist, and put some food before him' — and plunging into the sea he instantly disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Sitliarnat 仍躊躇了片刻，但熊繼續說道：「你若不隨我入海，就永遠回不了家。」牠奔跑向前，縱身一躍；他剛一潛下，便又升起，雙腳僅僅掠過水面，滑行而去，彷彿腳下是堅冰而非海浪——那海鷗也現了身，化作一座巨大的冰山，他攀了上去，兩個兄弟也跟了上來。老人轉向第四人：「我知道你也想回去；現在試試你的翅膀吧！」他躍入海中試圖飛翔，卻直往下沉，若不是那熊把他送上岸，他早已沒了氣息：「不行，你永遠回不了家，因為你的護身符是渡鴉；你只能像從前一樣回到我家去。」熊對三人說道：「閉上眼睛，緊緊坐在一起。你們若睜開眼，就永遠回不了家。我現在要把肩膀抵住冰山，把你們推走。」他們棲身之處在腳下開始震動，他們已踏上旅程，向前移動，直到感覺一陣震顫，彷彿觸到了什麼堅硬的東西。「睜開眼」——他們看見一片大地在眼前展開，認出那正是自己的故鄉，登陸之處就在他們從前居所略偏南的地方。他們請熊進屋，好報答牠一番；但牠說：「不必了，我不圖什麼報答——我只是想幫你們一把；不過到了冬天，你們若碰巧看見一頭禿了頭的熊，而你們的同伴準備去獵殺牠，那時就設法勸他們住手，並在牠面前放些食物」——說罷躍入海中，轉眼便不見了。

passages.text: The brothers went up to their former house and knew it to be inhabited because of little boys seen at play outside, named after them by their parents in remembrance of their lost friends. Their wives had all married again, but the other relatives rejoiced greatly at receiving those they had given up for lost. Asked about their companion, they answered they had left him 'on the opposite shore.' Perceiving that the husbands of their former wives feared them, they reassured them — 'We don't intend any harm towards you. Many thanks to you that ye have provided so well for our relatives' — but the wives, nevertheless, were given back to them. During the winter the bear was almost forgotten, till one evening when they were all at home some of the men exclaimed, 'A bear is making for the shore!' Collecting their arms, the brothers interfered, crying, 'Just wait a little; we must first have a look at him' — and instantly recognised their own bear: 'Without his good aid we should never have reached home again. Don't hunt that bear; make haste and give him a feast.' When the bear had got on shore he went right up to the house, sat down on his haunches before the entrance, head turned towards it; the people put several entire seals before him and beckoned him to eat, all the men gathered round him. When the meal was ended the bear lay down to sleep while the children played round him; after a while he awoke, having eaten a little more, arose, and following his own traces back to the beach, leapt into the sea, and was never seen any more. It is said that the descendants of Sitliarnat were very prosperous and multiplied greatly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 23 'Sitliamat'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾兄弟走上他們從前的屋子，知道裡頭住著人，因為看見幾個小男孩在外頭玩耍，他們的名字是父母為紀念失散的朋友而取的。他們的妻子都已改嫁，但其他親屬見到這些本已認定失蹤的人歸來，都萬分欣喜。問起他們的同伴，他們回答說把他留在了「對岸」。他們察覺到前妻的現任丈夫懼怕他們，便安慰道：「我們無意加害於你們。多謝你們把我們的親人照顧得這麼好」——然而那些妻子終究還是歸還給了他們。整個冬天，那熊幾乎被遺忘了，直到某天傍晚他們都在家時，有幾個男人喊道：「有頭熊正朝岸邊來！」眾兄弟拿起武器，上前攔阻，喊道：「且慢一慢；我們得先看看牠」——立刻認出正是他們的那頭熊：「若沒有牠的善助，我們絕不可能再回到家中。別獵那頭熊；快給牠備一頓盛宴。」熊上岸後徑直走向屋子，在門口蹲坐下來，頭朝向屋內；人們把好幾整隻海豹放在牠面前，招手示意牠吃，所有男人都圍攏過來。吃罷，熊躺下睡覺，孩子們在牠周圍玩耍；過了一會兒牠醒來，又吃了些，站起身，循著自己的足跡回到海灘，躍入海中，此後再無人見過牠。據說 Sitliarnat 的後裔十分興旺，繁衍眾多。

title.en: The Reindeer-Hunt of Merkisalik: The Bewitched Knuckle
title.zh: 梅基薩利克的獵鹿記：被咒的指骨

region.en: Inland reindeer valleys, Greenland
region.zh: 格陵蘭內陸馴鹿谷

period: Inuit oral tradition; compiled from two copies (one North Greenland, before 1828), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Visiting hunters mock the lone son of old Merkisalik — 'There must be any amount of animals in this place, since even Merkisalik's son is capable of getting at them' — and give him the last loophole. He alarms the herd, runs down the leaders over the hills, and returns cool and refreshed to their red-faced wrath. But the father of the visitors asks for a knuckle 'for a gimlet,' bewitches the knee-joint, and the swelling kills the son; Merkisalik makes a tupilak of whitened bones until it takes the shape of a little whale, and the hunters' sons vanish one by one from the north, harpooning 'a little whale,' until his wrath is somewhat appeased.
summary.zh: 造訪的獵隊譏誚梅基薩利克的獨子，逼他守最後一個射孔；他驚散鹿群、追過山脊，衣冠整齊地涼快而歸，令敵人紅著臉無言。然而仇家之父討走一根指骨『做手鑽』，暗中詛咒其膝關節——腫瘤日漸奪去兒子性命。老人以漂白的獸骨捏製圖皮拉克，直到它化作小鯨之形；此後北方的仇家子弟一個個『叉中小鯨』而消失，老人胸中恨意方才稍平。

sensitivity.note: Bewitched-gift motif (the requested knuckle as carrier of sorcery); tupilak-making as revenge, as in tale 13. Deaths recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Merkisalik had only one son to assist him in providing for his family; in the summer they always hunted along the shores of the same fiord without other company. Growing old and infirm, Merkisalik gave up hunting and left the providing to his son. Once, taken up at the fiord again with the son out hunting, the old people were left by themselves expecting no visitors — when they suddenly observed a boat sailing up the inlet right before the wind, accompanied by several kayakers. Merkisalik was much pleased, and ordered his wife to put out some dry meat for a bite on landing, rejoicing that his son should henceforth have companions on his hunting excursions. Among the visitors were a great number of men, some old and rather talkative and entertaining; the son returning from the mountains was likewise very glad of the company, treated them with the utmost hospitality, and invited them to the meal as soon as it was boiled and ready. They conversed very politely, and soon agreed in going out together the next day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: Merkisalik 只有一個兒子幫他養家；夏天他們總是在同一條峽灣沿岸狩獵，別無他人作伴。Merkisalik 年老體衰，便放棄了狩獵，把養家的擔子交給兒子。有一次，他們又來到那條峽灣，兒子外出打獵，老人們獨自留下，本不指望有客來訪——忽然他們看見一隻船順風駛入灣中，還有幾個划皮艇的人隨行。Merkisalik 大為高興，吩咐妻子拿出些乾肉，好讓客人上岸後吃點東西，他慶幸兒子今後打獵時能有伴了。訪客中有許多男人，有些上了年紀，頗為健談風趣；兒子從山上回來，也同樣為有伴而高興，極盡殷勤地款待他們，肉一煮好便邀他們一同用餐。他們交談甚為客氣，很快便約定次日一同出獵。

passages.text: Before long they came in sight of a number of animals feeding on the grass down in the valleys. The drivers were sent out, the hunters made walls of earth furnished with loopholes, and the visitors proposed that Merkisalik's son should be the last to shoot — he agreed; but when the drivers had surrounded the animals and began to drive them towards the loopholed walls, the thought struck him, 'What if they are too greedy to leave me any chance at all?' The others took aim and shot all that were to be got; he assisted in stripping off the skins, remaining a little behind on descending the hills towards the tents. At supper one of the men remarked, 'There must be any amount of animals in this place, since even Merkisalik's son is capable of getting at them.' The Merkisaliks heard the slight in silence; afterwards, sitting together in their own tent, the father said, 'It can't be otherwise; we must just let them have their way, seeing that they are so many.' The next day was spent in the same manner, the son allowed to take up his position as far away as possible from the drivers; the man who had scorned him spoke to him in a similar fashion again, at which he got into a great passion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，他們便望見一群動物在山谷下吃草。驅趕的人被派了出去，獵人們築起帶有射擊孔的土牆，訪客們提議讓 Merkisalik 的兒子最後一個射——他同意了；但當驅趕的人圍住獸群，開始把牠們趕向那些帶孔的土牆時，他心中忽然想到：「萬一他們太貪心，一點機會都不留給我呢？」其他人瞄準射擊，把所有能到手的都射殺了；他幫著剝皮，下山朝帳篷走去時稍稍落在後面。晚飯時，其中一人說道：「這地方準有數不清的動物，連 Merkisalik 的兒子都能獵到。」Merkisalik 一家默默聽著這番輕蔑之言；後來，父子二人在自家帳篷裡坐著，父親說：「這也是沒辦法的事；既然他們人多，我們只好由著他們。」第二天也照樣度過，兒子被允許盡可能遠離驅趕的人選定位置；那個曾輕蔑他的人又用類似的口氣對他說話，他於是勃然大怒。

passages.text: They set out together the next day to the entrance of a great valley almost overcrowded with reindeer, and as before ordered him to choose his hiding-place and make his loophole behind them all — at which he murmured to himself, 'If this is to go on, I shall never be able to get anything. I think I will give the beasts the alarm, that they may all run away.' When the flock approached, driven by the drivers, he feigned to be busy about something, was warned to be quiet, stopped a moment, and began to move about again. All of a sudden the leader stopped short, turned round, and bounded off as fast as possible; the others began to follow but dropped short one after another, so that at the other end of the valley but one had kept up with him, and that one soon tired out. Merkisalik's son disappeared on the other side of the hills, pursuing the fast-running animals. Slowly the men followed his traces; from the top of the hill they beheld numbers of deer with white bellies ready killed in the valley on the other side, and on a stone close by the huntsman seated, already quite cool and refreshed. The others arrived, faces all red with heat and wrath, and nobody spoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，他們一同出發前往一個幾乎擠滿了馴鹿的大山谷谷口，又像先前一樣吩咐他在所有人後面選好藏身之處、挖好射擊孔——他暗自嘟囔道：「若這樣下去，我什麼也獵不到。我看不如把獸群驚動起來，讓牠們全都跑掉。」當獸群被驅趕的人趕近時，他裝作忙於某事，被警告要安靜，停了一會兒，又開始動來動去。忽然間，領頭的那隻猛地停住，轉過身，飛也似地奔逃而去；其餘的也跟著跑，卻一隻接一隻地落了下來，結果到了山谷另一頭，只有一隻跟上了牠，而那隻也很快疲憊不堪。Merkisalik 的兒子消失在山丘的另一側，追趕著那些奔跑迅捷的動物。眾人緩緩循著他的足跡跟去；從山頂上，他們望見山谷另一側有許多白腹的鹿已被獵殺倒地，而獵人正坐在近旁的一塊石頭上，已然十分從容、精神恢復。其他人趕到時，個個滿臉通紅，又熱又怒，誰也沒有作聲。

passages.text: They set to work stripping the deer; while the others finished one, he stripped and cut up two, and packing his bundle said, 'Ye may all of you take as much as ye like.' The man who had formerly ridiculed him became quite mute and would not join the rest. Merkisalik's son got home first with his burden on his back; when the others came without anything, the Merkisaliks had all their pots and pans on the fire, and, after their wont, invited the foreigners to join them — but during the meal the host tried in vain to begin a conversation; all remained mute, and even their old father kept silent. Having done eating they retired, excepting the father, who now began to be a little talkative and, as if by chance, remarked, 'We want something that would do for a gimlet; would ye mind letting me have that knuckle?' Merkisalik gave it willingly: 'We have got lots of them.' The following morning the Merkisaliks were aroused by a clattering noise of poles — the visitors pulling down their tent and preparing to depart — and they were once more alone, the son again hunting by himself. One day, busy bringing down the deer he had stalked, he told them he had got a swelling at his knee; it grew in size, getting worse and worse, and at length he died — but not till he had made known to them that his disease was solely caused by the father of their former visitors, who, in order to hurt him, had bewitched the knee-joint he had asked of them, which had worked back upon him and killed him. The poor old people were inconsolable.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們著手剝鹿皮；別人只剝完一頭，他卻已剝好並切好了兩頭，一邊捆好他的包裹一邊說：「你們大家想拿多少就拿多少吧。」那個先前嘲笑過他的人變得十分沉默，不願與其他人為伍。梅爾基薩利克的兒子背著他的負擔最先回到家；當其他人空手而來時，梅爾基薩利克一家已把所有的鍋碗瓢盆都架在火上，並按照他們的習慣，邀請這些外來人一同用餐——然而席間主人徒勞地想開啟交談；所有人都保持沉默，甚至他們的老父親也默不作聲。吃完飯後，除了父親之外，眾人都退下了；父親這時開始有點健談起來，彷彿不經意地說道：「我們想要一樣可以當錐子用的東西；你介意把那隻指節給我嗎？」梅爾基薩利克欣然給了：「我們有很多呢。」第二天早晨，梅爾基薩利克一家被一陣木桿的碰撞聲驚醒——訪客們正在拆下他們的帳篷，準備離去——他們又一次孤身獨處，兒子又獨自去打獵了。有一天，他正忙著處理他悄悄接近並獵獲的鹿，卻告訴他們說他的膝蓋上長了一個腫塊；它越長越大，越來越嚴重，最後他死了——但直到臨終前，他才讓他們知道，他的病完全是由他們先前那些訪客的父親造成的：那人為了傷害他，對他向他們索要的那個膝關節施了巫術，那巫術反過來作用於他，害死了他。那可憐的老夫婦悲痛欲絕。

passages.text: It was now autumn; the little lakes began to be covered with ice, and it was time to leave the inland country for the sea-coast. They first wept at the tomb of their son, and, still wailing and complaining, went down the firth with a light easterly breeze. Having arrived at their winter-quarters, Merkisalik's mind was filled with hatred, always contemplating revenge: to carry it out he resolved to make a tupilak to destroy his enemies. Every day he collected bones of all sorts of animals, put them into the brook close by to whiten, then mixed them up with hairs taken from boat-skins; when he had got as many as he required, he made them alive and put them into the brook which flowed on to the sea. Watching the tupilak, he saw it taking the shape of an agpaliarsuk, which dived down and turned round to its owner; but he said, 'Thou art not the thing I want thee to be yet.' Instantly it dived and reappeared in the shape of a dovekie — 'That won't do neither.' It underwent many changes, taking the shape of all sorts of birds, then of all manner of seals and dolphins; at last, after another dive, its breath was heard like a mighty roar, and he beheld a small whale — 'This will do; thou shalt avenge us.' 'Where am I to go?' the animal seemed to inquire. 'To the hunting place of the many brothers' — it took one long breath, dived down into the sea, and the man returned home to bide his time. One evening a kayaker appeared rounding the northern point — a poor relative and very old man, quartered at the same place as their former visitors — who related: 'Some days ago an accident occurred up at our place; one of the many brothers has not returned home. The day before his departure he told us that he had harpooned a little whale, adding that he would now go out in search of it; but he has never yet returned.' The maker of the tupilak feigned compassion, but inwardly rejoiced. Again and again the old visitor returned, reporting 'Yesterday the same accident happened to another of the brothers' — and at last that the last of the brothers had now disappeared, the poor parents very much grieved because of their bereavement. On hearing this, Merkisalik's wrath was somewhat appeased.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 24 'The Reindeer-hunt of Merkisalik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此時已是秋天；小湖泊開始結冰，是時候離開內陸地區前往海岸了。他們先是在兒子的墳前哭泣，然後仍舊哀號抱怨著，乘著一陣輕柔的東風順著峽灣而下。到達他們的過冬居所後，梅爾基薩利克心中充滿了仇恨，總是盤算著復仇：為了實現它，他決心造一個圖皮拉克（tupilak）來消滅他的敵人。他每天收集各種動物的骨頭，把它們放進附近的小溪裡漂白，然後把它們與從皮艇蒙皮上取下的毛髮混合在一起；當他湊夠了所需的數量，便賦予它們生命，把它們放進流向大海的小溪裡。他觀察著那圖皮拉克，見它化作一隻阿格帕利亞爾蘇克（agpaliarsuk，一種海鳥）的形狀，潛下水去又轉向它的主人；但他說：「你還不是我想要你變成的東西。」它立刻潛下水去，再出現時化作一隻小海雀的形狀——「那也不行。」它經歷了許多變化，化作各種鳥類的形狀，又化作各種海豹和海豚的形狀；最後，又一次潛水之後，只聽它的呼吸聲如巨大的咆哮，他看見一頭小鯨——「這就行了；你要為我們復仇。」「我該去哪裡？」那動物似乎在詢問。「去那眾兄弟的打獵之地」——它長長地吸了一口氣，潛入海中，那人便回家等待時機。一天傍晚，一個皮艇手繞過北面的海角出現——那是一個窮親戚，一個很老的人，與他們先前的訪客住在同一處——他講述道：「幾天前我們那邊出了事；眾兄弟中的一個沒有回家。他出發的前一天告訴我們，他叉中了一頭小鯨，還說他這就要出去尋找它；但他至今仍未回來。」那造圖皮拉克的人假裝同情，心裡卻暗自歡喜。那位老訪客一次又一次地回來，報告說「昨天同樣的事故又發生在另一個兄弟身上」——最後又說眾兄弟中最後一個如今也失蹤了，那可憐的父母因喪親而悲痛萬分。聽到這些，梅爾基薩利克的怒火稍稍平息了些。

title.en: Namak: The Sling of the Avenger
title.zh: 納馬克：復仇者的投石索

region.en: North Greenland winter-house and northern enemy station
region.zh: 北格陵蘭冬屋與北方仇敵營地

period: Inuit oral tradition; single manuscript written down in North Greenland before 1828, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 25 'Namak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Orphaned when house-fellows killed both his parents, Namak is adopted by a foster-father who worries and provokes him on purpose — 'Namak, thy enemies have come to kill thee, too' — and gives him not a kayak but a sling. Cheated too often to stir, he rises only when he hears the tents clattering for real: lifting a thong-seal one-handed to cut his sling, he ambushes on the beach and sinks three boats with thrown stones, crews and all, his mind at rest. Years later father and son row to the enemy's northern station, tear the walrus-tooth pulling-thong with one hand, and out-pull the whole house, arms hooked one after another — never invited again.
summary.zh: 父母被同屋人殺害的孤兒納馬克，被一個故意激將的養父收養——『納馬克，敵人來殺你了』——給他的不是皮艇而是投石索。被騙多次的他直到親耳聽見拆帳聲才行動：單手翻轉長鬚海豹割取投石索，伏於石堆間，三塊飛石擊沉三艘敵船連人帶舟——心境自此安寧。多年後父子北訪仇敵，徒手扯斷鑲海象牙的拉繩，又逐一勾臂角力，無人能撼其分毫——仇人從此再不敢相邀。

sensitivity.note: The native writer's note (quoted by Rink): before Christianity strong men abounded because bad consciences induced them to cultivate strength — recorded here as part of the source. Boat-sinking killings recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: The parents of Namak were both killed by their house-fellows; while he was yet a weak and helpless child, a man happened to take pity on him and adopted him for his son. But this same foster-father was fond of worrying the boy, and inventing stories to frighten and excite him: sometimes, when the child was asleep, he would cry out, 'Namak, thy enemies have come to kill thee, too' — at first much alarmed, by degrees he got used to it. Sometimes the foster-father would say, 'Ah, how forgetful that Namak is! Here are his parents newly murdered, and he forgetting all about it' — at this Namak would get into a great rage. While still a child, his father one day made him a present of a sling, saying, 'I don't mean to give thee a kayak, because I believe that thy enemies will kill thee for all that; but take this sling and practise with it.' Namak instantly began, and soon got very clever in using it; in spring he would betake himself to solitary places, practising his sling, always pondering over the things his foster-father had said to stir up vengeance within him. At home he spoke little, but inwardly rejoiced at his growing strength; sometimes he brought in hares, sometimes ptarmigan, got entirely by means of his sling.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 納馬克的父母都被他們的同屋人殺害了；當他還是一個虛弱無助的孩童時，恰好有一個人憐憫他，收養他做了兒子。但這位養父卻喜歡捉弄這男孩，編造故事來嚇唬和刺激他：有時，當孩子睡著時，他會大喊：「納馬克，你的仇人來殺你了」——起初他大為驚恐，但漸漸地也就習慣了。有時，養父會說：「唉，納馬克多麼健忘啊！他的父母剛被殺害，他卻把這事全忘了」——聽了這話，納馬克便會勃然大怒。當他還是個孩子時，有一天父親送給他一個投石索，說道：「我並不打算給你一隻皮艇，因為我相信你的仇人終究會殺了你；但拿著這個投石索去練習吧。」納馬克立刻開始練習，很快就用得十分嫻熟；春天裡，他會獨自前往僻靜之處練習投石索，心裡總是想著養父說過的那些激起他復仇之心的話。在家裡他很少說話，但內心卻為自己日益增長的力量而歡喜；有時他帶回野兔，有時帶回雷鳥，全靠他的投石索獵得。

passages.text: In the summer he never slept at night, but always in the day-time. Sometimes, when he had gone to sleep, his father would bring home a seal, and he was then awakened to assist in carrying it up to the house; he would then hide his strength, making-believe it was very hard work for him. One day, however, he said that his sling was too weak, and his father went to cut him a stronger one out of a very thick piece of seal-skin — after that time he left off gibing the boy, because he began to fear him. During the winter it was reported that the enemies of Namak intended to remove farther to the north in spring; he got quite enraged at the thought that they would be going away before he could be revenged, and from that day his manner changed altogether. When spring came round and they left their winter-house for the tents, he one day said, 'I wish I could get myself a new sling' — the father went out in his kayak and had the good luck to catch a thong-seal, brought in while Namak was still asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夏天裡他從不在夜間睡覺，總是白天睡。有時，當他睡著時，父親會帶回一頭海豹，他便被叫醒去幫忙把它搬回家；這時他會隱藏自己的力量，裝作搬起來十分吃力。然而有一天，他說他的投石索太弱了，父親便去用一塊很厚的海豹皮為他割一條更結實的——從那以後，他就不再嘲弄這男孩了，因為他開始怕他。冬天裡，有消息說納馬克的仇人打算在春天遷往更北的地方；他一想到他們會在他能夠復仇之前就離開，便怒不可遏，從那天起他的舉止完全變了。當春天來臨，他們離開過冬的屋子住進帳篷時，有一天他說：「我真希望能給自己弄一個新投石索」——父親划著皮艇出去，幸運地捕到一頭帶皮條的海豹，在納馬克還在睡覺時帶了回來。

passages.text: When the women were busy flensing it and preparing the skin for boat-covers, the husband said, 'It just occurs to me that Namak is wanting a sling,' then roused him: 'Namak, thy enemies are making ready to depart.' He awoke and ran out, standing staring at the neighbours; on his way down to the beach his foster-father said to him, 'Just cut out a line for thy sling, wherever thou choosest.' Keeping an eye on his neighbours, he took the knife from his father, lifted up the seal by one of the forepaws with only one hand, and turning it over without any difficulty, cut himself a sling to his liking, all in one piece — on seeing this his foster-father got quite frightened. Some time after, their neighbours were really going to depart. Namak slept, and his father roused him: 'Namak, this time thou mayst believe me; thy enemies are in the very act of departing' — but Namak did not think fit to stir; he had been cheated too often. 'Now they are taking their tents away' — and as he himself could hear the clattering of the bars and poles, he rose and put on jacket and boots, but without getting into the sleeves of his jacket, and catching hold of his sling from under the ledge, hid it inside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當女人們忙著剝皮、準備把皮做成蒙船的材料時，丈夫說：「我剛想到納馬克正缺一個投石索」，然後叫醒他：「納馬克，你的仇人正準備離開。」他醒來跑出去，站著凝視鄰居們；在往海灘去的路上，養父對他說：「你就在你選的地方割一條做投石索的皮條吧。」他一邊留意著鄰居們，一邊從父親手中接過刀，只用一隻手抓住海豹的一隻前爪把它提起來，毫不費力地把它翻過來，為自己割了一條合意的投石索，整條一氣割成——養父見了，大為驚恐。過了些時候，他們的鄰居真的要離開了。納馬克睡著，父親叫醒他：「納馬克，這一次你可以相信我了；你的仇人正在離開」——但納馬克覺得不必動身；他被騙得太多次了。「現在他們正在拆帳篷了」——他自己也聽到了橫桿和木桿的碰撞聲，便起身穿上外套和靴子，卻沒有把胳膊伸進外套的袖子裡，又從擱板下抓起他的投石索，藏在外套裡面。

passages.text: Further down on the beach were some large stone-heaps; there he lay in ambush, and now that he had determined to revenge himself, no more concealed his strength. While some were yet bringing down their luggage, the first boat put out, rowing briskly, and when right athwart of him Namak put a big stone in his sling and threw it into the boat, where it made a large hole, so that it instantly began to sink — 'Alas! alas!' The other boat hurried on to rescue them, but underwent the same fate; the third tried to save itself by turning in time, but at that instant he flung the stone at it, hitting the prow and cleaving right through — and thus he destroyed three boats, crews and all, and his mind now got rest. One boat was saved from destruction, having gone out to sea at once instead of keeping along the shore. His enemies increased in number after they had established themselves somewhere in the north, and seeing they had reason to fear him, trained themselves to be as vigorous as he. Namak married, and though he had never had a kayak himself, taught his son to practise kayak-paddling; the son grew up an excellent kayaker and owned a boat as well as a tent. Reports reached them that their enemies were numerous and strong; at last he persuaded his son to go and look them up, and in spring they went northward in their boat, asking the people they met, 'Where are Namak's enemies?' — 'Farther north' was the constant answer. Learning that the station was close at hand, they rowed on incessantly instead of landing in the evening to take rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海灘更下方有一些大石堆；他埋伏在那裡，既然已決心復仇，便不再隱藏自己的力量。當一些人還在搬運行李時，第一隻船已划了出去，划得飛快，當它正好經過他面前時，納馬克把一塊大石頭放進投石索，朝那船擲去，在船上砸出一個大洞，船立刻開始下沉——「唉！唉！」另一隻船急忙趕去救他們，卻也遭了同樣的命運；第三隻船試圖及時掉頭自救，但就在那一瞬間，他把石頭擲向它，擊中船頭，直穿而過——就這樣他毀了三隻船，連人帶船，他的心裡這才得到了安寧。有一隻船倖免於難，因為它沒有沿著海岸走，而是一下子駛向了外海。他的仇人在北方某處安頓下來後，人數增多了，他們看出有理由懼怕他，便訓練自己像他一樣強健。納馬克結了婚，雖然他自己從未有過皮艇，卻教他的兒子練習划皮艇；兒子長大後成了一個出色的皮艇手，既擁有一隻船，也擁有一頂帳篷。有消息傳到他們那裡，說他們的仇人人多勢眾；最後他說服兒子去尋找他們，春天裡他們乘船向北而去，遇到人就問：「納馬克的仇人在哪裡？」——「再往北」總是回答。得知那地方已近在咫尺，他們便不停地划槳前進，而不在傍晚靠岸休息。

passages.text: On arrival they asked the people who came down to the beach to meet them, 'Where are Namak's enemies?' — but these made no reply, entering their houses, and the travellers had to make their way on shore by themselves; neither were they afterwards invited to visit. They took up their winter-quarters at that very place; in the beginning Namak advised his son to watch them closely, afterwards they got less suspicious. That same winter, one morning, it blew a gale from the south-west and the kayakers remained at home; on that day it was announced, 'They all want to see Namak' — ready in a moment, the son likewise going: thus they were going to visit their enemies for the first time. There was only set forth meat for two; the son did not taste much of it, but the father continued eating till the dish was nearly emptied. The visitors did not speak; at length one of the other party proposed different sports, saying, 'Ye ought to try strength at the pulling-thong first' — he took out the string fitted with walrus-teeth from beneath the ledge and threw it upon the skin spread on the floor for the champions. But Namak said, 'This is but child's-play for people who really want to try a match' — and so saying, took hold of and tore the thong asunder with one hand, then flung them down on the floor. Another offered to try strength with him, hooking their arms together and trying to pull each other over; Namak did not hesitate but at once sat down on the skin, and they tried one after another, nobody able to move his arm in the least. Seeing that they were not able to match him, they all departed. The son went home, but Namak never stirred but stayed on; at last he prepared to put on his outer coat, very slowly and deliberately, always expecting an attack. They were never invited afterwards. In spring they again wanted to go to the south, and at parting he let his house-fellows first go into the boat while he kept back, still expecting an attack from his enemies; but seeing that they did not come, he finally left the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 25 'Namak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 抵達之後，他們向那些下到海灘來迎接的人問道：「納馬克的敵人在哪裡？」——但這些人並未回答，逕自走進屋內，旅人只得自行上岸；此後他們也未曾受邀造訪。他們就在原地紮營過冬；起初納馬克囑咐兒子密切留意他們，後來他們便不那麼疑心了。就在那個冬天，某天早晨，西南方颳起一陣狂風，划皮艇的人們都留在家中；當天有人傳話說：「他們全都想見納馬克」——他立刻準備妥當，兒子也一同前往：他們就這樣頭一回去拜訪敵人。擺出來的肉只夠兩人吃；兒子沒吃多少，父親卻一直吃到盤子幾乎見底。來客並未開口；最後對方有一人提議比試各種競技，說道：「你們應當先試試拉皮條的力氣」——他從壁架下取出那條裝著海象牙的繩索，扔在鋪於地板供較量者使用的皮墊上。但納馬克說：「對真正想較量的人來說，這不過是兒戲罷了」——說著便一把抓住皮條，單手將其扯斷，然後扔在地上。另一人提出要與他較量力氣，彼此勾住手臂，試圖把對方拉倒；納馬克毫不遲疑，立刻在皮墊上坐下，他們一個接一個地試，卻誰也無法讓他的手臂動彈分毫。他們見自己不是他的對手，便全都離去了。兒子回了家，納馬克卻紋絲不動，留在原地；最後他才準備穿上外袍，動作極其緩慢從容，始終提防著襲擊。此後他們再也沒有受到邀請。春天時他們又想往南去，臨別之際，他讓同屋的人先上船，自己留在後面，仍提防著敵人的襲擊；但見敵人並未前來，他終於離開了那個地方。

title.en: Batara Guru Descends to Luwu: The Opening of the La Galigo
title.zh: 巴塔拉·古魯降臨盧武：《加利戈》開篇

region.en: Luwu, South Sulawesi (middle world of the Bugis)
region.zh: 南蘇拉威西盧武（布吉人之中界）

period: La Galigo (Sureq Galigo) epic tradition, dating from approximately the 14th century, rooted in oral tradition

summary.en: The Bugis myth par excellence: in the La Galigo, the most voluminous literary work known (an estimated 6,000 folio pages), the god Batara Guru descends from the upper world to the middle world in the land of Luwu, South Sulawesi, and his children and grandchildren people it — above all the hero Sawerigading and his son La Galigo, whose name the whole epic carries.
summary.zh: 布吉人至高之神話：在《加利戈》（Sureq Galigo，已知最浩繁之文學作品，約六千葉）中，神明巴塔拉·古魯自上界降臨南蘇拉威西盧武之地（中界），其子孫繁衍其間——尤以英雄薩維里加丁及其子加利戈為最，整部史詩即以其子命名。

sensitivity.note: Living Bugis identity-epic (Memory of the World, 2011); the epic is still performed (I La Galigo, 2004); paraphrase only, respect the community's ownership.

canonical_translation: Based on the standard La Galigo narrative as summarized in the UNESCO nomination and published bilingual editions (Bugis-Indonesian, 1995 and 2000); paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The La Galigo is the myth of the Bugis people par excellence — a poetic text in strict metre, composed in a difficult Bugis literary idiom, of pre-Islamic epic-mythological content, running to an estimated six thousand folio pages across manuscripts scattered from Makassar to Leiden, London and Washington. Its story opens in heaven and descends to Sulawesi.

BEGINNING: THE THREE WORLDS. The Bugis cosmos of the epic is arranged in levels: the upper world of the gods, the middle world of men, and the underworld. The upper world is troubled; its people seek a remedy in marriage and descent, and the god Batara Guru is sent down — or comes down of his own heroic motion — to the middle world, to the land of Luwu in the south of Sulawesi.

MIDDLE: THE DIVINE DESCENT IN LUWU. Batara Guru takes his place among the rulers of the middle world, and his marriage and his line fuse heaven with the Bugis country: his descendants are the heroic generations of the epic, endowed with the beauty, strength and appetites of gods living at human scale. The epic follows them through courtship, feud, voyage and ceremony — a chronicle of a world in which the divine continues to walk.

END: SAWERIGADING AND LA GALIGO. The greatest of the line is Sawerigading, the central hero, whose voyages andwhose doom the epic follows; his son La Galigo, born of the later generations, gives the work its name — 'Sureq Galigo', the song of Galigo. The two nominated manuscripts make this concrete: one holds the complete episode of the journey of Sawerigading and his son La Galigo to Senrijawa; the other, in twelve volumes by the Bugis queen Colliq Pujié of Pancana, preserves the longest known fragment. The epic thus ends where it is named: with the family of the descended god becoming the ancestry and identity of the Bugis people.

FUNCTIONS. The opening cycle (1) grounds Bugis kingship in divine descent landed at Luwu; (2) organizes the epic's moral world around marriages that join or sunder the levels; (3) makes Sulawesi's landscape the stage of divine biography; and (4) provides, in Sawerigading's line, the charter-hero of the southern Sulawesi courts. The epic's scale frames the descent: at an estimated six thousand folio pages the La Galigo exceeds every other epic on record, and no single manuscript contains the whole; the Makassar museum's 217-page manuscript holds the Senrijawa journey complete, and the Leiden twelve-volume copy — written by the Bugis queen Colliq Pujie of Pancana with the scholar B. F. Matthes — preserves the longest known fragment. The descent of Batara Guru is thus the doorway to a whole epic world of courts, voyages, weddings and wars in which divine qualities continue at human scale. The epic's standing in South Sulawesi is civic as much as literary: roads, museums and a university carry the names of La Galigo's heroes, and Robert Wilson's theatre adaptation I La Galigo carried the poetry to world stages in 2004 — a living myth whose afterlife is still being written.
narrative.zh: 《加利戈》乃布吉民族之至高神話——格律嚴謹、以佶屈之布吉文學語言寫成、前伊斯蘭時期之神話史詩，散於望加錫、萊頓、倫敦、華盛頓諸館之手稿合計約六千葉。其故事自天堂開篇而降至蘇拉威西。開篇：布吉宇宙分層——上界諸神、中界人間、下界冥府；上界有事，乃遣神明巴塔拉·古魯下降中界——南蘇拉威西盧武之地。中段：巴塔拉·古魯居中界諸王之間，其婚姻與後裔將天堂與布吉大地熔為一體：史詩追述諸英雄世代之求偶、仇殺、航行與儀典——神性仍行走人間之編年史。結尾：世系之最偉者薩維里加丁——史詩之中樞英雄——其航行與命運貫穿全篇；其子加利戈使全作得名『加利戈之歌』。兩部提名手稿為證：一部載薩維里加丁父子赴三里爪哇之完整篇章；另一部為潘恰納女君科利·普吉所書十二巨冊，存已知最長殘篇。史詩終於其得名處：降神之家成為布吉民族之祖源與認同。功能：以盧武降神立布吉王權之神裔、以聯姻組織史詩之道德世界、以蘇拉威西山水為神明傳記之舞臺、並為南蘇拉威西宮廷提供憲章英雄。

Organizes the epic's moral world around marriages that join or sunder the cosmic levels
Makes the landscape of South Sulawesi the stage of divine biography
Provides the charter-hero (Sawerigading's line) of the southern Sulawesi courts

title.en: Sawerigading and the Forbidden Twin: The Ship That Could Not Touch Home
title.zh: 薩維里加丁與禁忌的孿生：不能靠岸的船

region.en: Luwu and the open sea, South Sulawesi
region.zh: 南蘇拉威西盧武與外海

period: La Galigo epic tradition (Bugis); c. 14th century origins

source.archive: UNESCO Memory of the World Register (La Galigo)
source.work: La Galigo epic; Sawerigading cycle

summary.en: The central knot of the Sawerigading cycle: the hero's desire for his own twin sister is forbidden, and his punishment is the sea. He builds a great ship and sails away; the ship is fated never to touch the shore it longs for, and the hero's exile becomes the great Bugis image of the sea as the price of a broken boundary.
summary.zh: 薩維里加丁故事之樞紐：英雄欲娶自己孿生妹妹，此乃禁忌；其罰即是海洋。他造巨舟遠航；此船命定不能靠近思慕之岸——英雄之放逐，成為布吉人『破界之價是海』之偉大意象。

sensitivity.note: La Galigo core episode; incest-twin taboo treated as literary material.

passages.text: Sawerigading, the hero of the line of Batara Guru, desires the twin born with him — and the desire is impossible: the twin taboo stands across it as the boundary the Bugis world will not move. He builds a great ship and puts out to sea; the ship is fated never to come to rest at the shore of his desire, and his voyaging becomes the epic's image of exile — the sea as the price of the broken boundary.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the La Galigo Sawerigading cycle; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩韋里加丁，巴塔拉·古魯世系的英雄，渴望與他同時出生的雙胞胎——而這慾望是不可能實現的：雙胞胎禁忌橫亙其間，作為布吉世界不願逾越的界線。他建造了一艘大船出海；這艘船註定永遠無法在他慾望的岸邊停泊，他的航行遂成為史詩中流亡的意象——大海即是逾越界線的代價。

title.en: Sawerigading Goes Down: The Hero Becomes King of the Underworld
title.zh: 薩維里加丁下行：英雄成為冥府之王

region.en: Wewangriu and the underworld (Peretui), Bugis cosmos

summary.en: The Sawerigading cycle ends downward: the hero's returning ship breaks, and he does not drown but descends — taken to the underworld, where he becomes its king. The greatest hero of the middle world thus ends as the ruler of the level beneath it, closing the La Galigo's geography of three worlds with a king in each.
summary.zh: 薩維里加丁故事以向下收束：歸舟破碎，英雄未被溺斃而是下行——被接入冥府，並成為冥府之王。中界之至高英雄終為下界之君，使《加利戈》三界之地理各得一王而閉合。

sensitivity.note: Descent-to-underworld cluster, Bugis form.

passages.text: The ship of Sawerigading's return breaks, and the hero is not lost but taken: he descends to the underworld of the Bugis cosmos, where he becomes its king. The middle world's greatest hero thus ends as ruler of the level beneath it — the epic's three worlds each with its sovereign, and death transposed from drowning into coronation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the La Galigo Sawerigading cycle; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩韋里加丁歸返的船毀了，英雄並未就此消逝，而是被接納：他下到布吉宇宙的冥界，成為那裡的君王。中界最偉大的英雄於是終結為其下層世界的統治者——史詩的三界各有其君主，而死亡也由溺斃轉化為加冕。

Father and son travel the water-world of the Bugis epic, meeting the powers and courts that mark its geography; the episode carries the work's pattern of voyage, obligation and return that governs the whole La Galigo.

passages.zh: 英雄薩韋里加丁與其子拉加利戈前往森里賈瓦的旅程，是望加錫拉加利戈博物館手稿中所保存的《拉加利戈》完整篇章——一段穿越史詩中宮廷、風暴與儀典之海的航行。父子二人航行於布吉史詩的水上世界，遇見標誌其地理格局的種種權勢與宮廷；這一篇章承載了貫穿整部《拉加利戈》的航行、義務與歸返之模式。

title.en: Toar and Lumimu'ut: The Mother and Son Who Peopled Minahassa
title.zh: 托阿爾與盧米穆特：繁衍米納哈薩的母子

region.en: Minahassa peninsula, North Sulawesi
region.zh: 北蘇拉威西米納哈薩半島

period: Minahassa ancestral tradition; recorded in nineteenth-twentieth century ethnography

source.archive: Minahassa oral tradition (recorded in colonial-era ethnography)
source.work: The ancestral myth of Toar and Lumimu'ut (Minahassa tradition)

summary.en: The Minahassa begin with a mother and a son: Lumimu'ut, the first woman of the land, and her son Toar, who grew to be a giant. Separated so that neither knew the other's origin, mother and son met as strangers on the mountain, wed, and their children became the first peoples of the peninsula — the sibling-creator pair of North Sulawesi, whose boundary-taboo is told before every genealogy.
summary.zh: 米納哈薩以一對母子開篇：大地初女盧米穆特與其子托阿爾——長成巨人。母子相隔、互不知來歷，竟在山上如陌生人相遇而結合；其子孫遂為半島最早的族群——北蘇拉威西之『兄妹創世對』，其禁忌故事在每一份譜系之前被講述。

sensitivity.note: Minahassa ancestry charter; the incest-recognition pair is treated at tradition level.

canonical_translation: Based on the standard Minahassa ancestral account; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Minahassa peoples of the northern peninsula tell their beginnings as a story of two people who did not know what they were to each other.

BEGINNING: THE FIRST WOMAN AND HER SON. Lumimu'ut is the first woman of the Minahassa country; her son Toar grows in the wilds to marvellous size and strength. The two live apart, and the tale keeps them apart by a device: neither is ever told the origin of the other — the son does not know his mother, the mother does not know her grown son.

MIDDLE: THE MEETING ON THE MOUNTAIN. Mother and son meet as strangers on the mountain, exchange the courtesies of two young unmarried people, and wed. Only afterwards, when the signs of kinship are told to them by the old ones — in the standard tellings, by the story of the twin stones or the staffs of Lumimu'ut — do they understand what they have done.

END: THE CHILDREN AND THE DIVISION. The children of the union are the first peoples of the peninsula; their mother, understanding now the true relation of all the houses, gathers her descendants and divides them — the division told of in the companion record of the stone of Watu Pinawetengan — and the Minahassa nations set out from the mountain each to their own lands.

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) provides the sibling-creator pair of North Sulawesi; (2) uses the not-knowing device to keep the ancestral union within the law; (3) grounds the Minahassa nations' division of the land in the mother's act of ordering; and (4) makes genealogy-telling itself the ritual that repairs the broken knowledge. The Minahassa tellings keep the recognition mechanism visible rather than mysterious: in the standard forms, the tokens that reveal the kinship are Lumimu'ut's own — the twin staffs or stones by which a mother may know her son, held apart by the same device that kept the origin untold. The not-knowing is thus presented as an institution with a purpose: the first union is lawful because the law was not yet knowable, and the knowledge that arrives afterward is converted into the division of the children, the mother ordering her descendants to their lands. The stone of Watu Pinawetengan, with its old inscriptions, is the charter's monument: the place of division where Tonsea, Tondano, Tombulu and Tontemboan received their allotments. In Minahassa memory the myth does its work at every genealogy-recitation, where telling the descent is itself the rite that repairs the first broken knowledge — the community listening to the origin it once could not be told.
narrative.zh: 北蘇拉威西半島米納哈薩人以其開端為一對互不知身份者之故事。開篇：初女盧米穆特與其子在荒野中生長，成為力大無窮之巨人；二者分居，且故事以一設計使之相隔：誰也不被告知對方之來歷。中段：母子如陌生人於山上相遇，行未婚青年之禮而結合；及長者（標準敘述中為孿生石或盧米穆特之杖的故事）點明親緣之徵，二人方知所為。結尾：結合之子孫即半島最早之族群；母親既明諸家真實關係，乃聚其後裔而分之（其分地之事見『瓦圖·皮納韋滕甘石』篇）；米納哈薩各族遂自聖山而出，各赴其土。功能：供給北蘇拉威西之兄妹創世對、以『不知情』維繫祖源結合之合法性、以母親之秩序行為奠立米納哈薩民族分地之憲章、並使譜系講述本身成為修復所斷知識之儀式。

Keeps the ancestral union within the law by the device of mutual not-knowing
Grounds the division of the Minahassa nations in the mother's act of ordering
Makes genealogy-telling the ritual that repairs the broken knowledge
