passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minahassa ancestral myth; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 米纳哈萨地方的第一位女子卢米穆乌特，与她的儿子托阿尔，彼此分开居住；托阿尔已长成惊人的体格与力气。两人从未被告知对方的来历——儿子不认识自己的母亲，母亲也不认识已长大的儿子。

passages.text: Mother and son meet as strangers on the mountain and wed; when the old ones tell them the signs of their kinship, they understand what they have done, and the children of the union become the first peoples of the peninsula, divided and sent out by their mother to each his own land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minahassa ancestral myth; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 母子二人在山上以陌生人的身份相遇并结为夫妻；当长辈们向他们道出彼此血缘的种种迹象时，他们才明白自己做了什么，而这段结合所生的子女便成为半岛上最早的诸民族，由他们的母亲分派、遣往各自的地方。

title.en: The Stone of Watu Pinawetengan: Where the Peoples Were Divided
title.zh: 瓦圖·皮納韋滕甘石：分族之地

region.en: Watu Pinawetengan stone, Tomohon, North Sulawesi
region.zh: 北蘇拉威西托莫洪瓦圖·皮納韋滕甘石

period: Minahassa sacred-geography tradition

source.work: The tradition of Watu Pinawetengan (Minahassa stone of division)

summary.en: On the stone called Watu Pinawetengan — 'the place of division' — the first ancestress or the first ancestors gathered the descendants and marked out their lands: the four directions of the Minahassa peoples, the allotment of Tonsea, Tondano, Tombulu and Tontemboan. The stone still stands, its old inscriptions the charter of the peninsula's ethnography.
summary.zh: 在名為『分族之地』的瓦圖·皮納韋滕甘石上，初祖召集後裔、劃定各土：米納哈薩四向之民——通塞亞、通達諾、通布盧與通特姆布安之分配。石仍矗立，其古刻即半島族群地圖之憲章。

sensitivity.note: Living sacred site of the Minahassa; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: On the stone of Watu Pinawetengan the first ancestress gathered her descendants and divided the lands among them, fixing the allotments of the Minahassa peoples to the four directions. The stone still stands with its old inscriptions, and the Minahassa nations tell their origins from that place of division — genealogy, land and monument joined in one charter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Minahassa tradition of Watu Pinawetengan; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Minahassa tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在瓦图·皮纳韦滕甘之石上，第一位女祖先召集了她的后裔，将土地分给他们，把米纳哈萨诸民族的份地划定于四方。那块石头至今仍矗立着，上面刻着古老的铭文，米纳哈萨诸族皆从那分地之处讲述自己的起源——谱系、土地与纪念碑合于同一部宪章之中。

title.en: The Tumanurung of Gowa: The One Who Descended
title.zh: 戈瓦之圖瑪努倫：降臨者

region.en: Gowa (Makassar), South Sulawesi
region.zh: 南蘇拉威西戈瓦（望加錫）

period: Makassar lontara' chronicle tradition (Gowa dynastic origins)

source.work: The Tumanurung narrative of the Gowa chronicle (Makassar dynastic tradition)

summary.en: The founding myth of the Makassar kingdom of Gowa: a woman of heavenly radiance, the Tumanurung ('the one who descended'), appears in the land and is found by the people; she is wed to the chief and bears the line of the kings of Gowa — the white-blooded ancestress whose descent from above legitimizes the Makassar throne.
summary.zh: 望加錫戈瓦王國之開基神話：一位天光燦然之女子——『圖瑪努倫』（降臨者）——現於此地為民所見；她與酋長成婚，誕下戈瓦歷代國王之世系——這位血統純白、自天而降的女祖，為望加錫王座賦予合法性。

sensitivity.note: Dynastic charter of the Gowa chronicle tradition.

passages.text: The people of the land find a woman of heavenly radiance, the Tumanurung, 'the one who descended,' and cannot tell where she has come from; the chief takes her to wife, and from the marriage descends the line of the kings of Gowa. The descended ancestress is the charter of the Makassar throne: her children carry the whiteness and radiance of her origin, and the kingdom's legitimacy is told as descent rather than conquest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Gowa chronicle's Tumanurung narrative; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Gowa chronicle tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那片土地上的人们发现了一位有天赐光辉的女子，即图马努隆，“降临者”，却无法说出她来自何处；首领娶她为妻，戈瓦的历代国王便出自这桩婚姻。这位降临的女祖先乃是望加锡王位的宪章：她的子女承袭了她出身的洁白与光辉，而王国的正统性是以血统而非征服来讲述的。

title.en: The Tongkonan and the Horns: Toraja Houses That Remember
title.zh: 通科南與牛角：會記憶的托拉查之屋

region.en: Tana Toraja highlands, South Sulawesi
region.zh: 南蘇拉威西塔納托拉查高地

period: Toraja aluk to dolo tradition; recorded in twentieth-century ethnography

source.work: The tradition of the tongkonan ancestral house and the buffalo-horn genealogy (Toraja)

summary.en: The great boat-shaped houses of the Toraja (tongkonan) are not dwellings but genealogies: each is founded by an ancestor, oriented to the points of the Toraja cosmos, and its facade grows outward in horns — every pair of buffalo horns sacrificed at the house's feasts and funerals a further record of who owed and gave what to the family. The house remembers so that the living need not: rank, debt and descent are read off the wall.
summary.zh: 托拉查人船形大屋（tongkonan）非宅第而是譜系：每座由一位祖先奠基，朝向托拉查宇宙之方位；其立面以牛角向外生長——屋中歷次慶典與葬禮所宰水牛之每一對角，皆為『誰欠何物、誰予何物』之紀錄。屋替活人記憶：階級、債務與世系皆可自牆上讀出。

sensitivity.note: Living Toraja material religion; paraphrase respectfully, note the funeral economy without exoticizing it.

passages.text: The tongkonan houses of the Toraja are founded by named ancestors and oriented to the cosmos; the house is the family's seat of memory, not merely its shelter. At every great feast and funeral, buffalo are sacrificed and their horns added to the facade; the growing wall of horns is a public genealogy of the house — rank, debt and descent read off the architecture itself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Toraja tongkonan tradition as recorded in twentieth-century ethnography; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Toraja tongkonan tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 托拉查人的通科南房屋由具名的祖先所创建，并朝向宇宙；房屋是家族记忆的所在，而不只是栖身之所。在每一次盛大的宴席与葬礼上，人们献祭水牛，并将其角添置于屋面上；那不断增高的角墙便是这所房屋的公开谱系——身份、债务与血统皆可从建筑本身读出。

title.en: The Lonely Brothers and the Swift Kivigtok Bride
title.zh: 孤身兄弟與疾行的奇維托克新娘

region.en: Fiord of the west coast and the far side of the inland ice
region.zh: 西岸峽灣與內陸冰蓋彼端

period: Inuit oral tradition; abridged from one manuscript, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two housekeeping brothers steal a wife from a rocky point — a kivigtok, endowed with supernatural swiftness, who vanishes from between them and reappears mending their boots. Winning her confidence, they prosper until homesickness for her own brothers sends the whole family across the interior of Greenland; she leads at superhuman pace and is recognized by the little nephew who has never seen her. At the hook-and-crook feast the eldest visitor slowly pulls each host's arm to his breast, skinning it — then throws the giant champion a whole day's wrestle out among the spectators; the hosts' mysterious 'windlasses' prove to be walrus-teeth stuck in the ice for seal-hunting, and the brothers go home never to be seen again.
summary.zh: 操持家務的兩兄弟從巖角搶來一位妻子——疾行如飛的奇維托克人；她在他們之間憑空消失，又在家中補靴重現。贏得她的信任後家道興旺；她思親心切，竟領全家橫越格陵蘭內陸——她始終走在前面，令兩位獵手難以跟上。 hook-and-crook 摔跤宴上，長兄緩緩把每位主人的手臂拉到胸前、扯下臂皮；再與巨人冠軍摔足一整天，將其拋入觀眾之中。主人們的『絞盤』原來是插在冰上的海象牙獵具。歸途之後，兄弟們再也無人見過。

sensitivity.note: Kivigtok = those who fled from mankind to the desolate interior, believed to acquire supernatural swiftness and longevity (Rink's note). The cross-country journey is a transplanted motif per Rink.

passages.text: Two brothers had taken up their abode at a fiord, living alone, and having no female assistance were obliged to cook and make their garments themselves. One day out kayaking they passed a little rocky point, and turning their eyes landwards observed a woman standing on the beach. The eldest brother went ashore to fetch her, but when he approached she fled, at first slowly, till when he commenced to run she hurried on so that he gave her up and returned to his kayak. The younger brother ascended the beach, and as he approached she stood quiet, making no resistance, but let him take her down. They fastened the kayaks together with strings, and when she was seated behind the men she said to the eldest brother, 'I observed thy intention to be bad, so I fled; but thy brother there has a better disposition.' They paddled homewards keeping a sharp look-out upon her — but it happened they left off watching for a moment, and instantly they heard a clattering noise, and there she was gone; searching all around, no traces anywhere, they gave her up, saying, 'No matter, perhaps she was not a real woman' — that is, she had fled from mankind and was a Kivigtok, endowed with supernatural swiftness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有两兄弟在一处峡湾安了家，独自居住，没有女子相助，只得自己做饭、自己缝制衣物。一天，他们划着皮艇经过一处小小的岩石岬角，朝岸上望去，看见一名女子站在海滩上。兄长上岸去接她，但当他走近时，她却逃开了，起初慢慢地走，待他跑起来，她便急急奔去，于是他只好放弃，回到皮艇上。弟弟上了海滩，当他走近时，她却静静站着，毫不抗拒，任他把她带下来。他们用绳索把皮艇系在一起，当她坐在男人们身后时，她对兄长说：“我看出你心怀不善，所以我才逃走；但你那位弟弟性情较好。”他们朝家的方向划去，一路紧紧留意着她——可偏偏就在他们稍一松懈的片刻，他们立刻听到一阵咔嗒的响声，她已不见了踪影；他们四处搜寻，却毫无踪迹，只好作罢，说道：“罢了，也许她并不是真正的女人”——也就是说，她已逃离了人类，是个基维格托克，天生具有超乎寻常的迅捷。

passages.text: They again untied their kayaks and made for home — but lo, there she was, standing outside the tent mending their boots. They ran up to her in case she wanted to run away, but she said to them, 'Pray let go your hold of me, I don't want to leave you.' For the first few days they were unwilling to leave her alone; afterwards they started but did not leave her neighbourhood, and did not venture away for any length of time until she had said, 'I like to stop with you, and ye may go as far as ye like.' Employing all their time in hunting, having a woman at home to cook and sew, they got more prosperous than before. She bore a male child in due time; but from that period her manners were altered, and she grew restrained and silent. Questioned at night, she answered: 'It is because of our baby boy; I would like him so much to go and see his mother's brothers. I cannot forget those dear ones, and that is the reason why I have grown so silent.' The brothers agreed they could not deny her the pleasure, and would accompany her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們再次解開獨木舟，朝家鄉划去——可是瞧，她就在那兒，站在帳篷外替他們縫補靴子。他們奔上前去，生怕她想逃走，她卻對他們說：「請放開我，我不想離開你們。」起初幾天，他們不願留她獨自一人；後來他們動身外出，卻不遠離她的近旁，也不敢長時間走遠，直到她說：「我喜歡和你們待在一起，你們愛走多遠就走多遠吧。」他們把全部時間都用於打獵，家中又有個女人做飯縫衣，日子過得比從前更加興旺。時候到了，她生下一個男孩；但從那時起，她的舉止就變了，變得拘謹而沉默。夜裡問她，她答道：「都是因為我們的小男孩；我多麼想讓他去見見他母親的兄弟們。我忘不了那些親人，這就是我變得如此沉默的原因。」兄弟倆一致認為不能拂了她的心願，便決定陪她同去。

passages.text: Delighted at the prospect, she packed up a bundle of boots and several new pairs of soles, and they started to cross the country; the wife with the child in the amowt constantly went ahead, and the others could scarcely keep up. For several days they wandered on until she exclaimed, 'If my brothers be still alive, and are to be found in the old place, we shall certainly come in sight of their sea to-morrow; I recognise all the mountain-hills of my old home.' Towards evening they sighted an open water and all began crying for joy, obliged to stop a little; they lay down for the night and descended the hillside in the morning, where a great many tents appeared in the valley below. Pointing to one remarkable for its greater size, she cried, 'That is the tent belonging to my relatives, but I would fain go down by myself; meanwhile you must keep behind' — and so she went. An old woman came forth from a tent holding a child by one arm, carrying a large seal-skin for sole-leather in her other; all of a sudden the little one turned round, exclaiming, 'Why, is not that my aunt coming there?' — 'No, don't speak such foolish things. Thou knowest very well thy aunt fled away never to return any more, because of these quarrels and fights for her sake.' Still the boy went on, 'Indeed, indeed, it is my aunt, and there she is coming!' — she got into a passion and tore out the peg-holes in the skin; then for the first time she looked up and cried out, 'That is she, sure enough. Why did not I believe the little one?' and went on caressing the boy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她滿心歡喜，包了一捆靴子和好幾雙新鞋底，他們便動身穿越陸地；妻子把孩子裝在阿莫特（amowt，婦女背孩子的兜袋）裡，一路總是走在前面，其餘的人幾乎跟不上。他們走了好幾天，直到她喊道：「若我的兄弟們還活著，還住在老地方，我們明天一定能望見他們那片海；我認得我老家所有的山巒。」傍晚時分，他們望見一片開闊的水面，都歡呼起來，不得不停下來歇一歇；他們躺下過夜，第二天早晨下山，只見下面的山谷裡出現了許多帳篷。她指著一頂格外大的帳篷喊道：「那是我親戚家的帳篷，但我寧願獨自下去；你們暫且留在後面」——於是她就去了。一個老婦人從帳篷裡出來，一隻手臂抱著孩子，另一隻手提著一大張海豹皮，用來做鞋底皮；忽然那小孩轉過身來喊道：「咦，那不是我的姑母來了嗎？」——「不，別說這種傻話。你很清楚，你的姑母因為那些為她而起的爭吵和打鬥，早已逃走，再也不會回來了。」可那男孩仍舊說：「真的，真的，是我的姑母，她正朝這兒來呢！」她發了怒，把皮上的穿繩孔都扯破了；這時她才第一次抬頭看，喊道：「果然是她。我怎麼不信這孩子呢？」接著便不住地撫愛那男孩。

passages.text: Each of the brothers cried out, 'Oh, my dear sister! ye have not cared so much for her as I have; ye have not missed her so much neither; ye have not longed so much for her as I have done' — and each wanted to be the first to greet her and take hold of her, out of reverence for the eldest allowing him to give her welcome first. The men waiting on the mountainside were brought down, the tent entrance soon blocked with inquisitive neighbours eager to see the travellers who had crossed the whole breadth of the country; for joy at the meeting the brothers could do nought but sit down together and regard each other lovingly. In the evening the eldest proposed amusements, and they agreed to try strength at hook-and-crook: a skin was drawn forth, 'When strangers meet, one always likes to see which is the better man,' and the host undressed and seated himself on it; one of his own brothers sat down opposite, they hooked arms, and the eldest of the two beat his brother's back vigorously to encourage him to pull hard — yet neither he nor any of the brothers were able to stretch out his arm. The eldest of the visitors whispered to his brother, 'I shall first take my chance, then thou take thine' — undressed, sat down, hooked his right arm inside his adversary's, and gathering all his strength, slowly pulled on the arm till it touched his own breast; the other tried to draw him back, his features growing quite convulsed, the skin coming off his arms in the attempt. They tried the left arms with the same result; and at last the host rose: 'I now see that we have acquired some very strong friends... We, too, have got a man of great strength among us, and ye will scarcely escape him; I almost fear you won't come off alive.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兄弟們個個喊道：「哦，我親愛的妹妹！你對她的情意不如我深；你思念她不如我切；你對她的盼望也不如我久」——每個人都想第一個迎接她、拉住她，但出於對長兄的敬重，讓長兄先向她致意。等在山上的人也都被叫了下來，帳篷門口很快擠滿了好奇的鄰人，急著要看這些走遍全境而來的旅人；兄弟們因重逢而歡喜，什麼也做不了，只能一同坐下，彼此深情地對望。到了晚上，長兄提議玩些遊戲，大家便同意比一比鉤臂的力氣：一張皮子被鋪了開來，「陌生人相見，總想看看誰更強些」，主人脫了衣服坐上去；他的一個兄弟在對面坐下，兩人鉤住手臂，兩人中的長兄用力拍打他兄弟的背，鼓勵他使勁拉——然而他和他所有的兄弟都無法把手臂拉直。來客中的長兄對他的兄弟低聲說：「我先試一試，然後你來試」——他脫了衣服坐下，把右臂鉤進對手的臂彎裡，聚起全身力氣，慢慢地把那條手臂拉過來，直到貼上自己的胸膛；對方想把他拉回去，面容都扭曲了，皮子從他手臂上滑脫。他們又試左臂，結果相同；最後主人站起身來：「我現在看出，我們結交了一些非常強壯的朋友……我們這裡也有一個力氣極大的人，你們恐怕很難躲過他；我幾乎擔心你們不能活著脫身。」

passages.text: Next morning a call was heard outside: 'The visitors are requested to come and fight!' — a number of people ascending the heights to a plain where a still greater crowd formed a circle about a fellow with a frame like a giant. 'It won't do for thee to go first — thou dost look so very dejected; I had better go myself' — and at sunrise the elder brother suddenly rushed at the champion, taking him by surprise. At sunset they were still fighting; 'I must try to throw him over before I get too tired' — taking hold of him he slowly lifted him off his feet and held him swinging in the air; noticing a pole stuck up among some rocks, he did not choose to knock him down against that, but hurled him right out among the spectators, where he fell, the blood gushing from his mouth. A loud roar rose among the people — some rejoiced, others wept — and descending to the valley they all gathered around the eldest visitor merely to have the satisfaction of having touched him; some said, 'Thou shalt have my windlass in reward for that job,' which he did not understand at the time. The whole crowd vanished with one cry, 'Ye shall be our masters henceforth.' When frost set in, the visitors accompanied the men to see their ways of hunting: far beyond the shore they fell in with the frost-smoke and the first apertures in the ice, at the edge of which walrus-teeth had been stuck down — these were what they had been calling their windlasses. 'Do not try to harpoon the big ones, but aim at the little firth-seals, and leave the others to me' — each harpooned a small seal and wound his harpoon-string round one of the large walrus-teeth; when the seals were slaughtered and they prepared to return, letting the elder take the lead, he had not gone far before, turning round, he remarked, 'Now ye may go on just as ye like' — and went off as if carried by the wind. The others came home late; the brothers, forestalling them on another day with a large seal each, had the supper already before the master of the house on his entry: 'We fear the meat has got tough, and has lost its flavour; it is ever so long since we boiled it.' He was glad he had got such able and clever helpmates. When spring came on, the brothers began to long for their own home, and asked their former companion whether she preferred to stay or go with them — 'I will rather return with you.' Her parents making no objections, they went away together, and were never more seen or heard of by any of their kinsmen after the day of their departure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 26 'The Lonely Brothers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早晨，外面傳來一聲呼喚：「請來客們出來比試！」——一群人登上高地，來到一片平地上，那裡已圍成更大的一圈人，中央站著一個身材如巨人般的漢子。「你先上去不行——你看起來太消沉了；還是我自己去吧」——日出時分，兄長突然衝向那勇士，打了個措手不及。日落時他們仍在搏鬥；「我得趁還沒太累把他摔倒」——他抓住對方，慢慢把他舉離地面，讓他在空中搖晃；他注意到岩石間豎著一根杆子，不願把他撞在那上面，便把他直直地拋進圍觀的人群中，他落在那裡，口中鮮血直湧。人群中爆發出巨大的吼聲——有人歡喜，有人哭泣——他們下到山谷，全都圍到那位來客長兄身邊，只為能碰一碰他而感到滿足；有人說：「為了這一手，我的絞盤歸你」，他當時並不明白這話的意思。整群人隨著一聲呼喊消失了：「從今以後，你們就是我們的主人。」霜凍來臨時，來客們跟著那些人去看他們打獵的方法：在遠離海岸的地方，他們遇上了霜霧和冰面上最初的幾個孔洞，洞的邊緣插著海象牙——這就是他們所說的「絞盤」。「別去叉那些大的，瞄準那些小峽灣海豹，其餘的留給我」——各人叉住一隻小海豹，把叉繩繞在一顆大海象牙上；海豹宰殺完畢，他們準備回去，讓年長者領頭，他沒走多遠便轉過身來說：「現在你們愛怎麼走就怎麼走吧」——隨即像被風捲走一般離去。其餘的人很晚才到家；兄弟倆另一天各帶一隻大海豹先他們一步回來，主人一進門晚飯就已擺好：「我們怕這肉已經煮老了，失了鮮味；煮了好久了。」他很慶幸有了這樣能幹又聰明的幫手。春天來臨時，兄弟倆開始思念自己的家鄉，便問他們從前的同伴是願意留下還是跟他們走——「我寧願跟你們回去。」她的父母沒有反對，他們便一同離去，自離開那天起，他們的親族再也沒有人見過或聽過他們的消息。

title.en: Sikutluk: The Killing Sorrow That Devoured Him
title.zh: 西庫特盧克：噬人的殺戮之痛

region.en: Inland glaciers and the erkilek coast
region.zh: 內陸冰川與厄基萊克海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Persuaded to shoot his cousin's only dog, Sikutluk is trapped into a quarrel and shoots his beloved cousin dead — then stones the boat and tent and wanders off killing everything he meets: the she-amarok howling over her dead cubs ('Ah, my cousin, my beloved cousin, I murdered thee!'), the buck-carrying male, a kilivfak whose cave filled with its tumbling body. Fleeing across the glaciers, he and his wife fall in with men who are really erkileks; when he goes back for kinsmen and never returns, an angakok's clairvoyance names the male amarok as his devourer, and his wife lives on with the foreigners until her death.
summary.zh: 西庫特盧克被表兄設計射殺其唯一的狗，繼而在爭執中失手射死摯愛的表兄——用巨石封埋船與帳，攜妻遠走，見活物即殺：哀號於死崽之上的母狼（『唉，我的表兄，我的至愛表兄，是我害了你』）、銜鹿而歸的公狼、以及墜入洞穴的奇獸。穿越冰川後，他們投宿的『人們』其實是厄基萊克妖族；他返鄉尋親一去不返，巫師遙視斷言：是那頭公狼把他吞了。其妻遂與異族同住至終老。

sensitivity.note: Amarok (fabulous wolf), kilivfak (fabulous animal), erkilek (fabulous inlanders) per Rink's notes. Killing spree recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Sikutluk and his cousin were living together and loved each other dearly; at that settlement the cousin was the only one who possessed a dog. One day Sikutluk observed his cousin sitting before his tent doing some work, the dog beside him; when he came close up the cousin suddenly said, 'Pray, shoot my dog.' 'No, I won't, because we are friends.' But the cousin still persuaded him — 'Pray do it, nevertheless'; he brought his bow accordingly, but not yet satisfied, the cousin again inquired, 'But wilt thou not really get vexed when it is too late?' 'No, indeed, I shall not' — and the other killed the dog. The cousin, however, took offence for all that, and challenged his friend, saying he had a mind to kill him at once; but Sikutluk shot him right through the breast, and he fell down dead. Immediately after this Sikutluk went and covered his cousin's boat and tent all over with heavy stones, and left the place along with his wife; but the murder he had committed had made him thirst for blood, and he went on intending to kill whatever he met with — at first content with killing ptarmigan and reindeer, both bringing with them as many arrows as they were able to carry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西庫特盧克（Sikutluk）和他的表兄弟住在一起，彼此十分相愛；在那個住地，表兄弟是唯一養著一條狗的人。一天，西庫特盧克看見表兄弟坐在帳篷前做活，狗就在他身旁；他走近時，表兄弟忽然說：「請你把我的狗射死吧。」「不，我不幹，因為我們是朋友。」但表兄弟仍舊勸他——「儘管如此，還是請你射吧」；他於是拿來了弓，可表兄弟還不滿足，又問：「可是，事到臨頭，你真的不會生氣嗎？」「不會，真的不會」——於是對方把狗射死了。然而表兄弟還是動了怒，向他的朋友挑戰，說他真想立刻殺了他；西庫特盧克卻一箭射穿了他的胸膛，他當場倒地而死。此事過後，西庫特盧克立刻去用沉重的石頭把表兄弟的船和帳篷統統蓋住，然後帶著妻子離開了那個地方；但他所犯的殺人罪使他渴血，他一路走一路打算殺掉所遇到的一切——起初只滿足於殺雷鳥和馴鹿，兩人都盡其所能帶上許多箭。

passages.text: After a while they fell in with an aviarok. They first discovered the young ones, but towards evening the mother arrived with a young buck in her mouth; from their retreat they noticed her dropping the burden on finding that her young ones were killed, then sniffing the air, following the scent of human beings, and with a fearful howl coming running on towards them at full speed. The woman screamed, 'I fear she will devour us!' but he made no other reply than, 'Ah, my cousin, my beloved cousin, I murdered thee!' — and crept forth from his ambush, aimed at the beast, and killed it on the spot. They hid themselves again, and soon afterwards saw the male return, also carrying a buck between his teeth; after the same words, 'Alas, my cousin, my beloved cousin!' he shot this one also. They still wandered on and on, and killed everything living they met with on their way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了一陣，他們遇到一頭雌熊（aviarok）。他們先發現了幼崽，但到了傍晚，母熊回來了，嘴裡叼著一頭小公鹿；他們從藏身處看見她發現幼崽被殺後把獵物丟下，接著嗅了嗅空氣，循著人的氣味，發出一聲可怕的嚎叫，全速朝他們奔來。那女人尖叫道：「我怕她會把我們吃掉！」他卻只答道：「啊，我的表兄弟，我親愛的表兄弟，我殺了你！」——便從埋伏處爬出來，瞄準那野獸，當場把它射死。他們又躲了起來，不久便看見雄熊回來，嘴裡也叼著一頭公鹿；他照樣念了那句「唉，我的表兄弟，我親愛的表兄弟！」又把這一頭也射死了。他們仍舊一路走啊走，把路上遇到的一切活物都殺掉。

passages.text: One day the woman caught sight of a kilivfak, which stood scratching the earth with its feet. When the husband had also seen it, he first went to look out for a hole in the earth close by, where he ordered his wife to go and hide, and remain quiet till he should let himself down to her; he stole down to encounter the animal, bending to the ground whenever it turned to look round, creeping on when it stood scratching the earth. At last he had got quite close, ventured a shot at it, hurried back, and let himself fall down to his wife — after him came the wild beast tumbling down into the cave, where it entirely filled up the opening; but after much toil they got out again. They continued roaming further away, crossing the glaciers with him carrying his wife across the crevasses; at length he again reached the sea, and at the same time observed a kayaker close by, who said he would take them to his own place if they would wait while he brought a boat — but the crew were all men. They took up with these people, but soon found out they had come among erkileks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，那女人瞧見一頭基利夫法克（kilivfak），正站在那兒用腳刨地。丈夫也看見了牠之後，先去找附近地上的一個洞，吩咐妻子到那裡躲起來，安安靜靜待著，等他下來找她；他自己則悄悄潛近，去迎戰那頭野獸，每當牠轉頭張望時，他便伏向地面，等牠站著刨地時再悄悄爬近。最後他終於靠得極近，壯起膽子朝牠射了一箭，急忙退回，縱身跳下到妻子那裡——那頭野獸緊隨其後，翻滾著跌進洞裡，把洞口整個堵住了；但他們費了好大的勁，才又爬了出來。他們繼續往更遠處遊蕩，他背著妻子越過冰河上的裂隙；最後他又來到了海邊，同時望見附近有個划獨木舟的人，那人說，只要他們肯等他去把船帶來，他就願意載他們到自己的地方去——可是那船上的人全是男人。他們便與這些人結交，但很快就發現，自己已落入了厄基勒克人（erkileks）之中。

passages.text: One day Sikutluk told his wife that he would return and look for some of their kinsmen, naming a certain time by which they expected to be back; but in vain they waited for him. When the appointed time had elapsed, they promised an angakok a great reward if he could tell what had befallen the traveller. After some meditation he replied, 'I observed he killed a pair of amaroks with their brood.' The wife acknowledged it. 'And a female kilivfak besides?' 'Indeed he did so.' 'Then be assured the male beast devoured him.' But the wife of Sikutluk lived on with the foreigners until the time of her death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 27 'Sikutluk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，西庫特盧克（Sikutluk）對妻子說，他要回去尋找一些親族，並說定了某個時辰，預計屆時歸來；但他們白白等了他一場。約定的時辰過去之後，他們便向一位安加科克（angakok，巫師）許下重酬，只要他能說出那旅人遭遇了什麼。他沉思了一會兒，答道：『我見他殺了一對阿瑪洛克（amarok），連同牠們的幼崽。』妻子承認確有此事。『另外還有一頭雌的基利夫法克，對吧？』『他確實這麼做了。』『那麼你大可放心，那頭雄獸把他吃掉了。』然而西庫特盧克的妻子此後一直與那些外族人同住，直到她死去。

title.en: The Girl Who Fled to the Inlanders
title.zh: 投奔內陸人的少女

region.en: Inland lakes and stone-boat roads of the inlanders
region.zh: 內陸湖沼與內陸人的石舟之路

period: Inuit oral tradition; compiled from imperfect manuscripts, one of the oldest traditions, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Exiled for breaking her sister's precious reindeer-horn needle, a girl weeps on a stone until a tall inlander — exiled likewise for spoiling his brother's snare — takes her home over the hills, past his idiot sister's betrayal ('Ye haven't got a sister-in-law like mine, with beads and necklace — a real nice one'), through the stone-boat voyage with shut eyes, the dancing feats (reindeer, hare, and peeled-skin transformations, one dancer crushing a woman and child), the vermin-boots that grow her new inland flesh and swiftness, and the duck-trap triumph — until, their son dead, he returns to his own people and is seen no more.
summary.zh: 因折斷姐姐珍貴的鹿角針而被逐的少女，在石上啜泣——一位同樣因弄壞兄弟珍貴羅網而被逐的高大內陸人將她帶回家。白痴妹妹洩密（『你們可沒有我這樣的弟媳——戴著珠串項鍊的海濱美人』）、閉眼乘石舟、觀舞（化鹿、化兔、剝皮起舞，一名舞者竟踏斃一對母子）、以蟲豸之靴長新肉而得內陸人的敏捷、鴨籠滿載的勝利——直到兒子病亡，他返回族人之中，從此杳無音訊。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads the tale as preserving relations between Eskimo and Indians, with hints of the latter's dancing and disguising customs. Crushing death at the dance recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: There was once a young maiden who happened to break her elder sister's needle, made of reindeer-horn and very precious. The sister got dreadfully angry, although she lived in great prosperity, being well married — so angry that she told her sister she might as well take herself off, and henceforth keep away from the coast-people. The girl at once obeyed, and wandered about the country for many a day. One night, sitting down on a stone crying, she heard a voice beside her: 'Why dost thou cry thus?' — turning round she saw a very tall man, whom she recognised to be an inlander, standing beside her. 'For what art thou crying?' 'Because I broke my sister's needle, and she sent me away.' 'And I was sent away in the same manner because I spoiled my brother's precious snare.' Then he asked her to follow him, and they went away together to his house, where he made her a present of deer-skins, some for outer garments and some for inner clothes, and took her for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有個年輕姑娘，偶然弄斷了她姊姊一根用馴鹿角做的針，那針十分珍貴。姊姊勃然大怒——雖說她日子過得十分富足，也嫁得好——怒得竟對妹妹說，她乾脆走遠些，從此別再靠近海岸邊的人。姑娘立刻照辦，在鄉野間遊蕩了許多天。一天夜裡，她坐在一塊石頭上哭泣，聽見身旁有個聲音說：『你為什麼這樣哭？』她轉過身，看見一個非常高大的男人站在身旁，她認出那是個內陸人。『你為什麼哭？』『因為我弄斷了姊姊的針，她就把我趕走了。』『我也是這樣被趕出來的，因為我弄壞了哥哥珍貴的捕獸索。』接著他請她跟他走，他們便一同去了他的住處，他在那裡送她一些鹿皮，有些做外衣，有些做內衣，並娶她為妻。

passages.text: This inlander used to go and catch eider-ducks in a certain lake by wading out into the water and taking the birds by stealth. One day he proposed that she should accompany him on a visit to his relatives, telling her that when they came in sight of the house he would call out, 'Kung, kung-kuyo!' and they would know him at once. They went; as soon as from one of the hill-tops they could make out the house of his relatives in the valley, he made the sign, and they heard the children of the place calling out, 'Somebody is saying, Kung, kung,' and his mother appearing in the doorway repeating the same words. They descended and entered the house; he had a sister who was an idiot (considered a clairvoyant) and very talkative, and told her not to mention that a coast-woman had come among them, going to hide his wife in some remote corner of the broad ledge — but when his brothers came in they at once remarked, 'There is a smell of coast-people about the place!' and when the fool went outside she could not forbear saying to his neighbours, 'Ye haven't got a sister-in-law like mine, with beads and necklace — a real nice one — one of the coast-women!' After this the inquisitive people thronged about the window to get a peep at the stranger, some creeping up on the roof to make themselves a peep-hole, and in no time the house was quite full.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個內陸人常到某個湖裡去捉絨鴨，方法是涉水走進水中，偷偷把鳥捉住。有一天，他提議帶她一同去探望他的親族，並告訴她，等他們望見那屋子時，他就會喊『孔，孔—庫喲！』他們一聽便會認出是他。他們出發了；當他們從一座山頂上望見山谷裡他親族的屋子時，他便發出那信號，只聽得那地方的孩子們喊著：『有人在喊「孔，孔」呢！』他母親也出現在門口，重複著同樣的話。他們下山進了屋；他有個妹妹是個傻子（被視為能通靈的人），非常愛說話，他囑咐她不要提有個海岸女人來到他們中間，又把妻子藏到寬闊炕臺某個偏僻的角落——可是他的兄弟們一進來就立刻說道：『這地方有股海岸人的氣味！』而那傻子走到外頭時，忍不住對他的鄰居們說：『你們可沒有像我這樣的嫂子，戴著珠子和項鍊——真是個漂亮的——一個海岸女人呢！』此後，那些好奇的人便擠在窗邊想偷看那陌生人，有的還爬上屋頂挖個窺孔，轉眼間屋裡就擠得滿滿的。

passages.text: Subsequently there was talk of a boat shortly expected, and one morning it was announced to be coming — inuarutligaks, fabulous dwarf inlanders or mountain-elves. On coming up from the beach they stopped outside the house and commenced singing to one another, then brought forth gifts of skins, and stayed a whole month, enjoying each other's company, feasting a great deal, and singing songs continually. At one of their banquets an inlander stood forth and, by way of entertaining the assembly, sang and danced: during the dance he transformed himself into a reindeer, at which trick the children of the inuarutligaks got dreadfully frightened, so that he again quickly changed himself into a man. Another took upon himself the shape of a hare, but the inlanders' children cried out aloud and he hastened to re-change himself; another pulled the skin from off his whole body till it only adhered to a small portion between his eyes, putting it all right again when the urchins cried. At last one of the inuarutligaks came forth to dance, and he danced in such a way that the whole house soon leaned over, all the inmates rolling down to one side with such force that one woman and a child were crushed to death. The entertainment now ended, and the next day the inuarutligaks departed, after having first invited their late hosts to visit them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，大家談起有一條船不久就要到來，一天早晨，有人通報說船來了——是伊努阿魯特利加克人（inuarutligaks），即傳說中的矮小內陸人或山中精靈。他們從海灘上來後，停在屋外，彼此對唱起來，然後獻上毛皮的禮物，並待了整整一個月，彼此相伴甚歡，大擺宴席，歌聲不斷。在其中一次宴會上，一個內陸人站出來，為了娛樂眾人而唱歌跳舞：跳舞時他化身為一頭馴鹿，這個把戲把伊努阿魯特利加克人的孩子們嚇得魂飛魄散，於是他又趕緊變回人形。另一個把自己變成兔子的模樣，但內陸人的孩子們放聲大哭，他便急忙變了回來；又有一個把自己全身的皮從身上剝下來，只讓皮連在兩眼之間的一小塊地方，等那些小鬼哭起來時，他又把一切恢復原狀。最後，伊努阿魯特利加克人中的一個出來跳舞，他跳得整座屋子不久便歪斜了，屋裡所有人全都朝一邊滾去，力道之大，以致一個女人和一個孩子被壓死了。娛樂到此結束，第二天，伊努阿魯特利加克人便告辭離去，臨走前先邀請了他們方才的東道主前去拜訪。

passages.text: In a month's time they made preparations to start, and had a boat made of stone for the purpose. They agreed that the coast-woman might as well be of the party, but told her not to open her eyes during the voyage, the boat not moving on if she did so; she complied, but as soon as the crew could make out the sound of children's voices they permitted her to open them again, and she perceived a very little house, wondering how they should all get room in it — while she was looking at it, it seemed to grow bigger, the inuarutligaks knowing how to enlarge their houses by means of rubbing them. They went inside, bringing their bundles of skin, one for each person, and commenced feasting and merry-making. One of the inuarutligaks stepped forward, and after having performed a dance flung himself down on the ground transformed into an orsighiak-stone (a sort of white, glistering felspar); the inlanders tried to lift it, but being quite unable, he soon rose up in his proper shape. One of the inlanders now advanced, fell to the ground, and was transformed into a common stone; but the inuarutligaks managed to lift it, and flung it against the door, where it flew to pieces — in this manner the inlanders lost one of their people, and they left on the following day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個月後，他們準備動身，並為此造了一條石船。大家商定讓那海岸女人也一同前往，但囑咐她在航行途中不可睜眼，否則船便不再前行；她照辦了，可是等船上的人一聽出孩子們的聲音，便允許她再睜開眼，她看見一間很小的屋子，正納悶他們這麼多人怎麼擠得進去——就在她看著的時候，那屋子似乎越變越大，原來伊努阿魯特利加克人懂得用摩擦的辦法把屋子變大。他們走進屋裡，帶進各自的皮包袱，每人一個，然後開始宴飲作樂。伊努阿魯特利加克人中的一個走上前來，跳完一支舞後，便撲倒在地，化作一塊奧爾西希亞克石（orsighiak，一種白色閃亮的長石）；內陸人想把它抬起來，卻怎麼也抬不動，他隨即以本來的形貌站了起來。這時一個內陸人走上前，倒在地上，化作一塊普通的石頭；但伊努阿魯特利加克人竟把它抬了起來，朝門口扔去，石頭當場摔得粉碎——內陸人就這樣失去了一個同伴，他們便在第二天離去了。

passages.text: In the summer-time preparations were made for reindeer-hunting, and the coast-woman was to accompany them. She had two girls for her enemies because she married so early, and they were always molesting her and trying to make her ridiculous, saying she was not so smart and lightfooted on the march as the inlanders; one added, 'To-day I even pursued and overtook a young deer!' On hearing this, the old woman of the house produced a pair of boots which she filled with all kinds of vermin, ordering her to put them on and tightening them round her legs, the husband encouraging her — 'She must needs bear it in order to get agile and smart.' But presently she fell into a swoon, and the skin dropped off her feet and legs; when restored to her senses she perceived new flesh and new skin growing on them, and she had now become swift and nimble as the inlanders themselves. On their return from the reindeer-hunt she said she longed for her relatives and was desirous to go and see them; the next summer her husband accompanied her thither. Approaching the coast-side they hailed a kayaker and asked him to bring a boat to take them the remainder of the way; on getting into it the inlander was dreadfully afraid, falling down flat on his face at the bottom of the boat, where he remained till he landed close to their home. They stayed that winter at her parents, and once her father said, 'I wish I could have got another son-in-law instead of this one — one who knew how to trap eider-ducks' — the inlander had a habit of stopping in the house all day, but at these words he only asked a trap of him; one day he returned all covered with ducks. The other men of the place in the winter-time often used to ridicule him, and always wanted to persuade him to accompany them out on the ice for the viowpok-hunt (seal-hunt by watching the breathing-holes). In the summer he resolved to visit his countrymen, and on parting said to his wife, 'If I find our son in health, I will return with more companions.' He set off, and did not return till next spring, and then reported that their son had died. He told his wife it was now his intention to return to his own people; and when he left they never saw any more of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 28 'The Girl who fled to the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夏季來臨時，人們為獵捕馴鹿做準備，那位海岸女子也要隨行。她有兩個女孩與她為敵，因為她那麼早就出嫁，她們總是騷擾她，想讓她出醜，說她在行進中不如內陸人那般機敏輕快；其中一個還補上一句：「今天我甚至追上了一頭小鹿呢！」老婦人聽了這話，便拿出一雙靴子，往裡塞滿各種蟲子，命她穿上，並把靴子緊緊綁在她腿上，她的丈夫也慫恿她——「她非得忍受這個，才能變得靈活機敏。」可是不久她便昏了過去，腳和腿上的皮都脫落了；等她恢復知覺，發覺上面長出了新肉和新皮，如今她已變得和內陸人一樣迅捷靈巧。獵馴鹿歸來後，她說她思念親人，想去看看他們；第二年夏天，她的丈夫陪她前往。快到海岸邊時，他們向一個划獨木舟的人呼喊，請他划船來載他們走完剩下的路；內陸人一上船就嚇得要命，臉朝下趴在船底，一直趴到船靠岸、接近他們家為止。他們在她父母家過了那個冬天，有一次她父親說：「我希望能換個別的女婿，而不是這一個——一個懂得捕捉絨鴨的人」——那內陸人習慣整天待在屋裡，但聽了這話，他只向他要了一個捕鴨的陷阱；有一天他回來時，滿身都是鴨子。當地其他男人在冬天常取笑他，總想說服他隨他們到冰上去獵海豹（守候呼吸孔獵海豹）。夏天，他決心去探望自己的族人，臨別時對妻子說：「若我見我們兒子安康，我會帶更多同伴回來。」他動身離去，直到次年春天才回來，然後報告說他們的兒子已經死了。他告訴妻子，他現在打算回到自己族人那裡去；他離開之後，他們就再也沒見過他。

title.en: The Gods of Gunung Agung: Raffles' Account of Balinese Religion
title.zh: 阿貢山諸神：拉弗爾斯所記巴釐宗教

region.en: Gunung Agung, Bali
region.zh: 巴釐島阿貢山

period: Balinese religious tradition as recorded by Raffles in 1815 (published 1817), from a Balinese informant

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), Appendix (CCVIII-CCXI), the religion of Bali

summary.en: Raffles' appendix records the Balinese pantheon from an intelligent native informant: Batara Guru is 'the highest object of worship below the divinity, Sang Yang Tunggal (the lord who is one)'; the great deities of the island are Dewa Gede Segara (deity of the sea), Dewa Gede Dalam (emblematical of death), Dewa Gede Bali Agung, and above all Dewa Gede Gunung Agung, 'to whom all the Rajas and people of Bali pay adoration'; images of gold, silver, bell-metal and iron stand in temples on Gunung Agung, Batu, Batur-hakul and Predung.
summary.zh: 拉弗爾斯附錄自一位聰慧之巴釐本地人記錄島上神譜：巴塔拉·古魯為『至上神（桑·揚·通加爾，唯一之主）以下最高之崇拜對象』；島上大神為海神德瓦·格德·塞加拉、象徵死亡之德瓦·格德·達蘭、德瓦·格德·巴釐·阿貢，以及至高之德瓦·格德·阿貢山神——『巴釐列王與人民皆敬拜之』；金、銀、銅、鐵所鑄神像供於阿貢山、巴圖、巴圖爾-哈庫爾與普勒東之廟中。

sensitivity.note: Early-nineteenth-century record of living Balinese religion; paraphrase respectfully.

canonical_translation: Raffles 1817 (English); paraphrase

narrative.en:
Raffles' appendix to the History of Java preserves the earliest full English account of Balinese religion, given to him by 'an intelligent Mahometan, a native of the island' — a syncretic reporter describing the Hindu-Balinese system from within its neighbourhood.

BEGINNING: THE ONE AND THE HIERARCHY. The account places Batara Guru as the highest object of worship below the divinity Sang Yang Tunggal — 'the lord who is one.' Beneath this apex the Balinese pantheon distributes the island's sacred geography: Dewa Gede Segara is the deity of the sea; Dewa Gede Dalam is emblematical of death, with a temple near the kraton of the Raja; Dewa Gede Bali Agung is the deity in whose temple the common people worship on particular days; and Dewa Gede Gunung Agung is a deity still more generally worshipped, 'to whom all the Rajas and people of Bali pay adoration.'

MIDDLE: THE MOUNTAINS OF THE GODS. Images of the deities — some of gold, some of silver, some of bell-metal, some of iron — are housed in temples and dedicated places on Gunung Agung, Gunung Batu, Gunung Batur-hakul and Gunung Predung; 'but it is Gunung Agung that is the famous place for them, and those figures are the objects of worship to all the princes of Bali.' The volcano is the throne-room of the island's religion, and the rajahs' worship centres on its summit.

END: THE RUBRIC OF FESTIVALS. The informant closes with the calendar of devotion: at a tama'tum (festival on a grand occasion) all the Rajas with families and subjects repair to Gunung Agung and invoke the deities, the Maperwita Brahmana (the learned Brahmins called Padinda) conducting the ceremonies; marriages are sanctified by being witnessed by the Brahmanas and all the deities invoked; on the new moon and the eighth and twenty-third of the month all the deities are worshipped and 'thousands of people are afterwards fed with their consecrated fragments,' the Padinda administering holy water which the people drink and bathe with. On the day of the new year the deities are worshipped, ablutions performed, offerings made; cloths and money are offered twice a year; and there is the fast of Nyuapid, lasting a day and a night, during which food and sleep must be abstained from.

FUNCTIONS. The record (1) fixes the vertical theology of Bali (the One, Batara Guru, the Gede deities, the mountain temples); (2) ties the volcano to kingship and popular worship alike; (3) documents the priestly administration (Padinda) and the feeding of thousands on consecrated fragments; and (4) supplies the early external witness to the cycle of festivals still centred on the Day of Silence.
narrative.zh: 拉弗爾斯《爪哇史》附錄保存了巴釐宗教最早之完整英文記錄，出自『一位聰慧之本地穆斯林』之手——以鄰居身分描述印度教-巴釐體系。開篇：等級神學——桑·揚·通加爾（唯一之主）之下，巴塔拉·古魯為最高崇拜對象；其下分掌島之聖地：海神德瓦·格德·塞加拉、死亡之象徵德瓦·格德·達蘭（廟近王宮）、德瓦·格德·巴釐·阿貢，及至高之德瓦·格德·阿貢山神——『巴釐列王與人民皆敬拜之』。中段：諸神之山——金、銀、銅、鐵神像供於阿貢山、巴圖山、巴圖爾-哈庫爾與普勒東之廟；『阿貢山為其名區，諸像即巴釐列王崇拜之對象』——火山即全島宗教之寶座廳。結尾：節慶儀注——大節之日，列王攜家眷與臣民登阿貢山呼喚諸神，由瑪珀維塔婆羅門（即帕丁達）主持；婚禮須經婆羅門與所呼諸神見證；朔日與每月初八、廿三，眾神受拜，『成千之人以受祝之祭餘果腹』，帕丁達施聖水令民飲之浴之；新年之日拜神、行浴、獻祭；布與錢一年兩獻；另有『尼烏阿皮德』齋戒——一晝夜間絕食禁眠。功能：立巴釐縱向神學、繫火山於王權與民祀、記載帕丁達祭司之執禮與食聖餘之眾、並為今日『靜默日』節俗提供最早之外部見證。

functions: Fixes the vertical theology of Bali: the One, Batara Guru, the Gede deities, the mountain temples
Ties the volcano Gunung Agung to both kingship and popular worship
Documents the Padinda priesthood and the feeding of thousands on consecrated fragments
Provides the early external witness to the festival cycle of the Day of Silence

variants.name: Modern Balinese accounts (dewa acintya framing)
variants.summary: The contemporary system names the apex as Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa/Acintya; the Raffles informant's Sang Yang Tunggal is the same apex under an older name.

primary_sources.citation: Recorded 1815-1816 from a Balinese informant; published in Raffles, The History of Java, London 1817, Appendix pp. CCVIII-CCXI.

secondary_sources.work: Miguel Covarrubias, Island of Bali
secondary_sources.citation: Covarrubias 1937 — the standard modern portrait of the Balinese temple system (copyright; consulted as context only).

source_urls.description: Internet Archive scan of Raffles, History of Java, vol. II (1817) with the Bali appendix

sensitivity_guidance: Living Balinese Hindu tradition; paraphrase only; do not reproduce ritual instructions verbatim.

passages.text: Batara Guru is considered as the highest object of worship below the divinity, Sang Yang Tunggal (the lord who is one). The deity Dewa Gede Segara is the deity of the sea; Dewa Gede Dalam is emblematical of death; Dewa Gede Gunung Agung is a deity still more generally worshipped, and to him all the Rajas and people of Bali pay adoration.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴塔拉·古魯被視為神性之下最高的崇拜對象，即桑·揚·通加爾（唯一之主）。德瓦·格德·塞加拉是海神；德瓦·格德·達拉姆象徵死亡；德瓦·格德·古農·阿貢是更普遍受崇拜的神，峇里島所有的拉惹與人民都向他致敬。

passages.text: Images are made of the deities, some of gold, some of silver, some of bell-metal, and some in iron, and dedicated in temples on Gunung Agung, Gunung Batu, Gunung Batur-hakul and Gunung Predung; but it is Gunung Agung that is the famous place for them, and those figures are the objects of worship to all the princes of Bali.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 神像以各種材料製成，有些是金的，有些是銀的，有些是鐘銅的，有些是鐵的，供奉在古農·阿貢、古農·巴圖、古農·巴圖爾-哈庫爾與古農·普雷東的廟宇中；但古農·阿貢才是它們的著名之地，那些神像乃是峇里島所有王公的崇拜對象。

passages.text: When there happens to be a festival on a grand occasion, all the Rajas with their families and subjects repair to Gunung Agung and invoke the deities, the Maperwita Brahmana being summoned to conduct the ceremonies. Marriages are sanctified by being witnessed by the Brahmanas and all the deities invoked; on the new moon and the eighth and twenty-third of the month all the deities are worshipped, thousands of people are afterwards fed with their consecrated fragments, and the Padinda administers holy water which they both drink and perform ablutions with.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 每逢盛大場合舉行慶典時，所有拉惹帶著家眷與臣民前往古農·阿貢，祈求眾神，並召來馬佩爾維塔婆羅門主持儀式。婚姻因婆羅門的見證與祈求眾神而得以聖化；在新月之日以及每月初八與二十三日，眾神皆受崇拜，之後有數千人分食其祝聖過的餘食，而帕丁達則分發聖水，他們既飲用又用以淨身。

title.en: The Fast of Nyuapid: Bali's Day of Silence
title.zh: 尼烏阿皮德齋戒：巴釐靜默日

region.en: Bali (island-wide new year observance)
region.zh: 巴釐島（全島新年齋戒）

period: Balinese new-year fast recorded by Raffles (1817); observed annually to the present

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), Appendix, the fast of Nyuapid

summary.en: Raffles' informant closes the Balinese calendar with the fast of Nyuapid — 'which lasts a day and a night, during which time food and sleep must be abstained from,' held on the first or the fifteenth of the month. This is the early record of Nyepi, the Day of Silence with which the Balinese new year begins: the island shuts down, fires and lights are doused, and work stops, so that the demons sweeping over the island find it empty and pass on.
summary.zh: 拉弗爾斯之報告人以『尼烏阿皮德』齋戒收束巴釐曆法——『歷一晝夜，其間禁食禁眠』，行於每月之首或十五日。此即靜默日（Nyepi）之最早記錄——巴釐新年始於全島止息：熄火滅燈、停止勞作，使巡島之魔靈見島空無一人而過。

sensitivity.note: Living observance; the empty-island explanation is the folk rationale of the fast.

passages.text: There is also the fast of Nyuapid, which lasts a day and a night, during which time food and sleep must be abstained from; this fast must be held on the first or the fifteenth of the month. The Day of Silence begins the Balinese new year: the island goes dark and still — no fire, no light, no work, no travel — so that the demons who sweep over Bali at the year's turning find it empty and pass it by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Nyepi tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 還有紐阿皮德齋戒，持續一晝一夜，期間必須戒絕食物與睡眠；此齋戒須在每月初一或十五舉行。靜默日開啟峇里新年：全島陷入黑暗與寂靜——沒有火，沒有光，沒有勞作，沒有出行——好讓在歲末交替之際掃過峇里的惡魔發現島上空無一人，因而過門不入。

title.en: The Wayang of the New Year: Offerings at All the Market-Places
title.zh: 新年之哇揚：各集市之供品

region.en: Bali (market-places of the island)
region.zh: 巴釐島（各集市）

period: Balinese custom recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), Appendix, the new-year wayang offerings

summary.en: In Raffles' Balinese rubric, 'when it is Idn'uik wayang, which means the new year wayangs, offerings are made and placed at all the market-places, but no worship takes place' — and at the annual festivals of tampak kilwon offerings are made on account of all the different animals. The shadow-plays of the new year receive their own offerings, at the markets rather than the temples.
summary.zh: 拉弗爾斯所錄巴釐儀注：『值伊德努伊克·哇揚（即新年哇揚）之期，須備供品置於各集市，但不舉行崇拜』；歲末『坦帕克·基爾旺』節，並為各類動物備供。新年皮影戲自有其供——供於市場而非廟宇。

sensitivity.note: Market-place offerings recorded 1817; read alongside the wayang tradition's sacred status.

passages.text: When it is Idn'uik wayang, which means the new year wayangs, offerings are made and placed at all the market-places, but no worship takes place; and at the annual festivals of tampak kilwon there are offerings made on account of all the different animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了伊德努伊克皮影戲之時，意即新年皮影戲，人們備好供品置於所有市場，但不舉行崇拜；而在坦帕克·基爾翁的年度節慶上，則為各種不同的動物獻上供品。

title.en: Sakalan and Nikalan: The Two Halves of Balinese Religion
title.zh: 薩卡蘭與尼卡蘭：巴釐宗教之二分

region.en: Bali (island-wide division of religious labour)
region.zh: 巴釐島（宗教職分之二分）

period: Balinese religious division recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), Appendix, the two divisions of Balinese religion

summary.en: The religion of Bali, Raffles' informant explains, is divided into Sakalan and Nikalan: the first regards all worldly concerns — the orders of the prince, the laws of the land, the common affairs and transactions of life; the second comprehends all the duties and ceremonies of religion, 'the conducting of which is in the hands of the Maperwita, or learned Brahmins called Padinda.' Sacred and secular are one system with two offices.
summary.zh: 拉弗爾斯之報告人釋曰：巴釐宗教分為薩卡蘭與尼卡蘭：前者掌一切俗務——王者之命、國之法律、日常事務；後者總宗教之一切職責與儀典，『其主持之權在瑪珀維塔——即受學之婆羅門，名帕丁達』。聖俗一體，惟執掌有二。

sensitivity.note: Structural note on Balinese religious organization recorded 1817.

passages.text: The religion of Bali, as it exists on Bali, is divided into Sakalan and Nikalan. The first regards all worldly concerns, such as the orders of the prince, the laws of the land, and the common affairs and transactions of life; the second comprehends all the duties and ceremonies of religion, the conducting of which is in the hands of the Maperwita, or learned Brahmins called Padinda.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 峇里島的宗教，就其於峇里島實存之樣貌而言，分為薩卡蘭（Sakalan）與尼卡蘭（Nikalan）。前者關乎一切世俗事務，諸如君主的詔令、國家的律法，以及生活中日常的事務與往來；後者則涵蓋宗教的一切職責與儀典，其主持之責操於馬佩爾維塔（Maperwita），即稱為帕丁達（Padinda）的博學婆羅門之手。

title.en: Barong and Rangda: The Lion, the Widow and the Kris Dancers
title.zh: 巴龍與蘭達：獅、寡婦與持克里斯的舞者

region.en: Village temples of Bali
region.zh: 巴釐各村廟

period: Balinese ritual drama; early twentieth-century documentation (Spies and de Zoete 1938) on older village foundations

source.work: The Barong and Rangda drama (Calonarang play) of Balinese village temples

summary.en: At the temple festival the shaggy lion-barong — kept in the temple shed as a village treasure — dances against Rangda the widow-witch, fangs and mane of white hair, whose leyak followers swarm at her call. Young men with kris dance the baris between them; at the climax Rangda's power enters them and they turn the daggers on their own breasts, which cannot pierce — the play ends not with victory but with the community's evidence that both powers must be kept inside the village boundary.
summary.zh: 廟節之時，毛蓬蓬的獅形巴龍——作為全村之寶供於廟棚——與寡婦巫蘭達對舞：蘭達利齒白髮如鬣，其黎雅克徒眾聞呼而至。持克里斯的青年舞於兩者之間；高潮處蘭達之力入其身，他們反將短刃刺向自己胸膛——卻刺之不入。戲不以勝負收場，而以『兩種力量都必須留在村界之內』的明證作結。

sensitivity.note: Living ritual drama; treat with respect; do not describe as spectacle without its protective function.

canonical_translation: Based on the standard documentation of the Calonarang play; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Barong-Rangda drama is Bali's central living rite of the boundary between the village and the dangerous outside — performed at temple festivals in nearly every community, with the two faces of the myth carried by the same village.

BEGINNING: THE LION IN THE SHED. The barong is a shaggy lion-dragon mask worked in leather and mirror, kept in the temple's shed between performances and fed and honoured as a village treasure; it is the protective power of the community, led by comic followers, danced by two men inside the costume.

MIDDLE: THE WIDOW COMES. Rangda — the widow-witch whose legend goes back to Calon Arang of Girah — enters the square: fangs, pendulous breasts, and the mane of white hair; her followers, the leyak, swarm behind her, and she brings the sickness and madness that once plagued Airlangga's kingdom. The kris dancers of the village (the baris) dance against her; she casts her power at them, and at the climax the dancers turn their daggers on their own breasts in trance — the blades bending, unable to pierce.

END: THE BOUNDARY HELD. The play does not end in a victor: Rangda retreats toward the graveyard and the barong stands between; the trance is broken gently with incense and the dancers are led back to themselves. The village has tested its boundary — the destructive force was met, entered the young men's bodies even, and was returned outside the line. The drama is thus not a tale but an instrument: it maintains the edge where the community's protection stops and the wilderness of the leyak begins.

FUNCTIONS. The drama (1) maintains the village boundary against the leyak world; (2) transmits the Calon Arang legend as embodied memory; (3) manages possession safely inside ritual (the kris-on-breast climax under the priests' supervision); and (4) balances the village's two faces — the barong's nurture and Rangda's menace — as both necessary, both owned, both kept in the temple precinct. The performance's management is as carefully codified as its myth: the kris dancers are men chosen and prepared by the village, the trance is induced and released under the direction of the pemangku and the barong's handlers, and the blades that turn on the dancers' breasts are pressed flat, never driven — the danger is displayed and mastered in the same gesture. The two masks are owned, not opposed: villages keep both in the temple's sheds, feed and dress them on their days, and the drama's calendar follows the temple's odalan. The Rangda figure carries the Calon Arang legend's whole cargo — widowhood, grudge, plague, and the king's counter-plot — into dance, so that the historical narrative of the Pararaton lives as embodied memory in the square. Comparative mythologists read the pair as a boundary-instrument: the village's protective power and its projected menace, locked in a balance the community itself conducts.
narrative.zh: 巴龍-蘭達戲劇是巴釐『村界內外』核心活態儀式——幾乎各村廟節皆演，神話之兩面由同一村落承載。開篇：廟棚中的獅子——巴龍為皮革與鏡片所作之蓬鬆獅龍面具，演出間供奉於廟棚、受人餵養禮敬，是村社之護佑力，由二名舞者藏於道具之內，率丑角隨員起舞。中段：寡婦登場——其傳說上溯格拉鎮之加隆·阿朗——利齒、垂乳、白髮如鬣；黎雅克徒眾蜂擁其後，帶來昔年荼毒艾爾朗加國之病與瘋。村中持克利斯之青年（巴里）與之對舞；蘭達施力於其身，高潮處舞者入恍惚，反將短刃刺向己胸——刃彎而不入。結尾：戲不分勝負——蘭達退向墳場，巴龍立於其間；以香火輕撫喚醒恍惚者。村界經受考驗：毀滅之力被迎戰、甚至進入青年之身，終被送回界外。此戲非故事而是儀器：維持『村之護佑止於何處、黎雅克荒野始於何處』之邊界。功能：以戲維持村界對抗黎雅克世界、以身體記憶傳承加隆·阿朗傳說、在祭司監督下安全地管理附體（刺胸高潮）、並平衡村社兩面——巴龍之護與蘭達之險——兩者皆必需、皆為村所有、皆留在廟垣之內。

Manages trance-possession safely inside ritual, under priestly supervision
Balances protection and menace as both owned by the village

passages.text: The barong, the shaggy lion-dragon kept in the temple shed as a village treasure, dances against Rangda the widow-witch — fangs, pendulous breasts and the mane of white hair — whose leyak followers swarm behind her. The kris dancers of the village dance between the two powers; at the climax Rangda's power enters them and they turn the daggers on their own breasts in trance — the blades bending, unable to pierce — until incense breaks the trance and the dancers are led back to themselves. The play does not end in victory: Rangda retreats toward the graveyard, the barong stands between, and the village has tested its boundary — the destructive force met, entered, and returned outside the line where the community's protection stops.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Balinese Barong-Rangda drama; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Barong-Rangda drama; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Barong-Rangda drama; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴龍（barong），那頭毛茸茸的獅龍，被養在廟宇的棚舍中作為村落的珍寶，舞動著對抗寡婦女巫蘭達（Rangda）——獠牙、下垂的雙乳與一頭白髮——其萊雅克（leyak）隨從成群簇擁於她身後。村中的克里斯（kris）短劍舞者舞於這兩股力量之間；至高潮時，蘭達的力量進入他們體內，他們便在恍惚中將匕首轉向自己的胸膛——刀刃彎曲，無法刺入——直到香煙破除恍惚，舞者才被引回自身。此劇並不以勝利告終：蘭達退向墓地，巴龍立於其間，而村落已試探了自身的界線——毀滅之力被迎上、被進入，而後被送回界線之外，即社群庇護所止之處。

title.en: The Leyak: Headless Fliers of the Balinese Night
title.zh: 黎雅克：巴釐夜間的無首飛者

region.en: Crossroads and graveyards of Bali
region.zh: 巴釐的十字路口與墳場

period: Balinese night-lore; living tradition

source.work: The leyak cycle (Balinese night-lore)

summary.en: The leyak are the night-witches of Bali: men and women who at night detach their heads from their bodies, trailing their glowing entrails behind them like a fiery organ-light, to fly to graveyards and crossroads and feed on the unborn and the sick. Their queen is Rangda; against them hang the offerings and paper squares at every door, and the effigies that catch them at the crossroads.
summary.zh: 黎雅克乃巴釐之夜巫：男女於夜間自頸取首，臟腑發光如焰尾曳於身後，飛往墳場十字路口，吸食胎兒與病者之精氣。其後即蘭達；家家門前懸紙方與供品、路口立草人相迎相捕，皆為防黎雅克而設。

sensitivity.note: Living folklore; avoid applying witch-labels to any living person or community.

passages.text: The leyak of Balinese night-lore are humans who at night leave their bodies: the head flies with the glowing entrails trailing behind, to the graveyards and crossroads where the dead are fed, and to the houses of the sick and pregnant. Against them hang the small offerings and paper squares at every doorway, and the effigies set at the crossroads; Rangda is their queen, and the Barong-Rangda drama of the temple festival is the village's regular answer to their kind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Balinese leyak cycle; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 峇里島夜間傳說中的萊雅克（leyak）是夜裡離開軀體的人：其頭顱飛出，發光的臟腑拖曳於後，前往餵養死者的墓地與十字路口，也前往病人與孕婦的家中。為防範它們，家家戶戶的門口都懸掛著小供品與紙片，十字路口則設置了偶像；蘭達（Rangda）是她們的女王，而廟會節慶中的巴龍—蘭達（Barong-Rangda）戲劇，正是村落對其同類的例行回應。

title.en: The Ramayana in Bali: Sita's Abduction and the Monkey Chorus
title.zh: 巴釐的《羅摩衍那》：悉多被劫與群猴合唱

region.en: Temple courtyards of Bali
region.zh: 巴釐各廟庭

period: Balinese Ramayana tradition (Phalgunadi's Balinese Ramayana editions, 1990s, on older village cycles); kecak form c. 1930s

source.work: The Balinese Ramayana cycle (kecak and sendratari forms; I Gusti Putu Phalgunadi, The Balinese Ramayana)

license: Living tradition; paraphrase of copyrighted editions not permitted — narrative summarized

summary.en: Bali keeps the Ramayana as its own: the island's retellings give Sita's abduction, the burning of Alengka and Rawana's fall in Balinese names and Balinese metres, while the kecak — a sitting chorus of dozens of men chanting 'cak-cak-cak' — carries the war of the monkeys around the fire, Rangda and the barong breaking in at the edges as the play's spirits.
summary.zh: 巴釐視《羅摩衍那》為己有：島上之轉述以巴釐名與巴釐格律講述悉多被劫、焚阿楞迦與十首王之亡；而『克恰克』——數十男子圍火坐唱『恰恰恰』之合唱——載起群猴之戰，蘭達與巴龍則於劇之邊緣現身，作為其靈。

sensitivity.note: Living performance tradition; Phalgunadi's editions are copyrighted — narrative summarized, never quoted.

passages.text: The Balinese retellings of the Ramayana keep the whole arc — the golden deer, the abduction, Hanuman's burning of Alengka, Rawana's fall and Sita's ordeal — in Balinese idiom, with the island's own names for Rama's party and the rakshasa court.
passages.note: Summary of the Balinese Ramayana tradition (cf. Phalgunadi's Balinese Ramayana editions); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 《羅摩衍那》的峇里島改編本保留了整個故事脈絡——金鹿、擄走、哈奴曼焚燒阿楞卡（Alengka）、羅婆那（Rawana）的敗亡與悉多（Sita）的試煉——皆以峇里島的語彙呈現，並以島上自身的名稱稱呼羅摩（Rama）一方與羅剎（rakshasa）宮廷。

passages.text: In the kecak form the war of the monkeys is carried by a seated chorus of chanting men around fire and torchlight; the abduction is danced at the centre, and the drama closes with the entry of Rangda and the barong, the island's own spirits claiming the Ramayana stage as theirs.
passages.note: Summary of the kecak performance tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在凱恰克（kecak）形式中，猴群之戰由一群圍坐於火堆與火炬光旁、吟誦的男子承擔；擄走一幕在中央舞蹈，而戲劇以蘭達（Rangda）與巴龍（barong）的登場作結，島上自身的精靈將《羅摩衍那》的舞台據為己有。

title.en: The Crocodile That Became Timor
title.zh: 化為帝汶之鱷

region.en: Timor island
region.zh: 帝汶島

period: Timorese oral legend; recorded in twentieth-century collections

source.work: The legend of the crocodile and the boy (Timor island-origin legend)

summary.en: A crocodile, stranded far from the sea, is saved by a small boy who carries it back to the water; the grateful reptile promises to repay him, and years later comes for the boy — to carry him not to death but on a last voyage. The crocodile grows old swimming the seas, and when it dies its body becomes the island of Timor, shaped like a crocodile in the map; the Timorese, descendants of the boy, still call the crocodile grandfather and observe its taboos.
summary.zh: 一鱷離海擱淺，為一孩童所救，被背返水中；感恩的鱷允諾報答。多年之後，鱷來尋那孩子——不是索命，而是邀他同行最後一程。鱷游遍大海，垂垂老去；死後其身化為帝汶島——地圖上輪廓如鱷。島民（男孩之後裔）至今稱鱷為祖父，守其禁忌。

sensitivity.note: Island-origin legend shared by Timorese communities on both sides of the island.

canonical_translation: Based on the Timorese oral legend; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The best-known origin legend of Timor tells how the island itself is a relative.

BEGINNING: THE RESCUE. A crocodile, caught far from the sea on dry land, is found by a small boy; instead of killing it, he carries it on his back to the water and releases it. The crocodile promises to repay the service.

MIDDLE: THE CALL AND THE VOYAGE. Years pass; the crocodile returns — for the boy, now grown, is called by it. It carries him not to death but on a last voyage across the seas, as its guest and friend, and the two travel together as the crocodile grows old.

END: THE ISLAND. When the crocodile dies its vast body stays above the water and hardens into land: the island of Timor, which the map shows shaped like a crocodile, with the mountain ridges for its spines. The boy's descendants are the Timorese, who call the crocodile grandfather, ask its pardon before entering its rivers, and treat the animal as kin rather than vermin.

FUNCTIONS. The legend (1) makes the island a relative, with all the obligations of kinship toward crocodiles; (2) explains the island's shape as a body; (3) polices a shared ecology (the courtesy owed to crocodiles in river and sea); and (4) supplies the comparative island-from-animal motif of the eastern archipelago. The legend's ecology is its point: Timor's rivers and coasts are crocodile country, and the myth converts a lethal neighbour into a relative with a name, a genealogy and an etiquette. Fishermen and river-crossers acknowledge the grandfather crocodile, ask pardon before entering his waters, and distinguish the crocodile that takes a man from the grandfather who would not — a legal distinction inside a kinship. The island's shape seals the reading: on the map Timor's long ridged outline suggests the crocodile floating west to east, the mountain chain for its spines, so that geography confirms genealogy. Eastern-Indonesian parallels — islands from animals, canoes turned to reefs, ancestors as sharks or serpents — surround the Timor tale, but its warmth is distinctive: the island is not a defeated monster but a dying grandfather who carried the boy's line home. The legend also carries the eastern archipelago's oldest register of obligations: the boy's rescue of the stranded crocodile is an act of pity between unequals, and the crocodile's repayment — the last voyage, the island, the descendants — converts a debt between two individuals into a standing covenant between two peoples, the boy's line and the crocodile's. Timorese ritual speech still keeps the terms of that covenant in view: the crocodile is addressed as elder, not hunted as vermin, and the tellings insist that the few crocodiles who break the peace are not the grandfather but his lawless descendants. Read as charter, the myth does what island-origin legends do — it makes the land itself the body of an ancestor — but it does so with the unusual tenderness of a rescue repaid, which is why the tale survives so uniformly on both sides of the island's colonial border.
narrative.zh: 帝汶最著名之由來傳說謂此島本身即親族。開篇：一鱷離海擱於陸地，被孩童發現；男孩不忍殺之，背之返水而釋。鱷允諾報恩。中段：多年後鱷歸來——唤那已成少年的男孩；不是索命，而是邀他作客，同遊最後一程；人與鱷同游四海，鱷漸老。結尾：鱷死，其巨身留於水上硬化為陸——即帝汶島；地圖上其輪廓如鱷，山脊為其棘刺。男孩之後裔即帝汶人，至今稱鱷為祖父，入河下海前先請鱷恕罪，視之為親而非害獸。功能：以親屬關係釋島（對鱷負親族之義）、以屍身釋島形、規訓人鱷共居之生態禮俗、並為東部群島『動物化島』母題供給帝汶之形態。

functions: Makes the island a relative, with kinship obligations toward crocodiles
Explains the island's crocodile shape as a body at rest
Policing a shared ecology: the courtesy owed to crocodiles
Eastern-archipelago form of the island-from-animal motif

passages.note: Paraphrase of the Timor crocodile legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一隻擱淺在遠離大海之處的鱷魚被一個小男孩扛回水中，牠承諾報答這份恩情；多年之後，牠回來找那男孩——此時已長大成人——並非為了取他性命，而是作為他的東道與朋友，帶他踏上最後一次航行。

passages.text: The crocodile swims the seas until it dies, and its vast body hardens into land: the island of Timor, shaped like a crocodile with the ridges for spines. The boy's descendants are the Timorese, who call the crocodile grandfather and ask its pardon before entering its waters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Timor crocodile legend; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鱷魚在海中游動，直至死去，牠龐大的身軀硬化成陸地：帝汶島，形狀如鱷魚，脊背上有如脊椎的稜脊。那男孩的後代就是帝汶人，他們稱鱷魚為祖父，在進入牠的水域之前先向牠求恕。

title.en: The Pasola of Sumba: Riders on the Beach for the Rice-Worms
title.zh: 松巴島帕索拉：騎手為稻蟲而馳

region.en: Kodhi and Wanukaka coasts, Sumba
region.zh: 松巴島科迪與瓦努卡卡海岸

period: Sumba marapu tradition; annual observance

source.work: The pasola horse-battle tradition of West Sumba (marapu religion)

summary.en: The pasola of West Sumba opens the planting year: bands of horsemen from rival clans charge each other on the sea-shore with spears — a ritual battle fixed by the date the nyale sea-worms swarm ashore. The blood spilled on the sand is the field's fertilizer and the year's divination: the more it flows, the better the rice; the falling riders read the harvest to come.
summary.zh: 西松巴『帕索拉』開啟耕年：敵對氏族之騎手群於海灘持矛對衝——儀式性戰鬥，其日期由『尼亞勒』海蟲湧岸之日決定。灘上所流之血即田之肥與年之卜：血流愈盛，稻愈豐；墜馬之騎手，即為來年收成之兆。

sensitivity.note: Living ritual battle; note the real risks and the community's own rules.

passages.text: The pasola opens the planting year in West Sumba: horsemen of rival clans charge each other on the sea-shore with spears, the date fixed by the night the nyale sea-worms swarm ashore. The blood spilled on the sand is both fertilizer and oracle — the more it flows, the better the rice; the riders who fall are read as the harvest's signs, and the year's planting proceeds under marapu rules fixed by the battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sumba pasola tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 帕索拉節揭開西松巴的播種之年：敵對氏族的騎手在海濱持矛相互衝鋒，日期由夜裡「尼亞勒」海蟲湧上岸的那一夜決定。灑在沙上的血既是肥料也是神諭——血流得越多，稻米越好；落馬的騎手被解讀為收成的徵兆，當年的播種便在戰鬥所定的「馬拉普」規矩下進行。

title.en: Ngaben: The Return by Fire
title.zh: 火葬之歸：恩加本

region.en: Bali (village cremation grounds)
region.zh: 巴釐各村落火葬場

period: Balinese funerary tradition; living practice

source.work: The ngaben cremation rite (Balinese funerary cycle)

summary.en: In Bali the dead are not buried but burned: the ngaben sends the soul's five elements back to their sources — earth to earth, water to water, fire to fire, air to air — through the burning of the sarcophagus and the tower. Raffles' informant noted the Pembakaran, 'the place where the bodies of the princes are burned,' with figures of the deities installed beside it; the ashes go to the river, and the soul, element by element, goes home.
summary.zh: 巴釐亡者不入土而以火歸：『恩加本』將魂之五元素送還其源——土歸土、水歸水、火歸火、風歸風——藉棺槨與塔樓之焚化完成。拉弗爾斯之報告人亦記『彭巴卡蘭』——焚燒王族遺體之地，其旁立有諸神之像；骨灰入河，魂則元素逐一歸家。

sensitivity.note: Living funerary rite; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: The ngaben returns the dead by fire: the burning of the sarcophagus and the tower sends the soul's elements back to their sources — earth to earth, water to water, fire to fire, air to air — and the ashes are carried to the river. Raffles' informant records the Pembakaran, the place where the bodies of the princes are burned, with figures of the different deities installed in places made for their reception — the cremation ground itself a temple of the return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Balinese ngaben tradition; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), Appendix; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「恩加賓」火葬以火送還亡者：焚燒石棺與塔樓，將靈魂的元素送回其源頭——土歸土、水歸水、火歸火、氣歸氣——骨灰則被帶到河邊。萊佛士的報導人記載了「彭巴卡蘭」，即焚燒王子遺體之處，其中安置著不同神祇的塑像，設於為迎接祂們而造的位置——火葬場本身即是一座歸返之廟。

title.en: The Orphans and the Seal-Skin Disguise
title.zh: 孤兒姊弟與海豹皮偽裝

region.en: Winter settlement on the islets, Greenland
region.zh: 格陵蘭外島冬居地

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 29 'The Orphans', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Shut into an empty house by stone while the settlement moves off, the starving orphans bore through the roof, eat winter leavings, and — remembering their mother's magic songs — the sister rubs a thong-seal skin until it wraps the brother whole: he plays seal in the calm, and the unjacketed kayakers who chase him sink in the storm he sings up. Taken in, then fed a knee-pan as first bite by a new master, he grows strong; years later he makes the old man choose between a knee-pan and boiling train-oil — the scald kills him drinking — and the appeased orphan leaves on the first thaw.
summary.zh: 村民遷徙時用巨石封門，將姊弟二人鎖入空屋。饑餓中他們鑿穿屋頂而出，靠殘食度日；妹妹憶起母親所授咒歌，把長鬚海豹皮揉唱到能將弟弟整個裹住——他扮作小海豹引來追獵，唱起風暴咒，未著防水衣的皮艇客盡數翻沉。被收留後又被主人罰吞膝蓋骨；數年後他長成壯漢，回敬那老者：『吞膝骨容易，還是喝滾油容易？請您試試。』滾油燙喉，老者當場斃命，姊弟於初融時離去。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note lists related orphan fragments (ptarmigan-and-seals gifts, the fire that could never be extinguished, the orphan who walked on the ocean). Scalding death recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: In a well-peopled settlement there lived an old couple with an only son and a younger daughter; but the parents died before they were grown up. They soon got foster-parents, but these did not love them — always scolded, left to seek their food on the beach at low-water. One spring, when the people were going to start on their summer travels, they put the children into an empty house with a small portion of food, closed the entrance with large stones, and then left them. When the poor orphans were wellnigh starving, they rummaged about the empty room and fell to eating all the old leavings they could get hold of; when these were finished, the sister found an instrument for boring. As they could not reach the ceiling, they heaped up stones to stand upon, and in this way managed to make a hole in the roof to creep through — the brother first helping his sister to escape, then getting out himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 29 'The Orphans'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一個人口眾多的聚落裡，住著一對老夫婦，他們有一個獨子和一個年幼的女兒；但父母在他們長大之前便去世了。他們很快有了養父母，但養父母並不疼愛他們——總是責罵，任他們在退潮時到海灘上自行覓食。有一年春天，人們正要開始夏季的遷徙，便把這兩個孩子關進一間空屋，只留下少許食物，用大石封住入口，然後便離去了。可憐的孤兒們幾乎餓死，他們在空屋裡翻找，開始吃所有能找到的殘餘舊食；吃完了之後，妹妹找到一件鑽孔的工具。由於搆不到屋頂，他們便堆起石頭站上去，就這樣在屋頂上弄出一個洞爬了出去——哥哥先幫妹妹逃出，然後自己再出來。

passages.text: Outside they could see tents standing in rows on the islets, themselves on the mainland; by the smoke they knew the people to be cooking all the day, and could see the kayakers pursuing the seals. Hungry, they went to the place where the seals used to be stripped in the winter, hoping to find old bits, and were fortunate enough to find the head of a small thong-seal. Having eaten a part of it, the sister stripped off the skin, prepared it, and said to the brother: 'I am going to make a disguise for thee; dost not thou remember the magic song our mother taught us?' 'Indeed I do; and I even remember one for raising a storm. Make haste and get ready the skin.' She rubbed it hard, singing over it, and all the while it grew larger and larger; he tried it on — it only touched his knees — she rubbed still more, and at last he could wrap himself quite up in it. 'There, thou lookest just like a young thong-seal; now try the water' — he leapt down while she remained singing the magic lay, and when he reappeared she sang again, until at last: 'Well, now, thou art quite like a thong-seal; come!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 29 'The Orphans'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了外面，他們看見帳篷成排立在小島上，而他們自己在大陸上；從炊煙他們知道人們整天都在煮食，也能看見划皮艇的人追逐海豹。他們餓了，便走到冬天剝海豹皮的地方，希望能找到些舊的碎塊，幸運地找到一隻小帶紋海豹的頭。吃下一部分之後，妹妹剝下皮，加以處理，對哥哥說：「我要給你做一件偽裝；你不記得母親教我們的咒歌了嗎？」「我當然記得；我甚至還記得一首能興起風暴的。快點把皮準備好。」她用力搓揉那張皮，一邊對著它唱歌，皮便越變越大；他試穿了一下——只到他的膝蓋——她繼續搓揉，最後他終於能把自己整個裹進去。「好了，你看起來就像一隻小帶紋海豹；現在試試水吧」——她留在原地唱著咒歌，他跳了下去，當他再出現時她又唱，直到最後：「好了，現在你完全像一隻帶紋海豹了；來吧！」

passages.text: Next morning, fine weather and quite calm, and no kayaker from the islets having left land, he took a fancy to play the seal: putting on his disguise he leapt into the sea, and no sooner was he observed from the tents than they called out, 'There is a young seal; let us be off and chase it!' — plenty of joking and a great bustle, the men getting their kayaks down into the sea in a great hurry. In the meantime he dived; as he could not keep his breath all the time, he rose to the surface behind one of the kayakers and took breath without being observed. In the hurry of the moment some of the men had forgotten to put on their kayak-jackets, though rather far out at sea — these the disguised boy had picked out to wreak his vengeance on. He sang the lay for raising the wind, and all of a sudden a gale began to blow; the hunters hastened to put back and reach home, but those who were not in proper trim had their kayaks filled with water and perished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 29 'The Orphans'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早晨，天氣晴朗，風平浪靜，小島上沒有划皮艇的人離岸，他便起了興致要扮海豹：穿上他的偽裝，跳入海中，才剛被帳篷裡的人看見，他們便喊道：「那裡有一隻小海豹；我們快去追牠！」——一片嬉笑與大忙亂，男人們匆匆忙忙把皮艇推下海。與此同時他潛入水中；他無法一直屏住呼吸，便在其中一個划艇者的背後浮上水面換氣，沒有被察覺。匆忙之間，有些人忘了穿上他們的皮艇上衣，雖然已離岸相當遠——這些正是那偽裝的男孩挑出來要報復的對象。他唱起興風的咒歌，忽然間狂風大作；獵人們急忙掉頭回家，但那些裝備不齊的人，皮艇灌滿了水，就此喪命。

passages.text: When the brother came on shore he said to his sister: 'I believe we may safely venture to let them see we are still alive. Now they have lost some of their people, we may probably be of some use to them, and may be they will fetch us off' — and they made signs to attract attention. As soon as the people on the opposite islands observed them they said to one another, 'Let us get them over; we are in want of people' — a boat despatched, the orphans recovered. Later in the summer they were taken into a boat's crew as rowers and went up a firth for a deer-hunting station; but their master was not kind to them, and when he had got his first buck he gave the boy the knee-pan, saying, 'Until thou hast swallowed that, thou shalt have nothing else to eat' — almost choked, he managed to make it go down, then had his meal, but never forgot the knee-pan. When the deer-hunting was at an end in the autumn, some people were leaving for the north, the orphans among their party, thus leaving their former masters. Not yet quite grown up, they went on practising all manner of hard exercise to increase their strength, and both succeeded — the brother turning out to be an excellent seal-hunter besides. Some years afterwards they travelled back to the south and again came across the man who had made him swallow the knee-pan, now grown quite old. Game was scarce in the middle of winter, but the young man still went out and tried his luck, one day bringing home a large thong-seal, ordering the sister to boil down the blubber into train-oil. This done, he invited all their neighbours; when the meal was served up he addressed the old man: 'I would like to know whether it be easier to swallow a knee-pan or to drink boiling-hot oil? Just thou try, or otherwise thou wilt have no supper.' The old man hesitated, but drank it off at last; his throat got scalded, and he died in the act of drinking. The young man was thus appeased, and left the place on the first thaw.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 29 'The Orphans'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當哥哥上岸後，他對妹妹說：「我想我們現在可以放心讓他們看見我們還活著。如今他們已經損失了一些人，我們或許對他們還有些用處，說不定他們會把我們接過去。」於是他們做出手勢以引起注意。對面島上的人們一看見他們，便彼此說道：「讓我們把他們接過來吧；我們正缺人手。」於是派出一艘船，把這對孤兒接了回來。那年夏天晚些時候，他們被編入一艘船的船員中當槳手，溯著一道峽灣而上，前往一處獵鹿的營地；但他們的主人對他們並不和善，當他獵到第一頭雄鹿時，便把鹿的膝蓋骨交給那男孩，說道：「除非你把這個吞下去，否則你別想吃到別的東西。」他幾乎被噎住，好不容易才把它吞了下去，然後才吃了飯，卻始終沒有忘記那塊膝蓋骨。秋天獵鹿結束後，有些人要動身北上，這對孤兒也在其中，於是離開了他們從前的主人。他們尚未完全長大，便繼續操練各種艱苦的運動以增強體力，兩人都成功了——哥哥後來還成了一名出色的獵海豹能手。幾年之後，他們又南行，再次遇見了那個逼他吞下膝蓋骨的人，那人如今已十分衰老。隆冬時節獵物稀少，但這年輕人仍舊外出碰運氣，有一天帶回了一頭大皮帶海豹，吩咐妹妹把脂肪熬成魚油。熬好之後，他邀請了所有的鄰居；飯菜端上桌時，他對那老人說道：「我很想知道，究竟是吞下一塊膝蓋骨容易，還是喝下滾燙的油容易？你就試一試吧，否則你就別想吃晚飯。」老人猶豫了一下，最後還是把它喝了下去；他的喉嚨被燙傷，就在喝的當口死去了。年輕人這才消了氣，在第一次解凍時便離開了那個地方。

title.en: Alekatokak, Who Went Away in Search of Her Brother
title.zh: 阿蕾卡托卡克尋兄記

region.en: Inland valley of shadows and the northern camping plain
region.zh: 幽影之谷與北方營地草原

period: Inuit oral tradition; from two rather defective copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Blamed for her brother Asuvina's disappearance, Alekatokak flees her father's death-threat inland — past a giant who would not let her off, through a house of invisible shadows that feed her, to the camp where a kayaker tows a seal: 'Asuvina has got a seal!' Hidden from the clairvoyant idiot, she watches the chief crush his own feet with the lifting-stone and cures him with a young deer's entrails; married there, she swallows fox-entrails with shut eyes at her son's birth — the custom for clever children — and her boy grows a very swift runner, the family's descendants numerous in the place.
summary.zh: 兄長阿蘇維納失蹤，父親卻揚言要懲罰妹妹阿蕾卡托卡克；她攜衣物袋遠走內陸——躲過揚言不放她走的巨人，被一屋看不見的幽影留宿餵飯，終於在海邊營地聽見孩子們高喊『阿蘇維納獵到海豹啦！』。她藏身避開先知的白痴，眼看酋長舉圓石砸了自己雙腳，便疾奔追回幼鹿、以鹿腸為他療傷；在當地成婚生子，依習俗閉眼吞下狐腸——孩子長成飛毛腿，子孫繁衍於斯。

sensitivity.note: The place of shadows and the fox-entrails birth custom are documented as told; Rink notes the copies are defective.

passages.text: Alekatokak went away with her brother Asuvina to set up fox-traps. Having arrived at the place they had fixed upon, she told her brother that she wanted a flat stone to make a door for the trap, and asked him to bring her one; he went to get it, but as he was rather long in returning she went off to seek him — in vain; he had completely disappeared, and she was obliged to return by herself. On her coming home her father said, 'I suppose thou hast hurt him — perhaps even killed him: I shall be sure to punish thee.' He had often threatened to make away with her, having never liked her, but put her down as an idle wench, unable to make herself useful in any way. Her mother pitied her, and advised her to flee the society of men; accordingly she made up a little bag with some clothes, and went far into the country, wandering about, and could even overtake the reindeer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿萊卡托卡克和她的哥哥阿蘇維納一同外出設置捕狐陷阱。到了他們選定的地方後，她告訴哥哥她需要一塊平整的石頭來做陷阱的門，請他去取一塊來；他便去取了，但因為他去了好一陣還沒回來，她便去找他——卻白找一場；他完全消失了，她只好獨自返回。回到家後，她的父親說：「我猜你一定是傷了他——說不定還殺了他：我非得懲罰你不可。」他常常威脅說要除掉她，因為他從來就不喜歡她，只把她當作一個沒用的丫頭，認為她什麼事也做不好。她的母親憐憫她，勸她逃離人群；於是她就收拾了一個裝著些衣物的小包袱，遠走他鄉，四處流浪，甚至連馴鹿都能追得上。

passages.text: Having once passed a cleft in the mountains, she saw a little house down in a valley, with an opening in the centre of the roof; peeping down she observed a giant-like fellow, who returned the look and addressed her: 'What dost thou want here, thou miserable daughter of the coast-people? Dost thou think that I will let thee off like that?' He rushed out to seize her, but meanwhile she had found a hiding-place; when he had returned to his house she again hastened on farther into the country, and at last came to another house, which had three windows. She noticed that cooking was going on inside, as well as other business, without any people being visible — though not aware of it, she had been coming all the way to the place of shadows. A voice was heard saying, 'Thou little one from the coast-side, come in, come in!' — and when she had entered, a dish with boiled meat was set before her; her hunger stilled, the invisible shadows invited her to stay and sleep there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次她走過山間的一道裂縫，看見山谷下有一座小屋，屋頂中央有一個開口；她往下窺看，瞧見一個巨人般的傢伙，那人也回望她，對她說道：「你這海邊人的可憐丫頭，到這兒來做什麼？你以為我會就這麼放過你嗎？」他衝出來要抓她，但這期間她已找到了一個藏身之處；等他回到屋裡後，她又急忙往內陸更深處趕路，最後來到另一座房子，那房子有三扇窗戶。她注意到裡面正在煮東西，還有別的事情在忙活，卻看不見任何人——她並不知道，自己一路走來，竟來到了幽影之地。只聽得一個聲音說道：「你這海邊來的小傢伙，進來吧，進來吧！」她進去之後，一盤煮好的肉擺在了她面前；她止住了飢餓，那些看不見的幽影便邀她留下來在那裡過夜。

passages.text: After farther wanderings she at length reached the sea, and around a little creek observed a great many tents pitched up near the strand; waiting till evening before venturing down, she sat on a slope and heard the children of the place call out, 'A kayaker is coming! he is towing a seal!' — presently a kayaker appeared from behind a point, and they repeated, 'Asuvina has got a seal!' — and she felt sure she had found her lost brother.
