The people of the place had a chief whose tent was larger than all the rest, and beyond this a plain where they used to practise ball-playing; she recognised her brother accompanying the men thither, and saw that he was ordered to lift up a large round stone — not being able, the others threw him down. In the evening she descended the hill and went straight to his house; he wondered very much at her coming, told her he had lost his way in seeking the slab for her fox-trap, but was now married, his wife having a sister. There was an idiot at the place who, by clairvoyance, would probably soon be aware of her arrival — she had better hide herself a while behind the skin-hangings of the wall. Next morning the fool entered, saying, 'In the night I dreamt that a woman from the coast-side, and sister to Asuvina, came among us'; but Asuvina answered, 'I have got no sister' — and the other went away; Asuvina stayed at home the whole day long, enjoying his sister's company.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又流浪了一段路程之後，她終於來到了海邊，看見一個小灣周圍，緊挨著海灘搭起了許多帳篷；她等到傍晚才敢下去，坐在一道斜坡上，聽見那地方的孩童們喊道：「有個划獨木舟的人來了！他正拖著一頭海豹！」不一會兒，一個划獨木舟的人從一個岬角後出現，他們又重複喊道：「阿蘇維納打到一頭海豹了！」她便確信自己找到了失散的哥哥。那地方的人有一位首領，他的帳篷比其餘所有的都大，帳篷後面是一片平地，他們常在那裡玩球；她認出哥哥隨著那些男人往那裡去，又看見他被吩咐去舉起一塊大圓石——他舉不起來，其餘的人便把他摔倒。傍晚時分她下了山，徑直走到他的屋前；他對她的到來大為驚異，告訴她說，他當初為她找捕狐陷阱的石板時迷了路，如今已經娶了妻，妻子的妹妹也同住。那地方有一個傻子，憑著千里眼，大概很快就會察覺她的到來——她最好先在牆上的皮掛簾後面躲一陣子。第二天早晨，那傻子走了進來，說道：「我夜裡夢見一個海邊來的女人，是阿蘇維納的妹妹，來到了我們中間。」但阿蘇維納回答說：「我沒有妹妹。」那人便走了；阿蘇維納整天待在家裡，享受與妹妹相聚的時光。

passages.text: In the evening she went with them to the ball-play on the plain, disguised in the clothes of her sister-in-law. When the chief had lifted the round stone he made a false hit, and let it fall down upon his own feet, and fairly crushed them. Alekatokak now told them quickly to fetch a little dog; but on hearing that they had not got one in the whole place, she hurried away and soon overtook and brought back a young deer; she cut an opening into it, and let the chief put the sore feet down among the entrails, and in this way cured him. She got married there and had a son; at his birth they brought her an oblong dish with certain entrails of a fox, and ordered her to swallow them, shutting her eyes the while — this was the custom with them when they desired the new-born child to be clever and dexterous. After this remedy she was at once restored to her usual health, and her boy grew to be a very swift runner; and they remained in the place and had numerous descendants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傍晚時分，她換上嫂嫂的衣服，隨他們一同到平地上玩球。首領舉起那塊圓石時失了手，讓石頭砸落到自己的腳上，把腳砸得稀爛。阿萊卡托卡克當即叫他們趕快去牽一條小狗來；但聽說他們整個地方連一條狗也沒有，她便急忙離去，很快就追上並帶回了一頭小鹿；她在鹿身上割開一個口子，讓首領把受傷的腳伸進內臟裡，就這樣治好了他。她在那裡結了婚，生了一個兒子；孩子出生時，他們給她端來一個長方形的盤子，裡面盛著狐狸的某些內臟，吩咐她閉上眼睛把它們吞下去——這是他們的習俗，為的是讓新生兒聰明靈巧。用了這副藥之後，她立刻恢復了平日的健康，她的兒子也長成了一個跑得極快的飛毛腿；他們就留在了那個地方，子孫繁衍眾多。

title.en: The Dog: Origin of the Howling at the Last Point
title.zh: 狗：吠送行舟之俗的由來

region.en: Coast settlement and inlanders' camp
region.zh: 海岸聚落與內陸人營地

period: Inuit oral tradition; single manuscript, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 31 'The Dog', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Nursed at the ledge with her own milk after the inlanders hang her sons on an inaccessible rock, a mother adopts a magic whelp that scratches its face and asks 'What do I look like now?' — its scratching a charm to frighten people to death. It frightens a whole conjuring-house dead, fetches storehouse victuals to the starving family, and is abandoned when the boat sails, following along the shore to whine and howl at the last point — the origin, the teller says, of the dogs that follow the departing boat along the coast and go on howling at them from the last point of land.
summary.zh: 內陸人把兩個兒子倒吊於不可攀的危崖上；悲憤的母親領回一只有靈的狗崽，以乳汁哺於長凳之上。狗兒抓著自己的臉問『我現在好看嗎？』——那抓撓正是嚇死人的咒術。它使一座降神屋的人當場嚇死，又為絕糧的一家搬回存糧。開春船隻啟航時，母親藉口讓它回屋取物，隨即解纜而去；狗沿岸追至最後一處岬角，再無路可走，唯有對著船嗚咽長嚎——今日狗群追船吠送之俗，即由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Etiological ending documented in the source. The hanged sons and fright-killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: An old married couple had two sons and a little daughter; the sons were renowned for strength and for being able hunters, used to return with their seals towing in a long line behind them — but one day they did not return. While the parents were still expecting them, a man brought the sad news that he had seen them both hanging on an inaccessible rock, hung up by the feet, head downwards, nobody able to get at them to save them; this deed had been done by the inlanders. While the old parents were in deep affliction for their loss, they heard that some of their neighbours had a dog with a great many whelps; the mother sent the daughter away to fetch one, which she adopted, and had it always on the ledge beside her, nursing it with her own milk. In the winter she noticed that the dog, being endowed with magic power, sometimes went on scratching his face, and at the same time always commencing to speak, asking, 'What do I look like now?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 31 'The Dog'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一對老夫婦有兩個兒子和一個小女兒；兩個兒子以力大和善獵聞名，常常拖著長長一列海豹歸來——可是有一天他們沒有回來。正當父母還在盼望他們時，一個人帶來了噩耗，說他看見他們兄弟二人被倒吊在一處無法攀及的岩石上，腳朝上、頭朝下，誰也夠不著去救他們；這樁事是內陸人幹的。老夫婦正為失去兒子而悲痛欲絕時，聽說有些鄰居養了一條狗，生了許多小狗崽；母親便打發女兒去討一隻回來，她收養了它，總把它放在自己身旁的壁架上，用自己的奶餵養它。到了冬天，她發覺這條狗被賦予了法力，有時會抓撓自己的臉，同時總是開口說話，問道：「我現在看起來像什麼？」

passages.text: Towards the end of the winter they were in great want, having lost their protectors. The dog then said he was going for a walk into the country; one night he roused his foster-mother, and having given himself a scratching, inquired, 'Am I still good-looking? I shall be off to-morrow' — the reason for thus scratching itself was to frighten people to death by charm. He came upon the inlanders while they were busy conjuring spirits; the angakok soon foretold his coming, and cried, 'Fire! fire!' but the dog scratched his face and rushed into the passage, hiding itself there; when the people came out, bringing lights with them, the dog frightened them to death on the spot. Next he set off in search of their storehouse, and carried some victuals back to his foster-parents, showing them the place where they could find the rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 31 'The Dog'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 冬末時節，他們失去了保護者，陷入極度的匱乏之中。那隻狗便說要到鄉間去走走；某夜，他喚醒了他的養母，在自己身上抓撓了一番，問道：「我還算好看嗎？我明天就要走了。」——他這般抓撓自己，為的是以符咒將人嚇死。他遇上了那些內陸人，當時他們正忙著召喚神靈；那巫師（angakok）很快便預言了他的到來，喊道：「火！火！」但那隻狗抓撓自己的臉，衝進通道裡，藏身其中；當人們帶著燈火走出來時，那隻狗當場把他們嚇死了。接著他又動身去尋他們的儲藏屋，帶了些食物回去給他的養父母，並指給他們其餘食物所在的地方。

passages.text: But from that time upwards the woman began to fear him; and in the spring, when the boat was loaded and ready for starting, she asked the dog to go back to the house and bring her something she had forgotten. As soon as it had disappeared to obey her orders, they pushed off from land and set out on their journey. The dog went on following along the shore until they gained the last point, from which it could follow them no longer; there it remained whining and howling. It is supposed that this is the origin of the present custom with the dogs to follow the departing boat along the coast, and go on howling at them from the last point of land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 31 'The Dog'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但從那時起，那女人便開始懼怕他；到了春天，船已裝載妥當、準備啟程時，她叫那隻狗回屋裡去替她取一件她忘了的東西。他一消失去遵從她的吩咐，他們便推船離岸，踏上旅程。那隻狗沿著岸邊一路追隨，直到他們抵達最後一個岬角，從那裡他再也無法跟隨他們了；他便留在那裡，哀鳴嚎叫。據說，如今狗隻沿著海岸追隨離去的船、並在最後一處陸地對它們不停嚎叫的習俗，便是由此而來。

title.en: The Widow's Vengeance: The Bear and the Poisoned Loin
title.zh: 寡婦復仇記：靈熊與咒肉

region.en: Iceberg grounds and rival household, Greenland coast
region.zh: 格陵蘭冰山海面與仇家屋舍

period: Inuit oral tradition; one of the older manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Refused even a taviorasak of blubber, the widow charms an eider-duck, a small seal, and at last a completely furnished kayak into being; her son Kujanguak climbs the iceberg the brothers could not and flings down a bear stone-dead. When they set on him on the water, the sea-water-charm loosens their grip; across the breakers he rides the surf. A spelled piece of loin kills Sanak at the shared feast; the eldest shakes the house-pillars and tears off her jacket-points, but the widow, her back broken leaping the boat, flings the filth of her dead mother's corner at the enemies' house — sickness kills them all but the sister, who turns kivigtok.
summary.zh: 討一點油脂也被拒的寡婦，以咒術接連變出海雀、小海豹，乃至一艘配備齊全的皮艇；其子庫江瓜克登上連兄弟們都攀不上的冰山，把熊活活摔死海中。兄弟們在水上圍攻他，他蘸一口海水便令其鬆手，又踏浪越過碎浪帶。分肉的宴席上，一小塊被咒的腰肉使三納克窒息而死；長兄搖撼屋柱、撕她衣角，寡婦卻在跳船時折了背——臨終前她將亡母角落裡的穢物擲向仇家之屋，瘟疫隨之而至，唯其妹遁入內陸為奇維托克人。

sensitivity.note: Charm-made objects (duck, seal, kayak) and corpse-filth sorcery documented as told in the 1875 source. Multiple deaths recorded.

passages.text: There was a widow with a son named Kujanguak; beyond her house was another one, inhabited by a number of brothers, all clever at their profession and well off. Whenever they had brought home any seals, the widow, according to the custom, would send her son to get a taviorasak (little bit of blubber); but the men generally replied, 'Thou lazy beggar, thou never assisted us in providing anything; so thou wilt not get anything neither.' On his returning with this answer his mother only said, 'Never mind — just let them talk.' One day they caught a mamartok (a delicious kind of seal that has shed hair); the mother now took a stronger fancy than ever for a little morsel, and sent her son for it — he was treated as usual: the men took a bit of whatever they could lay hand on and flung it at him. When he came back and gave their message to his mother, she was in a great rage; taking one of her boots, she seated herself in a corner of the ledge to practise some charm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個寡婦，帶著一個名叫庫揚瓜克（Kujanguak）的兒子；她家屋外還有另一戶人家，住著一群兄弟，個個精於本行，家境富裕。每當他們帶回海豹時，那寡婦便依習俗派兒子去討一塊塔維奧拉薩克（taviorasak，一小塊鯨脂）；但那些男人通常回答：「你這懶叫化子，你從沒幫我們弄到過什麼東西；所以你也什麼都別想得到。」他帶著這答覆回來，母親只說：「別在意——隨他們說去。」有一天，他們捕到一頭馬馬爾托克（mamartok，一種已蛻去毛皮的鮮美海豹）；母親這回比以往更饞那一小塊肉，便派兒子去討——他照舊受到那般對待：那些男人隨手抓起什麼就朝他扔去。當他回來把他們的話轉告母親時，她勃然大怒；她拿起自己的一隻靴子，坐到炕沿的一角，施起符咒來。

passages.text: On the following morning, when her son looked into the pot, there was an eider-duck in it — 'Just take it' — part boiled, the rest put by for future use. In the evening she repeated her charms and spells, and a small seal was found in the water-tub. The third day, the son, to his great surprise, saw standing on the floor a completely furnished kayak; the mother took him down to the beach, and made him practise paddling, as well as upsetting and again righting, till he had got quite expert at these things. The following day she let him go out again, and pointing to an iceberg told him to round it in his kayak; the neighbours likewise set off, and saw Kujanguak attacking a bear, which at last took refuge on an iceberg. The eldest of the brothers tried to climb it, but was not able; after him Kujanguak made the attempt — having first asked the other to take care of his kayak, he clutched hold of the ice and scrambled up. At the very top he encountered the bear, and immediately fell upon it; taking hold of it by the neck, he flung it down into the sea, stone-dead. The youngest of the brothers, Sanak, cried out, 'I have got a bear!' — but Kujanguak quietly descended, got into his kayak, fastened his towing-line to the bear, and paddled home, followed by the other kayakers who had given him their assistance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早晨，她兒子往鍋裡一看，裡面有一隻絨鴨——「就拿去吧」——一部分已煮過，其餘的留作日後之用。到了晚上，她重施符咒法術，水盆裡便出現了一隻小海豹。第三天，兒子大為驚奇地看見地板上立著一艘配備齊全的皮划艇；母親帶他到海灘上，讓他練習划槳，以及翻艇和再把艇翻正，直到他對這些事都相當熟練為止。第二天，她又讓他出海，指著一座冰山叫他划著皮划艇繞過它；鄰人們也一同出發，看見庫揚瓜克正在攻擊一頭熊，那熊最後逃到一座冰山上避難。兄弟中年長的那個試圖爬上冰山，卻爬不上去；接著庫揚瓜克也來一試——他先請那人照看他的皮划艇，然後抓住冰面攀爬上去。到了最頂上，他遇上了那頭熊，立刻撲了上去；他抓住熊的脖子，把它扔進海裡，當場摔死。兄弟中最年幼的薩納克（Sanak）喊道：「我逮到一頭熊了！」——但庫揚瓜克不聲不響地下來，上了他的皮划艇，把拖繩繫在熊身上，划船回家，後面跟著那些曾助他一臂之力的其他划艇者。

passages.text: The mother went down to the beach accompanied by the sister of the brothers; while they were busy dragging the bear up to the house the mother mockingly observed, turning to her, 'Who knows how nourishing that flesh may be!' adding, 'Now haul it up the rest of the way thyself; I am going to fetch water.' Having finished this task, however, she returned to the bear, divided it into two equal parts, and gave her companion one: 'The skin thou mayst keep for a ledge-cover.' She boiled the flesh and invited the whole party to partake of it, seating the other woman on the main ledge; when she had served the meal up she remarked, 'It is a pity one cannot make sure whether there is any nourishment about this game of Kujanguak's' — the visitor said she had been longing ever so much for bear's meat lately, they all ate well, and on taking leave the female visitor thanked her, saying she had altogether found it a delicious and hearty feed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 母親由那群兄弟的姊妹陪同著下到海灘；當她們忙著把熊拖回家時，母親轉向她，語帶嘲諷地說：「誰知道那肉有多滋補呢！」又補上一句：「剩下的路你自己拖回去吧；我去打水。」然而，打完水之後，她回到熊那兒，把它分成相等的兩半，把一半給了她的同伴：「那張皮你留著做炕沿的鋪蓋吧。」她把肉煮了，邀請那一群人一同享用，讓另一個女人坐在主炕上；上完飯菜後，她說道：「可惜沒法確定庫揚瓜克這獵物到底有沒有滋補」——那來客說她近來一直非常想吃熊肉，大家吃得很好，告辭時那女客向她道謝，說她這一頓吃得十分鮮美又飽足。

passages.text: The following day Kujanguak again set off to the iceberg and got a large seal; returning towing it homewards, he chanced to encounter the brothers — happily his mother had advised him beforehand, 'If ever they venture to persecute thee, take some water out of the sea with thy left hand, and moisten thy lips with it.' He tried this as soon as they all came rushing in upon him; the eldest brother began the attack by catching hold of the kayak point, doing his utmost to upset it — no sooner had Kujanguak tasted the water with his lips than the other let it go. 'Look at the foaming breakers there! let us try which of us can first get beyond them' — all pushed on as fast as possible; Kujanguak, who had a seal on his line, was first obliged to tighten it, but this done, pushed on like a shot and soon came up with the eldest brother ahead of the others; while they rowed outside of the breakers, Kujanguak went right across them, carried along by the surf. When the waves retreated he jumped out upon the rocks; when the breakers came rolling on again, he hastened back into the kayak. On the way home the brothers secretly consulted to surround him; however, he made his escape from them. Meanwhile his mother suddenly missed a certain lock of hair, knowing this to be a bad omen for her son, very anxious about him until it shortly afterwards proved to be in its proper place on her forehead; reassured, she mounted the hills to look out for his return. On landing he was received on the beach by her along with the other woman, who asked him how her brothers had fared — 'I wonder thou carest to bother thyself about those stupid fellows!' When the flesh of the seal had been prepared and the men were supping upon the briskets, the mother of the many sons grew envious and resentful because she was not invited to share the good fare; on hearing this the widow cut a piece of the loin, and having pronounced a spell upon it, carried it to her by way of a present. When they sat down to eat it, Sanak was almost suffocated, and presently his old mother likewise cried for water — having got a drink she recovered; Sanak, however, expired. When the widow re-entered the room, the eldest brother accused her of the deed: 'You only fed them to work their destruction — it is none but thou who hast killed them!' — and rose and rushed against the house-pillars to shake it down and make it fall over her; but the widow replaced them quickly. Again he rose from his seat, and turning towards the widow herself, quickly snatched off the two points of her jacket, the one in front as well as the one behind. Little heeding this affront, she now ran out and told her son that two of their adversaries had now been despatched; in the enjoyment of the happy event they both bolted across the boat in great glee — however, the mother happened to break her back. When Kujanguak had got her indoors, she took some filth from beneath the place where her dead mother used to put all kinds of dirty refuse, and threw it out at the house of their enemies; this brought sickness upon them, from which all of them died excepting the sister, who turned kivigtok.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，庫揚瓜克又動身前往冰山，捕到一頭大漢豹；他拖著它回家，途中恰好遇上那群兄弟——幸好他母親事先囑咐過他：「倘若他們膽敢來迫害你，就用左手從海裡取些水，潤濕你的嘴唇。」他們一齊向他撲來時，他便試了這法子；年長的兄弟率先發難，抓住皮划艇的艇首，竭力要把它弄翻——庫揚瓜克剛用嘴唇嚐了那水，那人便鬆了手。「瞧那邊翻湧的浪花！咱們來比比誰先越過它們」——眾人盡力向前划；庫揚瓜克拖繩上繫著一頭海豹，只得先把它收緊，但收好之後，便如箭一般衝了出去，很快追上了領先眾人的年長兄弟；當他們在浪花外側划行時，庫揚瓜克卻乘著浪頭直穿而過。浪退時，他跳上岩石；浪花再次湧來時，他又急忙回到皮划艇裡。回家途中，那群兄弟暗中商議要圍住他；然而他還是逃脫了。與此同時，他母親忽然發覺少了一撮頭髮，知道這是兒子的凶兆，便為他十分焦慮，直到不久之後那撮頭髮又回到她額上原處；她這才安心，登上山丘去張望他歸來。他靠岸時，她與另一個女人在海灘上迎接他，那女人問她的兄弟們過得如何——「我倒奇怪你竟有興致去操心那些蠢貨！」海豹肉備好之後，男人們正吃著胸肉，那多子之母因未被邀共享這頓好菜而心生嫉妒與怨恨；寡婦聽說後，切下一塊腰肉，對它念了咒，拿去送給她當作禮物。他們坐下要吃時，薩納克幾乎噎死，不久他那老母親也喊著要水——喝了水便恢復了；薩納克卻斷了氣。寡婦再進屋時，年長的兄弟指控是她下的手：「你餵他們吃，就是要害他們的命——殺死他們的正是你！」——說罷起身衝向屋柱，要把屋子搖倒、壓在她身上；但寡婦迅速把柱子扶回原位。他又從座位上起身，轉向寡婦本人，飛快地扯下她外套上的兩個尖角，前襟的和後襟的都扯了。她對這番羞辱不甚在意，這會兒跑出去告訴兒子，說他們的對頭已有兩個被解決了；母子二人為這喜事歡欣雀躍，雙雙飛奔著跨過船——不料母親竟折斷了背。庫揚瓜克把她扶進屋後，她從她死去的母親從前堆放各種污穢廢物的地方底下取了些穢物，朝他們仇人的屋子扔去；這使他們染上疾病，除那姊妹之外全都死了，而那姊妹則變成了基維格托克（kivigtok）。

title.en: A Lamentable Story: The Cleft That Closed
title.zh: 悲慘的故事：合攏的石縫

region.en: Rock cleft by the sealing ice, Greenland
region.zh: 格陵蘭獵豹冰畔的石縫

period: Inuit oral tradition; one of the older manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 33 'A Lamentable Story', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: One shout from playing children, carrying their baby sisters and brothers in their hoods, spoils an old man's seal — and in his rage he cries 'Shut up, mountain-cleft!' — and it closes upon all of them, wide at the bottom, narrow at the top. The babies cry for thirst; the girls suck their fingers and hush them — 'When mother has finished soling the boots, she will come and suckle thee.' The mothers come and pour water down the cleft, trickling along the walls to be licked up, see the children plainly, and cannot get at them — and all of them are starved.
summary.zh: 孩子們背著兜帽中的弟妹在石縫間嬉戲，一聲歡呼驚走了老人的海豹。他盛怒喝道：『合上吧，山縫！』石縫應聲閉合，將孩子們全部困於底闊頂窄的巖窟之中。嬰兒啼哭要水，女孩們把手指塞進他們嘴裡哄道：『等媽媽補好靴底，就來餵你了。』母親們趕來，把水沿縫灌下，孩子們沿壁舔飲；母親們看得清清楚楚，卻無法救出——孩子們終究全數餓死。

sensitivity.note: Same motif family as Rasmussen's 'The man who became a star' (Nalaussartoq, cross-ref inuit-man-became-star); here without the star transformation. Child deaths recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: An old man had taken up his position on the ice watching the breathing-holes of the seals, in order to spear them as they appeared. Meanwhile some little girls were playing on shore in a cleft between some rocks, as usual, carrying their little baby sisters and brothers in the amowts (hoods) at their backs. Just as the old man was in the act of spearing a seal, the children happened to give a shout, and the terrified seal at once dived to the bottom. On this the old man got into a great passion, and cried out aloud, 'Shut up, mountain-cleft!' — and accordingly it closed upon all the playing children, who were not able to escape, but were now buried in a cavern, wide at the bottom, and narrow towards the top.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 33 'A Lamentable Story'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位老人站在冰上，守著海豹的呼吸孔，好趁牠們浮出時以魚叉刺之。與此同時，幾個小女孩在岸上岩石間的一道裂隙裡玩耍，一如往常，背上還用阿莫特（兜帽）背著她們的小妹妹和小弟弟。正當老人舉叉刺向一頭海豹時，孩子們恰好喊了一聲，那受驚的海豹立刻潛入水底。老人因此勃然大怒，高聲喊道：「閉嘴，山裂隙！」——於是裂隙便合攏起來，把那些正在玩耍的孩子全都封在其中，他們無法逃脫，就此被埋進一個底部寬闊、向上漸窄的洞穴裡。

passages.text: The babies soon began to cry for thirst, and the girls put their fingers into their mouths to suck at, trying to hush them by telling them, 'When mother has finished soling the boots, she will come and suckle thee.' At length the mothers came to the spot, and poured water down in the cleft; the water trickled along the walls, and they licked it up, and the mothers could very well see the children, but as it was impossible to get at them, all of them were starved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 33 'A Lamentable Story'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 嬰兒們不久便因口渴而哭了起來，女孩們把手指伸進他們嘴裡讓他們吮吸，又哄他們說：「等母親縫完靴子，就會來餵你。」終於，母親們來到那地方，往裂隙裡灌水；水沿著岩壁流下，孩子們便舔著喝，母親們能清清楚楚看見孩子，卻無法搆到他們，於是他們全都餓死了。

title.en: Uvikiak: The Mock-Song of the Murderers
title.zh: 烏維基亞克：兇手的嘲歌

region.en: Northern coast journey and the murderers' dancing ground
region.zh: 北航海岸與兇手們的舞場

period: Inuit oral tradition; one of the oldest manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 34 'Uvikiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Travelling north, Uvikiak's son is found dead at the landing-place — pierced beneath the arms, eyes covered with his own entrails. Following the murders from camp to camp, he hears first the mock-song ('they laughed and scorned him'), then a boat's crew singing very sadly about the young man they had killed. At the murderers' settlement, hidden under a keel-upturned boat and over the dancing-hill, he and his daughters seize two flushed, undressed young men fresh from the song, kill them, and set them up in exactly the position of the son — hearing the cry of vengeance from hiding before escaping home to the south.
summary.zh: 北行途中，烏維基亞克的兒子陳屍於約定的登岸處——腋下貫穿銳器、雙眼被自己的腸臟覆蓋。一路追蹤，他先聽見營中的嘲歌——『他們笑他、辱他』——後又聽得一船之人悲唱那被他們殺死的少年。到了兇手的聚落，父女藏身於翻扣的船底與舞山之後，擒住兩名剛唱完歌、汗流滿面赤身而來的年輕人，依其子之狀陳屍示眾，隱身聽得復仇的喊叫，方才安然南歸。

sensitivity.note: Graphic murder description recorded as told in the 1875 source. The mock-song as evidence motif recurs in Greenlandic feud tales.

passages.text: Uvikiak was travelling to the north, accompanied by one son and two daughters. Whenever he came to a favourable shore the son kayaked ahead of them, and when the others came up to the spot they had fixed to land upon, he was already standing in waiting. They generally remained on land for the night and travelled further the next day; in the evening the son roamed ahead, as usual, to await them ashore — but when they landed and looked for him he was not to be seen. They pushed off again, and having doubled a point of land and got into a bay, they saw his lifeless body, standing erect, pierced with sharp weapons beneath his arms, and his eyes covered with some of his entrails. At this sight his father groaned with despair, and left the place to get hold of the murderers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 34 'Uvikiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏維基亞克帶著一個兒子和兩個女兒向北而行。每逢來到一處適宜的岸邊，兒子便划著獨木舟先行，等其他人到達他們預定登陸的地點時，他已站在那裡等候了。他們通常上岸過夜，次日再繼續前行；傍晚時分，兒子照例先划到前頭，在岸上等候他們——可是當他們登岸尋他時，卻不見他的蹤影。他們再度離岸，繞過一個岬角，進入一處海灣，只見他的屍體直立著，腋下被銳利的武器刺穿，雙眼被一些內臟遮蓋著。見此情景，父親絕望地呻吟，隨即離開那地方，要去抓住兇手。

passages.text: Some way off he observed some tents, and went and asked, 'Have ye seen no travellers pass by this way?' — 'To be sure we have: yesterday a boat passed by; they were singing some kind of mock song about a young lad whose eyes had been covered with his entrails, and at which they laughed and scorned him.' At this report the father was still more provoked; always lamenting the lost one, they continued their journey of discovery, making inquiries at several other places, where they always got the same information, that a boat had newly passed by. Uvikiak still travelled on, with his wife and his two daughters, never now coming on shore in the night. At last they again reached some tents, and on making the usual inquiries got the answer that a boat had lately passed by, the crew of which were singing very sadly about a young man they had killed — and the wrath of the old Uvikiak somewhat subsided at their mild words.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 34 'Uvikiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 走了一段路，他望見幾頂帳篷，便前去問道：「你們可曾看見有旅人從這條路經過？」——「當然看見過：昨天有一艘船經過；他們唱著某種嘲弄的歌，唱的是一個眼睛被自己內臟遮住的少年，他們一邊唱一邊笑，嘲笑他。」聽到這番話，父親更加憤怒了；他們始終哀悼著失去的親人，繼續踏上追查之旅，又在好幾處地方打聽，得到的總是同樣的消息：有一艘船剛剛經過。烏維基亞克仍舊帶著妻子和兩個女兒前行，如今夜裡再也不上岸了。最後他們又來到幾頂帳篷前，照例打聽，得到的回答是：不久前有一艘船經過，船上的人正十分悲傷地唱著一個被他們殺死的年輕人——老烏維基亞克聽了他們溫和的話語，怒氣才稍稍平息。

passages.text: They continued their journey for several days without being able to sleep in the night for excitement; but at length they set foot on the spot where lived the murderers. They put in and landed somewhat at the back of their dwelling-place, and having got the boat on shore, placed it keel upwards, and gathered crowberry plants and grass to cover it up with; Uvikiak's wife betook herself under the boat, while he himself went away with his daughters across the isthmus. They soon heard a noise, and listening on one of the nearest hills, just above the spot where they used to have dancing and other games, they heard distinctly that one of them was singing about Uvikiak's son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 34 'Uvikiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們又繼續走了好幾天，夜裡因情緒激動而無法入睡；最後他們終於踏上了兇手們居住的地方。他們把船駛近，在那些人住處的後方一帶登陸，將船拖上岸，船底朝上放好，又採集了岩高蘭和草來遮蓋它；烏維基亞克的妻子躲到船底下，他自己則帶著女兒們越過地峽而去。他們不久便聽到一陣喧鬧，於是伏在離那地方最近的一座小丘上——正好在那些人平日跳舞嬉戲之處的上方——清楚地聽見其中一人在唱著關於烏維基亞克兒子的歌。

passages.text: The song being finished, two young men came walking up-hill, flushed with heat and quite undressed; the new-comers at once inquired something about the singers — 'It is our master; he was just singing about a young man whom we happened to meet with down in the south, and killed — it was mighty amusing.' In a great rage Uvikiak instantly seized the one of them, and the daughters the other; they soon got the better of both, and having killed them, put them in exactly the same position as that in which they had seen Uvikiak's son, after which they hid themselves at a little distance. They had not to wait long before they heard a cry of vengeance; but their hiding-place was not discovered, and they escaped without any harm, and then returned to their home in the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 34 'Uvikiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歌聲唱罷，兩個年輕人走上山來，熱得滿臉通紅，身上一絲不掛；這兩個新來的人立刻向他們打聽那些唱歌的人——「那是我們的主人；他剛才在唱一個我們在南邊偶然遇見並殺死的年輕人——真是有趣極了。」烏維基亞克勃然大怒，立刻抓住其中一人，女兒們抓住另一個；他們很快便制服了兩人，將他們殺死後，擺成與他們所見烏維基亞克兒子完全相同的姿勢，然後躲到不遠處。他們沒等多久便聽到一聲復仇的呼喊；但他們的藏身之處並未被發現，他們毫髮無傷地逃脫了，隨後返回南方的家園。

title.en: The Sun and the Moon: Sister's Fire, Brother's Smoke
title.zh: 日月神話：姊之焰與弟之煙

region.en: Old woman's house and the ascending skies
region.zh: 老嫗之屋與升天之空

period: Inuit oral tradition; translated from one of the oldest manuscripts; also known at Point Barrow, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 35 'The Sun and the Moon', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Announced by snow-bunting, wheat-ear, and raven, a beautiful woman visits a lonely wife and tells the incest tale: courting in the dark, she sooted her hands to mark her lover and found her own brother's white jacket besmeared — cutting off her breasts, 'Since my body seems to please thee, pray take these and eat them.' Racing about the room with lit moss, they are lifted into the air; his light goes out, hers keeps burning — she has become the sun, on her way higher up the skies to give warmth to the orphans and make summer. One last look shows her back a mere skeleton.
summary.zh: 雪鳥、穗鵖與渡鴉依次報信後，一位美貌婦人造訪獨守的老嫗，自述亂倫之罪：黑夜中擇偶嬉戲，她以煙灰塗掌辨認意中人，竟發現哥哥的白袍沾滿灰黑——她割下雙乳：『既然我的身體合你心意，就把這個也吃了吧。』二人持燃苔追逐，忽被舉上長空；他的光熄了，她的光長明——她已成為太陽，正升向更高的天際，『好讓陽光溫暖孤兒們，為大地帶來夏天』。臨別一瞥，她的背影已是枯骨一副。

sensitivity.note: Incest and self-mutilation recorded as told in the 1875 source. Rink notes a Point Barrow version (John Simpson, surgeon of the Plover) with nearly the same words — evidence of the tale's circumpolar spread.

passages.text: An old married couple remained at home while their children travelled about all the summer. One day the wife was left alone as usual while the husband was out kayaking; on hearing something moving about close by, she hastened to hide beneath her coverlet, and after a little while, when she ventured to peep above it, saw a little snow-bunting hopping about on the floor and chirping, 'Another one will soon enter, who is going to tell thee something.' In a little while she was alarmed by a still greater noise, and looking up again beheld a kusagtak (the wheat-ear), likewise hopping on the floor and singing, 'Somebody shall soon enter and tell thee something.' It left the room, and was soon followed by a raven; but soon after it had gone she heard a sound like the steps of people, and this time saw a very beautiful woman who entered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 35 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一對老夫婦留在家中，而他們的子女整個夏天都在外四處遊歷。有一天，妻子一如往常獨自留在家裡，丈夫則外出划獨木舟；她聽見近處有東西在動，便急忙躲到被子底下，過了一會兒，她壯起膽子從被子上方偷看，看見一隻小雪鵐在地板上跳來跳去，啾啾叫著：『另一個馬上就要進來了，他會告訴你一些事情。』過了一會兒，她被一陣更大的聲響嚇了一跳，再次抬頭看，看見一隻kusagtak（麥穗鳥），同樣在地板上跳著，唱著：『馬上就會有人進來，告訴你一些事情。』牠離開了屋子，不久之後一隻渡鴉跟了進來；但牠走後不久，她聽見像是人的腳步聲，這一次她看見一個非常美麗的女人走了進來。

passages.text: On asking whence she came, the stranger told: 'In bygone days we often used to assemble in my home to divert ourselves at different plays and games, and in the evening, when it was all ended, the young girls generally remained out, and the young men used to pursue and court us; but we could never manage to recognise them in the dark. One night I was curious to know the one who had chosen me, and so I went and daubed my hands with soot before I joined the others. When our play had come to an end, I drew my hands along his back, and left him, and was the first who entered the house. The young people came in, one after another undressed, but for some time I observed no marks. Last of all my brother entered, and I saw at once that the back of his white jacket was all besmeared with soot. I took a knife, and sharpened it, and proceeded to cut off my two breasts, and gave him them, saying, Since my body seems to please thee, pray take these and eat them.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 35 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她問那陌生人從何而來，陌生人說道：『從前我們常在我家裡聚會，玩各種遊戲消遣，到了晚上，一切結束之後，年輕女孩們通常留在外頭，年輕男子們便會追逐我們、向我們求愛；但我們在黑暗中始終認不出他們是誰。有一天夜裡，我很好奇想知道選中我的是哪一個，於是我在加入其他人之前，先去用煤煙塗抹了自己的雙手。等我們的遊戲結束後，我把雙手沿著他的背抹過去，然後離開他，第一個進了屋。年輕人一個接一個進來，脫下衣服，但有好一陣子我都沒看到任何痕跡。最後進來的是我哥哥，我立刻看見他那件白色外套的背上全沾滿了煤煙。我拿了一把刀，把它磨利，然後動手割下自己的兩個乳房，把它們交給他，說道：既然我的身體似乎令你歡喜，那就請拿去吃了吧。』

passages.text: 'He now began to speak indecently to me, and courted me more than ever, and while we raced about the room he caught hold of some bad moss and lit it, but I took some that was good, and also lit mine. He ran out, and I ran after him; but suddenly I felt that we were lifted up, and soared high up in the air. When we got more aloft my brother's light was extinguished, but mine remained burning, and I had become a sun. Now I am on my way higher up the skies, that I may give warmth to the orphans' — going, the teller explains, to make summer. Finally she said, 'Now close thy eyes.' The woman turned her eyes downwards; but perceiving that she was about to leave the house, she gave her one look, and observed that at her back she was a mere skeleton. Soon after she had left the house the old husband returned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 35 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『他這時開始對我說些下流話，比以往更加熱烈地追求我，我們在屋裡追逐時，他抓起一些壞苔蘚點燃了它，但我拿了一些好的，也點燃了我自己的。他跑了出去，我跟在他後面跑；但突然间我感覺我們被抬了起來，高高地升上空中。當我們升得更高時，我哥哥的光熄滅了，但我的仍舊燃燒著，而我已變成了太陽。現在我正往更高的天空去，好讓我能給孤兒們帶來溫暖』——說故事的人解釋道，她是去造夏天的。最後她說：『現在閉上你的眼睛。』那女人把眼睛朝下看；但察覺她即將離開屋子，便看了她一眼，發現她的背不過是一具骷髏。她離開屋子後不久，年老的丈夫便回來了。

title.en: Nivnitak: Strength Against Old Age
title.zh: 尼夫尼塔克：以膂力抗老

region.en: Northern hunting grounds and the foreign coast across the ice
region.zh: 北方獵場與冰海彼岸的異鄉

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Greyless among grown grandchildren, Nivnitak shames them back to the ice by hunting alone through the worst winter, following a sledge-track clean across the frozen sea to a foreign coast. Married there to two daughters of a faster hunter, he out-eats his host, out-hauls him, and — wearing a jacket of still-warm seal-entrails — wins the ball-play both ways, first knocked flat by his own wish 'I only wish I may do well,' then uncatchable. Slipping away in a glued-tight suit, he leaves a moss-stuffed decoy in a snow-hut for the pursuers to spear, and dies at last at home at a very old age, flesh shrivelled and shrunk.
summary.zh: 孫輩皆已成年而他猶無一根白髮的尼夫尼塔克，嚴冬獨自出獵，令賴床的子孫羞愧重返冰上。他循雪橇轍跡橫越冰海，抵達異鄉海岸；娶了比他更快的老獵手的兩個女兒——比食量、比拖曳、以尚帶體溫的豹腸新衣赴賽。擲球戲上他先是心願『但願我能打好』而被球擊倒，再戰則無人能敵。他縫製緊身衣夜遁，以塞苔草的假人誘敵刺殺，安然返鄉，直至壽終。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads the tale as enshrining the esteem for personal dexterity, strength, courage, and hardihood brought to bear against old age. Entrails-jacket detail documented as told.

passages.text: Nivnitak went away and settled far off to the north, at a certain place favourably situated for all kinds of hunting. He had many grandchildren, who all grew up to be skilled hunters while he was still in the prime of life; but none of them ever came to be a match for him. At last they also married in their turn and begat children before Nivnitak had got one grey hair. It once happened that the winter set in very severely, with hard weather every day; when the sea was getting all covered with ice the young people gradually left off hunting, while Nivnitak was constantly on the move, alternately on land and on the frozen sea. Later on the young men did not even rise from their couches. 'To-morrow I won't go out hunting, but I intend to climb the highest mountains to have a survey of the sea' — and returning late: 'I climbed the highest, and saw the frost-smoke at different places far out at sea. No doubt there will be animals to be got there; to-morrow I shall try.' When the midnight stars shone brightest he left the house, gained the outermost islets at dawn, and for the first time observed the haze hanging above the open water; pushing a seal on before him, he entered the house: 'If we are in want of game, I have found a hole where plenty of seals, large as well as small, are to be had.' His children and grandchildren only murmured and sulked a little, then asked for a morsel of blubber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 尼夫尼塔克離去，遠赴北方定居，選了一處便於從事各種狩獵的地方。他有許多孫子，在他仍正值壯年時，他們都已長成嫻熟的獵人；但他們之中沒有一個能與他匹敵。最後他們也各自成婚，在尼夫尼塔克還沒有一根白髮之前就生下了孩子。有一次，冬天來得極為嚴酷，天天都是惡劣的天氣；當海面漸漸全被冰封住時，年輕人一個接一個停止了打獵，而尼夫尼塔克卻不停地活動，時而在陸上，時而在冰封的海上。後來，年輕男子們甚至連床榻都不起身了。『明天我不出去打獵，但我打算爬上最高的山，察看一番海面的情況』——他很晚才回來：『我爬上了最高的山，看見遠方海面上好幾處地方冒著霜煙。那裡無疑有獵物可捕；明天我要去試試。』當午夜的星辰照耀得最明亮時，他離開了屋子，黎明時分抵達最外圍的小島，第一次注意到開闊水面上方懸浮的霧氣；他推著一隻海豹在前頭，走進屋裡：『如果我們缺獵物，我找到了一個洞，那裡有許多海豹，大的小的都有。』他的子女和孫子們只是咕噥抱怨了幾句，然後要了一小塊鯨脂。

passages.text: Again off at an early hour, he returned late at night covered with sweat with a very large seal; that day the young men had risen and were sitting on the ledge with their boots on; the following night they were mending their hunting tools, and on the ensuing morning some of the ablest accompanied him — but because of their slowness he ordered them not to attack the larger seals. At the aperture he detected the marks of a sledge leading right out to sea, examined them closely, lanced a couple of seals, and dragging them along by the tug-line made for home — but finding his grandchildren, each with but one seal, too slow for him, prepared to leave them: 'Ye know your way, of course, and can go on by yourselves,' reaching home much earlier. 'If the weather stands, it is quite a treat to go out hunting; now ye may stop at home if ye like: I will take care that we do not suffer from want of food.' On the morrow he left as usual, but in the evening they expected him back in vain: Nivnitak remembered the track of the sledge, and having found it, followed it across the sea; the mountains of his own country were lost to sight, others appeared ahead, and he landed on a foreign coast at the opposite side of the ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他又在一大早出門，深夜才回來，滿身是汗，帶著一隻非常大的海豹；那一天年輕男子們已經起身，穿著靴子坐在床沿上；第二天夜裡他們在修補狩獵工具，翌日早晨，幾個最能幹的跟著他去了——但因為他們動作太慢，他吩咐他們不要去攻擊較大的海豹。在冰洞口，他發現了一道雪橇的痕跡，一直通向海面，便仔細察看，用矛刺了兩隻海豹，拖著牠們的牽繩往家走——但發現他的孫子們每人只獵得一隻海豹，對他來說太慢了，便準備丟下他們：『你們當然認得路，可以自己走回去』，自己則早得多就到家了。『如果天氣持續這樣，出去打獵真是件樂事；現在你們若願意，盡可以留在家裡：我會確保我們不致缺糧。』翌日他照常出門，但到了晚上，他們等他回來卻白等了一場：尼夫尼塔克記起了那道雪橇的痕跡，找到之後，便循著它橫越海面；他自己國家的山巒已看不見了，前方出現了別的山，他登上了大洋對岸一片陌生的海岸。

passages.text: Passing through a valley he beheld a sheet of frozen water, and close by a little house with some poles stuck in the ground beside it; a woman emerged, and perceiving a stranger approaching by such an unwonted road, stood hesitating an instant, then asked him to come inside — two young girls sitting close to the wall, whom he secretly determined should be his future wives. He felt very hungry and hoped to be offered something to eat, but was disappointed; one of the women returned crying 'Yonder he is coming!' — through the window Nivnitak saw a man running along the ice at a great rate, tugging two seals after him, disappearing among the loose ice-blocks near the beach, then reappearing bounding towards the house — stopping at seeing the outer garments of a stranger hung on the poles. Having relieved himself of his clothes, the host took a bear-skin from beneath the ledge, spreading it mid-way on the floor: 'When two men meet for the first time they always try to outdo each other; let us have a try.' Nivnitak did not hesitate a moment, undressed, sat down opposite, hooked his hand into his adversary's arms, and pulled away with all might, almost succeeding in mastering him. The host seated himself on the main ledge and inquired if the visitor had got anything to eat — 'No' — 'Why, then, make haste and treat him to your best' — the women set forth several dishes, and when the host was going to begin the dish was already empty. He looked at the two girls flensing the seal on the floor, one cleaning the entrails, the other blowing them up; before the seal-flesh was boiled the entrails had been dried, and the girls were busy making a jacket of them for their father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他穿過一道山谷，看見一片結冰的水面，近旁有一間小屋，屋旁地上插著幾根竿子；一個女人走了出來，察覺有個陌生人經由這樣不尋常的路徑走近，便猶豫了片刻，然後請他進屋——兩個年輕女孩緊靠著牆坐著，他暗自決定要讓她們成為自己未來的妻子。他覺得非常飢餓，希望能有人給他點吃的，卻失望了；其中一個女人回來喊著『他在那邊來了！』——尼夫尼塔克透過窗戶看見一個男人在冰上飛快地奔跑，身後拖著兩隻海豹，消失在海灘附近鬆散的浮冰之間，然後又出現，蹦跳著朝屋子奔來——看見竿子上掛著陌生人的外衣，便停了下來。主人脫下自己的衣服，從床沿下取出一張熊皮，鋪在地板中央：『兩個人初次見面，總要較量一番；我們來比試比試。』尼夫尼塔克毫不猶豫，脫下衣服，在對面坐下，把手鉤住對手的臂膀，使盡全力拉扯，幾乎將他制伏。主人坐到主床沿上，問訪客有沒有吃過東西——『沒有』——『那還不快把你最好的東西端出來招待他』——女人們擺出好幾道菜，而當主人正要動手時，盤子已經空了。他看著那兩個女孩在地板上處理海豹，一個清理內臟，另一個把腸子吹脹；海豹肉還沒煮好，腸子已經晾乾了，女孩們正忙著用它們為父親縫製一件外套。

passages.text: 'I am in want of a companion on my hunting excursions; we have plenty of good hunting hereabout. Away on the ice is a place where the thong-seals have their breathing-holes... If thou wantest a wife, thou art welcome to take one of my daughters' — and thus Nivnitak became his son-in-law. Next day the father put on the jacket of seal-entrails from yesterday's hunt; they wandered a great distance on the ice till they reached the apertures made by the seals — 'As thou hast not got my alacrity thou hadst better not catch more than one at a time; it is as much as I can manage to drag along two of them.' Meanwhile he soon caught a couple; Nivnitak thought he should like to do the same, and when he had caught the first and the father-in-law had turned a little aside, hastened to pull up another, and thus had two. Hauling their seals along, the host continually observed the sun, guiding himself by it — 'I suppose thou knowest thy way by this time; I think I will leave thee to follow in my wake.' 'We cannot expect him before late, but still ye must keep a look-out for him,' said the father on entering the main room; the daughters kept waiting and waiting, but he did not come home till late in the night. The father-in-law never spoke to him, but the daughters were delighted to see him and at once cut up the animals — but when they were preparing to make the dress, the entrails had shrunk and got too small: this was the reason the father made such haste in returning, that the entrails might not get cold on the way, lest they should shrink and be unfit for use. He was now displeased at having got a son-in-law not as clever as he wished him to be.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「我打獵時正缺一個伴；這附近有的是好獵場。冰上遠處有個地方，是皮帶海豹的呼吸孔所在……你若想要個妻子，歡迎你娶我其中一個女兒。」——尼夫尼塔克就這樣成了他的女婿。第二天，岳父穿上昨日獵得的海豹腸衣外套；他們在冰上走了很遠，直到抵達海豹所開的孔洞——「既然你沒有我這般敏捷，最好一次只捕一頭；我拖兩頭已是極限了。」話雖如此，他很快便捕到兩頭；尼夫尼塔克覺得自己也該照做，當他捕到第一頭、岳父稍稍轉過身去時，便急忙再拉起一頭，於是也有了兩頭。他們拖著海豹前行，主人不時觀察太陽，藉以辨認方向——「我想你到這會兒該認得路了吧；我看我就讓你跟在我的足跡後頭走。」「我們不能指望他早歸，但你們仍得留意著他。」父親進主屋時說道；女兒們等啊等，他卻直到深夜才回家。岳父一句話也不同他說，女兒們見了他卻滿心歡喜，立刻動手切割獵物——但當她們準備製作衣物時，腸子已經縮小，變得太窄了：這正是父親急著趕回的原因，為的是不讓腸子在途中變冷，免得收縮而無法使用。他如今不高興了，因為招來的女婿不如他所期望的那般能幹。

passages.text: They went out together all the same next day with a similar result; on the way home the father again told him that as he could not keep up with him he would go on beforehand — but this time Nivnitak was saying to himself, 'To-day I should just like to run a race with him.' He soon lost sight of him and lost his way besides, but at the same time felt that his burden was getting lighter; continuing to run still faster, turning round he saw that his two seals were swinging round in the air after him. He passed by his host in a great circuit and was home in good time long before him; his wife instantly prepared the meal, and seeing the blown-up entrails clean and shining, Nivnitak did not doubt they would make him a nice jacket. He let the meat be kept ready dressed for his father-in-law, and the women had the jacket finished even before his arrival; putting it on at once he was standing outside mending his tools when the host made his appearance — at first sight he thought some visitor had arrived during his absence, and not till he had passed the iceberg did he recognise Nivnitak; on finding it to be him he was very well pleased, and again spoke familiarly: 'That's right, we will always succeed in the end' — but Nivnitak did not quite understand this speech. Seated at the meal, the host said, 'Why, it has been getting quite cold and dry' — he did not quite like it so; nevertheless he was as gay and talkative as could be. They now went on having the same good luck, and Nivnitak totally forgot his home and his grandchildren, and would not leave his young wives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日他們仍一同外出，結果也相仿；回家途中，父親又對他說，既然他跟不上自己，自己便先走一步——但這一回尼夫尼塔克暗自思忖：「今天我倒真想跟他賽一賽跑。」他很快便看不見對方，還迷了路，但同時覺得自己的負擔越來越輕；他繼續跑得更快，回頭一看，只見他那兩頭海豹竟在空中隨著他擺盪。他繞了個大圈越過主人，早早回到家，比他先到許久；妻子立刻備好飯食，尼夫尼塔克見那吹脹的腸子潔淨光亮，便不懷疑它們能為他做件好外套。他讓人把肉整治妥當，留給岳父，而女人們甚至在他回來之前就把外套做好了；他立刻穿上，站在外頭修整工具，這時主人現身了——乍看之下，他以為自己不在時來了訪客，直到繞過冰山才認出是尼夫尼塔克；發覺是他之後，他十分滿意，又親切地說：「這就對了，我們終究總會成功的。」——但尼夫尼塔克並不太明白這話。用餐時，主人說：「哎呀，這東西都變得又冷又乾了。」——他並不怎麼喜歡這樣；儘管如此，他仍舊談笑風生，興致極高。此後他們一直這般好運連連，尼夫尼塔克完全忘了自己的家鄉和孫兒，再也不願離開他年輕的妻子們。

passages.text: One day his father-in-law accosted him: 'The moon is now in the crescent, and our neighbours will be coming to pay us a visit and practice ball-playing; to-morrow I shall stay at home and make tools for the games, and we must all be smart and trim in new dresses.' Next day Nivnitak likewise stayed at home, and his father-in-law brought in six large shoulder-blades of walrus: 'When the play has begun, and the ball has been thrown, we must follow its course, and always be ready to strike it; if any one throws it wrong we shan't win; so thou must mind what thou art about. With this spoon-like instrument we hit the ball; I shall throw it to my wife, and she to her daughter, and they will send it on to thee; take care that thou dost not make any mistake, or miss catching it, lest we should be mocked and scorned.' At last a great many people appeared passing round the southern point, and Nivnitak, along with his new relations, quickly put on his new clothes and ran out to meet them on the ice, shouting to them, 'Here we are with our new relative Nivnitak! Let the play begin at once!' — the strangers answered with a loud yell. The ball, consisting of a large seal-skin stuffed with sand and clay, and fashioned like a real seal, was now brought out; the master determined that Nivnitak, being the most dexterous, should stand next to the adversaries, and began the play by throwing the ball to his wife; she running along beneath it thrust it to her younger daughter, she in her turn to her elder sister, and she to her husband — but when Nivnitak was about to strike it, he thought to himself, 'I only wish I may do well.' That instant the ball hit him with its whole force and knocked him down, so that he was unable to rise; the enemies shouted and yelled in great triumph and took up the ball, carrying it towards their dwelling-place, their opponents pursuing without any result. On turning round the host saw a multitude of people and not observing Nivnitak among them suspected some evil; hurrying to his assistance he found him almost dying, some filling his clothes with snow, others actually trampling on him. He drew him from out the heap, but the enemies left with great glee and loud halloos; Nivnitak's clothes had been quite spoiled with the snow and the mud, and in this state they got home — the father-in-law sullen and cross.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，岳父對他說：「如今月亮已呈彎鉤，鄰居們要來拜訪我們，玩擊球之戲；明日我留在家中製作遊戲用的器具，我們大家都得打扮得整齊漂亮，換上新衣。」翌日尼夫尼塔克也留在家中，岳父拿進六片巨大的海象肩胛骨：「遊戲開始、球擲出之後，我們必須跟著球的去向，隨時準備擊球；若有人擲偏了，我們就贏不了；所以你務必留心自己在做什麼。我們用這像湯匙的器具擊球；我把球擲給我妻子，她再擲給她的女兒，她們再傳給你；小心別出錯，也別漏接，免得我們遭人譏笑輕蔑。」終於，許多人繞過南邊的海角出現了，尼夫尼塔克與他的新親屬們迅速換上新衣，跑到冰上迎接他們，向他們喊道：「我們在這兒，帶著我們的新親戚尼夫尼塔克！讓遊戲立刻開始吧！」——陌生人以一聲高呼回應。那球是用一大張海豹皮填塞沙土做成，形狀仿如真海豹，這時被取了出來；主人決定讓最靈巧的尼夫尼塔克站在對手旁邊，並由他把球擲給妻子，開始了遊戲；她跑在球下方，把球推給年幼的女兒，她再傳給姊姊，姊姊又傳給丈夫——但當尼夫尼塔克正要擊球時，他暗自心想：「但願我能表現得好。」那一瞬間，球以全力擊中他，把他打倒在地，使他無法起身；敵方得意洋洋地又叫又嚷，拾起球往他們的住處帶去，對手們追趕卻毫無結果。主人回頭一看，見人群眾多，卻不見尼夫尼塔克在其中，便疑心出了什麼壞事；他急忙趕去相助，發現他幾乎死去，有人往他衣服裡塞雪，有人甚至踩踏他。他把他從人堆裡拉了出來，但敵人歡天喜地、高聲呼喝著離去；尼夫尼塔克的衣服已被雪和泥弄得不成樣子，他們就這樣回了家——岳父陰沉惱怒。

passages.text: 'It will soon be time for us to pay our neighbours a return visit; get everything ready' — on departing Nivnitak looked very nice in his new suit, but the father-in-law once more admonished him: 'We must do our utmost to vanquish them, and if thou doest wrong this time, we will have nothing more to do with thee' — Nivnitak did not deign to answer. Approaching the abode of the neighbours, a tumultuous roar was raised to welcome them, the ball brought down on the ice, and they posted themselves as before. When it was Nivnitak's turn to strike, he gave the ball such a blow that it turned round in the air and then flew straight forward; the father-in-law's turn to run for it, but Nivnitak had already reached it and hit it a second time; the adversaries advanced to give it a stroke, but Nivnitak always forestalled them, sending it higher and higher aloft — nobody could cope with him, and thus he went on pursuing the ball until he at length reached home. Their rivals had at last to give in and retired very much dejected, and Nivnitak's host cried out to them, 'To-day ye lost the game, better luck next time!' On the way home he kept constantly repeating, 'That's right, we will always succeed in the end' — it was only now that Nivnitak understood what the other had meant by saying so before. Some time after, Nivnitak began to think of his old relatives whom he had left in poverty and want; one day returning from his hunt he said to his wives, 'Make me a suit of tight clothes, jacket, breeches, and boots' — they fitted him as if they had been glued on to his body, and where they were a little too wide he at once had them altered; he made the suit into a bundle and went to hide it beneath the boat, and from this time secretly planned to return to his own country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「很快就輪到我們回訪鄰居了；把一切都準備好。」——出發時，尼夫尼塔克穿著新衣顯得十分俊俏，但岳父又一次告誡他：「我們必須竭盡全力擊敗他們，這回你若出了差錯，我們就再也不與你相干。」——尼夫尼塔克不屑回答。接近鄰人的住處時，一陣喧騰的吼聲響起，歡迎他們到來，球被帶到冰上，他們又如先前那般各就各位。輪到尼夫尼塔克擊球時，他奮力一擊，球在空中打了個轉，隨即筆直飛去；輪到岳父去追球，但尼夫尼塔克早已趕到，又擊了第二下；對手們上前要擊球，尼夫尼塔克卻總是搶先一步，把球越送越高——無人能與他匹敵，他就這樣一路追著球，直到最後回到了家。他們的對手終於不得不認輸，十分沮喪地退去，尼夫尼塔克的主人向他們喊道：「今天你們輸了這一局，下次好運！」回家途中，他不住地重複：「這就對了，我們終究總會成功的。」——直到這時，尼夫尼塔克才明白對方先前說這話是什麼意思。過了些時日，尼夫尼塔克開始想起被他留在貧困匱乏中的舊親人；有一天打獵歸來，他對妻子們說：「替我縫一套緊身的衣服，外套、褲子和靴子。」——她們替他做得貼身，彷彿黏在他身上一般，凡稍嫌寬鬆之處，他立刻叫人改過；他把這套衣服打成一個包裹，拿去藏在船底下，從此暗中盤算著要回到自己的家鄉。

passages.text: One night, when the others were sound asleep, he tried to leap down on the floor; but on touching the edge of the bench one of his wives awoke, and he again went back and quietly lay down beside them — for several nights he repeated his attempts, always obliged to turn in again. One night he succeeded in getting down without anybody awaking; to make quite sure they were all fast asleep he again stepped up on the ledge, and finding the noise had awakened nobody, jumped down on the floor above the entrance of the room and gliding out noiselessly dressed himself in his tight clothes, then in his outer coat hanging on the poles outside. Taking hold of his spear he climbed the low roof of the house and sallied forth in the opposite direction he wanted to take, making circular tracks in the snow; after a while he jumped and crossed the little promontory, got down on the ice which stretched away as far as his own country, again making large round tracks, always leaping from one side to the other so that his family should not be able to be guided by his footmarks. Reaching a coast with a steep ascent covered with heath, he once more formed plenty of round circles on the ice, jumped ashore, climbed an edge of the rock, stuffed his outer coat well with moss, and again leaped down; on the ice he built a snow-hut and placed the stuffed coat inside it, spear in hand, with the back turned outwards, that it might resemble a living man. After this he again went back and climbed the steep rock, awaiting the arrival of the pursuers. At sunrise several people who had come out in search of him were to be seen on the ice, sometimes single, sometimes making joint efforts to find the track; at last, halting at the snow-house, they approached it cautiously — no sooner had the foremost detected the figure in the doorway than he thrust his spear straight at it, and Nivnitak heard them call out, 'Well, well, we ought to have kept a better watch upon him while he was with us, showing well enough that he was not a real man; but anyhow we have done with him now' — and they returned, satisfied that they had killed him. When they had quite disappeared, Nivnitak again leapt down the rocks. The sun was then high in the heavens; but before it had quite set he reached the shore of his own country and found his grandchildren, who had totally given him up, prospering and doing well. In the spring-time, when the ice had vanished, he got a fancy to go and see his native place; but having arrived there he determined to spend the rest of his days in this place, and did not travel any more. He lived to see his grandchildren's grandchildren, but at length the flesh of his body became all shrivelled and shrunk; and finally, at a very old age, he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天夜裡，趁其他人都熟睡時，他試著跳到地板上；但一碰到床沿，他的一個妻子便醒了，他只好又回去，悄悄在她們身旁躺下——一連幾夜他都重複嘗試，卻總是被迫再躺回去。有一夜，他總算在無人驚醒的情況下跳了下來；為確保她們全都熟睡，他又踏上床沿，發覺聲響並未驚醒任何人，便跳到門廊上方的地板上，無聲無息地溜出去，穿上他那套緊身衣，再穿上掛在外頭木桿上的外袍。他拿起長矛，爬上屋子的低矮屋頂，朝與他想去的方向相反之處出發，在雪地上繞出圓形的足跡；過了一會兒，他縱身躍過那小海角，落到向著自己家鄉延伸的冰面上，又繞出大大的圓圈，總是從一邊跳到另一邊，好讓家人無法循著他的足跡追蹤。他來到一處長滿石南、坡勢陡峭的海岸，又在冰上繞出許多圓圈，跳上岸，攀上一處岩緣，用苔蘚把外袍塞得鼓鼓的，再跳下去；他在冰上築了一座雪屋，把塞滿的外袍放在裡頭，手持長矛，背朝外，好讓它像個活人。之後他又折返，攀上陡峭的岩石，等待追兵到來。日出時分，冰上出現了幾個出來搜尋他的人，時而分散，時而合力尋找足跡；最後，他們在雪屋前停下，小心翼翼地靠近——最前頭的人一發覺門口的人影，便舉矛直刺過去，尼夫尼塔克聽見他們喊道：「唉，唉，他在我們這裡時，我們就該把他看緊些，他分明顯出不是個真人；不過無論如何，我們如今總算擺脫他了。」——他們便回去了，確信已將他殺死。等他們完全消失後，尼夫尼塔克又從岩石上跳下來。那時太陽高懸天上；但還沒等它完全落下，他已抵達自己家鄉的海岸，找到他那早已對他絕望的孫兒們，他們過得興旺順遂。春天冰消之後，他起了念頭想去看看自己的故鄉；但到了那裡之後，他決定在此地度過餘生，不再遠行。他活著見到了孫兒們的孫兒，但到最後，他身上的肉全都乾癟皺縮；終於，在極其高齡之時，他死去了。

title.en: The Brother Who Went to Akilinek: Invention of the Dog-Sledge
title.zh: 遠赴阿基利內克的兄長：狗橇的發明

region.en: Frozen sea crossing and Akilinek, the country beyond
region.zh: 冰海橫渡與彼岸的阿基利內克

period: Inuit oral tradition; nearly literally translated from one manuscript, widely known in Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: His sister vanished from the islets, leaving only a sledge-track leading seaward, the matchless hunter brings home — one by one, to his little sister's horror — a bear, an amarok, and an agshik to draw the sledge his father makes of hard knotted wood; rounding the coast at a day's drive that would take a boat from spring to autumn. Trusting the unbroken ice, he drives straight across the sea to Akilinek, finds his sister married with a baby, matches teams with her reindeer-driving husband, and carries home the children's clothes as a promise — fulfilled when the sledges come, the merry little sister leaps the boat-stands and frightens the visitors off, and the furious agshik, loosed in punishment, returns bloody-muzzled, having probably devoured them all.
summary.zh: 妹妹在外島失蹤，冰上只餘一道指向海中的雪橇轍跡。無敵的獵手先後領回——令幼妹驚呼的——一頭熊、一頭狼靈、一隻阿格希克怪獸，拉動父親特製的硬木雪橇；沿岸疾馳，一日之程抵舟行春至秋之遙。他賭冰未裂，直駛海心抵達阿基利內克，尋得已為人母的妹妹；與其馴鹿橇夫比試獸力，又攜外甥的衣物作為歸約。雪橇如約而至，活潑的小妹歡躍過船架，卻嚇得客人掉頭而逃；盛怒的阿格希克被放去追擊，歸來時嘴邊血污——多半把他們全數吞了。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads the tale as probably resting on a historical basis: the invention of dog-sledging or the teaming and training of some wild animal from which the Eskimo dog descended. Rink's note records a kukissook variant in which the cousin-version ends with the Akilinek brother-in-law torn to pieces and the child killed. The devouring ending recorded as told.

passages.text: An old man had a son and two daughters; his son being a first-rate hunter and provider, the father at length gave up kayaking himself. His son could overtake and outrun every animal on shore, and at sea was an excellent hand at harpooning; his eldest sister used to follow him along the shore, amusing herself by catching partridges in little traps, and generally got a good many. At a time when the sea was frozen over, they one day went away to the outermost islets; there the brother saw a fox and set off to pursue it. After a short absence among the islets he returned with the fox — but meanwhile the sister was gone. He looked for her everywhere and called out, but she did not come; at length he detected the trace of a sledge, but as it was growing dark, he had to go home without his sister. On his return he grew silent and reserved, but after a while said to his father, 'Oh how much I should like to have a sledge!' The father favoured the idea and at once set about making him one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個老人，有一兒兩女；他兒子是頭等的獵手和養家之人，父親後來便不再自己划獨木舟了。他兒子在陸上能追上並跑贏任何野獸，在海上則是極擅長用魚叉的好手；他的大姊常沿著海岸跟著他，以在小陷阱裡捕捉雷鳥為樂，往往收穫不少。有一回海面結了冰，他們某天一同前往最外圍的小島；在那裡，弟弟看見一隻狐狸，便動身去追。他在小島間離開不久，便帶著狐狸回來——但這段期間，姊姊卻不見了。他四處尋找、呼喊，她卻沒有來；最後他發現了一道雪橇的痕跡，但天色漸暗，他只得沒帶姊姊先回家。回來之後，他變得沉默寡言，但過了一陣子，他對父親說：「唉，我多麼想要一輛雪橇啊！」父親贊同這個主意，立刻動手替他做了一輛。

passages.text: Next morning the son set out on foot, returned at nightfall without having killed anything, and went to sleep without a word. In the morning he asked his father to provide him with some cords, saying he wanted to fetch home an animal to pull his sledge for him, and went off. Towards evening a strange noise was heard, and the little sister went outside to see what it was, but instantly returned in great alarm, exclaiming, 'Oh, what dreadful monster is this my dear brother has brought home with him?' When he entered, the father asked him what beast it was — 'Why, it is only a little bear I have caught to drag my sledge; I hope thou wilt make a harness for it; I want him to be trained shortly.' The father complied, and the son left off hunting for a while in order to train the bear. Another time he again returned late in the evening quite exhausted; the following morning he asked his father for still stronger cords, went away, and in the evening a strange noise was again heard, the little sister returning quite horrified, saying it was still more frightful than the last time — 'Oh, it's nothing but a little amarok I have caught to match the bear.' These two, however, could not agree, and he had often to use his whip to part them when they were going to fight; after training they pulled very well together. He wanted a third one, and having set out for it in the morning did not return till late at night, when his parents had long been quite miserable on account of his long absence; the next morning he applied for strings and lashings, but this time none but the very strongest would serve him. In the evening there was a terrible noise outside, for now he had got the bear, the amarok, and an agshik fighting each other; at length he had them all tamed and trained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日清晨，兒子徒步出發，直到夜幕低垂才歸來，一無所獲，一言不發便睡下了。早晨，他請父親給他一些繩索，說他想帶一頭野獸回家替他拉雪橇，隨後便動身離去。近黃昏時，傳來一陣奇怪的聲響，小妹妹走到外頭去看個究竟，卻立刻驚慌失措地奔回屋內，喊道：「哎呀，我親愛的哥哥帶回家來的這是什麼可怕的怪物啊？」他進屋時，父親問他是什麼野獸——「唉，不過是我捉來拉雪橇的一頭小熊罷了；希望您能給牠做一副挽具；我想不久就訓練牠。」父親照辦了，兒子便暫時停止打獵，專心訓練那頭熊。又一次，他直到深夜才歸來，疲憊不堪；翌日早晨，他請父親給他更結實的繩索，便離去了，到了傍晚又傳來一陣奇怪的聲響，小妹妹回來時驚恐萬分，說這次比上次還要可怕得多——「哎呀，不過是我捉來與那頭熊配對的一頭小阿瑪洛克（amarok）罷了。」然而這兩頭卻合不來，每當牠們要打鬥時，他往往得用鞭子把牠們分開；經過訓練之後，牠們拉起來配合得極好。他想要第三頭，早晨出發去尋，直到深夜才歸來，他的父母因他久久未歸早已十分憂愁；翌日早晨，他索取繩索與皮帶，但這一次非得最結實的才合用。傍晚時分，外頭傳來可怕的聲響，因為這回他讓熊、阿瑪洛克與一頭阿格希克（agshik）互相打了起來；最後他總算把牠們全都馴服並訓練好了。

passages.text: His father, quite willing, made him a sledge of very hard wood with many knots in it; when the sea was frozen over he went out to try his team, following the coast southwards, and returned towards evening the same day. Questioned as to how far he had been, he answered: 'If thou wert to leave with a boat early in spring, thou wouldst not have reached the place I got at to-day before autumn. In going home we made great speed, but the bear got tired, and I was obliged to take him into the sledge beside me; but the agshik is incapable of tiring, and will be of great use to me.' The next day he travelled on in the same manner to the north, returning home at night, adding, 'The agshik, I find, is soon provoked, and goes off in a fury; he will be rather dangerous for strangers to encounter.' The ice now covering the sea all over, not having broken up although it had been very stormy, he supposed he might trust himself out on it; and the weather again became settled and beautiful. 'Don't ye remember the day I wandered out on the ice with my sister and lost her there? Since that day I have sought her far and near all over our country: where can she have gone to? Not even the bones of her corpse did I find; but on the day I lost her, in looking for her, I noticed the marks of a sledge on the ice, leading right to sea. Any other trace of her I have never seen; and therefore I should now like to go across to Akilinek, as I shall certainly not be at rest until I have found her.' The parents tried to persuade him to stay — 'It does not matter for thy sister, who has been lost to us for such a great length of time; don't go away in search of her as far away as that, but bear in mind thou art now our only provider. Out yonder is a cleft in the ice so wide that thou mayst never cross it' — 'To be sure my animals cannot swim; the bear only in some degree is capable of that: but if I don't succeed, I shall, of course, return.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他父親十分樂意，為他造了一架用多節的堅硬木材製成的雪橇；海面結冰之後，他便出去試他的牲隊，沿著海岸向南而行，當天傍晚便回來了。有人問他走了多遠，他答道：「倘若你開春時節乘船出發，到了秋天也到不了我今日所到之處。回家時我們走得極快，但那頭熊累了，我只好把牠抱上雪橇，放在我身旁；不過那頭阿格希克是不會累的，對我大有用處。」翌日，他又以同樣的方式向北行去，夜裡回家，又補了一句：「我發覺那頭阿格希克很容易被激怒，一發怒便狂奔而去；陌生人遇上牠，恐怕相當危險。」如今海面全被冰封，雖曾風暴大作，冰卻未曾裂開，他心想或許可以放心到冰上去；天氣又變得平靜而美好。「你們還記得我與妹妹在冰上漫遊、卻在那裡失去她的那一天嗎？自那日起，我走遍我們這片土地，遠近各處尋她：她究竟去了何處呢？我連她屍骨的骨頭都沒找到；但在我失去她的那一天，我尋她時，曾注意到冰上有一架雪橇的痕跡，筆直通向海上。除此之外，我再沒見過她任何蹤跡；因此我如今想渡海到阿基利內克（Akilinek）去，因為在找到她之前，我定然無法安心。」父母試圖勸他留下——「你妹妹的事倒不打緊，她已失蹤這麼長久了；別為了尋她跑到那麼遠的地方去，要記得你如今是我們唯一的供養者。那邊有一道冰裂縫寬得你或許永遠過不去」——「我的牲口當然不會游泳；那頭熊多少還能游一點：但倘若我不成功，我自然會回來的。」

passages.text: At the exact spot where he had formerly seen the trace of a sledge he turned right seawards, and after a while lost sight of the land; the bear got tired as before, and being only a hindrance, he took it on the sledge. Driving continually straight on, he again came in sight of land and observed the tracks of many sledges, seeing them in all directions on approaching the shore. Making fast his animals to an iceberg near the strand, he went to shore himself, and had not walked long before he saw a number of houses; after a while he advanced, found an entrance, walked up to a large house and went inside — and at once recognised his sister sitting down with a baby on her lap. Seating himself on the side bench, she also recognised him, and they began to speak to each other: 'On the same day thou left me to pursue thy fox, a man in a sledge happened to pass by; and in no time I was taken up and carried away to this place, and that is the reason why thou seest me here. I am married, but at present my husband is out as usual. However, I expect him home very soon, and when he comes thou must look at him well.' 'Since that day I have done nothing but try to find thee out; all over the country I have travelled in search of thee; how lucky it is that I find thee at last!' Whilst they sat waiting some one called out, 'There he is coming!' — looking out at the window the brother saw his sister's husband driving on towards the house with a number of young reindeer pulling his sledge; though he sped on at a good rate, the other thought his own animals still swifter, and considering himself quite a match for the new-comer, again seated himself without any further remark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在他從前見過雪橇痕跡的那個確切地點，他轉向正對海面，過了一會兒便看不見陸地了；那頭熊一如先前般疲倦，只成了累贅，他便把牠抱上雪橇。他一路筆直向前奔馳，又望見了陸地，並觀察到許多雪橇的痕跡，接近岸邊時，只見四面八方都是。他把牲口拴在灘邊的一座冰山上，自己上了岸，沒走多遠便看見許多房屋；過了一會兒，他走上前去，找到一個入口，走到一座大屋前便走了進去——立刻認出他妹妹正坐在那裡，膝上抱著一個嬰兒。他在側邊的長凳上坐下，她也認出了他，兩人便交談起來：「就在你離開我去追你的狐狸的那一天，恰好有一個乘雪橇的男人經過；轉眼之間我便被帶走，給帶到這個地方來，這就是你在此見著我的緣故。我已婚配，但眼下我丈夫一如往常出門去了。不過我料他很快就會回家，他回來時你可得好好瞧瞧他。」「自那日起，我什麼都不做，只一心尋你；我走遍全國各地尋你；如今終於找到你，真是何等幸運！」他們坐著等候時，有人喊道：「他回來了！」——哥哥從窗戶望出去，只見妹妹的丈夫趕著一群年輕的馴鹿拉著他的雪橇朝屋子駛來；雖說他奔得極快，哥哥卻覺得自己的牲口還要更快，自忖足以與這新來者匹敵，便又一言不發地坐了下來。

passages.text: When the husband entered he kept his eyes constantly fixed on the visitor sitting beside his wife, and without a word to any one leaned back on the ledge, so that nothing but his heels resting on the edge of it were visible. The relatives being thus interrupted left off speaking for a time; however, she told her brother it was for fear of her husband, who used to speak very little, being of a shy disposition; on hearing this he came a little closer to them, and they began to converse together. The guest spoke of his happiness in seeing his sister so well off, and said that seeing she had such a good provider he would not trouble himself any more about her in future, further proposing that they should come and visit him and his parents on the opposite shore — but his brother-in-law did not fancy this much, giving as a pretext that the cold would be too severe for the children. Both now wanted to persuade him to stay, but he said he must needs go and look after his animals, without mention of what kind they were; his relatives gave him some of the children's clothes for a gift to the parents — he put them on his shoulders, went to his sledge, and departed. When he had got so far that he had lost sight of the land the bear again got tired, and was taken in beside him; on his return his parents rejoiced greatly at seeing the clothes of their daughter's little children, and on hearing that their long-missed daughter was coming to visit them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 丈夫進屋後，目光始終緊盯著坐在他妻子身旁的訪客，也不對任何人說一句話，便仰身靠在壁台上，只露出兩隻腳跟擱在台沿。親屬們就這樣被打斷，一時停止了交談；不過，她告訴哥哥，這是因為她丈夫向來寡言少語，生性羞怯；他聽了這話，便稍稍向他們靠近了些，他們便開始交談起來。客人說他很欣慰見到妹妹過得這般好，又說既然她有這樣好的供養者，他今後便不再為她操心了，還提議他們不妨到對岸來探望他和他的父母——但他妹夫卻不大中意這個主意，託辭說天寒地凍，對孩子們來說太過嚴酷。這會兒兩人都想勸他留下，但他說他非得回去照看他的牲口不可，卻沒提是什麼牲口；他的親屬給了他一些孩子們的衣物，作為送給父母的禮物——他把衣物搭在肩上，走到雪橇旁，便離去了。當他走得遠到看不見陸地時，那頭熊又累了，便被抱上雪橇，坐在他身旁；他歸來時，父母見到他們女兒幼小子女的衣物，又聽說他們久盼的女兒要來探望他們，都大喜過望。

passages.text: One day during fine weather, when they were anxiously expecting them, sledges were seen coming across the ice, which made them all very happy, the little sister, of a merry temper, hardly able to contain her joy. When her sister's sledge had come still closer she gave a jump and bounded over the boat, which was put up on the boat-pillars — but all of a sudden the sledgers were seen to put about, probably taking fright at seeing her brother's animals and at the girl indulging in such wild pranks. They now called out loudly for them, and the parents were very much distressed and wept together. This sight made the son take pity on the old people, and to punish the fugitives he let loose the agshik, being the most furious of the lot, to pursue them. In a moment the sledgers as well as the agshik disappeared; but on his return the agshik was all bloody around the muzzle. In all likelihood he devoured them all; the brother did not go in search of them, as he did not expect any of them to be alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某日天氣晴好，他們正焦急地盼著，忽見雪橇從冰上駛來，這讓大家都很歡喜，那小妹妹生性快活，幾乎按捺不住滿心的喜悅。當她姐姐的雪橇駛得更近時，她縱身一跳，躍過了架在船柱上的那條船——可是忽然間，只見那些乘雪橇的人掉頭折返，大概是見到她哥哥的牲口，又見那姑娘這般撒野胡鬧，給嚇著了。他們於是高聲呼喚他們，父母十分悲痛，一同哭泣起來。這情景讓兒子對兩位老人起了憐憫之心，為了懲罰那些逃走的人，他便放開那頭最為兇猛的阿格希克去追他們。轉眼之間，那些乘雪橇的人連同那頭阿格希克都不見了；但阿格希克回來時，口鼻周圍盡是血跡。十之八九牠把他們全都吞吃了；哥哥並沒有去尋找他們，因為他不指望他們之中還有誰活著。

title.en: Ussungussak or Savnimersok: The Inlander's Seal-Trap
title.zh: 烏蘇恩瓜舒克：內陸人的捕豹陷阱

region.en: Gulf of the earth and the inland meadow
region.zh: 大地之灣與內陸草甸

period: Inuit oral tradition; two of the older manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Scolded empty-handed once too often, Ussungussak follows a beach-stranger inland through the fearful precipice of the earth's gulf — nearly choked by a cord round his neck — to an inlander's comfortable house, whose shore-standing trap kills seals on the beach. Given leave to take one at a time, then two, greed carries him past the last of the lot; refused a return when he comes empty again, he is fairly strangled at the precipice — and the kayaker sent to find him avenges him with harpoon, bladder, and arrow, putting a knee on the nape of the giant he has cut up.
summary.zh: 又一次空手而歸、被妻子痛罵的烏蘇恩瓜舒克，跟隨岸邊的陌生人走進內陸——穿越大地之灣的可怕絕壁，頸上繩索勒得他幾乎斃命——抵達內陸人舒適的家。那內陸人立於岸上以陷阱獵豹，沙灘上堆滿死豹。許他一次取一、再取兩頭；貪心令他把最後一頭也搬空。空手再來時，他在絕壁處被活活勒死；出海尋找他的皮艇客以魚叉、浮囊、箭連環報仇，踩著已肢解的巨人後頸。

sensitivity.note: Rink gives the tale for its apparent mythological reference, noting it is otherwise fragmentary and obscure. The earth's gulf precipice is an otherworld threshold motif.

passages.text: A number of people once lived together in a large house; among them was a man named Ussungussak, who generally came home empty-handed when all the others returned with what they had caught, for which his wife used to scold him. One night she had gone on rating him worse than usual, and in the morning he had disappeared. He kayaked along shore, and having rounded a point saw a man standing on the beach; at first he was frightened, but then he thought a little and finally concluded, 'Why should I be afraid at the very moment I have resolved to go and lead a solitary life all by myself?' When the man on shore called him, he alternately approached and again turned back; but when he had come pretty close to the beach, the other threw out a trap, by which he drew him in, and ordered him to follow to the inland. They wandered along together and came to the gulf of the earth; there poor Ussungussak began to whine and howl, but the inlander put a cord round his neck, straining it so hard that he was nearly choked — when he again untied him, however, they had safely passed the fearful precipice. Having next crossed a beautiful meadow, they gained the house of the inlander, who had a wife but no children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一群人同住在一座大屋裡；其中有個名叫烏松古薩克（Ussungussak）的人，別人歸來時都帶著獵獲之物，他卻往往空手而回，為此他妻子常責罵他。有一天夜裡，她比往常罵得更兇，到了早晨他便不見了。他划著皮艇沿岸而行，繞過一個岬角後，看見岸邊站著一個人；起初他很害怕，但轉念一想，最後斷定：「我既然已決心獨自一人去過離群索居的生活，又何必害怕呢？」岸上那人喚他時，他一會兒靠近，一會兒又折返；但當他靠得離岸相當近時，那人拋出一具陷阱，把他拉了過去，命他跟著往內陸去。他們一同漫遊，來到了大地的深谷；在那裡，可憐的烏松古薩克開始哀號嚎叫，但那內陸人把一根繩索套在他脖子上，勒得他幾乎窒息——然而當他再解開繩索時，他們已安然渡過了那可怕的懸崖。接著他們又穿過一片美麗的草地，來到了那內陸人的家；他有妻子，卻沒有孩子。

passages.text: In the morning Ussungussak was ordered to remain at home, while the master of the house went away himself and returned very noisily in the evening with what he had taken; in this way several days went by, but at length Ussungussak got desirous to see his own home, and the inlander accompanied him on the way. This time they did not see the precipice; arriving at the coast they saw a great many killed seals on the beach, being those which the inlander, standing on shore, had caught in his trap. When Ussungussak was about to take leave, the inlander said, 'Henceforth thou canst take some of these seals, but mind, thou art not to be too greedy: thou mayst take one at a time to begin with; afterwards thou mayst take two.' He returned to his homestead and housemates, who were having good hunting at the time; the next day he again disappeared, but in the evening returned with two seals; the following day he brought home three — 'Out at the most seaward place,' he answered, when asked where he had got them, and they demanded whether they might not accompany him thither.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 早晨，烏松古薩克奉命留在家中，而屋主則獨自外出，傍晚時分帶著獵獲物、喧鬧異常地歸來；如此過了數日，烏松古薩克終於起了想看看自己家的念頭，那內陸人便陪他上路。這回他們沒見到那懸崖；抵達海岸時，他們看見灘上躺著許多被殺死的海豹，正是那內陸人站在岸上、以他的陷阱所捕獲的。烏松古薩克正要告別，內陸人說道：「從今以後，你可以取些這樣的海豹，但切記，不可太過貪心：起初你一次可取一隻；之後可取兩隻。」他回到自己的家園與同屋之人身邊，他們當時正獵運亨通；翌日他又不見了，但傍晚帶著兩隻海豹歸來；再一日他帶回三隻——「在最靠海的那一處，」當被問及從何處得來時他答道，而他們又問能否隨他同去那兒。

passages.text: But when he had carried away the very last of the lot, he one night returned without anything at all, and was again scolded by his wife. The day after he left as before, kayaking along shore he at length turned a point and again beheld the inlander; this time he willingly approached him when he was called and went along with him — but when they had gained the precipice, he did not get over this time, but was fairly strangled. When Ussungussak's relations and housemates had been expecting him in vain for five days, one of the kayakers went out in search of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但當他把那一批的最後一隻也搬走之後，有一夜他竟空手而歸，又遭妻子責罵。次日他照舊出門，沿岸划著皮艇，終於繞過一處岬角，又見到了那內陸人；這回他被呼喚時便欣然上前，隨他同行——但當他們來到那懸崖時，他這次沒能越過，而是著實被勒死了。烏松古薩克的親屬與同屋之人徒然等了他五日，其中一名划皮艇者便出海尋他。

passages.text: He encountered the inlander, and asked him whether he had not seen a man — 'To be sure I have, and I killed him myself!' At this the other thrust his harpoon at him, and he ran on with the hunting-bladder dragging behind him, and thus disappeared; the coastman now took his spear and bladder-arrow, following him swiftly, and found him drawing out the point — he lanced another spear at him, while the inlander kept running on so fast that the bladder flew up high in the air; finally he flung his arrow at him, and this at last did for him, and he expired, upon which the pursuer cut him up, and put his knee on the nape of his neck.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 38 'Ussungussak or Savnimersok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他遇見了那內陸人，問他可曾見到一個人——「當然見到了，而且是我親手殺的！」聽罷，那人便以魚叉刺他，他卻拖著身後的獵囊奔逃而去，就此消失；那海岸人於是取了他的矛與囊箭，疾速追趕，見他正把矛頭拔出——他又擲出一矛，而那內陸人只管飛奔，快得囊袋都高高飛起；最後他擲出箭，這一擊終於結果了他，他便斷了氣，追者於是將他肢解，並把膝蓋壓在他後頸上。

title.en: The Child-Monster with Great Big Teeth
title.zh: 巨齒嬰怪

region.en: Great rock and provision-house, inland country
region.zh: 巨巖與糧倉之間的內陸

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Born with great big teeth that tear the midwife's arm, the monster drags its own mother by the loose hair and devours the whole settlement — eating away the boat-pillars, ordering the refuge-rock itself to upset. Two boys and their sister escape to the provision-house, flee houses where the sleepers plot to kill them, spell one house-door dead with the brother's boot, and are saved by a giant reindeer-carrier — until the younger brother is torn asunder by the great serdlernak bird whose pouch is full of seal-bones. The sister kills it with her boot, singles out the bones, and carries them home moving in her hand until the brother revives, seemingly quite unhurt.
summary.zh: 嬰兒一落地便露出巨齒，咬傷接生婆的手臂；怪物拖著披頭散髮的生母，吃盡全村——啃斷船柱使避難者跌落，又令避難巨巖翻覆。兩兄弟與妹妹逃入糧倉，連夜逃過謀害他們的屋舍，以兄長的靴子加咒封死一戶之門；最後借宿半鹿在肩的巨人——幼弟卻被捕豹的巨鳥賽德勒納克撕裂。妹妹以靴擊殺巨鳥，從其滿貯豹骨的嗉囊中揀出兄弟的骨頭，攜行途中骨已蠕動——一到家，兄弟便復原如初。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note: such monsters generally figure as revengers of atrocity — in one version the imbecile child Tungavik devours all its housemates except two orphans who showed kindness. Graphic devouring recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Amongst a number of people who lived in the same house, one woman was in the act of childbirth when all of a sudden the midwife attending her cried out in great dismay, 'Ah, it is a monster, with great big teeth; it is tearing my arm!' As she spoke, all the inmates fled away to the boat, which was turned keel upwards, and to the top of a great rock; only two boys with their sister could find no room there, and they therefore hurried out to the provision-house. Meantime the monster appeared, dragging along his own mother, her hair all loose and flying about her, and it soon turned upon those on the boat: not being able itself to climb, it ate away the pillars beneath, so that, when they gave way, all the people came tumbling down and were devoured. It next came to the rock, and those who had taken refuge on it pushed and knocked against each other for horror, till all but one lost their footing and came down heads over heels; the monster now ordered the rock to upset, and the very last of them was made away with.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一群同住一屋的人當中，有一名婦人正在分娩，忽然間，照料她的產婆驚恐萬分地叫道：「哎呀，是個怪物，長著好大的牙齒；它正在撕扯我的手臂！」她話音剛落，屋裡所有人便逃向那艘底朝上翻扣的船，以及一塊巨岩之頂；只有兩個男孩和他們的妹妹在那兒找不到容身之處，於是急忙奔往儲糧屋。其間那怪物現了身，拖著自己的母親，她的頭髮全散開、四下飄飛，它隨即撲向船上那些人：它自己爬不上去，便啃斷底下的支柱，支柱一塌，所有人便紛紛跌落，被它吞食。接著它來到岩石前，那些在石上避難的人驚駭之下互相推擠碰撞，直到除一人外全都失足，頭朝下栽落；怪物於是命岩石翻覆，最後一人也被結果了。

passages.text: When these were all killed, the beast turned against the provision-house, but stopping, entered the main house instead; this process was repeated several times, and it always remained inside a little longer each time. During the last interval the children fled out of sight, and went far into the country until they came in sight of a house; they went in and told their story and the cause of their flight, and stayed there for the night. Most of the inmates had gone to sleep; the sister, however, did not dare to do so, and kept awake. At midnight she heard some one saying, 'They have probably themselves put their housemates to death, though they tell us a different story. The safest thing will be to have them killed in the morning.' At this speech she got greatly alarmed, and when the others had gone off to sleep she roused her brothers, and once more they fled on and reached another house, where they met the very same fate. But when they made their escape from this place the second night, the sister took one of her brother's boots and thrust it several times against the house-door, at the same time pronouncing a spell, that the people within might all perish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 待這些人都被殺盡，那野獸便轉向儲糧屋，卻又停下，改而進了正屋；這般情形重複了好幾回，而它每次在屋內停留的時間都稍長一些。趁著最後那段間隙，孩子們逃得不見蹤影，一路遠走進鄉野，直到望見一戶人家；他們走進去，訴說了自己的遭遇與逃亡的緣由，並在那兒過夜。屋裡大多數人都已入睡；那妹妹卻不敢睡，一直醒著。午夜時分，她聽見有人說道：「他們多半是自己把同屋之人害死了，卻對我們編出另一套說辭。最穩妥的辦法，是明早把他們殺了。」聽了這番話，她大為驚恐，待其他人睡去後，她喚醒兩個哥哥，他們再度逃亡，來到另一戶人家，卻又遭遇同樣的命運。但當他們第二夜從這地方逃出時，那妹妹取了她哥哥的一隻靴子，朝屋門連連猛擊數下，同時念了一道咒，好讓屋裡的人全都喪命。

passages.text: Pursuing their way, they fell in with a man of extraordinary size, carrying one half of a reindeer on his shoulders; the sister said to the youngest brother, 'Go and try to make him understand why we have come here,' telling him how to put his words. When the boy had finished, the big man took them along to his own house, the interior nicely furnished and hung with reindeer-skins all along the walls; there they remained and made a meal upon some dry meat.
