This done, the girl said to her brothers, 'Reindeer-meat is good eating, no doubt; but what would make it eat still better?' — 'Mixing it up with some nice partridges, to be sure' — off they went, a flapping of wings presently heard, and lots of birds brought into the house. 'Partridges are very nice, sure enough; but what would make them eat still better?' — 'Mixing them up with some nice hares, to be sure!' — and so they went on with all kinds of game and fowls, until at last she said, 'Young serdlernaks are exceedingly nice, but the large ones — oh, be quick, be quick!' The huge man said, 'I never hunted that fowl without some misgivings; when she is hatching her eggs on the lee side of yonder point, and catches the seals, she is rather dangerous.' Still they all ran out to have a look at it; but seeing it perched on its rock, and sometimes rising to snatch at them, they were afraid and again retired — only the younger brother remained, and was torn asunder by it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們繼續趕路，遇見一個身形奇大的人，肩上扛著半隻馴鹿；那妹妹對最小的哥哥說：「去，想法子讓他明白我們為何來到這裡，」並教他該怎麼措辭。男孩說完之後，那大漢便領他們到自己的屋裡，屋內陳設齊整，四壁盡掛著馴鹿皮；他們就在那兒留下，吃了一頓乾肉。吃罷，那女孩對哥哥們說：「馴鹿肉固然好吃；可要怎樣才能更好吃呢？」——「當然是摻上些鮮美的松雞嘍」——他們便出去了，隨即聽得一陣振翅之聲，許多鳥兒被帶進屋裡。「松雞固然鮮美；可要怎樣才能更好吃呢？」——「當然是摻上些鮮美的野兔嘍！」——他們就這樣把各樣野味與禽鳥一一弄來，直到最後她說：「小塞德勒納克鳥極其鮮美，可那大隻的——哦，快，快！」那巨漢說道：「我獵那鳥時從沒有不心存疑慮的；當牠在那岬角的背風處孵蛋，又捕食海豹時，可是相當危險的。」他們卻仍都跑出去看牠；但見牠棲在岩石上，時而騰起向他們撲抓，眾人害怕，又退了回來——只有那最小的哥哥留著，被牠撕成了兩半。

passages.text: Then the sister shouted, 'It is now time for me to interfere,' upon which they all ran out together; she quickly pulled out her boot, struck at the bird with it, and killed it on the spot. She now cut it up, and found its pouch filled with seal-bones, among which she likewise found those of her brother; when these had all been singled out, she carried them with her. While she was yet on the way she felt them move; and when they got close to the house she put them down, and the brother quickly revived, seemingly quite unhurt, and they all of them reached home safely.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 39 'The Child-monster'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是妹妹喊道：「現在該我出手了。」說罷，他們一同奔了出去；她迅速抽出自己的靴子，拿它朝那隻鳥打去，當場將牠打死。她隨即把牠剖開，發現牠的囊袋裡裝滿了海豹骨，其中她也找到了她哥哥的骨頭；她把這些骨頭一一挑出後，便帶在身上。她還在路上時，就感覺那些骨頭在動；等他們走近屋子時，她把它們放下，哥哥立刻甦醒過來，看上去毫髮無傷，他們全都平安回到了家。

title.en: The Kivigtok: The Brother Who Would Not Come Home
title.zh: 奇維托克：不願歸家的兄長

region.en: Rock cave in an out-of-the-way place
region.zh: 僻遠之地的巖穴

period: Inuit oral tradition; an old manuscript, sample of a very popular subject, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A man's second son turns kivigtok — flees the society of mankind — and the family spends two summers searching until they find his reindeer-skin-lined rock cave, dragging home a whole deer. Given his word that he will follow on the last load down, he vanishes instead with the remaining provisions, and later terrifies the searchers by yelling from the summit of a steep and altogether inaccessible rock, how he got there they could not make out, and finding it impossible to follow him they were obliged to give him up for lost.
summary.zh: 某家的次子成了奇維托克——拋開人世遁入荒野。全家兩度放棄狩獵之夏四處尋找，終於發現他鋪著馴鹿皮的巖穴，穴中儲滿乾肉與皮張；他扛著整鹿而歸，立誓最後一趟搬運時隨家人下山——卻帶著剩下的存糧憑空消失。此後他立於絕不可攀的崖頂對尋找他的家人長嚎示威；他如何上去無人知曉，家人只得放棄，任他失踪。

sensitivity.note: Kivigtok lore (supernatural swiftness, longevity, clairvoyance) recurs across the collection; this is a sample record per Rink.

passages.text: There was once a man who had several sons; of these, the second son turned kivigtok — that is, fled the society of mankind. This happened in the winter-time; but next summer the father, as well as his other sons, went away from home in order to search for the fugitive. In this manner summer went by and winter came round, but still they had not found him. When summer was again approaching, they made all preparations for another search, this time to other places, along another firth; late in autumn they at length chanced to find out his solitary abode, in an out-of-the-way place, after having traversed the country in every direction for ever so long. His habitation was a cave or hollow in a rock, the inside being covered with reindeer-skin, and the entrance carefully closed up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個人，他有好幾個兒子；其中次子成了基維格托克——也就是逃離了人類社會。這事發生在冬天；但到了次年夏天，父親連同其他幾個兒子都離家外出，去尋找那個逃亡者。就這樣，夏天過去，冬天又來，他們卻始終沒有找到他。當夏天再度臨近時，他們做好一切準備，要再搜尋一次，這回是去別的地方，沿著另一條峽灣；直到深秋，他們在走遍各地、尋了許久之後，終於偶然發現了他那孤零零的居所，位於一處偏僻之地。他的住處是岩石中的一個洞穴或凹窟，裡面鋪著馴鹿皮，入口被仔細地封住。

passages.text: At the time of their arrival the kivigtok was still out hunting; but a little later they saw him advance towards the place from the inland, dragging a whole deer along with him. The brothers were lying in ambush for him; when he came close to them they seized hold of him, and he recognised them at once, giving a loud cry like that of a reindeer, and saying, 'Do let me off; I shan't flee.' The father now asked him to return with them, adding, 'This is the second summer in which we have given up our hunt in order to find thee out, and, now we have succeeded, thou really must come home with us' — 'Yes, that I will.' They remained in the cave during the night, enjoying each other's company; next day they had much to do with the things that had to be taken back, the store-room, besides his dwelling-place, being filled with dry meat and skins.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們到達時，那個基維格托克仍在外打獵；但過了一會兒，他們看見他從內陸方向朝這地方走來，拖著一整頭鹿。兄弟們埋伏著等他；當他走近他們時，他們一把抓住他，他立刻認出了他們，發出一聲像馴鹿般的叫喊，說道：「放了我吧；我不會逃的。」父親於是請他跟他們回去，又說：「這是我們為了尋你而放棄打獵的第二個夏天了，如今我們總算找到了你，你真的一定得跟我們回家。」——「好，我願意。」他們在洞穴裡過了一夜，彼此相伴甚歡；第二天他們忙著收拾要帶回去的東西，因為除了他的住處之外，儲藏室裡也裝滿了乾肉和獸皮。

passages.text: Tying up bundles to be taken down one by one to the tent of his relatives, pitched at some distance near the firth by which they were to travel home, they wanted him to follow them with the first loads; he excused himself — 'When ye go down the last time I shall follow; but I must stay and take care of these things.' They went without him; but on their return the kivigtok had disappeared, and taken the remainder of the provisions with him, and the brothers grew exceedingly vexed with themselves that they had thus relied on his word, without leaving any one in charge of him — all too late.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們把東西捆成包裹，準備一件件運到親屬的帳篷去，那帳篷紮在稍遠處、靠近他們返家所要經過的峽灣；他們要他帶著第一批東西跟他們走；他推託道：「你們最後一趟下去時我就跟著來；但我得留下來看管這些東西。」他們沒帶他就走了；但等他們回來時，那個基維格托克已經不見了，還帶走了剩下的糧食，兄弟們對自己極為懊惱，竟這樣信了他的話，沒留一個人看守他——一切都太遲了。

passages.text: Some time afterwards, when they had gone out again to look for him, he terrified them by yelling and howling at them from the summit of a steep and altogether inaccessible rock. How he had got there they could not make out, but finding it impossible to follow him, they were obliged to give him up for lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 40 'The Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了些時候，當他們又出去找他時，他從一座陡峭且完全無法攀爬的岩頂上對他們又叫又吼，把他們嚇得驚恐萬分。他們弄不明白他是怎麼上去的，但既然無法跟著他上去，只好認定他已失蹤，不得不放棄他。

title.en: Nagguanguak: The Wife in the Gull's Mound
title.zh: 納瓜恩瓜克：鷗丘中的妻子

region.en: Gull's mound and the ingnersuit house under ground
region.zh: 鷗丘與地下的因格內爾舒特人居所

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Left behind on purpose by scolding hunting companions, Nagguanguak is courted by a man stepping out of a gull's mound whose hill-house is walled with reindeer-skins, and bears him a son to be named Imitlungnarsunguak — 'It did not matter; he would take care to make a great huntsman of him.' Claiming the boy's first catch, the father pulls the first seal through the floor of the passage; the mother shouts her son's garments out of the house and follows them down beneath the lifted coast-ice to the ingnersuit house under ground, where she finds him tied hands and feet, loosens him, hurries him into his clothes, and brings him away.
summary.zh: 被斥責她的獵伴故意丟下的納瓜恩瓜克，被一名自鷗丘中現身的男子娶為妻；丘中之屋四壁掛滿馴鹿皮，舒適異常。她為他生子，父親要為孩子取名伊米特隆納孫瓜克——『無妨，我會把他調教成偉大的獵手』，並索要孩子的頭獵。第一頭海豹竟從甬道地板下被拽走；母親高喊讓兒子的衣物自己飛出屋外，追著它們下到升起的海冰之下——地底的因格內爾舒特人屋中，她尋見被縛手縛腳的兒子，解開繩索、披上衣物，帶他逃了出來。

sensitivity.note: Ingnersuit (ingnersuat): elves or spirits having their abodes in the rocks along the sea (Rink's note). Parallel to the atliarusek corpus (cross-ref inuit-girl-atliarusek-husband).

passages.text: It once happened that two men went out deer-hunting, accompanied by a woman. On the way they scolded her, at which she got vexed, and tied up her boots in order to remain behind; they waited a while for her, but at length went along without her, and soon lost sight of her, as she had purposely hidden herself behind some large heaps of stones. She heard them seeking for her close beside her hiding-place, and lamenting their loss; but nevertheless she remained quiet until they were gone. When she was thus left alone she crept forth and went off in an opposite direction. After some time she came to a gull's mound, and observed a man coming out from it; she tried to escape, but he seized hold of her, and asked her to follow him to his dwelling-place in the gull's-hill, as he wished to marry her. She followed him reluctantly; but when he opened it to her, she noticed that it was covered with reindeer-skins on the walls, and on the whole looked quite comfortable. She now left off crying, entered the hill, and became his wife, and in due time she bore him a child, whom the father wanted to be named Imitlungnarsunguak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，兩個男人帶著一個女人出去獵鹿。路上他們責罵她，她因此生氣，便把靴子綁好，要留在後頭；他們等了她一會兒，最後還是沒帶她先走了，很快便看不見她，因為她故意躲在一些大石堆後面。她聽見他們就在她藏身處旁邊尋找她，哀嘆失去了她；但她仍然一聲不響，直到他們離去。她這樣被獨自留下後，便悄悄爬出來，朝相反的方向走去。過了些時候，她來到一座海鷗丘，看見一個男人從裡面走出來；她想逃，卻被他抓住，他請她跟他到他位於海鷗丘中的住處去，因為他想娶她。她勉強跟著他；但當他為她打開門時，她注意到裡面牆上鋪著馴鹿皮，整體看來相當舒適。於是她不再哭泣，走進丘中，成了他的妻子，後來屆時為他生下一個孩子，父親想給孩子取名為伊米特隆納松瓜克。

passages.text: The wife remonstrated, saying that she had not got any relatives of that name; but the husband answered her, 'It did not matter; he would take care to make a great huntsman of him' — and then she let him call the boy as he liked. When he grew on, and his mother had spent a good many winters in this place, she longed for her former home and wished to return; the husband merely answered her, 'I claim his first catch, mind!' and then she left him along with her son, and went back to her old relatives and housemates, and once more lived with them. When the other children played with her son, she used to tell them not to do him any harm, and for fear of his unknown father they desisted. When he was quite grown up and saw the men prepare for the hunt, he was very desirous to join them; his mother observing this went outside and shouted out aloud, 'Now get him some tools!' — when she came out next morning she found them lying on the ground close beside the entry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 妻子勸阻他，說自己並沒有叫這個名字的親戚；但丈夫回答她說：「那無妨；他自會留心把他造就成一個了不起的獵人。」於是她就任憑他隨意給那男孩取名。當他漸漸長大，他母親已在此地度過了許多個冬天，她思念從前的家鄉，想要回去；丈夫只回答她說：「他的第一件獵獲物歸我，記住！」於是她就帶著兒子離開了他，回到舊日的親戚與同住的人那裡，重新和他們住在一起。別的孩子和她兒子玩耍時，她常叮囑他們不要傷害他，他們因懼怕他那不知名的父親，便不再那樣做。當他完全長大，看見男人們準備去打獵，便非常渴望加入他們；他母親察覺到這一點，就走到外面高聲喊道：「現在給他弄些工具來！」——第二天早晨她出去時，發現那些工具就放在入口緊旁的地上。

passages.text: When the son brought home what he had caught for the first time, she again went out and cried with all her might, 'Imitlungnarsunguak has caught a seal!' — and when she was about to re-enter, the people were all very busy in dragging this seal into the house; when they had reached the farther end of the passage it could not be lifted across the threshold into the room, but rolled back, and in no time had vanished — the father, of course, had taken it away. His next catch the mother got; but when he went out hunting the third time, he remained away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當兒子第一次把他所獵得的東西帶回家時，她又走出去，用盡全力喊道：「伊米特隆納爾松瓜克捉到一隻海豹了！」——當她正要再進屋時，眾人正忙著把這隻海豹拖進屋裡；他們拖到通道的盡頭時，卻無法把它抬過門檻送進屋內，它反而滾了回去，轉眼間便消失無蹤——當然，是父親把它取走了。他下一次的獵獲物由母親得到了；但當他第三次出去打獵時，就一去不返。

passages.text: His mother now mended his clothes and put them to rights, and in the evening went outside as before, shouting something at the pitch of her voice, upon which his garments came flying out of the house, and she hurried after them; when they had got as far as the beach, the coast-ice appeared to be lifted up, and left room for the clothes to slip down beneath — the mother following them closely. She now came to a house under ground belonging to ingnersuit, and there found her son, tied hands and feet; loosening him she hurried him into his clothes, and brought him away with her. Her own name was Nagguanguak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 41 'The Woman who got connected with the Ingnersuit or Under-world People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他母親這時縫補好他的衣服，把它們整理妥當，傍晚時又如先前一樣走到外面，用最高的嗓門喊了些什麼，於是他的衣物便從屋裡飛了出來，她急忙跟在後面追；當他們到了海灘那麼遠的地方，沿岸的冰似乎被掀了起來，讓出空隙好讓衣服滑落下去——母親緊緊跟隨著它們。她這時來到一座屬於因格爾蘇伊特（ingnersuit）的地下房屋，在那裡找到了她的兒子，手腳都被捆綁著；她解開他，急忙替他穿上衣服，把他帶了回來。她自己的名字叫納瓜瓜克（Nagguanguak）。

title.en: The Children of Two Cousins: The Pet Calf and the Jealous Bow
title.zh: 兩表兄弟的孩子：寵鹿與嫉妒之弓

region.en: Shared winter-station and the strong man's coast
region.zh: 共用的越冬地與大力士的海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 42 'About the Children of Two Cousins', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two childless cousins part with 'we will see who first gets a child.' One prospers south and fathers a boy; the other, childless still, trains a young deer until it understands human speech. When the calf knocks the playmate-boy over once too often, the boy's father shoots it — dearly as he loves his cousin — and the childless man, furious, meets him armed with bows and shoots him on the spot, then drowns himself in tears. The orphan son returns full-grown, too late for the murderer, and kills instead the enormously strong wife-robber, restoring the women to their husbands.
summary.zh: 一對膝下無子的表兄弟分別時約定：『且看誰先得子。』南行的表弟得子；留守的表兄依舊無嗣，馴養一頭幼鹿直至通曉人言。小鹿與小主人嬉戲，卻屢屢把他撞翻——孩子的父親雖深愛表兄，仍舉弓射殺幼鹿；暴怒的無子者立即應戰，弓箭相見，當場射殺表弟，隨後痛哭失聲。遺孤長成後返鄉復仇，仇人已亡；轉而挑戰搶妻的巨力者，將其摔殺，把被搶的婦女一一送還其夫。

sensitivity.note: Killing and grief recorded as told in the 1875 source. The trained-calf motif parallels the animal-training sledge tales.

passages.text: There were once two cousins living together at the same winter-station, and at the time their wives were both childless. In spring they parted from each other, saying, 'Well, we will see who first gets a child.' One travelled away to the south, and established himself for the coming winter; at this place he lived in prosperity, and his wife bore him a child. When the boy grew up, the father took a fancy to return to his cousin; he, however, had still no children, and for this reason he caught a young deer and trained it up for his amusement — at length it improved so much that it could understand human speech. About that period the cousin returned, and first beheld the calf running about outside the house; the cousins once more lived together, and the boy and the calf became playmates. The calf, however, soon grew stronger, and sometimes knocked over the boy, at which he wept; for this reason the boy's father went and shot the calf, though he loved his cousin dearly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 42 'About the Children of Two Cousins'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有兩個表兄弟同住在一個冬季營地，那時他們的妻子都沒有生育。春天他們彼此分別，說道：「好吧，我們看看誰先得子。」一個往南去了，在那裡安頓下來準備過冬；他在這地方生活富足，他的妻子為他生了一個孩子。當男孩長大，父親起了回去找表兄弟的念頭；然而那人仍然沒有孩子，因此他捉了一隻小鹿，訓練牠以供消遣——最後牠進步得那麼多，竟能聽懂人話。大約就在那時，表兄弟回來了，首先看見那隻小鹿在屋外跑來跑去；兩個表兄弟又重新住在一起，那男孩和小鹿成了玩伴。然而小鹿很快長得更強壯了，有時把男孩撞倒，男孩便哭了起來；為此男孩的父親便去把那隻小鹿射死了，儘管他深愛著他的表兄弟。

passages.text: The childless man got into a great rage at this, and at once challenged his cousin, and they met armed with their bows; the childless man shot his cousin on the spot, but was very much afflicted afterwards, and burst into a flood of tears. The son of the man that had been thus killed removed to a distance, for he could not endure the sight of his father's cousin. When he was full-grown and strong he returned to the place, but he had come too late — the cousin was no more. He heard some rumour of an enormously strong man who used to rob other men of their wives; he challenged him to a wrestling-match, and overcame and killed him, and returned the women to their own husbands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 42 'About the Children of Two Cousins'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那沒有孩子的人為此大發雷霆，立刻向他的表兄弟挑戰，他們便帶著弓相會；那沒有孩子的人當場射死了他的表兄弟，但事後非常悲痛，淚如泉湧。那被這樣殺死的人的兒子遷到了遠處，因為他無法忍受看見父親的表兄弟。當他長大成人、身強力壯時，他回到了那地方，但他來得太遲了——那表兄弟已不在人世。他聽到一些傳聞，說有一個力大無窮的人常奪走別人的妻子；他向那人挑戰，要比一場角力，結果戰勝並殺死了他，把那些婦女送還給她們各自的丈夫。

title.en: The Girl Who Was Stolen by an Inorusek
title.zh: 被內陸巨人擄走的少女

region.en: Salmon river highlands and the inorusek huts
region.zh: 鮭魚河高地與內陸巨人的營地

period: Inuit oral tradition; obscure and fragmentary, related to tales 28 and 30, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Carried inland by an inorusek while salmon-fishing, a girl is fed deer-heart fat and tallow she will not touch, and warned by a bones-and-joints skeleton — once a stolen girl like her, whose boots were filled with reptiles until the flesh was all gone. The giant flings the crawling boots away into the corner, and at last she wins his trust — 'I have no intention of leaving thee now' — escapes over the hills to her parents' tent, bursting through the door-curtain: 'Let us be off at once and remove to some other place; the inlanders are sure to come and seek me here' — and the family never again ventured to pitch their tents on the continent.
summary.zh: 採鮭時被內陸巨人擄走的少女，拒食鹿心脂與普通油脂；一具瘦骨嶙峋的「人形」爬過長凳警告她：『別哭了，免得他們像對我那樣對你——當年他們把我的靴子裝滿蟲豸，脫下時，我的肉已經沒了。』巨人把蠕動的靴子擲向屋角，她才止住啼哭。她假意溫順——『我無意離開你』——趁其出獵翻山越嶺直奔父母帳篷，撞破門簾而入：『快搬走吧！內陸人一定會來找我的。』全家遷往外海小島，從此再不敢在大陸紮營。

sensitivity.note: Inorusek: fabulous giant-like inlanders (Rink's note). Details in the different manuscripts of tales 28, 30, and 43 are confounded and intermixed per Rink. The vermin-boots punishment recorded as told.

passages.text: A brother and a sister once lived together, and were very much attached to each other. The sister, very desirous of going off for the salmon-fishing, asked her brother to take her up to a salmon river; not being able to deny her, he put the boat into the sea and went with her to the fishing-place — but when they had landed and discharged the boat, putting all their things on the beach, she climbed a little way up the rocks and went across a smooth level to the brook. All at once she saw an inorusek close beside her; stupefied with terror, she tried to escape, but he caught hold of her and carried her further and further inland. The others plainly heard her shrieks for help, and hurried off to rescue her; but she was already gone, and her cries soon died away among the mountains. In the meantime the inorusek carried her up through the highlands till they stopped at a place with a number of huts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一對兄妹同住在一起，彼此非常友愛。妹妹非常想去捕鮭魚，便求哥哥帶她到一條鮭魚河去；他無法拒絕她，就把船推下海，和她一同前往捕魚的地方——但當他們上岸、卸下船上的東西，把一切物品都放在海灘上之後，她爬上岩石一小段路，穿過一片平坦光滑的地面，走向那條小溪。忽然她看見一個伊諾魯塞克（inorusek）就在她身旁；她驚恐得發呆，想要逃走，但他抓住她，把她往內陸越帶越遠。其他人清楚地聽見她呼救的尖叫聲，急忙趕去救她；但她已經不見了，她的呼喊聲很快便在山間消逝。與此同時，那伊諾魯塞克把她帶上高地，直到他們停在一個有許多小屋的地方。

passages.text: He intended to marry her, but first brought her to the house of a neighbour, where he put her down on the ledge and seated himself in front of her; she cried incessantly, but whenever she tried to run away he took hold of her like a little child and put her down again. While she was thus sitting an old woman peeped across the screen of the ledge, asking her, 'What wouldst thou like to eat? Dost thou like talu?' — the unhappy girl thought to herself, 'I wonder what talu is like!' She soon heard the old woman step down to fetch something, and though still weeping, peeped through her fingers, and perceived it to be the fat of a deer's heart they were giving her; however, she would not take it, and the old woman again retired. 'Wouldst thou like some ernowt?' — 'What may it be like?' — this time she saw the old hag produce some common tallow, saying, 'Now do eat that and be quiet'; but she would not take that either. Being very disheartened she continued to weep; the old woman now menaced her and threatened to take away her boots, at which she cried still more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他打算娶她為妻，但先把她帶到鄰人的屋裡，將她放在窗台邊的坐板上，自己坐在她面前；她哭個不停，可是每當她想逃走，他便像對待小孩子一樣抓住她，再把她放回去。她這樣坐著的時候，一個老婦人從窗台的隔板後探出頭來，問她：『你想吃什麼？你喜歡吃塔魯嗎？』——這不幸的姑娘心裡想：『不知塔魯是什麼滋味！』她不久便聽見老婦人走下去取東西，雖然仍在哭泣，卻從指縫間偷看，發覺她們給她的是鹿心的脂肪；然而她不肯吃，老婦人便又退了下去。『你想吃點艾爾瑙特嗎？』——『那會是什麼滋味呢？』——這一次她看見那老妖婆取出一些普通的油脂，說道：『現在就吃了吧，安靜下來。』但她也不肯吃。她十分沮喪，繼續哭泣；老婦人這時恐嚇她，說要脫掉她的靴子，她於是哭得更厲害了。

passages.text: Then she heard a rattling noise, and peeping through her fingers saw a strange figure, all bones and joints, creeping along the ledge towards her. This creature warned her, saying, 'Leave off crying, lest they should treat thee as they did me. I was once like thee; I was stolen and brought to this place, and because I would not leave off crying, they took away my boots and gave me others filled with reptiles, spiders, and vermin. They fastened them on my legs, and when they were taken off, the flesh was all gone.' When the skeleton had done speaking, she cried all the more; the old hag now in an outburst of ill temper and vexation approached, and she saw her holding a pair of boots in which she observed something crawling about — but the giant took hold of them and flung them away into the corner of the room, and then at length she was able to leave off crying.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著她聽見一陣格格作響的聲音，從指縫間偷看，只見一個奇怪的形體，滿身骨頭與關節，沿著坐板朝她爬來。這東西警告她說：『別再哭了，免得他們像對待我那樣對待你。我從前也和你一樣；我被擄來帶到這個地方，因為我不肯停止哭泣，他們便脫掉我的靴子，給我換上一雙裝滿爬蟲、蜘蛛和害蟲的靴子。他們把靴子綁在我腿上，等脫下來時，肉全都沒有了。』那骷髏說完之後，她哭得更加厲害；老妖婆這時因脾氣發作、心煩意亂而走近前來，她看見她拿著一雙靴子，裡面有東西在爬動——但巨人抓住那雙靴子，把它們扔到屋角去了，她這才終於能夠停止哭泣。

passages.text: Her husband, however, kept a close watch upon her, and led her by the hand whenever she wished to go out. One day she said to him, 'Don't go on watching me so; I have no intention of leaving thee now; I like thee very much, and thou mayst safely leave me and go out deer-hunting as usual.' After that she feigned to go behind the house, but started from her hiding-place and ran up and down hill, and continued running towards the coast until she reached the tent of her parents, where she burst right through the door-curtain, not giving herself time to draw it before entering. She hastened to say, 'Let us be off at once and remove to some other place; the inlanders are sure to come and seek me here.' They at once left the mainland to settle down on one of the farthest-off islets; and after that time they never again ventured to pitch their tents on the continent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 43 'The Girl who was stolen by an Inlander'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而她的丈夫嚴密地看守著她，每當她想出去，便牽著她的手。有一天她對他說：『別再這樣看著我了；我現在無意離開你；我很喜歡你，你可以放心地留下我，像往常一樣出去獵鹿。』此後她假裝走到屋後，卻從藏身之處起身，翻山越嶺地奔跑，一直朝海岸跑去，直到抵達她父母的帳篷，她直衝過門簾，連掀開門簾進去的時間都不給自己。她急忙說道：『我們立刻走吧，搬到別的地方去；內地人一定會到這裡來找我。』他們立刻離開大陸，定居在一個最遙遠的小島上；此後他們再也不敢在大陸上搭帳篷了。

title.en: Tungnerdluk: The Child Taken by the Inlanders
title.zh: 通格內爾盧克：被內陸人奪走的孩子

region.en: Fiord winter-quarters and the inlanders' large house
region.zh: 峽灣冬居與內陸人的大屋

period: Inuit oral tradition; one manuscript plus a verbal narration, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 44 'The Child that was stolen by the Inlanders', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Gathering berries with her only child, Tungnerdluk's wife turns away a moment and the inlanders have him. His father, guided by an angakok cousin, creeps hands and knees into the great house where two hags fight over the weeping boy — a huge helper sprung from the coast people hands the child over and warns of pursuit. Harpooning one pursuer from the beach, Tungnerdluk rows off; but the child sickens, and a second angakok, renowned at headlifting, flies to fetch the child's spirit back from the inlanders — restoring it, the baby recovers, and the mockers who come with whalebones are respectfully silenced by his storehouse.
summary.zh: 採莓時一轉身，通格內爾盧克夫人的獨子已被內陸人奪走。其父求教於巫師表親，獨自潛入大屋——兩個老嫗正為啼哭的孩子爭執不休；一名自稱源出海濱人的巨漢出手相助，把孩子交還並警告後有追兵。海灘上一叉刺翻一名追兵後，他們舉家出海；孩子卻病倒了——精於抬頭術的巫師飛往內陸，把孩子的靈魂帶回，嬰兒旋即康復。攜鯨骨前來嘲弄的訪客，在見識過他的鯨骨庫藏後悻悻而退。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note records an amarsiniook variant (monster of the inland ice) in which the falcon-tornak vanquishes the monster. Spirit-restoration (headlifting, angakok flight) documented as told.

passages.text: A man, whose name was Tungnerdluk, had his fixed abode by a firth, from which he made his regular excursions into the highlands to hunt the reindeer, and generally he was lucky; in winter he carried on seal-hunting at the mouth of the firth. One summer he was out chasing the deer as usual, and during his absence his wife went away to gather berries among the heather with their only child. She put the boy down on the sod and left him a moment; she had hardly turned away before she heard him crying out — although she instantly turned back, she did not find him in his place, but only heard his lamentations a long way off from where she was standing. She returned to the tent in great affliction, and told how she had suffered her child to be taken by the inlanders, adding that she feared her husband's anger. In the evening he returned heavily laden — 'I have got plenty of reindeer-flesh for thee' — and on finding that nobody answered, at once knew that some mischief had befallen them in his absence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 44 'The Child that was stolen by the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個名叫通納德盧克的人，固定住在一個峽灣旁，從那裡定期到高地去獵馴鹿，通常都很幸運；冬天他則在峽灣口獵海豹。有一年夏天，他照常出去追鹿，在他不在的時候，他的妻子帶著他們唯一的孩子出去，在石南叢中採漿果。她把男孩放在草皮上，離開了片刻；她幾乎還沒轉身，就聽見他叫喊起來——雖然她立刻折返，卻沒有在原地找到他，只聽見他的哭聲從她所站之處很遠的地方傳來。她悲痛萬分地回到帳篷，訴說她如何讓孩子被內地人擄去，又說她害怕丈夫發怒。傍晚他滿載而歸——『我給你帶了好多馴鹿肉』——發現無人回應，立刻明白在他不在時他們遭遇了禍事。

passages.text: He hurried in, and breathlessly asked if his son had died; the wife made no answer, but the others enlightened him: 'She let the inlanders take him.' Tungnerdluk asked his trembling wife to put new soles on his boots — he wanted to go and consult his cousin, who was an angakok. This man pointed out the place to which the boy had been taken, and accompanied the father on his way to find him. At a good distance they reached a large house, and the angakok told him he must go up to it alone, and that he himself would have to return. Tungnerdluk peeped in at the window, and saw two terrible women quarrelling and fighting about his weeping child; he leapt down into the outer passage, creeping on hands and feet to get through the inner one up into the main room. Having at last succeeded, he made his way up to the two hags to snatch his child — but whenever he tried to take it from one woman, she directly handed it to the other, and thus they went on a good while.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 44 'The Child that was stolen by the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他急忙進去，氣喘吁吁地問兒子是不是死了；妻子沒有回答，但其他人告訴了他：『她讓內地人把他擄走了。』通納德盧克請他顫抖的妻子給他的靴子換上新鞋底——他想去請教他的表親，那人是一位安加科克（巫師）。這人指出了男孩被帶去的地方，並陪父親一同上路去尋找他。走了好一段路，他們來到大屋前，巫師告訴他必須獨自上前，而他自己則必須回去。通納德盧克從窗戶往裡窺看，看見兩個可怕的女人正為他哭泣的孩子爭吵打鬥；他跳進外側的通道，手腳並用地爬過內側通道，進入正屋。終於成功之後，他朝那兩個妖婆走去，想奪回自己的孩子——但每當他從一個女人手中奪取孩子，她便立刻把孩子遞給另一個，就這樣持續了好一陣子。

passages.text: A huge man at length entered, who said he would assist him, declaring that he had sprung from the coast people: 'Thou'dst better run on beforehand: be sure I will soon come after with the child; but mind be quick — my house-fellows will soon be pursuing us.' Tungnerdluk came running at full speed and entered his tent, saying, 'Make ready to depart at once' — and meanwhile the other entered with the child. They folded their tents and quickly loaded their boat; at the very moment they pushed from shore they saw their enemies descending the hills. When they had fairly got down to the beach, Tungnerdluk could not resist putting back to fight them, and soon despatched one of them with his harpoon, then followed his own people out of the firth. After this his son fell sick, and he consulted an angakok who was not able to find out the cause; he then called another, renowned as a performer of headlifting, who conjured and called up spirits, lying down on his back, first letting go his breath, then rising up and beginning to breathe again, saying, 'The child's spirit is still with the inlanders.' 'Then lose no time in preparing for an angakok-flight to bring it back and restore it to us' — and he flew away to the inlanders, fetching the spirit of the child home with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 44 'The Child that was stolen by the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後進來一個魁梧的男子，說他願意幫助他，聲稱自己出身於海岸的人：『你最好先跑；放心，我很快就會帶著孩子跟來；但要快——我的屋中同伴很快就會追我們。』通納德盧克全速奔跑，進入自己的帳篷，說道：『立刻準備出發』——同時那人也帶著孩子進來了。他們收起帳篷，迅速把船裝載好；就在他們離岸的那一刻，他們看見敵人正從山上下來。當他們確實到達海灘時，通納德盧克忍不住掉轉船頭與他們交戰，很快用魚叉結果了其中一人，然後跟著自己的人們駛出峽灣。此後他的兒子病了，他請教一位安加科克，那人無法查出病因；於是他又請來另一位以行「舉頭術」聞名的巫師，那人施法召喚精靈，仰面躺下，先呼出氣息，然後起身重新呼吸，說道：『孩子的靈魂仍與內地人在一起。』『那就趕快準備一次安加科克飛行，把它帶回來還給我們』——於是他飛往內地人那裡，把孩子的靈魂帶回了家。

passages.text: On his return to the parents he heard the voice of the child growing weaker; but by restoring the spirit to it the baby soon recovered. Tungnerdluk paid the angakok well with different kinds of victuals, adding, 'Whenever thou shouldst happen to be in any distress, I will gladly assist thee.' Shortly afterwards two visitors came on purpose to mock him, one carrying a lot of whalebones: 'We have heard of the celebrated Tungnerdluk, who fetched his child back from the inlanders; pray tell us some of thy achievements: we will make thee a present of our whalebones in return.' 'I am not in want of any such thing' — he took them to his storehouse, where he showed them his large stock of whalebones as well as of walrus-teeth; seeing this, they respectfully retired and left the place without so much as entering the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 44 'The Child that was stolen by the Inlanders'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他回到父母身邊時，聽見孩子的聲音越來越微弱；但把靈魂還給孩子之後，嬰兒很快就復原了。通格訥德盧克以各式各樣的食物厚厚酬謝了那位巫師，還補上一句：「日後你若有任何危難，我必樂意相助。」不久之後，有兩個人特地前來嘲弄他，其中一人帶著許多鯨鬚：「我們聽說過大名鼎鼎的通格訥德盧克，他從內陸人那裡把自己的孩子取了回來；請講幾件你的功績給我們聽聽：我們就把這些鯨鬚送給你作為回報。」「我並不缺這種東西。」他領他們到自己的庫房，給他們看自己囤積的大量鯨鬚以及海象牙；兩人見了，便恭恭敬敬地告退離去，連屋子都沒進去。

title.en: The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek
title.zh: 巫師飛行阿基利內克

region.en: Akilinek, the fabulous country beyond the ocean
region.zh: 海外幻境阿基利內克

period: Inuit oral tradition; three tales under one number (North Greenland before 1830; southernmost Greenland c. 1860; author's verbal narration), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Three angakok-flight tales: a father initiates his son at the graves — hand thrust into the corpse's flesh, warned to flee at a spark falling from the setting sun — until the boy flies past his father's limit to Akilinek, where his iceberg-tornak séance is wrecked by a hairy woman's misstep, killing the house. The novice Ipisanguak finds the house of the bloody sword and exchanges places nightly with its dim-eyed angakok, until a topknot-ribboned girl with an anghiak wrecks his own iceberg séance and the Kagsimiut avenger is stoned back. A boy forced to sit on his conjuring father's knee hears stars dropping into the old grave, faints at the maggot-smell of its ghost, and wakes clairvoyant in the grave — to fly at last to Akilinek and share the wreck of a kivinngak iceberg that an anghiak turns upon the house.
summary.zh: 三則巫師飛行故事：父親在墓場為兒子行入門禮——手探屍身、囑其見落日滴下火花即逃——兒子終於飛越父親的界限抵達阿基利內克；降靈召來冰山靈，卻因毛婦失足而屋毀人亡。新手伊皮桑瓜克尋得『血劍之屋』，與其瞇眼巫師夜夜互換位置，直至繫彩帶、攜死胎鬼（安吉亞克）的少女令他的冰山降靈翻覆；復仇的巫師也被眾人擲石擊退。被父親按在膝上聽降神的小兒，眼見星辰落入古墓，嗅得蛆蟲之氣昏厥，醒來已在墓中、通曉千里——末了同往阿基利內克，又逢安吉亞克令冰山傾覆、全屋覆滅。

sensitivity.note: Documents angakok science: grave initiation, tornaks, headlifting, anghiak, kivinngak iceberg-tornak. House-destruction deaths recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: (1) There was once a very clever angakok. When he was about to practise his art, and his limbs had been tied and the lamps extinguished, he took flight, and having found the wind favourable, flew across the sea, but did not sight the opposite shore before daybreak, when he was obliged to return. Several times he tried to get farther away, but was never able to pass beyond this mark; and therefore he determined to educate his son for an angakok, hoping that he might possibly be brought to excel him. When the boy was grown up he went through all the grades and branches of the angakok-science; but when the father proposed to give up teaching him, the son turned very moody and low-spirited — 'Is there any part of the science thou thinkest we have overlooked, and neglected to practise?' 'I think there is.' After due meditation the father asked, 'Didst thou visit the graves?' — he had not — 'Well, I will take thee thither this evening.' At the burying-grounds the father opened one of the graves, undid the pall of a corpse beneath the waist, and made his son thrust his hand right into the flesh of the deceased body; this done, he left him as if nothing at all were the matter, remarking, 'As yet thou hast observed nothing particular at this tomb; but wait till thou seest the last rays of the setting sun, and take not thy eyes from its splendour: but the moment thou dost notice a spark of light falling down from it, beware, and flee the place at once.' While he stood gazing at the declining sun, the father suddenly beheld something glistening through the brightness of the sky, at the sight of which he immediately took flight — but the son remained with his hands attached to the corpse, unable to extricate himself. Not until midnight did he return, all smiles and joy; and now the father deemed him thoroughly tried and expert in his art.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: (1) 從前有一位非常高明的巫師。當他準備施展法術、四肢被綁好、燈火被熄滅之後，他便騰空飛起；見風向順遂，便飛越海面，但直到破曉仍未望見對岸，只得折返。他屢次試圖飛得更遠，卻始終無法越過這個界限；因此他決心把兒子培養成巫師，希望或許能使他青出於藍。男孩長大後，學遍了巫術科學的各個等級與門類；但當父親打算停止教他時，兒子卻變得十分鬱鬱寡歡——「你認為我們還有哪一部分學問忽略了、沒有加以演練嗎？」「我想是有的。」父親沉思良久後問道：「你去過墓地嗎？」——他沒有去過——「那麼，今晚我帶你去。」在墓地，父親打開其中一座墳，解開一具屍體腰部以下的裹屍布，叫兒子把手直直插進死者的肉裡；做完之後，他若無其事地離開他，只說道：「到目前為止，你在這座墳前還沒注意到什麼特別的東西；但等著看落日最後的光芒吧，別把眼睛從那光輝上移開：可是，一旦你看見有一點火光從中落下，就要當心，立刻逃離此地。」當他站在那裡凝視著西沉的太陽時，父親忽然看見有什麼東西透過天空的明亮閃爍而下，一見此景便立刻逃走——但兒子卻雙手黏在屍體上，無法脫身。直到午夜他才回來，滿臉笑容、滿心歡喜；這時父親便認為他已受過徹底的考驗，精通此術了。

passages.text: On the night of the following day he resolved to bind him for his first flight; when the lamps had been extinguished the son flew out, and having no particular end or aim, only went backwards and forwards, seeing nothing very remarkable — questioned concerning the currents of the air, he had not happened to take note of any. The next day he again prepared for an angakok flight, observing that the wind was favourable; he crossed part of the sea, and soon perceived that he was taking the same course as his father. At last great perpendicular rocks arose in front of him, and he had reached the limit of his father's journey; continuing his flight towards it and with some difficulty passing it, he saw an extensive country, crossed it in a southerly direction, and came upon a small house with two windows, alighting close beside it. Peeping within, he saw one man standing at each window, watching him closely; one of the men went out, beckoned to a woman, and invited the stranger to step inside. Seated on the side-ledge to the right, on the opposite side he saw a squint-eyed person whose breath was like fire (peculiar to angakut, and also only to be observed by them), bone-chips at his feet at which he had been working; further away a woman whose body was all over hairy. 'Why dost thou thus stare at me?' — 'Oh, I was only looking at the chips at thy feet.' — 'In the summer I have not got time to make chips, and that is why I am at it now.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日夜晚，他決定為兒子的初次飛行把他綁好；燈火熄滅後，兒子飛了出去，但沒有特定的目的或目標，只是來回飛翔，沒看見什麼特別值得注意的東西——問起氣流的情況，他恰好沒有留意到任何一點。第二天他又準備作一次巫師飛行，觀察到風向順遂；他飛越了一部分海面，很快便發覺自己正循著與父親相同的路線前進。最後，他面前矗立起巨大的垂直岩壁，他已到達父親旅程的極限；他繼續朝那裡飛去，費了些力氣才飛越過去，看見一片廣闊的國度，便朝南橫越而過，來到一間有兩扇窗戶的小屋，在屋旁降落。他往裡窺看，看見每個窗口各站著一個男人，正緊緊盯著他；其中一人走了出去，向一個女人招手，並邀請這陌生人進屋。他坐在右側的邊台上，在對面看見一個斜眼的人，其氣息如火（這是巫師特有的，也只有巫師才看得見），腳邊放著他一直在削的骨屑；再過去是一個全身長滿毛髮的女人。「你為什麼這樣盯著我看？」——「哦，我只是在看您腳邊的骨屑。」——「夏天我沒空削骨屑，所以才趁現在做。」

passages.text: Some of them said, 'Perhaps our visitor would like to show us some of his art?' — 'Why, I am not unwilling, though it is but the second time I have practised angakok science.' They all repaired to the kagse, their house of festivities; the squint-eyed person, always keeping close at the visitor's heels, asked him what fearful tornak he had got at his service — 'If I succeed, a large iceberg will presently appear.' They all entered the dark kagse, where he also observed the hairy woman, the sight of whom he did not like, suspecting her to be dangerous to his purpose. When the conjuring had begun and he felt that his tornak was drawing nigh, he said, 'I fancy that something is approaching us' — they looked out at the window and whispered, 'A monstrous iceberg is close upon the beach.' 'Let a young man and a maiden step forth and post themselves in the middle of the floor' — a tremendous noise proceeded from the iceberg bouncing ashore and suddenly calving; then a married couple was ordered out on the floor, and a loud roar from without followed; thus they were all called forth one after the other, and at last it was the turn of the ugly woman to step out — she missed her footing on one of the flags, got beyond the proper stepping-stones, and at the same time the iceberg turned over, came tumbling over the shore, and crushed the house to atoms. Only the angakok visitor and the man with the squint came out unhurt; tying his limbs, he rose high in the air and returned, accompanied by a swarm of croaking ravens. Silent and dejected — 'I am heavy with grief because I have practised my art badly: I did wrong in calling forth the hairy woman; and by this fault of mine many happy and vigorous people have perished.' Next day the squint-eyed person made his appearance: 'Perhaps I too may be allowed to exhibit my art? I too am an angakok.' 'My son there is just telling me that he has killed many brave and strong people by his want of experience.' 'So he did, the bad one.' Tied hand and foot, the squint-eyed began his flight in the house, and as soon as they began singing flew out of it; suspecting he might be dangerous, they extinguished the lamps to prevent his re-entering — but looking out at the window, they saw him take a direction towards his own homestead, and soon after proceeded to light the lamps, concluding that at any rate he would not return the same night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們當中有人說：「也許我們的訪客願意給我們露幾手他的法術？」——「唉，我倒不反對，雖說這只是我第二次施展巫術。」他們全都前往卡格塞，也就是他們的慶會屋；那個斜眼的人始終緊跟在訪客腳後，問他役使的是什麼可怕的托爾納克（精靈）——「若我成功，馬上就會出現一座巨大的冰山。」他們全都進入漆黑的卡格塞，他在那裡也看見了那個多毛的女人，見了她他並不喜歡，懷疑她會妨礙他的目的。當法術開始、他感到自己的托爾納克正逼近時，他說：「我覺得有什麼東西正朝我們靠近。」他們從窗口望出去，低聲說：「一座龐大的冰山正逼近海灘。」「讓一個年輕男子和一個少女走上前去，站到地板中央。」冰山撞上岸、突然崩裂，發出震天巨響；接著又命一對已婚夫婦走到地板上，外面隨即傳來一聲巨吼；就這樣他們一個接一個被叫出去，最後輪到那個醜陋的女人走出去——她在一塊石板上失了足，越出了該踩的墊腳石，與此同時冰山翻了過來，滾過海岸，把屋子壓得粉碎。只有那位巫師訪客和那個斜眼的人安然無恙；他綁好四肢，高高升上空中離去，伴隨著一群呱呱叫的渡鴉。他沉默而沮喪——「我心中沉重，因為我法術施展得不好：我錯在召來了那個多毛的女人；由於我這個過失，許多快樂而健壯的人都喪了命。」第二天，那個斜眼的人出現了：「也許也允許我展示一下我的法術？我也是個巫師。」「我兒子剛才正告訴我，他因經驗不足害死了許多勇敢強壯的人。」「他確實如此，這個壞傢伙。」斜眼的人手腳被綁好，在屋內開始飛行，他們一開始唱誦，他便飛了出去；他們懷疑他可能有害，便熄滅燈火以防他再進來——但從窗口望出去，他們看見他朝自己家的方向而去，不久之後便重新點燈，斷定他無論如何當夜不會再回來了。

passages.text: (2) Of an angakok called Ipisanguak, who was still a novice in his art, this tale is told: On a certain evening, when he was just ready to set out on a flight, he said, 'I intend to go away in search of the little house my forefathers have often spoken of, outside of which lies the bloody sword.' Having spoken thus he set off, making a circuit all round the horizon without having anything particular to relate on his return; but the next time he flew straight across to Akilinek, and alighted right in front of a house where lay the bloody sword which was to be taken by him. A man emerged from the entrance whose eyes were all dim, like those of an unborn seal; he re-entered without noticing the stranger, and another man appeared whose eyes were like the blackest berries, asking him to step inside, the inmates welcoming him: 'Thou art just in time to join us at our meal.' After a while the angakok observed, 'I want another to fill my place at home to-night, otherwise my relatives will not believe that I have been here' — 'I should very much like to be thy substitute, but I am rather a slow one.' They proceeded to have him tied; presently he was lifted up within the house and soared out into the open air, while Ipisanguak enjoyed a happy night in the company of his pleasant hosts. At dawn of day he broke off — 'The night is done; I must be off' — and again crossed the sea; about midway he saw a glare as of a great fire shining about him, which appeared to be from his substitute, who likewise was on his way home, and thus meeting, both aimed at each other. Ipisanguak again visited Akilinek next evening, and at the same time his substitute exclaimed, 'I hear him coming; behold, there he is!' — and again they encountered each other on the way, smiled as they met, and returned in the same way at daybreak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: (2) 關於一位名叫伊皮桑瓜克、法術尚屬初學的巫師，有這樣一則故事：某天晚上，他正準備出發飛行，說道：「我打算去尋找我先祖們常提起的那間小屋，屋外放著那把血淋淋的劍。」說完這番話他便動身，繞著地平線飛了一圈，回來時卻沒什麼特別的事可講；但下一次他直飛橫越至阿基利內克，正好降落在一間屋前，屋外放著那把要由他取走的血淋淋的劍。一個男人從門口出來，雙眼昏暗，像未出生的海豹的眼睛；他沒注意到陌生人便又進去了，接著又出現另一個男人，眼睛黑得像最黑的漿果，請他進屋，屋裡的人歡迎他：「你來得正好，跟我們一起吃飯吧。」過了一會兒，巫師說道：「我今晚需要有人在家裡替我頂替，否則我的親屬不會相信我來過這裡。」——「我很願意做你的替身，只是我動作相當慢。」他們便把他綁好；不久他被舉到屋內，又騰空飛入戶外，而伊皮桑瓜克則在愉快的主人們陪伴下度過了歡樂的一夜。天亮時他打住——「夜已盡，我該走了」——於是再度橫越海面；約莫到了中途，他看見一道如大火般的光在他四周閃耀，似乎是從他的替身那裡發出的，那替身也正趕路回家，兩人如此相遇，便互相對準了對方。伊皮桑瓜克第二天晚上又造訪阿基利內克，與此同時他的替身喊道：「我聽見他來了；瞧，他在那裡！」——他們又在途中相遇，相視而笑，並在破曉時以同樣的方式各自返回。

passages.text: On the following day, when Ipisanguak returned from a trip in his kayak, he said he had met several kayakers from an adjoining place called Kagsimiut, and likewise reported that he had heard them say of himself, 'Ipisanguak has turned angakok, and almost every day exchanges place with an angakok from Akilinek. Let us go and hear him.' On the following day a great many kayakers and several boats' crews arrived; and when he suffered himself to be tied and left for Akilinek, he was soon replaced by his comrade, who entered the house and entertained the guests all the night long. Some time after this Ipisanguak paid a visit to Kagsimiut; during his stay one of the seal-hunters said, 'Seals are rather scanty with us at present: a clever hunter can hardly get one at a time; thou mightest bring on the seals, I should think, and thus improve the hunting.' At the same time Ipisanguak observed a handsome young woman, to whom he at once took a fancy, standing outside the house. In the evening he conjured spirits; during that interval an immense iceberg appeared fast approaching the beach — he now let the women advance one by one, but she to whom he had taken a liking would not come; at length one appeared with a fine new ribbon round her topknot, and at that very moment the iceberg began to waver and shake: the angakok immediately sank down beneath the floor and reached his own house by an underground way, while the iceberg came rolling on, tumbling right across the beach, crushing the house to atoms. On getting home he had all the lamps lighted; but in less than a moment the angakok from Kagsimiut made his appearance to avenge his people — they hit him with stones and drove him back, and his voice had become inaudible. The following day Ipisanguak went to have a look at the destroyed house, but not a trace was left of it. The girl with the new topknot was possessed of an anghiak (the ghost of an abortion, or a child born in concealment), and it was all owing to her that Ipisanguak had been the cause of the accident that had happened to her housemates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日，伊皮桑瓜克划獨木舟出遊歸來，說他遇見了幾個來自鄰近地方卡格西繆特的獨木舟手，並說他聽見他們談到自己：「伊皮桑瓜克當上巫師了，幾乎每天都跟阿基利內克的一位巫師交換位置。我們去聽聽他吧。」第二天，許多獨木舟手和好幾船的人來了；當他讓人把自己綁好、動身前往阿基利內克時，他的同伴很快便來頂替，進屋整夜款待賓客。此後過了些時候，伊皮桑瓜克造訪卡格西繆特；逗留期間，一名獵海豹的人說：「我們這裡現在海豹相當稀少：高明的獵人一次也難得獵到一隻；我想你或許能把海豹引來，這樣就能改善狩獵。」與此同時，伊皮桑瓜克注意到屋外站著一位漂亮的年輕女子，立刻對她一見傾心。晚上他召喚精靈；在這期間，一座巨大的冰山出現，迅速逼近海灘——他於是讓女人們一個接一個走上前去，但他所中意的那位卻不肯來；最後有一個女人出現，髮髻上繫著一條漂亮的新緞帶，就在那一刻，冰山開始搖晃震動：巫師立刻沉入地板之下，經由地下的通道回到自己家中，而冰山則滾滾而來，橫越海灘，把屋子壓得粉碎。他到家後把所有的燈都點亮；但不到片刻，來自卡格西繆特的巫師便現身，要為他的人民報仇——他們用石頭打他，把他趕了回去，他的聲音已變得聽不見了。第二天，伊皮桑瓜克去看那座被毀的屋子，卻連一點痕跡也沒留下。那個繫著新髮髻的女孩身上附著一個安吉阿克（墮胎的鬼魂，或私生子的鬼魂），全是因為她，伊皮桑瓜克才釀成了她同屋之人所遭遇的那場災禍。

passages.text: (3) A great angakok at his conjurations always used to talk of his having been to Akilinek, and his auditors fully believed him. Once he forced his little son to attend his conjurations, sitting upon his knee; the boy, horribly frightened, said, 'Lo! what is it I see? The stars are dropping down in the old grave on yonder hill.' The father said, 'When the old grave is shining to thee, it will enlighten thy understanding.' Lying down in his lap for a while, the son again burst out, 'What is it I now see? — the bones in the old grave are beginning to join together.' The father only repeating his last words, the son grew obstinate and wanted to run away; but the father still kept hold of him. Lastly, the ghost from the grave came out, and being called upon by the angakok, entered the house to fetch the boy, who only perceived a strong smell of maggots, and then fainted away. On recovering his senses he found himself in the grave quite naked, and when he arose and looked about, his nature was totally altered — he found himself able at a sight to survey the whole country away to the farthest north, and nothing remained concealed from him; all the dwelling-places of man appeared to be close together, side by side, and on looking at the sea he saw his father's tracks stretching across to Akilinek. Going down to the house, he observed his clothes flying through the air, and had only to put forth his hands and feet to make them cover his body again; but on entering the house he looked exceedingly pale, because of the great angakok wisdom he had acquired down in the old grave. After having become an angakok himself, he once went on a flight to Akilinek, and entered a house where a number of men were assembled, one of whom he observed to be dim-eyed. By help of his angakok sense he discovered this man also to be an angakok, and remarked some bone-chips lying at his feet — probably supernatural ones, and only visible to a clairvoyant, which the dim-eyed man had in vain tried to get rid of, because they arose from some work he had taken in hand before the appointed days of mourning for some person deceased had gone by, thereby provoking the invisible rulers. While staying here, the angakok visitor was requested to make a conjuration in order to procure a plentiful seal-hunting: he summoned his tornak called a kivinngak — an iceberg, steep on one side but sloping down on the other, all covered with seals. The iceberg quickly approached with the latter side towards them, bending over, just about to cast off all the seals into the water — but it so happened that among the housemates who had stepped forth on the floor there was a woman with an anghiak, which immediately made the iceberg turn on its steep side; and tumbling over with a tremendous roar, it crushed the house and all the people within, all of whom perished excepting the two angakut, who took care to make their escape at the right moment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 45 'The Angakok's Flight to Akilinek'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: （3）有一位偉大的安加科克（angakok，巫師）在行法術時，總愛談起自己曾到過阿基利內克（Akilinek），而聽他說話的人也都深信不疑。有一次，他硬要他的小兒子來看他行法術，讓他坐在自己膝上；那孩子嚇得魂飛魄散，說道：「哎呀！我看見的是什麼？星星正一顆顆落進那邊山丘上的舊墳裡呢。」父親說：「當那座舊墳在你眼前發光時，它就會照亮你的悟性。」兒子在他懷裡躺了一會兒，又突然嚷道：「我現在看見的是什麼？——舊墳裡的骨頭開始拼合起來了。」父親只是重複他最後說的話，兒子便倔強起來，想要逃走；但父親仍舊緊緊抓住他。最後，墳裡的鬼魂走了出來，受安加科克召喚，進屋來捉那男孩；男孩只聞到一股濃烈的蛆蟲氣味，隨即昏了過去。等他恢復知覺，發現自己赤條條地身在墳中；他起身四望，本性已全然改變——他發現自己一眼便能望遍整個地方，直到最遠的北方，什麼也瞞不過他；所有人類的居所看來都緊挨在一起，並排而立；他朝海上看去，只見父親的足跡一路延伸到阿基利內克。他走下山到屋裡去，看見自己的衣服在空中飛翔，只消伸出手腳，衣服便又覆蓋住他的身體；但進屋時他面色極為蒼白，因為他在那座舊墳裡獲得了極大的安加科克智慧。後來他自己也成了安加科克，有一次他飛往阿基利內克，進入一間聚集了許多人的屋子，他注意到其中一人目光昏濁。藉著安加科克的感知，他發現這人也是個安加科克，並注意到他腳邊散落著一些骨屑——大概是超自然的骨屑，只有能透視的人才能看見；那目光昏濁的人曾徒勞地想擺脫它們，因為它們源自他為某個死者服喪的規定日子尚未過去之前就著手的一件活計，因而觸怒了那些無形的主宰者。在此逗留期間，這位來訪的安加科克被請求行一場法術，以求獵得大量海豹：他召來他名為「基文加克」（kivinngak）的托爾納克（tornak，精靈）——那是一座冰山，一面陡峭，另一面則向下傾斜，全覆滿了海豹。冰山迅速靠近，以傾斜的那一面朝向他們，彎下身來，正要將所有海豹傾入水中——但恰巧在同屋的人當中，有一個帶著安吉阿克（anghiak）的女人走上了地板，這立刻使冰山轉向陡峭的那一面；冰山轟然一聲巨響翻倒下來，壓碎了房屋和裡面所有的人，全都喪命，只有那兩個安加科克及時逃脫。

title.en: The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit
title.zh: 被惡意因格內爾舒特人俘虜的皮艇客

region.en: Sea-shore rocks of the ingnersuit
region.zh: 因格內爾舒特人的海濱巖窟

period: Inuit oral tradition; abridged variations of a popular theme, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 46 'The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Three captivity tales of the sea-shore gnomes: Kuvitsina's rock opens of itself, his kayak smashed, his nose cut off — until the tornak Napatarak severs his strings with 'What have ye been doing to Kuvitsina?' and the warning that earth-folk vanquish the very whales; his nose comes whirling home through the air to fit itself awry. Katauk, capsized without a bladder, is nose-cut and tied beneath the roof-beams — three tornaks relieve him, his killed erkungassok is breathed back to life, and the cut-up binding-thong becomes amulets for good kayakers. Ulajok is drawn by his own turning prow behind a white kayak into the lifted rock.
summary.zh: 三則海底精靈的擄俘故事：庫維茨納的巖石自動開合、皮艇被砸碎、鼻被割去——靈助納帕塔拉克喝問『你們對庫維茨納做了什麼？』替他解縛，並訓誡：『地上之人連我們所懼的鯨都能降服，你們更當敬畏他們。』他的鼻子飛旋歸位，只是稍有歪斜。無浮囊翻艇的卡塔烏克同遭割鼻縛樑；三靈助救他脫險，被殺的智靈被他呵氣復生；被割成小段的縛繩成了少年們習泳的護身符。烏拉約克的艇首自轉，被他身後的白艇一路引入升起的巖石之中。

sensitivity.note: Ingnersuit: gnomes of the sea-shore (Rink's Introduction). Nose-cutting and maiming recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: (1) Kuvitsina left the boat and the crew who had been his companions on their summer journey, whom he had followed down the firth, and in his lonely kayak went along the shore. As he approached a low steep rock, it opened of its own accord, and seeing this, he entered; no sooner had he got inside than he was surrounded by ingnersuit, who tore his kayak from him and smashed it to pieces. They took him away into the house, and put him down on the side-ledge, and their old housewife first sharpened her knife, went up to him, and cut off his nose, and tied him to one of the pillars. In this plight he at length bethought himself of his tornaks; the first he called, however, were not at all noticed by the ingnersuit, and had no effect upon them. It then occurred to him to call forth two tornaks he had amongst the benevolent ingnersuit; their approach was instantly heard, and one of them was named Nepingasuak, the other Napatarak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 46 'The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: （1）庫維齊納（Kuvitsina）離開了船，也離開了他夏季旅程中的同伴——他本是跟著他們順著峽灣下行的——獨自划著他的皮艇沿岸而行。當他靠近一塊低矮陡峭的岩石時，那岩石自行裂開，他見狀便鑽了進去；他剛一進去，就被英格納蘇特（ingnersuit）團團圍住，他們奪走他的皮艇，把它砸得粉碎。他們把他帶進屋裡，放在側邊的平台上，他們的老主婦先磨快了刀，走到他跟前，割掉了他的鼻子，又把他綁在一根柱子上。身處這般困境，他終於想起了他的托爾納克；然而他首先召喚的那些，英格納蘇特全然不睬，對他們毫無作用。這時他想到召喚他所有的那兩個屬於善良英格納蘇特的托爾納克；他們的到來立刻被聽見了，其中一個名叫內平加蘇阿克（Nepingasuak），另一個名叫納帕塔拉克（Napatarak）。

passages.text: The latter of the two was the first to hasten to the spot, crying loudly, 'What have ye been doing to Kuvitsina?' He was in a terrible passion, and at once severed the strings, and further gave Kuvitsina an amulet, saying, 'Make haste, and be off!' — and he had thus escaped even before Nepingasuak arrived. On coming down to his ruined kayak, Nepingasuak merely breathed upon it, which soon made it all right; and thus he again returned to his own world, while Napatarak warned the ingnersuit, saying, 'Ye should never lay hand on the people who live on the face of the earth: ye ought much more to hold them in awe, because they can vanquish the beings we hold in fear, such as whales, which they catch by means of the bladder.' Kuvitsina had another name, which was Akamak. On his way home he met Nepingasuak, and at the same time observed a strange noise overhead: this was his nose, which came whirling along in the air, and adjusted itself in its proper place — only it became a little awry; and thus Kuvitsina reached his home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 46 'The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這兩個中，後者最先趕到現場，高聲喊道：「你們把庫維齊納怎麼了？」他怒不可遏，立刻割斷了繩索，又給了庫維齊納一件護符，說道：「快走，趕快離開！」——於是他在內平加蘇阿克到達之前就已逃脫了。內平加蘇阿克來到他那被毀的皮艇前，只對它吹了一口氣，皮艇便很快完好如初；於是庫維齊納又回到了自己的世界，而納帕塔拉克則警告英格納蘇特說：「你們絕不該動手碰那些住在地面上的人類：你們更應當敬畏他們，因為他們能制服我們所畏懼的生靈，比如鯨魚，他們用膀胱就能捕到。」庫維齊納另有一個名字，叫阿卡馬克（Akamak）。在回家的路上，他遇見了內平加蘇阿克，同時注意到頭頂上方有一陣奇怪的聲響：那是他的鼻子，正旋轉著在空中飛來，自行安回它應在的位置——只是稍微歪了一點；庫維齊納就這樣回到了家。

passages.text: (2) Katauk, a very skilful hunter, used to catch seals by fastening the harpoon-line to his kayak without any hunting-bladder. Once, however, he happened to be capsized and drawn out of his kayak; being on the point of drowning, he gave himself up for lost, when all of a sudden he was surprised at the sound of kayakers approaching from the shore. He saw that they were the ingnersuit, and of the malignant sort; but still he thought it better to be captured by them than drown. He was carried off to their place, put down on the window-bench, and encouraged to talk — but seeing that he remained quite mute, they first cut off his nose, and then tied him up beneath the roof-beams. Being in the greatest distress he called his tornaks, three of whom instantly appeared and relieved him after a hard struggle; on going outside he found his erkungassok (the wise man among the tornaks) prostrate and killed, but quickly made him revive again by breathing on him. When he had pushed off in his kayak he heard a voice calling behind him, and a whistling besides; turning his face round, he beheld his nose, which came flying through the air, sent by his erkungassok; it soon fitted itself into its due place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 46 'The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: （2）卡陶克（Katauk）是個非常嫻熟的獵手，慣於把魚叉繩繫在皮艇上而不帶任何獵用膀胱來捕海豹。然而有一次，他碰巧翻了艇，被拖出了皮艇；眼看就要淹死，他自認沒救了，忽然間，他驚訝地聽到有皮艇手從岸邊划來的聲音。他看出他們是英格納蘇特，而且是凶惡的那一種；但他仍覺得被他們捉去總比淹死好。他被帶到他們的地方，放在窗台上，又被鼓勵說話——但見他始終一聲不吭，他們便先割掉他的鼻子，然後把他綁在屋樑下面。他身處極度的痛苦之中，於是召喚他的托爾納克，其中三個立刻現身，經過一番苦鬥把他解救出來；他走到外面，發現他的「埃爾孔加索克」（erkungassok，托爾納克中的智者）倒在地上被殺死了，但他對它吹了一口氣，很快又使它復活。當他划著皮艇離開時，他聽見身後有聲音在呼喚，此外還有呼嘯聲；他轉過臉去，看見自己的鼻子正由他的埃爾孔加索克送來，在空中飛翔；它很快就自行安回它應在的位置。

passages.text: In the evening, when he had gained his home, he felt a pain around his waist and loins, and looking at them, perceived one of the thongs with which he had been tied still attached; he cut it up in small bits, which he gave to young people for amulets, for the purpose of making them good kayakers. (3) Ulajok, while looking for seals outside the islands, came to a rock which was being washed by a heavy swell; at the same time he observed a bright kayak making great haste towards him — getting sight of Ulajok, the white kayak turned back and made for the rock again. Suspecting that he might be an ingnersuak, Ulajok wanted to turn his kayak homeward, but tried it in vain: the prow of his kayak always kept turning round, pointing anew at the rock, and insensibly he was drawn behind the white kayak. When close to the rock he saw it being lifted high up, and within, houses and people presented themselves; Ulajok was pulled to the shore, where the people put by his kayak and paddle, conducting him into a large house. (The rest of the story is much like the preceding two.)
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 46 'The Kayakers in Captivity with the Malignant Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傍晚他回到家中，感到腰部和腰側一陣疼痛，一看，發現綁過他的那些皮條中還有一根附在身上；他把它切成小塊，分給年輕人作護符，為的是使他們成為出色的皮艇手。（3）烏拉約克（Ulajok）在島外尋找海豹時，來到一塊正被洶湧的浪潮拍打的岩石旁；同時他注意到一隻明亮的皮艇正急速朝他駛來——那白色皮艇一見到烏拉約克，便掉頭又朝岩石駛去。烏拉約克懷疑那可能是個英格納蘇阿克（ingnersuak），便想把皮艇掉頭回家，卻怎麼也辦不到：他皮艇的船頭總是轉回來，重新指向那塊岩石，不知不覺間他被拖在那白色皮艇後面。靠近岩石時，他看見岩石被高高抬起，裡面顯出房屋和人群；烏拉約克被拉到岸上，那裡的人收起了他的皮艇和槳，領他走進一間大屋。（其餘的故事與前面兩則大致相同。）

title.en: The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik
title.zh: 孤兒伊利亞索基克

region.en: Crowded winter-house by the frozen sea
region.zh: 封凍海畔擁擠的冬屋

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Passed family to family until 'cast him out on the dunghill at once,' Iliarsorkik is taken in by a widow whose single lamp burns when all the others are dark. Sandpipers one a day, then partridges, then seals from the breathing-hole the mist revealed — he feeds the starving house, shares his seals with another starving widow on the way home, and kills an ice-covered bear by hollowing a cave in an iceberg and spearing it with his ice-pick at every pass. On the flensing road they find the corpses of those who died trying to reach the bear.
summary.zh: 被輾轉寄養、終被喝令『扔到糞堆上去』的孤兒伊利亞索基克，被一位寡婦收留——全屋燈熄之際，唯她的燈還亮著。磯鷸日增一只，繼而雷鳥，再繼而自霧中尋得的海豹呼吸孔——他餵活了一屋饑民，歸途又分海豹救了另一家瀕死之人；以鑿冰器環冰山鑿穴藏身，逐圈刺擊冰封巨熊，直至其倒斃。剝皮路上，他們見到那些試圖走到熊跟前而餓斃路旁的屍體。

sensitivity.note: Famine deaths recorded as told in the 1875 source. Widow-provider pattern recurs across the collection.

passages.text: In a house which was occupied by a great number of people lived a married couple with only one son; the parents, however, both died while he was quite a baby. Another family adopted him; but on finding that he gave them more trouble than they had expected, they soon grew tired of him, and he became nothing but a bore to them; others took him up, but in a little time neglected him; and thus it befell that all the families in a house came to take charge of him by turns. His last foster-parents had him for rather a long time; but on a certain day when the man happened to return home without any catch, and was cross and moody, he addressed his wife, saying, 'This boy is a mere good-for-nothing; cast him out on the dunghill at once.' Meantime a widow, whose son had just commenced to try his hand at seal-hunting, took him in; she brought him up, and he did well, and was well provided for from that time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一間住著許多人的屋子裡，住著一對夫婦，他們只有一個兒子；然而這孩子的父母在他還是個嬰兒時就都死了。另一家人收養了他；但他們發現他帶來的麻煩比預想的多，很快就厭煩了他，他對他們來說只是個累贅；別的人家接過手去，可沒過多久又把他丟在一邊；於是事情就成了這樣：屋裡所有的人家輪流照管他。他最後的養父母養他的時間倒比較長；但有一天，那男人碰巧一無所獲地回到家，脾氣暴躁、悶悶不樂，便對妻子說：「這孩子簡直一無是處；乾脆把他扔到糞堆上去。」這時，有個寡婦，她的兒子剛開始試著捕海豹，便收留了他；她把他撫養長大，他表現得很好，從那時起也得到了妥善的供養。

passages.text: One autumn the weather turned bad with heavy gales, and snowdrifts coming on earlier than usual, there had hardly been a chance of any catch for the inhabitants. Before the days had begun to lengthen the sea was quite frozen over, and the bad weather still continuing, the many hunters and providers about the place entirely ceased to go out; all their provisions had been spent, and the lamps were not lighted in the evening. The only lamp still burning was that of the widow, and the only person that made any attempt at hunting was her adopted son Iliarsorkik. One of his housemates, a man who did not possess any kayak, used to take him by the hand every morning and give him a run uphill; by continuing this exercise he soon got to be very swift and agile. Meanwhile the inmates of the crowded house all remained in bed for hunger and cold; but every evening the widow went to her little store and took out a handful of angmagsat (dried capelins, the chief winter provision), bestowing a small share upon each — her own son got four, her adopted son three, and the others half a one, all with a little morsel of blubber besides.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一年秋天，天氣轉壞，狂風大作，雪堆也比往常來得早，居民們幾乎沒有機會捕到任何獵物。白晝尚未開始變長，海面就已完全凍結，而壞天氣仍持續不斷，當地眾多獵人和養家者完全不再外出；他們的存糧都已用盡，晚上也不點燈了。唯一還亮著的燈是那位寡婦的，而唯一還試圖打獵的人，是她的養子伊利亞索基克。與他同住的一個人，一個沒有皮划艇的男子，每天早上都會牽著他的手，帶他往山上跑；藉由持續這項鍛鍊，他很快就變得非常迅捷靈活。與此同時，這擁擠屋子裡的所有人都因飢寒而躺在床上；但每天晚上，寡婦都會走到她的小儲藏處，取出一把凍乾小魚（angmagsat，即乾燥的毛鱗魚，是主要的冬季食糧），分給每人一小份——她親生兒子得四條，養子得三條，其餘的人各得半條，另外還都配上一小塊鯨脂。

passages.text: One morning at low tide Iliarsorkik saw some small spots off the rocky shore free of ice, and coming nearer saw a great number of little sandpipers there; he at length caught one and brought it to the house. 'Look here, what I have got!' — the men who lay on the ledge cried out, 'Oh, he has actually got a sandpiper!' and reproached each other for having driven him out, saying he might now have been able to provide for them. The mother cut the little bird through at all its joints, giving every one their share, but still some one went on crying for more. The next day Iliarsorkik brought two, and every succeeding day one more; the widow always divided them and gave their house-fellows something, each in turn. One day he again met the man who used to give him a turn up the hills, who pointed out to him a spot where the partridges were sitting in the snow with their black beaks peeping forth, directing him how to get at them; he brought one home the first day, every following day the number increased, and the men were constantly repeating, 'What a pity we ever cast him off from us!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一天早晨退潮時，伊利亞索基克看見岩岸外有些沒有結冰的小斑點，走近一看，發現那裡有許多小磯鷸；他終於捉到一隻，帶回屋裡。「看哪，我弄到了什麼！」——躺在床板上的男人們喊道：「哦，他竟然真的捉到一隻磯鷸！」他們互相責怪當初把他趕了出去，說他如今或許本可養活他們。母親把那隻小鳥從每個關節處切開，分給每人一份，但仍有人一直喊著要更多。第二天伊利亞索基克帶回兩隻，此後每天多一隻；寡婦總是將牠們分好，給同屋的人一些，輪流分給各人。有一天他又遇到那個常帶他上山跑的人，那人指給他看一處地方，那裡有幾隻雷鳥蹲在雪中，黑色的喙露在外面，並指點他如何接近牠們；第一天他帶回一隻，此後每天數目都增加，男人們不斷重複說：「我們當初把他趕走，真是太可惜了！」

passages.text: One day when he was away among the mountains in search of partridges with his friend, he observed a mist hanging above the waters, at one time growing thicker, and shortly after dissolving — his companions hailed it as a good sign, a sure token of holes in the ice kept open by the sea animals gathered there to breathe. They climbed a still higher mountain to make sure of the place; in the evening Iliarsorkik said to his brother, 'To-morrow I don't intend to hunt on shore; I shall just take a walk on the ice, and give a look round to find out the breathing-holes' — his foster-brother answered, 'Yonder beneath the boat thou wilt find my hunting-tools... but mind they are put deep down in the snow.' Early in the morning he was off, fell in with the frost-haze, followed its direction, and soon arrived at the brim of the aperture, where he saw the seals diving up and down and playing about in large crowds in the open water. Finding it difficult to get a sure footing on the slippery edge, he lost no time, took aim at once, and fixed his harpoon into one of the smaller seals; hauling it up on the ice, fastening it to his towing-line, he made the best of his way home. When the starving creatures heard him dragging a seal along through the house-passage a great clamour and strife ensued; the widow first cut very thin slices of blubber and skin together and handed them round — 'Each of you will get a piece in his or her turn' — took a piece of flesh of the size of a hand and boiled it after having lit some lamps; but even this meal did not satisfy them, and in the night some of them came creeping across the floor to steal the raw flesh, so faint they could not get back and climb the ledge. Iliarsorkik brought a larger seal on the following day, the widow now able to light all the lamps and warm up the house, though still very careful in sharing out very small rations; from this day forth Iliarsorkik every day brought home seals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他和朋友在山中尋找雷鳥時，看見水面上籠罩著一層霧氣，一時變得濃厚，不久又消散——他的同伴們認為這是好兆頭，是海獸聚集在那裡呼吸、使冰洞保持敞開的可靠徵兆。他們爬上一座更高的山以確認地點；晚上伊利亞索基克對他的兄弟說：「明天我不打算在岸上打獵了；我要到冰上走走，四處看看，找出那些呼吸孔。」他的義兄弟回答：「在那邊船底下，你會找到我的打獵工具……但要記得它們埋在雪深處。」一大早他就出發了，遇上那層霜霧，順著它的方向走，很快就來到那個開口的邊緣，看見海豹在開闊的水中成群地上下游動、嬉戲。他發覺在滑溜的邊緣難以站穩，便毫不耽擱，立刻瞄準，將魚叉扎進一隻較小的海豹；他把牠拖上冰面，繫在拖繩上，盡快趕回家。那些飢餓的人聽見他拖著一隻海豹穿過屋子的通道時，頓時一片喧嚷爭搶；寡婦先切下鯨脂和皮混合的極薄片分給大家——「你們每人輪流都會分到一塊」——又取了一塊手掌大小的肉，點亮幾盞燈後煮了；但即使這一餐也沒能讓他們吃飽，夜裡有些人爬過地板來偷生肉，虛弱得回不去、爬不上床板。第二天伊利亞索基克帶回一隻更大的海豹，寡婦如今能點亮所有的燈、把屋子暖和起來，但仍非常小心地分配極少的份額；從這天起，伊利亞索基克每天都帶回海豹。

passages.text: One time when he had got two very big ones and was already half-way home, he was suddenly caught in an easterly gale with a snowstorm blowing right in his face, so that he was not able to see anything at all; continuing to walk straight against the wind, as it hauled round to the south he took a wrong direction and lost his way. Towards evening he concluded he must have gained the coast-side by the loose blocks of ice scattered about; leaving his seals on the beach, he stepped up on shore and came across a house. On entering it he saw only the foremost lamps burning, behind this a widow and a young man sitting, the latter with his chin buried deep in the fur collar of his jacket, but behind, in the more remote corner of the house, the lamps all extinguished. 'I have not absolutely come here on a visit, but I was not aware that the wind had changed, and thus lost my way in the snow-drift.' 'Then thou hadst better stay here till to-morrow; and when the weather alters for the better thou mayst return to thy home.' 'If ye have any fancy at all, ye are very welcome to one of my seals' — no sooner had he uttered these words than a faint sound of wailing was heard from the dark corners of the room: these people were likewise starving, and he had just come in time to save them. The weather being fine on the following day he reached his home, and when he had told his mother how he had solaced the hungry and starving, she answered him, 'Always act in that way, and the number of thy captured animals will always increase.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，他獵到兩隻非常大的海豹，已在回家途中走了一半，突然遭遇東風暴，夾著暴雪直吹他的臉，使他什麼也看不見；他繼續頂風直走，當風向轉為南風時，他走錯了方向，迷了路。到了傍晚，他判斷自己一定是靠著散落的浮冰來到了海岸邊；他把海豹留在海灘上，走上岸，遇到一戶人家。進去後，他只看見最前面的幾盞燈亮著，後面坐著一個寡婦和一個年輕人，那年輕人下巴深埋在外套的毛領裡，而更後面、屋子較遠的角落裡，燈全都熄滅了。「我並非專程來拜訪，只是沒察覺風向變了，因此在雪堆中迷了路。」「那你最好留在這裡到明天；等天氣好轉，你再回家。」「如果你們不嫌棄，非常歡迎你們拿一隻我的海豹。」——他話音剛落，就聽見房間黑暗的角落裡傳來微弱的哀號聲：這些人同樣在挨餓，他正好及時趕到救了他們。第二天天氣晴朗，他回到家中，當他告訴母親自己如何救助了那些飢餓待斃的人時，她回答他：「永遠這樣做，你捕獲的獵物數量就會不斷增加。」

passages.text: Another time when he was just making ready what he had caught to carry it home, he suddenly heard a tremendous roar, and the ice seemed to quake beneath his feet; looking round and seeing nothing but icebergs right and left, he thought it might have been one of them calving. When the roaring sound was again heard, and had come much nearer, he again turned round and saw that what he had taken for an iceberg was a great bear, all covered with ice, standing erect before him. When he saw the beast preparing to attack him he ran on towards an iceberg at some distance, kept running about always pursued by the bear; each time he rounded it he managed to hit a blow in the same spot on the iceberg, and in this manner he had soon made a cave, into which he hastened to creep, while the animal still hurried and followed the scent of his footmarks. Whenever the bear passed him he thrust at it with his tok (tool for making holes in the ice); each time he thus hit it some of the ice-cover dropped down from its back, and at length some bleeding was visible — snorting and roaring, it circled round the iceberg, but at length stopped short and fell down motionless. Iliarsorkik descended and found it to be dead; he cut out a piece of the flesh and made the best of his way home. Having arrived safely, he gave notice at the dwelling-places in the neighbourhood that whoever chose might go and fetch away some of the bear's flesh, and went along with his house-fellows, who had in the meantime fully recovered, to flense and cut it up on the following day. Having gone on for some time he saw a black spot on the ice which soon appeared to be the body of a dead man; further on they came across another one, and so on all the way — the corpses of people who had been on the point of starvation and had expired in making their attempt to reach the bear; a few of them had succeeded in reaching it and getting a bite of the flesh, but afterwards dropped on their way home, worn out with hunger and fatigue.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 47 'The Orphan Boy Iliarsorkik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 另一次，他正準備把獵物收拾好帶回家，突然聽見一聲巨響，腳下的冰似乎都在震動；他環顧四周，左右只見冰山，便以為是其中一座在崩裂。當那轟鳴聲再次響起、而且近得多時，他又轉過身，看見他原以為是冰山的東西，竟是一隻渾身覆冰的大熊，直立在他面前。他見那野獸準備攻擊他，便朝遠處的一座冰山跑去，一直奔跑，那熊始終追趕；每次繞過冰山時，他總設法在同一處地方擊打冰山，就這樣很快鑿出一個洞穴，急忙鑽了進去，而那野獸仍循著他的腳印氣味緊追不捨。每當熊經過他身邊，他就用他的「托克」（在冰上鑿洞的工具）刺牠；每次刺中，牠背上的一些冰殼便掉落下來，最後終於見了血——牠噴著鼻息、咆哮著繞冰山轉圈，最後終於停下，一動不動地倒下。伊利亞索基克下來，發現牠已經死了；他割下一塊肉，盡快趕回家。平安到家後，他通知附近各住處，誰願意都可以去取些熊肉，並在第二天與其間已完全康復的同屋人一同前去剝皮切肉。走了一段時間，他看見冰上有一個黑點，不久看出那是一具死人的屍體；再往前，他們又遇到一具，一路都是如此——這些都是瀕臨餓死之人的屍體，他們在試圖到達那隻熊的途中喪了命；其中少數人成功到達並吃到了些肉，但隨後在回家路上因飢餓和疲憊而倒下。

title.en: The Brothers Who Were Lost on Their Journey Up the Fiord
title.zh: 峽灣遇難的兄弟

region.en: Upper fiord of the murderers
region.zh: 兇手盤踞的峽灣上游

period: Inuit oral tradition; from two copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 48 'The Brothers who were lost on their Journey up the Fiord', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: One by one the kayakers who went up the fiord disappeared; the elder of the two brothers left is drawn by two old sorcerers to a shore of their many sons, his kayak smashed, a dish of berries offered with a human hand sticking up among them. Unable to be beaten at hook-and-crook, he is kept alive; his brother follows, gets his own kayak snatched to safety by the feigning brother, and at midnight escapes while the brother delays the pursuit by breaking every oar. Revenge comes in winter — the elder brother betrays the hiding cave, arrows kill all but one, and the last, escaping as a bird, is shot by an orphan boy's arrow and cut to pieces, his entrails sunk in the ocean's depths and left where the sun never shone.
summary.zh: 凡上峽灣的皮艇客一個接一個消失。留下的兄弟中，兄長先去尋人——被兩個老巫引上岸，皮艇被砸碎，一盆漿果中竟插著半只人手。他摔跤無人能敵，才保住性命；弟弟循跡而至，假裝不相識的兄長把他的皮艇搶到高處藏好，半夜放他逃走，又在追擊中逐一折斷船槳。冬日大軍復仇——兄長出賣藏身的巖洞，箭雨之中僅餘一人化鳥飛出，卻被練弓的孤兒一箭射中，屍遭肢解，腸臟一半沉入海底，一半留在太陽照不到的地方。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note records two variants: the old bachelor suffocated by the women's caresses; the sorcerer who flew at visitors like a bird striking off their heads, killed by a trained boy's arrow. Massacre and mutilation recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Several men were living together in the mouth of a fiord; each of them used to go out kayaking by himself, but it so happened that all those who went up the fiord entirely disappeared one after another. Two brothers, both strong and able men, were still left, and of these the eldest first went out in search of the lost ones. He kept close along shore; but having arrived at a certain spot, he could not master the strong tide, but was carried along by it to a place where two old people were standing, who by magic drew him to their shore. When he got upon land he saw numbers of people, who were all sons of the old couple; they seized his kayak, smashed it asunder, and put the pieces of it on the top of the turned-up boat. He was then asked to enter the house, and a dish of berries was put before him — but perceiving part of a human hand sticking up among them, he left it untouched. The people he had thus encountered were the murderers of his lost friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 48 'The Brothers who were lost on their Journey up the Fiord'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有幾個人一同住在一個峽灣的灣口；他們每個人都習慣獨自划皮划艇出去，但事情竟是這樣：所有往峽灣上游去的人，一個接一個全都消失了。還剩下兩兄弟，兩人都強壯能幹，其中哥哥首先出去尋找那些失蹤的人。他緊貼著海岸前行；但到了某個地方，他抵擋不住強勁的潮流，被它帶到一處，那裡站著兩個老人，他們用魔法把他引到他們的岸邊。他上岸後，看見許多人，全都是那對老夫婦的兒子；他們抓住他的皮划艇，把它砸成碎片，並把碎片放在翻過來的船頂上。然後他們要他進屋，在他面前擺上一盤漿果——但他察覺其中插著一隻人手的一部分，便沒有動它。他這樣遇到的人，正是殺害他那些失蹤朋友的兇手。

passages.text: At nightfall they entered to attack him also, and with this view they as usual took out a sealskin and spread it on the floor for a trying-match at hook and crook; seeing, however, that nobody was able to conquer him in this way, they dared not downright kill him. His kayak being destroyed, he was deprived of all means of returning. His brother in vain awaited his arrival, and therefore at length resolved to follow him; he took the very same course, and had the same fate, being likewise drawn towards the shore by the two old people — but before the young men could seize hold of his kayak, his own brother, who all the while had feigned to know nought of him, caught it up and placed it in safety on the top of the boat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 48 'The Brothers who were lost on their Journey up the Fiord'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 黃昏時分，他們也上前來攻擊他；為此，他們照例取出一張海豹皮，鋪在地上，要與他比試鉤拉之戲；然而他們見無人能在這方面勝過他，便不敢逕行殺他。他的獨木舟已被毀壞，他因而失去了一切歸返之途。他的兄弟徒然等候他歸來，於是終於決意追隨他；他循著完全相同的路線，也遭遇了同樣的命運，同樣被那兩位老人引向岸邊——但就在年輕人還來不及抓住他的獨木舟之前，他那始終佯裝不認識他的親兄弟卻一把將舟抓起，安然置於大船之上。

passages.text: At night he said to the men of the place that they might as well go to sleep, and that he would take charge of the stranger; but at midnight he suffered him to escape, and not till he believed he had gained a safe distance did he awake the people of the house and make known to them what had happened. The boat was quickly got down and put out in pursuit; the brother, who was given charge of the steering-oar, feigned to be pulling exceedingly hard, and in so doing purposely broke every oar he got in hand in order to delay the pursuit. Meanwhile the fugitive escaped them, and on reaching home went off in search of helpmates to the north as well as to the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 48 'The Brothers who were lost on their Journey up the Fiord'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夜裡，他對當地的人說，他們不妨去睡，由他來看管這陌生人；但到了半夜，他卻任他逃走，直到他相信那人已逃至安全距離之外，才喚醒屋中眾人，告知他們所發生之事。大船迅速被放下水，出海追趕；那兄弟被派去掌舵槳，佯裝奮力划槳，卻藉此故意弄斷他手中每一支槳，以延緩追擊。與此同時，那逃亡者已逃脫他們，回到家鄉後，便往北方與南方去尋求幫手。

passages.text: In the ensuing winter they started in great numbers to take revenge on the fiord people. When the latter had been apprised of their approach, the elder brother, who was still staying with them, said he would rescue them, and they had better go and hide themselves in a cave close by — but no sooner had the assailants arrived than the brother hastened to point out their hiding-place, and they commenced the attack, pouring their arrows into the cave, killing all but one, for whom there was not an arrow left. Presently, however, a bird came flying out of the cave; one of them quickly got an arrow from an orphan boy, who had just been practising bow-shooting, and hit the bird with it — and when they came to look more closely at it, the bird turned out to have been one of the men. They cut him to pieces, and at once took out his entrails; part of them were sunk in the depths of the ocean, and the rest brought to a place on which the sun never shone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 48 'The Brothers who were lost on their Journey up the Fiord'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌年冬天，他們大批出發，要向峽灣之人報仇。峽灣之人獲悉他們逼近後，那仍與他們同住的兄長說他會救他們，他們最好去躲進附近的一個洞穴——但襲擊者一到，那兄弟便急忙指出他們的藏身之處，於是他們開始進攻，將箭矢紛紛射入洞中，除一人之外盡皆殺死，因為已無箭可射。然而不久，一隻鳥從洞中飛出；其中一人迅速從一個方才正在練習射箭的孤兒男孩那裡取得一支箭，射中了那隻鳥——而當他們更仔細察看時，那隻鳥竟原來是其中一人。他們將他切成碎塊，立刻取出他的內臟；一部分沉入海洋深處，其餘的則帶到一處太陽永不照耀之地。

title.en: The Solitary Kayaker: Grief, Blood, and the White Whale
title.zh: 獨釣客：哀、血與白鯨

region.en: Northern three-windowed house and the solitary hunting-ground
region.zh: 北方的三窗大屋與獨享獵場

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A talkative rival pre-empts the solitary kayaker's private hunting-ground day after day — until the rival falls silent: his wife is dying. Going to console the widower, the visitor is seized by the throat, flung into the doorway, and has his spine broken against the door-posts; a widow's son whets his knife and cuts the murderer's back open, and a terrible slaughter ensues. The survivors ration dried capelins until the son drags home an immense white whale — the blood-filled boots chill the stepdaughter, who breaks in twain dead at the entrance, and is restored to life by the son's secret angakok spell.
