summary.zh: 一名健談的對手日日搶佔獨釣客的私人獵場——直到對方一言不發：他的妻子快死了。登門慰問的訪客被扼喉、擲入甬道，脊背撞上門柱而死；寡婦之子磨利尖刀，從背後將那喪妻者剖開，血濺滿屋，一場屠殺隨之而起。倖存者靠定量分食乾魚度日，直到兒子拖回一頭巨大的白鯨——魚血灌靴的繼女雙腳冰冷、看山成雙，彎身入門時斷成兩截倒斃；兒子於燈滅之夜施咒，將她救活。此後三人安居，他娶了義妹。

sensitivity.note: Mourning-violence and sudden slaughter recorded as told in the 1875 source. The angakok son's secret identity is the tale's turn.

passages.text: There was once a kayaker who had only one certain hunting-place to which he always resorted, and whither he was never accompanied by any one else; he was well skilled in his craft, and generally brought home a great quantity of seals. Not far off, to the north of his habitation, lived a number of other people in a large house with three windows. One day he had started as usual for his solitary hunting-ground, but for the first time found it preoccupied by another hunter — on coming closer he recognised in him one of his northern neighbours. This man spoke to him and was so talkative that the other found it rather difficult to mind his work; at home he reported, 'To-morrow I intend to be off earlier and try to forestall him' — but on reaching the place the other man had already arrived, and was even more loquacious than on the first day; it was almost daybreak before they had begun their work. Trying again, starting while it was still pitch-dark, the other was on the spot, rowing close up to him — but to-day he did not speak at all; not until daybreak did he utter a single word, and then went away. The next day it was the same thing over again, he never spoke till sunrise: 'To-day she remained in bed altogether; the day before yesterday she fell sick, and all the while she is growing worse and worse' — speaking of his wife, and this was the reason why he had thus changed. 'If thou dost not meet me here to-morrow, thou mayst judge that she is still worse, and then pray look in upon us to-morrow and see how we are doing.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個划獨木舟的人，他只有一個固定的狩獵之地，總是在那裡打獵，從未有別人與他同往；他精於此道，通常帶回大量海豹。在他住所北面不遠處，另有一群人住在一座有三扇窗戶的大屋裡。有一天，他照常出發前往他獨自的獵場，卻頭一次發現那裡已被另一個獵人佔據——走近一看，他認出那是他北方的鄰人之一。這人與他說話，且十分健談，以致對方覺得頗難專心工作；他回家後稟報說：「明天我打算更早出發，設法搶在他前頭」——但到了那地方，那人早已抵達，而且比第一天更為多話；他們幾乎到破曉才開始工作。他又試了一次，趁天還漆黑便出發，那人卻已在場，並划近他身旁——但今天他全然不開口；直到破曉他才說了一句話，隨即離去。第二天又是同樣情形，他直到日出才開口：「今天她整日臥床不起；前天她病倒了，而她的病情一直越來越重」——他說的正是他的妻子，而這便是他如此轉變的原因。「倘若你明日不在此處與我相見，你便可斷定她病情更重了，那麼請你明日來我們家看看我們的情形。」

passages.text: He did not meet his new comrade the next day, and therefore called on him the day after; entering the house he found all the men within, not one of them out kayaking that day. He entered the room and there remarked a man sitting far back upon the ledge and staring straight before him, and soon recognised him to be his former companion: his wife had died and he had already buried her. Observing the general silence, he rose and moved alongside the widower, saying, 'I have come to give thee some solace; thou wilt be sure to stand in need of some one to talk to thee at such an unhappy time: and if thou wouldst like it, I will bethink me of something to tell thee' — but at this the widower uttered some unintelligible words, at the same time looking very fierce and angry, suddenly advanced, took hold of the visitor by the throat, and threw him down into the doorway. Taking it all for a jest, he quickly got up and re-entered the room; but he was again seized and thrust right against the door-posts and broke his spine, which immediately caused his death. The murderer again with downcast eyes seated himself on the ledge; meanwhile a youth, the son of a widow, coolly proceeded to whet his knife, and when he had got it well sharpened, sprang up behind the widower and made a long cut on each side of his back; the blood rushed out, and in a few minutes he fell down dead. At this sight they all got infuriated and took to their knives, and a terrible slaughter ensued; the widow and her son, with an adopted daughter, were the only ones that remained unhurt, and having made their escape through the window, went to take up their abode in the storehouse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天他沒有遇見他的新夥伴，於是隔天便去拜訪他；進屋後，他發現所有男人都在屋內，那天沒有一人外出划獨木舟。他走進房間，注意到有一人遠遠坐在土榻後方，直視前方，不久便認出那正是他先前的同伴：他的妻子已死，而他已將她安葬。他察覺到一片沉默，便起身走到那鰥夫身旁，說道：「我來給你一些慰藉；在這樣不幸的時刻，你必定需要有人與你說話；若你願意，我會想些話來對你說」——但此言一出，那鰥夫卻發出一些聽不懂的話，同時神色兇狠憤怒，突然上前，掐住訪客的喉嚨，將他摔倒在門口。他以為這全是玩笑，便迅速起身，再次走進房間；但他又被抓住，猛力撞向門柱，折斷了脊骨，當即喪命。那兇手又垂下眼簾，坐回土榻上；與此同時，一個寡婦的兒子從容地磨起他的刀來，磨得鋒利之後，便躍到那鰥夫身後，在他背部兩側各劃了一道長長的口子；鮮血湧出，幾分鐘後他便倒地而死。見此情景，眾人皆怒不可遏，紛紛拔刀，隨即發生了一場可怕的屠殺；只有那寡婦和她的兒子，以及一個養女毫髮無傷，他們從窗戶逃出，前往倉庫棲身。

passages.text: But subsequently the winter became very severe, and the frost fearfully keen, so that the widow's son at last had to give up hunting and remain indoors. They had almost finished their stock of provisions, only a few angmagsat (small dried fish) and a small bag with blubber still left, and accordingly could not afford to eat their fill every day; not till supper-time did the widow venture to share out their portions — the son then got two and a half fish, while she herself and her stepdaughter had one and a half. Owing to this sensible management they kept alive, though badly enough, because they always got a morsel of blubber besides. For three succeeding days they went on like this, but on the fourth the young man disappeared — he had only gone out to take a look round from some of the neighbouring heights. In the evening he put his weapons and tools to rights, and on the very next day returned home dragging an immense white whale with him; the women were transported with joy, and at once began to flense and cut it up — but presently the daughter complained of her feet being so dreadfully cold: the blood of the fish had got into her boots and filled them. Her mother pretended not to heed her, and told her to go on helping her; a little afterwards the girl said that she saw all the mountains double, and then she was ordered to go inside — the moment she bent down to descend through the entrance she broke in twain, and was dead on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但後來冬天變得極為嚴酷，寒霜可怕地刺骨，以致寡婦的兒子最後不得不放棄打獵，留在家中。他們的存糧幾乎吃盡，只剩下幾條小乾魚和一小袋鯨脂，因此無法每天吃飽；直到晚飯時，寡婦才敢分發他們的口糧——兒子分到兩條半魚，而她自己和繼女則各分到一條半。由於這般精打細算，他們得以活命，雖然過得十分艱難，因為他們總還能分到一點鯨脂。接連三天他們都這樣過活，但到了第四天，那年輕人卻不見了——他只是出去到附近幾處高地上察看一番。傍晚，他整理好他的武器和工具，就在第二天便拖著一頭巨大的白鯨回家；女人們欣喜若狂，立刻開始剝皮切割——但不久那女兒便抱怨她的腳冷得厲害：魚血滲進了她的靴子，灌滿了靴筒。她母親佯裝不理，叫她繼續幫忙；過了一會兒，女孩說她看見所有的山都成了雙重，於是她被吩咐進屋去——就在她彎身要從入口下去的那一刻，她裂成兩半，當場死去。

passages.text: In the evening the son wrought a spell upon the body of the deceased, and not till then was her mother aware of his being an angakok; they extinguished the lamps and he called forth the spirits, and restored her to life and health. They all remained living together at this place, and he afterwards married his adopted sister; at length they died there without removing to any other place, and without any accidents ever happening to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 49 'The Solitary Kayaker'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了傍晚，兒子對死者的遺體施了法術，直到那時她母親才曉得他是個安加科克（angakok，薩滿）；他們熄滅了燈，他召喚出神靈，使她重獲生命與健康。他們全都繼續同住在此地，他後來娶了他的養妹；最後他們就死在那裡，未曾遷往他處，也未曾遭遇任何變故。

title.en: Kasiagsak, the Great Liar
title.zh: 大話家卡西亞克薩克

region.en: Seal-hunters' coast, Greenland
region.zh: 格陵蘭獵豹海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The wife's watchful hope, the stolen seal with its walrus-tooth towing-line, the stone rolled into the sea for a phantom walrus, the kayak hammered and stuffed with ice for a phantom iceberg calving, the fatted boasts to a starving father-in-law boiling dog's flesh, the raven-trap 'Two! — alas! one made its escape,' the dead daughter's name 'Nepisanguak' — until the last lie, a floating bit of whale-skin as a whale-carcass, leads the whole boat-fleet ness after ness to nothing, and they stop all his fibs by killing him then and there.
summary.zh: 妻癡望於門，他竊取同伴的海豹、炫耀海象牙拖繩；把石頭滾入海中冒充中叉的海象；把皮艇砸爛、懷揣冰塊，謊稱冰山崩塌壓頂；到斷糧煮狗肉的岳父家誇耀『倉庫都塞滿了』；以『抓到兩只——唉，跑了一只』的渡鴉陷阱哄騙；冒用亡女之名『尼皮桑瓜克』騙取珠串炊鍋。最後他拾起一片漂浮的鯨皮謊稱鯨屍，引得全隊大舟一岬又一岬地空尋——眾人厭極，就地將他殺死，斷了他所有的謊。

sensitivity.note: Same liar-type as Rasmussen's Qasiagssaq (cross-ref inuit-qasiagssaq-great-liar) but a different telling with distinct episodes. Killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Kasiagsak, who was living with a great many skilful seal-hunters, always returned in the evening without a catch of his own; when he was out, his wife, named Kitlagsuak, was always restless and fidgety, running out and in looking out for him, in the hope that he might be bringing home something — but he generally returned empty-handed. One day, being out in his kayak, he observed a black spot on a piece of ice, and it soon turned to be a little seal; his first intention was to harpoon it, but he changed his mind: 'Poor little thing! it is almost a pity. Perhaps it has already been wounded by somebody else; perhaps it will slide down in the water when I approach it, and then I need only take hold of it with my hands.' So saying he gave a shout, at which the seal was not slow to get down; presently it appeared close before the point of his kayak, but he called out still louder than before, and the seal went on diving up and down quite close to him. At length he made up his mind to chase and harpoon it; but somehow it always rose at a greater distance, and was soon entirely lost to him. 'Ye silly thing! ye are not easy to get at; but just wait till next time.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡西亞格薩克與許多嫻熟的海豹獵人同住，卻總是在傍晚空手而歸；他外出時，他那名叫基特拉格蘇阿克（Kitlagsuak）的妻子總是坐立不安、心神不寧，跑進跑出地張望等候他，盼著他也許能帶回些什麼——但他通常都是空手而返。有一天，他划著皮艇外出，瞧見一塊浮冰上有個黑點，不久便看出那是一隻小海豹；他起初打算用魚叉刺牠，卻又改變了主意：「可憐的小東西！幾乎讓人不忍心。說不定牠已經被別人弄傷了；說不定我一靠近，牠就會滑進水裡，那我只需用手抓住牠就行了。」說著他便喊了一聲，那海豹倒也不慢，立刻潛了下去；不一會兒牠又出現在他皮艇前端附近，但他比先前喊得更大聲，海豹便緊挨著他上上下下地潛游。最後他下定決心去追趕並用魚叉刺牠；但不知怎的，牠總是在更遠的地方浮起，很快便完全消失無蹤。「你這蠢東西！你可真不容易得手；不過且等下一回吧。」

passages.text: Another day he went seaward in bright fine weather; looking towards land he got sight of the other kayakers, and observed that one of them had just harpooned a seal, the others all hurrying on to his assistance. As to himself he never stirred, but remained quite unconcerned in his former place; he also noticed that the one who had caught the seal tugged it to the shore and made it fast to a rock on the beach, intending to return in pursuit of others. He instantly put further out to sea; when he had got quite out of sight he returned to the beach by a roundabout way, made straight for the other man's seal, and carried it off — the towing-line all around ornamented with walrus-teeth, and he greatly delighted at the prospect of getting home with this prize. His wife, wandering about in expectation, cried out at last, 'There is a kayak!' — shading her eyes with her hand, 'It looks like Kasiagsak, and he moves his arms like one tugging something along with him. Well, I suppose it will now be my turn to give you a share, and ye shall all get a nice piece of blubber.' As soon as he landed she hastened to ask, 'Where didst thou get that beautiful tugging-line?' 'This morning at setting out I thought it might come in handy, as I was bent on having a catch, and so I brought it out with me; I have kept it in store this long time.' She began the flensing and carving business, putting the head, the back, and the skin aside, all the rest as well as the blubber to make a grand feast upon; the other kayakers successively returned, and she took care to inform each separately that a seal was already brought home. But while they were sitting down to supper in the evening a boy entered: 'I have been sent to ask for the towing-line; as to the seal, that is no matter.' 'Didst thou tell me an untruth?' — 'To be sure I did' — 'What a shame it is that Kasiagsak behaves thus!' — he only made a wry face, 'Bah!' which made her quite frightened; and when they lay down to rest he went on pinching her and whistling until they both fell asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一天，天氣晴朗美好，他划向海面；朝陸地望去，他看見了其他划皮艇的人，並注意到其中一人剛用魚叉刺中一隻海豹，其餘的人都趕去相助。他自己卻一動也不動，仍舊若無其事地待在原處；他也注意到，那捕到海豹的人把牠拖上岸，繫在灘上的一塊岩石上，打算再回去追捕其他的。他立刻更向海面划去；等划到完全看不見的地方，他便繞道回到灘上，徑直走向那人的海豹，把牠帶走了——那拖曳繩上滿是海象牙裝飾，他想到能帶著這戰利品回家，心中大為歡喜。他的妻子來回走動、滿懷期待，最後喊道：「有一艘皮艇！」——她用手遮著眼睛，「看起來像卡西亞格薩克，他擺動手臂的樣子像是拖著什麼東西。好啊，這回想必輪到我分給你們一份了，你們都能分到一塊上好的鯨脂。」他一上岸，她便急忙問道：「你從哪兒弄來那條漂亮的拖曳繩？」「今早出門時我想它也許派得上用場，因為我一心想要有所捕獲，就把它帶了出來；我存著它好久了。」她開始動手剝皮切肉，把頭、背和皮擱在一邊，其餘的連同鯨脂都留著辦一場盛大的宴席；其他划皮艇的人陸續回來，她還特意一一告訴每個人，說海豹已經帶回家了。可是傍晚他們正坐下來吃晚飯時，一個男孩走了進來：「我是被派來討那條拖曳繩的；至於那隻海豹，那倒無所謂。」「你先前是對我說了謊嗎？」——「那當然啦。」——「卡西亞格薩克這般行徑，真是丟人！」——他只做了個鬼臉，「呸！」這倒把她嚇得不輕；等他們躺下歇息時，他仍不停地捏她、吹口哨，直到兩人都睡著了。

passages.text: Another day, rowing about in his kayak, he observed a black spot away on a flake of ice; on nearing it he made it out to be only a stone. He glanced round towards the other kayakers, then suddenly feigned to be rowing hard up to a seal, lifting the harpoon ready to lance it — but presently went to hide behind a projecting point of the ice, from which he managed to climb it and roll the stone into the sea with a splash, making it all froth and foam; getting into his kayak again he made a great roar to call the others to his assistance. When they came up to him they observed he had no bladder — 'A walrus has just gone down with my bladder; do help me to catch sight of him; meantime I will turn back and tell that I have lanced a walrus.' He hurried landwards; his wife again shouted, 'A kayaker!' — 'I almost do believe it is Kasiagsak; do ye hear him in there?' Meantime he had approached the shore: 'In chasing a walrus I lost my bladder; I only came home to tell you this.' His wife came running into the house, in such a hurry she broke the handle of her knife — however, she did not mind: 'Now I can get a handle of walrus-tooth for my knife, and a new hook for my kettle.' In the evening Kasiagsak had chosen a seat on the hindermost part of the ledge, so that only his heels were to be seen; the other kayakers stayed out rather long, but the last of them on entering brought a harpoon-line and a bladder along with him: 'I think it is thine; it must have been tied round some stone and have slipped off; here it is.' 'Hast thou been telling us new lies?' — 'Why, yes; I wanted to play you a trick, you see.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一天，他划著皮艇四處游弋，望見遠處一片浮冰上有個黑點；靠近一看，才認出那不過是塊石頭。他朝其他划皮艇的人瞥了一眼，隨即忽然裝作奮力划向一隻海豹，舉起魚叉準備刺下——但不久便躲到一處突出的冰角後面，從那裡設法爬上冰面，把那塊石頭滾進海裡，濺起嘩啦一聲，激起一片泡沫浪花；他重新坐上皮艇，大聲呼喊，召喚其他人前來相助。他們趕到他身邊時，發現他沒有了浮囊——「一隻海象剛帶著我的浮囊潛下去了；請幫我留意找找牠；這期間我先回去，告訴大家我刺中了一隻海象。」他急忙朝陸地划去；他的妻子又喊道：「一個划皮艇的！」——「我幾乎可以肯定那就是卡西亞格薩克；你們聽見他在裡頭的聲音了嗎？」這期間他已靠近岸邊：「我追一隻海象時丟了浮囊；我回來只是為了告訴你們這件事。」他的妻子跑進屋裡，匆忙間竟把刀柄弄斷了——不過她並不在意：「這下我可以給我的刀配個海象牙的柄，再給我的鍋配個新掛鉤了。」傍晚，卡西亞格薩克挑了炕台最靠後的位置坐下，只露出兩隻腳跟；其他划皮艇的人在外頭待得相當久，但最後一個進屋的人帶回了一條魚叉繩和一個浮囊：「我想這是你的；它準是綁在某塊石頭上又滑落了；喏，還給你。」「你又對我們編了新謊話嗎？」——「唉，是啊；你知道，我就是想捉弄你們一下。」

passages.text: Another day, kayaking along the coast, he remarked some loose pieces of ice away on a sandy beach at some distance; rowing up he went ashore, two women gathering berries watching his doings all along. They saw him fill his kayak with bits of broken ice, then wade down into the water till it reached his very neck, turn back and get upon the beach, set to hammering his kayak all over with stones, and having finally stuffed his coat with ice, turn towards home. At some distance he commenced shrieking aloud and crying, 'Ah me! a big iceberg went calving right across my kayak, and came down on the top of me' — his wife repeated his ejaculations, adding, 'I must go and see about some dry clothes for him'; large bits of ice came tumbling out of his clothes while he went on lamenting as if with pain — 'I had a very narrow escape' — his wife repeating the tale of his misfortunes to every kayaker on his return home. At last the two women who had seen him returned, and at once exclaimed, 'Is not that he whom we saw down below the sand-cliffs, stuffing his clothes with ice' — 'Dear me! has Kasiagsak again been lying to us?' Subsequently Kasiagsak went to pay a visit to his father-in-law: 'Why, what's the matter with you that your lamps are not burning, and ye are boiling dog's flesh?' — 'Alas!' answered the master, pointing to his little son, 'he was hungry, poor fellow! and having nothing else to eat we killed the dog.' Kasiagsak boastingly answered, 'Yesterday we had a hard job at home. One of the women and I had our hands full with the great heaps of seals and walruses that have been caught. I have got both my storehouses choke-full with them; my arms are quite sore with the work.' 'Who would ever have thought that the poor little orphan boy Kasiagsak should turn out such a rich man!' — and so saying he began crying with emotion; Kasiagsak feigned crying likewise. On parting the following day he proposed that his little brother-in-law should accompany him to bring back some victuals, adding, 'I will see thee home again'; on reaching home Kasiagsak busied himself in making a trap, taking scraps of frizzled blubber from his wife's lamp to thrust out as baits for the ravens — suddenly he gave a pull at the string, crying out, 'Two! — alas! one made its escape' — and then ran out and brought back a raven, which his wife skinned and boiled; his brother-in-law had to look to the other people for some food, and at his departure likewise received all his presents from them, and not from Kasiagsak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一天，他沿著海岸划皮艇，注意到遠處一片沙灘上有幾塊鬆散的浮冰；他划近後上了岸，兩個採漿果的女人自始至終都注視著他的舉動。她們見他把碎冰塊裝滿皮艇，然後涉水而下，直到水沒到他的脖子，又折返上岸，動手用石頭把皮艇四處敲打，最後把冰塊塞滿自己的外套，便朝家的方向走去。走了一段距離後，他開始放聲尖叫哭喊：「哎呀！一座大冰山崩裂，正砸在我的皮艇上，又壓到我身上」——他的妻子跟著重複他的哀號，還加上一句：「我得去給他找些乾衣服。」大塊的冰從他衣服裡滾落出來，他則繼續哀嘆，彷彿疼痛難忍——「我真是九死一生」——他的妻子逢著每個划皮艇回家的人，都複述一遍他遭遇的不幸。最後，那兩個看見他所作所為的女人回來了，立刻嚷道：「那不就是我們在沙崖下看見、往衣服裡塞冰塊的人嗎？」——「天哪！卡西亞格薩克又對我們撒謊了嗎？」後來，卡西亞格薩克去拜訪他的岳父：「咦，你們這是怎麼了，燈也不點，還在煮狗肉？」——「唉！」主人指著他的小兒子答道，「他餓了，可憐的孩子！我們沒有別的可吃，就把狗殺了。」卡西亞格薩克誇口答道：「昨天我們家裡可忙壞了。我和其中一個女人忙著處理捕來的一大堆海豹和海象。我的兩座倉庫都塞得滿滿的；我的胳膊都累得酸痛了。」「誰能想到，那可憐的小孤兒卡西亞格薩克竟會變成這樣一個富翁！」——說著他便感動得哭了起來；卡西亞格薩克也裝作一同哭泣。次日臨別時，他提議讓他的小舅子陪他回去取些食物，還加上一句：「我會再送你回家。」到家後，卡西亞格薩克忙著做一個陷阱，從妻子燈裡取了些焦脆的鯨脂碎屑，伸出去作誘餌捕烏鴉——忽然他猛拉繩子，喊道：「兩隻！——唉！有一隻逃掉了」——然後跑出去帶回一隻烏鴉，他妻子把牠剝皮煮了；他的小舅子只得向其他人討些食物，臨走時同樣是從那些人而非卡西亞格薩克那裡得到他所有的禮物。

passages.text: Another day he set off in his kayak to visit some people at a neighbouring station; having entered one of the houses he soon noticed that some of the inmates were mourning the loss of some one deceased. He questioned the others, and on hearing they had lost a little daughter named Nepisanguak, hastened in a loud voice to state, 'We have just got a little daughter at home, whom we have called Nepisanguak' — the mourning parents and relations exclaimed, 'Thanks be to thee that ye have called her by that name,' and wept, Kasiagsak also making believe to be weeping, but peeping through his fingers all the while. Later in the day they treated him richly; he went on, 'Our little daughter cannot speak plainly as yet; she only cries apangaja!' — the others said, 'She surely means scipangaja (sapangat, beads); we will give thee some for her' — at his departure he was loaded with gifts, such as beads, a plate, and some seal-paws; one of the men cried out to him, 'I would fain buy a kayak, and I can pay it back with a good pot; make it known to the people in thy place' — 'Give it to me; I have got a new kayak, but it is a little too narrow for my size.' At length he started along with his presents, the pot stuck upon the front part of his kayak; at home he said, 'Such a dreadful accident! a boat must surely have been lost; all these things I bring you here, I have found tossed about on the ice' — his wife hastened into the house to give her cracked old pot a smash, threw away the shoulder-blades that till now had served her instead of plates, ornamented her coat with beads, and proudly walked to and fro to make the pearls rattle. The next day a great many kayakers were announced; Kasiagsak instantly kept as far back on the ledge as possible. As soon as the kayakers put in to shore they called out, 'Tell Kasiagsak to come down and fetch off some victuals we have brought for their little daughter' — 'Why, they have got no daughter at all.' 'Go and ask Kasiagsak for the new kayak I bought of him' — 'He certainly has no new kayak.' At this information they quickly got up to the house, entered, taking their several gifts back, and last of all cutting the flaps ornamented with beads away from the wife's jacket; when the strangers were gone she said as before, 'Kasiagsak has indeed been telling a lie again.' His last invention: one day he found a small bit of whale-skin floating on the top of the water, and bringing it home said, 'I have found the carcass of a whale; follow me and I will show you it' — the boat was got out and they started; after a good while they asked him, 'Whereabout is it?' — 'Away yonder' — a little bit further, 'We shall soon get at it' — but when they had gone a long way from home without seeing anything like a floating whale, they got tired of Kasiagsak, and put a stop to all his fibs by killing him then and there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 50 'Kasiagsak, the Great Liar'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 又一天，他划著皮艇去拜訪鄰近住地的幾戶人家；走進其中一間屋子後，他很快便注意到有些家中人正在哀悼某個亡故之人。他向其他人打聽，聽說他們失去了一個名叫內皮桑瓜克（Nepisanguak）的小女兒，便急忙高聲說道：「我們家裡剛添了個小女兒，我們給她取名內皮桑瓜克」——那哀悼的父母和親屬們嚷道：「感謝你給她取了這個名字，」說著便哭了起來，卡西亞格薩克也裝作哭泣，卻一直從指縫間偷看。當天稍晚，他們盛情款待他；他接著說：「我們的小女兒還說不清楚話；她只會喊『阿潘加亞（apangaja）』！」——其他人說：「她準是想說『西潘加亞（scipangaja）』（薩潘加特 sapangat，即珠子）；我們送些珠子給你，好給她」——臨走時他被塞滿了禮物，諸如珠子、一隻盤子和一些海豹爪；其中一個男人朝他喊道：「我很想買一艘皮艇，我可以拿一口好鍋來抵；請你轉告你們那兒的人」——「給我吧；我有一艘新皮艇，只是對我的身量來說窄了些。」最後他帶著禮物出發，那口鍋擱在他皮艇的前部；回到家裡他說：「真是場可怕的事故！準是有條船失事了；我帶給你們的這些東西，都是我從浮冰上撿來的」——他的妻子急忙跑進屋裡，把她那口裂了縫的舊鍋砸個粉碎，扔掉了至今權當盤子用的肩胛骨，用珠子裝飾她的外套，得意地走來走去，讓那些珠子叮噹作響。第二天，聽說有許多划皮艇的人要來；卡西亞格薩克立刻盡量往炕台最靠後的地方躲。那些划皮艇的人一靠岸便喊道：「叫卡西亞格薩克下來，把我們帶給他們小女兒的食物取走」——「咦，他們根本沒有女兒呀。」「去問卡西亞格薩克要我向他買的那艘新皮艇」——「他肯定沒有什麼新皮艇。」聽到這些話，他們急忙上到屋裡，走了進去，各自取回自己的禮物，最後還把妻子外套上綴著珠子的衣襟割了下來；那些外人走後，她像先前一樣說道：「卡西亞格薩克果然又撒謊了。」他最後一個發明：有一天，他發現水面上漂著一小塊鯨皮，便把它帶回家說：「我發現了一具鯨魚的屍體；跟我來，我指給你們看」——他們把船弄出來便出發了；過了許久，他們問他：「它到底在哪兒？」——「就在那邊遠處」——再往前一點，「我們很快就到了」——可是當他們離家走了很遠，卻始終沒見到什麼漂浮的鯨魚時，他們對卡西亞格薩克厭煩透了，就當場把他殺了，從此結束了他所有的謊言。

title.en: The Revived Youth and the Under-World People
title.zh: 復活的少年與地下之民

region.en: Rock-cliff of the ingnersuit and the cliff-top house
region.zh: 地下之民的巖崖與崖頂之屋

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 51 'The Revived who came to the Under-world People', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Left before the five mourning days were over, the dead son is dug up by starving old housemates and chanted back to life — running headlong at the man, the woman, and himself until they all lie fallen. His father returns, disbelieves, kills him by touching him, and the old people revive him a second time; 'No, no! ye left me before the five mourning days were over, and therefore I will remain with those who have revived me.' Married to an ingnersuak-woman, he leads his foster-parents to the cliff that opens — 'do not look back' — but at the sight of the beautiful country with heaps of flesh and matak they turn for joy, the prow smashes on the rock, and they are left apart for ever, fed daily by the ingnersuit from their cliff-top house.
summary.zh: 喪期未滿五日便被拋下的死者，被斷糧的老夫婦掘出、唱咒復生——他橫衝直撞，把漢子、婦人、連自己都撞倒在地。生父不信，伸手一碰，他又倒斃；老夫婦再度唱咒救活。『不！你們喪期未滿就丟下我，我要留在救活我的人身邊。』娶了地下女子後，他引養父母去那會開合的巖崖——『千萬別回頭』——然而一見崖內美景與成堆的肉與鯨皮，二人歡喜忘誡回頭相望，船頭撞上峭壁粉碎，從此永隔；老夫婦在崖頂築屋，日日由地下之民送飯。

sensitivity.note: Five-day mourning period and grave-revival chant documented as told. Orpheus-type backward-glance taboo parallels the Greek cluster.

passages.text: A husband and a wife, with an only son, were living together with an old married couple who had got no children at all. On a certain day, while together on the fishing-place, the former lost their son, and left the place before the five subsequent mourning days were over, leaving the old childless people behind. Not knowing anyway to get food without assistance, the man said to his wife, 'Let us go up to the tomb' — 'Thou being a woman, must open the grave' — 'Thou being the man, ought to do so.' However, she proceeded to take away the top-stone, after which the man set himself to open the grave. When they had got the corpse taken out and had done chanting over it, it began to move, and after a while it rose up, and began running straight against the man. The woman now said to her husband, 'Stand steady' — the very same moment he was overturned, in the next she was herself thrown over, and lastly the youth also fell down. The old man first rose, and going up to him said, 'Now, dear, come along and stay with us' — and the revived youth went home with them, got a kayak, and became their provider.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 51 'The Revived who came to the Under-world People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一對夫妻，帶著一個獨生子，與一對全然沒有子女的老夫婦同住。某日，他們一同在捕魚處，那對夫妻失去了兒子，未等五日的服喪期屆滿便離開了該地，將那對無子的老夫婦拋在後頭。那男子不知如何在無人相助之下取得食物，便對妻子說：「我們上墳去吧。」——「你是女人，須由你開墳。」——「你是男人，理當由你來做。」然而，她還是動手移開了頂石，隨後那男子便著手開墳。待他們將屍體取出、為之誦咒完畢，屍身便開始動了起來，過了一會兒，它立起身來，逕直朝那男子奔去。那女人此時對丈夫說：「站穩了。」——就在同一剎那，他被掀翻在地，接著她自己也遭掀倒，最後那少年也倒了下來。那老者先起身，走上前去說道：「來吧，親愛的，跟我們一同住下。」——那復活的少年便隨他們回家，得到了一艘獨木舟，成了他們的供養者。

passages.text: Once his real father came back to see what had become of the old people, who he almost expected had starved for want of food. Coming round the point, and seeing blood upon the stones on the beach, he thought, 'They must have been to the grave and taken away the corpse' — but coming closer, he observed marks of seal-flensing besides, and therefore inquired, 'Whoever might have caught these for you?' They made answer, 'Thy own son, whom we have restored to life again' — but he at once prepared to kill them, because he doubted the truth of this assertion and believed they were mocking him. The old man now said, 'Just wait a little; and if he then does not come, it is time enough to kill us!' Before he had finished speaking the son appeared from behind the point; they both cried out, 'Don't touch him at once!' — but the father could not forbear so doing, and consequently he again fell down dead on the spot. The old people again sang some magic lay over him, and by this means restored him to life; once more he moved, rose up, and ran right up to his father, whom he threw down, and likewise his foster-mother, but then stopped. His father would fain have taken him home to his true mother, but the son answered him, 'No, no! ye left me before the five mourning days were over, and therefore I will remain with those who have revived me' — and the father started off by himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 51 'The Revived who came to the Under-world People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，他的生父回來看看那對老夫婦究竟如何了，他幾乎料定他們已因缺食而餓死。繞過岬角，看見海灘石上有血，他心想：「他們必定是上墳去把屍體取走了。」——但再走近些，他又察覺到旁有剝海豹皮的痕跡，於是問道：「這些究竟是誰替你們捕來的？」他們答道：「是你自己的兒子，我們已使他復生。」——但他當即準備殺了他们，因為他不信此言為真，以為他們在嘲弄他。那老者此時說道：「且稍待片刻；若他屆時不來，再殺我們也不遲！」話未說完，那兒子便從岬角後現身；兩人齊聲喊道：「先別碰他！」——但那父親按捺不住，還是動了手，於是當場又倒地而死。老夫婦再次在他身上唱起某種咒歌，藉此使他復生；他又一次動了起來，立起身，逕直奔向他的父親，將他掀倒，也同樣掀倒了養母，隨後便停了下來。他的父親極想帶他回家去見生母，但兒子回答他說：「不，不！你們未等五日的服喪期屆滿便拋下了我，因此我要留在使我復活的人身邊。」——那父親便獨自離去了。

passages.text: One day the youth returned in his kayak, but in a strangely silent mood — 'Why doestn't thou speak, dear?' — to which the son answered that he had gone and taken an ingnersuak-woman for a wife. The old people were sorry that he should have to leave them, and asked him if they might not accompany him; one day, on meeting an ingnersuak, he inquired of him whether he could bring them with him — he answered that they might come, but at the same time told him to warn them not to look back when they approached the rock which enclosed the abode of the ingnersuit, lest the entrance should remain shut for them. He told them this, and impressed on them all the way to keep their eyes fixed on the point of his kayak; they then instantly loaded the boat and made ready to depart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 51 'The Revived who came to the Under-world People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某日，那少年划著獨木舟歸來，卻神情異常沉默——「你為何不說話呀，親愛的？」——兒子回答說，他已前去娶了一位因格爾蘇阿克（ingnersuak）女子為妻。老夫婦為他不得不離開他們而難過，便問他可否讓他們同行；某日，他遇見一位因格爾蘇阿克，便問他能否將他們一同帶去——那人回答說他們可以來，但同時囑他告誡他們，在接近那圍繞因格爾蘇伊特（ingnersuit）居所的岩石時切莫回頭，以免入口對他們閉合。他將此事告訴了他們，並再三叮囑他們一路上要將目光緊盯著他獨木舟的船頭；他們隨即裝好船，準備啟程。

passages.text: When they had reached the cliff and were rowing up to it, it forthwith opened; and inside was seen a beautiful country, with many houses, and a beach covered with pebbles, and large heaps of flesh and matak. Perceiving this, the old people for joy forgot the warning and turned round, and instantly all disappeared: the prow of the boat knocked right against the steep rock, and was smashed in, so that they all were thrown down by the shock. The son said, 'Now we must remain apart for ever; but build your house on yonder cliff: they will no doubt provide you with food.' They built their house on the cliff, and every day they got their meals without trouble from the ingnersuit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 51 'The Revived who came to the Under-world People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們抵達那崖壁、正划舟而上時，崖壁隨即敞開；裡面可見一片美麗的國土，有許多房屋，海灘上鋪滿卵石，還有大堆的肉與瑪塔克（matak）。老夫婦見此，一時欣喜，竟忘了告誡，回過頭去，剎那間一切盡皆消失：船頭正撞上陡峭的岩壁，被撞得粉碎，他們也全都因這震擊而跌倒。兒子說道：「如今我們只得永遠分離了；不過你們就在那邊的崖上造屋吧：他們定會供給你們食物。」他們在崖上造了屋，每日都毫不費力地從因格爾蘇伊特那裡得到飯食。

title.en: The Old Bachelor and the Flying Song
title.zh: 老鰥夫與飛行咒歌

region.en: Coast firth and the mountain peak
region.zh: 海灣與山巔

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A bachelor who hates singing hears a boat going up the firth unrowed against the wind, singing 'Let us be taken aloft!' — lifted through the air with it, he stays with the flying household, learns their magic lay, and flies home with a victual-laden kayak. Pausing on a steep peak, he finds the song gone from his memory and tumbles down the precipice catching at words — 'immaketja! no... kinajaja! no, that's not it neither' — until the true verse returns an arm's length above the stone-heaps. He lands inside his own house, kayak-point crushing the wall, and that was his first and last journey through the air.
summary.zh: 討厭唱歌的老鰥夫聽見一艘逆風不用槳、憑歌上溯的船——『讓我們飛上天吧！』——他隨船凌空而去，寄住飛行人家、習得咒歌，載滿食物飛返家鄉。在陡峭山巔稍歇之際，歌詞忽然從記憶中消失；他一邊哭一邊抓住隻言片語往下滾落——直到離亂石堆一臂之遙才想起正句，凌空獲救。最後他駕艇直衝自家屋內，艇首撞上內牆——那是他第一次、也是最後一次的空中之旅。

sensitivity.note: Flying-boat song (kangatarsa) motif; documented as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: There was once a queer old bachelor who had a singular dislike to singing: whenever he heard people sing, he would take himself off immediately. One day, being out at his hunting-place off the coast, he heard people singing, and it proved to proceed from the crew of a boat which was going up the firth right against the wind, and without being rowed. This song pleased him; he went up to the boat, which he several times noticed to be lifted up into the air, soon to sink down again on the surface of the water, and constantly advancing, although the crew seemed resting on their oars all the while.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個古怪的老單身漢，對唱歌懷有一種奇特的厭惡：每逢聽見人唱歌，他便立刻走開。某日，他正在離岸的捕獵處，聽見有人唱歌，發覺那歌聲來自一艘船的船員，那船正逆著風向上游峽灣駛去，且無人划槳。這歌聲令他歡喜；他走近那船，屢次注意到它被舉升到空中，隨即又沉落回水面，且不斷前進，儘管船員們似乎始終倚在槳上歇息。

passages.text: He now asked leave to be one of the party; the steersman said he might follow them if he chose, but that he must keep close to them — they tied his kayak to the boat, and then continued singing, Kangatarsa, Kangatarsartigut! (let us be taken aloft!) imakaja, ah, ha, ha — they were instantly lifted up and taken away across the country. Being now on the top of a very high mountain they took a little rest, but soon after travelled on through the air until they alighted close beside a house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他於是請求加入他們一夥；掌舵的說他若願意便可跟隨他們，但必須緊靠著他們——他們將他的獨木舟繫在船上，接著繼續唱道：Kangatarsa, Kangatarsartigut！（讓我們被舉升上天吧！）imakaja，啊，哈，哈——他們剎那間便被舉起，橫越陸地而去。此時他們已在一座極高的山頂上，稍作歇息，但不久又穿越空中前行，直到降落在一座房屋的近旁。

passages.text: He discharged the boat and got out of his kayak on land, entered a house to pay them a visit, came to like them, remained with them, and learned their magic song. But at length he bethought himself of his relatives, who were sure to be missing him and concerned about his fate, and resolved to return; his hosts proceeded to fill his kayak with victuals, after which he got in, and singing the magic lay, flew away in the same direction he had formerly come from — but when he reached the high mountain, he got a strong fancy to repose for a while on the summit of it, which happened to be a very steep peak. After a while he wanted to be off again, but found that he had suddenly forgotten the lay, and then he sat down all at a loss on the steep mountain-side; at last he lost his balance, and was about to fall down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他把皮艇推下水，從陸地上走出獨木舟，走進一間屋子去拜訪他們，漸漸喜歡上他們，便與他們同住，並學會了他們的魔法之歌。但到後來，他想起了自己的親人，他們必定正惦念著他、為他的命運擔憂，於是決意回去；主人們著手用食物裝滿他的皮艇，之後他坐進去，唱起那支魔法之歌，朝著他先前來時的方向飛去——但當他抵達那座高山時，忽然強烈地想要在山頂上歇息片刻，而那山頂恰是一個非常陡峭的峰。過了一會兒，他想再度啟程，卻發現自己竟突然忘了那支歌，於是他一籌莫展地坐在陡峭的山坡上；最後他失去平衡，眼看就要跌落下去。

passages.text: He tried to catch hold of the proper words, and sang, 'Immaketja!' — no; not quite that; 'Kinajaja!' — no, that's not it neither — and now he began crying and tumbling down the precipice. When he was quite close to the stone-heaps at the foot of the mountain he remembered the song, and was again carried through the air, and thus saved from destruction. At last he saw his dwelling-place, where his house-fellows had quite given him up for lost; they were just assembled outside when all at once they heard a song from above, and looking upwards perceived a kayaker overhead rushing through the air, and before long recognised their own old bachelor. He directed his course straight towards the entrance, never stopping until he sat right down on the ledge, his kayak's point crushing against the wall of the room — and this was his first and last journey through the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 52 'The Old Bachelor'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他試著抓住正確的歌詞，唱道：「Immaketja！」——不對；不完全是那個；「Kinajaja！」——不對，也不是那個——於是他開始哭喊，並從懸崖上滾落下去。當他十分接近山腳下的石堆時，他想起了那支歌，便又再度被托上空中，因而免於毀滅。最後他望見了自己的住處，那裡與他同屋的人早已認定他失蹤了；他們正聚在屋外，忽然聽見從上方傳來一支歌，抬頭一看，只見一個划皮艇的人從頭頂上飛掠而過，不久便認出那是他們自己的老單身漢。他筆直朝入口飛去，一直不停，直到正好落在窗臺上，皮艇的尖端撞上了屋子的牆壁——而這便是他第一次也是最後一次空中之旅。

title.en: Salik the Kivigtok and His Namesake
title.zh: 奇維托克薩利克與同名者

region.en: Northern solitude and the great glacier
region.zh: 北方荒野與大冰川

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Ice-bound north, Salik returns for a forgotten axe and is surprised in the dark house by his own namesake — a clairvoyant scrap-gatherer who heard everything but his steps. The visitor tells his life: ten children fed plate after plate, a mother's words about a mother's-brother who fled mankind for his wife's scolding — words he could not swallow, so he ran into the interior, killed a buck in a snowstorm with a finger-length knife, matched his speed with any animal, hunted an amarok across the glacier clefts, and was entertained by little hare-women mocking the 'wicked little foxes' and the hare that sits down at the word itek. Paid with a knife from the boot, he ran off as swiftly as a flying raven.
summary.zh: 北地冰封，薩利克回頭取遺落的斧頭，卻在黑屋中被同名者撞見——一位先知的拾荒客，萬物之聲皆入其耳，唯獨聽不見腳步。客人自述一生：十個孩子一盤接一盤地吃；母親一句『我舅父就是被妻子罵了才遁世』的話哽在喉頭，使他奔入內陸；雪暴中以一指長的刀刃獵殺公鹿；練就與百獸賽跑的腳力；冰川裂隙間追逐狼靈阿馬洛克；又得兔化少女相伴，笑談『狡猾的小狐狸』與一聲『itek』便坐地不動的野兔。臨別，他自靴筒抽出一把小刀相贈，隨即如飛掠的渡鴉般疾奔而去。

sensitivity.note: Kivigtok clairvoyance and hare-women (transformation) motifs. Domestic quarrel origin of the flight recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Salik went off to the north; and during his journey the frost set in, and cut off his passage home, and he established himself for the winter at a very solitary place. The following spring he drew still farther north; after some hours' travelling he remembered that they had left their axe fixed in one of the cross-beams of their deserted house. He at once returned and entered the dark house through the open window; just as he was going to take hold of the axe he heard something moving about beside the ledge, down on the floor, and on looking more closely caught sight of a man. The stranger began to whistle aloud, but soon after spoke thus: 'Though I am always aware of what is going to happen, thou hast for once chanced to take me by surprise. This is the way in which I manage: being very quick, it is my wont to go about from one place to another, picking up odd scraps and leavings after people move away to other parts... I think it is the custom when meeting a man for the first time to ask him his name.' 'My name is Salik' — 'Why, so is mine; and since thou hast, to a certain degree, outdone me, who have never before been taken aback, I shall relate the history of my life to thee.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩利克往北而去；旅途中嚴寒降臨，截斷了他回家的路，他便在一個十分荒僻的地方安頓下來過冬。次年春天，他更往北行；走了幾個時辰之後，他想起他們把斧頭留在了那座棄屋的一根橫樑上。他立刻折返，從敞開的窗子進入那間昏暗的屋子；正當他要伸手去拿斧頭時，他聽見窗臺旁的地板上有什麼東西在動，仔細一看，瞥見一個男人。那陌生人開始大聲吹口哨，但不久便這樣說道：「雖然我總是預知將要發生的事，你卻偏偏有一次出其不意地撞見了我。我行事的方式是這樣的：我動作極快，慣於從一處到另一處遊走，撿拾人們遷往別處後留下的零碎雜物和殘餘……我想，初次遇見一個人時問他姓名，該是慣例吧。」「我的名字叫薩利克。」——「哎呀，我的名字也是；既然你某種程度上勝過了我，而我從未被人這樣出其不意地撞見過，我便把我的生平講給你聽吧。」

passages.text: His history: ten children leaving the house every morning with their father, spending the day practising bow-shooting and flinging stones, fed plate after plate on their return — 'But we were ten children, and therefore the plate had to be filled thrice before we were quite satisfied.' One evening they found the lamps tumbled bottom-up, the parents' manners altered; the father said, 'These will probably be hungry: I am not going to do like my mother's brothers, who fled from mankind because he had been scolded by his wife' — and the mother replied, 'If he had any sense at all, he would not speak in that way.' The angmagsat-fishing, the dykes for the salmon, the lancing and drying — 'My brothers enjoyed that busy time; but I had not yet learned to forget those words of my mother's, and my spirits grew more and more depressed.' At the dam he turned to his youngest brother — 'I think I see a partridge yonder: pray take my lot of salmons along with thee while I pursue the bird' — and darting off, ran straight on for the interior, never stopping his flight till nightfall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的生平：十個孩子每天早晨隨父親出門，整天練習射箭和投石，回來時一盤接一盤地吃——「但我們是十個孩子，所以那盤子得添滿三次，我們才吃得心滿意足。」一天傍晚，他們發現燈都翻倒了，底朝上，父母的態度也變了；父親說：「這些孩子大概是餓了：我可不打算像我母親的兄弟們那樣，因為被妻子責罵就逃離人群」——母親回答說：「他若有一點見識，就不會那樣說話。」捕安格馬格魚、為鮭魚築堰、用矛刺魚並曬乾——「我的兄弟們享受那段忙碌的時光；但我還沒學會忘掉母親的那些話，我的心情越來越消沉。」在堰壩邊，他轉向最小的弟弟——「我想我看見那邊有一隻雷鳥：請你替我把分給我的那份鮭魚帶走，我去追那隻鳥」——說罷便飛奔而去，直往內陸跑，一路不停，直到天黑。

passages.text: All the summer he roamed about snaring partridges, and in the autumn built himself a house for the winter. One morning, in a terrible snow-fall, he saw a large male reindeer seeking food beneath the snow — dreadfully hungry, he could not suppress a loud cry on seeing it: 'The knife I have got here — showing a stump of a knife hardly a finger's-length — was then considerably longer: I took hold of it, and crept up to the animal very cautiously... rushing at it, thrusting my knife several times into its flanks, following up its bloody tracks until I got it killed' — a fat buck, providing him sufficiently for the winter. Next summer he travelled to a place abounding in those animals and became well skilled in hunting them, but constantly got very low-spirited, going in search of more daring excitement — he only happened to meet with some poor old kivigtut. He had got to be very nimble-footed, and could run a race with any animal that ever was.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 整個夏天他四處遊走，用套索捕捉雷鳥，到了秋天便為自己蓋了一間過冬的屋子。一天早晨，大雪紛飛，他看見一頭巨大的雄馴鹿在雪下覓食——他餓得厲害，一看見牠便忍不住大叫一聲：「我這裡帶著的刀——他亮出一截還不到一指長的刀柄——那時要長得多：我握住它，非常小心地朝那動物爬過去……朝牠猛撲過去，把刀刺進牠的腰腹好幾次，循著牠的血跡追趕，直到把牠殺死」——那是一頭肥壯的公鹿，足夠他過冬。次年夏天，他前往一個盛產這種動物的地方，獵捕牠們的技藝變得十分嫻熟，但心情卻時常十分低落，便去尋求更為大膽的刺激——他卻只偶爾遇到一些可憐的老基維格托特。他的腳力已變得十分敏捷，能與任何曾有過的動物賽跑。

passages.text: Once he ascended the highlands to the verge of the large glacier and climbed his way on to an ice-bound land; his boots poor and soaked, he took out the skin-stockings to dry — and surveying the immense plain, perceived a tiny black spot at some distance: a raven, then more like a fox, then the size of a reindeer, then like an amarok. Having all the time been in search of something appalling enough to rouse his dejected spirits, he resolved to front and attack the animal — on its approach, however, he found himself turning somewhat irresolute. The beast bent down, the ice flying about it on every side; it bounded right towards him, and he took to his heels trying to gain the ice where it was less smooth and slippery, thinking all his diversion would likely end in being devoured by a monster. He reached some large clefts in the ice — when obliged to leap, the monster merely took a long stride over — and looked out for a very wide crevice, thinking it would be quite as well to fall down the precipice as to be swallowed up by the beast. He barely managed to cross it; no sooner had he gained the other side than he heard a fearful yell, and turning round beheld the monster hanging perched on the edge of the icy rocks, unable to get up again. He sprang towards it, but before he had time to kill it, it was tumbling down the precipice — and thus he lost his prize. At the beginning of every winter he filled two storehouses with victuals, remembering the terrible want of the first winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次他登上高地，來到大冰川的邊緣，一路攀爬上一片冰封之地；他的靴子破舊濕透，便取出毛皮襪來晾乾——他眺望那廣袤的平原，發現在不遠處有一個小小的黑點：先是一隻渡鴉，接著像一隻狐狸，然後有馴鹿那麼大，再然後像一頭阿瑪洛克。他一直都在尋找足以激起他那消沉心緒的可怕之物，於是決意迎上前去攻擊那動物——然而當牠逼近時，他發現自己竟有些猶豫不決。那野獸俯下身來，冰塊在牠四周飛濺；牠直朝他躍來，他便拔腿飛奔，想逃到冰面不那麼平滑滑溜的地方，心想自己這番消遣恐怕要以被一頭怪物吞食告終。他跑到冰上一些巨大的裂縫處——每當必須跳躍時，那怪物只消大步一跨便躍過——他尋找一道極寬的裂隙，心想與其被那野獸吞掉，倒不如跌下懸崖也無妨。他勉強跨了過去；剛一到達對岸，便聽見一聲可怕的嚎叫，回頭一看，只見那怪物懸在冰岩的邊緣上，再也爬不上來。他朝牠躍去，但還沒來得及殺死牠，牠便滾落懸崖——他就這樣失去了獵物。每年初冬，他都會把兩座儲藏屋裝滿食物，記著第一個冬天那可怕的匱乏。

passages.text: One evening, seated at his work, he suddenly heard somebody passing through the entry, and two little women presently appeared before him, both light-haired with a cleft in their upper lips, each carrying a bag with berries — no room left in the little house when they sat down. He treated them civilly as his very first visitors; they poured out their berries and begged him to eat with them, and he brought in grease and meat, of which they would take nothing, being much amused at their lively talking all the evening through. 'When people don't keep an eye upon their stores, the wicked little foxes will come and carry them off; and then, when they happen to take them by surprise, they will run away, the tails turned right out' — laughing till out of breath; he joined their merry laughter and felt very happy indeed. At length they left him, taking their bags, and he now perceived for the first time that his guests had been hares disguised in the shape of women. Another evening two other little women entered — darker complexion, larger tufts of hair, still more amiable: 'These silly little hares, whenever they happen to meet folks, they sit down staring at them — they look so very funny with their cloven lips; and when they take to run, and people only say itek, they sit down on the spot.' 'Now I have got practised in running, and skip about from place to place whenever I know that people have newly left. Accordingly I came here. Thou alone hast taken me by surprise; otherwise I seem to hear everything. When the partridges sit down yonder behind the high mountain-ridges, I shall be sure to hear them as if they were quite close by: but thy steps I have not heard.' From the upper part of his boot the first Salik produced a knife and handed it to the narrator — 'I have got nothing else wherewith to pay thee back the pleasure thou hast given me.' 'I feel a little indisposed immediately after the meal, but just follow me with a look' — and off he ran, up the high sloping hill as swiftly as a flying raven that soars smoothly along, barely touching the earth, and thus quickly out of sight; Salik often repeated the interesting tale of his namesake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 53 'Salik the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某天傍晚，他正坐着干活，忽然听见有人穿过入口，随即两个身材矮小的女子出现在他面前，两人都是浅色头发、上唇有裂口，各自提着一袋浆果——她们一坐下，这间小屋便再无余地。他待她们彬彬有礼，视作自己最早的访客；她们倒出浆果，请他同吃，他则取来油脂和肉，她们却一概不取，整晚都因她们活泼的谈笑而十分开心。「人们若不看管好自己的储粮，那些淘气的小狐狸就会跑来把它们叼走；可要是冷不防撞见它们，它们就逃之夭夭，尾巴直挺挺地翘着」——笑得上气不接下气；他也跟着她们一同欢笑，心里着实快活。最后她们提着袋子离去，他这才第一次发觉，自己的客人原来是化作女子模样的野兔。又有一晚，另两个矮小女子走了进来——肤色较深，发簇较大，更为和蔼可亲：「这些傻乎乎的小野兔，一碰上人，就坐下来直盯着人家看——那副裂唇的模样真是滑稽极了；可它们一跑起来，人们只要喊一声『itek』，它们就当场坐下。」「如今我已练熟了奔跑，一知道有人刚离开，就从一个地方蹦到另一个地方。因此我来到了这里。只有你出其不意地逮住了我；否则我似乎什么都能听见。当那些雷鸟落在那边高山脊背后时，我准能听见它们，仿佛近在咫尺：可你的脚步声我却没听见。」第一个萨利克从靴筒上部取出一把刀，递给讲述者——「我别无他物可以报答你给我带来的乐趣。」「我饭后立刻就觉得有点不适，不过你只管用目光跟着我」——说罢他便跑开，奔上那高高的斜坡山丘，快得像一只飞翔的渡鸦，平稳地翱翔，几乎不触地面，转眼便不见了踪影；萨利克常常反复讲述他这位同名者那引人入胜的故事。

title.en: Coyote and Buffalo: Why There Are No Buffalo in the West
title.zh: 郊狼與野牛：西部何以無野牛

region.en: Plains east of the Salish country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩利什故地以東之平原（象徵定位）

period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (8) Coyote and Buffalo' (Okanagon)

summary.en: Coyote urinates on the skull of a dead buffalo-bull and is chased at full speed by the living bull — 'Because you urinated on my head while I was dead.' He makes peace, sharpens the bull's horns with pitchy pine points, and helps him kill the rival who took his wives; the grateful bull gives him a fat buffalo-cow to wife with the rule that he must not sleep with her for three nights. Coyote breaks the rule, loses her, wins her back, kills and eats her as she comes up a defile — and then cannot defecate himself, so the meat-eating birds and animals strip the carcass while he stands helpless and Wolverene runs off with the pelvic bones. Had he carried his wife home, there would now be buffalo all over the Okanagon country; buffaloes do not go farther west than the place where Coyote killed his wife, and since the marrow was spilled on the water, some lakes have oil on their surface.
summary.zh: 郊狼溺於死牛頭骨之上，活牛狂奔而來復仇：『爾於吾死時辱吾首！』郊狼求和，以松脂尖為其磨角，助其誅殺奪妻之敵。牛以肥母牛妻之，惟誡：『三夜不得同寢。』郊狼破戒失妻，復得之，後竟於峽谷中射殺烹食；而己卻腹脹難便，百鳥百獸群集而食，狼獾更銜其骨而去。若其攜妻還家，則今奧卡諾根之地當遍野牛。野牛西行至郊狼殺妻之處而止；髓脂瀉入水中，故今有湖面浮油。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling about, and went northward from the Salish to the Blackfoot country. He found the skeleton of an old buffalo-bull, urinated on the skull, and passed on. Presently he heard a noise like wind behind him; he looked back but saw nothing. The noise grew louder, and he looked again: a buffalo-bull was approaching at full speed — it was the bull whose skull he had insulted. Coyote ran away, but the Buffalo gained on him; he ran round and round a large bowlder until exhausted, and shouted, 'Why do you chase me?' The Buffalo replied, 'Because you urinated on my head while I was dead.' 'What killed you?' — 'I became old, and a younger bull killed me. My horns were dull.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 76-77 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼四处游荡，从萨利什人的地方向北行去，来到黑脚人的地界。他发现一具老公牛的骸骨，朝那头骨上撒了尿，便继续前行。不久他听见身后有像风一样的声响；他回头张望，却什么也没看见。那声响越来越大，他又回头看：一头公牛正全速奔来——正是他侮辱了其头骨的那头公牛。郊狼拔腿就跑，可公牛渐渐逼近；他绕着一块大圆石一圈又一圈地跑，直到筋疲力尽，喊道：「你为何追我？」公牛答道：「因为我在死时，你朝我头上撒了尿。」「是什么害死了你？」——「我老了，一头年轻的公牛杀死了我。我的角钝了。」

passages.text: Coyote said, 'If you will promise not to hurt me, I will sharpen your horns after I have had a rest.' Buffalo stopped. Coyote gathered pitchy roots of the yellow pine, which have sharp points, and attached them to the ends of Buffalo's horns, then told him to go toss an old log to test them. Buffalo did as directed, and his horns stood the test. He was very glad, and said, 'I will be your friend. My rival, who took my wives, is somewhere around. Let us go and find him! I will kill him and take back the women, and will give some of them to you.' On the plain they found Buffalo's enemy surrounded by a band of women; Buffalo tore him in two, and said to Coyote, 'Friend, pick out one of these women, whichever you like.' Coyote asked for a fat one, 'for my home is far away, and she will get thin while travelling with me.' Buffalo picked out a very fat one, and said, 'This one will be your wife. You must not sleep with her for three nights. After that everything will be well.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 77 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼说：「你若答应不伤害我，等我歇息过后，就替你磨尖双角。」公牛停了下来。郊狼采集了黄松那带尖刺的含脂树根，把它们安在公牛的角尖上，然后叫他去挑一根旧木头来试试。公牛照做，他的角经受住了考验。他非常高兴，说道：「我要做你的朋友。那个夺走我妻妾的对手就在附近某处。我们去找他吧！我要杀死他，夺回那些女人，再分几个给你。」在平原上，他们发现公牛的仇敌被一群女人簇拥着；公牛把他撕成两半，对郊狼说：「朋友，从这些女人中挑一个吧，随你喜欢哪个。」郊狼要一个胖的，「因为我家远，她跟着我赶路会变瘦的。」公牛挑出一个非常胖的，说道：「这个就做你的妻子。你三夜之内不可与她同寝。过了这三夜，一切都会顺遂。」

passages.text: Coyote started homeward with his new wife. The second night he said to himself, 'The time that he named is too long. No one since the beginning of the world has had a wife for three nights without sleeping with her' — and she became invisible and returned to her band. He went back and found Buffalo-Bull, who was angry but forgave him, giving her back with the reminder, 'Now you must remember, three days.' This time was sufficient to cross the mountains; then he lay with his wife and was glad. On the succeeding day he was hungry, and thought how fat she was: 'My wife is only a trouble to me. I will kill and eat her.' He sent her up a defile, ran around the hill, met her coming up, shot her twice from above, and cut her up — she was very fat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 77-78 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼带着新妻子踏上归途。第二夜，他自言自语道：「他定的期限太长了。自开天辟地以来，还没有人娶了妻子三夜却不与她同寝的」——于是她变得无影无踪，回到了她的族群。他折返回去，找到公牛，公牛虽恼怒却宽恕了他，把妻子还给他，并提醒道：「如今你务必记住，三天。」这一回时间足够翻过山岭；随后他与妻子同寝，心中欢喜。到了第二天，他饿了，心想她多么肥：「我的妻子只会给我添麻烦。我要杀了她吃掉。」他打发她上一处峡谷，自己绕山跑过去，迎上她走来，从上方朝她射了两箭，把她切成块——她非常肥。

passages.text: Now Coyote tried to defecate, but could not; he was seized with violent pains and could not stand up. Magpie came and alighted on the carcass, then Eagle, Buzzard and Raven, all the birds that eat meat; Wolf came, and all the animals that eat meat, and they ate the buffalo-cow while Coyote could only call them nasty names. The bones were picked clean and scattered; Wolverene stuck his head into the pelvic bones and ran away with them. At last Coyote passed a little dung, was angry at his excrement, beat it flat on a rock, and blamed it for the loss of the fine meat. He found some bones, cooked and broke them, filled his wife's bladder with the marrow and set it in a lake to cool — and when Muskrat swam past he scared it for fun, until it ducked its head suddenly and tore the bladder, spilling all the marrow, which Coyote could not catch. The foolish Coyote had lost both his wife and his meat. Had he been wise and carried his wife home, there would now be buffaloes all over the Okanagon country. Buffaloes do not go farther west than the place where Coyote killed his wife; and since the marrow was spilled on the water, some lakes have on their surface oil, or something that appears like oil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 78-79 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 这时郊狼想排便，却排不出；他腹中剧痛，站都站不起来。喜鹊飞来，落在尸体上，接着是鹰、鹫和渡鸦，所有吃肉的鸟都来了；狼来了，所有吃肉的兽也都来了，它们吃着那头母牛，而郊狼只能骂它们下流。骨头被啃得干干净净，散落一地；狼獾把头钻进骨盆里，叼着它跑走了。最后郊狼排出一点粪便，他对自己的排泄物大为恼怒，把它在石头上拍扁，怪它害自己丢了那上好的肉。他找到一些骨头，煮熟敲碎，把骨髓灌进妻子的膀胱，放在湖里冷却——麝鼠游过时，他为了取乐去吓它，直到它猛地扎下头，撕破了膀胱，骨髓全洒了出来，郊狼怎么也捞不回来。愚蠢的郊狼既丢了妻子，又丢了肉。倘若他当初明智些，把妻子带回家，如今奥卡纳根一带便会遍地是野牛了。野牛向西不会越过郊狼杀妻的那个地方；又因为骨髓洒在了水里，有些湖面上便浮着油，或类似油的东西。

title.en: Coyote's Sons and Grizzly-Bear's Daughter
title.zh: 郊狼諸子與灰熊之女

region.en: Grizzly-Bear's home across the river (symbolic pin at Okanagon River)
region.zh: 河彼岸灰熊之家（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

period: Collected by Franz Boas; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (10) Coyote and Grizzly-Bear' (Okanagon, collected by Boas)

summary.en: Coyote's eldest son goes to marry Grizzly-Bear's daughter; the Bear steps on his arrow-points, sends him to shoot a bear from below, and the bear kills him. The second son fares the same. The youngest makes two stone-pointed arrows, stands above the bear instead of below, shoots it twice, cuts off its head, and throws it into his father's tent, where Coyote tests the mourners by producing stone, dung and a little bush from himself as the Bear investigates the laughter. Finally Coyote escapes over a river-log he has secretly had the Wood-worm riddle through the middle — Grizzly-Bear follows his directions, and the log breaks under him in midstream.
summary.zh: 郊狼長子往娶灰熊之女；熊踐其箭鏃，遣其自下射熊，熊反殺之。次子亦然。幼子製石鏃箭二支，居高位而射，二箭斃熊，割其首擲入父帳。熊聞笑聲入帳察看，郊狼先後化石、化糞、化小灌木戲之。最後郊狼賄木蠧蟲暗蛀過河之木，佯稱木堅；灰熊依其言踏木過河，至中流木斷墜水。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative collected by Boas (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote lived with his children. His eldest son said, 'Father, I am going to see the daughter of Grizzly-Bear.' He made arrows and started. When he arrived, the Bear said, 'Have you arrived, son-in-law?' He told his daughter to go to dig roots, then went out and stepped on the arrow-points of the son-in-law. He said, 'Come, son-in-law, shoot for me that bear, that I may eat it!' — and told him, 'Stand below the bear and shoot it.' Coyote's son went and shot at the bear, which pursued him and killed him. Coyote's second son found out what had happened, made arrows, went to marry the Grizzly-Bear's daughter, and was killed in the same way as his elder brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 79 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼和他的孩子们住在一起。他的长子说：「父亲，我要去见灰熊的女儿。」他做了些箭便出发了。到了那里，灰熊说：「你来了吗，女婿？」他吩咐女儿去挖根茎，然后走出去，踩在女婿的箭尖上。他说：「来吧，女婿，替我射那头熊，好让我吃它的肉！」——又对他说：「站到熊的下方去射它。」郊狼的儿子前去射那熊，熊追赶他，把他杀死了。郊狼的次子探明了发生的事，做了些箭，前去娶灰熊的女儿，也以同样的方式被杀死，和他哥哥一样。

passages.text: Finally the youngest son went. He made two arrows with stone points and said, 'Father, I shall go to find out what happened to my brothers.' When he arrived, the Bear said, 'Have you arrived, son-in-law?' and sent his daughter to dig roots; then went out and stepped on the weapons of his son-in-law. 'Come, son-in-law, shoot that bear for me, that I may eat it!' The boy took his arrows and sat down in his canoe, crossed the river, climbed the hill, and stood above the bear. He went down towards the bear and shot it; he shot it again, and the bear rolled down. He ran after it and cut off its head, then sat down in his canoe and went down the river to his father's tent, throwing the head into the tent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 79-80 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最後，最小的兒子出發了。他做了兩支石鏃箭，說道：「父親，我要去查明我的兄長們遭遇了什麼事。」當他抵達時，熊說道：「你來了嗎，女婿？」便派女兒去挖根莖；隨後走了出去，踩在女婿的武器上。「來吧，女婿，替我射那頭熊，好讓我吃牠！」男孩拿起他的箭，坐進獨木舟，渡過河，爬上山丘，站在熊的上方。他朝熊走下去並射牠；他又射了一箭，熊便滾落下去。他追上前去，砍下牠的頭，然後坐進獨木舟順流而下，來到父親的帳篷，把頭顱扔進帳篷裡。

passages.text: When the Bear came and heard the people laughing, he entered and saw a stone on the floor; he was going to bite it, but said, 'No, my teeth will break,' and went out again. After he had gone some distance he heard laughter, turned back, and saw dung on the floor: 'No, it is very bad.' Again he heard laughter and entered; there was a little bush which scratched him. Then Coyote jumped out laughing and ran away, and the Bear pursued him. Coyote transformed himself into a bush; the Bear went on, saw the bush, and Coyote laughed at him from a distance. Again pursued, Coyote transformed himself into a stick; the Bear saw it and said, 'This is a nice stick.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 80 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當熊前來，聽見人們的笑聲，便走了進去，看見地上有一塊石頭；他正要咬它，卻說道：「不，我的牙齒會斷的。」於是又走了出去。他走了一段距離後，聽見笑聲，便折返回來，看見地上有糞便：「不，這太糟糕了。」他又聽見笑聲，便走了進去；那裡有一叢小灌木，刮傷了他。這時郊狼笑著跳了出來，逃走了，熊便追趕他。郊狼把自己變成一叢灌木；熊繼續前行，看見那叢灌木，郊狼便從遠處嘲笑他。熊再次追趕，郊狼把自己變成一條木棍；熊看見了，說道：「這是一根好木棍。

passages.text: I will use it as a walking-stick' — then, 'No, it is too heavy. I will leave it,' and dropped it. Still pursued, Coyote walked over a log that lay across a river; he paid the Wood-worm and said, 'Make a hole in the middle of this log that lies across the river.' When Grizzly-Bear arrived he asked which way Coyote had gone, and Coyote replied, 'I came over this log. Is it strong? Yes, it is very strong. Come!' The Bear jumped on the log and was walking along; when he reached the middle of the stream, the log broke in the middle, and he fell into the water. Then Coyote went on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 80 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我要拿它當拐杖」——接著又說：「不，它太重了。我還是把它留下吧。」便把它丟下。熊仍舊追趕，郊狼走過一根橫跨河流的木頭；他付錢給木蠹蟲，說道：「在這根橫跨河流的木頭中間鑽一個洞。」當灰熊抵達時，他問郊狼往哪個方向去了，郊狼回答：「我是從這根木頭上過來的。它結實嗎？是的，它非常結實。來吧！」熊跳上木頭，正走著；當他到達河流中央時，木頭從中間斷裂，他掉進了水裡。於是郊狼繼續前行。

title.en: Coyote's Work Finished: The Chief Comes Down
title.zh: 功成身退：主神下凡驗工

region.en: Okanagon country, Washington (symbolic pin at Okanogan River)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根故地，華盛頓州（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

period: Told by Red-Arm (Nespelim/Lower Okanagon); collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 2. Old-One' (Coyote's rest and return; Okanagon, told by Red-Arm)

summary.en: Coyote transforms the good ancients into Indian pairs settled across the country with different names and languages — the ancestors of the tribes — and teaches people to eat, dress, build, hunt and fish; but he is too fond of tricks, often selfish, boastful, vain and foolish, and duped by those he meant to dupe. When his work is done, the Chief comes down as a poor old man, challenges the boastful traveller ('If you are Chief, take that lake and place it yonder' — Coyote does it, but cannot put it back), and dismisses him to a prepared home: Coyote disappears, and no one knows where he is. The Chief will return with all the spirits of the dead when the Earth-Woman is very old; then the Earth-Woman will revert to her natural shape and live as a mother among her children, and there will be much happiness.
summary.zh: 郊狼化善古者為印第安夫妻，散居各地，賜以族名與語言——諸族之祖；又教民飲食、衣著、築屋、狩獵、捕魚。然其性好戲謔，時而自私自誇，愚而受騙。功成之際，主神化身貧老下凡相驗：『汝若主神，能移彼湖否？』郊狼移之，卻不能復位；主神一移即回。乃曰：『汝功已成，行遠勞苦，善事亦多。今有居所為汝備矣。』郊狼遂隱，無人知其所在。主神言：待大地之母極老之時，彼將偕亡者諸靈重返；屆時大地復為母親之身，與兒女同樂，萬事皆善。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Eschatological closing of the Coyote mission cycle; the informant's narration includes Christian elements noted by Teit. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote then travelled on the earth, and did many wonderful things. He destroyed the powers of all the monsters and evil beings that preyed on the people. He transformed the good ancients into Indians, and divided them into groups or pairs, and settled them in different places; for the Chief desired the earth to be inhabited everywhere, and not only in a few places. He gave each people a different name and a different language. These pairs were the ancestors of all the present Indian tribes; and that is why there are so many Indian tribes and languages now, and why Indians live all over the country. He taught the people how to eat, how to wear clothes, make houses, hunt, fish, and more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 82 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼隨後在大地上遊歷，做了許多奇妙的事。他摧毀了所有捕食人類的怪物與邪惡存在的力量。他把善良的古人變成了印第安人，將他們分成群體或成對，安置在不同的地方；因為首領希望大地處處都有人居住，而不只是少數幾個地方。他賜給每個民族不同的名字和不同的語言。這些成對的人便是現今所有印第安部落的祖先；這就是為什麼如今有這麼多印第安部落和語言，也是為什麼印第安人遍布全國。他教導人們如何飲食、如何穿衣、如何建造房屋、狩獵、捕魚，以及更多的事。

passages.text: Coyote did a great deal of good, but he did not finish everything properly. Sometimes he made mistakes; and although he was wise and powerful, he did many foolish things. He was too fond of playing tricks for his own amusement; he was also often selfish, boastful, and vain; he sometimes overreached himself, and occasionally was duped by persons whom he intended to dupe. He was ugly, and women generally did not like him; he often used cunning to gain his ends. He was immortal, and did not die as we die. Coyote had done nearly everything he could think of, and was travelling from place to place to learn of other things that remained to be done. Chief looked over the earth, and said, 'Coyote has now done almost everything that he is capable of doing. I will relieve him.' Chief came down, and travelled in the shape of a poor old man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 82-83 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼行了許多善事，但他並沒有把每件事都妥善完成。有時他會犯錯；儘管他睿智而強大，他仍做了許多愚蠢的事。他太喜歡為了自娛而耍弄詭計；他也常常自私、自誇、虛榮；他有時會弄巧成拙，偶爾還會被他本想愚弄的人所騙。他相貌醜陋，女人們大多不喜歡他；他常常用狡詐來達到目的。他是不死的，並不像我們那樣死去。郊狼幾乎做盡了他所能想到的一切，正四處遊歷，以了解還有哪些事尚待完成。首領俯瞰大地，說道：「郊狼如今幾乎做盡了他力所能及的一切。我要讓他卸下職責。」首領降臨，以一個可憐老人的模樣遊歷。

passages.text: He met Coyote, who said to him, 'I am Coyote. Who are you?' Chief answered, 'I am Chief of the earth. It was I who sent you to set the world right.' Coyote said, 'No, you never sent me. I don't know you. If you are Chief, take that lake and place it yonder.' Chief said, 'No. If you are the wonderful Coyote, let me see you do it!' Coyote did it. Chief said, 'Place it back again.' Coyote tried, but could not do it; he thought this strange. Chief placed it back. Coyote said, 'Now I know you are Chief.' Chief said, 'Your work is finished. You have travelled far and long, and done much good. Now, you shall go to where I have prepared a home for you.' Coyote disappeared, and no one knows where he is.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 83 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他遇見了郊狼，郊狼對他說：「我是郊狼。你是誰？」首領回答：「我是大地之首領。正是我派你去把世界導正。」郊狼說：「不，你從未派過我。我不認識你。如果你是首領，就把那座湖拿起來，放到那邊去。」首領說：「不。如果你就是那位神奇的郊狼，就讓我看看你做得到！」郊狼做到了。首領說：「把它放回原處。」郊狼試了，卻做不到；他覺得這很奇怪。首領把它放回原處。郊狼說：「現在我知道你是首領了。」首領說：「你的工作已經完成。你遠行已久，行了許多善事。現在，你要前往我為你準備好的家園。」郊狼消失了，沒有人知道他身在何處。

passages.text: The Chief prepared to leave also. He said, 'I will send messages to earth by the souls of people that reach me, but whose time to die has not come. They will carry messages to you from time to time; and when their souls return to their bodies, they will revive, and tell you their experiences. Coyote and myself will not be seen again until the Earth-Woman is very old. Then we shall return to earth, for it will require a new change by that time. Coyote will precede me by some little time; and when you see him, you will know that the time is at hand. When I return, all the spirits of the dead will accompany me, and after that there will be no spirit-land. All the people will live together. Then will the Earth-Woman revert to her natural shape, and live as a mother among her children. Then will things be made right, and there will be much happiness.' The Earth-Woman is now very old, and even her bones (the rocks) are crumbling away; therefore the time cannot be far away when the earth will be transformed again, and when the spirits of the dead will come back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 83-84 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 酋長也準備離開。他說：「我會藉由那些來到我這裡、但死期尚未到來之人的靈魂，向大地傳遞訊息。他們會不時把訊息帶給你們；當他們的靈魂回到身體時，他們會甦醒，並告訴你們他們的經歷。郊狼和我自己不會再被看見，直到大地之母非常年老。那時我們將重返大地，因為到那時又需要一次新的變革。郊狼會比我早一些時候；當你們看見他時，你們就知道時候近了。當我回來時，所有死者的靈魂都會伴隨我而來，在那之後就不再有靈魂之地了。所有人都會一同生活。那時大地之母將恢復她原本的形貌，像母親一樣生活在她的子女之間。那時一切將被導正，會有許多幸福。」大地之母如今已非常年老，甚至她的骨頭（岩石）也在崩解；因此，大地再次轉變、死者靈魂歸來的時候，必定不遠了。

title.en: The Creation: The Man Who Was Also a Wolf
title.zh: 創世：狼人之初

region.en: Similkameen country, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Princeton)
region.zh: 西米爾卡米恩故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於普林斯頓）

period: Collected from Similkameen; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 3. The Creation' (Okanagon, from Similkameen)

summary.en: The Chief above made the earth, small at first, letting it increase and rolling it out until it was very large; he covered it with a white dust that became the soil. He made three worlds, one above another — the sky world, the earth we live on, and the underworld — all connected by a pole or tree that passes through the middle of each. Then he created the animals, and at last a man who was also a wolf; from this man's tail he made a woman. These first people, called 'Tai'en' by the old people who knew the story well, were the ancestors of all the Indians.
summary.zh: 上界主神造大地，初甚小，任其增大，輾轉鋪展至廣；覆以白塵，即為土壤。又造三界，上下相疊——天界、人間、冥界——中有神柱（或神樹）貫通。後造百獸，終造一人，其身亦狼；自此人之尾造出一女。二人乃初民，古之知者稱之為『Tai'en』，印第安諸族皆其後裔。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon (Similkameen) creation narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Chief above made the earth. It was small at first, and he let it increase in size. He continued to enlarge it, and rolled it out until it was very large. Then he covered it with a white dust, which became the soil. He made three worlds, one above another — the sky world, the earth we live on, and the underworld. All are connected by a pole or tree which passes through the middle of each. Then he created the animals. At last he made a man, who, however, was also a wolf. From this man's tail he made a woman. These were the first people. They were called 'Tai'en' by the old people, who knew the story well, and they were the ancestors of all the Indians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 84 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 上方的酋長造了大地。起初它很小，他讓它增大。他繼續使它變大，將它滾展開來，直到它非常巨大。然後他用一層白色的塵土覆蓋它，那塵土就成了土壤。他造了三個世界，一個在另一個之上——天空世界、我們所居住的大地，以及地下世界。三者都由一根穿過各自中央的柱子或樹木相連。然後他創造了動物。最後他造了一個男人，然而這人同時也是一隻狼。他用這男人的尾巴造了一個女人。這些就是最早的人。熟知這個故事的老人們稱他們為「Tai'en」，他們是所有印第安人的祖先。

title.en: Origin of the Earth and People: The Red Earth of the Indians
title.zh: 大地與人民之始：紅土造印第安人

region.en: Okanagon Lake country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根湖故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected at Okanagon Lake; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 4. Origin of the Earth and People' (Okanagon, from Okanagon Lake)

summary.en: The Chief made seven worlds, of which the earth is the central one — three above, three below (some say the first priests or white people told us this, but some of us believe it now). He stretched the earth out with its head to the west: the west is the head of the earth, the place of the dead, and the direction the great rivers flow and the souls take, following the course of the waters. Perhaps in the beginning the earth was a woman: the Chief stretched her body across the world, feet east and head west, transformed her into the earth we live on, and made the first Indians out of her flesh, the soil — out of balls of red earth or mud, which is why we are reddish-colored. Other races were made from soil of different colors, and their mingling accounts for the intermediate shades; and as red earth is more nearly related to gold and copper, the Indians are nearer to gold and finer than other races.
summary.zh: 主神造七界，人間居中——上三下三（或云此說出自初來之傳教士與白人，然今亦有人信之）。神鋪展大地，首在西：西方乃大地之首、亡者之鄉，大河西流，魂魄亦隨水西去。或謂太初大地本為女子：神展其身橫亙世界，足東首西，化其為大地；又取其肉（即土壤）搓紅泥為丸，造出第一批印第安人——故吾儕膚色微紅。他族以異色之土造成，諸族相遇雜處，遂生中間膚色。紅土與金銅同氣，故印第安人近金而貴於他族。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Chief (or God) made seven worlds, of which the earth is the central one. There are three worlds above, and three below. Maybe the first priests or white people told us this, but some of us believe it now. When the Chief made the earth, he stretched it out with its head to the west; therefore the west is the head of the earth. Heaven, or the place of the dead, is in that direction, and the great rivers all flow westward. West is the direction the souls take; some say they follow the course the waters take.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 84 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 酋長（或神）造了七個世界，大地是其中居中的一個。上方有三個世界，下方也有三個。也許是最初的祭司或白人告訴我們這件事的，但我們當中有些人現在相信它。當酋長造大地時，他將它伸展，使其頭朝西；因此西方是大地的頭。天國，或死者之地，就在那個方向，而大河全都向西流。西方是靈魂所取的方向；有人說他們循著水流的方向而去。

passages.text: Perhaps in the beginning the earth was a woman. Some Indians say so, and state that the Chief stretched her body across the world (probably the water), and that she lay with her feet east and her head west. He transformed her into the earth we live on, and he made the first Indians out of her flesh (which is the soil). Thus the first Indians were made by him from balls of red earth or mud, and this is why we are reddish-colored. Other races were made from soil of different colors. Afterwards some of these different races met at certain points and intermingled, and thus the intermediate shades of color have arisen. As red earth is more nearly related to gold and copper than other kinds of earth, therefore the Indians are nearer to gold, and finer than other races.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 84 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 也許起初大地是一個女人。有些印第安人這麼說，並聲稱酋長將她的身體伸展橫跨世界（大概是水域），她躺著，腳朝東、頭朝西。他將她轉變成我們所居住的大地，並用她的肉（也就是土壤）造出了最早的印第安人。因此，最早的印第安人是他用紅土或泥團造出來的，這就是為什麼我們呈紅色的緣故。其他種族則是用不同顏色的土壤造出來的。後來，這些不同種族中的一些在某些地點相遇並混雜，於是便產生了中間的各種色調。由於紅土比其他種類的土壤更接近金與銅，因此印第安人更接近金，也比其他種族更精緻。

title.en: War with the Sky People: The Chain of Arrows Broken
title.zh: 與天族之戰：箭鏈之斷

region.en: Okanagon Lake country, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根湖故地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

period: Collected at Okanagon Lake; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 5. War with the Sky People' (Okanagon, from Okanagon Lake)

summary.en: The people resolve to make war on the Sky people — some say to procure fire from there — and Grizzly-Bear, their chief, calls everyone to shoot arrows at the sky; all fall short, even Fish, Snakes and Toads. Only Chickadee is left, and no one expects him to hit — but his arrow strikes the sky. In turn the others shoot arrows into each nock until a chain reaches the ground, and up it they climb, leaving only Grizzly-Bear and Black-Bear, who quarrel over who shall climb next, chase each other around the ladder, and knock it down. In the sky the attackers are defeated and flee; finding the lower part of the chain gone at mid-descent, they hesitate, the crowd above breaks the ladder with its weight, and all fall — those left above kill themselves in the drop, the rest are killed by the Sky people, and the Fish fare worst: Sucker broke all his bones.
summary.zh: 族人欲征天族（或云為奪火），熊酋召眾射天；眾箭皆墮，魚、蛇、蟾亦然。最後唯剩山雀，人皆不望其能中——然其箭竟釘天。於是眾輪流以箭續射，鏈成及地，攀之登天；僅灰熊與黑熊未上，因爭先後而追逐，竟撞倒箭梯。天上攻者敗退；退至半空，發覺下段箭鏈已失，猶豫不敢跳，而上空人潮愈擠愈重，箭梯竟斷，全體墜落——空中餘者躍下自斃，其餘為天族所誅。魚類最慘，胭脂魚遍體骨碎。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Arrow-chain ascent to the sky, a widespread Plateau motif. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once upon a time the people wanted to make war on the Sky people (some informants say they wanted to procure fire from there). Grizzly-Bear, who was chief, called all the people together to shoot arrows at the sky. Each animal and bird shot, but all the arrows fell short. The Fish, Snakes, and Toads also tried. At last only Chickadee (or Wren?) was left, and no one expected that he could hit the sky; Coyote said he did not need to try, when he himself had failed. However, Chickadee's arrow hit the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 85 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，人們想向天空之民開戰（有些提供消息的人說他們想從那裡取得火）。首領灰熊召集所有人向天空射箭。每隻動物和鳥都射了，但所有箭都射不到。魚、蛇和蟾蜍也試了。最後只剩下山雀（還是鷦鷯？），沒有人料到牠能射中天空；郊狼說牠不必試，因為他自己都失敗了。然而，山雀的箭射中了天空。

passages.text: The others all shot in turn again, and Chickadee shot an arrow which stuck in the nock of the first one. They kept on shooting until a chain of arrows had been made which reached the ground, and on this they climbed to the sky. Grizzly-Bear and Black-Bear only remained. They quarrelled as to who should climb next: Black-Bear said Grizzly was too heavy and would break the ladder. They chased each other around the ladder, and finally knocked it down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 85 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其他人又輪流射了一遍，山雀射出一支箭，插進了第一支箭的箭尾凹口。他們繼續射，直到形成一條觸及地面的箭鏈，他們便沿著它爬上了天空。只有灰熊和黑熊留了下來。他們爭吵著接下來該誰爬：黑熊說灰熊太重，會弄斷梯子。他們繞著梯子互相追逐，最後把它撞倒了。

passages.text: Meanwhile the people who had reached the sky had attacked the people there, and had been defeated. They fled; and when the first ones reached the hole in the sky, they descended one after another. When they reached half way down, they found the lower part gone, and hesitated to drop so far. Meanwhile the people crowded so thickly on the ladder above that their weight broke it, and they all fell down. Those left above threw themselves down and killed or hurt themselves, while the remainder were killed by the Sky people. The Fish, who had no wings, fared worst: Sucker broke all his bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 85 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 與此同時，那些已抵達天空的人攻擊了那裡的人，卻被擊敗了。他們逃走了；當第一批人抵達天空的洞口時，他們一個接一個地往下爬。當他們爬到半途時，發現下半段已經不見了，便猶豫著不敢往下跳那麼遠。與此同時，上面的人密密麻麻地擠在梯子上，他們的重量把梯子壓斷了，於是他們全都掉了下去。留在上面的人縱身跳下，摔死或摔傷了自己，而其餘的人則被天空之民殺死。魚沒有翅膀，境況最慘：吸盤魚摔斷了全身的骨頭。

title.en: Dirty-Boy: Sun Descends to Wed the Chief's Daughter
title.zh: 髒小子：太陽下凡娶酋長之女

region.en: Large camp of the Okanagon country (symbolic pin at Okanogan River)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根故地大營（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 6. Dirty-Boy' (Okanagon)

summary.en: The chief's two beautiful daughters have refused every suitor, and Sun and Star, brother and sister in the sky, descend to test them — Sun as a dirty, sore-eyed boy, Star as a decrepit grandmother, in a ruined mat lodge at the camp's edge. In the shooting contest the disguised boy kills the eagle through his lodge-door while Coyote misses twice and is stripped of his extra arrows; in the fisher-trapping contest his two willow dead-falls by the lodge-door hold the only two prime fishers, while Coyote's ten traps catch nothing. The chief keeps his word, but one daughter detours to marry Raven's ugly eldest son; the other attends the 'sick, dying' boy as commanded, and on the third night Sun and Star resume their true forms — a skin lodge richer than the Blackfeet's, a copper kettle, a woman clothed in stars, and a man whose hair shines like sun-rays. The rejected sister falls four times trying to walk the golden-dust trail, and when game grows scarce Sun turns over dried droppings on the plain until every one becomes living game driven into the chief's pit — the last, a gaunt steer that is nearly all fat. The steer-hairs become cattle; the wise sister's line prospers and the foolish one is shamed.
summary.zh: 酋長二美拒不嫁，太陽與星（天上兄妹）下凡試之：太陽化為目爛身污之小兒，星化為襤褸老嫗，營邊搭破爛草席之屋。射雕之賽，髒小子於門內發箭連中雕心；郊狼兩射皆空，多箭被奪。捕貂之賽，老嫗於門旁置柳木陷阱二，竟得毛色一明一暗之上等貂二張；郊狼十陷無獲。酋長守諾，令二女下嫁；長姊途徑渡鴉家入而嫁其醜子，幼妹守命侍『病篤』之夫。第三夜，兄妹復本相：帳化皮帳華過黑腳族，釜化銅釜，老嫗星衣熠熠，男兒髮光如日。被拒之姊四度踏上金塵之路而四度跌倒。獵物匱乏之時，太陽翻轉原上乾糞，糞皆化活獸，驅入酋長深坑；最後一頭瘦牛，剖之幾全為脂。牛毛化家牛，故今家畜多於野獸；賢姊之後昌，愚姊蒙羞。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Celestial bridegroom tale (star-husband cluster). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The people of a certain region were living together in a very large camp. Their chief had two beautiful daughters of marriageable age; many young men had proposed to them, but all had been refused. The chief said, 'Whom do my daughters wish to marry? They have refused all the men.' Sun and Star, who were brother and sister, lived in the sky, and had seen all that had happened. Sun said to his sister, 'The chief's daughters have rejected the suits of all our friends. Let us go down and arrange this matter! Let us try these girls!' They made clothes, and at night descended to earth, erecting a lodge on the outskirts of the camp with the appearance of being very old and belonging to poor people — old poles, tattered tule-mat covering, beds of dried brush, kettles and cups of poorly made bark. Star had assumed the form of a decrepit old woman dressed in rags, and Sun that of a dirty boy with sore eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 85-86 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 某個地區的人們聚居在一個非常大的營地裡。他們的酋長有兩個正值婚齡的美麗女兒；許多青年男子向她們求婚，但全都被拒絕了。酋長說：『我的女兒們想嫁給誰呢？她們拒絕了所有的男人。』太陽和星星是兄妹，住在天上，看到了所發生的一切。太陽對妹妹說：『酋長的女兒們拒絕了我們所有朋友的求婚。讓我們下去把這件事安排好吧！讓我們試試這些姑娘！』他們做了衣服，夜裡降落到地上，在營地邊緣搭起一座小屋，外表看起來非常破舊，像是窮人的住處——破舊的柱子、破爛的燈心草蓆屋頂、乾枯灌木鋪成的床、做工粗劣的樹皮鍋和杯子。星星化作一個衣衫襤褸的衰弱老婦，太陽則化作一個眼睛紅腫的骯髒男孩。

passages.text: The chief resolved to find husbands for his daughters, announcing a shooting contest in four days: an eagle would perch on the tall tree, and whoever killed it should have the chief's daughters.
