passages.zh: 動物們到達天空後，發現自己身處一個湖邊的山谷，天空的人們正在那裡捕魚。郊狼想當偵察兵，卻被抓住了。於是麝鼠沿著湖岸挖了許多洞，河狸和老鷹便出發去取火。河狸鑽進其中一個魚簍裡裝死；他們把他抬到首領的屋裡，那裡的人們開始剝他的皮。這時，老鷹停落在帳篷附近的一棵樹上；人們一看見老鷹，便跑了出去，河狸立刻抓起一只裝滿熾熱炭火的蛤殼逃走。他跳進湖裡，人們試圖用網抓住他，但湖水從麝鼠挖的洞裡流光了。

passages.text: The animals ran back to the arrow-chain, which they found broken. Then each bird took a quadruped on its back, and they flew down with them. Only Coyote and the Sucker were left above. Coyote tied a piece of buffalo robe to each paw and jumped down; he sailed down on the skin, and finally landed on a pine-tree. On the following morning he showed off his wings, but was unable to take them off again, and was transformed into a bat. The Sucker had to jump down, and was broken to pieces; the animals fitted his bones together, and, since some were missing, they put pine-needles into his tail. Therefore the sucker has many bones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 108 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 動物們跑回箭鏈處，發現箭鏈已經斷了。於是每隻鳥背起一隻四足動物，帶著牠們飛了下去。只有郊狼和吸盤魚還留在上面。郊狼在每隻腳掌上綁了一片水牛皮，然後跳了下去；他乘著那塊皮滑翔而下，最後落在一棵松樹上。第二天早晨，他炫耀自己的翅膀，卻再也無法把它們取下來，於是變成了一隻蝙蝠。吸盤魚不得不跳下去，結果摔得粉碎；動物們把他的骨頭拼湊起來，因為缺了一些，就把松針放進他的尾巴裡。因此，吸盤魚才有許多骨頭。

title.en: The Eagles: Bald-Head Left on the Ledge
title.zh: 雙鵰記：禿首困於鷹巢

region.en: Eagle-nest ledge between Omak Lake and Omak Creek (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧馬克湖與奧馬克溪之間鷹巢崖（象徵定位）

period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 11. The Eagles'

summary.en: Bald-Headed Eagle falls in love with the wife of his elder brother Hail-Storm, and lures him to an eagle's nest between Omak Lake and Omak Creek to gather head-dress feathers; lowered by rope to the ledge, he is deserted by his brother. Attacked by the mother-eagle on her return, he catches her wing and ties her; three days later he ties the male too, ties the young eagles to the same rope, and jumps — carried safely down. His friends then kill the treacherous brother.
summary.zh: 禿首鵰戀其兄雹暴之妻，誘兄同往奧馬克湖與奧馬克溪之間採鷹羽製冠；以繩縋至鷹巢之崖，兄竟棄之而去。母鵰歸巢攻之，其人擒翼縛之；三日後公鵰亦被縛。遂縛雛鵰於同繩，躍崖而下，群鵰負之安全著地。歸後，友人誅其不義之兄。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Gould notes it is told as a true story. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Bald-Headed Eagle (Pakamiaken) fell in love with the wife of his elder brother Hail-Storm (Selusken). One day Bald-Head found an eagle's nest between Omak Lake and Omak Creek. He asked his brother to accompany him and to get feathers for a head-dress. The brothers made a rope, and Hail-Storm let down his elder brother to the ledge on which the eagle's nest was located; there his brother deserted him. He found the young eagles in the nest, and a dead ground-hog which the old eagles had left there. When the mother-eagle returned, she attacked the man, who, however, succeeded in catching her wing and tying her. Three days later the male eagle appeared, and he tied him also. Then he tied the young eagles to the same rope, jumped down, and was carried down safely by the eagles. After he had returned, his friends killed the treacherous brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 108 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 禿頭鷹（帕卡米亞肯）愛上了他兄長冰雹風暴（塞盧斯肯）的妻子。有一天，禿頭在奧馬克湖與奧馬克溪之間發現了一個鷹巢。他請兄長陪他同去，為頭飾採集羽毛。兄弟倆做了一條繩子，冰雹風暴把兄長縋下到鷹巢所在的那處岩臺；到了那裡，他的兄長卻拋棄了他。他在巢中發現了幼鷹，以及老鷹留在那裡的一隻死土撥鼠。母鷹回來時攻擊了這個人，然而他卻成功抓住了她的翅膀，把她綁了起來。三天後，雄鷹出現了，他也把牠綁了起來。接著，他把幼鷹綁在同一條繩子上，跳了下去，由鷹群安全地帶了下去。他回來之後，他的朋友們殺死了那個背信棄義的兄長。

title.en: The Poisoned Arrows: Hesken's Revenge
title.zh: 毒箭復仇：海斯肯誅熊記

region.en: Mountain den of the five grizzly sisters, Sanpoil country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地五熊姊妹之山穴（象徵定位）

period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 12. The Poisoned Arrows'

summary.en: The girl who disobeys her grandmother and picks berries up the brook is killed by the she-grizzly Kelauna; her unborn son is laid unharmed on a rock, found and reared as Hesken by the old woman, who keeps revenge before him. Tested at twelve, he paints a grizzly's head on a rock of power; on a high peak he fasts twelve days, wins a guardian-spirit bird and a song, and is told where to find poison; from his grandfather's spirit, the huge supernatural snake whose eyes shoot lightning, he begs the front tooth — 'Touched with that poison, a victim gives one look and dies.' With five poisoned arrows he waits by the dim trail of the five sisters, chants defiance in the war-lodge of Kimhist — 'I will kill and tear to pieces every grizzly bear I meet' — and picks off the sisters one by one as they climb out at sunrise, scattering their feet to the four winds. The last sister flees through the forest, and he lets her go, deciding not to destroy the whole grizzly-bear race; then Kimhist reveals herself as the spirit of his mother, well pleased with his courage.
summary.zh: 女童違祖母之誡，上溪採莓，為母熊格拉烏納所殺；腹中嬰孩被棄石上而無恙，祖母拾回撫養，取名海斯肯，時時以復仇勉之。十二歲受試，繪熊首於神石；登絕頂絕食十二日，得守護靈鳥與神歌，並獲示毒之所在。至巨蟒之穴——其目閃電、舌吐火——三求毒牙，終得門牙：『觸此毒者，一瞥即斃。』製毒箭五支，伏於五熊姊妹晨出之徑；於金姨之戰舍中朗聲應戰：『凡遇灰熊，必誅而碎之，散其屍於大地！』破曉逐一射殺四姊，斷其足擲於四方，使之不得復返噬人。第五妹遁入林中，海斯肯不追，存灰熊一脈。金姨現身，原為其母之靈，嘉其勇毅。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Monster-slaying hero cycle. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: An old woman warned her daughter not to go up a brook when picking service-berries, because Kelauna, a female grizzly bear, lived there and would attack her. Since berries grew thick and large there, the girl disobeyed; while she picked berries, the grizzly killed her. Her unborn child was laid upon a rock and left unharmed. When the young woman did not return, her grandmother searched for her and found the infant boy, took him home and cared for him, and named him Hesken; when he was a year old she told him of his mother's death, and always kept the idea of revenge before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 109 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位老婦人警告她的女兒，採摘越橘時不要沿著一條小溪往上游走，因為那裡住著一頭名叫凱勞娜的雌性灰熊，會攻擊她。由於那裡的漿果長得又密又大，女孩沒有聽從；就在她採摘漿果時，那頭灰熊殺死了她。她未出生的孩子被放在一塊岩石上，安然無恙。年輕女子沒有回來，她的祖母便去尋找她，發現了那個男嬰，把他帶回家撫養，給他取名赫斯肯；當他滿一歲時，祖母告訴他母親的死訊，並且始終把復仇的念頭放在他心中。

passages.text: When he was twelve years old, she wanted to test his courage, and sent him at night to a rock of supernatural power, which he was to mark with a painting of his own design; the next day she found he had drawn a grizzly bear's head. A summer and winter passed; then he was sent across two mountain-ranges, across two valleys, and to a high peak, where he built a monument and remained twelve days without eating or sleeping. His guardian-spirit came to him in the form of a bird, and a song was given to him; he became very brave, and was told by a voice where to find poison with which to tip his arrows to revenge his mother's death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 109-110 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他十二歲時，祖母想考驗他的勇氣，便在夜裡派他去一塊具有超自然力量的岩石，要他在上面畫一幅自己設計的圖案作為標記；第二天，她發現他畫的是一個灰熊的頭。一個夏天和一個冬天過去了；接著，他被派去翻越兩道山脈、穿過兩座山谷，來到一座高峰，在那裡壘起了一座紀念碑，並且不吃不睡地待了十二天。他的守護神以鳥的形態來到他面前，賜給他一首歌；他變得非常勇敢，並有一個聲音告訴他何處可以找到毒藥，用來塗在箭頭上，為母親的死復仇。

passages.text: His grandmother sent him to a distant mountain on which dwelt in a cave a huge supernatural snake: 'When you enter the cave, do not be afraid, although his eyes shoot forth lightning and his tongue flame.' The boy went to the cave and saw the great snake, which lay coiled in the centre. The Snake spoke to him, and he answered, 'I am not afraid of you, for you are the spirit of my grandfather, and I have come to you for poison with which to tip my arrows to avenge my mother's death.' The Snake saw that he had courage and knowledge; he took a tooth from his mouth and offered it to him, but the boy refused it, and another tooth also. He put his arms around the Snake's neck and begged for the real poison, the deadliest the Snake had; then the Snake gave him a front tooth, saying, 'Touched with that poison, a victim gives one look and dies.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 110 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的祖母派他去一座遙遠的山，山上的一個洞穴裡住著一條巨大的超自然之蛇：「當你走進洞穴時，不要害怕，儘管牠的雙眼射出閃電，舌頭噴出火焰。」男孩走到洞穴，看見了那條大蛇，牠盤繞在中央。蛇對他說話，他回答說：「我不怕你，因為你是我祖父的靈，我來找你，是要取得毒藥，塗在我的箭頭上，為我母親的死復仇。」蛇看出他有勇氣和見識；牠從口中取下一顆牙齒遞給他，但男孩拒絕了，第二顆牙齒也拒絕了。他雙臂環抱住蛇的脖子，懇求牠給出真正的毒藥，也就是蛇所擁有的最致命的毒藥；於是蛇給了他一顆門牙，說道：「一旦被那毒藥觸及，受害者看一眼便會死去。」

passages.text: Hesken made five arrows and covered the flint tips with poison from the snake-tooth. In the spring he climbed a mountain and found a dim trail made by five sisters; he waited under a pine-tree, then met an old woman named Kimhist, who told him of a war-dance at her house and, after refusing at first — there were five sisters there who did not like strangers — let him come along, telling him to stand behind her back. When they stepped into the lodge there was a heavy growl; the eldest sister, Kelauna, began a chant telling of her intention to destroy every human being in the spring: 'I will kill and tear to pieces every human being I meet, and scatter his body over the face of the earth.' Hesken chanted after her, 'I will kill and tear to pieces every grizzly bear I meet, and scatter his body over the face of the earth.' The woman would have attacked him if Kimhist had not been there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 110 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 赫斯肯做了五支箭，用蛇牙上的毒藥塗滿了燧石箭頭。春天，他爬上一座山，發現了一條由五姐妹踩出的模糊小徑；他在一棵松樹下等候，隨後遇見了一位名叫金希斯特的老婦人，她告訴他她家要舉行一場戰舞會，起初拒絕了他——那裡有五姐妹，不喜歡陌生人——後來還是讓他一起去了，叫他站在她背後。當他們走進屋裡時，響起了一聲沉重的低吼；大姐凱勞娜開始吟唱，訴說她打算在春天毀滅每一個人：「我要殺死並撕碎我遇到的每一個人，把他的屍體撒遍大地。」赫斯肯跟在她後面吟唱：「我要殺死並撕碎我遇到的每一頭灰熊，把牠的屍體撒遍大地。」若不是金希斯特在那裡，那女人早就攻擊他了。

passages.text: Before daybreak, while the bears slumbered, Hesken stole out and returned to the tree, climbed it and waited. At sunrise the eldest sister came out of the den, depressed and sad, the tears rolling from her eyes; as she climbed the trail and passed under the pine-tree, Hesken whistled, she looked up, and he killed her with one of his poisoned arrows. He came down, cut off her feet, and threw them to the four winds, scattering them so far that they could not return to devour the Indians of that place. The next morning her sister came out and climbed the trail, and he shot her in the same manner; on the third and fourth days he killed two more of the sisters. On the fifth day the last one came out, but she did not climb the trail; she turned and went off through the forest, and Hesken did not go in pursuit — he decided not to destroy the whole grizzly-bear race. As he descended the mountain he met a black bear, who told him she was Kimhist and the spirit of his mother: 'I was allowed to protect you from the grizzly bears. Now that my death has been avenged, I am well pleased with your courage.' Then she went away. Hesken went back to his grandmother and told her all she had wished to know, and she gave a great feast in his honor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 110-111 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天亮之前，趁著熊群酣睡，赫斯肯偷偷溜了出去，回到那棵樹下，爬上樹等候。日出時，大姐走出洞穴，神情抑鬱悲傷，淚水滾落眼眶；當她沿著小徑往上走、經過松樹底下時，赫斯肯吹了聲口哨，她抬頭張望，他便用一支毒箭射死了她。他下樹來，砍下她的雙腳，拋向四方之風，將它們散得極遠，使它們無法回來吞食當地的印第安人。第二天早晨，她的妹妹走了出來，沿著小徑往上走，他以同樣的方式射殺了她；第三、第四天，他又殺了她們之中的兩個姊妹。第五天，最後一個走了出來，但她沒有沿小徑往上走；她轉身穿過森林離去，赫斯肯沒有追趕——他決定不將整個灰熊族趕盡殺絕。他下山時遇見一頭黑熊，黑熊告訴他，她就是金希斯特，是他母親的亡靈：「我被允許保護你免受灰熊之害。如今我的死已得報償，我對你的勇氣十分欣慰。」說罷她便離去了。赫斯肯回到祖母那裡，把她想知道的一切都告訴了她，祖母便為他舉辦了一場盛大的宴會。

title.en: The Race between Turtle and Frog
title.zh: 龜蛙賽跑

region.en: Rolling meadow race-course, Sanpoil country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地起伏草坡賽道（象徵定位）

period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 13. The Race between Turtle and Frog'

summary.en: A race between Turtle and Frog is proposed over uneven ground, and all the people bet that Frog will win; Mud-Turtle asks three days' grace and bets his back against Frog's tail. Given a head start, Turtle keeps disappearing over the low places ahead of Frog, who hurries faster and faster without ever overtaking him, and crosses the line just as the last low ground is passed. Frog has to give up his tail — it took six turtles to beat him — and now pollywogs have to lose their tails before they can become frogs.
summary.zh: 龜蛙相賽於起伏之地，眾皆押蛙勝；泥龜求三日寬限，以背注蛙尾。龜得先發，每於窪地隱沒復現於前；蛙愈追愈急，終不能及，龜已越線。蛙輸其尾——六龜接力方勝一蛙——故今蝌蚪必先失尾方能化蛙。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: At one time there was a race proposed between Turtle and Frog. All the people bet that Frog would win. Mud-Turtle asked for three days to let his friends know about the race; the race-course was very uneven — low and high ground, rolling meadow. Turtle bet his back against Frog's tail. On the third day Turtle was given a head start. Frog stood there taking more bets; finally he started, and ahead in a low place he saw Turtle going out of sight. Each time he looked ahead he saw Turtle going out of sight; he hurried faster and faster, but did not overtake him. Just as he crossed the last low ground he saw Turtle over the line. He had to give up his tail. It took six turtles to beat him, but he lost the race. Now the pollywogs have to lose their tails before they can become frogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 111 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，烏龜和青蛙相約賽跑。所有人都下注賭青蛙會贏。泥龜請求給他三天時間通知朋友們這場比賽；賽道非常崎嶇不平——有低地也有高地，是起伏的草甸。烏龜以自己的背殼賭青蛙的尾巴。第三天，烏龜獲准先跑。青蛙站在那裡繼續接受更多的賭注；最後他終於起跑，在前方一處低地看見烏龜正走出視野。他每次往前看，都看見烏龜正走出視野；他越跑越快，卻始終沒有追上。就在他穿過最後一片低地時，他看見烏龜已過了終點線。他只得交出尾巴。要六隻烏龜才贏得了他，但他輸了這場比賽。如今蝌蚪都得先失去尾巴，才能變成青蛙。

title.en: The Origin of the Different Languages: The Dispute over the Ducks
title.zh: 諸語之始：群鴨之爭

region.en: Wintering grounds of the ducks on the Sanpoil rivers (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦諸河群鴨越冬之地（象徵定位）

period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 14. The Origin of the Different Languages'

summary.en: Two hunters who have each taken one duck quarrel over whether the whistling-noise the rising ducks make comes from bill or wings, and neither will yield; the chief, whose dead ducks cannot answer, calls a council. The people go down to the river to hear for themselves, and split over the answer — bill or wings — quarrelling violently and separating in an ugly mood. The hatred grows all winter until in spring part of the Indians move south for new homes: the first division of the people into tribes. New objects bring new words, each split brings a new chief and different words and meanings, and thus the tribes slowly scattered, and dialects and even new languages were formed.
summary.zh: 二獵人各得一鴨，為群鴨起飛時之哨聲究竟出自喙或翼而爭執不下。酋長所獲二鴨已死無從對證，遂召集議。眾親往河邊聽之，仍各執一詞，忿然分開。積怨一冬，翌春部分族人南遷覓新居——是為部落之分。新物生新詞，每分一支，即立一酋，言語漸異。諸族由此四散，方言之別乃至新語之立，皆由此起。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Language-separation ethnogony. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: In a certain place in the winter months, the ducks (lulluUo) collected in great numbers; when any one approached them, they would rise and fly away, making a whistling-noise. One morning two hunters went down to a river to kill some ducks; they had each obtained one, when a dispute arose over the question whether the whistling-noise was made with the bill or with the wings when they rose to fly. Neither could convince the other, and the words became bitter; finally they agreed to take it to the chief and let him settle the dispute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 111 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在某個地方，冬季時節，鴨子（lulluUo）成群聚集；一有人靠近，牠們便會飛起離去，發出呼嘯般的聲響。一天早晨，兩名獵人下到河邊去打幾隻鴨子；他們各自打到了一隻，這時卻起了爭執，爭的是鴨子飛起時那呼嘯聲究竟是用嘴喙還是用翅膀發出的。兩人誰也說服不了誰，話越說越難聽；最後他們商定把這事交給酋長，由他來裁決。

passages.text: The chief heard the story and looked at the ducks; both of them were dead and could not make any noise. Therefore he called a council to listen to the dispute. The people came from all around to deliberate; they spoke one language and had only one chief. The ducks were brought in, and the chief explained the question. The people said, 'We do not wish to be unjust, we will go to the river and hear for ourselves; these ducks can do us no good.' So they went down to the river and frightened the ducks, which flew over their heads. Part of the Indians said the noise was made with the bills; part said it was made with the wings. They could not agree; therefore the ducks were made to fly once more, and the people began to quarrel violently, and separated in an ugly mood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 111-112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 酋長聽完事情經過，看了看那些鴨子；兩隻都已死了，發不出任何聲響。於是他召集了一次議會來聽這場爭執。人們從四面八方前來商議；他們只說一種語言，也只有一位酋長。鴨子被帶了進來，酋長說明了爭議的問題。眾人說：「我們不願有失公道，我們要親自到河邊去聽個明白；這些鴨子對我們也幫不上什麼忙。」於是他們下到河邊，驚起鴨子，鴨子從他們頭頂飛過。一部分印第安人說那聲響是嘴喙發出的；一部分說是翅膀發出的。他們無法達成一致；於是又讓鴨子再飛一次，眾人便激烈地爭吵起來，最後不歡而散。

passages.text: All during the winter the feeling grew, until in spring the mutual hatred drove part of the Indians south to hunt for new homes. This was the first division of the people into tribes. They selected a chief from their own division, and called themselves by another name. Finding new objects, and having to give such objects names, brought new words into their former language; and thus after many years the language was changed. Each split in the tribe made a new division and brought a new chief; each migration brought different words and meanings. Thus the tribes slowly scattered; and thus the dialects, and even new languages, were formed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 整個冬季，這種情緒不斷滋長，到了春天，彼此的仇恨終於驅使一部分印第安人南遷，去尋找新的家園。這是人群第一次分裂成各個部落。他們從自己這一部分人中選出一位酋長，並以另一個名字自稱。他們發現了新的事物，又不得不為這些事物命名，於是新的詞語進入了他們原有的語言；如此經過許多年，語言便改變了。部落每分裂一次，便形成一個新的分支，產生一位新的酋長；每一次遷徙都帶來不同的詞語和含義。部落就這樣慢慢四散；方言乃至新的語言，也就這樣形成了。

title.en: The Weeping Woman
title.zh: 哭泣之婦

region.en: Headwaters of a Sanpoil stream (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦河源頭（象徵定位）

period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 15. The Weeping Woman'

summary.en: Chatalem lures hunters to their death with her beautiful, sad wailing, always keeping out of sight; one brave hunter follows the stream to its source, camps and sweats there, and when she rises and floats away like a cloud as he approaches, he turns the other way. Later she comes to him unseen while he has killed a deer; in mid-winter he wakes to find her cooking for him — carrying a child with its head down — and she promises to meet him at the forest's edge if he returns alone. His wife insists on accompanying him the next fall, hears the wailing, asks what it is, and he will not tell her; then a high wind and a terrible storm kill her, and the angry hunter returns to his own people and does not go back to the weeping woman.
summary.zh: 恰塔勒姆以哀婉哭聲引獵人送命，始終隱形於視線之外。一勇獵人循溪至源，結廬汗浴；其近前時，婦如雲飄去，他掉頭他往。其後獵鹿之時，婦聲不見形；隆冬一覺醒來，見婦為其炊飯——背上倒懸一孩——並許諾：若獨自歸來，願於林口相候。翌年其妻執意同行，聞哭聲而問，夫不答；旋即狂風暴雨大作，妻為所斃。獵人憤而歸族，不再往見哭泣之婦。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Chatalem lured away hunters by her beautiful, sad wailing. She always kept at a distance from them, so that they could not see her; they followed her until they perished. One brave hunter followed the stream to its source; then he camped and built a sweat-house, and every morning at dawn he heated rocks and took a bath. One morning, when he came back to his tent, he saw a beautiful woman sitting in the doorway. He fell in love with her, and made up his mind to ask her to remain; however, as he approached, she rose and floated away like a cloud, wailing. He was strongly tempted to follow her, but he turned and went the other way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 查塔萊姆以她美妙而哀傷的慟哭引誘獵人離開。她總是與他們保持距離，使他們看不見她；他們跟隨著她，直到喪命。有一位勇敢的獵人沿著溪流走到它的源頭；於是他紮了營，搭起一座汗屋，每天清晨破曉時分都燒熱石頭沐浴。一天早晨，他回到帳篷時，看見一個美麗的女子坐在門口。他愛上了她，決心請她留下；然而當他走近時，她卻起身，像雲一般飄然離去，一路哀哭。他深受誘惑，想要跟隨她，但他轉過身，朝另一個方向走去。

passages.text: Later on, she came to him when he had killed a deer; he heard her voice, but did not see her. He thought of her often; he also thought of his wife and children whom he had left at home, and tried to forget her. One day in mid-winter he slept soundly, and when he awoke she was cooking for him; then for the first time he saw her back: she carried a child with its head down. She told him she had come to keep him company, and when he left for home she told him to come back alone, and promised to meet him at the entrance of the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，當他殺了一頭鹿時，她來到他身邊；他聽見她的聲音，卻看不見她。他時常想起她；他也想起留在家中的妻子和兒女，並試圖忘掉她。隆冬某日，他睡得很沉，醒來時她正在為他煮食；這時他第一次看見她的背：她背著一個頭朝下的孩子。她告訴他，她來與他作伴；當他離去回家時，她囑咐他獨自回來，並答應在森林入口與他相會。

passages.text: In the fall of the year he prepared to go hunting, and his wife wished to accompany him; at first he refused her request, but when she insisted he told her she might go as far as the forest. The next year she desired to accompany him again; as before, he refused, but she insisted. She went as far as the forest, but then she would not return; she followed him and heard a wailing-sound. She asked him what it was, but he would not tell her. Then came a high wind and a terrible storm, and the man's mortal wife was killed. This made the hunter angry, and he returned at once to his own people, and did not go back to the weeping woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那年秋天，他準備去打獵，他的妻子想隨他同去；起初他拒絕了她的請求，但當她堅持時，他告訴她可以走到森林為止。第二年她又想隨他同去；他像先前一樣拒絕，但她堅持要去。她走到森林為止，但隨後不肯回去；她跟隨他，聽見一陣哀號聲。她問他那是什麼，他不肯告訴她。接著刮起大風，來了可怕的暴風雨，那人的凡人妻子被殺死了。這使獵人十分憤怒，他立刻回到自己的族人那裡，不再回到那哭泣的女人身邊。

title.en: Timtimenee, or the Island of Death
title.zh: 提姆提姆內：死亡之島

region.en: Island in the River of Death (symbolic pin on the Sanpoil Columbia)
region.zh: 死亡之河中島（象徵定位於桑普瓦哥倫比亞河段）

period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 16. Timtimenee; or, The Island of Death'

summary.en: A handsome warrior and great hunter takes a plain second wife and brings her most of his meat; the first wife and children starve, the boy sent to the father's tent is rebuffed, and the new wife laughs. The mother whittles three sharp bones from a deer's antler, kills her two children as they sleep, and drives the last into her own breast. Grieved, the father takes his bow and arrows and leaves the camp, crossing the plain to a river with a large island where he sees canoes and camps but no sign of life; a woman comes out of an open tent, paddles across, and he recognizes his first wife, who lands him and takes him into the large tent — inside only skeletons, his children's among them, and then his wife a skeleton too, and himself without flesh. He had crossed the River of Death.
summary.zh: 俊勇獵人另娶陋女，以其居別帳，肉食多歸之。前妻與子女飢寒交迫；其子往父帳求食，遭拒，新婦笑之。母聞子言，削鹿角為三枚銳骨，夜殺二子，最後一枚刺入自己胸膛。父悲痛，携弓箭離營，過平原至一河，河中大島上有舟有帳而無人跡。一婦自開敞之帳出，划舟渡來——乃其前妻。登島入大帳，帳內唯骸骨；子女之骨俱在，妻亦白骨，自顧亦無肉身——原來他已渡過死亡之河。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Contains family-violence narrative as recorded; presented as collected. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was once a camp by a river. Among the people there was a handsome man, who was a brave warrior and a great hunter; he had two children. His wife was beautiful, and he loved her dearly. One day he met a very plain maiden; she attracted him. He took her for his wife, and put her in another tent, and took most of his meat to her. Then the first wife and his children grew hungry; the younger child cried, and the mother sent her son to his father for meat. The boy went to the tent and stood in the doorway; when his father asked him what he wanted, he said that they were hungry. He was sent back without any food, and the new wife laughed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前河邊有一個營地。族中有一個英俊的男子，是勇敢的戰士，也是出色的獵人；他有兩個孩子。他的妻子很美，他深愛著她。有一天他遇見一個相貌十分平庸的少女；她吸引了他。他娶她為妻，把她安置在另一座帳篷裡，並把大部分的肉都帶給她。於是第一個妻子和她的孩子們挨餓；年幼的孩子哭了起來，母親便打發兒子去向父親要肉。男孩走到帳篷前，站在門口；父親問他要什麼，他說他們餓了。他沒拿到任何食物就被打發回去，而新妻子還笑了起來。

passages.text: The boy returned and told his mother that he had been rebuffed and scolded, and that his father's new wife had laughed at him. His mother listened to his words, took a deer's antler, and whittled three sharp bones out of it. With two of these she killed her children while they were asleep; the last one she drove into her own breast. In the morning the grandmother of the children came with food and found them dead. She raised a wail, and the people came to see what had happened; then the father was grieved. He took his bow and arrows and left the camp.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 112 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 男孩回來告訴母親，他遭到冷遇和責罵，父親的新妻子還嘲笑他。母親聽了他的話，取來一隻鹿角，削出三根尖銳的骨刺。她用其中兩根在孩子們熟睡時殺了他們；最後一根她刺進自己的胸膛。早晨，孩子們的祖母帶著食物前來，發現他們都死了。她放聲哀號，人們前來查看發生了什麼事；於是父親悲痛不已。他拿起弓箭，離開了營地。

passages.text: He crossed the plain, and came to a river in which was a large island. He saw canoes and camps on it, but he did not see any signs of life. He became sleepy. One tent on the island was open; a woman came out, boarded a canoe, and paddled across. He recognized his first wife, who took him across. They landed, and she pulled the canoe up on shore; she took him into the large tent. Inside there were only skeletons. He saw his children's skeletons. Then he saw that his wife too was a skeleton. He looked at himself, and he saw that he had no flesh. He had crossed the River of Death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 113 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他穿過平原，來到一條河邊，河中有一座大島。他看見島上有獨木舟和營地，卻看不到任何生命的跡象。他睏倦起來。島上有一座帳篷敞開著；一個女人走出來，登上一艘獨木舟，划了過來。他認出那是他的第一個妻子，她載他過河。他們上了岸，她把獨木舟拖上灘；她帶他進入那座大帳篷。裡面只有骸骨。他看見孩子們的骸骨。接著他看出他的妻子也是骸骨。他看看自己，發現自己沒有血肉。他已渡過了死亡之河。

title.en: Starvation: The Elk that Appeared at Sunrise
title.zh: 飢冬：日出之鹿

region.en: Snowbound camp of the Sanpoil winter (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 桑普瓦故地雪冬之營（象徵定位）

period: Told to Marian K. Gould; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sanpoil Tales, 17. Starvation'

summary.en: Deep snow, no game; hearing his wife tell the children 'Your father may bring us some nice meat to-day,' a hunter is too downcast to enter his own tent. In a dream a voice tells him, 'Don't leave this place! Awake, and look towards the rising sun!' — and at sunrise an elk appears, which he shoots; whenever he needs meat, an elk appears, and in this way they live through the winter.
summary.zh: 大雪封山，獵無所獲。獵人歸而未入帳，忽聞妻對子女言：『你父親今天或許會帶好肉回來。』他羞慚欲絕。夜夢中有聲音說：『勿離此地！醒來朝東方日出處看！』日出之時，麋鹿自現，一箭而獲；此後每有所需，鹿必自現。一家遂安然度過嚴冬。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sanpoil narrative collected by Marian K. Gould (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: One winter there was a very heavy snow, and the people were starving. A man lived alone with his wife and children; on account of the snow he was unable to kill any game. One night when he returned, he heard his wife saying to the children, 'Your father may bring us some nice meat to-day.' He felt very much downcast when he heard this, and went back without entering the tent. He lay down to sleep, and in his dream he heard a voice saying, 'Don't leave this place! Awake, and look towards the rising sun!' When he awoke and the sun rose, an elk appeared, which he shot. Whenever he needed meat, an elk would appear. In this way they lived through the winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 113 (Gould, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一年冬天雪下得極大，人們都在挨餓。一個男人與妻子兒女獨自住著；由於大雪，他無法獵到任何獵物。一天夜裡他回家時，聽見妻子對孩子們說：『你們的父親今天也許會給我們帶些好肉回來。』他聽到這話，感到非常沮喪，沒進帳篷就折了回去。他躺下睡覺，夢中聽見一個聲音說：『不要離開這個地方！醒來，朝日出之處看！』他醒來，太陽升起時，出現了一頭麋鹿，他射中了牠。每當他需要肉時，就會出現一頭麋鹿。他們就這樣度過了冬天。

title.en: Coyote, Wren, and Grouse
title.zh: 郊狼、鷦鷯與松雞

region.en: Ridge and cliff above Pend d'Oreille country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 彭德奧雷伊故地山嶺與斷崖（象徵定位）

period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 1. Coyote, Wren, and Grouse'

summary.en: Coyote mocks Wren's tiny bow — 'You can't shoot far with those' — and Wren promises to shoot him on the distant ridge, where the arrow strikes his heart; Fox pulls out the arrow and jumps over him, and Coyote comes to life claiming a long nap. Later Coyote gambles everything away from Wren, sings 'I won from the Kalispel,' cooks the ten grouse children in a hole in their own lodge, and is ambushed by the revenged parents and Wren on a ridge by a steep cliff: one grouse flies at his head, another between his legs, and he falls over the cliff while they pluck him of his winnings as he falls, restoring everything to Wren, who restores the children to life.
summary.zh: 郊狼譏鷦鷯弓小射不遠；鷦鷯言能於遠嶺射中其心。郊狼果於嶺上中箭斃命；狐拔箭躍其身，郊狼復活，自稱久眠。其後郊狼賭盡鷦鷯弓箭衣物，唱『我勝了卡利斯佩爾人』；又於松雞家中掘坑，以燒石烹其十個孩子。松雞夫婦與鷦鷯合謀復仇：於崖嶺上，一雞撲其面，一雞穿其襠，郊狼墜崖；眾雞趁其墜落拔光其贏來之物，歸還鷦鷯；鷦鷯則令松雞孩子復生。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative told by Michel Revais and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once Coyote met Wren (tsEska'n), and laughed at his small bow and arrows. He said, 'You can't shoot far with those.' Wren answered, 'Yes, I can shoot far. If you go to that distant ridge, I will shoot you while you are there.' Coyote laughed, and said, 'That ridge is so far away that we can hardly see it.' Soon afterwards Coyote was walking along this ridge, and Fox was following him; he had forgotten about his talk with Wren. Presently he heard something coming, and Wren's arrow struck him in the heart; he gave two jumps and fell down dead. Fox pulled out the arrow, and jumped over Coyote, who came to life, and said, 'I must have slept a long time.' Fox said, 'You were not sleeping, you were dead. Wren's arrow struck your heart. Why do you fool with Wren? You know he can shoot better than any one.' Coyote took the arrow from Fox, and said, 'I shall get even with him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 114 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，郊狼遇見了鷦鷯（tsEska'n），便嘲笑他那小小的弓和箭。他說：「用那些東西，你射不遠。」鷦鷯回答：「不，我能射得很遠。你若走到那道遙遠的山脊上，我就在那裡射你。」郊狼笑了，說：「那道山脊那麼遠，我們幾乎都看不見它。」不久之後，郊狼沿著這道山脊走著，狐狸跟在他後面；他已經忘了自己與鷦鷯說過的話。過了一會兒，他聽見有東西飛來，鷦鷯的箭射中了他的心；他跳了兩下，便倒地而死。狐狸拔出那支箭，從郊狼身上跳過去，郊狼便活了過來，說：「我一定是睡了很久。」狐狸說：「你不是在睡覺，你是死了。鷦鷯的箭射中了你的心。你為什麼要跟鷦鷯胡鬧？你知道他比誰都射得好。」郊狼從狐狸手中接過那支箭，說：「我會找他算帳的。」

passages.text: Some time after this, Coyote met Wren, and proposed to gamble with him: 'I have an arrow which looks like yours. Now you have a chance to win it back.' They played a game of throwing arrows; Coyote beat Wren every time, won all his arrows, then his bow, and later all his beautiful clothes. Wren was left practically naked. Coyote went off singing, 'Alpano'n e Kalispe'' ('I won from the Kalispel'), and Wren followed him at some distance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 114 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後過了些時候，郊狼遇見鷦鷯，提議與他賭博：「我有一支箭，看起來和你的那支一樣。現在你有機會把它贏回去。」他們玩了一種擲箭的遊戲；郊狼每次都贏了鷦鷯，贏走了他所有的箭，接著是他的弓，後來又贏走他所有美麗的衣裳。鷦鷯幾乎落得一絲不掛。郊狼唱著歌離去：「Alpano'n e Kalispe'」（「我從卡利斯佩爾人那裡贏來的」），鷦鷯則隔著一段距離跟在他後面。

passages.text: Coyote passed by the lodge of Willow-Grouse, who had ten young children, their parents being off in the hills. He mocked their parents' names, went into the lodge, dug a small hole near the fire, and said to the children, 'Carry those red bearberries into the hole, and watch me cook them for you.' They did so, and crowded around the edge to watch him; he pushed them into the hole and threw earth and hot ashes on top of them, then went on. Their parents came home and, finding their children dead, they cried. Wren came along and told them, 'I have a grudge against Coyote, too. I want my things which he won from me.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 114-115 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼經過柳雷鳥的住所，柳雷鳥有十個年幼的孩子，他們的父母到山裡去了。他嘲弄他們父母的名字，走進屋裡，在火邊挖了一個小洞，對孩子們說：「把那些紅色的熊果放進洞裡，看我替你們煮。」他們照做了，並擠在洞邊看他；他把他們推進洞裡，把泥土和熱灰撒在他們上面，然後繼續上路。他們的父母回到家，發現孩子們死了，便哭了起來。鷦鷯走了過來，對他們說：「我也對郊狼懷恨在心。我要討回他從我這裡贏走的東西。

passages.text: If you can get them back for me, I will restore your children to life.' Coyote was then passing over a high ridge, close to a steep cliff. Grouse made a detour, and hid ahead of him on the upper side; when Coyote was opposite them, one flew out suddenly at his head — he bent back over the cliff to avoid it — then the other flew between his legs, and he lost his balance and fell over the cliff. Grouse hastened and plucked him as he was falling: they plucked away his bow and arrows and quiver and clothes, and gave them back to Wren, who restored the children to life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 114-115 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 你們若能替我討回來，我就讓你們的孩子復活。』當時郊狼正走過一道高高的山脊，緊鄰著陡峭的懸崖。雷鳥繞了路，躲在他前方上坡的一側；當郊狼走到與他們相對的位置時，一隻突然朝他的頭飛撲而來——他向後仰，越過懸崖以避開牠——接著另一隻從他兩腿之間飛過，他失去平衡，從懸崖上摔了下去。雷鳥急忙趕上，在他墜落時啄拔他：他們拔走了他的弓、箭、箭袋和衣裳，交還給鷦鷯，鷦鷯便讓孩子們復活了。

title.en: The Iron Chamber and the South Sea at Kandang West
title.zh: 鐵室與西部康丹之南海

region.en: Pakuan Pajajaran and the southern coast (Kandang West)
region.zh: 帕庫安·巴查查蘭與南海岸（西部康丹）

period: Sundanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817), vol. II ch. X

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X (the iron-smith and the king)

summary.en: A youth of the Sundanese court excels in every kind of iron-work, fashioning red-hot iron with his fingers, and is made chief of the smiths. He constructs an iron chamber that attracts the prince, persuades him to step inside, and closes the door — burning him alive, or, in some accounts, casting him into the South Sea at Kandang West, fulfilling the devotee's prophecy. The smith assumes the government, and the Pajajaran succession passes through blood and betrayal — the legend in which the smith's art kills the king and the South Sea receives him.
summary.zh: 巽他宮廷一名青年精於一切鐵藝，徒手拈紅鐵，遂為鐵匠之長。他造鐵室吸引王子，誘其入內閉門——或焚之於室內，或據另說擲之於西部康丹之南海——應了苦行者之預言。鐵匠遂奪政權；帕查查蘭王統由血與背叛傳承——匠人之藝弒王、南海受王之軀。

sensitivity.note: Sundanese dynastic legend; the South Sea at Kandang West is the region later bound to the sea-queen Ratu Kidul.

passages.text: The youth soon excelled in the manufacture of all kinds of iron-work, and in the wild tradition of the country he is said to have fashioned the red hot iron with his fingers; in a short time he was made chief of the Pandi or iron-smiths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這青年很快就在製造各種鐵器方面出類拔萃，而依照當地粗野的傳說，據說他能用手指捏塑燒紅的鐵；不久之後，他就被推舉為潘迪（Pandi），即鐵匠之首。

passages.text: Having constructed an iron chamber or cage which particularly attracted the attention of the prince, he succeeded in persuading him to step in it; when closing the door, he according to some accounts burned him alive, or according to others caused him to be thrown into the South Sea at Kandang West, thus fulfilling the prophecy of the devotee.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他造了一間鐵室或鐵籠，特別引起了王子的注意，並成功說服王子走了進去；關門之時，據某些說法，他將王子活活燒死，而據另一些說法，他命人將王子投入坎當西（Kandang West）的南海之中，如此應驗了那位苦修者的預言。

title.en: The Bitter Maja Fruit: How Majapahit Got Its Name
title.zh: 苦摩賈果：馬卓帕希特之名的由來

region.en: Majapahit, East Java
region.zh: 東爪哇馬卓帕希特

period: Javanese chronicle tradition (Javan year 1221 / AD 1299), recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the founding of Majapahit

summary.en: Raden Tanduran, defeated and fleeing east with three followers, takes refuge with a widow and with his sister performing penance on Mount Chermai; following the course of a bird she releases for the purpose, he reaches Wirasaba. There he sees the maja fruit entwined round a tree, bites it and finds it extremely bitter, throwing it away — 'Then let us stop here and establish our kingdom, and let us call it Majapahit': the empire named from a mouthful of bitterness.
summary.zh: 敗逃的拉德恩·坦都蘭攜三隨從東行，借宿寡婦之家，又遇其妹在徹瑪伊山修行；他循其妹所放之鳥飛行之路抵維拉薩巴。見纏繞樹上之摩賈果，一口咬下苦不可忍，隨即吐棄——『就停在此建國，就叫它馬卓帕希特（苦摩賈）』——帝國以一口之苦命名。

sensitivity.note: Name-etiology of Majapahit in the chronicle tradition.

passages.text: Raden Tanduran arriving at the river of Grissee took refuge at the house of a widow, and afterwards meeting with his sister, who was performing a penance on the mountain Chermai, he was encouraged by her to proceed further east, following the course of a bird which she desired that he would let loose for the purpose, till he reached the district of Wirasaba.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉登·丹杜蘭抵達格里西河畔，寄居於一名寡婦家中；後來他與正在切爾邁山上苦修的妹妹相遇，妹妹鼓勵他繼續向東前行，跟隨一隻鳥的飛向——她請他為此放飛那隻鳥——直到他抵達維拉薩巴地區。

passages.text: Here he observed a plant called the maja, entwined round a tree; he wished to eat of the fruit, but finding it extremely bitter threw it away. 'Then let us stop here and establish our kingdom, and let us call it Majapahit' — for maja and pahit both signify 'bitter' — the name given in the Javan year 1221.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在此他看見一種名為「瑪賈」的植物纏繞在一棵樹上；他想吃那果實，卻發現它極其苦澀，便將它丟棄。「那麼我們就留在此地建立我們的王國，就叫它滿者伯夷吧」——因為瑪賈（maja）與帕希特（pahit）都意指「苦」——此名定於爪哇曆一二二一年。

title.en: The Stone Column of Tigil: The Boundary of Two Kingdoms
title.zh: 提吉勒石柱：兩國之界

region.en: Tigil, near Semarang, Central Java
region.zh: 中爪哇三寶瓏附近提吉勒

period: Javanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the treaty of the two princes

summary.en: The armies of Pajajaran and Majapahit meet at the centre of the island, and the general engagement proves indecisive; as the two chiefs are about to close in personal combat, it is mutually agreed that henceforth the countries to the west shall be subject to Pajajaran and those to the east to Majapahit — a line drawn due south from a stone column placed near the spot in commemoration of the agreement. The column is still to be seen at Tigil, a few miles west of Semarang.
summary.zh: 巴查查蘭與馬卓帕希特兩軍會於島之中部，大戰不分勝負；正當兩王將要親自決鬥之際，雙方協定：自此以西諸地屬巴查查蘭、以東屬馬卓帕希特——自主柱石向南畫一直線為界，立柱以紀此約。該柱至今猶存於三寶瓏以西數里之提吉勒。

sensitivity.note: Boundary-treaty legend; the standing column as charter.

passages.text: Both princes moved with their respective armies towards the centre of the island; a general engagement took place, which proving indecisive, a personal combat between the two chiefs was about to occur, when it was mutually agreed that thenceforth the countries to the west should be subject to Pajajaran, and those to the east to Majapahit. A line was drawn due south from a stone column placed near the spot in commemoration of the agreement; the column is still to be seen at Tigil, a few miles west of Semarang.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩位親王各自率軍向島嶼中部進發；一場大戰爆發，結果未分勝負，兩位首領正要進行單挑，此時雙方共同議定：自此以後，西邊各國歸屬巴查查蘭，東邊各國歸屬滿者伯夷。為紀念此約，人們在該地附近立下一根石柱，並自石柱向正南畫出一條界線；那根石柱至今仍可見於三寶壟以西數英里處的蒂吉爾。

title.en: Brama Hedali and the Eighty Smiths
title.zh: 婆羅摩·赫達利與八十鐵匠

region.en: From Pajajaran to Majapahit across the river Pamali
region.zh: 自帕查查蘭跨帕馬利河至馬卓帕希特

period: Javanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the emigration of the smiths

summary.en: Heavy demands made upon the people set off emigrations from Pajajaran: Brama Hedali at the head of eighty Pandi, or iron-smiths, with their families, deserts the country; pursued as far as the river Pamali in Brebes, the smiths effect their escape and are received with open arms at Majapahit. When the king demands that the smiths be delivered up, the refusal is positive — and war follows.
summary.zh: 帕查查蘭苛捐重斂，民乃外遷：婆羅摩·赫達利率八十名鐵匠（Pandi）攜家出走；追兵直逼布利貝斯之帕馬利河，鐵匠們逃脫成功，在馬卓帕希特受到張臂歡迎。王者索要工匠，對方斷然拒絕——戰爭隨之而來。

sensitivity.note: Migration legend; the smith-caste's allegiance as political capital.

passages.text: In a short time considerable emigrations took place from Pajajaran, in consequence of the heavy demands made upon the people: among others, Brama Hedali, at the head of eighty Pandi or iron-smiths with their families, deserted their country. They were pursued as far as the river Pamali in Brebes, but effected their escape, and were received with open arms at Majapahit; Chiong Wandra, on demanding that the Pandi should be delivered up, received a positive refusal, and in consequence declared war against his half brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久之後，由於對人民課以沉重的負擔，巴查查蘭發生了大规模的遷徙；其中，布拉瑪·赫達利率領八十名潘迪（鐵匠）及其家眷，離開了他們的國家。他們被追至布雷貝斯的帕馬利河，但成功逃脫，並在滿者伯夷受到熱烈歡迎；瓊·萬德拉要求交出這些潘迪，卻遭到斷然拒絕，於是向他的同父異母兄弟宣戰。

title.en: Batara Kala: The Devourer of Children and the Ruwatan of the Dalang
title.zh: 卡拉神：食子之神與達朗的淨儀

region.en: Wayang purwa cycle, Central and East Java
region.zh: 哇揚戲班，中爪哇與東爪哇

period: Javanese wayang purwa tradition (the Murwakala cycle); documented in the wayang repertoire

source.archive: Javanese wayang tradition (documented in the wayang lakon repertoire)
source.work: The Murwakala legend of Batara Kala (wayang purwa)

summary.en: The wayang's great explanation of child-death: Batara Kala, the ogre of time, devours children — the deaths of the young are his appetite walking through the village. The dalang performs the play Murwakala as a ruwatan, a cleansing: the puppet rite stands between Kala and the household, teaches the ogre his limits, and sends the family out from the performance washed of the debt his hunger represents.
summary.zh: 哇揚戲對夭折之解釋：卡拉神——時間之巨魔——吞噬孩童；幼兒之死即其食慾巡行於村。達朗（戲偶師）以哇揚戲《穆爾瓦卡拉》行『魯瓦坦』淨儀：偶戲立於卡拉與家宅之間，教知巨魔其限，使全家自戲場洗淨其飢餓所代表之債。

sensitivity.note: Living wayang ritual theology; paraphrase respectfully.

canonical_translation: Based on the wayang purwa tradition of the Murwakala play; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Batara Kala cycle is the wayang's charter of mourning: it explains why children die and what the community can do about it.

BEGINNING: THE OGRE OF TIME. In the wayang theology Batara Kala is the devourer set over the span of things — the great ogre whose hunger is time itself. Children are his proper prey; the death of a child in the village is his passing, and the fear of him hangs over every cradle.

MIDDLE: THE PLAY AS BARGAIN. The dalang answers with the play Murwakala, performed as a ruwatan — a cleansing rite — for households under threat: the story of Kala's origin and his restraint. In the play's theology Kala was created in the beginning as a force of consumption, and the gods themselves had to negotiate the terms of his eating: the boundaries within which he may take, and the signs by which a child is spared.

END: THE CLEANSING OF THE HOUSE. The performance is the medicine: the family that watches the play from beginning to end — the dalang's voice speaking the ogre's part, the shadows falling on the screen — stands inside the pact, and the child at risk is presented to the story and passed through it. The ruwatan closes with the community's eating together; the debt the ogre represents has been paid in spectacle.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle (1) explains child-mortality theologically without blaming the parents; (2) gives the dalang his highest office — exorcist, not entertainer; (3) charters the wayang performance as a protective rite (the play performed for endangered children); and (4) supplies the origin-of-death cluster with the Javanese devourer-of-children form. The ruwatan's choreography gives the theology its practice: households sponsor the play for children whose births or circumstances mark them, the dalang recites the ogre's origin and his negotiated limits, and the family sits inside the story's shelter from the first shadow to the last. The wayang's protective office explains the dalang's social standing: he is not an entertainer who happens to chant sacred tales but a ritual technician whose night-work stands between Kala and the cradle. The theology's compassion is its distinctive note: the child's death is laid to the ogre's appetite rather than to the parents' fault, and the community's answer is spectacle rather than accusation — the debt represented by hunger is paid in a story told to its face. In the wayang repertoire the Murwakala stands beside the Mahabharata plays as one of the few lakon performed for necessity rather than occasion.
narrative.zh: 卡拉神故事乃哇揚戲之喪慟憲章：解釋孩童何以夭折、社群能做何事。開篇：哇揚神學中，卡拉神是掌管時限之吞噬者——其飢餓即時間本身；孩童乃其應得之獵物，村中幼兒之死即是他的路過，其名高懸於每一搖籃之上。中段：達朗以《穆爾瓦卡拉》一劇行魯瓦坦淨儀，為受威脅之家宅演出——講述卡拉之起源與其節制：劇中神學謂卡拉於太初受造為吞噬之力，諸神被迫與之談判其食之條界——他可取之界、以及孩童得免之徵。結尾：演出即是藥：全家自首至尾觀戲——達朗之聲代巨魔發言、影落幕上——即立於盟約之內；受險之孩童被呈於故事之前、並穿越之。魯瓦坦以社區共食作結；巨魔所代表之債已以演劇償付。功能：不咎父母而神學地解釋夭折、賦達朗以最高職分（驅邪者而非娛樂者）、以哇揚演出為護佑之儀（為危孩而演）、並為『死亡之由來』母題群供給爪哇式『食子者』形態。

functions: Explains child-mortality theologically without blaming the parents
Assigns the dalang his highest office: exorcist of the devourer
Charters the wayang performance itself as a protective rite for endangered children
Javanese form of the origin-of-death cluster: the devourer of children

variants.name: Murwakala play variants
variants.summary: Village and court tellings differ in Kala's parentage and in the terms of his restraint.

primary_sources.citation: Javanese wayang purwa tradition; the play performed as ruwatan cleansing; paraphrased from the repertoire's standard documentation.

secondary_sources.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java
secondary_sources.citation: Worsfold 1893 — the wayang performance context and the dalang's recitation of legendary tales.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive full text of Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893) — wayang context

sensitivity_guidance: Living ritual theology of mourning; paraphrase respectfully; do not reproduce exorcism instructions.

passages.text: Batara Kala is the devourer set over the span of things, the great ogre whose hunger is time itself; children are his proper prey, and the death of a child in the village is his passing — the fear of him hangs over every cradle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the wayang purwa tradition (Murwakala cycle); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴塔拉·卡拉是掌管萬物壽數的吞噬者，是那以時間本身為飢餓的巨魔；孩童是他理所當然的獵物，村中孩童之死便是他的經過——對他的恐懼籠罩著每一張搖籃。

passages.text: The dalang answers with the play Murwakala performed as a ruwatan, a cleansing rite: the story of Kala's origin and of the terms the gods negotiated for his eating — the boundaries within which he may take, and the signs by which a child is spared. The family that watches the play from beginning to end stands inside the pact.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the wayang purwa tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達朗以戲劇《穆爾瓦卡拉》作為魯瓦坦——一種淨化儀式——來回應：講述卡拉起源的故事，以及眾神為他的進食所議定的條件——他得以取食的界限，以及孩童得以倖免的徵兆。從頭到尾觀看此劇的家庭，便立於這項盟約之內。

title.en: Nyi Roro Kidul: The Queen of the Southern Sea
title.zh: 南海女王：洛羅·兀魯

region.en: Pelabuhan Ratu and the south coast of Java
region.zh: 爪哇南海岸與『女王港』

period: Javanese court tradition (documented from the Mataram court period); earlier South-Sea motifs recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: The legend of the Queen of the Southern Sea (Javanese court tradition); cf. Raffles 1817, the South Sea at Kandang West

summary.en: The green-clad spirit-queen of Java's south coast: Nyi Roro Kidul rules the Indian Ocean from the southern sea, is consort and guardian to the kings of Mataram and their successors, and takes to her green waters those she favours and those who offend. Green is her colour and not to be worn on her shore; the kings keep her chamber in their palaces; the harbour where her legend concentrates is named Pelabuhan Ratu — 'the harbour of the queen.'
summary.zh: 爪哇南海岸之綠衣靈后：洛羅·兀魯統轄南印度洋，為馬打藍諸王及其後嗣之后與守護者；受其寵者與犯其忌者皆被收於碧波之中。綠為其色，臨其岸不可著綠衣；歷代君王於宮中設其專室；其傳說所聚之港名『女王港』（Pelabuhan Ratu）。

sensitivity.note: Living court devotion and popular belief; paraphrase respectfully; note the earlier South-Sea casting legend recorded by Raffles as a motif-root.

passages.text: Nyi Roro Kidul, the queen of the southern sea, rules the ocean along Java's south coast; she is consort and guardian to the kings of Mataram and their successors, and the green sea-belt takes those she favours as it takes those who offend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese court legend of the Queen of the Southern Sea; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 南海女王妮·羅羅·基杜爾（Nyi Roro Kidul）統治著爪哇南岸一帶的海洋；她是馬打蘭諸王及其後繼者的配偶與守護者，而那條綠色海帶會帶走她所眷顧的人，正如它帶走冒犯她的人一樣。

passages.text: Green is her colour and is not worn on her shore; the palaces of the kraton keep a chamber for her visits, and the harbour of her legend is named Pelabuhan Ratu — the harbour of the queen. The south coast's casting legends recorded in the older chronicles — the king thrown into the South Sea at Kandang West — are the motif's roots.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese court legend, with the Raffles (1817) South-Sea motif noted; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 綠色是她的顏色，在她岸邊不可穿著；克拉頓（kraton）的王宮為她的來訪保留一間房室，而她傳說中的港口名為「巴拉布漢·拉圖」（Pelabuhan Ratu）——女王之港。較古老的編年史所記載的南岸放逐傳說——國王在甘當西（Kandang West）被投入南海——正是此一母題的根源。

title.en: The Princess of Gunung Ledang: A Phial of the Raja's Blood
title.zh: 利芒山公主：一瓶國王之血

region.en: Gunung Ledang (Mount Ophir), Malay Annals geography
region.zh: 利芒山（歐菲爾山，《馬來紀年》地理）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. XXVII (the embassy to the Princess Gunung Ledang), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Sultan Mahmud of Malacca, widowed, sends Tun Mamed up the musical mountain to ask for the Princess Gunung Ledang. The way up runs through groves of spontaneously melodious bamboo and a garden where flowers recite pantuns, to a hall of bone roofed with hair; the princess, in the guise of an old woman, sets her price: stairs of gold and of silver from Malacca to the mountain, a gnat's heart and a moth's heart each seven platters broad, a vat of human tears, a vat of young betel-nut juice, a phial of the raja's blood — and one of the young prince's. The king consents to all but the blood.
summary.zh: 滿剌加蘇丹馬末喪偶後，遣敦·馬末登『樂音之山』向利芒山公主求婚。登山之途經自鳴之竹林與花樹吟班頓詩之園，至骨為牆、髮為頂之大殿；公主化為老嫗索價：自滿剌加至山之金梯銀梯、闊七盤之蚊心與蛾心、人淚一缸、嫩檳榔汁一缸、國王之血一瓶——及幼王子之血一瓶。王允一切，惟血不可。

sensitivity.note: The Annals' most famous supernatural-wooing episode; the blood-price is the moral hinge.

passages.text: The king said, 'I want to ask the Princess Gunung Ledang'; and Tun Mamed, sent first to clear the way, ascends a mountain of violent gusts and unsupportable cold, where the bamboos are spontaneously melodious, the forest deer are enchanted by their melody, and a garden of wonderful beauty holds flowers that recite pantuns and fruits that laugh and smile.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XXVII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 國王說：「我想向勒當山公主（Princess Gunung Ledang）求親」；先被派去開路的敦·馬梅德（Tun Mamed）登上一座狂風猛烈、寒冷難耐的山，那裡竹子自發地奏出旋律，林中的鹿為這旋律所迷醉，而一座美妙絕倫的花園裡，花朵吟誦著班頓詩（pantun），果實則歡笑盈盈。

passages.text: At a hall whose materials are of bone and its roof of hair, the princess — in the guise of an old woman, hunch-backed and bent threefold — delivers her answer: if the raja of Malaca wishes for her, he must first make a flight of stairs of gold, and another of silver, from Malaca to Gunung Ledang; and present a gnat's heart seven platters broad, a moth's heart seven platters broad, a vat of human tears, a vat of the juice of the young betel nut, one phial of the raja's blood, and one phial of the Prince Raja Ahmed's blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XXVII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在一座以骨為材、以髮為頂的廳堂裡，公主——化身為一位駝背、彎腰三折的老婦——給出了她的答覆：倘若馬六甲（Malaca）的拉者（raja）想要她，他必須先從馬六甲到勒當山築起一道金階梯，再築一道銀階梯；並獻上七盤寬的蚊心、七盤寬的蛾心、一缸人淚、一缸檳榔嫩果的汁液、一小瓶拉者之血，以及一小瓶拉者阿末王子（Prince Raja Ahmed）之血。

passages.text: The whole is related to Sultan Mahmud Shah, who says that all these requests may be complied with, but that the taking of blood is an unpleasant business, and he has no inclination for it at all — the bride-price declined at the exact point where it asked for the life of his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XXVII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 整件事稟報給蘇丹馬末沙（Sultan Mahmud Shah），他說這些要求皆可照辦，但取血乃是不愉快之事，他全然無意為之——這份聘禮恰在索求他兒子性命之處被回絕了。

title.en: The Maro Cycle: The Dema Theology of Western Seram
title.zh: 瑪羅循環：西塞蘭之德瑪神學

region.en: Western Seram (Ceram), Maluku
region.zh: 馬魯古群島西塞蘭

period: Recorded 1937-38 by the Frobenius Institute expedition (Ad. E. Jensen); published Jensen, Hainuwele, 1939, and Myth and Cult, 1963

source.work: The dema corpus of the Wemale of western Seram, incl. the Maro dance cycle (recorded with named informants)

license: Jensen 1939/1963 quoted only as summary (copyright); dema narratives are community heritage — paraphrase only

summary.en: Around Hainuwele, the Frobenius expedition recorded the Wemale dema cycle: the primordial world of the dema-beings, the origin of the nine-night maro dance and its exchange, and the theology that all culture — dance, planting, death — rises from the acts and deaths of the dema. The corpus frames Hainuwele's murder as one episode in a complete moral history: killing is the price of sustenance, and the maro dance re-enacts it.
summary.zh: 弗羅貝尼烏斯探險隊於海努韋萊之外又錄得西塞蘭瓦馬勒人之德瑪故事群：原初德瑪存在之世界、九夜『瑪羅』舞與交換之起源、以及『一切文化——舞、耕、死亡——皆自德瑪之行與死而生』的神學。該故事群將海努韋萊之死納入完整道德史：殺戮為取食之代價，瑪羅舞即其重演。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (1937-39), flagged; Seram communities hold the heritage — paraphrase only.

canonical_translation: Jensen 1939 (German, copyright); paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The dema theology of western Seram, as reconstructed from the Jensen expedition's recordings, is Maluku's most systematic myth-cycle — the frame within which the Hainuwele story stands.

BEGINNING: THE WORLD OF THE DEMA. Before the present order, the world is inhabited by the dema — beings of the primordial time, neither gods nor animals, who act and die in ways that fix what the world will be. Their acts are the templates of things: each dema-death or dema-deed founds a species of plant, an instrument, a custom.

MIDDLE: THE MARO DANCE AND THE EXCHANGE. The great institution of the dema-time is the maro — the nine-night festival of dance and gift-exchange recorded with the Hainuwele story, in which the circle of dancers closes around the giver at the centre. The cycle tells how the maro was founded in the dema era and how its exchange binds clans to clans; the girl whose death defines the festival is buried at the dance-ground, and her body becomes the food plants — so that the festival's gifts are, in the theology, pieces of her, redistributed.

END: THE FALL INTO THE PRESENT. With the dema-era deaths, the world hardens into its present form: men are separated from the dema, death becomes the human condition, and the rituals — the maro, the funeral, the planting — are what remain of the passage. Jensen's famous reading is that the corpus encodes a theology of the origin of culture in primordial murder: killing is the price of sustenance, and ritual re-enacts it; the anthropological debate about his 'dema' category continues, but the corpus itself is Seram's, not the theory's.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle (1) grounds the maro festival as charter; (2) explains agriculture, exchange and death in one system; (3) supplies the dismembered-culture cluster with its eastern-Indonesian food-and-dance form; and (4) documents — through the named informants of the expedition notebooks — a complete regional theology before its twentieth-century transformations. The corpus's regional depth repays notice: the Frobenius expedition of 1937-38 recorded the Wemale narratives with named informants in its notebooks, and the published corpus in Jensen's Hainuwele (1939) and the later Myth and Cult arranged them into the dema-theology that became a benchmark of the history-of-religions school — a framework that later scholarship has both used and contested. What belongs to Seram itself is the narrative system: a primordial population whose deaths fix the world, a festival whose gifts are pieces of a buried girl, and an origin of culture in which killing is not an accident but the founding transaction. The maro's nine nights give the theology its calendar, and the funeral its doctrine: burial is planting, and the dead are the seed of the next crop. In comparative view the cycle stands with Hainuwele at the junction of the dismembered-creator myths (Purusha, Ymir, Pangu) and the exchange-festival charters of Melanesia and eastern Indonesia — producing, unlike the cosmic versions, not a universe but a meal, and not by a god's hand but by a community's.
narrative.zh: 據詹森探險隊錄音重建之西塞蘭德瑪神學，乃馬魯古最系統之神話群——即海努韋萊故事所處之框架。開篇：現存秩序之前，世界由德瑪居住——原初時代之存在者，非神非獸，其行與死規定世界之所將是；每一德瑪之死或行皆奠定一種植物、一件器物、一項習俗之原型。中段：德瑪時代之偉大制度即瑪羅——與海努韋萊故事一併錄得之九夜歌舞交換節；舞圈環繞居中之贈者而合攏。故事群敘述瑪羅如何奠基於德瑪時代、其交換如何綁定氏族；定此節日之少女葬於舞場，其身化為食糧之植物——故節日之贈品在神學上即她的碎片之再分配。結尾：隨德瑪時代之死亡，世界凝為今形：人與德瑪分離，死亡成為人之境遇；瑪羅、葬禮、耕作等儀式即通道之所餘。詹森之著名解讀：故事群以原初謀殺編碼『文化起源』之神學——殺戮為取食之代價、儀式即其重演；其『德瑪』範疇之爭論持續，但故事群本身屬於塞蘭，而非理論。功能：以憲章立瑪羅節、於一系統內解釋農耕、交換與死亡、為『碎身文化』母題群供給東印尼之『食與舞』形態、並經探險隊筆記中有名之報告人記錄了二十世紀轉型之前完整之區域神學。

functions: Charters the nine-night maro festival of dance and exchange
Explains agriculture, exchange and death within one system
Eastern-Indonesian form of the dismembered-culture cluster: food and dance from a dema body
Documents a complete regional theology through named informants before its modern transformations

variants.name: Hainuwele (the central dema myth)
variants.summary: The coconut-girl whose dismembered body becomes the clans' food plants — the corpus's central episode.

variants.name: Jensen's dema-theory debate
variants.summary: The 'dema' category as Jensen's interpretive frame; the corpus is Seram's heritage independent of the theory.

primary_sources.citation: Recorded 1937-38 by the Frobenius Institute expedition (Ad. E. Jensen) among the Wemale of western Seram; informants named in the expedition notebooks; published in Jensen, Hainuwele, Frankfurt 1939 (copyright), and Myth and Cult among Primitive Peoples, 1963.

secondary_sources.work: Adolf E. Jensen, Myth and Cult among Primitive Peoples
secondary_sources.citation: Jensen 1963, Chicago: University of Chicago Press — the dema-theology framework.

source_urls.description: Frobenius Institute — Jensen expedition archive

sensitivity_guidance: Colonial-era expedition materials; Seram and Maluku communities hold the heritage — paraphrase only, no verbatim ritual text.

passages.text: Before the present order the world is inhabited by the dema — beings of the primordial time whose acts and deaths fix what the world will be: each dema-death founds a species of plant, an instrument, a custom. The maro — the nine-night festival of dance and gift-exchange — is founded in the dema era; the girl whose death defines the festival is buried at the dance-ground and her body becomes the food plants, so that the festival's gifts are, in the theology, pieces of her redistributed among the clans.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Wemale dema corpus as summarized in the Jensen expedition materials; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Wemale dema corpus; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在現今秩序之前，世界由德瑪（dema）所居——他們是原初時代的存在，其行為與死亡奠定了世界將成的樣貌：每一樁德瑪之死都創生出一種植物、一件器具、一種習俗。馬羅（maro）——為期九夜的舞蹈與交換禮物之節慶——即奠基於德瑪時代；那位以其死亡界定此節慶的少女被葬於舞場，她的身體化為食用植物，因此在神學中，節慶的禮物便是她被分送給各氏族的碎片。

title.en: The Spectre Huntsman of the Malay Hills
title.zh: 馬來山中之魅影獵手

region.en: Selangor hills, Malay Peninsula (collected by Skeat)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪山丘（斯凱特採錄）

period: Recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. V

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. V, the Spectre Huntsman

summary.en: The Spectre Huntsman rides the forest trails at night with hound and spear — the leader of the spectral chase of the Malay hills, whose weapons are named in the charm-books: the lance singkabuana ('lion of the world'), the kris salngkisa. He is blamed for deaths in the forest, and his passing is read in the baying of unseen dogs.
summary.zh: 魅影獵手夜騎於林間小徑，帶獵犬與長矛——馬來山丘幽冥獵隊之主；符咒書中記其武器之名：長矛『辛卡布瓦納』（世界之獅）、克利斯『薩恩基薩』。林中暴斃皆歸咎於他；其過處，以無形獵犬之吠聲可辨。

sensitivity.note: Wild-huntsman folklore recorded 1900; paraphrase.

passages.text: The Spectre Huntsman rides the forest trails of the Malay hills at night with hound and spear, leader of the spectral chase; the charm-books name his weapons — the lance singkabuana, 'lion of the world,' and the kris salngkisa. Deaths in the forest are laid to his passage, and his approach is known by the baying of unseen dogs — the Malay wild huntsman in the Skeat collection's fullest figure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. V; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Skeat (1900); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 幽靈獵人帶著獵犬與長矛，夜間騎行於馬來山丘的林間小徑，是幽靈狩獵隊伍的首領；符咒書記載了他的武器——名為「singkabuana」（意為「世界之獅」）的長槍，以及名為「salngkisa」的馬來短劍。林中發生的死亡皆歸因於他的經過，而他的接近則以看不見的狗群吠聲為人所知——他是斯基特（Skeat）蒐集資料中最完整的馬來野獵人形象。

title.en: Men Who Are Tigers: The Malay Were-Beast Lore
title.zh: 化虎之人：馬來獸化傳說

region.en: Malay Peninsula and Sumatra (shared lore, collected by Skeat)
region.zh: 馬來半島與蘇門答臘（共享傳說，斯凱特採錄）

period: Recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic (1900)

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), the tiger and were-beast beliefs of the Malays

summary.en: In Malay belief certain men are tigers: the village tiger that passes by night may be a neighbour in his beast-shape, whose human clothes are found folded where the animal slept; such were-tigers do not eat their kin, spare their friends' herds, and can be recalled to human shape by recognition — a beast whose beastliness is a temporary and negotiable condition.
summary.zh: 馬來信仰中，某些人即是虎：夜行過村之虎可能是鄰人化身，其衣摺疊於獸睡之處；如此『化虎者』不食親屬、饒過友人之牛群，且可因相認而復人形——獸性在此是暫時可談判的狀態。

sensitivity.note: Were-beast folklore recorded 1900; careful not to frame any living community practice.

passages.text: In Malay belief certain men are tigers: the tiger that passes the village by night may be a neighbour in his beast-shape, his human clothes found folded where the animal slept. The were-tiger does not eat his kin and spares his friends' herds, and can be recalled to human shape by recognition — the beastliness a temporary and negotiable condition in the Skeat collection's tiger lore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Skeat (1900); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在馬來人的信仰中，某些人是老虎：夜間經過村莊的老虎，可能是某位鄰人以獸形現身，而他的衣物被發現摺疊在野獸睡臥之處。人虎不食其親族，並饒過友人的牲畜，且能因被認出而召回人形——在斯基特的老虎傳說中，獸性是一種暫時且可商議的狀態。

title.en: The Sword-Fish and the Plantain Rampart: Hang Nadim's Idea
title.zh: 劍魚與芭蕉堤：漢·納丁之策

region.en: Coast of Singhapura
region.zh: 獅子城海岸

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. X (the todak sword-fish), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The sword-fish todak come upon the coast of Singhapura, springing ashore to pierce men through and through, until none dare live on the beach. Paduka Sri Maharaja marches out and orders a rampart of his men's legs — until a boy among the people says: 'Of what use is a rampart of our legs? It would be much better to make a rampart of plantain stems.' The beaks bury themselves in the banana trunks and the fish are slain in heaps; and the great men, awed by the boy's understanding, counsel the raja to kill him before he grows — 'and he was accordingly put to death, but the guilt of his blood' remains in the chronicle's telling.
summary.zh: 劍魚（todak）湧至獅子城海岸，躍上岸穿透人體，海灘無人敢居。帕杜卡·斯里·摩訶拉賈親征，命部下以腿築壘——人群中一男孩言：『以腿築壘何用？不如以芭蕉莖為堤。』魚喙盡沒入蕉莖，劍魚成堆被殺；而大臣們懼此童之才，勸王於其長成前除之——『於是殺之，然其血之罪』永載紀年。

sensitivity.note: The Hang Nadim episode; the killing of the clever child is the chronicle's own commentary on royal fear.

passages.text: A species of sword-fish named todak came upon the coast of Singhapura, and springing ashore killed a great number of persons on the beach — striking the breast they pierced through the body to the back; so many were slain that nobody durst reside on the shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. X (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一種名為「todak」的旗魚來到新加坡（Singhapura）海岸，躍上岸來，在海灘上殺死了許多人——牠們刺穿胸膛，穿透身體直達背部；被殺者如此之多，以致無人敢居住在岸邊。

passages.text: Paduka Sri Maharaja marched out with all his ministers and warriors, and ordered a rampart to be formed of the legs of his men; but the sword-fish sprung out and pierced their limbs through and through. Among the people there was a boy who said: 'Of what use is it for us to form a rampart with our legs? It would be much better to make a rampart of plantain stems.' The raja heard and assented; the sword-fish rapidly struck their beaks into the plantain stems, and remaining there the people came and slew them in great numbers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. X (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴杜卡·斯里·馬哈拉惹（Paduka Sri Maharaja）率領全體大臣與戰士出動，下令以他部下的腿築成一道防壘；但旗魚躍出，將他們的肢體一一刺穿。人群中有一名男孩說道：「我們用腿築成防壘有什麼用？倒不如用芭蕉莖來築防壘。」拉惹聽後同意了；旗魚迅速將喙刺入芭蕉莖中，就此卡住，人們便前來大量殺死牠們。

passages.text: All the great men represented to him: 'Sire, if this boy, though so young, possesses such an uncommon understanding, what will he do when he grows up? It will be best for us to kill him.' He was accordingly put to death, but the guilt of his blood stays with the tellers — the chronicle's verdict on the fear of clever children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. X (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 所有顯貴都向他進言：「陛下，這男孩雖如此年幼，卻有這般不凡的見識，等他長大後會做出什麼事來？我們最好殺了他。」於是他被處死，但殺害他的罪責仍歸於講述此事的人——這是編年史對畏懼聰慧孩童所作的評斷。

title.en: The Albicore That Carried Him Ashore: The Taboo of the Alu-alu Fish
title.zh: 載他登岸的鰹魚：禁食鰹魚之禁忌

region.en: Jambu Ayer roadstead, Malay Annals geography
region.zh: 占布·阿耶爾泊地（《馬來紀年》地理）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. XI (Mani Farendan's shipwreck), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Prince Mani Farendan sails for Malacca with a fleet; at Jambu Ayer a violent storm sinks his ship, and fallen into the sea he leaps upon an albicore — the alu-alu fish — by which he is conveyed to land, catching hold of a ganda-suli tree to reach the shore. 'This is the reason that Mani Farendan forbade all his descendants to eat of the fish alu-alu, or to wear the flower of the ganda-suli' — the house's thanksgiving fixed as a food and flower taboo.
summary.zh: 瑪尼·法倫丹王子率船隊往滿剌加；至占布·阿耶爾，暴風驟起沉其船。他墜海中，躍上鰹魚（alu-alu）之背，被載至岸邊，攀住格達-蘇利樹而登陸。『故瑪尼·法倫丹禁其子孫食鰹魚、佩格達-蘇利之花』——家族之感恩定為食禁與花禁。

sensitivity.note: Fish-rescue etiology fixing a family taboo.

passages.text: When Mani Farendan arrived at Jambu Ayer, the wind arose, and a violent storm succeeded, and the ship of Mani Farendan sunk; and he having fallen into the sea leapt upon an albicore, or alu-alu fish, by which he was conveyed to land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當馬尼·法倫丹（Mani Farendan）抵達占布·阿耶爾（Jambu Ayer）時，風起了，隨即颳起猛烈的風暴，馬尼·法倫丹的船沉沒了；他落入海中，躍上一條長鰭鰹魚，即「alu-alu」魚，被牠載到了陸地。

passages.text: When he reached the shore he caught hold of a ganda-suli tree, and in this manner reached the land. This is the reason that Mani Farendan forbade all his descendants to eat of the fish alu-alu, or to wear the flower of the ganda-suli — the rescuers of the prince made forever untouchable by his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他抵達岸邊時，他抓住了一棵甘達蘇里樹，就這樣登上了陸地。正因如此，馬尼·法雷丹禁止他所有的後代食用阿魯阿魯魚，或佩戴甘達蘇里的花——王子的救命恩人，從此被他的家族永遠視為不可觸碰之物。

title.en: The Fisher-King: Raja Kasim Selling Fish to the Stranger Ship
title.zh: 漁夫王：向異船賣魚的卡西姆王子

region.en: Roadstead of Malacca
region.zh: 滿剌加泊地

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. XIII (Raja Kasim in disguise), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Dispossessed by his father's widow's party, Raja Kasim lives unregarded in the house of a fisherman and plies the fisher's trade at sea. When a vessel from the regions above the wind anchors, all the fishing prows come out to sell fish — among them Raja Kasim; and the merchant Moulana Jelal-ed-din, seeing him, calls him aboard and treats him with all the dignity of his rank. 'Why do you pay respect to me, a poor fisherman?' — 'Of a truth, you are the son of this country, and will certainly become raja of Malaca.'
summary.zh: 被庶母一黨剝奪繼承的卡西姆王子，匿身漁夫之家，操舟賣魚。一艘上風之邦的商船來泊，漁船盡出賣魚——卡西姆亦在其中；船上商人毛拉納·哲拉魯丁見之，請他登船、以王者之禮相待。『緣何禮遇賣魚之窮漁夫？』——『足下實為此國之子，必將為滿剌加之王。』

sensitivity.note: Disguised-king recognition episode; the blessing of the stranger merchant.

passages.text: Raja Kasim went unregarded and lived in the house of a fisherman, and for a long period plied the trade of a fisher at sea. When a vessel from the regions above the wind drew near the land, all the fishing prows and boats approached to sell fish to the people of the vessel; among the rest came Raja Kasim to sell his fish, in the dress of a fisherman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XIII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉惹·卡辛無人理會，住在一名漁夫的家中，長久以來在海上從事漁夫的行當。當一艘來自風之上地域的船隻靠近陸地時，所有的漁船和小舟都前來向船上的人們賣魚；拉惹·卡辛也混在其中，穿著漁夫的裝扮前來賣他的魚。

passages.text: The merchant Moulana Jelal-ed-din, as soon as he saw Raja Kasim, called him on board and treated him with all the dignity due to his rank. 'Why do you pay respect to me, a poor fisherman selling my fish?' — 'Of a truth, you are the son of this country, and will certainly become raja of Malaca' — the stranger's blessing that begins the restored reign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XIII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 商人毛拉納·傑拉爾-埃德-丁一見到拉惹·卡辛，便把他喚上船，並以與其身份相稱的尊榮款待他。「您為何對我這賣魚的窮漁夫如此禮敬？」——「說實話，您是本鄉之子，日後必將成為馬六甲的拉惹」——這異鄉人的祝福，開啟了復位的統治。

title.en: The Pursuit of Dewa Sura: Numbers, Names and the Mound of 'Gently, Gently'
title.zh: 追捕德瓦·蘇拉：數、名與『慢慢來』之丘

region.en: Jaram-kwoi mound, Malay Annals geography
region.zh: 賈拉姆-誇伊丘（《馬來紀年》地理）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals (the pursuit of Maha Raja Dewa Sura), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Ordered to pursue the fugitive Maha Raja Dewa Sura, the champion Sri Vija di Raja amuses himself — snaring apes, fishing with nets — while everyone else races for the reward. 'How do you youngsters know?' he answers: 'On trying his name by the power of numbers, it is subservient, and his time is also subservient to mine; how then can he escape from my hands?' The fugitive's boat grounds at a mound he names with a cry — kwoi! kwoi! 'gently, gently' in Siamese — the mound keeps the name Jaram-kwoi, and the fugitive is taken at the old woman's hut, without fetters, 'according to the custom of Princes.'
summary.zh: 奉命追捕逃亡的德瓦·蘇拉，勇士斯里·維賈·迪·拉賈卻自得其樂——捕猿、撒網——而人人爭先逐賞。『你們少年人懂什麼？』他答：『以數之力驗其名，其名已服；其時亦服於我時——他豈能逃出我手？』逃者之舟擱於一丘，他以暹語呼『誇伊！誇伊！』（慢慢來）而名之曰賈拉姆-誇伊；逃者在老嫗之屋被擒，不加縛鎖——『依王子之禮相待』。

sensitivity.note: Name-numerology (ilmu) applied to pursuit; the mound-etiology inside the episode.

passages.text: Sri Vija di Raja went on the pursuit, but he amused himself with catching the wild buffalo, piercing the rhinoceros, and snaring the ape, and wherever the sand of the river was fine, there he amused himself in fishing with nets. 'How do you youngsters know?' he said; 'on trying his name by the power of numbers, it is subservient, and his time is also subservient to mine; how then can he escape from my hands?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Malay Annals pursuit episode (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯里·維賈·迪·拉惹繼續追擊，但他卻以捕捉野牛、刺殺犀牛、設網捕猿為樂，凡是河水沙細之處，他便在那裡以網捕魚為樂。「你們這些年輕人怎麼知道？」他說；「以數術之力推算他的名字，他是順服的，他的時辰也順服於我；那麼他怎能逃出我的手心？」

passages.text: Maha Raja Deva Sura's boat grounded at the foot of a mound at the mouth of a small river, when he exclaimed 'kwoi! kwoi!' — 'gently, gently' in Siamese; hence the name of the mound is still Jaram-kwoi. There the Malaca men came up with him, and he was taken at the old woman's house and delivered up to the bandahara without fetters or bonds, treated according to the custom of Princes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Malay Annals pursuit episode; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬哈·拉惹·德瓦·蘇拉的船擱淺在一條小河河口的一座土丘腳下，他驚呼「kwoi！kwoi！」——在暹羅語中意為「輕些，輕些」；因此這座土丘至今仍名為賈蘭-奎。馬六甲的人們在那裡追上了他，他在老婦人的屋中被擒，未戴腳鐐手銬便被交給班達哈拉，並依王子的禮制受到對待。

title.en: The First Damasked Krises of Majapahit
title.zh: 馬卓帕希特首批大馬士革紋克利斯

region.en: Majapahit, East Java
region.zh: 東爪哇馬卓帕希特

period: Javanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the krises of Majapahit

summary.en: In the chronicle's account of the Majapahit period, the smiths' art reaches its highest perfection: 'the first damasked krises were now made by the pandi (smiths) from Pajajaran, who became so distinguished that they were appointed to the charge of districts with a thousand chaka each.' The kris afterwards placed on the tomb of Sunan Giri is said to have been manufactured at this time from a piece of old iron found by the prince — the weapon of state carried from found iron to holy tomb.
summary.zh: 編年史述馬卓帕希特之世，匠藝臻於極盛：『首批大馬士革紋克利斯由帕查查蘭來之鐵匠（pandi）鍛成，彼等名聲大著，各獲授千戶（chaka）之地之職。』後供於蘇南·吉里墓上之克利斯，據云即此時以王子所拾之一塊廢鐵鍛成——武器由拾得之鐵至聖墓完成旅程。

sensitivity.note: Smithing charter of the pusaka-kris tradition.

passages.text: The first damasked krises were now made by the pandi, or smiths, from Pajajaran, who became so distinguished that they were appointed to the charge of districts with a thousand chaka each — the smiths raised to lords of land by their art.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最初的達馬斯克紋短劍此時由來自帕查查蘭的潘迪，即鐵匠們所打造，他們聲名顯赫，以至於被任命掌管各區，每區各有一千查卡——鐵匠們憑其技藝被擢升為一方之主。

passages.text: The kris which was afterwards placed on the tomb of Sunan Giri is said to have been manufactured at this time from a piece of old iron found by the prince — found iron hammered into the holiest of blades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說，後來被安放在蘇南·吉里墓上的那把克里斯短劍，便是此時以王子所發現的一塊舊鐵鍛造而成——那塊尋獲的鐵被錘鍊成最神聖的劍刃。

title.en: The Prince in Commoner's Dress: The Arrow of Jaya Langkara's Iron
title.zh: 布衣王子：耶亞·蘭卡拉之鐵箭

region.en: Janggala, East Java
region.zh: 東爪哇章格拉

period: Madura-tradition legend recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the death of Ino Kerta Pati

summary.en: Finding the battle going against him, the prince of Nusa Antara remembers the guru's advice, the loss of his wife, and the insults of Ino Kerta Pati; throwing off his princely attire he disguises himself as a common man, arms himself with an arrow made from the iron of Jaya Langkara, and goes in search of his enemy — who falls dead at the first shot, 'it having been foretold that this chief could not be killed except by the iron staff of Jaya Langkara, of which the prince of Nusa Antara had made his arrow.'
summary.zh: 戰局逆轉之際，努薩·安塔拉王子想起上師之訓、亡妻之痛與伊諾·克爾塔·巴迪之辱；褪去王服、扮作常人，以耶亞·蘭卡拉之鐵所製之箭為兵器，尋仇而去——一箭而斃，『蓋預言曾云：此人唯耶亞·蘭卡拉之鐵杖能殺，而努薩·安塔拉王子之箭正是以此鐵所製』。

sensitivity.note: Completes the invulnerability-prophecy episode (batch-220).

passages.text: This prince, finding the battle going against him, recollected the advice of Guru Bramana Kdenda, the loss of his wife, and the many insults he had received from Ino Karta Pati; then throwing off his princely attire he disguised himself as a common man, and arming himself with an arrow mixed with the poison of Jaraga went in search of Ino Kerta Pati.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這位王子見戰事對己不利，便想起古魯·布拉馬納·克登達的勸告、自己喪妻之痛，以及他從伊諾·卡爾塔·帕蒂那裡所受的種種屈辱；於是脫下王子裝束，喬裝成平民，以一支摻了雅拉加毒藥的箭武裝自己，前去尋找伊諾·卡爾塔·帕蒂。

passages.text: He had no sooner found him than he discharged his arrow, and Ino Kerta Pati fell dead — it having been foretold that this chief could not be killed except by the iron staff of Jaya Langkara, of which the prince of Nusa Antara had made his arrow, arm and knife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他一找到對方，便射出箭矢，伊諾·卡爾塔·帕蒂當即倒地身亡——因為曾有預言說，這位首領除非被查亞·朗卡拉的鐵杖所殺，否則無法喪命，而努沙·安塔拉王子正是以那鐵杖製成了他的箭、臂甲與刀。

title.en: The Mountain That Thunders: Plague, Ash-Darkness and the Flight to Sea
title.zh: 轟鳴之山：瘟疫、灰暗與出海之逃

region.en: Mount Kelud, East Java, and the western coast
region.zh: 東爪哇克盧特山與西岸

period: Javanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the sickness and eruption of Kelud

summary.en: A dreadful sickness prevails in the eastern districts of Java, and the young prince quits his capital to found a new one in the west — while the first recorded eruption of Mount Kelud discharges 'like thunder,' its ashes involving the country 'in impenetrable darkness.' The sickness continuing after the prince's departure, the inhabitants who remained 'embarked in vessels and proceeded to sea, no one knowing whither they went or hearing more of them' — Java's legend of a people swallowed by its own volcano.
summary.zh: 東爪哇瘟疫大作，少年王子離棄都城，西行另建新都——與此同時，克盧特山首次大爆發，聲如雷鳴，火山灰使舉國陷入『不可穿透之黑暗』。王子去後疫情不止，留居之人『乘舟出海，無人知其所往，亦再無音訊』——爪哇民族自述為自家火山所吞。

sensitivity.note: Catastrophe-migration legend around Kelud's first recorded eruption.

passages.text: The causes which induced him to leave his capital are related to have been a dreadful sickness, which at that period prevailed in the eastern districts of Java, and the designs of his minister. The first eruption of the mountain Kelud, of which tradition makes mention, is recorded to have taken place at this time, when the discharges from it are represented to have been like thunder, and the ashes to have involved the country in impenetrable darkness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說，促使他離開都城的原因，是當時肆虐於爪哇東部各區的一場可怕疫病，以及他大臣的圖謀。傳說中提及的克盧德山第一次噴發，據記載便發生在此時，當時從山中噴出的物質被形容為如雷鳴一般，火山灰使整個地區陷入伸手不見五指的黑暗。

passages.text: The sickness having continued to prevail after the departure of the prince, the inhabitants who had remained are said to have embarked in vessels and proceeded to sea, no one knowing whither they went or hearing more of them — the vanished fleet of the eastern kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 王子離去之後，疫病仍持續肆虐，據說留下的居民便登上船隻出海而去，無人知道他們去了何處，也再無人聽聞他們的消息——那支東王國消失的船隊。

title.en: The Rice-Soul: Carrying the Rice-Child Home Under an Umbrella
title.zh: 稻之魂：以傘護送稻童歸家
