region.en: Selangor rice-fields, Malay Peninsula (collected by Skeat)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪稻田（斯凱特採錄）

period: Ceremony recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. V (vegetation charms)

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), the rice-soul ceremony (semangat padi)

summary.en: The rice has a soul, and the harvest is a rescue: the pawang leads a procession to the 'mother-sheaf', warning the herons and the 'spectral reapers' to retire; the cradle-basket of the Rice-child holds white cloth, parti-coloured thread, a hen's egg, a candle-nut, a cockle shell and a long iron nail; the first seven heads are cut into the cradle, rice is strewn over the sheaf and over the reapers' heads with 'kur semangat!' — 'cluck, cluck, soul!' — and the First Bearer slings the basket at her neck and opens an umbrella to shield the Rice-child from the sun on the road home.
summary.zh: 稻有魂，收穫即是救援：巫師（pawang）率隊至『母稻束』，先命蒼鷺與『幽靈收割者』退散；稻童之搖籃籃中置白布、五色線、雞蛋、蠟燭果、蛤殼與長鐵釘；先割七穗入籃，向母束與眾人頭上撒米，口中呼『庫·瑟瑪加！』——『咯咯，魂啊！』——首抬者以紅布將籃懸於頸間，撐傘遮陽，護『稻童』踏上歸家之路。

sensitivity.note: Rice-soul ceremony recorded 1900; paraphrase respectfully; the rice-mother theology parallels Dewi Sri across the archipelago.

passages.text: A shaped basket bound with the ribu-ribu creeper, standing in front of the three rice-baskets, was intended to serve as the cradle of the Rice-soul, or Rice-baby; it contained a strip of white cloth, parti-coloured thread, a hen's egg, a hard jungle-nut (candle-nut), a cockle shell, and a long iron nail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), the rice-soul ceremony; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一隻以里布—里布藤蔓捆綁的成形籃子，立在三隻稻籃之前，本是要充當稻魂或稻嬰的搖籃；籃中放著一條白布、雜色線、一枚雞蛋、一顆堅硬的林中果實（油桐果）、一枚鳥蛤殼，以及一根長鐵釘。

passages.text: On reaching the rice the procession filed through a lane already made until the mother-sheaf was reached from which the Rice-soul was to be taken; the pawang warned the herons of the region to roost on his bow-shaft and bade the Spectral Reapers retire. The first seven heads were cut and deposited as before in the basket; rice was strewn over the sheaf, and tossed backwards over the reapers' heads, with the cry 'kur semangat, kur semangat!' — cluck, cluck, soul!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat (1900); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 抵達稻田後，隊伍魚貫穿過一條早已開闢好的小徑，直到來到那束母稻前——稻魂即將從中取出；帕旺（pawang，巫師）警告該地的蒼鷺棲息在他的弓桿上，並命幽靈收割者退下。最先的七個稻穗被割下，如前一般放入籃中；稻米撒在稻束上，並越過收割者的頭頂向後拋擲，同時高喊「kur semangat, kur semangat!」——咯咯，咯咯，魂啊！

passages.text: The First Bearer slung the basket of the Rice-child about her neck and opened an umbrella to shield the Rice-child from the effects of the sun; without the umbrella, the recorders were told, the Rice-child could not be carried home — the harvest as a rescue of a soul small enough to sunburn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat (1900); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第一位持籃者將盛著稻童的籃子掛在頸上，並撐開一把傘，以遮蔽稻童免受日曬之苦；據告訴記錄者的說法，若無這把傘，稻童便無法被帶回家——收穫即是一場拯救，拯救一個小到會被曬傷的魂。

title.en: Male Floods and Female Floods
title.zh: 雄洪與雌洪

region.en: Selangor rivers, Malay Peninsula (collected by Skeat)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪諸河（斯凱特採錄）

period: Belief recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic (1900)

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), floods due to heavy rain (male and female floods)

summary.en: Floods, like other moving things, are conceived as male and female: floodwater 'due to heavy rain is conceived to be caused' by one sex of the water and the sudden spate that rolls down a river-bed by the other — the gendered taxonomy of the river's two tempers, recorded from the river-folk of Selangor.
summary.zh: 洪水如其他流動之物，亦有雌雄之分：驟雨之洪屬其一性，河道中奔突之暴漲屬另一性——雪蘭莪河民對河流兩副脾氣之性別分類。

sensitivity.note: River-lore record; read alongside the world-buffalo and tide-tree cosmologies.

passages.text: Floods, like other moving things, are conceived to be 'male' and 'female': the belief is that floods due to heavy rain are of one kind and the flood which sometimes rushes down a river-bed another — the river's two tempers given a gendered taxonomy in the Selangor river-lore collected by Skeat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洪水如同其他會動的事物一般，被設想為「雄性」與「雌性」：人們相信，因大雨而致的洪水屬於一種，而有時沿河床奔湧而下的洪水則屬於另一種——河流的兩種性情，在斯基特（Skeat）所搜集的雪蘭莪河川傳說中被賦予了性別化的分類。

title.en: Sri Tri Buana Buried on the Hill: The Offices of the New Court
title.zh: 三界之主葬於山丘：新朝廷之職官

region.en: Hill of Singhapura
region.zh: 獅子城之丘

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. IV (the death of Sri Tri Buana and the institution of the court offices), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When his earthly period was completed, Sri Tri Buana was buried on the hill of Singhapura; his son succeeds under a new title, and the court's constitution is fixed in the same breath as the mourning: the first bandahara Tun Parpatih Parmuka Barjaja, who occupies the sovereign's place when the sovereign will not show himself; the mantri opposite him; the pangulu bandahari; the chief hulubalang over all champions — the offices that will govern Malacca instituted at the founder's grave.
summary.zh: 斯里·三界之主壽終，葬於獅子城之丘；其子襲位並受新號；朝廷之憲制亦於此時同時確立：首位首相（bandahara）敦·帕帕提·帕爾穆卡·巴爾賈賈——王不露面時即代王位；其對座之大臣；彭古魯·邦達哈里；統領眾勇士之首席呼魯巴蘭——統治滿剌加之官制，即於開國者之墓前定立。

sensitivity.note: Court-constitution charter fixed at the founder's burial.

passages.text: After a long time, when his earthly period was completed, Sri Tri-buana departed this life, and was buried on the hill of Singhapura; he was succeeded by Raja Kichil Besar under the title of Paduca Sri Vicrama Vira. The constitution of the court was fixed with the mourning: Tun Parpatih Parmuka Barjaja became the first bandahara, and whenever the sovereign did not choose to show himself, his place was occupied by this minister; under him the pangulu bandahari, and the chief hulubalang who was over all the champions — the offices instituted at the founder's grave and carried on to Malacca.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. IV (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 許久之後，當他在人間的歲月圓滿，斯里·特里布阿納（Sri Tri-buana）辭別此生，葬於辛加普拉（Singhapura）山上；拉惹·基吉爾·勿沙（Raja Kichil Besar）以帕杜卡·斯里·維克拉瑪·維拉（Paduca Sri Vicrama Vira）之號繼承其位。宮廷的體制隨喪儀而定：敦·帕爾帕蒂·帕爾穆卡·巴爾賈賈（Tun Parpatih Parmuka Barjaja）成為首位班達哈拉（bandahara，首相），每當君主不願露面時，便由這位大臣代居其位；其下為彭古魯·班達哈拉（pangulu bandahari），以及統轄所有勇士的首領胡魯巴朗（hulubalang）——這些官職創設於創建者的墓前，並一直沿襲至馬六甲。

title.en: The Dalang's Night: Chanting the Legends Behind the Screen
title.zh: 達朗之夜：幕後吟唱古老傳說

region.en: West Javanese plantation district (a wayang night)
region.zh: 西爪哇種植園區（哇揚之夜）

period: Performance recorded by Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893)

source.work: W. Basil Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893), the wayang kulit performance observed

summary.en: The wayang night observed in the round: the dalang sits cross-legged before the lamp, sticking the puppets into a banana-stem log taken from a box at his side; he chants 'a long legendary tale taken from the ancient Javan literature, dealing with the times before the European occupation of the island'; at intervals he breaks into dialogue, working the puppets' arms and legs with wires, while the gamelan orchestra behind him punctuates the play — and the audience sits 'listening for hours, far into the night, without getting tired.'
summary.zh: 哇揚之夜全景：達朗盤坐燈前，身側木箱取偶、插於香蕉莖座；他吟唱『取自古爪哇文學之長篇傳說，所述乃歐人據島之前時代之事』；不時轉入對白，以鐵絲操縱戲偶手足；身後加美蘭樂隊點擊伴奏——觀眾『久坐傾聽，直到深夜而不倦』。

sensitivity.note: The wayang performance as sacred recitation; read with the Batara Kala ruwatan record for the rite's protective office.

passages.text: The dalang sat before the lamp with the puppets stuck in a banana-stem log taken from a box placed by his side; he chanted a long legendary tale taken from the ancient Javan literature, dealing with the times before the European occupation of the island; at intervals he broke into a dialogue, when he worked the puppets' arms and legs with wires, so that they seemed to be acting their several parts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Worsfold, A Visit to Java (1893); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達朗（dalang，操偶師）坐在燈前，傀儡插在他身旁一只箱子取出的香蕉莖段上；他吟唱一段取自古代爪哇文學的悠長傳說，內容涉及歐洲人佔領該島之前的時代；他不時轉為對白，此時他以細線操動傀儡的手腳，使它們彷彿各自扮演著自己的角色。

passages.text: Behind the dalang was a gamelan, a series of gongs on a wooden frame struck with wooden hammers by other members of the company; and it was interesting to observe the deep attention with which the audience followed the movements of the puppets and listened to the recitations — they would sit there listening for hours, far into the night, without getting tired.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Worsfold (1893); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 達朗身後是一組甘美朗（gamelan），即架在木框上的一排鑼，由戲班其他成員以木槌敲擊；觀察觀眾如何全神貫注地追隨傀儡的動作、聆聽吟誦，著實有趣——他們會坐在那裡聆聽數小時，直至深夜，也不覺疲倦。

title.en: Sleeping at the Chief's Grave: The Dream-Bargain with a Dead Man
title.zh: 睡於酋長墓旁：與亡者的夢中交易

region.en: Klemantan and Sea Dayak country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸克勒曼丹與海上達雅克之地（象徵性定位）

period: Cult practice recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the cult of deceased chiefs

summary.en: A recently deceased chief of exceptional capacity becomes the object of a cult: men go to sleep beside his grave hoping for good dreams, invoking the dead man's aid in acquiring health or wealth or whatever a man most desires; Sea Dayaks fix a tube of bamboo leading from just above the eyes of the corpse to the surface of the ground, and address the dead man through it — the making of a god from a remembered ruler.
summary.zh: 才略超群之新亡酋長遂成崇拜之對象：人們睡於其墓旁以求吉夢，呼其助己得康健、財富或心之所欲；海上達雅克人並自死者眼上方插一竹管通至地表，隔管與亡者言語——由被記憶的統治者鑄成一位神明。

sensitivity.note: Ancestor-deification practice recorded 1912; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: A recently deceased chief of exceptional capacity and influence becomes not infrequently the object of a certain cult among Klemantans and Sea Dayaks: men will go to sleep beside his grave or tomb, hoping for good dreams and invoking the aid of the dead chief in acquiring health, or wealth, or whatever a man most desires.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位近日過世、能力卓越且影響力非凡的酋長，往往會成為克萊曼丹人與海達雅克人之間某種祭祀的對象：人們會睡在他的墳墓或陵墓旁，期盼獲得吉夢，並祈求這位已故酋長相助，以求得健康、財富，或任何人最渴望之物。

passages.text: Sea Dayaks sometimes fix a tube of bamboo leading from just above the eyes of the corpse to the surface of the ground; they will address the dead man through it — the grave becoming a speaking-place, and the dead chief a god in the making.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 海達雅克人有時會固定一根竹管，從死者雙眼正上方一直通到地面；他們會透過它向死者說話——墳墓於是成了說話之所，而這位已故酋長則成了正在成形中的神。

title.en: Bali Sungei: The Dragon at the Bottom of the River
title.zh: 巴利·松蓋：河底之龍

region.en: Kenyan and Kayan rivers, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸肯雅與加揚諸河（象徵性定位）

period: Religious tradition recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the river-gods of the Kenyahs

summary.en: Bali Sungei is embodied in a huge serpent or dragon living at the bottom of the river; he causes the violent swirls and uprushes of water that appear on the surface in times of flood, is regarded with fear, and is held responsible for the upsetting of boats and the drownings in the river — the river's temper given a body in the deep water.
summary.zh: 巴利·松蓋化身為一條居於河底之巨蛇或龍；洪水之時水面猛旋猛湧，皆其所為；人對之懷畏，舟覆溺亡之禍皆歸其身——河流之脾氣在深水之中獲得了身體。

sensitivity.note: River-dragon record; compare the Batak Naga Padoha and the Malay Ular Naga.

passages.text: Bali Sungei is thought of as embodied in a huge serpent or dragon living at the bottom of the river; he is supposed to cause the violent swirls and uprushes of water that appear on the surface in times of flood, and is held responsible for the upsetting of boats and drownings in the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴里雙溪被認為化身為一條巨大的蛇或龍，棲居於河底；據信是牠造成了洪水時河面出現的猛烈漩渦與湧流，船隻翻覆與河中溺斃之事也被歸咎於牠。

passages.text: He is regarded with fear; and it is not clear that he is the spirit of the river itself, for floods and the various changes of the river do not seem to be attributed to him — only the sudden violence of the deep water is his.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人們對牠心懷畏懼；而牠是否即為河流本身的精靈，則並不清楚，因為洪水與河流的種種變化似乎並不被歸因於牠——唯有深水突發的狂暴才是牠的作為。

title.en: The Batu Tuloi: Stones That Grow and Move of Themselves
title.zh: 巴圖·圖洛伊：自行生長移動之石

region.en: Kenyan longhouses, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸肯雅長屋（象徵性定位）

period: Practice recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the batu tuloi of the Kenyah altar-posts

summary.en: Peculiar adjuncts of the Kenyah altar-posts are the deep-red dracaena plant and a number of large spherical stones, the batu tuloi — perpetual possessions of the house. Their history is unknown; they are supposed to grow gradually larger and to move spontaneously when danger threatens the house; and when a household removes to build a new home, the stones are carried to the new site with some ceremony.
summary.zh: 肯雅祭柱旁有深紅龍血樹與數枚大圓石——巴圖·圖洛伊，為家宅永傳之物。其來歷無人知曉；相傳其體漸長，且於家宅有險時自行移動；家戶遷居建新屋之日，諸石須行禮遷往新址。

sensitivity.note: Animate-stone possession record; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: Peculiar adjuncts of the altar-posts of the Kenyahs are the dracaena plant and a number of large spherical stones, batu tuloi; these are perpetual possessions of the house, whose history is unknown, but they are supposed to grow gradually larger and to move spontaneously when danger threatens the house. When a household removes and builds for itself a new home, these stones are carried with some ceremony to the new site — the house's luck travelling with its stones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 肯雅人祭壇柱的特殊附屬物，是龍血樹植物與若干大型球狀石頭，即「巴圖圖洛伊」；這些是屋子的永久所有物，其來歷不明，但據信它們會逐漸變大，並在屋子遭遇危險時自行移動。當一戶人家遷移並為自己建造新居時，這些石頭會伴隨若干儀式被帶往新址——屋子的運氣隨著它的石頭一同遷移。

title.en: Bali Flaki: The Carrion Hawk That Ate a War-God's Job
title.zh: 巴利·弗拉基：吞沒戰神職分的食腐鷹

region.en: Kenyan country, interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲內陸肯雅之地（象徵性定位）

period: Religious tradition recorded by Hose & McDougall (1912)

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the cult of Bali Flaki

summary.en: A special position in the Kenyah system is occupied by Bali Flaki, the carrion hawk — the principal omen bird of war. Alone among the many omen-birds he has an altar-post of his own, sometimes surmounted by a wooden image of the hawk; and Hose and McDougall judge that the bird has driven into the background, 'and more or less completely taken the place of, a god of war whose name even has been forgotten by many of the Kenyahs, if not by all of them.'
summary.zh: 肯雅體系中，食腐之鷹巴利·弗拉基佔有特殊之位——其為戰事占卜之首要靈鳥。眾多占卜鳥中唯他有專屬祭柱，柱頂或立木鷹之像；霍斯與麥克杜格爾論曰：此鳥已將戰神擠入幕後，『或多或少完全取代了一位戰神——其名為許多肯雅人（若非全部）所遺忘』。

sensitivity.note: A documented case of an omen-bird displacing its god.

passages.text: A special position in the Kenyah system is occupied by Bali Flaki, the carrion hawk, the principal omen bird observed during the preparation for and conduct of war; an altar-post before the house is assigned to him, in some cases surmounted by a wooden image of the hawk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在肯雅人的體系中，食腐鷹巴里弗拉基佔有特殊地位，牠是備戰與作戰期間所觀察的主要預兆鳥；屋前有一根祭壇柱被指派給牠，有時柱上還立著一尊木製的鷹像。

passages.text: The Kenyahs have carried further the tendency to let the omen birds figure so prominently in their rites as to obscure the gods whose messengers they are; Bali Flaki has in this way taken the place of a god of war whose name even has been forgotten by many of the Kenyahs, if not by all of them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 肯雅人更進一步發展了這種傾向：讓預兆之鳥在他們的儀式中佔據如此顯著的地位，以致遮蔽了那些以牠們為使者的神祇；巴厘弗拉基便這樣取代了一位戰神的位置，而這位戰神的名字，即使不是全體肯雅人，也已被許多肯雅人所遺忘。

title.en: The Flattened Skull: The Midwife Who Made a Second Alexander
title.zh: 扁顱嬰兒：產婆造就的第二位亞歷山大

region.en: Singhapura (Malay Annals geography)
region.zh: 獅子城（《馬來紀年》地理）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VI (the birth of Raja Secander Zulkarneini the second), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The queen Dasya Putri bears a son 'whose skull was flattened in the birth by the midwife, and who was named Raja Secander Zulkarneini' — the Annals gives its future Malacca founder the name of Alexander the Great himself, marked at birth by the flattened head of a hard delivery.
summary.zh: 王后達夏·普特里產下一子，『因產婆之手而顱骨扁平』——命名為『拉賈·西坎德·祖勒卡爾奈尼』。《紀年》以亞歷山大大帝之名賜予其未來滿剌加開國之主，其出生之印記竟是難產造成的扁顱。

sensitivity.note: Birth-omen and name-inheritance in the Annals' genealogy.

passages.text: The raja's queen, Dasya Putri, became pregnant, and produced a son whose skull was flattened in the birth by the midwife, and who was named Raja Secander Zulkarneini — the name of Alexander the Great, given to the Annals' future founder of Malacca.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉惹的王后達西亞·普特麗懷了孕，產下一子，這嬰兒在出生時被接生婆壓扁了頭骨，取名為拉惹·塞坎德爾·祖爾卡內尼——即亞歷山大大帝之名，此名被賦予《年鑑》中未來馬六甲的建立者。

title.en: The Deathbed Charge of Sultan Malac al Salih
title.zh: 馬立克·薩利赫臨終之囑

region.en: Samudra, north Sumatra
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘三摩陀

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VII (the dying charge of Sultan Malec al Salih), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Summoning his two sons and the great men of Samadra to his deathbed, the first sultan of Sumatra charges them: 'Do not covet the wealth of others, and do not desire the wives of others, but agree with each other like brothers, and do not quarrel'; and to the two guardians of the princes, Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din and Sidi Ali Ismayemdi: 'Carefully bring up these my children, and do not suffer two brothers to quarrel' — a charge they swear to 'by the great God, the Creator of all.'
summary.zh: 三摩陀開國蘇丹臨終召集二子與國中重臣，囑曰：『勿覬他人之財，勿慕他人之妻；兄弟相睦，勿相爭。』又囑二位王子之監護人西迪·阿里二人：『善養吾子，勿使兄弟相爭。』二人『憑創造萬物之偉大神明』立誓。

sensitivity.note: Royal testament episode; the brother-peace charge as dynastic ethic.

passages.text: Sultan Malec al Salih, sickening, summoned his two sons with all the great men of Samadra and addressed them: 'O my two sons, and you my friends, I am at the point of death; may you remain happy after I have left you: and you, my sons, do not covet the wealth of others, and do not desire the wives of others, but agree with each other like brothers, and do not quarrel.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 蘇丹馬列克·阿爾·薩利赫病重，召來他的兩個兒子以及薩馬德拉的所有顯貴，對他們說道：「啊，我的兩個兒子，還有你們，我的朋友們，我已臨近死亡；願你們在我離去之後依然幸福；而你們，我的兒子們，不要貪圖他人的財富，不要覬覦他人的妻子，而要像兄弟一般和睦相處，不要爭吵。」

passages.text: To Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din and Sidi Ali Ismayemdi he said: 'Carefully bring up these my children, and do not suffer two brothers to quarrel; adhere firmly to your fidelity to them, and do not join yourselves to other rajas.' They assented in profound grief, swearing by the great God, the Creator of all, that they would faithfully maintain their allegiance to the princes his sons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他對西迪·阿里·蓋亞斯·埃德丁與西迪·阿里·伊斯邁耶姆迪說道：「要小心撫育我這些孩子，不要讓兩兄弟爭吵；要堅定地對他們保持忠誠，不要與其他拉惹結交。」他們在深切的悲痛中應允，並向偉大的神、萬物的創造者發誓，他們將忠實地對諸位王子——他的兒子們——保持效忠。

title.en: Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok
title.zh: 卡科爾托克首領翁戈爾托克

region.en: Kakortok (Julianehaab district), South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭卡科爾托克（尤利安娜霍布一帶）

period: Inuit oral tradition; West Greenland tradition of the ancient Scandinavian settlers, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The only trace of the ancient Scandinavian settlers: taunted into killing a shell-gathering Kavdlunak, the kayaker kills a second and the Kavdlunait revenge themselves with axes, sparing only two brothers — the younger losing an arm before Kaisape's eyes ('As long as thou livest thou won't surely forget thy poor brother'). Years on, Kaisape builds a false iceberg of white seal-skins in a hollowed spar, drifts it up to Kakortok, fires the house with juniper fagots, and hunts Ungortok with a barren woman's boot-shelf arrow charmed by an Eastlander — through the sleeping wife's throat, past the thin-as-a-shadow dodge, until the charmed shaft goes through the protruding chin.
summary.zh: 關於古斯堪地那維亞移民的唯一口傳：皮艇客被戲弄著射殺撿貝的卡夫德盧納克，再殺第二人——仇家提斧屠村，兄弟二人僅以身免，幼弟斷臂，兄長卡伊薩佩銘記於心。多年後他以白海豹皮裝入掏空浮木，偽裝冰山漂至卡科爾托克，以杜松柴火焚其屋；再向東地人求得『不孕婦靴架之木』所製的神箭——穿過熟睡妻子的咽喉、避過扁如薄影的閃避，最終穿透首領昂出的下巴，報了斷臂之仇。

sensitivity.note: Rink: the only trace of intelligence concerning the ancient Scandinavian settlers found in the country; Kakortok = Julianehaab with Scandinavian ruins 8 miles distant. Graphic mutilation and killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: It once happened that a kayaker from Arpatsivik came rowing up the firth, trying his new bird-javelin as he went along. On approaching Kakortok, where the first Kavdlunait had taken up their abode, he saw one of them gathering shells on the beach, and presently he called out to him, 'Let us see whether thou canst hit me with thy lance.' The kayaker would not comply, although the other continued asking him; at last, however, the master of the place, named Ungortok, made his appearance, and said, 'Since he seems so very anxious about it, take good aim at him' — and soon the kayaker sent out his spear in good earnest, and killed him on the spot. Ungortok, however, did not reproach him, but only said, 'It certainly is no fault of thine, since thou hast only done as thou wast bidden.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，一個來自阿爾帕齊維克的皮艇手划著艇沿峽灣而上，一邊划一邊試用他那支新的鳥形標槍。當他接近卡科爾托克——首批卡夫德盧奈特人已在那裡定居——時，他看見其中一人在海灘上拾貝殼，不久便朝他喊道：「讓我們看看你能不能拿長矛刺中我。」皮艇手不肯照辦，儘管那人一再請求他；最後，這地方的首領、名叫溫戈爾托克的人現身了，說道：「既然他似乎如此急切，你就好好瞄準他吧」——皮艇手隨即認真地擲出長矛，當場將他殺死。然而溫戈爾托克並未責備他，只說道：「這當然不是你的過錯，因為你不過是照吩咐行事罷了。」

passages.text: When winter came it was a general belief that the Kavdlunait would come and avenge the death of their countryman; but summer came round again, and even two summers passed quickly by. At the beginning of the third winter the same kayaker again rowed up to Kakortok, provided with the usual hunting tools, bladder and all. This time he again happened to see a Kavdlunak gathering shells, and somehow took a fancy to kill him too: rowing up on the sunlit side of the water, launching his spear, he killed him at once, returned home unobserved, and told how he had done away with one of the Kavdlunait. They reproached him with not having let their chief know of this — 'The first time I only killed him because I was asked over and over again to do so.' Some time after, a girl sent out to draw water in the evening noticed the reflection of something red down in the water; turning round she was horrified at seeing a great crowd of Kavdlunait — so confounded that she left the pail behind and hurried into the house. The enemies posted themselves in front of the door and the windows; one of the inmates ran out but was soon killed with an axe and cast aside — they were all despatched in this way, only two brothers remaining unhurt, who happily escaped out on the ice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 冬天來臨時，人們普遍相信卡夫德盧奈特人會前來為他們同胞的死復仇；但夏天又再度來臨，甚至兩個夏天也匆匆過去了。第三個冬天開始時，同一個皮艇手又帶著慣常的狩獵工具——包括浮囊等一應俱全——划艇來到卡科爾托克。這一次他又碰巧看見一個卡夫德盧奈克人在拾貝殼，不知怎地又起了念頭想把他一併殺掉：他划到水面向陽的一側，擲出長矛，當場將他殺死，未被察覺地返回家中，並講述了自己如何除掉了一個卡夫德盧奈特人。他們責備他沒有讓首領知道此事——「第一次我殺他，只是因為我一再被請求那樣做。」過了些時候，一個女孩在傍晚被派出去打水，她注意到水下有某種紅色之物的倒影；她轉過身來，驚恐地看見一大群卡夫德盧奈特人——她驚慌失措，丟下水桶便急忙跑進屋裡。敵人部署在門前和窗前；屋內一人跑了出去，但很快被斧頭砍死並棄置一旁——他們就這樣被一一解決，只有兩兄弟毫髮無傷，僥倖逃到冰上。

passages.text: The Kavdlunait soon caught sight of them: 'Those are the last of the lot; let us be after them' — and at once began the pursuit, their leader claiming to be the quickest. The brothers' speed was greatly retarded, the younger having new soles to his boots which made them slippery and often cost him his footing. They reached the opposite shore; Kaisape, the elder, succeeded in climbing the icy beach, but the younger fell and was quickly overtaken. Ungortok cut off his left arm, and held it up before his brother, saying, 'Kaisape! as long as thou livest thou won't surely forget thy poor brother.' Kaisape, unarmed, could render him no assistance, but quickly took to his heels, crossing the country for Kangermiutsiak where his father-in-law was living. He remained there all winter, was presented with a kayak, kayaked south in summer to learn some magic lay that had power to charm his enemies, wintered again, and went north to find himself a companion — at every place inquiring first if there happened to be a couple of brothers, then examining the inside fur of their boots to see whether they had any lice in them, travelling far and wide before he found two brothers of whom the younger was altogether without lice. This one he persuaded to assist him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡夫德魯奈特人（Kavdlunait）不久便望見了他們：「那些是最後一批了；我們追上去吧」——隨即展開追擊，他們的首領自稱跑得最快。兩兄弟的速度大為受阻，弟弟的靴子換了新底，走起來很滑，使他屢屢失足。他們抵達對岸；哥哥凱薩佩（Kaisape）成功爬上了結冰的海灘，但弟弟跌倒了，很快便被追上。溫戈托克（Ungortok）砍下他的左臂，舉在哥哥面前說：「凱薩佩！只要你活著，想必不會忘記你可憐的弟弟。」凱薩佩手無寸鐵，無法救他，只得趕快拔腿奔逃，穿越陸地前往他岳父所居的康格爾米烏齊亞克（Kangermiutsiak）。他在那裡待了整個冬天，獲贈一艘獨木舟，夏天便划舟南下去學某種能魅惑敵人的法術，又過了一冬，再往北去尋找同伴——每到一處，他都先打聽那裡是否恰有兩兄弟，然後察看他們靴內的毛皮，看有沒有蝨子，走了很遠很廣，才找到兩兄弟，其中弟弟身上完全沒有蝨子。他說服了這人來協助他。

passages.text: Very intent on catching seals, of all he caught he had the hairs removed from the skins to be used for white skins; then he found a large piece of driftwood, excavated it with his knife until it was all hollow like a tube, made a cover to fit tightly at one end, furnished both sides with little holes and stoppers of wood. He put all the white skins inside the hollow space, shut it up, put it down into the water, and all the kayakers joined in towing it down the inlet to Pingiviarnek, where, having got out the skins and attached strings, they hoisted and spread them like sails, so that the boat came to have the appearance of a somewhat dirty iceberg. The people got in, the boat was pushed off, Kaisape gave the order 'Let the skins be spread!' — and the people on shore were astonished to see how very like it was to an iceberg floating slowly along. When the fair wind set in, the firth filled with broken bits of ice; several boats followed in his wake, their crews landing a little north of Kakortok to gather fagots of juniper, while Kaisape and his helpmates, well hidden in the hollow wood and keeping a constant look-out through the peep-holes, drifted straight on towards the house. Once they distinctly heard it announced, 'The Kaladlit are coming!' — all came running out, but when the master had reassured them, 'It is nothing but ice,' they again retired, and Kaisape said, 'Now, quick! they won't be coming out for a while, I think.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他非常專注於捕海豹，凡他所捕得的，都把皮上的毛除去，以作白色皮料之用；接著他找到一大塊浮木，用刀把它挖空，直到整塊中空如管，又做了一個能嚴密合於一端的蓋子，兩面都裝上小孔和木塞。他把所有白皮放進中空的空間裡，封好，放入水中，所有划獨木舟的人一同把它拖下海灣，拖到平吉維亞爾內克（Pingiviarnek），在那裡取出皮子、繫上繩索，把它們升起張開如帆，使那船看上去像一座略帶污濁的冰山。眾人上了船，船被推離岸，凱薩佩下令「把皮子張開！」——岸上的人驚異地看到它多麼像一座緩緩漂流的冰山。順風吹起時，海灣裡滿是碎冰；好幾艘船跟在他的船後，船上的人在北距卡科爾托克（Kakortok）不遠處登岸，採集杜松柴束，而凱薩佩和他的幫手們則藏身於中空的木頭裡，透過窺孔不斷瞭望，徑直向那屋子漂去。有一次他們清楚地聽見有人宣告：「卡拉德利特人（Kaladlit）來了！」——所有人都跑了出來，但當主人安撫他們說「不過是冰罷了」，他們便又回去了，凱薩佩說：「現在，快！我想他們一時半刻不會再出來了。」

passages.text: They got out on shore, and, well loaded with juniper fagots, surrounded the house; Kaisape filled up the doorway with fuel and stuck fire to it, so that all the people inside were burned, and those who tried to escape through the passage were also consumed. But Kaisape cared little for the people in general; his thoughts all centred in Ungortok — 'Kaisape! the man whom thou seekest is up there.' The chief had left the burning house through a window and was flying with his little son in his arms; at the lake the father threw his child into the water that it might rather die unwounded, and Kaisape, not being able to overtake his antagonist, was forced to return to his crew. Ungortok ran on till he reached Igaliko, and established himself with another chief named Olave; on finding that Kaisape would not leave him at peace he removed to the head of the firth Agdluitsok, settling at Sioralik, while Kaisape established himself at the outlet of the same firth. The following summer he again left in pursuit, Ungortok getting to the coast opposite the island of Aluk, Kaisape tracing him to the north side of the same island, where he took up his abode; there he consulted the Eastlanders with regard to some means of killing Ungortok, and at last one stood forth: 'I will get thee a bit of wood from a barren woman's boot-shelf, out of which thou must shape thine arrow' — having pronounced some spell upon it, he handed it over, and Kaisape acknowledged the gift: 'If it comes true that this shall help me, I will be bound to give thee my aid in hunting and fishing.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們上了岸，滿載杜松柴束，包圍了那屋子；凱薩佩用柴薪堵住門口，點上火，於是屋裡所有人盡被燒死，那些想從通道逃出的人也被燒死了。但凱薩佩對一般人並不在意；他的心思全集中在溫戈托克身上——「凱薩佩！你要找的人就在上面。」首領已從窗戶逃出著火的屋子，抱著他的小兒子奔逃；到了湖邊，父親把孩子扔進水裡，寧願他不帶傷痕地死去，而凱薩佩追不上他的對手，只得回到他的同伴那裡。溫戈托克一路奔逃，直到伊加利科（Igaliko），與另一位名叫奧拉夫（Olave）的首領同住；發覺凱薩佩不肯讓他安寧，便遷到阿格德盧伊措克（Agdluitsok）灣的灣頭，定居於西奧拉利克（Sioralik），而凱薩佩則在同一海灣的出口處安頓下來。次年夏天他又出發追擊，溫戈托克逃到阿盧克島（Aluk）對岸的海岸，凱薩佩追蹤他到同一島的北側，在那裡住了下來；他在那裡向東地人（Eastlanders）請教殺死溫戈托克的辦法，終於有一人站出來說：「我要給你一小塊取自不孕婦人靴架的木头，你必須用它削成你的箭」——他對它念了些咒語，便交了出去，凱薩佩領受了這份贈禮：「倘若這真能助我，我必當在狩獵和捕魚上助你。」

passages.text: He made as many arrows as could be contained in a sealskin quiver, adding last of all the precious charmed one, and with his helpmates left for the great lake in front of Ungortok's house, sticking all the arrows in the ground at a certain distance from each other, and finally the charmed one. Letting his companion remain below by the lake, he cautiously mounted high hills, from whence he could see Ungortok striding to and fro outside his house, talking to himself and mentioning the name of Kaisape. In the dusk he stole away to the house and looked in at the window, holding his bow ready bent; Ungortok was passing up and down as swiftly as a shadow, making a sure aim impossible — so Kaisape levelled his bow at Ungortok's wife, who lay sleeping with a baby at her breast; hearing a noise, Ungortok gave a look at his wife and perceived the arrow sticking fast in her throat. Kaisape ran back to the lake to fetch another arrow while Ungortok sped after him with the uplifted axe that had formerly killed his brother; the second arrow was escaped by falling down and making himself so thin that nothing but his chin remained visible, and before long Kaisape had spent all his arrows without having hit his mark — Ungortok broke them in twain and threw them into the lake. But at last Kaisape caught hold of the charmed arrow, and this went straight through the protruding chin down into the throat. As Ungortok did not expire immediately, Kaisape took flight, shortly followed by the wounded Ungortok; running a good long while, he suddenly felt his throat getting dry and fell down totally exhausted — remembering Ungortok, he rose again and ran back to find his dead body lying close by. He cut off his right arm and held it up before the dead man, repeating his own words, 'Behold this arm, which thou wilt surely never forget!' He also killed the orphan child, and taking the old Eastlander with him, travelled back to Kangermiutsiak, where he sustained the old man, whose bones, according to report, were laid to rest in that same place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他做了滿滿一個海豹皮箭袋所能裝下的箭，最後加上那支珍貴的施咒之箭，便與他的幫手們前往溫戈托克屋前的大湖，把所有箭按一定距離一一插在地上，最後插上那支施咒之箭。他讓同伴留在湖邊下方，自己小心翼翼地登上高丘，從那裡可以望見溫戈托克在屋外來回踱步，自言自語，提到凱薩佩的名字。暮色中他悄悄潛到屋前，從窗戶望進去，把弓拉滿待發；溫戈托克如影子般迅疾地來回走動，使人無法瞄準——於是凱薩佩把弓對準溫戈托克的妻子，她正摟著嬰兒睡著；溫戈托克聽見聲響，朝妻子一看，發覺那支箭已牢牢插在她喉嚨上。凱薩佩奔回湖邊去取另一支箭，溫戈托克則舉起那柄曾殺死他弟弟的斧頭疾追其後；第二支箭被他伏倒在地、把自己縮得極薄，只露出下巴而躲過，不久凱薩佩的箭已用盡，卻一支也沒射中目標——溫戈托克把它們折成兩段，扔進湖裡。但最後凱薩佩抓起了那支施咒之箭，它直穿那突出的下巴，深入喉嚨。由於溫戈托克並未立即斷氣，凱薩佩便逃走了，受傷的溫戈托克隨即追來；跑了很長一段路後，他忽然覺得喉嚨發乾，精疲力竭地倒下——想起溫戈托克，他又站起來跑回去，發現他的屍體就躺在近旁。他砍下他的右臂，舉在死者面前，重複著他自己的話：「看這條手臂，你必定永遠不會忘記！」他又殺死了那孤兒，帶著那位年老的東地人，返回康格爾米烏齊亞克，在那裡贍養老人，據說老人的遺骨就安葬在那同一個地方。

title.en: The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait
title.zh: 格陵蘭人與古卡夫德盧納人的初遇

region.en: Kangersunek and Pisigsarfik, Godthaab district
region.zh: 努克地區康格蘇內克與射箭山

period: Inuit oral tradition; Godthaab narrators, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 54 (2) 'The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait in Greenland', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A boat's crew landing at Nook finds the fiord already settled by the first Kavdlunak settlers, who treat them kindly — but they hasten away afraid, returning with many boats until the two peoples learn each other's language. At Kapisilik a Kavdlunak and a Kalalek become inseparable friends, first-rate archers whose arrows always fall side by side — until the wager 'he who fails shall be thrown down the precipice' is accepted against the Greenlander's protest, the Kavdlunak misses, the Kalalek pierces the skin target in the centre, and the mountain has been called Pisigsarfik (the shooting-place) ever since.
summary.zh: 一支大舟在努克登岸，發現峽灣裡早住著第一批卡夫德盧納克移民；對方以禮相待，格陵蘭人卻驚懼而去——直至眾舟齊至、兩族互學語言。在卡皮西利克，一名卡夫德盧納克與一名格陵蘭人結成莫逆，箭術相當、箭箭並落——直到前者執意立誓：『射不中者墜崖而死。』格陵蘭人勸阻無效；卡夫德盧納克脫靶，格陵蘭人正中皮靶，前者依願墜崖，族人只道他自取其禍。此山自此名為皮西格薩爾菲克——射箭之地。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note: compiled from six manuscripts, localised for the Julianehaab (Easterbygd) and Godthaab (Westerbygd) districts; linked to tale 18 (Navaranak) to explain the beginning of the warfare. Suicide by wager recorded as told.

passages.text: In former times, when the coast was less peopled than now, a boat's crew landed at Nook (Godthaab); they found no people, and traversed the fiord to Kangersunek. Half-way up to the east of Kornok, near Ivangiusak, they came upon a large house; but on getting closer to it they did not know what to make of the people, seeing that they were not Kaladlit — in this manner they had quite unexpectedly come across the first Kavdlunak settlers. These likewise for the first time saw the natives of the country, and treated them kindly and civilly; but the Greenlanders nevertheless feared them, and made for their boats.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (2) 'The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait in Greenland'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，海岸上的人煙比現在稀少，有一船人登陸努克（Nook，即戈特霍布 Godthaab）；他們沒見到人，便穿過峽灣來到康格爾蘇內克（Kangersunek）。在往東上行至科爾諾克（Kornok）半途、伊萬吉烏薩克（Ivangiusak）附近，他們遇見一座大屋子；但走近一看，他們不知該如何看待那些人，因為他們不是卡拉德利特人——他們就這樣意外地遇上了第一批卡夫德魯納克（Kavdlunak）移民。這些人也同樣是第一次見到這地方的土著，待他們和善而有禮；然而格陵蘭人仍然懼怕他們，便奔向自己的船。

passages.text: On getting farther up the fiord they found many Kavdlunait stationed; however, they did not put in anywhere, but hastened away as fast as possible. When the boat and its crew returned from their summer trip in the fiord, they told their countrymen all around of their encounter with the foreigners, and many of them now travelled up to see them. Many boats having thus reached Kangersunek, they now began to have intercourse with the Kavdlunait, seeing that they were well disposed towards them; later on in the summer many more Kaladlit arrived, and the foreigners began to learn their language.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (2) 'The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait in Greenland'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 再往峽灣上游走，他們發現駐有許多卡夫德魯奈特人；然而他們沒有在任何地方靠岸，而是盡快離去。當那船及其船員結束夏季的峽灣之行歸來時，他們向四周的同胞講述了與外來人的相遇，如今許多人便上行去看他們。許多船就這樣抵達康格爾蘇內克，他們於是開始與卡夫德魯奈特人往來，因為見他們對自己心懷善意；那年夏天稍晚，又有更多卡拉德利特人來到，外來人也開始學他們的語言。

passages.text: At Kapisilik a Kavdlunak and a Kalalek, it is said, became such fast friends that they would not be separated, but were constantly together; they tried to excel each other at different games and feats of dexterity, and their countrymen on both sides were greatly diverted as lookers-on — but being both first-rate archers, their arrows always fell side by side. One day the Kavdlunak said, 'Come, let us climb yon lofty hill; but first we will stretch a skin for a target to aim at on that little islet yonder; then we will try which of us can hit the mark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (2) 'The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait in Greenland'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說在卡皮西利克，有個卡夫德魯納克人和一個卡拉萊克人成了莫逆之交，誰也離不開誰，總是形影不離；他們在各種遊戲和比試身手上一較高下，兩邊的同胞作為旁觀者都大為開心——但兩人都是頂尖的射手，他們的箭總是並排落下。有一天，卡夫德魯納克人說：『來吧，我們去爬那邊那座高山；不過我們先在那邊的小島上繃一張皮子當靶子；然後我們比試比試，看誰能射中靶心。』

passages.text: He who fails shall be thrown down the precipice, and the other remain the conqueror.' 'No, I will not agree to that, because we are friends, and none of us shall perish' — but the Kavdlunak persisted so long that his own countrymen at last said, 'Well, let him be thrown down as it is at his own will,' and the Kalalek at last gave in, and they climbed the mountain together, accompanied by a crowd of spectators. The Kavdlunak was the first to shoot, but altogether failed; then the Kalalek came in for his turn, and pierced the skin in the centre. According to his own desire the Kavdlunak was hurled down the precipice, and his countrymen only thought it served him right for having thus recklessly pledged his life. From that day until the present this mountain has been called Pisigsarfik (the shooting-place).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (2) 'The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait in Greenland'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『射不中的那個就從懸崖上扔下去，另一個留下來做勝者。』『不，我不會同意這個，因為我們是朋友，我們誰都不該喪命』——但卡夫德魯納克人堅持了那麼久，最後連他自己的同胞都說：『好吧，既然是他自己的意願，就讓他被扔下去吧。』卡拉萊克人最後也讓了步，他們便一同爬上山去，跟著一大群看熱鬧的人。卡夫德魯納克人先射，卻完全沒有射中；接著輪到卡拉萊克人，他一箭射穿了皮子的正中央。按照他自己的意願，卡夫德魯納克人被從懸崖上扔了下去，他的同胞只覺得他這樣輕率地拿性命打賭，是咎由自取。從那天直到如今，這座山一直叫做皮西格薩菲克（射箭之地）。

title.en: The Ancient Kavdlunait's Ruin Near Arsut
title.zh: 阿爾舒特古移民遺跡

region.en: Iminguit bay and Ikat, near Arsut, South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭阿爾舒特附近的伊明圭特灣與伊卡特

period: Inuit oral tradition; common tradition at Arsut, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 54 (3) 'The Ancient Kavdlunait's Ruin near Arsut', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A kayaker striking the sides of a Kavdlunait tent at Iminguit silences their jesting — peeping in, he finds them all dead with fear. At Ikat the Kavdlunait taken by surprise flee with their children upon thin ice and are drowned — it is said only a few years ago they might be seen at the bottom of the sea; and the common tradition at Arsut holds that whenever they become visible it is a sure foreboding that one of the people will die.
summary.zh: 一名皮艇客在伊明圭特灣敲擊卡夫德盧納克的帳篷，戲語漸息——窺看之下，他們竟全數嚇死。伊卡特處的移民攜子逃上薄冰，破冰溺斃——據說數年前還能在海底看見他們；阿爾舒特當地相傳：這些身影一旦顯現，便是村中有人將死的預兆。

sensitivity.note: Place-legend attached to actual Scandinavian ruins; drowning recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: A kayaker one day went to the bay of Iminguit to catch thong-seals. Arriving there he observed a tent belonging to some Kavdlunait. He heard them jesting and prating inside, and was strongly minded to go and look in upon them; accordingly he left his kayak, went up to the place, and began to strike on the sides of the tent. This made them apprehensive, and they now became quiet, which only encouraged him to continue all the more, until he succeeded in silencing them altogether. Then he took a peep in at them, and behold! they were all dead with fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (3) 'The Ancient Kavdlunait's Ruin near Arsut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，一個划皮艇的人到伊明古伊特灣去捕帶狀海豹。到了那裡，他看見一座屬於幾個卡夫德魯納特人的帳篷。他聽見他們在裡面說笑閒聊，便極想過去瞧瞧他們；於是他離開皮艇，走到那地方，開始拍打帳篷的側面。這使他們心生恐懼，他們便安靜了下來，這反倒更助長了他，越發拍打不停，直到他終於使他們完全沒了聲息。然後他往裡窺探，瞧啊！他們全都嚇死了。

passages.text: At Ikat the Kavdlunait living there were also taken by surprise by the Kaladlit, and four fathers fled with their children out upon the ice, which, however, being too thin, broke through with them, so that all were drowned — and it is said that only a few years ago they might be seen at the bottom of the sea. It is a common tradition at Arsut that whenever they become visible it is a sure foreboding that one of the people will die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (3) 'The Ancient Kavdlunait's Ruin near Arsut'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在伊卡特，住在那裡的卡夫德魯納特人也遭到卡拉德利特人的突襲，四位父親帶著孩子逃到冰上，然而冰太薄，隨著他們一起破裂，於是全都淹死了——據說就在幾年前，還能在海底看見他們。阿爾蘇特有一個普遍的傳說：每當他們顯現，就必定預示著族人中將有一人要死去。

title.en: Encounter of Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait on the Ice
title.zh: 冰上的遭遇戰

region.en: Frozen lake of the south country, North Greenland telling
region.zh: 南方凍湖（北格陵蘭講述本）

period: Inuit oral tradition; tale received from North Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 54 (4) 'Encounter of Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait on the Ice', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Attacked in autumn when the lakes are frozen, a house is put to the axe while the newly delivered housewife is sorceried through a window; a mother is dragged across the frozen lake by a rope tied to her tuft of hair. Hidden among stone-heaps, the enraged son sends two girls out on the ice as bait — the slippery Kavdlunait fall on their backs, sideways, tottering — and with spear and spare spear he despatches the whole enemy before the girls reach the open sea, then pierces them through their bellies to complete his vengeance.
summary.zh: 秋日湖凍之際，仇家提斧攻屋；產婦被巫術送出窗外，老母被繩縛髮髻拖過凍湖。藏於石堆的兒子怒極，遣兩名少女上冰為餌——卡夫德盧納克人在冰上連連跌倒；他執叉攜備叉衝上冰面，未等少女抵達海面便殺盡來敵，又逐一刺穿其腹，以完復仇——歸屋所見，盡是同袍屍骸。

sensitivity.note: Graphic massacre and dragging of the mother recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: It is said that the Kaladlit of the south country at times were attacked in the autumn season, when the lakes were frozen over, and the sea-shore was all bordered with ice. It once happened that a man had been out hunting, and came home with two white whales; in the evening a couple of girls came running into the house crying, 'The enemy is coming upon us!' At which the man got into a passion, and tore the fishing-line which he was busily winding up; but when he was about to go out, the Kavdlunait were already making an onset upon the house. The housewife, who had been newly delivered of a child, was by means of sorcery got through a window, and several escaped the same way; but all those who attempted to get through the entrance were miserably killed. The master of the house, who had escaped along with his wife, returned to bring his mother out, but finding her badly wounded had to leave her to her fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (4) 'Encounter of Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait on the Ice'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說南方之地的卡拉德利特人有時會在秋季遭到襲擊，那時湖泊已經結冰，海岸也盡是冰。有一次，一個男人外出打獵，帶著兩頭白鯨回家；傍晚時分，兩個姑娘跑進屋裡哭喊：『敵人朝我們來了！』那男人聽了大發脾氣，扯斷了他正忙著纏繞的釣魚線；但當他要出去時，卡夫德魯納特人已經開始攻打屋子了。那家的主婦剛生了孩子，靠巫術從一扇窗戶送了出去，有幾個人也從同一條路逃走了；但所有想從門口出去的人都被慘殺。那家的男主人與妻子一同逃出後，又折回去要把他母親帶出來，卻發現她受了重傷，只好任她聽天由命。

passages.text: Some had in this manner escaped and hastened away to hide themselves among the stone-heaps, from whence they heard the enemy's wild shouts of triumph; the man had to witness his mother being dragged across the frozen lake by a rope fastened to her tuft of hair. Though greatly enraged he tried to keep quiet in his hiding-place, but ordered the two girls down on the ice: 'Now ye go on to the edge of the water, and when they overtake you plunge yourselves into the sea.' Sobbing and crying they did as they were bid; no sooner had they been observed by the Kavdlunait than they were seen to run out after them — but the ice was too slippery for them, and they lost their footing, some falling on their backs, others sideways, and some going tottering about.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (4) 'Encounter of Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait on the Ice'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有些人就這樣逃了出來，急忙躲到石堆之間，從那裡他們聽見敵人狂野的勝利呼喊；那男人不得不眼睜睜看著自己的母親被一根拴在她髮髻上的繩子拖過結冰的湖面。他雖然怒火中燒，卻盡力在藏身之處保持安靜，只吩咐那兩個姑娘到冰上去：『現在你們往水邊去，等他們追上你們，就跳進海裡。』她們抽泣哭喊著照做了；卡夫德魯納特人一發現她們，就見他們跑出去追——但冰對他們來說太滑了，他們腳下一滑，有的仰面摔倒，有的側身跌倒，有的踉踉蹌蹌地晃來晃去。

passages.text: The angry Kalalek now asked his people how many of the enemy had gone out on the ice and whether any of them were still on shore; they did not agree about this, but at last one said that all of them had now got down. Immediately the furious Kalalek rushed out on the ice, spear in hand, and another one in store: the first of the Kavdlunait he met was instantly speared; the others fell on approaching him, and were likewise killed. When the point of his spear had got too sticky with blood he would only take time to blow it away; and before the girls had reached the open sea he had despatched the whole of them. However, he turned back again, and pierced them through their bellies in order to complete his vengeance, and then returned to the house, where he found the inmates all killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (4) 'Encounter of Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait on the Ice'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 憤怒的卡勒萊克此時問他的族人，敵人有多少人上了冰面，是否還有人留在岸上；眾人對此意見不一，但最後有一人說，他們現在全都下來了。滿懷怒火的卡勒萊克立刻手持長矛衝上冰面，另備一支長矛在身：他遇到的第一個卡夫德魯奈特人當場被刺死；其餘的人一靠近他便倒下，也同樣被殺。當他的矛尖沾血過多而黏滯時，他只肯花時間把血吹掉；在女孩們抵達外海之前，他已將她們全數解決。然而他又折返，刺穿她們的腹部以完成復仇，然後回到屋裡，發現屋內的人全都被殺了。

title.en: Pisagsak and the Kivigtok: The Ladder of the Cliff
title.zh: 皮薩克薩克與奇維托克：崖上的長梯

region.en: Steep mountain-wall with a suspended ladder, inland plain
region.zh: 懸梯高崖與內陸棉草平原

period: Inuit oral tradition; received from one narrator, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Carried by his sport to a mountain-wall hung with a long ladder, Pisagsak is claimed by a shivering old kivigtok — 'I would like thee for my companion' — and learns the hidden plain: boots on the cross-bar, reindeer from the pot, wife-stealing at the Kavdlunait's water-spring (his own catch deliberately a wrinkled old woman who stays gladly), until the day the Kavdlunait assault from the sea-side: the ladder is loosened at the top, a tremendous cry, and the Kavdlunait are all swallowed up by the sea, not one escaping. The old woman dies of sheer old age, Pisagsak goes home with the kivigtok's warning, and never afterwards leaves home.
summary.zh: 逐獵忘返的皮薩克薩克來到一道垂著長梯的絕壁下，被一個瑟縮的老奇維托克收留——『我要你做我的伴』——習得隱谷生活：橫樑上的靴串、鍋中燉鹿、以及在卡夫德盧納人泉邊搶親（他自己故意搶回一位皺紋滿面的老嫗，老嫗卻樂意留下）。仇家自海面來犯之日，老者於崖頂鬆開梯索——一聲慘叫，卡夫德盧納人盡葬海中。老嫗壽終，皮薩克薩克攔下老者的口信回到族人之中，此後再未離家。

sensitivity.note: Rink notes the tale doubtful for inclusion among the Kavdlunait stories. Drowning of the assault party recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Pisagsak one day went out kayaking in order to try his new bird-javelin, and in the excitement of the sport was carried far away from his homestead; at length he arrived at the foot of a steep mountain-wall, from the top of which a long ladder was suspended, and having reached the top with great trouble surveyed a little plain spreading below on the other side, covered with cotton-grass, the down carried along by the wind. The plain was bordered by another mountain-wall, which he climbed likewise, and far below on the other side beheld a little house; stealing along to it he peeped in at the window, but only saw one old kivigtok sitting at his work. When he was about to withdraw as noiselessly as he had come, the old man accosted him: 'Of course I have seen thee, so please to come inside' — all shaky and shivering, in a peevish voice, 'I would like thee for my companion; thou hadst better stop with me.' He went out and returned with some dried meat and tallow; Pisagsak satisfied his hunger, and his host then took some boiled reindeer out of a large pot, which pleased him even more. At night Pisagsak could hardly sleep for fear of his aged housemate; in the morning the old man had gone off, and on looking round he perceived a great number of boots dangling on the cross-bar beneath the roof — he took them, overhauled them, put them up to dry, and proceeded to do the cooking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，皮薩格薩克划著皮艇出去，想試試他的新鳥矛，卻在狩獵的興奮中被帶得遠離家園；最後他來到一道陡峭山壁的腳下，山壁頂端垂下一道長梯，他費了極大氣力才爬到頂上，望見另一側下方展開一片小平原，長滿棉草，草絮隨風飄揚。平原邊緣是另一道山壁，他也照樣爬了上去，望見另一側遠下方有一間小屋；他悄悄潛近，從窗戶往裡窺看，卻只看見一個老基維格托克坐在那裡做活。他正要像來時那樣無聲無息地退走，老人卻叫住他：「我當然看見你了，請進來吧。」——聲音顫抖哆嗦，語氣慍怒，「我想讓你做我的同伴；你最好留下來陪我。」他走出去，帶回一些乾肉和油脂；皮薩格薩克滿足了飢餓，接著主人又從一個大鍋裡取出煮熟的馴鹿肉，這更令他歡喜。夜裡，皮薩格薩克因害怕這位年邁的同屋人而幾乎無法入睡；到了早晨，老人已經出去了，他環顧四周，發現屋頂下方的橫樑上掛著許多靴子——他把它們取下來，翻檢一番，拿去晾乾，然後動手做飯。

passages.text: In the evening he heard a noise, and soon saw the old man coming along with two large bucks: 'Here is some work for thee to put thy hand to; come away and skin them at once.' Pisagsak remained with him and took charge of the household work; he learned to snare partridges and shoot reindeer, and after some time grew very dexterous as a sportsman. One evening the old kivigtok went on, saying, 'To-morrow is the day when the women of the Kavdlunait use to come here to fetch water. I dare-say there will be some young girls among them: we will go and have a look at them.' They arrived at a place from whence they could see a great many houses, beyond which a spring was visible, and hid themselves behind some large stones; about sunrise the first girl came, filled her pail, and retired, others following, some handsome, some old and slow. A young and very beautiful woman approached, had just put down her pail and commenced pouring in water, when Pisagsak noticed that the old man was getting very excited and trembled all over — the next moment he sprang on the young girl and carried her away, having first stuffed her mouth to keep her from calling out; Pisagsak of course followed them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傍晚，他聽到一陣聲響，不久便看見老人帶著兩頭大公鹿回來：「這裡有些活兒給你搭把手；快過來，立刻把它們剝皮。」皮薩格薩克留下來與他同住，掌管家中事務；他學會了用套索捕捉雷鳥、射殺馴鹿，過了一段時日，便成了非常嫻熟的獵手。一天傍晚，老基維格托克接著說道：「明天是卡夫德魯奈特人的女人們慣常來這裡取水的日子。我敢說她們當中會有些年輕姑娘：我們去瞧瞧她們。」他們來到一處能望見許多房屋的地方，房屋後方看得見一處泉水，兩人便躲在大石頭後面；大約日出時分，第一個姑娘來了，裝滿水桶便回去了，其餘的陸續跟來，有的標緻，有的年老遲緩。一個年輕而極美的女子走上前來，剛放下水桶開始舀水，皮薩格薩克便發覺老人變得非常激動，渾身發抖——下一刻，他撲向那年輕女子，先塞住她的嘴不讓她叫喊，然後把她擄走；皮薩格薩克自然跟在他們後面。

passages.text: Having reached their house, they took away her boots to prevent her from running away, and only went out to hunt by turns in order to keep watch on her; however, the girl at length got reconciled to her fate and gave up all idea of flight, and they could now venture to leave the house together — on their return they always found the work of the house ready done, and their clothes and boots mended. Another day Pisagsak again accompanied the old man to the spring to look at the girls; this time the old man ordered Pisagsak to catch a nice one, but he lingered and waited till an old woman, wrinkled all over, made her appearance, then rushed on and took hold of her and brought her home — and when the old woman had passed one day with them she came to like them, and did not care to go back. Now they had two women in the house, and they did exceedingly well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 回到他們的屋子後，他們脫下她的靴子，以防她逃走，並且只輪流外出打獵，以便看守她；然而那姑娘終於順從了自己的命運，放棄了逃跑的念頭，他們這才敢一同離家——每次回來，總發現家務已經做好，衣服和靴子也已縫補妥當。又一天，皮薩格薩克再次陪老人去泉邊看那些姑娘；這回老人吩咐皮薩格薩克去抓一個漂亮的，他卻磨蹭著，一直等到一個滿臉皺紋的老婦人出現，這才衝上前去抓住她，把她帶回家——那老婦人與他們共處一日之後，便喜歡上了他們，不願再回去了。如今他們屋裡有了兩個女人，日子過得極好。

passages.text: One day the kivigtok said to Pisagsak, 'To-morrow the Kavdlunait will be making an assault on us from the sea-side; let us go and look out for them.' They went away to the top of the high cliff where the ladder was made fast, and saw several boats approaching the coast: 'Now they begin to land; but when they have all got on shore and try to climb the ladder, I will loosen it on the top, and then thou wilt see a sight.' Pisagsak stood in great expectation; presently they had all got on the ladder, but not until the first of them appeared wielding his lance above the summit of the steep mountain-side did the kivigtok loosen the cords from the stone — a tremendous cry now followed, and the Kavdlunait were all swallowed up by the sea; not one escaped. After this catastrophe the others for some time lived on in their usual way, but the old woman at length took ill and died from sheer old age, and after that Pisagsak began to long for his own home. When he told his master he did not object, but remarked, 'Tell the Kavdlunait yonder that they had better not attack me; if they do, I shall certainly destroy them.' Pisagsak now returned to his relatives, who had totally given him up, brought them the message of the kivigtok, and never afterwards left home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，基維格托克對皮薩格薩克說：「明天卡夫德魯奈特人會從海那邊來攻打我們；我們去察看他們吧。」他們來到長梯所繫的高崖頂上，看見幾艘船正逼近海岸：「現在他們開始登陸了；等他們全都上了岸，試圖攀爬長梯時，我就把梯子頂端鬆開，那時你就會看到一番景象。」皮薩格薩克滿懷期待地站著；不久他們全都爬上了長梯，但直到第一批人揮舞長矛出現在陡峭山壁的頂端之上，基維格托克才把繩索從石頭上解開——隨即響起一聲巨大的呼喊，卡夫德魯奈特人全都被大海吞沒，無一逃脫。這場災難之後，其餘的人又照常生活了一段時日，但那老婦人終於因年邁而病倒死去，此後皮薩格薩克便開始思念自己的家鄉。當他告訴主人時，主人並不反對，只說道：「告訴那邊的卡夫德魯奈特人，他們最好別來攻擊我；若他們來，我必定消滅他們。」皮薩格薩克於是回到親人身邊，他們本已完全放棄了他；他帶給他們基維格托克的口信，此後再未離開家園。

title.en: Tugtutsiak: The Child Who Played Angakok
title.zh: 托格托夏克：玩降靈的孩子

region.en: Great house and the sea-mother's dark shore
region.zh: 大屋與海底老嫗的幽暗海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; one copy, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 56 'The Angakok Tugtutsiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Playing angakok with the other children left berry-gathering, Tugtutsiak's slabs fly from the floor and chase the fleeing playmates. Forced by bad hunting to conjure for the village, he is flung bear-and-walrus across the sea to a dark house where a dishevelled sufferer — eyes, nostrils, and mouth stuffed with filth — waits; he cleans her, dresses her hair, and she sends little flat-nosed and crook-nosed people streaming from the wall — 'Kah, kah — sa, sa!' — which he scratches on the forehead to know again. Returned wounded head to foot by the bear's and walrus's teeth, sung whole through the night, he brings gales, auks, and dovekies in thousands — and far off at Illulissat a thong-seal and a spotted seal are caught with a mark right between the eyes.
summary.zh: 採莓的人群離家後，孩子們玩起降靈；托格托夏克的咒術令地板的石板騰空追趕逃散的玩伴。獵運衰敗，村人強令他召喚海獸——他被熊與海象輪流拋擲，拋過重洋，抵達一間幽暗的屋子：頭髮散亂的老嫗五官塞滿穢物。他為她清潔梳髮；她自牆中放出成群的小矮人——扁鼻的、鷹鉤鼻的，叫聲如海鳩——他在美者的額頭留下記號。帶著遍體齒傷被歌聲治癒歸來後，他喚來大風與滿海的海鳩；遠在伊盧利薩特，人們捕到額間有記號的海豹。

sensitivity.note: Documents the angakok-poolik process (playing at shaman) frequently mentioned by older authors, per Rink. The sea-mother cleaning is the Sedna-rite (cross-ref sedna-sea-mother).

passages.text: Tugtutsiak and his sister were a couple of orphans, and lived in a great house. It once happened that all the grown-up people went away berry-gathering, leaving all children at home; Tugtutsiak, the eldest of them, said, 'Let us try to conjure up spirits' — some proceeded to make up the necessary preparations, while he himself undressed, covered the door with his jacket, and closed the opening at the sleeves with a string. He now commenced the invocation, while the other children got mortally frightened and were about to take flight — but the slabs of the floor were lifted high in the air and rushed after them. Tugtutsiak would have followed them, but felt himself sticking fast to the floor, and could not get loose until he had made the children come back and ordered them to uncover the door and open the window, on which it again became light in the room and he was enabled to get up. He told his companions not to mention it to the old ones when they returned — but as soon as the boat landed in the evening some of the younger children forgot their promise: 'We have had great fun to-day; Tugtutsiak played at angakok, and when we got frightened and took to our heels, the slabs rose up from their place on the floor and followed after us.' The elder people were astonished, but agreed to let him try it over again in the evening — at this proposal Tugtutsiak got frightened and took to crying; but afterwards, when the hunting became bad, they wanted him to conjure up the sea-animals, and he was made to sit down and call forth a bear and a walrus, which were soon roaring outside the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 56 'The Angakok Tugtutsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 圖格圖齊亞克和他的妹妹是一對孤兒，住在一間大屋裡。有一次，所有成年人都外出採漿果，把孩子們全留在家裡；圖格圖齊亞克是孩子中年紀最大的，他說：「我們來試著召喚神靈吧。」有些人著手做必要的準備，他則自己脫下衣服，用外套遮住門，並用繩子封住袖口的開口。他隨即開始念咒召喚，其他孩子嚇得要命，正要逃走——但地板的石板卻高高升到空中，朝他們追去。圖格圖齊亞克本想跟著他們跑，卻覺得自己被牢牢黏在地板上，直到他叫孩子們回來，命他們揭開門上的遮蓋、打開窗戶，屋裡才重又亮了起來，他才能站起身。他叮囑同伴們，等大人們回來時不要提起此事——可是傍晚船一靠岸，幾個年幼的孩子就忘了承諾：「我們今天玩得可開心了；圖格圖齊亞克玩安加科克，我們一害怕拔腿就跑，地板上的石板就從原位升起，追著我們跑。」大人們大為驚訝，卻同意讓他晚上再試一次——聽到這個提議，圖格圖齊亞克嚇得哭了起來；但後來，當狩獵收成變差時，他們便要他去召喚海中動物，他被迫坐下，喚出一頭熊和一頭海象，牠們很快就在屋外咆哮起來。

passages.text: The bear went ashore and took hold of Tugtutsiak, and flung him along to the walrus, which again hurled him out to the bear — in this manner Tugtutsiak alternately was thrust from the walrus to the bear, and from the bear to the walrus, until he lost sight of his native country, and at length a new land rose in front of him, lower than the one he had left. Close to the shore the bear for the last time seized hold of him and threw him upon the beach; having got there, his senses revived, and close beside him he observed a house, and on the roof, above the passage leading to it, a terrible dog, which, showing his white teeth, howled and snarled at him when he drew nigh. Nevertheless he approached, and for the first time observed that a bridge as narrow as a knife's edge led into the inner room, which appeared totally dark; still he proceeded and made his way to the main room, where the female owner of the house lay on the ledge suffering great pain, her hair all loose and dishevelled, her face turned to the wall. On seeing Tugtutsiak she started to her feet, crying out aloud, 'What hast thou come for? thou canst not take away what makes me suffer' — but from the narrow passage he rushed right upon her, took hold of her by the hair, and flung her against the door-post; having got his hands entangled in her long hair he was himself dragged along with her, and could not extricate himself. He tried to throw her off, but his hands could not be got loose — and she surrendered herself to him, saying, 'Now I see thou mayst be capable of removing my sufferings.' On closer examination Tugtutsiak found her eyes, nostrils, and mouth stuffed with dirt and filth; he cleaned it away and threw it outside, after which the hideous woman grew somewhat composed, and after a while resumed, 'Now do my hair.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 56 'The Angakok Tugtutsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那頭熊上岸抓住圖圖齊阿克，把他拋向海象，海象又把他拋回熊那裡——圖圖齊阿克就這樣被海象拋向熊、又被熊拋向海象，直到他再也看不見自己的故鄉，最後在他面前浮現出一片新的陸地，比他離開的那片低矮。熊在近岸處最後一次抓住他，把他扔到海灘上；到了那裡，他的神智恢復過來，他發現在自己身旁有一間屋子，而在屋頂上、通往屋內的過道上方，有一隻可怕的狗，當他走近時，那狗露出白牙，朝他嚎叫咆哮。儘管如此，他還是走上前去，這才第一次注意到有一道像刀刃一樣窄的橋通向內室，內室看起來一片漆黑；他仍舊往前走，來到主室，屋子的女主人正躺在石臺上，痛苦萬分，頭髮全都散亂蓬鬆，臉朝著牆。一看見圖圖齊阿克，她便跳起身來，大聲喊道：『你來做什麼？你無法拿走使我受苦的東西』——但他從那狹窄的過道直衝向她，抓住她的頭髮，把她摔向門柱；他的雙手纏在她的長髮裡，自己也被她拖著走，無法脫身。他試圖把她甩開，雙手卻鬆不開——於是她向他屈服，說道：『現在我看出你也許能夠除去我的苦痛。』圖圖齊阿克仔細一看，發現她的眼睛、鼻孔和嘴裡都塞滿了泥土和污穢；他把這些清理掉，扔到外面，之後那醜陋的女人稍稍平靜了些，過了一會兒又說道：『現在給我梳理頭髮吧。』

passages.text: He put it up in the usual tuft, upon which she took down some eagles' wings from a nail in the wall and stirred up the smoking lamp so as to make it burn brightly; for the first time he could see the walls hung with skins like those used for boat-covers, though he could not distinguish any objects in the more remote parts of the room, which were in total darkness. A moment after he heard the horrible woman saying, 'My guest ought not to go alone; let some one accompany him out' — and presently a little man with a very short nose emerged from out of the wall, and after him a host of similar creatures, who all passed out of the doorway; when the last had vanished they were all heard to cry out, 'Kah, kah — sa, sa!' just like the shrieks of auks. Other varieties followed soon — some with flat noses and others with crooked ones; but when they were getting too numerous she cried 'Stop!' When the last were about to pass Tugtutsiak he scratched some of them in the forehead, because he noticed that they were transfigured as soon as they passed the doorway, and put a mark upon some of the most beautiful specimens, that he might know them again if he happened to catch them. Afterwards several other curious creatures appeared, some of them with large heads and great beards, and as soon as they were getting too numerous she again cried 'Stop!' When these had all passed by, he observed that the lamp burned still brighter, and the way through the passage was now quite smooth and sufficiently wide, and the dog wagged his tail quite amicably at him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 56 'The Angakok Tugtutsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他把她的頭髮盤成通常的髮髻，她便從牆上的一根釘子上取下幾隻鷹翅，把冒煙的燈挑旺，讓它明亮地燃燒；他這才第一次看清牆上掛著像蒙船皮那樣的獸皮，不過屋子較遠的地方一片漆黑，他分辨不出任何東西。片刻之後，他聽見那可怕的女人說道：『我的客人不該獨自出去；讓誰陪他出去吧』——隨即一個鼻子極短的小人從牆裡鑽了出來，跟在他後面又出來一大群類似的生物，全都從門口走了出去；當最後一個消失時，只聽他們全都喊道：『咔，咔——薩，薩！』就像海雀的尖叫聲一樣。接著又來了別的種類——有的鼻子扁平，有的鼻子彎曲；但當他們變得太多時，她喊道：『停下！』當最後一批要從圖圖齊阿克身邊經過時，他抓傷了其中幾個的額頭，因為他注意到他們一經過門口就變了形，於是在幾個最漂亮的樣本上做了記號，以便日後若碰巧再捉到他們時能認出來。之後又出現了幾個別種奇怪的生物，其中有些大腦袋、大鬍子，當他們變得太多時，她又喊道：『停下！』當這些全都過去之後，他發現燈火燒得更亮了，穿過過道的路現在十分平坦，也足夠寬，那隻狗還十分友好地朝他搖尾巴。

passages.text: Simultaneously with all these strange doings his house-fellows at home observed that his belongings were shaking; on his way home he was again alternately thrown along by the bear and the walrus, the last time by the bear, and he gained his homestead, where his relatives sat singing for him on his return. Being apprised of his arrival through the noise caused by his entrance, a great man among them gave orders, 'Light the lamp for him' — and they could now see that no single spot of his body had remained unwounded: this arose from the teeth of the bear and the walrus, and they could not hear him breathe. The lamps were again extinguished, and the singing commenced; some time after he began to revive a little, but at daybreak they saw that his wounds were not yet healed, and so they continued the singing. There happened to be among them one ostentatious fellow, who on the following morning went out to have a look at the ice; on his return he exclaimed, 'I guess it will be a meagre hunt he will procure us' — but Tugtutsiak only muttered, 'Wait a bit — let my wounds first heal, and then we will see.' When they began healing a gale from the south-east had suddenly set in; a man who had gone out to reconnoitre quickly returned reporting that the ice was rapidly receding from the shore, and instantly afterwards auks and dovekies were seen in numbers. The inhabitants soon hastened out with their fowling-spears, and had their kayaks filled before evening; the boaster, however, only got one bird. When they began to catch seals they gave to the angakok the first one they caught, of all varieties; he examined all he got closely, hoping to find out those he had marked, but all in vain — some time after, however, the report came that far away at Illulissat there had been caught a thong-seal and a spotted seal both with a mark right between the eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 56 'The Angakok Tugtutsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在這些怪事發生的同時，他家中的人發現他的物件在震動；在回家的路上，他又被熊和海象輪流拋擲，最後一次是熊拋的，他回到了自己的家園，他的親屬們正坐著為他的歸來唱歌。他們從他進門的聲響得知他到了，其中一位大人物吩咐道：『為他點燈』——這時他們才看清他身上沒有一處不是傷痕：這是熊和海象的牙齒造成的，而且他們聽不到他呼吸。燈又被熄滅，歌聲重新響起；過了些時候他開始稍稍甦醒，但天亮時他們看出他的傷口還沒癒合，於是他們繼續唱歌。他們當中恰好有一個愛吹噓的傢伙，第二天早晨出去看了看冰面；回來時他嚷道：『我猜他給我們弄來的將是一次貧乏的狩獵』——但圖圖齊阿克只是低聲說：『等一等——先讓我的傷口癒合，然後我們再看。』當傷口開始癒合時，東南方向突然刮起一陣大風；一個出去偵察的人很快回來報告說，冰正迅速從岸邊退去，緊接著就看見大批海雀和小海雀。居民們很快帶著捕鳥矛趕了出去，還沒到傍晚就把獨木舟裝滿了；那個吹噓的人卻只打到一隻鳥。當他們開始捕海豹時，他們把捕到的第一隻、各種各樣的都給了那位巫師；他仔細察看所得到的一切，希望能找出他做過記號的那些，卻一無所獲——然而過了些時候，有消息傳來，說在遙遠的伊盧利薩特捕到了一隻皮條海豹和一隻斑海豹，兩隻的記號都正好在兩眼之間。

title.en: The Witchcraft of Kulange
title.zh: 庫蘭格的巫術

region.en: New grave and the kayakers' shore
region.zh: 新墳與皮艇客的海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 57 'The Witchcraft of Kulange', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The carrier of hunting-tools catches his friend opening a new grave, cutting a morsel of flesh and the bladder from the dead — 'I want it to work some witchcraft... dry the morsel of dead man's flesh and put it beneath the point of the hunter's harpoon; dry the bladder and, when the other is asleep, press the air out upon him.' Kulange tests both: the harpooned kayaker fails day after day until the flesh is cleaned off, and the bladder blown on his offended daughter-in-law swells her whole side — until the angakok names him, he confesses, the bewitching objects are sunk deep in the sea, and the wicked friend is put to death.
summary.zh: 替獵手搬運工具的庫蘭格撞見朋友掘開新墳、割取屍肉與膀胱——『我要拿它行巫術……把屍肉曬乾、塞進獵手的魚叉尖下；把膀胱吹脹，趁他熟睡對他放氣。』他逐一試驗：肉下的獵手日日空手而歸，直到肉被清出方才復運；膀胱之氣令冒犯他的兒媳半身浮腫——巫師遙指其名，他坦白交出凶器；巫物沉入深海，那邪惡的朋友則被處死。

sensitivity.note: Corpse-flesh and bladder sorcery documented as practice-belief. Killing of the friend recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: It was Kulange's business to bring up and down the fishing implements, tools, and arms of the kayakers; having no kayak of his own, he only roamed about the country. He had but one friend; and on a certain day he saw his friend engaged in opening a new grave and cutting a piece out of the dead body — he had taken a morsel of flesh and the bladder. He approached silently, and after having watched his proceeding asked him what he was about; the friend turned round, explaining to him, 'I want it to work some witchcraft.' But having thus been taken by surprise he got ashamed and wished to make it over to Kulange, saying that he might use it advantageously any time he wanted to injure some great hunter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 57 'The Witchcraft of Kulange'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫蘭格的職責是替划獨木舟的人搬上搬下漁具、工具和武器；他自己沒有獨木舟，只是在全國各地遊蕩。他只有一個朋友；某一天，他看見他的朋友正忙著挖開一座新墳，從屍體上割下一塊——他取了一小塊肉和膀胱。庫蘭格悄悄走近，看了一會兒他的舉動之後，問他在做什麼；那朋友轉過身來，向他解釋道：『我要用它來施些巫術。』但這樣被撞見之後，他感到羞愧，想把它讓給庫蘭格，說他隨時想害某個大獵人時都可以拿它來派上用場。

passages.text: He informed him that he ought to dry the morsel of dead man's flesh, and put it beneath the point of the hunter's harpoon, and that in this manner he might in less than a moment turn a clever hunter into a very poor one; the bladder he was likewise to dry, and if ever he happened to get an enemy, he was to blow it up, and, while the other was asleep, press the air out upon him. At length Kulange accepted the gift, and after making the grave up anew they both departed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 57 'The Witchcraft of Kulange'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他告訴庫蘭格，他應該把那塊死人肉晾乾，放在獵人魚叉的尖端下面，這樣他就能在不到片刻之間把一個能幹的獵人變成一個很差的獵人；那膀胱他也同樣要晾乾，倘若他日後碰巧有了仇人，就把它吹脹，趁那人睡著時，把裡面的氣擠到他身上。最後庫蘭格接受了這份贈禮，他們把墳重新填好之後，兩人都離開了。

passages.text: Kulange put by the things, intending to try them on the first occasion. About the beginning of winter one of his house-fellows had a particularly good hunt and consequently got quite rich; Kulange at once determined whether he could put an end to his great good luck, and with this view put a bit of the flesh beneath the point of his harpoon while the owner was sleeping, after which he sneaked silently away to his couch. On the return of the kayakers the following evening it happened that only he on whose harpoon the bit of flesh had been concealed was unsuccessful, and this continued from day to day until one day Kulange again took it away and cleaned the point well where it had been deposited — no sooner had this been done than the kayaker returned tugging a large seal after him like all the rest, and he had the same good luck ever afterwards. Kulange now thought that he had sufficiently tested the magic power of the flesh, and only awaited an opportunity to make somebody angry with him in order to try the effect of the bladder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 57 'The Witchcraft of Kulange'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫蘭格把這些東西收起來，打算一有機會就試一試。初冬時節，他的一個同屋人打獵特別順利，因而變得相當富有；庫蘭格立刻決定要看看自己能否終結他的大好運氣，於是趁那主人睡覺時，把一小塊肉放在他魚叉的尖端下面，然後悄悄溜回自己的鋪位。第二天傍晚划獨木舟的人們回來時，恰好只有那個魚叉下藏了肉塊的人一無所獲，而且這種情況一天天持續下去，直到有一天庫蘭格又把那塊肉取走，把放過肉的地方好好擦乾淨——剛一擦淨，那划獨木舟的人就像其他人一樣拖著一隻大個海豹回來了，此後他也一直有同樣的好運氣。庫蘭格現在認為自己已經充分試驗了那塊肉的魔力，只等一個機會讓某人對他發怒，以便試試那膀胱的效力。

passages.text: It so happened that his daughter-in-law got offended with him, and in her wrath called him 'the nasty Kulange.' The next day it blew a gale from the south, and he went out to fill the bladder with air; when she was asleep in the evening he went up beside her and let the air out upon her. At dawn she awoke with a swelling in her side, and later in the day she was swollen all over; her husband instantly rowed away to fetch an angakok from a neighbouring place. He came back with him, and after having practised his incantations for some time in the darkened room he knew enough to tell that the misdeed had been done by Kulange, who immediately confessed his guilt, saying, 'I certainly did it, and here are the implements given me by my friend.' Having heard the whole state of the case, the bewitching objects were sunk deep in the sea; but the wicked friend was put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 57 'The Witchcraft of Kulange'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來他的媳婦得罪了他，一怒之下罵他「可惡的庫蘭格」。第二天南風大作，他出去把膀胱灌滿了氣；到了晚上她睡著時，他走到她身旁，把氣放出來吹在她身上。天亮時她醒來，腰側腫了起來，到了白天她全身都腫了；她的丈夫立刻划船離去，到鄰近的地方請一位巫師（angakok）來。他帶著巫師回來，巫師在昏暗的屋裡念了好一陣咒之後，便明白過來，說這樁惡事是庫蘭格所為；庫蘭格當即認罪，說道：「確實是我做的，這是我朋友給我的法器。」聽罷全部案情之後，那些施咒之物被深深沉入海中；但那邪惡的朋友卻被處死了。

title.en: The Old Men's Revenge
title.zh: 老翁復仇記

region.en: Sun-glittered sea north of the outermost islands
region.zh: 外島以北陽光閃爍的海面

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 58 'The Old Men's Revenge', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Their sons killed by a giant kayaker known as a formidable man-slayer, two old men re-arm themselves — a bird-javelin pointed with sharp bone for want of iron, a lance pointed with a seal's rib — and keeping in the glittering sunshine, spear the manslayer between them. Tugging him to his own coast, they tell his daughter 'He killed our sons, and we have paid him back in the same manner'; she agrees — 'it is only what he deserved' — then begs them up to the house, undresses naked to the water-edge, gnashes 'Would I could kill them both like this!' crushing wood between her fingers, and carries down the boat on her back — until the old men are safely out of sight.
summary.zh: 兒子被遠近聞名的殺人巨漢所害，兩位老翁重新武裝——鐵器匱乏，以銳骨為鳥鏢鏃、以海豹肋為長矛鏃——藏身陽光閃爍處，合力刺殺了那殺人者。他們把屍體拖回其海岸，對他的女兒說：『他殺了我們的兒子，我們以同樣方式償還。』女兒答道：『這是他應得的。』隨後她裸身立於水邊，咬牙切齒——『恨不得就這樣把你们俩都殺了！』——指間捏碎木塊，獨力將大舟扛下海。老翁們遠遁，餘悸猶存。

sensitivity.note: Nudity of the daughter presented as told in the archival source. Killing recorded as told.

passages.text: Two men were living together, each of them having a son; when the young men were beginning to provide for them, the old ones resolved to abandon hunting altogether and gave themselves up to their ease and comfort. One of them, who most valued a life of idleness and ease, soon got rid of all his tools and implements, while the other one had still a few left. Their sons used both to start in the morning as well as to return together at night, accustomed to brave the fiercest gales, so that the parents were never alarmed on their account. Nevertheless, one day when they had left with fair weather in the morning they happened not to return as usual in the evening: they had fallen in with a man of more than common strength, well known in those parts as a formidable man-slayer, and he had killed them both. Under these circumstances the old men had again to take to their kayaks; but as one of them had no hunting-tools, he made a bird-javelin, the point of which he fashioned out of a sharp-edged piece of bone for want of iron, and for the point of his lance, having nothing better, used the rib of a seal. 'We may as well run the risk and be off; we are not of much account anyhow.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 58 'The Old Men's Revenge'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有兩個人住在一起，各有一個兒子；當年輕人開始供養他們時，老人們便決心完全放棄打獵，一心圖安逸舒適。其中一人最看重閒散安逸的生活，很快就把自己的工具和器具全都丟棄了，另一人卻還剩下幾件。他們的兒子們習慣於早晨一同出發，晚上一同歸來，慣於頂著最猛烈的狂風，因此父母從不為他們擔憂。然而有一天，他們早晨趁好天氣出發，晚上卻偏偏沒有像往常那樣回來：他們遇上了一個人，力氣遠勝常人，在那一帶以兇悍的殺人者著稱，他把他們兩個都殺了。在這種情況下，老人們只得又操起獨木舟；但其中一人沒有打獵的工具，便做了一支獵鳥標槍，因沒有鐵，槍尖是用一塊鋒利的骨片削成的，而他的長矛尖，因為沒有更好的材料，就用了海豹的肋骨。「我們不妨冒一冒險，走吧；反正我們也沒什麼要緊。」

passages.text: Early the next morning they set off in their kayaks, and soon lost sight of the outermost islands; turning more to the north they took care to keep right in the glittering sunshine, that they might not so easily be perceived. After a little while they detected an almost giant-like kayaker hunting to the north of them; they quickly paddled up to him all the time keeping in the sun — while he was stooping down resting on his paddle they had recourse to charms, and hoped by this means to get the better of him. 'When thou thinkest him to be within thy aim, lose no time in thrusting thy harpoon at him: if he sees us beforehand he will be sure to catch us both.' Rushing forward he lifted his harpoon, but while in the act of throwing took fright and whispered, 'Where? where? when?' — at length he did fling it, but in the meantime the murderer had heard the noise, and as he turned round to look for the cause the other missed him, only hitting the kayak. 'Did not I tell thee to be quick lest he should forestall thee and make us both his prey? Now look well after thy bladder.' — 'Now is thy turn; lance thy javelin into him.' It cleft the air with a whizzing sound, and though it first went beyond him, quickly rebounded and struck the man-slayer on the crown of his head with a crack; he was seen to stagger and fall over on one side, and the first kayaker launched his spear at him, another splash heard. When they had thus killed him between them they examined his body and found that the javelin with the bone point had killed him without even penetrating as far as the barbs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 58 'The Old Men's Revenge'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天一早，他們便乘獨木舟出發，不久就望不見最外邊的島嶼了；他們轉向偏北，留心一直待在閃爍的陽光裡，好不那麼容易被發現。過了一會兒，他們發覺有一個幾乎像巨人般的划舟人在他們北邊打獵；他們迅速划槳追上去，一路都待在陽光裡——當他俯身靠在槳上歇息時，他們便施展法術，希望藉此勝過他。「你估摸他到了你的射程之內，就趕快把魚叉刺向他：要是他先看見我們，準會把我們兩個都逮住。」他衝上前去舉起魚叉，可正要投擲時卻害怕起來，低聲問：「哪兒？哪兒？什麼時候？」——最後他終於投了出去，可就在這時那兇手已聽見聲響，轉過身來查看緣由，這一下那人沒刺中他，只刺中了獨木舟。「我不是叫你快些嗎，免得他搶先下手，把我們兩個都當了獵物？現在好好看住你的膀胱。」——「現在輪到你了；把你的標槍刺向他。」標槍呼嘯著劃破空氣，雖然先飛過了他，卻很快彈了回來，啪的一聲擊中那殺人者的頭頂；只見他踉蹌了一下，倒向一邊，第一個划舟人又朝他投出長矛，又聽得一聲水響。他們就這樣合力殺了他，隨後查看他的屍體，發現那支骨尖標槍殺死了他，甚至連倒鉤都沒扎進去。

passages.text: 'If we leave him here his relatives will know nothing of him; let us rather bring him to the coast' — tying him to their kayaks they tugged him to the shore, where they soon discovered his house near the beach, and saw a person emerge from it, shading her eyes with her hands, taking a survey of the sea, and then re-entering. This person was the daughter of the strong man, not expecting any other kayak, only on the look-out for her father. She soon came out again, and seemed greatly astonished that the strange kayakers had already gained the coast; they now called out to her, 'This is only what thou mightst expect. He killed our sons, and we have paid him back in the same manner.' She remained quite motionless for some time, but at last said in a low voice, 'You are in the right; it is only what he deserved' — but she briskly added, 'Ye ought to come up and visit our house.' She could not help wondering that those two wretches had been able to conquer her powerful father; when she went on urging them to come up, and herself came further down the beach to welcome them, one whispered to the other, 'Since the father was so fearfully strong, the daughter, no doubt, is not less so, so don't go.' Though they had already started, she followed them running along the water-side still beseeching them to come — but the old men were only the more afraid of her, and though they had made a great distance from the shore they could still see how she undressed herself, first taking off her jacket, then her boots, and at last her breeches, and seated herself thus naked on the water-edge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 58 'The Old Men's Revenge'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 「要是把他丟在這裡，他的親屬就什麼也不知道了；我們不如把他帶到岸邊去」——他們把他綁在獨木舟上，拖到岸邊，很快就在海灘附近發現了他的屋子，看見一個人從屋裡出來，用手遮著眼睛眺望海面，然後又走了進去。這人是那大力士的女兒，她沒料到會有別的獨木舟，只是在張望她的父親。她很快又出來了，似乎大為驚訝，那些陌生的划舟人竟已到了岸邊；這時他們朝她喊道：「這不過是你意料之中的事。他殺了我們的兒子，我們也照樣回敬了他。」她一時紋絲不動，最後才低聲說：「你們做得對；這是他罪有應得」——但她又爽快地補了一句：「你們該上來我們家坐坐。」她不禁納悶，那兩個可憐蟲竟能制服她強悍的父親；她繼續催促他們上來，自己又往海灘下走來迎接他們，其中一人對另一人低聲說：「既然父親那麼可怕地強壯，女兒無疑也不比他弱，別去。」他們雖然已經動身離開，她卻沿著水邊跑著追趕他們，仍懇求他們過來——可老人們只是越發怕她，雖然他們已離岸很遠，仍能看見她脫去衣服，先脫下短外套，再脫下靴子，最後脫下褲子，就這樣赤身裸體地坐在水邊。

passages.text: One of the old men seeing this thought it good fun and wanted to go back to her; but his companion rebuked him — 'What is it thou art about? She will be sure to take thy life if thou goest' — he gave up his intention, and having put further out to sea they once more looked round and saw the woman jump up and run up to the house without ever minding her clothes. 'Being so strong, she will very likely pursue us in her boat' — and he was not mistaken: immediately they saw her creeping down beneath the boat, intending to carry it down on her back, and could still hear her gnashing her teeth, calling out, 'Would I could kill them both like this!' at the same time crushing a piece of wood to atoms between her fingers. They at length lost sight of her; at home they related how they had despatched the well-known murderer, and their mind was somewhat relieved by having had their revenge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 58 'The Old Men's Revenge'; not verbatim.
