passages.zh: 其中一個老人見了，覺得挺有趣，想回去找她；可他的同伴責備他——「你在幹什麼？你要是去了，她準會要了你的命」——他打消了念頭，又往海上划遠了些，再回頭一看，只見那女人跳起身來，跑回屋裡去，全然不顧自己的衣服。「她這麼強壯，很可能會划船來追我們」——他沒有料錯：他們立刻看見她悄悄溜到船底下，打算把船背起來帶走，還聽得見她咬牙切齒，喊道：「我恨不得就這樣把他們兩個都殺了！」同時用手指把一塊木頭捏得粉碎。他們終於望不見她了；回到家裡，他們講述了如何結果了那個有名的殺人者，報了仇，心裡也稍稍寬慰了些。

title.en: Aterfio: The Unwoundable Father and the Falcon-Swift Son
title.zh: 阿特爾菲奧：不傷之父與隼速之子

region.en: Skerries and islands, and the Southlanders' coast
region.zh: 群礁外海與南方人的海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 59 'Aterfio', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Fed and taught patience by his widowed mother ('let him go on as he likes, only thou shun his companionship'), Aterfio endures Sukalassok's harpoons, capsizings, and arrows — until the third arrow draws his own, and Sukalassok dies. The dead man's relatives come in many boats; harpoons break in three pieces on him, wrestlers die 'as easily as if he had been a fox,' and the whole assaulting party is killed on the way home. Trained to all daring feats, his son Akeralik skims the surface like a falcon — and when the Southlander Tajarnek comes with boats for a match, father and son throw the challengers, then slay Tajarnek and all the rest, ending their days unwounded and renowned.
summary.zh: 寡母以食哺之、以忍教之——『隨他去吧，只是別與他同行』——阿特爾菲奧連忍蘇卡拉克的魚叉、掀艇與冷箭，直至第三箭破空，他反手一叉將其刺斃。仇族的船隊前來，魚叉在他身上斷成三截，摔跤對手『如狐狸般』輕易斃命，來犯者盡誅於歸途。其子阿克拉利克被訓練得如隼掠水——南方大力士塔雅爾內克率船隊前來挑戰，父子先摔後殺，盡誅來者；此後父子名滿海岸，至死未嘗一傷。

sensitivity.note: Massacre of the Southlanders recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Two widows, having each a son, had chosen their winter quarters at no great distance from one another. Both of them happened to have several neighbours; but though these principally consisted of rich and prosperous people, they did not think of assisting the poor orphans. Having lost their supporters, the widows suffered much from want, and they therefore admonished their young sons to be wise and kind to the other children, lest they should be deprived of the scanty help they now enjoyed; at last, however, the relatives furnished the orphans with kayaks. He who lived furthest south was named Aterfio, and the other one living to the north was called Sukallassok; they grew up to be much renowned for their strength and vigour. They always chose their hunting-places far off the coast, and even in hard weather and heavy gales went out, and never came home empty-handed; on their return they always used to give the orphans a plentiful repast, and had special stores of provisions set apart for orphan children against hard times.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 59 'Aterfio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩個寡婦各有一個兒子，她們把過冬的住處選在彼此相距不遠的地方。她們碰巧都有幾個鄰居；雖說這些鄰居多為富裕殷實之人，卻沒想到要幫助這些可憐的孤兒。寡婦們失去了依靠，受盡貧困之苦，因此告誡年幼的兒子們要懂事、善待別家的孩子，免得失去眼下這點微薄的幫助；不過到最後，親戚們還是給孤兒們置辦了獨木舟。住在最南邊的那個叫阿特菲奧（Aterfio），住在北邊的那個叫蘇卡拉斯索克（Sukallassok）；他們長大後以力氣和精力充沛而聞名。他們總是把打獵的地方選在遠離海岸之處，即使天氣惡劣、狂風大作也照樣出海，從不空手而歸；歸來時，他們總要讓孤兒們飽餐一頓，還專門留出一些食物儲備，以備艱難時日供孤兒孩子們之用。

passages.text: One day Aterfio had gone out hunting beyond the skerries and islands, the wind northerly and the sky clear; he had already got two seals, and, expecting to catch some more, still rowed on, till all of a sudden he heard a noise, and turning round beheld Sukalassok with raised arm aiming his harpoon at him. Not being able to make any resistance he was obliged to await his fate; keeping his eyes on him, he capsized his kayak towards him so as to make the harpoon only touch the side of it. As soon as he again had risen, the thought flashed through him to revenge himself on Sukalassok; but he gave up the idea and turned towards home, not mentioning the matter at all. Some time later, in a gale from the north, the same thing happened over again; he forebore to take revenge, but this time told those at home that Sukalassok had twice attempted to kill him — his mother bade him not take revenge: 'Never mind; let him go on as he likes, only thou shun his companionship.' Soon after, Aterfio being busy in his hunting-grounds suddenly heard a whizzing sound close by, and presently afterwards was grazed by an arrow which fell into the water alongside of him; his wrath was now up and he could not resist paying him back — in less than no time he levelled his harpoon at Sukalassok and killed him right off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 59 'Aterfio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，阿特菲奧越過礁石與島嶼出海打獵，北風吹拂，天空晴朗；他已捕得兩隻海豹，還想再捕一些，便繼續划槳前行，忽然間他聽見一陣聲響，回頭一看，只見蘇卡拉斯克舉起手臂，正以魚叉瞄準他。他無力抵抗，只得聽天由命；他目不轉睛地盯著對方，將皮艇朝他那邊翻側，好讓魚叉只擦到艇身側面。他一重新坐直，心中便閃過向蘇卡拉斯克報仇的念頭；但他打消了這個主意，轉而朝家的方向划去，對此事絕口不提。過了些時日，在北方吹來的一陣狂風中，同樣的事又發生了一次；他忍住沒有報仇，但這一回他告訴家中的人，說蘇卡拉斯克已兩次企圖殺他——他母親囑咐他不要報仇：『不必在意；隨他去吧，你只要避開與他往來便是。』不久之後，阿特菲奧正在他的獵場上忙碌，忽然聽見近旁傳來一陣呼嘯聲，緊接著便被一支箭擦過，那箭落在他身旁的水中；他這下怒火中燒，再也按捺不住要還以顏色——轉眼之間他便將魚叉對準蘇卡拉斯克，當場將他殺死。

passages.text: At home he reported his deed and said he would flee to the south, thinking it probable the relatives of Sukalassok might take part with the slain and pursue him; but his mother told him he need not fear his new enemies, and he remained at the old place as before. Soon after he married and got a son, whom he called Akeralik. One day an old man came to visit them, who reported that the relatives of Sukalossok were ill-minded towards Aterfio — 'They are quite welcome to anything; and thou mayst tell them that I myself, my little son, and the rest of the household, are ready to receive them whenever they like.' From that day they grew suspicious, and not long afterwards a great many strange boats appeared off the coast. Aterfio went in, relieved himself of his jacket, went straight down to the beach, and seated himself on a flat stone with his back turned to the sea; rowing on, the kayakers deliberated among themselves who should be the first to wound him — the foremost took up his harpoon to strike him, and although it hit the mark it did him no harm, but the harpoon broke in three pieces; the next kayakers likewise unlaunched their harpoons at him, but had them broken in the same manner without wounding him in the least. They now held a council and agreed in landing to try a match with him on shore; Aterfio willingly attended, the strangers stayed the night over, and early the next morning four stout and powerful men made their way through the entrance — 'My house is too small, let us fight in the open air.' Having reached the meadow above, one of the strong men instantly rushed in upon Aterfio to try a wrestling-match with him; but Aterfio only turned to him and thrust him down as easily as if he had been a fox, upon which he soon died. The foreigners now made a general assault on him, but he shook them off like children, and on the way home he killed the whole of them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 59 'Aterfio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他回到家中稟報了自己的所作所為，並說他要逃往南方，心想蘇卡拉斯克的親族多半會站在被殺者一邊來追殺他；但他母親告訴他不必畏懼這些新的仇敵，於是他便如往常一樣留在原地。不久之後他娶了妻，得了一個兒子，取名為阿克拉利克。有一天，一位老人前來拜訪他們，說蘇卡拉斯克的親族對阿特菲奧心懷不善——『他們要什麼都儘管來；你可以告訴他們，我本人、我的小兒子，以及家中其餘的人，隨時都準備好迎接他們，隨他們高興。』從那天起他們便起了疑心，不久之後，海岸外出現了許多陌生的船隻。阿特菲奧走進屋裡，脫下外衣，徑直下到海灘，背朝大海坐在一塊平坦的石頭上；那些划艇的人一邊划近，一邊彼此商議誰該先傷他——最前頭的人舉起魚叉刺他，雖然擊中了目標，卻絲毫傷不了他，魚叉反而斷成三截；接著的划艇者也同樣朝他擲出魚叉，卻都以同樣的方式折斷，一點也傷不了他。他們於是商議了一番，決定上岸與他在陸上較量；阿特菲奧欣然應允，那些陌生人留宿了一夜，次日清晨，四個強壯有力的人穿過入口進來——『我的屋子太小了，我們到空地上打吧。』到了上方那片草地，其中一個壯漢立刻撲向阿特菲奧，要與他比試摔跤；但阿特菲奧只是轉身朝他，輕而易舉地將他摔倒，彷彿他是一隻狐狸，那人不久便死了。那些外來者於是合力圍攻他，但他把他們像孩童一般甩開，並在回家的路上將他們全部殺死。

passages.text: After this Aterfio trained his son to all kinds of daring feats on land as well as at sea; and thus Akeralik grew to be a man, and was still stronger and even more fearless than his father. His hunting-ground was far out at sea, and he hunted seals and white whales alike, and could keep his breath under water as well as any seal. One day when they were a long way off the coast a small-topped cloud rose on the horizon — 'Dost thou see the cloud yonder? When the mists come up from that side it will not be child's-play; let us put back with all speed.' They put their seals on the top of their kayaks and made them fast with the harpoon-lines, and headed for the shore, each having captured two seals. Scarcely had they put about before a heavy gale came rushing down upon them, turning the sea into one mass of foam and completely hiding the land; a roaring noise was heard — 'Take care we don't smash together; keep further away from me' — and he saw a great sea topped with foam close upon them, turning side on and bolting across them; but notwithstanding, they kept their breath and rowed away under water until they soon afterwards both emerged on the surface. At last his son got a tear in his thick outer jacket; then he spoke to his father, 'Now mind thine own self, I must needs speed on' — and he skimmed the surface like a falcon pursuing his prey, and was lost to sight in less than a moment. Both safely reached home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 59 'Aterfio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後，阿特菲奧訓練他的兒子在陸上與海上做各種大膽的技藝；阿克拉利克就這樣長大成人，比他父親更為強壯，甚至更加無所畏懼。他的獵場遠在海上，他捕海豹，也同樣捕白鯨，還能像海豹一樣在水下屏住呼吸。有一天，當他們離海岸很遠時，地平線上升起一朵頂端細小的雲——『你看見那邊那朵雲了嗎？當霧從那一邊升起時，那可不是鬧著玩的；我們趕快回去吧。』他們把海豹放到皮艇頂上，用魚叉繩綁牢，然後朝岸邊划去，每人各捕得了兩隻海豹。他們剛一掉轉方向，一陣猛烈的狂風便朝他們撲來，把海面攪成一片泡沫，將陸地完全遮蔽；只聽得一陣轟鳴聲——『當心別撞在一起；離我遠一點』——他看見一道巨浪帶著泡沫逼近他們，浪頭側轉過來，從他們身上橫掃而過；儘管如此，他們仍屏住呼吸，在水下划行，不久之後兩人便都浮出了水面。最後他兒子的厚外衣被撕開了一道口子；於是他對父親說：『現在你自己當心，我必須趕路了』——他如獵鷹追捕獵物般掠過水面，轉眼之間便消失得無影無蹤。兩人都平安回到了家。

passages.text: About this time the Southlanders happened to hear the fame of the mighty Aterfio and of his son Akeralik, who with his kayak matched a falcon in speed; among this people of the south there was a strong man named Tajarnek, who greatly longed to have an encounter with Aterfio. One day Aterfio and all his family remained at home, the air clear and the weather fine; they saw a great many boats and kayaks apparently passing by their place — but Aterfio came down to the water's edge and hailed them, shouting, 'Where are ye for? It is late in the evening; ye had better put in and take shelter with us for the night.' One of the men replied, 'We have heard of the mighty Aterfio, and have come to offer him a match.' 'He whom ye see is nothing extraordinary, but his son is a man of great strength' — so saying, he pointed to him as he stood at his side; the kayakers stopped short in great amazement, never thinking him to be the person in question. 'But here is a first-rate landing-place, and ye can pass the night here.' Accordingly they landed; after a needful rest they all resorted to a level spot above the houses. Tajarnek first seized Aterfio, but was soon thrown over without being hurt; several times they closed with him, but Aterfio was as staunch as a rock. Akeralik now thought it time for him to interfere; every man he touched was soon thrown down. At first they turned them over without injuring them further, but at length they slew Tajarnek and all the rest — all the Southlanders, women and children included, were thus put to death. From this time upwards Aterfio roamed all along the coast-side, and father and son were equally renowned; and they both ended their days without ever having been wounded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 59 'Aterfio'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大約在這時，南方人偶然聽聞了強大的阿特菲奧及其兒子阿克拉利克的名聲，說他划著皮艇能與獵鷹比快；在這南方民族之中，有一個名叫塔亞爾內克的壯漢，極想與阿特菲奧一較高下。有一天，阿特菲奧與全家人都待在家中，空氣清朗，天氣晴好；他們看見許多船隻和皮艇似乎正經過他們住處附近——阿特菲奧便走到水邊向他們招呼，高聲喊道：『你們要往哪裡去？天色已晚；你們最好靠岸，到我們這裡過夜避一避。』其中一人回答說：『我們聽聞了強大的阿特菲奧，特來向他挑戰。』『你們所見的這個人並沒有什麼了不起，倒是他的兒子是個力大無窮的人』——說著，他指了指站在他身旁的兒子；那些划艇的人大吃一驚，停了下來，萬萬沒想到他就是所說的那個人。『不過這裡是個極好的登岸處，你們可以在這裡過夜。』於是他們便上了岸；歇息妥當之後，他們全都聚集到屋舍上方的一塊平地上。塔亞爾內克首先抓住阿特菲奧，但很快便被摔倒，並未受傷；他們與他扭打了好幾回，但阿特菲奧穩如磐石。阿克拉利克這時覺得該輪到自己出手了；凡被他碰到的人，很快便被摔倒。起初他們只是把對方摔倒，並未進一步傷害，但到最後他們殺死了塔亞爾內克及其餘所有的人——所有的南方人，連婦孺在內，都這樣被殺死了。自此以後，阿特菲奧沿著海岸一帶四處遊歷，父子二人同樣聲名遠播；他們兩人都終其天年，從未受過傷。

title.en: Inugtujusok: The Man-Slayer in the Snow-Cave
title.zh: 伊努格圖尤蘇克：雪穴中的殺人者

region.en: Five-windowed house and the fox-trap cave in the snow
region.zh: 五窗大屋與雪中捕狐陷阱

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 60 'Inugtujusok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Waylaying the bridegroom from a fox-trap cave, the wicked angakok forces his girl to help tire him out — 'if thou canst not I will kill you both.' The brothers defer revenge until the angakok has a son reared to catch beaked whales with ordinary kayak tools, then lure the ageing man north with a sick child, treat him kindly, and beat his brains out at daybreak. His son rows on with oar-strokes lifting the prow — 'I suppose ye have done for him!' — but yields to the warning that avengers always turn up, and report says they were reconciled.
summary.zh: 邪惡的巫師伊努格圖尤蘇克自捕狐雪穴中埋伏求婚的新郎，逼他的姑娘幫忙拖垮情郎——『辦不到就連你們一起殺。』兄弟們隱忍復仇，直到巫師北去養出一個能以普通漁具捕捉喙鯨的兒子；再以病兒為餌，善意款待年邁的仇人，黎明時亂棍擊碎其頭顱。其子划槳如飛——『你們把他解決了吧！』——終被勸阻：『復仇者總會出現。』據說他們就此和解。

sensitivity.note: Murder by mob violence and coerced pursuit recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Several brothers lived in a large house with five windows; about the time when the youngest of them had grown to manhood, a widow with one beautiful daughter happened to live at a place not far off. The brothers were very kindly disposed towards the widow, and when the youngest had made the daughter his sweetheart they grew still more intimate, and the brothers never failed to bring her part of their hunt. Every night the bridegroom used to cross the country to see his bride, but unhappily there lived in that neighbourhood a wicked angakok, a man-slayer, named Inugtujusok: he had made himself a hiding-place by digging out a cave in the snow like those formerly used for fox-trapping, close by the way on which the young man used to pass on going to his girl, and went to hide himself there in order to waylay or murder him. One evening the young woman accompanied her lover home; when all of a sudden they caught sight of Inugtujusok emerging from the cave. On seeing him armed with a lance they both took flight, and he pursued them closely, crying out to the girl, 'Help me to tire him out; if thou canst not I will kill you both.' The girl pitied her lover, but being obliged to help the dreadful angakok she pretended to be pursuing him, and before long he was overtaken and killed. She returned home and mentioned naught about the matter to her mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 60 'Inugtujusok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有幾兄弟同住在一座有五扇窗戶的大屋裡；大約在他們之中最小的那個長大成人時，恰好有一位寡婦帶著一個美麗的女兒住在不遠的地方。兄弟們對那寡婦十分友善，而當最小的那個與那女兒相戀之後，他們往來更加親密，兄弟們每次打獵總不忘分一份獵物給她。新郎每夜都越過原野去見他的新娘，但不幸的是，那一帶住著一個邪惡的安加科克（巫師），一個名叫伊努克圖尤索克的殺人者：他在那年輕人前往會情人的必經之路旁，像從前捕狐用的陷阱那樣，在雪中挖出一個洞穴，為自己造了一個藏身之處，並到那裡躲藏，以便埋伏或殺害他。有一天傍晚，那年輕女子送她的情人回家；忽然間他們瞥見伊努克圖尤索克從洞穴中鑽了出來。見他手持長矛，兩人便雙雙逃跑，他在後面緊緊追趕，對那女子喊道：『幫我把他拖累；你若辦不到，我就把你們兩個都殺了。』那女子憐憫她的情人，卻又不得不幫助那可怖的安加科克，便假裝在追趕他，不久之後他便被追上殺死了。她回到家中，對母親隻字未提此事。

passages.text: The following morning the brothers all came up to her house, calling out, 'Where is our brother?' — no reply was made; again they cried, 'Where is our brother?' but again no answer came. At last they tore a hole in the window, and constantly repeating their question went on to break down the roof — nor until the mother said, 'They have begun to unroof our house, do give them an answer,' did she exclaim, 'Yesterday, on his return from our house, I accompanied him on the way, and saw him killed by Inugtujusok,' and then burst into tears. The brothers likewise returned in tears, filled with hatred towards Inugtujusok; well knowing that he was a great angakok they durst not attack him at once, but gradually prepared themselves to defy him. At this time they heard that Inugtujusok intended to leave for the north for fear of his enemies; he travelled all the summer and did not settle down till late in the autumn, in the far north, where he got a son, whom he brought up with great care, saying that since they had many enemies he ought not to grow up a good-for-nothing. When he was full-grown he was so clever and dexterous that he could catch the very tikagugdlik (beaked whale) with nothing but the ordinary kayak tools; when he had attained to his perfection, and could not be conquered by mere human beings, they remained no longer where they were, but travelled back to the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 60 'Inugtujusok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天早晨，兄弟們全都來到她家門前，喊道：『我們的兄弟在哪裡？』——沒有人回答；他們又喊道：『我們的兄弟在哪裡？』但依然沒有回音。最後他們在窗上撕開一個洞，一面不停地重複著他們的問話，一面動手拆毀屋頂——直到母親說：『他們已經開始拆我們的屋頂了，你就給他們一個回答吧』，那女子才哭喊著說：『昨天他從我們家回去時，我送了他一程，親眼看見他被伊努克圖尤索克殺死了』，隨即放聲大哭。兄弟們也哭著回去了，心中對伊努克圖尤索克充滿仇恨；他們深知他是個法力高強的安加科克，不敢立刻向他動手，只得慢慢準備，以便與他對抗。這時他們聽說伊努克圖尤索克因畏懼仇敵，打算遷往北方；他走了整整一個夏天，直到深秋才在極北之地定居下來，在那裡得了一個兒子，他悉心撫養這兒子，說既然他們有許多仇敵，這孩子就不該長成一個沒用的人。當這孩子長大成人後，他聰明靈巧，單憑普通的皮艇器具便能捕到那所謂的提卡古格德利克（喙鯨）；當他達到爐火純青之境，單憑凡人之力已無法將他制伏時，他們便不再留在原地，而是遷回了南方。

passages.text: The brothers had not meanwhile left their abode; hearing that their enemy was drawing nigh they went on to meet him half-way. One had furnished himself with a girdle of whalebone three fingers wide: he had first made it out of the skin of a thong-seal and tried to burst it open by pressing back his breath, but this was not nearly strong enough, then proceeded to make the one of whalebone, as much tougher — this man was thought the hardiest and strongest of all the brothers. While they had gone to lie in wait for him on the islands outside the country, Inugtujusok and his son happened to set off in their boat, but on seeing their enemies would not go back there, but went to the place where the brothers had formerly lived; discovering their intention, Inugtujusok did not proceed but returned to his former quarters, and the brothers said, 'Let us rather remain where we are, that we may not frighten them away.' Winter had now set in, and a little daughter belonging to one of the brothers was taken very ill: 'Let us call in the angakok Inugtujusok that he may come and try his art upon her; and when he has done we will of course put him to death.' An old bachelor who lived in the house with them was sent off on this errand, and when he had brought his message to Inugtujusok the angakok answered, 'Well, let it be so.' His son was away at the time; but he was beginning to think that in the course of time their feelings had probably softened and their thoughts of revenge been given up — he was himself beginning to grow old, and he accompanied the bachelor back. On entering, the brothers cried, 'Poor thing, thou art getting rather aged!' 'I am so,' he answered; and this was all he spoke. They treated him to a good meal, and in the evening the invocation commenced; soon they agreed that the little girl improved at once. 'Thou mayst sleep without fear, and go back to-morrow' — when he awoke and found himself all alone he suspected evil and started up; on raising his head in stepping over the door-sill of the outer entrance he encountered a man standing close by, who accosted him, saying, 'It is very fine weather, but it is only daybreak, and rather dark yet.' On hearing these words he trembled; after speaking, the man, though not he with the strong girdle, struck him on the head and almost stunned him, upon which the others rushed in upon him, beating him so that his head was bruised, and the brain gushed forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 60 'Inugtujusok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這期間兄弟們並未離開住所；聽說仇敵正逼近，他們便前去半路迎擊。其中一人備了一條三指寬的鯨骨腰帶：他先以海豹皮的皮條製成一條，試著屏住呼吸將它撐破，但這遠不夠結實，於是又著手製成鯨骨的那條，堅韌得多——此人被認為是眾兄弟中最強悍、最健壯的。當他們已前往境外島嶼埋伏等候他時，伊努克圖尤索克與其子恰巧駕船出發，但一見仇敵便不願再回那裡，而轉往兄弟們從前居住之地；伊努克圖尤索克察覺其意圖，便不再前行，折返舊居，兄弟們說：『我們還是留在原地吧，免得把他們嚇跑。』此時已入冬，兄弟中一人的小女兒病得很重：『我們去請巫師伊努克圖尤索克來，讓他來對她施法；等他做完，我們自然要將他處死。』與他們同住的一名老單身漢被派去傳話，當他把話帶給伊努克圖尤索克時，巫師答道：『好，就這麼辦。』他的兒子當時不在；但他開始覺得，隨著時日推移，他們的情感大概已緩和，復仇之念也已放棄——他自己也開始老了，便隨那單身漢一同回去。進門時，兄弟們喊道：『可憐的人，你老了些了！』『是啊，』他答道；他只說了這些。他們給他吃了一頓好飯，到了晚上便開始召靈；不久他們一致認為小女孩立刻好轉了。『你可以安心睡覺，明天就回去吧』——當他醒來發現自己孤身一人時，他疑心有詐，猛然起身；在跨過外門門檻時一抬頭，他遇見一個人站在近旁，那人對他說：『天氣很好，不過才剛破曉，還相當暗呢。』聽到這些話，他發起抖來；那人說完，雖不是佩強韌腰帶的那個，卻朝他頭上打去，幾乎把他打昏，接著其餘的人一擁而上，將他痛打，打得他頭破血流，腦漿迸出。

passages.text: The next morning the son of Inugtujusok came on, ready for them; he was taking such strokes with his oars that the prow of his kayak rose right out of the water, and he exclaimed, 'I suppose ye have done for him!' They made answer from land, 'If thou venturest to approach this place we shall send thee straight after him.' At these words he rushed on in a great passion; but they stood ready to receive and shake him off — finding it quite impossible to get on shore he at length gave it up, and wheeled round, crying, 'To-morrow ye shall be my spoil!' The old bachelor, however, warned him, saying, 'Thou hadst better give it up, and leave thy father alone. He was only paid back according to his deserts, being himself a man-slayer.' And the son of Inugtujusok responded, 'Let it be as thou proposest; perhaps I shall only get new foes if I carry out my thoughts of vengeance. People seeming to have no relatives, when they get enemies generally have some relations (viz., avengers) turning up.' And report says that in this manner they were reconciled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 60 'Inugtujusok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日早晨，伊努克圖尤索克的兒子來了，準備與他們一戰；他划槳用力之猛，使皮艇的船首直翹出水面，他喊道：『我想你們已經把他結果了吧！』他們從岸上答道：『你若敢靠近此地，我們就立刻送你隨他而去。』聽聞此言，他滿腔怒火地衝上前；但他們嚴陣以待，要將他擊退——他發覺根本無法上岸，終於放棄，掉轉船頭，喊道：『明天你們就要成為我的獵物！』然而那老單身漢警告他說：『你最好放棄，別再管你父親的事。他不過是罪有應得，他自己就是個殺人者。』伊努克圖尤索克的兒子回答：『就照你說的辦吧；也許我若實行復仇之念，只會招來新的仇敵。看來沒有親屬的人，一旦結了仇，通常總會有些親戚（即復仇者）冒出來。』據說他們就這樣和解了。

title.en: The Sons Who Avenged Their Mother
title.zh: 為母復仇的眾兄弟

region.en: Mother's grave by the fiord and the far land beyond the sea
region.zh: 峽灣畔的母親墳墓與海外遠邦

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 61 'The Sons who avenged their Mother', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Watching their mother's grave, the brothers catch an old neighbour rummaging it and kill him — 'Thy father shall recompense me through his daughter' — taking his eldest girl to wife. Stabbed in the bosom by her knife one night, the eldest dies silently; the widow-murderess rows out with her family, breaking every oar, steering for the far south. There her son is rubbed with the inuarutligaks' whetstone — 'Child! be as hard as this stone' — until the avenging brothers, landing years later across Akilinek, try their knife on the named boy and find it glides off him, broken. The brothers cross the sea home; the fugitives remain, their bones said to rest there.
summary.zh: 眾兄弟守護母親的墳墓，捉住盜墓的老鄰居並將其殺死——『叫你父親用女兒來賠我』——強娶其長女為妻。新婚夜，她持刀刺入丈夫胸口，無聲而亡；殺夫的她攜全家出海，一路折斷所有船槳，直駛南方遠邦。其子在出生時被以山中精靈的磨刀石摩挲——『孩子！要像這石頭一樣硬』——復仇的兄弟們多年後渡海而至，以刀試那以亡父之名命名的孩子，刀刃竟滑開折斷。兄弟們渡海返鄉，逃亡者留居新地，遺骨據說至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Uxoricide and forced marriage recorded as told in the 1875 source. The whetstone-invulnerability charm is a documented Greenlandic belief.

passages.text: A great many brothers were living in a house together, with but one female — their old mother. Beside the house they occupied was another inhabited by an old couple, whose children consisted of girls only, and they never left their parents. When the brothers removed to the other side of the fiord in search of provender the old people followed them, and took up their abode a little further down the coast; here the mother of the many men died, and being bereft of their housewife the youngest brother had to do the general work. On alternate days the elder ones went out kayaking, and repaired to their mother's grave to mourn her death. At last they moved back to their usual winter station, and the old people likewise resorted to their hut; from this place also the brothers continued alternately to go out hunting one day, and visit their mother's grave the next, whereas the youngest always stopped at home to flense the seals and attend to the other house-work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 61 'The Sons who avenged their Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 許多兄弟同住一屋，只有一名女子——他們的年邁母親。他們所住的屋子旁邊還有另一間，住著一對老夫婦，他們的孩子全是女兒，從不離開父母。當兄弟們遷往峽灣對岸尋找食物時，老夫婦也跟了過去，在沿海稍遠處安了家；在那裡，這許多人的母親去世了，失去了主婦，最小的弟弟只得承擔一切家務。兄長們隔日輪流划皮艇外出，並前往母親的墳墓哀悼她的死。最後他們遷回慣常的過冬之地，老夫婦也同樣回到他們的小屋；從此地起，兄弟們仍舊輪流一日外出打獵，次日去母親墳前，而最小的弟弟總是留在家中剝海豹皮、料理其他家務。

passages.text: One day, on reaching the grave, they noticed that the top-stones had been disturbed and were out of their proper place; the day after they again went to the tomb, and after hiding their kayaks concealed themselves behind some heaps of great rocks. When dawn had changed into broad daylight they saw a kayaker putting off from their own shore, and when he came nearer recognised him as their own old neighbour; they first supposed him to be going to a small uninhabited house down on the coast, but this he passed by, and went right up to the grave, where he at once began to rummage about. 'There is plain proof; he is the criminal; let us kill him to-morrow.' They saw the old man descending to his kayak and pulling back across the fiord to his own home, and followed him; the next morning they sought him in his tent — he had not yet arisen. The eldest brother went first, and after him followed the others; the leader accosted the old man: 'It is not without reason we have thus come to thee, but because the tomb of our mother has recently been disturbed.' 'But who could possibly have done it? I am but a poor decayed fellow, and am hardly able to get up to the little house on the shore.' 'Notwithstanding, I know thou art the trespasser, inasmuch as we all saw thee pilfering about the grave yesterday' — so saying he rushed upon him, and hauling him outside the tent killed him on the spot. This done he returned to the hut, and going right up to the eldest girl said to her, 'Thy father shall recompense me through his daughter' — upon which he brought her home and took her for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 61 'The Sons who avenged their Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他們到了墳前，發現墳頂的石頭被動過，不在原位；第二天他們又去墳墓，把皮艇藏好後，躲在一些大石堆後面。當黎明化為大白天時，他們看見一個划皮艇的人從他們自己的岸邊出發，等他靠近些，認出正是他們的老鄰居；他們起初以為他是要去海岸下游一間無人居住的小屋，但他經過那裡，逕直划向墳墓，一到便開始翻找。『證據確鑿；他就是罪犯；明天我們殺了他。』他們看見老人下到皮艇，划過峽灣回自己家去，便跟蹤他；第二天早晨他們在他的帳篷裡找他——他還沒起身。大哥先進去，其餘的人跟在後面；為首的對老人說：『我們這樣來找你並非無故，而是因為我們母親的墳近來被人動過。』『可這會是誰幹的呢？我不過是個衰弱可憐的老頭，連走到岸邊那間小屋都幾乎辦不到。』『儘管如此，我知道你就是那個擅闖者，因為我們昨天都看見你在墳邊鬼鬼祟祟地翻找』——說著他撲向他，把他拖出帳篷，當場殺死。辦完之後他回到屋裡，逕直走到大女兒面前對她說：『你父親要透過他的女兒來補償我』——於是把她帶回家，娶她為妻。

passages.text: The next day the younger brothers were to watch her during the absence of the elder ones, lest she should make her escape; she remained there for a long while, but continued to be very obstinate, and could not be made to lie down on the ledge, but remained sitting up till dawn of day. At last she determined to kill her husband: he always used to put his knife in front of the lamp on coming in for the night; one evening when all were fast asleep and her husband lay beside her, she took hold of the knife, having first tied on her boots well. The thought struck her, however, 'If the others awake at his cry, they will no doubt turn upon me at once; but let them take my life too, as they have already taken that of my poor father.' Putting aside her fears she stabbed him in the bosom, and in a moment he silently expired; without drawing the knife back she hurried away to her mother's house, saying, 'Pack up thy things speedily and let us be off; I have killed the eldest brother.' That same night the boat was loaded and they started.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 61 'The Sons who avenged their Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，兄長們外出時，由較年幼的弟弟們看守她，免得她逃走；她在那裡待了很久，卻始終十分倔強，怎麼也不肯躺到床板上，一直坐到天亮。最後她決心殺死丈夫：他每晚進屋時總把刀子放在燈前；一天晚上，眾人都熟睡，她丈夫躺在她身旁，她先把自己的靴子繫好，然後握住刀子。然而她心中忽然閃過一念：『若是別人被他的叫聲驚醒，必定立刻撲向我；但就讓他們取我性命吧，反正他們已經取了我那可憐父親的命。』她撇開恐懼，刺入他的胸膛，他頃刻間無聲地死去；她沒有拔出刀子，便匆匆趕往母親的屋子，說：『快收拾你的東西，我們走吧；我殺死了大哥。』當夜船便裝載完畢，他們出發了。

passages.text: She who had slain her husband questioned the man at the steer-oar, 'What way are we going?' — 'I shall follow the coast up north' — but she thought the pursuers would most probably likewise take that direction; when he turned to the south she feared they would do the same when they had sought them in vain to the north, and she advised him to steer right to sea. No sooner had they turned their prow off the land than the foremost of the women-rowers broke her oar; she asked for that of her neighbour, but broke that too, and thus went on to break them all one after another, at last wanting the steersman to give up his too — 'What wouldst thou have me steer with?' — 'With thy kayak-paddle, of course.' They now rowed on with the only oar left, he steering with his paddle; the mother, who had her place in the bottom of the boat, said to her son the steersman that they would soon be in sight of land ahead of them, and told him to steer straight towards the sun and follow the coast southwards. As she had said, a great looming land soon broke upon their sight, and observing a house on the shore they landed there; it so happened that only one man was standing outside, with this exception all there happened to be women — they were invited to come in and accordingly entered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 61 'The Sons who avenged their Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那殺死丈夫的女子問掌舵的人：『我們往哪個方向走？』——『我要沿著海岸往北。』——但她想追兵很可能也會朝那個方向去；當他轉向南時，她又怕他們在北邊搜尋無果後也會照樣南下，便勸他直向海上駛去。他們的船首剛一離開陸地，划槳婦女中最前頭的那個便折斷了槳；她向鄰座要槳，卻又把那支也折斷了，就這樣一支接一支地全折斷了，最後竟要掌舵的人也把他的槳讓出來——『那你要我用什麼掌舵？』——『當然是用你的皮艇槳。』他們如今只用僅剩的一支槳划行，他則用皮艇槳掌舵；坐在船底的母親對掌舵的兒子說，他們不久就會看見前方的陸地，並叫他朝著太陽的方向直駛，沿海南下。正如她所說，一片高聳的陸地不久便映入眼簾，他們望見岸上有一間屋子，便在那裡登陸；恰巧只有一個男人站在外面，除此之外那裡碰巧全是女人——他們被邀進屋，於是便進去了。

passages.text: In the meantime the brothers of the murdered man, left behind in their former place, awoke and found him stabbed and steeped in blood beside them; they hastened along to the house of their neighbours, and finding it empty at once made ready to pursue them. First they scanned the coast to the north, asking intelligence of everybody they met with; not gaining the information they sought they put about, and having again passed by their own place now rowed south — there they had no better luck, and having roamed about for a long time only returned home in time to get settled for the winter. Next summer they also put out to sea, intending to cross the sea for Akilinek, but having reached the land on the other side made to the north instead of to the south; having put many inquiries to different people they happened to meet with on the coast, they gave up the chase and settled down there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 61 'The Sons who avenged their Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在此期間，被殺者遺留在原居地的兄弟們醒來，發現他被刺死、浸在血泊之中躺在他們身旁；他們急忙趕往鄰人的屋子，見屋內空無一人，便立刻準備追趕他們。他們先察看北面的海岸，向所遇到的每一個人打聽消息；得不到所要的情報，便掉轉船頭，再次經過自己的居所，如今向南划去——在那裡運氣也好不了多少，遊蕩了許久，只來得及趕回家安頓過冬。次年夏天他們也出海，打算渡海前往阿基利內克，但抵達對岸陸地後卻往北去而非往南；他們向沿海偶然遇到的各色人等多方打聽，終於放棄追尋，就在那裡定居下來。

passages.text: Meantime the second of the sisters that had escaped had got married to the only man of their place, and their brother on his side had chosen a wife among the sisters of his brothers-in-law; on getting a son he called his name after that of his poor deceased father. The grandmother ordered them, 'Bring me my bag!' — and having got it she produced the whetstone of the inuarutligaks (mountain-elves) from the bottom of it, and rubbing the new-born baby with it went on repeating: 'Child! be as hard as this stone' (viz., invulnerable by charm); each time the child got a new suit of clothes she would give him a rub with the stone, repeating the words, 'Be hard.' In course of time, when the son had got more children, he one day chanced to ask whether there were no more people in that country — 'Ah, yes, to the north of us are plenty of people, but having never been there we don't know them.' He tried to persuade his brother-in-law to follow him thither; at first he would not consent to go to these strange people, but when the other went on entreating he at last agreed, and they started with only one boat. After a rather long journey they passed by a foreland under shelter of which they saw a great many tents pitched round a little bay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 61 'The Sons who avenged their Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在此期間，逃脫的姊妹中排行第二的那位已嫁給了她們居所中唯一的男子，而她們的兄弟則在姻親的姊妹中擇了一妻；得了一個兒子後，他便以他那可憐的亡父之名為兒子命名。祖母吩咐他們：『把我的袋子拿來！』——拿到之後，她從袋底取出山精（inuarutligaks）的磨刀石，用它摩擦那初生的嬰兒，一面反覆念道：『孩子！要像這石頭一樣堅硬』（即刀槍不入、不受咒術所傷）；每當孩子換上一套新衣，她便用石頭為他摩擦一遍，反覆念著：『要堅硬。』時日流轉，當這兒子又有了更多子女之後，有一天他偶然問起那地方是否再沒有別的人了——『啊，有的，我們北邊人煙稠密，只是我們從未去過，不認識他們。』他試圖說服他的姻親隨他前往那裡；起初他不肯去見這些陌生的人，但對方一再懇求，他終於答應，兩人只乘一條船出發。經過相當漫長的一段旅程，他們駛過一處海岬，在海岬的掩蔽下，他們看見一個小海灣周圍搭著許多帳篷。

passages.text: The fugitive next morning ascended a hill; seeing a kayaker shove off from land he hastened down and likewise got into his kayak to make his acquaintance — on getting up with him he thought he knew his features, thinking them to be those of the next younger brother he had been living with in his former home. On their way to the hunting-place he went on to question him: 'Art thou a native of this country?' 'Yes, I was born here.' 'Art thou also grown up here?' 'No, I am neither born nor grown up here, but in the country opposite. When our eldest brother was killed by his wife we left our land in search of her, hoping to find her out, and finally landed here.' 'Art thou married?' 'Yes, I am.' 'Are all thy brothers married?' 'Yes, excepting the youngest.' 'Hast thou got any children?' 'Yes, two — both boys.' 'Have thy brothers got children?' 'Yes, and all of them boys.' On his return from the hunt, after having been seated a little while in the tent, the inmates heard a noise of many people outside, and presently all those brothers came rushing in; he who was now the eldest sat down opposite to his former sister-in-law, and at once exclaimed, 'These people are easily recognised.' 'Maybe we are easily recognised, but so ye are too, although ye pretend to be foreigners.' 'Can we possibly let them remain alive, now that we have at length fallen in with them?' Their old adversary, the woman who had committed the murder, was busy making sewing-thread; her brother said, 'They say that womankind are not fit to revenge themselves on men' — and taking up a large knife gave it to the other, saying, 'Look here; that poor boy is named after my father, whom ye killed; appease your thirst of vengeance by killing him first.' The bad man at once thrust his knife at the boy, who was standing erect in the centre of the tent — but the knife glided off him, and a sound was heard as if it had struck against something hard; on finding they were not able to pierce him through he examined the knife and found it broken, returned it to the owner, and they all left the tent. Shortly after, the former fugitive went outside and saw to his amazement the people preparing to leave the place; he then determined to do the same, and both parties started at the same time — the brothers crossed the sea to go to their own country, but the fugitives remained for good at their new place of abode, where they lived, they and their successors, and where their bones are said to rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 61 'The Sons who avenged their Mother'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 次日早晨，那逃亡者登上山丘；看見一名划著獨木舟的人離岸而去，便急忙下山，也坐上自己的獨木舟去與他結識——趕上他之後，他覺得認得他的容貌，認為那正是他從前在家時與之同住的次幼弟。在前往獵場的途中，他繼續問他：『你是這地方的人嗎？』『是的，我生在這裡。』『你也是在這裡長大的嗎？』『不，我既不是生在這裡，也不是在這裡長大的，而是在對岸的地方。我們的大哥被他的妻子殺死後，我們便離開故土尋找她，希望能找到她，最後在此登陸。』『你成親了嗎？』『是的，我成親了。』『你的兄弟們都成親了嗎？』『是的，只有最小的那個還沒有。』『你有孩子嗎？』『有，兩個——都是男孩。』『你的兄弟們有孩子嗎？』『有，而且全都是男孩。』他打獵歸來，在帳篷裡坐了一會兒之後，帳中的人聽見外面有許多人喧嘩的聲音，隨即那些兄弟全都衝了進來；如今身為長兄的那人坐在他從前的嫂嫂對面，立刻喊道：『這些人很容易認出來。』『也許我們很容易認出來，但你們也一樣，儘管你們假裝是外地人。』『既然我們終於碰上了他們，難道還能讓他們活著嗎？』他們的老對頭，那個犯下殺人的女人，正忙著做縫線；她的兄弟說：『人家都說女人不適合向男人報仇』——說著拿起一把大刀遞給另一人，說道：『瞧；那可憐的孩子取的是我父親的名字，而你們殺了他；先殺了他，以解你們復仇之渴吧。』那惡人立刻把刀刺向那直立在帳篷中央的孩子——但刀從他身上滑開，並發出像是撞在什麼硬物上的聲響；他們發覺無法刺穿他，便察看那把刀，發現它已折斷，於是把它還給主人，眾人便都離開了帳篷。不久之後，先前的逃亡者走到外面，驚愕地看見那些人正準備離開此地；他於是決定也照樣做，兩方同時出發——兄弟們渡海返回自己的故鄉，而逃亡者則永久留在他們新的居所，他們和他們的後裔都住在那裡，據說他們的遺骨也安息於此。

title.en: Ernersiak the Foster-Son
title.zh: 義子厄內爾夏克

region.en: Brothers' house and the red-walrus coast of the north
region.zh: 兄弟之家與北方的紅海象海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 62 'Ernersiak the Foster-son', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Blamed for the youngest brother's death, little Ernersiak's stepmother is struck dead while he sets fox-traps; the strong man of the place adopts him with a bit of his dead mother's backbone for an amulet, lifting him off his couch by the hairs, teaching hook-and-crook. Struck down twice by a lurking ball-player, he flings his assailant bleeding to the ground — the spears break on his back, the crowd cannot throw him, and he hurles them all bleeding by the fur collars. Given his first kayak, he kills from behind at the tents that once knew him, drives them from the coast with a warning, and spears the red walrus in the north where his tools were 'not likely ever to have more use.'
summary.zh: 么弟病亡，眾兄弟遷怒於厄內爾夏克的繼母，趁他外出設狐陷阱時將老人打死。村中的大力士收養了他，以亡母脊椎骨一段為護身符，清早僅提髮將他從床上拎起，教他角力與投石。兩度被埋伏的球童擊暈後，他把偷襲者拎著衣領掄轉、擲地見血；長矛在他背上寸寸折斷，圍攻者反被他一個個擲翻。得了皮艇後，他在昔日相識的營地背後一叉殺人，並放話威懾；北上紅海象之海，他一叉斃巨獸——那裡的人曾說他的工具『不會再有用了』。

sensitivity.note: Killing of the stepmother and of the kayaker recorded as told in the 1875 source. Backbone amulet motif documented.

passages.text: Little Ernersiak lived with an aged stepmother at a place where a number of men, who were all brothers, housed together, and at that same place there was also an immensely strong man. In the autumn the youngest brother fell sick, and getting worse and worse at length died; they all agreed in suspecting Ernersiak's mother of having caused his death, and only waited a time when they should find her alone in the house to charge her with the deed. One morning Ernersiak furnished himself with some strings and went away to set up fox-traps, and the brothers, profiting by his absence, entered and struck the old woman dead. But the strong man took pity on Ernersiak; when he saw him returning he went out to meet him and said, 'Don't thou go into the tent; thou won't see her any more; the brothers killed her this morning as soon as thou wert gone' — and the strong man adopted him, and for want of a better gave him a bit of his dear mother's backbone for an amulet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 62 'Ernersiak the Foster-son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 小埃爾納西亞克與一位年邁的繼母同住，那地方有一群全是兄弟的男子同住一處，而在同一地方還有一個力大無窮的人。秋天，最小的弟弟病倒了，病情越來越重，終於死去；他們都一致懷疑埃爾納西亞克的母親造成了她的死，只等有朝一日發現她獨自在家時，便向她問罪。一天早晨，埃爾納西亞克帶了些繩子出去設置捕狐陷阱，兄弟們趁他不在，進屋把老婦人打死。但那大力士憐憫埃爾納西亞克；見他回來，便出去迎他，說道：『你別進帳篷了；你再也見不到她了；今早你一出門，兄弟們就把她殺了』——大力士收養了他，因沒有更好的東西，便從他親愛母親的脊骨上取下一小塊給他作護身符。

passages.text: The strong man brought him up and trained him according to the rules of strength: early in the morning he lifted him off his couch by the hairs only, and the boy did not awake till he was put down on his feet; his new parents gave him a suit of clothes, but these did not last long, because he had always to exercise himself throwing and carrying stones. One evening, when they were late up, his new father took a skin and spreading it on the floor began to teach him how to draw hook and crook, admonishing him not to join the other children at ball-playing — for this reason Ernersiak was always seen standing with one arm out of his sleeve (a token of modesty), regarding them from a safe distance. One day, however, while he was thus looking on he got a severe stroke on the top of his head, at which he fell to the ground in a swoon; when he came to himself nobody was near. Another time he was again struck down in the same manner, but on rising plainly saw some one sneaking away; hurrying after him he found him hiding behind a rock, and making right up to him took hold of him by the collar of his jacket, and hurling him several times round in the air flung him to the ground with such force that the blood gushed out of his mouth and nose. 'Ernersiak has been up to mischief' was now all the cry, a large skin produced to carry the wounded boy away upon, while Ernersiak seated himself on a little mound in front of the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 62 'Ernersiak the Foster-son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大力士撫養他，並按力量的規矩訓練他：清晨他只憑頭髮把他從床上提起來，男孩直到被放下站穩才醒來；他的新父母給了他一套衣服，但這些衣服穿不了多久，因為他總得練習投石和搬石。一天晚上，他們很晚還沒睡，他的新父親拿了一張皮鋪在地上，開始教他如何彎腰屈背（拉弓射箭之姿），告誡他不要和其他孩子一起玩球——正因如此，人們總看見埃爾納西亞克一隻手臂露在袖子外站著（這是謙遜的標誌），從安全的距離外觀看他們。然而有一天，他正這樣觀看時，頭頂挨了重重一擊，昏倒在地；等他醒來，身旁已無一人。又一次，他又以同樣的方式被打倒，但起身時清楚地看見有人偷偷溜走；他急忙追去，發現那人躲在一塊岩石後面，便逕直走到他跟前，抓住他夾克的衣領，在空中把他掄了好幾圈，然後猛力把他摔在地上，以致血從他口鼻中湧出。『埃爾納西亞克闖禍了』如今成了眾人的喊聲，有人拿出一大張皮來抬走那受傷的男孩，而埃爾納西亞克則在屋前的一個小土墩上坐了下來。

passages.text: Soon after the kayakers were seen to return, and they were welcomed with the same cry; when his foster-father heard this he speedily loosened his towing-line, and running up to Ernersiak said that they intended to kill him. The brothers by this time had also got on shore, and hearing what had happened one among them ran to fetch his spear, the others all following him; the father of the wounded boy flung his lance with all his strength at Ernersiak, who remained sitting, his back turned towards them — though Ernersiak remained unhurt, the lance was broken in pieces; the others now tried their lances, but with no better luck. In this manner we are told his foster-mother's amulet wrought its first wonder. They now gathered round him and caught hold of him; though they were so many that he could hardly be seen in the crowd, they were not able to throw him over — all of a sudden he turned round upon them, seized them one by one by their fur collars, and hurled them all bleeding to the ground. His foster-father now advised him to stop, lest he should get too many enemies, upon which he followed him into the house, where he seated himself but could not be made to eat or speak. In the evening his foster-father fetched him some liver, hoping he would relish that, and on entering with it remarked, 'The very last boat is now leaving us, and we shall have no neighbours henceforth.' On hearing this he leaned forward and chuckled grimly, well knowing that he had been the cause of their hasty departure; he enjoyed the idea vastly, and from that moment he began to find his appetite.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 62 'Ernersiak the Foster-son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久之後，有人看見划獨木舟的人回來了，他們也以同樣的喊聲迎接；他的養父聽到這喊聲，急忙解開拖繩，跑到埃爾納西亞克跟前，說他們打算殺他。這時兄弟們也已上岸，聽到發生的事，其中一人跑去取他的長矛，其餘的人都跟著他；那受傷男孩的父親用盡全力把長矛擲向埃爾納西亞克，而埃爾納西亞克仍背對著他們坐著——雖然埃爾納西亞克毫髮無傷，長矛卻斷成了幾截；其餘的人現在也試著擲長矛，但運氣也好不了多少。據說他的養母的護身符就是這樣第一次顯靈。他們現在圍住他，抓住他；儘管人數眾多，幾乎看不見他在人群中的身影，他們卻無法把他扳倒——忽然他轉身面對他們，一個接一個抓住他們的毛皮衣領，把他們全都摔得流血倒地。他的養父這時勸他住手，免得結下太多仇敵，他於是跟著他進了屋，在屋裡坐下，卻怎麼也不肯吃東西或說話。傍晚，他的養父拿了些肝來，希望他會喜歡吃，進屋時說道：『最後一條船現在也要離開我們了，從今以後我們就沒有鄰居了。』聽到這話，他向前傾身，陰沉地輕笑起來，心裡明白自己正是他們匆匆離去的原因；他非常喜歡這個念頭，從那一刻起，他開始有了胃口。

passages.text: His father, who now deemed it only fair that he should have his own kayak, set to building him one, and subsequently began to teach him how to manage it; before long the pupil proved himself very apt at paddling as well as hunting in kayak. When his father awoke in the morning his son had already fetched his kayak-jacket, and when the father went away for his own the son was already seated in his kayak waiting, invariably returning home with some capture. One day he had been waiting in his kayak for his father to come down and start with him; but thinking him too long about it he paddled away alone, following the coast southwards, and there behind a cape suddenly fell in with another kayaker — this man did not recognise Ernersiak, because he left him before he had got his kayak. He asked him to go with him and visit his people; presently they came upon a place covered with tents, in front of which a number of people were engaged in building boats, kayaks, &c. — on catching sight of Ernersiak and his companion they shouted, 'Look there! Ernersiak has turned a kayaker.' At this moment Ernersiak's companion paddled on in advance of him intending to make the shore before him; but Ernersiak followed him close, and almost before 'He is going to kill thee' had escaped the bystanders, Ernersiak lifted his harpoon and killed him from behind, then paddling up to him drew it out and turned his back upon them. Having passed the cape he put ashore and climbed the top there to await his pursuers; but when night set in and no one had as yet appeared he again set off for home, sulking and refusing to eat. His father guessed he had been guilty of some murder, and went on warning him against making too many enemies for himself; after this he was again persuaded to take some food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 62 'Ernersiak the Foster-son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的父親如今認為，讓他擁有自己的獨木舟才算公平，於是著手為他造了一艘，隨後便開始教他如何操縱；不久，這學生便證明自己非常擅長划槳，也擅長在獨木舟上狩獵。父親早晨醒來時，兒子已取來他的獨木舟外套；而當父親去取自己的外套時，兒子早已坐進獨木舟裡等候，而且總會帶著獵物回家。有一天，他一直在獨木舟裡等父親下來與他一同出發；但嫌父親耽擱太久，便獨自划走了，沿著海岸向南而行，在那裡繞過一處海岬後，忽然遇見另一個划獨木舟的人——這人沒認出厄訥西阿克，因為他在厄訥西阿克還沒坐上獨木舟時就已離開了他。他邀厄訥西阿克與他同行，去拜訪他的族人；不久他們來到一處滿是帳篷的地方，帳篷前有許多人正忙著造船、造獨木舟等等——他們一見厄訥西阿克和他的同伴，便喊道：『瞧那邊！厄訥西阿克也成了划獨木舟的人了。』就在這時，厄訥西阿克的同伴划到他前頭，想搶先上岸；但厄訥西阿克緊隨其後，幾乎在旁觀者那句『他要殺你了』還沒出口之前，厄訥西阿克便舉起魚叉，從背後將他殺死，隨後划近他，拔出魚叉，背對著眾人而去。繞過海岬後，他靠岸，爬上那裡的頂端等候追兵；但夜幕降臨，仍不見有人出現，他便又動身回家，悶悶不樂，不肯進食。父親猜到他是犯了殺人之事，便繼續告誡他不要樹敵太多；此後他又被勸服，吃了些食物。

passages.text: The following day the father kayaked the same way past the cape and came in sight of the tents with the people at work outside them; he paddled quite close to the beach and cried out, 'If ye remain in this neighbourhood I and my son Ernersiak won't fail to despatch the whole of you; but I have heard of plenty good hunting away to the north, and I will encourage him to go thither.' After this speech he returned and did not fail to tell his son the exciting report, finding him very anxious to try that place. In the spring they left their old quarters and travelled northwards the whole summer-time; just as the frost was beginning to harden the earth a little they got to a place with many tents, and being hailed from land to put in there went ashore accordingly — very civilly received, not allowed to trouble themselves about their luggage, the inhabitants unloading and carrying it all up for them. It happened that Ernersiak, being somewhat fatigued with kayaking, had seated himself in the boat for a rest; on finding his tools and weapons so heavy that they had to carry them on their shoulders, the people remarked that he was not likely ever to have more use for them. The foster-father overhearing their talk repeated it to Ernersiak in the evening, who, tickled at the idea, burst out laughing — this was his first mirth since the murder. In this place they passed the winter. One morning, coming outside, Ernersiak was astonished not to see any one about the houses as usual, but on glancing round observed them standing on a hilltop looking out upon the sea — 'We are watching the red walrus.' Ernersiak, on seeing the ocean all a foam, hastened down to his kayak and set off towards them; he soon detected a large walrus comparatively quiet, and when he came close to it the animal lifted its head above the surface, holding back its breath quietly regarding him — but when it had come quite close it tossed back its head, blew a great puff of air at him, and rushed towards him, while he kept steadily moving in upon it. About the distance of an arrow-shot he aimed his weapon at it, and when the animal bent down and curved its back he lanced and thrust, instantly despatching it; having towed it ashore he went back to catch one more before he landed for good himself. Towards spring they again prepared to go south, their hosts inviting them to come back and pass the winter with them — they thanked them very kindly, but being once more in the south they stopped, and never afterwards visited the north.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 62 'Ernersiak the Foster-son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，父親沿同一路線划獨木舟經過海岬，望見那些帳篷，人們正在帳篷外幹活；他划到離海灘很近的地方，高聲喊道：『你們若留在這一帶，我和我兒子厄訥西阿克定會把你們全部解決掉；但我聽說北邊有許多極好的獵場，我會鼓勵他去那裡。』說完這番話，他便回去了，並且不忘把這令人振奮的消息告訴兒子，發現兒子非常渴望去那個地方一試。春天，他們離開舊居，整個夏天都向北行進；就在嚴霜開始使土地稍稍變硬之時，他們來到一處有許多帳篷的地方，岸上有人招呼他們靠岸，他們便依言上岸——受到十分客氣的接待，人家不讓他們為行李操心，居民替他們卸下並把所有東西都搬了上去。恰巧厄訥西阿克因划獨木舟有些疲倦，坐在船裡歇息；眾人發現他的工具和武器重得必須用肩扛，便議論說他今後大概再也用不著這些東西了。養父無意中聽到他們的話，晚上便轉述給厄訥西阿克，他覺得這念頭有趣，不禁大笑起來——這是自那次殺人以來他第一次開懷。他們就在這地方過了冬。一天早晨，厄訥西阿克走到屋外，驚訝地發現屋舍周圍不像往常那樣有人，但環顧四周，卻見眾人站在一座山頂上眺望大海——『我們在看紅海象。』厄訥西阿克見海面盡是泡沫，急忙奔向自己的獨木舟，朝他們划去；他很快發現一頭相當安靜的大海象，當他靠近時，那動物把頭抬出水面，屏住呼吸，靜靜地打量他——但當他靠得相當近時，牠把頭往後一甩，朝他噴出一大股氣，向他衝來，而他則穩穩地向牠逼近。大約在一箭之遙的距離，他瞄準牠擲出武器，當那動物俯身弓背時，他刺了進去，當即將牠殺死；把牠拖上岸後，他又回去再捕一頭，然後才正式上岸。臨近春天，他們又準備南歸，主人們邀他們再回來與他們共度冬天——他們非常懇切地道謝，但既已回到南方，便留了下來，此後再未去過北方。

title.en: The Old Southlander: The Face Like the Full Moon
title.zh: 南方老翁：滿月般的臉

region.en: Agdluitsok, South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭阿格盧伊茨奧克

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 63 'The Old Southlander', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Told that the middlemost of the famous brothers has murdered his only son, the old man of the south resumes kayaking after years of eating and sleeping — driftwood wrought into harpoon and lance, a new bladder — kills the murderer from the sun-glitter, and calls ashore: 'Since your brother wanted to get rid of his life, I have done away with it.' Defending his lonely tent with arrows in three portions at three points, he next refuses weapons altogether: singing his face enlarged till it resembled the full moon, he pokes it through the entrance — 'A face! a face!' — and no one dares enter again; the counter-lay restores it, and with two tremendous bladder-arrows he snatches the wounded seal from amid the whole hunting-fleet.
summary.zh: 聞說著名的兄弟中居中者殺害了自己的獨子，南方老翁重拾皮艇——以浮木打造魚叉長矛、備新浮囊——自陽光反光處一擊斃敵，遙呼岸上：『你們的兄弟既想送命，我便成全了他。』他以三份箭守三處岬角退敵，繼而索性棄械：高唱咒歌使己面脹大如滿月，自帳門探出——『一張臉！一張臉！』——來犯者無人再敢登岸。解咒復原後，他以兩支巨大的浮囊箭闖入整支獵隊之中，奪走被叉傷的海豹，令敵人再不敢輕舉妄動。

sensitivity.note: Face-enlarging magic lay documented as told in the 1875 source. Killing and vengeance recorded as told.

passages.text: In days of yore there was an old man who lived down south with his only son, a very dexterous and able sportsman, in the country near Agdluitsok (South Greenland). When this son was able to supply their wants the father left everything to his care, and for his part lived only to eat and sleep. One day the son did not return as usual in the evening; it was the season for the large hooded seals (bladder-nose), and the father thought he was lost. In sight of his abode was a plain with many tents, the inhabitants of which consisted partly of a number of brothers, among whom there was one of great fame; there also was a cousin of the old man living there, and whilst the latter was bewailing and mourning the loss of his son this cousin came to see him and informed him that his son had been put to death, and that the middlemost among the brothers was the transgressor. The old man was greatly enraged at this intelligence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 63 'The Old Southlander'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 往昔，有一位老人與他唯一的兒子住在南方，就在阿格德盧伊措克（南格陵蘭）附近的鄉間，那兒子是個非常靈巧能幹的獵手。當這兒子足以供養他們所需時，父親便把一切都交給他照料，自己則只顧吃喝睡覺。一天，兒子沒有像往常那樣在傍晚回家；當時正是大冠海豹（囊鼻海豹）的季節，父親以為他失蹤了。他住所望得見一片滿是帳篷的平原，那裡的居民中有一部分是許多兄弟，其中有一個名聲極大；老人的一個表親也住在那裡，當老人正為失去兒子而悲嘆哀悼時，這表親前來看他，告訴他他的兒子已被殺害，而行凶者正是那群兄弟中居中的那一個。老人聽到這消息，勃然大怒。

passages.text: That same spring he secured a large piece of driftwood, which he cut up and wrought out of it various heavy tools, such as a harpoon and a lance; he also provided himself with a new bladder. From that time he resumed all his former habits — going out kayaking, always hoping to find an opportunity to avenge his son. One morning early he went off to one of the hunting-grounds farthest out at sea; after a while he came back inside the reefs, and on approaching the shore encountered a kayaker towing a seal and making for the land — this was the murderer of his son. Keeping right in the sunlight he looked carefully about to see if they were alone, and having first made sure of his man, who did not detect him, being blinded by the sun, suddenly rushed in upon him, and lifting his weapon gave him the death-stroke. He towed him towards land; on seeing an iceberg driven up on the rocks by the tide he made him fast to this, and leaving him there pursued his way landwards to let his brothers know what had happened. They were all at home, and his cousin was among them, sitting in the open air outside their tents, when they suddenly beheld him paddling in with unwonted speed; he stopped short and called aloud to those on shore, 'Since your brother wanted to get rid of his life, I have done away with it' — he then turned quickly away and made for his own abode. They all stood gazing wonderingly at him while he was making such way through the rushing waters all foaming about him; then the brothers began to cry and prepared to fetch home their dead — they found him awfully massacred. But the old man again ceased kayaking and hunting from the time he had killed the murderer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 63 'The Old Southlander'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在那年春天，他弄到一大塊浮木，把它切開，從中打造出各種沉重的工具，如魚叉和長矛；他還為自己備了一個新的浮囊。從那時起，他恢復了以往的一切習慣——划獨木舟出海，總盼著能找到機會為兒子報仇。一天清晨，他前往最遠的一處海上獵場；過了一會兒，他回到礁石內側，在靠近岸邊時遇見一個划獨木舟的人，正拖著一頭海豹向陸地駛去——這人正是殺他兒子的凶手。他正好處在陽光中，仔細察看四周是否只有他們兩人，在確認了目標之後——那人被陽光晃得眼花，並未察覺他——便突然向他撲去，舉起武器給了他致命一擊。他把那人拖向陸地；看見一座被潮水衝上岩石的冰山，便把他綁在上面，將他留在那裡，自己繼續向陸地而去，好讓他的兄弟們知道出了什麼事。他們都在家，他的表親也在其中，正坐在帳篷外的空地上，忽然看見他以異乎尋常的速度划來；他猛地停住，向岸上的人高聲喊道：『既然你們的兄弟想丟掉性命，我就替他了結了。』——說完便迅速轉身，朝自己的住所而去。當他這樣破浪而行、四周盡是翻騰的泡沫時，他們都站著驚愕地望著他；隨後兄弟們開始痛哭，準備去把死者接回家——他們發現他被殺得慘不忍睹。但老人自從殺死凶手之後，便又不再划獨木舟、不再打獵了。

passages.text: Whilst he still had his tent pitched alongside of his winter-house his cousin one day came to tell him that the brothers had been calling several relatives together with a view to attacking him in company; when he heard this he employed himself in making a great supply of arrows, but otherwise remained quietly at his place, not leaving home at all. One day he espied the long-expected kayakers crossing the bay to attack him in his loneliness; he went to fetch his bow, and dividing his arrows into three portions brought each portion down to a different little point on the beach. Having thus prepared for them he stood awaiting his enemies with no other arms than his bow: one of the men was just making ready to jump ashore when the old man, perceiving it in time, came running on to the nearest point, pulling out one of his arrows aimed at him, whereat the other retreated; another now tried to land on the second cape, but the old man as quickly reached it and had his bow ready bent for him; at the third point they fared no better, and becoming awed by his great expertness they soon retreated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 63 'The Old Southlander'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他的帳篷仍搭在過冬屋旁時，有一天他的表親前來告訴他，那群兄弟已召集了好幾個親戚，打算聯手來攻擊他；他聽說後，便忙著製作大量箭矢，除此之外仍舊安靜地待在自己的地方，完全不離家。一天，他望見期盼已久的划獨木舟者正橫渡海灣，要來攻擊孤身一人的他；他去取來弓，把箭分成三份，各放一份在海灘上三個不同的小岬角。這樣為他們準備妥當後，他便只憑一張弓，別無其他武器，站著等候敵人：其中一人正要縱身跳上岸時，老人及時察覺，跑到最近的岬角，抽出一支箭瞄準他，那人便退了回去；另一個又想從第二個岬角登陸，但老人同樣迅速地趕到那裡，為他拉弓待發；在第三個岬角，他們也沒占到便宜，被他高超的技藝震懾，不久便退走了。

passages.text: Subsequently he was again informed of an intended attack, and that they were coming in still greater number — but he said, 'They may come whenever they please; this time I am not even going to use any weapons; I only intend to show my face.' His tent, they say, lay just above the water-mark; the tide happened to be full, and there he sat within singing a magic song to have his face enlarged, and as he sang it grew in size, but he went on until it fairly resembled the full moon. He then went out into the front part of the tent, hiding himself among the skin-curtains; at this time one of the men had just got out of his kayak and prepared to enter — but turning round he started at seeing the terrible face which the old man poked out towards him through the entrance. 'A face! a face!' was all he could utter in his terror, and almost capsizing his kayak he put about and quickly rowed away; another was now ready to enter but met the same face — and merely by showing his face he succeeded in keeping them all off, and was attacked no more. When they were all gone he sang a counter-acting lay to get his face to its proper shape again. Next spring he heard that his enemies, in company with some others, were chasing spotted seals; he now made himself a couple of very large bladder-arrows, and one fine day kayaked away to have a look at them. Before long he heard them shouting, and catching sight of them rowed right in amidst them; the foremost of them had just flung his arrow at a seal, but on thus suddenly beholding the old man with his tremendous arrow both he and his companions were startled — whilst they all sat staring at him the wounded seal dived up in front of the old man's kayak. He darted on to pierce it with his two big arrows, and tearing out the first one threw it contemptuously to the owner; with one hand he lifted the seal upon the kayak behind him, and left his enemies in utter amazement. They never afterwards ventured to attack one who, notwithstanding his great age, had such strength and vigour left; the old man at length died in peace without being killed or even wounded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 63 'The Old Southlander'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來他又得到消息，說有人打算來襲，而且這次來的人更多——但他說：『他們愛什麼時候來就什麼時候來；這回我連武器都不打算用；我只打算讓他們看看我的臉。』據說他的帳篷就搭在水線上方；當時恰逢滿潮，他就坐在裡面唱一首咒歌，好讓自己的臉變大，唱著唱著，臉便越變越大，他一直唱到那張臉活像一輪滿月。然後他走到帳篷的前部，把自己藏在皮簾之間；這時其中一人剛從獨木舟上下來，準備進帳——但他一轉身，看見老人從入口朝他探出的那張可怕的臉，便嚇得跳了起來。『一張臉！一張臉！』他驚恐之下只說得出這句話，幾乎把獨木舟弄翻，掉轉船頭便迅速划走了；另一個這會兒也準備進來，卻遇到同一張臉——他就這樣單憑露臉，便成功地把他們全都擋了回去，此後再無人來攻擊他。等他們全都走了，他又唱了一首反咒的歌，讓自己的臉恢復原狀。次年春天，他聽說他的敵人會同另外一些人正在追捕斑海豹；這回他為自己做了兩支非常大的浮囊箭，在一個晴朗的日子划獨木舟去看他們。不一會兒，他聽見他們的喊聲，望見他們後便逕直划進他們中間；最前頭的那人剛把箭投向一頭海豹，但突然看見老人帶著他那兩支巨大的箭，他和同伴們都大吃一驚——正當他們都坐著瞪眼看他時，那頭受傷的海豹在老人獨木舟前方浮了上來。他衝上前去，用兩支大箭刺中牠，拔出第一支，輕蔑地扔還給它的主人；他一手把海豹提上身後自己的獨木舟，留下敵人萬分驚愕。此後他們再也不敢攻擊一個雖已年邁，卻仍有如此力氣與精力的人；老人最終安然去世，既未被殺，甚至未曾受傷。

title.en: Naujarsuak and Kukajak: The Fox-Holes in the Store-Stones
title.zh: 納烏亞舒克與庫卡雅克：石蓋上的狐洞

region.en: Store-places on the coast and Amerdlok (Holsteinsborg)
region.zh: 海岸貯藏地與霍爾斯泰因斯堡

period: Inuit oral tradition; a tale from South Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 64 'Naujarsuak and Kukajak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Foxes find holes freshly cut in Kukajak's stone store-covers, and the jealous friend made them. Despite the murder, he goes visiting — 'Thou hast been wrong in coming so late to look after thy stores' — then harpoons Naujarsuak from behind before his little son on the beach. The grandfather takes the boy to Amerdlok, where he never smiles, and years later, whalebone-rich, he greets the aged murderer, loads him with gifts — then fixes the bone-point with a loud jerk (a charm), and outside his own house sends the lance crashing into Kukajak's body: 'I saw him treat my father in the same way; and I have only paid him back.'
summary.zh: 庫卡雅克的石蓋貯藏所被狐狸搬空——石蓋上留著新鑿的狐洞，那是嫉妒的朋友所為。他按捺不住思友之情仍登門拜訪，卻在兒子親眼目睹下自背後一叉刺死納烏亞舒克。祖父攜孤兒遷居霍爾斯泰因斯堡——孩子從此不再展顏；多年後他滿載鯨骨南歸，熱情款待年邁的仇人，臨別時『咔』地一聲釘上骨鏢尖（咒術），在自家屋前把長矛轟入庫卡雅克體內——『我親眼看見他這樣對我父親；如今不過是以牙還牙。』

sensitivity.note: Murder and revenge-killing recorded as told in the 1875 source. Never-smiling mourning observance documented.

passages.text: Naujarsuak and Kukajak were friends, and both skilled hunters; they lived apart, but being very fond of each other they were often together. In spring, when the first seals had made their appearance, they used to bring full-loaded boats with dried meat to their storehouses. Once Kukajak happened to have put by a greater store than his friend, and this made Naujarsuak jealous. Kukajak used to go away deer-hunting in the spring, and did the same that summer; on his way home in the autumn he was as usual to pass by his store-places on the coast and take out some dried seal-meat for a welcome feast at home, longing greatly for some dried seal-flesh himself — but on arriving at his stores he found that the foxes had been there beforehand, and had left nothing for him. On a close examination he found out that some one had been making little holes in the stone coverings, just large enough for a fox to pass through; he got extremely vexed, and at home learned that Naujarsuak had made the holes during his absence — at this intelligence he became still more angry, but nevertheless could not help longing for his friend, and started on a visit to him the day after.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 64 'Naujarsuak and Kukajak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 納烏亞爾蘇阿克與庫卡亞克是朋友，兩人都是技藝精湛的獵人；他們分居兩處，但因彼此情誼深厚，常相聚在一起。春天，當第一批海豹出現時，他們慣常載著滿船的乾肉，運往自己的儲藏庫。有一次，庫卡亞克恰巧囤積了比朋友更多的存糧，這使納烏亞爾蘇阿克心生嫉妒。庫卡亞克春天常外出獵鹿，那年夏天也是如此；秋天返家途中，他照例要經過海岸邊的儲藏處，取出一些乾海豹肉，以備到家後設宴款待，他自己也極渴望吃些乾海豹肉——然而抵達儲藏處時，他發現狐狸早已捷足先登，一點也沒給他留下。仔細察看後，他發現有人在石頭覆蓋處挖了些小洞，大小恰好夠一隻狐狸鑽過；他極為惱怒，回家後得知那些洞是納烏亞爾蘇阿克趁他不在時挖的——聞此消息，他更加憤怒，卻仍不禁思念朋友，次日便動身前去拜訪他。

passages.text: Naujarsuak, in his turn, was longing as much to see Kukajak; as soon as the other had arrived he hastened to draw his kayak on land and take him to his house. During the meal Kukajak carelessly observed, 'I also had a small portion of dried meat put by, but the foxes have carried it all off, which has never happened to me before' — Naujarsuak remarked, 'Thou hast been wrong in coming so late to look after thy stores.' At this speech Kukajak got inwardly enraged; having passed the night beneath his friend's roof, he as usual invited him to accompany him home to have some dried reindeer-flesh. While they were thus talking they saw from land some kayakers stopping outside, lying in wait for seals, when all of a sudden Kukajak came upon his friend from behind and sent his harpoon right through him. The little son of Naujarsuak was standing on the beach and saw his father being killed, while Kukajak called out, 'I paid him back, because he spoiled my stores,' and then turned his back upon them and rowed home. The old father of Naujarsuak now took away the corpse of his son and had it buried; and when the usual days of mourning had gone by he accosted the little one thus: 'Now thou hast seen thy father killed, it will not do for thee to grow up in idleness.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 64 'Naujarsuak and Kukajak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 納烏亞爾蘇阿克也同樣渴望見到庫卡亞克；對方一到，他便趕緊把獨木舟拖上岸，領他進屋。用餐時，庫卡亞克漫不經心地說：「我也存了一小份乾肉，但狐狸全給叼走了，這種事我以前從未遇過」——納烏亞爾蘇阿克說道：「你這麼晚才來查看存糧，是你自己不對。」聽聞此言，庫卡亞克心中暗自惱怒；他在朋友屋簷下過了一夜，照例邀他一同回家吃些乾馴鹿肉。兩人正說著話，忽見岸邊有些划獨木舟的人停在外頭，伏候海豹；就在此時，庫卡亞克冷不防從背後撲向朋友，將魚叉直刺穿他的身體。納烏亞爾蘇阿克的小兒子正站在海灘上，親眼看見父親被殺，而庫卡亞克喊道：「我報復了他，因為他糟蹋了我的存糧」，隨即背對他們，划船回家。納烏亞爾蘇阿克的老父親於是收殮兒子的屍體，將他安葬；待慣常的哀悼期過去後，他對那小孩說道：「如今你已親眼看見父親被殺，你再這樣閒散度日可不行了。」

passages.text: He then resolved to leave his place, where he was continually reminded of his lost son; they travelled on to Amerdlok (the present Holsteinsborg), where they established themselves for the winter. Here the boy grew up under the constant care and unceasing admonitions of his grandfather, and he was never seen to smile. While they were still at Amerdlok he grew to manhood, assisted at the whale-fishing, and turned out an able and expert kayaker; under these circumstances the old man advised him to go southwards and revenge himself on Kukajak, if he were still alive, and during this last winter he carefully secured the whalebones whenever a whale was caught, knowing them to be a rare article much in request in the south. When the first thaw set in they started, and at every place they passed by they inquired, 'Have ye heard nothing of Kukajak?' — invariably the answer was, 'No; we don't know him.' Far away south, however, they met some people who told them: 'Kukajak! ah, yes; he is all right! but getting rather old now, and has taken to frog-fishing.' At length they reached their former home and settled there for good; all their relatives immediately came to see them after their long absence, and on leaving presented them with some of the longest and best whalebones — they had many unexpected visitors, some of whom only came in the hope of getting their share of whalebones, which were well known to be desired for gifts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 64 'Naujarsuak and Kukajak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他於是決心離開這個不斷令他想起亡子的地方；他們遷往阿梅爾德洛克（即今日的霍爾斯泰恩斯堡），在那裡安頓下來過冬。男孩在祖父無微不至的照料與不斷的告誡下長大，從未有人見他笑過。他們仍住在阿梅爾德洛克時，他已長大成人，協助捕鯨，並成為一名能幹嫻熟的獨木舟手；在這種情況下，老人勸他南下，若庫卡亞克尚在人世，便向他報仇，而在這最後一個冬天，每當捕到鯨魚，他便細心收好鯨鬚，因為他知道鯨鬚是南方極為搶手、需求甚殷的稀有之物。初融之際，他們便啟程，每到一處便打聽：「你們可曾聽過庫卡亞克的消息？」——得到的回答總是：「沒有；我們不認識他。」然而在遙遠的南方，他們遇到一些人告訴他們：「庫卡亞克！啊，是的；他過得不錯！只是如今上了年紀，捕起蛙來了。」他們終於抵達舊日的家園，從此定居下來；久別之後，所有親戚立刻前來探望，臨別時贈予他們一些最長、最好的鯨鬚——他們有許多不速之客，其中有些人只是希望能分得一份鯨鬚，因為眾所周知，鯨鬚是人人想得到的贈禮。

passages.text: As time wore on they had to change their tent for a winter hut; but as yet Naujarsuak's son had had no opportunity of avenging the murder of his father. He one day requested his grandfather to make him a very big harpoon with a strong line to match; the grandfather got it ready for him the very next day, and regarding it with great satisfaction the son smiled, and thanked him, and concealed it carefully beneath the ledge. Some time after, Kukajak took a great fancy to go and ask the son of his betrayed friend for a piece of whalebone for his fishing-line, but on further consideration gave up the idea, fearing that he might bring down vengeance upon himself if he carried it out; however, the people thereabout were always telling him of the gifts they had received — 'If thou goest, thou wilt be sure to get some too: it was only the other day the old man said that he longed much to see thee.' On hearing this he could resist no longer, and started the very next day. He got a friendly welcome, and was beginning to think they had forgotten all about the murder; a plentiful repast was soon served up before him, and the talk went merrily round all the evening — but somehow, whenever there was a short silence, he always thought, 'there, now, it all returns to them.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 64 'Naujarsuak and Kukajak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 時日推移，他們不得不把帳篷換成過冬的屋舍；然而納烏亞爾蘇阿克的兒子至今仍無機會為父親的被害報仇。有一天，他請祖父為他打造一支極大的魚叉，並配上相稱的粗繩；祖父次日便為他備妥，他滿意地端詳著，露出了笑容，向祖父道謝，然後小心地把它藏在壁架底下。過了些時日，庫卡亞克忽然很想去找他那被背叛的朋友之子，討一塊鯨鬚做釣線，但再一想便打消了念頭，生怕付諸實行會給自己招來殺身之禍；然而那一帶的人總是向他提起他們收到的贈禮——「你若去，一定也能分到一些：就在前幾天，那老人還說他極想見你呢。」聽聞此言，他再也按捺不住，次日便動身前往。他受到友善的款待，正開始覺得他們已把殺人之事忘得一乾二淨；不久，豐盛的飯菜端到他面前，整個晚上談話都歡快融洽——但不知怎的，每當短暫的沉默出現，他總覺得：「這下，他們又想起那件事了。」

passages.text: At daybreak the following morning, when Naujarsuak's son went outside the house, the thought struck him it was just on such a day that his father was killed; the air was soft, and light clouds appeared and passed by overhead — at this his former wrath awoke with full force, but on entering the house he looked quite guileless. At Kukajak's departure he also was presented with whalebones; still he apprehended some evil, and kept glancing back to be sure that he was not pursued, and thus succeeded in getting a considerable way off. Now, however, was the time for Naujarsuak's son to make use of his new weapon: he took the bone-point which his grandfather had made, brought it down, and fixed it with a loud jerk — Kukajak heard the sound and recognised the meaning (viz., charm) of it, and seeing his enemy in full pursuit hastened on as quickly as he could, but found his strength fast failing. Perceiving this, his enemy pursued him more slowly, and Kukajak began thinking that he might reach home unharmed; at that moment, however, his adversary again darted on, and just outside his own house took aim and sent his lance with a great crash into Kukajak's body. The son of Naujarsuak now turned to the bystanders, saying, 'I saw him treat my father in the same way; and I have only paid him back; if ye care for his corpse, ye may take it.' Having finished this speech he left for home; and from that day his father was not always in his thought, though he never quite forgot him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 64 'Naujarsuak and Kukajak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 次日破曉，納烏亞爾蘇阿克的兒子走出屋外時，忽然想到，父親正是在這樣的一天被殺的；空氣柔和，淡淡的雲朵出現又從頭頂飄過——此時，他昔日的怒火猛然復燃，但一進屋，他卻顯得若無其事。庫卡亞克臨走時，也獲贈了鯨鬚；他仍心存疑懼，頻頻回頭張望，確認無人追來，就這樣走出了相當遠的一段路。然而，此時正是納烏亞爾蘇阿克的兒子使用新武器之時：他取出祖父打造的骨製矛尖，猛地一擊將其固定，發出響亮的喀嗒聲——庫卡亞克聽見聲響，領會了其中的含意（即咒力），見敵人全力追來，便拼命奔逃，卻發覺自己的力氣迅速衰竭。敵人察覺後，便放慢追擊，庫卡亞克開始以為自己或許能安然到家；就在那一刻，對手又猛然衝上前，就在他家門外瞄準，將長矛帶著巨響刺入庫卡亞克的身體。納烏亞爾蘇阿克的兒子轉向旁觀的人說道：「我親眼見他這樣對待我父親；我不過是以其人之道還治其人之身；你們若顧惜他的屍體，儘管拿去。」說完這番話，他便動身回家；從那天起，父親雖不再時刻縈繞於他心頭，他卻從未真正忘懷。

title.en: The Two Friends Rescued by the Benevolent Ingnersuit
title.zh: 善因格內爾舒特人救友記

region.en: High island of the ingnersuit, under-world
region.zh: 地下之民的高島

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 65 'The Two Friends rescued by the Benevolent Ingnersuit', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Three times his friend tries to harpoon him from behind; the third time the victim answers in kind, runs his kayak-point across the capsized boat, and drowns him — then leaks and sinks himself, saved by three ingnersuit kayakers who stopper the leak with blubber and string his seals for warmth. In the under-world house, the wrinkled-skin old man sends for more brothers — among them the murdered friend, restored like himself — and the wrestling-match puts the living strangers to shame: give up quarrelling and be friends again. On the sixth day he meets his friend alive at the old hunting-place, both angakut with tornaks among the ingnersuit, and they are reconciled.
summary.zh: 摯友三度自背後舉叉相向；第三次他反手回擊，以艇首壓住翻覆的皮艇將其溺斃——自己卻也漏水下沉，幸得三位地下之民的皮艇客相救：以油脂塞漏、解下成串海豹讓他拖曳取暖。在地下之屋中，皺皮覆眼的老者又召來眾兄弟——其中竟有被他殺死的朋友，與他同樣復生；摔跤較技令活人羞愧——『從此息爭，重修舊好。』第六日離去時，他在舊獵場重逢復活的朋友——二人皆為巫師、靈助同在地下之民中——就此和解。

sensitivity.note: Under-world restoration of the drowned documented as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: One widow lived all alone with her son at a winter station; and a little more to the south another widow, also with an only son, had her residence. The young men were fast friends, and used to go out kayaking and perform their several tasks in company. But one morning the one who was to the north, seeing the clear bright sky and a light breeze from the east, resolved on going to the hunting-place by himself without waiting his friend's arrival; after he had been on the hunting-ground for some time he suddenly heard a noise from the sunny side of the bay, and turning round saw his friend with gloomy looks and hand uplifted about to throw his harpoon at him. Having no other choice he kept his look steadily fixed on him; the moment the harpoon came flying towards him he upset himself, kayak and all, so that the weapon touched the edge of the kayak and fell splashing into the water beside him, after which he again rose by means of his paddle. The other now proceeded to coil up his harpoon-line; without further reference to the matter the friends as usual remained together, catching their seals, and speaking pleasantly to each other on the way home — still he kept an eye upon his companion, but did not find anything to rouse his suspicion. Another time he again left home without waiting the arrival of his friend, and the same thing happened; after a third similar attempt, however, he resolved to revenge himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 65 'The Two Friends rescued by the Benevolent Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個寡婦帶著兒子，孤零零地住在一個過冬的營地；稍往南一些，另一個寡婦也帶著獨子居住。兩個年輕人是要好的朋友，常一同划獨木舟出海，結伴完成各自的活計。然而有一天早晨，住在北邊的那一個見天空晴朗明亮，東風微拂，便決定不等朋友到來，獨自前往獵場；他在獵場待了一陣，忽然聽見海灣向陽的一側傳來聲響，回頭一看，只見朋友面色陰沉，舉起手來正要向他擲出魚叉。他別無選擇，只能目不轉睛地盯著對方；魚叉飛來的那一刻，他連人帶舟一併翻覆，那武器只擦過獨木舟的邊緣，濺著水花落在他身旁，隨後他又靠槳重新浮起。對方接著便開始收捲魚叉的繩索；此事不再提起，兩人照舊廝守在一起捕海豹，歸途中彼此和氣交談——但他仍留意著同伴，卻未發現任何可疑之處。又一次，他又不等朋友到來便離家外出，同樣的事再度發生；然而在第三次類似的情形之後，他決心報復。

passages.text: He did so in the following way: as soon as he rose above water after having capsized his kayak as before, he aimed his harpoon at his friend, who, however, averted the danger by likewise upsetting himself — but before he was able to get his kayak righted the other was by his side and kept him from rising by running the point of his own kayak right across the one that lay bottom upwards. After having killed his friend in this manner he rowed towards land; but before he reached the first islets he noticed the water coming fast into his kayak. He pulled as quickly as possible, but all in vain, and was only kept above water by means of the bladder; he then happily remembered that he was himself an angakok, and that he had several tornaks (guardian spirits) among the ingnersuit (under-world people). No sooner had he called them than he saw three kayakers coming straight towards him: two of the strangers put their paddles, one from each side, into the sinking kayak to hold it up, and at the same time the third mended the kayak as well as possible by filling the leak with blubber, and hastened to give the drowning man his dry breeches to put on. He was now again placed in his kayak, to which they made fast their seals, all strung together in a long row, and told him to tug them along that he might get warm; he rowed in front and they closely followed him with the greatest speed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 65 'The Two Friends rescued by the Benevolent Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他是這樣做的：當他像先前那樣翻覆皮划艇後一浮出水面，便立刻把魚叉對準他的朋友；然而那朋友也照樣翻覆自己的艇，藉此避開了危險——但在他還來得及把皮划艇扶正之前，另一人已來到他身旁，將自己皮划艇的艇首橫壓在那艘底朝上的艇上，使他無法浮起。他以這種方式殺死朋友之後，便向陸地划去；但還沒抵達最初的幾座小島，他就發覺海水迅速灌進自己的皮划艇。他盡可能快地划，卻全然徒勞，只靠那浮囊才勉強浮在水面；這時他慶幸地想起自己就是個安加科克（angakok，巫師），而且在因格爾蘇特（ingnersuit，地下世界的人）之中有幾個托爾納克（tornaks，守護靈）。他剛一呼喚他們，就看見三個划皮划艇的人筆直朝他而來：其中兩個陌生人各從一邊把槳伸進那艘下沉的皮划艇，將它托住；同時第三個人盡可能地修補皮划艇，用鯨脂堵住裂縫，並趕緊把自己乾燥的褲子遞給那溺水的人穿上。他如今又被安置在自己的皮划艇裡，他們把各自的獵海豹繫在他的艇上，全部串成長長的一列，叫他拖著牠們走，好讓他暖和起來；他在前頭划，他們以最快的速度緊緊跟隨其後。

passages.text: They came to a high island with only one house; there they landed and at once entered. When they had seated themselves he saw the master of the house, a man so very old that his wrinkled skin was hanging and almost hiding his eyes; the old man pushed it aside a little and looked at the new-comers. Presently some one called out that two kayakers were approaching tugging seals along with them; those whose business it was to bring them up to the house soon returned with hauling-thongs ornamented with fittings of bright walrus-bone, and then followed the seal-hunters themselves. On entering the house they accosted their brothers and reproached them, saying, 'Why were ye not quicker in giving him your assistance before he got to be so cold?' — 'He did not call for our aid till then.' They now ordered the women to bring some dry meat; after the meal the old man moved aside the wrinkled skin from off his eyes, gave a look out of the window, and said, 'Go and call our other relatives' — the youngest immediately went away, and after some time came back covered with sweat. The stranger on seeing him reflected, 'Where can he have been, since no house seems to be near?' and soon after five other brothers, much like his hosts and also accompanied by an old man, entered the house; there was also another man, who turned out to be his former friend and companion whom he had killed in his kayak — he sat down right opposite and hardly dared to look up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 65 'The Two Friends rescued by the Benevolent Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們來到一座只有一間屋子的高島；他們在那裡登陸，隨即走了進去。當他們坐下之後，他看見屋主是個極其年邁的人，那皺巴巴的皮膚垂掛著，幾乎遮住了他的眼睛；老人把皮膚稍稍推開一點，看了看這些新來的人。不久有人喊道，有兩個划皮划艇的人正拖著獵海豹靠近；那些負責把獵物搬進屋裡的人很快便帶著飾有明亮海象牙配件的拖繩回來，隨後那些獵海豹的人也跟著進來了。他們一進屋便招呼自己的兄弟，並責備他們說：「他還沒冷成這樣之前，你們為什麼不趕快幫他一把？」——「他到那時才呼喚我們相助。」他們現在吩咐女人們拿些乾肉來；吃過飯後，老人把皺皮從眼睛上移開，朝窗外望了一眼，說道：「去把我們其他的親戚叫來」——最年輕的那個立刻離去，過了些時候滿身大汗地回來。那陌生人見了心想：「既然附近似乎沒有屋子，他究竟能到哪裡去呢？」不久之後，另外五個兄弟走進屋裡，他們與主人們十分相像，也由一位老人陪同；此外還有一個人，原來就是他從前那位朋友兼同伴，那個他在皮划艇裡殺死的人——他正坐在對面，幾乎不敢抬頭。

passages.text: When they had had their meal the eldest brother brought out a skin, spread it on the floor, and first tried a wrestling-match with his own brothers and afterwards with the visitors — no one was able to hold his own against him. The master of the house now challenged the other old man, who, however, had to give in to him. Having thus been vanquished and put to shame the strangers prepared to leave their hosts; these reproved them sharply for their former behaviour and told them henceforth to give up quarrelling and be friends again. When the rest had all withdrawn the stranger who had been saved remained five days longer, but on the sixth he left; on passing his usual hunting-place he encountered his friend, who had been restored to life in the same manner as himself, and they spoke to each other. It so happened that they were both angakut, and that each of them had his tornaks among the ingnersuit — from this time they were quite reconciled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 65 'The Two Friends rescued by the Benevolent Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們吃過飯後，最年長的兄弟拿出一張獸皮，鋪在地上，先與自己的兄弟們試了一場角力，隨後又與來客們比試——沒有人能敵得過他。屋主這時向另一位老人挑戰，那老人卻不得不向他認輸。來客們既已如此被擊敗、蒙受羞辱，便準備告別主人；主人嚴厲責備他們先前的行徑，並吩咐他們從今以後不要再爭吵，重新做朋友。其餘的人都退下之後，那位獲救的陌生人又多留了五天，到第六天才離去；他經過平日狩獵的地方時，遇見了他的朋友，那朋友也像他一樣被救活了，兩人便交談起來。原來他們兩人都是安加科克，各自在因格爾蘇特之中有自己的托爾納克——從此以後，他們便完全和解了。

title.en: The Strong Man on the Island of K'erka
title.zh: 克爾卡島上的力士

region.en: K'erka islet north of Pamiut (Frederikshaab)
region.zh: 帕米烏特（腓特烈斯哈布）以北的克爾卡島

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 66 'The Strong Man on the Island of K'erka', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The lone kayaker of K'erka, whose paddle had to be cut narrower where it was to be grasped, is blown by a north gale to the homestead of his adversary — who is inside practising the nith-song with which to abuse him in spring; he memorizes every taunt, and when the singing-match comes he knows them all beforehand and gains an easy victory. His southern enemies attack in numbers: gliding kayak and all into a great cave in an iceberg, lance lifted, he spears each man as he comes in front of the cave — all fared alike except two, left alive to inform their countrymen of what had happened.
summary.zh: 克爾卡島的獨居力士——槳粗得須在握把處削細——被北風吹到仇家的村莊；屋內那人正在練習開春辱罵他的諷歌。他逐句默記，春季對歌時早有備而來，輕取對手。南方仇家大舉來犯：他連人帶艇滑入冰山的巨洞，長矛高舉——來者一一被他刺翻，只留兩人活口回去報信。南方人本欲殺他，反倒自己送了命。

sensitivity.note: Nith-song (satirical song) duel documented as told. Killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Little north of Pamiut (Frederikshaab) there is an island called K'erka.
