In olden times there lived on this islet a man who had no equal in kayaking; his paddle was so thick that he had to cut it narrower where it was to be grasped. He was alone in this place. Once in the winter time, when he was far out on the open sea, he was suddenly caught in a furious gale from the north; he tried hard to make the land, but the coast had altogether vanished in the tempest. At length, however, he knew by the great breakers that he must be right off Tulugartalik (close to the large glacier); having passed those isles, land soon appeared ahead, and he observed a light from a window on shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 66 'The Strong Man on the Island of K'erka'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在帕米烏特（Pamiut，即腓特烈斯霍布）以北不遠處，有一座名叫克爾卡（K'erka）的島。古時候，這座小島上住著一個划皮划艇無人能及的人；他的槳粗得他必須在握槳之處把它削窄。他獨自住在這個地方。有一回冬天，當他遠在遼闊的外海時，突然遭遇一陣猛烈的北風；他奮力想靠岸，但海岸在暴風中已全然消失無蹤。然而最後，他從巨大的碎浪判斷出自己必定正位於圖盧加爾塔利克（Tulugartalik，靠近大冰川）外；駛過那些島嶼之後，前方不久便出現了陸地，他看見岸上一扇窗戶透出燈光。

passages.text: Landing his kayak he went up towards the house, and stopped short on hearing some one singing within; after listening for a while he found that he had unawares landed on Ukevik, the homestead of his adversary, who happened to be practising a nith-song (satirical song) with which to abuse him when they met in the spring. He took great care to impress the exact words on his memory, and then went silently down to his kayak, leaving the place in the dark; and having again crossed the heavy surf about Tulugartalik, reached his own home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 66 'The Strong Man on the Island of K'erka'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他把皮划艇靠岸後，便朝那屋子走去，卻在聽見屋內有人唱歌時猛然停住；聽了一會兒之後，他發覺自己竟不知不覺地登上了烏克維克（Ukevik），那正是他對頭的住處，而那人恰好在練習一首尼特歌（nith-song，諷刺歌），準備在春天相遇時用來辱罵他。他極其小心地把確切的歌詞牢記在心，然後悄悄回到自己的皮划艇，在黑暗中離開了那個地方；他再次穿過圖盧加爾塔利克附近洶湧的碎浪，回到了自己的家。

passages.text: The following spring his adversary came from Ukevik to have a singing match with him; but as he had well remembered, and knew all the taunts and spiteful things beforehand, he soon gained an easy victory over him. The lonely resident of K'erka also had some enemies among the southern people; during the summer, when he was one day out at sea kayaking in fine calm weather, he noticed some kayakers coming from the south, and from their numbers guessed they were his enemies coming to attack him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 66 'The Strong Man on the Island of K'erka'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 次年春天，他的對頭從烏克維克前來與他比賽唱歌；但由於他記得很牢，事先便已知道所有那些嘲諷和惡毒的話，所以很快就輕易地勝過了他。這位獨居克爾卡的人在南邊的人當中也有一些仇敵；那年夏天，有一天他在風平浪靜的好天氣裡出海划皮划艇，他注意到有些划皮划艇的人從南邊而來，從他們的人數判斷，他猜想是他的仇敵前來攻擊他。

passages.text: On this surmise he fled towards the shore, with the rest in full pursuit after him; reaching a large iceberg, he happened to observe a great cave on the opposite side of it, and quickly glided in, kayak and all — the prow turned outwards, and holding his lance ready lifted he lay in wait for his enemies. When the first man came up in front of the cave he speared him, at once drawing his lance back; the second met the same fate, and all the others fared alike, excepting two, whom he left alive that they might inform their countrymen of what had happened. All those Southlanders had intended to kill their foe, but happened to be killed themselves instead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 66 'The Strong Man on the Island of K'erka'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他憑著這個猜想，便往岸邊逃去，其餘的人緊追在後；他來到一座大冰山前，恰好望見冰山對面有個大洞穴，便迅速滑了進去，連人帶皮艇一併鑽入——艇首朝外，他舉起長矛持於手中，埋伏著等候敵人。第一個人來到洞口前，他一矛刺去，隨即把長矛抽回；第二個人也落得同樣下場，其餘眾人皆如此，只有兩人他留了活口，好讓他們回去告訴同鄉發生了何事。那些南地人本來都想殺死他們的仇敵，結果反倒自己送了命。

title.en: Niakunguak: The Modest Hunter and the Crushed Liver
title.zh: 尼亞孔瓜克：謙遜的獵手與捏碎的肝

region.en: Little bay of the south coast and the Southlanders' winter quarters
region.zh: 南岸小灣與南方人的越冬地

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 67 'Niakunguak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Weary of his boisterous brothers, Niakunguak coasts south until hailed into a bay of tents, marries the youngest daughter, and is loved for his modesty. A conceited Southlander abandons him in a gale — 'thy silly father will never return; there is no kayaking in such weather' — and comes home behind two black spots of speared seal on the foam: 'In such a sea and such weather one might go out even in a very poor kayak.' Forced at last into a ball-play grapple, he hurls the braggart so hard his bowels burst; and when the dead man's sons later raise the dried-liver challenge, Niakunguak's son crushes it to dust between his fingers, and the enemies depart peaceably in spring.
summary.zh: 厭倦了喧鬧兄弟的尼亞孔瓜克南下，被迎入帳篷環列的小灣，娶了幼女，以謙遜得眾人喜愛。一個自負的南方人在風暴中棄他而去——『你那傻父親再也回不來了，這種天氣划不了艇』——而他卻踏浪而歸：『這樣的海與風，就是破艇也能出海。』球賽中被逼應戰，他把那誇口者摔得腸破血流；數年後死者的兩個兒子以硬如石的乾肝叫陣——尼亞孔瓜克之子兩指一捏，肝碎如塵。春天一到，仇家和平離去。

sensitivity.note: Bursting-bowels killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: A number of brothers always used to have their fixed winter quarters at a certain place, while several of the older ones were married; Niakunguak, one of the younger brothers, had as yet no wife. His disposition differed greatly from the others, who were all wild and boisterous; he would never join in any of their noisy pastimes and wanton tricks, although they tried to persuade him to do so. At last he got so weary of their company that he would stay with them no longer: one morning he did not join them in their day's excursion, but as soon as they were well off betook himself to his kayak, put out from land, and coasted away south. He travelled on for many days without seeing a human being, and had fairly given up the hope of falling in with any, when suddenly he was hailed from shore, and at the same time discovered a little bay with many tents pitched round it, people shouting to him to land. When he reached the beach he was received by a crowd of men, who welcomed him very civilly, although he did not know any one of them; an old man now invited him to come to his tent, where there were only his two daughters inside, but before long it was crowded with visitors, all very friendly and pleasant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 67 'Niakunguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一群兄弟總是在某個固定的地方過冬，其中幾個年長的都已娶妻；尼亞孔瓜克是較年幼的兄弟之一，尚未娶妻。他的性情與其他人大不相同，那些人個個粗野喧鬧；他從不參與他們任何吵鬧的消遣和放肆的惡作劇，儘管他們曾試圖勸他加入。最後他對他們的陪伴厭倦至極，再也不願與他們同住：一天早晨，他沒有隨他們一同外出，等他們走遠之後，他便上了自己的皮艇，離岸向南沿岸划去。他航行了許多天，未見一個人影，幾乎已放棄了遇見人的希望，忽然岸上有人向他呼喚，同時他望見一個小海灣，灣邊搭著許多帳篷，人們高聲喊他靠岸。他抵達灘頭時，一群人前來迎接，十分有禮地歡迎他，儘管他一個也不認識；一位老人邀請他到自己的帳篷去，裡面只有他的兩個女兒，但不久帳篷裡便擠滿了來訪的人，個個都很友善和氣。

passages.text: The visitors having left, the old man said, 'In case thou wouldst like one of my daughters, thou mayst choose for thyself' — he took the youngest for his wife, and henceforth became the support and provider of the old man. The people there got very fond of him and liked him for his great modesty, and he too felt very happy amongst them; when they assembled for social intercourse boasting was not heard nor boisterous manners displayed. When the days lengthened and seals got scarce Niakunguak chose his hunting-place at a good distance out; his wife in the meantime had borne him a son, and during his childhood a boat's crew of Southlanders arrived and took up their winter abode among them. It soon appeared that one of the strangers was presumptuous and full of conceit, though Niakunguak in his modesty felt loath to contradict him. One morning after the winter solstice, when the cold was very severe, Niakunguak was the only man of the place who thought of starting; the bragging stranger on seeing this offered to go with him, and both put out to sea in quest of seals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 67 'Niakunguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 訪客離去後，老人說道：「倘若你想要我的一個女兒，你可以自行挑選」——他娶了最年幼的那個為妻，從此便成了老人的依靠和供養者。那裡的人非常喜歡他，因他十分謙遜而喜愛他，他在他們中間也感到非常快樂；當他們聚會交往時，聽不到自誇，也見不到粗野的舉止。當白晝漸長、海豹漸少時，尼亞孔瓜克選了一處相當遠的地方作為獵場；其間他的妻子為他生了一個兒子，在兒子幼年時，一群南地人乘船而來，在他們中間過冬。不久便看出其中一個外來者傲慢自負，而尼亞孔瓜克出於謙遜，不願與他爭辯。冬至後的一個早晨，天氣嚴寒，尼亞孔瓜克是當地唯一想到要出發的人；那個誇口的外來者見狀，便提出與他同去，兩人便一同出海獵海豹。

passages.text: Meantime the wind increased; but Niakunguak, nothing daunted, lanced his seal, hoping his companion would come and help him to kill the animal — however, he showed no such intention, but had already turned homewards, frightened at the fury of the gale. Niakunguak made his seal fast to the tug-line, but did not return till he had got another. Meantime his companion had gained the shore, where Niakunguak's little son was standing on the beach gazing out upon the heaving sea, on the look-out for his father; the boy at once inquired about his father, having seen them go out together — the other answered, 'Thou mayst as well go home; thy silly father will never return; there is no kayaking in such weather.' The boy entered the house and kept tranquil and silent — he was already of an age to understand the ways of mourning — but the other men still kept outside the house on the look-out for Niakunguak's kayak. The opening of the bay was a very narrow one, and consequently a mass of foaming surf; towards evening they espied two little black spots upon the white foam — his seals with the spears still sticking in them, tossed along by the breakers setting in upon the shore. A third black spot on the surf appeared to be himself, carried quickly on across the heavy seas; having got on shore and reached his house his son told him what the other man had said — that no kayak could live in such a sea — and the father replied, 'In such a sea and such weather one might go out even in a very poor kayak.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 67 'Niakunguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其間風勢漸強；但尼亞孔瓜克毫不畏懼，用矛刺中了他的海豹，指望同伴過來幫他殺死獵物——然而對方並無此意，早已被狂風的怒號嚇得掉頭回家了。尼亞孔瓜克把海豹繫在拖繩上，但直到又獵得一隻才返回。其間他的同伴已回到岸上，尼亞孔瓜克的幼子正站在灘頭，凝望著起伏的大海，等候父親歸來；那男孩一見他們曾一同出海，便立刻問起父親——那人答道：「你還是回家去吧；你那傻父親再也不會回來了；這種天氣根本划不了皮艇。」男孩進了屋，保持平靜，默不作聲——他已到了懂得哀悼之道的年紀——但其他人仍留在屋外，張望尼亞孔瓜克的皮艇。海灣的出口非常狹窄，因此激起一片翻騰的浪花；傍晚時分，他們在白沫上望見兩個小黑點——那是他的海豹，矛還插在上面，被湧向岸邊的碎浪顛簸著。浪花上又出現第三個黑點，似乎就是他本人，正被巨浪迅速推送過來；他上岸回到家中，兒子告訴他那人所說的話——說這種海面根本沒有皮艇能存活——父親答道：「這樣的海面、這樣的天氣，就是划一隻很差的皮艇也能出海。」

passages.text: When the briskets were boiled the men were invited to partake of the meal; when the dish was ready served and the guests all assembled Niakunguak during a pause remarked, 'When I had harpooned my second seal, I looked about in vain for a kayaker to assist me in securing it' — later on the guests grew talkative and all passed the evening pleasantly, excepting his companion of the morning, who never spoke a word. When the days grew still longer and there were no seals to be had the men entertained themselves with ball-playing; once there was a general calling for Niakunguak to come and join the ball-players — though not disposed to do so he at once obeyed their summons, but only went to look on at some distance. While occupied in watching the ball-players, and standing modestly with one arm drawn out of the sleeve of his jacket, the other kayaker owing him a grudge now approached and threw him down; while Niakunguak was rising and shaking the snow from his garments the men gathered round him, saying, 'Is Niakunguak going to stand this?' On hearing this his antagonist seized hold of Niakunguak, who, seeking no strife, only tried to keep his footing — but finding that the other would not let go his grasp he was forced to defend himself, and a struggle ensued ending in favour of Niakunguak, who soon got the better of his adversary and hurled him to the ground with such force that his bowels burst and the blood gushed from his mouth. His brothers instantly left off playing and brought him into the house, where he soon expired. Niakunguak had now, much against his will, made himself enemies, and he told his young son that he ought to mind this, and train himself to endure hardships that he might attain strength and vigour: he should no longer practise lifting and flinging stones, but should try to pull up shrubs and bushes by the root. Afterwards he taught him everything belonging to kayaking; before long he came to be his father's equal every way, and even in the roughest weather chased the seal far out seawards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 67 'Niakunguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 胸肉煮好後，眾人被邀來用餐；菜餚備好、賓客齊聚時，尼亞孔瓜克趁著靜默的間隙說道：「我刺中第二隻海豹時，四處張望，卻找不到一個划皮艇的人來幫我把它弄到手」——後來賓客們談笑風生，整個晚上都過得很愉快，只有他早晨的那個同伴一言不發。當白晝更長、再也獵不到海豹時，男人們便以玩球自娛；有一次大家齊聲呼喚尼亞孔瓜克來加入玩球的人——他雖無意於此，卻立刻順從了他們的召喚，但只是遠遠地在一旁觀看。他正站著觀看玩球的人，謙遜地一隻手臂從外套袖子裡抽了出來，那個與他結怨的划艇人這時走上前來，把他推倒在地；尼亞孔瓜克起身抖落衣服上的雪時，眾人圍了上來，說道：「尼亞孔瓜克就打算這樣忍下去嗎？」他的對手聽聞此言，便抓住尼亞孔瓜克，而尼亞孔瓜克本不求爭鬥，只想站穩腳跟——但發覺對方不肯鬆手，他被迫自衛，一場扭打隨之而起，結果尼亞孔瓜克占了上風，他很快制伏了對手，把他猛力摔在地上，以致對方肚破腸流，鮮血從口中湧出。他的兄弟們立刻停止玩球，把他抬進屋裡，他不久便斷了氣。尼亞孔瓜克如今違背自己的意願，為自己結下了仇敵，他告訴年幼的兒子應當記住此事，並鍛鍊自己忍受艱苦，以求獲得力量與精力：他不應再練習舉石擲石，而應試著把灌木連根拔起。此後他教會兒子一切划皮艇的本領；不久兒子在各方面都與父親不相上下，甚至在最惡劣的天氣裡也能遠赴海外追逐海豹。

passages.text: Once another party of Southlanders arrived, and among them were two sons of the man whom Niakunguak had formerly killed; they also had been reared to manly exercise in order to promote their strength. The strangers were polite and friendly enough, and chose to settle with them for the winter; the equinoctial gales proved very strong that autumn, with much bad weather, and often no kayaking was possible. On such a day Niakunguak with his son and other housemates was invited to the foreigners; they were well received, and afterwards regaled with many dainties, and there was no want of lively talking at the meal. At last there was silence, and during this one of the two brothers stood forth, and taking a bit of dried liver (this being exceedingly hard) raised his voice, saying, 'I have been told that I have an enemy in Niakunguak' — at the same time he tried to crush the piece of liver he held in his hand, but failing to do so he again put it by. Silence still prevailed, when Niakunguak's son advanced, and taking up the same bit crushed it to atoms with his fingers, so that it fell like dust upon the floor; all were utterly amazed, and not a word was spoken. Niakunguak and his relations still felt some suspicion of their enemies; but these departed peaceably as soon as spring came on, and henceforth the Niakunguaks remained undisturbed until their death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 67 'Niakunguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，又一群南地人來到，其中有尼亞孔瓜克從前所殺那人的兩個兒子；他們也自幼受男子漢的鍛鍊，以增強體力。這些外來者相當有禮友善，選擇與他們一同過冬；那年秋天，春分時的暴風異常猛烈，壞天氣很多，常常無法划皮艇。就在這樣的一天，尼亞孔瓜克帶著兒子和同屋的人應邀前往外來者處；他們受到熱情接待，隨後又以許多美味款待，席間談笑風生，毫不冷場。最後眾人靜了下來，就在此時，兩兄弟中的一個站了出來，拿起一小塊乾肝（這東西極硬），提高聲音說道：「我聽說我在尼亞孔瓜克這裡有個仇人」——同時他試圖捏碎手中那塊肝，卻捏不碎，只好又放了回去。眾人仍然一片沉默，這時尼亞孔瓜克的兒子走上前來，拿起同一塊肝，用手指把它捏得粉碎，碎屑如塵土般落在地上；眾人無不驚愕萬分，一句話也說不出來。尼亞孔瓜克和他的親屬對這些仇敵仍存幾分疑心；但春天一到，那些人便平安離去，此後尼亞孔瓜克一家直到去世都未再受侵擾。

title.en: Augpilagtok and the Tossed Amulet
title.zh: 奧格皮拉格托克與擲出的護身符

region.en: Kangek firth of Godthaab and Antangmik
region.zh: 努克峽灣康格克與安唐格米克

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 68 'Augpilagtok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Frost-bound before reaching the famous hunting-grounds of Kangek, Augpilagtok eats his dog raw and frozen, then finds the auk-entrails on the dunghill of the very place he sought. Warned that some kayakers 'it would be no joke to disturb,' he tosses up his amulet crying 'Whomsoever!' — kayaks overturn one by one till all are drowned but father and son. Fleeing north, the son endures his companion's 'only in fun' harpoon-throws twice before killing him and bringing the seal home tail-foremost; at the brothers' frozen-liver feast Augpilagtok cuts his own belly open and heals it with a stroke of the hand, and the roof falls in by sorcery — 'The Southlanders are rather deep; we had better leave them alone.'
summary.zh: 霜凍封路，未能抵達康格克獵場的奧格皮拉格托克生食凍犬；翌日卻在心儀獵場的糞堆上吞下海鳩內臟。有人警告『有些皮艇客招惹不得』——他高呼『憑誰都好！』擲出護身符，皮艇一艘接一艘翻覆沉沒。北遷後，兒子兩度躲過同伴『只是玩笑』的魚叉，第三次反手將其擊斃，尾前拖豹歸家示眾；在兄弟們的凍肝宴上，他剖開自己的肚腹、一抹即癒，屋頂又應咒塌落——『南方人詭計多端，還是別招惹他們。』

sensitivity.note: Drowning by tossed amulet and belly-cutting self-display recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Augpilagtok, who was living in the southern part of the country, chanced to hear that Kangek (at the firth of Godthaab) was an excellent place for seal-hunting; he accordingly started for it — but the autumn set in, and the ground was hard with frost before he arrived, so on coming across an old deserted house at Ikarisat, not far from Kangek, he decided to stop there and set about preparing an abode for the winter. At first he had fair hunting, so much was he able to store up that it might have been thought the seals came to his house of their own accord; heavy northern gales were blowing, and the fall of snow was so great that he was forced to take his store of seals into the house and live entirely upon them — at last, however, they were finished. The weather was getting calmer, but the sea was still covered with ice; in these circumstances he made himself a small harpoon for hunting on the ice, but first went out to reconnoitre and find out the breathing-holes of the seals. The first day he roamed all around the bay Ameralik without finding one opening in the ice; the next he tried Kapisilik, but also in vain; the third day, having had the same bad luck at Kangersunek and having nothing to eat, he set to whetting his knife in the evening. He had a dog with drooping ears, and his knife was intended for this poor animal: he killed it, and cut a piece from the loin, which he ate raw, skin and all, only scraping off the hairs; when the rest had been boiled he again ate with a hearty appetite.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 68 'Augpilagtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧格皮拉格托克（Augpilagtok）住在這片土地的南部，偶然聽說坎格克（Kangek，位於戈特霍布峽灣口）是獵海豹的絕佳之地；於是他便動身前往——然而秋季已然來臨，他還沒抵達，地面就已凍得堅硬，因此當他在離坎格克不遠的伊卡里薩特（Ikarisat）遇見一間廢棄的舊屋時，便決定停在那裡，著手準備過冬的住所。起初他狩獵順利，貯存之物多到令人以為海豹是自己跑到他家來的；強勁的北風陣陣吹颳，降雪極大，他不得不把貯存的海豹搬進屋裡，完全靠牠們過活——然而最後，牠們還是吃完了。天氣漸趨平靜，但海面仍覆滿冰層；在這種情況下，他為自己在冰上狩獵做了一支小魚叉，但先出去偵察，尋找海豹的呼吸孔。第一天他在阿梅拉利克（Ameralik）灣四周漫遊，卻沒找到一處冰上的開口；第二天他試了卡皮西利克（Kapisilik），同樣徒勞無功；第三天，他在坎格爾蘇內克（Kangersunek）也遭遇同樣的壞運氣，且已無物可食，便在傍晚開始磨起他的刀來。他養著一隻垂耳狗，那把刀正是為這可憐的畜生準備的：他殺了牠，從腰肉上割下一塊，連皮帶肉生吃，只把毛刮掉；其餘的煮熟之後，他又胃口大開地吃了一頓。

passages.text: The following day he remained in the house; on the next he climbed the highest mountains to survey the neighbourhood, and discovered an opening in the ice not far from his dwelling-place, but it was then too late to start. The following morning he set off, carrying his kayak on his head as far as the water's edge; having rowed for some time along the margin of the ice he unexpectedly detected a number of huts, and the beach was also red with blood from sea-animals which had been killed. He pulled away, and on arriving had a friendly welcome from the inmates, who asked him to their huts — this place was that Kangek which, for want of better knowledge of the locality, he had not been able to reach before the winter overtook him. In ascending the beach he saw the frozen entrails of some auks thrown out upon the dunghill, and not till he had swallowed some of these could they get him to go inside, where he soon got a proper meal and had his kayak filled with stores for his departure. A short time after this he removed with all his household to Kangek; every day he alternately went out seal-hunting and spearing birds, and during this period his little son was provided with a kayak of his own. When auk-hunting his father told him, 'When thou goest out for auks and I am not with thee, thou needest not look so much for my kayak, but be watchful of the others; there are those among them whom it would be no joke to disturb while they are busy at their hunt.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 68 'Augpilagtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 翌日他留在屋裡；再過一天，他爬上最高的山嶺察看周遭，發現離住處不遠處的冰上有一處開口，但當時動身已太晚。次日清晨他出發，把獨木舟頂在頭上一直扛到水邊；沿著冰緣划了一陣之後，他意外地發現了許多小屋，海灘也被獵殺海獸的血染得通紅。他划了過去，抵達時受到屋中人的友善歡迎，他們邀他進屋——這地方正是坎格克，只因他對當地不熟悉，才未能在冬季降臨前抵達。他登上灘岸時，看見糞堆上扔著一些海雀的凍內臟，直到他吞下一些，他們才肯讓他進屋；進屋後他很快便吃了一頓像樣的飯，離去時他的獨木舟也裝滿了補給。此後不久，他帶著全家遷往坎格克；他每天輪流外出獵海豹和叉鳥，這段期間，他的小兒子也有了自己的獨木舟。獵海雀時，父親對他說：「當你出去獵海雀而我不在你身邊時，你不必太留意我的獨木舟，倒要提防其他人；他們之中有些人，在忙著狩獵時被打擾可不是鬧著玩的。」

passages.text: One day, however, when they had gone out together after birds, Augpilagtok had got to a little distance from his son; suddenly he heard angry voices, and turning round saw the small kayak surrounded by the other men. Augpilagtok, who at once suspected something wrong, quickly produced his amulet from out the edging of his jacket, and hiding it inside his mouth rowed on as fast as possible; having reached them he tossed up the amulet, saying, 'Whomsoever!' — at which one was instantly overturned, then a second, then a third, and so on, till all were drowned excepting himself and his son, who returned home together. Not feeling secure in this place any longer, they removed farther north to Antangmik in the spring; during their stay there the father recommended the son to exert himself to grow a match for his enemies, from whom they might expect an assault some day or other. The son soon became a first-rate kayaker, and chased the sea-animals at the remotest places; on his excursions he was often accompanied by the middlemost of several brothers living at the same settlement.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 68 'Augpilagtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 然而有一天，他們一同出去獵鳥，奧格皮拉格托克離兒子稍遠了些；忽然他聽見憤怒的叫嚷聲，轉頭一看，只見那隻小獨木舟被其他男人團團圍住。奧格皮拉格托克立刻察覺不對，迅速從外套的鑲邊中取出他的護符，藏進嘴裡，盡可能快地划過去；到了他們跟前，他把護符往上一拋，說道：「無論是誰！」——當下便有一人翻覆，接著第二個、第三個，如此這般，直到全都被淹死，只剩他和兒子，兩人一同回家。他們在這地方不再感到安全，便於春天往北遷到安坦米克（Antangmik）；在那裡逗留期間，父親勸兒子要努力鍛鍊，成長為能與敵人匹敵之人，因為敵人總有一天會來襲擊。兒子很快便成了一流的獨木舟手，遠至最偏遠的地方追逐海獸；外出時，常與同一聚落中幾兄弟裡居中的那位結伴同行。

passages.text: One day when he thought himself quite alone he was surprised to hear a sound like that of an approaching kayak, and turning round saw with some amazement his usual companion deliberately aiming at him with his harpoon; he narrowly escaped by overturning his kayak, and when he rose again the other said it was only in fun, although it had been an attempt on his life in good earnest. At home he told his father of this occurrence, but he advised him to take no notice of it, lest he should stir up more foes for himself; the next day the same thing happened, and he barely escaped — the third time he resolved to revenge himself, and killed his antagonist. After the deed he returned home, having first put the seal on his kayak, but turned tail foremost; by this sign his father at once knew what had happened, but the brothers of the deceased, who were standing outside the house-door, thought he had placed it the wrong way to ease the kayak while rowing against the wind. Augpilagtok's son on landing said, 'I have put it thus because it was the next one after a man; he thrice attempted my life, and was in the act of killing me; if ye are longing for him ye may go and look for him.' At this news they all began to cry, and entered the house to observe the usual mourning ceremonies. After this the youth became cautious, and never started except when the weather was too bad for the others to venture out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 68 'Augpilagtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，他自以為完全獨處，卻驚訝地聽見一陣像是獨木舟逼近的聲音，轉頭一看，詫異地發現他平日的同伴正刻意用魚叉瞄準他；他靠著翻覆獨木舟才勉強逃過一劫，當他再度浮起時，對方卻說那只是開玩笑，儘管那其實是貨真價實的殺機。回家後他把這件事告訴父親，父親卻勸他別放在心上，免得為自己招來更多敵人；第二天同樣的事又發生了，他勉強逃脫——第三次他決心報復，殺死了他的對手。事後他先將海豹放上獨木舟，卻把牠頭朝船尾擺放，然後回家；父親一見這徵兆便立刻明白發生了什麼事，而死者的兄弟們站在屋門外，還以為他是為了逆風划行時減輕獨木舟的負擔，才把海豹放反了方向。奧格皮拉格托克的兒子登岸後說：「我這樣擺放，是因為牠是緊接在一個人之後的；他三度企圖取我性命，當時正要殺我；你們若思念他，盡可去找他。」聽到這消息，他們全都哭了起來，並進屋舉行慣常的哀悼儀式。此後這青年變得謹慎，除非天氣惡劣到其他人都不敢外出，否則絕不出發。

passages.text: Once in the spring he was invited with his father to visit the brothers; Augpilagtok said to his son, 'We may as well make a bold entrance, and I will go first, and take a good leap across the doorway, right to the entrance of the room.' They thus entered, and saw all the brothers stretched out at full length on the ledge, only their feet visible on its outer edge (a sign of wrath); they were treated to some frozen liver in an oblong dish, but when they had got only half through with it the frozen roof fell in and covered the dish with turf-dust. The eldest brother now said, 'When the roof falls down like this, it only can be by sorcery. The Southlanders are rather deep, and know a thing or two; we had better leave them alone.' Augpilagtok now said to his son, 'Slip off thy clothes' — and taking a knife cut up his belly; but when the entrails began to fall out he merely drew his hand across the cut, and instantly it healed. Some time after they once more repaired to the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 68 'Augpilagtok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一年春天，他與父親受邀去拜訪那幾兄弟；奧格皮拉格托克對兒子說：「我們不妨大膽地進去，我先走，一躍跳過門檻，直達內室的入口。」他們就這樣進了屋，只見所有兄弟都直挺挺地躺在長榻上，只有雙腳露在榻的外緣（這是憤怒的徵兆）；他們被招待吃一盤長方形盤子裡的凍肝，但才吃到一半，凍結的屋頂便塌了下來，把草皮屑撒滿了盤子。這時長兄說道：「屋頂這樣塌下來，只可能是巫術所致。南方人城府頗深，懂得一些門道；我們還是別招惹他們為妙。」奧格皮拉格托克這時對兒子說：「把衣服脫掉」——接著拿刀剖開他的肚子；但當腸子開始掉出來時，他只用手在傷口上一抹，傷口便立刻癒合了。過了些時日，他們又再度南行。

title.en: The Angakok Ataitsiak and the Withering Aunt
title.zh: 巫師阿泰茨夏克與枯萎的姑母

region.en: Ingnersuit land beneath the new shore
region.zh: 新岸之下的地下之民

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 69 'The Angakok Ataitsiak practising his Art with the Benevolent Ingnersuit', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Capsized by his own harpooned seal, Ataitsiak is fished out by his ingnersuit tornaks, towed seaward ('Take care that the blood of the seal does not drop to earth; for in that case he will never see his home again'), and warmed in the under-world house. Asked to examine a failing hunter, he sees the sick man's aunt — her ghost, she being a witch — creeping to touch him: 'From that day I determined to blast and wither him, and but for thee I would have touched him now.' The witch escapes beneath the floor dragging the harpoon-line, her foot bleeding on her couch; the young man recovers, and later brings gifts and the news that the base old hag had died.
summary.zh: 被自己叉中的海豹掀翻的巫師阿泰茨夏克，被地下之民的靈助們救起——『千萬別讓海豹的血滴到地上，否則他永遠回不了家』——被抬入地下之屋烤火復甦。眾人請他診視一位日漸衰弱的年輕獵手；他看見那青年的姑母——其魂魄，她本是巫婆——正爬近欲觸其身：『自那日起我便決意詛咒枯萎他，若非你來，此刻已得手。』巫婆拖著魚叉繩遁入地板之下，臥床時腳底淌血；青年痊癒，日後攜禮來謝，並報知那老嫗已死。

sensitivity.note: Withering witchcraft and the seal-blood taboo of the under-world journey documented as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Ataitsiak was a very celebrated angakok, who had his hunting-place close to his abode, and used to frequent it all by himself; if he ever wanted company he used to invoke some of his tornaks belonging to the ingnersuit, and they always came at his call. One day he had just harpooned a seal and was about to slacken the line, when suddenly the seal gave a pull which capsized his kayak, throwing him headlong out of it; he could barely keep his head above the water by taking hold of the line. It was not till he began to grow stiff with cold that he thought of calling his tornaks — no sooner had he done so than they appeared, coming from the shore in their kayaks; the foremost called out to the others, 'Quick, or he may be drawn down; make haste!' When the first was taking hold of his kayak he perceived that he was already lifted up, and when the others came up he saw that the kayak was emptied of the sea-water, whilst others supported his weak limbs. They then replaced him in his kayak, giving him dry warm clothes; being well propped up he noticed that his seal and kayak were being towed along by the others, and that they carried him out seawards. They soon saw a great new land, and the oldest said, 'Take care that the blood of the seal does not drop to earth; for in that case he will never see his home again.' When they were near enough to hear what was said ashore they heard people cry that a dolphin was probably caught; to which they answered that they were only bringing their old angakok.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 69 'The Angakok Ataitsiak practising his Art with the Benevolent Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿泰齊亞克（Ataitsiak）是一位極負盛名的安加科克（angakok，巫師），他的狩獵地就在住處附近，常獨自一人前往；若他想有伴，便會召喚他那些屬於因格內爾蘇伊特（ingnersuit）的托爾納克（tornak，精靈），而牠們總是有召必至。有一天，他剛叉中一頭海豹，正要鬆開繩索，忽然那海豹猛地一拉，把他的獨木舟掀翻，使他整個人頭朝前地被拋出船外；他抓著繩索，才勉強把頭保持在水面之上。直到他開始冷得僵硬，才想到召喚他的托爾納克——他剛一召喚，牠們便出現了，划著獨木舟從岸邊趕來；為首的那個對其他人大喊：「快，否則他會被拖下水去；快點！」當第一個抓住他的獨木舟時，發覺他已浮了上來；等其他人趕到，他看見獨木舟裡的海水已被舀空，而另一些則扶著他虛弱無力的四肢。接著他們把他放回獨木舟，給他乾燥溫暖的衣物；他被妥善支撐著，注意到他的海豹和獨木舟正被其他人拖著走，而他們把他帶向海的方向。他們很快便看見一片廣闊的新陸地，其中最年長的說：「小心別讓海豹的血滴到地上；否則他將再也見不到自己的家。」當他們靠近到能聽見岸上話語時，他們聽見人們喊著說大概是捕到一頭海豚了；他們回答說，他們只是把他們的老安加科克帶回來了。

passages.text: Having got him inside, all the lamps were lighted; they first laid him naked down on the floor and covered him well up, and after a while he again recovered his lost senses and began to walk. In the evening they served all kinds of victuals before him; during the meal he noticed a poor young man, very ill, lying down on the ledge. The oldest among them said, 'A most distressing case with the lad yonder; he is failing fast. When he chased the reindeer in the autumn we feasted and were well off; he was equally clever at stalking deer and chasing white whales; and even in the worst season was always lucky; will you examine his case to-night? There must be something particular the matter with him, preventing his recovery.' He said he would fain do it; but as he was going to set about it he noticed the sick man's aunt (viz., her soul or ghost, she being a witch) going close up to him in order to touch him — on seeing this he said, 'It would be an easy matter, and he would look to it the day after.' When he began his conjurations the following night he saw the woman approaching still nearer to the sick youth, and then said, 'In the practice of my art I must speak the truth; it is the woman there that does him the mischief.' They cried with one voice, 'Take her, do take her away' — 'I must first question her.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 69 'The Angakok Ataitsiak practising his Art with the Benevolent Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 把他帶進屋後，所有的燈都點了起來；他們先讓他赤身裸體躺在地上，把他蓋得嚴嚴實實，過了一會兒，他又恢復了失去的知覺，開始走動。傍晚，他們在他面前擺上各式各樣的食物；吃飯時，他注意到一個可憐的年輕人，病得很重，躺在炕沿上。他們中年紀最大的人說：『那邊那個小夥子的情況最令人揪心；他正迅速衰弱下去。秋天他追趕馴鹿時，我們有吃有喝，日子過得很好；他無論是潛近鹿群還是追捕白鯨，都同樣在行；即使在最糟的季節，他也總是運氣很好；你今晚願意察看一下他的病情嗎？他身上一定有什麼特別的毛病，使他無法康復。』他說他樂意去做；但正當他要著手時，他注意到病人的姑母（即她的靈魂或鬼魂，因為她是個女巫）湊近他，想要碰他——見此情景，他說：『這本是件容易的事，他會在後天留意處理。』第二天夜裡他開始施法時，看見那女人更加靠近那個生病的年輕人，於是說道：『在施展我的法術時，我必須說真話；正是那邊那個女人在害他。』他們異口同聲地喊道：『抓住她，務必把她帶走』——『我必須先審問她。』

passages.text: The base woman now explained, 'Whenever he returned from the hunt he used to supply me abundantly with sundry good things; but the last time he was out, though he brought home deer as well as dolphins, and I was in the highest expectation, he never gave me a bit. From that day I determined to blast and wither him, and but for thee I would have touched him now.' Ataitsiak turned to the others, saying, 'If you really want the young man to recover I must slay her; but mind you hold the harpoon-strings fast.' He was about to hit her, but as long as she looked at him he could not conquer her; as soon, however, as she turned to the wall, he thrust at her, and a loud cracking noise ensued — but she, having watched him sharply, as soon as he moved let herself down beneath the floor, and the harpoon only caught the sole of her foot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 69 'The Angakok Ataitsiak practising his Art with the Benevolent Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那個卑劣的女人這時解釋道：『每當他打獵回來，總會給我送來大量各式各樣的好東西；但上一次他外出時，雖然帶回了鹿，也帶回了海豚，我滿心期待，他卻一點兒也沒給我。從那天起，我就決心要毀掉他、讓他衰弱下去，若不是你，我現在早就碰到他了。』阿泰齊亞克轉向其他人說：『你們若真想讓這年輕人康復，我就必須殺了她；但你們務必把魚叉繩牢牢抓住。』他正要刺她，但只要她盯著他看，他就制不住她；然而她剛一轉向牆壁，他就朝她刺去，隨即發出一聲響亮的爆裂聲——但她一直機警地盯著他，他一動，她就讓自己沉到地板下面去了，魚叉只鉤住了她的腳底。

passages.text: She went dragging the line down with her, so that the men with all their strength could hardly stop her; one after another they let go their hold — at last there was only one man at the line when Ataitsiak was happily in time to help him, and catching hold of a bit of bone made fast to the line he entirely stopped it. After a while he said, 'Now go and see how his aunt is'; she lived in a little house close by — they returned and reported that she lay on her couch with a bleeding foot. On the ensuing morning Ataitsiak went back to his home loaded with gifts; his family had not as yet given him up, being assured he would return before the three days were over. One day, at a later period, when he happened to be out in his hunting-ground, a great many kayakers were seen approaching, and first among them was the sick young man whom he had restored to health, bringing many gifts for Ataitsiak, and at the same time reporting that his aunt, the base old hag, had died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 69 'The Angakok Ataitsiak practising his Art with the Benevolent Ingnersuit'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 她拖著繩子往下沉，那些人用盡全力也幾乎拉不住她；他們一個接一個地鬆了手——最後只剩一個人抓著繩子，幸好阿泰齊亞克及時趕來幫他，抓住繫在繩上的一塊骨頭，才完全把它止住。過了一會兒，他說：『現在去看看他姑母怎麼樣了』；她住在附近的一間小屋裡——他們回來報告說，她躺在臥榻上，腳在流血。第二天早晨，阿泰齊亞克滿載著禮物回家去了；他的家人還沒有放棄他，因為他們確信他會在三天之內回來。後來有一天，他碰巧外出到他的獵場去，看見許多划獨木舟的人駛近，走在最前面的正是他使之恢復健康的那個生病年輕人，他給阿泰齊亞克帶來了許多禮物，同時報告說他的姑母，那個卑劣的老巫婆，已經死了。

title.en: The Strong Man on Umanak and the One-Bladed Kayariak
title.zh: 烏馬納克力士與單葉槳的幽靈艇客

region.en: Isle of Umanak in the Isortok firth, South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭伊索爾托克峽灣的烏馬納克島

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 70 'The Strong Man on Umanak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The strong man of Umanak carries his two big seals on the kayak itself and returns before the sun turns west — until his trained son fails to come home. Out where the southern islands turn shadowy he hears 'Eek!' and finds a kayariak, a fabulous kayaker with a paddle of one blade shifted side to side — his son's arm lashed on the after-part. He harpoons him, finds a second with the other arm, then the father of both carrying the body: 'Canst thou revive him there?' — touched, the drowned revive; the limbs are joined on a floe, a giant kayak is lent with 'do not let any one look into it,' and the one unbeliever who looks is frightened to death, while the borrower goes lame. Then the father's pipe blown to the four quarters raises the gale that drives him home around Cape Farewell.
summary.zh: 烏馬納克的力士把兩頭大豹直接縛在艇上，日未西斜便滿載而歸——直到受訓的兒子一去不返。遠至南島只剩暗影之處，他聽見『咦——』的呼聲，尋見一個幽靈艇客：單葉槳左右換手划動，艇尾竟縛著兒子的手臂。他一叉斃之，再殺其持另一臂的兄弟，最後找到載著兒子屍身的兩人之父——『你能讓他復活嗎？』觸之即生；浮冰上接合斷肢，又借得巨艇——『千萬別讓人往艇裡看』——偷看者被嚇死，借艇者跛了腿。其父向四方吹響煙管，召來風暴，繞過費爾韋爾角歸家。

sensitivity.note: Dismemberment and revival documented as told in the 1875 source. Kayariak = fabulous kayaker (Rink's usage).

passages.text: On the isle of Umanak in the Isortok firth (South Greenland) lived a very strong man, besides a great many other people. He gained great fame from his extraordinary strength, and was likewise considered a first-rate hunter and skilled angakok; he was in fact a principal provider for the whole place, and their angakok into the bargain. He used to take his little son on his knee when conjuring, in order to teach him his art. The people themselves had no lack of good hunting off the coast in the autumn season; but after the winter solstice the angakok used to roam about on the open sea all by himself, and when he had caught a couple of big seals he used to put them upon his kayak, one in front and the other behind (viz., instead of towing them), making them fast with his harpoon-line. Before the sun had gone round to the west he was sure to have reached home with his two seals, and then lost no time in ordering the women to cook the briskets. When the meal was served the men sat down to it, and generally the angakok started the conversation by saying, 'I was again caught in a heavy snowstorm from the north' — this seemed very strange, for on shore the weather had been fine, and far away seawards only a small mist-band had been noticed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 70 'The Strong Man on Umanak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在伊索托克峽灣（南格陵蘭）的烏馬納克島上，住著一個非常強壯的人，此外還有許多別的人。他因力氣非凡而聲名遠揚，同時也被認為是一流的獵手和熟練的安加科克（巫師）；事實上，他是整個地方的主要供養者，而且還是他們的安加科克。他施法時常把小兒子抱在膝上，以便把自己的法術傳授給他。秋天時節，人們在近海一帶並不缺少好獵獲；但冬至之後，這位安加科克常常獨自到外海去遊蕩，當他捕到兩隻大海豹時，就把牠們放在獨木舟上，一隻在前，一隻在後（即不用拖曳的方式），用魚叉繩把牠們綁牢。太陽還沒轉到西邊，他必定已經帶著兩隻海豹回到家了，然後趕緊吩咐女人們煮海豹胸肉。飯菜端上來後，男人們坐下吃飯，通常由這位安加科克先開口說話：『我又遇上從北方來的猛烈暴風雪了』——這似乎很奇怪，因為岸上天氣一直很好，只在遠離海岸的地方看到過一小條霧帶。

passages.text: Being a man of such rare qualities he naturally wished his son to come up to his own standard, and carefully trained him with this view; when full grown the son also would go far out to sea in all weathers and bring big seals home with him. From that time the father grew quite easy about him, and occasionally remained at home himself, though perfectly hale and hearty. Once in the long days the son had started by himself, and at night the father in vain expected his return; the next morning at daybreak he set out in search of him. When so far from land that the southern islands looked quite dim and shadowy he heard a voice calling out 'Eek!' — on hearing this strange voice, which he soon knew did not belong to any of his countrymen, he hastened on southwards steering towards the sun, and in a little while suddenly stopped short, again hearing a voice shouting 'Where?' Soon after he came in sight of an immense kayak, and on nearing it found it to be a kayariak (fabulous kayaker); the huge kayaker had a paddle with only one blade, which he plied vigorously by shifting it alternately from one side of the kayak to the other. Approaching him from behind he discovered one of his son's arms lashed on to the after-part of the kayariak — at this sight he got into such a rage that he instantly darted his harpoon and killed the kayaker; having drawn out the harpoon, whose point was the length of half an arm, he kayaked still further along until he heard the former cry repeated. He answered it, and continuing his way soon fell in with another kayaker, who carried the second arm of his son aft on his kayak; having killed him also he stood out to sea till the high mountains of his own country were almost lost to sight. He again heard a deep rough voice belonging to a similar kayaker, who was the father of the two he had already killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 70 'The Strong Man on Umanak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他既是這樣一個稟賦罕見的人，自然希望兒子能達到自己的水準，便懷著這個目的精心訓練他；兒子長大成人後，也能在各種天氣下遠航出海，帶回大隻的海豹。從那時起，父親對他十分放心，偶爾自己也留在家裡，儘管他身體依然十分健壯。有一次，在漫長的白晝裡，兒子獨自出發了，到了夜裡，父親白白盼望他回來；第二天黎明，他便動身去找兒子。當他離陸地很遠，南邊的島嶼看上去已十分模糊朦朧時，他聽見一個聲音喊著『咦！』——聽到這奇怪的叫聲，他很快便知道那不是任何同鄉人發出的，於是他加快向南，朝著太陽的方向划去，不一會兒突然停住，又聽到一個聲音喊著『在哪裡？』。不久之後，他望見一隻巨大的獨木舟，靠近一看，發現那是一個卡亞里亞克（傳說中的獨木舟人）；那巨大的獨木舟人只有一支單葉槳，他把槳在獨木舟兩側輪流換著，用力划動。從後面靠近他時，他發現兒子的一條手臂被綁在卡亞里亞克獨木舟的後部——見此情景，他勃然大怒，立刻擲出魚叉，殺死了那個獨木舟人；拔出魚叉後——那叉尖有半條手臂那麼長——他繼續划著獨木舟向前，直到又聽見先前那樣的喊聲。他應了一聲，繼續前行，不久又遇到另一個獨木舟人，這人把兒子的第二條手臂放在獨木舟後部；他也把這人殺死，然後向外海划去，直到本國的高山幾乎都看不見了。他又聽到一個低沉粗啞的聲音，屬於一個與先前相似的獨木舟人，這人正是他已經殺死的兩個人的父親。

passages.text: The weather being calm, with a swell from the south-west, he put in his oar, and having secured it by means of the kayak-line drifted along, steering only with his hands; approaching the great kayaker thus he discovered his son's body behind him on his kayak. He did not throw his lance, but rowed right in upon him and kept alongside of him by hooking his oar into the stranger's kayak-straps; this somewhat startled the former, and he was heard to exclaim, 'Where are those whom I am seeking?' — and then the angakok understood of whom he was speaking. Turning landwards they soon fell in with one kayak floating bottom up; the angakok now inquired, 'Canst thou revive him there?' — 'Why, yes, I could' — and lifting the wounded man up he merely touched him and brought him to life again; then they reached the next, and the father did the same to him. Being now four in number the angakok went on, 'Perhaps ye would not mind making him alive too whom ye have got there on your kayak' — 'It might be done if a fitting place can be found to manage it properly.' On reaching a piece of floating ice they landed upon it, and when the kayariak had joined the severed limbs together and had revived him that had been slain, the father said, 'What is to be done next? He has got no kayak; can't we have the loan of one of those?' — 'Well, take it, but be sure ye bring it back immediately, and when ye land do not let any one look into it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 70 'The Strong Man on Umanak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天氣平靜，西南方向湧來一陣浪，他把槳放好，用獨木舟繩把它固定住，任憑漂流，只用雙手掌舵；這樣靠近那個巨大的獨木舟人時，他發現兒子的屍體就在那人身後的獨木舟上。他沒有擲出長矛，而是徑直划過去，用槳鉤住那陌生人的獨木舟綁帶，與他並排而行；這讓那人有些吃驚，只聽他喊道：『我正在找的那些人在哪裡？』——這時這位安加科克才明白他指的是誰。他們轉向陸地，不久便遇到一隻底朝上漂浮的獨木舟；安加科克這時問道：『你能讓那裡的那個人復活嗎？』——『嗯，能啊，我可以』——於是把那受傷的人舉起來，只碰了他一下，就使他重新活了過來；接著他們又到了下一隻獨木舟旁，父親也照樣使他復活。現在一共四個人了，安加科克接著說：『也許你們不介意把你們獨木舟上載著的那個人也弄活吧』——『若能找到合適的地方妥善處理，倒是可以辦到。』他們到了一塊浮冰上，便登了上去，等卡亞里亞克把斷開的肢體接合起來，使被殺的人復活之後，父親說：『接下來該怎麼辦？他沒有獨木舟；我們能不能借用其中一隻？』——『好吧，拿去吧，但務必立刻送回來，而且你們上岸時，不要讓任何人往裡面看。』

passages.text: The angakok now returned with his son, who found his kayak such a size that he went down into it to the pit of his arms; on reaching land he cried out that no one must look down into the big kayak — but one unbeliever among their placemates did so, in consequence of which the son of the angakok who had made use of it grew lame in his legs; the unbeliever also was found close by, having been frightened to death at something he had seen inside the big kayak. Meantime the angakok brought the kayak back to the big man, who stood waiting for him on the ice; the sons now both descended into their kayaks, but the father remained a while, and first took a general view of the whole horizon, then producing a small pipe he had hidden in his own boat blew it successively towards the four quarters of the horizon, and then repaired to his boat. When the angakok left them the weather was fine and calm, but he was hardly off before clouds arose, the sky became overcast, and all of a sudden a heavy gale was blowing; the wind rushing on from different quarters almost prevented his making the land — however, he went ahead undauntedly, having a first-rate kayak covered with skins joined together lengthways. When the storm abated and the stars again shone out, a high land became visible which he recognised to be Akilinek, on the shore opposite his own; he was again caught in a tempest, but this having also subsided he landed at the southernmost point of our country (Cape Farewell), and finally reached his own home, where his family had long believed him dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 70 'The Strong Man on Umanak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這時，那位安加科克（angakok，巫師）帶著兒子回來了；他兒子發現自己的皮划艇竟大得能讓他坐進去直到腋下。上岸時，他高聲喊道，誰都不許往那艘大皮划艇裡張望——但他們同村的人中有一個不信邪的偏偏照做了，結果，那個曾使用過這艘皮划艇的安加科克的兒子雙腿竟瘸了；那個不信邪的人也被人發現倒在近旁，原來他是被自己在這艘大皮划艇裡看到的某樣東西給活活嚇死了。與此同時，安加科克把皮划艇還給了那個大個子，那人正站在冰上等他；兩個兒子這會兒都坐進了自己的皮划艇，但父親卻逗留了一會兒，他先是縱覽了整個地平線，然後取出一根藏在自己船裡的小管子，朝著地平線的四個方向依次吹了一遍，之後才回到自己的船上。安加科克離開他們時，天氣晴好而平靜，可他剛一走，雲便湧了上來，天空陰沉下來，轉眼間便刮起了猛烈的狂風；風從四面八方呼嘯而來，幾乎使他無法靠岸——然而，他毫不畏懼地向前行進，因為他有一艘上好的皮划艇，是用獸皮縱向拼接覆蓋而成的。當風暴平息、星辰重又閃耀時，一片高地顯現出來，他認出那便是阿基利內克（Akilinek），就在他自己家鄉對岸的海岸上；他再次遭遇了一場暴風雨，但這場風暴也平息之後，他在我們國土的最南端（法韋爾角）登了陸，最終回到了自己的家，而他的家人早已長久地以為他死了。

title.en: Coyote and the Snake-Monster of the Jocko Valley
title.zh: 郊狼誅喬科谷巨蛇

region.en: Jocko valley, between Evaro and Ravalli (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喬科谷，埃瓦羅與拉瓦利之間（象徵定位）

period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 2. Coyote and the Snake-Monster'

summary.en: A huge rattlesnake-monster occupies the Jocko valley, its tail at Snlpo' near Evaro, its mouth at Skul'io' near Ravalli, its stomach near Jocko: travellers walk into its mouth thinking it a valley, sicken in its stomach and die. Coyote travels through with two long tamarack poles on his shoulder, finds the dying people inside ('You have been swallowed. You are in its stomach now'), plants the poles upright — two tamaracks grow there to-day — and dances under the hanging heart with a sharp arrow-stone dagger fixed on his head until he has killed the monster. Its heart is Butte near Jocko; the props hold the mouth open and the cut tail is the canyon near Evaro, so that people pass through without harm, and the valley is as we see it to-day.
summary.zh: 巨蛇盤踞喬科谷：尾在埃瓦羅附近 Snlpo'，口在拉瓦利附近 Skul'io'，胃近喬科。行人誤以為山谷而入其口，至胃則病亡。郊狼肩扛兩根長落葉松桿入谷，遇垂死之人方知已在蛇胃；遂立桿於地（今彼處仍生兩株落葉松），頭頂利箭石，於懸垂之蛇心下起舞跳擊，直至誅蛇。蛇心即今喬科附近之孤丘；口被撐開、尾被剖開——埃瓦羅附近之峽谷即其割痕。行人從此往來無恙，山谷遂如今貌。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative told by Michel Revais (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Landscape etiology for Jocko valley features. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a huge rattlesnake-monster which occupied the Jocko valley. Its tail was at Snlpo' (Come-Out or Emerge), a place near Evaro; and its mouth, at Skul'io', near Ravalli. Its stomach was near Jocko. It swallowed people without their knowing it: they walked into its mouth, and passed on to its stomach, thinking they were going through a valley, and not knowing that they were inside a monster. When they reached the stomach, they became sick, and ere long died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 115 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一隻巨大的響尾蛇怪物盤踞在喬科（Jocko）山谷。牠的尾巴在斯恩爾波（Snlpo'，意為「出來」或「現身」），那是埃瓦羅附近的一個地方；牠的嘴在斯庫爾伊奧（Skul'io'），靠近拉瓦利。牠的胃在喬科附近。牠吞食人時，人們渾然不覺：他們走進牠的嘴裡，一路前行到了牠的胃裡，還以為自己是在穿過一個山谷，全然不知自己正身處一隻怪物的腹中。當他們到達胃裡時，便生了病，不久就死了。

passages.text: Coyote was travelling with Fox, and reached that district. The people told him of the monster, and he said he would go and kill it. Fox advised him not to go, because he would be killed. Coyote, however, started; and when near the monster's head, he cut two long tamarack-poles, and carried them along on his shoulder, thinking, 'I will use these in case he tries to close his mouth on me.' He passed through the monster's mouth without knowing it. When he reached a place near Arlee, he saw a number of people in all stages of dying, and asked them what they were doing there. 'The monster has killed us,' they answered. 'Where is he? I am looking for him. I don't see anything here to kill you.' — 'You have been swallowed. You are in its stomach now.' Then he placed his poles upright: therefore two tamaracks grow at this place to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 115-116 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正與狐狸同行，來到了那一帶。人們把怪物的事告訴了他，他說他要去把那怪物殺掉。狐狸勸他別去，因為他會被殺死的。然而郊狼還是出發了；當他走近怪物的頭部時，他砍了兩根長長的落葉松木桿，扛在肩上，心裡想：「要是牠想用嘴把我合住，我就用這些來對付。」他走進了怪物的嘴裡，卻渾然不覺。當他走到阿爾利附近的一個地方時，他看見許多人正處於各種瀕死的狀態，便問他們在那裡做什麼。「怪物把我們害死了，」他們回答。「牠在哪兒？我正在找牠。我在這兒可沒看見什麼能害死你們的東西。」——「你已經被吞下去了。你現在就在牠的胃裡。」於是他把自己的木桿豎立起來：所以今天這個地方長著兩棵落葉松。

passages.text: Not very far from there he saw the monster's heart hanging down. Coyote was wearing a sharp arrow-stone fastened upright on his head. He began to dance; and whenever he jumped up, the dagger pierced the heart. Thus he kept on dancing until he had killed the monster. Its heart may still be seen in the shape of Butte, near Jocko. Coyote supported its mouth so that it could not close, and opened its tail; the cut he made may be seen as a canyon near Evaro. Thus Coyote made it possible for people to pass through without hindrance or harm, and the valley was as we see it to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 116 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 離那裡不遠，他看見怪物的心臟懸垂下來。郊狼頭上正豎直地綁著一塊鋒利的箭石。他開始跳起舞來；每當他向上躍起，那匕首便刺中那顆心臟。他就這樣不停地跳著，直到把怪物殺死。據說牠的心臟至今仍可見，就是喬科附近那座孤山（Butte）的形狀。郊狼撐住了牠的嘴，使牠無法合攏，又剖開了牠的尾巴；他割開的那道口子至今仍可見，就是埃瓦羅附近的一處峽谷。就這樣，郊狼使人們得以通行無阻、不受傷害，而那山谷也就成了我們今日所見的模樣。

title.en: Coyote and Mountain-Sheep: The Rock at Amtkane'
title.zh: 郊狼與大角羊：阿姆特坎之石

region.en: Amtkane', five miles below Missoula (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿姆特坎，米蘇拉以南五英里（象徵定位）

period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 3. Coyote and Mountain-Sheep'

summary.en: At Amtkane', about five miles below Missoula, a large rock stands on the edge of a high cliff and moves when pushed; there lives the Mountain-Ram who kills people — inviting passers-by to push the rock over, then to look over the cliff at the sheep on the rocks below, pushing them over while they look. Coyote, armed, is invited to shoot the sheep, goes to look, and is pushed over and killed; Fox revives him by jumping over him. Returning, Coyote feigns not to see the sheep until Ram leans out over the cliff to point them out — and Coyote shoves him over: 'Had you kept on living and doing this way, you would have exterminated the people.'
summary.zh: 阿姆特坎高地崖邊有一巨石，推之則動。彼處住殺人大角羊：先請過客推石下崖，再請俯瞰崖下石上之羊，趁其觀望推之墜崖。郊狼攜弓矢而來，被請射羊，俯視之際被推落斃命；狐躍其身救活。郊狼復往，佯裝不見羊群；大角羊探身崖外指點，郊狼推其墜崖，曰：『若任爾如此下去，人類將被爾滅絕。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came to Amtkane', about five miles below Missoula, where a large rock is standing on the edge of a high cliff; it moves when it is pushed. Here lived the Mountain-Ram who killed people. He invited passers-by to push the rock over the cliff; when they failed, he invited them to look over the cliff at the sheep on the rocks below. Then, while they were looking, he would push them over, and thus kill them. As Coyote was passing, Bighorn shouted to him; Coyote went up and asked him what he wanted. He saw that Coyote was armed, so he said, 'You have bow and arrows. I should like you to shoot those sheep among the rocks below.' Coyote went to look at them; then Bighorn pushed him over, and he was killed on the rocks below.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 116 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在旅行，來到了阿姆特卡內（Amtkane'），那地方在米蘇拉下游約五英里處，有一塊大岩石立在一道高崖的邊緣上；一推它，它就會動。這裡住著一隻害人性命的山羊。牠邀請過路的人把那塊岩石推下懸崖；當他們推不動時，牠便邀他們探身望向崖下，去看下面岩石上的羊群。然後，趁他們張望之際，牠就把他們推下去，就這樣害死他們。郊狼路過時，大角羊朝他喊叫；郊狼走上前去，問牠想要什麼。牠看出郊狼帶著武器，於是說道：「你有弓和箭。我想請你射死下面岩石間的那些羊。」郊狼便去看那些羊；這時大角羊把他推了下去，他就在下面的岩石上摔死了。

passages.text: Later Fox came along, and jumped over him. Then Coyote moved, rubbed his eyes, and said, 'I must have slept a long time.' Fox answered, 'You were dead. I told you not to come here.' Coyote said, 'I will be revenged.' Coyote went the same way; and as he was passing, Bighorn shouted as before, and said, 'You have bow and arrows. I want you to shoot these sheep.' Coyote went cautiously to the edge of the cliff, and pretended not to see the sheep; Bighorn pointed them out, but Coyote said he did not see them. Ram leaned out over the cliff to show them to Coyote, and the latter shoved him over and killed him. He said, 'Had you kept on living and doing this way, you would have exterminated the people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 116 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來狐狸走了過來，從他身上跳了過去。於是郊狼動了動，揉了揉眼睛，說道：「我一定是睡了很久。」狐狸回答說：「你死了。我早就告訴過你別到這兒來。」郊狼說：「我要報仇。」郊狼沿著同一條路走去；當他路過時，大角羊像先前一樣朝他喊叫，說道：「你有弓和箭。我要你射死這些羊。」郊狼小心翼翼地走到懸崖邊上，假裝沒看見那些羊；大角羊把牠們指給他看，可郊狼說他沒看見。山羊便探身到懸崖外，想把牠們指給郊狼看，後者卻一把將牠推了下去，把牠摔死了。他說：「你要是繼續活著、繼續這樣幹下去，早就把人趕盡殺絕了。」

title.en: Coyote and the Skukula'na Women
title.zh: 郊狼與斯庫庫拉納婦人

region.en: Bitter-Root River bank (symbolic pin near Hamilton)
region.zh: 比特魯特河岸（象徵定位於漢密爾頓附近）

period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 4. Coyote and the Skukula'na Women'

summary.en: On the Bitter-Root River Coyote hears women dancing in the tall grass singing 'He goes up the ridge' as he crosses, 'He goes down the ridge' as he descends, and joins them; they take him by each hand, dance him toward the river, and drag him up and down until he is drowned — 'It does not matter about clothes in the other world where you are going.' Fox revives him by jumping over his body, and Coyote fires the grass all around them: scorched as they rush through to the river, the women are transformed — 'You shall be Skukula'na, and people shall put you into the fire and eat you' — which is why these fresh-water shellfish appear as if burned on one side.
summary.zh: 比特魯特河畔，郊狼聞高草間眾女歌舞：其上嶺則唱『彼上嶺矣』，下嶺則唱『彼下嶺矣』，遂入其群。眾女左右執其手，舞向河邊，將其拖入水中上下拽曳，直至溺斃——『來世之中，衣衫何足惜哉。』狐躍其屍救活。郊狼復返，縱火焚其四周之草；眾女穿火奔河，皆被灼傷，遂被化為斯庫庫拉納貝：『人將置爾於火中而食之。』故此類貝如今似半邊火烤之狀。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and went up Bitter-Root River. There he saw a number of women dancing among tall grass on the bank. He approached, crossing a ridge; he heard them singing, 'He goes up the ridge.' He said, 'They have noticed me. They mean me.' When he went down over the ridge, they sang, 'He goes down the ridge.' Coyote thought, 'They refer to me.' He went down and joined the women. They took him by each hand, and danced with him towards the river. They said, 'We are going into the water.' Coyote said, 'Let me go. My clothes will get wet. I will take them off.' They answered, 'You need not mind. It does not matter about clothes in the other world where you are going.' They took him into the water, and dragged him up and down until he was drowned. They left his body on the bank; and Fox came along, and brought him to life by jumping over him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 116-117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在旅行，沿著苦根河而上。他在那裡看見許多女人在岸邊的高草叢中跳舞。他越過一道山脊走近；他聽見她們唱著：「他正走上山脊。」他說：「她們注意到我了。她們說的是我。」當他越過山脊往下走時，她們唱著：「他正走下山脊。」郊狼心想：「她們指的是我。」他走下去，加入了那些女人。她們各牽著他的一隻手，與他一同朝河邊跳舞。她們說：「我們要進水裡去了。」郊狼說：「放開我。我的衣服會濕。我要把它們脫掉。」她們回答：「你不必在意。你要去的另一個世界裡，衣服是無關緊要的。」她們把他帶進水裡，拖著他上上下下，直到他淹死。她們把他的屍體留在岸上；狐狸走了過來，從他身上跳過，使他復活。

passages.text: Coyote said, 'I shall get even with these women.' He went back, and found them dancing in the same place. He set fire to the grass all around them, and they ran together to get away from the fire; when they saw that it would reach them, they rushed through and ran for the river. As they passed through the fire, they were scorched. Coyote transformed them, saying, 'You shall be Skukula'na, and people shall put you into the fire and eat you.' For this reason these shell-fish appear as if burned on one side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼說：「我要跟這些女人算這筆帳。」他回去，發現她們仍在同一處跳舞。他放火燒了她們四周的草，她們便一起奔跑，想逃離火勢；當她們看出火會燒到她們時，她們衝過火堆，奔向河邊。她們穿過火焰時被燒焦了。郊狼把她們變形，說道：「你們將成為斯庫庫拉納（Skukula'na），人們會把你們放進火裡烤了吃。」正因如此，這些貝類看起來就像有一面被燒過一樣。

title.en: Coyote and the Elk-Monster of Few-Trees-on-Prairie
title.zh: 郊狼誅草原麋怪

region.en: StsE'ltsaltsEle' near Hamilton on the Bitter-Root River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 比特魯特河漢密爾頓附近 StsE'ltsaltsEle'（象徵定位）

period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 5. Coyote and Elk'

summary.en: At StsE'ltsaltsEle' (Few-Trees-standing-on-Prairie) near Hamilton, an Elk-Monster lies on a butte commanding the whole prairie, sucking in its breath to swallow every traveller it sees. Coyote has his wife, the Short-Tailed-Mouse, tunnel an underground passage up to the Elk, then emerges right beneath the monster — 'How did you come here? I never saw you. I see everything.' — until Elk believes Coyote's powers are greater than its own. Coyote asks the Elk to attack some people crossing the prairie 'as we do in the world whence I come,' relieves the Elk of its too-large stone dagger 'that will make you tired,' and stabs him to death, cutting out his heart: 'Henceforth you shall be a common elk, and people shall eat you, instead of your eating people.'
summary.zh: 比特魯特河畔漢密爾頓附近之孤丘上臥麋怪，瞰制全原，吸氣即吞所見行旅。郊狼命其妻短尾鼠自丘後掘地道直達麋怪腹下，忽然現身。麋怪大驚：『爾何從至此？吾明察秋毫，未見爾蹤！』遂疑郊狼神通更廣。郊狼唆其出擊原上行人，並借口替其扛那『累人之』巨石匕首而卸其兵，刺之而死，剜其心：『自此爾為凡麋，人食爾，非爾食人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote went to StsE'ltsaltsEle' (Few-Trees-standing-on-Prairie), a place near Hamilton on the Bitter-Root River, where an Elk-Monster lived. It lay on a butte there, from which it could see a long distance over the adjoining prairie; nothing could pass over the prairie without being seen by it. When it saw people, it drew in its breath, and they were sucked into its mouth and swallowed; it had thus killed many people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼前往斯采爾察爾策萊（StsE'ltsaltsEle'，意為「草原上矗立的幾棵樹」），那是苦根河畔漢密爾頓附近的一個地方，住著一頭麋鹿妖。牠躺在那裡的一座孤丘上，從那裡可以望見遠方毗連的草原；任何東西都無法經過那片草原而不被牠看見。牠一看見人，就吸氣，把他們吸進嘴裡吞下；牠就這樣殺死了許多人。

passages.text: Coyote took his wife, the Short-Tailed-Mouse, with him, and ordered her to dig an underground passage to the Elk. She began to work behind a hill, and tunnelled up to the Elk. Then her husband told her to move camp across the prairie. Coyote went through the passage, and came out right under the Elk-Monster, which was surprised and said, 'How did you come here? I never saw you. I see everything.' Coyote answered, 'I came right across the prairie. You must be blind if you did not see me.' Elk became afraid, for he thought Coyote must have greater powers than he had.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼帶上他的妻子短尾鼠，吩咐她挖一條通往麋鹿妖的地下通道。她在一座山丘後面開始挖掘，一直挖隧道通到麋鹿妖那裡。然後她丈夫叫她拔營橫越草原。郊狼穿過通道，正好從麋鹿妖的正下方出來，麋鹿妖大吃一驚，說道：「你怎麼來到這裡的？我從沒見過你。我什麼都看得見。」郊狼回答：「我就是橫越草原過來的。你若是沒看見我，一定是瞎了。」麋鹿妖害怕起來，因為牠認為郊狼的本領必定比牠大。

passages.text: Just then Coyote saw the people crossing the prairie. He asked Elk if he saw them, and he answered, 'Yes.' Coyote said, 'Then go and attack them. In the world whence I come we do that. When we see strangers, we go out to attack them and try to take their scalps.' Elk agreed, and Coyote accompanied him. Elk had a large stone dagger. Coyote said, 'That knife will make you tired. It is too large and heavy for you to carry. Let me carry it for you.' Elk gave him the knife, and thus disarmed himself. Then Coyote attacked him, stabbed him to death, and cut out his heart. He said, 'Henceforth you shall be a common elk, and people shall eat you, instead of your eating people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 117 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在這時，郊狼看見那些人正橫越草原。他問麋鹿妖有沒有看見他們，牠回答：「看見了。」郊狼說：「那就去攻擊他們。在我來的那個世界裡，我們就是這麼做的。我們一看見陌生人，就出去攻擊他們，設法剝下他們的頭皮。」麋鹿妖同意了，郊狼便陪著牠。麋鹿妖有一把大石匕首。郊狼說：「那把刀會使你疲累。它太大太重，你帶著不方便。讓我替你拿吧。」麋鹿妖把刀交給了他，就這樣解除了自己的武裝。於是郊狼攻擊牠，把牠刺死，挖出了牠的心。他說：「從今以後，你將成為一頭普通的麋鹿，人們會吃你，而不是你吃人。」

title.en: The Wren and the War on the Sky
title.zh: 鷦鷯與征天之戰

region.en: Arrow-chain from the Pend d'Oreille country to the sky (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自彭德奧雷伊故地直上天際之箭鏈（象徵定位）

period: Told by Michel Revais; collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Pend d'Oreille Tales, 6. The Wren'

summary.en: The Earth people, under Grizzly-Bear their chief, make war on the Sky people; every arrow falls short of the moon until little Wren's shot sticks fast, and the chain of arrows reaching to the ground is climbed — Grizzly-Bear last, whose weight breaks it. Springing for the upper part, he pulls the arrows out at the top and the whole chain falls, stranding the army in the sky. The Earth people defeat the Stars in the first battle but are routed in the second; at the broken ladder each prepares for the fall as best he can: Flying-Squirrel spreads his small robe like wings (hence his wings), Whitefish looks down the hole and puckers his mouth (hence his small puckered mouth), and Sucker jumps unprepared and breaks every bone (hence his bones all through his flesh). At that time there were a number of different animals on earth that are not here now; they were killed in this war and transformed into stars — those we have now are only the survivors.
summary.zh: 地人奉灰熊為酋，征伐天族（星辰）；眾箭皆不及月，唯鷦鷯之箭釘天。箭鏈及地，眾攀之而上，灰熊殿後，體重斷鏈。其躍抓上段，反將頂端之箭拔出，全鏈墜地，征天大軍困於天界。首戰地人勝，再戰為星辰所敗；箭梯已斷，各設法下跳：鼯鼠展小裘如翼，故今有翼；白鮭俯瞰深淵，噘嘴後縮，故其口小而噘；胭脂魚貿然跳下，骨碎遍體，故其骨散於肉中。當時世間尚有多種今已不存之獸，皆歿於此戰，化為星辰——今日之獸，唯其倖存者。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Pend d'Oreille narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Arrow-chain war-on-sky cycle with etiological endings. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Earth people wanted to make war on the Sky people. Grizzly-Bear was their chief, and he called all the warriors together. They were told to shoot in turn at the moon (or sky); all did as directed, but their arrows fell short. Only Wren had not shot his arrow. Coyote said, 'He need not shoot. He is too small, and his bow and arrows are too weak.' However, Grizzly-Bear declared that Wren must have his turn. Wren shot his arrow, and it hit the moon (or sky) and stuck fast. Then the others shot their arrows, which stuck each in the nock of the preceding one, until they had made a chain reaching from the sky to the ground. Then all the people climbed up, Grizzly-Bear going last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 118 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 地上的人們想向天上的人們開戰。灰熊是他們的酋長，他召集了所有的戰士。他們奉命輪流朝月亮（或天空）射箭；大家都照著做了，但他們的箭都射不到。只有鷦鷯還沒射他的箭。郊狼說：「他不必射。他太小了，他的弓和箭也太弱了。」然而，灰熊堅持鷦鷯也必須輪到。鷦鷯射出他的箭，箭射中月亮（或天空），牢牢釘住。接著其他人射出他們的箭，每一支都插進前一支的箭尾凹口，直到他們連成一條從天空垂到地面的鏈子。於是所有人都爬了上去，灰熊走在最後。

passages.text: He was very heavy; and when he was up more than half way, the chain broke by his weight. He made a spring, and caught the part of the chain above him; and this caused the arrows to pull out at the top, where the leading warriors had made a hole to enter the sky. The whole chain fell down, and left the people without means of descending. The Earth people attacked the Sky people (the Stars), and defeated them in the first battle; but the latter soon gathered in such numbers that they far outnumbered the Earth people, and in the next battle routed them, killing a great many — at that time there were a number of different animals on earth that are not here now, but they were killed in this war and transformed into stars: those we have now represent only the survivors of the war.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 118 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他非常沉重；当他爬到一半以上时，锁链因他的重量而断裂。他纵身一跃，抓住了上方的那段锁链；这使得箭矢在顶端被拔出，那里正是先头 warriors 挖洞进入天空的地方。整条锁链坠落下来，使人们失去了下降的途径。地上的人攻击天上的人（星辰），并在第一场战斗中击败了他们；但后者很快聚集了如此众多的人数，远远超过了地上的人，并在下一场战斗中击溃了他们，杀死了许多人——那时地上有许多如今已不在此处的不同动物，但它们在这场战争中被杀死并化作了星辰：我们如今所见的那些仅仅代表了战争的幸存者。

passages.text: The defeated Earth people ran for the ladder, many being overtaken and killed on the way. When they found the ladder broken, each prepared himself the best way he could, so as not to fall too heavily, and one after another jumped down. Flying-Squirrel was wearing a small robe, which he spread out like wings when he jumped: therefore he has something like wings now, and came down without hurting himself. Whitefish looked down the hole before jumping; when he saw the great depth, he puckered up his mouth and drew back: therefore he has a small puckered mouth at the present day. Sucker jumped down without first preparing himself, and his bones were broken: therefore the sucker's bones are found in all parts of its flesh now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 118 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 战败的地上人奔向梯子，许多人在途中被追上并杀死。当他们发现梯子已断时，各自尽其所能做好准备，以免摔得太重，一个接一个地跳了下去。飞鼠穿着一件小袍子，跳下时将它展开如翅膀：因此它如今有类似翅膀的东西，并且安然无恙地落了下来。白鱼在跳下前朝洞里望去；当它看到那巨大的深度时，它皱起嘴缩了回去：因此它如今有一张皱起的小嘴。吸盘鱼没有先做好准备就跳了下去，它的骨头断裂了：因此如今在吸盘鱼的肉中各处都能找到它的骨头。

title.en: Conditions in Mythological Times
title.zh: 神話時代之世情

region.en: Coeur d'Alene country, Idaho (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地，愛達荷州（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 1. Conditions in Mythological Times'

summary.en: Long ago the earth was different: much wind and heat, little rain or snow, very dry, thunder frequent and lightning killing many people, and many monsters killing them. Gradually these conditions were changed by Coyote and others, who made transformations beneficial to the people; Coyote also introduced the salmon, made fishing-places, and taught the people many arts. Giants and dwarfs of several kinds inhabited mountains and forests, and Coyote did not transform all of them — some are said to exist at the present day, as do many 'mysteries' both land and water; even many beings that Coyote transformed had not all their evil powers taken from them, and sometimes harm people still.
summary.zh: 上古之世，天地異於今：多風多熱，雨雪稀少，大地乾燥；雷聲頻繁，閃電殺人；怪物橫行。後郊狼與諸賢漸次整治，多行利民之變；郊狼又引鮭魚、闢漁場、授民諸藝。山林之間，巨人與矮人族類繁多，郊狼未及盡化——至今猶有存者；水陸諸『神祕』亦然。即為郊狼所化者，惡力未必盡除，今仍有害人之時。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A long time ago conditions on the earth were different from what they are now, and people had a hard time to live. There was much wind and heat, and little rain or snow; it was very dry. Some say thunder was frequent, and lightning killed many people. Many monsters lived on earth and killed people. Gradually these conditions were changed by Coyote and others, who made many transformations beneficial to the people. Coyote also introduced the salmon, made fishing-places, and taught the people many arts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 119 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，地上的状况与现在不同，人们生活艰难。风多热多，雨雪稀少；非常干燥。有人说雷声频繁，闪电杀死了许多人。许多怪物生活在地上并杀人。渐渐地，这些状况被郊狼和其他人所改变，他们做出了许多对人们有益的转变。郊狼还引入了鲑鱼，开辟了捕鱼之地，并教给人们许多技艺。

passages.text: Giants and dwarfs of several kinds inhabited some parts of the country, particularly mountains and forests. Coyote did not transform all of them, and some are said to exist at the present day. In the same way some 'mysteries' — both land and water beings — continue to exist. Even many beings that Coyote transformed had not all their evil powers taken from them, and they sometimes harm people at the present day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 119 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 几种巨人和矮人居住在该地区的某些地方，尤其是山区和森林。郊狼并没有将他们全部转变，据说有些至今仍然存在。同样，一些“奥秘”——包括陆地和水的存在物——继续存在。甚至许多被郊狼转变的存在物也没有被完全剥夺其邪恶的力量，它们如今有时还会伤害人们。

title.en: Old-One of the Coeur d'Alene: The Chief Who Became the Moon
title.zh: 柯達倫之老者：化月之神

region.en: Coeur d'Alene country, Idaho (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地，愛達荷州（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 2. Old-One'

summary.en: Spoxani'tcElt was a chief and a great man, often appearing in the shape of an old man and helping the people: he travelled about, visited the people, learned what they did, and when he saw that they did not know how to act, he taught them. He did many good, helpful, and kind things, and never fooled people, like Coyote. He was like Christ of the whites, because he did many wonderful things, and always spoke good and did good; at last he ascended to the sky, and was transformed into the moon.
summary.zh: Spoxani'tcElt 乃酋長偉人，常化為老翁濟世：遊歷四方，訪問民眾，察其所為，見其不知者則教之。行善濟人，從不像郊狼那樣捉弄人。彼如白人之基督，多行奇事，言必善，行必善；終升天界，化為明月。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The informant's Christian analogy is part of the recorded telling. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Spoxani'tcElt was a chief and a great man. He often appeared in the shape of an old man, and helped the people; he travelled about, visited the people, and learned what they did. When he saw that they did not know how to act, he taught them. He did many good, helpful, and kind things, and never fooled people, like Coyote. He was like Christ of the whites, because he did many wonderful things, and always spoke good and did good. At last he ascended to the sky, and was transformed into the moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 119-120 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: Spoxani'tcElt 是一位酋长，也是一位伟人。他常以老人的形象出现，帮助人们；他四处游历，拜访人们，了解他们所做之事。当他看到他们不知如何行事时，便教导他们。他做了许多善良、有益和仁慈的事，从不象郊狼那样愚弄人们。他象白人的基督一样，因为他做了许多奇妙的事，总是说好话、行善事。最后他升上天空，化作了月亮。

title.en: Coyote's Son: The Tree to the Sky and the Spider Rope
title.zh: 郊狼之子：通天樹與蜘蛛索

region.en: Eagle tree grown to the sky; spider country (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 通天之鷹樹與蜘蛛之國（象徵定位於柯達倫）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 3. Coyote's Son'

summary.en: Jealous of his son To'rtorsEmstEm, Coyote lures him to climb for an eagle's nest, blinking his eyes all the while — 'I am afraid some dust may get into my eyes and blind me' — each blink making the tree grow taller until it reaches the sky. In the new country the youth finds two Spider people quarrelling over Indian-hemp; deaf to beads and necklaces, they listen at once to two fathoms of hemp apiece, and let him down to earth by a rope in a basket — stop four times, turn over, not rise, tug the rope when he hears the grass of his own country. Home again, he found his father and killed him.
summary.zh: 郊狼妒其子 To'rtorsEmstEm，誘其攀樹取鷹雛；攀高之際，郊狼頻頻眨眼——『怕灰塵入眼』——每眨一次，樹便長高一截，直至通天。其子在天上新國遇蜘蛛二人爭論印第安大麻之爭；珠鏈項圈皆不動心，唯各得兩庹大麻方止爭，遂以繩繫籃縋其下凡——途中四停，每停須翻轉不可上升；聞故鄉草聲即可出籃。既歸，尋得其父而殺之。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Sky-ascent cycle (cf. Thompson name parallels noted by Teit). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was jealous of his son To'rtorsEmstEm, and wanted to get rid of him. He told him that he knew of an eagle's nest in a tree, and induced him to go there with him and climb for it, saying that he wanted the young eagles for their tail-feathers. When up quite high, the youth looked down and saw his father blinking his eyes. 'Why are you doing that, father?' Coyote answered, 'I am afraid some dust may get into my eyes and blind me.' By blinking his eyes Coyote made the tree grow tall: each time he blinked, the tree grew. To'rtorsEmstEm looked down again, and saw his father still looking up and blinking his eyes. The tree grew up until it reached the sky, and there To'rtorsEmstEm found himself in a new country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 120 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼嫉妒他的儿子 To'rtorsEmstEm，想要除掉他。他告诉儿子他知道一棵树上有一个鹰巢，并诱使儿子与他同去爬树取巢，说他想用雏鹰的尾羽。当爬到相当高时，年轻人向下望去，看见父亲在眨眼。“父亲，你为什么这样做？”郊狼回答说：“我怕有些灰尘会进入我的眼睛，使我失明。”郊狼通过眨眼使树长高：每当他眨眼，树就长高。To'rtorsEmstEm 再次向下望去，看见父亲仍在向上看并眨着眼睛。树一直长高，直到触及天空，在那里 To'rtorsEmstEm 发现自己身处一个新的国度。

passages.text: He travelled about, and at last came to a lodge where he heard talking: two Spider people inside were quarrelling about Indian-hemp, one saying it grew one way and belonged to him, the other saying it grew another way and belonged to him. 'Grandchildren, I want you to take me back to my country,' he addressed them, but they paid no attention; beads and necklaces were offered, and still no heed. Then he offered them each two fathoms of Indian-hemp, and at once they ceased their quarrelling and became attentive, promising to let him down to his country by a rope. They put him into a basket with the rope fastened to it: 'You will stop four times on your way down. You must not rise, but turn over; then the basket will proceed. When the basket stops the fourth time, you will be on the earth; and when you hear the grass, you will know that you are in your own country. Then step out of the basket and tug the rope, and we will pull it up.' He did as directed, and they pulled it up. To'rtorsEmstEm went home, found his father, and killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 120-121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他四處遊歷，最後來到一間小屋，聽見裡頭有說話聲：兩個蜘蛛人在屋內為印第安大麻爭吵，一個說它朝某個方向生長、是屬於他的，另一個說它朝另一個方向生長、是屬於他的。「孫子們，我希望你們帶我回到我的家鄉。」他向他們說道，但他們毫不理會；他獻上珠子和項鍊，他們依然不加理睬。於是他給他們每人兩噚長的印第安大麻，他們立刻停止爭吵，變得專心起來，答應用繩子把他垂降到他的家鄉。他們把他放進籃子，並把繩子繫在籃上：「你在下墜途中會停四次。你不可起身，而要翻身；這樣籃子便會繼續前進。當籃子第四次停下時，你就到了地上；當你聽見草的聲音，就知道自己已身在自己的家鄉。那時你便跨出籃子，拉一拉繩子，我們就把繩子拉上來。」他照著指示做了，他們便把繩子拉了上來。托爾托爾塞姆斯泰姆回到家，找到他的父親，把他殺了。

title.en: Coyote and the Sun: The Stolen Heart
title.zh: 郊狼與太陽：竊心記

region.en: Drinking-place of the Sun at the edge of the earth (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 大地邊界太陽飲水處（象徵定位於柯達倫）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 4. Coyote and the Sun'

summary.en: The Sun had killed Coyote's children, and Coyote resolved on revenge: lying in wait, he kills the Sun as it comes down from the sky to drink, and cuts out its heart — whereupon the earth becomes totally dark. Carrying the heart home, each step he takes he treads on the Sun (or Sun's body), can make no progress, and at last, exhausted, places the heart back on the Sun; the Sun comes to life at once, and there is light over the world as before.
summary.zh: 太陽殺郊狼諸子，郊狼誓報：伏於太陽下凡飲水之處，殺之剜心。剎那間天地全黑。郊狼攜心歸家，然而每跨一步，必踏太陽之軀，寸步難行；力竭之餘，將心放回太陽之身。太陽頃刻復生，世界重見光明。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Sun-capture cluster. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Sun had killed Coyote's children, and Coyote resolved to take revenge. He lay in wait; and when the Sun came down from the sky to drink, he killed him and cut out his heart. At once the earth became totally dark. Coyote tried to go home carrying Sun's heart; but each time he made a step, he trod on the Sun (or Sun's body). He could make no progress; and at last he was exhausted, and placed the heart on the Sun. The latter at once came to life, and there was light over the world, as before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 太陽殺了郊狼的孩子們，郊狼決心報仇。他埋伏等候；當太陽從天上下來喝水時，他殺了太陽，並挖出他的心臟。大地立刻變得一片漆黑。郊狼帶著太陽的心臟想回家；但他每走一步，都踩在太陽（或太陽的屍身）上。他寸步難行；最後他筋疲力盡，把心臟放回太陽身上。太陽立刻復活，世界又像從前一樣有了光明。

title.en: Coyote Introduces Salmon to the Coeur d'Alene
title.zh: 郊狼引鮭：柯達倫版本

region.en: Dam of the four women on the Columbia River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河四女之壩（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 5. Coyote introduces Salmon'

summary.en: Four women on the Columbia River hold the salmon back from the interior with a dam, attacking and eating whoever comes near. Coyote changes himself into a board, floats down to the dam, becomes a baby, and is taken in to be reared by the husbandless, childless women; slipping out 'for a drink,' he undermines the dam for three days, and on the fourth, found out, he tears out the last pieces under their clubs — his armor protecting him — and leaps to the opposite bank as the water bursts through. Great numbers of salmon ascend the river, and Coyote conducts them up the streams, introducing them in many places; thus he benefited his people, for before this the Indian tribes of the interior had no salmon.
summary.zh: 哥倫比亞河上四女築壩攔鮭，近者皆遭其噬。郊狼化為木板漂流至壩，再化為嬰兒，被無夫無子之四女拾回收養。借口出壩飲水，三度潛掘壩基；第四日事發，四女持棒亂擊其手足，然其有甲護身。郊狼拆去最後幾塊，水決而出，他躍至對岸。群鮭上溯，郊狼引之溯流而上，遍置於諸水——故內陸諸族自此始得鮭魚，民受其惠。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Salmon-liberation cycle, Coeur d'Alene version. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Four women who lived on the Columbia River had a dam which held the salmon from ascending to the interior. Whoever came near them was attacked and eaten by them. Coyote heard of them and their salmon, and resolved to go and break the dam. He changed himself into a board, and floated down the stream until he reached the dam; then he changed himself into a baby. The women were out on the dam catching salmon; they saw him, and, thinking that he was a baby, said they would take him to their house and rear him as their son, for they were glad to have a child, having neither husbands nor children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 住在哥倫比亞河畔的四個女人築有一道水壩，擋住鮭魚，使牠們無法溯游到內陸。凡是走近她們的人，都會遭到她們攻擊並被吃掉。郊狼聽說了她們和她們的鮭魚，決心前去破壞水壩。他把自己變成一塊木板，順流漂下，直到抵達水壩；然後他把自己變成一個嬰兒。那些女人正在壩上捕鮭魚；她們看見了他，以為他是個嬰兒，便說要把他帶回家撫養，當作自己的兒子，因為她們既無丈夫也無子女，很高興能有個孩子。

passages.text: After Coyote had been with them a while, he wanted to go out on the dam to have a drink, and they gave their permission. He began to undermine and break up the dam, but did not stay very long for fear of arousing their suspicions; he did so on three days, and the dam was nearly broken through. On the fourth day he stayed longer than usual, and the women went to see what was the matter. When they came to the river-bank and looked down, they saw Coyote tearing down their dam. They rushed at him and clubbed him over hands and arms, but he was protected by armor. Coyote tore out the last pieces; now the water rushed through the break, and Coyote jumped to the opposite side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼與她們同住了一段時日後，想要到壩上喝水，她們便准許了。他開始從底下掏挖、破壞水壩，但不敢待得太久，怕引起她們的疑心；他這樣做了三天，水壩幾乎被鑿穿了。第四天他待得比平常久，那些女人便前去查看是怎麼回事。她們來到河岸往下一看，只見郊狼正在拆毀她們的水壩。她們朝他衝去，用棍棒打他的手和手臂，但他有護甲保護。郊狼扯下最後幾塊；此時河水從缺口奔湧而出，郊狼便跳到了對岸。

passages.text: Most of the dam was carried away, and great numbers of salmon ascended the river. Coyote conducted them up the streams, introducing them in many places; thus Coyote benefited his people, for before this the Indian tribes of the interior had no salmon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 121 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 水壩大部分都被沖走了，大批鮭魚溯河而上。郊狼引領牠們沿各條溪流而上，在許多地方放流牠們；郊狼就這樣造福了他的族人，因為在此之前，內陸的印第安部族是沒有鮭魚的。

title.en: Coyote and Wewel'tc: The Big-Mouthed Pass Monster
title.zh: 郊狼與韋韋爾茨：隘口巨口怪
