region.en: Passes between the hills of the Coeur d'Alene country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地山隘（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 6. Coyote and Wewel'tc'

summary.en: A monster used to set his head in the gaps between hills with his mouth wide open; people crossing the hills walked into his mouth and on into his stomach without noticing it, and many were thus swallowed and eaten. 'Oh, he is nothing! I shall go and kill him,' said Coyote, taking a long tamarack pole; a voice at the pass called, 'Where are you going, Coyote?' — and when Coyote answered that he was seeking the man-eating monster, 'Don't kill him!' — 'Well, if you promise not to eat people, I will spare you.' The monster promised, and Coyote transformed him into the wewel'kc-bird: 'You shall be a bird with a big mouth, but shall not be able to eat people any more.'
summary.zh: 有怪居於山隘，張巨口以待：越山人不知不覺步入其口，直達其胃，多有被吞者。郊狼聞之曰：『區區小怪！吾往誅之。』携長落葉松桿上山；臨隘有聲問：『郊狼欲往何處？』郊狼答：『尋食人之怪。』聲曰：『勿殺之！』郊狼曰：『若允諾不復食人，可留汝命。』怪允諾。郊狼遂化其為韋韋爾茨鳥：『自此爾為大口之鳥，不得再食人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a monster who used to go to the passes between hills, and place his head in the gap with his mouth wide open. People crossing the hills walked into his mouth, and on into his stomach, without noticing it; thus he had swallowed and eaten many people. Coyote heard of this monster, and said, 'Oh, he is nothing! I shall go and kill him.' He took a long pole of tamarack, and went up the hills. As he neared a pass, he heard a voice saying, 'Where are you going, Coyote?' He answered, 'I am seeking the monster who eats men. I will find him, and learn if he eats men. I do, but he does not.' Coyote went on. Again the voice said, 'Don't kill him!' Coyote answered, 'Well, if you promise not to eat people, I will spare you.' The monster promised. Then Coyote transformed him into the wewel'kc-bird, saying, 'You shall be a bird with a big mouth, but shall not be able to eat people any more.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 121-122 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個怪物，常到山丘之間的山口去，把頭擱在隘口裡，張開大嘴。翻越山丘的人走進他的嘴裡，一路走進他的肚子，卻渾然不覺；他就這樣吞下並吃掉了許多人。郊狼聽說了這個怪物，說道：「唉，他算不了什麼！我要去殺了他。」他拿了一根長長的落葉松木桿，往山上走去。當他走近一處山口時，他聽見一個聲音說：「郊狼，你要去哪裡？」他回答：「我在尋找那個吃人的怪物。我要找到他，弄清楚他是否吃人。我吃人，但他不吃。」郊狼繼續往前走。那聲音又說：「別殺他！」郊狼回答：「好吧，如果你答應不再吃人，我就饒了你。」怪物答應了。於是郊狼把他變成威威爾克鳥，說道：「你將成為一隻大嘴的鳥，但再也不能吃人了。」

title.en: Division of the Cannibal's Body
title.zh: 分食人魔之屍

region.en: Mouth of the Palouse River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕盧斯河口（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 7. Division of the Cannibal's Body'

summary.en: A large monster around the mouth of the Palouse River had killed many people; a man gifted with magic attacked him in his house, and after a long combat the monster died. The victor threw his ornaments and clothing about, cut up the body, and threw a piece to each tribe: the head down the river to the Wishram (big heads), the scalp to the Crows (long hair), the ribs and chest to the Nez Perce (large-bodied), the legs to the Blackfeet (a tall people), the heart to the Coeur d'Alene — noted ever after as brave fighters of cruel disposition — and pieces to the Salish, the Columbias and all the rest. Two tribes had been forgotten; finding no scraps, he wiped his knife with a bunch of grass and threw the knife to one tribe, probably the Thompson, and the grass to the SEntatuu'li of Hangman's Creek, Spokane — who therefore have never been a numerous people.
summary.zh: 帕盧斯河口巨魔殺人無算；有神通者入其宅與之鬥，久戰而誅之。勝者散其飾物衣物，剖其屍分擲諸族：頭擲下游之威什拉姆人——故其頭大；髮皮擲烏鴉——故其髮長；肋胸擲內茲珀斯人——故其軀偉；腿擲黑腳人——故其身高；心擲柯達倫人——故其族以勇戰剛烈著稱；餘肉分與薩利什、哥倫比亞等各族。尚有二族被遺忘；遍尋無餘屑，乃以草拭刀，擲刀與一族（或即湯普森人），擲草與斯波坎漢人溪之 SEntatuu'li——故其族人丁始終不旺。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Dismemberment ethnogony parallel (Ymir/Pangu/Purusha cluster). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once a large monster inhabited the country around the mouth of the Palouse River. He had killed many people. Coyote, or some other man gifted with magic, made up his mind to rid the country of this evil being. He went to his house and attacked him; the combat lasted a long time, and ended with the monster's death. Then the victor took off the ornaments and clothing of his victim, and threw them about; then he cut up the body, and threw a piece to each tribe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 122 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一隻巨大的怪物居住在帕盧斯河口一帶的地方。牠殺害了許多人。郊狼，或另一位具有法力的男子，下定決心要為這地方除去這個邪惡的存在。他前往牠的住處攻擊牠；這場搏鬥持續了很久，最後以怪物的死亡告終。接著，勝利者脫下他獵物的飾物與衣物，將它們四處拋擲；然後他切開屍體，把一塊扔給每一個部族。

passages.text: He threw the head down the river to the Wishram: therefore they now have big heads. He threw the scalp to the Crows, for they have long hair. He cut out the ribs and chest and threw them to the Nez Perce: therefore they are large-bodied. He threw the legs to the Blackfeet: therefore they are a tall people. He threw the heart to the Coeur d'Alene: therefore they became noted as brave fighters, and of cruel disposition. Thus he threw pieces to all the tribes — to the Salish, to the Columbias, and so on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 122 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他把頭顱扔向下游的威什拉姆人：因此他們如今頭很大。他把頭皮扔給烏鴉族，因為他們頭髮長。他切下肋骨與胸膛，扔給內茲珀斯人：因此他們體格魁梧。他把腿扔給黑腳人：因此他們是身材高大的人民。他把心扔給科達倫人：因此他們以勇猛的戰士著稱，性情殘酷。他就這樣把一塊塊扔給所有的部族——給薩利什人、給哥倫比亞人，諸如此類。

passages.text: He thought every one had received a piece; then he remembered that two tribes had been forgotten. He looked around, but could find no scraps to give them. He took his knife, and, after wiping it with a bunch of grass, threw it to one tribe, probably the Thompson; he threw the grass to the SEntatuu'li. Therefore the latter have never been a numerous people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 122 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他以為每一個人都分到了一塊；然後他想起有兩個部族被遺忘了。他環顧四周，卻找不到任何碎塊可以給他們。他拿起自己的刀，用一束草擦拭過後，把刀扔給其中一個部族，大概是湯普森人；他把草扔給森塔圖烏利人。因此後者從來不是一個人口眾多的民族。

title.en: The Sun and the Moon: Choosing the Carriers
title.zh: 日月擔夫

region.en: Sky above the Coeur d'Alene country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地上空（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 8. The Sun and the Moon'

summary.en: The people could not manage the sun: carriers went too near — killing many by heat — too far, or zigzag, and were deposed one after another. Robin was elected, but soon came so near that the people fled into the water and stayed immersed all day, until even the water got hot; then a one-eyed man, .s.tsakozaltsasa'-xkEn, was chosen, who keeps a straight and even course and carries the sun yet. The moon fared as badly: Coyote offered to carry it, and in his nightly travels called out people's names and told what they were doing — loudly, when he saw married people together — until the annoyed people deposed him and asked Spoxani'tcElt (Old-One) to take his place; he did his work perfectly, and carries the moon yet.
summary.zh: 世人苦於日行無度：擔日者或太近灼人、或太遠失明、或曲行無定，相繼被廢。眾乃選知更鳥擔日，然其不久便贴近大地，人皆整日泡於水中，連水都燒熱了。於是改選獨眼人 .s.tsakozaltsasa'-xkEn，其行路平直有度，至今擔日。月亦然：郊狼自薦，夜行時高唱人名，揭露各人所為——見夫婦同寢，更是聲震四野——眾人不堪其擾，遂廢之，請老者 Spoxani'tcElt 代之；其行事盡善，至今擔月。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The people had trouble with the sun. They could not manage to make it go right. They tried different people to carry it, but they did not do it properly, and the people deposed them: most of them did not carry it at the right distance from the earth; some went in a zigzag course, sometimes too far away, then too near; those who carried it too near killed many people by the heat. Then the people chose Robin to carry the sun, for they could not do without heat and light; he had to travel only in the daytime, for at night the moon was carried instead. Robin carried the sun, but soon came so near to the earth that the people had to flee to the water and keep themselves immersed all day; soon even the water got hot. Therefore they deposed Robin, and elected a one-eyed man called .s.tsakozaltsasa'-xkEn in his stead. This man was able to keep a straight and even course in the sky, and carries the sun yet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 123 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人們與太陽起了麻煩。他們無法讓它正常運行。他們試過讓不同的人來搬運它，但他們都做得不對，人們便將他們撤換：他們大多沒有讓太陽與大地保持適當的距離；有些人走的是曲折的路線，時而太遠，時而太近；那些把它搬得太近的人以酷熱殺死了許多人。於是眾人選了知更鳥來搬運太陽，因為他們不能沒有熱與光；他只能在白天行進，因為夜間改由月亮來搬運。知更鳥搬運太陽，但不久便離大地太近，人們只得逃到水裡，整日泡在水中；不久連水也變熱了。因此他們撤換了知更鳥，改選一位名叫 .s.tsakozaltsasa'-xkEn 的獨眼人代替他。這個人能在天空中保持筆直而平穩的路線，至今仍搬運著太陽。

passages.text: At the same time the people had trouble with the moon. They had tried several people to carry it, but none of them had done it properly. Coyote had offered to carry it, but the people did not trust him; at last they thought they would try him. In his nightly travels he called out people's names, and told what they were doing. When he saw married people together, he called out their names loudly, so that every one could hear, and told what they were doing. This so much annoyed the people that they deposed him, and asked Spoxani'tcElt to take his place. The latter did his work perfectly, and carries the moon yet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 123 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同時，人們與月亮也起了麻煩。他們試過好幾個人來搬運它，但沒有一個人做得妥當。郊狼曾自願搬運它，但人們不信任他；最後他們想不妨一試。他在夜間行進時呼喊人們的名字，並說出他們正在做什麼。當他看到夫婦在一起時，便大聲喊出他們的名字，讓每個人都能聽見，並說出他們正在做什麼。這使人們極為惱怒，於是將他撤換，並請斯波哈尼特塞爾特接替他的位置。後者把工作做得完美無缺，至今仍搬運著月亮。

title.en: Toad and the Moon
title.zh: 蟾蜍與月

region.en: Feast of the moon at Spoxani'tcElt's house (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 老者家中月神之宴（象徵定位於柯達倫）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 9. Toad and the Moon'

summary.en: After Spoxani'tcElt took up the duty of being moon, he invited the people to a feast, and the house was soon crowded. Toad came along, found it full, was told 'There is no place to sit,' went home angry, and made a heavy rain that penetrated everything, putting out lights and fires. Driven from tent to tent, under canoes, the people followed a light to Toad's house, dry inside, and crowded in; then Toad jumped on Spoxani'tcElt's face and sat there, and at once the rain stopped. The people tried to pull Toad off his face and did not succeed — the marks of Toad may still be seen on the moon.
summary.zh: 老者既擔月，設宴款眾；屋中人滿。蟾蜍至，問座處，答曰：『無隙可坐。』蟾怒歸，召大雨，透屋滅燈熄火。眾人倉皇避雨，自帳至舟底皆滲漏；見一光，趨之——乃蟾蜍之屋，內中乾爽——遂擠入。蟾蜍一躍而上，坐在老者面上，雨立止。眾欲拽之不下——月面上蟾蜍之影，至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: After Spoxani'tcElt had taken up the duty of being moon, he invited the people to a feast; so many people went to the feast that his house was soon crowded. Toad came along, and found the house full. She asked where she was to sit, and he answered, 'There is no place to sit.' She became angry, and returned to her own house; then she made a heavy rain, which penetrated everything and put out lights and fires.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 123 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 斯波哈尼特塞爾特擔起月亮的職責之後，邀請人們赴宴；赴宴的人如此之多，他的屋子很快就擠滿了。蟾蜍來了，發現屋裡已滿。她問自己該坐在哪裡，他回答：『沒有位子可坐了。』她勃然大怒，回到自己的屋子；接著她降下一場大雨，雨水滲透一切，澆熄了燈火與爐火。

passages.text: As more people arrived, they crowded inside, saying, 'Chief, where are we to sit? It is wet outside.' At last, as the rain came pouring through the roof of the house, all the people cried aloud, 'Chief, where are we to sit? Where can we go to be out of the rain?' They went from tent to tent, but it rained through them all; they went under canoes, but it rained through them also. Finally they saw a light, and went to it: it was in Toad's house, and inside it was quite dry. They crowded in. Then Toad jumped on Spoxani'tcElt's face, and sat there; at once the rain stopped. The people tried to pull Toad off his face, but did not succeed. The marks of Toad may still be seen on the moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 123-124 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨著更多人抵達，他們擠進屋內，說道：「酋長，我們該坐哪裡？外頭濕透了。」最後，當雨水從屋頂傾瀉而下時，所有人都大聲喊道：「酋長，我們該坐哪裡？我們能去哪裡避雨？」他們從一頂帳篷走到另一頂帳篷，但雨水穿透了每一頂；他們躲到獨木舟下，雨水也同樣穿透了獨木舟。最後他們看見一道光，便朝它走去：那光在蟾蜍的屋裡，屋內十分乾燥。他們擠了進去。接著蟾蜍跳到斯波克薩尼特塞爾特（Spoxani'tcElt）的臉上，坐在那裡；雨立刻停了。人們試圖把蟾蜍從他臉上拉下來，卻沒有成功。蟾蜍的痕跡至今仍可在月亮上見到。

title.en: The Wind in Coyote's Snare
title.zh: 郊狼縛風

region.en: Windy plains of the Coeur d'Alene country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地多風之原（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 10. The Wind'

summary.en: The wind used to blow hard all the time; the people had no peace, and many were hurt. Coyote made a snare and tried to catch the Wind, but Wind always passed through it; he made his snare smaller and smaller, and finally caught the Wind. Then he took away its power of hurting the people, and released it — since then the wind has been as we know it to-day.
summary.zh: 古時終日狂風，民無寧日，多受其害。郊狼結網捕風，風屢穿網而過；網愈結愈小，終於縛住風。郊狼收其害人之力，然後放風歸山——故今日之風，溫馴如常。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The wind used to blow hard all the time. The people had no peace, and many were hurt. Then Coyote made a snare and tried to catch the Wind, but Wind always passed through his snare. He made his snare smaller and smaller, and finally caught the Wind. Then he took away his power of hurting the people, and released it. Since then the wind has been as we know it to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 124 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前風總是猛烈地吹著。人們不得安寧，許多人受了傷。於是郊狼做了一個套索，想捕捉風，但風總是穿過他的套索。他把套索做得越來越小，終於捉住了風。接著他奪走了風傷害人們的力量，然後將它釋放。自那時起，風便如我們今日所知的那般。

title.en: The Hot and Cold Winds
title.zh: 熱風與寒風

region.en: Between the far north and the south, wind-bag countries (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南北風囊之國之間（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 11. The Hot and Cold Winds'

summary.en: Formerly the Earth was vexed with hot and cold winds caused by the Wind people striving with each other: the Cold-Wind people in the far north pressed the bag in which they kept the wind, and a cold wind rushed south; the Hot-Wind people, becoming cold, pressed their own wind-bag, and a hot wind rushed north, making the Cold-Wind people sick, who pressed their bag again. Thus the conflict continued constantly between the two, until some one made peace between these people, or curtailed their powers — therefore cold and warm winds blow as they do now.
summary.zh: 上古之世，風族相爭，冷熱之風肆虐大地。寒風族居極北，按其風囊，寒風南掃；熱風族覺冷，急按己囊，熱風北襲，寒族遂病，復按其囊。兩族相持不休。後有賢者為之和解，或削其力——故今之冷暖二風，各行其道，不復相殘。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Formerly the Earth was vexed with hot and cold winds, caused by the Wind people, who were striving with each other. The Cold-Wind people lived in the far north, and the Hot-Wind people in the south. The Cold-Wind people would press the bag in which they kept the wind in their house, and immediately a cold wind would rush out, and blow over the country. When it reached the Hot-Wind people, they became cold, and at once pressed their wind-bag, and a hot wind rushed north. When it reached the Cold-Wind people, they became sick, and they pressed their bag. Thus the conflict continued constantly between the two. Some one made peace between these people, or curtailed their powers; therefore cold and warm winds blow as they do now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 124 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，大地飽受熱風與冷風之苦，這是由風族人所引起的，他們彼此爭鬥。冷風族人住在極北之地，熱風族人則住在南方。冷風族人會擠壓他們存放在屋內的風袋，立刻便有一陣冷風衝出，吹過大地。當冷風抵達熱風族人那裡，他們便感到寒冷，立刻擠壓自己的風袋，於是一陣熱風向北衝去。當熱風抵達冷風族人那裡，他們便生了病，於是擠壓自己的風袋。兩族之間的衝突就這樣持續不斷。有人在這些人之間調停，或削減了他們的力量；因此冷風與暖風便如現今這般吹拂。

title.en: Heat and Cold: The Two Brothers
title.zh: 熱與寒：兄弟之戰

region.en: South journey of Heat; winter of Cold (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 熱神南遊，寒神肆虐（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 12. Heat and Cold'

summary.en: Heat and Cold were two brothers, the former good-looking and the latter ugly. One fall Heat travelled south, and then Cold made up his mind to kill the people: he made the weather so cold that most of them died. Heat hurried back to save them, and made the weather so hot that he killed his brother, and the frost and ice and snow he had made disappeared. It was then ordained that cold should not prevail long at a time, and should always be driven away by heat — we see the killing of Cold by his brother every spring.
summary.zh: 熱與寒本為兄弟，兄俊弟陋。一年秋天，熱神南遊；寒神趁機肆虐，天寒地凍，民多凍斃。熱神聞訊急返，天氣頓熱，寒神竟被熱死，冰雪霜霜俱消。自此天命：寒不得久居，必為熱所驅——每年春天，我們都看見兄弟殺寒的這一幕。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Season-cycle myth. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Heat and Cold were two brothers, the former good-looking, and the latter ugly. One fall Heat travelled south, and then Cold made up his mind to kill the people: he made the weather so cold that most of the people died. Heat hurried back to save them, and made the weather so hot that he killed his brother, and the frost and ice and snow which he had made disappeared. It was then ordained that cold should not prevail long at a time, and should always be driven away by heat. We see the killing of Cold by his brother every spring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 124 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 熱與冷是兩兄弟，前者相貌俊美，後者醜陋。某年秋天，熱向南而去，冷便下定決心要殺死人們：他把天氣弄得極為寒冷，以致大多數人都死了。熱急忙趕回拯救他們，把天氣弄得極為炎熱，因而殺死了他的兄弟，於是他所造的霜、冰與雪都消失了。當時便定下規矩：寒冷不得長久持續，且總應被炎熱驅走。我們每年春天都能見到冷被其兄弟殺死。

title.en: Thunder and His Feather Dress
title.zh: 雷神與羽衣

region.en: House of Thunder in the high mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 高山雷神之居（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 13. Thunder'

summary.en: Thunder used to kill many people by shooting down large arrow-stones; when he wanted rain, he sang. A man went to his house in the high mountains and tore up his dress, which was made of feathers; after this the thunder was only able to thunder when it was about to rain, and could not kill people any more.
summary.zh: 雷神常擲大箭石殺人；欲雨則歌。一人上高山雷神之居，撕其羽衣。自此雷唯在欲雨之時作聲，再不能殺人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Thunder used to kill many people by shooting down large arrow-stones. When he wanted rain, he sang. A man went to his house in the high mountains, and tore up his dress, which was made of feathers. After this the thunder was only able to thunder when it was about to rain, and could not kill people any more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 124-125 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 雷從前會射下巨大的箭石，殺死許多人。當他想要下雨時，便歌唱。有一個人前往他位於高山上的屋子，撕破了他那件以羽毛製成的衣裳。此後，雷便只能在即將下雨時打雷，再也無法殺人了。

title.en: The Champions in the Chests: Avidichu Takes a Raja Alive
title.zh: 箱中勇士：阿維迪朱活擒蘇丹

region.en: Samudra, north Sumatra (Malay Annals geography)
region.zh: 北蘇門答臘三摩陀（《馬來紀年》地理）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VIII (Avidichu's stratagem), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The raja of Shaher al Nawi hears of rich Samudra and asks who will take its raja alive; the champion Avidichu asks for four thousand warriors and a hundred prows, sails in merchant's guise, presents himself as an ambassador — and sends forty daring warriors to the palace in chests that open from within, 'as containing the presents of Raja Shaher al Nawi.' At the moment of audience the chests burst open and the raja is seized; his own warriors stand down under the threat to his life, and the captive sultan is set to keeping hens.
summary.zh: 薩赫爾·納維之王聞三摩陀富庶，問誰能生擒其王；勇士阿維迪朱請兵四千、船百艘，喬裝商賈而來，自稱使節——並以『內可自內開啟之箱』送四十勇士入宮，詐稱『薩赫爾·納維王之禮』。覲見之際群箱迸裂，蘇丹被擒；三摩陀武士因王在敵手而不敢拔刃，被俘之蘇丹竟被罰去養雞。

sensitivity.note: Chest-trojan ruse; the humiliation (henkeeper) as narrative wound driving the rescue.

passages.text: Avidichu placed forty daring warriors in chests which opened from within, and sent them forward to the palace as containing the presents of Raja Shaher al Nawi, directing them that when he should appear before the raja to receive audience, they should suddenly issue forth and seize the raja.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VIII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿維迪楚（Avidichu）將四十名勇猛的戰士安置在可從內部開啟的箱子裡，把他們送往宮殿，聲稱箱中裝著拉惹沙赫爾·阿爾·納維（Raja Shaher al Nawi）的禮物，並指示他們：當他出現在拉惹面前接受覲見時，他們便應突然衝出，擒住拉惹。

passages.text: Avidichu proceeded to the presence of the raja and presented the letter, which was read in due form; meantime the champions started from their chests and seized the raja of Samadra. The warriors of Samadra flew to their arms, but were assured that the instant they commenced their attack the raja would be slain — and Avidichu returned with his prisoner, whom the conquering raja appointed his henkeeper.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VIII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿維迪楚前往拉惹面前，呈上書信，書信依禮宣讀；在此期間，那些勇士從箱中躍出，擒住了薩瑪德拉的拉惹。薩瑪德拉的戰士們急忙奔向兵器，卻得到保證：他們一旦發動攻擊，拉惹便會被殺——於是阿維迪楚帶著他的俘虜返回，得勝的拉惹任命他為養雞人。

title.en: The Golden Tree, the Gemmed Chessboard, the Golden Ducks: Buying Back a King
title.zh: 金樹、寶棋、金鴨：贖回君王

region.en: Shaher al Nawi and Samudra (Malay Annals geography)
region.zh: 薩赫爾·納維與三摩陀（《馬來紀年》地理）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. VIII (Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din's ransoming gifts), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din answers the humiliation with a ruse of generosity: three voyages, three gifts — a golden tree whose fruits are gems worth a bahara of gold, a gemmed chessboard worth a bahara, and two golden ducks embossed with diamonds, swimming in a basin and pecking each other of their own accord. Each time the delighted raja offers any request and each time the envoys decline; only when he swears an oath does the request come: 'present us with the man that feeds your fowls' — 'he is the raja of Pasei, but if you ask him I will give him.' The henkeeper is bathed, robed in royal vestments, and carried home.
summary.zh: 西迪·阿里以慷慨之計復仇：三次航程、三件禮物——結寶石之金樹（值一巴哈爾金）、寶石棋盤（值一巴哈爾）、鑲鑽金鴨一對，於盆中自行游動相互啄咬。王大悅，屢問所求而使者屢辭；直至王發誓必允，使者乃言：『請賜餵雞之人』——『他乃帕賽之王，但你既求，我便給你。』『養雞人』受浴、被以王服，被迎歸國。

sensitivity.note: The three-gift ruse as royal restoration; the ducks' self-motion as the marvel that unlocks the oath.

passages.text: Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din fitted out a ship with Arab merchandise, arrayed all his crew in Arab dress, and carried first a golden tree whose fruits were of various kinds of gems worth a bahara of gold, then a golden chess board whose squares were of gems, and last two ducks of gold embossed with diamonds, placed in a basin of water in which they moved and swam of their own accord and pecked each other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VIII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西迪·阿里·蓋亞斯·埃德丁裝備了一艘載有阿拉伯貨物的船，讓全體船員穿上阿拉伯服飾，先運來一棵金樹，其果實為各式各樣的寶石，價值一巴哈拉黃金；接著是一副金棋盤，其方格皆為寶石；最後是兩隻鑲嵌鑽石的金鴨，置於一盆水中，牠們在水中自行移動、游動，並互相啄擊。

passages.text: The raja, surprised at the skill, confirmed by an oath that he would grant whatever they wanted; then Sidi Ali Gheyas ed-din said: 'If you will extend to us the royal favour, present us with the man that feeds your fowls.' — 'He is the raja of Pasei, but if you ask him I will give him.' The sultan was bathed, dressed in a raja's vestments, and carried aboard amid a rising wind to Samudra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. VIII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉惹對這般技藝感到驚奇，以誓言確認他將賜予他們所想要的任何東西；於是西迪·阿里·蓋亞斯·埃德丁說道：『若您願向我們施予王室恩寵，請把餵養您家禽的人賜給我們。』——『他是帕塞的拉惹，但若你們向他請求，我便把他給你們。』蘇丹沐浴之後，穿上拉惹的服飾，在漸起的風中被帶上船，送往薩穆德拉。

title.en: The White Mouse-Deer and the Malacca Tree: The Founding of Malacca
title.zh: 白鼠鹿與滿剌加樹：滿剌加建城

region.en: Bertam river, Malacca
region.zh: 滿剌加伯淡河

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. IX-X (the founding of Malacca), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Driven from Singhapura by its conquest, Raja Secander Shah hunts at the banks of the river Bertam, standing under a spreading tree, when one of his dogs rouses a white mouse-deer — which turns and attacks the dog, driving it into the water. 'This is a fine place,' says the raja, 'where the very mouse-deer are full of courage; let us found a city here'; and asking the name of the tree above him — the malacca tree — he names the city Malacca.
summary.zh: 獅子城陷落後，西坎德·沙王流亡至伯淡河畔行獵，立於大樹濃蔭之下；獵犬驚起一隻白鼠鹿——鼠鹿竟反撲獵犬，將其逐入水中。王喜曰：『此地甚佳，連鼠鹿都如此勇敢；就在此建城。』問得頭頂之樹名為『滿剌加樹』，遂以之名城。

sensitivity.note: The best-known Malay foundation myth after the lion of Singhapura; courage of the small animal as the site's omen.

passages.text: Raja Secander Shah returned to the shore of the sea, to the banks of a river named Bertam, where he hunted, standing under the shade of a spreading tree; one of his dogs roused a white pelandok, or mouse-deer, which attacking the dog drove it into the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉惹·塞坎德爾·沙阿回到海邊，來到一條名為貝爾坦的河的岸邊，他在那裡打獵，站在一棵枝葉繁茂的樹蔭下；他的一隻狗驚起了一隻白色的鼠鹿，鼠鹿攻擊那隻狗，把牠逼入水中。

passages.text: The raja was pleased and said: 'This is a fine place, where the very mouse-deer are full of courage; let us found a city here.' Enquiring the name of the tree under which he was standing, he was informed it was named the malacca tree; 'Then let the name of the city be called Malacca' — the empire named from a tree and a fight between a mouse-deer and a dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉惹十分欣喜，說道：『這是個好地方，連鼠鹿都充滿勇氣；讓我們在此建立一座城吧。』他詢問自己所站的那棵樹的名字，得知它名叫馬六甲樹；『那麼就讓這座城取名為馬六甲吧』——這個帝國因一棵樹以及一隻鼠鹿與一隻狗之間的搏鬥而得名。

title.en: The Rotten Fort: Work Undone Every Night
title.zh: 爛城：夜夜崩解的工程

region.en: Malay Annals coast geography
region.zh: 《馬來紀年》海岸地理

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals (the fort that would not stand), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Driven from one station by stinking crocodiles, Raja Secander Shah begins building a fort at another place; by day the workmen labour, 'but at night their work all decayed' — and the place takes its name from the failure, Kota-buru, the rotten fort. The land refuses a city until the raja reaches the ground that will hold one.
summary.zh: 因惡臭之鱷而棄一地之後，西坎德·沙王於另一處築城；晝間工匠施工，『夜間工程盡毀』——其地遂以此得名『科塔布魯』，即『爛城』。大地拒絕建城，直至王抵達那片能承載城池的土地。

sensitivity.note: Failed-foundation episode inside the Malacca migration.

passages.text: Raja Secander Shah was obliged to desert the station and move to another place, where he began building a fort; by day he caused his workmen to labour, but at night their work all decayed, and the name of this place was hence called Kota-buru, the rotten fort.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉惹·塞坎德爾·沙阿不得不捨棄該地，遷往另一處，並在那裡開始築造一座堡壘；白天他讓工匠們勞作，但到了夜裡，他們的工程全都朽壞，因此這個地方便得名哥打布魯，意即腐朽之堡。

title.en: The Prophet's Dream at Malacca: The Ship from Jidda at Daybreak
title.zh: 滿剌加之夢：破曉自吉達而來之船

region.en: Malacca (court of the raja)
region.zh: 滿剌加（王庭）

period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals (the dream of Nabi Muhammed and the ship from Jidda), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Raja Kichil Besar dreams that he sees Nabi Muhammed, who testifies 'that God is the one God, and that Muhammed is his prophet'; the raja does as directed and receives the name Sultan Muhammed. 'Next morning at daybreak,' says the prophet, 'there will arrive a ship from Jidda, and will land on the shore of Malacca' — the dream and the arriving ship together fix Malacca's conversion as prophecy kept to the hour.
summary.zh: 拉賈·基奇爾·貝薩爾夢見先知穆罕默德，先知作證『上帝乃唯一之神，穆罕默德為其使者』；王依所示而行，受名『蘇丹穆罕默德』。先知言：『明晨破曉，將有一船自吉達來，泊於滿剌加海岸』——夢與船同時應驗，滿剌加之皈依遂成準時之預言。

sensitivity.note: Malacca's conversion legend; respectful treatment of the prophetic dream.

passages.text: Raja Kichil Besar dreamed one night that he saw Nabi Muhammed, who said to him: 'I testify that God is the one God, and that Muhammed is his prophet'; and Raja Kichil Besar did as he was directed by the prophet, who conferred on him the name of Sultan Muhammed. 'Next morning,' said the prophet, 'at daybreak, there will arrive a ship from Jidda, and will land on the shore of Malacca' — the promised ship that carries the new faith to the port the mouse-deer's courage had chosen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 拉惹·基奇爾·勿沙有一夜夢見先知穆罕默德，先知對他說：「我作證：真主是唯一的神，穆罕默德是他的先知」；拉惹·基奇爾·勿沙便照先知所囑而行，先知賜予他蘇丹穆罕默德之名。「明日清晨，」先知說，「破曉時分，將有一艘船自吉達抵達，並在馬六甲海岸登陸」——那艘應許之船，載著新的信仰，駛向那由鼠鹿之勇所選定的港口。

title.en: Stealing the Semangat: The Soul That Can Be Taken
title.zh: 竊取瑟瑪加：可被奪走的靈魂

region.en: Selangor, Malay Peninsula (collected by Skeat)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪（斯凱特採錄）

period: Belief recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic (1900)

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), the soul (semangat) and its abduction

summary.en: In Malay folk-theology the semangat — the soul or vital principle — is a portable object that can be coaxed, escaping 'riang semangat', or stolen outright: 'mengambil semangat orang', to take away a person's soul-power, and induce it to pass into the thief's keeping. Illness, wasting and misfortune read as soul-loss; the magician's trade is recovery, the thief's art abduction — the same verb in both crafts.
summary.zh: 馬來民間神學中，瑟瑪加（semangat，靈魂/生命力）乃可攜之物：或被誘離（riang semangat），或被 outright 竊取——『mengambil semangat orang』即取走他人之靈力，並誘其入竊者掌中。病弱衰敗皆讀作失魂；術師之業是尋回，竊者之術是奪走——二者用的是同一個動詞。

sensitivity.note: Soul-belief record; careful framing around accusations of sorcery.

passages.text: The semangat, the vital principle of Malay folk-theology, is portable: it may be escaping (riang semangat) or deliberately taken — mengambil semangat orang, to abduct a person's soul-power and induce it to pass into the taker's keeping. Sickness and wasting are read as soul-loss, and the two crafts that answer it — the magician's recovery and the thief's abduction — are mirror arts using the same verb; the soul is an object with a location, and that is what makes both possible.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Skeat (1900); not verbatim.
passages.zh: semangat，即馬來民間神學中的生命本原，是可遷移的：它可能自行逸出（riang semangat），也可能被刻意取走——mengambil semangat orang，即擄走某人的靈魂之力，誘使其轉入取者之手。疾病與消瘦被解讀為失魂，而應對失魂的兩種技藝——術士的召回與竊者的擄取——乃是使用同一動詞的鏡像之術；靈魂是一個有處所之物，而這正是兩者皆得以成立的原因。

title.en: A God Evolved in the Interior: Hose and McDougall on Bali Penyalong
title.zh: 內陸自生之神：霍斯與麥克杜格爾論巴利·珀尼亞隆

region.en: Kenyan and Madang country, remotest interior Borneo (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 婆羅洲最深內陸肯雅與馬當之地（象徵性定位）

period: Argument published by Hose & McDougall (1912), from a paper of some ten years before

source.work: Charles Hose & William McDougall, The Pagan Tribes of Borneo (1912), the origin of the Kenyah belief in a Supreme Being

summary.en: Hose and McDougall argue against borrowing as the origin of the interior's supreme god: the belief is a living one among the Madangs, 'a Kenyah tribe that inhabits a district in the remotest interior and has had no intercourse with Malays,' while the Ibans, who have had far more intercourse with Malays, show least trace of it. They conclude that the Kenyahs and Kayans evolved the conception themselves — Bali Penyalong the war-god exalted by the importance of his department — and note the difficult step: gods of abstract function like Bali Atap, who guards the house, evolved out of nature-spirits like Balingo the thunderer and Bali Sungei of the rivers.
summary.zh: 霍斯與麥克杜格爾反駁『至上神乃借自馬來人』之說：此信仰在馬當人——『居於最深內陸、從未與馬來人交往之肯雅部族』——中活著；而與馬來人交往遠多之伊班人卻幾無此觀念之痕跡。二人斷言：肯雅人與加揚人自生此概念——巴利·珀尼亞隆本為戰神，因職司之重而被抬高；最難的一步是『抽象職能之神』（如守屋之巴利·阿塔普）自自然精靈（雷神巴利諾、河神巴利·松蓋）中演化而出。

sensitivity.note: A documented argument in the comparative study of supreme beings; the recorders' hypothesis, flagged as theirs.

passages.text: It might be thought that the conception of a beneficent Supreme Being has been borrowed directly or indirectly from the Malays; but the recorders do not think this view tenable, in face of the fact that the conception is a living belief among the Madangs, a Kenyah tribe inhabiting the remotest interior with no intercourse with Malays, while the Ibans, who have had far more intercourse with Malays, show least trace of it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 或許有人會認為，一位仁慈的至高存在之觀念，是直接或間接從馬來人那裡借來的；但記錄者們認為此說難以成立，因為這一觀念乃是馬當人活生生的信仰，而馬當人是一個居住在極偏遠內陸、與馬來人毫無往來的肯雅族部落；反之，與馬來人往來遠為頻繁的伊班人，卻幾乎不見此觀念的痕跡。

passages.text: They are inclined to suppose that the tribes of the interior evolved the conception for themselves — Bali Penyalong of the Kenyahs being their god of war exalted above all others by the importance of the department he presides over — the difficult step being gods of abstract function, such as Bali Atap who guards the house, evolved out of nature-spirits like Balingo and Bali Sungei.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Hose & McDougall (1912); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們傾向於設想，內陸各部落是自行演化出這一觀念的——肯雅人的巴利·佩尼亞隆，因其司掌之領域的重要性而被尊崇於諸神之上，成為他們的戰神——而艱難的一步，則在於由巴林戈與巴利·蘇蓋之類的自然精靈，演化出司掌抽象職能的神祇，例如守護家宅的巴利·阿塔普。

title.en: Kigutikak Carried Off by the Whalers
title.zh: 被捕鯨船擄走的基古提卡克

region.en: Ameralik shore and the European whale-ships
region.zh: 阿梅拉利克海岸與歐洲捕鯨船

period: Inuit oral tradition; founded on a real event of violence by the first European visitors, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 71 'Kigutikak who was carried off by the Whalers', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Seized kayak and all by malevolent whalers, Kigutikak rides out a deck-sweeping wave alone, holding the gunwale while the sea tears the rest away. In Europe he follows the captain's heels through gnat-swarms of gawkers, fends off sword-wielding jokers with a knobbed rope, buries two men who would kill him on his partridge walks, and — finding his brother — pools their money to buy and build a ship. Mast-cutting lands him in a cave of pleasant solitary women who fill his pockets; his brother dies, and he burns his own ship, sinks his stores in the sea, and slips home from the last whaler, pockets stuffed with old iron.
summary.zh: 被惡意的捕鯨者連人帶艇擄上船的基古提卡克，在巨浪橫掃甲板時獨自抓緊船舷——海水撕裂其餘船舷而獨留他立身之處。在歐洲，他緊跟船長的鞋跟穿過圍觀的人群，以帶結的繩索擊退持劍戲弄者，又在采雷鳥的路上埋葬了兩個要殺他的人；尋得兄弟後，二人合資造船備航。伐木取桅時他被引進一群快樂的獨居女子之穴，滿袋金錢而歸；兄弟病亡，他焚燬自造的船、將物資沉海，趁最後一班捕鯨船返航之機揣著滿袋舊鐵溜回故土。

sensitivity.note: Kidnapping of Greenlanders by European ships is a documented historical practice (Rink's note analyses the tale's development from Kigutikak's own reported account). Killing and the cave-women episode recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: In former times when European ships used to come to the Ameralik shore, the whalers and natives met for trading. Once a whaler warned Kigutikak and his brother: 'Ye had better beware of approaching my countrymen yonder; they intend some evil.' One day Kigutikak had got some gifts from the sailors; his brother on seeing this envied his good luck, and gathering some of his goods for barter went off to the malevolent whalers. Kigutikak also collected some trifles and followed his brother; but when the brother approached the ship a well-manned boat came off to meet him — they seized him and hoisted him on deck, kayak and all. Kigutikak having shared the same fate, the ship weighed anchor and stood out to sea. When fairly clear of land the wind rose and the sea ran high; once a great wave came sweeping the deck, and the sailors all rushed below for safety. Kigutikak alone remained on deck, and as the sea washed over he took firm hold of the gunwale — except a small space where Kigutikak had planted himself, the sea carried away every part of the gunwale with a loud crash; and when the sailors appeared on deck they could not but see that he had been in great danger. Afterwards, when the storm had passed and they had made a good distance off the land, which was now out of sight, it blew another gale — this time the sailors persuaded him to go below with them before they shipped another sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 71 'Kigutikak who was carried off by the Whalers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，當歐洲船隻常來阿梅拉利克海岸時，捕鯨者與當地人會面進行交易。有一次，一名捕鯨者警告基古提卡克和他的兄弟：「你們最好當心，別靠近那邊我的同胞；他們心懷不軌。」有一天，基古提卡克從水手那裡得到了一些禮物；他的兄弟見此，嫉妒他的好運，便收拾了一些貨物前去與那些心懷惡意的捕鯨者交易。基古提卡克也收集了一些小物件，跟隨兄弟而去；但當兄弟靠近船隻時，一艘滿載人手的划艇駛來迎他——他們抓住他，連同皮划艇一併吊上甲板。基古提卡克也遭遇了同樣的命運，船便起錨出海。當船完全離開陸地後，風起了，海面波濤洶湧；一次，一個巨浪掃過甲板，水手們全都衝到艙下避險。唯有基古提卡克留在甲板上，當海水沖刷而過時，他緊緊抓住船舷——除了基古提卡克所立的一小塊地方之外，海水伴著一聲巨響把船舷的其餘部分全都沖走了；當水手們出現在甲板上時，他們不得不看出他方才身處極大的危險之中。後來，風暴過去，他們已遠離陸地，陸地此時已不見蹤影，又刮起了一陣大風——這一次，水手們勸他在再進一次海水之前與他們一同下艙。

passages.text: Approaching their own country they shortened sail, although the wind was fair, lest it should be known whom they had brought with them; only at midnight they stood in for the land and anchored. People on shore were heard to call out, 'The trading ships are coming' — at this news all the houses were quickly illuminated, and afterwards the seamen were invited to come on shore, but the captain would not leave the ship before next morning. The following day he went on shore taking the Kalaleks (Greenlanders) with him; people having got news of their presence gathered like gnats in great swarms to catch sight of them. In the boat the captain gave orders to them saying, 'When I am going among people on shore, ye must not be staring about you, but keep your eyes fixed on my heels; if ye don't mind my words and take your eyes off my heels, ye are sure to be lost in the throng' — they answered, 'Well, we will follow thee closely.' On landing there was not a spot to plant their feet, such was the crowd; at last a soldier appeared and undertook to clear a passage for them by dividing the masses, and following in his wake they managed to get through. Arriving at the captain's house the brother of Kigutikak was missing; in looking round he had lost his way, but had fortunately been picked up by some other great man with whom he remained. When Kigutikak entered with the captain they found his wife moody and sulking — fancy the idea! she had a fit of jealousy; however, when the captain produced a doll from his pocket and put it on the table before her, her good temper was somewhat restored.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 71 'Kigutikak who was carried off by the Whalers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接近他們自己的國度時，儘管順風，他們仍收帆減速，以免被人知道他們帶了誰回來；直到午夜，他們才朝陸地駛去並下錨。只聽岸上的人喊道：「商船來了」——這消息一傳開，所有房屋迅速亮起了燈，隨後水手們被邀請上岸，但船長在次日早晨之前不肯離船。第二天，他帶著卡拉萊克人（格陵蘭人）一同上岸；人們得知他們在場的消息後，便如蚊蚋般成群結隊地聚集起來，爭相一睹他們的容貌。在船上，船長向他們下令道：「當我走在岸上的人群中時，你們不可東張西望，而要將目光緊盯我的腳後跟；如果你們不聽我的話，把目光從我的腳後跟上移開，你們必定會在人潮中走失」——他們回答：「好的，我們會緊緊跟隨你。」登岸時，人群擁擠得連落腳之地都沒有；最後，一名士兵出現，自告奮勇為他們分開人群、開闢通道，他們跟在他的身後，總算擠了過去。抵達船長的住所時，基古提卡克的兄弟卻不見了；他四處張望時迷了路，但幸運地被另一位大人物收留，便留在了那人那裡。當基古提卡克隨船長進屋時，他們發現船長的妻子悶悶不樂、滿臉怒氣——想想看！她竟起了嫉妒之心；然而，當船長從口袋裡掏出一個玩偶，放在她面前的桌上時，她的好脾氣才稍稍恢復。

passages.text: During Kigutikak's stay at their house one day as he was going out to the privy, on getting outside he was somewhat surprised by two big Europeans menacing him from either side with their long swords; greatly alarmed he ventured to tell his master, who forthwith gave him a bit of a rope with a large knob at one end, saying, 'Now go and open the door and hit away among them with all thy might' — having taken the rope's end he did as he was told, hitting right and left without ever looking at them. Having thus cleared a way for himself and being again ready to enter, he saw them peeping round a corner of the house covering their faces with a handkerchief, for in lashing them with the rope he had sorely hurt their eyes; his master merely said it served them quite right. During his stay at the captain's house Kigutikak sometimes went out to chase partridges; on one of these excursions he happened to meet a great big European who wanted to kill him, but he forestalled him and killed him instead — in order that no one should find out the deed he buried him on the spot and afterwards made the gravel quite smooth on the top; at home he put on an unconcerned air as if nothing at all had happened. The next day he encountered another big Kavdlunak who had the same bad fortune; but on meeting one on the same road the third day, whom he was just about to despatch, he suddenly in time recognised his brother. After having questioned each other about various matters they both fell a-weeping, and then Kigutikak asked his brother where he had come to live — 'My present master is a very grand gentleman; in following you the other day I only turned to look about once, but from that instant losing sight of you, I was happily taken up by him, and am there in want of nothing.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 71 'Kigutikak who was carried off by the Whalers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天，基古提卡克住在他們家時，正當他外出如廁，一走到屋外，便有些驚訝地發現兩名高大的歐洲人從兩側以長劍威脅他；他大為驚恐，壯著膽子去告訴他的主人，主人立刻給了他一截一端有個大結的繩子，說道：「現在去開門，用盡全力在他們中間打。」他接過繩端，照著吩咐去做，左右揮打，從不去看他們。如此為自己清出一條路後，他正準備再進屋，卻見他們從屋角探出頭來，用手帕遮著臉，因為他用繩子抽打時，重重傷了他們的眼睛；他的主人只說他們活該。基古提卡克住在船長家期間，有時外出獵捕鷓鴣；有一次這樣的遠行，他恰巧遇見一名高大魁梧的歐洲人想殺他，但他先發制人，反倒殺了對方——為了不讓任何人發現此事，他就地將他埋了，事後又把上面的礫石弄得十分平整；回到家裡，他裝作若無其事，彷彿什麼也沒發生。第二天，他又遇到另一名高大的卡夫德魯納克，同樣遭了厄運；但第三天在同一條路上又遇到一個，他正要將他解決時，卻及時認出了那是他的兄弟。彼此詢問了種種事情之後，兩人都哭了起來，接著基古提卡克問他兄弟住在何處——「我現在的主人是一位非常顯貴的紳士；那天我跟著你，只回頭張望了一次，但從那一刻起就失去了你的蹤影，我幸運地被他收留，如今在那裡什麼也不缺。」

passages.text: When Kigutikak told him what had become of the two big Kavdlunait the brother rejoined that the other day on a similar provocation he had acted the same way; they agreed to meet the day after the following, whereat they parted and each returned to his place. At the next encounter Kigutikak exclaimed, 'What a lot of money I have got!' and the brother replied, 'The same have I' — and they began to deliberate whether by adding the money together they could not buy a ship with it; the brother decided that it would not be a bad plan and should be carried out, and thus they parted. At home Kigutikak took his master into counsel: 'Could we not put our money together and buy a ship, my brother and I? Pray count it over.' 'Why, ye have plenty to get one for' — and Kigutikak soon proceeded to carry out his plan, finding materials and hiring the workmen; the hull being finished in springtime he began to talk to his master about the masts. 'They are easily got; a little south of this is a place with many straight and tall trees, just the thing for masts' — and when the time for his departure arrived his master added, 'But mark my words: when you cut trees, have great care in looking about on all sides and listen attentively. If you happen to hear any noise, then flee at once, and if you think the way hither too long, betake yourself to a steep rock a little to the north, and there you will find people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 71 'Kigutikak who was carried off by the Whalers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當基古提卡克告訴他那兩名高大的卡夫德魯納伊特遭遇了什麼之後，兄弟回答說，前幾天在類似的挑釁下，他也做了同樣的事；他們約定後天再見，於是就此分別，各自回到自己的地方。下一次相遇時，基古提卡克驚呼：「我得了好多錢！」兄弟回答：「我也一樣」——他們便開始商議，把錢合在一起，是否就能買一艘船；兄弟認定這主意不壞，應當實行，於是兩人又分別了。回到家裡，基古提卡克向主人討教：「我和我兄弟把我們的錢合起來，能不能買一艘船？請算一算吧。」「哎呀，你們的錢足夠買一艘了」——基古提卡克很快便著手實行他的計畫，找來材料，雇用工人；船體在春天完工後，他開始和主人談起桅杆的事。「那容易弄到；這兒往南不遠有個地方，長著許多又直又高的樹，正適合做桅杆」——到了他該動身的時候，主人又補了一句：「但記住我的話：砍樹的時候，務必小心環顧四周，仔細傾聽。萬一聽到什麼聲響，就立刻逃走；如果你覺得回這裡的路太遠，就往北邊不遠處的一座陡峭岩石去，在那裡你會找到人。」

passages.text: Starting for the forest he at length reached it, and soon found out the highest and most beautiful trees, very cautiously beginning to cut them down; when he was about to fell the second one he fancied he saw another tree moving, and at the same time heard a noise, but did not take any notice of either as long as he saw nothing (although he had been warned beforehand). No sooner had he caught sight of a horrid beast emerging from among the trees than he flung down his axe and took to running with all his might; on turning round he plainly saw that the beast was gaining upon him, his master's home being too far off — he retreated towards the cave, which opened all of itself and closed in the same manner as soon as he had got within, and almost instantly he heard the pursuing beast bounding against the door with a terrible roar. Inside the cave he found a lot of dissolute women, with whom he remained without caring much for getting home; as time passed and he did not return his master supposed him to have been devoured by the wild beast, but at that very time he was preparing for his departure, having first had his pockets filled with money by the women as a recompense for having slept with them. On his way home he first repaired to the forest to cut down the second tree and fetch off the tools, and then returned to his master — 'I thought the wild beast had made thee his prey; where hast thou been all this while?' — 'I was with the solitary women in the cave; they made themselves very pleasant towards me.' 'Oh, that's just what they always do; when once one gets in to them, it is no easy matter to free one's self from them and get away.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 71 'Kigutikak who was carried off by the Whalers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他動身前往森林，終於抵達，很快便找出最高最美麗的樹木，非常謹慎地開始砍伐；當他正要砍倒第二棵時，他覺得自己看見另一棵樹在移動，同時也聽到一聲響，但只要什麼也沒看見，他就不去理會（儘管事先已受過警告）。他一瞧見一頭可怕的野獸從樹林間現身，便立刻扔下斧頭，拼命奔跑；回頭一看，他清楚地看見那野獸正漸漸追上他，而主人的家又太遠——他便朝那洞穴退去，洞穴自行敞開，他一進去又同樣自行閉合，幾乎立刻他就聽見追趕的野獸以可怕的吼聲猛撞洞門。在洞裡他發現許多放蕩的女人，他便與她們廝混，不太在意回家；時間過去，他仍未歸來，他的主人以為他被野獸吞食了，但就在那時，他正準備動身，先前那些女人已把他的口袋塞滿了錢，作為與她們同寢的報酬。回家途中，他先繞到森林砍倒第二棵樹，取回工具，然後回到主人那裡——「我以為那野獸已把你當作獵物了；你這些時候都上哪兒去了？」——「我和洞裡那些獨居的女人在一起；她們對我十分殷勤。」「哦，她們一向如此；一旦有人進了她們那裡，要脫身離開可不是容易的事。」

passages.text: When the ship had been masted and was ready for sea it was put into the water, and two men set to work loading it; but on going to leave port they were only three for the ship all told — viz., the brothers and a cook. At this time the brother unfortunately fell ill, and getting worse and worse at length died, whereupon Kigutikak set on fire and burned his ship, and buried all his stores in the sea — this was about the usual time of departure for the whalers going to Greenland. His master said, 'Thou art sad and low-spirited; a walk would be a change and diversion for thee'; they set out, and arriving at a small lake found a boat moored off the shore — in this they rowed across to the other side, soon reaching another lake and a small boat, crossed this in the same manner, then proceeded to the next lake where they likewise found a boat, such being the regular means of conveyance for travellers going this way. Having moored the last boat and proceeded on their way they soon arrived at a town in the middle part of the country, where they entered a house to get refreshments; whilst they were eating they heard a cry, 'The whalers are leaving! the whalers are off!' At this news Kigutikak started, and leaving his meal unfinished he sped down and unmoored the boat, his master following at a little distance; he travelled back across the lakes all by himself, his master being continually somewhat behind. When Kigutikak at last reached the main harbour he heard that the whaling ships were all gone excepting one, whose crew had just gone ashore to undo the cables — Kigutikak was just in time to jump into the boat and get on board. His master, who all this time had been unable to keep pace with him, was now calling to the sailors to take good care of him, and watch him closely during their stay in Greenland.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 71 'Kigutikak who was carried off by the Whalers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 船裝好桅杆、準備出海後，便被放入水中，兩個人著手裝載；但等到要離港時，整艘船總共只有三人——即那對兄弟和一名廚子。這時，兄弟不幸病倒，病情越來越重，終於死去，於是基古提卡克放火燒了他的船，並把他所有的補給品都沉入海中——這大約正是捕鯨船前往格陵蘭的慣常出發時節。他的主人說：「你憂傷消沉；散散步對你來說會是個轉換和消遣」；他們出發，來到一個小湖，發現岸邊繫著一條船——他們乘這條船划到對岸，很快又到了另一個湖和一條小船，同樣渡了過去，接著前往下一個湖，那裡也同樣有一條船，這正是往這個方向去的旅人慣用的交通工具。繫好最後一條船，繼續上路，他們很快來到國土中部的一座城鎮，進了一戶人家想用些點心；正吃著，他們聽到一聲喊叫：「捕鯨船要走了！捕鯨船出發了！」聽到這消息，基古提卡克猛然起身，飯也沒吃完就飛奔而下，解開船纜，他的主人稍隔一段距離跟在後面；他獨自一人渡過各個湖泊往回趕，他的主人則始終稍稍落後。當基古提卡克終於抵達主港時，他聽說捕鯨船全都走了，只剩一艘，其船員剛上岸去解纜——基古提卡克正好及時跳上小船，登上了大船。他的主人一路都跟不上他，這時正呼喚水手們好好照顧他，在他們停留格陵蘭期間密切看管他。

passages.text: After a voyage of many days they got sight of the southern point of the land; from that time Kigutikak would no more undress himself — he wanted to make use of his time and collect as many odd bits of old iron as he could with which to stuff his pockets before leaving the Europeans. As soon as he recognised his own country, and the places where he used to live, he proposed to the sailors to land and go out partridge-shooting; to this they consented, but without leaving him alone for a single moment, fearing he would either be lost or run off for his home. Kigutikak then told them, 'Ye need not fear my being lost, but just go after your game' — so they left him for a short time; no sooner had they turned their backs upon him than he hid himself in a deep cleft, and immediately after he heard them shouting for him and saying to each other, 'We were charged to keep a good watch over him, and it will be a bad job for us if he is not found.' As soon as he thought them sufficiently far off he emerged and proceeded onwards; having wandered a long while he observed a steep rock and began to descend it — half-way down he was somewhat perplexed at finding himself utterly unable either to advance or retreat; at length he determined to ease himself of all the things he had carried away in his pockets, and slid down the rest of the way. He proceeded still further and came in sight of a great many tents; seeing him approach, people came running and crying aloud, 'Kigutikak is coming!' — and then all the rest hastened out to have a look at him. He asked them in the Kavdlunak language, 'Where is my family?' but they could not understand him; asking them in their own language, however, their place of abode was pointed out to him. His own people had long ago given him up, and since then an old bachelor had undertaken to provide for them — Kigutikak rewarded him by allowing him to choose himself some trifles among the pieces of iron he had brought along with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 71 'Kigutikak who was carried off by the Whalers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 航行多日之後，他們望見了這片土地的南端；從那時起，基古提卡克再也不肯脫下衣服——他想利用時間，盡可能收集各種舊鐵碎片，好在離開歐洲人之前塞滿自己的口袋。他一認出自己的國土，以及他從前居住的地方，便向水手們提議上岸去打鷓鴣；他們同意了，但一刻也不讓他獨處，怕他走失或跑回家去。基古提卡克於是對他們說：「你們不必擔心我會走失，只管去打你們的獵物吧」——於是他們離開了他一小會兒；他們一轉身背對他，他便躲進一道深裂隙裡，隨即就聽見他們呼喊他，彼此說道：「我們奉命好好看管他，要是找不到他，我們可就糟了。」等他覺得他們已走得夠遠，他便出來繼續前行；走了很久，他看見一座陡峭的岩石，便開始往下走——走到半途，他發覺自己進退兩難，有些不知所措；最後他決定把口袋裡帶出來的東西全都卸下，然後滑下剩下的路程。他繼續往前走，看見了許多帳篷；見他走近，人們跑來高聲喊道：「基古提卡克回來了！」——其餘的人也都趕出來看他。他用卡夫德魯納克語問他們：「我的家人在哪裡？」但他們聽不懂；於是他用他們自己的語言再問，他們便指給了他住處。他自己的親人早已以為他死了，此後由一位老單身漢承擔起供養他們的責任——基古提卡克報答他，讓他在自己帶來的那些鐵塊中挑選些小玩意兒。

title.en: The Origin of Death: The Twins' Unfinished Argument
title.zh: 死亡之始：雙生子未完之辯

region.en: Coeur d'Alene village lodge (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫村落屋內（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 14. Origin of Death'

summary.en: A woman leaves her twin children, who seem to faint away (or only sleep); she notices tracks like theirs around the house and thinks they come to life and play in her absence. One day she steals on them unseen and finds them arguing inside the lodge — one says, 'It is better to be dead,' the other, 'It is better to be alive.' When they saw her they stopped talking; and since then people die from time to time, always some being born and some dying, some living ones and some dead ones. Had she remained hidden and allowed them to finish their argument, one would have prevailed over the other, and there would have been either no life or no death.
summary.zh: 一婦人晨出暮歸，其雙生子女終日昏睡（或云實乃假寐）。她見屋周有其足跡，疑其醒時嬉戲。一日她悄然而入，竟聞二子於屋內爭論：一言『死勝於生』，一言『生勝於死』。二子見母，言止。自此人乃有生死之別，生者死者並存於世。若婦人隱而不出，任其辯畢，則其一必勝——世間將或有生無死，或有死無生。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Origin-of-death cluster (interrupted-debate variant). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once a woman had twin children (some say brother and sister) who fainted away; possibly they only slept. Their mother left them in the morning; and when she returned in the evening, they were still lying there. She noticed tracks like theirs around the house: therefore she thought they must come to life and play during her absence. One day she stole on them unseen, and found them arguing with each other inside the lodge. One said, 'It is better to be dead'; and the other said, 'It is better to be alive.' When they saw her, they stopped talking; and since then people die from time to time. There are always some being born and some dying at the same time, always some living ones and some dead ones. Had she remained hidden, and allowed them to finish their argument, one would have prevailed over the other, and there would have been either no life or no death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 125 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有個女人生了一對雙胞胎（有人說是兄妹），他們昏了過去；也許他們只是睡著了。他們的母親早晨離開他們；傍晚回來時，他們仍躺在那裡。她注意到屋子周圍有像他們那樣的足跡：因此她想，他們一定是在她不在時活過來玩耍。有一天，她悄悄潛近，未被察覺，發現他們在屋裡互相爭論。一個說：「死了好」；另一個說：「活著好。」他們看見她，便不再說話；從那時起，人們便不時死去。總是有一些人在出生的同時，有一些人在死去，總是有一些活著的人，也有一些死去的人。倘若她一直躲著，讓他們把爭論結束，一個就會勝過另一個，那麼便會要麼沒有生，要麼沒有死。

title.en: Qo'zqozt: Badger Steals Coyote's Child
title.zh: 庫茲庫茲特：獾拐郊狼之子

region.en: Star group probably the Pleiades and two stars near them (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 星群，疑為昴星團及其附近雙星（象徵定位於柯達倫）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 15. Star Myths, (1) Qo'zqozt'

summary.en: Once Badger stole Coyote's favorite child, and Coyote chased them; as he was nearly overtaking them, they became transformed into stars — a group probably the Pleiades and two stars near them, which the Thompson consider a group of people, some saying they are Coyote's children. Coyote thus lost his child, and the group of people who were looking on were also transformed into stars.
summary.zh: 獾拐走郊狼最寵愛的孩子，郊狼窮追不捨；追及之際，三者俱化為星辰——即昴星團附近之星群（湯普森人謂其為一群人，或云郊狼之子）。郊狼自此失子；圍觀之眾亦化為星。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene star-myth recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The pin is symbolic (the sky). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once Badger stole Coyote's favorite child. Coyote chased them; and as he was nearly overtaking them, they became transformed into stars (the group Qo'zqozt, probably the Pleiades, and two stars near them; the Thompson consider the Pleiades to have been a group of people, and some say they are Coyote's children). Coyote thus lost his child. A group of people who were looking on were also transformed into stars.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 125 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，獾偷走了郊狼最心愛的孩子。郊狼追趕他們；就在他幾乎要追上時，他們變成了星星（即 Qo'zqozt 星群，大概是昴宿星團，以及附近兩顆星；湯普森人認為昴宿星團曾是一群人，有人說他們是郊狼的孩子）。郊狼就這樣失去了自己的孩子。一群旁觀的人也被變成了星星。

title.en: Sgwelkai'len: The Women Cooking Camas
title.zh: 斯格威爾凱倫：煮卡瑪斯之婦

region.en: Earth oven by the camas beds (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 卡瑪斯田畔地灶（象徵定位於柯達倫）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 15. Star Myths, (2) sgwelkai'len'

summary.en: Some women were cooking camas in an earth oven; the roots nearly done, they sat down in a circle round the pit. Skunk went there to spoil the camas but could not reach it because the women encircled the pit, and sat down a little distance off to wait. As they were thus seated, they were transformed into stars — the group Sgwelkai'len, seemingly the large stars of Auriga and Perseus, which the Thompson call 'The Women Cooking Roots.'
summary.zh: 眾婦以地灶煮卡瑪斯根，將熟之際環灶而坐。臭鼬欲毀其根，然婦人環灶而守，無從下手，只得稍退以待。眾人坐間，俱化為星——即斯格威爾凱倫星群，疑為御夫座與英仙座之亮星；湯普森人稱之為『煮根之婦』。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene star-myth recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The pin is symbolic (the sky). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Some women were cooking camas in an earth oven. The roots were nearly done, and the women sat down in a circle round the pit. Skunk went there to spoil the camas, but could not reach it, because the women encircled the pit; he sat down a little distance off to wait. As they were thus seated, they were transformed into stars (the group Sgwelkai'len, seemingly the large stars of Auriga and Perseus, called by the Thompson 'The Women Cooking Roots').
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 125 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有些婦女正在土窯裡煮卡馬斯（camas，一種百合科塊根植物）。根快煮熟了，婦女們便圍著土坑坐成一圈。臭鼬前去想破壞那些卡馬斯，卻搆不著，因為婦女們圍住了土坑；他便在稍遠處坐下等候。就在她們這樣坐著的時候，她們被變成了星星（即 Sgwelkai'len 星群，似乎是御夫座和英仙座的大星，湯普森人稱之為「煮根的婦女」）。

title.en: Temexa'tcasqat: The Grizzly-Bear Hunt in the Sky
title.zh: 特梅夏茨卡沙特：天上獵熊

region.en: The Great Bear constellation (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 大熊星座（象徵定位於柯達倫）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 15. Star Myths, (3) temexa'.tcasqat'

summary.en: Three brothers had a brother-in-law who was a Grizzly Bear; the youngest brother was a good friend of the Bear, but the other two disliked him and said they would kill him. The Bear went off hunting one day, and the youngest brother was following him; the other brothers overtook them, and were about to shoot the Bear. The youngest brother called out, 'Brother-in-law, they are going to shoot you!' Just as they were in the act of shooting, they were transformed into stars — the group Temexa'tcasqat, evidently the Great Bear, called by the Thompson 'The Grizzly-Bear' or 'The Grizzly-Bear and Hunters.'
summary.zh: 三兄弟之姊夫乃灰熊；幼弟與之交好，二兄惡之，欲殺。一日熊出獵，幼弟隨行；二兄追至，正欲放箭。幼弟急呼：『姊夫，他們要射你！』眾人舉弓之際，俱化為星辰——即特梅夏茨卡沙特星群，顯為大熊座；湯普森人稱之為『灰熊』或『灰熊與獵人』。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene star-myth recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The pin is symbolic (the sky). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Three brothers had a brother-in-law who was a Grizzly Bear. The youngest brother was a good friend of the Bear; but the other two brothers disliked him, and said they would kill him. The Bear went off hunting one day, and the youngest brother was following him. The other brothers overtook them, and were about to shoot the Bear. The youngest brother called out, 'Brother-in-law, they are going to shoot you!' Just as they were in the act of shooting, they were transformed into stars (the group Temexa'tcasqat, evidently the Great Bear, called by the Thompson 'The Grizzly-Bear' or 'The Grizzly-Bear and Hunters').
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 126 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 三兄弟有一個姐夫（或妹夫）是灰熊。最小的弟弟與熊交好；但另外兩個兄弟不喜歡他，說要殺了他。有一天熊出去打獵，最小的弟弟跟在他後面。另外兩個兄弟追上了他們，正要射殺那熊。最小的弟弟喊道：「姐夫，他們要射你了！」就在他們正要放箭之際，他們被變成了星星（即 Temexa'tcasqat 星群，顯然就是大熊座，湯普森人稱之為「灰熊」或「灰熊與獵人」）。

title.en: The Arrow-Chain of the Coeur d'Alene
title.zh: 柯達倫之箭鏈

region.en: Chain of arrows from earth to sky (symbolic pin at Coeur d'Alene)
region.zh: 自大地直達天際之箭鏈（象徵定位於柯達倫）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 16. The Arrow-Chain'

summary.en: The people wanted to go to the sky; they assembled and shot their arrows upward until an arrow reached the sky and stuck there, and then shot arrows at its nock until a chain of arrows reached down to the earth. The informants claimed this story used to be told often, but they had forgotten the details; Eagle and Coyote were mentioned in it, and they thought Coyote was the one who shot the arrow that hit the sky.
summary.zh: 世人慾登天界，聚眾向上射箭，終有一箭釘天；再續射其箭尾，箭鏈垂地乃成。相傳此事古時常有人講述，然細節已佚；據云鷹與郊狼亦在其中，而釘天之箭，當屬郊狼所射。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Details were reported forgotten by the informants. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The people wanted to go to the sky. They assembled, and shot their arrows upward. At last an arrow reached the sky, and stuck there. Then they shot arrows at the nock of this one, and gradually they formed a chain of arrows which reached down to the earth. The informants claimed this story used to be told often, but they had forgotten the details; Eagle and Coyote were mentioned in it, and they thought Coyote was the one who shot the arrow that hit the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 126 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 人們想要到天上去。他們聚集起來，朝上射箭。終於有一支箭射到了天，並插在那裡。接著他們朝這支箭的箭尾射箭，漸漸地形成了一條一直垂到地面的箭鏈。提供資料的人說，這個故事以前常被講述，但他們已忘了細節；故事中提到鷹和郊狼，他們認為射中天空那支箭的是郊狼。

title.en: The Water-Mystery near Cheney
title.zh: 奇尼附近之水靈

region.en: Small lake near Cheney, Spokane territory (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 斯波坎故地奇尼附近小湖（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 17. The Water-Mystery'

summary.en: A number of people were dancing at a small lake near Cheney, in Spokane territory, when they became aware of a strange smell; one of them said at once, 'That is .stsomkestci'nt.' All looked where he was looking, and saw four men standing about an equal distance apart from each other, all wearing buffalo-skins around the shoulders, hair-side out, each with his hair done up so that it stood out to the side. As the people looked, they disappeared, and four bushes grew up where they disappeared — these bushes were there lately, and probably may still be seen.
summary.zh: 斯波坎故地奇尼附近小湖畔，眾人正舞，忽聞異香。一人即呼：『此乃 .stsomkestci'nt 也！』眾皆循其目而望，見四人分立四處，皆肩披野牛皮，毛面向外，髮束向上外揚。眾人凝視之際，四人不見，原處生出四叢灌木——此灌木近年猶在，或至今尚存。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Teit compares the Uta'mqt stories of land-mysteries and giants changing into trees. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once a number of people were dancing at a small lake near Cheney, in the territory of the Spokane. Suddenly they became aware of a strange smell; and one of them at once said, 'That is .stsomkestci'nt.' The man looked around, and all the people looked to where he was looking. They saw four men standing about an equal distance apart from each other; all wore buffalo-skins around the shoulders, hair-side out, and each had his hair done up so that it stood out to the side. As the people looked, they disappeared, and four bushes grew up where they disappeared. These bushes were there lately, and probably may still be seen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 127 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，一群人在斯波坎人領地內切尼附近的一個小湖邊跳舞。突然他們察覺到一股奇怪的氣味；其中一人立刻說：「那是 .stsomkestci'nt。」那人環顧四周，所有人也都朝他看的方向望去。他們看見四個人站著，彼此間隔大致相等；四人都肩披水牛皮，毛面朝外，而且每人的頭髮都束起，向側邊翹出。就在人們看著的時候，他們消失了，而在他們消失的地方長出了四叢灌木。這些灌木不久前還在那裡，或許現在仍可見到。

title.en: The Water-Buffalo of Coeur d'Alene Lake
title.zh: 柯達倫湖中水牛靈

region.en: Coeur d'Alene Lake shore bush (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫湖畔灌木處（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 18. The Water-Buffalo'

summary.en: There was a water-mystery in Coeur d'Alene Lake with horns like a buffalo, otherwise somewhat like a buffalo. Once a man paddling his canoe along the shore in the dark found, opposite a bush growing near the shore, that his canoe stood still; he paddled hard, but the canoe would not move, and feeling along the gunwales he discovered a horn holding the canoe on each side — he knew the Water-Buffalo had caught him. He asked it to let him go, and gave it a present; at once it settled in the water, and the man paddled away. Ever afterwards people were careful to pray and make an offering at this place, the offerings being placed near the bush.
summary.zh: 柯達倫湖中有一水靈，其角如野牛，形亦近似。昔有人夜航沿湖而行，至湖畔灌木處，舟忽不動；奮力划槳，舟仍不移。以手探舷，兩側各有一角扣舟——知為水牛靈所擒。其人獻禮求釋，水牛靈遂沉入水中，舟行如常。自是行舟至此者，必祈禱獻祭於灌木之旁，以為定例。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a water-mystery in the Coeur d'Alene Lake. It had horns like a buffalo, and is said to have been otherwise somewhat like a buffalo. Once a man was paddling his canoe along the shore in the dark. When opposite a place where a bush grows near the shore, his canoe stood still. He paddled hard, but the canoe would not move. Then he felt along the gunwales of the canoe, and discovered a horn holding the canoe on each side. He knew the Water-Buffalo had caught him. He asked him to let him go, and gave him a present; at once he settled in the water, and the man paddled away. Ever afterwards people were careful to pray, and make an offering at this place; the offerings were placed near the bush.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 127 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 科達倫湖裡有一個水之謎（water-mystery）。它長著像水牛一樣的角，據說其他方面也多少像水牛。有一次，一個人在黑暗中沿著岸邊划獨木舟。當他划到岸邊有一叢灌木的地方對面時，他的獨木舟停住不動了。他用力划，獨木舟卻動不了。於是他沿著獨木舟的舷緣摸索，發現兩側各有一隻角夾住了獨木舟。他知道是水牛（Water-Buffalo）抓住了他。他求它放他走，並送了它一份禮物；它立刻沉入水中，那人便划船離去。此後人們總是小心地在此處祈禱並獻上供品；供品就放在那叢灌木附近。

title.en: The Nka'mEmEn Water-Mystery
title.zh: 恩卡梅門湖之水靈

region.en: Lake Nka'mEmEn (Swallowing) near the head of San Joe River (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 聖喬河源頭之恩卡梅門湖（意為『吞沒』）（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 19. The Nka'mEmEn Water-Mystery'

summary.en: Near the head of San Joe River is a lake called Nka'mEmEn (Swallowing): when people look at it, sticks jump out of the water. Once two brothers came out on the ridge above this lake, thirsty from hunting; the elder asked the other to bring him water, and the younger refused — 'No one goes near this lake' — until the elder said he would die without it. The younger descended, drew water quickly, ran uphill as fast as he could, and set down his bucket beside his brother before running down the other side; looking back, he saw a wave rise over the top of the ridge where his brother was and stand there for a while. When it disappeared, he went back and found his elder brother drowned.
summary.zh: 聖喬河源頭有湖，名恩卡梅門，意為『吞沒』：人望湖時，水面即有木棍躍出。昔有兄弟二人狩獵至此嶺，渴甚；兄命弟取水，弟拒之：『無人敢近此湖。』兄曰：『不得水，吾必死。』弟遂疾下湖畔，匆匆汲水，飛奔上山，置桶於兄旁，即越嶺而逃。回首一望，見巨浪騰越山嶺，罩於兄之所在，聳立片刻而沒。弟返尋兄，兄已溺斃。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Near the head of San Joe River is a lake called Nka'mEmEn (Swallowing). When people look at it, sticks jump out of the water. Once two brothers came out on the ridge above this lake; they had been hunting, and were very thirsty. The elder brother asked the other to bring him some water. The younger brother refused, saying, 'No one goes near this lake.' The elder said, 'I shall die if water is not brought to me.' The younger then descended, drew some water quickly, and ran uphill as fast as he could; he put down his bucket alongside his brother, and ran down the other side. He looked back, and saw a wave rise over the top of the ridge where his brother was, and stand up there for a while. When it disappeared, he went back and found his elder brother drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 127 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在聖喬河源頭附近有一座湖，名叫恩卡梅門（意為「吞嚥」）。人們朝湖裡看時，會有木棍從水中跳出。從前有兩兄弟來到這座湖上方的山脊；他們一直在打獵，口渴得厲害。哥哥叫弟弟去給他取些水來。弟弟不肯，說：「沒有人會靠近這座湖。」哥哥說：「要是不給我取水來，我就會死。」弟弟於是下山，快快地取了水，又盡可能快地跑上山；他把水桶放在哥哥身旁，便往山的另一邊跑去。他回頭一看，只見一道波浪從哥哥所在的山脊頂上湧起，在那裡立了一會兒。波浪消失後，他回去一看，發現哥哥已經淹死了。

title.en: The Water-Mystery of the Upper San Joe River
title.zh: 上聖喬河之水靈

region.en: Deep water of the upper San Joe River and a small mystery lake (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 上聖喬河深水與鄰近小靈湖（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 20. The Water-Mystery of the Upper San Joe River'

summary.en: Long ago some women were picking service-berries a long way up the San Joe River, four sisters among them; in the hot weather the sisters said they would have a swim, and seeing a large fish out in the deep water, said, 'Let us see who can reach him first!' They swam out; and when they came near, the fish went down — the sisters went down too, and were never seen again. The other women said, 'That was not a fish, it was the tongue of the water-mystery.' Shortly afterwards, some people on a nearby mountain with a small 'mystery' lake found on the shore the hair of the four sisters; they reported their find to the parents, who went and took away the hair. The people thus learned that there was a water-passage between this small lake and the river, and that it was used by the water-mystery.
summary.zh: 昔有眾女上聖喬河採莓，中有姊妹四人。天熱，姊妹戲言下水同泳；見深水處有大魚，遂呼：『且比誰先游到！』四人並進，將近之時，魚忽沉——姊妹亦隨之而沒，從此無蹤。眾女曰：『此非魚也，乃水靈之舌。』未幾，有人於鄰山小靈湖畔拾得四姊妹之髮，報於其親，其親往取之。眾人始知此小湖與大河之間有水道相通，為水靈往來之路。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: One time long ago some women were picking service-berries a long ways up the San Joe River. Four sisters were among them. It was hot weather, and the sisters said they would have a swim. They saw a large fish out in the deep water, and said, 'Let us see who can reach him first!' They swam out; and when they came near, the fish went down. The sisters also went down, and were never seen again. The other women said, 'That was not a fish, it was the tongue of the water-mystery.' Shortly afterwards some people were on a mountain near by where there is a small 'mystery' lake. There they found on the shore the hair of the four sisters; they reported their find to the parents of the sisters, who went and took away the hair. The people thus learned that there was a water-passage between this small lake and the river, and that it was used by the water-mystery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 128 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 很久以前，有些婦女在聖喬河上游很遠的地方採摘唐棣果。其中有四姐妹。天氣炎熱，姐妹們說要去游水。她們看見深水裡有一條大魚，便說：「咱們看看誰先夠到牠！」她們游了過去；快靠近時，那魚沉了下去。姐妹們也沉了下去，此後再沒有人見過她們。其他婦女說：「那不是魚，那是水之謎靈的舌頭。」不久之後，有些人在附近一座山上，那裡有一個小小的「謎靈」湖。他們在岸上發現了四姐妹的頭髮；他們把發現的事告訴了姐妹們的父母，父母前去把頭髮取了回來。人們由此得知，這個小湖與那條河之間有一條水道，而且水之謎靈會經由它往來。

title.en: The Rolling Head
title.zh: 滾動之首

region.en: Firewood stands of the Coeur d'Alene country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 柯達倫故地拾柴之地（象徵定位）

period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coeur d'Alene Tales, 21. The Rolling Head'

summary.en: A young woman gathering fire-wood, about to rise with her load, notices a man's head on her dress, which says, 'You must be my wife.' She rises, the head falls off and rolls after her, entering the lodge close behind; when she sits down it rolls onto her dress, and she takes it up to decorate it with beads. One line of beads is strung from the back of the head to the brow, and as she works another line around from ear to ear her sister comes home, angry, and tells her to let it alone; she strikes her hand to make her stop — so the beading was never finished. The head stayed with her as her husband.
summary.zh: 少女拾柴，負重將起，忽見裙上有男子之首，且言：『汝當為吾妻。』少女起身，首落而滾，緊隨其後入屋；少女坐，首又滾上裙，遂拾起以珠飾之。自後腦至額已串珠一行，正自耳至耳再串一行，其姊歸而大怒，令其罷手，並擊其手以止之——故飾珠未竟。此首遂留其身畔，以為夫。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Coeur d'Alene narrative recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Rolling-head motif; cf. the Thompson rolling-bowlder tale. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once there was a young woman gathering fire-wood. She made up a load, and, having attached her pack-strap to it, sat down to place it over her head. As she was about to rise with her load, she noticed a man's head on her dress. It said to her, 'You must be my wife.' She rose up, and the head fell off her dress; she went home, and the head rolled after her. She entered the lodge, and it followed close behind her. When she sat down, it rolled on her dress. She took it up, and thought she would decorate it with beads. She had put one line of beads from the back of the head to the brow, and was engaged in putting on another line around the head from ear to ear, when her sister came home. She was angry when she saw her beading the head; she told her to let it alone, and have nothing to do with it, but the young woman kept on beading. Then her sister struck her hand to make her stop; therefore she did not finish the beading. The head stayed with her as her husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 128 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有一個年輕女子在拾柴。她捆好一捆柴，把背帶繫在柴捆上，坐下來要把柴捆頂到頭上。她正要背起柴捆站起來時，發覺自己的衣裙上有一顆男人的頭。那頭對她說：「你必須做我的妻子。」她站起身來，那頭便從她的衣裙上掉了下去；她走回家去，那頭就跟在她後面滾。她走進屋裡，那頭緊緊跟在她身後。她坐下時，那頭便滾到她的衣裙上。她把頭拿起來，心想可以用珠子把它裝飾一番。她已經從後腦到額頭綴了一排珠子，正忙著從一隻耳朵到另一隻耳朵再綴一排時，她的妹妹回家了。妹妹看見她在給那頭綴珠子，很生氣；她叫姐姐別去碰它，不要和它有任何瓜葛，可是那年輕女子仍舊繼續綴珠子。於是妹妹打了她的手，叫她停下來；因此她沒有把那排珠子綴完。那頭便留下來做她的丈夫。

title.en: Coyote and his Son: The Eagle-Tree to the Sky Country
title.zh: 郊狼父子：通天之樹

region.en: Eagle-tree mountain near Snake River, up to the sky country (symbolic pin at Waha Lake)
region.zh: 斯內克河畔神樹之山，直上天界（象徵定位於瓦哈湖）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; edited by Theresa Mayer; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 1. Coyote and his Son' (collected by Farrand)

summary.en: Old-Coyote, coveting his son's white Duck wife, sends him to strip and climb for eaglets in a tree that rises with every wink of the father's eye until it carries the youth beyond the clouds into the sky country. There he finds a five-doored tent of his grandfathers, who spend five days making rope enough to lower him in a huge spoon through five cloud-obstacles — 'Roll over when you feel the spoon stop' — down to the earth. In the meantime Old-Coyote has donned the son's clothes and deceived the Duck wife, while the sceptical Beetle wife leaves with her baby; the returned son overtakes them, Raven proves Old-Coyote a liar, the people shout the true news, and Duck, ashamed, becomes a duck in the river forever.
summary.zh: 老郊狼覬覦其子之白鴨妻，誘其脫衣攀樹取鷹雛；父每眨眼一次，樹便升高一截，終將其子送上雲霄天界。其子在天界遇五位祖父之五門大帳，祖父等費五日搓繩，以巨勺盛之，穿五重雲障縋其下凡——『勺停即翻身』。其間老郊狼穿上其子衣物，騙得鴨妻；多疑之甲蟲妻携子離去。其子歸來追上妻兒，渡鴉揭穿老郊狼謊言，眾人齊呼真相；鴨妻羞愧，化為鴨，永居河中。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin (Yakama-area) narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Two further versions are recorded in the source. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote had a son who was a chief and a good man. He went up a mountain near Snake River; one morning he kicked a log, and fire came, which would burn to warm people, and he used to tell the people to hunt deer — all considered him the greatest chief. Coyote's son had two wives, Beetle, who was black, and Duck, who was white, and Beetle had a son. One day Old-Coyote made a fire of willows, saw the women's privates between their legs as the sparks flew, and coveted Duck. He resolved to kill his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 135 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼有一個兒子，是酋長，也是個好人。他登上蛇河附近的一座山；有一天早晨，他踢了一根木頭，火便出來了，這火可以用來燃燒取暖，他常叫人們去獵鹿——大家都認為他是最偉大的酋長。郊狼的兒子有兩個妻子：甲蟲，是黑色的；鴨子，是白色的。甲蟲有一個兒子。有一天，老郊狼用柳枝生了一堆火，火星飛濺時，他看見了那兩個女人兩腿之間的私處，便貪戀起鴨子來。他決心要殺死自己的兒子。

passages.text: He told the women that there was an eagle with several young ones on the top of a tree, and they immediately said they wanted the feathers; Old-Coyote told his son to get the eaglets at once, since they would fly away in about ten days. They came to a mountain covered with trees, and Coyote showed his son the eyry on a tree that did not seem very high and was easy to climb; he said he could not climb it himself, and sent his son, telling him to strip off his clothes so they should not be spoiled — Old-Coyote wanted the clothes for himself. The youth had gone a little way when the old man winked his eye at him, and the eyry rose; he winked again, and it rose still higher. The youth turned and scolded his father, who said he was just watching him. The youth kept on climbing until he was out of sight: the tree carried him up beyond the clouds, into the sky country, and when he left the tree it had shrunk back to its original size.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 135 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
