passages.zh: 他告訴那兩個女人，說有一棵樹頂上有一隻鷹和幾隻雛鷹，她們立刻說想要那些羽毛；老郊狼便叫兒子馬上去把雛鷹取來，因為大約十天之後牠們就會飛走。他們來到一座長滿樹木的山上，郊狼把樹上的鷹巢指給兒子看，那樹看上去並不很高，也容易爬；他說自己爬不上去，就打發兒子去，叫他脫下衣服，免得弄壞了——老郊狼其實是想把那些衣服據為己有。少年才爬了一小段路，老人就朝他眨了一下眼，那鷹巢便升高了；他又眨了一下眼，鷹巢升得更高了。少年轉過身來責罵父親，父親說自己只是在看著他。少年繼續往上爬，直到看不見為止：那棵樹把他帶到雲層之上，進了天空之國；等他離開那棵樹時，樹又縮回原來的大小。

passages.text: The sky country was just like our earth. After a while he saw a large tent with five doors; at the first the people shouted that it was cold, at the next they seized their spears to attack him, and at the last they tried to hit him with their spears — until he shouted, 'Stop, grandfather!' They answered, 'Our only grandchild is Coyote's son.' — 'I am he,' he said, and they welcomed him, gave him food, and promised to send him down. They had long ropes piled up in coils, and told him it would take five days to make enough to reach down to the earth, asking him to fill the spoon with deer-tallow to rub on their hands, which would be sore from letting him down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 135-136 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天空之國和我們的大地一模一樣。過了一會兒，他看見一座有五扇門的大帳篷；在第一扇門前，人們喊著說天氣冷；在第二扇門前，他們抓起長矛要攻擊他；在最後一扇門前，他們試圖用長矛打他——直到他喊道：「住手，祖父！」他們回答說：「我們唯一的孫子就是郊狼的兒子。」——「我就是他，」他說。於是他們歡迎他，給他食物，並答應把他送下去。他們把長繩盤成一圈圈堆著，告訴他要花五天工夫才能搓出夠長、能垂到地面的繩子，並請他把勺子裝滿鹿油，塗在他們的手上，因為放他下去會把手磨痛。

passages.text: At the end of five days they put him into a spoon as large as a huge dish, instructing him to roll over in it whenever he felt it stop. He went down through the sky, struck obstacles five times — the clouds through which he was passing — and rolled over each time; finally he struck solid ground, and when the spoon did not move he knew he had reached the earth. He untied himself, hunted deer as requested, filled the spoon with tallow, and pulled the rope as a signal that he had arrived. In the meantime Old-Coyote had gone home and taken the Duck wife, deceiving her by pretending to be her husband; he danced all the time, telling the people he had persuaded his father to climb up, and most of the people believed him, because he looked so different. Duck actually thought he was her husband, but Beetle disbelieved him, put reeds on her back, placed her baby on them, and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 136 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 五天之後，他們把他放進一只大如巨盤的匙子裡，囑咐他每逢覺得匙子停住，就在裡面翻個身。他穿過天空往下落，先後撞上五道障礙——那正是他一路穿過的雲層——每撞一次便翻一個身；最後他撞上了堅實的地面，匙子不再動彈，他便知道自己已抵達大地。他解開繩索，照吩咐獵了一頭鹿，把匙子裝滿鹿脂，然後拉動繩子，作為他已到達的信號。與此同時，老郊狼已回到家中，娶了鴨妻，假冒她的丈夫欺騙她；他終日跳舞，告訴眾人他已說服父親攀上天去，大多數人都信了他，因為他的模樣大不相同。鴨子當真以為他就是自己的丈夫，甲蟲卻不信，她把蘆葦披在背上，把孩子放在上面，便離去了。

passages.text: Coyote's son followed her, passing ten of her camp-sites, taking along the boy's bow found at the last. Looking down over a hill, he saw his wife carrying the child and crying; the boy saw his father and cried, 'Father has my bow!' — 'Your father is dead,' said the mother. Catching up to them, he held her by stepping on her rawhide strap, and said, 'Don't strike the boy! You are hurting him.' Then they sat down, and he related all that had happened; she told him how the people had missed him, because without him they did not kill many deer. He told his wife to wrap him up in reeds, place the boy on top of him, and stop at some distance from the camp; she was to keep crying, because her child was hungry, and inform him if the people caught a fat deer. Mosquito volunteered to look through a hole in the tent-cover and was driven back; Raven slipped in silently under the tent, saw Coyote's son eating, recognized him, and told what he had seen, proving that Old-Coyote was a liar. The old people gave orders to everybody to shout, 'Coyote's son has come back!' Old-Coyote pulled off his clothes, jumped into the fire, and cried over his boy; Duck was ashamed and turned into a duck, and has been in the river ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 136-137 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼之子跟隨著她，走過她十處宿營之地，並帶上在最後一處找到的男孩的弓。他從一座山丘上往下望，看見妻子抱著孩子哭泣；男孩看見父親，便喊道：『父親拿著我的弓！』——『你父親已經死了，』母親說。他追上他們，踩住她的生皮帶把她攔住，說道：『別打孩子！你弄疼他了。』於是他們坐下來，他講述了發生的一切；她則告訴他眾人如何惦念他，因為沒有他，他們獵不到多少鹿。他吩咐妻子用蘆葦把他裹起來，把孩子放在他身上，並在離營地一段距離處停下；她要一直哭，就說孩子餓了，若眾人獵到肥鹿便來告知他。蚊子自告奮勇從帳篷頂的洞裡張望，卻被趕了回去；渡鴉悄悄從帳篷底下溜進去，看見郊狼之子正在吃東西，認出了他，便把自己所見告訴眾人，證明老郊狼是個騙子。老人們下令眾人齊聲高呼：『郊狼之子回來了！』老郊狼扯下自己的衣服，跳進火裡，為他的孩子痛哭；鴨子羞愧難當，變成了一隻鴨子，從此一直住在河裡。

title.en: Backbone Ridge: Old-Coyote Punished
title.zh: 脊骨嶺：懲罰老郊狼

region.en: Hill named Backbone (Kupkup) close to the river, near Waka Lake (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河畔之脊骨嶺（Kupkup），瓦哈湖附近（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 1. Coyote and his Son' (revenge on Old-Coyote)

summary.en: From that time on Old-Coyote was treated like a slave, and Coyote's son decided to take revenge. Hunting on a ridge near Waka Lake, close to the river by the hill named Backbone (Kupkup), he killed a fat deer, butchered it and left it there, then sent Old-Coyote to bring in the carcass with a strap Beetle had painted to look like a tump-line. The strap broke five times; hot and exhausted, Old-Coyote could go no farther, and Coyote's son threw the backbone down the hill, saying, 'Henceforth this shall be Backbone Ridge' — and Old-Coyote sat down ashamed.
summary.zh: 自那時起，老郊狼形同奴僕。郊狼之子謀復仇，於瓦哈湖附近脊骨嶺（Kupkup）下河邊獵得肥鹿，剖而留之，遣老郊狼以甲蟲妻繪成背帶之假革帶負屍而歸。革帶五斷；天熱力竭，老郊狼寸步難行。郊狼之子遂擲鹿脊下山，曰：『自此此嶺名脊骨嶺。』老郊狼愧而坐地。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: From that time on, Old-Coyote was treated like a slave. Coyote's son decided to take revenge. He went hunting on a ridge near Waka Lake, and came to a hill named Backbone (Kupkup); there, close to the river, he killed a fat deer, butchered it, and left it there. Then he went home and asked Old-Coyote to bring in the carcass. Beetle had painted a gut like a tump-line; they gave it to Old-Coyote to carry the carcass. When Old-Coyote reached the deer, he took a great piece off and ate it; then he tied up the pack and started to carry it home. He had gone but a little way when the strap broke. His son told him to tie it together and go ahead. The strap broke five times, and finally he had nothing with which to carry his burden; he grew very tired. It was hot, and he could not go any farther. Then Coyote's son threw the backbone down the hill, saying, 'Henceforth this shall be Backbone Ridge.' Then Old-Coyote sat down ashamed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 137 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從那時起，老郊狼便像奴隸一樣被使喚。郊狼之子決定報仇。他到瓦卡湖附近的一道山脊上打獵，來到一座名叫脊骨（庫普庫普）的山丘；在那裡，緊挨著河邊，他獵到一頭肥鹿，把它開膛分割，留在原地。然後他回家，叫老郊狼去把獵物搬回來。甲蟲畫了一條像馱帶一樣的腸子；他們把它交給老郊狼去背獵物。老郊狼到了鹿那裡，扯下一大塊吃了；然後他把獵物捆好，開始往家背。他沒走多遠，帶子就斷了。他兒子叫他接上再走。帶子斷了五次，最後他再沒有東西可以捆綁重物；他疲憊不堪。天氣炎熱，他再也走不動了。於是郊狼之子把脊骨扔下山去，說道：『從今以後，這裡就叫脊骨嶺。』老郊狼羞愧地坐了下來。

title.en: Coyote Liberates the Salmon
title.zh: 郊狼釋鮭記

region.en: Swallow dams on the Columbia and Snake rivers (symbolic pin at the Dalles)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河與斯內克河燕子姊妹之壩（象徵定位於達爾斯）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 2. Coyote liberates the Salmon' (collected by Farrand)

summary.en: Five Swallow girls own a dam and fish-trap that hold all the salmon back from the upper river. Coyote turns himself into a crying infant drifting on a reed-and-buffalo-skin raft; the girls, who have always wanted a child, race for him, and the eldest wins. The baby grows with unnatural speed, calls every part of her body 'my mother's', cries his way to a full meal and all their water, and when sent for more runs like a man between terraces. At the hut he eats the stores, tears down the dam — 'There shall no longer be a dam in this river. Many Indians will come here to live' — shouts the news, ties a head-sized spoon on as a helmet against their blows, and vanishes into a cloud of black paint. The salmon crowd up the river behind him; when his old reed blanket tears at every catch, Beaver advises the club, and the killed salmon is cooked while Coyote sleeps.
summary.zh: 五燕子姊妹壩上蓄魚，阻鮭上溯。郊狼化為啼哭嬰兒，臥蘆葦野皮筏順流而下；眾姊妹久盼子嗣，競游搶之，長姊得勝。嬰孩速長，凡觸母身皆喚『吾母之……』；索食索水，撒潑放賴，得令自取則人立而行，過兩層臺地仍佯為嬰孩爬行。至屋飽食存糧，拆壩放水——『此河從此無壩，印第安人將大量遷來』——以勺為盔禦棒擊，撒黑漆遁入黑暗。鮭魚成群上溯；其舊葦毯屢捕屢裂，河貍教以棍擊，烹鮭而眠。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Three versions are recorded in the source; the salmon-liberation element is common to all. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote knew of five girls who prevented the salmon from coming up the river. He went in that direction, and sat down to think out how he might obtain the salmon. 'I will turn into an infant and float down on a bed of reeds,' he said to himself. 'The women will take care of me and raise me until I know their customs.' When the girls saw the infant drifting on the water, they rescued it; the oldest girl said, 'He shall be my son.' She kept him; and when he grew up and came to be a young man, he saw that the salmon were kept in a pound. He cut a ditch and made a channel, which enabled the salmon to go up the river; he showed his mother how he had broken the dam. The women tried to kill him, but he escaped and came back home; then he went down and freed all the people who were held captive in the form of fishes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 139 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼得知有五個姑娘阻擋鮭魚溯河而上。他朝那個方向走去，坐下來思量怎樣才能得到鮭魚。『我要變成一個嬰兒，躺在蘆葦筏上順流漂下，』他自言自語道。『那些女人會收養我、撫育我，直到我摸清她們的習性。』姑娘們看見嬰兒在水上漂流，便把他救了起來；最年長的姑娘說：『他就做我的兒子吧。』她把他留下；等他長大成人，他看見鮭魚被圈在魚欄裡。他挖了一條溝，開出一條水道，使鮭魚得以溯河而上；他讓母親看他是怎樣破開堤壩的。那些女人想殺他，但他逃脫了，回到家裡；隨後他下去，把所有被囚禁成魚形的人都釋放了。

passages.text: In the second version, he swam all the way down the Snake River without once turning around, and came to the dam of five Swallow girls who owned it and a fish-trap. He turned into a little boy drifting down on a raft of reeds and buffalo-skin, crying lustily; the girls had always wanted a child, and raced to see who should get this one — Coyote winked his eye at the oldest, who drew ahead and won. They had had him but two days when he began to eat; in three days he began to creep about and to talk. Sleeping beside his mother, he felt of her head, her hair, her body, repeating 'my mother's' of every part; the youngest of the girls knew the baby was Coyote, and every time she said so he began to cry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 140-141 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在第二個版本中，他一路游下斯內克河，一次也沒有回頭，來到五個燕子姑娘所擁有的堤壩和魚梁前。他變成一個小男孩，躺在蘆葦和野牛皮做的筏子上順流漂下，放聲大哭；姑娘們一直想要個孩子，便爭先恐後地跑去看誰能得到這一個——郊狼朝最年長的姑娘眨了眨眼，她便跑在前面贏了。她們收養他才兩天，他就開始吃東西；三天之內，他就開始爬來爬去、開口說話。他睡在母親身旁，摸她的頭、她的頭髮、她的身體，每摸到一處便重複說『我母親的』；姑娘中年紀最小的那個知道這嬰兒就是郊狼，每次她這麼說，他就哭起來。

passages.text: Five days elapsed in this manner; on the sixth they planned to dig roots and took the baby along with water and food. He ate everything and drank all the water, then cried for more, until they told him to go and get it himself. He crawled down the hill, got up and ran when out of sight at the first terrace, crawled again in sight, and ran once more after the second; soon he arrived at the house, ate all the food in it, and tore down the dam in the river, digging around it. When the water began to come through he sat down and called out, 'Come down, the dam is broken!' The youngest said, 'I know that is Coyote's work.' The fish were running up in shoals; Coyote had made a spoon just the size of his head and tied it on, so that when his mother hit him on the head he did not feel it and just laughed. He untied a bag of black paint, and immediately it became dark so they could not see him; from a hill he called down to them to take care of his children if he should have any — 'The youngest one knew me, so perhaps she will not have a baby' — nevertheless he gave them all names.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 141 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就這樣過了五天；第六天，她們打算去挖根莖，帶著嬰兒以及水和食物一同前往。他把東西全吃光、水全喝光，然後哭著還要，直到她們叫他自個兒去拿。他爬下山丘，一到看不見的第一層台地便站起身跑，到了看得見的地方又爬，過了第二層台地又跑；不一會兒他就到了家，把屋裡的食物全吃光，又在河邊繞著堤壩挖掘，把它拆毀。當水開始湧出時，他坐下來喊道：『下來吧，堤壩破了！』最小的姑娘說：『我知道這是郊狼幹的。』魚成群結隊地往上游；郊狼做了一只正好有他腦袋那麼大的匙子綁在頭上，這樣他母親打他頭時他毫無感覺，只是發笑。他解開一袋黑色顏料，天色立刻變黑，使她們看不見他；他從一座山丘上朝她們喊話，說倘若他有了孩子，請她們照料——『最小的那個認出了我，也許她不會生孩子』——儘管如此，他還是給她們都取了名字。

passages.text: In the third version the Swallow girls lived at the Dalles on the Columbia River, where they had made a dam to prevent the salmon from going upstream. The baby grew up very quickly, and the youngest girl suspected there was something strange about him and concluded it was Coyote and no real baby at all. When he had finished eating the stores, he began to tear down the dam, saying, 'There shall no longer be a dam in this river. Many Indians will come here to live'; when he had broken it, he shouted, 'Mother, come down! Our dam is broken, and the water is gone.' The youngest scolded the others and told them the baby was none other than Coyote. The salmon now crowded up the river, and Coyote followed them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 142-143 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在第三個版本中，燕子姑娘們住在哥倫比亞河畔的達爾斯，她們在那裡築了一道壩，阻止鮭魚往上游去。那嬰兒長得極快，最小的姑娘懷疑他有些古怪，斷定他是郊狼，根本不是真正的嬰兒。當他吃完了儲糧，便開始拆毀那道壩，說道：「這條河裡再也不許有壩了。許多印第安人會到這裡來居住。」當他拆毀了壩，便喊道：「母親，下來吧！我們的壩破了，水也流走了。」最小的姑娘責罵其他幾位，告訴她們那嬰兒正是郊狼。鮭魚如今成群湧上河來，郊狼便跟隨著牠們。

title.en: The Wolves Eat Coyote's Guts
title.zh: 群狼竊食郊狼之腸

region.en: Riverbank cook-fire of the Columbia-Salmon country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞鮭鄉河畔炊火處（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 2. Coyote liberates the Salmon' (the Wolves and the eggs)

summary.en: Five Wolves smell the cooked salmon and, careful not to awaken Coyote, eat it all, then slit his anus from behind, take out the gut and roast it for him; waking, Coyote thanks his 'grand-daughter' for the food and eats it until a bird shouts, 'You are eating your own guts!' Feeling up to his elbow in the cavity, he puts the last piece back, then hits his hip so that dung becomes boys, all but the youngest returning into him — the youngest tells him the thieves were the Wolves and a Fox. Coyote follows them, eats their ground-oven eggs but leaves one for each, remodels their faces asleep — pulling out noses, pushing in cheeks, making them gray as wolves are now — rubs Fox with egg-yolk for his color, makes Skunk black and white, and laughs at them from the hill; Fox, the swiftest, catches up and sits down with him to talk, for he is Coyote's best friend.
summary.zh: 五狼嗅得熟鮭，躡足盡食，又自後割開郊狼後竅，取出其腸烤以奉之。郊狼醒，謝『孫女』贈食，食之津津；飛鳥高呼：『爾正食己腸！』探手入腔至肘，方納最後一段歸位。再擊其臀，糞化童子，皆歸其身，唯幼者留外告之：竊賊乃五狼一狐。郊狼追至狼巢，食其地灶之蛋，每獸留一枚；趁其酣睡重塑其面——拉長其鼻、按平其頰、染其灰色——以蛋黃塗狐定其色，以黑白定臭鼬之色，立於山頭大笑。狐最捷，追及，然與郊狼並坐而談——蓋狐乃其至交。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Five Wolves smelled the fish and came close to the fire; they found the salmon and ate it, careful not to awaken Coyote. When they had eaten it all, they cut open Coyote's anus, took out the gut, and cooked it for him. When Coyote awoke, he thought, 'There is my fish cooking for me' — but nothing was left but the bones. When he saw the guts, he said, 'My grandchild must have left these guts here,' and began to eat them. A bird saw him, and shouted, 'You are eating your own guts!' Nevertheless he kept on eating, until he felt behind him and ran his hand clear up to his elbow, finding but a little piece of his intestines left, which he put back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 141-142 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 五隻狼聞到了魚的氣味，便走近火堆；他們找到了鮭魚，把它吃了，小心翼翼地不驚醒郊狼。他們把魚吃光之後，便剖開郊狼的肛門，取出腸子，替他煮了。郊狼醒來時心想：「那是我的魚在替我煮著呢。」——可是除了骨頭什麼也沒剩下。當他看見那些腸子，便說：「準是我的孫兒把這些腸子留在這裡的。」於是開始吃了起來。一隻鳥看見了他，喊道：「你吃的正是你自己的腸子！」儘管如此，他還是繼續吃，直到他往身後摸去，把手一直伸到肘部，才發現自己的腸子只剩下一小截，便把它放了回去。

passages.text: Then he hit his hip a second time, and the dung which appeared turned into boys as before; all but the youngest went back into him. He told Coyote that the thieves were the Wolves and a Fox, who were cooking some eggs and had taken his salmon while he had been asleep. Coyote was very angry, and started out to hunt the Wolves. He came to the place where they were cooking eggs; not far away the Wolves were asleep. The eggs were done, and Coyote began to eat them — he did not eat all, however, but left six, one for each of the animals, and covered them up as they had been before. The Wolves and the Fox slept on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 142 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著他又拍了一下自己的髖部，出現的糞便像先前一樣變成了男孩；除了最小的那個，全都回到了他體內。那男孩告訴郊狼，偷東西的是那些狼和一隻狐狸，他們正在煮一些蛋，趁他睡著時拿走了他的鮭魚。郊狼非常憤怒，便動身去追獵那些狼。他來到他們煮蛋的地方；不遠處那些狼正睡著。蛋煮好了，郊狼便開始吃——不過他並沒有全吃光，而是留下了六個，每隻動物一個，並照原樣把它們蓋好。那些狼和那隻狐狸仍舊睡著。

passages.text: Coyote took some charcoal and painted their faces to make them look ugly; he painted Fox with the yolk of an egg, and put charcoal on the tips of his ears. When he had finished, Coyote went to a notch on the hill and waited to see what would happen, carrying five bags of black paint. Soon one of the Wolves awoke and called the others; they went to get the eggs, and each took one. Coyote, way up on the hill, laughed to himself; when they went to get another egg, they found nothing but shells, and wondered what the trouble was. One looked at another: 'Why, what is the matter with you?' Then they teased one another about their looks — Fox was yellow all over. They came to the conclusion that this was Coyote's handiwork, and indeed there was Coyote laughing at them. They gave chase, and Fox almost caught him; but Coyote said, 'We are friends,' opened a sack of paint and disappeared in the darkness. When it cleared up, he was on the other side of the canyon, still laughing; so they decided to leave him alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 142 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼拿了些木炭，把他們的臉塗得醜陋不堪；他用蛋黃塗了狐狸，又把木炭塗在他的耳尖上。塗完之後，郊狼帶著五袋黑顏料，走到山丘上的一處凹口，等著看會發生什麼事。不久，一隻狼醒了，叫醒了其他幾隻；他們去取蛋，各自拿了一個。郊狼在高高的山上暗自發笑；當他們去取另一個蛋時，卻只發現蛋殼，便納悶出了什麼岔子。一個看著另一個：「咦，你這是怎麼了？」接著他們互相取笑彼此的模樣——狐狸全身都是黃的。他們斷定這是郊狼的傑作，而郊狼果然正在嘲笑他們。他們追了上去，狐狸幾乎抓住了他；但郊狼說：「我們是朋友。」便打開一袋顏料，消失在黑暗之中。等天色清朗時，他已到了峽谷的另一邊，仍舊笑著；於是他們決定不再理他。

title.en: Coyote and the Goose Girl
title.zh: 郊狼與雁女

region.en: Goose brothers' camp across the river (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雁兄營地，河之彼岸（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 3. Coyote and the Geese' (the marriage)

summary.en: After the strange object that struck his face and cooked like fat meat cost Coyote all his teeth, he finds the camp of five white geese who have flown across the river to hunt deer, leaving their pretty sister alone making clothes, with the promise that any man who chances to their camp shall be her husband. Peering through the tent-hole, Coyote magically provides five eagle feathers tipped with black, five fine men's dresses and five bows and arrows, has made himself a handsome man with nice long hair — but cannot bite the meat she sets before him and must be satisfied with pounded meat. Asleep with open mouth, he is given a set of mountain-sheep teeth by the girl: 'My teeth always do that, they grow while I sleep.' When the five brothers come home and crowd him toward their sister, the eldest says, 'Don't be mean!' — and Coyote married the girl.
summary.zh: 郊狼誤食擊面之異物，牙齒盡落。行至五白雁之營——雁兄五人已渡河獵鹿，留美貌之妹獨自縫衣，且曾言：『凡至此營之男子，不論老幼，皆為其夫。』郊狼窺帳見之，以法術備禮：黑尖鷹羽五支、男服五套、弓箭五副，又自化俊男、蓄美髯。惜無齒難噬，只得就肉糜。睡中張口，雁女見其無齒，乃取大角羊齒一套納其口中：『吾齒向來如此，睡中自長。』五兄歸，屢令其挪位擠向其妹，長兄斥曰：『休得無禮！』郊狼遂娶雁女。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The opening episode in which Coyote cooks and eats a mysterious object and loses his teeth is summarized plainly, as recorded. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote went on up the river. He heard a noise, and saw what he believed to be a duck flying above him. It came nearer, and, as he turned around to look at it, it slapped him in the eye and stuck there. Only with the most strenuous efforts could he dislodge it; when he finally succeeded in removing it, he looked at it, but even then he did not know what it was. He threw it into the river and went on his way; this happened four times. When it struck him the fifth time, he decided to cook it: he pulled it off, cut it up, made a fire of pine-cones, and broiled it on a stick. It smelled just like fat meat; when it was done, he tasted it, and found it tasted like cow-teats. He ate it all up, and when he had finished, he regretted that he had eaten it. He was thirsty, and looked for water; soon he found a good spring, and stooped over to drink. As he opened his mouth, all his teeth fell out; not a single one was left. So he went his way without any teeth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 144-145 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼繼續沿河而上。他聽見一陣聲響，看見一個他以為是鴨子的東西在他上方飛。那東西越飛越近，當他轉過身去看它時，它啪地打在他眼睛上，黏在那裡。他費了極大的力氣才把它弄下來；當他終於把它取下時，他看了看它，可即便如此，他仍不知道那是什麼。他把它扔進河裡，繼續趕路；這樣的事發生了四次。當它第五次打中他時，他決定把它煮了：他把它扯下來，切碎，用松果生起火，串在棍子上烤。它聞起來就像肥肉；烤好之後，他嚐了嚐，覺得味道像母牛的乳頭。他把它全吃光了，吃完之後，又後悔吃了它。他口渴了，便去找水；不久他找到一處好泉眼，便彎下腰去喝。他剛一張嘴，滿口的牙全掉了下來；一顆也沒剩下。於是他就這樣沒了牙，繼續趕路。

passages.text: He came to a place where five white geese had their camp. They had flown over the river to hunt deer, and had left their pretty sister at home alone making clothes; before leaving her they had told her that any man who chanced to come to their camp would be her husband, no matter whether he was old or young. Coyote came along, and when he saw the big tent he peeked in through a hole: the girl was sitting making fine things, and he saw how handsome she was. He went back some distance, and by magic procured five eagle's feathers tipped with black, five fine dresses for men, and five bows and arrows, leaving these outside; he had previously made himself a handsome man with nice long hair. The girl received him, cooked food for him, and gave him a fork made of bone; Coyote took a big piece, for he had forgotten all about the loss of his teeth, and could not bite it — he had to be satisfied with pounded meat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 145 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他來到一個地方，那裡有五隻白雁紮了營。她們飛過河去獵鹿，把美麗的妹妹獨自留在家中做衣服；臨走前她們告訴她，任何碰巧來到她們營地的男人，無論老少，都將成為她的丈夫。郊狼走了過來，看見那座大帳篷，便從一個孔洞往裡窺看：那姑娘正坐著製作精美的物件，他看出她有多麼標緻。他退後了一段距離，施法術弄來五根尖端帶黑的鷹羽、五套精美的男裝，以及五副弓箭，把這些留在外面；他先前已把自己變成一個英俊的男子，留著漂亮的長髮。姑娘接待了他，為他煮了食物，給了他一把骨製的叉子；郊狼叉了一大塊，因為他早把掉牙的事忘得一乾二淨，咬不動它——只好將就著吃些搗碎的肉。

passages.text: When he had finished eating, he lay on his back and sang a song, and soon fell asleep. As he lay there, his mouth was open, and the girl saw that he had no teeth; she took a set of teeth of a mountain-sheep and put them into his mouth, then awakened him. She gave him more food, and he found he could eat with ease. 'My teeth always do that,' he said to the girl; 'they grow while I sleep.' He soon finished all she had placed before him, and told her, 'Here are some clothes that I brought for your brothers.' She thought well of his liberality, and told him her five brothers would be home in the evening. Soon they heard them approach: the eldest came in and threw down his deer, and Coyote thought what a handsome man he was. He told Coyote to move over, and Coyote moved closer to the girl; so with each one of them, until finally the fifth came in and told him to move still closer — by this time he was almost on the girl's lap. The eldest said, 'Don't be mean!' Then Coyote married the girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 145-146 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他吃完後，仰面躺下唱了一首歌，不久便睡著了。他躺在那裡時，嘴巴張開，女孩見他沒有牙齒；她取來一副大角羊的牙齒，放進他嘴裡，然後把他喚醒。她又給他更多食物，他發覺自己能夠輕鬆進食。「我的牙齒總是這樣，」他對女孩說；「我睡覺時它們就會長出來。」他很快便把她擺在他面前的食物全都吃完了，並對她說：「這是我帶來給你兄弟們的一些衣服。」她對他的慷慨頗為讚許，並告訴他她的五個兄弟傍晚就會回家。不久他們便聽見他們走近：老大走了進來，扔下他的鹿，郊狼心想他真是個英俊的男子。他叫郊狼挪開一點，郊狼便移近女孩一些；他們每一個人都這樣做，直到最後第五個走進來，叫他再挪近一些——此時他幾乎已坐在女孩的腿上。老大說：「別這麼小氣！」於是郊狼便娶了那女孩。

title.en: The Goose Flight and the Sister's Revenge
title.zh: 雁行墜水與妹之復仇

region.en: Flight across the river of the goose brothers (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雁兄弟渡河飛翔之處（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 3. Coyote and the Geese' (the flight and death of Coyote)

summary.en: Allowed at last to hunt with the brothers, Coyote clings to two of them as they fly across the river uttering the goose-cry — until he screams and all fall. He shoots a fawn, swims with the guts tangled around him in shame, and on the crossing home he shouts in midstream despite their rebukes; the youngest says, 'Let us drop him! It is Coyote,' and he falls — 'Be feathers' lets him float down gently, 'Be a limb' drops him again, until, close to the water, he mistakes and says 'Be a limb,' strikes the bottom of the river, and kills himself. At home the girl sews until she breaks her needle — five needles before she lays down her work — puts her heart into her little finger, and shoots her brothers, killing three; only the two youngest are spared, and the elder of these shoots the end of her little finger, killing his sister.
summary.zh: 郊狼終得隨雁兄狩獵：眾雁脱衣化雁，銜其飛渡大河，囑其勿聲。行至中流，郊狼大呼，眾皆墮地。獲幼鹿後，他携腸下水，腸纏其身，羞愧難當；歸途再渡，中流又呼，弟曰：『丟下他吧！是郊狼！』眾乃棄之。郊狼下墜，呼『化為羽毛』而緩降，呼『化為枯枝』而復墜；臨水誤呼『枯枝』，觸河底而亡。家中雁女縫衣屢折針——折五針方罷——知其夫已死；藏心於小指，取弓射兄，誅其三；二弟倖免，弟射其小指尖，妹亦斃。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The brothers considered Coyote a fine man, and were greatly pleased with the presents he had given to them. Coyote stayed at home one day; the following day he wanted to accompany the brothers when they went hunting. His wife told him that the brothers were accustomed to hunt on the other side of the river, and did not want him to go along because they were going so far that he could not follow them; but the youngest brother said, 'Oh, let him come along!' They came to the river, where they took off their clothes and started to fly across, telling Coyote to utter no sound. Then they flew up into the air, while he clung to two of them; they uttered the goose-cry, and thus they crossed the river. It did not take long before Coyote began to scream, and as soon as he did so, they all fell down. They rebuked him and told him to keep quiet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 146 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兄弟們認為郊狼是個好人，對他送給他們的禮物大為滿意。有一天郊狼留在家裡；第二天他想跟兄弟們一同去打獵。他的妻子告訴他，兄弟們習慣到河的對岸去打獵，不願他跟著去，因為他們要走得太遠，他跟不上；但最小的弟弟說：「哎，讓他一起來吧！」他們來到河邊，在那裡脫下衣服，開始飛越河面，吩咐郊狼不要發出任何聲音。接著他們飛上空中，他緊抓住他們兩個；他們發出雁的叫聲，就這樣飛過了河。沒過多久郊狼便開始尖叫，他一叫出聲，他們便全都掉了下來。他們責備他，叫他保持安靜。

passages.text: They went on for a short distance, hunting for mountain-sheep and other big game. Soon a fawn appeared, and Coyote shot it; he skinned it and went down to the river, thinking that he had done enough. He took the guts and all with him, and after having walked down along the bank a little way, went in swimming. The Goose brothers came up to him to see what he had caught; they took the fawn and threw it into the river, and the guts caught Coyote around the body. He was ashamed. Then the oldest brother suggested that they cross back; they made ready their packs and prepared to cross, putting Coyote on top of them. They flew up and uttered their cry; in the middle of the stream Coyote began to shout, and they fell down fast. They told him to keep still, but he refused to do so. The youngest brother then said, 'Let us drop him! It is Coyote.' They did so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 146 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們繼續走了一小段路，獵捕大角羊和其他大獵物。不久出現了一隻幼鹿，郊狼射中了牠；他剝下鹿皮，走下河邊，自以為已經做得夠多了。他把內臟連同其他東西一併帶著，沿著河岸走了一小段路後，便下水游泳。雁兄弟們上前來看他捕到了什麼；他們拿過幼鹿，把牠扔進河裡，那些內臟便纏住了郊狼的身體。他感到羞愧。接著最年長的哥哥提議他們渡河回去；他們收拾好行囊，準備渡河，把郊狼放在他們上面。他們飛起來，發出叫聲；到了河中央，郊狼開始大喊，他們便急速下墜。他們叫他保持安靜，他卻不肯。最小的弟弟於是說：「我們把他丟下吧！他是郊狼。」他們便這樣做了。

passages.text: When he was just above the surface of the water, he said to himself, 'Be feathers,' and he floated through the air gently; when he rose to a great height, he said, 'Be a limb,' and he fell again rapidly. He kept this up until he finally made a mistake, saying, when he was close to the water, 'Be a limb.' He fell, struck the bottom of the river, and killed himself. The girl at home kept on sewing until she broke her needle; then she knew that her brothers had killed her husband. She broke five needles before she laid down her work; then she took the bows and arrows, put her heart into her little finger, and made ready to kill her brothers. When they came near, she began to shoot; they shouted, 'Don't be angry, your husband was Coyote!' She, however, killed three of her brothers, and spared only the two youngest ones. The younger one then said to the elder, 'Shoot the end of her little finger.' He did so, and so killed his sister. Then they decided to leave the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 146-147 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他正好在水面之上時，他對自己說：「變成羽毛吧。」他便輕輕地在空中飄浮；當他升到極高處時，他說：「變成樹枝吧。」他又急速墜落。他這樣反覆不停，直到最後出了差錯，在接近水面時說：「變成樹枝吧。」他墜落下來，撞到河底，摔死了。家中的女孩一直縫著，直到把針弄斷；於是她知道她的兄弟們殺了她的丈夫。她躺下歇工之前，一共弄斷了五根針；接著她拿起弓箭，把心放進她的小指裡，準備殺她的兄弟們。當他們走近時，她開始射箭；他們喊道：「別生氣，你的丈夫是郊狼！」然而她殺了她的三個兄弟，只饒了兩個最小的。最小的弟弟於是對哥哥說：「射她小指的指尖。」他照做了，就這樣殺了他的姊姊。然後他們決定離開這個地方。

title.en: The Daughters of Winter and Summer
title.zh: 冬夏之女

region.en: House of Winter and house of Summer (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 冬之屋與夏之屋（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 3. Coyote and the Geese' (Winter and Summer)

summary.en: Fifteen days without food after killing their sister, the two surviving goose brothers eat their bowstring and bow-backing, then reach the house of an old gray-haired giant full of ice without a fire, stark naked, whose little daughter Winter calls her four elder sisters from their underground house to cook for him; hearing how the visitors were treated, the brothers leave. Soon they come to the tent of Summer, very warm, where a fine-dressed little girl brings five dishes of meat — one tiny, four large; the brothers can hardly finish the tiny dish, and the girl's elder sisters comb their tangled hair, so the brothers had two wives. They built a sweat-house, repaired their bows, hunted ten deer a day, and had plenty of meat.
summary.zh: 誅妹之後，二雁弟絕糧十五日，食弓弦與弓背筋而活。終至一灰髮老怪之家：滿屋是冰，無火，老怪裸體，幼女冬兒奉命召四姊出地窖為其炊食。二弟見狀即離去。旋至夏神之帳，暖如春暉；小女衣著華美，奉上五盤肉——一小四大。二弟連小盤亦難食盡。老怪命諸女為客梳其糾結之髮，二弟遂得二妻。二人搭汗屋，修弓矢，日獵十鹿，衣食豐足。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Season-house episode. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: They went on, taking along only their bows and arrows. They took no food with them, and had nothing to eat for fifteen days; the younger brother almost starved. His brother took his bowstring and the backing of the bow, both of which were made of sinew, and gave them to him to eat. Finally they came in sight of a large house. They went in. An old gray-haired giant was living there who had four grown daughters and a little one; the youngest girl's name was Winter (xa'lpxa'lp). The house was full of ice and without even a little fire; the old man was stark naked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 147 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們繼續前行，只帶著弓箭。他們沒有帶食物，十五天來什麼也沒吃；弟弟幾乎餓死了。他的哥哥拿了他的弓弦和弓背，兩者都是用筋腱製成的，給他吃。最後他們望見一座大房子。他們走了進去。那裡住著一個頭髮灰白的老巨人，他有四個成年的女兒和一個小女兒；最小的女孩名叫冬天（xa'lpxa'lp）。屋裡滿是冰，連一點小火也沒有；那老人赤身裸體。

passages.text: The four older girls had an underground house to themselves, and were working on beautiful clothing outside the house. The giant sent Winter to call her sisters: as she threw the door open, they shouted, 'You dirty thing! why do you come here?' She delivered her message, and the sisters promised to come soon, cooking a large dishful of food for their father; while they were leaving, the little girl brought two spoons and ate the food with her father, and between them they ate it all. When the young men saw all this, they left.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 147 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 四個較年長的女孩有一座屬於自己的地下房屋，正在屋外製作美麗的衣物。巨人派冬天去叫她的姊姊們：她一推開門，她們便喊道：「你這髒東西！你來這裡做什麼？」她傳達了訊息，姊姊們答應很快就來，並為她們的父親煮了滿滿一大盤食物；她們正要離開時，小女孩拿來兩把勺子，和父親一同吃那食物，兩人把它全都吃光了。兩個年輕人看到這一切，便離開了。

passages.text: Soon they came to another tent, which belonged to Summer. They entered, and saw an old man and a small girl in a fine dress; the house was very warm. The old man sent the girl to ask her sisters to cook a meal, and they came and prepared five dishes of meat — a very tiny one and four large ones. The brothers asked the old man and the little girl for some food, and were given spoons; the younger one began to eat, and could not finish what was given to him; the elder one then ate, and was hardly able to finish what his brother had left. Thereupon the old man told the girl to put away the rest of the food for them. The hair of the brothers was very much entangled; therefore the old man sent the girl to call her sisters, who were to comb the hair of the brothers — the oldest two girls combed the hair of the elder brother, while the younger girls combed the hair of the younger one, so they had two wives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 147-148 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久他們來到另一座帳篷，那是屬於夏季的。他們走進去，看見一位老人和一個穿著華美衣裳的小女孩；屋裡非常溫暖。老人派那女孩去叫她的姊妹們煮一頓飯，她們便來預備了五盤肉——一盤極小，四盤很大。兄弟倆向老人和小女孩討些食物，得到了湯匙；弟弟先吃，卻吃不完給他的份量；哥哥接著吃，也幾乎吃不完弟弟剩下的。於是老人吩咐女孩把其餘的食物收起來留給他們。兄弟倆的頭髮十分糾結；因此老人派女孩去叫她的姊妹們來為兄弟倆梳理頭髮——兩個年長的女孩為哥哥梳頭，年幼的女孩們則為弟弟梳頭，於是他們各有了兩位妻子。

passages.text: The brothers made their home there. They built a sweat-house and repaired their bows, the strings and backing of which they had eaten. The old man told them that there were many deer in the canyons; they set out before daylight and killed ten, which they carried home. They went out to hunt every day, and had plenty of meat, part of which they dried.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 148 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兄弟倆就在那裡安了家。他們蓋了一座汗屋，又修好了他們的弓，因為弓弦和弓背都被他們吃掉了。老人告訴他們，峽谷裡有許多鹿；他們在天亮前出發，獵得十隻鹿，扛回家中。他們每天外出打獵，肉食充足，其中一部分他們曬乾了。

title.en: Winter's War on Summer
title.zh: 冬神征夏

region.en: From Winter's ice-house to Summer's warm tent (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自冬之冰屋至夏之暖帳（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 3. Coyote and the Geese' (Winter's war on Summer)

summary.en: Winter, insulted by the meat Summer's people threw at her, resolved to wage war on Summer; her four sisters drove her away with a stick and refused to go, so the old giant and his youngest daughter set out alone on a white bob-tailed horse made of ice, with ice-spears, ice-arrows and ice hanging all over their bodies. Summer saw a fog coming and knew what it was; when the girl told him they were close by, he shook his blanket — the deer's liver and lungs his daughter used — and all the ice melted and fell off their bodies. 'You have no power. Take all the meat you want,' said Summer, and they loaded their horse and went home.
summary.zh: 冬女受夏族擲肉之辱，誓師征夏。四姊以棍驅之，拒不從行。冬神乃與幼女獨往：乘冰製白短尾馬，携冰矛冰箭，周身掛冰。夏神見霧氣而來，已知其故；聞女報『敵至』，抖動其毯（其女所用鹿肝肺）——冰甲盡融墜地。夏神曰：『爾等已無能為。要肉便拿去。』父女載肉而歸。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Season-war myth closing the Winter/Summer episode. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The girl returned home and found her father sitting in the house; she threw the meat at him, just as Summer had done to her, and he picked it up likewise and ate it. He decided, however, to wage war on Summer, and told his youngest daughter to summon her sisters. They drove her away with a stick, and refused to go; therefore the giant and his youngest daughter prepared to go without them. They took a white bob-tailed horse made of ice, ice-spears, and ice-arrows; ice was hanging all over their bodies. They came to Summer's house, the girl riding behind the old man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 148 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 女孩回到家中，發現父親坐在屋裡；她把肉朝他扔去，正如夏季當初對她所做的那樣，他也照樣撿起來吃了。然而他決定向夏季開戰，並吩咐他最年幼的女兒去召集她的姊妹們。她們用棍子把她趕走，拒絕前去；於是巨人便帶著他最年幼的女兒準備獨自前往。他們帶了一匹冰做的白短尾馬、冰矛和冰箭；冰掛滿了他們全身。他們來到夏季的屋前，女孩騎在老人身後。

passages.text: Summer saw a fog, and knew what was coming. When his daughter told him that they were close by, he shook his blanket — the little girl used a deer's liver, the old man a deer's lungs, to drive them away — and all the ice melted and fell off from their bodies. When they came nearer, Summer said to them, 'You have no power. Take all the meat you want.' They loaded their horse and went home. That is the end of the story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 148 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 夏季看見一團霧，便知道將有什麼事臨到。當他的女兒告訴他他們已近在咫尺時，他抖動他的毯子——小女孩用鹿肝，老人用鹿肺，來把他們驅退——所有的冰都融化了，從他們身上脫落。當他們走得更近時，夏季對他們說：『你們沒有力量。你們要多少肉就拿多少吧。』他們把馬裝載好，便回家去了。故事到此結束。

title.en: Coyote and the Swallowing Monster of Kamiah
title.zh: 郊狼誅卡米亞吞人魔

region.en: Kamiah on the Clearwater, monster's body across the valley (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 清水河卡米亞，魔軀橫跨河谷（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 4. Coyote and the Swallowing Monster'

summary.en: Coyote ties himself with wild grape-vine in three places, hides behind a bundle of grass with pitch and fire-sticks in his quiver, and challenges the monster Iltswe'tsix at Kamiah: 'Let us swallow each other!' Drawn in against his ropes, breaking one after another, he insists on entering by the mouth — tramples Rattlesnake flat-nosed for not biting the monster, reproaches Grizzly-Bear for not killing him — and reaching the hanging heart, stabs it, builds a fire under it, and orders the people to step out before the monster dies, himself last. The monster may be seen at Kamiah to-day, and the heart is there too.
summary.zh: 郊狼以野葡萄藤三處縛身，以草束遮身潛近卡米亞之魔 Iltswe'tsix，挑戰曰：『吾倆互吞如何！』魔吸之，藤索逐一崩斷；郊狼堅持自其口而入——踩扁響尾蛇之鼻（斥其不噬魔）、叱灰熊不誅魔——終至懸心之處，以刀刺之，於心下燃火，令眾人於魔死前奪路而出，己則殿後。卡米亞至今猶見魔之遺骸，其心亦在。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Monster-slaying culture-hero cycle; a second version places the monster on Salmon River. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote came back westward through Idaho. On his way he heard that a monster was swallowing the people. Coyote tied himself with a wild grape-vine in three different places, and then crawled over the mountains to see the monster. He hid behind a bundle of grass that he carried in front of himself; he had pitch and fire-sticks in his quiver. He met the monster at Kamiah, and then he mocked him, saying, 'Iltswe'tsix — that was the monster's name — let us swallow each other!' The monster was so surprised that he did not know what to say. He told Coyote to swallow him first; Coyote said that he preferred him to begin, but finally he gave in and agreed to swallow the monster first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 148-149 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼向西穿過愛達荷返回。途中他聽說有個怪物正在吞食人們。郊狼用野葡萄藤在三處把自己綁住，然後翻山越嶺去看那怪物。他躲在自己身前攜帶的一捆草後面；他的箭袋裡裝著瀝青和取火棒。他在卡米亞遇見了那怪物，便譏笑他說：『伊爾茨韋齊克西——那是怪物的名字——讓我們互相吞了對方吧！』怪物驚訝得不知該說什麼。他叫郊狼先吞他；郊狼說他寧願由對方先開始，但最後他讓步了，同意先吞那怪物。

passages.text: Coyote drew in his breath, and the monster could hardly withstand the suction: 'Doggone you! you are stronger than I thought.' Coyote then said, 'Now it is your turn.' The monster tried hard to move Coyote, but he was tied fast; Coyote then tried a second time, and was able to move the monster a little. When the monster tried again, one of the ropes that held Coyote broke; the next time all the ropes broke, and Coyote was drawn towards the monster. He argued with him, because they could not agree on the way Coyote should enter his body: the monster tried to get him to go in through the anus or the ears; Coyote insisted on going in through the mouth, and at last the monster consented. He opened his mouth, and Coyote went in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 149 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼吸了一口氣，那怪物幾乎抵擋不住這股吸力：『該死的你！你比我想的還要強。』郊狼於是說：『現在輪到你了。』怪物使勁想拉動郊狼，但他被綁得牢牢的；郊狼接著又試了第二次，能把怪物稍微拉動一點。當怪物再試一次時，綁住郊狼的一條繩子斷了；下一次所有的繩子都斷了，郊狼被拉向怪物。他與怪物爭論，因為他們無法就郊狼該從何處進入他的身體達成一致：怪物想讓他從肛門或耳朵進去；郊狼堅持要從嘴巴進去，最後怪物同意了。他張開嘴，郊狼便進去了。

passages.text: Inside he met Rattlesnake, who wanted to bite him; Coyote trampled him under foot, thereby flattening his nose, and reviled him for not biting the monster. Farther in he met Grizzly-Bear, and reproached him for not killing the monster. Finally he reached the place where the monster's heart was hanging; he stabbed it with his knife. The monster now tried to coax Coyote to come out, but he refused, and proceeded to build a fire directly under the heart; then he cut it. He ordered the people to get ready to step out before the monster should die; they went out, Coyote last of all. The monster may be seen at Kamiah to-day, and the heart is there too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 149 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在裡面遇見響尾蛇，響尾蛇想咬他；郊狼用腳踩踏牠，因而把牠的鼻子踩扁了，並斥責牠不去咬那怪物。再往裡走，他遇見灰熊，責備牠不去殺那怪物。最後他來到怪物心臟懸掛之處；他用刀刺它。怪物這時試圖哄騙郊狼出來，但他拒絕了，並逕自在心臟正下方生起火來；然後他把心臟割下。他命令眾人準備在怪物死前走出去；他們走了出去，郊狼走在最後。今日在卡米亞（Kamiah）仍可見到那怪物，心臟也在那裡。

title.en: Coyote Butchers the Monster: The Making of the Tribes
title.zh: 郊狼剖魔分族

region.en: Butchering-place of the monster at Kamiah (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡米亞魔屍剖分之地（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 4. Coyote and the Swallowing Monster' (the division of the body)

summary.en: Coyote decided to cut up the monster and divide it among the people: out of its feet he made the Blackfeet; the Crow, the Sioux, and the Bannock were all made out of different parts of its body. Asked what he took for himself, he answered, 'To be wise (?).' Then he called for water, washed his hands and scattered the water, saying, 'You shall be the Nez Perces, a small tribe, but you shall be the most powerful of all the people.' In the second version he threw the skin to Montana — 'This shall be the Blackfoot Indians, and they shall be tall, stout men' — made the tribes from the other parts, and when Fox objected that he had done nothing for the place where they were living, sprinkled the blood left on his hands and on the ground: 'This blood shall be Indians in the future. They shall be good warriors and strong, but they shall be few in number.' These were the Nez Perce Indians.
summary.zh: 郊狼剖魔分肉：以其足造黑腳人；烏鴉、蘇人、班諾克各族，皆取魔身不同部位而成。人問其自取何物，答曰：『取智（？）。』復索水洗手上之血，將水潑灑，曰：『爾等將為內茲珀斯人，族小人少，然為萬族中最強者。』另一異文：皮擲蒙大拿——『是為黑腳人，身長體壯』——餘體分造諸族。狐嫌其未為本地居民做任何事，郊狼遂將手上與地上之血灑於斯：『此血將化為印第安人，勇敢強健，然人數不多。』是即內茲珀斯人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Dismemberment ethnogony parallel (Ymir/Pangu/Purusha cluster). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Then Coyote decided to cut up the monster and to divide it among the people. Out of its feet he made the Blackfeet. The Crow, the Sioux, and the Bannock were all made out of different parts of its body. While Coyote was standing there, some one said, 'What did you take yourself?' and he replied, 'To be wise (?).' Then he called for water. He washed his hands and scattered the water, saying, 'You shall be the Nez Perces, a small tribe, but you shall be the most powerful of all the people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 149 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是郊狼決定把怪物切開，分給眾人。他用牠的腳造出黑腳人（Blackfeet）。烏鴉人（Crow）、蘇人（Sioux）與班諾克人（Bannock）都是由牠身體的不同部位造出的。郊狼站在那裡時，有人說：『你給自己取了什麼？』他回答：『做個有智慧的（？）。』然後他要水。他洗了手，把水灑出去，說：『你們將成為內茲珀斯人（Nez Perces），一個小部落，但你們將成為所有人中最強大的。』

passages.text: In the second version Coyote now began to butcher the monster. He threw the skin to Montana, and said, 'This shall be the Blackfoot Indians, and they shall be tall, stout men.' The other parts of the body he threw in different directions, and thus made the different tribes. After the body had been entirely dismembered, Fox, who was watching him, said, 'You have done nothing for the place where we are now living.' There was some blood left on his hands and on the ground; Coyote sprinkled it over the place, saying, 'This blood shall be Indians in the future. They shall be good warriors and strong, but they shall be few in number.' These were the Nez Perce Indians.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 151 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在第二個版本中，郊狼這時開始宰割怪物。他把皮扔向蒙大拿（Montana），說：『這將成為黑腳印第安人（Blackfoot Indians），他們將是高大、壯碩的人。』身體的其他部分他扔向不同方向，就這樣造出了不同的部落。身體被完全肢解之後，在一旁觀看的狐狸說：『對於我們現在居住的這個地方，你什麼也沒做。』他手上和地上還留有一些血；郊狼把血灑在那地方，說：『這血將來要成為印第安人。他們將是優秀的戰士，強壯，但人數稀少。』這些就是內茲珀斯印第安人。

title.en: Coyote's Wars: The Humming-Birds of the Canyon
title.zh: 郊狼之戰：峽谷雙蜂鳥

region.en: Canyon ridge with the two white heart-sticks (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 峽谷山脊，雙白心柱所在（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 5. Coyote's Wars' (the Humming-Birds)

summary.en: Two Humming-Birds, the only living things about, challenge Coyote — 'Let us have war!' — kill him and throw him into the river; he drifts ashore where Magpie pecks his eyes awake. 'I was just dreaming about getting some girls at the head of the canyon,' says Coyote; Magpie tells him those birds were put there when the world was first made, and teaches the secret: their hearts are two white sticks with two white feathers on the hill-top — seize the poles, break the feathers, and they die. Transformed into an old man, Coyote baits them — 'Come down and kill me' — slips up the other side, reaches the poles with the birds almost upon him, breaks the feathers, and kills both: 'Hereafter you shall just be pretty little birds, and not kill people.'
summary.zh: 兩蜂鳥乃當地唯一生靈，向郊狼挑戰：『來戰！』殺之而投諸河。其屍漂至岸邊，喜鵲啄其目而醒。郊狼曰：『吾方夢見峽源之美女。』鵲告之：此二鳥乃開天闢地時所置，專司殺人；欲誅之，須奪其命根——山頂兩根白柱，上各插白羽，是即其心。化為老翁誘敵：『來殺我吧！』趁其下谷，反向山頂疾奔，搶得木柱，折其白羽——二鳥遂死。郊狼曰：『爾等從此只為小鳥，不得再殺人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. First of the Coyote's-wars episodes. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling upstream. He heard a noise like the sawing of wood, and stood still and listened: two Humming-Birds were there, the only living things about. They said to Coyote, 'Let us have war!' Coyote heard them, and, throwing his bow and arrow down in front of him, replied, 'That is what I have been looking for, a light.' With that he jumped about, ran up the ridge toward them; and they came down the canyon, and rushed at him from both sides. They killed Coyote, and told him that he was to be nothing but Coyote. They dragged him to the river and threw him into the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 151 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正沿河而上。他聽見一種像鋸木頭的聲音，便站住傾聽：那裡有兩隻蜂鳥，是附近僅有的活物。牠們對郊狼說：『我們來打仗吧！』郊狼聽見了，把他的弓和箭扔到面前，回答：『這正是我一直在找的，一道光。』說著他便跳來跳去，沿著山脊向牠們奔去；牠們則從峽谷下來，從兩邊向他衝來。牠們殺死了郊狼，並告訴他，他什麼也不是，只是郊狼。牠們把他拖到河邊，扔進水裡。

passages.text: He floated down the stream until his body drifted ashore. Magpie saw him lying dead, and began pecking at his eyes, which awakened Coyote. 'That is not right. I was just dreaming about getting some girls at the head of the canyon,' he said to Magpie, who replied, 'There are two Humming-Birds up there who kill everybody, and they are the ones who killed you. They were put there when the world was first made. Listen to what I tell you now! Return the way you came. Make yourself an old man, and, should they say anything to you, tell them to kill you because you are tired. When they come up over the hill, there will be two white sticks with two white feathers on them on the top of the hill. These are their hearts. Take the canyon trail and run as hard as you can toward the sticks; keep going until you get them. Then take hold of the poles, break the feathers, and thus kill them. That is the only way to destroy them.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 152 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他順流漂下，直到屍體被沖上岸。喜鵲看見他躺在那裡死了，便開始啄他的眼睛，這把郊狼弄醒了。『這可不對。我剛才正夢見在峽谷上頭弄到幾個姑娘呢，』他對喜鵲說。喜鵲回答：『那上面有兩隻蜂鳥，牠們見誰殺誰，就是牠們殺了你。世界初造之時，牠們就被安置在那裡。現在聽我告訴你！循原路回去。把自己變成一個老人，要是牠們對你說什麼，就告訴牠們殺了你吧，因為你累了。當牠們翻過山頭上來時，山頂上會有兩根白棍子，上面各插著兩根白羽毛。那就是牠們的心。走峽谷的小路，盡全力朝那些棍子跑去；一直跑，直到拿到它們。然後抓住那些桿子，折斷羽毛，這樣就能殺死牠們。這是毀掉牠們的唯一辦法。』

passages.text: He transformed himself into an old man and went off, in accordance with Magpie's instructions. He met the Humming-Birds, who said, 'Let us have war!' — 'Come down and kill me,' was Coyote's reply as he lay down on his back. When they started towards him, he ran up on the other side, and was half way up when they got down. They turned, and saw that he was fairly close to the two poles, and started after him. When he reached the two poles, they had almost caught up with him; he seized the poles, however, broke the feathers, and thus killed both of them. Then Coyote said to the Humming-Birds, 'There are other people coming. Hereafter you shall just be pretty little birds, and not kill people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 152 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他把自己變成一個老人，依照喜鵲的指示出發了。他遇見蜂鳥，牠們說：『我們來打仗吧！』——『下來殺我吧，』郊狼仰面躺下回答。當牠們朝他走來時，他從另一邊跑上山去，牠們下來時他已跑到半山腰。牠們轉身，看見他相當接近那兩根桿子，便開始追他。當他到達那兩根桿子時，牠們幾乎追上他了；然而他抓住桿子，折斷羽毛，就這樣把牠們兩隻都殺死了。然後郊狼對蜂鳥說：『還有別的人要來。從今以後，你們就只做漂亮的小鳥，不再殺人。』

title.en: The Mountain-Sheep Woman
title.zh: 大角羊女

region.en: Bluff above the river where the forked-stick woman waits (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河上峭壁，分叉木杖女子伏擊處（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 5. Coyote's Wars' (the mountain-sheep woman)

summary.en: A handsome girl with a forked white stick calls travellers to come and lie with her, then bids them look down at a big mountain-sheep and pierces their necks with the forked stick as they stoop, pushing them over and into the river. Magpie revives Coyote a second time and tells him the woman has always been there to kill everybody: when she calls again, climb up, ask her for the stick because you are tired, and push her over. Coyote does so — 'Now, grandchild, show me where to look' — and knocks her head off as she looks down. 'That is easy; but hereafter when people come, they shall eat you, for from now on you shall only be a mountain-sheep.'
summary.zh: 一美貌少女持白色分叉木杖，喚旅人曰：『來與吾同臥！』待其近前，又令其俯視崖下大角羊；趁其彎腰，以杖刺其頸，推落河中。郊狼二度為喜鵲所救。鵲曰：『此女常伏於此殺人。』教其計策：她再喚時，登崖索杖——『吾倦矣』——趁其俯視，推其下崖。郊狼依計而行，一刀擊落其首。臨終言：『此事易耳。然自此以後，人將食爾——爾已化為凡獸大角羊矣。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: He continued his journey up the river. Soon he heard a woman: 'Whoever you are, come and lie with me!' When he came up to her, he saw that she was a handsome girl, with in her hand a forked white stick. Coyote asked, 'Grandchild, what do you want?' She told him to look down, and he would see a big mountain-sheep. As he stooped down to do so, she pierced his neck with her forked stick, pushed him over, and killed him. She went to see whom she had killed, and saw that it was Coyote; she was afraid that his decaying body would smell, so she threw it into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 152 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他繼續沿河而上。不久他聽見一個女人說：「不管你是誰，過來與我同臥吧！」當他走到她面前，看見她是個標緻的姑娘，手裡拿著一根分叉的白木棍。郊狼問道：「孫女啊，你想要什麼？」她叫他往下看，他便會看見一頭大盤羊。當他彎下腰去看時，她用那根分叉的木棍刺穿了他的脖子，把他推倒，殺死了他。她前去查看自己殺死的是誰，發現是郊狼；她怕他腐爛的屍體發臭，便把他扔進了河裡。

passages.text: It floated down and drifted ashore at the same place as before. Magpie pecked at his eyes and cured him. Coyote told him that he was dreaming about some woman, and Magpie told him that the woman had always been there to kill everybody: 'When she does so again, climb up to her; and when she tells you to look, ask her to come down because you are tired. Then push her over and kill her. She is a mountain-sheep.' Coyote went up, listened, and heard her calling him; he climbed up and pretended to be tired, and asked her for the stick. 'Now, grandchild,' he said, 'show me where to look.' She stepped to the bluff; and when she looked down, he knocked her head off and killed her. 'That is easy,' he said, 'but hereafter when people come, they shall eat you, for from now on you shall only be a mountain-sheep.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 152 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他順流漂下，又漂到先前同一個地方擱了淺。喜鵲啄他的眼睛，把他治好了。郊狼告訴喜鵲，他正夢見某個女人，喜鵲便告訴他，那女人一直待在那裡殺害每一個人：「等她再這樣做時，你爬到她那裡去；當她叫你往下看時，你就說你累了，請她下來。然後把她推倒，殺死她。她是一頭盤羊。」郊狼上去，側耳傾聽，聽見她在呼喚他；他爬上去，假裝疲倦，向她要那根木棍。「現在，孫女啊，」他說，「指給我看該往哪裡看。」她走到崖邊；當她往下看時，他砍掉了她的頭，殺死了她。「這很容易，」他說，「但從今以後，當人們來時，他們要吃你，因為從現在起你只會是一頭盤羊。」

title.en: The Mussel Girl and the Leech Woman
title.zh: 蚌女與螞蟥婦

region.en: Spring-side opening on the river bank (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 河畔泉邊空地（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 5. Coyote's Wars' (the Mussel and the Leech)

summary.en: A fine-dressed girl on the hillside calls 'Come and lie down with me!' — and when Coyote obeys, her sexual organs bite and kill him. Magpie names her the Mussel and teaches the remedy: a notched bone to pry her open. Killed in turn, she is dragged to the river: 'You shall never move about again. You shall be called Mussel, and people shall eat you.' Farther up, a fat girl with red paint on her dress can say only 'U u u!' and 'E e e!'; she chokes Coyote with her grip and throws him in. Magpie names her the Leech and tells Coyote to make a big fire and push her into it; crawling out, she is pushed back and killed — 'Sometimes you will get on to children and crawl into them, but not many will die from your bites. Good people are coming, and you shall not harm them.'
summary.zh: 衣飾華美之少女立於坡上，呼曰：『來同臥！』郊狼從之，竟為其下體咬斃。喜鵲告之：此乃蚌女，當以帶齒之骨撬之。郊狼依計誅之，棄屍於河：『爾從此不得移動，名為蚌，人將食爾。』再上，遇一肥女，裙染紅彩，唯能發『嗚嗚』之聲；抱郊狼至窒息，擲之於河。鵲名之為螞蟥，授計以大火焚之。郊狼積薪燃火，以長棍推之入火；她爬出，再推，遂斃。郊狼曰：『爾偶附孩童爬入其身，然死者無多。善人將至，不得害之。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote now resumed his way upstream. It was not long before he met a woman who called him: 'Come and lie down with me!' He looked at her, and saw that she wore a fine dress down to her waist; the girl stood on the hillside. Coyote climbed up to her, and asked her what she had said. 'Lie with me,' was the answer. When he obeyed, her sexual organs bit and killed him. The girl then dragged him to the river and threw him in, as the others had done. He floated down to the same place as on the previous occasions, and Magpie found him and revived him. 'You brown-eye!' Coyote said, 'why are you running about here? I was just getting some girls from the head of the canyon.' — 'That was the Mussel who killed you,' Magpie said. 'Go back and take a bone with notches in it, and then, when she lies down, run it into her and pry her open.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 152-153 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼現在又繼續溯流而上。沒過多久，他遇到一個女人呼喚他：「過來與我同臥吧！」他看了看她，見她穿著一件垂到腰際的漂亮衣裳；那姑娘站在山坡上。郊狼爬到她那裡，問她剛才說了什麼。「與我同臥，」她回答。當他照做時，她的性器咬住他，殺死了他。那姑娘隨後把他拖到河邊，扔了進去，就像其他人所做的那樣。他順流漂到先前幾次同一個地方，喜鵲發現了他，使他甦醒過來。「你這個褐眼睛！」郊狼說，「你為什麼在這裡跑來跑去？我剛才正從峽谷上頭弄來幾個姑娘呢。」——「殺死你的是貽貝，」喜鵲說。「回去拿一根帶缺口的骨頭，然後，等她躺下時，把它刺進她體內，把她撬開。」

passages.text: Coyote went back, and the girl called to him as before, 'Come and try me, whoever it is that is going up there!' Coyote went to her and killed her, as instructed by Magpie. Then he dragged her to the river and threw her in, saying, 'You shall never move about again. You shall be called Mussel, and people shall eat you. Soon other people will come.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 153 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼回去了，那姑娘像先前一樣呼喚他：「不管往那上頭去的是誰，過來試試我吧！」郊狼走到她那裡，照喜鵲的指示殺死了她。然後他把她拖到河邊，扔了進去，說道：「你再也動彈不得了。你要被叫作貽貝，人們要吃你。不久別的人們就要來了。」

passages.text: He went on up the stream. He came to an opening where he saw a fat girl; she had red paint on her dress. Coyote asked her, 'Why are you sitting there?' All she answered was, 'U u u!' — she could not say anything else. Coyote then thought he would take her along. 'Must I carry you on my back?' Her reply was, 'E e e!' He lifted her up; and when he was ready to put her down, he said to her, 'Let go! Here is a good place to stop.' The girl, however, only tightened her hold until she choked Coyote. She recognized him, and threw him into the river, and Magpie revived him as before. 'That was a leech,' Magpie told him. 'When you go back, she will be there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 153 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他繼續沿溪而上。他來到一處空地，看見一個胖姑娘；她的衣裳上有紅色的塗料。郊狼問她：「你為什麼坐在那裡？」她只回答：「嗚嗚嗚！」——她說不出別的話。郊狼於是心想，他要帶她一起走。「我非得背你不可嗎？」她的回答是：「咿咿咿！」他把她舉起來；當他準備把她放下時，他對她說：「鬆手！這裡是個停下來的好地方。」然而那姑娘只是把他摟得更緊，直到把郊狼勒得喘不過氣。她認出了他，把他扔進河裡，喜鵲像先前一樣使他甦醒過來。「那是一隻水蛭，」喜鵲告訴他。「你回去時，她會在那裡。

passages.text: Ask her if she is cold, and she will say, E e e! Then make a big fire, take a stick, and burn her.' Coyote went up, reached the woman, and said to her, 'My cousin, I see you are still here. Are you not cold sitting in the spring?' — 'E e e!' was her answer. He gathered a load of wood and made a big fire; then he pulled her toward it, and with a long stick pushed her in. When she tried to crawl out, he pushed her back and killed her. Then he said, 'Your name shall be Leech. Sometimes you will get on to children and crawl into them, but not many will die from your bites. Good people are coming, and you shall not harm them.' That was the end of Coyote's journey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 153 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 問她冷不冷，她會說：咿咿咿！然後生一大堆火，拿一根棍子，把她燒了。」郊狼上去，走到那女人那裡，對她說：「我的表親，我看你還在這兒。坐在泉水裡你不冷嗎？」——「咿咿咿！」她回答。他拾了一捆柴，生了一大堆火；然後把她往火邊拉，用一根長棍把她推了進去。當她試圖爬出來時，他又把她推回去，殺死了她。然後他說：「你的名字要叫水蛭。有時你會爬到孩子們身上，鑽進他們體內，但不會有多少人因你的咬而死去。好人們就要來了，你不可傷害他們。」那就是郊狼旅程的終結。

title.en: Coyote and Crane: The Stingy Fisherman
title.zh: 郊狼與鶴：吝嗇漁夫

region.en: Middle of the current where the long-legged fisherman stands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 長腿漁夫立於急流中央（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 7. Coyote and Crane'

summary.en: A long-legged man stands in the middle of the current catching fish with a long pole, a pile of fish on the bank; twice Coyote asks for a fish and is refused — the second time mocked with his own words. When the man starts to ford the river, the angry Coyote throws a rock that breaks his legs, and he floats down the river repeating 'Your load was too heavy and broke your legs!' until only bubbles rise. 'Henceforth you shall be a crane, and people shall make fun of you. From now on, when a man kills much game, he shall give others some.'
summary.zh: 長腿漁夫立於急流中央，以長竿捕魚，岸邊魚積如山。郊狼兩度乞魚，均遭拒絕，且受其嘲弄。漁夫涉水而返之際，郊狼怒擲石塊，斷其雙腿；漁夫順流而下，口中喃喃：『負荷太重，腿為之折！』終至滅頂，唯見氣泡。郊狼曰：『從今為鶴，任人取笑。此後凡獵得多者，當分與他人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote continued his travels up the river, and met a man with long legs, who stood in the middle of the current, catching fish with a long pole; a pile of fish lay on the bank of the river. Coyote spoke to him, but the man did not answer; he kept on catching fish, which he strung up. Coyote asked him for a fish, but his request was refused. He asked a second time, and this time the man mocked him, repeating Coyote's words: 'Give me one.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 155 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼沿河繼續他的旅程，遇見一個長腿的男人，那人站在水流中央，用一根長竿捕魚；河岸上堆著一堆魚。郊狼對他說話，那人卻不回答；他只顧繼續捕魚，把魚串起來。郊狼向他要一條魚，卻遭到拒絕。他第二次開口，這回那人嘲弄他，重複郊狼的話：「給我一條。」

passages.text: After a while the man started to ford the river. Coyote, who was very angry, threw a rock at him, hit his legs, and broke them. The man floated down the river; and Coyote called after him, 'Your load was too heavy and broke your legs!' The man repeated the words after him. As he was sinking, Coyote spoke again; but when the man tried to answer, all that could be seen were bubbles on the surface of the water. Coyote said, 'Henceforth you shall be a crane (mu'k'a), and people shall make fun of you. From now on, when a man kills much game, he shall give others some.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 155 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了一會兒，那人開始涉水過河。郊狼非常憤怒，朝他扔了一塊石頭，打中他的腿，把腿打斷了。那人順流漂下；郊狼在他身後喊道：「你的負擔太重，把你的腿壓斷了！」那人跟著重複他的話。當他往下沉時，郊狼又開口；但那個人試著回答時，水面上只看得到氣泡。郊狼說：「從今以後，你將是一隻鶴（mu'k'a），人們會取笑你。從今以後，當一個人獵到許多獵物時，他應當分一些給別人。」

title.en: The Eye-Juggler: Coyote Loses His Eyes
title.zh: 拋眼戲：郊狼失明記

region.en: Woods where Wildcat plays ball with his eyes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 野貓戲眼之林（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 8. The Eye-Juggler'

summary.en: Hearing some one sing 'Come back, my eyes!', Coyote finds Wildcat playing ball with his eyes and resolves to try; his first eye drops back into its socket when called, but Wildcat, knowing it is Coyote, knocks the eye aside with his horn so it does not return. Taking out the other so that 'both will come back to me,' he throws them both at once — Wildcat knocks both away, and Coyote becomes totally blind. He comes to a tent where an old woman sings that it is a good thing Coyote lost his eyes; he kills her, skins her, eats the meal and seeds, and assumes her shape. The grand-daughters who dance about Coyote's eyes come home, the youngest alone recognizing him; they carry 'grandmother' to the dance, each elder dropping her in turn at his touch, until at the dance he demands his eyes, puts back his own, throws off the disguise and scatters black paint behind him five times to darken the pursuers' way until, weary, they give up — and Coyote got his eyes back.
summary.zh: 郊狼聞歌『回來吧，吾眼！』見野貓以眼為球而戲，羨而效之。拋出之眼一呼即回；然野貓識其為郊狼，以其角擊偏其眼，使之不返。郊狼自以為：『取出另一眼，二眼皆歸。』雙拋之際，野貓又擊——郊狼全盲。行至一帳，老嫗歌唱『郊狼失眼，真是好事』；郊狼殺之、剝其皮、食其糧、披其衣，假扮老嫗。其眾孫女自郊狼之眼舞會歸來，唯幼女識破。眾女輪流背『祖母』赴會，長者皆因被他觸碰而棄之；至會場，郊狼索回己眼，褪去偽裝而逃，沿途五次撒黑漆遮蔽追者，眾人疲而罷追——郊狼復得雙眼。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Eye-juggler cycle. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and heard some one singing, 'Come back, my eyes!' Soon he saw Wildcat playing ball with his eyes. He said, 'I wish I could do that! If I could do that and do it at Qualp, I should do great things.' Coyote decided to try; he went into the woods, and when he tried to take out his eye, it hurt so that he screamed. Finally he succeeded in removing it; he threw it up into the air and called to it to come back, and it dropped back into its socket. 'Now I can do it,' he said to himself. Wildcat heard him, and, knowing it was Coyote, took his horn, and, when Coyote threw his eye up again, knocked it out of the way, so that it did not return. Coyote called several times, but the eye did not come back. Coyote now said, 'My eye must be near. If I take out the other one, they will both come back to me.' So he took it out and threw it up; both came back. 'That's a fine trick,' Coyote said. Now he threw both at the same time; this time Wildcat knocked both away, and Coyote became totally blind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 155-156 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正在旅行，聽見有人唱著：「回來吧，我的眼睛！」不久他看見野貓用自己的眼睛玩球。他說：「但願我也能那樣做！如果我能那樣做，而且在Qualp做，我就能成就大事。」郊狼決定一試；他走進樹林，當他試著取出自己的眼睛時，痛得他尖叫起來。最後他總算把眼睛取了出來；他把它拋向空中，喚它回來，它便落回眼窩裡。「現在我會了，」他自言自語。野貓聽見了，知道那是郊狼，便拿起他的號角，當郊狼再次把眼睛拋上去時，把眼睛撞到一旁，使它沒有回來。郊狼呼喚了好幾次，眼睛卻沒有回來。郊狼這時說：「我的眼睛一定就在附近。如果我把另一隻也取出來，它們兩隻都會回到我身上。」於是他取出另一隻，拋了上去；兩隻都回來了。「這真是個好把戲，」郊狼說。這回他同時拋出兩隻；這一次野貓把兩隻都撞開，郊狼便完全瞎了。

passages.text: When Coyote came to a tent, he found an old woman living there. He listened outside, and heard her sing about Coyote's eyes: 'It is a good thing he lost his eyes.' Coyote went in and saw the woman grinding seeds very fine. 'What are you singing about?' — 'Coyote lost his eyes. That is why I am singing. People are gathered here from all over, dancing about Coyote's eyes. My grand-daughters have gone there. They will come back to me soon.' The woman then gave some seeds to Coyote, who said to himself, 'I must kill this old woman.' 'I must go out a minute,' he told her, went out to get two stones, returned, said, 'I am glad Coyote lost his eyes,' and hit her on the head with a stone, killing her. He took his knife and skinned her, hid the body outside, cooked and ate all the meal and seeds, then put on her skin and clothes and assumed her shape, keeping on pounding the meal and seeds until towards evening.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 156 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼來到一座帳篷前，發現那裡住著一個老婦人。他在外面傾聽，聽見她唱著關於郊狼眼睛的歌：「他失去了眼睛，這是件好事。」郊狼走進去，看見那婦人正把種子磨得很細。「你在唱什麼？」——「郊狼失去了眼睛。這就是我在唱的原因。人們從四面八方聚集到這裡，圍著郊狼的眼睛跳舞。我的孫女們都到那裡去了。她們很快就會回到我這裡來。」那婦人隨後給了郊狼一些種子，郊狼自言自語道：「我必須殺死這個老婦人。」「我必須出去一下，」他對她說，出去拿了兩塊石頭，回來，說：「我很高興郊狼失去了眼睛，」便用石頭打她的頭，把她打死了。他拿出刀，剝下她的皮，把屍體藏到外面，把飯和種子全都煮了吃掉，然後穿上她的皮和衣服，變成她的模樣，繼續搗著飯和種子，直到傍晚。

passages.text: The oldest daughter came in, then the next younger, and the others in order, the youngest one coming last. She looked at Coyote and recognized him, and decided that he had killed her grandmother; the other girls rebuked him for not grinding the seeds properly — 'The meal is much too coarse' — and he answered, 'My legs hurt. I was shot in the thigh a long time ago, and it hurts so that I cannot do much pounding now.' The girls went back into the tent, and, being tired, went to sleep. Coyote put his hand on the privates of the four elder girls; as he approached the youngest, she awoke and kicked him, knowing he was Coyote: 'What are you doing?' At this the other girls awoke too, and rebuked her for acting so toward her grandmother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 156 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 最大的女兒走了進來，接著是次大的，其餘的依次進來，最小的最後一個到。她看著郊狼，認出了他，斷定是他殺了她的祖母；其他女孩責備他沒有把種子磨好——「這飯磨得太粗了」——他回答說：「我的腿疼。很久以前我的大腿中過箭，疼得我現在搗不了多少。」女孩們回到帳篷裡，因為疲倦，便睡著了。郊狼把手放在四個年長女孩的私處；當他靠近最小的那個時，她醒了過來，踢了他一腳，知道他正是郊狼：「你在做什麼？」其他女孩也因此醒來，責備她竟這樣對待自己的祖母。

passages.text: The following day they said to her, 'Grandmother, they want you at the dance to dance about Coyote.' — 'I am so weak, I doubt if I could get there.' — 'We will carry you,' the girls said. The oldest one carried him first; Coyote told her to raise up her dress and let him slide down lower on her back, and with that she felt him touch her and dropped him — 'I did not mean to drop her,' she said. The next one tried, and the same thing happened; and so with all four of them. Then they told the youngest that she must do her share, but she refused; when they reached the hill and could see the houses, Coyote said, 'I can walk from here on.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 156-157 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，她們對她說：「祖母，他們要你去跳舞，圍著郊狼跳舞。」——「我太虛弱了，恐怕到不了那裡。」——「我們會抬你去，」女孩們說。最大的那個先背他；郊狼叫她撩起裙子，讓他滑到她背上更低的地方，這麼一來她感覺到他碰了自己，便把他摔了下來——「我不是故意摔她的，」她說。下一個試了，同樣的事又發生了；四個人都是如此。然後她們告訴最小的那個，她也必須盡自己的一份力，但她拒絕了；當她們到達山丘，能看見那些房屋時，郊狼說：「從這裡起我可以自己走了。」

passages.text: When they arrived at the place, they heard a loud noise and saw the people dancing, and there was another Coyote at the camp. This one, when he caught sight of them, called out, 'The old woman is coming to dance with us!' The disguised Coyote began to dance and sing, and forgot all about his lameness. 'Where are Coyote's eyes? Let me have them!' he said. 'Let her have them!' some one said; the people crowded together and made room for her to dance. As soon as he had his eyes, he took out the other ones and put back his own; then he took off his disguise and ran away. The people wondered at first, then saw they had been deceived, and pursued him. Fox caught up with him; Coyote then scattered some of the black paint that he had, and it grew dark. The pursuers lost their way, while Coyote sat on a hill a little way off; when it cleared, they gave chase again, and Coyote eluded them as before. This happened five times. At last they grew weary and gave up the chase. So Coyote got his eyes back. Later on he went back and gave names to the children of the girls whom he had deceived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 157 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們抵達那個地方時，聽見一陣巨響，看見人們正在跳舞，而營地裡還有另一個郊狼。這個郊狼一瞧見他們，便喊道：「老婦人來和我們一起跳舞了！」那偽裝的郊狼開始跳舞唱歌，完全忘了自己跛腳的事。「郊狼的眼睛在哪裡？讓我拿到它們！」他說。「讓她拿去吧！」有人說道；眾人擠在一起，讓出地方給她跳舞。他一拿到眼睛，便取出另外那雙，換回自己的；接著他脫下偽裝，逃走了。眾人起初感到驚異，隨後發覺自己受了騙，便追趕他。狐狸追上了他；郊狼於是撒出一些他帶著的黑色顏料，天色便暗了下來。追趕的人迷失了方向，而郊狼則坐在不遠處的一座小丘上；天色轉晴時，他們又追了上來，郊狼又如先前那樣甩脫了他們。這樣的事發生了五次。最後他們疲倦了，便放棄追趕。於是郊狼取回了自己的眼睛。後來他回去，為那些他曾欺騙過的女孩所生的孩子取名。

title.en: The Rival Suitors: The False Accusation
title.zh: 求婚之爭：誣陷與登天

region.en: Hunters' lodge, then the tree climbed to the sky (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 獵戶之宅，繼而通天之樹（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 9. The Rival Suitors' (the false accusation)

summary.en: The younger of two great hunter brothers, making arrows by the fire, is called out by his sister-in-law to shoot a little bird for her; while he is gone she scratches her own face with the bird's claws and lies accusing him — but the grizzly-bear dog saw everything. The elder brother breaks the boy's arrows in the fire; the boy takes his bow and wanders off with the dog, crosses five mountains, undresses, and climbs a tree higher and higher until out of sight — he climbed into the sky and entered Spider's house, never coming back. The dog howls at the tree-foot for days; the repentant brother crosses three mountains to find it, learns the whole truth from the bear-dog, and leaves him there: 'You shall be a grizzly bear. You shall kill people when you must, but not always. I shall go home and kill my wife, and then go to the village to live.' Walaetitsa shoots his wife and swallows all his fine things, becoming small and extremely ugly.
summary.zh: 獵戶兄弟中，弟於火旁製箭，嫂喚其出射小鳥；乘其在外，嫂以鳥爪自抓其面，誣其非禮——然灰熊犬目睹一切。兄折其箭投火；弟携弓與犬出走，越五重山，脫衣攀樹，愈攀愈高，直至不見——入天界蜘蛛之屋，永不復返。犬於樹下日夜悲嚎。兄自責，越三山尋至，從灰熊犬口中得知真相，留之於山中：『汝當為灰熊。必不得已時方可殺人。吾將歸而誅吾妻，再往村中居住。』瓦萊提察射殺其妻，吞盡其珍寶，變得又矮又醜。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Sahaptin narrative collected by Farrand (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. First half of the rival-suitors cycle. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was the leading man in a certain village; Eagle was the second in rank. There were two brothers who lived some distance away. They were great hunters and very wealthy, honored by all, but preferring to live by themselves. The older one was married; his name was Walaetitsa, his wife's name Ti'pti'-ptle'ya (a small bird). The younger one had a dog, the Grizzly-Bear, who was in love with the younger brother, though he paid no attention to her. One day the younger man said to his brother, 'My arrows are broken, I want to get some wood for shafts. You may go hunting alone to-day.' The elder brother set out by himself; the younger one cut sticks, made several arrows, and put them near the fire to dry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 157 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼是某個村莊裡的首領人物；鷹的位次居第二。有兩兄弟住在離此一段距離的地方。他們是了不起的獵人，非常富有，受眾人尊敬，卻寧願獨自居住。年長的那個已經成婚；他的名字叫瓦萊提察（Walaetitsa），他妻子的名字叫提普提普勒雅（Ti'pti'-ptle'ya，一種小鳥）。年幼的那個養了一條狗，即灰熊，她愛上了弟弟，儘管他對她毫不理會。有一天，年幼的那個對他的兄長說：「我的箭都斷了，我想弄些木頭來做箭桿。你今天可以獨自去打獵。」兄長獨自出發了；弟弟則砍削樹枝，做了幾支箭，把它們放在火邊烘乾。

passages.text: While he was working, his sister-in-law called him from outside: 'Come out and shoot this little bird for me!' He refused, saying, 'Why do you want the bird?' She coaxed him; and finally he went out, shot the bird with a broken arrow, and threw it at her, saying, 'There is the bird. What do you want it for?' Then he went in. Soon he came out again to cut more arrow-sticks; while he was gone, his sister-in-law went in and scratched her face with the claws of the bird, then lay down. The young man's dog saw the whole performance. When her husband came home and saw her lying there, he asked what ailed her; finally she replied impatiently, 'See what your brother has done to me! He tried to force me; and when I resisted, he scratched my face.' The grizzly-bear dog lay there and watched, and heard everything. The man turned around, and, seeing the boy's arrows, broke them and threw them into the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 157-158 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他正做工時，他的嫂嫂從外面喚他：「出來替我射這隻小鳥！」他拒絕了，說道：「你為什麼要那隻鳥？」她百般哄勸他；最後他走了出去，用一支斷箭射下那隻鳥，把它扔給她，說道：「鳥在那兒。你要它做什麼？」然後他便進屋去了。不久他又出來砍削更多做箭的木枝；趁他不在時，他的嫂嫂走了進去，用那隻鳥的爪子抓破自己的臉，然後躺下。那年輕人的狗目睹了這一切。她的丈夫回家後，看見她躺在那裡，便問她怎麼了；最後她不耐煩地回答：「看看你弟弟對我做了什麼！他想強迫我；我抵抗時，他就抓破了我的臉。」那條灰熊狗躺在那裡看著，把一切都聽在耳裡。那男人轉過身來，看見那男孩的箭，便把它們折斷，扔進火裡。

passages.text: The young man came in and asked, 'Where are my arrows?' No one answered; then he saw the ends in the fire. Finally his brother spoke, and said, 'So you did not want to go out hunting this morning, did you? You wanted to force your sister-in-law.' The boy got up, took his bow and arrows, and went out, his dog following him; he left the house and wandered off on his travels. He crossed five mountains; the fifth mountain was very high. Here he undressed, and told the dog to stay below and wait, while he climbed a tree, higher and higher until he was out of sight — he climbed into the sky and entered Spider's house, and never came back. The dog waited at the foot of the tree several days, howling all the time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 158 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那年輕人走了進來，問道：「我的箭在哪裡？」沒有人回答；接著他看見箭頭在火裡。最後他的兄長開口說道：「這麼說，你今天早上不想出去打獵，是吧？你想強迫你的嫂嫂。」那男孩站起身，拿起他的弓和箭，走了出去，他的狗跟隨著他；他離開屋子，踏上旅途四處遊蕩。他翻過了五座山；第五座山非常高。他在這裡脫下衣服，吩咐狗留在山下等候，自己則爬上一棵樹，越爬越高，直到不見踪影——他爬進了天空，進了蜘蛛的家，再也沒有回來。那狗在樹腳下等了好幾天，一直嚎叫不停。

passages.text: His brother now began to reproach himself: 'What have I done? I have wronged my brother.' He went out and followed his trail, and when he had crossed three of the mountains, he heard the dog howling; crossing the fourth, the sound became much more distinct, and soon he came to the place where the dog was. He approached him, and the dog growled, acting as if it wanted to kill the man, until Walaetitsa begged and begged: 'O dog! where is your master?' The dog at last replied, 'You cruel man! You have done wrong. My master has left me, and I am here alone... He has ascended the tree, saying he would not come back. He has gone for good.' Walaetitsa asked how it all happened, and the dog gave an account of everything — how the wife had scratched her own face, and how his master had done no wrong. 'If that is so, I shall leave you here as a grizzly bear. You shall kill people when you must, but not always. I shall go home and kill my wife, and then go to the village to live.' With that they parted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 158-159 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的兄長這時開始自責：「我做了什麼？我冤枉了我的弟弟。」他走出去，循著弟弟的足跡追尋，當他翻過三座山時，聽見那狗的嚎叫；翻過第四座山時，聲音變得清晰得多，不久他便來到狗所在的地方。他走近牠，那狗便低吼起來，一副想要殺死他的樣子，直到瓦萊提察再三哀求：「噢，狗啊！你的主人在哪裡？」那狗最後回答：「你這殘忍的人！你做錯了事。我的主人離開了我，我獨自在此……他爬上了那棵樹，說他不會回來了。他永遠地走了。」瓦萊提察問這一切是怎麼發生的，那狗便把一切經過述說了一遍——妻子如何自己抓破了自己的臉，他的主人如何沒有做錯任何事。「既是如此，我就把你留在這裡，讓你做一頭灰熊。你必要時可以殺人，但不可總是如此。我要回家殺了我的妻子，然後到村裡去住。」說罷，他們便分別了。

passages.text: Walaetitsa approached his home, and saw his wife outside dressing a skin. He drew his bow and arrow and aimed at her. 'Are you going to shoot me?' she asked him, laughing. He did not answer, but merely drew his bow and killed her. Then he went into the house, swallowed all his fine things, and went to the village. Walaetitsa was a rather large man; but when he had swallowed all those things, he became very small and extremely ugly — he and his brother had been the best-looking men in the village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 159 (Farrand, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 瓦萊提察走近自己的家，看見妻子在外面鞣製一張獸皮。他拉開弓，搭上箭，瞄準她。「你要射我嗎？」她笑著問他。他沒有回答，只是拉開弓，把她射死了。然後他走進屋裡，把他所有精美的物品都吞了下去，便前往村莊。瓦萊提察本是相當高大的男子；但當他吞下所有那些東西之後，他變得非常矮小，而且極其醜陋——他和他的弟弟曾是村裡相貌最俊美的男子。

title.en: The Bungling Host: Coyote Visits his Sons-in-Law
title.zh: 笨拙之主：郊狼拜訪女婿

region.en: Winter ice-holes of the Sahaptin rivers (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩哈普廷諸河冬季冰洞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Livingston Farrand, 1902; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Sahaptin Tales, 10. The Bungling Host'
