I left my work undone because of the victuals, that always seem to be drawing me on' — however, she did not give over, but ate all the more, till her tongue at length was so sore that it turned quite awry, and crying out, 'Sakak, my tongue! I am growing matak myself,' she suddenly died. People say that while she lived a noxious whale-monster used to appear above the water whenever she left the house, but after her death it was seen no more; the principal wife being gone the others were now at liberty to share out as they liked. In the following spring Kepigsuak returned to Kangamiut; he was afterwards baptised and called Egede, and is buried at Kangamiut.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 74 'Utereetsok's Journey to the Far North'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 凱皮格蘇阿克在康加米烏特住了一段時間後，計劃南行，去了卡科爾托克；他在那裡逗留期間，一個名叫薩卡克的人捕獲了一頭長鬚鯨。薩卡克有四個妻子，其中最後一位伊格帕克非常傲慢，而且貪得無厭；長鬚鯨的消息傳開後，許多訪客前來，但伊格帕克卻沒有什麼可招待客人的。薩卡克親自邀請一位老人到他家，可老人剛一坐定，伊格帕克就粗魯地嚷道：『哎呀，說真的，這回上門來看我們的老人可真不少啊』——老人回敬道：『就我而言，我不過是因為被邀請才來的。』聽了這話，她給了他一塊鯨皮，還有一把切鯨皮的刀；然而他拒絕了那把刀，說他只想把它帶回家去。伊格帕克一向吃個不停，彷彿永遠吃不飽，過了一會兒又這般說道：『我這是怎麼了？我這是怎麼了？我因為這些吃的丟下了手頭的活兒，它們總像是在引誘著我』——然而她並沒有停下來，反而吃得更多，直到舌頭終於疼得厲害，完全歪到了一邊，她大喊：『薩卡克，我的舌頭！我自己都要變成鯨皮了』，隨即突然死去。人們說，她活著的時候，每當她離家外出，水面上總會出現一頭有害的鯨形怪物，但她死後就再也沒見過那怪物了；正妻既已不在，其餘的人如今便可隨意分配了。次年春天，凱皮格蘇阿克回到康加米烏特；他後來受了洗禮，取名埃格德，葬於康加米烏特。

title.en: Savanguak and the Derelict Whaler
title.zh: 薩萬瓜克與無人捕鯨船

region.en: Kangerdlugsuatsiak and Kassigissat, South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭康格盧克蘇瓦夏克與卡西吉薩特

period: Inuit oral tradition; a story from South Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 75 'Savanguak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Rowing out to a deserted ship with her father-in-law Niumak, Savanguak's household becomes rich — beads like the whalers', sails for tent-covers, peas, sugar, and molasses poured into the sea — the finest beads all hers. When her baby dies, a vile old Southlander crone mocks the bereaved mother; Savanguak drowns herself in the little lake, and the mourning turns on the hag: a pail of icy water, the ledge-boards torn out from under her companions, the household moving to Kassigissat. The famished boat-crew from dead Sakak's place are fed by young Habakuk, the future prophet, and row on southward.
summary.zh: 與公公尼烏馬克劃向一艘無人的船後，薩萬瓜克一家暴富——捕鯨人式的珠串、帆布做帳篷外罩；豌豆、糖與糖蜜盡數倒進海裡；最好的珠子全歸她。幼嬰夭折後，一名可憎的南方老嫗竟拿自家孫兒嘲弄喪子的母親；薩萬瓜克投湖自盡——喪禮之後，一桶冰水當頭淋下、長凳板被拆起拋出窗外，全家遷往卡西吉薩特。從死絕的薩卡克家逃出的飢民小舟，由未來的先知少年哈巴庫克分豹相贈、飽食而南去。

sensitivity.note: Suicide of Savanguak recorded as told in the 1875 source. Rink's note identifies Habakuk as the native prophet of 1790, head of a Christian sect independent of the missionaries.

passages.text: Near Kangerdlugsuatsiak there lived a man called Niumak, with his wife Kujapigak; both were very anxious to get a suitable wife for their only son. Niumak, from his early youth, had neither fancied nor taken any part in singing or dancing entertainments — at the dancing parties he would turn away from the performers seeming to take no notice of them; but if a wrestling match or a trial of strength was going to come off he was always on the alert. At last Niumak fixed upon a girl named Savanguak for the wife of his son, and he became very fond of his daughter-in-law. In summer-time he had one day gone out kayaking by himself, and on landing from a hill perceived a ship approaching; he lost no time in getting out his kayak and rowed away to meet it. Having got alongside the vessel he saw a rope-ladder hanging down the side, but not a single man was seen on deck, and no one answering his repeated calls he went on board and entered the cabin — all was desolate there as elsewhere, and he concluded that the crew had recently left the ship, omitting to furl the sails. The ship having run in among the islands and grounded, he left it to fetch a boat; returning with this he established himself and his people on board, and they soon ascertained that the cargo was in no way injured. In the cabin they found beads like those they had been accustomed to get from the whalers, and having possessed themselves of them thought themselves very rich; they also overhauled the cargo, but being totally unacquainted with it poured into the sea such articles as peas, sugar, and molasses. Having taken from the ship all they could lay hands on they tore down the sails in order to make use of them as an outside cover of their tents — all the finest beads were given to Savanguak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 75 'Savanguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在康格爾德盧格蘇阿齊亞克附近，住著一個名叫紐馬克的人，與他的妻子庫亞皮加克；兩人都非常急切地想為他們唯一的兒子找一個合適的妻子。紐馬克從少年時代起，就既不喜歡也不參與任何唱歌或跳舞的娛樂——在舞會上他總是背對著表演者，似乎對他們毫不理會；但若是有摔跤比賽或較量力氣的活動要舉行，他總是格外警覺。最後，紐馬克選定了一個名叫薩萬古阿克姑娘做他兒子的妻子，並且非常喜愛這個兒媳。夏天有一天，他獨自划著皮艇出海，從一座山丘上岸時，看見一艘船正駛近；他連忙取出皮艇，划過去迎它。靠上船後，他看見船舷上垂下一條繩梯，但甲板上一個人也看不到，他連聲呼喊也無人應答，便上了船，走進船艙——那裡和其他地方一樣荒涼，他斷定船員們不久前棄船而去，忘了收帆。船駛入群島之間擱淺了，他離開船去取一艘小船；帶著小船回來後，他把自己和手下的人安頓在船上，他們很快查明貨物絲毫未損。他們在船艙裡發現了一些珠子，和他們一向從捕鯨人那裡換來的一樣，拿到這些珠子後便自以為非常富有；他們還翻檢了貨物，但由於對這些東西全然不識，便把豌豆、糖和糖蜜之類的東西倒進了海裡。他們把船上能拿的東西都拿光之後，又扯下船帆，用來做帳篷的外罩——所有最好的珠子都給了薩萬古阿克。

passages.text: Afterwards, when Savanguak had already got several children, some Southlanders arrived whom Niumak invited to come and stay at his house. In the beginning of winter the younger baby of Savanguak died, and they were all very sorry; one day when her husband was absent a vile old crone belonging to the Southlanders went on mocking the bereaved mother, holding up her own grandchild before her in a provoking manner unobserved by the others — this roused Savanguak's suspicion against her. On the same day her husband was expected back, her mother-in-law brought all the reindeer-skins in to have them looked over; while every one's attention was taken up with this Savanguak ran outside to take the air. On finding she did not return Kujapigak turned to some of the larger children: 'Go and look after your sister-in-law' — 'She is standing outside the house' — as she still remained out they all ran off to fetch her back; following her tracks they had to cross a hill, and at length found her at the bottom of a little lake close by. Nobody was able to draw her out; at the same time they perceived Niumak in his kayak making for the shore — no one dared to call him and tell him what had happened, but getting suspicious from their silence he put in at once and hurried to them. On looking round for information one of the bystanders screamed out, 'Thy daughter-in-law is lying dead at the bottom of the lake.' Without uttering a single word he proceeded to draw her out, and tried every means for reviving her; these proving all in vain he let the others bring her to the house, on carrying her in bringing all their things out according to custom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 75 'Savanguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，薩萬古阿克已經有了好幾個孩子，一些南方人來到此地，紐馬克邀請他們到他家來住。入冬之初，薩萬古阿克最小的嬰兒死了，大家都很悲傷；有一天她丈夫外出時，南方人中一個卑劣的老太婆竟嘲弄這位喪子的母親，趁別人不注意，把自己孫子舉到她面前挑釁——這引起了薩萬古阿克對她的懷疑。就在她丈夫預定回來的那天，婆婆把所有的馴鹿皮都拿進來查看；趁大家的注意力都集中在這上面時，薩萬古阿克跑到外面去透氣。見她沒有回來，庫亞皮加克便對幾個大些的孩子說：『去看看你們的嫂子』——『她站在屋外呢』——她仍然待在外面，於是大家都跑出去找她回來；循著她的足跡，他們得翻過一座山丘，最後在附近一個小湖的湖底找到了她。誰也無法把她拉出來；就在這時，他們看見紐馬克划著皮艇向岸邊駛來——沒有人敢呼喊他，告訴他出了什麼事，但他從他們的沉默中起了疑心，立刻靠岸，急忙趕到他們身邊。他環顧四周想打聽情況，人群中一個人大聲喊道：『你的兒媳婦死了，躺在湖底。』他一言不發，上前把她拉了出來，想盡一切辦法使她甦醒；種種辦法都徒勞無效之後，他便讓別人把她抬回屋裡，抬進去時，按照習俗把他們所有的東西都搬了出來。

passages.text: The husband of the deceased, who was named Taterak, also arrived calling out that he had got a white whale; the servant-maid of the house silently went down to receive and help him — feeling assured that something was amiss he asked her to draw his kayak on shore; obeying her master she pulled up the boat but did it hurriedly without the usual care, at which he looked inquiringly at her but got no answer. On stepping ashore his father met him and gave him the sad intelligence that his wife had drowned herself; without undressing he quickly entered the house, and the father as well as the son went up and down the room deliberating upon how to find out the cause of her death — meanwhile some of the others were whispering, 'Now we will soon have done with the old hag,' but the two men never heard them; unable to discover any reason they broke out into loud lamentations joined by all the rest, the old hag only excepted, who was busy eating matak. Some time after a baby of the place was called Savanguak in memory of the deceased; it happened that one of Niumak's house-fellows told him that the old woman had been heard to mock and ridicule the baby's namesake. When the little one was learning to walk the old hag one day took to scolding it — on hearing which Niumak and his son rose up together, saying, 'Now we see who is the real culprit'; and so saying he poured out a pailful of icy water upon the naked woman, afterwards throwing the pail out of the window. Her companions quietly kept their seats in a row on the ledge; but they were soon upset by Niumak, who tore away the ledge-boards beneath them, which were likewise thrown outside, and he removed all his belongings out of the house. They departed from thence to Kassigissat, leaving their wicked house-fellows behind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 75 'Savanguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 死者的丈夫名叫塔特拉（Taterak），也回来了，高声呼喊说自己捕到了一头白鲸；屋里的女仆默默地下去迎接并帮他——他感到事情有些不对，便叫她把自己的皮划艇拖上岸；她听从主人的吩咐把船拉了上来，但拉得匆忙，不像平常那样小心，他便探询地看了她一眼，却没有得到回答。他上岸时父亲迎上来，把妻子投水自尽的噩耗告诉了他；他连衣服都没脱就急忙进了屋，父亲和儿子一同在屋里来回踱步，思量着如何查明她的死因——与此同时，其余一些人正在窃窃私语：“现在我们很快就能收拾掉那个老妖婆了。”但那两个男人始终没有听见。他们查不出任何缘由，便放声痛哭起来，其余所有人都跟着哭，只有那个老妖婆例外，她正忙着吃马塔克（matak）。过了一些时候，当地的一个婴儿被取名为萨万瓜克（Savanguak），以纪念死者；恰好尼乌马克（Niumak）的一个同屋人告诉他，有人听见那老妇人讥笑嘲弄与婴儿同名的人。当那小孩学走路时，有一天老妖婆责骂起他来——尼乌马克和儿子听到这话便一同站起身来，说道：“现在我们知道谁是真正的罪魁祸首了。”说着，他把一桶冰水泼在那赤身裸体的女人身上，随后把桶扔出窗外。她的同伴们静静地一排坐在壁架上；但尼乌马克很快就把她们掀翻了，他扯掉她们身下的壁架木板，那些木板也同样被扔到了外面，然后他把自己的所有财物都搬出了屋子。他们离开那里，前往卡西吉萨特（Kassigissat），把那些邪恶的同屋人抛在了身后。

passages.text: During their stay at Kassigissat several other people came to encamp there, waiting for the migratory seal; about that time Habakuk, a youth whose parents had likewise pitched their tents there, one day kayaked northwards to meet the seals, and was suddenly surprised on seeing a boat coming down upon him rowed by a single man. Habakuk on his part made up to them and rowed on alongside of them, being too modest to address them first — at last their old woman Ajugaussak began: 'We are almost starving; give us a little of thy new-caught seal. We came away from Sakak, where all our house-fellows died of famine, and we have travelled all this way south without once taking our boat ashore for drying; our only provisions have been half-dried boat-skins.' When she had ended Habakuk went closer to them, saying, 'Well, take the skin of my seal with blubber and all, and the liver besides' — they forthwith tried to get the animal out of the boat but were too weak and exhausted to do it without his help; their old woman proceeded to cut it up and gave each a little piece of the blubber, and having their hunger appeased for the present they followed him home, where a meal was instantly set before them. However, they were at first only able to take a very little food, and then went off to sleep, having first asked their old woman to light a lamp — she trimmed it with blubber accordingly, but missing the stick to stir it up with had to make a shift with her forefinger, at the same time exclaiming, 'What a length of time I have longed for the sight of this!' The strange travellers began to recover by the nourishing food they were getting, but still they often fell asleep in the midst of their meal; on awaking they fell to again, and at last grew so fat that they could hardly get on their boots — soon afterwards they prepared to leave, intending to go still further to the south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 75 'Savanguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他们在卡西吉萨特逗留期间，又有另外几个人来此扎营，等候洄游的海豹；大约就在那时，哈巴库克（Habakuk）——一个父母也同样在那里搭起帐篷的青年——有一天划着皮划艇向北去迎海豹，忽然吃惊地看见一条船朝他驶来，船上只有一个男人在划。哈巴库克这边便迎上前去，与他们的船并排划行，因为过于腼腆，没有先开口——最后他们的老妇人阿尤高萨克（Ajugaussak）开口道：“我们快要饿死了；把你新捕的海豹分一点给我们吧。我们是从萨卡克（Sakak）来的，那里我们的同屋人都饿死了，我们一路往南走了这么远，一次也没把船拖上岸晾干；我们唯一的食物就是半干不干的船皮。”她说完后，哈巴库克靠得更近了些，说道：“好吧，把我这海豹的皮连脂肪一起拿去，还有肝脏也拿去。”他们当即想把那动物从船里弄出来，却太虚弱疲惫，没有他的帮助弄不动；他们的老妇人便动手把它切开，给每人分了一小块脂肪，暂时止住了饥饿，他们便跟着他回了家，一到家就立刻给他们摆上了饭食。然而他们起初只能吃下很少一点食物，随后便去睡了，睡前先请他们的老妇人点上一盏灯——她便用脂肪把灯捻好，可是找不到拨灯芯的棍子，只好用食指凑合，同时喊道：“我盼望见到这盏灯盼了多久啊！”这些陌生的旅人靠着吃到的滋养食物开始恢复，但仍常常在吃饭时睡着；醒来后又接着吃，最后长得胖得几乎穿不上靴子——不久之后他们便准备离开，打算继续往更南边去。

title.en: Inuarutligak, Whose Christian Name Was Peter Rantholl
title.zh: 山中精靈伊努阿魯特利亞克

region.en: Kutserfik and Noosak on the continent, the elves' northern migration
region.zh: 庫策爾菲克與大陸上的努薩克——精靈北遷之路

period: Inuit oral tradition; a tale from North Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 76 'Inuarutligak — whose Christian name was Peter Rantholl', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: After a man killed one of them, the dwarf-inlanders withdrew to hollows in the earth, arming themselves with a fist-sized willow-root weapon with black and red stones — the pointing weapon that kills what it is pointed at. Migrating north over years of earth-hollow winters, they meet dog-bodied archers, cover a house with the six-legged kilivfak's skin, shrink the country by kneeling and spreading their arms to the mountain-tops, and stride across the contracted parts in the leader's tracks. Sold for knives, bearskin, and twisted whalebone lines to a childless angakok at Noosak, the youngest slips into the wife's womb at night — born with full consciousness — and his people renew their youth five times by falling headlong down a precipice.
summary.zh: 自從一名族人被人殺害，山中精靈便遁入地穴，以柳根雕成拳大的『指向武器』——黑石在下、紅石在上，所指即亡。他們北上遷徙，冬季居於地穴；途遇犬身弓手，以六足奇獸奇利夫法克之皮覆屋——吃盡其肉，骨上復生其肉，凡六次；又以跪地張臂收攏山河、跨步而過。幼子被無子的巫師以三把刀、熊皮與絞成的鯨骨釣線買去——夜裡鑽入其妻腹中，故生而全知。其族人五度墜崖以返老還童，謂之伊努特松納爾托克。

sensitivity.note: Inuarutligak: fabulous dwarf-inlander or mountain-elf (Rink's note). The youth-renewing precipice fall (inutsungnartok) documented as told.

passages.text: In times far back the ancestors of this same Inuarutligak (viz., fabulous dwarf-inlander or mountain-elf) are said to have lived at the southernmost point of the country, at a place called Kutserfik, and this was before they had learned to be shy of human beings. Just about that time a lasting enmity sprang up between them on account of an Inuarutligak being killed by a man, and ever after they say that the gnomes have resorted to desert places, making hollows in the earth for their abodes and shunning the society of man. Thirsting for vengeance they in return killed a man whom they chanced to meet with on one of their excursions; being sadly in want of proper arms they found a large willow-bush on the sunny side of the Kutserfik-mount, its form like a man bending down on his knees and supporting his hand against the ground. From one of its roots they made a weapon not larger in size than a closed fist, shaped like a pistol; at the end they put a little black stone with a little red one on the top of it — this instrument, when finished, they named the pointing weapon. Knowing and fearing its killing powers for their own kith and kin they are said always to have carried it in their hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 76 'Inuarutligak — whose Christian name was Peter Rantholl'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 据说在很久以前，这同一个伊努阿鲁特利加克（Inuarutligak，即传说中的矮小内陆人或山精灵）的祖先们住在国土最南端一个叫库策尔菲克（Kutserfik）的地方，那时他们还没有学会躲避人类。大约就在那时，因为一个伊努阿鲁特利加克被一个人杀死，他们之间结下了持久的仇恨，此后人们便说这些地精迁往荒僻之地，在地上挖出洞穴居住，避开与人类交往。他们渴望复仇，便反过来杀了一个在一次外出时偶然遇见的人；由于极其缺乏合适的武器，他们在库策尔菲克山向阳的一面找到一大丛柳树，形状像一个屈膝弯腰、一手撑地的人。他们用其中一条根做成了一件武器，大小不超过一个握紧的拳头，形状像手枪；在末端他们放了一小块黑石，上面又放了一小块红石——这件器具做成后，他们称之为“指向武器”。他们知道并畏惧它对自家亲族的杀伤力，据说总是把它拿在手里。

passages.text: At this time the Inuarutligak of our tale was born; his father's name was Malerke, that of the eldest son Kinavina, of the second Kook, of the third Asarfe, and of the fourth Sersok, of whom we are going to tell. Being given to moving about his parents and relatives set out on a journey to the north and travelled on for several years successively, always passing the winter in hollows in the earth and starting again in the early spring. It is told that they once met with some singular people whose upper limbs were those of human beings, but below the waist they were shaped like dogs — these creatures were armed with bows, dreadful to behold, and could catch the scent of man and beast against the wind like animals. One winter they covered the whole inside of their abode under ground with a single skin — that of the large beast called kilivfak, the one with six legs; the story goes that when they had eaten the flesh of this animal the bones were covered anew with flesh, but only up to the sixth time — despite its strength and size they killed it with the above-mentioned instrument by merely pointing at it. They also knew how to diminish the distance from one place to another by drawing the various parts of the country closer, and performed this by merely kneeling down together and spreading their arms out towards the mountain-tops; but finding some of them too high to spread their arms over, the foremost crossed the already contracted parts with one long stride, the others one by one following in his tracks — whenever one of them was unfortunate enough to make a false step, several of them were left far behind for a long time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 76 'Inuarutligak — whose Christian name was Peter Rantholl'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 就在这个时候，我们故事中的伊努阿鲁特利加克出生了；他父亲名叫马勒克（Malerke），长子名叫基纳维纳（Kinavina），次子名叫库克（Kook），三子名叫阿萨尔费（Asarfe），四子名叫塞尔索克（Sersok），我们要讲的就是他。由于他们喜好迁徙，他的父母和亲属们便踏上了向北的旅程，一连走了好几年，总是在地洞里过冬，早春又再出发。据说他们曾遇到一些奇特的人，他们的上肢是人的，但腰部以下却像狗——这些生物手持弓箭，模样可怕，还能像野兽一样逆风嗅出人和兽的气味。有一个冬天，他们用一张皮——那种叫基利夫法克（kilivfak）、长着六条腿的大兽的皮——把他们地下住所的整个内部都铺盖起来；故事说，他们吃完这动物的肉后，骨头会重新长出肉来，但只到第六次为止——尽管它强壮巨大，他们只用上述那件器具对着它一指就把它杀死了。他们还懂得把各地的距离缩短，把国土的各部分拉近，做法只是大家一同跪下，朝山顶张开双臂；但发现有些山顶太高，双臂张不过去，最前面的人便用一大步跨过已经缩短的部分，其余的人一个接一个循着他的足迹跟上——每当他们中有人不幸踏错一步，就有好几个人被远远落在后面，很久才能赶上。

passages.text: After a journey of several years they arrived at Ikerasarsuak (at the mouth of Wygat Straits), a place where lived Inuarutligaks as well as Inoruseks; there they settled to wait till the frost should cover the ground with ice and make it possible to join those on the other side. Starting again in spring and passing several winters at different places they at length reached Noosak on the continent and came to their long-wished-for relatives, and there they lived for many winters. People say that at the beginning of the journey to the north the high mountains were still without ice and Ikerasarsuak without any glacier. These elves had two different ways of clothing themselves — one suit fitting their natural size, the other large enough to fit a man; during their wandering they wore their own proper clothes carrying the large ones with them ready to put on in case they should get some heavy load to carry — they could then, by beating themselves, reach human size. Their way of regaining their natural appearance was by bending down to enter their cave and hitting the crown of their heads against the roof, on which they dwindled down to their ordinary smallness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 76 'Inuarutligak — whose Christian name was Peter Rantholl'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 走了几年之后，他们到达伊凯拉萨尔苏阿克（Ikerasarsuak，在维加特海峡〔Wygat Straits〕口），那里住着伊努阿鲁特利加克，也住着伊诺鲁塞克（Inoruseks）；他们便在那里定居下来，等候寒霜把地面覆上冰，好与对岸的人会合。春天他们又出发，在不同的地方过了几个冬天，终于到达大陆上的努萨克（Noosak），来到他们盼望已久的亲属那里，在那里住了许多个冬天。人们说，在他们开始北行之时，高山还没有冰雪，伊凯拉萨尔苏阿克也还没有冰川。这些精灵有两种不同的穿衣方式——一套合他们天生的身材，另一套大得足以套进一个人；在漫游途中他们穿着自己本来的衣服，随身带着那套大衣服，以备要背负沉重的东西时穿上——那时他们只要拍打自己，就能达到人的身材。他们恢复本来面貌的办法，是弯腰进入洞穴，用头顶撞上洞顶，于是一下子缩回平常的矮小身材。

passages.text: An angakok at Noosak whose wife was childless wanted to buy a child from the Inuarutligaks, and offered to pay for him with three knives, a piece of bearskin, and some whalebones already twisted into fishing-lines; Malerke, on seeing them, grew very desirous of these things, and having got them gave the knives to his three sons — but the fourth and youngest he sold in exchange for them. His new father brought him home and went to hide him behind the house; at night, however, he got inside and at once slipped into the womb of his mother, on which account it was said that he was in a state of perfect consciousness while he remained in his mother's womb. These elves were long in turning old; their youth was renewed five times over — on getting old the first time they let themselves fall headlong down a precipice, and in this way regained the vigour and elasticity of youth; after repeating this five succeeding times it was useless to try a sixth. This practice of letting themselves fall down they called Inutsungnartok. They never die young, but only after having undergone their five separate ages, excepting those who are killed by snowslips.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 76 'Inuarutligak — whose Christian name was Peter Rantholl'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 努萨克有一个安加科克（angakok，巫师），他的妻子没有孩子，他想从伊努阿鲁特利加克那里买一个孩子，提出用三把刀、一块熊皮和一些已经搓成钓线的鲸须来换；马勒克一见到这些东西就非常想要，得到之后把刀分给了他的三个儿子——但第四个、最小的那个，他却拿来换了这些东西。他的新父亲把他带回家，去把他藏在屋后；然而到了夜里，他钻进了屋里，一下子溜进了他母亲的子宫，因此据说他在母亲子宫里时处于完全有意识的状态。这些精灵衰老得很慢；他们的青春能更新五次——第一次变老时，他们让自己头朝下从悬崖上跳下去，这样就重获了青春的活力和柔韧；这样接连重复五次之后，再试第六次就没有用了。他们这种让自己跳崖的做法，他们称之为伊努聪纳尔托克（Inutsungnartok）。他们从不会年轻时就死，只有在经历了五个不同的年龄段之后才会死，除非是被雪崩压死的。

title.en: Akutak and Inuinak: The Wife Who Ran on the Water
title.zh: 阿庫塔克與伊努伊納克：踏水而行的瘋婦

region.en: Brothers' hamlet and the haunted house, Greenland coast
region.zh: 格陵蘭海岸的兄弟村與鬧鬼之屋

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 77 'Akutak and Inuinak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Inuinak wins the only sister of many brothers; Akutak, refused, bewitches her from afar. Caressing her husband beyond endurance, she gnaws a piece of grindstone like ice, and the brothers cut their boat's lashings and flee. Pursued night after night, she walks the water after his kayak; a streak of little ripples turns her back wailing. At last found stone-dead in a cave, she becomes a shroud-dragging ghost that the orphan boy with his dog barely escapes — the ghost's house left windowless — and the boy, telling a brave lie, is loaded with boots, a knife, and presents, all exchanged for his own first kayak.
summary.zh: 伊努伊納克娶得眾兄弟的獨妹；被拒的阿庫塔克遠程施咒離間夫妻。新婦愛撫無度，竟啃咬磨石如冰；兄弟們割斷船繩倉皇而逃。此後她夜夜追趕丈夫的皮艇——踏水如履堅冰——直到一道漣漪令她哀泣折返。最終人們在巖洞中尋見她蜷縮死去；其魂魄拖著裹屍布成為幽靈，攜犬的孤兒千鈞一髮逃過——他謊稱『無事』，換得雙靴、美柄小刀與滿身贈禮，全都換成了自己的第一條皮艇。

sensitivity.note: Bewitchment and haunting recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Several brothers had an only sister whom they loved dearly and were very loath to part with; to the north of them was another hamlet where lived Akutak and Inuinak. One day when out kayaking Akutak said, 'Let us go and give the brothers yonder a call' — Inuinak surmised they would only get a cold reception. However, they started, but not a man did they find at home; the women of the place could not give them any welcome, their husbands having strictly ordered them not to receive any unmarried man whatever during their absence. The strangers nevertheless entered the house, where they found the lonely sister occupying a seat on the southern side of the ledge, where her bedding also could be seen most handsomely piled up; though seats were offered to them at the northern end they preferred a settle facing the unmarried sister. They now proceeded to relieve themselves of their jackets, Akutak displaying a skin as fair and soft as that of a white whale, while Inuinak on stripping himself came out as black as a raven. Thus they remained a short time; before food had been offered to them the men of the place were hailed returning with their prey, the women running down to assist them in bringing up their seals — no sooner had they re-entered the house than a voice was heard in the passage and a man entered, and in a grumbling voice broke out, 'Well, to be sure, we are having visitors.' This was the middle brother, soon followed by the rest of them; 'There thou art right; however, we were not very anxious to come at all,' answered Akutak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 77 'Akutak and Inuinak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有幾兄弟，他們只有一個姊妹，對她疼愛有加，極不願與她分離；在他們北邊有另一個小村落，住著阿庫塔克與伊努伊納克。有一天，阿庫塔克划著獨木舟外出時說：「咱們去拜訪那邊那幾兄弟吧。」伊努伊納克猜想他們只會受到冷淡的接待。然而他們還是出發了，卻一個男人也沒在家中找到；那地方的女人無法款待他們，因為她們的丈夫臨行前嚴厲吩咐過，在他們外出期間不得接待任何未婚男子。這些陌生人仍舊進了屋，發現那位孤單的姊妹坐在炕沿南側的座位上，她那鋪疊得極其齊整美觀的床褥也清晰可見；雖然有人請他們到北端就座，他們卻偏要坐在正對那位未婚姊妹的長凳上。接著他們便脫下外套，阿庫塔克露出一身像白鯨般白皙柔嫩的皮膚，而伊努伊納克一脫下衣服，卻黑得像隻渡鴉。他們就這樣待了一小會兒；還沒有人端上食物，就聽得有人呼喊，說這地方的男人們帶著獵物回來了，女人們紛紛跑下去幫他們把海豹搬上來——他們才剛重新進屋，通道裡便傳來一個聲音，一個男人走了進來，用抱怨的口氣說道：「哎呀，可不是嘛，咱們這兒來客人了。」這是中間那個兄弟，其餘的人隨後也跟著進來；「你說得沒錯；不過我們本來也不太想來。」阿庫塔克回答。

passages.text: The middle brother then ordered some meat to be served up to them; after a plenteous feast there was a good deal of talking, but the whole of the evening the visitors kept their seats never turning their looks off the maiden sister. At length the brothers, longing for rest, lay down to sleep, reclining in their different places — only the middlemost of them determined to keep watch, having pulled off his boots and leaned back keeping an eye on the strangers all the while. Presently he heard Inuinak call out in a loud voice, 'Young girl, make up a bed for me!' The sister at once complied, and he lay down beside her; the brothers first thought of interfering but soon gave up the idea and took no further notice of them. Akutak being now left by himself was beginning to feel rather lonely, and not addressing any one in particular simply cried out, 'Make up a bed for me, too!' — the brothers only glanced at him, saying, 'Why, thou art raving; just lie down by thyself.' Somewhat abashed he went off to sleep; in the morning, when the others awoke, they found he was gone — in his anger he had bewitched the sister, in order to set her against her new husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 77 'Akutak and Inuinak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著，中間那個兄弟吩咐給他們端上些肉；飽餐一頓之後，大家談了不少話，但整整一晚，這兩位客人始終坐在原位，目光一刻也沒離開那位年輕的姊妹。最後，兄弟們睏倦了，便各自躺下睡覺，各據一方——只有排行中間的那個決意守夜，他脫下靴子，向後靠著，一直盯著那兩個陌生人。不久，他聽見伊努伊納克大聲喊道：「姑娘，給我鋪張床吧！」那姊妹立刻照辦，他便在她身旁躺下；兄弟們起初想出面干涉，但很快便打消了念頭，不再理會他們。阿庫塔克此時被獨自撇下，開始覺得有些孤單，也不特別對著誰，只是喊道：「也給我鋪張床吧！」——兄弟們只瞥了他一眼，說道：「哎呀，你這是胡言亂語；自個兒躺下就是了。」他有些羞愧地睡去了；第二天早晨，其他人醒來時，發現他已不見了——他在盛怒之下對那姊妹施了咒，好讓她與新婚丈夫反目。

passages.text: Early in the morning the brothers all left in their kayaks, but the brother-in-law remained in bed till after sunrise, when he likewise started, having first put on his kayak-jacket; ere long it was announced that he was putting back and had some spoil in tow — he had already captured two seals, and his young wife was soon on the alert for flensing and cutting them up. This done she fell upon her husband's neck, caressing him incessantly, and would not leave him alone a single moment; when night set in and the brothers had all returned he actually began to be afraid of her, and removed to another corner of the room, seating himself behind a lamp always keeping her off — but still she would not leave him at peace, and catching hold of him with one hand at last took up a piece of a grindstone with the other, eating away at it as if it had been a morsel of ice. At sight of this the brothers exclaimed, 'Our sister has gone raving mad; let us be off from here' — away they fled, having first cut asunder all the lashings of their boat, and at their departure one of them said to their brother-in-law, 'If people are like this one, nothing is to be done; and thou hadst better come with us.' 'I will take my chance, and stay, if it be only for this one night' — the others all started off while he remained with his wife; she went on pursuing him all the night and he kept running away from her scarcely able to escape her clutch. At dawn of day however he succeeded in making a bold leap from the floor right down the house passage, and rushing along to seize his kayak quickly got into it — but at the very moment he was ready to push off she again reached him and made an attempt to catch hold of the kayak-point, in which she did not succeed; at first she seemed determined to follow him on the water, but all of a sudden turned back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 77 'Akutak and Inuinak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一大早，兄弟們都划著獨木舟出去了，但那位妹夫卻一直躺在床上，直到日出之後才起身，先穿上他的獨木舟外套，然後也出發了；不一會兒便有人通報說他正划回來，還拖著些獵物——他已經捕到兩隻海豹，他那年輕的妻子立刻忙著剖割切塊。做完這些，她便摟住丈夫的脖子，不停地愛撫他，一刻也不肯離開他身邊；夜幕降臨，兄弟們全都回來後，他竟開始怕起她來，便挪到屋子的另一個角落，坐在一盞燈後面，始終與她保持距離——但她仍不肯讓他安寧，最後一手抓住他，另一手拿起一塊磨石，像啃冰塊似地啃了起來。兄弟們見狀驚呼：「咱們的姊妹發瘋了；咱們快離開這兒吧。」——他們先割斷了船上的所有纜索，然後逃走了，臨走時其中一人對妹夫說：「人要是成了這副樣子，就沒法可想了；你還是跟我們一起走吧。」「我還是碰碰運氣留下來吧，哪怕只留這一晚也好。」——其他人都動身走了，他則與妻子留在一起；她整夜追著他，他不停地躲逃，幾乎逃不過她的抓握。然而到了黎明時分，他總算從地板上一躍跳進屋子的通道，一路奔去抓住自己的獨木舟，迅速坐了進去——但就在他準備推舟離岸的那一刻，她又追上了他，試圖抓住獨木舟的船頭，卻沒有得逞；起初她似乎決意要在水上追他，卻忽然轉身回去了。

passages.text: The poor husband hastened away to a small island off the coast where he knew the brothers had established themselves; the middlemost came out inquiring how she was, and being informed how she was remarked as before, 'If people are like her, there is nothing to be done but keep away from them.' When ten days had elapsed one morning the husband said, 'I must go and look after her; she may possibly be starving for want of food' — the others tried to dissuade him, but he insisted on going. Having reached the place he only pulled his kayak half-way out of the water and then proceeded to the house; for fear of his wife he did not venture to enter at once but only peeped in at the window, and there perceived her lying on the ledge, her hair all loose and dishevelled. When he addressed her she answered him back in the blandest manner, saying, 'I am quite well; come inside' — he went in at her bidding; but no sooner had he entered the room than she jumped up and made a furious rush at him, upon which he again started back and narrowly escaped through the doorway. She quickly followed him, and after vainly attempting to catch the prow of his kayak he suddenly observed her walking on the water as if it had been solid ice; hearing her voice he turned round, and seeing her close by cried, 'Why did I go and see this wicked thing? Probably she is going to eat me up.' As the only way to keep her off he began swinging to and fro in his kayak; presently her voice grew weak, and on turning round saw her nearly falling — but always giving her time to get up he at last brought her towards the brothers. On seeing her approach they cried, 'Why didst thou bring her over? She will kill us all' — while they were thus exclaiming and the husband could not persuade himself to leave her altogether, she saw before her a streak of little ripples on the water; when she came to them she suddenly turned and went back wailing and lamenting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 77 'Akutak and Inuinak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那可憐的丈夫急忙趕往離岸不遠的一座小島，他知道兄弟們已在那裡安頓下來；排行中間的那個出來問她怎麼樣了，聽了她的情況後，仍像先前那樣說道：「人要是成了她那副樣子，就沒法可想了，只能離得遠遠的。」過了十天，有一天早晨，丈夫說：「我得去看看她；她也許正因為沒有食物而挨餓呢。」——其他人試圖勸阻他，但他執意要去。到了那地方，他只把獨木舟從水裡拉出一半，然後便朝屋子走去；因為怕妻子，他不敢立刻進去，只從窗戶往裡窺看，只見她躺在炕上，頭髮蓬亂散開。他跟她說話時，她卻用最溫和的語氣回答他，說：「我很好；進來吧。」——他聽了她的話便進去了；可是他才一進屋，她便跳起來，怒氣沖沖地朝他撲去，於是他又退了出來，勉強從門口逃脫。她迅速跟了出來，在徒然試圖抓住他獨木舟船頭之後，他忽然發覺她竟像走在堅冰上一樣在水面上行走；聽見她的聲音，他轉過身來，見她就在近旁，便喊道：「我為什麼要來看這邪惡的東西？她多半是要把我吃掉。」為了擋住她，他唯一的辦法就是在獨木舟裡來回搖晃；不久，她的聲音漸漸微弱，他轉頭一看，見她幾乎要跌倒——但他總是給她時間再站起來，最後終於把她引向兄弟們那邊。兄弟們見她靠近，便喊道：「你把她帶過來做什麼？她會把我們全都殺了的。」——就在他們這樣驚呼、而丈夫又狠不下心完全撇下她的時候，她看見前方水面上有一道細細的漣漪；她走到那裡，忽然轉身回去，哀號悲泣不已。

passages.text: The husband now left off visiting her for a long time; at last one day he said, 'I must go and see her once more; she is probably dead' — on arriving at the place he found the house empty, and at last discovered her sitting in a cave all shrunk together and stone-dead; having buried her remains and covered the grave well with stones he returned. They now resolved upon giving up the house for good, and settled down for the coming winter on the outermost of the islets, soon after which the sea was frozen over. About this time a poor orphan boy, living in the house of Akutak, said to his house-fellows, 'I am in great want of boots, and intend to go to the brothers and offer them my little dog in exchange for a pair of old boots' — accordingly he betook himself to their old place. On arriving there in the morning he wondered at seeing the house without windows; however, he went up to it and found it still well provisioned, but he could neither see a boat nor any person about the place — on entering he found all the skin-hangings of the walls torn down and spread on the floor. Knowing no other inhabited house in the neighbourhood he soon made up his mind to stay the night over, and at dark went to fetch some blubber, trimmed a lamp and lighted it; he then pulled off his ragged boots, having put them up above the lamp to dry, and seated himself at the south end of the ledge. At first his little dog had followed him into the house and rolled itself up at his feet on the floor; but while his boots were drying the dog began to sniff and yell, running outside, its barking gradually becoming more distant — some time after it again returned, lying down before its master looked at him very sharply, then rushed out howling as before, this time re-entering immediately. The orphan thought, 'Dogs are not unconscious of anything' — he then put on his boots and rushed out, soon followed by the dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 77 'Akutak and Inuinak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 丈夫此後很久都不再去看她；最後有一天，他說：「我得再去看她一次；她大概已經死了。」——到了那地方，他發現屋子空無一人，最後才發現她蜷縮著坐在一個洞穴裡，已經僵死了；他埋葬了她的遺骸，用石頭把墳墓嚴嚴實實地蓋好，然後回去了。他們如今決意永遠捨棄那座屋子，搬到最外邊的一座小島上安頓下來過冬，不久之後海面便結了冰。大約在這時候，一個住在阿庫塔克家的可憐孤兒對同屋的人說：「我極需要一雙靴子，打算去找那幾兄弟，把我的小狗送給他們，換一雙舊靴子。」——於是他就動身前往他們從前住的地方。早晨到達那裡時，他詫異地發現那屋子沒有窗戶；然而他還是走上前去，發現屋裡仍儲備充足，但他既看不見船，也看不到那地方周圍有任何人——進屋後，他發現牆上所有的皮製掛飾都被扯了下來，鋪在地上。他不知附近還有別的人家，很快便打定主意在此過夜，天黑時去取了些鯨脂，修剪好一盞燈並點燃；然後他脫下破爛的靴子，把它們放在燈上方烘乾，自己則坐在炕的南端。起初他的小狗跟著他進了屋，在地板上蜷縮在他腳邊；但就在他的靴子烘著的時候，那狗開始嗅聞、吠叫，跑到外面去，叫聲漸漸遠去——過了一會兒它又回來，趴在主人面前，非常銳利地看著他，隨後又像先前那樣嚎叫著衝了出去，這次卻立刻又進來了。那孤兒心想：「狗是不會無緣無故這樣的。」——於是他穿上靴子衝了出去，那狗隨即跟上。

passages.text: Before they had made their way through the house passage, on looking out he caught sight of the ghost making towards him through the entrance, dragging its shroud behind it; the boy being in the middle part of the passage pressed himself close up to the wall, and the dog also. At the very moment he expected to be discovered by the ghost it passed by, on which the dog instantly jumped noiselessly out, followed by his poor master; both now hastened down to the ice — but before they had got far the spectre was seen emerging from the house in full pursuit of them. It did not however get hold of them, for at a little distance the fugitive had to pass by a large iceberg, and seeing a cave on one side of it stepped quickly in, and there awaited the coming day. At dawn he issued forth again, not knowing which way to wend his steps; his first plan was to go back to his own home, when he suddenly espied a number of people on one of the outer islets and at once turned towards them — they apparently got much excited at seeing him, thinking it might be the mad woman; not till he was quite close did they recognise the poor orphan boy, when they all asked whether he had not slept in the haunted house and whether he had seen anything amiss there. 'No; I observed nothing particular' — in so saying he told a lie, as he had barely escaped being devoured by the ghost. When they asked him why he had gone there at all he made answer, 'Because I wanted to barter away my little dog for a pair of boots.' The middle brother now said, 'Well, thou art a hearty little fellow for thy age' — and with these words gave him two pairs of boots without taking his dog; when the boy was about to leave he asked a gift of a knife with a pretty handle — all the other brothers likewise loaded him with little presents of various kinds; on reaching home however he exchanged all these things for a kayak of his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 77 'Akutak and Inuinak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們還沒穿過屋子的通道，他往外一看，就瞥見那鬼魂正穿過入口朝他而來，身後拖著它的裹屍布；那男孩身處通道中段，便緊貼著牆壁，那狗也一樣。就在他以為自己要被鬼魂發現的那一刻，鬼魂卻走了過去，那狗立刻悄無聲息地跳了出去，可憐的主人緊隨其後；兩人當下急忙奔向冰面——但還沒走多遠，就看見那幽靈從屋裡出來，全力追趕他們。然而它並沒有抓住他們，因為逃命的人在不遠處必須經過一座大冰山，他看見冰山一側有個洞穴，便迅速鑽了進去，在那裡等待天明。黎明時分他又出來了，不知該往哪個方向走；他最初的打算是回自己的家去，這時忽然瞥見外邊一座小島上有許多人，便立刻朝他們走去——那些人見到他顯然十分激動，以為可能是那個瘋女人；直到他走得相當近了，他們才認出是那可憐的孤兒，於是眾人紛紛問他，是不是在那鬧鬼的屋子裡睡了一夜，有沒有在那裡看到什麼不對勁的東西。「沒有；我沒注意到什麼特別的。」——他這樣說是在撒謊，因為他差點就被那鬼魂吞吃了。當他們問他究竟為什麼要去那裡時，他回答說：「因為我想把我的小狗換一雙靴子。」中間那個兄弟這時說道：「嗯，以你這年紀來說，你倒是個挺有膽量的小傢伙。」——說著便給了他兩雙靴子，卻沒有要他的狗；男孩臨走時，又討要一把刀柄漂亮的刀子作禮物——其餘的兄弟也都紛紛送他各種小禮物；然而他回到家後，把這些東西全都換成了一艘屬於自己的獨木舟。

title.en: Arnarsarsuak, the Kivigtok Woman and Her Bear Children
title.zh: 奇維托克婦人阿納薩舒亞克與其熊子

region.en: The interior and the far-away islands
region.zh: 內陸與遙遠的外海島嶼

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 78 'Arnarsarsuak, the Kivigtok Woman', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Overhearing 'who ever will care to be troubled with the charge of that wretch Arnarsarsuak is going to give birth to,' the pregnant girl drops her pails in the passage and flees mankind, bearing a kingulerak — the anghiak that stays attached to a kivigtok mother until she has revenged herself. Summoned by her own song sung far away, she joins the grown-up orphans she once fed, flenses both seals and sews while cooking, and bears them child after child — a little bear cub and a real child, nursed together — until the bear-sons swim alongside the boat to a well-peopled place, popping their muzzles bashfully above water: 'Don't be ashamed; remember ye also are of human extraction.'
summary.zh: 聽見妯娌譏語『誰願意照管那賤人阿納薩舒亞克要生的東西』，懷孕的她把水桶一放，遁入內陸拋開人世——生下一名附身不離的昆古勒拉克（死胎鬼，纏住遁世之母直至復仇完畢）。多年後，她循著遠方有人唱起自己的歌而來，投奔昔日善待的兩名孤兒——剥豹炊飯兼縫衣，一胎又一胎：熊崽與真孩同榻而哺。熊子們隨舟泅向人煙之地，羞怯地把吻部探出水面——『別害臊；你們也是人類的後代。』

sensitivity.note: Kingulerak: an anghiak who remained attached to the mother on account of her being kivigtok until she had revenged herself (Rink's note). Bear-children birth recorded as told.

passages.text: Arnarsarsuak was a pretty girl, much courted by the best seal-hunters of the neighbourhood; her brother being unwilling to let her get married she at length took up with a fellow and lived with him as his concubine. Before long she was with child, but notwithstanding her brother still continued loving her dearly. One day she had been out to fetch water, and at the very moment she was about to enter she chanced to hear her sisters-in-law within talking about her, saying to each other, 'I wonder who ever will care to be troubled with the charge of that wretch Arnarsarsuak is going to give birth to.' On hearing these words she at once put down her pails in the passage and ran off far to the inland, away from humankind; during her flight she perceived that the time had come when she should be delivered — she fell into a deep swoon, and on recovering found she had given birth to a kingulerak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 78 'Arnarsarsuak, the Kivigtok Woman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿納薩蘇阿克是個漂亮的姑娘，附近最出色的獵海豹人都爭相向她求愛；她的兄長不願讓她出嫁，她終於跟了一個男子，做了他的妾，與他同居。不久她便有了身孕，然而兄長依舊深愛著她。有一天她外出取水，正當她要進門的時候，偶然聽見嫂子們在屋裡談論她，彼此說道：『我倒想知道，究竟有誰願意費心去照料阿納薩蘇阿克將要生下的那個孽種。』聽到這番話，她立刻把水桶放在過道裡，逃往內陸的遠方，遠離人群；在奔逃途中，她發覺臨盆的時候到了——她陷入深深的昏厥，醒來時發現自己生下了一個金古列拉克。

passages.text: Formerly, in the days of her prosperity, she had been kind and charitable to two orphan children, a boy and a girl, who lived among them; many years after, when Arnarsarsuak's brothers were all dead, the two orphans took up their abode at a solitary place out on some far-away islands. When the brother was following his trade in his kayak the sister felt miserably lonely — to make up for which however when he again returned she felt as if the house were full of visitors. One evening when they were sitting chatting together the brother suddenly said, 'I think I shall try to recall the song that Arnarsarsuak used to sing' — the sister advised him rather to desist, saying, 'Remember that Arnarsarsuak now belongs to those of uncommon kind, having fled from mankind during her pregnancy. I have heard that such people have the gift of hearing their own songs a long way off.' However, the brother would not give up his intention; no sooner had he commenced singing than a voice was heard outside, 'On hearing my song I could not resist coming, and here I am' — the brother and sister looked at each other in great alarm, knowing that their house was far away from any one. However, they soon recognised the voice to be Arnarsarsuak's, on which the sister resumed, 'Did not I tell thee she would be sure to hear thee singing? Now go and answer, thou being the best talker of us' — the brother did not stir, and the voice was again heard, 'Ye need not be afraid of me; I only want to get inside.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 78 'Arnarsarsuak, the Kivigtok Woman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前，在她境況順遂的日子裡，她曾善待並施恩於兩個孤兒，一男一女，他們就住在他們中間；許多年後，當阿納薩蘇阿克的兄弟們全都死去，這兩個孤兒便在一處偏僻之地、遠方的一些島嶼上安了家。當兄長划著皮艇外出營生時，妹妹感到十分孤寂——然而為了彌補這一點，當他歸來時，她總覺得屋子裡彷彿擠滿了訪客。一天傍晚，他們坐在一起閒談，兄長忽然說道：『我想試著回想阿納薩蘇阿克從前常唱的那首歌。』妹妹勸他還是作罷，說道：『別忘了阿納薩蘇阿克如今已屬於非同尋常的一類，她懷孕時逃離了人群。我聽說這樣的人有本領在很遠的地方聽見自己的歌聲。』然而兄長不肯放棄他的念頭；他剛一開口唱，外面就傳來一個聲音：『一聽見我的歌，我就忍不住要來，我這就到了』——兄妹二人驚恐地互相對視，因為他們知道自己的屋子遠離任何人煙。然而他們很快便聽出那是阿納薩蘇阿克的聲音，於是妹妹接著說道：『我不是告訴過你，她一定會聽見你唱歌嗎？現在去答話吧，你比我們都會說話。』兄長一動不動，那聲音又響了起來：『你們不必怕我；我只想進屋裡去。』

passages.text: Seeing her brothers could find no words the sister said, 'Well, come in' — presently a sound was heard of something creeping along the passage, while the two shrank back on the ledge in silence with a sure foreboding that the next moment they would be frightened to death; the sound rapidly approached, they only ventured a timid glance towards the entrance, and immediately after Arnarsarsuak entered, prettier than ever, and said, 'I was lately far from this place, in the interior, whence I was suddenly lured by some voice calling me hither.' The sister now took courage to say, 'It was only for a pastime he tried to sing thy lay' — Arnarsarsuak continued, 'Ye know why I fled; it was because I heard my sisters-in-law observing that no one would be found willing to provide for my poor offspring. On that day I ran far off into the interior, when I was soon to give birth to a kingulerak, which ever since adhered to my body till a few days ago. In my present state ye have nothing to fear from me, and I would be very glad to come and stay with you.' Seeing that they had no choice and could not get rid of her they allowed her room on the farthest end of the ledge, and themselves lay down leaving a wide space between them — still they were quite unable to fall asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 78 'Arnarsarsuak, the Kivigtok Woman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 妹妹見兄長們說不出話來，便說道：『好吧，進來吧。』不久便聽見有什麼東西沿著過道爬行，而二人默默縮回炕上，心中確信下一刻就會被嚇死；那聲音迅速逼近，他們只敢怯怯地朝入口瞥了一眼，緊接著阿納薩蘇阿克便走了進來，比從前更加美麗，說道：『我近來在離此地很遠的內陸，忽然被某個呼喚我的聲音引到了這裡。』妹妹這時鼓起勇氣說道：『他不過是為了好玩，才試著唱你的歌。』阿納薩蘇阿克接著說道：『你們知道我為何逃走；是因為我聽見嫂子們說，沒有人會願意供養我可憐的孩子。那天我逃到內陸的遠方，不久便要生下一個金古列拉克，它從那時起一直附在我身上，直到幾天前才脫離。以我現在的狀況，你們不必怕我，我很願意來和你們同住。』他們見別無選擇，也擺脫不了她，便讓她在炕的最遠一端佔了一席之地，自己則躺下，與她之間留出寬闊的空隙——然而他們仍然完全無法入睡。

passages.text: The following day the brother wanted to go out hunting; his sister however persuaded him to stay at home on account of her new housemate, whom they still considered rather a doubtful personage — on the ensuing day he went out kayaking but kept so near to the house as not to lose sight of them for any length of time. In the evening however he returned bringing with him two seals, and the sister at once ran down as usual to flense and cut up the animals, but Arnarsarsuak would not allow it, taking all the work on herself; having quickly flensed both seals she made up a fire, and while she did the cooking she sewed at the same time. As time went by and their fears subsided the brother resolved to marry her; but when she came to be pregnant the sister began to fear she would bear no human offspring, and in that case said, 'Whither am I to flee? Seeing we live on an island I can only rush down to the sea.' When her time had come the brother as well as the sister determined to run away from the house — but when the brother turned back to have a last look through the window his wife turned towards him, saying, 'It is all over, and the birth has taken place. Do not fear, but come in to me.' On hearing this he hastened to bring his sister back; when they returned Arnarsarsuak sat smiling kindly on them and said, 'Behold the object of your fears, my two babes' — she then showed them a little bear cub and a real child. Both were nursed together, and when the bear had begun to go about by himself she again bore a child and another little bear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 78 'Arnarsarsuak, the Kivigtok Woman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，兄長想外出打獵；妹妹卻因這位新來的同住者而勸他留在家中，他們仍覺得她是個相當可疑的人物——到了翌日，他划著皮艇出去了，但始終靠屋子很近，不曾長時間看不見他們。然而到了傍晚，他帶著兩隻海豹回來，妹妹照例立刻跑下去剝皮、切割獵物，但阿納薩蘇阿克不許她動手，把全部活計都攬到自己身上；她很快剝好了兩隻海豹，生起火來，一邊做飯一邊縫紉。日子一天天過去，他們的恐懼漸漸消退，兄長便決意娶她；但當她懷了孕，妹妹開始擔心她生下的不會是人類的後代，若果真如此，她說：『我該往哪裡逃呢？我們既然住在島上，我只能奔向大海了。』臨產之時，兄長和妹妹都決意逃離屋子——但當兄長回頭從窗戶最後望一眼時，他的妻子轉向他說道：『一切都結束了，孩子已經生下。不要害怕，進來吧。』他聽了這話，連忙把妹妹帶回來；他們回來時，阿納薩蘇阿克坐著，和善地對他們微笑，說道：『看看你們所懼怕的東西吧，我的兩個寶寶。』她隨即給他們看一隻小熊崽和一個真正的人類孩子。兩個孩子一同哺育，當那隻熊開始自己四處走動時，她又生下了一個孩子和另一隻小熊。

passages.text: In due time the father gave his boys kayaks, and the bears of their own account went out for provender; at length the father could afford to take things easy and rest from work. Subsequently he proposed that they should all set out together in search of other people, thinking that the children ought not to live always at such a desolate place; accordingly they started northwards, the sons following in their kayaks, while the bears kept swimming alongside the boat. Travelling on thus they at length came in sight of a well-peopled place; on this the bears stuck closer to the boat and out of bashfulness only popped their muzzles above water — the father remarked, 'Don't be ashamed; remember ye also are of human extraction.' However, on landing a little south of the settlement they were received by a number of people, who on seeing two large bears ran off for their weapons; but on the father calling to them, 'What are you thinking of? They also are my children,' they desisted. The new-comers took up their winter quarters at this place, where the sons both got married and all lived happy together; when the weather was too bad for the men to go out hunting the bears went off in their stead. After wintering there they again broke up for their old home, and were joined by several people of the place who accompanied them thither, where their bones now rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 78 'Arnarsarsuak, the Kivigtok Woman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 到了適當的時候，父親給兒子們皮艇，那些熊則自行外出覓食；終於，父親得以安閒度日，不必再勞作。後來他提議大家一同出發去尋找別的人群，認為孩子們不該總住在這樣荒涼的地方；於是他們向北進發，兒子們划著皮艇跟隨，熊則一直沿著船邊游著。這樣一路行來，他們終於望見一處人煙稠密的地方；見此，熊緊貼著船，出於羞怯只把鼻吻探出水面——父親說道：『不必害羞；別忘了你們也出自人類血統。』然而，他們在聚落稍南處登岸時，受到一群人的迎接，那些人一見兩隻大熊便跑去取武器；但父親向他們喊道：『你們想幹什麼？它們也是我的孩子。』他們便住了手。新來的人在此地過冬，兒子們都娶了妻，大家和睦度日；天氣太壞、男人們無法外出打獵時，熊便代他們出去。在此過冬之後，他們又動身返回舊居，當地有幾個人與他們同行，一同前往那裡，如今他們的遺骨就安息在那裡。

title.en: Avatarsuak, Baptised Nathan: The Tupilak on His Stern
title.zh: 受洗者內森（阿瓦塔舒亞克）：艇尾的圖皮拉克

region.en: Trading route to Pamiut (Frederikshaab)
region.zh: 通往帕米烏特（腓特烈斯哈布）的商路

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 79 'Avatarsuak, who was baptised Nathan', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Grandfather-raised to harm 'not the meanest dog,' Avatarsuak is suspected of killing two missing traders — and rides home with a tupilak on his stern crying 'I shall soon make a feast on thy entrails,' until it wails 'I see I have made a mistake, and climbed up to one of uncommon kind.' Wedged as if glued, it is levered off by women with oars — stuffed with bones of birds, walruses, and seals — and sunk in the sea and old tombs. Later an iceberg calving presses him under; his grandparents escort him beneath the waves, warn him off the spring designed for those perishing at sea, and land him at the great house of dogs-in-shape-of-men, where he lies five days and rows home on his own drifted kayak — no witchcraft working on him ever after.
summary.zh: 由祖父撫養成人、被告誡『莫傷最卑賤的狗』的阿瓦塔舒亞克，被疑殺害兩名失蹤商人——歸途中艇尾竟騎上一隻圖皮拉克，嘶叫『我很快就要享用了你的腸子』，直到它哀鳴『我看錯了，爬上了一位不凡之人』。被女子們以槳撬下——內藏鳥、海象與海豹之骨——沉海並藏入古墓。其後冰山崩裂將他壓入水中；祖父母護送他潛行海底，囑他莫飲『海上溺亡者之泉』，最後抵達犬形人守衛的大屋——躺臥五日後，乘著漂回的自己的皮艇歸家，從此再無巫術能近其身。

sensitivity.note: Grandparent-guardian spirits and the sea-death spring documented as told. Rink notes Avatarsuak was a historical baptized man (Nathan).

passages.text: It is said that his grandfather, being likewise called Avatarsuak, was a wise man; it was he who took charge of his younger namesake, whose own father had been early called away from home. The grandfather admonished him not to harm the meanest dog, and never to be uncivil towards old people, not even on being reproved by them. When he came to possess a kayak of his own he remarked that his grandfather, when pushing him off the beach, was always heard to pronounce some strange words, at the same time uncovering his head by pulling the hood back behind the ears — but though the youth listened carefully he could not make out the meaning of the words. About the time when he first commenced seal-catching his grandfather died, and being left alone he took up his winter quarters at a place where the Southlanders had to pass by when on their trading excursions to the European settlement at Pamiut (Fredrikshaab). At length two kayakers on their voyage to this place passed by his residence, whom he expected for ever so long to see return but in vain; at length he learned from the south that both were missing, and at the same time that he was suspected of having killed them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 79 'Avatarsuak, who was baptised Nathan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說他的祖父也叫阿瓦塔蘇阿克，是個有智慧的人；正是他照管了與他同名的孫兒，這孩子的父親早早便離家而去。祖父告誡他不可傷害最卑賤的狗，對老人也絕不可無禮，即使受到他們責備時也不例外。當他有了自己的皮艇時，他注意到祖父在岸邊推他下水時，總會念出一些奇怪的話，同時把頭巾向後拉到耳後，露出頭來——但這少年雖然仔細傾聽，卻聽不出那些話的意思。大約在他初次開始捕海豹的時候，祖父去世了，他獨自一人，便在一處南方人前往帕繆特（腓特烈斯霍布）的歐洲人聚落做買賣途中必經之地過冬。終於，有兩個划皮艇的人在前往該地的途中經過他的住處，他盼著他們歸來，盼了很久卻始終不見；最後他從南方得知，兩人都失蹤了，同時也得知自己被人懷疑殺了他們。

passages.text: Some time after, being in want of a skin for a hunting-bladder he went off in search of a firth-seal; it was fine weather and so calm that the breathing of the larger seals was plainly audible — as for the small firth-seals however he saw none, and was getting farther and farther into the bay. Suddenly something emerged from the water coming up close behind him and beating the top of his kayak — and lo! it was nothing less than a tupilak (monster made by sorcery). It accosted him, saying, 'How lucky I met thee thus alone, as I am longing for some entrails!' Stupefied with awe he felt the creature creeping up on the top of the kayak behind him, constantly repeating, 'I shall soon make a feast on thy entrails,' at the same time pressing down the stern of the kayak so deep as to make the prow rise in the air; never before had he, who was wont to carry spotted seals, had such a weight on board. Feeling his strength giving way and knowing nothing better he tried to capsize his kayak to the left, but was greatly perplexed to find his oar striking against a hard substance below, though out in deep water — at this he got up; but in attempting to turn his kayak to the right he again hit something hard, on which he slowly righted himself and rowed away, at the same time perceiving that he was regaining his strength. But though he pulled homewards with all his strength he found it impossible to make his kayak go straight; it kept turning round carrying him towards uninhabited places.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 79 'Avatarsuak, who was baptised Nathan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 過了些時日，他因缺少一張皮來做獵囊，便出去尋找峽灣海豹；天氣晴朗，海面平靜得連大隻海豹的呼吸聲都清晰可聞——然而他卻一隻小峽灣海豹也沒看見，而且愈划愈深入灣中。忽然有東西從水中冒出，緊跟在他身後浮上來，拍打著他的皮艇頂部——瞧！那竟是一隻圖皮拉克（以巫術造出的怪物）。牠向他搭話說：「我竟能這樣獨自遇上你，真是幸運，我正饞著要吃些內臟呢！」他驚愕得發愣，只覺那怪物在他身後爬上艇頂，不斷重複著：「我很快就要拿你的內臟飽餐一頓。」同時把艇尾壓得極深，使艇首翹向空中；他平日慣於載運斑海豹，卻從未有過這般沉重的負載。他感到力氣漸失，又別無他法，便試著把皮艇往左翻，卻大為困惑地發現自己的槳在深水之中竟撞到某種堅硬的東西——他於是坐直起來；但當他試圖把皮艇轉向右邊時，又撞到硬物，這才慢慢把艇扶正，划了開去，同時發覺自己的力氣正在恢復。然而儘管他竭盡全力往家的方向划，卻發現皮艇怎麼也划不直；它不斷打轉，把他帶往無人居住的地方。

passages.text: The tupilak now cried, 'Thou hateful creature, I see I have made a mistake, and climbed up to one of uncommon kind' (viz., a man endowed with a certain degree of angakok power) — he noticed it struggling hard to get down but without being able to detach itself. Thus he went on pulling away to the sunny side of the firth; when they were quite close to the beach the tupilak said, 'I see I shall not get through with thee, and I think I shall be made thy prize.' Just then the man on looking round discovered a boat occupied by women who had been farther up the firth getting angmagsat (capelins); he called out to them, 'I have got something on my kayak that is not a seal; put ashore yonder and come round this way quickly' — when they had done as he told them he went on saying, 'Don't attack it in front, as it might be dangerous to you.' The foremost among them on seeing the beast fled in terror; the kayaker again began to lose strength, but at length his repeated calls caused the women to come back bringing with them oars, intending to use them as levers, the beast sticking fast as if glued to the kayak — at length it gave way, and a cracking noise was heard, whereupon he was able to get out and look at the monster, which proved to be the size of a large firth-seal. Turning to the oldest of the women he said, 'I do not care to touch it; ye cut it up; I shall repay you hereafter.' In expectation of the reward she at once fell to and cut open the tupilak, which she found stuffed with all kinds of bones, such as of birds, walruses, and seals; they had it entirely destroyed by sinking part of it in the sea and hiding the rest of it in some old tombs. This done he prepared to row home, but first said to the women, 'Thanks to you and your roaming thus about, without which I wonder how I had fared. I will take care to repay you; I am not likely to forget you.' At home he told his adventure, and all now felt sure that it must have been the tupilak which had formerly killed the two traders; after this all travellers were unmolested, and the women were well paid by Avatarsuak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 79 'Avatarsuak, who was baptised Nathan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那圖皮拉克這時叫道：「你這可惡的東西，我看我是弄錯了，竟爬上了個與眾不同的人身上」（即一個具有某種安加科克法力的人）——他察覺牠正拼命想下去，卻無法脫身。於是他繼續往峽灣向陽的一側划去；當他們十分靠近灘岸時，圖皮拉克說：「我看我是擺脫不了你了，我想我就要成為你的獵獲物了。」就在這時，那人回頭一看，發現一條船，船上盡是婦女，她們原是在峽灣上游捕撈安格馬薩特（毛鱗魚）的；他向她們喊道：「我艇上載著個不是海豹的東西；你們在那邊靠岸，快從這邊繞過來。」她們照他的話做了之後，他又接著說：「別從正面攻擊牠，那對你們可能有危險。」她們當中為首的一人一見那怪物便驚恐地逃開了；划皮艇的人又開始力氣不支，但經他一再呼喊，婦女們終於帶著槳回來，打算用槳當槓桿撬開，那怪物卻像黏在皮艇上一般牢牢附著——最後牠終於鬆脫，只聽得一聲爆裂的聲響，他這才得以脫身出來察看那怪物，原來牠有大峽灣海豹那般大小。他轉向婦女中年紀最長的一位說：「我不想碰牠；你們把牠切開吧；我日後會報答你們的。」她一心盼著報酬，立刻動手剖開那圖皮拉克，發現牠肚裡塞滿了各式各樣的骨頭，有鳥的、海象的、海豹的；她們把牠徹底毀掉，一部分沉入海中，其餘的藏進幾座舊墳墓裡。辦完之後，他準備划船回家，但先對婦女們說：「多虧你們，也多虧你們這樣四處遊走，否則我真不知會落得什麼下場。我一定會好好報答你們；我是不會忘記你們的。」回到家裡，他講述了自己的遭遇，如今大家都確信，從前殺死那兩名商人的一定就是這隻圖皮拉克；此後所有旅人都平安無事，而那些婦女也得到了阿瓦塔蘇克豐厚的報酬。

passages.text: Some time now elapsed without anything remarkable happening. Towards spring however he found himself in want of several necessaries, such as lead, powder, and tobacco, and set out for the European settlement at Pamiut; having finished his business there and rested during the night he turned homewards, rather uneasy about a quantity of drift-ice which had accumulated at the mouth of a firth he had to cross. Before he reached the spot the land wind set in and came storming down upon him, and the sky looked black and threatening; still he tried to cross the firth winding his way through the small passages between the broken ice — at length however he found himself almost entirely stopped, and at the same time saw a large iceberg drifting down upon him. He tried to escape, but presently heard the roar of its calving right alongside him, and pressing him deep under the waters; however he rose on the other side of the broken piece and again sped along — but on the shady side of the firth he was once more overturned by a much larger iceberg, and this time he quite lost his senses. How long he was in this state of stupor is not known; but on reviving he noticed the strings of his kayak-jacket rattling about and smiting his back with the quick motion, while he was pushed on towards the land beneath the waves — he had no kayak, but found himself sitting down, the loose bottom skin of his kayak fastened round him, having his kayak-stick for an oar, and with one leg somewhat bent. In front he saw some one in a large hood rushing on and cleaving the waters for him, and behind he heard some one talking, but without being able to make out the words — these companions proved to be his grandparents protecting their grandson.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 79 'Avatarsuak, who was baptised Nathan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後又過了些時日，並無任何異事發生。然而到了春天將近時，他發覺自己缺少幾樣必需品，諸如鉛、火藥和菸草，便動身前往帕米烏特的歐洲人聚落；他在那裡辦完事，歇了一夜，便啟程回家，心裡卻頗為不安，因為他必須橫渡的一處峽灣口積聚了大量浮冰。他還沒到那地方，陸風便起了，朝他猛烈吹襲而下，天色也顯得陰沉險惡；他仍試著橫渡峽灣，在碎冰之間的小水道中迂迴穿行——然而最後他發現自己幾乎完全被阻住，同時又看見一座巨大的冰山朝他漂流而來。他試圖逃開，卻立刻聽見冰山就在他身旁崩裂的轟鳴，把他深深壓入水中；不過他在那碎冰的另一側浮了上來，又繼續疾行——但在峽灣背陰的一側，他又被一座大得多的冰山掀翻，這回他完全失去了知覺。他在這種昏沉狀態中過了多久，無人知曉；但當他甦醒過來時，察覺自己皮艇外套的繫帶在急速的動作中噼啪作響，拍打著他的背，而他正被推著往陸地而去，身處波浪之下——他沒有皮艇，卻發現自己正坐著，皮艇鬆脫的底皮裹在他身上，手裡拿著皮艇桿當槳，一條腿還微微彎曲。他看見前方有人穿著一件大兜帽，正為他破水疾行，又聽見身後有人在說話，卻聽不清說的是什麼——這兩位同伴原來是他的祖父母，正在庇護他們的孫兒。

passages.text: When they came nearer to the islets he felt exceedingly thirsty, and presently discovering an iceberg with a fine spring flowing from it wanted to go and quench his thirst — but at that moment he heard a warning voice behind him saying, 'Dear grandson, do not drink of the fountain designed for those perishing at sea; if thou drinkest thou wilt never return.' At length he was carried far towards the head of the firth and saw light from the windows of a very large house; presently a woman in a white jacket came out of the doorway, then another, and at last a man in a reindeer cloak followed by others, all being dogs in shape of men, running down on the beach to him. When he entered the house there were people sitting together at its southern end keeping watch over a dying brother; having got inside he fell down beside the first lamp, but still could hear one of the men say, 'An anghiniartok has come among us' — at that instant, on being handled by them and touched upon his bare skin, he lost all consciousness, but soon after revived hearing a sweet tune of a song from his childhood. At the very moment he revived the sick man breathed his last. The people of the house put a new skin underneath him and let him remain perfectly quiet in his own clothes for five succeeding days, after which he began to stir about a little and long to get home, but he had no kayak — one day however a woman went down along the beach to gather the red sea-weed and returned saying, 'Only fancy! I have found a complete kayak drifted ashore to us.' When they had gathered on the beach and duly inspected it they made it out to be the kayak of their anghiniartok, in perfect order, lying just above high-water mark and well closed by the half-jacket; on opening this they also found his goods, not a single implement amissing. The next day he returned; and from that time upwards he became still more of a wise man, and no witchcraft could ever work upon him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 79 'Avatarsuak, who was baptised Nathan'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們靠近那些小島時，他感到口渴難耐，隨即發現一座冰山上有清澈的泉水湧出，便想去解渴——但就在那一刻，他聽見身後有個警告的聲音說：「親愛的孫兒，別喝那專為在海上喪命之人預備的泉水；你若喝了，就再也回不來了。」最後他被帶到峽灣上游很遠的地方，看見一座極大的屋子窗戶透出燈光；不久，一個穿白外套的女人從門口出來，接著又是一個，最後是一個穿馴鹿皮斗篷的男人，後面還跟著其他人，他們全都是化作人形的狗，一齊奔下灘岸朝他而來。他進屋時，屋子的南端坐著一群人，正守望著一個垂死的兄弟；他進去之後，便倒在第一盞燈旁，卻仍聽得其中一個男人說：「有個安吉尼亞爾托克來到我們中間了。」就在那一瞬間，當他們扶起他、觸碰到他裸露的皮膚時，他完全失去了知覺，但不久又因聽見一首他童年時的歌謠的甜美曲調而甦醒過來。就在他甦醒的那一刻，那病人嚥下了最後一口氣。屋裡的人在他身下鋪了一張新皮，讓他穿著自己的衣服完全安靜地躺了接連五天，之後他開始稍稍活動，渴望回家，但他沒有皮艇——然而有一天，一個女人下到灘岸去採紅海藻，回來時說：「你想想看！我發現一隻完好的皮艇漂到我們這岸上來了。」等他們聚到灘岸上仔細察看，才認出那正是他們那位安吉尼亞爾托克的皮艇，完好無損，就擱在滿潮線上方，還被那半截外套嚴嚴實實地封蓋著；打開一看，他們也找到了他的物品，一件器具都不缺。第二天他便回去了；從那時起，他愈發成為一個有智慧的人，任何巫術都再也奈何不了他。

title.en: The Firth-People Who Rode the Surf
title.zh: 峽灣人踏浪登岸

region.en: Kangek at the mouth of the Godthaab firth
region.zh: 努克峽灣口的康格克

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 80 'About the Men from the Firth visiting the People at the open Sea-shore', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Firth-born brothers who had never faced the outer sea-coast are mocked by the surf-men: 'It is plain the firth-people yonder know nothing about surf; now we will have some fun with them' — 'We never land anywhere but at the point yonder.' The eldest lets a monstrous wave carry him right in upon the rocks, loosens his jacket at the break, leaps ashore, and hauls his kayak in on the next roller — not a word from the mockers, who stood in great consternation; the second does it with even greater agility. 'Poor worthless fellows like us are little fit to come here; but our younger brother would just be the man for you... we dare not venture out on account of the dreadful surf from the glacier' — fed on auks (entrails preferred, more like their gulls'), they load up and turn homewards.
summary.zh: 從未見過外海的峽灣兄弟遭衝浪好手嘲弄：『這些峽灣人分明不懂衝浪，正好戲弄他們一番』——『我們向來只在那處岬角登岸。』長兄任憑巨浪把艇推上礁石，浪頭破碎之際鬆開外套躍上岸，再借下一道浪把艇拖上岸——嘲弄者啞口無言、驚惶失色；次兄登岸更為敏捷。『我們這等無用之人不配來此；但我弟弟正是你們要找的人……只是冰川碎浪兇險，我們不敢冒險出海』——他們飽餐海鳩（偏愛內臟，酷似慣吃的鷗腸），滿載而歸。

sensitivity.note: Surf-landing technique tale; ethnographic as well as narrative interest per Rink.

passages.text: There once lived three brothers at the head of a firth not far from Nook (Godthaab); they were born firth-people, and never thought of approaching the outer sea-coast. But on learning that great flocks of auks were to be met with at Kangek, at the mouth of the firth, they agreed to make a trip thither; when they were ready for their departure however the youngest changed his mind and would not be of the party, so the other two went off by themselves. Arrived at Kangek they first intended to land at the outermost point, not being aware of the heavy surf setting in upon it; when the men of the place saw them in their trouble they said to each other, 'It is plain the firth-people yonder know nothing about surf; now we will have some fun with them.' Meantime the visitors had put back, and were looking for a place nearer the habitations where the landing was easier; but the men called out to them, 'We never land anywhere but at the point yonder: it is rather an awkward thing, and cannot be done without letting the surf roll over you; however, that is the way to do it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 80 'About the Men from the Firth visiting the People at the open Sea-shore'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 從前有三兄弟住在離努克（戈特霍布）不遠的一處峽灣上游；他們生來就是峽灣人，從沒想過要靠近外海海岸。但當他們得知峽灣口的康格克一帶可以見到成群結隊的大海雀時，便相約到那裡走一趟；然而到了準備出發的時候，最小的那個卻改變了主意，不肯同行，於是另外兩個便自行出發了。到了康格克，他們起初打算在最外端的岬角登陸，卻不知道那裡正湧著洶湧的拍岸浪；當地人見他們陷入困境，便彼此說道：「那邊的峽灣人顯然對拍岸浪一無所知；這下我們可有樂子瞧了。」其間那兩位訪客已經折返，正尋找一處離住屋較近、較易登陸的地方；但那些人卻朝他們喊道：「我們從不在別處登陸，只在那邊的岬角登陸：那是有點棘手的事，非得讓浪頭從你身上滾過去不可；不過，就是要那樣做才行。」

passages.text: The two poor fellows retired abashed, and paddling back to the great breakers outside the cape almost doubted their words; however, as the men on shore continued encouraging them, the eldest brother first paddled back, and when at the right distance from shore suffered himself to be carried right in upon the rocks by a monstrous wave, while he quickly made fast his oar by his kayak-strings — at the moment the wave broke over him he had loosened his jacket from the kayak, and took a leap, jumping on shore, where he waited the next roller which brought in his kayak, which he grasped hold of at the right moment hauling it up. Not a word was uttered by any of the mockers, who stood in great consternation on seeing this daring act, which no one among them would have been able to accomplish; while the poor visitor was drawing up his kayak the other prepared to land in the same way, and achieved it with even greater agility and swiftness than the brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 80 'About the Men from the Firth visiting the People at the open Sea-shore'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那兩個可憐人羞愧地退開，划回海岬外的大浪處，幾乎不敢相信他們的話；然而岸上的人仍不斷鼓勵他們，於是大哥先划了回去，等到了離岸適當的距離，便任憑一道巨浪把他直直沖向岩石，同時他迅速用皮艇的繫帶把槳綁牢——就在浪頭打在他身上的那一刻，他已把外套從皮艇上解開，縱身一躍，跳上了岸，在那裡等候下一道滾浪把他的皮艇送來，他在恰當的時機一把抓住，把它拖了上去。那些嘲弄他的人誰也沒說一句話，他們見了這大膽的舉動，都驚愕地站著，因為他們之中沒有一個人能辦得到；就在那可憐的訪客拖上皮艇的時候，另一個也準備以同樣的方式登陸，而且比他的兄弟更加敏捷迅速地做到了。

passages.text: After this the men on shore took a sudden fancy to them, and vied with each other in inviting them to their houses; the elder, who had by this time found out their former intention of mocking them, replied, 'Poor worthless fellows like us are little fit to come here; but our younger brother would just be the man for you. However, he had no fancy for coming. In summer, when the mighty glaciers are throwing off the icebergs into the firth, and when the spotted seals appear, we always want to get at them, but we dare not venture out on account of the dreadful surf from the glacier.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 80 'About the Men from the Firth visiting the People at the open Sea-shore'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 此後，岸上的男人們忽然對他們起了興致，爭相邀請他們到自家作客；那位年長者此時已看穿他們先前想嘲弄自己的意圖，便答道：「像我們這般沒用的可憐人，實在不配到這裡來；不過我們的弟弟倒正合你們的意。只是他無意前來。夏天，當巨大的冰川把冰山拋入峽灣，當斑海豹出現時，我們總想捕到牠們，卻因冰川湧來的可怕碎浪而不敢貿然出海。

passages.text: We only stand watching our brother, when he heedless of the danger crosses the firth; so you see that we are not at all the right ones to call in here.' Still not a word escaped the others. After having put their kayaks and implements ashore they entered the houses and were regaled with auks, which they liked very much — however they preferred the entrails to the flesh itself, thinking them more like the entrails of gulls which were their usual food. The day after they went with the men auk-catching, and having loaded their kayaks again turned homewards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 80 'About the Men from the Firth visiting the People at the open Sea-shore'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 我們只能站著看我們的弟弟，他不顧危險橫渡峽灣；所以你看，我們根本不是該受邀請到這裡來的人。」其餘的人依舊一言不發。他們把獨木舟和器具搬上岸後，便進了屋，受到以海雀款待，他們非常喜歡——不過比起雀肉，他們更愛雀的內臟，覺得那更像他們平日常吃的海鷗內臟。第二天，他們隨那些男人去捕海雀，把獨木舟重新裝滿後便掉頭返家。

title.en: The Deserted Woman and Her Foster-Daughter: The Magic Water-Hole
title.zh: 被棄婦人與養女：魔法水坑

region.en: Deserted windowless house, Greenland coast
region.zh: 格陵蘭海岸無窗的空屋

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 81 'The Deserted Woman and her Foster-daughter', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Abandoned with 'Ye only eat our food; we won't take you along,' the widow and her docile foster-daughter settle in the one windowless house with hangings left, living on leavings then a whole seal's entrails. A hole dug beneath the window-ledge and filled with sea-water becomes her magic pool: frog-fish, nepisak, eider-duck, firth-seal, saddleback, dolphin, white whale, narwal — until the flensing-place runs red, the aged kinsman comes to bury them and finds a feast, and the offended spirits still her incantation for ever because she gave the gifts to other people.
summary.zh: 被拋下時只聽得『你們白吃我們的糧食，我們不帶你們走』；寡婦與聽話的養女住進唯一窗戶被封、牆皮猶存的空屋，靠殘食與整副海豹內臟度日。窗台下掘坑注滿海水，便成她的魔法之池：鮟鱇、圓鰭魚、絨鴨、環斑海豹、鞍紋海豹、海豚、白鯨、一角鯨——剝皮台血流成河，年邁的親戚本是來收屍的，卻見盛宴滿桌。然而她把獵物分贈他人，觸怒了水中的靈——咒歌自此永寂。

sensitivity.note: Starvation survival and magic-pool hunting documented as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: A woman, who had no brothers or sisters, lived with a little foster-daughter at the house of a great seal-hunter; the daughter was very docile, and always obeyed at the least word. Once during spring all the people belonging to the place went away fishing; the chief hunter only lingered behind, harbouring wicked intentions. One calm morning he went outside the house and re-entered, saying, 'Pack up your things; we must be ready to start' — they now made all speed, and the lonely woman was not the least busy among them, working away as she never did before. When she had put her own poor bundles into the boat she hurried up for her ledge-cover; but when she came outside again she observed the foster-daughter still standing on shore watching their master closely — and when she herself came down he leaped into the boat, and shoving off called out to them, 'Ye only eat our food; we won't take you along.' So saying their housemates turned their backs upon them and got under way. The poor creatures, whose scanty belongings had all been put into the boat excepting the ledge-cover, on seeing the boat depart faced each other in blank despair and then burst into tears; however, when the boat was out of sight the widow wiped her eyes and said, 'Never mind, my dear; we must just do without them' — but the child was not so easily consoled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 81 'The Deserted Woman and her Foster-daughter'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個沒有兄弟姊妹的女人，帶著一個小小的養女，住在一位了不起的捕海豹獵人屋裡；那女孩非常順從，只要一句話便總是照辦。有一回正值春天，當地所有人都外出捕魚；只有那位首領獵人留了下來，心懷歹意。一個風平浪靜的早晨，他走出屋外又折回來，說道：「收拾你們的東西；我們得準備出發了」——於是眾人急忙行動，那孤單的女人也忙得不可開交，幹得比以往任何時候都賣力。她把自己可憐的幾包東西放進船裡後，又趕回去取她的窗臺遮皮；可是當她再出來時，她看見養女仍站在岸上，緊緊盯著她們的主人——而當她自己也走下來時，他卻跳上船，把船撐開，對她們喊道：「你們只會吃我們的糧食；我們不會帶你們走。」說著，同屋的人便背對她們，啟程離去。這些可憐人除了那張窗臺遮皮外，微薄的家當都已裝上了船，眼看船離去，只能面面相覷，茫然絕望，繼而放聲大哭；然而，等船影消失後，那寡婦擦乾眼淚說道：「別難過，親愛的；我們只好沒有他們也過下去」——但那孩子卻沒那麼容易得到安慰。

passages.text: When at length she stopped crying her mother said, 'Let us go and find out a house to make our home'; they went through all the deserted huts, but everywhere the walls were bare and the hangings removed, till at length they came into one without windows where the skins still hung on the walls, and the old one said, 'Here, in the southern corner, we'll take up our quarters' — she at once proceeded to make a room of suitable size dividing it from the rest of the house with the skins. This done she continued, 'Let us now go outside and try to find something to eat at the flensing-place'; she took the child by her hand and they soon found some small bits of blubber and skin which they greedily devoured, having had no food the whole day; after this meal they lay down to rest but were unable to sleep because of the cold. The next day after a similar search they found the entrails of an entire seal; after this however they found nothing more and had only the entrails to live upon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 81 'The Deserted Woman and her Foster-daughter'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 等她終於停止哭泣，母親說道：「我們去找一間屋子安家吧」；她們走遍了所有廢棄的屋子，但到處牆壁光禿、掛飾盡去，最後她們走進一間沒有窗戶的屋子，那裡的牆上仍掛著獸皮，老婦人便說：「這裡，在南邊的角落，我們就安頓下來」——她立刻動手，用獸皮隔出一間大小合適的房間，與屋子的其餘部分隔開。做完之後，她接著說：「現在我們出去，到剖鯨的地方找點吃的吧」；她牽著孩子的手，很快便找到一些零碎的鯨脂和皮，她們一整天沒吃東西，便狼吞虎嚥地吃了下去；吃過這頓，她們躺下休息，卻因寒冷而睡不著。第二天，她們又照樣搜尋，找到了一整隻海豹的內臟；然而此後便再也找不到別的東西，只能靠這些內臟過活。

passages.text: It was just when the herds of seals are passing along the coast that their stock of entrails was exhausted; one morning, having taken a small morsel, they noticed that there was only a bit left for their supper at night. Then the widow said to her daughter, 'Child, thou art more strong and active than I: thou must go and dig a hole over yonder beneath the window-ledge' — the daughter obeyed at once and began to dig up the loose earth. When she had finished the mother repeated, 'Thou art more brisk and active than I: run away and fill the hole with water' — the daughter continued fetching water from the sea, and before evening the hole was filled. That evening they took their last bit of food and went to rest, but without being able to sleep. In the early morning the mother said, 'I shall probably not succeed; still I think I will try to procure something (by magic)' — the daughter did not like the idea, nor did she believe in it; but the mother rejoined, 'When I commence my incantation, as I repeat it again and again, thou must listen attentively.' She soon began, and as she went through it warned her daughter to attend well; the child listened, and presently heard a splash — 'Mother dear, there is something moving in the water.' When the old woman told her to see what it was she ran off to look, and seeing a little frog-fish called out, 'Ah, mother, it is a frog-fish!' The mother told her to kill it with the old grindstone (probably an amulet); the little girl obeyed, and the fish was boiled and cut in two, putting aside one-half for their evening meal. Next morning the mother repeated her incantation and they got a nepisak-fish (lump-sucker); the next day in the same way an eider-duck — and so on the following days, a firth-seal, a saddleback-seal, a small dolphin, a white whale, and at last a narwal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 81 'The Deserted Woman and her Foster-daughter'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正當成群的海豹沿著海岸經過時，她們的內臟存糧吃完了；一天早晨，她們吃了一小口，便發覺只餘下一點點留作當晚的晚飯。於是寡婦對女兒說：「孩子，你比我強壯靈活：你得去那邊窗臺簷下挖個坑」——女兒立刻照辦，開始挖鬆軟的泥土。挖好之後，母親又說：「你比我輕快活潑：跑去把坑灌滿水」——女兒便不斷從海裡取水，還沒到傍晚，坑就灌滿了。那天晚上，她們吃了最後一點食物便去休息，卻睡不著。清晨，母親說：「我大概不會成功；不過我想我還是試試（用魔法）弄點什麼來」——女兒不喜歡這主意，也不相信；但母親接著說：「等我開始念咒，一遍又一遍念的時候，你得仔細聽。」她很快便開始念，一邊念一邊叮囑女兒好好留意；孩子聽著，不久便聽到潑水聲——「親愛的母親，水裡有東西在動。」老婦人叫她去看看是什麼，她便跑去瞧，看見一條小小的蛙魚，便喊道：「啊，母親，是一條蛙魚！」母親叫她用那塊舊磨石（大概是護身符）把牠打死；小女孩照辦了，魚被煮了，切成兩半，留下一半作當晚的飯食。第二天早晨，母親又念咒，她們得到一條內皮薩克魚（圓鰭魚）；再一天，同樣得到一隻絨鴨——此後幾天，又依次得到一隻峽灣海豹、一隻鞍背海豹、一隻小海豚、一頭白鯨，最後是一頭一角鯨。

passages.text: When she had done flensing the captured animals the following day large quantities of different kinds of provisions were heaped up outside the house; towards evening they went to the top of a rock sloping south to cut the flesh in thin slices for drying — while there engaged the daughter exclaimed, 'I almost think I see a kayak coming in,' and in this she was quite right. The lonely woman had one relative, a very aged man; this poor fellow having lately heard of the manner in which she had been abandoned and left in an empty house now came to see if she had not starved to death, bringing with him a frog-fish as a gift in case she was still alive. When he saw the flensing-place all red with blood he could not believe his own eyes but thought it all a delusion — and when he observed the two women standing on the rock and slicing large pieces of flesh for drying, and when they afterwards came running down to receive him, he accosted them, 'Here am I, expecting to find you starved to death: I actually came to bury you.' 'Silly old thing thou art! just get thee out of thy kayak, and partake of our good fare here' — the poor old man went ashore but tasted nothing till he had pulled his kayak properly up on the beach; the women had meanwhile boiled him a nice dish, he took his fill for once, and when he wanted to start they stuffed his kayak with such a supply that it was almost ready to sink. On leaving he said, 'As it is, there is no fear of your starving to death; when all your provisions are ready prepared I shall come to fetch you off.' When he was gone they went to rest, and the morning after she again made ready to practise her art — however she chanted and invoked, and chanted again, and the daughter watched and listened as usual, but neither breathing nor splashing was heard: the reason was that they had taken offence at her having made the gifts over to other people, and from that time upwards she never succeeded in calling forth anything. When her magic spell had wholly lost its effect and she had finished drying her stock of flesh her poor old relative came and fetched her off to his own homestead, and there she remained the rest of her days with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 81 'The Deserted Woman and her Foster-daughter'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第二天，她剖完捕獲的獵物後，屋外便堆起了大量各式各樣的儲糧；傍晚時分，她們到一塊朝南傾斜的岩石頂上，把肉切成薄片晾曬——正忙著時，女兒忽然喊道：「我好像看見一隻獨木舟划進來了」，她說得一點不錯。那孤單的女人有一個親戚，是個很老的人；這可憐人近來聽說了她被拋棄、被留在空屋裡的情形，如今便來看看她是否已餓死，還帶了一條蛙魚作禮物，以備她仍活著。當他看見剖鯨場血跡斑斑，簡直不敢相信自己的眼睛，只當全是幻覺——而當他望見兩個女人站在岩石上，切著大塊的肉晾曬，隨後又見她們跑下來迎接他時，他便對她們說：「我來了，本以為會發現你們餓死：我其實是來埋葬你們的。」「你這傻老頭！快從獨木舟上下來，嚐嚐我們這裡的好東西」——那可憐的老人上了岸，卻直到把獨木舟好好拖上灘才肯吃東西；女人們 meanwhile 已為他煮了一盤好菜，他這回吃了個飽，等他要動身時，她們又往他的獨木舟裡塞了那麼多補給，幾乎要把船壓沉。臨走時他說：「既然如此，就不怕你們餓死了；等你們的儲糧全都備好，我就來接你們走。」他走後，她們便去休息，第二天早晨她又準備施展法術——然而她念了又念，召了又召，女兒照常看著聽著，卻既聽不到呼吸聲，也聽不到潑水聲：原因是她們惱她竟把禮物轉送給了別人，從那時起，她便再也召不出任何東西。等她的法術完全失效，她也把存肉全都晾曬完畢，那可憐的老親戚便來接她回自己的家，此後她便與他同住，度過餘生。

title.en: Isigarsigak: The Amulet Split and the Oldest Old Age
title.zh: 伊西加利西亞克：分符與至壽

region.en: Akilinek across the ocean and the favourite bird-cliff
region.zh: 海外阿基利內克與心愛的鳥崖

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 82 'Isigarsigak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Rowing with the villagers to Akilinek — 'Much as we long to be off, we dare not risk it yet' — Isigarsigak hunts reindeer beyond the dark stripe, wins the singing-match by sending his clever wife forward, and parts from his brother over a shared health-amulet broken in two: a bit like coal from a fireplace. Dying at Akilinek-free Greenland older than anyone — 'he got quite as old as Nivnitak' — he is carried like a child, breath tested with a bit of down, and sings a feeble bird-cry at his favourite gull-cliff until the feather does not stir; through his brother, the teller says, we are related to the people of Akilinek.
summary.zh: 隨村人渡海往阿基利內克——『雖然心切，尚不敢輕舉妄動』——他在『黑帶』彼端獵鹿，歌唱比賽上派出的機敏妻子技壓全場；臨別時把合用的健康護身符（一塊爐中黑炭）掰為兩半。歸鄉後他壽冠格陵蘭——『與尼夫尼塔克同壽』——被孫輩如孩童般抬抱，以絨毛探息，在心愛的海鷗崖上哼出細如鳥鳴的歌，直到那根絨毛不再顫動。據說正是他弟弟的後代，使我們與阿基利內克的人民有了血緣。

sensitivity.note: Akilinek migration legend and extreme-longevity motif; ethnohistorical claim of kinship across the ocean.

passages.text: Isigarsigak and his younger brother once set out on a journey northwards, and did not stop till the frost obliged them to establish themselves for the winter before they had reached their goal; not till the middle of next summer did they arrive at their place of destination, where they found a number of people all friendly and well inclined, and therefore resolved to pass the next winter with them.
