Winter went by in the usual way; but when spring came round some of the people at times would say, 'At midsummer-time we shall no doubt again see the dark stripe' — this implied the intention of going a trip to Akilinek (the country beyond the ocean), but the strangers did not understand their meaning. One day a man came up to Isigarsigak saying, 'We all of us intend to go a voyage out seawards to Akilinek; with that view thou wouldst do well to gather skins for a double coating to thy boat.' He followed this advice; when all had got their boats new coverings he noticed that every morning the inhabitants mounted the top of a hill to take a survey of the ocean — sometimes he joined them, and then they used to say, 'Much as we long to be off, we dare not risk it yet.' But at length the rattling noise of the tent-poles woke him one morning, and when he saw the others had almost finished carrying their things down to the boats he hastened to pull down his tent; being also ready the boats started. They stood to sea at once; when the outer covers got wet and began to slacken their speed they cut their fastenings and cast them off — Isigarsigak dropped astern a little, and had almost given up hope of seeing land again, when suddenly he heard land-shouts ahead of him: as he listened again he could make out that they cried, 'The broad dark stripe,' and presently he saw it looming out — when he rose and stood upright he beheld a broad expanse of land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 82 'Isigarsigak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊西加西加克與他的弟弟曾有一次向北遠行，一直不曾停歇，直到嚴霜迫使他們在尚未抵達目的地之前先安頓下來過冬；直到次年仲夏，他們才抵達了目的地，在那裡發現一群人全都友善而心懷善意，於是決定與他們共度下一個冬天。冬天照常過去；但當春天來臨時，有些人偶爾會說：『到了仲夏時節，我們無疑又會見到那道暗色的條紋了。』——這暗示著他們打算前往阿基利內克（大洋彼岸之國）一遊，但這些外來者並不理解他們的意思。有一天，一個人走到伊西加西加克面前說：『我們全都要出海航行前往阿基利內克；為此，你最好採集些獸皮，好給你的船做雙層包皮。』他聽從了這個建議；當所有人都給船換上新包皮後，他注意到每天早晨居民們都會登上山頂眺望海洋——有時他也一同前去，那時他們便會說：『儘管我們多麼渴望出發，我們還是不敢冒這個險。』但終於有一天早晨，帳篷支柱的碰撞聲將他吵醒，當他看到其他人幾乎已把東西都搬到船上時，他趕緊拆下自己的帳篷；一切就緒後，船隻便出發了。他們立刻駛向大海；當外層包皮浸濕、開始拖慢他們的速度時，他們便割斷繫繩，將包皮拋棄——伊西加西加克稍稍落在後面，幾乎已放棄再見到陸地的希望，這時他突然聽見前方傳來陸地的呼喊聲：他再仔細聆聽，便能辨出他們喊的是『那寬闊的暗色條紋』，不久他便看見它隱約浮現——當他起身直立時，他望見一片廣闊的陸地。

passages.text: The travellers now broke out into exulting shouts that they had reached the opposite shore without a gale, and on coming close to the land found it abounding with reindeer; they moored their boats and at once went off shooting, but Isigarsigak and his brother slew the greatest number, deciding on staying at this place for a season. Some time after there was heard a cry of 'Boats' — Isigarsigak went out and saw a great number coming down from the north; these travellers also took up their quarters there, but Isigarsigak did not care to assist them and remained in his tent. Before long however there was a cry at the entrance, 'Isigarsigak and his brother are called upon to come out for a singing match' (nith-songs or satirical songs); although Isigarsigak had no idea of singing they made themselves smart and went outside — they saw an enormous crowd of people all going up hill, the men in front, the women following. As soon as they were seen there was another shout, 'Let the men from East step forward' — the brother of Isigarsigak first performed a dance and retired; Isigarsigak himself was now summoned, but as he did not know much about either singing or dancing he proposed to his wife to advance, who was so smart and clever that nobody could match her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 82 'Isigarsigak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 旅人們這時爆發出歡呼，因為他們未遇狂風便抵達了對岸，靠近陸地時發現那裡遍地是馴鹿；他們將船繫泊好，立刻前去打獵，但伊西加西加克與他的弟弟獵得最多，決定在此地停留一季。過了些時候，傳來一聲呼喊：『船來了』——伊西加西加克走出去，看見一大群船從北方順流而下；這些旅人也在此地安頓下來，但伊西加西加克無意幫助他們，便留在自己的帳篷裡。然而不久，入口處傳來一聲呼喊：『伊西加西加克與他的弟弟被召喚出來參加歌唱比賽』（即尼特歌或諷刺歌）；儘管伊西加西加克根本無意唱歌，他們還是打扮了一番，走到外面——他們看見一大群人全都往山上走去，男人在前，女人在後。他們一被看見，又傳來一聲呼喊：『讓東方來的人上前來』——伊西加西加克的弟弟先表演了一支舞便退下；現在輪到伊西加西加克本人被召喚，但他對唱歌和跳舞都不甚在行，便提議讓他的妻子上前，她如此俏麗聰慧，無人能與之匹敵。

passages.text: The brother of Isigarsigak being unmarried now took a wife in this place; as his brothers-in-law came to like him uncommonly well they would not allow him to leave them — the year being far advanced they all prepared to cross to their own land, giving their boats new covers. Though Isigarsigak had been greatly attached to his brother and did not like the idea of leaving him, he wished to die in his own country, and therefore made ready to follow his countrymen; at length they started — but a little way off land Isigarsigak said to his people, 'It occurs to me that I forgot to divide our healing remedy (viz., amulet for health and longevity). What a pity! We shall have to go back.' Accordingly they went back and unpacked the things again; opening an old box he produced something like a small bit of coal from a fireplace — this being an amulet given to him and his brother in common. He broke it into two pieces, and gave one of them to his brother; the boat was again loaded, and steering right out to sea he turned round to see the last of his brother, who stood watching them on the beach in his white reindeer jacket — they were never to meet again, so he did not take his eyes off him till he was quite lost to sight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 82 'Isigarsigak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊西加西加克的弟弟尚未婚娶，此時在此地娶了妻；由於他的妻舅們格外喜愛他，便不肯讓他離開他們——時令已晚，他們全都準備渡海回到自己的家鄉，給船換上新包皮。儘管伊西加西加克與弟弟感情深厚，不願與他分離，但他希望死在自己的故土，因此準備跟隨他的同胞們；終於他們出發了——但離岸不遠，伊西加西加克便對他的族人說：『我想起來了，我忘了把我們的療癒之物（即保健康長壽的護身符）分開。多可惜啊！我們得回去一趟。』於是他們折返，重新卸下東西；他打開一隻舊箱子，取出某樣像壁爐裡一小塊煤的東西——這是同時賜予他與他弟弟的護身符。他把它掰成兩半，將其中一半給了弟弟；船再次裝載妥當，他將船頭直直駛向大海，然後回頭最後望了一眼弟弟，弟弟穿著白色馴鹿皮外套，站在海灘上目送他們——他們此後再未相見，因此他一直目不轉睛地望著他，直到他完全消失於視線之外。

passages.text: The boats safely reached their own shore without encountering any storm; Isigarsigak now began seal-hunting with his children, but in time these grew old and died successively — then he went out in company with his grandchildren, as yet without losing strength himself; it was not till his grandchildren were getting aged that he began to feel a little less handy himself. He was much beloved by his grandchildren, and they often went with him to a craggy reddish cliff, a favourite spot of his, where a number of gulls had built their nests, and the grandchildren's children would call to him, saying, 'Here we are at thy favourite cliff; do sing to us' — he had a fine voice, and could also imitate the cries of birds, which delighted the urchins beyond everything. This generation also died, and their children became his companions; but his grandchildren's grandchildren had to carry him in a boat, and to treat him like a child — his strong frame had now grown thin and shrunk like that of a baby; he ate almost nothing, and to know whether he still breathed they used to hold a bit of down before his nose. In passing by the bird's-cliff they would say, 'Now we are at thy favourite spot; do sing a song' — and listening sharply they could hear a small feeble sound like the cry of a bird. At length he began to suck his coverlet; one day when they came to take him out as usual they observed that the feather before his mouth did not stir — he had breathed his last. Isigarsigak never had his like with regard to old age in this country (Greenland); he got quite as old as Nivnitak. His younger brother may even have outlived him, but he had never been heard of. It is through him that we are related to the people of Akilinek.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 82 'Isigarsigak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 船隻安然無恙地抵達了自己的海岸，未遇任何風暴；伊西加西加克此時開始與他的孩子們一同獵海豹，但隨著時間流逝，這些孩子相繼年老死去——於是他便與他的孫輩們一同外出，而他自己尚未失去力氣；直到他的孫輩們也漸趨年老，他才開始感到自己稍稍不那麼靈便了。他深受孫輩們的喜愛，他們常與他一同前往一處崎嶇的紅色崖壁，那是他鍾愛之地，那裡有許多海鷗築了巢，而孫輩們的孩子會呼喚他，說：『我們到你鍾愛的崖壁來了；給我們唱首歌吧』——他有一副好嗓子，還能模仿鳥兒的鳴叫，這讓那些小鬼頭們欣喜至極。這一代人也死去了，他們的孩子成了他的伴侶；但到他孫輩的孫輩時，他們不得不把他抬上船，像對待孩子一樣照料他——他那強壯的身軀如今已變得瘦削萎縮，如同嬰兒一般；他幾乎什麼都不吃，為了知道他是否還有呼吸，他們常把一小片絨羽放在他鼻前。經過鳥崖時，他們會說：『我們現在到你鍾愛的地方了；唱首歌吧』——他們仔細傾聽，能聽見一個微弱細小的聲音，如同鳥兒的鳴叫。終於，他開始吮吸自己的被褥；有一天，當他們照常來帶他出去時，他們注意到他嘴前的絨羽不再動了——他已嚥下最後一口氣。就高壽而言，伊西加西加克在這個國家（格陵蘭）從未有過能與之相比的人；他活得和尼夫尼塔克一樣長壽。他的弟弟甚至可能比他活得更久，但從未有人聽聞過他的消息。正是透過他，我們才與阿基利內克的人們有了親緣關係。

title.en: Atalianguak: The Wife in the Fox-Hole
title.zh: 阿塔利安瓜克：狐穴中的妻子

region.en: Bachelor house and the lakeside fox-hole
region.zh: 單身漢之屋與湖畔狐穴

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 83 'Atalianguak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A pretty little woman in white boots with a newly-dressed hair-tuft waits outside the bachelor's tent; married home, she is betrayed by 'What a very peculiar smell I perceived' — a fox-tail dangling at her back as she passes the doorway. He breathes upon the entrance of her fox-hole and enters: walls covered with flies, dirt-flies, beetles, and all kinds of reptiles sing him down — 'Atalianguak, sleep, sleep; at spring we will rouse thee again' — and waking of his own accord after ages, he makes water that turns to a whole river, and gives up all thought of womanhood.
summary.zh: 穿白靴、髮髻新梳的嬌小女子候在單身漢的帳外；娶歸家後，一句『好奇怪的氣味』洩了底——她跨出門檻時，身後垂著一條狐狸尾巴。他對狐穴入口呵氣而入：四壁爬滿蒼蠅、家蠅、甲蟲與各種蟲豸，齊聲唱他入睡——『阿塔利安瓜克，睡吧睡吧；春天我們再喚醒你』——不知過了多少歲月他自行醒來，一泡尿竟化作整條大河。從此他對女人心灰意冷。

sensitivity.note: Fox-wife and sleeping-enchantment motifs; parallels Rink tale 11 (fox-wife) and the Insects tale of Rasmussen.

passages.text: Atalianguak was an excellent seal-hunter, and lived as a bachelor in a large house together with several cousins; at spring-time he used to go out all by himself in his boat in order to fish angmagsat (capelins). One evening when he returned to his tent, having been out kayaking, he was much surprised at seeing a pretty little woman standing outside of it — she wore a pair of white boots, and her hair-tuft was newly dressed. Atalianguak ran quickly up beside her, and taking hold of her hand brought her into the tent, and afterwards married her; when the fishing season came to an end he repaired homewards in his boat, his wife rowing while he himself took the helm. In autumn he again settled down in the house of his cousins.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 83 'Atalianguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿塔利安瓜克是一位出色的獵海豹者，與幾個表親一同住在一座大房子裡，過著單身生活；春天時，他常獨自划著小船出海捕撈安格馬克薩特（即毛鱗魚）。有一天傍晚，他划著皮艇歸來，回到帳篷時，驚訝地看見帳篷外站著一個嬌小美麗的女子——她穿著一雙白色的靴子，髮髻是新梳理過的。阿塔利安瓜克快步跑到她身旁，牽起她的手將她帶進帳篷，後來娶了她；捕魚季節結束後，他划船返家，妻子划槳，他自己掌舵。到了秋天，他又在表親們的屋子裡安頓下來。

passages.text: One evening just as his wife had risen from her seat on the ledge to go outside one of the other people, whom she happened to pass by, remarked, 'What a very peculiar smell I perceived' — his housemates told him to take great care not to offend her, as they had observed that she was not a woman of the common kind. The same thing however happened again; this time the little woman hearing them speak of a strange smell rushed quickly out, and the moment she passed the doorway the people observed a fox-tail dangling at her back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 83 'Atalianguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一天傍晚，正當他的妻子從坐榻上起身要走到外面時，她恰好經過的一個人說道：『我聞到一股多麼奇怪的氣味啊』——他的同屋人叫他千萬小心，別冒犯了她，因為他們已察覺她並非尋常女子。然而同樣的事又發生了一次；這一次，那嬌小的女子聽見他們談論一股奇怪的氣味，便迅速衝了出去，就在她穿過門口的那一刻，人們看見她背後垂著一條狐狸尾巴。

passages.text: Atalianguak pursued her to the border of a lake; in a fox-hole close by he noticed a light, and peeping in saw his wife sitting on a ledge — 'I feel so cold, let me come in.' 'Well, come.' 'But in what way am I to enter?' 'Thou hast only to breathe upon the entrance and thou wilt easily get in.' Thus he entered, and sitting down beside his wife exclaimed, 'It is dreadfully cold — do make me warm.' At the same time he saw one of the walls covered with flies, dirt-flies, beetles, and all kinds of reptiles; she now raised up her head and ordered them to lull Atalianguak to sleep, and presently they all began singing, 'Atalianguak, sleep, sleep; at spring we will rouse thee again' — and he slept for ever so long. At last he awoke of his own accord, and when he rose and went outside the sun was high in the sky, while the cave itself swarmed with flies and reptiles; he went to make water, and forthwith it turned to a whole river — from that time he gave up all thought of womanhood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 83 'Atalianguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿塔利安瓜克一路追她到一座湖的邊界；在近旁一個狐狸洞裡，他瞧見一點光亮，往裡一望，看見妻子坐在一處岩架上——「我覺得好冷，讓我進去吧。」「好，進來吧。」「可是我要怎麼進去呢？」「你只要朝洞口吹一口氣，就能輕易進去了。」於是他就進去了，在妻子身旁坐下，喊道：「冷得要命——快讓我暖和起來。」同時他看見其中一面牆上爬滿了蒼蠅、糞蠅、甲蟲和各式各樣的爬蟲；這時她抬起頭來，命令牠們哄阿塔利安瓜克入睡，不一會兒牠們全都開始唱道：「阿塔利安瓜克，睡吧，睡吧；到了春天我們再把你喚醒」——他就這樣睡了不知多久。最後他自己醒了過來，起身走到外頭，太陽已高掛天空，而那洞穴本身則爬滿了蒼蠅和爬蟲；他去解手，那尿當即化作一整條河——從那時起，他便斷了對女人的一切念頭。

title.en: A Visit to the Giants: Inoosarsuk the Little Amulet
title.zh: 巨人之旅：小護身符伊努薩舒克

region.en: Wild firth of the giants and Akilinek
region.zh: 巨人的蠻荒峽灣與阿基利內克

period: Inuit oral tradition; English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 84 'A Visit to the Giants', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Beaten for a used kayak and driven to flight by a lost half-jacket, the orphan Inoosarsuk plants a quannek stalk on the drift-ice — 'Thus shalt thou remain standing erect' — and rows for Akilinek past the cannibals' black smoke to the white-smoked women who take fish by bladders at low tide. Taken up kayak and all by an enormously big kayaker as an amulet for his little daughter, he nearly becomes her midnight meal, is covered with the giant's cloak — 'Thou shalt grow as big as that, as big as that' — grows to the daughter's height, is fitted with a giant kayak, and rows home to find his foster-parents buried beneath their wasted house.
summary.zh: 因艇被私用而挨打、又因丟失半件防水衣而惶恐出逃的孤兒伊努薩舒克，在浮冰上插下一根當歸莖——『你就這樣直立不動吧』——直駛阿基利內克：先過黑煙裊裊的食人族，再到白煙裊裊、退潮時以浮囊捕魚的女子們那裡受到善待。一名巨大皮艇客把他連人帶艇一手提起，帶回去給小女兒做護身符；半夜他差點成了她無意中的點心。巨人为他披上大氅——『你會長得這麼大，這麼大』——他很快長到與其女等高，獲贈巨艇；劃回故里時，只見舊屋傾頹、養父母已葬於瓦礫之下。

sensitivity.note: Giant-country geography (black vs white smoke) parallels Rasmussen's Insects tale; growth charm recorded as told.

passages.text: The orphan boy Inoosarsuk was greatly loved by his foster-mother, but not by his foster-father. One day when the father was out on a seal-hunt the mother told Inoosarsuk she was tired of seal-flesh, and ordered him out in her husband's other kayak to catch some frog-fish; he remonstrated, saying that his father had forbidden him to take the kayak — but still she went on desiring him to go, at the same time assuring him she would clean and put it back all right in its place. Notwithstanding, the father coming home observed that it had been used, and beat Inoosarsuk till he could not move for pain. Another day his mother went on persuading him in the same way to take the kayak in order to go out and get her some quannek (the eatable stalk of Angelica), growing near the shore a little up the firth; but when he had ascended the hills in order to fetch her some and came back to the beach he found, to his great alarm, that the tide had carried away the half-jacket belonging to his foster-father's kayak. On approaching home he got so frightened at the thought of his foster-father that he passed it by and turned right out to sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 84 'A Visit to the Giants'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 孤兒伊努薩蘇克極受養母疼愛，養父卻不疼他。有一天，父親外出獵海豹，母親對伊努薩蘇克說她吃膩了海豹肉，命他划丈夫的另一艘獨木舟出去捕些蛙魚；他出言反對，說父親禁止他動用那艘獨木舟——可她仍舊要他前去，同時向他保證她會把它清洗乾淨、原樣放回原處。儘管如此，父親回家後仍發覺獨木舟被人用過，把伊努薩蘇克打得痛得動彈不得。又一天，母親照樣勸他划那艘獨木舟出去，替她採些 quannek（當歸可食的莖），那東西長在稍往峽灣上游一點的岸邊；可是當他爬上丘陵替她採了些回來、走到海灘時，卻驚恐地發現潮水已把養父獨木舟上的那件半截外套沖走了。快到家時，他一想到養父就嚇得厲害，於是過門不入，逕直轉向大海而去。

passages.text: Having rowed beyond the outermost islands he suddenly remembered his two amulets, a quannek and an old whetstone; jumping out on a flake of drift-ice he planted one of his newly-gathered stalks, calling out, 'Thus shalt thou remain standing erect' — an invocation to secure him calm weather. Like Giviok, he passed by the ocean-lice for Akilinek, and having first encountered the cannibals afterwards fell in with the women who captured fishes by putting bladders to them at low tide; from the cannibals' chimney a black smoke arose in the air, but from that of the latter a white smoke was seen. Among these he was very kindly treated, but still he at last grew tired of his sojourn; one day pretending to row a little in the neighbourhood he took himself far off and fled to the south. At length he arrived at a wild firth; thinking it too long to enter he resolved merely to cross the inlet to the opposite shore — when half-way across he saw what he fancied was a rock, but on coming closer found it to be an enormously big kayaker, who took hold of him and lifted him up quite easily, kayak and all, in one hand, and put him down before himself on his own vessel, intending to take him home as an amulet for his little daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 84 'A Visit to the Giants'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 划過最外圍的島嶼之後，他忽然想起自己的兩件護身符：一根 quannek 和一塊舊磨刀石；他跳上一塊漂流冰，插下他新採的一根莖，喊道：「你就這樣直立著吧」——這是一句祈求風平浪靜的咒語。他像吉維奧克一樣，避開海蝨，朝阿基利內克而去；他先遇上食人族，後來又碰上那些趁退潮把魚鰾放到魚身上捕魚的女人；食人族的煙囪冒出黑煙升上天空，而那些女人的煙囪則見白煙。他在這些女人中間受到極好的款待，但待久了終究厭倦；有一天他假裝在附近划一划，便遠遠離去，逃往南方。最後他來到一處荒僻的峽灣；他覺得進去太遠，便決定只橫渡這道水灣到對岸——划到一半時，他看見一個以為是岩石的東西，靠近一看，才發現是個身形巨大的划獨木舟者，那人一把抓住他，輕而易舉地連人帶舟用一隻手把他舉起，放到自己船上、自己身前，打算把他帶回家給小女兒當護身符。

passages.text: When they approached the homestead of the giant something like a big iceberg was standing in front of the house; on closer inspection it proved to be an enormous gull, which the giant's daughter was in the act of catching. Inoosarsuk was now brought up to the house and put upon a shelf near the window; during the night he took a fancy to some very nice-looking eatables lying behind the lamp — he managed to slide down on the side ledge, but finding it quite filled up by the giant's sleeping daughter without any room left where to put down his foot he had no choice left but to step along her one leg; unfortunately he lost his footing and fell down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 84 'A Visit to the Giants'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當他們接近那巨人的住處時，屋前立著一個像大冰山似的東西；走近細看，原來是一隻巨大的海鷗，巨人的女兒正動手去捉牠。伊努薩蘇克這時被帶到屋裡，放在窗邊的一塊擱板上；夜裡他看中了燈後一些看來很好吃的食物——他設法沿著側邊的岩架滑下去，卻發現那兒被巨人熟睡的女兒佔得滿滿的，連落腳的地方都沒有，他別無選擇，只好踩著她的一條腿過去；不幸的是他腳下一滑，摔了下去。

passages.text: The giant's daughter on being awakened in this way and unconsciously grasping him had nearly eaten him up, but luckily remembered that he was her little amulet. The giant seeing Inoosarsuk's dismay and utter dejection at length put him down on the floor and covered him up with his large cloak, saying, 'Thou shalt grow as big as that, as big as that' — he forthwith commenced to grow, and was soon as tall as the daughter, after which the giant furnished him with a kayak of suitable size. He now remembered his foster-parents; longing to take revenge for the many blows he had formerly got he crossed the ocean, and soon found the place where they had formerly lived — but the house was laid waste, and the old people buried beneath its ruins. He then returned to pass the rest of his days at Akilinek.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 84 'A Visit to the Giants'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巨人的女兒這樣被驚醒，下意識地一把抓住他，差點把他吃掉，幸好想起他是自己的小護身符。巨人見伊努薩蘇克驚惶失措、萬分沮喪，最後把他放到地上，用自己寬大的斗篷蓋住他，說道：「你要長得那麼大，那麼大」——他當即開始長大，很快就長得和那女兒一般高，之後巨人給他配了一艘大小合適的獨木舟。這時他想起自己的養父母；他渴望報復從前挨的許多頓打，便渡過大洋，很快找到了他們從前住的地方——可是那屋子已荒廢，兩位老人葬身於廢墟之下。他於是返回阿基利內克，度過餘生。

title.en: Kagsuk: The Manslayer and the Two Old Men's Bows
title.zh: 卡克舒克：殺人者與二老的短弓

region.en: Karsit islands outside Amerdlok (Holsteinsborg) and Satok
region.zh: 霍爾斯泰因斯堡外卡爾西特群島與薩托克

period: Inuit oral tradition; localised in the districts of Holsteinsborg and Sukkertoppen, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 85 'Kagsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Wounded by his brothers-in-law, Kagsuk's son heals every knife-stroke with a rub of the hand and knocks them all down — and the vengeance of the invincible man-slayer destroys the people of Satok, a boy and a girl spared. Hospitality mixed with menace for two snow-lost kayakers ('Take care that none of your people come hither to visit us, lest we should take their lives'), the greedy visitors never returning — until the sons of two spell-cunning old men come at last: the toogdlik perched on the roof cries warning, but the old men steal on unseen from behind, and an arm's-length bow shoots him dead on the spot.
summary.zh: 內兄弟的刀傷被他一抹即癒，反被逐一擊倒；『堅不可摧的殺人者』卡克舒克當夜屠盡薩托克全族，僅留一對孤兒。他對迷路的獵人殷勤款待又嚴詞警告——『別讓你們的人再來，否則性命難保』——貪圖存糧的訪客有去無回。最後，兩位精於咒術的老人為亡子製成一臂長的小弓：屋頂報訊的巨潛鳥一叫，他答道『我看見你們了』——卻不知隱身咒下的老人已自背後偷襲，一箭將他射斃當場。

sensitivity.note: Massacre of Satok and the greedy visitors recorded as told in the 1875 source. Rink's note links the tale to Kagsagsuk (tale 1) continuations with the walrus-tooth rattle entrance.

passages.text: It is said that Kagsuk once had his wintering-place on the Karsit islands outside of Amerdlok (Holsteinsborg), and that his son married the only sister of some men living at Satok, near Maneetsok (Sukkertoppen). Kagsuk, as well as his son, were powerful and strong men; the former was also a man-slayer, invincible to his enemies. Once, when the son had been out during the day with his brothers-in-law, at evening, when it was growing dark, he had some talk with his wife that ended in a quarrel; her brothers, fearing his strength, at first kept silence — but soon after, when he gave her a kick, they all went up to him and seized him in order to protect their sister. He tried to appease their wrath but in vain, and at last they struck him with a knife — every time he was wounded he only rubbed the place with his hand, and directly it healed, after which he knocked them all down, one after another. From this time however he did not trust his brothers-in-law; once at dark night he escaped from the house, leaving his kayak behind, and taking his way across the fast ice to the north, where he stayed a while with some other people, and at length came to the house of his father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 85 'Kagsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說卡格蘇克曾在阿梅德洛克（霍爾斯泰因斯堡）外海的卡爾西特群島設過冬居所，他的兒子娶了住在馬尼特索克（蘇克托彭）附近薩托克的一些人的獨生姊妹。卡格蘇克和他兒子都是強壯有力的人；前者還是個殺人者，對敵人戰無不勝。有一次，兒子白天隨妻舅們外出，到了傍晚天色漸暗時，他和妻子說了些話，結果吵了起來；她的兄弟們畏懼他的力氣，起初默不作聲——可是不久之後，他踢了她一腳，他們便一齊上前抓住他，以保護自己的姊妹。他試圖平息他們的怒氣，卻徒勞無功，最後他們用刀砍他——每當他被砍傷，他只是用手揉一揉傷處，傷口立刻癒合，隨後他把他們一個接一個全都打倒在地。然而從此以後他不再信任妻舅們；有一次趁黑夜，他從屋裡逃出，把獨木舟留在原處，取道堅冰向北而去，在那裡和另一些人住了一陣，最後來到他父親的家。

passages.text: When Kagsuk came to know how his son had been treated he got into a great rage; in vain the son tried to persuade him to delay his revenge — 'If they have struck thee with a knife, we will set out and destroy the people of Satok this very night.' And off they went the same day for Satok and slew the whole of them, only sparing a boy and a girl. On returning to Karsit Kagsuk became a still more desperate murderer; the people of Amerdlok, on becoming aware of this, did not venture themselves far away from the shore. Kagsuk and his son being both very suspicious agreed on the following mode of life: if the weather was fine the son went out kayaking alone, and when the father went out the son remained at home, unless it happened to blow very hard, in which case, and then only, they went out together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 85 'Kagsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當卡格蘇克得知兒子所受的對待後，勃然大怒；兒子試圖勸他暫緩報仇，卻是徒勞——「若他們曾以刀擊你，我們今晚就出發，滅盡薩托克的人。」當日他們便動身前往薩托克，殺盡了所有人，只饒過一個男孩和一個女孩。回到卡爾西特後，卡格蘇克成了更加凶殘的殺人者；阿梅德洛克的人察覺此事後，不敢遠離海岸。卡格蘇克與兒子都極為多疑，於是約定如下生活方式：若天氣晴好，兒子便獨自划皮艇外出；父親外出時，兒子則留在家中；除非風颳得極猛，唯有在那種情況下，兩人才一同外出。

passages.text: One winter, when the days were beginning to lengthen, two kayakers from Amerdlok, while out seal-hunting, were overtaken by a snowstorm and could not make out their own land; bewildered, they came to Kagsuk's house — at seeing which they got very frightened, lest he would kill them. As soon as they saw him come out of his house and before he could utter a word they said, 'Chance brought us hither, and no intention of visiting you. We lost our way on account of the snow, and could not advance against the storm.' Kagsuk asked them to come on shore, adding that as soon as the weather abated they might set off for home — on hearing this they were reassured and entered the house, which was very hot. Kagsuk talked a great deal the whole day; but in the evening, when it was still blowing a gale and snowing as fast as ever, he suddenly became silent — at length he inquired, 'Which kayak is he using to-day?' The housemates answered, 'The narrow one.' 'I was rather uneasy about him; but if he has taken that kayak I have no fear.' Later in the evening there was a cry that he had arrived tugging a walrus; when the people whose business it was to haul it up on shore had gone out Kagsuk said, 'They don't intend to stop, but having lost their way chanced to come in here much against their will' — the guests looking round then first discovered that he was speaking to his son, who appeared in the entrance and already had bent his bow and was aiming at them, but now drew back, and directly after entered, asking if the guests had been offered something to eat. On hearing that they had as yet had nothing he ordered different dishes to be set before them, saying he would share the repast with them; they afterwards went to rest and slept quietly until Kagsuk roused them up, saying that now the weather was fine they might as well start for their home. At their departure he ordered their kayaks to be filled with provisions, but at the same time added, 'Take care that none of your people come hither to visit us, lest we should take their lives' — they then pushed off and arrived safely at their home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 85 'Kagsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一年冬天，白晝開始漸長，兩個來自阿梅德洛克的皮艇手在外捕海豹時遭遇暴風雪，辨不清自家的陸地；他們迷了路，來到卡格蘇克的屋前——見此情景，他們大為驚恐，生怕他會殺了他們。他們一看見他走出屋門，不等他開口便說道：「我們是偶然來到此地，絕無拜訪您之意。我們因大雪迷了路，無法頂著風暴前行。」卡格蘇克請他們上岸，並說天氣一緩，他們便可啟程回家——聽聞此言，他們安下心來，走進屋內，屋裡十分炎熱。卡格蘇克整日說了許多話；但到了傍晚，風仍颳得猛烈，雪也下得和先前一樣急，他卻突然沉默下來——最後他問道：「他今天用的是哪隻皮艇？」同屋的人答道：「那隻窄的。」「我本來有些擔心他；但若他取了那隻皮艇，我便不懼了。」夜裡稍晚，有人喊道他回來了，正拖著一頭海象；當那些負責把海象拖上岸的人出去後，卡格蘇克說道：「他們無意停留，只是迷了路，極不情願地偶然來到這裡。」——客人們這時環顧四周，才初次發覺他是在對兒子說話；那兒子已出現在門口，早已彎弓搭箭瞄準他們，此刻卻退了回去，隨即走進屋來，問客人是否已給了些吃的。聽說他們至今什麼也沒吃，他便吩咐擺上不同的菜餚，說要與他們一同用餐；之後他們去歇息，安睡無擾，直到卡格蘇克把他們叫醒，說現在天氣好了，他們不妨啟程回家。臨行時，他吩咐把他們的皮艇裝滿食物，但同時又補了一句：「當心別讓你們的人來此拜訪我們，免得我們取了他們的性命。」——他們於是推艇離岸，平安抵家。

passages.text: But when the people of Amerdlok saw the stores they had brought with them they were all keen to visit Kagsuk; notwithstanding their being repeatedly warned by those two chance visitors of what Kagsuk had threatened, several among them would not desist from trying their chance — they went accordingly but never returned. Among the kayakers lost in this way were the sons of two old men who were very clever in magic spells; they prepared bows of an arm's length, and having finished these said to their place-fellows, 'Now we will set out to punish Kagsuk: while ye approach his house from the sea-side, we will come on from behind.' Kagsuk had for his amulet a toogdlik (the Great Northern Diver) perched on the roof of his house, giving him notice of every impending danger; one day on hearing its cry he went out, and observing the kayakers approaching said, 'All right; I see you.' But at the same moment the two old men, having escaped observation by means of magic spells, came stealing on from behind and shot him dead on the spot — the kayakers coming on shore killed all his housemates, with the exception of his son, who happened not to be at home, and afterwards fled to the north.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 85 'Kagsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但阿梅德洛克的人看到他們帶回的儲糧後，個個都急於去拜訪卡格蘇克；儘管那兩個偶然來訪者一再警告他們卡格蘇克的威脅，其中仍有數人不肯罷休，想要一試運氣——他們果然去了，卻再也沒有回來。如此喪命的皮艇手中，有兩個老人的兒子，那兩位老人極擅魔法咒語；他們製作了長一臂的弓，做成之後對同伴們說：「現在我們要出發去懲治卡格蘇克：你們從海邊接近他的屋子，我們則從背後而來。」卡格蘇克的護身符是一隻棲在他屋頂上的圖格德利克（大北方潛鳥），每逢危險將至便向他示警；一天他聽到牠的叫聲便走了出去，望見皮艇手們正靠近，說道：「好吧；我看見你們了。」但就在同時，那兩位老人藉魔法咒語避開了注意，從背後悄悄逼近，當場將他射死——皮艇手們上岸殺光了他所有的同屋人，只有他的兒子因恰巧不在家而倖免，之後他們逃往北方。

title.en: The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik
title.zh: 阿卡馬利克的夢與皈依

region.en: South Greenland and the bright country above the abyss
region.zh: 南格陵蘭與深淵之上的光明之國

period: Inuit oral tradition; event mentioned by Crantz as of the year 1743, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Grief for a dead cousin and the lack of a namesake drive Akamalik to kick and awl-pierce his wife — until a new-born babe named for the friend lets him sleep five nights, and then the dream comes: led by a woman over a plain like the ocean's surface, past ball-playing dead men, up three impossible steps, across a fiery abyss to the place so dazzling he had never seen — where the Saviour preaches and leads the song, reproaches his sins, points out tornarsuk in the depths, and bids him seek instruction at Nook. Re-entering his maggot-covered body, he wakes, repents, and is baptised by the Moravian missionaries — a Christian by name, a good man and a loving husband.
summary.zh: 喪友之痛與無名可承，使阿卡馬利克遷怒於妻——踢打錐刺；直到一名嬰兒承了亡友之名，他連睡五夜安枕，夢便來了：一位女子引他越過如海面般的原野，經過擲海象頭球戲的亡者群，躍上三級不可攀的石階，跨過深淵烈火，抵達他從未見過的光明之鄉——救主親自講道領唱，責其罪愆，指出深淵中的托那舒克，並囑他明夏往努克求教。他重入爬滿蛆蟲的軀殼醒來，懺悔前非，受洗於摩拉維亞傳教士——名為基督徒，實為善人與慈夫。

sensitivity.note: Christian-vision syncretism documented as an Inuit-voiced tradition of 1743 (per Crantz); missionary framing retained from the source. Domestic violence recorded as told.

passages.text: In the days when missionaries had come to Nook (Godthaab with New-Herrnhut), but people in other places were still heathens, there lived in the south a clever and skilful seal-hunter named Akamalik, who had a cousin of whom he was very fond. However, it chanced that this friend of his fell ill and died, which caused him much grief and sorely depressed his spirits; as chance would have it, the women of the place at that time brought forth no sons, and his own wife being childless, he could get no namesake for his deceased friend. He henceforth fell into the habit of ill-treating his wife, kicking her and piercing her skin with an awl. After some time it was rumoured that a woman of a neighbouring place had borne a child and named it after his friend; on hearing this Akamalik at once hastened thither, and was so glad at seeing the babe that he was quite unable to sleep for five succeeding nights. Having returned home sleep at length was again restored to him, and then he dreamt as follows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在傳教士已來到努克（即新赫恩胡特的戈特霍布），而其他地方的人仍是異教徒的時代，南方住著一個聰明而嫻熟的捕海豹者，名叫阿卡馬利克，他有一個非常疼愛的堂表兄弟。然而，這位朋友不幸患病身亡，令他悲痛萬分，精神極為消沉；恰巧當時此地婦女皆未生男，他自己的妻子又無子嗣，他無法為亡友找到同名者。此後他養成了虐待妻子的習慣，踢她，用錐子刺她的皮膚。過了些時，有傳聞說鄰地一名婦女生了孩子，並以他朋友之名命名；阿卡馬利克聞訊立刻趕往那裡，見到嬰兒時欣喜若狂，接連五夜完全無法入睡。回家之後，睡眠終於再度降臨於他，隨後他做了如下之夢。

passages.text: Some one peeped in at the window, and calling out for him said that he was to come and get his piece of blubber from a young whale which was just being caught; he at once went out and followed the voice, the owner of which he now perceived was a woman. In running after her he came across a vast plain stretching forth like the surface of the ocean and gradually rising; it became brighter and always brighter — he passed over heaps of sand rolling dreadfully like a mountain-river, and saw a crowd of people playing at ball with a walrus-head. Akamalik would fain have stopped and joined the players, but the woman hurried him on, and almost against his will he constantly followed her; he wondered greatly, for in those people on close view he plainly recognised men who had died a number of years ago. He then came to three high steps which it appeared impossible to ascend; but merely looking at his guide he gave a leap and almost unwillingly mounted them. From the top he again saw before him a great plain and a crowd of people in beautiful clothing — among them he recognised a man in the murder of whom he himself had taken an active part many years ago, and could not but be astonished at hearing people talk in answer to what he was thinking of but had not yet spoken out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有人從窗外窺視，呼喚他，說他該去領取他那份鯨脂，那是一頭剛被捕獲的小鯨；他立刻出門，循聲而去，此時才發覺那聲音的主人是一名女子。他追趕她時，來到一片廣闊的平原，那平原如海面般延展開去，並漸漸升高；天色越來越亮，始終越來越亮——他越過一堆堆如山河般可怕翻滾的沙丘，看見一群人正用海象頭玩球。阿卡馬利克很想停下來加入玩球的人，但那女子催他前行，他幾乎身不由己地不斷跟隨她；他大為驚異，因為細看那些人，他清楚地認出了一些多年前死去的人。接著他來到三級高臺階前，看來無法攀登；但他只是望了望他的嚮導，便縱身一躍，幾乎不情願地登了上去。從高處他又看見眼前一片大平原和一群衣著華美的人——其中他認出一個多年前他自己曾積極參與殺害的人，並且不禁驚異地發現，人們竟能回答他心中所想卻尚未說出的話。

passages.text: Voices were then heard calling the crowd to divine service; the people all sallied forth, and he followed their steps, passing over a dreadful abyss with fires burning down in the depths — then they ascended still higher to a place so dazzlingly bright and beautiful as he never had seen before. Here the Saviour Himself was preaching and leading the song of innumerable people; the Saviour spoke to Akamalik, reproaching him with his sins, at the same time pointing out to him the abyss, where He told him that tornarsuk resided in the depths, and advised him, saying, 'Next summer thou must repair thee to Nook for the purpose of getting instructed.' The Saviour guided him on his way back across the abyss, and thus going downwards on approaching the earth again he (viz., his soul) beheld his own poor body walking backwards and forwards all void of intellect, people believing him to be mad — it appeared very uncouth in his sight, all covered with maggots; but though he greatly abhorred it he nevertheless entered into it, having no other abode.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後有聲音呼喚眾人去做禮拜；人們全都湧了出去，他跟隨他們的腳步，越過一道可怕的深淵，淵底燃燒著火焰——然後他們升得更高，來到一個明亮耀眼、美麗得他從未見過的地方。在這裡，救主親自講道，並領著無數的人歌唱；救主對阿卡馬利克說話，責備他的罪，同時指給他看那深淵，告訴他托爾納爾蘇克住在深處，並勸告他說：「明年夏天你必須前往努克，為的是接受教導。」救主引他踏上歸途，越過深淵，於是向下行，接近大地時，他（即他的靈魂）看見自己那可憐的軀體來回走動，全無理智，人們都以為他瘋了——那軀體在他眼中十分怪異，佈滿了蛆蟲；儘管他極為厭惡它，卻仍舊進入了其中，因為他別無居所。

passages.text: Having thus put on the garb of his body he became like dead and lay in a swoon; by-and-by he recovered his reason and was awake. He then repented his profligate life, went to Nook in the spring, and was baptised by the Moravian missionaries — he not only became a Christian by name, but also a good man and a loving husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 86 'The Dream and Conversion of Akamalik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他這樣披上自己肉身的衣袍之後，便如同死去一般，昏厥地躺著；過了一會兒，他恢復了神智，醒了過來。他隨後悔恨自己放蕩的生活，於春天前往努克，由摩拉維亞傳教士為他施洗——他不僅在名義上成了基督徒，也成了好人與慈愛的丈夫。

title.en: Sangiak: The Worm-Born Twin-Harpooner
title.zh: 蟲生神射手桑吉亞克

region.en: Open-sea hunting grounds
region.zh: 外海獵場

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 87 'Sangiak, or Nerngajorak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A worm fetched from a child's cry at sea and thrown on a barren wife begets Sangiak, who as a small boy strikes two seals with one throw and learns to take the whole flock at a cast. Envious of the double-armed kayaker beloved by all — two harpoons, one in each hand — he picks a quarrel alone at sea and kills him, announces the murder himself, and flees in a kayak his enemies hole at the bottom, stopping the leaks with the stones he fills it with, and returning safe and sound.
summary.zh: 循海上孩啼覓得的蠕蟲擲於不孕之妻身上，遂生桑吉亞克；孩童時代他便一擲雙豹，更練得『一叉收全群』的神技。嫉妒那位雙手各持一叉、受人愛戴的雙叉獵手，他獨自出海尋釁殺之，並親自向其親屬報信；敵人在他的艇底鑿洞追殺，他卻以滿艇石塊堵洞，安然返鄉。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note. Murder recorded as told.

passages.text: A man whose wife could beget no children was advised by an old wise man to set off in his kayak and go out to the open sea, and when he heard a voice like that of a child crying proceed in that direction, and would then find a worm, which he was to take home and throw upon the body of his wife. Having done it the worm disappeared in the body of his wife, who soon gave birth to a son whom they called Sangiak. While he was yet a small child he asked his father for a kayak, and when following his father out to sea surprised him by hitting two seals though he only threw his harpoon once — he acquired the art of always taking the whole flock of seals by only throwing at one of them; at last his father hardly knew how to bring home all the seals he captured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 87 'Sangiak, or Nerngajorak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個男人的妻子無法生育，一位年老的智者勸他划著獨木舟出海，前往遼闊的外海；當他聽見像是孩童啼哭的聲音時，便朝那個方向前進，就會找到一條蟲，他要把它帶回家，扔在妻子的身上。他照做之後，那條蟲便消失在妻子的身體裡，她不久便生下一個兒子，他們給他取名為桑吉阿克。他還是個小孩子的時候，就向父親要一艘獨木舟；當他跟隨父親出海時，他只擲了一次魚叉，卻擊中兩隻海豹，令父親大為驚訝——他學會了只朝其中一隻擲叉，就總能獵得整群海豹的本領；到最後，他父親幾乎不知道該如何把他捕獲的所有海豹都帶回家。

passages.text: Once Sangiak happened to get acquainted with another seal-hunter who could also take two seals at a time, but only by means of two harpoons which he threw one with each hand at once; this double-armed kayaker being much beloved by his companions Sangiak grew envious of him — once when he went out alone with him to sea he picked a quarrel with him and killed him. He then told his father what had happened, and that he would give the relatives of the double-armed notice of the murder; the relatives would fain have avenged it, but he took flight in his kayak, which though his enemies had cut holes in its bottom did not sink — having filled his kayak with stones he stopped the holes with them, and returned to his father safe and sound.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 87 'Sangiak, or Nerngajorak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一次，桑吉阿克偶然結識了另一位捕海豹的獵人，那人也能一次獵得兩隻海豹，但只能靠兩支魚叉，同時一手各擲一支；這位雙臂划舟的獵人深受同伴喜愛，桑吉阿克因而嫉妒他——有一次，他與那人單獨出海時，便尋釁與他爭吵，將他殺死。他隨後把發生的事告訴了父親，並說他要向那雙臂獵人的親屬通報這樁兇殺；那些親屬本想報仇，但他划著獨木舟逃走了，儘管敵人在船底鑿了洞，船卻沒有沉——他把石頭裝滿獨木舟，用石頭堵住了那些洞，安然無恙地回到父親身邊。

title.en: Atlunguak: Bear, Amarok, and Kilivfak
title.zh: 阿特隆瓜克：熊、狼靈與六足獸

region.en: Behind the mother's lamp
region.zh: 母親油燈之後

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 88 'Atlunguak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Despised behind his mother's lamp, fed on what others brought home, Atlunguak bestirs himself only when a deed of special daring which no one else cared to undertake is on hand: he first kills an ice-covered bear, then an amarok, and finally a kilivfak — all fabulous animals.
summary.zh: 被譏為終日蹲在母親油燈後的白食者，阿特隆瓜克唯有在無人敢為的壯舉面前才挺身而出：先殺冰封之熊，再斃狼靈阿馬洛克，終誅六足奇獸奇利夫法克。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note ('only the principal parts selected').

passages.text: Atlunguak was a miserable hunter, despised and mocked by his housemates, who only saw in him a poor wretch always sitting behind his mother's lamp, and feeding upon what the others brought home. But when some deed of special daring which no one else cared to undertake was on hand he at length bestirred himself and braved the danger alone — thus he first killed an ice-covered bear, then an amarok, and finally a kilivfak (all fabulous animals).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 88 'Atlunguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿特倫瓜克是個可憐的獵人，被同住的人輕視和嘲笑，他們只把他看作一個可憐蟲，總是坐在母親的燈後面，吃著別人帶回家的東西。但當有某件特別大膽、無人願意承擔的事需要去做時，他終於振作起來，獨自面對危險——就這樣，他先殺死了一頭覆冰的熊，接著殺死了一隻阿瑪洛克，最後殺死了一隻基利夫法克（皆為傳說中的動物）。

title.en: Nakasungnak: Inside the Ice-Bear, Outside the Gnat-Clouds
title.zh: 納卡孫納克：熊腹之中，蚊雲之下

region.en: The far north among boat-people
region.zh: 遠北用船人的居地

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 89 'Nakasungnak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Presumptuous among boat-people who have no kayaks, Nakasungnak ignores every warning: he leaps knife-in-hand down the ice-bear's open mouth and comes out between its ribs hairless and shivering; he scorns the advice for catching the birds that can speak and the little fishes with both eyes on one side, and gets none; he stays outside when the gnat-clouds the size of sea-fowls with arrow-point stings roll in like broken clouds from the south — and only a skeleton is found beneath the boat.
summary.zh: 在只有船沒有皮艇的北方人之中狂妄自負的納卡孫納克，無視一切告誡：持刀躍入冰熊張開的大口，從肋間破壁而出，毛髮盡脫、寒戰不止；不聽捕會說話的鳥與雙眼同側小魚的指點，一無所獲；蚊雲如碎雲自南方壓境——群鳥大小、蝟刺如鏃——他獨自留在外面，眾人尋見的只是艇底下一副骸骨。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note; death by gnats recorded as told.

passages.text: Nakasungnak travelled far up north, and settled down with some people who used boats, but no kayaks; he was very presumptuous and obstinate. His new place-fellows told him that before long the ice-covered bear would make its appearance, that it was very dangerous, and for mere men a deed impracticable to slay it — but Nakasungnak, nothing heeding, set out to encounter the terrible animal; on discovering it he ran in upon it only armed with a knife, and instantly disappeared down its open mouth. The bear was then seen to totter, and soon after fell down dead; on approaching it they observed a knife sticking out between its ribs — when the hole was widened Nakasungnak jumped out of it, but his hair as well as the skin of his face had come off, and shivering with cold and ague he ran away to the house. In the meantime the bear's flesh served them for food the greater part of the winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 89 'Nakasungnak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 納卡松納克遠赴北方，與一些使用船隻、但不使用獨木舟的人定居下來；他非常傲慢固執。他的新同伴告訴他，不久覆冰的熊就會出現，那熊非常危險，單憑人力是無法殺死牠的——但納卡松納克毫不理會，動身去迎戰那可怕的動物；他一發現牠，只帶著一把刀就衝上前去，隨即消失在那熊張開的嘴裡。隨後有人看見那熊搖晃起來，不久便倒地而死；他們走近一看，發現一把刀插在牠的肋骨之間——把那個洞擴大之後，納卡松納克從裡面跳了出來，但他的頭髮以及臉上的皮膚都脫落了，他冷得發抖、打著瘧疾，跑回了屋裡。與此同時，那熊的肉成了他們整個冬天大半時間的食物。

passages.text: Afterwards they told Nakasungnak how to behave when they were going to catch the birds that could speak, and the little fishes with both eyes on one side; the swarms of birds and fishes appeared — but Nakasungnak would not follow the advice they gave him, and consequently got none. Lastly they told him that gnats were soon expected, the size of sea-fowls, and with stings like the point of an arrow; when the swarms were approaching and seen to come on like broken clouds from the south the people had to retreat to their tents and close them with all care — Nakasungnak however again disregarded their warnings and took no notice of what they had said. When the clouds appeared and all the others sped into their tents he remained outside; when all was over and they went out to look for Nakasungnak they found only a skeleton lying beneath the boat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 89 'Nakasungnak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 後來，他們告訴納卡松納克，當他們要去捕捉那些會說話的鳥，以及兩隻眼睛長在同一邊的小魚時，該怎麼做；成群的鳥和魚出現了——但納卡松納克不肯聽從他們給的忠告，因此一無所獲。最後他們告訴他，不久就會有蚊子出現，有海鳥那麼大，螫刺像箭尖一樣；當那群蚊子逼近，被人看見像破碎的雲朵般從南方湧來時，人們必須退進帳篷，並小心翼翼地把它封好——然而納卡松納克又一次不理會他們的警告，對他們所說的話毫不在意。當那些雲朵出現，其他所有人都奔進帳篷時，他仍留在外面；一切結束之後，他們出去尋找納卡松納克，卻只發現一具骷髏躺在船底下。

title.en: The Anghiak: The Dog-Skull Kayak
title.zh: 死胎鬼：犬首為艇

region.en: The brothers' kayaking waters and the rubbish-heap refuge
region.zh: 兄弟們的獵海與垃圾堆中的藏身處

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 90 'The Anghiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Reproached into a secret miscarriage, the only sister's child gains intellect and becomes an anghiak: a dog's skull for a kayak, a man's arm-bone for a paddle — nightly at the mother's breasts, daily capsizing her kayaking brothers one after another. Its revenge done, it repents, flees north, frightens a conjuring-house to death, and hides in a rubbish-heap; when the angakok's examination draws out the mother's confession — 'What I brought forth was no real child' — the anghiak feels a pain in its head and dies as she tells her tale.
summary.zh: 在兄弟的斥責下偷偷流產的獨妹，其胎兒竟得神智化為安吉亞克：以犬首為艇、人臂骨為槳——夜夜伏在母親胸前吮乳，日日逐一掀翻獵海中的舅舅們。復仇既畢，它心生悔意，北遁嚇死一座降神屋的人，藏身垃圾堆中；巫師勘問之下，母親終於吐實——『我生的不是真正的孩子』——話音未落，安吉亞克頭痛欲裂，隨她的講述氣絕而亡。

sensitivity.note: Concealed-birth ghost (anghiak) and infanticide recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: A company of brothers had a single sister and would not allow her to marry; nevertheless, having many suitors, she finally came to be with child, and because of her brothers' reproaches secretly had a miscarriage — but the child got intellect and became an anghiak. It picked up the skull of a dog using it as a kayak, and the bone of a man's arm for a paddle; every night it used to creep into the house and lie down to suckle its mother's breasts, but during the day-time it was about pursuing her brothers when they were kayaking, and made them capsize and perish one after another. Having accomplished its revenge it repented its deeds and fled to the north, where it slipped down in the doorway of a house in which a conjuration was going on — the angakok (by means of his second-sight) at once observed its approach, and when the people of the house had got a light and went to look for it they were all frightened to death. It then became still more powerful, but went back again to its mother's abode and found a refuge in a heap of rubbish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 90 'The Anghiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一群兄弟，他們只有一個姊妹，卻不許她出嫁；然而她雖有許多求婚者，最終還是懷了孕，又因兄弟們的責罵而暗中流了產——但那孩子卻得了靈性，成了安吉阿克（anghiak）。它拾起一隻狗的頭骨當作獨木舟，又拿人的臂骨作槳；每到夜裡，它便潛入屋中，躺下吮吸母親的乳房，而白天則趁兄弟們划獨木舟時追逐他們，使他們翻船，一個接一個地喪命。報完了仇，它卻悔恨自己的所作所為，逃往北方，在一戶正在行法術的人家的門口滑倒跌落——那安加科克（angakok，即巫師）憑藉其第二視覺立刻察覺到它的到來，待屋裡的人取了燈來尋它時，他們全都嚇死了。此後它變得更加強大，卻又回到母親的住所，在一堆垃圾中找到了藏身之處。

passages.text: It now happened that the angakok of the place was about to perform a conjuration for the purpose of finding out what had caused the brothers' destruction; the sister, on being examined, first denied but finally confessed her sin, saying, 'What I brought forth was no real child' — no sooner had she pronounced these words than the anghiak felt a pain in its head, and while she continued her tale it lost its senses and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 90 'The Anghiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這時，當地的安加科克正要行一場法術，以查明是什麼導致了那些兄弟的毀滅；那姊妹受審問時，起初否認，最終還是承認了自己的罪，說道：「我生下的並不是真正的孩子」——她話音剛落，那安吉阿克便感到頭痛，而她繼續講述時，它便失了知覺，死了。

title.en: Kanak's Flight to the Moon
title.zh: 卡納克飛月記

region.en: The moon-man's house above the earth
region.zh: 地上空明月神之屋

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Kanak), IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Fleeing mankind, Kanak is lifted up in the way of the dead to the moon-man's house — guarded by a terrible dog, entered past a skeleton-backed serving woman, regaled while an old hag licks her own back to tempt him to laugh (the little-finger nail under the knee is the antidote) — until she leaves knife and platter behind, threatening to overthrow the pillars of heaven. Shown the hatch from which the moon-man blows the snow upon the earth, Kanak is pushed down through the opening, guided home by his grandmother's spirit, and grows a celebrated angakok.
summary.zh: 遁世的卡納克被舉上亡者之路，抵達月神之屋——大犬守門、龍骨架背的侍女上菜；一名舔着自己後背、百般逗人發笑的老嫗舞入堂中（以小指指甲擦膝即可忍笑）——她倉皇逃走，留下刀與盤，揚言『不還我便掀翻天柱』。月神自地板的活門向人間吹雪，最後把卡納克推下天梯；祖母的魂魄一路護送他回到地面——他日後成為名震一方的巫師。

sensitivity.note: Moon-man cycle (compare Rink tale 19's Moon Man and the obstinate man, cross-ref inuit-obstinate-man-moon). Fragmentary form per Rink.

passages.text: Kanak, on fleeing from mankind, felt himself lifted up from the ground, and following the way of the dead; at length he lost his senses, and on awakening again found himself in front of the house where the spirit (or owner) of the moon resided. This man of the moon assisted him to get inside, which was a perilous undertaking, the entrance being very large and guarded by a terrible dog; the moon-man having then breathed upon Kanak in order to ease the pain that racked his limbs and having restored him to health spoke thus: 'By the way thou earnest no man ever returned; this is the way thou must take' — upon which he opened a door and pointed out to him a hole in the floor from which he could overlook the surface of the earth with all the dwelling-places of man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Kanak); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡納克（Kanak）逃離人類時，覺得自己被從地面舉起，循著亡者之路而去；終於他失去了知覺，醒來時發現自己已置身於月之精靈（或月之主）所居的屋前。這月之人助他進入屋內，而這是一件凶險之事，因為那入口極大，且有一頭可怕的狗守衛著；月之人隨後向卡納克吹氣，以緩解折磨他四肢的疼痛，使他恢復了健康，然後這樣說道：「你來的這條路，從沒有人回來過；你必須走的是這條路」——說罷，他打開一扇門，指給他看地板上的一個洞，從那裡他可以俯瞰大地的表面，以及人類所有的居所。

passages.text: He regaled him with eating which was served and brought in by a woman whose back was like that of a skeleton; Kanak was getting afraid on perceiving that, on which the moon-man said, 'Why, that's nothing; but lo! soon the old woman will appear who takes out the entrails of every one she can tempt to laugh. If thou canst not withhold thy smiles thou only needst to rub thy leg underneath the knee with the nail of thy little finger.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Kanak); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他以食物款待他，那食物是由一個背脊如骷髏的女人端送進來的；卡納克見此心生恐懼，月之人便說：「這算不了什麼；可是瞧！那老婦人馬上就要出現了，凡是被她誘得發笑的人，她都要取出其內臟。你若忍不住要笑，只需用小指的指甲搓一搓你膝蓋下方的腿便可。」

passages.text: Soon after the old hag entered dancing and whirling about, licking her own back and putting on the most ridiculous gestures; but when Kanak rubbed his leg with the nail of his little finger she gave a sudden start, at which the moon-man seized her and threw her down in the entrance — she went off, but afterwards a voice was heard, 'She has left her knife and her platter, and if she does not get both she says she will overthrow the pillars of heaven.' The moon-man having thrown the knife and platter down the entrance again opened the hatch in the floor, and blowing through a great pipe showed Kanak how he made it snow upon the earth; lastly he said to him, 'Now it is time to leave me, but do not be the least afraid, lest thou never shalt come alive' — he then pushed him down through the opening, on which Kanak swooned; on recovering he heard the voice of his grandmother, whose spirit had followed and taken care of him, and at length reached the earth's surface, arose and went to his home, after which he grew a celebrated angakok.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Kanak); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 不久，那老妖婆便進來了，一邊跳舞一邊旋轉，舔著自己的背，做出種種最滑稽的姿態；但當卡納克用小指的指甲搓腿時，她突然一驚，月之人便趁勢抓住她，把她摔倒在入口處——她走了，但隨後傳來一個聲音：「她落下了她的刀和她的盤子，她說若不能兩樣都拿回，就要掀翻支撐天穹的柱子。」月之人把刀和盤子從入口扔下去，又打開地板上的艙口，透過一根大管子吹氣，向卡納克展示他如何使雪降在大地上；最後他對他說：「現在是你離開我的時候了，但千萬不要害怕，免得你再也活不回來」——說罷，他便把他從那開口推了下去，卡納克隨即昏厥；醒來時他聽見祖母的聲音，她的靈魂一路跟隨並照料著他，最後他到達地面，起身回家，此後他成了一位著名的安加科克。

title.en: The Barren Wife Taken by the Moon-Man
title.zh: 被月神娶走的不孕婦

region.en: Winter night and the moon-man's sledge
region.zh: 冬夜與月神之橇

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (A Barren Wife), IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Ill-treated by her husband, a barren wife goes off one winter night and meets the moon-man driving in his sledge, who takes her home with him; many days after, in spring, she appears again and returns to her husband — ere long perceiving she is with child, she gives birth to a son, who when he grows up is taken away by the moon-man.
summary.zh: 被丈夫苛待的不孕婦於某個冬夜離家，遇見駕橇而來的月神，被帶回月宮；次年春天她重返夫家——不久便覺有孕，產下一子；孩子長大後被月神接走。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary moon-myth; divine-marriage cluster parallel.

passages.text: A Barren Wife, who was treated badly by her husband, went off one winter night and met with the moon-man, who came driving in his sledge, and took her along with him to his home. Many days after in spring she again appeared and went to live with her husband; ere long she perceived that she was with child, and gave birth to a son who when he grew up was taken away by the moon-man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (A Barren Wife); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個不孕的妻子，受丈夫虐待，在一個冬夜出走，遇見了月之人，他駕著雪橇而來，帶她一同回到他的家。許多天之後，時值春天，她又出現了，回去與丈夫同住；不久她發覺自己有了身孕，生下一個兒子，這兒子長大後被月之人帶走了。

title.en: Manguarak and the Moon-Man: The Wolffish Boast
title.zh: 曼瓜拉克與月神：狼魚之誇

region.en: Winter ice and the moon-sledge ride
region.zh: 冬日冰面與月神之橇

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Manguarak), IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Ignoring his father's warnings, Manguarak catches a white whale with a black spot on one side — one of the chase-animals set apart for the spirit of the moon — and is challenged to fight on the ice. The duel becomes a boast-tally of every bird, seal, and whale ever chased; at the halibut-fishing he once helped haul up a keraK (wolffish), at which the moon-man exclaims 'What art thou saying, man?' — as a child he was so terrified at seeing such a fish hauled up that he never dared pursue it. 'Now that I know thou hast caught an animal which I never ventured to pursue, I will do thee no harm... come along with me and see my place' — one dog, a flying sledge, the dark cliff of the entrail-cutting hag.
summary.zh: 不聽父親告誡的曼瓜拉克，獵得側身帶黑斑的白鯨——那是月神專屬的獵物——被月神下戰書到冰面。比武竟成了『生平獵物大清點』；說到捕大比目魚時曾順手拉上一條狼魚，月神失聲——『你說什麼？』——他幼時見人拉起此魚嚇破了膽，從此不敢獵它。『既然你擒住了我從不敢追的野獸，我便不傷你……隨我去看我的居所吧』——單犬駕橇、凌空而馳，途經那割取內臟的老嫗棲身的黑崖。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary moon-myth; the boast-duel inverts the usual combat. Fragmentary form per Rink.

passages.text: Manguarak, unheeding the warnings of his father, caught a white whale which, having a black spot on one side, was known to belong to the animals of chase set apart for the spirit of the moon. On a fine winter night the moon-man was heard to call him outside and challenge him to fight; when he came down upon the ice the moon-man said, 'Well, we will presently begin, but first let us name all the animals of chase we have caught during our lifetime' — they then, each in his turn, named the different sorts of birds, seals, and whales they had chased; and beginning with the fishes Manguarak went on to tell how he once assisted at a halibut-fishing when they happened to haul up a keraK (wolffish).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Manguarak); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曼瓜拉克不聽父親的警告，捕獲了一頭白鯨；這頭白鯨一側有黑斑，眾所皆知牠屬於專為月之精靈保留的獵物。在一個晴朗的冬夜，有人聽見月人喚他外出，向他挑戰決鬥；當他下到冰上時，月人說道：「好，我們馬上就開始，但先讓我們一一說出我們一生中所捕獲的各種獵物。」於是他們輪流說出各自追逐過的各種鳥、海豹與鯨魚；曼瓜拉克從魚類說起，接著講到他有一次如何協助捕撈大比目魚，當時他們恰好拖上來一尾凱拉克（狼魚）。

passages.text: On hearing this the moon-man exclaimed, 'What art thou saying, man? Now just wait, and listen to me' — he then went on to tell how, when a child and still living among mankind, he had once seen some people haul up a fish of that same kind, at which he was so terrified that he had never since tried to catch that fish. 'And now that I know thou hast caught an animal which I never ventured to pursue, I will do thee no harm. I begin, in fact, rather to like thee; so come along with me and see my place.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Manguarak); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 月人一聽此言便驚呼道：「你在說什麼，人啊？且慢，聽我說。」接著他便講述自己年幼時仍生活在人類之中，有一次曾見一些人拖上來一尾同類的魚，他當時嚇得魂飛魄散，自此再也不敢嘗試捕那種魚。「如今我既知你捕獲了一種我從不敢追逐的動物，我便不會傷害你。事實上，我反倒開始有些喜歡你了；那麼就隨我來，看看我的住處吧。」

passages.text: Manguarak accordingly went up to ask his father's permission, which having gained he returned to the ice, where he found the moon-man waiting with a sledge drawn only by a single dog; when he had taken his place on the sledge away they drove at a great pace, and gradually rising from the ground seemed to fly through the air. At midnight they came to a high land upon which they still travelled on; they went through a valley covered with snow, and had to pass by a dark-looking cliff inside of which lived the old hag who was wont to cut out the entrails of people who could not forbear laughing — as to the rest of the adventures of Manguarak they are much the same as those encountered by Kanak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 91 'The Moon' (Manguarak); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曼瓜拉克於是前去請求父親的許可，得到允許後便回到冰上，發現月人正等著他，拉的雪橇只由一隻狗牽引；他坐上雪橇後，他們便以極快的速度馳去，並漸漸離地升起，彷彿在空中飛翔。午夜時分，他們來到一片高地，仍繼續前行；他們穿過一個積雪覆蓋的山谷，還得經過一座陰森森的懸崖，崖內住著那個老巫婆，她慣於割出那些忍不住發笑之人的內臟——至於曼瓜拉克其餘的冒險經歷，則與卡納克所遭遇的大致相同。

title.en: Arnarkuak, the Woman Who Wanted to Be a Man
title.zh: 自居男子的女人阿納庫阿克

region.en: Interior of the country
region.zh: 內陸之地

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 92 'The Woman who wanted to be a Man', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Never ceasing to scold her son for his want of skill in hunting and other manly pursuits, Arnarkuak forces her daughter-in-law under threat of death to flee with her to the interior, where she disguises herself like a man and takes her daughter-in-law Ukquamak for a wife — but the son finds out their place of refuge, and kills his despicable mother.
summary.zh: 因兒子獵藝不精而無休止斥罵的阿納庫阿克，以死相逼，迫使兒媳烏夸馬克隨她遁入內陸；她扮作男子，把兒媳當作妻子——然而兒子尋得他們的藏身之處，殺死了那可憎的母親。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note; matricide recorded as told.

passages.text: A woman named Arnarkuak would not give up scolding her son on account of his want of skill in hunting and other manly pursuits. Once in his absence, when he had gone out kayaking, she forced her daughter-in-law, by threatening her with death, to flee with her to the interior of the country, where she disguised herself like a man, and had her daughter-in-law Ukquamak for a wife — but the son found out their place of refuge, and killed his despicable mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 92 'The Woman who wanted to be a Man'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個名叫阿爾納夸克的女人，因兒子不擅狩獵及其他男子漢的技藝而不住地責罵他。有一次趁他外出划皮艇時，她以死相脅，逼迫媳婦隨她逃往內陸；在那裡她女扮男裝，娶媳婦烏克夸馬克為妻——但兒子找到了她們的藏身之處，殺死了他那可鄙的母親。

title.en: An Angakok Flight: The Thong-Bound Wizard
title.zh: 巫師飛行：皮繩縛身的降靈

region.en: Inland houses of women and inlanders
region.zh: 內陸的女人之屋與內陸人營地

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 93 'An Angakok Flight', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Bound in a seal-skin thong from toe to head, the great angakok lifts the roof off his house and flies inland: a house inhabited only by women whose enchanted husband — a house-pillar — emits sparks of fire and lead at his approach; a second flight ends in the inlanders' ball-play, hurled nearly dead between them until his tornak rescues him; the third brings him to his sister lost many years before, now married to an inlander, who gives him a piece of reindeer-skin as a token that he had really been with her.
summary.zh: 以海豹皮繩自趾纏頭的大巫師，飛起時掀開屋頂；第一次飛行入內陸，遇一屋只有女人——那被施咒的丈夫（屋柱）見他靠近便迸出火星與鉛丸；第二次飛行落入內陸人手中，被他們當球拋擲，幾近喪命，賴靈助相救；第三次飛行尋得多年杳無音信的妹妹——她已嫁給內陸人，贈他一片馴鹿皮作為『確曾相會』的信物。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note; documents angakok flight binding ritual.

passages.text: A great angakok, being once called upon to perform a conjuration, took a thong of seal-skin, and having in one end cut a hole for his toe he twisted it round his body and made fast the other end to his head. When the lamps had been all extinguished he was lifted up, and soaring about the house he made the roof lift and give way to him. Having escaped through the opening he flew to the inland and came to a house inhabited only by women — but as soon as he tried to approach any of them the house-pillar (their enchanted husband) began to emit sparks of fire and lead towards him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 93 'An Angakok Flight'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一位法力高強的安加科克，有一次應召施行法術，取來一條海豹皮鞭帶，在一端割出一個洞供腳趾穿過，將它纏繞在自己身上，並把另一端繫牢在頭上。當所有燈火都被熄滅後，他被舉起，在屋中翱翔，使屋頂掀起並為他讓路。他從那開口逃出後，便飛往內陸，來到一間只住著女人的屋子——但他一試圖接近其中任何一人，屋柱（她們那受魔法驅使的丈夫）便開始向他迸出火花並朝他逼近。

passages.text: The next time he flew to the inland he was seized hold of by the inlanders, who essayed to play at ball with him, hurling him backwards and forwards between them till he was nearly dead, when he called his tornak, who quickly rescued him. The third time he came to his sister, who had disappeared many years before, but whom he now found married to an inlander; she gave him a piece of reindeer-skin as a token to take home with him in order to convince people of his really having been with her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 93 'An Angakok Flight'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 下一次他飛往內陸時，被內陸人抓住，他們試圖拿他當球玩，將他在彼此之間拋來擲去，直到他幾乎死去，他才呼喚他的托爾納克，托爾納克迅速將他救出。第三次他來到他姊姊那裡；她多年前便已失蹤，但他如今發現她嫁給了一個內陸人；她給了他一塊馴鹿皮作為信物帶回家，以便使人相信他確實曾與她在一起。

title.en: The Means for Getting Children: The Two Little Dried Fishes
title.zh: 求子之方：兩尾小魚乾

region.en: Far north and far south quest
region.zh: 遠北與遠南的尋求之旅

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 94 'The Means for getting Children', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Travelling a summer north and a summer south for a means to get children, a husband wins from an old woman two small dried fishes — male for a son, female for a daughter — but stricken with hunger on the long road home he reasons 'What is the use of keeping this spawner? A son is what we desire' and swallows the male fish. Growing bigger and bigger till he can hardly slip into his kayak, he is delivered by a skilful old woman's charm of what was encumbering his inside: a fine little daughter.
summary.zh: 為求子而一夏北上、一夏南下的丈夫，終於從老嫗處得來兩尾小魚乾——雄魚得子、雌魚得女；歸途飢餓難耐，他暗想『留著這尾雄魚何用？我們要的本是兒子』——一口吞下。此後他日益腹脹，連皮艇都難以容身；最後由一位通靈的老嫗施法，替他『分娩』出腹中之物——竟是個可愛的女兒。

sensitivity.note: Rink doubts whether the rest of the tale is of genuine Eskimo origin — noted as part of the source.

passages.text: A married couple had in vain been in hope of getting children; at length the man set out in search of some means to attain their desire. The first summer he travelled as far as he could get to the north, and the next as far as possible to the south, before he succeeded in finding an old woman who promised to help him. From the bottom of her bag she produced two small dried fishes, a male and a female, of which he was to give his wife the former to eat if he wanted a son, and the latter in case they preferred a daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 94 'The Means for getting Children'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一對已婚夫婦一直盼望能得子，卻始終徒勞無功；最後，那男子便動身去尋求某種能達成他們心願的辦法。頭一個夏天，他盡可能往北走得極遠；第二年夏天，他又盡可能往南走得極遠，這才總算找到一位答應幫助他的老婦人。她從袋底取出兩條小小的乾魚，一雄一雌；他若想要兒子，就把前者給妻子吃，若他們更想要女兒，就給後者。

passages.text: He received the fishes and started on his way home; but having to travel very far and not always being able to get any victuals, once in a great strain for something to eat began to consider, 'What is the use of keeping this spawner? A son is what we desire' — on which he swallowed the one little fish. After a while he began to feel very ill at ease, at the same time growing bigger and bigger, till at length he could hardly manage to slip down in his kayak. A skilful old woman who lived at a place where he happened to land soon suspected what was the matter with him, and hit on a charm to deliver him of what was encumbering his inside, which soon proved to be a fine little daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 94 'The Means for getting Children'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他接過那兩條魚，便啟程回家；但因路途十分遙遠，又不總能弄到食物，有一回在極度困頓、急需吃食之際，他開始尋思：『留著這條產卵的魚有什麼用？我們要的是兒子。』於是他就把那條小魚吞了下去。過了一陣，他開始感到十分不適，同時身子越長越大，到最後幾乎連坐進皮划艇裡都辦不到了。他偶然登岸之處住著一位精通法術的老婦人，她很快就察覺出他出了什麼事，並想出一個咒法，替他把他腹中那累贅之物解脫出來，而那物不久便顯出是一個漂亮的小女兒。

title.en: Kanginguak's Son: The Falcon-Overtaking Rower
title.zh: 康瓜克的兒子：追上獵隼的划手

region.en: Umanarsuak, high island of South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭烏馬納舒阿克高島

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 95 'Kanginguak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The son of the southerner Kanginguak rows so expertly that he overtakes falcons in their flight and kills them with a blow of his paddle-oar; he rows out so far that Umanarsuak appears like a seal diving up and down among the waves — but in a match with a celebrated kayaker he is killed by his rival. His father afterwards goes to the place where he was buried, brings out his body again, and carries it along with him till he finds an angakok who restores it to life.
summary.zh: 南方人康瓜克之子划技超群：能追上飛掠的獵隼、以槳一擊斃之；出海之遠，使烏馬納舒阿克島看來如波間起伏的海豹——然而與名艇客比試時，他死於對手之手。父親隨後掘出他的遺體，一路攜行，直到尋得一位巫師將他救活。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note.

passages.text: Kanginguak was a native of the south, who set forth on a journey and took up his abode near Umanarsuak (a high island of South Greenland). He had a son named Tunerak, who was such an expert rower that he used to overtake the falcons in their flight and killed them with a blow of his paddle-oar; he went out to sea so far as to make Umanarsuak appear like a seal diving up and down among the waves — he also tried matches with celebrated kayakers, but on one of these occasions he was killed by his rival. His father afterwards went to the place where he was buried, brought out his body again and carried it along with him till he found an angakok who restored it to life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 95 'Kanginguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 康金古阿克是南方人，他出外遠行，在烏馬納爾蘇阿克（南格陵蘭的一座高島）附近定居下來。他有一個兒子名叫圖內拉克，划船技藝極為嫻熟，常能追上飛行中的隼，並用槳一擊將其打死；他出海划得極遠，遠得使烏馬納爾蘇阿克看上去就像一頭在海浪間上下浮沉的海豹——他也曾與著名的皮划艇手較量，但在其中一次較量中，他被對手殺死。他的父親後來去到埋葬他的地方，把他的屍體重新挖出，帶著它一路前行，直到找到一位巫師，使他復活。

title.en: Kigdlinararsuk: The Merganser Amulet in the Prow
title.zh: 基格德利納拉舒克：艇首的秋沙鴨符

region.en: The old hags' coast, northward quest
region.zh: 老嫗們的海岸，北行之路

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 96 'Kigdlinararsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Out to avenge his sister's murder, Kigdlinararsuk seeks an old woman who can give an amulet for giving swiftness to a boat: the first confesses she has grown old to no purpose — 'I am only clever in...' (the words untranslatable, per Rink's note, being the humblest of crafts) — but has an elder sister more cunning farther north, who gives him a small bit of a dried merganser. Inserted into the prow so no marks or joints are visible, tried twice until the boat can run down a flying merganser, he starts at last to encounter his adversaries.
summary.zh: 為妹復仇的基格德利納拉舒克，尋求能賜舟以速的護身符：第一位老嫗自承『我白活了這把年紀，只會……』（其原話按注無從譯出，是一門最低微的手藝），但北邊有位更精明的姐姐——贈他一小片秋沙鴨乾。他把符片嵌入艇首，接口無痕；試了兩次，直到船能追上飛掠的秋沙鴨，方才啟程尋仇。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; Rink's note explains the omitted modest formula.

passages.text: Kigdlinararsuk, in order to avenge the murder of his sister, went out in search of an old woman who could assist him in getting an amulet for giving swiftness to a boat. The first one he came to replied, 'I have grown rather old to no purpose (viz., without having acquired wisdom), I am only clever in...' [words omitted] '...but farther north I have an elder sister more cunning than I; first try thy luck with her, and if thou dost not succeed I'll see what can be done.' He then went farther and came to another old hag, who gave him for an amulet a small bit of a dried Merganser; this he inserted in the prow of the boat with such care that no marks or joints were visible — twice he tried it before the boat appeared swift enough to run down a flying Merganser, and not till then did he start to encounter his adversaries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 96 'Kigdlinararsuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 基格德利納拉爾蘇阿克為了替妹妹報仇，便出去尋找一位能幫他取得護符、使船行迅捷的老婦人。他找到的第一位回答說：『我白白活到這把年紀（即未曾獲得智慧），我只擅長……』〔文字從略〕『……但更往北去，我有一位比我更精明的姐姐；你先去她那裡試試運氣，若不成，我再看看能怎麼辦。』於是他繼續往前，來到另一位老巫婆那裡，她給了他一小塊乾的秋沙鴨作為護符；他極其小心地把它嵌進船頭，以致看不出任何痕跡或接縫——他試了兩回，船才顯得足夠迅捷，能追上飛行的秋沙鴨，直到那時他才動身去迎戰他的仇敵。

title.en: The Man of Karusuk and His Ingnersuak Companion
title.zh: 卡魯舒克與其精靈同伴

region.en: Karusuk in the firth of Godthaab and Kangek
region.zh: 努克峽灣的卡魯舒克與康格克

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 97 'A Man living on Karusuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Every day a man of Karusuk repairs the twenty-four miles to Kangek to hunt auks, companioned by an ingnersuak who is also the tornak of an angakok farther up the firth at Tukak — in the short winter days it comes to Karasuk, waits till the man is ready to start, follows and takes care of him the whole day, and returns with him to Karusuk, whence it goes on to its home at Tukak. Two distinct kayaks seen at a distance become one close up: an ingnersuak, invisible excepting from a great distance.
summary.zh: 卡魯舒克的一名男子日日往返二十四哩外的康格克獵海鳩，同行者是一位精靈——同時也是上游圖卡克一位巫師的靈助。冬日晝短，精靈來到卡魯舒克，候他整裝出發，一路照看整日，隨他歸來後再自行返回圖卡克。遠處明明是兩條皮艇，近前只剩一條——那便是精靈：唯遠望可見。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale documenting ingnersuak companionship belief (compare tale 46).

passages.text: A man living on Karusuk (in the firth of Godthaab) every day used to repair to Kangek (about 24 miles distant) for the purpose of hunting auks. For his companion he had an ingnersuak, who at the same time was the tornak of an angakok living farther up the firth at Tukak. It is said that even nowadays many kayakers have an ingnersuak for their companion, and every now and then they become visible; sometimes a kayaker observing two distinct kayaks at a distance on coming nearer will only meet with one, who on being questioned is not aware of any other having been with him — in such cases people believe it to have been an ingnersuak, on account of their being invisible excepting from a great distance. The said ingnersuak in the short winter days came to Karasuk, waited until he saw the man ready to start for Kangek, and then followed and took care of him the whole day, and returned with him to Karusuk, from whence he went on to his home at Tukak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 97 'A Man living on Karusuk'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 住在卡魯蘇克（在戈特霍布峽灣內）的一個人，每天都到康格克（約二十四英里之遙）去獵海雀。他有一個因格內爾蘇阿克作伴，這因格內爾蘇阿克同時又是住在峽灣更上游圖卡克的一位巫師的托爾納克。據說即便如今，許多皮划艇手也有因格內爾蘇阿克作伴，而且不時會顯形；有時皮划艇手遠遠望見兩隻分明的皮划艇，走近卻只遇見一隻，問起來那人也不知道有別人與他同行——這種情形下，人們便相信那是因格內爾蘇阿克，因為他們除非在極遠處，否則都是隱形的。所說的這因格內爾蘇阿克在短促的冬日裡來到卡魯蘇克，等到看見那人準備動身前往康格克，便跟隨其後，整天照看他，再隨他回到卡魯蘇克，然後從那裡回到自己在圖卡克的家。

title.en: Atarsuatsiak: A Row of Murder-Marks Across the Forehead
title.zh: 阿塔舒阿茨夏克：額際一排殺人刺青

region.en: Country about Upernivik, North Greenland
region.zh: 北格陵蘭烏珀納維克一帶

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 98 'Atarsuatsiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Atarsuatsiak and his brothers were a set of fearful man-slayers living in the country about Upernivik, who had their heads tattooed with a separate mark for each murder they had committed — on Atarsuatsiak these marks formed a whole row along his forehead from one side to the other. At last the people of the neighbouring places resolved upon having him killed at a place to which he used to resort in order to visit his concubine.
summary.zh: 阿塔舒阿茨夏克與其兄弟是烏珀納維克一帶令人聞風喪膽的殺人者，每殺一人便在頭上刺一記號——阿塔舒阿茨夏克額際的刺青已連成一排，橫貫兩鬢。最後，鄰近各處的人合謀，在他常去會情婦的地方將他結果。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note.

passages.text: Atarsuatsiak and his brothers were a set of fearful man-slayers, living in the country about Upernivik (Greenland), who had their heads tattooed with a separate mark for each murder they had committed; on Atarsuatsiak these marks formed a whole row along his forehead from one side to the other. At last the people of the neighbouring places resolved upon having him killed at a place to which he used to resort in order to visit his concubine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 98 'Atarsuatsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿塔爾蘇阿齊阿克和他的兄弟們是一夥可怕的殺人者，住在烏佩尼維克（格陵蘭）一帶；他們每殺一人，便在頭上刺一個單獨的記號；在阿塔爾蘇阿齊阿克頭上，這些記號沿著他的額頭從一邊到另一邊排成一整行。最後，鄰近各地的人們決意趁他常去探望其妾的一處地方把他殺掉。

title.en: Among the Last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak
title.zh: 康格盧克蘇瓦夏克的末代巫師

region.en: Kangerdlugsuatsiak, East Greenland
region.zh: 東格陵蘭康格盧克蘇瓦夏克

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 99 'Among the last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Kapiarsuak and Avangnanersuak go out daily all winter to catch partridges and never bring any home, never seen to eat — a curious child accompanying them watches Kapiarsuak strike a flat rock with his staff and murmur certain words: an opening appears in the ground, out of which they angle up different kinds of food, giving the child a small fish to swallow after which it loses all remembrance — not until full-grown, many years after, does it suddenly recollect the event. Kuvatsiak, whose brother was seized by the ingnersuit, dreams like Akamalik, meets his dead brother at sea laboring under a black impediment on his kayak that alone hinders him from leaving the under-world people, and when the first missionary comes a dream induces him to get baptised.
summary.zh: 康加皮亞舒克與阿萬格納內舒亞克整個冬天日日外出『獵雷鳥』，卻從不帶回、也從不見進食；一個好奇的孩子隨行，目睹前者以杖擊平石、低聲念咒——地面裂開，二人自穴中垂釣取出各色食物，並給孩子吞下一尾小魚令其忘卻所見——多年後長大成人，他才驀然憶起此事。庫瓦茨夏克的兄弟被地下之民擄走；他得了一個類似阿卡馬利克的夢，老年時常在海上遇見亡弟——艇上那件黑物正是阻止他離開地下之民、重返人間的唯一障礙；首批傳教士到來時，一夢引他受洗。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tales documenting the last angakut generation; Christian syncretism noted in the source.

passages.text: Among the last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak (Greenland) was a man named Kapiarsuk, and a woman called Avangnanersuak, who every day during the whole winter used to go out together to catch partridges, but never brought any home, and never were seen to eat anything at all. At last a child who was anxious as to their doings one day asked leave to accompany them, and soon observed that they never looked for any partridges at all — but having come a good way up the country Kapiarsuak commenced to strike a flat rock with his staff, and murmuring certain words an opening appeared in the ground, out of which they went on angling and hauling up different kinds of food, allowing the child to partake of the good fare. On going home they gave it a small fish to swallow, after which it lost all remembrance of what it had seen — not until he was full grown, many years after, did he suddenly recollect the event and narrate it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 99 'Among the last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在康格爾德盧格蘇阿齊亞克（格陵蘭）最後一批安加庫特之中，有一個名叫卡皮亞爾蘇克的男人，和一個名叫阿萬格納內爾蘇阿克的女人；整個冬天他們每天都一同外出捕捉雷鳥，卻從不帶任何獵物回家，也從未有人見他們吃過任何東西。最後，一個對他們的行徑感到好奇的孩子某天請求允許同行，不久便察覺他們根本不在尋找任何雷鳥——而是往內陸走了好一段路之後，卡皮亞爾蘇阿克開始用手杖敲擊一塊平坦的岩石，並喃喃念著某些話語，地上便裂開一個洞口，他們從中垂釣並拖上各種不同的食物，還讓那孩子一同享用這豐盛的一餐。回家時，他們給他一條小魚吞下，之後他便完全失去了對所見之事的記憶——直到多年以後他長大成人，才突然回想起這件事並講述出來。

passages.text: Another angakok of the same place, named Kuvatsiak, had two brothers, Usuinak and Igpak, of whom the former having gone out kayaking did not return and entirely disappeared — in the evening they saw the clothes of the missing brother moving about by themselves. Kuvatsiak forthwith began to conjure, by means of which he found out that he had been seized by the ingnersuit. Kuvatsiak had a dream somewhat like that of Akamalik; and when he began growing old he often met with his deceased brother out at sea — he observed some black thing lying on the top of his brother's kayak, who laboured in vain to rid himself of it, saying that that was the only impediment hindering him from leaving the under-world people and returning to the land of the living. When the first missionary came to the country Kuvatsiak had a dream that induced him to get baptised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 99 'Among the last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 同一地方的另一位安加庫克名叫庫瓦齊阿克，有兩個兄弟，烏蘇伊納克和伊格帕克；其中前者划著皮划艇出海後沒有回來，完全消失了——傍晚時他們看見那失蹤兄弟的衣服自行移動。庫瓦齊阿克隨即開始施法，藉此查出他已被因格內爾蘇伊特捉去。庫瓦齊阿克做了一個有些像阿卡馬利克那樣的夢；當他開始年老時，他常在海上看見已故的兄弟——他注意到有某樣黑色的東西擱在他兄弟的皮划艇上，他兄弟徒勞地想擺脫它，並說那正是唯一阻礙他離開冥界之人、返回生者之地的障礙。當第一位傳教士來到這個地方時，庫瓦齊阿克做了一個夢，促使他接受了洗禮。

title.en: Atungak: A Tale from Labrador
title.zh: 阿通加克：拉布拉多故事

region.en: Labrador coasts, cannibal land, and the lame people
region.zh: 拉布拉多海岸、食人之地與跛足人之鄉

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale from Labrador, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 100 'Atungak, a Tale from Labrador', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Pursuing a runaway wife, Atungak is feasted by cannibals on man's-and-wolves'-brains, then child's-and-walrus' flesh, eating dried reindeer with appetite while children's brains are sucked out around him; a sling-boy felled by a pyrites-stone leaves one booted leg under the bench — 'Ye have done very ill in taking that miserable Ajajusek, who ought to have served his younger brother for food.' Fleeing past the lame people ('they hopped about like so many ravens' — the wife's laugh is fatal), cutting all their sledge-lashings, past two fighting black bears and a pot boiling of itself, they meet at last a watcher at a seal's breathing-hole: their own son, left behind a child. They have travelled over the whole world without changing or getting old.
summary.zh: 追回逃妻的阿通加克被食人族以人腦拌狼腦、再以孩童肉拌海象肉設宴；夫婦只肯吃乾鹿肉，而席間孩童的腦髓正被吸食。持套索的少年被黃鐵礦石擊斃，凳下只剩一隻穿靴的腿——『你們抓走那可憐的阿亞尤塞克真是造孽，他本該留著給弟弟當飯吃的。』逃過跛足人之鄉（其妻笑他們『像一群跳躍的渡鴉』，險釀大禍）、割斷所有橇繩、穿過兩頭搏鬥的黑熊與自行沸騰的鍋，最後在呼吸孔旁守候的獵人竟是幼時遺落的兒子——他們環遊世界而容顏未改。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; Rink notes its curious similarities with the next (East Greenland) fragment from the most widely severed Eskimo countries. Cannibalism recorded as told.

passages.text: A man named Atungak had two wives; one of them having run away he pursued her in his sledge and soon overtook her.
