They then travelled together and came to cannibals, whose chief invited them to his house and set before them a dish of man's and wolves' brains mixed together; when they declined eating it another was served consisting of the flesh of a child and of a walrus — and this also being rejected, they brought in dried reindeer-flesh which they ate with hearty appetite. Meanwhile the people got hold of some children, and feigning to pet them they killed them and sucked out their brains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 100 'Atungak, a Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個名叫阿通加克的男人有兩個妻子；其中一個逃走後，他乘雪橇追趕，很快就追上了她。於是他們一同前行，來到食人族那裡；食人族的首領邀請他們到家中，在他們面前擺上一盤人腦與狼腦混合而成的菜；當他們拒絕吃時，又端上另一道由孩童之肉與海象肉做成的菜——這道也被拒絕後，他們便拿來乾馴鹿肉，兩人便津津有味地吃了起來。與此同時，那些人抓住了一些孩子，假意撫愛他們，卻將他們殺死並吸食其腦髓。

passages.text: A young lad was also there who carried a sling wherewith to entangle strangers; when he approached Atungak with this design he was struck on the head with a piece of pyrites-stone and fell to the ground. Afterwards when his mother came from another house to look for him she only found one of his legs left lying under the bench with the boot still on it, by means of which she recognised it — she then exclaimed, 'Ye have done very ill in taking that miserable Ajajusek, who ought to have served his younger brother for food.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 100 'Atungak, a Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那裡還有一個年輕小夥子，帶著一條用來纏住陌生人的投石索；當他帶著這個意圖走近阿通加克時，被一塊黃鐵礦石擊中頭部，倒在地上。後來他母親從另一間屋子來找他時，只發現他的一條腿留在長凳下，靴子還穿在上面，她藉此認出了他——她隨即驚呼：「你們把那個可憐的阿賈尤塞克帶走，實在做得太壞了，他本該留給他的弟弟當食物才對。」

passages.text: Atungak and his wife travelling on came to a country the people of which were all lame; before they reached them the chief came to receive them and warned them against his people as being a very ill-natured set. Nevertheless when Atungak's wife saw their ball-playing she could not help laughing, and said that they hopped about like so many ravens — Atungak got very much afraid when he heard the bystanders repeating this.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 100 'Atungak, a Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿通加克和妻子繼續前行，來到一個居民全是跛子的地方；在他們抵達之前，首領前來迎接他們，並警告他們提防他的族人，說他們是一群性情極壞的傢伙。然而當阿通加克的妻子看見他們玩球時，仍忍不住笑了起來，說他們蹦蹦跳跳活像一群渡鴉——阿通加克聽到旁觀者複述這番話時，非常害怕。

passages.text: He at once cut asunder all the lashings of the sledges belonging to the lame people so that they could not pursue them; hastening from there they came to two black bears engaged in a fight, and no other way being left they were obliged to pass between them — after which they came to a pot boiling of itself which they could not avoid crossing over. Lastly they came to a man watching at the breathing-hole of a seal, and on speaking to him they recognised him as Atungak's son whom they had left behind a child — they had travelled over the whole world without changing or getting old. In the north caves and clefts in the rocks are still to be seen in which they are said to have rested.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 100 'Atungak, a Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他立刻割斷了那些跛子所有雪橇的綁繩，使他們無法追趕；他們從那裡急忙離去，來到兩隻正在搏鬥的黑熊面前，別無他路，只得從牠們之間穿過——之後他們來到一口自行沸騰的鍋前，無法避開，只得跨過它。最後他們來到一個守在海豹呼吸孔旁的男人面前，與他交談後認出他正是阿通加克留在身後還是個孩子的兒子——他們走遍了整個世界，卻既未變樣也未衰老。在北方，至今仍可見到據說他們曾歇息過的岩洞與岩縫。

title.en: Malarsuak: A Story from East Greenland
title.zh: 馬拉爾舒亞克：東格陵蘭故事

region.en: East Greenland cannibal coast
region.zh: 東格陵蘭食人海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale from East Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 101 'Malarsuak, a Story from East Greenland', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Sledding in search of his lost sister, Malarsuak finds her domesticated among cannibals; a hideous-looking youth comes into the house and is killed by a bear's tooth fastened into a stick — 'Is this not my miserable son here — I mean the one who ought to serve as food for his brothers?' Returning with wife and child, the cannibals rob them of the child; warned by the brother-in-law to cut all his place-fellows' sledge-lashings, Malarsuak forgets one — it comes speeding after him, he kills the driver, and makes his escape himself.
summary.zh: 乘橇尋妹的馬拉爾舒亞克在食人族中找到已為人婦的妹妹；一名奇醜的少年入屋，被他以縛棍的熊牙刺穿頭顱——『這不就是我不成器的兒子嗎？他本該留著給兄弟們當飯吃的。』攜妻帶子重訪時，孩子被食人族奪走；臨別依小舅子之勸割斷眾人橇繩，卻漏了一架——那橇疾追而來，他殺了趕橇人，自己逃出生天。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; parallel to tale 100 (Labrador) per Rink's note. Child-stealing recorded as told.

passages.text: A man named Malarsuak started in search of his lost sister. Travelling by sledge he came to houses inhabited by cannibals, with one of which he found his sister domesticated. A hideous-looking youth came into the house, whom Malarsuak killed by piercing his head with a bear's tooth fastened into a stick, whereupon the host threw the dead body under the bench — some time after a woman appeared, saying, 'Is this not my miserable son here — I mean the one who ought to serve as food for his brothers?' Malarsuak travelled homewards, but came back on a visit, bringing his wife and a little child with him; the cannibals robbed them of their child. When going to leave the brother-in-law tried to persuade him first to cut all the lashings of his place-fellows' sledges in order to prevent their pursuing the travellers — Malarsuak took his advice, but happened to forget one of the sledges, which came speeding after him; he killed the driver and made his escape himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 101 'Malarsuak, a Story from East Greenland'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個名叫馬拉蘇阿克（Malarsuak）的男人動身尋找他失散的妹妹。他乘雪橇而行，來到幾間住著食人者的屋子，在其中一間裡他發現妹妹已被收養在家中。一個相貌醜陋的少年走進屋裡，馬拉蘇阿克將一顆熊牙固定在木棍上，刺穿他的頭部把他殺死，於是主人便把屍體扔到長凳底下——過了一陣，一個女人出現，說道：「這不就是我那可憐的兒子嗎——我是說，那個本該充當他兄弟們食物的人？」馬拉蘇阿克動身回家，但後來又帶著妻子和一個幼小的孩子回來探訪；食人者們奪走了他們的孩子。臨走時，妹夫先勸他把同伴們雪橇上所有的綁繩都割斷，以免他們追趕旅人——馬拉蘇阿克聽從了他的建議，卻恰好漏掉了一架雪橇，那雪橇飛速追了上來；他殺死了駕馭者，自己逃脫了。

title.en: Sikuliarsiujuitsok: The Giant Tied by His Feet
title.zh: 西庫利亞修尤伊特索克：縛足而亡的巨人

region.en: Labrador coast
region.zh: 拉布拉多海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale from Labrador, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 102 'A Tale from Labrador', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Too big to walk on new ice, Sikuliarsiujuitsok caught a whale from his kayak all by himself — dreaded and hated, never sleeping in strange places until persuaded into a snow-hut where, too big for room, he lay doubled up and let his feet be tied. Hauled out and killed — but not before killing four men in the struggle. His three sisters, one with three powerful sons, kept a stone-fenced enclosure into which they enticed all those they intended to kill.
summary.zh: 因身量過大而無法踏上新冰的西庫利亞修尤伊特索克，竟能獨自以皮艇捕鯨——人人畏懼憎恨，他從不在生地過夜；直到被勸入雪屋，體大難容、蜷縮而臥，任人縛住雙足。他被拖出殺害——臨死猶擊斃四人。他的三個姊妹（其一有三個強悍的兒子）築起石圍，專用來誘殺仇人。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary Labrador tale per Rink.

passages.text: Sikuliarsiujuitsok, on account of his great size, was unable to walk upon new ice; he all by himself caught a whale from his kayak. But he was much dreaded and hated, and never ventured to sleep in strange places — he was however once persuaded to stay for a night in a snow-hut; being too big to find room in it he lay all doubled up, and allowed his feet to be tied together. In this condition he was hauled out and killed, but not before he himself had killed four men in the struggle. He had three sisters, one of whom had three sons likewise powerful men; they had an enclosure fenced in with stones into which they enticed all those they intended to kill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 102 'A Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西庫利亞爾修尤伊措克（Sikuliarsiujuitsok）因身材巨大，無法在新結的冰上行走；他獨自一人從皮划艇上捕獲了一頭鯨。但他深受畏懼與憎恨，從不敢在陌生的地方睡覺——然而有一次他被說服在一間雪屋裡過夜；由於他體型太大，屋裡容不下他，他便蜷縮著躺下，任人把他的雙腳綁在一起。就在這種狀態下，他被拖了出去殺死，但在此之前他已在搏鬥中親手殺死了四個人。他有三個姐妹，其中一個也有三個同樣強壯的兒子；他們用石頭圍出一塊圈地，把他們打算殺死的人全都誘騙進去。

title.en: Aklaujak: Drowning the Reindeer by the Antlers
title.zh: 阿克勞雅克：執角溺鹿的力士

region.en: Reindeer lakes and the lookout hill, Labrador
region.zh: 拉布拉多的馴鹿湖與瞭望山

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale from Labrador, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 103 'Aklaujak, a Tale from Labrador', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Of immense strength, Aklaujak returns from a reindeer-hunt to find his brothers have robbed him of his wife — but his mother, watching from a high hill as he sits in his kayak seizing two large reindeers by the antlers and drowning them by holding them under water, hastens down and persuades the wife to return to him, on which the brothers take flight.
summary.zh: 力大無窮的阿克勞雅克獵鹿歸來，發現兄弟們搶走了他的妻子；而他的母親在高山上望見他坐在皮艇中，雙手執住兩頭大鹿的鹿角、按入水中將其溺斃——她急忙下山勸妻子回到他身邊；兄弟們見狀倉皇而逃。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary Labrador tale per Rink.

passages.text: A man named Aklaujak was of immense strength. Once, when away on a reindeer-hunt, his brothers robbed him of his wife; but the mother, who from a high hill observed him sitting in his kayak and seizing two large reindeers by the antlers and drowning them by holding them under water, hastened down and persuaded the wife to return to him, on which the brothers took flight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 103 'Aklaujak, a Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個名叫阿克勞雅克（Aklaujak）的男人力大無窮。有一次他外出獵馴鹿時，他的兄弟們奪走了他的妻子；但母親從高山上望見他坐在皮划艇裡，抓住兩頭大馴鹿的鹿角，把它們按在水下淹死，便急忙下山，勸說妻子回到他身邊，於是兄弟們便逃走了。

title.en: The Giant of Kangersuak: The Marshy Plain
title.zh: 康格蘇克的巨人與沼澤平原

region.en: Kangersuak or Cape Farewell, South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭康格蘇克（費爾韋爾角）

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 104 'The Giant of Kangersuak or Cape Farewell', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: At war, the northern people's powerful champion sat on the top of Kangersuak watching the Southlanders passing by. A man he had killed left a son who practised angakok science and revenged his father by inducing the giant to walk with him over a marshy plain, where he went down — and from beneath pierced the feet of the giant, and afterwards killed him.
summary.zh: 兩族交戰，北方人的強悍冠軍坐鎮康格蘇克山頂，專候過往的南方人。被他殺害的一人遺下一子，修習巫術，誘巨人與他同走沼澤平原——巨人陷入沼中，他自水底刺穿巨人的雙足，再將其擊斃，為父報仇。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: The people from the south (or east) and those from the north (or west) were at war with each other; the latter had a powerful champion who was sitting on the top of Kangersuak to watch the Southlanders passing by. A man who had been killed by him left a son, who practised angakok science and revenged his father by inducing the giant to walk with him over a marshy plain, where he went down — and from beneath pierced the feet of the giant, and afterwards killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 104 'The Giant of Kangersuak or Cape Farewell'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 南方（或東方）的人與北方（或西方）的人彼此交戰；後者有一位強大的勇士，坐在康格爾蘇阿克（Kangersuak）的山頂上監視路過的南方人。一個被他殺死的人留下了一個兒子，這兒子修習安加科克（angakok）法術，為父報仇，誘使那巨人與他一同走過一片沼澤平原，巨人陷了下去——他便從下方刺穿巨人的雙腳，隨後將他殺死。

title.en: The Kidnappers: The Magic Lay and the Dolphins' Speech
title.zh: 劫人者：咒歌與海豚之言

region.en: Coast of the girl and the gale
region.zh: 少女與風暴的海岸

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 105 'The Kidnappers', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A band of brothers tried to carry off a girl by force, but her mother by means of a magic lay caused them all to perish in a sudden gale. Some time after, an angakok who had been out kayaking stated that he had seen a shoal of dolphins — and listening to their speech made them out to be those brothers, who had been thus transformed.
summary.zh: 一夥兄弟企圖強搶少女，其母以咒歌召來驟風，令他們全數葬身海中；此後一名巫師出海時遇見一群海豚——聽其言語，正是那夥兄弟化為的形體。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: A band of brothers tried to carry off a girl by force; but her mother, by means of a magic lay, caused them all to perish in a sudden gale. Some time after an angakok who had been out kayaking stated that he had seen a shoal of dolphins, and listening to their speech made them out to be those brothers, who had been thus transformed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 105 'The Kidnappers'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一群兄弟企圖強行擄走一個女孩；但她的母親憑藉一首魔法歌謠，使他們全都在一場突如其來的狂風中喪命。過了些時候，一個曾出海划皮划艇的安加科克說他看見了一群海豚，細聽它們的言語，認出它們正是那些兄弟，他們就這樣被變成了海豚。

title.en: The Visiting Animals: Reindeer, Fox, and Hare
title.zh: 來訪的動物：鹿、狐與兔

region.en: Lonely winter-house by the son's grave
region.zh: 兒子墳旁的孤獨冬屋

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 106 'The Visiting Animals', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Grieving at his son's grave, an old man is surprised by three visitors: one tall and long-nosed, one smaller and flat-nosed, the last very small and white as snow — the flat-nosed one asking for a piece of sole-leather, the white one for a piece of walrus-tooth. Seeing the departing guests bound off in the shape of a reindeer, a fox, and a hare — it is said the hare had need of something for a new tooth.
summary.zh: 在兒子墳前守喪的老人，夜裡迎來三位客人：一個高挑長鼻、一個矮小塌鼻、最後一個瘦小而白如雪——臨別時，塌鼻者討走一塊皮底，白者討走一截海象牙。老人目送他們離去，驚見三人分別化作馴鹿、狐狸與野兔奔跳而去——據說那野兔正需要一件東西來換新牙。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: An old man, while staying in a firth to fish for salmon, lost his son, who died at some distance up the country; in his grief he could not persuade himself to leave his son's grave, and therefore put up his winter-house on the spot. In this lonely abode they were once surprised by seeing three men entering the house, one of them tall and long-nosed, the other smaller and with a flat nose, and the last of very small stature and white as snow. After passing the evening talking with the host the short-nosed man before starting asked for a piece of sole-leather, and the white one wanted a piece of walrus-tooth; the old man saw the departing visitors out, but when they left him stood dumfoundered at seeing them bounding off in the shape of a reindeer, a fox, and a hare — it is said that the hare had need of something for a new tooth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 106 'The Visiting Animals'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個老人住在海灣裡捕鮭魚時，失去了他的兒子，兒子死在內陸稍遠的地方；他悲痛不已，無法說服自己離開兒子的墳墓，於是就在那裡搭起了他的冬屋。在這孤寂的居所裡，他們有一次驚訝地看見三個男人走進屋來，其中一個身材高大、鼻子很長，另一個較矮、鼻子扁平，最後一個身材極小、白如積雪。與主人交談了一晚之後，那短鼻子的男人臨走前討要了一塊鞋底皮，那白色的則想要一塊海象牙；老人把離去的訪客送出門，但當他們離開他時，他目瞪口呆地看著他們化作一頭馴鹿、一隻狐狸和一隻野兔跳躍而去——據說那隻野兔需要點東西來長一顆新牙。

title.en: Avigiatsiak: Taken by the Whale, Reborn from the Seal
title.zh: 阿維吉阿茨夏克：鯨奪豹生

region.en: Beach where the knife was ground
region.zh: 磨刀的海灘

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 107 'Avigiatsiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Grinding her knife on the beach, the young woman Avigiatsiak is taken by a whale; living for a time with the whales she flees and is transformed into a seal — caught, hauled upon the ice, cut to pieces all excepting the head thrown beneath the bench — from thence she slips into the womb of the man's wife who had harpooned her, and is afterwards born anew, and called Avigiatsiak.
summary.zh: 在海灘磨刀的少女阿維吉阿茨夏克被鯨擄走；與鯨同處一段時日後逃出，化身為海豹——被人叉獲、拖上冰面肢解，唯頭顱被拋於長凳之下——她自那裡鑽入叉她之人的妻子腹中，重生為人，仍名阿維吉阿茨夏克。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: Avigiatsiak was the name of a young woman who, while grinding her knife on the beach, was taken by a whale; after living for a time with the whales she fled and was transformed into a seal, living with the seals. As such she was caught by a man, hauled upon the ice, and cut to pieces, all excepting the head which was thrown beneath the bench — from thence she slipped into the womb of the man's wife who had harpooned her, and was afterwards born anew and called Avigiatsiak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 107 'Avigiatsiak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿維吉亞齊阿克（Avigiatsiak）是一個年輕女子的名字，她在海灘上磨刀時被一頭鯨魚擄走；與鯨魚同住了一段時日之後，她逃了出來，並化為一頭海豹，與海豹們一同生活。正因如此，她被一個男人捕獲，拖上冰面，並被切成碎塊，唯有頭部倖免，被扔到長凳底下——她從那裡溜進了那個曾以魚叉刺中她的男人的妻子腹中，後來重新降生，取名為阿維吉亞齊阿克。

title.en: The Bird's Cliff: The House of Black and White People
title.zh: 鳥崖：黑民與白民之屋

region.en: Fog-bound sea and the cave in the rock
region.zh: 迷霧之海與巖中洞穴

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 108 'The Bird's Cliff', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Chased by a kayariak far off the land, father and son strike their persecutor dead from a flake of ice — but before sinking he spats repeatedly to all parts of the horizon, raising a dense fog that makes them wander. Landing at last, the angakok father perceives a house: one side inhabited by black people, the other by white ones; leaving after talk with both sides, they look back and see the house was a cave in the rock, the inhabitants gulls and ravens, and a drollish visitor staying with them, a falcon.
summary.zh: 父子在遠海被幽靈艇客追趕，自浮冰上將其擊斃——但那怪客沉海之前不斷向四方吐唾，霎時濃霧四起，父子迷失歸途。登岸後，身為巫師的父親覓得一屋：一側住著黑人，一側住著白人；與兩側居民交談作別後回望——那屋竟是巖中洞穴，居民原是海鷗與渡鴉，還有一位滑稽的訪客——獵隼。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: A father and his son, while kayaking far off the land, fell in with a kayariak who at once gave chase to them; they fortunately escaped by jumping out on a flake of ice, from which they struck their persecutor dead — but before sinking into the sea he spat repeatedly, turning round to all parts of the horizon, on which a dense fog arose causing them to wander and preventing their gaining their home. At last they reached land, and the father being angakok soon perceived a house and entered it — they found one side of it inhabited by black people and the other by white ones. After staying a while and having some talk with the inmates on both sides they left the house; but on looking behind them saw that the house was a cave in the rock, the inhabitants gulls and ravens, and a drollish visitor staying with them, a falcon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 108 'The Bird's Cliff'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位父親和他的兒子在遠離陸地的海上划著皮艇時，遇上了一名卡亞里阿克（kayariak），那人立刻向他們追來；他們僥倖逃脫，跳上一塊浮冰，從那塊浮冰上將追擊者擊斃——但那人沉入海中之前反覆吐唾沫，並向地平線四面八方轉動，於是升起一片濃霧，使他們迷失方向，無法歸家。最後他們終於抵達陸地，父親身為安加科克（angakok），很快便察覺到一座房屋並走了進去——他們發現房屋的一側住著黑人，另一側住著白人。待了一會兒，與兩側的居民都交談了幾句之後，他們便離開了那座房屋；但回頭一看，卻發現那房屋不過是岩石中的一個洞穴，居民是海鷗與渡鴉，還有一位滑稽古怪的訪客與他們同住，那是一隻隼。

title.en: Kuanak: The Angakok Who Came Back from the Sea-Bottom
title.zh: 庫阿納克：自海底歸來的巫師

region.en: South Greenland flight-roads and Pisugfik
region.zh: 南格陵蘭的飛行之路與皮蘇格菲克

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 109 'Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Head and feet tied for flight, Kuanak escapes the amarsiniook by dropping beneath sea and earth and emerging from his own house-floor; his drum soars of itself when he is found almost dying, an old kayak-cover having frightened him into his fall. Capsized by his own harpooned seal, he wakes at the sea-bottom with his grandmother, who ties his jacket close and pushes him up in a piece of skin — three landings scare him off (a urine-tub, a woman dressing her hair), the third fright would have lost him to the living for ever; at Pisugfik two dice-playing old men touch him senseless and chant him back, and his relatives, mourning-days done, hear his song from the boat that brings him home.
summary.zh: 縛首縛足而飛的庫阿納克，自山中竄出的阿馬爾西尼奧克魔掌下躍海而逃——穿海床、穿地底，從自家地板浮出；他的神鼓自行飛舞，而他幾乎凍斃於雪地——嚇他的是一張舊皮艇罩。被自己叉中的海豹掀翻後，他在海底醒來，祖母替他縛緊外套、以一塊皮為艇送他上升；三次登岸皆受驚逃（一盆尿、一個梳髮的女子），第三次若再受驚便永無生還之機——在皮蘇格菲克，兩個擲骰的老人觸他昏厥又以咒歌喚醒，送他還鄉；喪期已滿、幾已將他遺忘的親人，聽見送他回村的舟上唱起了庫阿納克的歌。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; documents anghiniartok revival at Pisugfik (compare tale 79).

passages.text: Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland, started for a flight, having previously had his feet and his head tied together; while passing along between two high rocks an amarsiniook rushed out from the mountain-side and wanted to take him into his hood — he made his escape by dropping into the sea, and proceeding onwards beneath the surface of the sea and the earth finally emerged from the floor of his own house. Another time when he had gone off on a flight his drum, which he had left in the house, was lifted up by itself and soared about in the room till at length it stopped and fell down; at that same moment a voice was heard from without, and hastening to look whence it came they found him in an almost dying state lying upon the snow, an old skin-cover from a kayak having frightened him and caused his downfall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 109 'Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫阿納克（Kuanak）是南格陵蘭的一位安加科克，他出發進行一次飛行，事先將自己的雙腳與頭部綁在一起；當他從兩塊高岩之間穿行而過時，一個阿馬爾西尼奧克（amarsiniook）從山腰衝出，想把他收進自己的兜帽裡——他跳入海中才得以逃脫，並繼續在海面與地面之下前行，最終從自己家中的地板下鑽了出來。另一次，當他外出飛行時，他留在屋裡的鼓自行升起，在房間裡飄來飄去，直到最後停下並落了下來；就在同一時刻，外面傳來一個聲音，他們趕忙去看聲音從何而來，發現他躺在雪地上，奄奄一息，原來是一張舊的皮艇皮罩嚇著了他，使他墜落。

passages.text: Kuanak was once capsized by a seal he had just harpooned; but being an anghiniartok his senses again returned, and he found himself at the bottom of the sea in company with his grandmother — she tied his kayak-jacket close to his body leaving no part of it uncovered, and then supplying him with a piece of skin by way of kayak pushed him upwards. When he emerged from the water he first betook himself far out to sea and thence made the land again, but happened to touch at an inhabited place where somebody was emptying out the urine-tub which scared him away from the shore — he tried to land on another place, but here a woman dressing her hair on the beach scared him away; if he had a third time taken fright he would never have returned to the land of the living.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 109 'Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 庫阿納克有一次被他剛用魚叉刺中的一頭海豹掀翻；但身為安吉尼亞爾托克（anghiniartok），他的知覺又恢復了過來，發現自己身處海底，與他的祖母在一起——她將他的皮艇上衣緊緊貼著他的身體綁好，不讓任何部位裸露在外，然後給他一塊皮子權當皮艇，把他向上推去。當他從水中浮出時，他先游向遠海，再從那裡重新靠岸，卻碰巧在一個有人居住的地方登陸，那裡有人正在倒尿桶，把他嚇得離開了海岸——他又試圖在另一處登陸，但這裡有一個女人在海灘上梳理頭髮，也把他嚇跑了；倘若他第三次受驚，便再也無法回到生者的世界了。

passages.text: But he happened to land at Pisugfik where a couple of old men were sitting playing at dice — they at once knew him to be an anghiniartok, and on merely touching his naked body he dropped down senseless; but on their chanting a magic lay he revived. They then brought him back to his homestead, where his relatives, who had already finished their days of mourning and nearly forgotten him, were gladly surprised at hearing the crew of the boat that brought him home intuning Kuanak's song.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 109 'Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 但他碰巧在皮蘇格菲克（Pisugfik）登陸，那裡有兩位老人正坐著擲骰子——他們立刻認出他是個安吉尼亞爾托克，僅僅碰了一下他赤裸的身體，他便失去知覺倒了下去；但當他們吟唱起一首咒歌時，他又甦醒過來。隨後他們把他帶回了他的家園，他的親屬們早已結束了哀悼的日子，幾乎把他忘卻，此刻聽到載他回家的那條船上的人們唱起庫阿納克的歌，都又驚又喜。

title.en: An Angakok on Kekertarsuak: The Funeral Kayak-Cover
title.zh: 凱克爾塔舒亞克的巫師：喪用艇罩

region.en: Kekertarsuak, the married sister's island
region.zh: 已婚姊妹所居的凱克爾塔舒亞克島

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 110 'An Angakok on Kekertarsuak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: His dogs stop dead before his sister's house; inside, all the people lie lifeless, eyes open and staring — his sister alone creeps towards him chewing, mouth widely opened as if to devour him, and the dogs start at the last moment. A conjuration and an angakok flight examine the place: those people had been frightened to death by the sight of a skin-cover from a kayak, which had been used at a funeral to carry the corpse upon.
summary.zh: 犬隊在妹妹的屋前僵立不前；屋內之人橫躺直坐、圓睜雙目、氣息全無——唯有妹妹蠕動著嘴如咀嚼狀，大張著口向他爬來，犬隊在最後關頭方才驚起。巫師歸家降神、飛往勘察：那些人都是被一張皮艇罩嚇死的——那正是喪禮上用來抬屍的艇罩。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; mass fright-death documented.

passages.text: An Angakok on Kekertarsuak set off in his sledge to visit his married sister; on approaching the house his dogs suddenly stopped. After in vain trying to urge them on with his whip he alighted and went up to the house on foot — but seeing no people about he looked in at the window, and was horror-struck at seeing all the people lying or sitting about lifeless, their eyes open and staring. His sister alone showed signs of life, and seeing her brother began to move her mouth as if chewing, and crept towards the entrance; at sight of this he was struck with terror and fled to his dogs, but was again unable to make them stir — not until the sister had come quite close, her mouth widely opened as if to devour him, did they suddenly start, and thus he escaped to his home. Afterwards he performed a conjuration and undertook an angakok flight to examine the place — on his return he reported that those people had been frightened to death by the sight of a skin-cover from a kayak (viz., which had been used at a funeral to carry the corpse upon).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 110 'An Angakok on Kekertarsuak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 凱克塔爾蘇阿克（Kekertarsuak）的一位安加科克乘著雪橇出發去探望他已出嫁的妹妹；快到他妹妹家時，他的狗突然停了下來。他用鞭子催促牠們前進，卻徒勞無功，於是下了雪橇，步行走向那座房屋——但見四周不見人影，他便從窗戶往裡張望，驚恐地看到所有人都橫七豎八地躺著或坐著，毫無生氣，眼睛睜得大大的，直直瞪著。唯有他的妹妹還顯出幾分生氣，她看見哥哥，便開始像咀嚼似地動起嘴來，並朝門口爬去；見此情景，他驚恐萬分，逃向他的狗，卻又無法讓牠們動彈——直到妹妹已爬得相當近，嘴巴大張，彷彿要把他吞下，牠們才猛然起步，他這才逃回了家。後來他施行了一場法術，並進行了一次安加科克飛行去察看那個地方——歸來後他報告說，那些人都是被一張皮艇皮罩（即葬禮時用來搬運屍體的那種）的景象給嚇死的。

title.en: Singajuk and His Descendants: Mangilak, Baptised Moses
title.zh: 辛亞尤克家世：受洗名摩西的曼吉拉克

region.en: Kangek near Godthaab
region.zh: 努克附近的康格克

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 111 'Singajuk and his Descendants', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A miscarried child swaddled in eider-duck skin, fostered with the utmost care to keep it alive, Mangilak becomes one of the most powerful of men — his first deed killing an ingnersuak. Caught in a gale, he learns a calm-spell by listening to a gull swimming in a solitary patch of smooth water, and from that time was not to be equalled in kayaking. Widowed, he visits his wife's grave and talks with the deceased, who gives him a mussel-shell containing a drink to endow him with angakok wisdom; he married again, and his son Akajarok died a Christian, while Mangilak himself, baptised and named Moses, was too full of angakok wisdom to become more than a nominal Christian.
summary.zh: 一個流產的嬰孩被裹在絨鴨皮中、悉心哺育才得存活——曼吉拉克長成為最強悍的人之一，首功便是誅殺一名地下精靈。海上遇風暴時，他聽著靜水窪中泅游的海鷗之聲習得止風咒，從此划艇無人能敵。喪妻後他常去墳前與亡妻交談，她以貝殼盛來一杯賦予巫智的飲液；再娶得子，其孫女正是講述此故事者之祖母。其子阿卡亞洛克以基督徒身分离世；曼吉拉克自己受洗名摩西，卻因巫智太深，始終只是個掛名的基督徒。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale with genealogical frame (the narrator's own ancestor); Christian syncretism noted in the source.

passages.text: Singajuk was a celebrated hunter living in Kangek (near Godthaab); his wife miscarried and brought forth a poor little wretch of a child that was swaddled in the skin of an eider-duck, and had to be fostered with the utmost care to keep it alive — this child was called Mangilak, and became one of the most powerful of men. His first deed was killing an ingnersuak; afterwards he was once caught in a gale of wind at sea, but espying a solitary spot of smooth water and a gull swimming in it, by dint of listening to its voice he learned a spell for procuring a calm, and from that time he was not to be equalled in kayaking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 111 'Singajuk and his Descendants'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 辛加尤克是住在坎格克（近哥特哈布）的一位著名獵人；他的妻子流產，生下一個瘦弱可憐的小嬰孩，這孩子被裹在絨鴨皮裡，必須極其小心地撫養才能活下來——這孩子名叫曼吉拉克，後來成為最強壯的人之一。他的第一件功績是殺死了一隻因格納蘇阿克；之後有一次他在海上遭遇狂風，但他望見一小片平靜的水面，有一隻海鷗在其中游著，他憑著傾聽牠的聲音學會了一道能招來平靜的咒語，從那時起，他在划皮艇方面便無人能及。

passages.text: His mother then persuaded him to marry, and he took a wife who however shortly afterwards died; being almost a wizard he used to visit her grave and talk with the deceased, and on one occasion she gave him a mussel-shell containing a drink to endow him with angakok wisdom. Mangilak married a second wife and got a son called Akajarok, whose daughter became the grandmother of the man who related this story (to the author); Akajarok died a Christian — Mangilak also was baptised and named Moses, but was too full of angakok wisdom to become more than a nominal Christian.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 111 'Singajuk and his Descendants'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的母親隨後勸他娶妻，他便娶了一個妻子，然而她不久之後就死了；他幾乎算是個巫師，常去她的墳前與死者交談，有一次她給了他一個貽貝殼，裡面盛著飲料，能賦予他安加科克的智慧。曼吉拉克又娶了第二個妻子，生了一個兒子名叫阿卡亞羅克，阿卡亞羅克的女兒成了（向作者）講述這個故事之人的祖母；阿卡亞羅克死時是基督徒——曼吉拉克也受了洗，取名摩西，但他滿腦子都是安加科克的智慧，只能算是名義上的基督徒。

title.en: The Cousins: The Toolik's Red-Hot Weapon
title.zh: 表兄弟：托洛克之赤熱兇器

region.en: The enemies' house and the flying angakok
region.zh: 仇家之屋與飛行的巫師

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 112 'The Cousins', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Like tale 15 but with the revenge brought on by an angakok who assisted the cousins on a flight: staying with them he invoked his tornak the toolik, who carried a red-hot weapon and destroyed the house and all its inhabitants by fire while the angakok flew homewards. Narrating the deed to his people, a laughing voice was heard from without, recognised as that of his erkungasok (the ingenious and cunning adviser, but rather powerless and boasting dweller among the tornaks), come to give notice of his having also assisted at the destruction of his enemies.
summary.zh: 與故事十五同型，但復仇由巫師促成：他在飛行中陪伴表兄弟，召來手持赤熱兇器的靈助托洛克——趁巫師飛回之際，一把火燒燬仇家之屋及其全部居民。歸家講述戰果時，屋外傳來笑聲——那是他的厄爾孔加索克（靈助中足智多謀卻無甚本事、慣於自誇的傢伙）——特地前來表功：那場火他也有份。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: This tale is somewhat similar to No. 15, but in the present version the revenge is brought on by an angakok who assisted the cousins on a flight; while staying with them he invoked his tornak the toolik, who carried a red-hot weapon and destroyed the house and all its inhabitants by fire while the angakok flew homewards. After his return to his house while narrating the deed to his people a laughing voice was heard from without, recognised as that of his erkungasok (the ingenious and cunning adviser, but rather powerless and boasting dweller among the tornaks), who came to give notice of his having also assisted at the destruction of his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 112 'The Cousins'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個故事與第十五則有些相似，但在本版本中，復仇是由一位協助表兄弟們逃亡的安加科克所促成的；他與他們同住時召喚了他的托爾納克——圖利克，圖利克帶著一件燒得通紅的武器，在安加科克飛回家時，以火毀掉了那座房子和其中的所有居民。他回到自己的房子後，正向族人講述此事時，外面傳來一個帶笑聲的聲音，聽出是他的埃爾孔加索克（那位機敏狡猾的謀士，但其實相當無力且愛吹噓，棲身於托爾納克之間），他前來告知自己也曾參與毀滅他的敵人。

title.en: Manik: The Boat-Crew of Rowing Girls
title.zh: 馬尼克：一船划槳的姑娘

region.en: Coast to the far north
region.zh: 海岸至遙遠北方

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 113 'Manik', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A bachelor till the day he suddenly ordered his mother to make ready the boat: he carried away the chief hunter's daughter crying and struggling in vain, pushed off north with all speed, and at every inhabited place carried away another woman — until he had got a complete boat's crew of rowing girls. Wintering in the far north he had an adventurous meeting with the ghost of a deceased woman, and found people feasting upon various meats hauled from the ground by magic lays; next year he returned all the women to their relatives excepting the first one, kept for his wife.
summary.zh: 孑然一身的馬尼克忽然命母親備船：他搶走大獵手的女兒——她哭喊掙扎皆屬徒勞——飛速北去；途經每一處村落便再搶一名女子，直到湊齊一船划槳的姑娘。遠北過冬時，他奇遇一名亡婦之魂，又見一屋之人以咒歌自地底拉出各色肉食宴飲；翌年南歸，他把女子們一一送還親屬，只留下第一個作為妻子。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; abduction presented as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Manik was a great seal-hunter, but his mother in vain urged him to take a wife; he continued a bachelor till one day he suddenly ordered his mother to make ready the boat for removing from the place. As soon as she had made all ready he hastened up to the house of the chief hunter, who at the time was absent, and carried away his daughter, crying and struggling in vain to be released. Having placed her on the boat he at once pushed off and made for the north with all speed; at the first inhabited place they came past he again carried away a woman, and this continued until he had got a complete boat's crew of rowing girls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 113 'Manik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬尼克是個了不起的海豹獵人，但他的母親勸他娶妻卻徒勞無功；他一直單身，直到有一天他突然吩咐母親備好船，要離開這個地方。她剛把一切準備妥當，他便趕到首領獵人的屋前，那人當時不在，他擄走了他的女兒，她哭喊著、掙扎著，卻無法脫身。他把她安置在船上後，立刻撐船離岸，全速向北而去；在他們經過的第一個有人居住的地方，他又擄走了一個女人，如此繼續，直到他湊齊了整整一船划槳的女孩。

passages.text: He continued his voyage the whole season till at length, having reached the far north, the frost set in and for the time obliged him to take up his quarters there; while wintering here and making excursions into the country he once came to a solitary house where he had an adventurous meeting with the ghost of a deceased woman, and from there came to another where he found the people feasting upon various meats which they kept hauling from the ground by help of magic lays. The next year he set out for his own country, returning to their relatives all the women excepting only the first one, whom he kept for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 113 'Manik'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他整個季節都在繼續航行，直到終於抵達極北之地，霜凍來臨，一時迫使他就在那裡落腳；他在此過冬並到鄉間遊歷時，有一次來到一座孤零零的房子，在那裡與一個死去女人的鬼魂有過一場驚險的相遇，又從那裡來到另一處，發現人們正享用各種肉食，他們靠著魔法咒歌把這些肉從地裡拉出來。第二年他動身返回自己的家鄉，把所有的女人都送還給她們的親人，只留下第一個，娶她為妻。

title.en: The Land of the Isarukitsok Bird
title.zh: 大海雀之鄉

region.en: The sunken promontory south of Godthaab
region.zh: 努克以南已沉沒的海岬

period: Inuit oral tradition; a story from South Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 114 'The Land of the Isarukitsok Bird', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Lost in fog, three kayakers come to a high promontory of one continuous steep inaccessible cliff inhabited by crowds of isarukitsoks (the great auk); resting and filling their kayaks with birds, they put off again and pass by one of the monstrous gulls which are in the habit of picking up kayakers and giving them as food to their young ones — but reach home in safety. Before the land of the isarukitsok sank, there were plenty of these birds about Nook (Godthaab).
summary.zh: 霧中迷航的三名皮艇客，來到一道綿延陡峭、人不可攀的海岬——其上棲滿大海雀；他們飽餐海鳥、滿載皮艇而歸，途中經過一隻慣於抓起皮艇客餵雛的巨鷗——幸而平安到家。據說在大海雀之鄉沉沒之前，努克一帶這種鳥還很多。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; the great auk (Pinguinus impennis) extinction is embedded in the legend.

passages.text: Two young men with one elder companion lost their way when kayaking in foggy weather, and having roamed about without being able to sight any land came to a high promontory, showing one continuous steep and inaccessible cliff, inhabited by crowds of isarukitsoks. By following the coast they at last came to a landing-place, and found a nice situation where they rested themselves and had their strength restored by eating birds — having also filled their kayaks with them they put off to sea again, and happened to pass by one of the monstrous gulls which are in the habit of picking up the kayakers and giving them as food to their young ones; but they reached their home in safety. It is told that before the land of the isarukitsok sank there were plenty of these birds about Nook (Godthaab).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 114 'The Land of the Isarukitsok Bird'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩個年輕人和一位年長的同伴在霧天划皮艇時迷了路，他們四處遊蕩，始終望不見任何陸地，後來來到一座高聳的海角，只見一道連續不斷的陡峭懸崖，無法攀登，上面棲息著成群的伊薩魯基措克。他們沿著海岸走，終於來到一處登陸點，找到一個不錯的地方，便在那裡休息，吃了些鳥，體力得以恢復——他們也把皮艇裝滿了鳥，然後再次出海，途中恰好經過一隻巨大的海鷗，這種海鷗慣於抓起划皮艇的人，拿去餵牠們的幼鳥；但他們平安回到了家。據說在伊薩魯基措克之地沉沒之前，努克（哥特哈布）一帶有許多這種鳥。

title.en: The Kuinasarinook: Uvnek Summons the Amarsiniook
title.zh: 庫伊納薩里努克：烏夫內克召喚山魔

region.en: Firth of Godthaab and the monster-mountains
region.zh: 努克峽灣與魔怪之山

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 116 'The Kuinasarinook', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Uvnek, one of the last angakut at the firth of Godthaab, on one of his spirit-flights narrowly escaped being taken by an amarsiniook; after his return he once performed a conjuration and summoned the amarsiniook — a brightness was observed, and a voice from above the house: 'If thou hadst not happened to be an angakok thou wouldst never have escaped; it was I who killed the kuinasarinook (another monster dwelling in certain mountains), because it had torn a man to pieces.' The auditors remembered how some time ago a man had been found dead, his body terribly mutilated, nobody able to make out how the murder was committed till it was thus explained by Uvnek.
summary.zh: 努克峽灣末代巫師之一的烏夫內克，在一次靈魂飛行中險遭山魔阿馬爾西尼奧克擄走；歸來後他降神召其現身——屋頂上方亮光一閃，傳來聲音：『若你不是巫師，斷難逃脫。是我殺了庫伊納薩里努克（另一種居於某些山中的魔怪），因為它把一個人撕成了碎片。』眾人這才想起：先前確有一人陳屍荒野、殘缺難辨，兇手成謎——直到烏夫內克一語道破。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: Uvnek, one of the last angakut at the firth of Godthaab, on one of his spirit-flights narrowly escaped being taken by an amarsiniook. After his return he once performed a conjuration and summoned the amarsiniook — a brightness was observed, and a voice was heard from above the house saying, 'If thou hadst not happened to be an angakok thou wouldst never have escaped; it was I who killed the kuinasarinook (another monster, dwelling in certain mountains), because it had torn a man to pieces.' The auditors then remembered how some time ago a man had been found dead and his body terribly mutilated; but nobody had been able to make out how the murder was committed till it was thus explained by Uvnek.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 116 'The Kuinasarinook'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 烏夫內克是戈特霍布峽灣最後幾位安加庫特（巫師）之一，有一次他在神遊途中險些被一隻阿馬西尼奧克（amarsiniook）擄去。歸來之後，他曾施行一次召魂術，召來了那隻阿馬西尼奧克——眾人看見一道亮光，又聽見屋上傳來一個聲音說：「若不是你恰好是個安加庫克，你絕逃不脫；殺死庫伊納薩里努克（kuinasarinook，另一種怪物，棲居於某些山中）的正是我，因為它把一個人撕成了碎片。」聽者這才想起，前些時候曾發現一人死去，屍體被殘害得慘不忍睹；可是誰也弄不清這樁兇殺是如何犯下的，直到烏夫內克如此解明。

title.en: Ajagutarsuk and Ularpana: The Tornaks' Duel
title.zh: 阿亞古塔舒克與烏拉爾帕納：靈助對決

region.en: The cave and the dried-up lake
region.zh: 巖穴與乾涸的湖底

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 117 'An Old Man who was always anxious to outdo other People', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Two old men anxious to outdo everyone bet in turn on whose wife should first get a son, then which son should become the greatest angakok: Ajagutarsuk attained angakok wisdom in a cave, Ularpana acquired it in a dried-up lake. The latter flew to visit the former, who called forth his tornaks belonging to the inlanders — but Ularpana invoked his, the upper ingnersuit, who totally defeated the inlanders.
summary.zh: 兩位事事爭勝的老人先賭誰的妻子先得子，再賭誰的兒子能成為最偉大的巫師：阿亞古塔舒克在巖穴中修得巫智，烏拉爾帕納在乾涸的湖底得道。後者飛往探望前者——阿亞古塔舒克召出內陸人的靈助；烏拉爾帕納則喚出上位因格內爾舒特人，把內陸人殺得大敗。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: An Old Man who was always anxious to outdo other People had laid a bet with his friend as to whose wife should first get a son, and afterwards as to which of their sons should in course of time become the greatest angakok. One of them, Ajagutarsuk, attained angakok wisdom in a cave; and the other, named Ularpana, acquired it in a dried-up lake. The latter went on an angakok flight to the first, and while staying with him Ajagutarsuk called forth his tornaks which belonged to the inlanders, and instantly appeared — but Ularpana invoked his tornaks, being the upper ingnersuit, who totally defeated the inlanders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 117 'An Old Man who was always anxious to outdo other People'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個老人總想勝過別人，他先與朋友打賭，看誰的妻子先得兒子，後來又賭他們的兒子日後誰能成為最偉大的安加庫克。其中一人名叫阿亞古塔爾蘇克，在一處洞穴中修得安加庫克之智；另一人名為烏拉爾帕納，則在一座乾涸的湖中修得此智。後來烏拉爾帕納作安加庫克之遊，飛往前者處；當他留居其間時，阿亞古塔爾蘇克召出了他那些屬於內陸人的托爾納克（tornaks），它們立刻現身——但烏拉爾帕納也召出了他的托爾納克，即上方的因格內爾蘇伊特（ingnersuit），它們把那些內陸人徹底擊敗。

title.en: The Revenging Animals: The Merganser's Eggs
title.zh: 復仇的動物：秋沙鴨之卵

region.en: Midsummer islands
region.zh: 仲夏的島嶼

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 118 'The Revenging Animals', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A great angakok seized by a longing for eggs carries off a merganser's whole nest — and on the way home the robbed seals voice their plan: fetch a piece of ice and return as umiarissat. The filth thrown on the beach turns their seal-manned boat to a piece of ice; later the gooseander's head emerges from the entrance with dreadfully enlarged eyes — come to fetch its eggs back by a charm that made him forget them in his kayak; had he not left them it certainly would have frightened them all to death. Another angakok in a similar case was bereft of his angakok power by the merganser.
summary.zh: 貪食鳥蛋的大巫師搬空了秋沙鴨的整巢——歸途上被搶的海豹群商議：『去搬塊冰來，化作幽靈之舟報仇！』灘上潑灑的穢物令那艘海豹駕驭的大舟現出冰塊原形；入夜，鵲鴨之頭自門口探出、雙眼脹得駭人——它是來討回鳥蛋的，靠咒術使他忘了蛋還在艇上；若非他恰好忘帶，必把全屋的人嚇死。另一位犯下同樣過錯的巫師，則被秋沙鴨奪去了全部法力。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; umiarissat = the avenging boat-people of overkilled seals (compare tale 14 note).

passages.text: A great angakok, while kayaking about at midsummer, suddenly took a longing for eggs; landing upon an island he found a merganser's nest with plenty of eggs, all of which he carried away. On his way home he met with a flock of seals of which he harpooned one — but after having taken it he heard voices from among the rest encouraging each other to go and get hold of a piece of ice and return as umiarissat. On getting home he walked up to his house forgetting the eggs in his kayak, but ordered his housemates to throw down on the beach all manner of filthy stuff to frighten away the umiarissat — in the evening a boat was seen to arrive manned with seals, but as soon as they scented the filth they all jumped into the water and the boat appeared as a piece of ice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 118 'The Revenging Animals'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位偉大的安加庫克在仲夏時節划著皮艇，忽然極想吃到鳥蛋；他登上一個島，發現一個秋沙鴨的巢，裡面有許多蛋，便把它們全都帶走了。回家途中他遇到一群海豹，便叉中了一隻——可是捕獲之後，他聽見其餘海豹中間有聲音在互相慫恿，要它們去取一塊冰來，然後化作烏米亞里薩特（umiarissat）回來。到家後他走上屋子，卻把皮艇裡的蛋忘了，只吩咐家中的人把各種污穢之物扔到海灘上，好把烏米亞里薩特嚇走——傍晚時分，只見一隻船載著海豹駛來，可是它們一聞到那污穢之氣，便全都跳入水中，那隻船也現形為一塊冰。

passages.text: Later in the evening a voice was heard outside, and the head of the gooseander emerged from the entrance with dreadfully enlarged eyes; addressing itself to the angakok it scolded him for having robbed it of its descendants, but now it had come to fetch its eggs back, having by help of a charm caused him to forget them and leave them in his kayak — if he had not left them it certainly would have frightened them all to death. Another angakok in a similar case was bereft of his angakok power by the merganser.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 118 'The Revenging Animals'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當晚更晚些時候，外面傳來一個聲音，那隻秋沙鴨的頭從入口探了進來，眼睛脹得可怕地大；它對安加庫克說話，責備他奪走了它的子孫，但它如今是來取回它的蛋的，因為它藉助一道符咒使他忘了那些蛋，把它們留在了皮艇裡——倘若他沒有留下它們，它必定會把他們全都嚇死。另一位安加庫克在類似的情形下，則被那隻秋沙鴨奪去了安加庫克的法力。

title.en: The Igdlokok: The Guest with One Footprint
title.zh: 伊格德洛洛克：只留一隻腳印的客人

region.en: Lonely house of the mourning man
region.zh: 守喪者的孤屋

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 119 'The Igdlokok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Having seen his beloved cousin torn to pieces by a sorcery-made bear, a man braves every danger for excitement and first kills an amarok — then a talkative stranger drops into his lonely house, also mourning a brother, and spends the evening pleasantly until the hostess serves the boiled amarok-flesh: 'But I see the dish is all aslope' — and the same instant he vanishes through the entrance. His footsteps in the snow are made by only one foot: the guest must have been an igdlokok, whose body is only the one half of the human body cut in twain.
summary.zh: 親眼目睹摯友被術造之熊撕碎的男子，為求刺激而歷險，先殺一頭狼靈阿馬洛克；夜裡一名健談的陌生人不請自入——同樣是喪失兄弟而四處歷險的人——賓主盡歡，直到女主人端上燉好的狼靈肉。客人連聲稱贊其香其色，卻忽然說：『可惜這盤子是斜的。』話音未落便穿門而去。雪地上的腳印只有一隻——原來那是伊格德洛洛克：軀體只有人被剖開的一半。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; note records a variant where the vanishing guests appear as the stars Siagtut or Qilugtussat.

passages.text: A man had lost his beloved cousin and friend, who in his sight had been torn to pieces by one of those bears that are made by sorcery. In his despair he went out to encounter and brave all kinds of danger by way of excitement, and first killed an amarok. One evening when staying at home he was surprised in his lonely house by a stranger dropping in, who explained that he also having lost his brother was roaming about for excitement; being very talkative he spent the evening there very pleasantly, until the hostess who had boiled some flesh of the amarok came and served it before the men. The guest then burst out in loud praises of its delicious flavour and tempting appearance — but before he had taken a morsel he went on, 'But I see the dish is all aslope,' and the same instant arose and vanished through the entrance. The host immediately followed him; and on examining his footsteps in the snow found them to be made by only one foot, so that the guest must have been an igdlokok (whose body is only the one half of the human body cut in twain).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 119 'The Igdlokok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個人失去了他心愛的堂兄弟兼摯友，那人曾在他眼前被一頭由巫術造出的熊撕成碎片。他在絕望中外出，藉以尋求刺激，去迎戰並冒盡種種危險，首先殺死了一頭阿馬羅克（amarok）。一天傍晚，他待在家中，獨居的屋裡忽然闖進一個陌生人，令他大吃一驚；那人解釋說，他也失去了兄弟，正四處遊蕩尋求刺激；他十分健談，在那裡度過了非常愉快的一晚，直到女主人煮了些阿馬羅克的肉，端來擺在兩個男人面前。那客人隨即大聲讚歎肉味鮮美、色相誘人——可是還沒吃上一口，他又接著說：「但我看這盤子是歪的。」話音剛落便起身，從入口消失了。主人立刻跟了出去；在雪地裡察看他的足跡，發現那隻有一隻腳踩出的印子，可見那客人必定是個伊格德洛科克（igdlokok，其身體只是被劈成兩半的人體之一半）。

title.en: Iviangersook Travelled All Around the Coast of Greenland
title.zh: 伊萬格舒克環格陵蘭海岸記

region.en: Cape Farewell, the eastward light-haired people, and Ilulissat Sound
region.zh: 費爾韋爾角、東岸淺髮族人與伊盧利薩特水道

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 120 'Iviangersook travelled all around the Coast of Greenland', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Starting for the south and passing Cape Farewell, Iviangersook came on the eastward to some light-haired people of European complexion, and lastly returned through the Sound, which was formerly open from east to west, near Ilulissat (Jakobshavn). When approaching his home near Godthaab he lost his brother, who was buried upon a small island after them named Uviarniak — one who travelled all around.
summary.zh: 伊萬格舒克南行繞過費爾韋爾角，在東岸遇見淺色頭髮、面貌如歐人的部族；最後經由昔日貫通東西的水道——伊盧利薩特附近——返航。將抵努克家園時失去了兄弟；他被葬在一座小島上，島從此以他們命名為烏維亞尼亞克——『環行一周者』。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; cross-ref inuit-inhabitants-akilinek (Rink tale 128).

passages.text: Iviangersook travelled all around the Coast of Greenland: he started for the south, and having passed Cape Farewell came on the eastward to some light-haired people of European complexion, and lastly returned through the Sound which was formerly open from east to west near Ilulissat (Jakobshavn). When approaching his home near Godthaab he lost his brother, who was buried upon a small island after them named Uviarniak (one who travelled all around).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 120 'Iviangersook travelled all around the Coast of Greenland'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊維安格爾蘇克繞行格陵蘭海岸一周：他先向南出發，過了法韋爾角便向東行，來到一些淺髮、具歐洲人膚色的人那裡，最後經由那道海峽返回——那海峽從前在伊盧利薩特（雅各布港）附近是自東向西敞開的。當他走近戈特霍布附近的家時，失去了他的兄弟；兄弟被葬在一個小島上，那島後來便以他們之名稱為烏維亞爾尼亞克（意為「繞行一周者」）。

title.en: The Childless Couple Who Were Both Angakok
title.zh: 雙巫夫妻的無子之嘆

region.en: Foreign place with the witch's ghost
region.zh: 巫婆之魂出沒的異鄉

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 121 'A Married Couple remained childless on account of their both being Angakok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Kayaking together as always, the angakok couple finds a young man almost dying in a foreign place; the man conjures the witch, detects her ghost approaching to touch the youth with her black hands, thrusts his harpoon at her heel — and almost at the same moment the aunt dies in the next house, proved to have been the witch. Envying the playing children — 'That crowd of boys might almost make people envious' — they are answered: 'The boys yonder are the namesakes of those whom the monster-gulls carried off as food for their young ones' — and the whole assembly at once becomes silent.
summary.zh: 相偕出海的巫師夫婦在異鄉遇見一名垂死的青年；丈夫降神召出害人的巫婆——識得她的鬼魂正要以黑手觸碰病者——一叉刺中她的腳跟；幾乎同時，隔壁的姑母死了，正是那巫婆。羨慕屋中嬉戲的孩子——『這群男孩簡直叫人嫉妒』——得到的回答是：『他們都是被巨鷗抓去餵雛的那些人的承名者』（即葬身海上者）——滿屋霎時寂然。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: The husband and wife always used to go out kayaking together; once they happened to come to a foreign place where a young man was found in an almost dying state. The angakok-man began a conjuration summoning the witch who had caused his sickness — he detected the ghost of the witch approaching the sick youth in order to touch him with her black hands, but the angakok thrust his harpoon at her, hitting her heel; almost at the same moment the aunt of the sick youth died in the next house and proved to have been the witch. While spending the rest of the evening there eating and talking in a pleasant way the visitors noticed the children playing on the floor; and thinking of their own childless state burst out, 'That crowd of boys might almost make people envious' — they were answered, 'The boys yonder are the namesakes of those whom the monster-gulls carried off as food for their young ones' (viz., who perished in kayaks); whereupon the whole assembly at once became silent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 121 'A Married Couple remained childless on account of their both being Angakok'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那對夫妻從前總是結伴划皮艇出遊；有一回他們偶然來到一處陌生的地方，發現一名年輕人奄奄一息。那名巫師男子開始施法，召喚導致他生病的女巫——他察覺到女巫的鬼魂正逼近這名生病的青年，想用她那雙黑手觸碰他，但巫師朝她擲出魚叉，擊中了她的腳跟；幾乎在同一時刻，生病青年的姑母在隔壁屋裡死去，事後證明她就是那個女巫。他們在那裡度過當晚餘下的時光，愉快地吃喝閒談，來客注意到孩子們在地板上玩耍；想到自己膝下無子，便脫口而出：「那一群男孩真叫人幾乎要嫉妒了」——他們得到的回答是：「那邊那些男孩，是那些被巨鷗叼去餵雛鳥的人的同名者」（即那些葬身皮艇的人）；此言一出，滿座頓時鴉雀無聲。

title.en: The Old Man Who Killed the Inlander Using the Fog as Kayak
title.zh: 以霧為艇：老人誤殺內陸人

region.en: The son's grave up the firth
region.zh: 峽灣深處兒子的墳墓

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 122 'An Old Man lost his only Son', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Visiting his son's reindeer-hunting grave, an old man sees an inlander pulling himself through the water without any kayak — 'using the fog as kayak' — and after some angry words kills him. Another time an inlander questions his grief — 'Yonder wretched heap of stones is the only object of my distress' — and tells how he also lost a son seal-hunting: the old man makes out it must have been the one he had killed, pretends to be expected home, pushes off in his skiff, and never more visits the grave of his son.
summary.zh: 常去峽灣深處兒子墳前憑弔的老人，一日見一名內陸人不駕艇而自行划水而來——『以霧為艇』——爭執幾句後將其殺死。再訪墳塋時，另一名內陸人問他何以悲傷——『那一堆可憐的石頭便是我全部的哀愁』——並說自己也折了一個出海的兒子；老人認出那正是被他殺死的年輕人，謊稱家人等他回去，掉槳而去，從此再不上墳。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: An Old Man lost his only Son when they were both reindeer-hunting up the country; after returning home he often used to visit his son's grave. Kayaking up the firth with this view he once right before him saw an inlander pulling himself through the water without any kayak ('using the fog as kayak'), and after some angry words killed the inlander. Another time when he was again visiting the grave he was surprised at the sight of an inlander who questioned him as to the cause of his grief — 'Yonder wretched heap of stones is the only object of my distress,' he answered. The inlander then told him how he also had some time ago lost a son who had been seal-hunting; the old man made out that it must have been the one he had killed — on which he pretended to be expected home, pushed off in his skiff, and never more visited the grave of his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 122 'An Old Man lost his only Son'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名老人與他唯一的兒子一同在內陸獵馴鹿時失去了兒子；返家之後，他常常去兒子的墳墓探望。有一次，他為此划著皮艇溯灣而上，忽然就在正前方看見一名內陸人不用任何皮艇、只憑自身在水中前行（「以霧為皮艇」），經過一番怒言相向之後，他殺死了那名內陸人。另一次，他再度前去掃墓時，驚見一名內陸人，那人問他為何如此悲傷——「那邊那堆可憐的石頭，就是我唯一傷心之物。」他答道。那內陸人於是告訴他，自己不久前也失去了一個獵海豹的兒子；老人推斷那必定就是他所殺的那一個——於是他假稱家中有人等他回去，推開小艇離去，此後再也不曾去兒子的墳前探望。

title.en: Angakorsiak: Shame Turned Him into a Reindeer
title.zh: 安加科夏克：羞愧化鹿

region.en: The northern angakok's island
region.zh: 北方巫師的島嶼

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 123 'Angakorsiak was very proud of his Angakok Wisdom', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Proud of his angakok wisdom, Angakorsiak challenges a northern rival in broad daylight: he cuts off his arm near the shoulder, replaces it drinking the blood, swallows an arrow-point and makes it appear again, opens his stomach with a knife — the rival repeats all with the utmost perfection and proposes a kayak-race, casting a harpoon into a rock so it enters the stone and blood springs from it. Angakorsiak fails, harpoon broken and lost, capsizes from shame and sinks — a reindeer immediately emerges and runs up the beach; shame having thus transformed him, he turns man again and hastens away, resolved to give up all kind of emulation in future.
summary.zh: 自負巫智的安加科夏克向北方同行下戰書：當眾斬臂、接臂飲血、吞箭吐箭、剖腹示腸——對手分毫不差地重演一遍，還提議賽艇：一叉擲入巖石，入石三分、石上迸血。安加科夏克如法炮製卻叉斷柄折；歸途羞愧低頭、翻艇沉底——轉瞬一頭馴鹿出水奔上山坡：羞愧把他變成了鹿。他復為人形後倉皇而去，發誓從此不再與人爭勝。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; several variants exist of the angakut's deeds.

passages.text: Angakorsiak was very proud of his Angakok Wisdom, and always roamed about seeking opportunities of emulating other angakut; when he happened to surpass them he used to mock and ridicule them in a most overbearing manner. Once he visited an angakok far up north and challenged him to a match, at which, in broad daylight, they were to contend in working the wonders of their art before an assembly. Angakorsiak began his performance by cutting off his arm near the shoulder, inserting it again and drinking the blood from the wound; after which he swallowed an arrow-point and made it appear again, opened his stomach with a knife, and so on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 123 'Angakorsiak was very proud of his Angakok Wisdom'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 安加科爾西亞克對自己的巫師智慧極為自負，總是四處遊走，尋找與其他巫師較量的機會；每當他勝過他們，便以最盛氣凌人的姿態嘲弄譏笑他們。有一次，他遠赴北方拜訪一位巫師，向他挑戰，約定在大白天於眾人面前較量法術神通。安加科爾西亞克先表演：他在近肩處砍下自己的手臂，再把它接回去，並飲下傷口流出的血；接著他吞下一枚箭頭又使它重現，用刀剖開自己的肚子，如此等等。

passages.text: When he had finished the other angakok repeated the same feats with the utmost perfection, and then remarked, 'Well, what we have yet done amounts to nothing; but I should now like to try a kayak-race with thee.' They went down in their kayaks, and the angakok of the place taking his way to an island threw his harpoon at a rock with such force as to make it enter the stone and blood to spring from it — Angakorsiak on trying this entirely failed, his harpoon being broken and lost. On their way back to the shore he bent down his head from shame, capsized his kayak, and sank — but directly afterwards a reindeer emerged from the water and ran up on the beach. Shame having thus transformed him into a reindeer he afterwards turned a man again, and hastened away, resolved to give up all kind of emulation in future.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 123 'Angakorsiak was very proud of his Angakok Wisdom'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他表演完畢後，另一位巫師以極其完美的身手重複了同樣的技藝，然後說道：「唉，我們至今所做的都不算什麼；不過我現在倒想與你比一場皮艇競速。」他們乘皮艇下水，當地那位巫師划向一座島嶼，朝一塊岩石擲出魚叉，力道之大竟使魚叉插入石中，並有血從石中湧出——安加科爾西亞克一試之下徹底失敗，他的魚叉折斷失落。在返回岸邊的途中，他羞愧地低下頭，翻覆了皮艇，沉了下去——但緊接著一頭馴鹿從水中浮現，奔上灘岸。羞愧就這樣把他變成一頭馴鹿，他後來又變回人形，匆匆離去，決心今後放棄一切爭勝之心。

title.en: Tuagtuanguak: Five Days at the Precipice
title.zh: 圖阿格圖安瓜克：懸崖五日

region.en: The northern flight-road and the ingnersuit country
region.zh: 北行之路與因格內爾舒特之地

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 124 'A Girl named Tuagtuanguak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Fleeing her persecuting brother-in-law across the ice, Tuagtuanguak falls through, gets up, and runs on north viewing a black spot before her — swooning several times, acquiring angakok power between swoons, five successive days to a precipice whose leap wafts her back through the air for five days more. Settling and marrying in the north, she visits the ingnersuit and receives presents — but carrying them homewards the gifts are wafted out of her hands and fly back to their first owners.
summary.zh: 為逃避姑丈糾纏而踏冰奔逃的圖阿格圖安瓜克落入冰縫又爬起，一路向北追著眼前的黑點——幾度昏厥，昏醒之間漸得巫力；連行五日至絕崖，躍而過之，卻被一股氣流送回原處，如是者五日。北地安家成婚後，她往訪因格內爾舒特人並受贈禮——然而攜禮歸途，禮物竟脫手飛回原主。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: A Girl named Tuagtuanguak fled from her brother-in-law who persecuted her; running across the ice she fell through, but having again got up she ran on and on to the north constantly viewing a black spot before her. Swooning several times and again seeing the black spot on awaking she meanwhile acquired angakok power; going on in this way for five successive days she came to a precipice, and setting out from its edge leaped across — but was somehow wafted back through the air to the same spot; this process she continued for five days. She then pursued her journey north and came to an inhabited place where she took up her abode and afterwards got married. She visited the ingnersuit and received presents from them — but while carrying them homewards the gifts were wafted out of her hands and flew back to their first owners.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 124 'A Girl named Tuagtuanguak'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名名叫圖阿克圖安瓜克的女孩為躲避迫害她的姐夫而逃走；她奔過冰面時掉了下去，但重新爬起後又繼續向前跑，一路向北，眼前始終看見一個黑點。她數次昏厥，醒來又見那黑點，在此期間她獲得了巫師之力；就這樣走了連續五天，她來到一處懸崖，從崖邊縱身躍過——卻不知怎地被氣流送回了原處；如此反覆了五天。她於是繼續北行，來到一處有人居住的地方，在那裡定居下來，後來結了婚。她拜訪了因格爾蘇特人，並從他們那裡得到禮物——但當她把禮物帶回家時，這些禮物卻從她手中飄走，飛回了原主那裡。

title.en: The Gifts from the Under-World: The Two Boats
title.zh: 冥界之贈：兩條小舟

region.en: The stone-covered entrance to the under-world
region.zh: 巨石封閉的冥界入口

period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 125 'The Gifts from the Under-world', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Envious of a younger man's luck and favour with women, an old bachelor is sent by his mother to a large stone: moving it aside, an opening leads straight to the under-world and a lake with two boats — let the first pass, apply to the second. Eating the matak from the second boat gives him astonishing luck; the young man, coached with the first boat substituted, secures only the worst luck in his hunting — and the old man, returning for more, finds himself quite unable to move the stone.
summary.zh: 嫉妒年輕人獵運亨通、深受女子青睞的老鰥夫，依母親指點挪開巨石，循孔道直下冥界之湖：兩舟並至，讓頭舟過，向次舟求取——吞下那片鯨皮，獵運驚人。年輕人追問法門，老鰥夫故意把『頭舟』『次舟』對調相告——年輕人求得的卻是最壞的運氣；老鰥夫食畢再去，巨石卻再也搬不動了。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink.

passages.text: An old bachelor, feeling envious of a younger one because of his better luck in hunting and his finding more favour with women, applied to his mother for counsel and aid. She pointed out to him a certain spot where he would find a large stone, and moving it aside an opening would appear leading straight to the under-world, where he would come to a lake; and on seeing two boats he was to let the first one pass but was to apply to the second.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 125 'The Gifts from the Under-world'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名老光棍因為一名較年輕的男子獵運較佳、更得女人歡心而心生嫉妒，便向母親求教求助。母親指點他一處地方，說他在那裡會找到一塊大石，把石頭移開便會出現一個直通下界的洞口，他會在那裡來到一座湖邊；看見兩艘船時，他要放第一艘過去，而向第二艘求助。

passages.text: Acting upon her advice he received a piece of matak (whale-skin) from the second boat, by eating which he acquired astonishing good-luck in hunting; the young man noticing this change of fortune questioned him as to the cause of his recent success, when he imparted to him the information he had gained from his mother only substituting the first boat for the second — the young man in this way also got a piece of matak, by eating which he only secured the worst luck in his hunting. Meanwhile the old man had consumed his piece and went to fetch more; but when he came to the spot the second time he found himself quite unable to move the stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 125 'The Gifts from the Under-world'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他聽從她的建議，從第二艘船上得到了一塊瑪塔克（鯨皮），吃下之後，他在狩獵上獲得了驚人的好運；那年輕人注意到他運勢的轉變，便問他近來成功的原因，於是他把自己從母親那裡得來的情報告訴了對方，只是把第一艘船說成了第二艘——那年輕人用這法子也得到了一塊瑪塔克，但吃下之後，他在狩獵上卻只落得最壞的運氣。與此同時，老人已吃完了自己那一塊，便前去再取一些；可是當他第二次來到那地方時，卻發現自己完全無法搬動那塊石頭。

title.en: Coyote's Wars: The Mountain-Sheep Girl
title.zh: 郊狼之戰：大角羊女

region.en: Cliff above the up-river trail, Nez Perce country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯故地上行小道旁峭壁（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 1. Coyote's Wars' (Mountain-Sheep Girl)

summary.en: A girl at the top of a cliff calls Coyote to come finish killing a mountain-sheep for her; as he looks over the edge she catches his neck with her forked stick and pushes him over, throwing the body into the river when she finds her victim is only Coyote. Magpie pecks his eyes awake — 'You were in no battle; you were pushed over the cliff and killed by Mountain-Sheep Girl' — and tells him how to even the score. Going up a second time, Coyote asks to take the stick and be shown where to stand; as she shows him, he catches her with the forked stick, pushes her over the cliff, and kills her.
summary.zh: 崖頂少女呼郊狼代其射殺大角羊；郊狼俯崖張望之際，她以分叉木杖鉤其頸推落。見死者竟是郊狼，棄屍河中。喜鵲啄其目使醒——『爾未曾征戰，乃為大角羊女推落崖下』——並授以報復之策。郊狼二度上山，反求持杖並請其指示站位；少女俯身指點之際，郊狼持杖鉤之，推落懸崖，反殺其人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling up the river. He heard some one calling to him from far off: a woman's voice said to him, 'Come here and finish killing him for me!' He looked, and saw a girl standing at the top of a cliff. She had a bow and arrows, but could not use them, and she was trying to kill Mountain-Sheep; so Coyote went up to help her. Besides the bow and arrows, she had a forked stick. She asked Coyote to look over the cliff and see how best they could get at Mountain-Sheep; and while he was doing this, she caught his neck with the forked stick and pushed him over the cliff. Then she went down where he had landed; and when she saw that her victim was only Coyote, she threw the body into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 180 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼正沿河而上。他聽見有人在遠處呼喚他：一個女人的聲音對他說：「到這兒來，替我把他殺死！」他望去，看見一個姑娘站在懸崖頂上。她帶著弓和箭，卻用不了，她正想殺死大角羊；於是郊狼上前去幫她。除了弓和箭，她還有一根帶叉的棍子。她請郊狼探身到懸崖外看看，他們怎樣才能最好地接近大角羊；就在他這麼做的時候，她用那根帶叉的棍子鉤住他的脖子，把他推下了懸崖。隨後她下到他落地的地方；當她看出自己的受害者不過是郊狼時，便把屍體扔進了河裡。

passages.text: Coyote floated down the river a bend and a half, and stranded. Magpie came flying up the river, and when he saw Coyote he thought to himself, 'I wonder if there is matter in his eyes!' When Magpie began pecking at the eyes of Coyote, however, the latter came to, and said to Magpie, 'Why are you flying around here? I myself have just been to battle, capturing women.' Magpie replied, 'You were in no battle; you were pushed over the cliff and killed by Mountain-Sheep Girl.' Then Magpie told Coyote what to do to play even.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 180 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼順流漂了一個半河灣，擱淺了。喜鵲沿河飛來，看見郊狼時，心裡想：「不知他眼裡有沒有東西可啄！」可是，當喜鵲開始啄郊狼的眼睛時，後者卻甦醒過來，對喜鵲說：「你為什麼在這兒飛來飛去？我剛剛才去打仗，擄了女人回來。」喜鵲回答說：「你根本沒去打什麼仗；你是被大角羊姑娘推下懸崖殺死的。」於是喜鵲告訴郊狼該怎麼做才能報復。

passages.text: So Coyote travelled upstream a second time, and again he heard her call. He went up to her; and when she asked him to do the same thing, he replied, 'Now, let me take the stick, and then you show me just where I have to stand in order to see Mountain-Sheep plainly.' When she went to show him, Coyote caught her with the forked stick, pushed her over the cliff, and killed her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 180 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是郊狼第二次溯流而上，又聽見了她的呼喚。他走到她跟前；當她請他做同樣的事時，他回答說：「這回讓我拿著棍子，然後你指給我看，我究竟該站在哪裡才能清楚地看見大角羊。」當她上前指給他看時，郊狼用那根帶叉的棍子鉤住她，把她推下懸崖，殺死了她。

title.en: The Mussel-Shell Woman
title.zh: 蚌殼女

region.en: Riverbank trysting-place, Nez Perce country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯故地河畔相會處（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 1. Coyote's Wars' (Mussel-Shell Woman)

summary.en: A woman by the river calls Coyote to come and lie with her; in the embrace she kills him, and throws the body into the water when she sees it is only Coyote. Magpie, feeding on his eyes, wakes him — 'No, you were over there with Mussel-Shell Woman, who cut off your penis and killed you' — and teaches the counter-trick. Coyote goes up the river a third time, and at the same place the woman calls to him again; but now Coyote has a bone which he uses instead, so he kills her, saying, 'You will be only a mussel-shell, and Indians will eat you, but you will not be able to hurt any one.'
summary.zh: 河畔婦人呼郊狼前來相就；相擁之間，郊狼被其陰所傷而斃。婦見死者不過郊狼，棄屍入水。喜鵲啄目使醒——『爾非征戰，乃為蚌殼女所殺』——並教以破解之法。郊狼三度前往，其地婦人又呼；此番郊狼以獸骨代身，反殺其人：『爾從此只是蚌殼，印第安人將食爾，然不能再傷人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Sexual motif summarized plainly as recorded. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Then Coyote resumed his journey up river; and by and by he heard another woman, who called to him to come and lie with her. He arrived where the woman was; then he embraced her. His organ was cut off, and he died. When the woman saw that it was only Coyote she had killed, she threw the body into the water, and it drifted down the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 180 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後郊狼繼續沿河而上；不久他又聽見另一個女人，她喚他過去與她同寢。他來到那女人所在之處；接著他擁抱了她。他的陽具被割掉了，他死了。當那女人看出自己殺死的不過是郊狼時，便把屍體扔進水裡，屍體順流漂了下去。

passages.text: Again Magpie saw the body, and came to feed on the matter in the eyes. Coyote came to, and said, 'Why did you wake me up? I have been to war, capturing women.' Then Magpie answered, 'No, you were over there with Mussel-Shell Woman, who killed you.' So again Magpie told him what to do to kill her in turn. He went up the river, and at the same place the woman called to him again; but now Coyote had a bone which he used instead of his member. So he killed her, and said, 'You will be only a mussel-shell, and Indians will eat you, but you will not be able to hurt any one.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 180-181 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 喜鵲又看見了那具屍體，便來啄食他眼裡的東西。郊狼甦醒過來，說：「你為什麼把我叫醒？我剛去打仗，擄了女人回來。」喜鵲回答說：「不對，你是在那邊跟貽貝殼女人在一起，是她殺了你。」於是喜鵲又告訴他該怎麼做，好輪到他殺死她。他沿河而上，在同一個地方，那女人又喚他；但這回郊狼帶了一根骨頭，用來代替他的陽具。於是他就殺死了她，並說：「你只會成為一隻貽貝殼，印第安人會吃你，但你再也傷害不了任何人。」

title.en: The Bungling Host: Coyote and his Four Sons-in-Law
title.zh: 笨拙之主：郊狼與四女婿

region.en: Winter camps of the Nez Perce, ice-holes on the river (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯冬季營地，河上冰洞（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 2. The Bungling Host'

summary.en: Visiting Elk, Mountain-Sheep, Otter and Fish-Hawk in turn, Coyote watches each son-in-law's magic — a bent green stick cooked in ashes becoming elk marrow-gut, excrement becoming camas, a piece of his wife's dress boiled into mountain-sheep meat, five thorn sticks through five ice-holes strung with fish, a dive from a leaning tree bringing up salmon-trout — and attempts every one at home: the withhe burns and the stick straightens, killing his wife (whom he brings back to life); only blood comes when he tries Elk's trick; his wife's dress stays elk-skin; diving under the ice he drifts to the rapids, nearly drowned, until Otter rescues him and fills all five sticks himself; and diving head-first from the tree, Coyote misses the hole and breaks his head against the ice — coming to only to find his visitor gone.
summary.zh: 郊狼依次拜訪麋、大角羊、水獺、魚鷹四位女婿，暗記其魔法：彎枝燼埋即成麋骨髓腸；穢物化卡瑪斯根；割妻裙入釜即成羊脂美肉；五荊枝穿五冰洞，枝枝掛魚；自斜樹俯衝冰洞，滿載鱒鮭。返家一一效仿：藤燃枝直，火燄四射，擊斃其妻（復活之）；仿麋術，唯得鮮血；仿羊術，裙仍為皮；潛冰逐流，漂至急灘，幾乎滅頂，賴水獺相救並代為滿掛五枝；自樹頭俯衝，失準撞冰，昏死——醒時賓客已散。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: One of Coyote's daughters had married an Elk, one a Mountain-Sheep, one an Otter, and one a Fish-Hawk; moreover, Coyote had a little boy. 'My son, let us go and see your oldest sister to-morrow!' said Coyote in the evening. When Coyote got to the house, they went in and sat there for a while. Soon Coyote saw Elk step outside to cut off a stick about as big as an arm and as long as two arms. Elk brought the stick into the tent and built a big fire; then Coyote saw the green stick roasting in the fire. Soon Elk took the stick out, turned the ends together so that it formed a hoop, dug a hole in the ashes and buried the bent stick. Pretty soon the stick was cooked; and when Elk took it out, it had turned into the marrow gut of an elk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 181 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 郊狼有一個女兒嫁給了麋鹿，一個嫁給了山綿羊，一個嫁給了水獺，還有一個嫁給了魚鷹；此外，郊狼還有一個小男孩。「兒子，我們明天去看看你的大姐吧！」郊狼在傍晚說道。郊狼到了那戶人家，他們便走進去坐了一會兒。不久，郊狼看見麋鹿走到外面，砍下一根約有手臂粗、兩臂長的木棍。麋鹿把木棍拿進帳篷，生起一堆大火；接著郊狼看見那根青木棍在火中烤著。不久，麋鹿把木棍取出來，將兩端彎攏在一起，使它形成一個圈，在灰燼中挖了一個洞，把彎曲的木棍埋了進去。不一會兒，木棍就熟了；麋鹿把它取出來時，它已經變成了麋鹿的髓腸。

passages.text: Elk gave Coyote a flint knife and told him to begin eating. 'Well, I never eat stick,' said Coyote to himself, so he gave the knife to his boy; but soon Coyote turned his head and saw the boy eating the stick, and it seemed so very rich that he took it away from him. When they had eaten as much as they could, they had used up only half. After this meal Elk asked for a winnowing-basket, went outside with the basket and knife, and Coyote ran to the door and peeked out through a hole: he saw Elk squat over the basket and stick the knife up his anus. When Elk brought in the basket and set it down, Coyote would not eat, because he had seen how Elk had obtained this food; so he gave it to the boy, saying he would eat after nobody. When the boy liked the food, however, Coyote also began to eat: it was camas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 181 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 麋鹿給了郊狼一把燧石刀，叫他開始吃。「唉，我從來不吃木棍的。」郊狼自言自語道，於是他把刀遞給了兒子；可是不一會兒，郊狼轉過頭，看見兒子正在吃那根木棍，那東西看起來滋味極美，他便從兒子手裡奪了過來。他們盡可能地吃，卻只吃掉了半根。吃完這頓飯後，麋鹿要來一個簸箕，帶著簸箕和刀走到外面，郊狼跑到門口，從一個小孔往外偷看：他看見麋鹿蹲在簸箕上方，把刀捅進自己的肛門。麋鹿把簸箕拿進來放下時，郊狼不肯吃，因為他看見了麋鹿是怎樣得到這食物的；於是他把食物給了兒子，說自己等別人吃完再吃。可是，當男孩吃得津津有味時，郊狼也開始吃了：那是卡馬斯（camas）。

passages.text: Before leaving Elk's camp, Coyote told Elk to be sure and return the visit the next day. Next morning Elk dressed himself up and went over; Coyote jumped up and ran outside to look for a good green stick, brought it in, built up a big fire, bent the hot stick and tied the ends together with a withe, dug a hole in the ashes and buried the stick. When the withe burnt through, the stick straightened out and threw the fire out of the fireplace and all over the tent; Coyote's wife was sitting near the door, and the stick hit her in the back and killed her. Coyote brought his wife back to life, and told his boy to get him a winnowing-basket; he stepped outside to do as Elk had done, stuck his knife up his anus, but all he could get was blood. Coyote could not produce his guest's dinner by magic; so Elk took pity on him, cut a stick as before, put it into the fire, telling Coyote to take it out when it was done, and also filled up the basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 181-182 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 離開麋鹿的營地之前，郊狼叮囑麋鹿務必第二天回訪。第二天早上，麋鹿打扮整齊，走了過去；郊狼跳起來跑到外面，找了一根上好的青木棍，拿進屋裡，生起一堆大火，把燒熱的木棍彎曲，用柳條把兩端綁在一起，在灰燼中挖了一個洞，把木棍埋了進去。柳條燒斷後，木棍便伸直了，把火從火塘裡甩了出來，甩得滿帳篷都是；郊狼的妻子正坐在門邊，木棍打中了她的背，把她打死了。郊狼把妻子救活，又叫兒子給他拿一個簸箕來；他走到外面，照麋鹿的做法去做，把刀捅進自己的肛門，可是弄出來的只有血。郊狼無法用魔法為客人變出晚餐；於是麋鹿可憐他，像先前那樣砍了一根木棍，放進火裡，叫郊狼熟了就拿出來，同時也把簸箕裝滿了。

passages.text: That night Coyote said to his boy, 'We will go and see the next oldest girl.' They set out next morning. Mountain-Sheep heated water in a willow basket; his wife was sitting with her back to the fire, and Mountain-Sheep took hold of her dress and cut away a piece of it at the back, and put this piece into the cooking-basket. Coyote shut his eyes; and when he opened them, the dress of the woman was whole again. When the food was cooked, Coyote thought, 'I do not care at all about eating my daughter's dress' — but when the boy started to eat it, Coyote saw that it was the very best mountain-sheep meat, so he ate it too. The next morning Mountain-Sheep went to Coyote's camp, where Coyote heated rocks, sharpened his flint knife, caught his wife by the back of the dress and cut the dress away as far down as the waist — 'You crazy old woman! I must have some meat for my son-in-law' — cut up the back of the dress in small pieces and put them into the boiling water, but what he took out was nothing but elk-skin. When Mountain-Sheep saw that Coyote was trying to imitate him, he pulled off his shirt and cut away all below the waist, telling Coyote to boil this; the shirt-tails came back on Mountain-Sheep's shirt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 182 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那天晚上，郊狼對兒子說：「我們去看看下一個大女兒。」第二天早上他們就出發了。山綿羊在柳條籃裡燒水；他的妻子背對著火坐著，山綿羊抓住她的衣服，從背後割下一塊，把這塊布放進煮食籃裡。郊狼閉上眼睛；等他睜開眼時，那女人的衣服又完好如初了。食物煮好後，郊狼心想：「我一點也不想吃我女兒的衣服。」——可是當男孩開始吃時，郊狼看出那是最好的山綿羊肉，於是他也吃了。第二天早上，山綿羊來到郊狼的營地，郊狼燒熱了石頭，磨利了他的燧石刀，抓住妻子衣服的後背，把衣服一直割到腰下——「你這個瘋老婆子！我得給我的女婿弄點肉」——把衣服後背切成小塊，放進滾水裡，可是撈出來的卻只是麋鹿皮。山綿羊看出郊狼是在模仿自己，便脫下自己的襯衫，把腰以下的部分全割下來，叫郊狼把這個煮了；那些襯衫下擺卻又回到了山綿羊的襯衫上。

passages.text: Coyote then visited Otter, who had five holes cut in the ice in a row near the middle of the river: laying down four sticks beside the farthest hole, he dove into the river with one stick, and when he came up, the stick was all strung with fish — five times, once at each hole, a string of fish each time. Coyote got up very early and cut five holes in the ice, got five good thorn switches, ran down to the last hole, laid down four of the sticks, and dove into the river with one of them; he drifted downstream under the ice and got no fish, drifting down to the rapids, and then came out almost drowned. Otter rescued Coyote and took him home; then he dove down as before and came up with the sticks full of fish. After a day or so, Coyote visited Fish-Hawk, whose camp had a dead tree leaning over the river and five small holes cut in the ice just under it: Fish-Hawk flew out of the house, circled around in the air, alighted on the tree, flew off, and dove for the lowest hole, coming back with a whole string of salmon-trout, two more strings of salmon-trout, and two strings of suckers. Coyote went home, cut five holes under a leaning tree, took the switches down to the river, climbed the tree, looked around a bit, and dove down head-first — he missed the hole, and broke his head against the ice. After a while Coyote came to; when he came to, he found that his visitor had gone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 183-184 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 接著郊狼去拜訪水獺，水獺在河中央附近的冰上鑿了一排五個洞：他在最遠的洞旁放下四根木棍，帶著一根木棍潛入河中，等他浮上來時，那根木棍上串滿了魚——一共五次，每個洞一次，每次一串魚。郊狼一大早就起來，在冰上鑿了五個洞，弄來五根上好的荊條，跑到最後一個洞邊，放下四根木棍，帶著其中一根潛入河中；他被水流沖到冰下，一條魚也沒弄到，一直漂到急流處，然後浮上來時幾乎淹死。水獺救了郊狼，把他帶回家；然後他又像先前那樣潛下去，浮上來時木棍上滿是魚。過了一兩天，郊狼去拜訪魚鷹，魚鷹的營地有一棵枯樹斜伸在河面上，樹下的冰上鑿了五個小洞：魚鷹從屋裡飛出去，在空中盤旋，落在樹上，又飛起來，朝最低的那個洞俯衝下去，回來時帶著滿滿一串鮭鱒，又兩串鮭鱒，還有兩串胭脂魚。郊狼回到家，在一棵斜伸的樹下鑿了五個洞，帶著荊條下到河邊，爬上樹，四下張望了一下，便頭朝下俯衝下去——他沒對準洞口，頭撞在冰上撞破了。過了一會兒，郊狼甦醒過來；他醒來時，發現他的客人已經走了。

title.en: Coyote and Fox Get Food: The Deer-Tick Man
title.zh: 郊狼與狐得食：鹿蝨翁

region.en: Camp door where the five packs fall (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 五袋食物墜落之營門（象徵定位）

period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 4. Coyote and Fox get Food'

summary.en: Coyote, the wise one, and Fox, the slow-witted, need food; Coyote wishes aloud — 'I wish that I and my friend could hear the sound of five packs of food falling at the door!' — and five sounds answer, tlitluk five times.
