passages.zh: 道有其法則，有其徵驗。它既無作為，亦無形體。它可以傳授，卻不能接受；可以獲得，卻不能看見。在天地存在之前，道就已存在。它自古以來恆存不變。神靈從它那裡獲得靈性，而宇宙則成為我們如今所見的模樣。對於道而言，天頂不算高，天底不算低；時間上沒有哪一點是久遠的，也沒有因歲月流逝而變老。

passages.text: Hsi Wei obtained TAO, and so set the universe in order. Fu Hsi obtained it, and was able to establish eternal principles. The Great Bear obtained it, and has never erred from its course. The sun and moon obtained it, and have never ceased to revolve. K'an P'i obtained it, and established the K'un-lun mountains. P'ing I obtained it, and rules over the streams. Chien Wu obtained it, and dwells on Mount T'ai.
passages.zh: 希韋獲得了道，因而使宇宙井然有序。伏羲獲得了它，因而能夠確立永恆的法則。北斗獲得了它，因而從未偏離其軌道。日月獲得了它，因而從未停止運轉。堪坏獲得了它，因而奠定了崑崙山。馮夷獲得了它，因而統轄河流。肩吾獲得了它，因而居住於泰山之上。

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor obtained it, and soared upon the clouds to heaven. Chuan Hsü obtained it, and dwells in the Dark Palace. Yü Ch'iang obtained it, and fixed himself at the North Pole. Hsi Wang Mu obtained it, and settled at Shao Kuang; since when, no one knows; until when, no one knows either. P'êng Tsu obtained it, and lived from the time of Shun until the time of the Five Princes. Fu Yüeh obtained it, and as the Minister of Wu Ting got the empire under his control. And now, charioted upon one constellation and drawn by another, he has been enrolled among the stars of heaven.
passages.zh: 黃帝獲得了它，因而乘雲飛升上天。顓頊獲得了它，因而居住於玄宮。禺強獲得了它，因而立身於北極。西王母獲得了它，因而定居於少廣；自那時起，無人知道；直到何時，也無人知曉。彭祖獲得了它，因而從舜的時代一直活到五伯的時代。傅說獲得了它，因而作為武丁的臣相，將天下掌控於手中。如今，他乘著一個星宿、由另一個星宿駕馭，已被列入天上的星辰之中。

title.en: Nü Yü Teaches the Tao in Nine Days (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 女偊教道（莊子）

region.en: The hermit's plot (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 隱者之圃（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei asks the aged Nü Yü why his countenance is like a child's; she answers that she has learnt the Tao. In three days Pu Liang I ceased to see the sublunary state; in seven more the external world; in nine he became unconscious of his own existence — first etherealised, then possessed of perfect wisdom, then without past or present, finally able to enter where life and death are no more.
summary.zh: 南伯子葵問乎女偊：子之年長矣，而色若孺子，何也？曰：吾聞道矣——三日而後能外天下；七日而後能外物；九日而後能外生；而後朝徹、見獨，而後能無古今；而後能入於不死不生。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the three-stage inner-cultivation scheme is the ancestor of later Daoist meditation grades. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "I fear not," said Nü Yü. "You are not the sort of man. There was Pu Liang I. He had all the qualifications of a sage, but not TAO. Now I had Tao, though none of the qualifications. But do you imagine that much as I wished it I was able to teach TAO to him so that he should be a perfect sage? Had it been so, then to teach TAO to one who has the qualifications of a sage would be an easy matter. No, Sir. I imparted as though withholding; and in three days, for him, this sublunary state had ceased to exist.
passages.zh: 「我不怕，」女偊說。「你不是那種人。從前有個卜梁倚。他具備了聖人的一切資質，卻沒有道。而我擁有道，卻沒有那些資質。可是你以為，儘管我如此希望，我能夠把道教給他，使他成為完美的聖人嗎？倘若如此，那麼把道教給一個具備聖人資質的人，便是輕而易舉的事了。不，先生。我傳授時彷彿有所保留；三天之後，對他而言，這塵世狀態便已不復存在。

passages.text: When he had attained to this, I withheld again; and in seven days more, for him, the external world had ceased to be. And so again for another nine days, when he became unconscious of his own existence. He became first etherealised, next possessed of perfect wisdom, then without past or present, and finally able to enter there where life and death are no more,--where killing does not take away life, nor does prolongation of life add to the duration of existence.
passages.zh: 當他達到這一境界時，我又有所保留；再過七天，對他而言，外在世界便已不復存在。如此再過九天，他便對自身的存在渾然不覺。他先是變得空靈，接著獲得了完美的智慧，然後沒有過去與現在，最後能夠進入那生死皆無之處——在那裡，殺戮不能奪去生命，延長壽命也不能增加存在的時長。

passages.text: "And how did you manage to get hold of all this?" asked Nan Po Tzŭ K'uei. "I got it from books," replied Nü Yü; "and the books got it from learning, and learning from investigation, and investigation from cö-ordination, and cö-ordination from application, and application from desire to know, and desire to know from the unknown, and the unknown from the great void, and the great void from infinity!"
passages.zh: 「那麼你是如何掌握這一切的？」南伯子葵問道。「我從書本中得來，」女偊回答；「而書本從學習中得來，學習從探究中得來，探究從協調中得來，協調從實踐中得來，實踐從求知的慾望中得來，求知的慾望從未知中得來，未知從太虛中得來，太虛從無窮中得來！」

title.en: Tzŭ Yü's Illness: Cock, Cross-bow, and Chariot (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子輿有病，曲僂發背（莊子）

region.en: The four friends' meeting-place (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 四子相與之地（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Four friends pledge that whoever can make Inaction the head, Life the backbone, and Death the tail of his existence shall be their friend. Tzŭ Yü falls ill, doubled up and deranged, and greets the change without fear: his left shoulder will become a cock to herald the morn, his right a cross-bow, his buttocks wheels with his soul for a horse — I obtained life because it was my time; I part with it in accordance with the same law.
summary.zh: 四人相與語曰：孰能以無為首，以生為脊，以死為尻？子輿有病，子祀往問；子輿曰：亡，予何惡——浸假而化予之左臂以為雞，右臂以為彈，尻以為輪，以神為馬，予因乘之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Four men were conversing together, when the following resolution was suggested:--"Whosoever can make Inaction the head, Life the backbone, and Death the tail, of his existence,--that man shall be admitted to friendship with us." The four looked at each other and smiled; and tacitly accepting the conditions, became friends forthwith. By-and-by, one of them, named Tzŭ Yü, fell ill, and another, Tzŭ Ssŭ, went to see him. "Verily God is great!" said the sick man. "See how he has doubled me up. My back is so hunched that my viscera are at the top of my body. My cheeks are level with my navel. My shoulders are higher than my neck. My hair grows up towards the sky. The whole economy of my organism is deranged. Nevertheless, my mental equilibrium is not disturbed."
passages.zh: 四人一同交談，其間有人提出這樣的主張：「誰能把無為當作頭，把生命當作脊梁，把死亡當作尾巴，這樣的人就可以和我們結為朋友。」四人相視而笑，默契地接受了這個條件，於是當下結為朋友。不久，其中一人名叫子輿的生了病，另一人子祀前去探望他。那病人說：「真是偉大啊，造物者！看祂把我彎曲成這副模樣。我的背駝得那麼厲害，以致五臟都跑到身體的上頭去了。我的面頰與肚臍齊平。我的肩膀高過脖子。我的頭髮朝天生長。我整個形體的生機都錯亂了。然而，我內心的平衡卻沒有受到擾亂。」

passages.text: "I am not [afraid]," replied Tzŭ Yü. "What have I to fear? Ere long I shall be decomposed. My left shoulder will become a cock, and I shall herald the approach of morn. My right shoulder will become a cross-bow, and I shall be able to get broiled duck. My buttocks will become wheels; and with my soul for a horse, I shall be able to ride in my own chariot. I obtained life because it was my time: I am now parting with it in accordance with the same law. Content with the natural sequence of these states, joy and sorrow touch me not. I am simply, as the ancients expressed it, hanging in the air, unable to cut myself down, bound with the trammels of material existence. But man has ever given way before God: why, then, should I be afraid?"
passages.zh: 子輿回答說：「我並不〔害怕〕。我有什麼好怕的呢？不久我就要分解了。我的左肩將變成公雞，我便來報曉清晨的到來。我的右肩將變成弩弓，我便能烤得野鴨來吃。我的臀部將變成車輪；以我的靈魂為馬，我便能乘坐自己的車子。我得到生命，是因為時機到了；如今我捨棄它，也是依照同樣的法則。安於這些狀態的自然更替，喜與憂便觸及不到我。我不過正如古人所說的，懸在半空中，無法把自己割下來，被形骸的羈絆所束縛罷了。然而人向來都是順服於造物者的：那麼，我又為什麼要害怕呢？」

title.en: Tzŭ Lai in the Smelting-Pot (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子來臨終：大冶鑄金（莊子）

region.en: The four friends' home (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 四子之家（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Tzŭ Lai lies gasping while his family weeps; Tzŭ Li drives them off and asks what God will make of him next — a rat's liver or a snake's shoulders. Tzŭ Lai answers that Nature is a man's parents: the universe is the smelting-pot and God the caster, and were he to cry 'Make of me a man!' he would be rejected as uncanny. I shall go whithersoever I am sent, as a man wakes from a dreamless sleep.
summary.zh: 子來有病，喘喘然將死；子犁往問，斥其妻子：無怛化！彼且以造化為父母——今一以天地為大爐，以造化為大冶，惡乎往而不可哉！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Creator-as-smelter image grounds the Taoist death-and-transformation cluster. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: By-and-by, another of the four, named Tzŭ Lai, fell ill, and lay gasping for breath, while his family stood weeping around. The fourth friend, Tzŭ Li, went to see him. "Chut!" cried he to the wife and children; "begone! you balk his decomposition." Then, leaning against the door, he said, "Verily, God is great! I wonder what he will make of you now. I wonder whither you will be sent. Do you think he will make you into a rat's liver or into the shoulders of a snake?"
passages.zh: 不久，四人中另一人名叫子來的生了病，躺著喘息不止，他的家人圍在旁邊哭泣。第四位朋友子犁前去探望他。「噓！」他對那人的妻兒喊道，「走開！你們妨礙他分解。」然後，他倚著門說：「真是偉大啊，造物者！我不知道祂現在要把你變成什麼。我不知道你將被送到哪裡去。你想祂會把你變成一隻老鼠的肝，還是變成一條蛇的肩膀呢？」

passages.text: "A son," answered Tzŭ Lai, "must go whithersoever his parents bid him. Nature is no other than a man's parents. If she bid me die quickly, and I demur, then I am an unfilial son. She can do me no wrong. TAO gives me this form, this toil in manhood, this repose in old age, this rest in death. And surely that which is such a kind arbiter of my life is the best arbiter of my death.
passages.zh: 子來回答說：「兒子必須到父母所吩咐的任何地方去。自然無異於人的父母。如果她吩咐我快快死去，而我卻猶豫不從，那我就是個不孝之子。她不會對我有所虧負。道給我這形體，給我成年時的勞碌，給我老年時的安閒，給我死亡時的休息。而那如此仁慈地安排我生命的，必定也是安排我死亡的最好主宰。

passages.text: "Suppose that the boiling metal in a smelting-pot were to bubble up and say, 'Make of me an Excalibur;' I think the caster would reject that metal as uncanny. And if a sinner like myself were to say to God, 'Make of me a man, make of me a man;' I think he too would reject me as uncanny. The universe is the smelting-pot, and God is the caster. I shall go whithersoever I am sent, to wake unconscious of the past, as a man wakes from a dreamless sleep."
passages.zh: 「假設熔爐裡沸騰的金屬冒起泡來說道：『把我鑄成一把寶劍吧；』我想鑄造的人會把那塊金屬當作不祥之物而丟棄。而如果像我這樣一個罪人對造物者說：『把我造成人，把我造成人；』我想祂也會把我當作不祥之物而丟棄。天地是熔爐，造物者是鑄造的人。我將被送到哪裡就到哪裡去，醒來時忘卻過去，就像人從無夢的睡眠中醒來一樣。」

title.en: The Song at Tzŭ Sang Hu's Corpse (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子桑戶死，孟子反琴曲（莊子）

region.en: The mourners' hall (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 吊喪之堂（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Three friends resolve to mount to heaven, roaming through the clouds beyond the limits of space. When Tzŭ Sang Hu dies, his two friends sing beside the corpse: 'Thou hast already returned to thy God, while we still remain here as men, alas!' Tzŭ Kung protests the breach of decorum; Confucius explains that these men look on life as a huge tumour from which death sets them free — for fishes are born in water, and man is born in TAO.
summary.zh: 子桑戶、孟子反、子琴張三人相與友；桑戶死，未葬，二子臨尸而歌：嗟來桑戶乎！而已反其真，而我猶為人猗！孔子曰：彼遊方之外者也，而丘遊方之內者也；魚相忘乎江湖，人相忘乎道術。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tzŭ Sang Hu, Mêng Tzŭ Fan, and Tzŭ Ch'in Chang, were conversing together, when it was asked, "Who can be, and yet not be? Who can do, and yet not do? Who can mount to heaven, and roaming through the clouds, pass beyond the limits of space, oblivious of existence, for ever and ever without end?" The three looked at each other and smiled; and as neither had any misgivings, they became friends accordingly. Shortly afterwards Tzŭ Sang Hu died; whereupon Confucius sent Tzŭ Kung to take part in the mourning. But Tzŭ Kung found that one had composed a song which the other was accompanying on the lute, as follows:--"Ah! Wilt thou come back to us, Sang Hu? Ah! Wilt thou come back to us, Sang Hu? Thou hast already returned to thy God, While we still remain here as men,--alas!"
passages.zh: 子桑戶、孟子反和子琴張三人一同交談，其間有人問道：「誰能有所作為而又無所作為？誰能登天，漫遊於雲端，超越空間的界限，忘卻存在，永遠永遠沒有終結？」三人相視而笑；由於彼此都沒有疑慮，於是便結為朋友。不久之後，子桑戶死了；於是孔子派子貢前去參與弔喪。但子貢發現，其中一人作了首歌，另一人彈著琴為他伴奏，歌詞如下：「唉！你會回到我們這裡來嗎，桑戶？唉！你會回到我們這裡來嗎，桑戶？你已經回到你的造物者那裡去了，而我們還留在這裡做人——唉！」

passages.text: "These men," replied Confucius, "travel beyond the rule of life. I travel within it. Consequently, our paths do not meet; and I was wrong in sending you to mourn. They consider themselves as one with God, recognising no distinctions between human and divine. They look on life as a huge tumour from which death sets them free. All the same they know not where they were before birth, nor where they will be after death. Though admitting different elements, they take their stand upon the unity of all things. ... They stroll beyond the dust and dirt of mortality, to wander in the realms of inaction. How should such men trouble themselves with the conventionalities of this world, or care what people may think of them?"
passages.zh: 孔子回答：「這些人，是行走於生死常規之外的人。而我，是行走於生死常規之內的人。因此，我們的道路並不相交；我先前派你去弔唁，是錯了。他們視自己與神合一，不承認人與神之間有何分別。他們把生命看作一個巨大的腫瘤，而死亡使他們從中解脫。儘管如此，他們不知自己生前在何處，也不知死後將往何方。他們雖承認萬物有別，卻立足於萬物的一體。……他們漫步於塵世塵垢之外，遨遊於無為之境。這樣的人，又怎會為世俗的禮法而自尋煩惱，或在意世人如何看待他們呢？」

passages.text: "Fishes," replied Confucius, "are born in water. Man is born in TAO. If fishes get ponds to live in, they thrive. If man gets TAO to live in, he may live his life in peace. Hence the saying, 'All that a fish wants is water; all that a man wants is TAO.'"
passages.zh: 孔子回答：「魚生於水。人生於道。魚若得池沼而居，便能茁壯。人若得道而居，便能安度一生。所以說：『魚所求的只是水；人所求的只是道。』」

title.en: Yen Hui Gets Rid of Everything (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 顏回坐忘（莊子）

region.en: The court of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯國曲阜

period: Zhuangzi ch. 6, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 6

summary.en: Yen Hui reports his progress three times to Confucius: first getting rid of charity and duty, then of ceremonial and music, finally of everything — I have freed myself from my body, discarded my reasoning powers, and become one with the Infinite. Confucius eagerly grants that if he has become one there can be no room for bias, and asks to follow in his steps.
summary.zh: 顏回曰：回益矣——忘仁義矣，忘禮樂矣，墮肢體，黜聰明，離形去知，同於大通，此謂坐忘。仲尼曰：同則無好也，化則無常也，而果其賢乎，丘也請從而後也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the 'sitting-and-forgetting' (zuowang) charter for Daoist meditation. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "I am getting on," observed Yen Hui to Confucius. "How so?" asked the latter. "I have got rid of charity and duty," replied the former. "Very good," replied Confucius, "but not perfect." Another day Yen Hui met Confucius and said, "I am getting on." "How so?" asked Confucius. "I have got rid of ceremonial and music," answered Yen Hui. "Very good," said Confucius, "but not perfect."
passages.zh: 顏回對孔子說：「我有進步了。」孔子問：「怎麼說？」顏回回答：「我已忘掉仁義了。」孔子說：「很好，但還不夠完美。」另一天，顏回又見到孔子，說：「我有進步了。」孔子問：「怎麼說？」顏回回答：「我已忘掉禮樂了。」孔子說：「很好，但還不夠完美。」

passages.text: On a third occasion Yen Hui met Confucius and said, "I am getting on." "How so?" asked the Sage. "I have got rid of everything," replied Yen Hui. "Got rid of everything!" said Confucius eagerly. "What do you mean by that?" "I have freed myself from my body," answered Yen Hui. "I have discarded my reasoning powers. And by thus getting rid of body and mind, I have become ONE with the Infinite. This is what I mean by getting rid of everything." "If you have become ONE," cried Confucius, "there can be no room for bias. If you have passed into space, you are indeed without beginning or end. And if you have really attained to this, I trust to be allowed to follow in your steps."
passages.zh: 第三次，顏回見到孔子，說：「我有進步了。」聖人問：「怎麼說？」顏回回答：「我已忘掉一切了。」孔子急切地說：「忘掉一切！你這是什麼意思？」顏回回答：「我已從自己的形體中解脫。我已捨棄了自己的思辨能力。如此捨棄形體與心智，我便與無限合而為一。這就是我所說的忘掉一切。」孔子驚呼：「你既已合而為一，便再無偏私的餘地。你既已進入虛空之境，便確實無始無終。你若真已達到這境界，我希望能追隨你的腳步。」

title.en: The Succession at the Hall of Banu Sa'idah
title.zh: 薩伊達亭堂的繼位

region.en: Medina, hall of Banu Sa'idah (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 麥地那薩伊達亭堂（象徵性定位）

period: Event 632 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate: Its Rise, Decline and Fall (1891), ch. 1

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate: Its Rise, Decline and Fall (Religious Tract Society, 1891), ch. 1

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The Prophet dies; the Ansar gather in the hall of Banu Sa'idah to choose a chief of their own. Abu Bakr and Umar come to them; Abu Bakr reminds them that the Arabs will not accept a chief outside Quraysh — 'the Arabs will not submit but to this tribe of Quraysh.' He takes the hand of Umar and of Abu Ubayda; the Ansar seize Abu Bakr's hand, and the homage is paid. In the hall of Aisha the party of Ali stands apart; but Abu Bakr's election carries, and the first caliph sends the army of Usama within days.
summary.zh: 先知歿；輔士聚於薩伊達亭堂欲自選首領。阿布·伯克爾與歐瑪爾往之；阿布·伯克爾言阿拉伯人必不認古萊氏之外者為主。他舉起歐瑪爾與阿布·烏拜達之手；輔士握阿布·伯克爾之手，效忠遂定。阿伊莎居室一方阿里派另立；然阿布·伯克爾之選成為公論，首任哈里發數日內即遣烏薩瑪之軍。

sensitivity.note: Historiographical tradition (Tabari, Ibn Ishaq) retold in Muir's 1891 narrative; the succession dispute remains a point of Sunni-Shi'i difference; presented as received narrative.

passages.text: While Abu Bakr and Umar were with the Prophet's family in Aisha's chamber, the Ansar gathered in the hall of Banu Sa'idah to choose a chief from among themselves. Abu Bakr and Umar went out to them. Sa'd ibn Ubada was sitting there, and Sad said: 'O company of the Ansar, you have precedence in religion and merit; there is no tribe like you in Islam; so let this matter be among you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當阿布·伯克爾與歐麥爾同先知的家屬在阿伊莎的房間裡時，輔士們聚集在薩伊達族的廳堂中，要從他們自己人中選出一位首領。阿布·伯克爾與歐麥爾出去見他們。薩阿德·伊本·烏巴達正坐在那裡，薩阿德說：「輔士們啊，你們在宗教與功績上居於前列；在伊斯蘭中沒有哪個部族比得上你們；所以讓此事在你們之中決定吧。」

passages.text: Abu Bakr answered: 'Noble as you are, the Arabs will acknowledge authority only in this tribe of Quraysh, who are the core of the Arab race.' Then he took Umar by the hand, and Abu Ubayda; and he said, 'Choose which of these two you will.' But the Ansar said: 'We will not have any but thee, Abu Bakr — thou wast the companion in the cave, the second of the two when they were in the cave.' They seized his hand, and the homage was paid; and the same day the army of Usama was sent forward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿布·伯克爾回答：「你們固然高貴，但阿拉伯人只承認古萊什這個部族的權威，因為他們是阿拉伯民族的核心。」然後他牽起歐麥爾的手，又牽起阿布·烏拜達的手，說道：「你們從這兩人中選一個吧。」但輔士們說：「除了你，阿布·伯克爾，我們誰也不要——你曾是洞中的同伴，當他們兩人在洞中時，你是二人中的第二位。」他們抓住他的手，宣誓效忠；就在同一天，烏薩瑪的軍隊被派往前線。

title.en: Yarmuk: The Day of Lost Eyes
title.zh: 雅爾穆克：失明之日

region.en: Yarmuk river gorge, southern Syria (literal pin)
region.zh: 敘利亞南部雅爾穆克河谷（實際定位）

period: Event 636 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 9; S. Ockley, History of the Saracens (1890)

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 9; Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890)

license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The Byzantine host of Heraclius' generals, five times the number of the Muslims, is drawn up at the Yarmuk. Khalid, fresh from the Iraq road, takes the command; the battle sways for days. The women of the Muslim camp fight in the last stand — 'the day of lost eyes', the day when so many lost their sight from the strain; the Byzantine line breaks, and the gorge is choked with fugitives. Syria is won.
summary.zh: 希拉克略諸將之拜占庭大軍，五倍於穆斯林，列陣雅爾穆克。自伊拉克戰場而來的哈立德受命；戰事連日拉鋸。營中婦女參與最後的防線——是日眾多戰士因力竭而失明，故名『失明之日』。拜占庭戰線崩潰，峽谷塞滿敗兵。敘利亞底定。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; battle narrative as received in Muir/Ockley from Tabari.

passages.text: Heraclius had gathered the forces of Byzantium at the Yarmuk — it was said eighty thousand or more — against the Muslim army of less than half the number, under Abu Ubayda, with Khalid ibn al-Walid as the fighting arm. The battle opened in the summer heat; for days the lines swayed back and forth along the gorge of the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 9; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 希拉克略在雅爾穆克集結了拜占庭的軍隊——據說有八萬人或更多——對抗由阿布·烏拜達率領、人數不到其半的穆斯林軍隊，哈立德·伊本·瓦利德則擔任作戰的主力。戰役在夏日的酷熱中展開；一連數日，戰線沿著河谷的峽谷來回搖擺。

passages.text: In the last stand the Muslim women came out to fight, and the warriors lost their sight from the heat and the strain — so the day was called 'the day of lost eyes.' The Byzantine line broke at last; the horsemen of the empire were driven back on the gorge, and the passage was choked with fugitives. Heraclius, at Antioch, heard the news and left Syria for Constantinople, saying: 'Peace be with thee, O Syria.' And the cities of the coast opened their gates one after another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 9; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在最後的抵抗中，穆斯林婦女也出來作戰，而戰士們因酷熱與勞累而失明——因此這一天被稱為「失明之日」。拜占庭的陣線終於崩潰；帝國的騎兵被逼退至峽谷，通道被逃亡者堵塞。希拉克略在安條克聽聞消息，便離開敘利亞前往君士坦丁堡，說道：「願平安與你同在，哦敘利亞。」沿海的城市則一座接一座地打開了城門。

title.en: Qadisiyya: Rustam's Armor and the Three Days
title.zh: 卡迪西亞：魯斯塔姆的鎧甲與三日之戰

region.en: Qadisiyya, near Hira, Iraq (literal pin)
region.zh: 伊拉克希拉附近的卡迪西亞（實際定位）

period: Event 637 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 13

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 13

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Rustam, the Sasanian commander, arrays the hosts of Persia at Qadisiyya, himself in cuirass and double mail with two coats of gold. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, sick, directs the battle from a castle. For three days and nights the lines fight; on the third night — the Night of Clangour — the Muslims carry the field; a gust of wind covers Rustam with dust, and he is struck down under his baggage-camel. The road to Ctesiphon is open.
summary.zh: 薩珊統帥魯斯塔姆於卡迪西亞列波斯大軍，身披胸甲與雙層鎖子甲，飾以金。賽爾德·本·阿比·瓦卡斯抱病於堡壘中指揮。三日三夜激戰；第三夜——『鏗鏘之夜』——穆斯林取勝；一陣風沙掩覆魯斯塔姆，他於其馱貨駱駝下被擊斃。通往泰西封之路開。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; narrative as received in Muir from Tabari.

passages.text: Rustam, the general of the Sasanian king, brought up the hosts of Persia to the plain of Qadisiyya, himself in a cuirass of gold, with two coats of mail, and a helmet; a herald cried before him. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, sick of the quinsy, directed the battle from the castle of the neighbouring monastery, watching from its towers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 13; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩珊國王的將領魯斯塔姆率領波斯大軍來到卡迪西亞平原，他本人身穿黃金胸甲，外罩兩層鎖子甲，頭戴頭盔；一名傳令官在他面前呼喊。薩阿德·伊本·阿比·瓦卡斯因患扁桃腺炎而病，從鄰近修道院的城堡中指揮戰役，從其塔樓上觀望。

passages.text: For three days and nights the two armies fought in relays; the third was the Night of Clangour, when neither host slept. In the last hour a storm of dust rose against the Persian lines, and Rustam hid himself under the baggage of his camel; a Muslim found him there and struck off his hand, and killed him. The army of Persia broke and fled; the elephant-guard died with their beasts; and the road to Ctesiphon, the royal city, lay open before the Arabs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 13; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 兩軍輪番交戰了三日三夜；第三夜是「喧囂之夜」，兩軍皆未入睡。在最後的時刻，一陣塵暴朝波斯陣線揚起，魯斯塔姆躲藏在他的駱駝的行李之下；一名穆斯林在那裡發現了他，砍斷了他的手，將他殺死。波斯大軍潰散奔逃；象衛隊與他們的象一同戰死；通往王城泰西封的道路在阿拉伯人面前敞開。

title.en: The Capture of Ctesiphon (Madain)
title.zh: 攻克泰西封（麥丹）

region.en: Ctesiphon / Madain, Sasanian capital on the Tigris (literal pin)
region.zh: 底格里斯河畔薩珊都城泰西封（實際定位）

period: Event 637 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 14

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 14

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The capital of the Sasanians falls after the siege of the canal line. The Great Hall of Khosrau is entered: the white elephant of the throne, the crown set with jewels, the carpet of the winter palace woven in one piece with its gardens of pearls — the fifth of the spoil set aside, the rest divided. Yazdegerd flees east, and the fire-temples of the Persian heartland are brought under tribute.
summary.zh: 圍攻運河防線後，薩珊都城陷落。庫斯老的偉大宮殿被入：寶座之白象、鑲寶之冠、冬宮以珍珠織成花園的整幅地毯——戰利品的五分之一歸庫，其餘分配。伊嗣俟東逃；波斯腹地的火廟納貢。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; the sack of the capital recorded as received narrative.

passages.text: After the victory of Qadisiyya the Arabs crossed the canal line in the storm, and the city of Madain — Ctesiphon, the capital of the Sasanians — was taken. The Great Hall of Khosrau was entered, and the treasure of the crown: the carpet of the winter palace was carried out whole, woven in a single piece with its gardens of gold and silver and pearls, and it was cut into shares by order of Umar, who said that such a thing should not be in one man's keeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 14; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 卡迪西亞勝利之後，阿拉伯人在風暴中越過了運河防線，馬達因城——即薩珊王朝的首都泰西封——被攻佔。科斯洛埃斯的大殿被進入，王冠的寶藏也被取走：冬宮的地毯被整幅搬出，它以金、銀和珍珠織成花園圖案，為一整塊織成，並奉歐麥爾之命被分割成若干份，歐麥爾說這樣的東西不應由一人獨佔。

passages.text: Yazdegerd fled eastward from city to city; the fire-temples of the Persian heartland were brought under tribute, and the Arabs recited at the palace: 'How often have they left their gardens and their fountains, their treasures and their splendid dwellings — so it was: and We gave them to the children of Israel for an inheritance.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 14; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 亞茲德格爾德向東逃亡，從一座城逃到另一座城；波斯腹地的火神廟被置於納貢之下，阿拉伯人在宮殿中誦道：「他們曾留下多少園圃和泉源，多少寶藏和華美的居所——事情就是這樣：我們使以色列的子孫繼承了它們。」

title.en: Umar Enters Jerusalem in His Patched Cloak
title.zh: 歐瑪爾披補丁斗篷入耶路撒冷

region.en: Jerusalem, the Aqsa sanctuary (literal pin)
region.zh: 耶路撒冷阿克薩聖所（實際定位）

period: Event 637-638 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 10

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 10

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The patriarch Sophronius surrenders the city on condition that the caliph come in person. Umar rides from Medina with a single camel-servant, the two riding turn about. He enters in a patched mantle, walking; the patriarch reads in his rags the abomination of desolation of Daniel. Terms are granted: the churches safe, the tributary tax; the caliph prays at the sanctuary of David, and the Aqsa is cleared of the city's refuse.
summary.zh: 主教索福羅尼烏斯以哈里發親臨為條件交城。歐瑪爾攜一名駱駝侍者自麥地那啟程，二人輪流騎乘。他徒步披補丁斗篷入城；主教於其襤褸中讀出但以理書之荒涼可憎之物。條款寬厚：教堂得保、納稅而存；哈里發於大衛聖所禮拜，並清出阿克薩的城中穢物。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; the Umar tradition underlies the later Covenant of Umar and Muslim-Jewish-Christian relations in the city.

passages.text: The patriarch Sophronius would surrender Jerusalem only to the caliph himself. Umar set out from Medina with one servant and a camel, which they rode turn about, he walking one day and his man the next. He came to the city in a patched mantle, walking, and entered by the gate; and the patriarch saw him in his rags, and said, sighing, that this was the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel the prophet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 10; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 宗主教索弗羅尼烏斯只願向哈里發本人投降，才肯交出耶路撒冷。歐麥爾從麥地那出發，只帶一名僕人和一頭駱駝，兩人輪流騎乘，他走一天，僕人走一天。他身穿補丁斗篷，徒步來到城下，從城門而入；宗主教見他衣衫襤褸，嘆息著說，這便是先知但以理所說的「那行毀壞可憎的」。

passages.text: Umar granted the terms: the churches were safe and their clergy free; the people paid the tribute of the protected. He walked through the city with the patriarch, and prayed in the sanctuary of the Temple Mount where the Rock of David stood, cleared of the refuse that the Christians had heaped there; and he prayed at the south of the sanctuary, that the Muslims might not take the place of the Christians' worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 10; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 歐麥爾允准了這些條件：教堂安全無虞，教士自由無礙；民眾繳納受保護者的貢稅。他與宗主教一同走過城中，在聖殿山上大衛之石所在的聖所祈禱，那裡已清除基督徒堆積的污穢；他又在聖所南側祈禱，以免穆斯林佔據基督徒禮拜之地。

title.en: Amr and the Books of Alexandria
title.zh: 阿慕爾與亞歷山大的藏書

region.en: Alexandria, Egypt (literal pin)
region.zh: 埃及亞歷山大（實際定位）

period: Event dated 642 CE in the story; English: S. Ockley, History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); Muir, The Caliphate (1891)

source.work: Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); William Muir, The Caliphate (1891) — with the historian's note that the tale is contested

license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic original 13th century)

summary.en: The story told by Ibn al-Qifti and repeated by Ockley: after the capture of Alexandria, John the Grammarian asks the caliph for the books of the library. Umar answers: if they agree with the Qur'an they are superfluous; if against it, they are pernicious; burn them. The books are used to heat the city baths for six months. Modern historians find the story in no early source and doubt it; the tale belongs to the lore of the conquests.
summary.zh: 伊本·基夫提所傳、奧克萊重述的故事：攻克亞歷山大後，文法家約翰向哈里發求藏書。歐瑪爾答：若與古蘭經相合則為多餘；若相悖則為有害；燒之。其書供城中浴場燒水六個月。現代史家未於早期史料中見此說而存疑；此乃征服傳說之軼事。

sensitivity.note: A famous legend of contested historicity, recorded in Ockley's eighteenth-century English with the caution repeated here; presented as story, not as established event.

passages.text: When Amr had taken Alexandria, John the Grammarian asked of the caliph the books of the library of the city, that they might not be given to the soldiers. Umar answered: 'If the books agree with the Book of God, they are superfluous; if they contradict it, they are pernicious; burn them.' And the books were distributed to the baths of the city, and burned in them for six months.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the story as told in Ibn al-Qifti and repeated in Ockley, History of the Saracens (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿姆爾攻下亞歷山大城後，文法學家約翰向哈里發請求城內圖書館的書籍，以免它們落入士兵之手。歐麥爾回答說：「若這些書與真主的經典相符，便是多餘的；若與之相悖，便是有害的；燒掉它們。」於是這些書被分發到城中的浴場，在浴場裡燒了六個月。

passages.text: The story is found in no early historian of the conquest; Muir records it with the caution that it is late and probably invented, and the modern reader should take it as a legend of the lore of the conquests — a tale about what it meant to burn a library, told long after the burning was forgotten or never happened.
passages.note: Historiographical note paraphrased from Muir, The Caliphate (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這個故事不見於任何早期記述征服史的史家；繆爾記載此事時告誡說，它出現得晚，很可能是編造的，現代讀者應把它看作征服傳說中的一則故事——一則講述燒毀一座圖書館意味著什麼的故事，講述於那場焚燒已被遺忘、或從未發生之後很久。

title.en: The Battle of the Camel: Aisha's Litter
title.zh: 駱駝之戰：阿伊莎的駝轎

region.en: Basra, Iraq (literal pin)
region.zh: 伊拉克巴士拉（實際定位）

period: Event 656 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 19

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 19

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Aisha, the widow of the Prophet, rides from Mecca to Basra to avenge Uthman; Talha and Zubayr are with her. Ali comes up from Kufa. In the battle the camel of Aisha carries her litter into the field, and the fighting gathers around it; Talha and Zubayr fall. Ali wins, and sends the Prophet's widow home with honour — but the companions' first war against companions has been fought.
summary.zh: 先知遺孀阿伊莎自麥加赴巴士拉，欲為奧斯曼復仇；塔拉哈與祖拜爾同行。阿里自庫法來。戰中阿伊莎之駝載其轎入陣，廝殺聚於其周；塔拉哈與祖拜爾皆歿。阿里勝，以榮遣先知之遺孀返歸——然聖門弟子間首度兵戎相見。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; the first civil war is read differently in Sunni and Shi'i memory; presented as received narrative.

passages.text: Uthman was slain in Medina, and Aisha, the widow of the Prophet, rode out to Basra to call his slayers to account, with Talha and Zubayr, two of the ten promised Paradise. Ali came up from Kufa to meet them; the parleys failed, and the two armies joined in battle under the walls of Basra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 19; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 奧斯曼在麥地那被殺，先知的遺孀阿伊莎與塔勒哈、祖拜爾——蒙應許入樂園的十人中的兩位——一同騎行前往巴士拉，要追究殺害他的人的責任。阿里從庫法前來迎擊；談判破裂，兩軍在巴士拉城牆下交戰。

passages.text: Aisha sat in a litter on her camel, and the fighting gathered around her as around a standard; the battle was called the Battle of the Camel. Talha fell; Zubayr left the field, and was slain in a ravine by a man who came only for the spoils. At last the camel was hamstrung, and the litter sank; Ali won the day, and sent the Prophet's widow home to Medina with every honour — but the companions had fought companions, and the wound did not close.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 19; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿伊莎坐在駱駝上的轎廂裡，戰鬥圍繞著她展開，如同圍繞著一面旗幟；此戰被稱為駱駝之戰。塔勒哈陣亡；祖拜爾離開戰場，在山谷中被一個只為戰利品而來的人殺死。最後駱駝的腿筋被割斷，轎廂傾覆；阿里贏得了這一天，以種種榮譽將先知的遺孀送回麥地那——但聖門弟子已與聖門弟子交戰，傷口未能癒合。

title.en: Siffin: Qur'ans on the Spears
title.zh: 綏芬：長矛上的古蘭經

region.en: Siffin, on the Euphrates (literal pin)
region.zh: 幼發拉底河畔的綏芬（實際定位）

period: Event 657 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Ali marches against Mu'awiya, governor of Syria. For days the armies fight; Amr ibn al-As, Mu'awiya's adviser, orders the soldiers to raise copies of the Qur'an on their spear-points and cry 'Let the Book of God decide.' The fight stops; Ali sees the trick — 'I knew them, O people; by night the pages were raised in sight of the Qur'an' — but his army compels him to arbitration. The arbitrators confer; the tide turns against Ali, and the Kharijites break away crying 'Judgment is God's alone.'
summary.zh: 阿里進軍敘利亞總督穆阿維亞。數日大戰；穆阿維亞謀士阿慕爾·本·阿斯令士兵將古蘭經抄本繫於矛端，高呼『讓主之經典裁決』。戰止；阿里識破詭計——『人們啊，我深知他們；夜間他們舉起書頁，卻不見古蘭經』——然其軍迫其行仲裁。仲裁者相商；局勢轉而不利於阿里，哈瓦利吉派高呼『惟主之裁決』而脫離。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; presented as received narrative.

passages.text: Ali marched against Mu'awiya, who had withheld his homage from Medina, and the armies met on the plain of Siffin by the Euphrates. For days the lines fought in relays; the spears and swords had decided nothing but the hour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿里進軍討伐穆阿維葉，穆阿維葉曾拒絕向麥地那宣誓效忠，兩軍在幼發拉底河畔的隋芬平原相遇。連日來，雙方輪番交戰；長矛與刀劍除了決定時辰之外，什麼也決定不了。

passages.text: Then Amr ibn al-As gave counsel to Mu'awiya: let the soldiers lift copies of the Qur'an on the points of their spears, crying, 'Let the Book of God judge between us.' And it was done; the battle stopped of itself. Ali said: 'I knew them — I tell you that these are the men of deception; by night they lifted pages that have nothing of the Qur'an in them.' But his army would not fight on, and compelled him to arbitration. The two arbitrators conferred at Adhruh; and the tide turned against Ali — and the strictest of his own soldiers broke away, crying, 'Judgment is God's alone; there is no arbitration between men.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是阿姆爾·伊本·阿斯向穆阿維葉獻策：讓士兵們把《古蘭經》的抄本挑在矛尖上，高喊：『讓真主的經典在我們之間裁斷吧。』事情就這樣做了；戰鬥自行停止了。阿里說：『我認識他們——我告訴你們，這些人是欺詐之徒；他們在夜裡舉起的那些書頁，裡面根本沒有《古蘭經》的內容。』但他的軍隊不願再戰，強迫他接受仲裁。兩位仲裁者在阿茲魯赫會商；形勢轉而對阿里不利——而他麾下最嚴格的士兵脫離了他，高喊：『裁斷只屬於真主；人與人之間沒有仲裁。』

title.en: The Martyrdom of Uthman
title.zh: 奧斯曼之殉難

region.en: Medina, house of Uthman (literal pin)
region.zh: 麥地那奧斯曼宅（實際定位）

period: Event 656 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The besiegers close on the house of Uthman; Ali sends his sons to guard the door. The rebels break in at last, and the old caliph is struck as he recites the Book; his blood runs on the verses — 'and God will suffice thee against them that mock' — read on to the end. Medina has seen its first civil blood; the copy of the Qur'an that he was reading is said to be the one his own commission produced.
summary.zh: 圍困者逼至奧斯曼宅；阿里遣其子守門。叛者終破門而入；年邁哈里發誦經時被擊；其血流於經文之上——『主必使你免受嘲笑者之害』——經誦讀至終。麥地那首見同室操戈之血；相傳其誦讀的抄本，正是他主持委員會所定。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; the first caliph slain by Muslims is treated with restraint in all traditions.

passages.text: The malcontents gathered in Egypt and Kufa marched to Medina and besieged the house of Uthman. Ali sent his sons to keep the door, and blood was shed before it. The rebels broke in at last; and the old caliph, seated with the Book before him, was struck, and his blood ran over the page where he had read: 'They will say, art thou the one whom God and His Messenger blessed? — and God will suffice thee against the mockers.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 心懷不滿的人聚集在埃及，庫法的人則進軍麥地那，圍困了奧斯曼的宅邸。阿里派他的兒子們守衛大門，門前流了血。叛亂者終於破門而入；這位年邁的哈里發正坐在那裡，面前攤著經典，遭到擊打，他的血濺流在他所讀的那一頁上：『他們將說，你不就是真主及其使者所祝福的那一位嗎？——真主必將替你抵禦那些嘲弄者。』

passages.text: It was the copy of the Qur'an which his own commission had gathered that lay before him, and the tale is told that he read to the end of the verse. His body was buried at night by his kin; Ali washed his hands, saying, 'God knows that I was innocent of his blood.' The Caliphate of Medina had seen its first civil blood, and the wound of the community was opened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 擺在他面前的，正是他親自委派編纂所匯集的那部《古蘭經》抄本，據說他讀到了那節經文的末尾。他的遺體由親屬在夜間安葬；阿里洗淨雙手，說道：『真主知道，我與他的血無關。』麥地那的哈里發政權見到了它最初的內戰之血，社群的傷口就此裂開。

title.en: The Martyrdom of Ali in the Mosque of Kufa
title.zh: 阿里殉於庫法清真寺

region.en: Kufa, mosque of Ali (literal pin)
region.zh: 庫法阿里清真寺（實際定位）

period: Event 661 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: A Kharijite, Ibn Muljam, waits for Ali at the dawn prayer of Ramadan in the mosque of Kufa. As the caliph is drawn from his couch of sleep and stands at prayer, the poisoned sword falls on the crown of his head. 'By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have succeeded'; the wound is mortal, and the words that follow are of the prayer, the fear of God, and the young man's death. Hasan buries him; the traditions read the murder as the price of arbitration.
summary.zh: 哈瓦利吉派刺客伊本·穆勒加姆於萊麥丹晨禮時候在庫法清真寺等候阿里。哈里發自睡榻起身立於禮拜時，淬毒之劍落於其頭頂。『以天房之主起誓，我已成功。』傷勢致命；臨終之言關乎禮拜、敬畏主、與青年刺客之死。哈桑葬之；諸傳統視此刺殺為仲裁之代價。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; Ali's martyrdom is a cardinal event of Shi'i devotion; presented as received narrative without sectarian framing.

passages.text: Ibn Muljam, a Kharijite of the breakaway sect, had bound himself to kill Ali, and waited for him in the mosque of Kufa at the dawn prayer of Ramadan. As Ali came out of his couch of sleep and stood at prayer, the man struck him on the crown of the head with a sword dipped in poison.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 伊本·穆爾賈姆，一個脫離派別哈瓦利吉派的成員，立誓要殺死阿里，並在齋月的晨禮時分於庫法的清真寺中等候他。當阿里從睡榻上起身站到禮拜中時，這人用一把浸過毒的劍擊中了他的頭頂。

passages.text: Ali cried, 'By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have succeeded.' The wound was mortal. He called his son Hasan, and spoke of the prayer, and of the fear of God, and of the young man who had killed him — 'Kill him gently, if I die of the wound, and do not mutilate him; I heard the Prophet say, do not mutilate even the dog.' And the First of the Muslims to be slain at prayer was buried in Kufa, and the caliphate passed out of the line of the companions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿里喊道：『以克爾白的主發誓，我成功了。』傷勢致命。他召來兒子哈桑，談到禮拜，談到對真主的敬畏，也談到殺死他的那個年輕人——『若我因這傷而死，就溫和地處死他，不要毀傷他的肢體；我聽先知說過，連狗都不要毀傷。』於是，第一位在禮拜中被殺的穆斯林葬於庫法，哈里發之位也從聖門弟子的世系中轉了出去。

title.en: Mu'awiya: 'I Use Cunning Where Thou Usest Chivalry'
title.zh: 穆阿維亞：「你用騎士之勇，我用權謀」

region.en: Damascus, court of Mu'awiya (literal pin)
region.zh: 大馬士革穆阿維亞宮廷（實際定位）

period: Events 650s-660s CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Mu'awiya, first of the Umayyads, rules twenty years from Damascus with the tools of the scribe and the soldier. To the last of the companions who reproach him he answers with the famous word: 'By God, I do not use against thee the sword, or the whip, or the market, or the crowding of men; I use cunning where thou usest chivalry.' The anecdote lore of the court gathers around him — the Kharijite who threw his sandal, the man who called out in the mosque, and the letter that ended: 'Do not write to me of women; write to me of power.'
summary.zh: 伍麥葉王朝首主穆阿維亞自大馬士革以文書與士兵之術執政二十年。對最後一位責難他的聖門弟子，他答以名言：『我不用劍，不用鞭，不用市場，不用人潮相逼；你用騎士之勇，我用權謀。』宮廷軼事圍繞他累積——投擲其靴之哈瓦利吉派者、清真寺中高呼者、以及結尾寫道：『勿與我言婦人；與我言權力』的書信。

sensitivity.note: Anecdote lore of the Umayyad court as gathered in Muir from the Arabic historians; Mu'awiya is judged differently in Sunni and Shi'i memory.

passages.text: Mu'awiya ruled from Damascus for twenty years, the first of the Umayyads. To the men of the Prophet's generation who reproached him for his rule by scribes and soldiers, he gave the famous answer: 'By God, I do not use against thee the sword, or the whip, or the market, or the crowding of men; I use cunning where thou usest chivalry.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote lore of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 穆阿維亞自大馬士革統治二十年，為伍麥葉家族之首。對於先知那一代中責備他以文書與士兵治國的人，他給了那句著名的答覆：「以真主之名，我不用劍、不用鞭、不用市場、不用人眾來對付你；你以騎士之風行事，我則以權謀應對。」

passages.text: The court anecdotes gather round him: the Kharijite who flung his sandal at him in the mosque and was told that he would be given his blood-money if he could find his equal; the man who cried out against him and was made to drink honey as a punishment; and the letter to a man who sought a wife: 'Do not write to me of women; write to me of power.' And he was said to be the most patient and the most clement of the caliphs, and the least of them to be provoked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote lore via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 宮廷軼事圍繞著他流傳：那名在清真寺裡向他擲鞋的哈瓦利吉派信徒，被告知若能找到與他相當之人，便可得其血金；那名高聲斥責他、卻被罰飲蜂蜜的人；以及他寫給一名求娶妻室之人的信：「不要寫信與我談女人；寫信與我談權力。」據說他是諸哈里發中最有耐性、最寬厚，也最不易被激怒的一位。

title.en: The Shaman and the Master of the Four Abysses (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 壺子示相，神巫季咸（莊子）

region.en: The State of Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國（今河南鄭州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 7, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 7

summary.en: In Chêng lives the magician Chi Han, who predicts death and life to a day. Lieh Tzŭ, dazzled, thinks his own tutor Hu Tzŭ inferior; but Hu Tzŭ shows the shaman four successive faces — the still earth, the dispassionate heaven, the nine-named abyss of equilibrium, and lastly the TAO before time was, a great blank existing of itself — at which the shaman turns and flees, and Lieh Tzŭ goes home to feed his pigs like human beings for three years.
summary.zh: 鄭有神巫曰季咸，知人之死生存亡。壺子四示其相：地文之靜、天壤之動、太衝莫勝之淵、而未始出吾宗——立未始出吾宗，而巫咸逃；列子三年不出，為其妻爨，食豕如食人。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the shaman-episode is the classic Taoist counter-narrative to divinatory magic. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: In the State of Chêng there was a wonderful magician, named Chi Han. He knew all about birth and death, gain and loss, misfortune and happiness, long life and short life,--predicting events to a day with supernatural accuracy. The people of Chêng used to flee at his approach; but Lieh Tzŭ went to see him, and became so infatuated that on his return he said to Hu Tzŭ, "I used to look upon your TAO as perfect. Now I know something more perfect still." "So far," replied Hu Tzŭ, "I have only taught you the ornamentals, not the essentials, of TAO; and yet you think you know all about it. Without cocks in your poultry-yard, what sort of eggs do the hens lay? If you go about trying to force TAO down people's throats, you will be simply exposing yourself. Bring your friend with you, and let me show myself to him."
passages.zh: 鄭國有一位神妙的巫者，名叫季咸。他通曉生死、得失、禍福、長壽與短命——預言事件，靈驗得能精確到某一天。鄭國的人一見他走近便紛紛逃走；但列子去見了他，竟為之傾倒，回來後對壺子說：「我從前以為您的道已臻完美。如今我才知道還有更完美的。」壺子回答：「到目前為止，我只教了你道的皮毛，還未教其精髓；你卻自以為全都懂了。你的雞欄裡沒有公雞，母雞又怎能下蛋？你若四處奔走，硬要把道塞進別人喉嚨裡，只會暴露你自己罷了。帶你的朋友來，讓我向他顯露一番。」

passages.text: So next day Lieh Tzŭ went with Chi Han to see Hu Tzŭ, and when they came out Chi Han said, "Alas! your teacher is doomed. He cannot live. I hardly give him ten days. I am astonished at him. He is but wet ashes." Lieh Tzŭ went in and wept bitterly, and told Hu Tzŭ; but the latter said, "I showed myself to him just now as the earth shows us its outward form, motionless and still, while production is all the time going on. I merely prevented him from seeing my pent-up energy within. Bring him again." Next day the interview took place as before; but as they were leaving Chi Han said to Lieh Tzŭ, "It is lucky for your teacher that he met me. He is better. He will recover. I saw he had recuperative power."
passages.zh: 於是次日列子帶著季咸去見壺子，出來時季咸說：「唉！你的老師命數已盡。他活不成了。我幾乎斷定他撐不過十天。我對他感到驚訝。他不過是濕灰罷了。」列子進去，痛哭失聲，告訴了壺子；壺子卻說：「我剛才向他顯露的，正如大地向我們顯露其外形，靜止不動，而生成卻始終在進行。我只是不讓他看見我內裡蓄積的元氣。再帶他來。」次日會面如前；但離開時季咸對列子說：「你的老師有幸遇見了我。他好些了。他會康復的。我看出他有恢復之力。」

passages.text: Next day a third interview took place, and as they were leaving, Chi Han said to Lieh Tzŭ, "Your teacher is never one day like another. I can tell nothing from his physiognomy. Get him to be regular, and I will then examine him again." This being repeated to Hu Tzŭ as before, the latter said, "I showed myself to him just now in a state of harmonious equilibrium. Where the whale disports itself,--is the abyss. Where water is at rest,--is the abyss. Where water is in motion,--is the abyss. The abyss has nine names. These are three of them." Next day the two went once more to see Hu Tzŭ; but Chi Han was unable to stand still, and in his confusion turned and fled.
passages.zh: 次日第三次會面，離開時季咸對列子說：「你的老師沒有一天與另一天相同。我無法從他的面相看出什麼。讓他變得有常規，我再來察看。」這話照樣轉告壺子，壺子說：「我剛才向他顯露的是和諧均衡的狀態。鯨魚嬉游之處，是深淵。水靜止之處，是深淵。水流動之處，是深淵。深淵有九個名稱。這是其中三個。」次日兩人又去見壺子；但季咸站不穩，慌亂之中轉身就逃。

passages.text: "I showed myself to him just now," said Hu Tzŭ, "as TAO appeared before time was. I was to him as a great blank, existing of itself. He knew not who I was. His face fell. He became confused. And so he fled." Upon this Lieh Tzŭ stood convinced that he had not yet acquired any real knowledge, and at once set to work in earnest, passing three years without leaving the house. He helped his wife to cook the family dinner, and fed his pigs just like human beings. He discarded the artificial and reverted to the natural. He became merely a shape. Amidst confusion, he was unconfounded. And so he continued to the end.
passages.zh: 壺子說：「我剛才向他顯露的，是道在時間之前顯現的樣子。我對他而言如同一片廣大的空白，自存自在。他不知道我是誰。他的臉色驟變。他慌亂了。於是便逃走了。」於是列子確信自己尚未獲得任何真正的學問，立刻認真用功，三年不出家門。他幫妻子做飯，餵豬如同待人。他捨棄人為，回歸自然。他僅成了一個形體。身處紛亂之中，他卻不為所惑。就這樣直到終了。

title.en: The Sage of the Yin Mountain Refuses the Empire (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 天根問治於蓼水之陽（莊子）

region.en: South of the Yin mountain, by the Liao river (symbolic pin: Liaoyang, Liaoning, China)
region.zh: 殷山之陽、蓼水之上（象徵定位：遼寧遼陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 7, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 7

summary.en: T'ien Kên meets a Sage by the Liao river and begs to ask about governing the empire; the Sage drives him off — borne on light pinions he can soar beyond the cardinal points to the land of nowhere — and on the second asking gives his whole doctrine: resolve your mental energy into abstraction, your physical energy into inaction, fall in with the natural order without admitting the element of self, and the empire will be governed.
summary.zh: 天根遊於殷陽，問為天下於聖人。聖人曰：去！汝鄙人也——予方與造物者為人，厭則又乘夫莽眇之鳥，以出六極之外，而遊無何有之鄉，以處壙垠之野。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Begone!" cried the Sage. "You are a low fellow, and your question is ill timed. God has just turned me out a man. That is enough for me. Borne on light pinions I can soar beyond the cardinal points, to the land of nowhere, in the domain of nothingness. And you come to worry me with government of the empire!" But T'ien Kên enquired a second time, and the Sage replied, "Resolve your mental energy into abstraction, your physical energy into inaction. Allow yourself to fall in with the natural order of phenomena, without admitting the element of self,--and the empire will be governed."
passages.zh: 「去吧！」聖人喊道。「你是個卑下之人，而且你問得不是時候。上天剛剛把我造就成一個人。這對我來說已經足夠了。乘著輕盈的羽翼，我能翱翔於四方之外，前往無何有之鄉，處於虛無之境。而你卻來以治理天下之事煩擾我！」但田開之再問了一次，聖人回答說：「把你的心神化為虛靜，把你的形體化為無為。讓自己順應萬物的自然秩序，而不容納自我之念——天下便會得到治理。」

title.en: Yang Tzŭ Chü Asks Lao Tzŭ What Makes a Wise Ruler (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 陽子居見老聃問明王（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's retreat (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 7, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 7

summary.en: Yang Tzŭ Chü asks whether an ardent, courageous, tireless seeker of the Tao would be a wise ruler. Lao Tzŭ answers that he would be a mere handicraftsman wearing out body and mind; the tiger suffers from the beauty of his skin. The wise ruler's goodness covers the empire, yet he himself seems to know it not — it is based upon the baseless, and travels through the realms of Nowhere.
summary.zh: 陽子居見老聃曰：有人於此，嚮疾強梁，物徹疏明，學道不倦——如是者可比明王乎？老聃曰：明王之治，功蓋天下而似不自己，化貸萬物而民弗恃；立乎不測，而遊於無有者也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yang Tzŭ Chü went to see Lao Tzŭ, and said, "Suppose a man were ardent and courageous, acquainted with the order and principles of things, and untiring in the pursuit of TAO--would he be accounted a wise ruler?" "From the point of view of a truly wise man," replied Lao Tzŭ, "such a one would be a mere handicraftsman, wearing out body and mind alike. The tiger and the pard suffer from the beauty of their skins. The cleverness of the monkey, the tractability of the ox, bring them both to the tether. It is not on such grounds that a ruler may be accounted wise."
passages.zh: 陽子居去見老子，說：「假設有一個人敏銳而勇敢，通曉事物的秩序與原理，並且孜孜不倦地追求道——他會被認為是明智的統治者嗎？」「從真正明智之人的觀點來看，」老子回答說，「這樣的人不過是個工匠，身心俱疲。虎豹因皮毛之美而受害。猴子的機巧、牛的順服，使牠們雙雙受制於繩索。統治者並非憑藉這類條件而被認為明智。」

passages.text: "The goodness of a wise ruler," answered Lao Tzŭ, "covers the whole empire, yet he himself seems to know it not. It influences all creation, yet none is conscious thereof. It appears under countless forms, bringing joy to all things. It is based upon the baseless, and travels through the realms of Nowhere."
passages.zh: 「明智統治者的善，」老子回答說，「覆蓋整個天下，然而他自己似乎並不知道。它影響萬物，然而沒有誰察覺到它。它以無數形態顯現，為萬物帶來歡樂。它立足於無所立足之處，並穿行於無何有之鄉。」

title.en: Karbala: The Martyrdom of Husayn
title.zh: 卡爾巴拉：侯賽因之殉難

region.en: Karbala, on the Euphrates, Iraq (literal pin)
region.zh: 伊拉克幼發拉底河畔卡爾巴拉（實際定位）

period: Event 680 CE; English: S. Ockley, History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 25

source.work: Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 25

license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Yazid is proclaimed caliph at Damascus; Husayn, grandson of the Prophet, refuses the oath and rides for Kufa. He is met by the army of Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad at Karbala, cut off from the Euphrates, and besieged for days without water. On the day of Ashura the seventy-two are struck down one by one; Husayn falls last, with his infant son in his arms. Zaynab carries the captives to Damascus, and the mourning for the family of the Prophet becomes the rite of Muharram.
summary.zh: 大馬士革擁立耶齊德為哈里發；先知之孫侯賽因拒誓，騎向庫法。於卡爾巴拉遇伊本·齊亞德之軍，被截於幼發拉底河之外，斷水圍困多日。阿舒拉之日，七十二人逐一被殺；侯賽因殿後而歿，懷中抱其幼子。宰乃布攜俘至大馬士革；先知家屬之哀悼成為穆哈蘭月之儀。

sensitivity.note: The martyrdom of Husayn is a cardinal devotion of Shi'ism and a grief-event in Sunni memory alike; recorded as the received narrative of Tabari/Ockley without sectarian framing.

passages.text: On the death of Mu'awiya his son Yazid was proclaimed caliph at Damascus. Husayn, the son of Ali and the grandson of the Prophet, refused the oath and rode from Medina towards Kufa, whose people had written to invite him. The governor Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad sent an army against him; his path was turned aside, and he was met at the plain of Karbala, two days from the Euphrates.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Ockley (1890) and Muir (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 穆阿維葉死後，他的兒子葉齊德在大馬士革被宣布為哈里發。阿里之子、先知之孫侯賽因拒絕宣誓效忠，並從麥地那騎行前往庫法，庫法的居民曾寫信邀請他。總督烏拜杜拉·伊本·齊亞德派軍迎擊他；他的道路被阻斷，他在距幼發拉底河兩日路程的卡爾巴拉平原上與敵軍相遇。

passages.text: Husayn was besieged with his family and companions — seventy-two fighting men, among them his brother Abbas and his young son — and the water of the river was denied them. On the tenth day of Muharram, the day of Ashura, they were struck down one after another; Abbas fell at the water, and the infant of Husayn died in his father's arms, an arrow through its neck. Husayn fell last, faint with thirst, crying the old cry: 'Is there any helper?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Ockley (1890); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 侯賽因與他的家人和同伴被圍困——七十二名戰士，其中有他的兄弟阿巴斯和他年幼的兒子——河水被斷絕不給他們。在穆哈蘭姆月的第十日，即阿舒拉日，他們一個接一個被擊倒；阿巴斯倒在水邊，侯賽因的嬰兒死在他父親的懷中，一支箭射穿了他的脖子。侯賽因最後倒下，因口渴而昏厥，呼喊著那古老的呼聲：『可有任何援助者？』

passages.text: His head was carried to Ibn Ziyad and then to Damascus; his sister Zaynab led the captives, and in the court of Yazid she spoke the protest that the tradition remembers. The mourning for the family of the Prophet — the weeping processions of Muharram, the ta'ziya recitations, the shrines of Karbala and Najaf — grew out of the plain where the seventy-two died; and the Sunni calendar keeps the tenth of Muharram as a fast of grief and of the Ark's resting alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the aftermath as told in Ockley (1890) and the Arabic historians; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的頭顱被送到伊本·齊亞德那裡，然後送到大馬士革；他的妹妹宰娜卜帶領俘虜，在葉齊德的宮廷中，她說出了傳統所銘記的抗議。對先知家族的哀悼——穆哈蘭姆月的哭泣遊行、塔齊耶的誦讀、卡爾巴拉與納傑夫的聖陵——都源自那七十二人死去的平原；而遜尼派曆法將穆哈蘭姆月的第十日既作為悲傷的齋戒，也作為方舟停泊之日來遵守。

title.en: Al-Mansur and the Death of Abu Muslim
title.zh: 曼蘇爾與阿布·穆斯林之死

region.en: Kufa and the Khurasan road (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 庫法與呼羅珊道（象徵性定位於巴格達）

period: Event 755 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Abu Muslim, the maker of the Abbasid revolution, has won Persia with the black banners. The caliph al-Mansur summons him to the court; the amir is warned, and comes. The caliph reproaches him with the name of Abu Muslim — 'Art thou Abu Muslim? I will make thee a prey to the dogs of the streets' — and the bodyguard does the rest. The revolution devours its maker; and Persia murmurs for twenty years.
summary.zh: 阿拔斯革命的締造者阿布·穆斯林已以黑旗得波斯。哈里發曼蘇爾召其入廷；封臣受警，仍前來。哈里發以『阿布·穆斯林』之名責之——『你是阿布·穆斯林嗎？我必使你為街犬之食』——衛士續行其事。革命吞其締造者；波斯怨憤二十年。

sensitivity.note: Early Abbasid historiography as received in Muir.

passages.text: Abu Muslim had made the Abbasid revolution in Khurasan and won Persia for the House. The caliph al-Mansur, grown uneasy before so great a man, summoned him to the court. The friends of Abu Muslim warned him; the astrologers warned him; and he came, saying that he had given thirty years to the House and would not refuse its summons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿布·穆斯林在呼羅珊發動了阿拔斯革命，為這個家族贏得了波斯。哈里發曼蘇爾面對如此偉大的人物，漸感不安，便召他入宮。阿布·穆斯林的朋友們警告他，占星家們也警告他；他還是來了，說他已為這個家族奉獻了三十年，不會拒絕它的召喚。

passages.text: He entered and saluted; the caliph reproached him, and then spoke the word the historians have kept: 'Art thou Abu Muslim? I will make thee a prey to the dogs of the streets.' The bodyguard closed; and the maker of the dynasty was slain in the caliph's tent. Persia murmured for twenty years after, and the sects that remembered him raised him to a hidden lord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 39; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他入內行禮；哈里發斥責了他，隨後說出了史家所記載的那句話：『你就是阿布·穆斯林嗎？我要讓你成為街頭群犬的獵物。』衛隊合圍；這位王朝的締造者便在哈里發的帳中被殺。此後波斯低聲怨憤了二十年，而那些記得他的教派將他奉為一位隱遁之主。

title.en: Al-Mansur Founds Baghdad: The Round City
title.zh: 曼蘇爾建巴格達：圓城

region.en: Baghdad, Tigris crossing (literal pin)
region.zh: 底格里斯河渡口的巴格達（實際定位）

period: Founded 762 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The caliph chooses the crossing of the Tigris and Sarat canals near the old Persian villages — 'a market for all the world, and nothing that the river brings can get past it.' Four thousand architects measure a city of concentric walls, Khuld the 'Eternal'; the trench is dug, the foundations laid of burned brick in rows of reed — 'O God, Thou art the Everlasting Lord; build Thou for me.' In four years the Round City stands, and it is called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace.
summary.zh: 哈里發擇底格里斯河與薩拉特運河交匯處，近古波斯村落——『天下之市集，河所載者無不經此』。四千名建築師量畫同心圓牆之城，名『永恆』（胡爾德）；掘溝，以蘆葦為行、焙磚為基——『主啊，你是永活之主；為我而建吧』。四年之間圓城立，名『和平之城』（麥地那·薩拉姆）。

sensitivity.note: Early Abbasid historiography; the founding is a landmark of urban and intellectual history.

passages.text: Al-Mansur sought a site for his capital and chose the crossing of the Tigris and the Sarat canals, by the villages of the old Persian name — a market for all the world, he said, with nothing that the river brings able to pass it. He had the ground measured by his engineers: a city of two concentric walls with a ditch between, the mosque and the palace at the centre under a golden dome.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 曼蘇爾為他的都城尋覓地點，選中了底格里斯河與薩拉特運河交匯之處，位於那些帶有古波斯名稱的村落旁——他說，這裡是全世界的市場，河運所帶來的一切都無法繞過它。他命工程師丈量土地：一座有兩道同心城牆、牆間設壕溝的城市，清真寺與宮殿居於中央，覆以金色圓頂。

passages.text: The trench was dug first, the caliph himself striking the first earth and praying: 'O God, Thou art the Everlasting Lord; build Thou for me; the world passes and Thy kingdom abides.' The walls were of burned brick laid in rows of reeds, the gates of iron; and in four years the Round City stood, called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace — and under its caliphs it became the seat of the translation of the sciences and of the lore of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 壕溝最先挖掘，哈里發親自掘下第一鏟土並祈禱：『真主啊，您是永恆的主；請為我建造；世界消逝，而您的國度長存。』城牆以燒磚砌成，磚層之間鋪以蘆葦，城門為鐵製；四年之後，圓城落成，名為和平之城（馬迪納特·薩拉姆）——在歷代哈里發治下，它成為翻譯科學與世界學問的中心。

title.en: Harun al-Rashid and the Fall of the Barmecides
title.zh: 哈倫·拉希德與巴爾馬克家族之傾覆

region.en: Baghdad, court of Harun (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴格達哈倫宮廷（實際定位）

period: Event 803 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Ja'far the Barmecide, vizier and playmate of Harun, is suddenly commanded to death; the tale is told that the caliph, feasting, had promised the hand of his sister Abbasa to Ja'far in jest, and that the jest was taken for a marriage. Whatever the cause, the sentence is carried in a night: Ja'far is struck in the hall of justice, his father Yahya cast into prison, the palaces of the family stripped. 'The cup of the Barmecides,' the Persian proverb runs, 'is broken.'
summary.zh: 巴爾馬克家族的賈法爾——哈倫的大臣與少年友伴——忽奉死命；相傳哈里發宴中戲許其妹阿巴西之婚，而戲言成真。無論其因，一夕行刑：賈法爾於議政廳被誅，其父葉海雅下獄，家族宮邸盡抄。波斯諺云：『巴爾馬克之杯已碎。』

sensitivity.note: Abbasid court historiography; the fall of the Barmecides is a locus classicus of the Arabic anecdote tradition.

passages.text: Ja'far the Barmecide had been the vizier of Harun al-Rashid and the companion of his boyhood; the House of Barmak had governed the East for a generation. In the year 803 the caliph commanded his death suddenly, without public cause; the tale is told that he had promised the hand of his sister Abbasa in jest at a feast, and that the jest had been taken for a marriage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴爾馬克家族的賈法爾曾任哈倫·拉希德的維齊爾，是他少年時代的伴侶；巴爾馬克家族已治理東方達一代人之久。803年，哈里發突然下令處死他，未給公開的理由；傳說他在一次宴會上戲言許諾將妹妹阿芭莎許配給他，而這句戲言竟被當作了婚約。

passages.text: The sentence was carried in a night: Ja'far was struck in the hall of justice, and his head sent to Baghdad; his father Yahya and his brother Fadl were cast into prison; the palaces of the family were stripped of their stuff. The Persian proverb kept the memory: 'The cup of the Barmecides is broken' — and the anecdote lore of the Arabs made the fall of the great House a byword for the turn of the king's favour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 46; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 判決在一夜之間執行：賈法爾在司法廳中被擊殺，首級送往巴格達；他的父親葉海亞與兄弟法德爾被投入監獄；家族的宮殿被抄掠一空。波斯諺語保存了這段記憶：『巴爾馬克人的酒杯碎了』——而阿拉伯人的軼事傳說使這個大家族之傾覆成為君王恩寵無常的代名詞。

title.en: The Brothers' War: Amin and Ma'mun
title.zh: 兄弟之戰：阿敏與馬蒙

region.en: Baghdad and Merv (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 巴格達與梅爾夫（象徵性定位於巴格達）

period: Events 809-813 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Harun divides the empire on his deathbed: Amin to reign at Baghdad, Ma'mun to hold Khurasan beyond the passes. The brothers' peace breaks; the Tahirid armies come west, Baghdad is besieged for a year, and Amin is taken in the last sally and slain on a bridge of boats. Ma'mun reigns from Merv, and the House is split between the two capitals for years.
summary.zh: 哈倫臨終分帝國：阿敏都於巴格達，馬蒙轄山外的呼羅珊。兄弟之約破裂；塔希爾軍西來，巴格達被圍一年，阿敏於最後的突圍中被擒，死於船橋之上。馬蒙自梅爾夫執政；王朝於兩都之間分裂数年。

sensitivity.note: Abbasid historiography as received in Muir.

passages.text: Harun al-Rashid on his deathbed divided his empire: Amin to reign at Baghdad, and Ma'mun to hold Khurasan beyond the passes, with his own guard and treasury. The peace of the brothers lasted as long as the guardians appointed; then Amin took the succession to himself, and Ma'mun refused, and the armies of Khurasan came west under Tahir.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈倫·拉希德在臨終之際分割了他的帝國：阿敏在巴格達執政，馬蒙則據有隘口之外的呼羅珊，並擁有自己的衛隊與財庫。兄弟之間的和平僅維持到受任的監護人尚在之時；其後阿敏將繼承權據為己有，馬蒙拒不承認，呼羅珊的軍隊便在塔希爾率領下西進。

passages.text: Baghdad was besieged for a year, house by house, the palaces burned and the people starved. In the last sally Amin was taken in a boat, and was slain on a bridge of the river by the men of Tahir; his head was sent to Merv. Ma'mun reigned from Khurasan, and did not come to Baghdad for years; and the House that Harun had divided never wholly joined again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 47; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴格達被圍攻一年，逐屋爭奪，宮殿遭焚，百姓饑困。在最後一次突圍中，阿敏於一條船上被擒，並在河上的一座橋上為塔希爾的人所殺；他的首級被送往木鹿。馬蒙自呼羅珊執政，多年未至巴格達；而哈倫所分割的那個家族，再也未能完全復合。

title.en: Tariq Crosses to the Rock of Gibraltar
title.zh: 塔里克渡至直布羅陀之岩

region.en: Gibraltar and Cadiz coast (literal pin)
region.zh: 直布羅陀與加的斯海岸（實際定位）

period: Event 711 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37 (Spanish conquest); S. Ockley (1890)

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; Simon Ockley, History of the Saracens (1890)

license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic originals 10th-11th centuries)

summary.en: Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses from Morocco to the rock that bears his name with seven thousand Berbers, and burns the boats: 'Where can you flee? The sea is behind you, the enemy in front.' Roderick the Visigoth comes against him with the hosts of Spain; the battle lasts a week, and the Visigothic kingdom falls. The rock keeps the commander's name; and Spain passes to the Muslims for eight hundred years.
summary.zh: 塔里克·本·齊亞德率七千柏柏爾人自摩洛哥渡至以他為名的岩地，並焚其舟：『你們能逃往何處？海在你身後，敵在你面前。』西哥特王羅德里克率西班牙大軍迎擊；戰事持續一週，西哥特王國傾覆。岩留統帥之名；西班牙歸穆斯林八百年。

sensitivity.note: Andalusi historiography as received in Muir/Ockley from Arabic sources.

passages.text: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from Morocco to the great rock of the strait with seven thousand Berbers, and burned the boats behind him. He spoke to them, in the speech the historians have kept: 'Whither can you flee? The sea is behind you, the enemy before you; you have nothing left but truth and courage.' And the rock took his name — Jabal Tariq, Gibraltar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Arabic accounts via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 塔里克·伊本·齊亞德率七千柏柏爾人自摩洛哥渡海，抵達海峽邊的那塊巨岩，並燒毀了身後的船隻。他以史家所保存的那番話對他們說道：『你們能逃往何處？大海在你們身後，敵人在你們面前；你們所剩的唯有真理與勇氣。』那塊巨岩遂取了他的名字——塔里克之山，即直布羅陀。

passages.text: Roderick, the last Visigothic king, came against him with the hosts of Spain. The battle lasted a week on the river of the south; the king fled or was drowned in the Guadalquivir, and his kingdom fell with him. The cities of Spain opened their gates one after another, and for eight hundred years the land of the Visigoths was the land of the Muslims, and its capital became Cordoba.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Arabic accounts via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 末代西哥德國王羅德里克率西班牙的大軍前來迎擊。戰鬥在南方的河畔持續了一週；國王或逃亡，或溺死於瓜達幾維河，他的王國也隨之傾覆。西班牙的各城逐一敞開城門，八百年間，西哥德人之地成了穆斯林之地，其都城則為科爾多瓦。

title.en: Abd al-Rahman and the Palm of Ronda
title.zh: 阿布杜·拉赫曼與隆達的棕櫚

region.en: Ronda, Andalus (literal pin)
region.zh: 安達魯西亞隆達（實際定位）

period: Event c. 756 CE; the poem preserved in Ibn Abd Rabbih's Arabic anthology; retold in later European histories

source.work: The palm-tree anecdote from the Arabic tradition (Ibn Abd Rabbih, al-Iqd al-Farid; retold in European histories of Spain); Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 38

license: Public domain (Arabic originals medieval; English edition 1891)

summary.en: The Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman, sole survivor of the massacre of his house, lands in Spain and builds his kingdom at Cordoba. Riding in the country of Ronda he finds a palm tree, the first he has seen since Damascus; he lays hold of it and speaks the lines the anthologies have kept: 'A palm like me, in exile far from home, parted from people and children... Turn to me, O palm, and hear me cry: as we are far from our people, so are you from yours.'
summary.zh: 伍麥葉王子阿布杜·拉赫曼——其家被屠之唯一倖存者——登陸西班牙，建都於科爾多瓦。行於隆達之鄉，見一棕櫚，乃其自大馬士革以來所見首株；他執其幹，誦出後世文集所存之句：『如我之棕櫚，離鄉萬里，與族人子女相隔……棕櫚啊，轉向我，聽我呼喊：我們離族人甚遠，你亦離你的族人甚遠。』

sensitivity.note: Anecdote lore of the Umayyad exiles of Spain; the palm poem is among the most quoted texts of Andalusi tradition.

passages.text: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya, the sole survivor of the Umayyad house after the Abbasid massacre, fled across half the world to Spain, and built his kingdom at Cordoba. Riding in the country of Ronda, he saw a palm tree — the first since Damascus — and laid hold of it, and spoke:
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote and poem as preserved in the Arabic anthologies; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 阿卜杜勒·拉赫曼·伊本·穆阿維葉，在阿拔斯王朝的大屠殺之後伍麥葉家族唯一的倖存者，逃越半個世界來到西班牙，在科爾多瓦建立了他的王國。他騎行於龍達鄉間，看見一棵棕櫚樹——自大馬士革以來所見的第一棵——便上前扶住它，說道：

passages.text: 'A palm like me, in exile far from home, parted from people and children, from kindred and from land: turn to me, O palm, and hear me cry — as we are far from our people, so are you from yours.' And the men of Spain wept to see their prince weep for a tree; and the kingdom of the exiles of Cordoba stood for three hundred years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote and poem as preserved in the Arabic anthologies; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 『一棵像我一樣的棕櫚，流亡遠離家園，與親人兒女分離，與族人與故土相隔：轉向我吧，棕櫚啊，聽我哭訴——正如我們遠離自己的族人，你也遠離你的。』西班牙的人們見他們的王子為一棵樹而哭泣，無不落淚；而科爾多瓦流亡者的王國存續了三百年。

title.en: The Assassins' Paradise at Alamut
title.zh: 阿拉穆特：刺客的樂園

region.en: Alamut fortress, Elburz mountains, Persia (literal pin)
region.zh: 波斯厄爾布爾士山阿拉穆特要塞（實際定位）

period: Legend told to Marco Polo c. 1270s; English: The Travels of Marco Polo (Marsden 1818 ed.); Persian sources of the 13th century

source.archive: Google Books (public domain scan of Marsden ed. 1818)
source.work: The Travels of Marco Polo, ch. on the Old Man of the Mountain (English, Marsden 1818 ed.); cf. Juvayni's Arabic-Persian history (13th century)

license: Public domain (English edition 1818; Arabic-Persian originals 13th century)

summary.en: The Venetian traveller tells of the Old Man of the Mountain, Hasan-i Sabbah, who kept at Alamut a secret garden watered with milk and honey, with boys and girls of beauty, to which he brought his young men drugged with wine and hemp; they woke in 'Paradise' and were cast out again, believing their master could return them at will. Hence, the legend says, the obedience of the Assassins to death. Modern historians find the garden only in the Western tellings; the fortress itself was taken by the Mongols in 1256.
summary.zh: 威尼斯旅人所述山中老人哈桑·薩巴赫於阿拉穆特蓄一秘密花園，水以乳與蜜，藏絕色男女；以酒與麻藥之青年入園，醒於『樂園』，復被逐出，信其主可隨意使之復返。相傳刺客由此捨死聽命。現代史家謂此花園僅見於西方敘述；要塞本身於1256年被蒙古人攻陷。

sensitivity.note: A Western legend about a Muslim sect, recorded by Marco Polo and doubted by modern historians of the Nizari Isma'ilis; presented as a story about how the East was told in Europe, not as an established fact.

passages.text: Marco Polo tells of the Old Man of the Mountain, who kept at Alamut a secret garden: he had it watered with milk and honey, and filled it with boys and girls of marvellous beauty, with palaces and music and wine. Thither he brought the young men of his following drugged with wine and a herb, and they woke among the delights and believed they were in Paradise; and after a season he cast them out, saying that Paradise could be theirs again if they did his bidding.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale in The Travels of Marco Polo (Marsden ed. 1818); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 馬可·波羅講述山中老人之事：他在阿拉穆特闢有一座秘密花園，命人以乳汁與蜂蜜澆灌，園中滿是容貌絕美的少男少女，並有宮殿、音樂與美酒。他將追隨他的青年以酒與一種草藥迷醉後帶到那裡，他們在歡愉中醒來，相信自己身處天堂；過了一季，他便將他們逐出，說只要聽從他的命令，天堂便可再度歸他們所有。

passages.text: So, the legend says, the young men went to their deaths without fear, obedient to the smallest word of the Old Man — whence the name Assassins, from the hashish of the drug, in the European tellings. The historians of the Mongol conquest of 1256, and the modern students of the Nizari Isma'ilis, find nothing of the garden in the Persian sources; the tale is the West's romance about a fortress it feared, and it is told here as a story about stories.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale and of the historiographical caution; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說如此記載，那些青年便毫不畏懼地赴死，對山中老人的片言隻語無不順從——阿薩辛之名即由此而來，在歐洲的講述中，出自那迷藥所用的哈希什。記述一二五六年蒙古征服的史家，以及研究尼扎里派伊斯瑪儀派的近代學者，在波斯文獻中都找不到這座花園的蹤跡；這個故事是西方對一座它所畏懼的城堡的浪漫想像，此處講述它，是把它當作一則關於故事的故事。

title.en: Al-Hajjaj: The Vizier of the Iron Rod
title.zh: 哈賈季：鐵棒之臣

region.en: Kufa and Wasit, Iraq (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊拉克庫法與瓦西特（象徵性定位）

period: Events 694-714 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The caliph Abd al-Malik sends al-Hajjaj to Kufa with no force: he rides into the mosque hooded, unmasks, and speaks the speech the historians have kept — 'I am he who trims the feather and sharpens the point, I am the punishment of God among you.' The city is governed by terror for ten years; the dialect of the mosque is corrected by the rod; and at his death the caliph says the tribute the biographers remember: 'I raised him when he was light, and he made himself heavy.'
summary.zh: 哈里發阿布杜·馬利克不遣一兵而遣哈賈季至庫法：他蒙面入清真寺，揭面而言史家所存之句——『我是削羽磨鋒之人，我是降於你們中間的主之懲罰。』城中以恐怖為治十年；清真寺之語以棒正音；其死時，哈里發言傳記所存之語：『我提拔他時他尚輕，而他自任為重。』

sensitivity.note: Umayyad anecdote lore as gathered in Muir.

passages.text: The caliph Abd al-Malik sent al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf to Kufa without an army. He rode into the mosque hooded, on a mule, and sat; then he unmasked and spoke: 'I am he who trims the feather and sharpens the point; I am the punishment of God among you.' And he governed the city and then the East by terror for ten years, it is said, and slew more men than the wars of his time had taken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈里發阿卜杜勒·馬利克派遣哈賈吉·本·優素福前往庫法，未帶一兵一卒。他蒙著面罩，騎著騾子進入清真寺，坐了下來；隨後他揭下面罩說道：「我就是修剪羽筆、削尖筆鋒之人；我就是你們之中真主的懲罰。」據說他以恐怖統治這座城市，繼而統治整個東方達十年之久，所殺之人多於他那個時代的戰爭所奪去的性命。

passages.text: The anecdote lore keeps his sayings: that he corrected the reading of the mosque by the rod; that he called the men of Kufa 'the dregs of the Arabs'; and that at his death the caliph said of him: 'I raised him when he was light, and he made himself heavy.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 31; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 軼聞傳說保留了他的話語：說他曾以杖矯正清真寺的誦讀；說他稱庫法之人為「阿拉伯人的渣滓」；又說他死時，哈里發如此評他：「他輕時我將他舉起，他卻使自己變得沉重。」

title.en: Al-Mutawakkil and the Poet's Rebuke
title.zh: 穆塔瓦基勒與詩人的譴責

region.en: Samarra, Abbasid capital (literal pin)
region.zh: 阿拔斯都城薩邁拉（實際定位）

period: Events 847-861 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The caliph al-Mutawakkil builds the great mosque of Samarra with its spiral minaret, keeps poets at his table, and dies of a court plot of his own son — the anecdote lore keeps the word said over him: 'He was the most magnificent of the caliphs and the most prodigal.' The Abbasid court at its height is here: the lute, the verses, the wine, and the sword behind the curtain.
summary.zh: 哈里發穆塔瓦基勒建薩邁拉大清真寺與其螺旋宣禮塔，蓄詩人於席，終死於其子主使之宮廷陰謀——軼事之集存其蓋棺之語：『他是最華麗的哈里發，也是最揮霍者。』阿拔斯宮廷之盛在此：琴、詩、酒，與幕後之劍。

sensitivity.note: Abbasid court anecdote lore as gathered in Muir.

passages.text: Al-Mutawakkil built the great mosque of Samarra, with its minaret wound like a screw into the sky, and kept the poets and singers of the age at his table. The anecdote lore remembers him as the most magnificent and the most prodigal of the caliphs: it was said that he built palaces without number and spent his nights in verse and wine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 穆塔瓦基勒建造了薩邁拉的大清真寺，其宣禮塔如螺絲般盤旋直上雲霄，並將當世的詩人與歌手留在自己的席間。軼聞傳說記得他是哈里發中最為輝煌、也最為揮霍的一位：據說他建造了無數宮殿，夜夜沉湎於詩歌與美酒。

passages.text: He was slain in his sleep by the guard of his own court, at the instance of his son; and the histories write the moral of the Abbasid height: the lute, the verse, the wine — and the sword behind the curtain. And the great mosque of Samarra stood, the largest mosque of the age, its spiral minaret the landmark of the desert capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 50; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在睡夢中被自己宮廷的衛兵所殺，此事由其子主使；史書寫下了阿拔斯王朝鼎盛之世的教訓：詩琴、詩歌、美酒——以及帷幕之後的刀劍。而薩邁拉的大清真寺依然矗立，那是當時最大的清真寺，其螺旋形的宣禮塔成為這座沙漠都城的標誌。

title.en: Horses' Hoofs: Poh Loh the Horse-Breaker (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 馬蹄：伯樂治馬（莊子）

region.en: The horse-pastures (symbolic pin: Zhangye, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 馬牧之野（象徵定位：甘肅張掖）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 9, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 9

summary.en: Horses have hoofs to carry them over frost and snow, and hair against the wind — palatial dwellings are of no use to them. Then Poh Loh appeared saying he understood the management of horses: he branded, clipped, halted, shackled and starved them until more than half died; and bridled and bitted, the horses learn to resist and bite — their natures become depraved, the fault of Poh Loh.
summary.zh: 馬蹄可以踐霜雪，毛可以禦風寒；及至伯樂曰我善治馬，燒之剔之，刻之雒之，饑之渴之，馬之死者已過半矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Horses have hoofs to carry them over frost and snow; hair, to protect them from wind and cold. They eat grass and drink water, and fling up their heels over the champaign. Such is the real nature of horses. Palatial dwellings are of no use to them.
passages.zh: 馬的蹄子可以踏霜雪而行，毛髮可以抵禦風寒。牠們吃草飲水，在草原上揚蹄跳躍。這便是馬的真性。華美的宮室對牠們毫無用處。

passages.text: One day Poh Loh appeared, saying, "I understand the management of horses." So he branded them, and clipped them, and pared their hoofs, and put halters on them, tying them up by the head and shackling them by the feet, and disposing them in stables, with the result that two or three in every ten died. Then he kept them hungry and thirsty, trotting them and galloping them, and grooming, and trimming, with the misery of the tasselled bridle before and the fear of the knotted whip behind, until more than half of them were dead.
passages.zh: 有一天伯樂出現了，說：「我懂得管理馬匹。」於是他給馬烙印、剪毛、削蹄，又給牠們套上籠頭，拴住頭部、絆住腳，把牠們安置在馬廄裡，結果每十匹中就有兩三匹死去。接著他又讓牠們挨餓受渴，驅使牠們奔馳，又替牠們刷洗修剪，前面有帶纓絡的勒口之苦，後面有皮鞭抽打的恐懼，直到大半的馬都死去。

passages.text: Horses live on dry land, eat grass and drink water. When pleased, they rub their necks together. When angry, they turn around and kick up their heels at each other. Thus far only do their natural dispositions carry them. But bridled and bitted, with a plate of metal on their foreheads, they learn to cast vicious looks, to turn the head to bite, to resist, to get the bit out of the mouth or the bridle into it. And thus their natures become depraved,--the fault of Poh Loh.
passages.zh: 馬生活在乾燥的陸地上，吃草飲水。高興時，牠們彼此摩擦脖頸。發怒時，牠們轉過身來互相踢蹄。牠們的天性所能達到的僅止於此。可是一旦套上籠頭、銜上嚼子，額上裝著金屬片，牠們便學會了斜眼怒視、扭頭咬人、抗拒、把嚼子從口中吐出或把籠頭咬進嘴裡。於是牠們的天性便敗壞了——這是伯樂的過錯。

title.en: The Strong Thief Carries Off the Till: T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ Steals Ch'i (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 胠篋：田成子竊齊（莊子）

region.en: The State of Ch'i (Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 齊國（今山東臨淄）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 10, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 10

summary.en: Locks and cords protect trunks from small thieves; a strong thief carries off the till with box and bag, his only fear being that the locks are not strong enough. So T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ slew the Prince of Ch'i and stole not only his kingdom but the wisdom-tricks of the Sages as well — and for twelve generations his descendants ruled, while the small States did not dare to blame him.
summary.zh: 為之斗斛以量之，則並與斗斛而竊之；為之仁義以矯之，則並與仁義而竊之。田成子一朝殺齊君而盜其國，所盜者豈獨其國邪？並與其聖知之法而盜之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The precautions taken against thieves who open trunks, search bags, or ransack tills, consist of securing with cords and fastening with bolts and locks. This is what the world calls wit. But a strong thief comes who carries off the till on his shoulders, with box and bag to boot. And his only fear is that the cords and locks should not be strong enough!
passages.zh: 防備那些開箱、探囊、撬櫃的盜賊所用的辦法，是用繩索捆綁、用插銷和鎖具加固。這便是世人所說的聰明。可是來了一個大盜，把櫃子扛在肩上，連箱帶囊一併拿走。而他唯一擔心的是繩索和鎖具不夠牢固！

passages.text: And within its four boundaries not a temple or shrine was dedicated, nor a district or hamlet governed, but in accordance with the rules laid down by the Sages. Yet one morning T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ slew the Prince of Ch'i, and stole his kingdom.
