And not his kingdom only, but the wisdom-tricks which he had got from the Sages as well; so that although T'ien Ch'êng Tzŭ acquired the reputation of a thief, he lived as comfortably as ever did either Yao or Shun. The small States did not venture to blame, nor the great States to punish him; and so for twelve generations his descendants ruled over Ch'i.
passages.zh: 而在其四境之內，沒有一座廟宇不被祭祀，沒有一個鄉邑不被治理，無不依照聖人所訂立的規矩行事。然而有一天早晨，田成子殺了齊君，竊取了他的國家。而且不僅是他的國家，連他從聖人那裡得來的智慧權術也一併竊取了；因此，田成子雖然得了盜賊的名聲，卻過得和堯、舜一樣安逸。小國不敢責備他，大國不敢懲罰他；於是他的子孫十二代統治齊國。

passages.text: One man steals a purse, and is punished. Another steals a State, and becomes a Prince. But charity and duty to one's neighbour are integral parts of princedom. Does he not then steal charity and duty to one's neighbour together with the wisdom of the Sages?
passages.zh: 有人偷了一個錢袋，便受到懲罰。另一個人偷了一個國家，便成了諸侯。而仁義正是諸侯之國不可分割的一部分。那麼他豈不是連同聖人的智慧一起，把仁義也偷去了嗎？

title.en: Robber Chê and the Tao of Thieving (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 盜亦有道（莊子）

region.en: Robber Chê's mountain fastness (symbolic pin: Mount T'ai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 盜跖之山寨（象徵定位：山東泰山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 10, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 10

summary.en: An apprentice asks Robber Chê whether there is Tao in thieving. Pray tell me of something in which there is not, he answers — the wisdom to locate booty, the courage to go in first, the heroism to come out last, the shrewdness to calculate success, the justice to divide the spoil equally; there has never yet been a great robber without these five. It was the appearance of Sages that caused the appearance of great robbers.
summary.zh: 跖之徒問於跖曰：盜亦有道乎？跖曰：何適而無有道邪——妄意室中之藏，聖也；入先，勇也；出後，義也；知可否，知也；分均，仁也。聖人不死，大盜不止。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); Robber Chê is Zhuangzi's trickster foil to Confucian virtue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: An apprentice to Robber Chê asked him saying, "Is there then TAO in thieving?" "Pray tell me of something in which there is not TAO," Chê replied. "There is the wisdom by which booty is located. The courage to go in first, and the heroism of coming out last. There is the shrewdness of calculating success, and justice in the equal division of the spoil. There has never yet been, a great robber who was not possessed of these five."
passages.zh: 盜跖的門徒問他說：「那麼，盜竊之中也有道嗎？」盜跖回答說：「你且告訴我，什麼地方沒有道呢？能猜測出屋裡所藏財物的，就是聖；帶頭先進去的，就是勇；最後退出殿後的，就是義；判斷能否下手成功的，就是智；分贓平均的，就是仁。從來沒有不具備這五種德行而能成為大盜的。」

passages.text: Drive out the Sages and leave the robbers alone,--then only will the empire be governed. As when the stream ceases the gully dries up, and when the hill is levelled the chasm is filled; so when Sages are extinct, there will be no more robbers, but the empire will rest in peace.
passages.zh: 趕走聖人，放過盜賊，天下才能治理得好。正如溪水乾涸，溝壑便會枯竭；山丘削平，深谷便會填滿；所以聖人絕跡，就不再有盜賊，天下也就安寧太平了。

title.en: The Golden Age of Knotted Cords (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 結繩而用之：至德之世（莊子）

region.en: The age of Yung Ch'êng, Ta T'ing, and Shên Nung (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 容成氏、大庭氏、神農之世（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 10, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 10

summary.en: In the Golden Age of the ancient rulers the people used knotted cords, were content with what food and raiment they could get, and lived simple and peaceful lives. Neighbouring districts were within sight, the cocks and dogs of one could be heard in the other — yet the people grew old and died without ever interchanging visits. In those days, government was indeed perfect.
summary.zh: 昔者容成氏、大庭氏、伯皇氏、中央氏、栗陸氏、驪畜氏、軒轅氏、赫胥氏、尊盧氏、祝融氏、伏羲氏、神農氏——當是時也，民結繩而用之，甘其食，美其服，鄰國相望，雞狗之音相聞，民至老死而不相往來。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Taoist Golden Age (parallel to the mythic first world). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Have you never heard of the Golden Age, the days of Yung Ch'êng, Ta T'ing, Poh Huang, Chung Yang, Li Lu, Li Hsü, Hsien Yüan, Hê Hsü, Tsun Lu, Chu Yung, Fu Hsi, and Shên Nung? Then the people used knotted cords.
passages.zh: 你難道沒有聽說過那黃金時代嗎？就是容成氏、大庭氏、伯皇氏、中央氏、栗陸氏、驪畜氏、軒轅氏、赫胥氏、尊盧氏、祝融氏、伏羲氏、神農氏的時代。那時，人民用結繩來記事。

passages.text: They were contented with what food and raiment they could get. They lived simple and peaceful lives. Neighbouring districts were within sight, and the cocks and dogs of one could be heard in the other, yet the people grew old and died without ever interchanging visits. In those days, government was indeed perfect.
passages.zh: 他們滿足於所能得到的食物和衣服，過著簡單而安寧的生活。鄰近的村落彼此相望，雞鳴狗吠之聲互相聽得見，然而人民直到老死也不互相往來。在那個時代，治理真是完善極了。

title.en: The Oilman and His Parrot
title.zh: 油商與其鸚鵡

region.en: Konya, shop of the oil-press (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞油坊（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887 (abridged), public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A parrot kept in the shop of an oilman speaks to the customers and drives away trade; the master threatens it, and the bird falls silent and shivers like a dead thing. The oilman carries it out and flings it on the dunghill. The bird rises on the wing, and the master learns that the parrot has taught the other parrots his own trade: silence is the one thing that cannot be talked about.
summary.zh: 油商鋪中一鸚鵡對客高談，趕走生意；主人威脅之，鳥遂默然顫抖如死物。油商攜之擲於糞堆。鳥振翅而起；主人方知鸚鵡已教眾鸚鵡他自己的營生：沉默乃無法言說之事。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: An oilman kept a parrot in his shop, a bird that could talk, and it talked the customers into and out of everything; trade went to ruin. The oilman threatened it, and the parrot fell silent and hung its head, and shivered, and made itself like a dead thing. The oilman grieved, and carried the bird out into the court, and flung it on the dunghill with the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Oilman and his Parrot'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個油商在店裡養了一隻鸚鵡，這鳥會說話，牠對顧客說這說那，把生意都說垮了。油商恐嚇牠，鸚鵡便沉默下來，垂著頭，瑟瑟發抖，裝得像死了一樣。油商心裡難過，把鳥帶到院子裡，扔在糞堆上，和死鳥放在一處。

passages.text: The parrot rose from the dunghill on the wing, and flew to the garden, and sat among the parrots of the garden. And when the master saw it fly, he understood: the bird had made itself dead that it might go free, and it had gone to teach the garden-parrots the one trade it knew — to be silent, and so escape the talker's snare. The moral of the tale is the speechlessness of the lover of God, who must be nothing, that he may be all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 鸚鵡從糞堆上振翅飛起，飛到花園裡，落在園中鸚鵡之間。主人見牠飛走，便明白了：這鳥裝死，是為了得自由，牠是去教園中的鸚鵡牠所懂得的唯一本領——沉默，藉此逃脫那多嘴者的羅網。這故事的寓意，就是愛神者的無言：他必須成為無，才能成為一切。

title.en: Moses and the Shepherd
title.zh: 穆薩與牧羊人

region.en: Wayside in the wilderness of Sinai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西奈曠野路旁（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 2 (composed c. 1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 2

summary.en: A shepherd on the road praises God in shepherd's words: 'I will comb thy hair, I will milk thee, I will kiss thy hand.' Moses rebukes him: 'Thou hast joined to God what does not become Him.' The shepherd tears his garment and departs. A voice comes to Moses: 'Thou hast come to unite, not to sever — I look not at the tongue and the speech; I look at the inward spirit.' Moses runs after the shepherd, who has understood: 'To each his own form of worship.'
summary.zh: 牧羊人以牧人言辭讚主：『我要為你梳髮、擠奶、吻你之手。』穆薩斥之：『你以不當之物配主。』牧人撕裂其衣而去。有聲臨穆薩：『你來是為聯合，非為割裂——我不看言與語，我看內在之靈。』穆薩追上牧人，牧人已悟：『各有各的敬拜形式。』

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment; the tale's theology is the poet's own, not scripture.

passages.text: A shepherd saw Moses on the road and said, 'Where art thou going, beloved of God?' Moses said, 'To pray to God, that He may pardon our sins.' The shepherd said, 'I will pray with thee'; and he prayed in shepherd's words: 'O God, I will comb Thy hair and wash Thy garments and kiss Thy hand and milk Thee, and bring Thee to my tent.' Moses said, 'What babbling is this? Thou hast joined to God what does not become Him: milk, and a comb, and sandals!' The shepherd tore his garment, sighed, and fled into the desert.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 2, 'Moses and the Shepherd'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名牧羊人在路上看見摩西，便說：『你要往哪裡去，神所愛的人啊？』摩西說：『去向上帝祈禱，求祂赦免我們的罪。』牧羊人說：『我要與你一同祈禱』；於是他以牧羊人的話語祈禱道：『噢上帝，我要為你梳理頭髮，洗滌你的衣裳，親吻你的手，為你擠奶，並領你到我的帳篷裡。』摩西說：『這是什麼胡言亂語？你將不合於祂的事物加諸上帝：奶、梳子與涼鞋！』牧羊人撕裂了自己的衣裳，嘆息一聲，便逃入沙漠之中。

passages.text: Then came a revelation to Moses: 'Thou hast come to unite, and thou hast severed. I look not at the tongue and the speech; I look at the inward spirit and the state. What are courtesy and the canons of speech? The light of the heart is my desire. Thou art gone to the temple and the law; and he has gone to be intoxicated with the Beloved. Thy way is good, his way is good too.' And Moses ran after the shepherd, who understood at last: 'To each his own form of worship; the Sufi has no kite and quarry but God.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 隨後有啟示臨到摩西：『你來是為要聯合，卻反倒割裂了。我不看舌頭與言語；我看的是內在的心靈與狀態。何謂禮節與言語的法則？心的光明才是我所願。你去了神殿與律法；而他卻去與所愛者同醉。你的路是好的，他的路也是好的。』於是摩西追趕那牧羊人，牧羊人終於領悟：『各人有各人的敬拜形式；蘇菲之徒除上帝外別無所逐、別無所獵。』

title.en: The Elephant in the Dark
title.zh: 黑暗中的大象

region.en: Konya, a dark house by night (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞夜間暗屋（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 3 (composed c. 1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 3

summary.en: An elephant is brought for show to a dark house; the visitors enter by a lamp each in turn and come out with different reports: a water-pipe, a fan, a pillar, a throne. They quarrel all night with candles in their hands. Had each held a candle, they had been one word short of truth — but each had only one lamp, and the elephant is only a figure of the Real, which each partial seer names after the part his hand has found.
summary.zh: 一象供觀賞置於暗屋；參觀者各持一燈輪流入，出而各異其辭：水管、扇、柱、御座。他們徹夜執燭相爭。若各持全燭，則離真理僅一詞——然每人只有一燈；象只是實在的比喻，各偏見者以手所觸之部分而名之。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: Some Hindoos were exhibiting an elephant, and all the people desired to see it; but the house was too dark, and so a lamp was provided, and the beholders went in one by one. In the dark they felt the beast with their hands, and each came out and gave a different report: one had found the trunk and cried 'A water-pipe!' another the ear and cried 'A fan!' another the leg and cried 'A pillar!' another the back and cried 'A throne!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3, 'The Elephant in the Dark'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有幾個印度人展示一頭大象，眾人都想觀看；但屋子太暗，於是備了一盞燈，觀看者便一個接一個地進去。他們在黑暗中用手摸那隻獸，各人出來後報告都不同：一人摸到象鼻，便喊『一根水管！』另一人摸到耳朵，便喊『一把扇子！』另一人摸到腿，便喊『一根柱子！』又一人摸到背，便喊『一張寶座！』

passages.text: They quarrelled all night with candles in their hands, each calling the others liars. If each had held a candle, the discrepancy would have gone out of their words — for all would have seen the one elephant. And the tale is told, says Rumi, of the seers and sects, who each see one member of the Real in the dark of this world, and each name it after the part his hand has found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他們手持蠟燭爭吵了一整夜，彼此互稱對方為說謊者。倘若各人手中都持一支蠟燭，他們言語中的分歧便會消失——因為眾人都會看見那同一頭大象。魯米說，這故事講的是那些有洞見者與各宗派，他們各自在這世界的黑暗中看見真實者的一個肢體，並各按自己手所摸到的部位為它命名。

title.en: The Travellers Who Ate the Young Elephant
title.zh: 食幼象的旅人

region.en: Wilderness road of India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印度曠野之路（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 3, Story I (composed c. 1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 3, Story I

summary.en: A party lost in the wilderness is starving; a sage shows them young elephants in the wood and warns them that the parents will track and avenge. They kill and eat one, and sleep; in the morning each has hidden in a different quarter, and the great elephants find them out one by one and trample them — every one, as the sage had said, except the man who told him where they were going.
summary.zh: 迷途之眾瀕餓；一智者示林中幼象，並警其父母必追而復仇。眾殺而食之一，睡去；晨間各匿不同方位，巨象逐一尋出踐踏——如智者所言，無一倖免，惟那位曾告訴智者去向者得免。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A party of travellers lost their way in a wilderness and were well-nigh famished. A sage came up and condoled with them, and told them there were many young elephants in the adjacent woods, one of which would furnish an ample meal; but he warned them that if they killed one, its parents would in all probability track them out and be revenged. They saw a plump young elephant, and could not resist killing and eating it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3, Story I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一群旅人在荒野中迷了路，幾乎餓死。一位智者前來慰問他們，告訴他們鄰近的樹林裡有許多小象，其中一頭便足以供一頓豐盛的餐食；但他警告他們，若殺了一頭，牠的父母十之八九會循跡找到他們並報復。他們看見一頭肥壯的小象，忍不住殺了牠並吃了。

passages.text: They slept, and each, it is said, hid himself in a different quarter, and one told the sage where they meant to hide. In the morning the great elephants came, and went from hiding-place to hiding-place, and trampled them one by one, every man of them — as the sage had said; and only the man who had told him where they were going came off alive. The moral, says Rumi, is of the men who slay the young of the Lord's creatures and think their hiding from the elephant is hiding from God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3, Story I; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說他們睡下之後，各人分別躲藏在不同的角落，其中一人告訴了智者他們打算躲藏的地方。到了早晨，那些大象來了，從一個藏身處走到另一個藏身處，將他們一一踩死，無一倖免——正如智者所言；唯有那告訴智者他們去向的人得以生還。魯米說，這則寓言的寓意在於那些人：他們殺害主所造之物的幼崽，還以為自己躲避大象便是躲避上帝。

title.en: The Fowler and the Bird
title.zh: 捕鳥者與鳥

region.en: Rooftop snare, Konya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞屋頂羅網（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A fowler snares a little bird on a roof, and the bird sings three songs to ransom itself: the first from the snare, the second from the hand, the third from the heart of the fowler — 'Three counsels I give in the mouth of thy three gates.' The first: 'Regret not what is past.' The second: 'Do not believe impossibilities.' The third: 'A pearl of great price lies in thy own garden; do not dig beyond it.' And the bird, escaping, mocks him gently: the pearl is its own body, which the fowler held and let go.
summary.zh: 捕鳥者於屋頂網得一鳥；鳥唱三歌贖身：第一歌贖自羅網，第二贖自手中，第三贖自捕者之心——『我以三言付汝三門之口』。其一：『勿悔既往。』其二：『勿信不可能之事。』其三：『至寶之珠在汝園中；勿掘園外。』鳥脫逃後溫言相嘲：珠即其身——捕者曾握而放之。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A fowler caught a little bird in a snare on the roof, and would have killed it; and the bird spoke: 'What wilt thou do with me? I am not a mouthful.' And it said, 'I will give thee three counsels, if thou let me go: the first on thy fingers, the second at the gate, the third in the heart of the field.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Fowler and the Bird'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個捕鳥人在屋頂上用網捕到一隻小鳥，正打算殺了牠；那鳥開口說道：「你要拿我怎麼辦？我還不夠你一口呢。」牠又說：「你若放我走，我就給你三條忠告：第一條在指頭上說，第二條在門口說，第三條在田野中央說。」

passages.text: The first counsel, given on the fingers: 'Regret not what is past.' The second, given standing free: 'Do not believe impossibilities — believe not that a bird should weigh six ounces and be heavier than an elephant.' And the third, given as it flew from the tree: 'In thy belly are thirty paces of pearl; but beyond thy own garden do not dig.' And the fowler stood repenting of his greed, and the bird called out: 'The pearl is my little body, which thou didst hold and didst let go.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第一條忠告，是在指頭上說的：「不要為過去的事懊悔。」第二條，是在牠自由站立時說的：「不要相信不可能的事——不要相信一隻鳥竟重達六盎司，比大象還重。」第三條，是在牠從樹上飛去時說的：「你腹中有三十步長的珍珠；但切莫在你自己的園子之外挖掘。」捕鳥人站在那裡，為自己的貪心懊悔不已，那鳥便喊道：「那珍珠就是我的小小身軀，你曾握在手中，又放走了它。」

title.en: The Sufi and the Qazi
title.zh: 蘇菲與法官

region.en: Court of the qazi, Konya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞法官法庭（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A qazi of the city judges by the letter; a wandering dervish is brought before him. The dervish tells the story of the jurist who slept with the light burning and demanded of the night why it had robbed him — and the tale turns the court's own grammar against it. The qazi is silent; the dervish goes; and the poem says the judge of the letter has never seen the day of the spirit.
summary.zh: 城中法官依字面而判；一行腳苦行僧被帶至其前。苦行僧講述一法官燃燈而眠、向夜索其被竊之光的故事——此喻反轉法庭自身之語法。法官默然；苦行僧離去；詩云字面之判者未嘗見靈之晝。

sensitivity.note: Sufi anecdote of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A qazi judged by the letter of the law, and a wandering dervish was brought before him. The dervish answered him with a tale: of a jurist who slept with his lamp burning, and rose and demanded of the night why it had stolen his light — and of the judge who fined the flood for wetting his shoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Sufi and the Qazi'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有位法官按律法的字面斷案，一個雲遊的德爾維希被帶到他面前。那德爾維希用一則故事回答他：說有位法學家點著燈睡覺，醒來便質問黑夜為何偷走了他的光——又說有位法官判洪水罰款，因為它弄濕了他的鞋。

passages.text: The court was silent; the dervish went his way; and the poem's moral is of the jurists who have the letter and not the spirit — 'The fish of the letter is caught in the net of the word, and the man of the sea has gone free.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 法庭一片寂靜；德爾維希徑自離去；這首詩的寓意，說的是那些徒有字面而無精神的法學家——「字面之魚落入了言語之網，而屬於大海的人卻已脫身而去。」

title.en: The King and His Three Sons
title.zh: 國王與其三子

region.en: Royal court and artisan quarter (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王廷與工匠坊（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: Three princes are set to learn a trade; one learns archery, one the manufacture of arrows, one the cure of men. War comes: the archer can no longer use his art, the arrow-maker's wares are taken, and only the healer is wanted. Rumi's moral: the art of healing souls is the trade that no misfortune dearness makes dearer or cheaper.
summary.zh: 三王子奉命習藝：一習射，一習製箭，一習醫人。戰事起：射者技無所用，製箭者貨物被奪，惟醫者受求。魯米之旨：醫治靈魂之藝乃無論窮通皆受求之業。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A king set his three sons to learn trades. One learned archery, and became the finest bowman of the age; one learned to make arrows, and his wares filled the market; and the third learned to heal the bodies and souls of men. War came, and the archer's art stood idle, and the arrow-maker's stock was seized for the king's men; only the healer was wanted, in war and in peace alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The King and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有位國王讓三個兒子去學手藝。一個學了射箭，成了當世最好的弓箭手；一個學了造箭，他的貨物擺滿了市集；第三個學了醫治人的身體與靈魂。戰爭來了，弓箭手的技藝閒置無用，造箭人的存貨被國王的兵士徵去；唯有那醫者為人所需要，無論戰時或平時皆然。

passages.text: Rumi's moral is of the science of the saints: the trade that is never dearer for need nor cheaper for peace — the healing of the soul, which every age requires, and which no misfortune can take from the man who has learned it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 魯米的寓意，說的是聖徒的學問：那門手藝，不因需要而更貴，也不因太平而更賤——即醫治靈魂，這是每個時代都需要的，也是任何不幸都無法從學會它的人身上奪走的。

title.en: The Man Who Was Tattooed
title.zh: 刺青之人

region.en: Konya, shop of the tattooer (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞刺青師鋪（象徵性定位）

period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A man goes to be tattooed with the figures of a lion on his shoulder, an eagle on his breast, a garland about his thigh. The needle touches his shoulder: 'What are you drawing?' — 'A lion.' 'Begin with the tail, for the shoulder is a tender place.' The needle touches his back: 'What now?' — 'An eagle.' 'Begin at the tail, for the back is tender.' — 'Begin at the thigh.' The artist throws down the needle: 'God never made a man with a tailless lion, a wingless eagle and a headless garland.'
summary.zh: 一人往刺青，欲肩繪獅、胸繪鷹、股繞花環。針及肩：『你畫什麼？』——『獅。』『先從尾開始，肩是嫩處。』針及背：『現在呢？』——『鷹。』『先從尾開始，背是嫩處。』——『從股開始。』刺青師擲針：『主造人從未有無尾之獅、無翼之鷹、無頭之花環。』

sensitivity.note: Sufi anecdote of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A man went to the tattooer to be marked with a lion on his shoulder, an eagle on his breast and a garland about his thigh. The needle began at the shoulder: 'What art thou drawing?' 'A lion.' 'Begin with the tail, for the shoulder is a tender place.' The needle began at the back: 'What now?' 'An eagle.' 'Begin at the tail, for the back is tender.' 'Then begin at the thigh.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Man who was Tattooed'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有一個人去找刺青師，要在肩上刺一頭獅子，胸前刺一隻鷹，大腿上刺一圈花環。針先從肩膀開始：「你在畫什麼？」「一頭獅子。」「從尾巴開始吧，因為肩膀是嬌嫩的地方。」針又從背部開始：「現在呢？」「一隻鷹。」「從尾巴開始吧，因為背部是嬌嫩的。」「那就從大腿開始吧。」

passages.text: The artist threw down the needle and said: 'God never made a man with a tailless lion and a wingless eagle and a headless garland.' The moral, says Rumi, is of the dervish who would have the delight of the path without its pain — who will be a lion in the spirit if he may be spared the needle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 刺青師丟下針說道：「真主從未造過沒有尾巴的獅子、沒有翅膀的鷹、沒有頭的花環。」魯米說，這則寓言的教訓，說的是那種想要修行之路的喜悅卻不要其痛苦的苦行僧——只要能免於針刺，他倒願意在精神上做一頭獅子。

title.en: The Human Heart: Ts'ui Chü Asks Lao Tzŭ (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 崔瞿問老聃：人心（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's retreat (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 11, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 11

summary.en: Ts'ui Chü asks how men's hearts can be kept in order if the empire is not governed. Lao Tzŭ answers: no bolt can bar, no bond can bind, such is the human heart — and blames the Yellow Emperor's charity for the chain of coercion that followed, ending with the Confucianists and Mihists preaching amid gyves and fetters. Abandon wisdom and discard knowledge, and the empire will be at peace.
summary.zh: 崔瞿問於老聃曰：不治天下，安藏人心？老聃曰：女慎無攖人心——一宅而寓於無形，不可內於靈臺；其居也淵而靜，其動也縣而天。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Be careful," replied Lao Tzŭ, "not to interfere with the natural goodness of the heart of man. Man's heart may be forced down or stirred up. In each case the issue is fatal. "By gentleness, the hardest heart may be softened. But try to cut and polish it,--'twill glow like fire or freeze like ice. In the twinkling of an eye it will pass beyond the limits of the Four Seas. In repose, profoundly still; in motion, far away in the sky. No bolt can bar, no bond can bind,--such is the human heart."
passages.zh: 「小心，」老子回答說，「不要干擾人心天然的本善。人心可以被壓抑，也可以被激盪。無論哪一種情形，結果都是致命的。」「以溫和之道，最堅硬的心也能被軟化。但若試圖去切割琢磨它——它便會如火般灼熱，或如冰般凍結。轉瞬之間，它便會越過四海的界限。靜止時，深邃而沉靜；運動時，遠馳於天際。沒有門閂能阻擋，沒有繩索能束縛——人心便是如此。」

passages.text: "Of old, the Yellow Emperor first caused charity and duty to one's neighbour to interfere with the natural goodness of the heart of man. In consequence of which, Yao and Shun wore the hair off their legs in endeavouring to feed their people. They disturbed their internal economy in order to find room for charity and duty to one's neighbour. They exhausted their energies in framing laws and statutes. Still they did not succeed.
passages.zh: 「古時，黃帝首先讓仁義干擾了人心天然的本善。因此之故，堯與舜為養育百姓而奔波得腿上毛都磨光了。他們擾亂了自身的內在秩序，以便為仁義騰出位置。他們耗盡心力制定法律典章。然而終究未能成功。」

passages.text: "Until I can say that the wisdom of Sages is not a fastener of cangues, and that charity and duty to one's neighbour are not bolts for gyves, how should I know that Tsêng and Shih are not the forerunners of Chieh and Chê? Therefore I said, 'Abandon wisdom and discard knowledge, and the empire will be at peace.'"
passages.zh: 「除非我能說聖人的智慧並非枷鎖的扣環，仁義並非鐐銬的門閂，我又怎能知道曾與史並非桀與跖的先驅呢？所以我說：『捨棄智慧，丟棄知識，天下便會太平。』」

title.en: The Yellow Emperor Visits Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ on Mount K'ung-t'ung (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 黃帝問道於空同廣成子（莊子）

region.en: Mount K'ung-t'ung (Kongtongshan, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 空同山（甘肅崆峒山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 11, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 11

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor, whose laws ruled the empire, climbs Mount K'ung-t'ung to ask the immortal Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ for the perfect Tao. Rebuffed once — for under his rule clouds rained before thickening and the sun's brightness paled — he abdicates for three months and kneels in the dust, and the master grants the inner teaching of seeing nothing and hearing nothing, of the gates of Great Light and Profound Mystery, of a self preserved twelve hundred years.
summary.zh: 黃帝立為天子十九年，聞廣成子在空同之上，往見之；再拜稽首而問：治身奈何而可以長久？廣成子曰：至道之精，窈窈冥冥——無視無聽，抱神以靜，形將自正。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the founding scene of the Yellow-Emperor-and-the-Immortal-Master topos in Daoist hagiography. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor sat on the throne for nineteen years, and his laws obtained all over the empire. Hearing that Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ was living on Mount K'ung-t'ung, he went thither to see him, and said, "I am told, Sir, that you are in possession of perfect TAO. May I ask in what perfect TAO consists? I desire to avail myself of the good influence of heaven and earth in order to secure harvests and feed my people. I should also like to control the Two Powers of nature in order to the protection of all living things. How can I accomplish this?" "What you desire to avail yourself of," replied Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ, "is the primordial integrity of matter. What you wish to control are the disintegrators thereof. Ever since the empire has been governed by you, the clouds have rained without waiting to thicken, the foliage of trees has fallen without waiting to grow yellow, the brightness of the sun and moon has paled, and the voice of the flatterer is heard on every side. How then speak of perfect TAO?"
passages.zh: 黃帝在位十九年，他的法令通行於整個天下。他聽說廣成子住在空同山上，便前往見他，說道：「我聽說，先生，您掌握了完美的道。請問完美的道究竟是什麼？我希望借助天地的好影響來確保收成、養育我的百姓。我還想掌控自然的兩種力量，以保護一切生靈。我怎樣才能做到呢？」廣成子回答說：「你所希望借助的，是物質的原初完整。你所希望掌控的，是使其分解的力量。自從天下由你治理以來，雲未及積聚便已降雨，樹葉未及變黃便已凋落，日月的光輝黯淡，諂媚者的聲音處處可聞。那麼還談什麼完美的道呢？」

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor withdrew. He resigned the Throne. He built himself a solitary hut. He lay upon straw. For three months he remained in seclusion, and then went again to see Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ. The latter was lying down with his face to the south. The Yellow Emperor approached after the manner of an inferior, upon his knees. Prostrating himself upon the ground he said, "I am told, Sir, that you are in possession of perfect TAO. May I ask how my self may be preserved so as to last?" Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ jumped up with a start. "A good question indeed!" cried he. "Come, and I will speak to you of perfect TAO.
passages.zh: 黃帝退下。他辭去了帝位。他為自己築了一間獨居的小屋。他臥於草蓆之上。他隱居了三個月，然後又去見廣成子。廣成子正仰面朝南躺著。黃帝以卑下者的禮節上前，跪行而前。他伏在地上說：「我聽說，先生，您掌握了完美的道。請問我該如何保養自身，使之長久？」廣成子猛然躍起。「問得好啊！」他喊道。「來吧，我來向你講述完美的道。」

passages.text: "See nothing; hear nothing; let your soul be wrapped in quiet; and your body will begin to take proper form. Let there be absolute repose and absolute purity; do not weary your body nor disturb your vitality,--and you will live for ever. For if the eye sees nothing, and the ear hears nothing, and the mind thinks nothing, the soul will preserve the body, and the body will live for ever.
passages.zh: 「什麼也不看；什麼也不聽；讓你的靈魂包裹於寂靜之中；你的身體便會開始呈現應有的形態。讓絕對的靜止與絕對的純淨存在；不要使你的身體疲憊，也不要擾亂你的生機——你便會永生。因為若眼無所見，耳無所聞，心無所思，靈魂便會保全身體，身體便會永生。」

passages.text: "Cherish that which is within you, and shut off that which is without; for much knowledge is a curse. Then I will place you upon that abode of Great Light which is the source of the positive Power, and escort you through the gate of Profound Mystery which is the source of the negative Power. These Powers are the controllers of heaven and earth, and each contains the other. ... I preserve the original ONE, while resting in harmony with externals. It is because I have thus cared for my self now for twelve hundred years that my body has not decayed." The Yellow Emperor prostrated himself and said, "Kuang Ch'êng Tzŭ is surely God...."
passages.zh: 「珍視你內在之物，閉塞你外在之物；因為廣博的知識是一種詛咒。然後我將把你安置於那大光明之居所，那是陽剛之力的源頭，並引領你穿過那深奧玄妙之門，那是陰柔之力的源頭。這兩種力量是天地的主宰，且各自包含對方。……我持守本初的太一，同時安處於與外物和諧之中。正因為我如此保養自身至今已有一千二百年，我的身體才沒有衰朽。」黃帝伏地而拜說：「廣成子必定是神……」

title.en: The Spirit of the Clouds Meets the Vital Principle (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 雲將遇鴻蒙（莊子）

region.en: The expanse of air east of Yu-sung (symbolic pin: Songshan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 過有宋之野而適遭鴻蒙（象徵定位：河南嵩山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 11, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 11

summary.en: The Spirit of the Clouds, passing east, falls in with the Vital Principle slapping his ribs and hopping about. He wishes to harmonise the six influences and nourish all living beings; three years later the answer comes: rest in inaction and the world will be good of itself — cast your slough, spit forth intelligence, become one with the infinite, release your mind, free your soul, be vacuous, be nothing.
summary.zh: 雲將東遊，過扶搖之枝而適遭鴻蒙；鴻蒙方將拊脾雀躍而遊。雲將曰：願合六氣之精以育群生——鴻蒙曰：意！心養。汝徒處無為，而物自化。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the cloud-spirit dialogue is a cosmogonic theophany scene. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The Spirit of the Clouds when passing eastwards through the expanse of Air happened to fall in with the Vital Principle. The latter was slapping his ribs and hopping about; whereupon the Spirit of the Clouds said, "Who are you, old man, and what are you doing here?" "Strolling!" replied the Vital Principle, without stopping. "I want to know something," continued the Spirit of the Clouds. "Ah!" uttered the Vital Principle, in a tone of disapprobation. "The relationship of heaven and earth is out of harmony," said the Spirit of the Clouds; "the six influences do not combine, and the four seasons are no longer regular. I desire to blend the six influences so as to nourish all living beings. What am I to do?" "I do not know!" cried the Vital Principle, shaking his head, while still slapping his ribs and hopping about; "I do not know!"
passages.zh: 雲神向東經過太虛之境時，偶然遇見了生機之靈。後者正拍著自己的肋骨跳來跳去；於是雲神說：「老人家，你是誰，在這裡做什麼？」「閒逛！」生機之靈答道，並未停下。「我想知道一些事情，」雲神繼續說。「啊！」生機之靈以不贊成的語氣發出聲音。「天地的關係失調了，」雲神說，「六氣不調和，四季也不再規律。我希望能調和六氣，以滋養一切生靈。我該怎麼做？」「我不知道！」生機之靈喊道，搖著頭，仍舊拍著肋骨跳來跳去；「我不知道！」

passages.text: "That the scheme of empire is in confusion," said the Vital Principle, "that the conditions of life are violated, that the will of God does not triumph, that the beasts of the field are disorganised, that the birds of the air cry at night, that blight reaches the trees and herbs, that destruction spreads among creeping things,--this, alas! is the fault of government." "True," replied the Spirit of the Clouds, "but what am I to do?" "It is here," cried the Vital Principle, "that the poison lurks! Go back!"
passages.zh: 「治國之策陷入混亂，」生機之靈說，「生命的條件遭到破壞，上帝的旨意不能彰顯，田野的走獸失序，空中的飛鳥夜啼，疫病侵及草木，毀滅蔓延於爬蟲之間——唉！這是為政者的過錯。」「不錯，」雲神回答，「但我該怎麼做？」「毒害就潛伏在這裡！」生機之靈喊道，「回去吧！」

passages.text: "Feed then your people," said the Vital Principle, "with your heart. Rest in inaction, and the world will be good of itself. Cast your slough. Spit forth intelligence. Ignore all differences. Become one with the infinite. Release your mind. Free your soul. Be vacuous. Be Nothing! Let all things revert to their original constitution. If they do this, without knowledge, the result will be a simple purity which they will never lose; but knowledge will bring with it a divergence therefrom. Seek not the names nor the relations of things, and all things will flourish of themselves."
passages.zh: 「那麼，用你的心，」生機之靈說，「去養育你的百姓。安處於無為，天下便會自行向善。蛻去你的軀殼。吐出你的智巧。忽略一切分別。與無限合而為一。釋放你的心。解脫你的靈魂。要空虛。要無！讓萬物回歸其本初的構成。若它們如此而行，不憑知識，結果將是一種它們永遠不會失去的單純純淨；但知識會帶來與此的背離。不要尋求事物的名稱與關係，萬物便會自行繁茂。」

title.en: Rabia's Fire and Water
title.zh: 拉比雅的火與水

region.en: Basra, streets of the woman-saint (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴士拉女聖徒的街市（實際定位）

period: Anecdotes preserved in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (Arabic-Persian, 12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), ch. on the Path; anecdotes of Rabia from Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Rabia al-Adawiyya, the freed slave-girl of Basra who became the mother of the Sufi doctrine of love, was seen one day carrying a torch in one hand and a pail of water in the other. 'I will burn the gardens of Paradise and drown the fires of Hell, that men may worship God neither for fear nor for reward — but for Himself alone.'
summary.zh: 巴士拉女奴出身的拉比雅·阿達維亞——蘇菲愛之學說的奠基者——一日手執火把與水桶而行。『我要燒盡樂園的園囿、澆熄火獄之火，使人敬拜主既非因懼亦非因賞——只為主自身。』

sensitivity.note: Sufi hagiography of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from public-domain sources.

passages.text: Rabia al-Adawiyya of Basra, the freed slave-girl who became the mother of the Sufi doctrine of love, was seen in the streets one day with a torch in one hand and a pail of water in the other. 'Why do you carry fire and water?' she was asked. She said: 'I will burn the gardens of Paradise with the one, and drown the fires of Hell with the other, that men may come to worship God without hope and without fear — for Himself alone.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote in Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴士拉的拉比亞·阿達維亞，本是獲釋的女奴，後來成為蘇菲愛之教義之母。某日，有人見她走在街上，一手持火炬，一手提水桶。「你為何帶著火與水？」有人問她。她說：「我要用這火燒盡天堂的花園，用這水澆熄地獄的烈火，好讓人們不求希望、不懷恐懼地來崇拜真主——只為祂本身。」

title.en: Ibrahim ibn Adham: The Prince Who Rode Away
title.zh: 易卜拉欣·本·阿丹：騎馬而去的王子

region.en: Balkh, capital of the prince (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴爾赫王子之都（實際定位）

period: Anecdotes preserved in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); anecdotes of Ibrahim ibn Adham from the Tadhkirat tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Ibrahim ibn Adham, king of Balkh, was hunting when a voice called after his horse: 'You were not created for this; nor were you created for that.' He looked and saw nothing; the call came again; the third time he rode away from his kingdom with his pilgrim's cloak, and took service as a watchman of orchards — the Prince who renounced, cousin of the Buddha's story told in the Islam of Khurasan.
summary.zh: 巴爾赫王易卜拉欣·本·阿丹狩獵之際，有聲自其馬後呼：『你非為此而受造；亦非為彼。』他環顧無所見；呼聲再至；第三次，他棄其王位，披朝聖者之氅而去，受雇為果園守夜人——放棄王位之王子，呼羅珊伊斯蘭中佛本生故事的親緣。

sensitivity.note: Sufi hagiography of a living devotional tradition; the renunciation tale parallels Buddhist and Christian withdrawal legends; cross-traditional motif tagging is interpretive.

passages.text: Ibrahim ibn Adham was king of Balkh. One day he was hunting, and a voice called after him on his horse: 'You were not created for this; nor were you created for that.' He looked and saw nobody. The call came again from behind him, and again; and the third time he took off his royal cloak and rode away from his kingdom, and became a watchman of the orchards and a waiter at the tables of others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote in Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 易卜拉欣·伊本·阿德漢是巴爾赫的國王。某日他外出狩獵，有個聲音在他馬後呼喚他：「你受造並非為此；你受造亦非為彼。」他環顧四周，不見一人。那呼喚又從他身後傳來，再來一次；到了第三次，他脫下王袍，騎馬離開了他的王國，成了果園的看守人，又在別人的餐桌旁當侍者。

passages.text: It is told of him that he served his years in silence, and that when his servants found him and would have brought him back, he said: 'My kingdom is not of Balkh.' The hagiographers make him the pattern of the great renunciation in the Islam of Khurasan; and the tale has travelled as far as the story of the prince who left the palace for the road, in every telling of it, from the Ganges to the Oxus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 關於他，有這樣的記載：他默默無聞地度過了那些年；當他的僕人找到他、想要帶他回去時，他說：「我的王國不在巴爾赫。」聖徒傳記的作者們將他塑造成呼羅珊伊斯蘭中偉大棄絕的典範；而這個故事，如同那位離開宮殿走上道路的王子之事，從恆河到阿姆河，在每一次講述中流傳至今。

title.en: Hallaj on the Gibbet: 'Ana al-Haqq'
title.zh: 哈拉吉於十字架：「我即真理」

region.en: Baghdad, gibbet of the Mansur gate (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴格達曼蘇爾門十字架（實際定位）

period: Event 922 CE; anecdotes in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); the Hallaj tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Al-Husayn ibn Mansur al-Hallaj, the Sufi of Baghdad, cried in the streets the word the jurists could not forgive: 'Ana al-Haqq' — I am the Truth. He was imprisoned for years, scourged, mutilated, and at last gibbeted; and the legend tells that his blood was two words written on the ground, and that passers-by asked him of the love of God as they walked beneath him.
summary.zh: 巴格達蘇菲胡賽因·本·曼蘇爾·哈拉吉於街市喊出法學家不能容之語：『我即真理』（Ana al-Haqq）。他被囚多年，受笞刑、殘肢，最後被釘於十字架；相傳其血於地上寫成兩個字，而行人在其下經過時仍向他問主之愛。

sensitivity.note: Sufi hagiography of a living devotional tradition; the trial and execution are matters of doctrine and history alike; presented as the received narrative.

passages.text: Al-Hallaj, the wool-carder of Baghdad, cried in the streets the word the jurists could not forgive: 'Ana al-Haqq' — I am the Truth. He was cast into prison for years, and scourged, and mutilated; and in the gibbet he was heard to pray: 'Pardon them; for if Thou hadst revealed to them what Thou hast revealed to me, they would not have done what they did.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Hallaj tradition as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), and Attar's Tadhkirat; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴格達的梳毛匠哈拉智在街頭高呼那句法學家們無法寬恕的話：「Ana al-Haqq」——我就是真理。他因此被投入監獄多年，遭受鞭笞，又被殘害肢體；人們聽見他在絞架上祈禱說：「赦免他們吧；因為倘若祢向他們啟示了祢向我啟示的一切，他們就不會做出他們所做之事。」

passages.text: The legend adds that when they questioned him on the gibbet he asked for his Lord, and that his blood wrote two words on the ground as it fell; and the Sufi poets took him for the martyr of the doctrine that the lover and the Beloved are one — and the jurists made of him a warning. Both readings have carried his name for a thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Hallaj tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說還補充道，當他們在絞架上審問他時，他呼求他的主；而他的血在滴落時，在地上寫下了兩個字。蘇菲詩人們將他視為「愛者與被愛者為一」這一教義的殉道者——而法學家們則以他為警戒。一千年來，這兩種解讀都承載著他的名字。

title.en: Bishr al-Hafi and the Scrap of Paper
title.zh: 比希爾·哈菲與紙片

region.en: Baghdad, street of the taverns (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 巴格達酒肆之街（象徵性定位）

period: Anecdotes in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); the Bishr al-Hafi tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Bishr ibn al-Harith, called al-Hafi (the Barefoot), the young rake of Baghdad, found one night in the street a scrap of paper bearing the name of God, trodden in the mud. He bought it, washed it, perfumed it, and buried it; and that night, the story says, he was told in sleep: 'Thou hast honoured My name; I have forgiven thee, and made thee and thy parents of My friends.' He rose barefoot, and was called the Barefoot ever after.
summary.zh: 巴格達的浪蕩青年比希爾·本·哈里斯——後稱『赤足者』（al-Hafi）——一夜於街上拾得一片寫著主名、陷於泥濘被踐踏的紙。他買下它，洗之、熏之、葬之；相傳當夜夢中被告知：『你尊崇了我的名；我已赦你，並使你與你的父母成為我的朋友。』他赤足而起，自是稱為赤足者。

sensitivity.note: Sufi hagiography of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from public-domain sources.

passages.text: Bishr ibn al-Harith, the young rake of Baghdad, found one night in the street a scrap of paper bearing the name of God, trodden in the mud. He bought it for a dinar from the man who had cast it away, and washed it and perfumed it, and buried it where the ground was clean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote in Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴格達的浪蕩青年比什爾·伊本·哈里斯，某夜在街上發現一片寫有真主之名的紙片，被踐踏在泥中。他從那個丟棄它的人手中以一第納爾買下，將它洗淨、薰香，然後埋葬在潔淨的土地裡。

passages.text: That night, the story says, he was told in sleep: 'Thou hast honoured My name; I have forgiven thee, and made thee and thy parents of My friends.' He rose barefoot, and gave up the tavern, and was called al-Hafi, the Barefoot, ever after; and his teacher Fudayl said of him: 'He was the wickedest of men, and he became one of the best.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 據說，那天夜裡，他在睡夢中被告知：「你已尊崇了我的名；我已赦免了你，並使你與你的父母成為我的朋友。」他赤足起身，捨棄了酒館，此後便被人稱為「赤足者」哈菲（al-Hafi）；他的老師富代勒談到他時說：「他曾是世人中最邪惡的，卻成了最善良者之一。」

title.en: Fudayl the Brigand Repents at the Wall
title.zh: 強盜福戴爾在牆下悔悟

region.en: City wall of Merv / Rayy (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 梅爾夫／賴夷城牆（象徵性定位）

period: Anecdotes in Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya (12th c.); English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); the Fudayl ibn Iyad tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: Fudayl ibn Iyad was a highwayman of Khurasan. He lay in wait one night and saw a traveller scaling the city wall, and asked him what he did. 'I am going to a woman I love.' 'And if you are seen?' — 'I fear being seen by men.' 'And do you not fear the sight of God?' The brigand wept, and left his trade at the foot of the wall, and became one of the masters of the age — the teacher of Bishr, the confessor of the road.
summary.zh: 呼羅珊的強盜福戴爾·本·伊亞德一夜埋伏，見一旅人攀城牆，問其何為。『去見我所愛的女子。』『若被見呢？』——『我怕人見。』『你豈不畏主之觀看？』強盜哭泣，棄其業於牆下，成為當代師表——比希爾之師、道路上的告解者。

sensitivity.note: Sufi hagiography of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from public-domain sources.

passages.text: Fudayl ibn Iyad was a highwayman of Khurasan, who lay in wait for caravans. One night he saw a traveller scaling the city wall, and asked him what he did there. 'I am going to a woman I love.' 'And if you are seen?' 'I fear being seen by men.' 'And do you not fear the sight of God?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote in Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 富代勒·伊本·伊亞德原是呼羅珊的攔路強盜，埋伏等候商隊。一天夜裡，他看見一名旅人翻越城牆，便問他在那裡做什麼。「我要去見我所愛的女人。」「若被人看見呢？」「我怕被人看見。」「你就不怕真主看見嗎？」

passages.text: The brigand wept at the foot of the wall, and left his trade there; and he became one of the masters of his age, the teacher of Bishr al-Hafi, and the man whose house the learned came to for the secrets of the fear of God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote tradition; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 那強盜在牆腳下痛哭，就此捨棄了他的行當；他後來成為當代宗師之一，是比什爾·哈菲的老師，也是學者們前來其家中探求敬畏真主之奧祕的那個人。

title.en: Junayd and the Boy on the Rooftop
title.zh: 朱奈德與屋頂上的男孩

region.en: Baghdad, rooftops of the city (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 巴格達城中屋頂（象徵性定位）

period: Anecdotes preserved in Arabic Sufi biographies; English: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), public domain

source.work: R. A. Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914), ch. on the Unitive State; Junayd traditions in Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya

license: Public domain (English edition 1914; Arabic originals medieval)

summary.en: Junayd of Baghdad, the shaykh of the sober school, was asked what he had learned of the love of God; he answered with the story of the boy who was set to watch the rooftops and saw the beloved's window lit — and climbed, and fell, and was carried home in silence. 'This is the love of God: it is not spoken of, it is climbed for.' The anecdote belongs to the doctrine that the mystic's state cannot be told, only lived.
summary.zh: 巴格達蘇菲師朱奈德被問及何謂主之愛；他以屋頂守望男孩的故事作答：男孩望見心上人窗中燈亮——攀之，墜之，默然被抬回家。『此即主之愛：不可言說，只可攀登。』此軼事屬「神秘狀態不可述、只可活」之教義。

sensitivity.note: Sufi anecdote of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from public-domain sources.

passages.text: Junayd of Baghdad, the shaykh of the sober school of Sufism, was asked what he had learned of the love of God, and answered with a tale: of a boy set to watch the rooftops, who saw the window of his beloved lit, and climbed, and fell, and was carried home in silence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴格達的朱奈德是蘇非主義中「清醒派」的長老，有人問他從對真主的愛中學到了什麼，他以一則故事作答：有個男孩被派去看守屋頂，他看見所愛之人的窗戶亮著燈，便攀爬而上，卻跌落下來，被人默默抬回家中。

passages.text: 'This,' said Junayd, 'is the love of God: it is not spoken of, it is climbed for; and the tongue of the lover is his falling, not his saying.' The doctrine of the school is that the mystic's state cannot be told, only lived — and the anecdote lore of Baghdad kept the lesson in a boy on a roof.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote as given in Nicholson, The Mystics of Islam (1914); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 朱奈德說：「這就是對真主的愛：它不靠言說，而是靠攀登；愛者的舌頭是他的跌落，而非他的言語。」該派的學說是：神祕者的境界無法言說，只能親身活出——而巴格達的軼事傳說，則把這一教訓寄託在一個屋頂上的男孩身上。

title.en: Saadi's Deaf Man and the Doctor
title.zh: 薩迪的聾人與醫生

region.en: Shiraz, house of the sick man (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 設拉子病者之家（象徵性定位）

period: Gulistan (Rose Garden), Book 4 (composed c. 1258); James Ross translation, 1823, public domain (Gutenberg #13060)

source.work: Sa'di, The Gulistan (Rose Garden), trans. James Ross (1823), Book 4 'Of the Benefit of Being Silent'

summary.en: A man whose relatives were sick resolved to visit them and cheer them: he asked a friend what questions he should be expected to ask, and what answers he should give. 'They will ask after thy health; say thou art well.' — 'And after the sickness?' — 'Say it is past.' — 'And what if he asks for medicine?' — 'Say the physician has ordered such and such.' The deaf man repeats the forms to the sick man's face — 'Are thy pains past?' 'Thanks to God, my pains are past' — and the sick man's friends hear him say what he never said: the comedy of the forms without the care.
summary.zh: 一人的親屬病重，決定探望並致慰：他問朋友該問什麼、該答什麼。『他們會問你的健康；說你很好。』——『那病呢？』——『說已痊癒。』——『若問藥呢？』——『說醫生囑如此。』聾人對病人當面復述套語——『你的病痛已過了嗎？』『感謝主，我的病痛已過』——病人之親聞其所從未言之語：徒有形式而無關懷之喜劇。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate wisdom tale (Saadi's Gulistan); paraphrased from the public-domain Ross translation.

passages.text: A man whose relatives were sick had never visited them; and being asked why, he said he was deaf and could not hear their questions. He resolved at last to go, and asked a friend what he should say when the sick man spoke to him. 'He will ask after thy health; say thou art well.' 'And after the sickness?' 'Say it is past.' 'And what if he asks for medicine?' 'Say the physician has ordered such and such.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sa'di, Gulistan (Ross 1823), Book 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 有個人親屬生病，他卻從未前去探望；有人問他緣故，他說自己耳聾，聽不見他們的問話。他終於決定前往，並問一位朋友：病人對他說話時，他該如何應答。「他會問候你的身體；你就說你很好。」「那問到病情呢？」「就說已經過去了。」「要是他問起藥呢？」「就說醫生吩咐了如此這般的藥。」

passages.text: So the deaf man went, and sat at the bed of the sick man, and put the questions in the order he had learned: 'How art thou?' The sick man answered, 'I am much worse.' — 'And thy pains?' 'They are increased.' — 'And hast thou taken the medicine?' 'No.' And the deaf man, pleased with the fitness of the forms, left him without asking anything more; and Saadi's moral is of the visit paid out of a book, in which the words are all right and the love is absent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sa'di, Gulistan (Ross 1823), Book 4; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 於是那聾人便去了，坐在病人的床邊，照著他所記熟的次序發問：「你好嗎？」病人答道：「我糟得很。」——「你的疼痛呢？」「越發加重了。」——「你吃過藥了嗎？」「沒有。」那聾人因這些問話的形式都恰當合宜而滿心歡喜，便不再多問一句就離開了他；薩迪的寓意，說的是照著書本去探病，話語全都沒錯，情意卻不在其中。

title.en: The Old Wrestler and the Ring
title.zh: 老摔跤手與擂台

region.en: Shiraz, wrestling-ground of the town (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 設拉子城中摔跤場（象徵性定位）

period: Gulistan, Book 1 (composed c. 1258); James Ross translation, 1823, public domain (Gutenberg #13060)

source.work: Sa'di, The Gulistan (Rose Garden), trans. James Ross (1823), Book 1 'Of the Customs of Kings'

summary.en: A wrestler grown old boasts before the king that he has never been thrown; a young man comes up and throws him twice. The old man asks him what he was before — 'I heard thee boast, and my hands grew strong.' Saadi's moral: the babbler's tongue is the wrestler's best adversary.
summary.zh: 一名老摔跤手在王前自誇從未被摔；一青年上場兩次摔倒他。老者問其先何為——『聞你自誇，我手便強。』薩迪之旨：饒舌者之舌乃摔跤手最佳對手。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate wisdom tale; paraphrased from the public-domain Ross translation.

passages.text: A wrestler grown old and stiff boasted before the king that he had never been thrown; and he said, 'I have no equal in the ring.' A young man came up and threw him twice. The old man asked him, 'Who art thou, and what hast thou been, that thou hast thrown me?' The young man said: 'I heard thy boast, and my hands grew strong.' Saadi's moral is of the talker: the babbler's tongue is the wrestler's best adversary, and the man who makes much of himself before others is beaten by the man who has nothing to say.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sa'di, Gulistan (Ross 1823), Book 1; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名年老而僵硬的角力士在國王面前誇口，說自己從未被人摔倒；他又說：「在角力場上我沒有敵手。」一個年輕人走上前來，把他摔倒了兩次。老人問他：「你是誰，從前是做什麼的，竟能把我摔倒？」年輕人說：「我聽見了你的誇口，我的手便強壯起來。」薩迪的寓意，說的是那好說話的人：饒舌者的舌頭，正是角力士最好的對手；而在人前把自己看得太重的人，總被那無話可說的人擊敗。

title.en: The Man Who Had No Shoes
title.zh: 無鞋之人

region.en: Great mosque of Kufa (literal pin)
region.zh: 庫法大清真寺（實際定位）

period: Gulistan, Book 3 (composed c. 1258); James Ross translation, 1823, public domain (Gutenberg #13060)

source.work: Sa'di, The Gulistan (Rose Garden), trans. James Ross (1823), Book 3 'On the Preciousness of Contentment'

summary.en: Saadi goes barefoot in the heat because he has no shoes, and is grieved; entering the great mosque of Kufa he sees a man who has no feet. 'Whereupon I thanked Providence for its bounty to myself.' The tale belongs to Saadi's doctrine of contentment, told from his own road.
summary.zh: 薩迪因無鞋而赤足行於烈日，心中愁苦；入庫法大清真寺，見一無足之人。『於是我感謝上天對我的恩賜。』此故事屬薩迪的知足學說，出自他自己的行路。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate wisdom tale; paraphrased from the public-domain Ross translation.

passages.text: One day, says Saadi, I had no shoes and was grieved with my lot, until I came into the great mosque of Kufa and there saw a man who had no feet. Whereupon I thanked Providence for its bounty to myself, and took up my burden as a gift.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sa'di, Gulistan (Ross 1823), Book 3; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 薩迪說，有一天我沒有鞋穿，為自己的命運而憂傷，直到我走進庫法的大清真寺，在那裡看見一個沒有腳的人。於是我為上天賜予我自己的恩惠而感恩，把自己的擔子當作禮物承擔起來。

title.en: The Dervish Who Would Not Ask
title.zh: 不開口的苦行僧

region.en: Shiraz, door of the dervish (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 設拉子苦行僧之門（象徵性定位）

period: Gulistan, Book 2 (composed c. 1258); James Ross translation, 1823, public domain (Gutenberg #13060)

source.work: Sa'di, The Gulistan (Rose Garden), trans. James Ross (1823), Book 2 'Of the Morals of Dervishes'

summary.en: A dervish sits at his door in contentment; a king passes and offers him wealth. 'Keep thy wealth, for I am rich without it.' 'How art thou rich?' — 'In that I ask nothing of the king.' The anecdote belongs to Saadi's second book, the morals of the dervishes, where the beggar is the rich man and the giver is the poor.
summary.zh: 一苦行僧滿足地坐在門前；一國王經過並許以財富。『留著你的財富，我無之而富。』『你何以為富？』——『在於我不向王求取。』此軼事屬薩迪第二卷「苦行僧之德」，其中乞者為富人，施者為窮人。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate wisdom tale; paraphrased from the public-domain Ross translation.

passages.text: A dervish sat at his door in contentment, and a king passing by offered him wealth. He said, 'Keep thy wealth, for I am rich without it.' The king said, 'How art thou rich?' The dervish said, 'In that I ask nothing of the king.' Saadi's moral is of the free man: the beggar who asks is the poor man, and the man who is contented is the rich — and the king went away the poorer of the two.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Sa'di, Gulistan (Ross 1823), Book 2; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一位苦行僧心滿意足地坐在自家門口，一位國王路過，要賜他財富。他說：「留著你的財富吧，沒有它我也是富足的。」國王說：「你怎麼算富足呢？」苦行僧說：「因為我不向國王求任何東西。」薩迪的寓意，說的是那自由的人：開口乞求的乞丐才是窮人，心滿意足的人才是富人——而國王離去時，反倒是兩人中較窮的那一個。

title.en: The Yellow Emperor's Magic Pearl (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 黃帝遺其玄珠（莊子）

region.en: The K'un-lun mountains (mythic range; symbolic pin: Kunlun, Xinjiang, China)
region.zh: 崑崙之丘（神話山系；象徵定位：新疆崑崙）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 12, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 12

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor travels north of the Red Lake and ascends the K'un-lun mountains, but on returning south loses his magic pearl. Intelligence, Sight, and Speech all fail to find it; finally he employs Nothing — and Nothing gets it. Strange indeed, quoth the Emperor, that Nothing should have been able to get it!
summary.zh: 黃帝遊乎赤水之北，登乎崑崙之丘而南還，還遺其玄珠。使知索之而不得，使離朱索之而不得，使喫詬索之而不得也。乃使象罔，象罔得之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the lost-pearl quest is the classic Taoist myth of knowledge versus negation. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The Yellow Emperor travelled to the north of the Red Lake and ascended the K'un-lun Mountains. Returning south he lost his magic pearl. He employed Intelligence to find it, but without success. He employed Sight to find it, but without success. He employed Speech to find it, but without success. Finally, he employed Nothing, and Nothing got it. "Strange indeed," quoth the Emperor, "that Nothing should have been able to get it!"
passages.zh: 黃帝往北行至赤水之北，登上崑崙之山。他向南歸來時，遺失了他的玄珠。他派智去尋找，沒有找到。他派離朱去尋找，沒有找到。他派喫詬去尋找，也沒有找到。最後，他派象罔去，象罔卻找到了。「真是奇怪啊，」黃帝說，「竟然是無心之象罔能夠找到它！」

title.en: Yao Declines Long Life, Wealth, and Sons (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 堯遊乎華，封人祝壽富多男子（莊子）

region.en: Hua, the border state (symbolic pin: Huayin, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 華封之地（象徵定位：陝西華陰）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 12, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 12

summary.en: Yao visits Hua, and the border-warden wishes him long life, plenty of money, and many sons — and Yao says Don't! to each. Many sons are many anxieties, plenty of money plenty of trouble. The true Sage dwells like the quail and feeds like a fledgeling; after a thousand years of this weary world he mounts aloft, riding upon the white clouds into the kingdom of God, whither the three evils do not reach.
summary.zh: 堯觀乎華，華封人三祝：使聖人壽、富、多男子；堯皆曰辭。封人曰：千歲厭世，去而上仙，乘彼白雲，至於帝鄉，三患莫至，身常無殃。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the 'riding white clouds to God's city' line is a classic ascension text. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Yao went to visit Hua. The border-warden of Hua said "Ha! a Sage. My best respects to you, Sir. I wish you a long life." "Don't!" replied Yao. "I wish you plenty of money," continued the border-warden. "Don't!" replied Yao. "And many sons," added he. "Don't!" replied Yao. "Long life, plenty of money, and many sons," cried the warden, "these are what all men desire. How is it you alone do not want them?" "Many sons," answered Yao, "are many anxieties. Plenty of money means plenty of trouble. Long life involves much that is not pleasant to put up with. These three gifts do not advance virtue; therefore I declined them."
passages.zh: 堯去拜訪華。華的守疆人說：「啊！一位聖人。我向您致以最崇高的敬意，先生。我祝您長壽。」「不必了！」堯回答。「我祝您財富充盈，」守疆人接著說。「不必了！」堯回答。「還有多子多孫，」他又補上一句。「不必了！」堯回答。「長壽、財富充盈、多子多孫，」守疆人高聲說，「這些都是人人所想要的。怎麼唯獨您不想要呢？」「多子多孫，」堯回答，「便是多憂多慮。財富充盈，便意味著多麻煩。長壽則牽涉許多令人難以忍受的事。這三樣贈禮並不能增進德行；所以我謝絕了它們。」

passages.text: "The true Sage dwells like the quail and feeds like a fledgeling. He travels like the bird, leaving no trace behind. If there be TAO in the empire, he and all things are in harmony. If there be not TAO, he cultivates virtue in retirement. After a thousand years of this weary world, he mounts aloft, and riding upon the white clouds passes into the kingdom of God, whither the three evils do not reach, and where he rests secure in eternity. What is there to put up with in that?"
passages.zh: 「真正的聖人，居處如鵪鶉，飲食如雛鳥。他出行如飛鳥，不留痕跡。若天下有道，他便與萬物和諧共處。若天下無道，他便退隱而修養其德。如此在這疲憊的世間歷經千年之後，他高升而去，乘著白雲進入上帝之國，那裡三種禍患無法到達，他也在永恆中安然歇息。那樣又有什麼需要忍受的呢？」

title.en: At the Beginning of the Beginning, Even Nothing Did Not Exist (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 泰初有無，無有無名（莊子）

region.en: The cosmogonic register (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宇宙開闢之初（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 12, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 12

summary.en: At the beginning of the beginning, even Nothing did not exist; then came the period of the Nameless. When One came into existence it was formless; things got their virtue; the formless but divided was called destiny; then the movement which gave life brought form — and form enclosing the spiritual part becomes nature, by whose cultivation we are carried back to virtue and to the beginning.
summary.zh: 泰初有無，無有無名；一之所起，有一而未形。物得以生，謂之德；未形者有分，且然無閒，謂之命；留動而生物，物成生理，謂之形；形體保神，各有儀則，謂之性。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); a priority Creation & Cosmology narrative. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: At the beginning of the beginning, even Nothing did not exist. Then came the period of the Nameless. When ONE came into existence, there was ONE, but it was formless. When things got that by which they came into existence, it was called their virtue.
passages.zh: 在太初之始，甚至連「無」都不存在。接著便到了無名的時期。當「一」出現時，就有了「一」，但它是沒有形體的。當萬物得到了它們藉以存在的東西，那便稱為它們的德。

passages.text: That which was formless, but divided, though without interstice, was called destiny. Then came the movement which gave life, and things produced in accordance with the principles of life had what is called form. When form encloses the spiritual part, each with its own characteristics, that is its nature. By cultivating this nature, we are carried back to virtue; and if this is perfected, we become as all things were in the beginning. We become unconditioned, and the unconditioned is great.
passages.zh: 那沒有形體卻有所分別、雖無間隙卻能劃分的，稱為命。接著便有了賦予生命的運動，而依生命之理產生的萬物便有了所謂的形體。當形體包裹住精神的部分，各自有其特徵，那便是它的本性。藉著修養這本性，我們便被帶回於德；若此得以完善，我們便如同萬物在太初之時一樣。我們成為無所依待的，而無所依待便是偉大。

title.en: The Gardener Who Refused the Well-Sweep (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 漢陰丈人拒桔槹（莊子）

region.en: Han-yin, on the Han river (Xiangyang, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 漢陰（漢水之南，今湖北襄陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 12, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 12

summary.en: Tzŭ Kung finds an old gardener watering a hundred plots with a hand-pitcher and offers him a well-sweep. The gardener flushes: those who have cunning implements are cunning in their dealings, cunning at heart, restless in spirit — not fit vehicles for TAO. I should be ashamed to use them. Tzŭ Kung slinks away and takes thirty li to recover his usual appearance.
summary.zh: 子貢南遊於楚，反於晉，過漢陰；見一丈人方將為圃畦，鑿隧而入井，抱甕而出灌。丈人曰：有機械者必有機事，有機事者必有機心。機心存於胸中，則純白不備；吾非不知，羞而不為也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the anti-machine gardener is Zhuangzi's most-cited technology parable. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Tzŭ Kung went south to the Ch'u State on his way back to the Chin State, he passed through Han-yin. There he saw an old man engaged in making a ditch to connect his vegetable garden with a well. He had a pitcher in his hand, with which he was bringing up water and pouring it into the ditch,--great labour with very little result. "If you had a machine here," cried Tzŭ Kung, "in a day you could irrigate a hundred times your present area. The labour required is trifling as compared with the work done. Would you not like to have one?" "What is it?" asked the gardener. "It is a contrivance made of wood," replied Tzŭ Kung, "heavy behind and light in front. It draws up water as you do with your hands, but in a constantly overflowing stream. It is called a well-sweep."
passages.zh: 子貢南遊於楚，返回晉國途中，經過漢陰。他在那裡看見一位老人正忙著挖一條溝渠，要把他的菜園與水井連接起來。他手裡拿著一個瓦罐，用瓦罐打水倒進溝渠裡——費了很大的力氣，成果卻極少。「這裡若有一部機械，」子貢高聲說道，「一天之內你就能灌溉比現在多一百倍的面積。所費的勞力比起所完成的工作微不足道。你難道不想有一部嗎？」「那是什麼東西？」園圃老人問道。「那是一種木製的裝置，」子貢回答說，「後面重而前面輕。它像你用手一樣把水提上來，卻是不斷湧流的泉水。它叫做桔槔。」

passages.text: Thereupon the gardener flushed up and said, "I have heard from my teacher that those who have cunning implements are cunning in their dealings, and that those who are cunning in their dealings have cunning in their hearts, and that those who have cunning in their hearts cannot be pure and incorrupt, and that those who are not pure and incorrupt are restless in spirit, and that those who are restless in spirit are not fit vehicles for TAO. It is not that I do not know of these things. I should be ashamed to use them."
passages.zh: 於是園圃老人臉色漲紅，說道：「我聽我的老師說過，凡有機巧器械的人，行事便機巧；行事機巧的人，心中便機巧；心中機巧的人，便不能純潔不腐；不能純潔不腐的人，精神便不得安寧；精神不得安寧的人，便不是承載道的器皿。並非我不知道這些東西。我只是羞於使用它們。」

passages.text: Tzŭ Kung changed colour and slunk away, being not at all pleased with this rebuff; and it was not before he had travelled some thirty li that he recovered his usual appearance. "What did the man we met do," asked a disciple, "that you should change colour and not recover for such a long time?" "I used to think there was only one man in all the world," replied Tzŭ Kung. "I did not know that there was also this man."
passages.zh: 子貢變了臉色，慚愧地退開，對這番責難甚為不悅；一直走了大約三十里，他才恢復平常的神色。「我們所遇見的那個人做了什麼，」一位弟子問道，「竟使你變了臉色，這麼久都恢復不過來？」「我從前以為全天下只有一種人，」子貢回答說，「我不知道還有這樣的人。」

title.en: Chun Mang by the Eastern Sea: The Divine Man Absorbed into Light (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 謫芒遊於東海，光芒畢照（莊子）

region.en: The shore of the eastern sea (symbolic pin: Yantai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 東海之濱（象徵定位：山東煙臺）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 12, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 12

summary.en: Setting out eastwards to the ocean, Chun Mang falls in with Yüan Fêng on the shore. Asked how the Sage governs, he answers that the officials confine themselves to their functions; then he describes the man of perfect virtue and finally the divine man who rides upon the glory of the sky, where his form can no longer be discerned — absorption into light, envelopment in darkness.
summary.zh: 謫芒將東之大壑，適遇苑風於東海之濱。謫芒曰：夫聖人之治也——至德之人：就藪澤，處閒曠，條達而福持。神人：乘彼昧光，盡其所懷乎！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: As Chun Mang was starting eastwards to the ocean, he fell in with Yüan Fêng on the shore of the eastern sea. "Whither bound?" cried the latter. "I am going to the ocean," replied Chun Mang. "What are you going to do there?" asked Yüan Fêng. "The ocean," said Chun Mang, "is a thing you cannot fill by pouring in, nor empty by taking out. I am simply on a trip."
passages.zh: 淳芒正要向東前往大海，在東海之濱遇見了苑風。苑風問道：「你要往哪裡去？」淳芒回答說：「我要去大海。」苑風問：「你去那裡做什麼？」淳芒說：「大海這東西，灌注進去也填不滿，取出來也掏不空。我不過是去走一趟罷了。」

passages.text: "The divine man," replied Chun Mang, "rides upon the glory of the sky where his form can no longer be discerned. This is called absorption into light. He fulfils his destiny. He acts in accordance with his nature. He is at one with God and man. For him all affairs cease to exist, and all things revert to their original state. This is called envelopment in darkness."
passages.zh: 淳芒回答說：「神人乘著天宇的光輝，他的形體已無法辨認。這叫做融入光明。他完成自己的天命，依循自己的本性行事。他與神合一，與人合一。對他而言，一切事務都不復存在，萬物都回歸本初的狀態。這叫做包藏於幽暗之中。」

title.en: Dimna's Slander: The Lion and the Ox
title.zh: 迪姆奈的讒言：獅與牛

region.en: Court of the lion-king, India of the fable (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 寓言印度的獅王之廷（象徵性定位）

period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah, Arabic by Ibn al-Muqaffa' (d. 759), from Persian; English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'Story of the Lion and the Ox'

license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: The lion-king befriends the ox Shanzabah, and the jackal Dimna, jealous of the newcomer's favour, whispers to each that the other plots against him. The friends are set at variance; the ox is killed in the quarrel; and the king, discovering the treachery, judges Dimna by the law of the beasts. The frame-story of the whole book: the philosopher Bidpai tells the tale to a king of India to warn him of tale-bearers.
summary.zh: 獅王善待公牛尚扎巴；豺狼迪姆奈嫉其新寵，向雙方各進讒言。二友失和；公牛死於爭端；獅王發現其奸，依獸法審判迪姆奈。全書框架故事：哲人白得巴向印度之王講述此篇，以警讒言者。

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable transmitted through Arabic (Kalilah wa-Dimnah) and long used in Islamic education; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation of the Syriac version.

passages.text: The lion-king took the ox Shanzabah into his friendship, and the jackal Dimna, who had served the king before him, grew jealous of the newcomer's favour. He went first to the ox and said: 'The king means to eat thee.' Then he went to the king and said: 'The ox has said among the beasts that he will take thy kingdom.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'Story of the Lion and the Ox'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 獅王與公牛善沙巴結為友誼，先前曾侍奉國王的豺狼迪姆納，嫉妒這新來者所受的寵愛。他先到公牛那裡說：『國王打算吃掉你。』然後又到國王那裡說：『公牛在群獸之中說過，他要奪取你的王國。』

passages.text: The friends were set at variance, and the ox was slain in the quarrel that the tale-bearer had made. The king discovered the treachery, and judged Dimna according to the law of the beasts; and the philosopher Bidpai, in the frame of the book, tells the story to a king of India: 'The tale-bearer is the wolf between two friends; and the throne that listens to him loses both.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這對朋友被挑撥離間，公牛便在搬弄是非者所挑起的爭鬥中被殺。國王發覺了這樁背叛，便依群獸之法審判迪姆納；而哲人比德派在本書的框架之中，向一位印度國王講述這個故事：『搬弄是非者就是兩個朋友之間的狼；聽信他的王座，會把兩者都失去。』

title.en: The War of the Owls and the Crows
title.zh: 貓頭鷹與烏鴉之戰

region.en: Owl fortress on a mountain, India of the fable (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 寓言印度的山上貓頭鷹堡（象徵性定位）

period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah (Arabic, 8th c.); English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'The Owls and the Crows'

license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: The owls have beaten the crows for years, because the crows cannot see by night. A young crow volunteers a desperate counsel: let him go over to the owls and be received as a deserter. He lives among them, learns the way to their fortress, gathers straw, and in the day sets fire to it while the owls sleep — and the war is ended in one morning. The moral: the counsel of the desperate is the sword of the desperate.
summary.zh: 貓頭鷹多年壓制烏鴉，因烏鴉夜不能視。一隻年輕烏鴉獻苦計：假投誠混入鴞群。他與之同住，探得其堡之路，積聚乾草；白晝鴞群酣睡時縱火——一晨之間戰爭終結。寓意：絕望者的計謀即絕望者的劍。

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation.

passages.text: The owls had beaten the crows for years, for the crows could not see by night and the owls came against them in the dark. A young crow stood up among the council and volunteered a desperate counsel: 'Let me go over to the owls and be received as a deserter, and I will learn the way to their fortress.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'The Owls and the Crows'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 貓頭鷹多年來一直擊敗烏鴉，因為烏鴉在夜裡看不見，而貓頭鷹總在黑暗中來襲。一隻年輕的烏鴉在議會中站起來，自願獻上一條孤注一擲的計策：『讓我投奔貓頭鷹，被當作叛逃者接納，我就能摸清通往他們堡壘的路。』

passages.text: He lived among the owls, and won their trust, and saw the fortress in which they slept by day. He gathered straw and laid it at the mouth of the cave; and one morning, while the owls slept, he set fire to the straw, and the war of the owls and the crows was ended. And the moral is of the counsel that is given only by him who is willing to be the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他住在貓頭鷹之中，贏得了他們的信任，看清了他們白天睡覺的堡壘。他收集稻草，堆在洞穴口；一天早晨，趁貓頭鷹熟睡之際，他點燃了稻草，貓頭鷹與烏鴉的戰爭就此結束。而這則寓言的教訓，是關於那種唯有甘願成為那團火的人才能給出的計策。

title.en: The Tortoise and the Ape
title.zh: 龜與猿

region.en: Riverbank of the fable (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 寓言的河岸（象徵性定位）

period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah (Arabic, 8th c.); English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'The Tortoise and the Ape'

license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: The ape and the tortoise are friends in the season of the flood; the ape is carried on the tortoise's back to an island, and in pride of his rescue mocks his preserver: 'Thy kind are but shells upon the sand.' The friendship is broken at a word, and both are lost in the next flood. The moral: the tongue that repays kindness with scorn breaks the boat that carries it.
summary.zh: 洪水季節猿與龜為友；龜載猿至島上；猿得救而傲，嘲其恩人：『你們一族不過沙上之殼。』一言友誼即斷，二人皆喪於下次洪水。寓意：以輕蔑報恩之言，自斷所乘之舟。

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation.

passages.text: In the season of the flood the ape and the tortoise were friends, and the tortoise carried the ape on his back to an island of safety. In pride of his rescue the ape mocked his preserver: 'Thy kind are but shells upon the sand.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'The Tortoise and the Ape'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 洪水季節，猿與龜為友，龜負猿於背上，載往安全之島。猿因獲救而自矜，反譏其救命之恩人曰：「爾之族類，不過沙上之貝殼耳。」

passages.text: The friendship was broken at a word; and when the next flood came, both were lost — for the tortoise would not carry again, and the ape could not swim. The moral of the tale is of the tongue that repays kindness with scorn, and breaks the boat that carries it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 友誼因一言而破裂；及至下次洪水來臨，二者俱亡——蓋龜不復肯負，而猿不能泅也。此故事之寓意，在於以輕蔑回報恩惠之舌，毀壞載己之舟。

title.en: The Ring-Dove and the Fowler's Net
title.zh: 斑鳩與捕鳥者的羅網

region.en: Forest of the fable (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 寓言的森林（象徵性定位）

period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah (Arabic, 8th c.); English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'Story of the Ring-dove'

license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: A ring-dove and her company are caught in the fowler's net; she lifts the net on her wings and flies with them all to the mouse's hole, and the mouse gnaws the strings and frees them one by one. The moral is spoken by the mouse: 'They who bear one another's burdens escape the net; they who peck at one another stay in it.'
summary.zh: 一斑鳩與同伴陷入捕鳥者羅網；她張翅舉網，攜眾飛至鼠洞；鼠逐一齧斷繩索而釋之。寓意出自鼠口：『彼此共負重軛者脫網；彼此相啄者困於網中。』

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation.

passages.text: A ring-dove and her company were caught in the fowler's net; and she lifted the net on her wings and flew with them all, dragging it to the hole of the mouse. The mouse gnawed the strings and freed them one by one, saving herself the last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'Story of the Ring-dove'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一斑鳩與其群侶為捕鳥者之網所困；斑鳩舉網於其翼上，與眾俱飛，曳網至鼠之洞穴。鼠齧斷繩索，逐一釋之，而自留於最後。

passages.text: The moral is spoken by the mouse: 'They who bear one another's burdens escape the net; they who peck at one another stay in it.' And the tale is told in the frame of the book as the counsel of unity to the king's court.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其寓意由鼠道出：「彼此分擔重負者，得脫於網；互相啄鬥者，仍留網中。」此故事於書中之框架內，乃作為對國王朝廷之團結勸諫而述。

title.en: The Trial of Dimna
title.zh: 迪姆奈受審

region.en: Court of the lion-king (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 獅王法庭（象徵性定位）

period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah (Arabic, 8th c.); English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'Dimnah's Defence'

license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: The jackal Dimna, accused of the ox's death, defends himself with a whole day of eloquence: he cites the law, the precedent of the wolves, the necessity of the state — and the assembly is nearly persuaded. Then the witnesses speak, and the sentence falls. The chapter is a satire on the advocate's art: the voice that can make wrong sound like justice.
summary.zh: 豺狼迪姆奈因公牛之死受審，以一整日雄辯自衛：引法度、援狼之先例、陳國家之需——眾幾乎被說服。繼而證人發言，判決落定。此章諷刺辯護術：能使非義聽似公義之聲音。

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation.

passages.text: The jackal Dimna, accused of the ox's death, defended himself with a whole day of eloquence: he cited the law, and the precedent of the wolves, and the necessity of the state, and the mercy that the king had shown to him who had only served him; and the assembly of the beasts was nearly persuaded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'Dimnah's Defence'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 豺狼迪姆納被控害牛致死，乃以終日之雄辯自辯：引述律法，援引群狼之先例，陳說國家之必要，並述國王對僅曾效勞於己者所施之恩慈；百獸之會幾乎為其所說服。

passages.text: Then the witnesses spoke, and the sentence fell; and the chapter is a satire on the advocate's art — the voice that can make wrong sound like justice — and a warning to the king's court of the tale-bearer at its own gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 其後證人發言，判決遂下；此章乃諷刺辯士之術——能令錯謬聽來如正義之聲——並為對國王朝廷之警戒，戒其自家門前之讒言者。

title.en: Shun Asks Yao How He Employs His Faculties (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 舜問堯天子之用心（莊子）

region.en: Yao's court at Fen-yang (Linfen, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 堯都汾陽（今山西臨汾）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 13, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 13

summary.en: Shun asks Yao how he employs his faculties. Yao describes his pity for the orphan and widow; Shun answers that this is good but not great — be passive like the virtue of God, whose sun and moon shine and seasons revolve without effort. Yao cries out that he has been making a muddle: You are in accord with God; I am in accord with man.
summary.zh: 舜問於堯：天王之用心何如？堯曰：吾不敖無告，不廢窮民，嘉孺子而哀婦人。舜曰：天德而出寧——日月照而四時行，若晝夜之有經，雲行而雨施矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Of old, Shun asked Yao, saying, "How does your Majesty employ your faculties?" "I am not arrogant towards the defenceless," replied Yao. "I do not neglect the poor. I grieve for those who die. I pity the orphan. I sympathise with the widow. Beyond this, nothing." "Good indeed!" cried Shun, "but yet not great." "How so?" inquired Yao. "Be passive," said Shun, "like the virtue of God. The sun and moon shine; the four seasons revolve; day and night alternate; clouds come and rain falls." "Alas!" cried Yao, "what a muddle I have been making. You are in accord with God; I am in accord with man."
passages.zh: 古時，舜問堯說：「天子是怎樣運用自己的心力的呢？」堯回答說：「我對無依無靠的人不敢傲慢，對貧困的人不敢遺棄，為死者哀傷，憐憫孤兒，同情寡婦。除此之外，便沒有別的了。」舜說：「好極了！然而還算不上偉大。」堯問：「這是什麼意思呢？」舜說：「要順任自然，像天地的德性那樣。日月照耀，四時運行，晝夜交替，雲氣興起而雨水降下。」堯說：「唉！我真是雜亂無章啊。你與天相合，我與人相合。」

title.en: Confucius Deposits His Works with Lao Tan (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孔子西藏書於周，往見老聃（莊子）

region.en: The Chou imperial library, Luoyang (Henan, China)
region.zh: 周室藏書（今河南洛陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 13, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 13

summary.en: Going west to place his works in the Chou imperial library, Confucius is counselled to interview the retired librarian Lao Tan — who interrupts the exposition of his twelve canons with 'This is all nonsense.' Charity and duty to one's neighbour, Lao Tzŭ argues, are not part of man's original nature: universal love contradicts itself, the elimination of self is a manifestation of self; follow the Tao of the unceasing sun and moon.
summary.zh: 孔子西藏書於周室，往見老聃。老聃曰：亦取其大要而已——子所言者，其人與骨皆已朽矣。仁義，先王之蘧廬也；無私，乃私也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Confucius-and-Laozi interview topos, paralleled in Shiji 63 and the Laojun hagiography. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Confucius was going west to place his works in the Imperial library of the House of Chou, Tzŭ Lu counselled him, saying, "I have heard that a certain librarian of the Chêng department, by name Lao Tan, has resigned and retired into private life. Now as you, Sir, wish to deposit your works, it would be advisable to go and interview him." "Certainly," said Confucius; and he thereupon went to see Lao Tzŭ. The latter would not hear of the proposal; so Confucius began to expound the doctrines of his twelve canons, in order to convince Lao Tzŭ. "This is all nonsense," cried Lao Tzŭ, interrupting him. "Tell me what are your criteria." "Charity," replied Confucius, "and duty towards one's neighbour."
passages.zh: 孔子打算往西去，把自己的著作收藏在周室的國家書庫中，子路勸告他說：「我聽說鄭地有一位掌管典籍的官吏，名叫老聃，已經辭官退隱，閒居在家。如今先生您想收藏自己的著作，不如前去見見他。」孔子說：「好。」於是便去見老子。老子不肯接受這個請求；孔子便開始闡述他的十二經的學說，想以此說服老子。老子打斷他說：「這全是些空話。告訴我你的準則是什麼。」孔子回答說：「是仁和義。」

passages.text: "Tell me," said Lao Tzŭ, "in what consist charity and duty to one's neighbour?" "They consist," answered Confucius, "in a capacity for rejoicing in all things; in universal love, without the element of self. These are the characteristics of charity and duty to one's neighbour." "What stuff!" cried Lao Tzŭ. "Does not universal love contradict itself? Is not your elimination of self a positive manifestation of self?
