Sir, if you would cause the empire not to lose its source of nourishment,--there is the universe, its regularity is unceasing; there are the sun and moon, their brightness is unceasing; there are the stars, their groupings never change; there are birds and beasts, they flock together without varying; there are trees and shrubs, they grow upwards without exception, Be like these; follow TAO; and you will be perfect. Why then these vain struggles after charity and duty to one's neighbour, as though beating a drum in search of a fugitive. Alas! Sir, you have brought much confusion into the mind of man."
passages.zh: 老子說：「請告訴我，仁和義究竟是什麼？」孔子回答說：「就是能夠對萬物感到喜悅，普遍地愛一切，而不帶有自我的成分。這些便是仁和義的特徵。」老子說：「這是什麼話！普遍地愛一切，豈不是自相矛盾嗎？你排除自我，豈不正是自我的一種明顯表現嗎？先生，你若想使天下不失去其滋養的根源——有宇宙，它的規律運行不息；有日月，它們的光明照耀不息；有星辰，它們的排列從不改變；有鳥獸，它們成群結隊而不散亂；有樹木叢草，它們無一例外地向上生長。像這些一樣，遵循大道，你便會完美無缺。那麼又何必這些徒勞的掙扎去追求仁和義，好像敲著鼓去追捕逃亡的人一樣呢。唉！先生，你給人心帶來了多大的混亂啊。」

title.en: The Wheelwright and the Dregs of the Ancients (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 輪扁斲輪（莊子）

region.en: The hall of Duke Huan of Ch'i (Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 齊桓公之堂（今山東臨淄）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 13, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 13

summary.en: Duke Huan reads in his hall while a wheelwright works below; flinging down his hammer, the wheelwright tells the Duke that the words of the dead Sages are only the dregs of the ancients. Wheel-making is a mysterious art of co-ordination between mind and hand that he cannot teach even his own son — and what the ancients could not impart died with them.
summary.zh: 桓公讀書於堂上，輪扁斲輪於堂下，釋椎鑿而上：君之所讀者，古人之糟魄已夫。斲輪徐則甘而不固，疾則苦而不入；得之於手而應於心，口不能言，臣不能以喻臣之子。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Duke Huan was one day reading in his hall, when a wheelwright who was working below, flung down his hammer and chisel, and mounting the steps said, "What words may your Highness be studying?" "I am studying the words of the Sages," replied the Duke. "Are the Sages alive?" asked the wheelwright. "No," answered the Duke; "they are dead." "Then the words your Highness is studying," rejoined the wheelwright, "are only the dregs of the ancients."
passages.zh: 有一天，桓公在堂上讀書，一個在堂下做工的輪扁放下手中的椎子和鑿子，登上台階說：「請問君上讀的是些什麼話？」桓公回答說：「我讀的是聖人的話。」輪扁問：「聖人還活著嗎？」桓公回答說：「不，他們已經死了。」輪扁接著說：「那麼君上所讀的，不過是古人的糟粕罷了。」

passages.text: "Let me take an illustration," said the wheelwright, "from my own trade. In making a wheel, if you work too slowly, you can't make it firm; if you work too fast, the spokes won't fit in. You must go neither too slowly nor too fast. There must be co-ordination of mind and hand. Words cannot explain what it is, but there is some mysterious art herein. I cannot teach it to my son; nor can he learn it from me. Consequently, though seventy years of age, I am still making wheels in my old age. If the ancients, together with what they could not impart, are dead and gone, then what your Highness is studying must be the dregs."
passages.zh: 輪扁說：「請讓我用自己本行的事來打個比方。製作車輪時，如果做得太慢，就不能牢固；如果做得太快，輻條就嵌不進去。必須不快不慢。這其中必須心與手相應。箇中的奧妙無法用言語說明，但確有某種神妙的技藝在其中。我不能把它教給我的兒子，我的兒子也不能從我這裡學到它。因此，我雖然已經七十歲了，到了這把年紀還在製作車輪。如果古人和他們所不能傳授的東西都已死去消失了，那麼君上所讀的，必定只是糟粕罷了。」

title.en: Had You Called Me a Horse, I Should Have Considered Myself a Horse (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 呼我牛也而謂之牛（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's retreat (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 13, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 13

summary.en: Shih Ch'êng Ch'i walks many stages to insult the Sage Lao Tzŭ for turning his sister out of doors while rats feast on his leavings. The Sage keeps silent; the next day he answers that he makes no pretension: had you called me an ox, I should have considered myself an ox — if men class you in accordance with truth and you reject the classification, you only double the reproach.
summary.zh: 士成綺見老子而問曰：吾聞夫子聖人也……觀於其室，不見其有所謂仁義也。老子曰：吾服也恆服，吾非以服有怍——呼我牛也而謂之牛，呼我馬也而謂之馬。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Shih Ch'êng Ch'i visited Lao Tzŭ, and addressed him, saying, "Having heard, Sir, that you were a Sage, I put aside all thought of distance to come and visit you. Travelling many stages, the soles of my feet thickened, but I did not venture to rest. And now I see you are not a Sage. While rats feasted off your leavings, you turned your sister out of doors. This is not charity. Though you have no lack of food, raw and cooked, you are stingy beyond all bounds."
passages.zh: 士成綺去拜訪老子，對他說：「我聽說先生是位聖人，便不顧路途遙遠前來拜見您。走了許多天的路程，腳底磨出了厚繭，也不敢歇息。如今我看先生並不是聖人。老鼠糟蹋您剩下的食物，您卻把妹妹趕出家門。這算不上仁。您生食熟食都不缺乏，卻吝嗇到了極點。」

passages.text: At this Lao Tzŭ was silent and made no reply; and the next day Shih Ch'êng Ch'i came again and said, "Before, I was rude to you; now, I am sorry. How is this?" "I have no pretension," replied Lao Tzŭ, "to be possessed of cunning knowledge nor of divine wisdom. Had you yesterday called me an ox, I should have considered myself an ox. Had you called me a horse, I should have considered myself a horse. For if men class you in accordance with truth, and you reject the classification, you only double the reproach. My humility is natural humility. It is not humility for humility's sake."
passages.zh: 老子默然不答；次日，士成綺又來，說道：「先前我對您無禮，如今我深感慚愧。這是怎麼回事呢？」老子答道：「我並沒有自負於機巧之智，也沒有自負於神明之慧。你昨日若稱我為牛，我便自認是牛；你若稱我為馬，我便自認是馬。因為若有人依循真實來評判你，而你卻拒絕這評判，那只會使責難加倍。我的謙卑是自然的謙卑，並非為謙卑而謙卑。」

title.en: The Fisherman and the Jinni
title.zh: 漁夫與妖靈

region.en: Seashore of the unnamed city, Indian Ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 無名之城的海濱，印度洋（象徵性定位）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 1 (1885), 'The Fisherman and the Jinni'

summary.en: A fisherman casts four times and draws up a copper jar sealed with the seal of Solomon; out of it rises a jinni who has sworn to kill whoever frees him. The fisherman tricks him back into the jar by asking how so huge a body could have come out of so small a vessel — and shuts the lid. The jinni bargains, and serves; and the fisherman, who would not open the jar a second time, tells the tale of the prudent man who believes a demon only once.
summary.zh: 漁夫四拋其網，撈起銅罐，上有素萊曼之印封；罐中升起妖靈，誓言必殺釋放他的人。漁夫以『如此龐大之軀如何出自如此小罐』之問誘其復入，蓋上蓋子。妖靈講條件而效力；不肯二次開罐的漁夫，講述只信魔鬼一次的智者的故事。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale (the Nights) belonging to the jinn lore of popular Islam; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A fisherman cast his net four times and drew up, the fourth time, a copper jar sealed with the seal of Solomon the son of David; and when he opened it there came out a jinni, huge as a cloud of smoke, who said: 'Now, that I have been a hundred years in the jar and no one came to free me, I swore in my anger to kill whoever should free me. Prepare to die.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), 'The Fisherman and the Jinni'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個漁夫撒網四次，第四次拉起一隻銅罐，上面封著大衛之子所羅門的印記；他打開罐子，裡面出來一個精靈，龐大如一團煙雲，說道：「如今我在罐中已一百年，無人前來釋放我，我便在憤怒中發誓，誰釋放我，我就殺誰。準備受死吧。」

passages.text: The fisherman said, 'Before I die, tell me: how could so huge a body come out of so small a jar?' The jinni stood and shook himself, and went back into the jar in a column of smoke; and the fisherman clapped the leaden lid upon it. 'Now choose thy death.' The jinni bargained, and swore by the Great Name to serve him if he let him out; and the fisherman let him out a second time only upon the oath — and the tale is told, the fisherman says, of the man who believes a demon once and no more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 漁夫說：「在我死之前，告訴我：如此龐大的身軀怎能從如此小的罐中出來？」精靈站起來抖了抖身子，化為一柱煙回到罐中；漁夫便將鉛蓋啪地蓋上。「現在選擇你的死法吧。」精靈討價還價，並以偉大之名發誓，若放他出來便服侍他；漁夫只因這誓言才第二次放他出來——漁夫說，這故事講的正是那種只相信一次魔鬼、絕不再信第二次的人。

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, First Voyage: The Whale-Island
title.zh: 辛巴達首航：鯨島

region.en: Indian Ocean trade route, whale-backed isle (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印度洋商路，鯨背之島（象徵性定位）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The First Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: Sindbad lands with his shipmates on what they take for an island and cook their dinner on it; the island moves — it is the back of a mighty fish — and dives, and the crew are left to the sea. Sindbad alone is saved by a wooden trough of the king's, is carried to the capital, and made superintendent of the port; and he tells his tale on his return to the porter Sindbad of the city, who has groaned under his load all day.
summary.zh: 辛巴達與船友登上一座以為是島的陸地，在上面生火做飯；島動了——那是一條巨魚之背——潛入水中，船員盡落海。僅辛巴達靠木盆獲救，被帶至都城，任港口之監督；歸來時向終日負重的腳夫辛巴達講述他的故事。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: Sindbad the sailor lands with his shipmates on what they take for an island — a green place, with a spring — and cook their dinner on it; and the island moves: it is the back of a mighty fish, and it dives, and the crew are thrown into the sea. Sindbad alone keeps hold of a great wooden trough that belongs to the king's supply-boat, and is carried on it to an island of the coast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The First Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 航海家辛巴達與同船夥伴登上一處他們以為是島嶼的地方——一片青綠之地，有一道泉水——並在上面煮晚餐；那島卻動了起來：原來那是一條巨魚的背，牠潛入水中，船員們都被拋入海中。唯有辛巴達抓住一隻屬於國王補給船的大木槽，被它載到海岸邊的一座島上。

passages.text: He is found there and carried to the capital, and made superintendent of the port; and on the strand he sees his own ship come in, with her crew, and recovers his goods. He returns to Baghdad rich, and tells his tale to the porter Sindbad of the city, who has groaned under his load all day; and the two Sindbads sit together in the evening, the bearer of burdens and the bearer of stories.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在那裡被人發現，帶到都城，被任命為港務總管；他在海灘上看到自己的船載著船員駛入，便取回了自己的貨物。他富足地回到巴格達，把自己的經歷講給城裡的腳夫辛巴達聽——那腳夫整日在他的重擔下呻吟；兩個辛巴達在傍晚同坐一處，一個是背負重擔的人，一個是背負故事的人。

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, Second Voyage: The Valley of Diamonds and the Roc
title.zh: 辛巴達二次航行：鑽石谷與神鷹

region.en: Valley of diamonds, Serendib (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 楞伽島鑽石谷（象徵性定位）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The Second Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: Sindbad sleeps in a valley ringed by mountains where the diamonds lie on the bottom and the serpents keep the night watch, and merchants come to the rocks to throw down carcases for the eagles. He binds himself to a carcase, and the roc carries him up to her nest on the mountain-top, from which he comes down with a bag of diamonds and makes his way home to Baghdad.
summary.zh: 辛巴達眠於群山環繞之谷，谷底鑽石遍地，毒蛇夜巡；商人們來到崖頂拋下獸屍引鷹。他將自己縛於獸屍，神鷹將他帶上山頂的巢；他攜一袋鑽石下山，返回巴格達。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: Sindbad is left on an island and sleeps in a valley ringed by mountains, where the diamonds lie on the bottom and serpents keep the night watch. Merchants come to the mountain heights and throw down carcases of beasts, which the eagles carry up to their nests; and the diamonds cling to the meat and are brought up with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The Second Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 辛巴達被遺留在一座島上，睡在一個群山環繞的山谷裡，谷底滿是鑽石，夜間有巨蛇守衛。商人們來到山巔，拋下獸屍，鷹便將獸屍銜回巢中；鑽石黏在肉上，隨之被帶了上去。

passages.text: Sindbad binds himself to a great carcase with his turban, and the roc carries him up to her nest on the mountain-top; he fills his pockets and his turban with diamonds, and makes his way down to the merchants, and home to Baghdad with wealth beyond reckoning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 辛巴達用頭巾把自己綁在一具巨大的獸屍上，大鵬鳥便把他帶上巢中，置於山頂；他將口袋與頭巾都裝滿鑽石，然後下山來到商人們那裏，帶著無法計數的財富回到巴格達。

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, Third Voyage: The Giant of the Island
title.zh: 辛巴達三航：島上巨人

region.en: Island of the giant, eastern seas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 東海巨人島（象徵性定位）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The Third Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: Shipwrecked, Sindbad's party reaches an island castle where a giant black eats the men one by one, roasting them on spits; the survivors blind him with two red-hot spits while he sleeps, and escape by raft — pursued to the shallows by stones. The tale is told as the oldest adventure of the East, cousin of Odysseus in the cave of the Cyclops.
summary.zh: 遇難後，辛巴達一行到達一島上城堡，黑色巨人逐一捕食眾人，於火上炙烤；倖存者趁其熟睡以兩支燒紅的烤叉刺盲其目，乘筏逃走——遭其擲石追至淺灘。此乃東方最古的冒險故事，為奧德修斯於獨眼巨人洞中之親緣。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the giant episode parallels the Odyssey's Cyclops; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: Shipwrecked, Sindbad's party reaches an island castle where a giant black, tall as a palm, sits at the door; he seizes the men one by one, roasts them on spits and eats them. The survivors blind him with two red-hot spits while he sleeps, and he falls roaring down the stair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The Third Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 辛巴達一行人遭遇船難，來到一座島上的城堡，那裏有個身高如棕櫚樹的黑色巨人坐在門口；他一個接一個抓住那些人，把他們串在鐵叉上烤熟吃掉。倖存者趁他熟睡時用兩根燒紅的鐵叉弄瞎他的雙眼，他咆哮著從階梯上滾落。

passages.text: The men escape by raft and are pursued to the shallows by the stones of the giant's fellows; Sindbad alone is carried to another shore, where he is treated well by a merchant who loads him with aloes-wood for the market of Baghdad. He returns and tells the tale, and adds that every voyage cost him more than the last, and every tale was shorter than the truth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 眾人乘木筏逃走，巨人的同伴們投擲石塊，一路追到淺灘；唯有辛巴達被沖到另一處海岸，那裏有位商人善待他，為他裝載沉香，運往巴格達的市集。他歸來後講述這段經歷，並補上一句：每一次航行都比前一次令他付出更大的代價，而每一個故事都比實情來得簡短。

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, Fifth Voyage: The Old Man of the Sea
title.zh: 辛巴達五航：海上老人

region.en: Indian Ocean, isle of the sea-ape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印度洋海上老人之島（象徵性定位）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The Fifth Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: A dwarfish old man with a face like an ape leaps on Sindbad's shoulders on the island shore and will not come off; he rides him for days, beating him with his heels, and drinks the water Sindbad brings him — the Old Man of the Sea. Sindbad carries a gourd of wine to the mariners' island, makes the sea-apes drunk, and loads a ship with their goods; and the Old Man rides no more.
summary.zh: 一貌似猿猴的侏儒老者躍上辛巴達之肩，不肯離去；他騎了他數日，以足跟夾擊，飲辛巴達取來之水——此即海上老人。辛巴達攜一葫蘆酒至海猿之島，使猿群醉倒，奪船載其貨而返；海上老人再不得騎人。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the Old Man of the Sea is one of the most quoted images of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: On the island shore a dwarfish old man with a face like an ape leaps on Sindbad's shoulders and will not come off; he rides him day after day, beating him with his heels, and drinks the water Sindbad fetches him — the Old Man of the Sea. The sailor carries him to the vines and squeezes grapes into his mouth, and at last the burden lightens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The Fifth Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在島岸上，一個面容如猿的矮小老人跳上辛巴達的肩頭，怎麼也不肯下來；他日復一日騎在他身上，用腳跟踢打他，還喝辛巴達為他取來的水——這便是海老人。水手把他帶到葡萄藤旁，將葡萄擠汁送入他口中，這重擔終於減輕了。

passages.text: Sindbad carries a gourd of wine to the island of the mariners, and the sea-apes drink and sleep, and he loads their ship with the goods of the dead crew. He escapes, and the Old Man rides no more; and the tale is the best known of the voyages, the picture of every burden a man carries that will not come off his back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 辛巴達帶著一葫蘆酒來到水手們的島上，海猿喝了酒便睡去，他便把死去船員的貨物裝上他們的船。他逃脫了，海老人也不再騎在他身上；這個故事是諸次航行中最為人熟知的一則，象徵著人背負在身上、怎麼也卸不下的每一副重擔。

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, Seventh Voyage: The Last Return
title.zh: 辛巴達七航：最後的歸航

region.en: Eastern seas and Baghdad (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 東海與巴格達（象徵性定位於巴格達）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The Seventh Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: On the last voyage the ship is wrecked on a coast of monkeys and pearls, Sindbad marries into the king's house, and learns the custom of the land: the husband is buried with the dead wife. He escapes from the grave of his wife by night, and lives for a while in the city of the buried living, until a ship takes him home — and he swears never to sail again. The seven voyages close with the formula: 'And I have recounted to thee, O my brother, all that befell me.'
summary.zh: 末次航行，船於猿猴與珍珠之岸遇難；辛巴達娶入王族，得知國俗：夫與亡妻同葬。他夜間自妻墓脫逃，於埋活人之城暫居，直至一船攜他歸家——他發誓不再航行。七次航行以慣用語收結：『兄弟啊，我已向你講完我的一切遭遇。』

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the buried-alive episode parallels descent narratives; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: On the last voyage the ship is wrecked on a coast of monkeys and pearls; Sindbad marries into the king's house, and learns too late the custom of the land: the husband is buried alive in the grave of the dead wife. He lies in the grave with the corpse, and escapes at night by the light of a fire kept at the mouth of the pit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The Seventh Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在最後一次航行中，船隻在一處滿是猴子與珍珠的海岸失事；辛巴達娶了國王家族的女子，卻太遲才得知此地的習俗：丈夫要活著被埋進亡妻的墳墓。他與屍體一同躺在墓中，夜裏靠著坑口所燃火光的照明逃了出來。

passages.text: He lives for a while in the city of the buried living, and strips the graves as the others do; till a ship takes him home, and he swears never to sail again. The seven voyages close with the formula: 'And I have recounted to thee, O my brother, all that befell me' — and the two Sindbads, the bearer of burdens and the teller of tales, sit down together to the evening meal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他在那座埋葬活人的城中住了一段時日，像其他人一樣盜掘墳墓；直到一艘船載他返鄉，他發誓再也不出海航行。七次航海以這樣的話語作結：「我的兄弟啊，我已把我所遭遇的一切都講述給你了」——於是兩位辛巴達，一個是背負重擔的人，一個是講述故事的人，一同坐下來共進晚餐。

title.en: The Three Apples
title.zh: 三個蘋果

region.en: Baghdad, the Tigris bank (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴格達底格里斯河岸（實際定位）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 1 (1885), 'The Three Apples'

summary.en: A fisherman draws up a chest from the river; inside is the body of a woman cut in pieces. The caliph Harun al-Rashid commands his vizier Ja'far to find the murderer in three days. The trail runs by a husband who bought three apples for his sick wife at a dinar each, a slave who mocked the purchase, a journey of murder and a journey of repentance — and ends with the slave's own cousin confessing to save the household, and the caliph's jest: 'I had thought to punish; instead I have bought a slave.'
summary.zh: 漁夫自河中撈起一箱；內有一被肢解的女子屍體。哈里發哈倫·拉希德限宰相加法爾三日內查明兇手。線索循一位曾以每枚一金幣為病妻買三個蘋果的丈夫、一位嘲笑其購買的奴隸、一次殺人之旅與一次懺悔之旅——終於奴隸之堂兄弟為保全家而自認，哈里發戲言：『本欲懲罰，結果買下一奴。』

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the murder mystery frame is one of the earliest detective narratives in world literature; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A fisherman draws up from the Tigris a heavy chest, and inside it the body of a woman cut in pieces. The caliph Harun al-Rashid commands his vizier Ja'far to find the murderer in three days, or die in his stead. Ja'far searches Baghdad in vain; on the last day the story is found at his own door, in the household of his own household's friend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), 'The Three Apples'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名漁夫從底格里斯河中拉起一只沉重的箱子，箱中是一具被切成碎塊的女子屍體。哈里發哈倫·拉希德命其宰相賈法爾在三日之內找出兇手，否則便代其受死。賈法爾在巴格達遍尋無果；到了最後一日，這故事卻在他自家門前被尋獲，就在他自家人的友人家中。

passages.text: The tale unravels from the murderer's own telling: a husband who bought three apples for his sick wife at a dinar each; a black slave who mocked the purchase and lied that he had had her love; the journey of murder; and the journey of repentance. A cousin confesses to save the husband, and the caliph's jest closes the case: 'I had thought to punish; instead I have bought a slave.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 這故事由兇手親口講述而層層揭開：一名丈夫為生病的妻子以每顆一第納爾的價錢買了三顆蘋果；一名黑奴嘲笑這樁買賣，並謊稱自己曾得到她的愛；一段行兇的旅程；以及一段悔悟的旅程。一名堂表親為救那丈夫而認罪，哈里發的一句戲言為此案作結：「我本以為是要懲罰；結果我反倒買了一名奴隸。」

title.en: The Hunchback's Tale: The Night of Four Guilty Tellers
title.zh: 駝背者的故事：四個自認兇手的夜晚

region.en: Kashgar to Cairo, road of the cycle (symbolic pin at Kashgar)
region.zh: 喀什噶爾至開羅的循環之路（象徵性定位於喀什噶爾）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 1 (1885), 'Tale of the Hunchback'

summary.en: A hunchback jester chokes on a fishbone at a tailor's supper; every host of the night believes himself the murderer — the tailor, the Christian broker, the Muslim steward, the Jewish physician, the barber of Kashgar and his brothers. Each buys off the dawn with the best story he can tell, and the barber, the last, revives the hunchback with a trick of the trade and the bone comes out. The tale is the great example of the story-cycle: five tales hung on one corpse.
summary.zh: 駝背弄臣於裁縫家晚宴上被魚刺哽死；當夜每一位主人皆自認是兇手——裁縫、基督徒經紀、穆斯林總管、猶太醫生、喀什噶爾理髮師及其兄弟。各人以最好的故事換取天亮；末位的理髮師以行當之技救活駝背人，魚刺取出。此乃故事循環之典範：五則故事繫於一具屍首。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the multi-narrator cycle is the Nights' signature device; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A hunchback jester chokes on a fishbone at a tailor's supper, and each host of the night believes himself the murderer — the tailor, the Christian broker, the Muslim steward, the Jewish physician of the town. Each buys off the dawn with the best story he can tell, and the tales are told in turn to the governor, who spares each teller for the sake of the tale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), 'Tale of the Hunchback'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名駝背的弄臣在裁縫家的晚餐上被魚刺噎住，那一夜的每一位主人都自以為是兇手——裁縫、基督徒經紀人、穆斯林管事、城中的猶太醫生。每個人都以自己所能講出的最好的故事來換取黎明時的赦免，而這些故事輪流講給總督聽，總督便看在故事的份上饒過了每一位講述者。

passages.text: The barber of Kashgar, last of the tellers, and the talker of six brothers, is brought in; he examines the dead man, feels his gullet, and draws out the bone with the instruments of his trade — and the hunchback revives. The tale is the great example of the story-cycle: five tales hung on one corpse, and a corpse that is not dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 喀什噶爾的理髮師，最後一位講述者，也是六個兄弟的談論者，被帶了進來；他檢視那死人，摸了摸他的咽喉，用他本行的器具取出那根骨頭——於是那駝背復活了。這故事是故事套故事的最佳範例：五個故事懸於一具屍體之上，而那屍體並未死去。

title.en: Nur al-Din Ali and Anis al-Jalis
title.zh: 努爾丁·阿里與蜜糖之光

region.en: Damascus and Baghdad (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 大馬士革與巴格達（象徵性定位於巴格達）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 2 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 2 (1885), 'Nur al-Din Ali and the Damsel Anis al-Jalis'

summary.en: The vizier of Damascus, dying, charges his son to bury his books with him and marry the daughter of a Cairene wazir. Nur al-Din Ali travels to Cairo, buys the singing-girl Anis al-Jalis for a thousand gold pieces, and is waylaid on the road home; the girl is taken to Baghdad and presented to the caliph, who will not take her — for she has told him whose she is. The lovers are restored, and the tale closes with the justice of the court.
summary.zh: 大馬士革宰相臨終，囑其子以書隨葬、娶開羅大臣之女。努爾丁·阿里赴開羅，以千金購歌女蜜糖之光（阿妮斯·賈利斯），歸途遇劫；女子被解至巴格達獻給哈里發，哈里發不肯納——因她告知其所屬。有情人得復聚；故事以宮廷之公義作結。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: The vizier of Damascus, dying, charges his son to bury his books with him and to marry the daughter of a Cairene wazir, and gives him a thousand gold pieces for her purchase. Nur al-Din Ali travels to Cairo and buys the singing-girl Anis al-Jalis, the light of sweetness; and on the road home the caravan is waylaid, and the girl is carried to Baghdad and presented to the caliph.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 2 (1885), 'Nur al-Din Ali and the Damsel Anis al-Jalis'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 大馬士革的宰相臨終時囑咐兒子將他的書與他一同埋葬，並娶一位開羅宰相的女兒，又給他一千金幣作為為她贖身的費用。努爾·丁·阿里前往開羅，買下了那歌女阿尼斯·阿爾-賈利斯，即「甘美之光」；而在返鄉途中，商隊遭人攔劫，那女子被帶到巴格達，獻給了哈里發。

passages.text: The caliph will not take her, for she has told him whose she is; and the tale closes with the justice of the court: the lovers are restored, the robbers are punished, and the two houses are joined by the marriage the dying father asked for.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 2 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 哈里發不會娶她，因為她已告訴他她是誰的人；故事以法庭的公正作結：戀人重聚，強盜受罰，兩家因那垂死父親所祈求的婚事而結為一體。

title.en: Abu Kir the Dyer and Abu Sir the Barber
title.zh: 染匠阿布·基爾與理髮匠阿布·西爾

region.en: Alexandria and Istanbul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 亞歷山大與伊斯坦布爾（象徵性定位）

period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 7 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 7 (1885), 'Abu Kir the Dyer and Abu Sir the Barber'

summary.en: Two neighbours of Alexandria — a cheating dyer and a generous barber — sail together to the capital. The dyer steals the barber's purse, has him branded a thief, and rises to be royal dyer by inventing colours no one knows; the barber washes in the hammam, is taken for a lord, and cures the king's scald-head with a salve of his own making. Justice is done at last at the table of the caliph; and the barber forgives the man who branded him — once.
summary.zh: 亞歷山大的兩位鄰居——行騙的染匠與慷慨的理髮匠——同船赴都城。染匠竊理髮匠錢袋，誣其為賊，並以發明無人知的顏色而晉升御用染匠；理髮匠於浴場洗浴，被誤為貴人，以自製藥膏治癒國王頭瘡。公義最終於哈里發席前得伸；理髮匠饒恕誣其之人——一次。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: Two neighbours of Alexandria sail together to the capital: Abu Kir the dyer, a cheat, and Abu Sir the barber, a generous man. The dyer steals the barber's purse, has him branded as a thief, and rises in the world by inventing colours no dyer has ever made; the barber washes in the hammam, is taken for a lord, and cures the king's scald-head with a salve of his own making.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 7 (1885), 'Abu Kir the Dyer and Abu Sir the Barber'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 亞歷山卓的兩個鄰居一同乘船前往都城：染匠阿布·基爾，一個騙子；理髮師阿布·希爾，一個慷慨之人。染匠偷了理髮師的錢袋，使他被烙上盜賊的印記，又憑著發明出沒有哪個染匠曾造出的顏色而飛黃騰達；理髮師在澡堂沐浴，被人當作貴人，並用自己調製的藥膏治好了國王的頭癬。

passages.text: Justice is done at last at the caliph's table: the dyer is brought to account for the branding, and the barber, offered his enemy's blood, forgives him once — and the tale closes with the rule the barber keeps: forgive a man once; do not forgive him twice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 7 (1885); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 正義終於在哈里發的餐桌上得到伸張：染匠因那烙刑而被追究，理髮師被獻上仇人的血，卻寬恕了他一次——故事以理髮師所守的準則作結：寬恕一個人一次；不要寬恕他兩次。

title.en: Abu Hassan, or the Sleeper Awakened
title.zh: 阿布·哈桑：醒來的沉睡者

region.en: Baghdad, caliph's palace (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴格達哈里發宮（實際定位）

period: Arabian Nights Supplemental Nights (Arabic, medieval); R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights, public domain (Gutenberg #3446)

source.work: R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 2 (1886), 'Abu Hassan, or the Sleeper Awakened'

summary.en: A broken merchant of Baghdad sleeps in the caliph's garden; Harun al-Rashid has him woken as the Commander of the Faithful, with a throne, a court and a purse — and, at evening, has him drugged and carried back to his own poverty. He wakes and cannot believe his year of power; and when the game is played a second time, he brings his wife, and the caliph's jest becomes the marriage of the household. The tale is the ancestor of every 'dream of the throne' told in the West since.
summary.zh: 巴格達一破產商人睡於哈里發花園；哈倫·拉希德命人以『信士長官』之禮喚醒他——寶座、廷臣與錢囊俱備——黃昏再以藥物使其昏睡，送回其貧舍。他醒來不信曾有掌權之年；第二次戲局時他攜妻同行，哈里發的戲言成全了這戶人家的婚姻。此故事為西方日後所有「王座之夢」敘事的先祖。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A broken merchant of Baghdad sleeps in the caliph's garden; Harun al-Rashid has him woken as the Commander of the Faithful, with a throne, a court, a purse, and a day of reign — and at evening has him drugged and carried back to his own poverty, where he wakes among his own debts and cannot believe his year of power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 2 (1886), 'Abu Hassan, or the Sleeper Awakened'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 巴格達一個破產的商人睡在哈里發的花園裡；哈倫·拉希德命人將他喚醒，讓他做信士的長官，賜他寶座、宮廷、錢袋和一天的統治——到了傍晚又命人給他下藥，把他送回自己的貧困之中，他在自己的債務堆裡醒來，無法相信自己那一年的大權。

passages.text: When the game is played a second time he brings his wife, and the caliph's jest becomes the marriage of the household; and the tale is the ancestor of every 'dream of the throne' told in the West since — the man who has been king for a day and wakes to his old shoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 2 (1886); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 當這場遊戲第二次上演時，他帶上了自己的妻子，哈里發的戲謔便成了這一家的婚事；而這個故事正是此後西方所講述的每一個「王座之夢」的祖先——那個做了一天國王、醒來卻面對舊鞋的人。

title.en: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves
title.zh: 阿里巴巴與四十大盜

region.en: Forest of the robbers, Persia of the tale (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 故事波斯的強盜森林（象徵性定位）

period: Story of the Galland cycle (18th c., from a Syrian storyteller); Arabic and French editions; R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights, public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 3 (1886), 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves'

summary.en: A poor woodcutter sees forty horsemen open a rock with the words 'Open, Sesame' and carries home a measure of gold. His rich brother Cassim goes, forgets the word, and is cut to pieces; the thieves return to find their cave betrayed, and hunt the household; and it is the slave-girl Marjaneh who outwits them — with the boiling oil in the oil-jars and the dance of the last thief — and marries the son of the house.
summary.zh: 窮樵夫見四十騎士以『芝麻開門』啟石入洞，帶回一量器黃金。其富兄卡西姆前往，忘卻口令，被剁成碎塊；群盜返洞察覺洩密，追索全家；機智的女奴瑪爾加娜以沸油灌罐、以及最後一盜之舞識破並剷除他們，嫁與家主之子。

sensitivity.note: A tale of the Galland cycle, of Syrian storyteller origin, now part of the Nights canon worldwide; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A poor woodcutter sees forty horsemen open a rock with the words 'Open, Sesame', and carries home a measure of gold on his three asses. His rich brother Cassim goes, forgets the word, and is cut to pieces at the door; his body is carried home sewn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 3 (1886), 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一個貧窮的樵夫看見四十名騎手用「芝麻開門」這句話打開了一塊岩石，便用他的三頭驢馱了一量器黃金回家。他那富有的哥哥卡西姆去了，卻忘了那句咒語，在門口被砍成了碎塊；他的屍體被縫合起來運回家中。

passages.text: The thieves return to find their cave betrayed, and hunt the household; and it is the slave-girl Marjaneh who outwits them — she marks the doors, then marks every door alike, and in the hiding of the oil-jars she pours the boiling oil on the men hidden in them, and dances before the last of the thieves and kills him with the dagger in her girdle. She marries the son of the house, and the cave is left shut for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 3 (1886); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 盜賊們回來，發現洞穴已被人出賣，便追查那戶人家；而識破他們的是女奴瑪爾佳娜——她在門上做了記號，隨後又把每一扇門都做上同樣的記號；在藏匿油甕一事上，她將滾燙的油澆在藏身甕中的人身上，又在最後一名盜賊面前起舞，用腰帶裡的匕首將他殺死。她嫁給了這戶人家的兒子，而那洞穴從此永遠封閉。

title.en: Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp
title.zh: 阿拉丁與神燈

region.en: City in China of the tale, and the Maghreb of the sorcerer (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 故事中的中國之城與術師的馬格里布（象徵性定位）

period: Story of the Galland cycle (18th c., from a Syrian storyteller); Arabic and French editions; R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights, public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1888), 'Ala al-Din and the Magical Lamp'

summary.en: A lazy boy of the city is sent by an African sorcerer into a cave for a lamp; the boy keeps the ring, and the slave of the lamp builds him a palace overnight. The sorcerer returns, tricks the princess out of the lamp by crying 'New lamps for old!', and carries palace and bride to Maghreb; the princess drugs the sorcerer's cup, and the boy returns — and the palace is set back where it stood.
summary.zh: 城中懶童受非洲術師遣入山洞取燈；少年保住戒指，燈奴一夜為他建成宮殿。術師重返，以『新燈換舊燈』之喚騙走公主手中神燈，連宮殿與新娘一併攜往馬格里布；公主以藥下其杯，少年歸來——宮殿復歸原位。

sensitivity.note: A tale of the Galland cycle, of Syrian storyteller origin; the most retold story of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A lazy boy of the city is sent by an African sorcerer into a cave for a lamp; the boy keeps the ring, and the slave of the ring brings him home; then the lamp is rubbed, and its slave builds him a palace overnight, with a garden of jewels and a marriage to the sultan's daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 6 (1888), 'Ala al-Din and the Magical Lamp'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 城裡一個懶惰的男孩被一名非洲術士派進洞穴去取一盞燈；男孩留下了戒指，戒指的精靈把他送回家；接著他摩擦那盞燈，燈的精靈一夜之間為他建起一座宮殿，其中有寶石的花園，並讓他娶了蘇丹的女兒。

passages.text: The sorcerer returns in the dress of a lamp-seller, crying 'New lamps for old!'; the princess, who does not know the lamp's worth, gives it, and palace and bride are carried away to the Maghreb. The princess drugs the sorcerer's cup with the sleeping draught the boy brings her, and the boy returns, slays him, and has the palace set back where it stood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 6 (1888); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 術士換上燈販的裝扮回來，高喊「新燈換舊燈！」；公主不知那盞燈的價值，便把它交了出去，於是宮殿與新娘都被帶往馬格里布。公主用男孩帶給她的安眠藥摻入術士的杯中，男孩歸來，殺了他，並讓宮殿回到原處。

title.en: The Ebony Horse
title.zh: 烏木馬

region.en: Persian court and Constantinople (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波斯宮廷與君士坦丁堡（象徵性定位）

period: Arabian Nights Supplemental Nights (Arabic, medieval); R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights, public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 2 (1886), 'The Ebony Horse'

summary.en: A Persian craftsman brings to the king of Persia an ebony horse that flies wherever its rider turns the pegs. The prince rides it to the king of Constantinople's daughter, and the two are carried off into the air; the girl is stolen from the sleeping prince by a king of the islands, and the prince wanders the world in the dress of a pilgrim to find her again. The tale is the Nights' most famous story of the flying machine.
summary.zh: 波斯工匠向波斯王獻上一匹烏木馬，騎者轉動其釘即可飛行。王子乘之至君士坦丁堡王之女兒處，二人被帶上天空；女子於王子熟睡時被群島之王竊去；王子著朝聖者之衣浪跡天下尋她。此乃《夜》中最著名的飛行器故事。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the flying horse is shared with the Persian and Indian romance tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A Persian craftsman brings to the king of Persia an ebony horse that flies wherever its rider turns the pegs in its neck. The prince rides it by night to the city of the king of Constantinople, and to the daughter of that king; and the two are carried off into the air together on the horse, and alight on a roof of the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 2 (1886), 'The Ebony Horse'; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名波斯工匠向波斯國王獻上一匹烏木馬，騎者轉動馬頸上的木栓，它便飛往任何地方。王子夜間騎著它飛到君士坦丁堡國王的城中，來到那位國王的女兒身邊；兩人一同騎馬騰空而去，降落在城中的一處屋頂上。

passages.text: The girl is stolen from the sleeping prince by a king of the islands, and the prince wanders the world in the dress of a pilgrim to find her again; the tale ends with the two restored, and the ebony horse returned to its maker — for the maker was the man who wanted the kingdom, and the flying machine was the price of the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 2 (1886); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名群島之王趁王子熟睡時擄走了那女孩，王子便扮作朝聖者走遍世界，只為再找到她；故事以兩人重聚、烏木馬歸還其製作者作結——因為那製作者正是覬覦王國之人，而那飛行機器便是王位的代價。

title.en: Who Turns the Sky? The Question of the Circling Heavens (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 天其運乎？地其處乎？（莊子）

region.en: The questioning of the heavens (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 問天之辨（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 14, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 14

summary.en: The sky turns round, the earth stands still, sun and moon pursue one another — who causes this? Clouds cause rain and rain causes clouds: whose kindly bounty is this? Wind comes from the north, blowing now east, now west, whirling aloft — who puffs it forth? I should like to know the cause of all this.
summary.zh: 天其運乎？地其處乎？日月其爭於所乎？孰主張是？孰維綱是？意者其有機緘而不得已邪？雲者為雨乎？雨者為雲乎？孰隆施是？風起北方，一西一東——孰噓吸是？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); a priority Cosmology narrative — Zhuangzi's cosmological interrogation of mechanism. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "The sky turns round; the earth stands still; sun and moon pursue one another. Who causes this? Who directs this? Who has leisure enough to see that such movements continue? "Some think there is a mechanical arrangement which makes these bodies move as they do. Others think that they revolve without being able to stop.
passages.zh: 「天旋轉；地靜止；日月相互追逐。是誰使然？是誰主宰？誰又有閒暇去察看這些運動如此持續不斷？有人認為有一種機械的安排，使這些天體如此運行。另一些人則認為它們旋轉不息，無法停止。」

passages.text: "The clouds cause rain; rain causes clouds. Whose kindly bounty is this? Who has leisure enough to see that such result is achieved? "Wind comes from the north. It blows now east, now west; and now it whirls aloft. Who puffs it forth? Who has leisure enough to be flapping it this way or that? I should like to know the cause of all this."
passages.zh: 「雲致雨，雨致雲。這是誰的仁慈恩澤？誰有閒暇去看到這樣的結果得以成就？風從北方吹來。它時而向東，時而向西；時而又盤旋而上。是誰把它吹出來的？誰有閒暇去這樣那樣地搧動它？我想知道這一切的緣由。」

title.en: The Yellow Emperor Plays the Han-ch'ih in the Wilds of T'ung-t'ing (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 黃帝張咸池之樂於洞庭之野（莊子）

region.en: The wilds of the T'ung-t'ing lake (Dongting, Hunan, China)
region.zh: 洞庭之野（今湖南洞庭湖）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 14, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 14

summary.en: Hearing the Yellow Emperor play the Han-ch'ih in the wilds of T'ung-t'ing, Pei Mên Ch'êng is first afraid, then amazed, then overwhelmed. The Emperor explains the music of God: a thundering peal without beginning or end; spirits of darkness kept to their domain while sun, moon, and stars pursued their appointed course; and lastly confusion, for confusion means absence of sense, and absence of sense means TAO, and TAO means absorption therein.
summary.zh: 黃帝將張咸池之樂於洞庭之野；北門成三聞之：懼、惑、愚——樂也者，始乎懼，次乎惑，卒乎愚；愚故道，道可載而與之俱也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the mythic performance of the Xianchi music. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Pei Mên Ch'êng said to the Yellow Emperor, "When your Majesty played the Han-ch'ih in the wilds of T'ung-t'ing, the first time I heard it I was afraid, the second time I was amazed, and the last time I was confused, speechless, overwhelmed." "You are not far from the truth," replied the Yellow Emperor. "I played as a man, drawing inspiration from God. The execution was punctilious, the expression sublime.
passages.zh: 北門成對黃帝說：「當陛下在洞庭的荒野演奏《咸池》時，我第一次聽到它時感到恐懼，第二次感到驚異，最後一次感到迷惑，啞口無言，不知所措。」「你離真相不遠了，」黃帝回答說。「我演奏時如同一個人，從神那裏汲取靈感。演奏一絲不苟，表現崇高莊嚴。

passages.text: "When I played again, it was the harmony of the Yin and Yang, lighted by the glory of sun and moon; now broken, now prolonged, now gentle, now severe, in one unbroken, unfathomable volume of sound. Filling valley and gorge, stopping the ears and dominating the senses, adapting itself to the capacities of things,--the sound whirled around on all sides, with shrill note and clear. The spirits of darkness kept to their domain. Sun, moon, and stars, pursued their appointed course. When the melody was exhausted I stopped; if the melody did not stop, I went on.
passages.zh: 「當我再次演奏時，那是陰陽的和諧，被日月的光輝照亮；時而斷續，時而延長，時而柔和，時而嚴厲，匯成一片連綿不斷、深不可測的音響。充滿山谷與峽谷，堵塞耳朵、主宰感官，順應事物的容量——聲音向四面八方迴旋，時而尖銳，時而清亮。幽暗的精靈各守其域。日月星辰各循其既定軌道。旋律耗盡時我便停止；若旋律未盡，我便繼續。

passages.text: "My music first induced fear; and as a consequence, respect. I then added amazement, by which you were isolated from consciousness of your surroundings. And lastly, confusion; for confusion means absence of sense, and absence of sense means TAO, and TAO means absorption therein."
passages.zh: 「我的音樂首先引發恐懼；因而產生敬畏。然後我加入驚異，使你與周圍環境的意識隔絕。最後是迷惑；因為迷惑意味著無感，無感意味著道，道意味著沉浸其中。」

title.en: The Straw Dog and the Frowning Hsi Shih (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 芻狗與西施之顰（莊子）

region.en: The Wei court (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 衛廷（今河南安陽一帶）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 14, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 14

summary.en: The musician Shih Chin tells Yen Yüan why his master Confucius is no success: the straw dog revered before sacrifice is trampled after it — and Confucius makes his disciples sleep alongside the ancients, already offered up. Pushing a boat on land, dressing a monkey in the robes of Chou Kung, and the ugly woman who knitted her brows because Hsi Shih's frown looked beautiful — all fail because they forget that customs change with the changing season.
summary.zh: 師金曰：芻狗之未陳也，盛以篋衍，巾以文繡；及其已陳也，行者踐其首脊。夫西施病心而矉其里；其里之醜人見而美之，歸亦捧心而矉其里——彼知矉美，而不知矉之所以美。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Before the straw dog has been offered in sacrifice," replied Shih Chin, "it is kept in a box, wrapped up in an embroidered cloth, and the augur fasts before using it. But when it has once been offered up, passers-by trample over its body, and fuel-gatherers pick it up for burning. Then, if any one should take it, and again putting it in a box and wrapping it up in an embroidered cloth, watch and sleep alongside, he would not only dream, but have nightmare into the bargain.
passages.zh: 「在芻狗被獻祭之前，」師金回答說，「它被保存在箱子裏，用繡花布包裹著，占卜者在用它之前要齋戒。但一旦被獻祭之後，路人便踩踏它的身體，拾柴的人把它撿去燒火。那麼，如果有人把它拿來，再次放進箱子裏、用繡花布包裹起來，守著它、睡在它旁邊，他不僅會做夢，還會做噩夢。

passages.text: "Now your Master has been thus treating the ancients, who are like the dog which has already been offered in sacrifice. He causes his disciples to watch and sleep alongside of them. Consequently, his tree has been cut down in Sung; they will have none of him in Wei; in fact, his chances among the Shangs and the Chous are exhausted. ... For travelling by water there is nothing like a boat. For travelling by land there is nothing like a cart. ... Now ancient and modern times may be likened unto water and land; Chou and Lu to the boat and the cart. To try to make the customs of Chou succeed in Lu, is like pushing a boat on land: great trouble and no result, except certain injury to oneself."
passages.zh: 「如今你的先生就這樣對待古人，古人就像那已經被獻祭過的芻狗。他讓弟子們守著它們、睡在它們旁邊。結果，他在宋國被砍倒了樹；衛國不要他；事實上，他在商、周之間的機會已經耗盡。……走水路沒有什麼比得上船。走陸路沒有什麼比得上車。……如今古今可以比作水與陸；周與魯比作船與車。試圖讓周的制度在魯國成功，就像在陸地上推船：極大的麻煩而沒有結果，除了必然給自己帶來傷害。」

passages.text: "When Hsi Shih was distressed in mind, she knitted her brows. An ugly woman of the village, seeing how beautiful she looked, went home, and having worked herself into a fit frame of mind, knitted her brows. The result was that the rich people of the place barred up their doors and would not come out, while the poor people took their wives and children and departed elsewhere. That woman saw the beauty of knitted brows, but she did not see wherein the beauty of knitted brows lay. Alas! your Master is emphatically not a success."
passages.zh: 「西施心中憂愁時，便皺起眉頭。村中一個醜女看見她皺眉的樣子十分美麗，回家之後，也勉強做出滿懷愁緒的神情，皺起眉頭。結果，當地的富人緊閉門戶不肯出來，窮人則帶著妻兒遠走他鄉。那女子看見了皺眉之美，卻沒看見皺眉之美究竟何在。唉！你們的先生實在算不上成功。」

title.en: I Saw a Dragon: Confucius Before Lao Tzŭ (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 吾乃今於是乎見龍（莊子）

region.en: P'ei, south of Lu (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 沛地（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 14, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 14

summary.en: Confucius at fifty-one seeks the TAO of Lao Tzŭ in numbers and the Yin-Yang and fails; Lao Tzŭ tells him the TAO cannot be presented like a gift. The chaff from winnowing blinds a man's eyes, mosquitoes keep him awake all night — and this talk of charity drives me nearly crazy. Back home, Confucius does not speak for three days: I saw a Dragon — which by convergence showed a body, by radiation became colour, and riding upon the clouds of heaven nourished the two Principles of Creation.
summary.zh: 孔子行年五十有一而不聞道，乃南之沛見老聃。歸三日不談；弟子問之，曰：吾乃今於是乎見龍——合而成體，散而成章，乘雲氣而養乎陰陽。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the dragon-appearance of Laozi paralleled in Shiji 63 and the Laojun hagiography. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Confucius had lived to the age of fifty-one without hearing TAO, when he went south to P'ei, to see Lao Tzŭ. "So you have come, Sir, have you? I hear you are considered a wise man up north. Have you got TAO?" "Not yet," answered Confucius. "I sought it for five years," replied Confucius, "in the science of numbers, but did not succeed. Then I spent twelve years seeking for it in the doctrine of the Yin and Yang, also without success."
passages.zh: 孔子活到五十一歲，尚未聽聞大道，於是南行至沛，去見老子。「您來了嗎，先生？我聽說北方人都認為您是位智者。您得道了嗎？」「還沒有。」孔子答道。「我花了五年時間，」孔子回答說，「在數術之中尋求它，卻沒有成功。後來我又花了十二年，在陰陽之說中尋求它，同樣沒有成功。」

passages.text: "The chaff from winnowing will blind a man's eyes so that he cannot tell the points of the compass. Mosquitoes will keep a man awake all night with their biting. And just in the same way this talk of charity and duty to one's neighbour drives me nearly crazy. Sir! strive to keep the world to its own original simplicity. And as the wind bloweth where it listeth, so let Virtue establish itself.
passages.zh: 「簸揚時飛出的糠屑會迷住人的眼睛，使他分辨不出東南西北。蚊蟲叮咬會使人整夜不得安眠。同樣地，這些仁義兼愛之說幾乎把我逼瘋。先生啊！請努力使天下回復其本然的淳樸吧。就像風隨其所欲而吹，讓德自行確立吧。

passages.text: On returning from this visit to Lao Tzŭ, Confucius did not speak for three days. A disciple asked him, saying, "Master, when you saw Lao Tzŭ, in what direction did you admonish him?" "I saw a Dragon," replied Confucius, "--a Dragon which by convergence showed a body, by radiation became colour, and riding upon the clouds of heaven, nourished the two Principles of Creation. My mouth was agape: I could not shut it. How then do you think I was going to admonish Lao Tzŭ?"
passages.zh: 孔子這次拜訪老子歸來之後，三天沒有說話。弟子問他說：「先生，您見到老子時，是從哪方面規勸他的呢？」「我看見了一條龍，」孔子回答說，「——一條龍，收斂時顯現其身，舒張時化為色彩，乘著天上的雲氣，涵養著創化的兩儀。我張口結舌，合不攏嘴。你想我怎麼還談得上規勸老子呢？」

title.en: Tigers and Wolves Have Charity (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 虎狼，仁也（莊子）

region.en: The Sung official's hall (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋大夫之堂（今河南商丘）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 14, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 14

summary.en: T'ang, a high official of Sung, asks Chuang Tzŭ about charity. Tigers and wolves have it, answers Chuang Tzŭ — the natural love between parents and offspring. Perfect charity does not admit of love for the individual: a man who travels southwards to Ying cannot see Mount Ming in the north, because he is too far off.
summary.zh: 商太宰蕩問仁於莊子。莊子曰：虎狼，仁也——至仁無親；夫至仁者，無親而不得其分：夫子之至德無以加矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: T'ang, a high official of Sung, asked Chuang Tzŭ about charity. Chuang Tzŭ said, "Tigers and wolves have it." "How so?" asked T'ang. "The natural love between parents and offspring," replied Chuang Tzŭ,--"is not that charity?" T'ang then inquired about perfect charity. "Perfect charity," said Chuang Tzŭ, "does not admit of love for the individual."
passages.zh: 宋國的高官蕩問莊子關於仁的問題。莊子說：「虎狼就有仁。」「怎麼說呢？」蕩問。莊子回答說：「父母與子女之間天生的愛，——這不就是仁嗎？」蕩於是又問什麼是至仁。莊子說：「至仁不容有對個別人的偏愛。」

passages.text: "A man who travels southwards to Ying cannot see Mount Ming in the north. Why? Because he is too far off. "True virtue does nothing, yet it leaves Yao and Shun far behind. Its good influence extends to ten thousand generations, yet no man knoweth it to exist. What boots it then to sigh after charity and duty to one's neighbour?"
passages.zh: 「一個南行到郢的人，是看不見北方的冥山的。為什麼呢？因為他離得太遠了。「真正的德無所作為，卻把堯舜遠遠拋在後面。它的善的影響延及萬代，卻沒有人知道它的存在。那麼，嚮往仁義又有什麼用呢？」

title.en: The People of the Bench (Ahl al-Suffa)
title.zh: 長凳之人（蘇法）

region.en: Medina, the mosque porch (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 麥地那清真寺廊簷（象徵性定位）

period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877); cf. Sahih al-Bukhari narrations on Ahl al-Suffa

license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: The homeless of the first Muslim community — men of no tribe and no house in Medina — are given the shadowed bench in the mosque, the Suffa. The Prophet sits with them; the wealthier Companions send them their supper; and the tradition counts among them the men who would become the first scholars and the first saints. The bench is the first institution of the poor of Islam.
summary.zh: 首個穆斯林社團中的無家者——無部落、無麥地那居所之人——被安置於清真寺的蔭廊長凳（蘇法）。先知與之同坐；富裕聖門弟子送晚飯；傳統中不乏日後的首批學者與聖徒。此長凳乃伊斯蘭窮人制度之始。

sensitivity.note: Sira/hadith tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: The homeless of the first Muslim community were given the shadowed bench at the back of the mosque of Medina — the Suffa — where they lodged and learned; men of no house in Medina, some of them of no tribe at all. The Prophet sat with them, and the wealthier Companions sent them their supper.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 第一批穆斯林社群中的無家者，獲賜麥地那清真寺後方那處有遮蔭的長凳——即蘇法（Suffa）——他們在此棲身並學習；他們是麥地那無家之人，其中有些甚至不屬於任何部落。先知與他們同坐，較富裕的聖門弟子則送來晚餐給他們。

passages.text: The tradition counts among the People of the Bench the men who became the first scholars and saints of Islam, and the story is told of one of them who had nothing but his cloak and his patience, and of the Prophet who said: 'Whoever of my people keeps one of these men shall keep his Prophet.' The bench is the first institution of the poor of Islam, and the first school.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳統將後來成為伊斯蘭首批學者與聖徒的人，列入長凳之民（People of the Bench）之中；相傳他們當中有個人，除了斗篷與耐心之外一無所有，而先知曾說：『凡我民中收留這些人之一者，便是收留了他的先知。』這長凳是伊斯蘭窮人的第一個機構，也是第一所學校。

title.en: The First Friday Prayer
title.zh: 首次主麻拜

region.en: Valley of Ranuna, near Quba (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫巴附近拉努納谷（象徵性定位）

period: Sira material from Ibn Ishaq (d. c. 767) via Ibn Hisham; English: Muir, Life of Mahomet (1877)

source.work: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (Arabic); English: William Muir, The Life of Mahomet (Smith, Elder, 1877)

license: Public domain (English edition 1877; Arabic original 9th century)

summary.en: On the road from Quba to Medina, on a Friday, the Prophet stops in the valley of Ranuna among the Banu Salim ibn Awf and leads them in the first congregational prayer of the new rite — the prayer of the congregation (jumu'ah), with the sermon. The mosque of Friday becomes the pattern of every mosque of the empire.
summary.zh: 自庫巴至麥地那途中，值周五，先知於拉努納谷薩里姆·本·奧夫部族中，率領首次新儀的集體禮拜——主麻拜，並講道。周五清真寺成為帝國每一座清真寺的範式。

sensitivity.note: Sira tradition of a living religion; paraphrased from public-domain Arabic/English sources.

passages.text: On the road from Quba to Medina, on a Friday, the Prophet stopped in the valley of Ranuna among the Banu Salim ibn Awf, and led them in the first congregational prayer of the new rite — the prayer of the congregation (jumu'ah), with its sermon; and a hundred men were present. It was the first Friday mosque of Islam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira (Muir 1877); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在從庫巴（Quba）前往麥地那的路上，某個星期五，先知在拉努納（Ranuna）山谷、薩利姆·伊本·奧夫（Banu Salim ibn Awf）族人之中停下，帶領他們舉行了這新儀式的第一次集體禮拜——即附有講道的聚禮（jumu'ah）；當時有一百人在場。那是伊斯蘭的第一座星期五清真寺。

title.en: The Twin-Sisters: Why Cain Slew
title.zh: 雙生姊妹：該隱殺弟之因

region.en: First settlement of Adam's children (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 阿丹子女的首處聚居地（象徵性定位）

period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, c. 8th-11th centuries CE); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Qisas al-Anbiya / tafsir legends (al-Tabari, al-Kisa'i); passages paraphrased from Arabic

license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: The legend fills the motive of the first murder: Adam's children were born in twin pairs, boy and girl, and the law of the time was that each brother should marry his own twin-sister from another pair — not his own. Abel's twin was the fairer; Cain refused to take his own and demanded his brother's; Adam bade them offer a sacrifice, and the fire from heaven decided. Cain slew, and the first city was built on the first grave.
summary.zh: 傳說補足首宗謀殺之動機：阿丹子女皆為雙生——一男一女；當時之法，各兄弟當娶另一對的雙生姊妹，而非自己的。亞伯的雙生妹貌美；該隱拒娶己妹而求其弟之妹；阿丹命二人獻祭，天火定奪。該隱殺之；首座城築於首個墳墓之上。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend of a living tradition; the twin-marriage motif parallels origin-of-death and sibling clusters; paraphrased from the Arabic original; motif tagging is interpretive.

passages.text: Adam's children, the legend says, were born in twin pairs, boy and girl together; and the law of that first age was that each brother should marry his twin-sister from another pair, but not his own. Abel's twin was the fairer of the two; and Cain refused to take his own sister and demanded his brother's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 傳說稱，亞當的子女皆成雙成對地出生，一男一女同胎；而那最初時代的律法是，每個兄弟應娶另一對中的雙生姊妹，而不可娶自己的雙生姊妹。亞伯（Abel）的雙生姊妹是兩人中較美的一位；該隱（Cain）拒絕娶自己的姊妹，卻要求娶他兄弟的。

passages.text: Adam bade them settle it by an offering: each to bring a sacrifice, and the fire from heaven to take the acceptable one. The fire came down on Abel's lamb and left Cain's sheaf; and Cain said to his brother, 'I will slay thee.' And he slew him — and the legend adds that the first city of the world was built by the line of Cain on the first grave of the world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 亞當吩咐他們以獻祭來解決此事：各人帶來一份祭品，由天降之火取走蒙悅納的那一份。火降在亞伯的羔羊上，卻撇下了該隱的麥束；該隱便對他的兄弟說：『我要殺你。』於是他殺了他——而傳說還補充道，世上第一座城，是由該隱的子孫建在世上第一座墳墓之上的。

title.en: Muhammad ibn Qasim and the Conquest of Sind
title.zh: 穆罕默德·本·卡西姆與信德征服

region.en: Indus delta, Debal and Daybul (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印度河三角洲，迪巴勒（象徵性定位）

period: Event 711-713 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37 (conquest of Sind); from the Arabic Chachnama tradition

license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic-Persian originals medieval)

summary.en: A girl taken by pirates from Sind calls on the caliph from the slave-market of Baghdad — 'I am a daughter of the chiefs of Sind.' Walid sends the young general Muhammad ibn Qasim with six thousand, and the fort of Debal is taken by the stone-thrower that was carried by five hundred men; the pirates' stronghold falls, and the Indus is opened. The young general is recalled, and the tale of his recall is one of the grey anecdotes of the caliphal court.
summary.zh: 一信德女子被海盜擄至巴格達奴市，向哈里發呼救——『我是信德酋長之女。』瓦利德遣青年統帥穆罕默德·本·卡西姆率六千人，以五百人抬運的投石機攻陷迪巴勒要塞；海盜巢穴傾覆，印度河開通。青年統帥被召回；其召回之事成為哈里發宮廷灰色軼事之一。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography of the eastern conquests; the Ibn Qasim episode opens eight centuries of Muslim presence in the subcontinent; paraphrased from Muir.

passages.text: A girl taken by pirates from the coast of Sind was set in the slave-market of Baghdad, and she called on the caliph in his own hall: 'I am a daughter of the chiefs of Sind; avenge me.' Walid sent the young general Muhammad ibn Qasim with six thousand men, and the fort of Debal, the pirates' stronghold, was taken by the great stone-thrower that was carried by five hundred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Chachnama tradition via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 37; not verbatim.
passages.zh: 一名從信德（Sind）海岸被海盜擄走的女子，被置於巴格達的奴隸市場上，她在他自己的殿堂裡向哈里發呼求：『我是信德首領們的女兒；為我復仇。』瓦利德（Walid）便派遣年輕的將領穆罕默德·伊本·卡西姆（Muhammad ibn Qasim）率領六千人前往，海盜的根據地德巴爾（Debal）堡壘，遂被那具由五百人抬運的巨大投石機攻下。

passages.text: The Indus was opened to the Arabs, and the towns of the river came under tribute; and the young general was recalled in the change of caliphs, and the tale of his recall is told among the grey anecdotes of the court. The conquest of Sind opened eight centuries of Muslim presence in the subcontinent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Chachnama tradition via Muir, The Caliphate (1891); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 印度河向阿拉伯人敞開，河畔城鎮皆納貢稱臣；而這位年輕的將領卻在哈里發更替之際被召回，其被召回之事，載於宮廷那些黯淡的軼聞之中。信德的征服，開啟了穆斯林在次大陸長達八百年的存在。

title.en: Stretching Like a Bear, Craning Like a Bird (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 吹呴呼吸，熊經鳥申（莊子）

region.en: The hygienists' court (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 導引之士（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 15, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 15

summary.en: Exhaling and inhaling, getting rid of the old and assimilating the new, stretching like a bear and craning like a bird — this is but valetudinarianism, affected by professors of hygiene and those who try to preserve the body to the age of P'êng Tsu. But in health without hygiene there is oblivion absolute coupled with possession of all things.
summary.zh: 吹呴呼吸，吐故納新，熊經鳥申，為壽而已矣；此導引之士，養形之人，彭祖壽考者之所好也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the earliest textual mention of daoyin health gymnastics, the aition of the breath-practices. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Exhaling and inhaling, getting rid of the old and assimilating the new, stretching like a bear and craning like a bird,--this is but valetudinarianism, affected by professors of hygiene and those who try to preserve the body to the age of P'êng Tsu.
passages.zh: 呼氣吸氣，吐故納新，像熊一樣伸展，像鳥一樣引頸——這不過是養生卻病之術，為講究衛生之人以及那些想保全身體以活到彭祖之年的人所施行。

passages.text: But in self-esteem without self-conceit, in moral culture without charity and duty to one's neighbour, in government without rank and fame, in retirement without solitude, in health without hygiene,--there we have oblivion absolute coupled with possession of all things; an infinite calm which becomes an object to be attained by all. Such is the TAO of the universe, such is the virtue of the Sage.
passages.zh: 然而，自尊而不自誇，修養道德而不施仁義於鄰人，治理政事而不慕爵位名聲，隱居而不孤寂，保養健康而不講衛生——如此便是絕對的遺忘，同時又擁有萬物；是一種無邊的寧靜，成為人人所當達到的目標。這就是宇宙之道，這就是聖人的德。

title.en: When Death Was Unknown: Primeval Man's Perfect Tranquillity (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 至一之世：莫之為而常自然（莊子）

region.en: The world's infancy (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 世界之幼年（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 16, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 16

summary.en: Primeval man enjoyed perfect tranquillity throughout life: the Positive and Negative were peacefully united, spiritual beings gave no trouble, the four seasons followed in due order, nothing suffered any injury — and death was unknown. Then virtue declined through the reigns of Sui Jen and Fu Hsi, Shên Nung and Huang Ti, until Yao and Shun introduced government and scattered man's original integrity.
summary.zh: 至德之世：陰陽和靜，鬼神不擾，四時得節，萬物不傷，群生不夭，人雖有知，無所用之——此之謂至一。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Taoist myth of the age before death, an origin-of-death cluster analogue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Primeval man enjoyed perfect tranquillity throughout life. In his day, the Positive and Negative principles were peacefully united; spiritual beings gave no trouble; the four seasons followed in due order; nothing suffered any injury; death was unknown; men had knowledge, but no occasion to use it. This may be called perfection of unity.
passages.zh: 上古之人終其一生享有完美的寧靜。在他們的時代，陰陽二氣和平交融；神靈不擾；四時依序而至；萬物不受損傷；死亡不為人知；人有知識，卻無使用的機會。這可以稱為合一的完美。

passages.text: By and by, virtue declined. Sui Jen and Fu Hsi ruled the empire. There was still natural adaptation, but the unity was gone. A further decline in virtue. Shên Nung and Huang Ti ruled the empire. There was peace, but the natural adaptation was gone. Again virtue declined. Yao and Shun ruled the empire. Systems of government and moral reform were introduced. Man's original integrity was scattered. Goodness led him astray from TAO; his actions imperilled his virtue.
passages.zh: 漸漸地，德衰落了。遂人與伏羲治理天下。那時仍有自然的順應，但合一已失。德又進一步衰落。神農與黃帝治理天下。那時有和平，但自然的順應已失。德再度衰落。堯與舜治理天下。治國之制與道德改革相繼引入。人原初的純真被離散了。善使他偏離了道；他的行為危及了他的德。

passages.text: Thus it may be said that the world destroys TAO, and that TAO destroys the world. And the world and TAO thus mutually destroying each other, how can the men of TAO elevate the world, and how can the world elevate TAO? TAO cannot elevate the world; neither can the world elevate TAO.
passages.zh: 因此可以說，世界毀滅了道，道也毀滅了世界。而世界與道如此互相毀滅，有道之人又怎能提升世界，世界又怎能提升道呢？道不能提升世界；世界也不能提升道。

title.en: The River Spirit and the Spirit of the North Sea (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 河伯與北海若（莊子）

region.en: The mouth of the Yellow River into the eastern sea (symbolic pin: Dongying, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 黃河入海處（象徵定位：山東東營）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: In the autumn floods every stream pours into the Yellow River, whose spirit laughs for joy that all the beauty of the earth is gathered to himself — until, travelling east to the ocean, he sees no limit to its waves. The Spirit of the Ocean tells him you cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog or of ice to a summer insect, and that the Four Seas are but puddles in the marsh of the universe.
summary.zh: 秋水時至，百川灌河；河伯欣然自喜，以天下之美為盡在己——順流而東行，至於北海，望洋向若而嘆。北海若曰：井蛙不可以語於海，夏蟲不可以語於冰。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the most famous of all Zhuangzi's mythic dialogues, between river-god and sea-god. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: It was the time of autumn floods. Every stream poured into the river, which swelled in its turbid course. The banks receded so far from one another that it was impossible to tell a cow from a horse. Then the Spirit of the River laughed for joy that all the beauty of the earth was gathered to himself. Down with the stream he journeyed east, until he reached the ocean. There, looking eastwards and seeing no limit to its waves, his countenance changed. And as he gazed over the expanse, he sighed and said to the Spirit of the Ocean, "A vulgar proverb says that he who has heard but part of the truth thinks no one equal to himself. And such a one am I."
passages.zh: 正當秋汛之時，百川灌注於黃河，河水暴漲，濁流滾滾。兩岸相距甚遠，遠得連牛馬都分辨不清。於是河伯欣然自喜，以為天下之美盡歸於己。他順流東行，直到抵達大海。到了那裡，向東望去，只見波濤無邊無際，於是神色大變。他望著那浩瀚的汪洋，喟然嘆息，對北海若說：「俗話說：聽聞了一點道理的人，便以為沒有人比得上自己。我就是這樣的人。」

passages.text: To which the Spirit of the Ocean replied, "You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,--the creature of a narrower sphere. You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,--the creature of a season. You cannot speak of TAO to a pedagogue: his scope is too restricted. But now that you have emerged from your narrow sphere and have seen the great ocean, you know your own insignificance, and I can speak to you of great principles.
passages.zh: 北海若回答說：「你不能對井底之蛙談論大海——牠是侷限於更狹小天地裡的生物。你不能對夏蟲談論冰雪——牠是侷限於一季的生物。你不能對迂腐的教書先生談論道：他的眼界太狹隘了。但如今你已走出你那狹小的天地，看見了浩瀚的大海，知道了自己的渺小，我才能同你談論大道。」

passages.text: "There is no body of water beneath the canopy of heaven which is greater than ocean. All streams pour into it without cease, yet it does not overflow. It is constantly being drained off, yet it is never empty. Spring and autumn bring no change; floods and droughts are equally unknown. And thus it is immeasurably superior to mere rivers and brooks,--though I would not venture to boast on this account, for I get my shape from the universe, my vital power from the Yin and Yang. In the universe I am but as a small stone or a small tree on a vast mountain. And conscious thus of my own insignificance, what is there of which I can boast?"
passages.zh: 「天下沒有比海更大的水體。百川不停地灌注其中，它卻從不滿溢。它不斷地被排洩，卻從不枯竭。春秋更迭不使它有所改變；水旱之災對它同樣無所影響。因此它遠勝於尋常的江河溪流——然而我也不敢以此自誇，因為我的形體來自天地，我的元氣來自陰陽。在天地之間，我不過如大山之上的一塊小石、一株小樹。既然自知如此渺小，還有什麼可誇耀的呢？」

passages.text: "The Four Seas,--are they not to the universe but like puddles in a marsh? The Middle Kingdom,--is it not to the surrounding ocean like a tare-seed in a granary? Of all the myriad created things, man is but one. And of all those who inhabit the land, live on the fruit of the earth, and move about in cart and boat, an individual man is but one. Is not he, as compared with all creation, but as the tip of a hair upon a horse's skin?"
passages.zh: 「四海——相對於天地，豈不就像沼澤中的小水窪嗎？中原之地——相對於環繞的大海，豈不就像糧倉裡的一粒小米嗎？在萬物之中，人不過是其中之一。而在所有居住於大地、以大地所產為食、乘車船往來的人之中，一個人不過是其中之一。他與萬物相比，豈不就像馬身上的一根毛的末端嗎？」

title.en: The One-Legged Walrus, the Centipede, the Snake, and the Wind (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 夔憐蚿，蚿憐蛇（莊子）

region.en: The creatures' colloquy (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 群物相語（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: The walrus envies the centipede; the centipede envies the snake; the snake envies the wind; the wind envies the eye; the eye envies the mind. Each explains its natural mechanism: the centipede works naturally like ejected saliva, the snake's mechanism is not a thing to be changed, and the wind can break huge trees and destroy large buildings though any one who can point at it excels it.
summary.zh: 夔憐蚿，蚿憐蛇，蛇憐風，風憐目，目憐心。夔謂蚿曰：吾以一足趻踔而行；蚿曰：天機之動，不知其然而也。蛇曰：夫天機之所動，何可易邪？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The walrus said to the centipede, "I hop about on one leg, but not very successfully. How do you manage all these legs you have?" "I don't manage them," replied the centipede. "Have you never seen saliva? When it is ejected, the big drops are the size of pearls, the small ones like mist. They fall promiscuously on the ground and cannot be counted. And so it is that my mechanism works naturally, without my being conscious of the fact."
passages.zh: 海若對蚿說：「我用一隻腳跳著走，卻走得不怎麼好。你這麼多腳，是怎麼支配它們的？」蚿回答說：「我並不支配它們。你沒見過唾沫嗎？噴出來的時候，大的像珠子，小的像霧。它們紛紛落在這地上，多得數不清。我的機理也是這樣自然而然地運作，我自己並不自覺。」

passages.text: The centipede said to the snake, "With all my legs I do not move as fast as you with none. How is that?" "One's natural mechanism," replied the snake, "is not a thing to be changed. What need have I for legs?" The snake said to the wind, "I can manage to wriggle along, but I have a form. Now you come blustering down from the north sea to bluster away to the south sea, and you seem to be without form. How is that?" "'Tis true," replied the wind, "that I bluster as you say; but any one who can point at me or kick at me, excels me. On the other hand, I can break huge trees and destroy large buildings. That is my strong point. Out of all the small things in which I do not excel I make one great one in which I do excel. And to excel in great things is given only to the Sages."
passages.zh: 蚿對蛇說：「我用這麼多腳，卻不如你沒有腳走得快。這是為什麼？」蛇回答說：「順任天然的機理，這不是可以改變的事。我要腳做什麼呢？」蛇對風說：「我能蜿蜒而行，但我有形體。如今你從北海呼嘯而來，又呼嘯著奔向南海，好像沒有形體。這是為什麼？」風回答說：「不錯，我正如你所說的那樣呼嘯；但凡是能指我、踢我的人，都勝過我。另一方面，我能折斷大樹、摧毀高樓。這正是我的長處。我從所有我不擅長的細小事物中，成就出一件我所擅長的大事。而擅長於大事，只有聖人才能做到。」

title.en: Confucius Encircled at K'uang Sings to His Guitar (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孔子遊於匡，弦歌不惙（莊子）

region.en: K'uang (Kuangyi, Wei State; symbolic pin: Changyuan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 匡地（衛國匡邑；象徵定位：河南長垣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: Mistaken for the fugitive Yang Hu, Confucius is closely surrounded by the men of Wei — yet goes on playing and singing to his guitar. To know that failure is fate and that success is opportunity, and to remain fearless in great danger: this is the courage of the Sage. My destiny is cut out for me.
summary.zh: 孔子遊於匡，衛人圍之數匝，而弦歌不惙。子路入見曰：何夫子之娛也？孔子曰：知窮之有命，知通之有時，臨大難而不懼者，聖人之勇也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Confucius visited K'uang, the men of Sung surrounded him closely. Yet he went on playing and singing to his guitar without ceasing. "How is it, Sir," enquired Tzŭ Lu, "that you are so cheerful?" "Come here," replied Confucius, "and I will tell you. For a long time I have been struggling against failure, but in vain. Fate is against me. For a long time I have been seeking success, but in vain. The hour has not come.
passages.zh: 孔子行經匡地，宋人將他團團圍住。然而他仍舊彈琴歌唱，不曾停歇。「先生，」子路問道，「您為何如此怡然自得？」「過來，」孔子答道，「我告訴你。長久以來，我一直與困厄相爭，卻徒勞無功。這是命啊。長久以來，我一直求取通達，卻徒勞無功。時機尚未到來。

passages.text: "To travel by water and not avoid sea-serpents and dragons,--this is the courage of the fisherman. To travel by land and not avoid the rhinoceros and the tiger,--this is the courage of hunters. When bright blades cross, to look on death as on life,--this is the courage of the hero. To know that failure is fate and that success is opportunity, and to remain fearless in great danger,--this is the courage of the Sage. Yu! rest in this. My destiny is cut out for me." Shortly afterwards, the captain of the troops came in and apologised, saying, "We thought you were Yang Hu; consequently we surrounded you. We find we have made a mistake." Whereupon he again apologised and retired.
passages.zh: 「行於水上而不避蛟龍，這是漁夫之勇。行於陸上而不避犀牛與猛虎，這是獵人之勇。白刃相交，視死如生，這是勇士之勇。知道困厄是命數、通達是時機，身處大難之中仍無所畏懼，這是聖人之勇。由啊！安於此吧。我的命運早已註定。」不久之後，領兵的將官進來謝罪，說道：「我們以為您是陽虎，因此將您圍住。如今發覺是我們弄錯了。」於是再次謝罪而退去。

title.en: The Frog in the Well and the Turtle of the Eastern Sea (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 埳井之蛙與東海之鱉（莊子）

region.en: The well-frog's domain (symbolic pin: Handan, Hebei, China)
region.zh: 埳井之蛙（象徵定位：河北邯鄲）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: The frog of the broken well invites the turtle of the eastern sea to visit his kingdom of rail, broken brick, mud, and unmatched tadpoles; the turtle's legs stick fast at the rim. A thousand li would not measure the sea's breadth; nine years of flood did not add to its bulk, seven years of drought did not narrow its span. The well-frog was considerably astonished, and knew not what to say next.
summary.zh: 埳井之蛙謂東海之鱉曰：吾樂與！出則跳梁乎井幹之上，入則休乎缺甃之崖；且夫擅一壑之水，而跨跱埳井之樂，此亦至矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); tagged flood for the Great Yü nine-floods line (interpretive). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "Have you never heard of the frog in the old well?--The frog said to the turtle of the eastern sea, 'Happy indeed am I! I hop on to the rail around the well. I rest in the hollow of some broken brick. Swimming, I gather the water under my arms and shut my mouth. I plunge into the mud, burying my feet and toes; and not one of the cockles, crabs, or tadpoles I see around me are my match. Why do you not come, Sir, and pay me a visit?'
passages.zh: 「你難道不曾聽說過那口古井裡的青蛙嗎？——青蛙對東海的巨龜說：『我真是快樂啊！我一躍便跳上井欄，歇息於破磚的凹洞之中。游水時，水托著我的兩腋，我閉住嘴巴。我躍入泥中，埋沒了雙腳與腳趾；而我四周所見的蛤蜊、螃蟹與蝌蚪，沒有一個比得上我。先生，您何不來我這裡一遊呢？』

passages.text: Now the turtle of the eastern sea had not got its left leg down ere its right had already stuck fast, so it shrank back and begged to be excused. It then described the sea, saying, 'A thousand li would not measure its breadth, nor a thousand fathoms its depth. In the days of the Great Yü, there were nine years of flood out of ten; but this did not add to its bulk. In the days of T'ang, there were seven years out of eight of drought; but this did not narrow its span. Not to be affected by duration of time, not to be affected by volume of water,--such is the great happiness of the eastern sea.' At this the well-frog was considerably astonished, and knew not what to say next.
passages.zh: 然而東海的巨龜左腳還未踏下，右腳便已卡住，於是它退了回來，婉言推辭。接著它描述大海，說道：『千里不足以量其廣，千仞不足以測其深。大禹之時，十年之中有九年洪水，卻不曾使海水增多。商湯之時，八年之中有七年大旱，卻不曾使海水減少。不為時間的長短所影響，不為水量的多寡所影響——這便是東海的大快樂。』井蛙聽罷，大為驚愕，不知接下來該說什麼才好。

title.en: The Sacred Tortoise Dead Three Thousand Years (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 楚之神龜，曳尾於塗中（莊子）

region.en: The river P'u in Ch'u (symbolic pin: Fuyang, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 濮水之濱（象徵定位：安徽阜陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: Fishing in the P'u, Chuang Tzŭ is offered the administration of the Ch'u State by two high officials. Without turning his head he asks whether the sacred tortoise dead three thousand years in its temple chest would rather be dead and venerated, or alive and wagging its tail in the mud — and sends them off: I too will wag my tail in the mud.
summary.zh: 莊子釣於濮水，楚王使大夫二人往先焉。莊子曰：吾聞楚有神龜，死已三千歲矣，王巾笥而藏之廟堂之上——寧其生而曳尾於塗中乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); tagged oracle-divination for the sacred tortoise-shell cult (interpretive). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ was fishing in the P'u when the prince of Ch'u sent two high officials to ask him to take charge of the administration of the Ch'u State. Chuang Tzŭ went on fishing, and without turning his head said, "I have heard that in Ch'u there is a sacred tortoise which has been dead now some three thousand years. And that the prince keeps this tortoise carefully enclosed in a chest on the altar of his ancestral temple. Now would this tortoise rather be dead and have its remains venerated, or be alive and wagging its tail in the mud?" "It would rather be alive," replied the two officials, "and wagging its tail in the mud." "Begone!" cried Chuang Tzŭ. "I too will wag my tail in the mud."
passages.zh: 莊子在濮水邊釣魚，楚王派了兩位高官前去，請他出任楚國的政事。莊子繼續釣魚，頭也不回地說：「我聽說楚國有一隻神龜，死去至今已有三千年了。楚王將這隻龜小心翼翼地盛在匣中，供奉於宗廟的祭壇之上。那麼，這隻龜寧願死去而讓它的遺骸受人尊崇，還是寧願活著而在泥中搖曳尾巴呢？」「它寧願活著，」兩位官員答道，「在泥中搖曳尾巴。」「去吧！」莊子喊道，「我也要在泥中搖曳我的尾巴。」

title.en: The Phœnix and the Owl's Rotten Rat (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 鵷鶵與鴟得腐鼠（莊子）

region.en: The Liang court (Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 梁廷（今河南開封）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: Hui Tzŭ, prime minister of Liang, fears that Chuang Tzŭ has come to take his place and hunts the state for three days and nights. Chuang Tzŭ answers with the yüan-ch'u phoenix that flies from the south sea to the north sea, alighting only on the wu-t'ung tree, eating only bamboo fruit, drinking only purest spring water — and the owl with a rotten rat's carcass who screeches at it as it passes. Are you not screeching at me over your kingdom of Liang?
summary.zh: 惠子相梁，莊子往見之；惠子恐，搜於國中三日三夜。莊子往見之曰：南方有鳥，其名為鵷鶵——非梧桐不止，非練實不食，非醴泉不飲。於是鴟得腐鼠，嚇之！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Hui Tzŭ was prime minister in the Liang State. Chuang Tzŭ went thither to visit him. Some one remarked, "Chuang Tzŭ has come. He wants to be minister in your place." Thereupon Hui Tzŭ was afraid, and searched all over the State for three days and three nights to find him.
passages.zh: 惠子在梁國做宰相。莊子前往那裡拜訪他。有人說道：「莊子來了。他想取代你的相位。」於是惠子心生恐懼，在國中遍尋他三天三夜。

passages.text: Then Chuang Tzŭ went to see Hui Tzŭ, and said, "In the south there is a bird. It is a kind of phœnix. Do you know it? It started from the south sea to fly to the north sea. Except on the wu-t'ung tree, it would not alight. It would eat nothing but the fruit of the bamboo, drink nothing but the purest spring water. An owl which had got the rotten carcass of a rat, looked up as the phœnix flew by, and screeched. Are you not screeching at me over your kingdom of Liang?"
passages.zh: 於是莊子去見惠子，說道：「南方有一種鳥，是鳳凰一類的。你知道嗎？牠從南海出發，飛往北海，不是梧桐樹不棲息，不是竹子的果實不吃，不是最潔淨的泉水不喝。有一隻貓頭鷹得到一隻腐爛的老鼠，抬頭看見鳳凰飛過，便發出怒叫。你莫非是為了你的梁國而向我怒叫嗎？」

title.en: The Pleasure of Fishes on the Hao Bridge (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 濠梁觀魚（莊子）

region.en: The bridge over the Hao river (Bengbu, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 濠水之梁（今安徽蚌埠）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 17, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 17

summary.en: Strolling on the bridge over the Hao, Chuang Tzŭ observes how the minnows dart about — that is the pleasure of fishes. Hui Tzŭ objects that he is not a fish; the dialectic goes back and forth until Chuang Tzŭ concludes: your very question shows that you knew I knew — I knew it from my own feelings on this bridge.
summary.zh: 莊子與惠子遊於濠梁之上。莊子曰：儵魚出遊從容，是魚之樂也。惠子曰：子非魚，安知魚之樂？莊子曰：我知之濠上也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ and Hui Tzŭ had strolled on to the bridge over the Hao, when the former observed, "See how the minnows are darting about! That is the pleasure of fishes." "You not being a fish yourself," said Hui Tzŭ, "how can you possibly know in what consists the pleasure of fishes?" "And you not being I," retorted Chuang Tzŭ, "how can you know that I do not know?"
