passages.text: But the fish (sea-calves) when they saw the lightning and fire, were killed, and swam dead upon the surface of the water, and a cloud of fire surrounded Thecla; so that as the beasts could not come near her, so the people could not see her nakedness. Yet they turned other wild beasts upon her; upon which they made a very mournful outcry; and some of them scattered spikenard, others cassia, others amomus... so that the quantity of ointment was large, in proportion to the number of people; and upon this all the beasts lay as though they had been fast asleep, and did not touch Thecla.
passages.zh: 但那些魚（海豹）一看見閃電與火，便被擊殺，死後浮在水面上；又有火雲環繞著特克拉；因此野獸既不能靠近她，眾人也看不見她的赤裸。然而他們又放出別的野獸來攻擊她；於是那些野獸發出極其悲鳴的叫聲；其中有些散佈甘松，有些散佈肉桂，有些散佈阿摩木……因此膏油的數量甚多，與人數相稱；於是所有的野獸都躺臥下來，彷彿熟睡了一般，並不觸碰特克拉。

passages.text: Then they put a cord round Thecla's waist, which bound also her feet, and with it tied her to the bulls, to whose privy-parts they applied red-hot irons, that so they being the more tormented, might more violently drag Thecla about, till they had killed her. The bulls accordingly tore about, making a most hideous noise; but the flame which was about Thecla, burnt off the cords which were fastened to the members of the bulls, and she stood in the middle of the stage, as unconcerned as if she had not been bound.
passages.zh: 於是他們把繩索繞在特克拉的腰間，這繩也捆住她的雙腳，又用這繩把她綁在公牛身上，並在公牛的私處烙上燒紅的鐵器，好叫牠們因受更多折磨，便更猛烈地拖拉特克拉，直到把她弄死。公牛果然狂奔亂竄，發出極其可怖的聲響；但環繞特克拉的火焰燒斷了繫在公牛身上的繩索，她便站在競技場中央，安然自若，彷彿從未被捆綁過一般。

title.en: Go and Teach the Word of the Lord
title.zh: 去把主的道傳開

region.en: Antioch to Iconium and Seleucia
region.zh: 安提阿至以哥念與西流基

period: Acts of Paul and Thecla, c. 180 CE (Wake trans., Hone, 1820)

source.work: The Forbidden Gospels and Epistles: Acts of Paul and Thecla, chap. 25 (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

license: Public domain (Wake translation, 18th c., ed. Hone 1820)

summary.en: Freed at last, Thecla finds Paul in Myra — 'I have been baptized, O Paul; for he who assists you in preaching, has assisted me to baptize' — and reports all that befell her in Antioch. Then she speaks her commission and receives the apostle's blessing: 'I am going to Iconium. Paul replied to her: Go and teach the word of the Lord.' She returns to preach at Iconium and withdraws to Seleucia, where a rock opens to receive her — the legend behind the great Thecla shrine at Maaloula and Selucia.
summary.zh: 終於獲釋的特格拉在密拉尋見保羅——「保羅啊，我已受洗；那協助你講道的，也協助了我受洗」——並述說在安提阿的一切。隨後她宣明己志：「我要往以哥念去。」保羅答：「去把主的道傳開。」她重返以哥念傳道，退居西流基，岩石裂開接納了她——敘利亞馬魯拉與西流基大聖堂傳說的本源。

sensitivity.note: Apocryphal; Thecla remains venerated (equal-to-the-apostles) in Eastern Orthodox and Maronite memory.

passages.text: Which when Thecla perceived, she said to him: I have been baptized, O Paul; for he who assists you in preaching, has assisted me to baptize. Then Paul took her, and led her to the house of Hermes; and Thecla related to Paul all that had befallen her in Antioch, insomuch that Paul exceedingly wondered, and all who heard were confirmed in the faith.
passages.zh: 特克拉察覺此事，便對他說：保羅啊，我已經受洗了；因為那協助你傳道的那一位，也協助我受了洗。於是保羅帶著她，領她到赫耳墨斯的家去；特克拉便把她在安提阿所遭遇的一切都告訴了保羅，以致保羅大為驚奇，凡聽見的人也都堅固了信仰。

passages.text: Then Thecla arose, and said to Paul, I am going to Iconium. Paul replied to her: Go and teach the word of the Lord. So Thecla went to Iconium. And when she came to the house of Onesiphorus, she fell down upon the floor where Paul had sat and preached, and, mixing tears with her prayers, she praised and glorified God: O Lord the God of this house, in which I was first enlightened by thee; O Jesus, son of the living God, who wast my helper before the governor, my helper in the fire, and my helper among the beasts; thou alone art God for ever and ever, Amen.
passages.zh: 於是特克拉起身，對保羅說：我要往以哥念去。保羅回答她說：去吧，傳講主的話。特克拉便往以哥念去了。她來到阿尼西母的家，就俯伏在保羅曾坐著講道的地上，淚水混著祈禱，讚美並榮耀神說：主啊，這家的神，我起初在你裡面得蒙光照；耶穌啊，永生神的兒子，你曾在總督面前幫助我，在火中幫助我，在野獸中間幫助我；惟獨你是神，直到永永遠遠，阿們。

title.en: The King of Glory at the Gates of Hell
title.zh: 榮耀之王在陰間之門

region.en: Hell's brass gates (vision-setting)
region.zh: 陰間黃銅之門（異象之境）

period: Gospel of Nicodemus, c. 4th-5th century CE (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

source.work: The Forbidden Gospels and Epistles: The Gospel of Nicodemus (formerly the Acts of Pontius Pilate), chaps. 16-17 (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

license: Public domain (Wake translation, 18th c., ed. Hone 1820)

summary.en: The descent into hell as Christian epic: a voice of thunder cries 'Lift up your gates, O ye princes... and the King of Glory shall come in'; David and Isaiah testify from among the dead; the prince of hell bars his brass gates 'with iron bars, and fight courageously, lest we be taken captives' — and the mighty Lord 'appeared in the form of a man, and enlightened those places which had ever before been in darkness. And broke asunder the fetters which before could not be broken.' The West's most quoted underworld scene, behind the Apostles' Creed's 'descended into hell' and the Paschal icons of Eastern Christianity.
summary.zh: 基督教史詩式的冥界下行：雷聲般呼喊「眾君侯啊，抬起你們的門……榮耀之王將要進來」；大衛與以賽亞在死者中作證；陰間君侯以鐵閂緊閃黃銅門「奮勇抵抗，免得我們被擄」——然而大能的主「以人的形像顯現，照亮了歷來的黑暗之地，掙斷了從前掙不斷的鎖鏈」。西方使徒信經「降在陰間」與東方復活節聖像的文本根源。

sensitivity.note: Apocryphal but theologically formative; the 'harrowing of hell' is one of the tradition's great underworld narratives, central to Paschal liturgy in the East.

passages.text: AND while Satan and the Prince of hell were discoursing thus to each other, on a sudden there was a voice as of thunder, and the rushing of winds, saying, Lift up your gates, O ye princes; and be ye lift up, O everlasting gates, and the King of Glory shall come in. When the prince of hell heard this, he said to Satan, Depart from me, and begone out of my habitations; if thou art a powerful warrior, fight with the King of Glory. And the prince said to his impious officers, Shut the brass gates of cruelty, and make them fast with iron bars, and fight courageously, lest we be taken captives.
passages.zh: 正當撒但與地獄之王如此彼此談論的時候，忽然有聲音如雷，又如疾風呼嘯，說：眾城門哪，抬起頭來；永久的門戶啊，你們要被舉起，榮耀的王將要進來。地獄之王聽見這話，就對撒但說：離開我，從我的居所出去吧；你若是強有力的勇士，就去與榮耀的王爭戰。那王又對他那些不敬虔的臣屬說：關上那殘酷的銅門，用鐵閂閂緊，勇敢爭戰，免得我們被擄去。

passages.text: But when all the company of the saints heard this they spake with a loud voice of anger to the prince of hell, Open thy gates, that the King of Glory may come in. And the divine prophet David cried out, saying, Did not I, when on earth, truly prophesy and say... For he hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder. After this, another prophet, namely, holy Isaiah, spake in like manner to all the saints, The dead men shall live, and they shall rise again who are in their graves. And I said in another place, O grave, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?
passages.zh: 但眾聖徒的會眾聽見這話，就怒聲向地獄之王大聲說：打開你的城門，讓榮耀的王進來。神聖的先知大衛也高聲呼喊說：我在世上的時候，豈不是曾真實地預言說……因為他打碎了銅門，砍斷了鐵閂。此後，另一位先知，就是聖以賽亞，也照樣對眾聖徒說：死人要復活，在墳墓裡的也要起來。我又在別處說：墳墓啊，你的得勝在哪裡？死亡啊，你的毒刺在哪裡？

passages.text: Then was there a great voice, as of the sound of thunder, saying, Lift up your gates, O princes; and be ye lifted up, ye gates of hell, and the King of Glory will enter in. The prince of hell perceiving the same voice repeated, cried out, as though he had been ignorant, Who is that King of Glory? David replied to the prince of hell... the Lord strong and powerful, the Lord mighty in battle: he is the King of Glory, and he is the Lord in heaven and in earth. And now, thou filthy and stinking prince of hell, open thy gates, that the King of Glory may enter in; for he is the Lord of heaven and earth. While David was saying this, the mighty Lord appeared in the form of a man, and enlightened those places which had ever before been in darkness. And broke asunder the fetters which before could not be broken.
passages.zh: 於是有一個大聲音，如同雷聲，說：眾君王啊，抬起你們的門來；地獄的門啊，你們要被舉起，榮耀的王將要進來。地獄的君王聽見這聲音一再重複，便彷彿一無所知地喊叫說：那榮耀的王是誰？大衛回答地獄的君王說……有力有能的耶和華，在爭戰中有大能的耶和華：他就是榮耀的王，他是天上地上的主。如今，你這污穢發臭的地獄君王，打開你的門，讓榮耀的王進來；因為他是天地的主。大衛正說這話的時候，有大能的主以人的形像顯現，照亮了那些向來黑暗的地方。又打斷了從前不能打斷的鎖鏈。

title.en: Come to Me, All Ye My Saints: Adam Led Up
title.zh: 凡我聖徒都到我這裏來：亞當被領上來

region.en: Depths of hell to Paradise
region.zh: 陰間深處至樂園

period: Gospel of Nicodemus, c. 4th-5th century CE (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

source.work: The Forbidden Gospels and Epistles: The Gospel of Nicodemus, chap. 19 (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

license: Public domain (Wake translation, 18th c., ed. Hone 1820)

summary.en: The second Adam reverses the first: 'Jesus stretched forth his hand, and said, Come to me, all ye my saints, who were created in my image, who were condemned by the tree of the forbidden fruit... Live now by the wood of my cross.' The Lord lays hold of Adam's hand, Adam sings the psalm 'O Lord thou hast brought up my soul from the grave', and 'taking hold of Adam by his right hand, he ascended from hell, and all the saints of God followed him' — David singing a new song behind. The classic image of the harrowing, Christ's hand in Adam's wrist, painted from the Easter icon westward.
summary.zh: 末後的亞當逆轉首先的亞當：「耶穌伸手說，凡我的聖徒，按我形像受造、因那棵禁果樹被定罪的，都到我這裏來……如今靠我十字架的木頭得以存活。」主握住亞當的手；亞當唱詩「主啊，你曾把我的靈魂從陰間救上來」；主「握住亞當右手，從陰間升上去，神的眾聖徒跟隨其後」——大衛在後高唱新歌。這「拉住亞當手腕」的經典畫面，自東方復活節聖像傳遍西方。

sensitivity.note: Apocryphal; the Adam-led-up image is the tradition's emblem of reversal of the fall (recapitulation).

passages.text: THEN Jesus stretched forth his hand, and said, Come to me, all ye my saints, who were created in my image, who were condemned by the tree of the forbidden fruit, and by the devil and death; Live now by the wood of my cross; the devil, the prince of this world, is overcome, and death is conquered. Then presently all the saints were joined together under the hand of the most high God; and the Lord Jesus laid hold on Adam's hand, and said to him, Peace be to thee, and all thy righteous posterity, which is mine.
passages.zh: 於是耶穌伸出手來，說：凡照我形像受造、因禁果之樹並因魔鬼與死亡而被定罪的眾聖徒，都到我這裡來；如今你們要因我十字架的木材而活；這世界的君王魔鬼已被制伏，死亡已被勝過。隨後，眾聖徒立刻在至高神的手下聚集聯合；主耶穌握住亞當的手，對他說：願你平安，也願你一切公義的後裔平安，他們都是屬我的。

passages.text: Then Adam, casting himself at the feet of Jesus, addressed himself to him with tears, in humble language, and a loud voice, saying, I will extol thee, O Lord, for thou hast lifted me up, and hast not made my foes to rejoice over me. O Lord my God, I cried unto thee, and thou hast healed me. O Lord thou hast brought up my soul from the grave; thou hast kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit.
passages.zh: 於是亞當俯伏在耶穌腳前，流著淚，用謙卑的言語、高聲對他說：耶和華啊，我要尊崇你，因為你曾提拔我，不叫仇敵向我誇耀。耶和華我的神啊，我曾呼求你，你醫治了我。耶和華啊，你曾把我的靈魂從陰間救上來；你保全我的性命，使我不至於下坑。

passages.text: O Lord, as thou hast put the ensigns of thy glory in heaven, and hast set up the sign of thy redemption, even thy cross on earth; so, Lord, set the sign of the victory of thy cross in hell, that death may have dominion no longer. Then the Lord stretching forth his hand, made the sign of the cross upon Adam, and upon all his saints. And taking hold of Adam by his right hand, he ascended from hell, and all the saints of God followed him. Then the royal prophet, David, boldly cried, and said, O sing unto the Lord a new song, for he hath done marvellous things; his right hand and his holy arm have gotten him the victory.
passages.zh: 主啊，正如你已將你榮耀的旗幟安置在天上，又在地上立起你救贖的記號，就是你的十字架；所以，主啊，也求你在地獄中設立你十字架得勝的記號，使死亡不再掌權。於是主伸出手來，在亞當和眾聖徒身上劃了十字架的記號。他又握住亞當的右手，從地獄升上去，神所有的聖徒都跟隨他。於是那君王般的先知大衛勇敢地高聲呼喊說：你們要向耶和華唱新歌，因為他行了奇妙的事；他的右手和他的聖臂為他取得了勝利。

title.en: The Letter of Abgar of Edessa
title.zh: 伊得撒王阿布加爾書信

region.en: Edessa, kingdom of Osrhoene
region.zh: 伊得撒城，奧斯若恩王國

period: Correspondence tradition, c. 4th-5th century CE (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

source.work: The Forbidden Gospels and Epistles: The Epistles of Jesus Christ and Abgarus King of Edessa, chaps. 1-2 (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

license: Public domain (Wake translation, 18th c., ed. Hone 1820)

summary.en: The sick king Abgar writes to Jesus: 'either that you are God himself descended from heaven... or the Son of God... My city is indeed small, but neat, and large enough for us both.' Jesus answers — 'Abgarus, you are happy, forasmuch as you have believed on me, whom you have not seen' — promising after his ascension to send a disciple who will cure him. Eusebius cites the letters; Edessa became the tradition's first royal Christian city, and the portrait-promise of the exchange seeded the Image of Edessa legends.
summary.zh: 患病的阿布加爾王寫信給耶穌：「或者你自己就是從天上降下的神……或者你是神的兒子……我的城雖小，卻整潔，足以容你與我。」耶穌回信道：「阿布加爾，你因未見而信，便是有福的」——應許升天後差門徒醫治。優西比烏引此書信；伊得撒遂為傳統首座基督徒王城，畫像之諾亦播下「伊得撒聖像」傳說的種子。

sensitivity.note: Legendary correspondence cited by Eusebius (Hist. Eccl. I.13); formative for Edessa's Christian royal legend.

passages.text: ABGARUS, king of Edessa, to Jesus the good Saviour, who appears at Jerusalem, greeting. I have been informed concerning you and your cures, which are performed without the use of medicines and herbs. For it is reported, that you cause the blind to see, the lame to walk, do both cleanse lepers, and cast out unclean spirits and devils, and restore them to health who have been long diseased; and raiseth up the dead. All which when I heard, I was persuaded of one of these two, namely, either that you are God himself descended from heaven; who do these things, or the Son of God. On this account therefore I have written to you, earnestly to desire you would take the trouble of a journey hither, and cure a disease which I am under. My city is indeed small, but neat, and large enough for us both.
passages.zh: 以德薩王押巴魯，致書於在耶路撒冷顯現的良善救主耶穌，問安。我已聽聞關於你和你所行醫治的事，這些醫治不用藥物和草藥。因為據說，你使瞎子看見，瘸子行走，又潔淨痲瘋病人，趕出污鬼和魔鬼，使久病的人恢復健康；並且使死人復活。我聽見這一切之後，便確信二者之一，就是：你要麼是從天降下、行這些事的上帝本身，要麼是上帝的兒子。因此我寫信給你，懇切地盼望你勞駕前來此地一行，醫治我所患的疾病。我的城雖小，卻整潔，也足以容納我們二人。

passages.text: ABGARUS, you are happy, forasmuch as you have believed on me, whom you have not seen. For it is written concerning me, that those who have seen me should not believe on me, that they who have not seen might believe and live. As to that part of your letter, which relates to my giving you a visit, I must inform you, that I must fulfil all the ends of my mission in this country, and after that be received up again to him who sent me. But after my ascension I will send one of my disciples, who will cure your disease, and give life to you, and all that are with you.
passages.zh: 押巴魯，你有福了，因為你雖未見我，卻已信了我。因為關於我經上記著說：那些看見我的人不當信我，好叫那些沒有看見的人可以相信而得生命。至於你信中提及我前去拜訪你的那部分，我必須告訴你：我必須在本國完成我使命的一切事，然後再被接升到差我來的那裡去。但我升天之後，將差遣我的一個門徒去，他必醫治你的病，並賜生命給你，以及一切與你同在的人。

title.en: Hermas Rebuked by the Heavenly Lady
title.zh: 天婦責備黑馬

region.en: Vision-place by the river Tyber, Rome
region.zh: 羅馬，台伯河邊異象之境

period: Shepherd of Hermas, Visions I-II, c. 90-140 CE (Wake trans., Hone, 1820)

source.work: The Forbidden Gospels and Epistles: The Shepherd of Hermas, Visions 1-2 (trans. Wake, in Hone, 1820)

license: Public domain (Wake translation, 18th c., ed. Hone 1820)

summary.en: Nearly canonical in some early lists, Hermas the former slave sees the woman he once coveted 'saluting me from heaven' with an accusation: 'the desire of naughtiness has risen up in thy heart... as for those who think wickedly in their hearts, they take to themselves death and captivity.' A later vision shows the church as an aged lady 'because she was created first of all', her chair of white wool, and a book of revelations she bids him copy — the Shepherd's visions became Rome's beloved manual of penitence.
summary.zh: 在某些早期正典目錄中近於正典的黑馬書：曾為奴的黑馬見昔日暗戀的婦人「從天上向我問安」並責備他：「淫念已在你心中興起……心中思想惡事的人，是自取死亡與捆鎖。」後續異象中，教會顯為「因先被造而顯老」的婦人，坐白羊毛之椅，授書命他抄錄——這位「牧者」的異象成為羅馬教會悔改生活的最愛讀本。

sensitivity.note: Apocryphal-but-beloved (Muratorian fragment debate); presented as early Christian vision literature.

passages.text: HE who had bred me up sold a certain young maid at Rome; whom when I saw many years after, I remembered her, and began to love her as a sister. It happened some time afterwards, that I saw her washing in the river Tyber; and I reached out my hand unto her, and brought her out of the river. And when I saw her I thought with myself, saying, How happy should I be if I had such a wife, both for beauty and manners. This I thought with myself; nor did I think any thing more.

And as I was praying, the heaven was opened, and I saw the woman which I had coveted, saluting me from heaven, and saying, Hermas, hail! and I looking upon her, answered, Lady, what dost thou do here? She answered me, I am taken up hither to accuse thee of sin before the Lord. God who dwelleth in heaven, and hath made all things out of nothing, and hath multiplied them for his holy church's sake, is angry with thee because thou hast sinned against me.

Then she, smiling upon me, said: the desire of naughtiness has risen up in thy heart. Does it not seem to thee to be an ill thing for a righteous man to have an evil desire rise up in his heart. It is indeed a sin, and that a very great sin, to such a one; for a righteous man thinketh that which is righteous. And whilst he does so, and walketh uprightly, he shall have the Lord in heaven favourable unto him in all his business. But as for those who think wickedly in their hearts, they take to themselves death and captivity.

title.en: The Secret Sayings of the Living Jesus
title.zh: 活著的耶穌之隱語

region.en: Nag Hammadi library find-spot, Upper Egypt (text)
region.zh: 上埃及拿戈瑪第文庫出土地（文本）

period: Gospel of Thomas, sayings tradition, c. 50-140 CE; Coptic MS c. 350 CE (Berlin Working Group trans., 1972; paraphrase)

source.work: Gospel of Thomas, prologue and logia 1-5 (sayings-gospel; paraphrased)

license: Paraphrase of the Coptic text tradition (public-domain basis); not verbatim

summary.en: A sayings gospel without narrative: 'These are the secret sayings which the living Jesus spoke, and Didymos Judas Thomas wrote down.' Whoever finds the interpretation of the sayings 'will not taste death'; the seeker is told to seek and not stop until found — and when found, troubled, then amazed, and to 'reign over the All.' The Thomas tradition's founding frame: salvation as interpretation.
summary.zh: 一部無敘事的語錄福音：「這些是活著的耶穌所說、迪迪摩斯·猶大·多馬記下的隱語。」找到解釋的人「必不嘗死味」；尋求者被囑「不可停止尋找，直到找著」——找著便憂傷，再驚異，並要「統管萬有」。多馬傳統的開篇框架：救恩即是解經。

sensitivity.note: Gnostic-adjacent sayings gospel; included as comparative text of the early Jesus movement, not endorsed as canonical.

passages.text: The opening frame: these are the hidden words that the living Jesus uttered, which Judas, who is also called Thomas, wrote down. Whoever discovers what the words mean will not taste death. The first saying turns the searcher inward: let one who seeks not cease from seeking until he finds, and when he finds he shall be troubled, and when he is troubled he shall marvel, and shall be king over all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, prologue and logia 1-2 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2; Berlin Working Group trans. 1972); not verbatim.

passages.text: Jesus answers the question of who may enter the kingdom: if those who lead you say the kingdom is in the sky, the birds will get there first; if they say it is in the sea, the fish will get there first — rather the kingdom is inside you and outside you, and when you know yourselves you will be known, and you will understand that you are children of the living Father. But if you do not know yourselves, you dwell in poverty, and you are that poverty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logia 3 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.

passages.text: The aged fisherman's image: a wise fisherman casts his net into the sea and draws up a full net of small fish, among which he finds one fine large fish — and throws all the small fish back into the sea without regret. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear. Thomas's version keeps the one-souls motif the Synoptics frame as a net that does not break.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logia 8 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.

title.en: Three Words: Jesus Takes Thomas Aside
title.zh: 三個字：耶穌領多馬到一旁

region.en: Sayings-dialogue setting (text)
region.zh: 對話語錄場景（文本）

period: Gospel of Thomas, sayings tradition, c. 50-140 CE; Coptic MS c. 350 CE (Berlin Working Group trans., 1972; paraphrase)

source.work: Gospel of Thomas, logia 13-14 (paraphrased)

license: Paraphrase of the Coptic text tradition (public-domain basis); not verbatim

summary.en: The disciples ask what Jesus is like; he compares them to the leaders of the world, from infants to the powerful — but takes Thomas aside and gives him three words. Asked to name them, Thomas answers that were he to tell them, bystanders would pick up stones to throw at him and fire would come from the stones to burn them up. Jesus renames him: 'you are no longer my disciple; you have become like me... I am not your master, because you have drunk, you have become intoxicated from the bubbling spring which I have measured out.'
summary.zh: 門徒問耶穌像誰；他將他們比作世上掌權者——自嬰孩到掌權者——卻領多馬到一旁，給他三個字。多馬若說出來，旁人必拾石投擲，石中亦必出火燒人。耶穌遂為他改名：「你不是我的門徒，你已像我……我不是你的師傅，因為你已喝了，你已從我量出的涌泉裏喝得陶醉。」

sensitivity.note: Gnostic-adjacent; the Thomas-elevation dialogue is the sayings gospel's charter scene.

passages.text: The disciples ask Jesus: who are you, that we should follow you? He compares them to men in the street who know neither where they are going nor who the masters are — and compares them, at one point, to infants and to the great ones of the world. Then he takes Thomas apart and speaks three words to him alone. When Thomas is asked to set them down in the world, he hesitates, saying that if he were to tell them, those who hear would take up stones to cast at him, and fire would come out of the stones and burn them up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logion 13 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.

passages.text: Jesus gives Thomas the hidden name: you are no longer my disciple, you have become like me, for you have drunk, you have become intoxicated from the bubbling spring that I have measured out. And whoever drinks from my mouth will become like me, and I myself will become that person, and the hidden things will be disclosed. The saying grounds the community's authority in Thomas's unique intimacy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logion 13, closing (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.

title.en: When You Make the Two Into One
title.zh: 當你使二成為一

region.en: Sayings collection (text)
region.zh: 語錄集（文本）

period: Gospel of Thomas, sayings tradition, c. 50-140 CE; Coptic MS c. 350 CE (Berlin Working Group trans., 1972; paraphrase)

source.work: Gospel of Thomas, logia 22 and 37 (paraphrased)

license: Paraphrase of the Coptic text tradition (public-domain basis); not verbatim

summary.en: The nursing infants at the master's feet: 'when will the new world come?' — 'when you make the two into one, and when you make the inner as the outer and the outer as the inner, and the above as the below... then you shall enter the kingdom.' Asked when he will appear, Jesus says he will not appear — his kin are those who wash off their garments and 'tread under foot the garments of shame, as little children.'
summary.zh: 在師傅腳前的乳養嬰孩：「新世界何時來到？」——「當你使二成為一，使內如外、外如內，上如下……那時你將進入神的國。」又問「你何時向我們顯現？」耶穌答「我不顯現」——他的親屬是那脫去衣裳、把羞恥的衣裳踏在腳下如小孩子的人。

sensitivity.note: Gnostic-adjacent; the androgyny-reunion motif is a gnostic baptism image; presented comparatively.

passages.text: Little children are brought, those who are being nursed, and the disciples ask what the kingdom resembles. Jesus answers: the nurslings who suck are like those who enter the kingdom — and expands: when you make the two into one, and make the inner as the outer and the outer as the inner, and the upper as the lower; and when you make male and female into a single one, so that the male is not male and the female not female; when you make eyes in place of an eye, a hand in place of a hand, a foot in place of a foot, an image in place of an image; then you shall enter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logion 22 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.

passages.text: The disciples ask: when will you appear to us, and when shall we see you? Jesus answers that he does not appear as he is — his kin are those who hear his word and accept it for themselves; they shall see him. And again: when they strip without shame and tread their garments under their feet, as little children, they shall see the son of the living one and shall not fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logia 37 and related (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.

title.en: I Am the Light: The Splinter and the Beam
title.zh: 我是光：梁木與刺

region.en: Sayings collection (text)
region.zh: 語錄集（文本）

period: Gospel of Thomas, sayings tradition, c. 50-140 CE; Coptic MS c. 350 CE (Berlin Working Group trans., 1972; paraphrase)

source.work: Gospel of Thomas, logia 26, 77, 113 (paraphrased)

license: Paraphrase of the Coptic text tradition (public-domain basis); not verbatim

summary.en: The splinter-and-beam saying in its Coptic form: 'you see the splinter in your brother's eye but do not see the beam in your own eye' — cast the beam out of your own eye and then you will see clearly. And the great identity saying that closes and opens the collection: 'I am the light that is over all things. I am all: from me all came forth, and to me all extends. Split a piece of wood; I am there. Lift up the stone, and you will find me there.'
summary.zh: 多馬本「梁木與刺」：「你看得見弟兄眼中的刺，卻看不見自己眼中的梁木」——先除去你眼中的梁木，才看得清楚。以及首尾呼應的大認同語：「我是普照萬物之光。我是萬有：萬有自我而出，萬有歸我而止。劈開一塊木頭，我在那裏；舉起一塊石頭，你在那裏找到我。」

sensitivity.note: Gnostic-adjacent; the panentheist identity saying (77) is the collection's most quoted text.

passages.text: You see the splinter that is in your brother's eye, but you do not see the beam that is in your own eye. When you cast the beam out of your own eye, then you will see clearly to cast the splinter out of your brother's eye. The saying keeps the proverb's force while trimming the Synoptic frame: the eye of judgment is the obstruction of vision.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logion 26 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.

passages.text: Jesus says: I am the light that is over all things. I am all: from me all came forth, and to me all extends. Split a piece of wood; I am there. Lift up the stone, and you will find me there. The saying's scattering-through-creation grounds the collection's closing claim that the kingdom is spread upon the earth, and people do not see it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logion 77 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.

title.en: Peter and Mary at the Collection's End
title.zh: 語錄之末：彼得與馬利亞

region.en: Sayings collection (text)
region.zh: 語錄集（文本）

period: Gospel of Thomas, sayings tradition, c. 50-140 CE; Coptic MS c. 350 CE (Berlin Working Group trans., 1972; paraphrase)

source.work: Gospel of Thomas, logia 114 (paraphrased)

license: Paraphrase of the Coptic text tradition (public-domain basis); not verbatim

summary.en: The collection closes with the gendered rivalry scene: Simon Peter objects, 'let Mary leave us, for women are not worthy of life.' Jesus answers, 'I myself shall lead her, in order to make her male, so that she too may become a living spirit resembling you males' — 'every woman who will make herself male will enter the kingdom of heaven.' One of the tradition's most-debated texts on women, quoted as the closing image of the sayings community.
summary.zh: 語錄以性別之爭收尾：西門彼得說「讓馬利亞離開我們吧，女人不配得生命」。耶穌答「我要親自引導她，使她成為男性，好叫她也成為與你們男性相像的活靈」——「凡使自己成為男性的女人，都必進入天國。」這是傳統關於女性最具爭議的文本之一，作為語錄群體的收尾意象而載。

sensitivity.note: Gnostic-adjacent; the 'become male' language reflects ancient ascetic spirit-flesh symbolism and is presented with that historical framing, not endorsed.

passages.text: Simon Peter says to them: let Mary leave us, for women are not worthy of life. Jesus answers: I myself shall lead her, in order to make her male, so that she too may become a living spirit resembling you males. For every woman who will make herself male will enter the kingdom of heaven. The final logion thus reopens, at the very end, the dispute over who counts as the community's bearer of life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logion 114 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 西門彼得對他們說：讓馬利亞離開我們吧，因為女人不配得生命。耶穌回答說：我將親自引導她，使她成為男子，好讓她也能成為一個活著的靈，與你們這些男子相像。因為凡使自己成為男子的女人，都將進入天國。這最後一則語錄，於全篇之末，重新開啟了關於誰才算作團體之生命承載者的爭論。

passages.text: In the same closing register stands the rivalry saying over who Jesus loves: the disciples' question about the beloved and Peter's privileging claims are answered by turning status inside out — whoever comes to know the father and the mother will be called the child of a whore, but shall be the son of the king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logion 105-107 range (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 在同一收尾的語調中，還有那則關於耶穌愛誰的爭競之言：門徒們關於那蒙愛者的提問，以及彼得自居優先的主張，皆以顛倒身份來作答——凡認識父與母的，將被稱為娼妓之子，卻要成為君王之子。

title.en: The Kingdom Is Spread Upon the Earth
title.zh: 國已鋪展於大地

region.en: Sayings collection (text)
region.zh: 語錄集（文本）

period: Gospel of Thomas, sayings tradition, c. 50-140 CE; Coptic MS c. 350 CE (Berlin Working Group trans., 1972; paraphrase)

source.work: Gospel of Thomas, logia 51-52, 109 (paraphrased)

license: Paraphrase of the Coptic text tradition (public-domain basis); not verbatim

summary.en: Asked about the new world's rest, Jesus answers, 'what you look forward to has already come, but you do not recognize it.' Asked by the disciples about the old age's end, he answers with the twenty-four prophets who spoke in Israel and 'all of them looked in upon you' — 'you search the scriptures, because you think you have eternal life in them; but it is they that testify of me.' And the treasure in the field the owner unknowingly plows: the buyer finds the treasure and lends money at interest to everyone.
summary.zh: 問及新世界的安息，耶穌答「你們所期待的那位早已來到，只是你們不認識他」。門徒問舊世代何時終結，他以以色列二十四位先知作答——「他們都到你們這裏來過」——「你們查考聖經，以為其中有永生；其實它們正是為我作見證。」又有田中藏寶之喻：地主耕田而不知，購得者尋著寶藏，便放債給眾人。

sensitivity.note: Gnostic-adjacent; the realized-eschatology logia are the collection's counterpoint to apocalyptic expectation.

passages.text: His disciples ask him: when will the repose of the dead come, and when will the new world come? He answers: what you look forward to has already come, but you do not recognize it. The disciples then ask about the end of the old age, and he answers with the twenty-four prophets who spoke in Israel and looked in upon them — and warns that they search the scriptures thinking to find life in them, while the living one stands in their midst and they do not know him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logia 51-52 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 他的門徒問他：死者的安息何時到來？新世界何時到來？他回答說：你們所盼望的已經來了，只是你們認不出它。門徒接著問舊世代的終結，他便以那二十四位在以色列中說話、並察看他們的先知作答——又警告說，他們查考聖經，以為在其中能尋得生命，然而那活著的卻站在他們中間，他們卻不認識他。

passages.text: The kingdom is like a man who had a hidden treasure in his field, unknown to him; and after he died he left it to his son, and the son knew nothing of it either. He took the field and sold it, and the buyer went plowing, found the treasure, and began to lend money at interest to whomever he wished. The unknowing inheritance and the discovered treasure frame the collection's imagery of finding without seeking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gospel of Thomas, logion 109 (Coptic Nag Hammadi II.2); not verbatim.
passages.zh: 天國好比一個人，他的田裡藏著寶貝，他卻不知道；他死後把它留給兒子，兒子也一無所知。他接過那塊田，把它賣了；買主去耕地，發現了寶貝，便開始隨心所欲地把錢借給人取利。這不知情的繼承與被發現的寶貝，構成了這部集子中「不尋而遇」的意象。

title.en: Dante in the Dark Wood: The She-Wolves of Mid-Life
title.zh: 但丁入幽暗森林：中年的三猛獸

region.en: Dark wood beneath a sunlit hill, the dream-journey
region.zh: 向陽山下的幽暗森林，夢遊之境

period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 1, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 1

summary.en: Lost in the middle of life, Dante meets the three beasts — the spotted leopard of lust, the lion of pride, the gaunt she-wolf of avarice that 'makes the mountains tremble' — and the shade of Virgil, sent by Beatrice, who offers the guided passage through Hell and Purgatory to the stars. The Comedy's frame-poem: everyman's mid-life crisis turned into the West's master-journey of the soul.
summary.zh: 人生中途迷途的但丁遇三獸——斑斕的豹、雄獅、以及「令群山顫抖」的瘦母狼——並遇奉貝雅特麗齊之命而來的維吉爾之影，允諾引其穿越地獄與煉獄，直至繁星。全詩框架由此立定：常人的中年危機化作西方靈魂之旅的總綱。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary-religious imagination (not scripture); presented as comparative underworld-journey narrative.

passages.text: In the midway of this our mortal life, I found me in a gloomy wood, astray gone from the path direct: and e'en to tell it were no easy task, how savage wild that forest, how robust and rough its growth, which to remember only, my dismay renews, in bitterness not far from death. But when a mountain's foot I reach'd, where clos'd the valley, that had pierc'd my heart with dread, I look'd aloft, and saw his shoulders broad already vested with that planet's beam, who leads all wanderers safe through every way.
passages.zh: 在我們這凡俗生命的半途，我發現自己身處一片幽暗的林中，迷失了正路：而即便述說，也非易事——那森林何等荒蠻，其生長何等茁壯粗糲；單是回想，便令我驚惶復萌，其苦澀幾近於死。但當我抵達一座山腳，那曾以恐懼刺透我心的山谷在此終止，我舉目仰望，見那山肩寬闊，已披上那顆行星的光輝——它引領一切迷途者安然走過各樣道路。

passages.text: My weary frame after short pause recomforted, I again took the road, and left the steep, plucking the sloping brake with foremost foot, till at a hole in the valley I arriv'd whose dreadful thrills would render vain my verse. And poison'd without humour of a god, my good Virgil with gentle accents moved me to the view, and bade me behold the three that came in sight: the spotted panther, the lion that did make my flesh to tremble, and the famish'd she-wolf, that of all losses most appals the man who wins.
passages.zh: 我疲憊的身軀稍作歇息便重得慰藉，我又踏上路途，離開那陡坡，以最前的一隻腳攀折著斜生的灌木，直到我來到山谷中的一處窟窿，其可怖的震顫將使我的詩句徒然無力。而我那善良的維吉爾，被神明的氣息所感，以溫和的語調打動我，引我觀看，命我注視那映入眼簾的三者：那斑斕的豹，那令我肌膚顫抖的獅子，以及那飢餓的母狼——在一切損失之中，最令得勝之人驚恐的便是牠。

passages.text: Then the courteous spirit answered me: Thou shalt not make thy passage without me; for the road I take is round about the mountain that bars thee from the shining height of thy dear home. And I: What needeth me to go? And he: Thou shalt indeed go, and yet not of thyself; for thou art one whose path is held in fee by him, who by his wisdom shall be thy guide through every place thou hast to see. The she-wolf makes the mountains tremble; and the man whom thou must follow by long experience, till he place thee in the sight of her, whose beauty hath such power, that she shall be thine aidance through the darkest and most rugged path.
passages.zh: 於是那有禮的幽靈回答我：你不可沒有我便走你的路；因為我所行的道路，是繞過那座山的，那山阻擋你，使你到不了你親愛家園的光明高處。我便說：我為何必須前往？他答道：你固然必須前往，卻不是憑你自己；因為你是那種人，其路途由他所掌管，他將憑他的智慧作你的嚮導，領你走過你必須觀看的每一處地方。那母狼使群山顫抖；而你必須憑長久的經驗跟隨那人，直到他把你置於她的眼前，她的美貌有如此的力量，她將在最为幽暗、最為崎嶇的路上作你的援助。

title.en: The Gate of Hell and the Souls That Lived Without Disgrace and Without Praise
title.zh: 地獄之門與「無譽無辱」的靈魂

region.en: Hell's gate, fore-courts of the abyss
region.zh: 地獄之門，深淵前庭

period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 3, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 3

summary.en: The gate's inscription — 'Through me you pass into the city of woe... All hope abandon ye who enter here' — opens the Comedy's most feared geography. Beyond it wail the wretched neutrals, 'who lived without disgrace and without praise', mixed with the angels that sided neither with God nor Satan in the rebellion, following a banner that never stops: 'let us not speak of them, but look, and pass on.' At Acheron, Charon the demon boatman threatens the living passenger who will not ride in the dark bark.
summary.zh: 門上銘文——「由我這裏，直通悲慘之城……入此門者，當捨棄一切希望」——開啟全詩最可怖的地域。門內哀號者是被斥為「一生無譽亦無辱」的騎牆者，與叛天時既不從神亦不從撒但的天使同列，追隨一面永不停歇的旗幟——「莫談他們，且看且行」。阿刻戎河上，惡鬼船夫卡戎恐嚇不肯乘上黑舟的活客。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary-religious imagination; the gate inscription is among the West's most quoted lines.

passages.text: Through me you pass into the city of woe: through me you pass into eternal pain: through me among the people lost for aye. Justice the founder of my fabric mov'd: to rear me was the task of power divine, supremest wisdom, and primeval love. Before me things create were none, save things eternal, and eternal I endure. All hope abandon ye who enter here.
passages.zh: 經由我，你們進入苦難之城：經由我，你們進入永恆的痛苦：經由我，你們進入永遠沉淪的人群之中。正義推動了我的建造者：為使我矗立，乃是神聖的力量、至高的智慧與太初的愛之任務。在我之前，除了永恆之物，別無受造之物；而我也永恆長存。凡進入此處者，當捨棄一切希望。

passages.text: Then I look'd round me and beheld, on each side of me, extended in long array, a troop of souls, that seem'd without all hope. With straining eyes, we then gaz'd on a bough which never should have left its parent stem; and, from amid that multitude, innumerable, who had not part in glory, 'let us not speak of them, but look, and pass on,' thus spake my master, 'without disgrace and without praise they lived.'
passages.zh: 於是我環顧四周，見我兩旁，排成長長的隊列，伸展著一群靈魂，似乎全無希望。我們隨即以緊繃的目光，凝視一根本不該離開其母幹的樹枝；而在那群不可勝數、與榮耀無分的人眾之中，「我們不必談論他們，只須觀看，然後走過，」我的導師如此說道，「他們活著，既無恥辱，也無讚譽。」

passages.text: And now the foul boat skimming the bank at last approaches, with a ghastly demon, a ferryman, Who all asunder tore me from their griefs: And bore me to the bark, and cried to the gathered souls: 'Go where the rest, eternal and for evermore, await your doom.' And like to autumn leaves, that one by one fall and are still, upon the bosom of the stream the guilty seeds of Adam's race, that once were told of, now departing, wait upon the sign, and fall one after other in the stream, as little birds at winter's season rush to land, all on their migration bent, when they must cross.
passages.zh: 如今那污穢的船掠過河岸，終於靠近了，船上有一個猙獰的惡魔，一個擺渡者，他把我從他們的悲苦中全然分開：並把我帶上船，向聚集的靈魂喊道：「去吧，到其餘的人那裡，永恆地、永遠地等候你們的命運。」如同秋葉，一片接一片落下，靜止於溪流的水面上，亞當族類那些有罪的種子，先前曾被提及的，如今離去，等候那徵兆，一個接一個落入溪流，如同小鳥在冬季時節奔向陸地，全都一心嚮往遷徙，當牠們必須飛越之時。

title.en: Limbo: The Great Souls Who Served Not God Aright
title.zh: 靈薄獄：未曾正確事奉神的偉大靈魂

region.en: First circle of Hell
region.zh: 地獄第一圈

period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 4, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 4

summary.en: No torment but eternal sighing 'not caus'd by tortures, but from grief felt by those multitudes' — the unbaptized of every age, where Virgil himself dwells: 'For these defects, and for no other evil, we are lost; only so far afflicted, that we live desiring without hope.' Dante meets Homer, Horace, Ovid, and Lucan, the philosophers, and the towered noble castle of the great souls of antiquity, amid whom he is a sixth amid so much worth.
summary.zh: 此處無刑罰，只有永遠的歎息——「非因折磨，乃因悲傷」——即歷代未受洗者之群，維吉爾本人亦在其中：「因這些缺失，而非別的罪惡，我們滅亡；所受的苦，只是無望而活著渴想。」但丁在此遇荷馬、賀拉斯、奧維德與盧坎，並入先賢名哲的高貴城堡，置身「如此多英靈之中，我居第六位」。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; Limbo (limbus patrum/infantium) is a contested doctrine Dante crystallizes.

passages.text: Here, as mine ear could note, no plaint was heard except of sighs, that made th' eternal air tremble, not caus'd by tortures, but from grief felt by those multitudes, many and vast, of men, women, and infants. Then to me the gentle guide: Inquir'st thou not what spirits are these, which thou beholdest? Ere thou pass farther, I would thou know, that these of sin were blameless; and if aught they merited, it profits not, since baptism was not theirs, the portal to thy faith. If they before the Gospel liv'd, they serv'd not God aright; and among such am I.
passages.zh: 在此，就我耳朵所能察覺，除了嘆息之外，聽不到任何哀號，那嘆息使永恆的空氣顫動，並非由折磨所致，而是出於那些眾多而廣大的人群——男人、女人和嬰孩——所感受的悲傷。於是我那溫和的嚮導對我說：你豈不問這些你所看見的靈魂是誰嗎？在你更往前去之前，我願你知道，這些人在罪上是無可指責的；而他們若有何功德，也無益處，因為他們沒有洗禮，那是你信仰的門戶。他們若生活在福音之前，便未曾正確地事奉神；而我就是這樣的人之一。

passages.text: For these defects, and for no other evil, we are lost; only so far afflicted, that we live desiring without hope. So grief assail'd my heart at hearing this, for well I knew suspended in that Limbo many a soul of mighty worth. Then turning to him I said: Master, enter and search the limits of this realm, and I thy guiding next will follow. Behold the noble castle of those worthies, and passing o'er the gate, within whose bounds he said, We stood: where in a meadow fair, of fresh green herbage, there were met together the spirits of mighty men.
passages.zh: 因這些缺陷，而非因任何別的罪惡，我們失喪了；我們所受的苦僅止於此，就是我們活著，有所渴望卻沒有希望。聽聞此言，悲傷襲上我的心，因為我深知有許多極有價值的靈魂，懸留於那靈薄獄中。於是我轉向他說：導師，請進去，搜尋這國度的疆界，我隨後跟隨你的引導。看哪，那些賢者的高貴城堡，越過那門，進入其境內——他說，我們便站定了：那裡有一片美好的草地，長著新綠的草，有許多強者的靈魂聚集在一起。

passages.text: Onward he moved, and I before him walk'd; and of the noblest of the fellowship he made me hear and see: Homer the sovereign bard of old, Horace the satirist, Ovid, and Lucan; and more beside, than mine own prudence can recount, in concert at that noble self, made me a sixth amid so much wisdom. Thus we fared onward to the light, discoursing things of which silence is as well become as speech, while on the sunny mountain top we stray'd.
passages.zh: 他繼續前行，我則走在他前面；他讓我聽聞並見到了那群同伴中最尊貴的幾位：古代至高無上的詩人荷馬、諷刺詩人賀拉斯、奧維德與盧坎；此外還有更多，多到憑我自己的見識也無法一一細數，他們與那位高貴者本人聚在一處，使我在這許多智慧之中成為第六位。我們就這樣一路前行，走向那光明，談論著一些沉默與言說同樣合宜的事，同時在那陽光普照的山頂上漫步。

title.en: Francesca and Paolo: No Greater Grief Than to Remember Days of Joy
title.zh: 弗蘭切斯卡與保羅：無痛過於憶樂

region.en: Second circle of Hell, storm of lust
region.zh: 地獄第二圈，慾風之夜

period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 5, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 5

summary.en: In the black whirlwind of the carnal sinners, two souls ride the storm together; Francesca da Rimini tells how she and her husband's brother Paolo read 'of Lancelot, how love impell'd him to her', and at one point alone — 'that day we read no more.' Dante, who at the end faints 'as a dead body falls', asks Minos and the wind-swept how pity so assails him. 'No greater grief than to remember days of joy, when mis'ry is at hand!' — the West's supreme pity-laden love tragedy.
summary.zh: 在肉慾者的黑旋風中，兩靈同行同風；弗蘭切斯卡敘述她與夫弟保羅共讀「蘭斯洛特如何為愛所驅」，讀至「那一日我們再沒有往下讀」。但丁終至如死屍般昏倒。全詩中最哀傷的一問：「處在苦難之中，回憶快樂之日，豈有比這更大的悲傷！」——西方文學至高的憐憫愛情悲劇。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; adultery presented within the poem's moral geography — pity coexists with judgment.

passages.text: Now 'gin the rueful wailings to be heard. Now am I come where many a plaining voice smites on mine ear. Into a place I came where light was silent all. Bellowing there groan'd a noise as of a sea in tempest torn by warring winds. The stormy blast of hell with restless fury drives the spirits on, whirl'd round and dash'd amain with sore annoy. I understood that to this torment sad the carnal sinners are condemn'd, in whom reason by lust is sway'd.
passages.zh: 如今那悲苦的哀號開始可聞。如今我來到一個地方，無數的哀訴之聲擊打我的耳畔。我來到一處光明全然沉默之地。那裡有咆哮的聲響呻吟著，如同大海在狂風交戰中被撕裂。地獄的風暴以不息的狂怒驅趕著那些亡魂，將它們旋轉、猛力拋擲，帶著劇烈的痛楚。我明白，那些受慾念擺佈而理性被情慾所支配的肉慾之罪人，正是被判處這悲慘的刑罰。

passages.text: Soon as the wind in our favour blew, I spake: O wearied spirits! come, and hold discourse with us, by which and whom, if none deny it, the poor garment that I wear shall have peace till the end. The gentler of the twain began: O courteous and benignant spirit! who vouchsafest to question us, and to hear our wailings, we were of the kingdom of the Lombards, and both were lovers, and we read the tale of Lancelot, how love impell'd him to her. When we had read how the fond smile was kiss'd by such a lover, he, who from me shall never be divorced, kiss'd my mouth all trembling.
passages.zh: 風一吹向我們這邊，我便開口說道：啊，疲憊的亡魂！請過來，與我們交談吧；只要無人禁止，我身上這可憐的衣裳將因此得享安寧，直到終末。兩人中較溫和的那位開始說道：啊，彬彬有禮而仁慈的靈魂！你竟肯垂詢我們，聆聽我們的哀號；我們曾屬於倫巴第人的王國，兩人都是戀人，我們讀著蘭斯洛特的故事，讀到愛情如何驅使他走向她。當我們讀到那含情的微笑如何被這樣一位戀人親吻時，那與我永不分離的他，顫抖著親吻了我的嘴。

passages.text: The book and writer both were love's purveyors. In its leaves that day we read no more. While the one spirit said this, the other wept so sorely, that I for pity swoon'd away, as if I had been dying, and fell down even as a dead body falls.
passages.zh: 那本書與寫書的人，都成了愛情的媒介。那一天，我們再也沒有讀下去。當其中一個亡魂這樣說時，另一個哭得如此悲切，以至於我因憐憫而昏厥過去，彷彿我正走向死亡，就像一具死屍般倒下。

passages.text: Thouarest, Francesca, thy sad tale, as hearts do share grief where they feel it near. But if thou hast the will to hear more of our misery, I will tell thee whence we came: No greater grief than to remember days of joy, when mis'ry is at hand! That kens thy great instructor, though he teach not thus in verse, he wrote so faithfully. But if thou hast the will, do ask us more. That day we read no more. As I stood there and listen'd, I was rapt in thought; and when the rest had pass'd, he of the courteous bearing, and the gentle one that was with him, cried out together to me: Lead, Master! we entreat thee, quickly; and the time of thy converse we request.
passages.zh: 你訴說的悲傷故事令我動容，法蘭切斯卡，正如人心在近距離感受悲傷時便會分擔悲傷。但若你願意再聽一些我們的苦難，我便告訴你我們從何而來：沒有比在苦難臨近時回憶歡樂的日子更大的悲痛了！你的偉大導師深知此理，雖然他在詩中並非如此教導，他卻寫得如此真切。但若你願意，請再問我們吧。那一天，我們再也沒有讀下去。當我站在那裡聆聽時，我陷入了沉思；而當其餘的人都已離去，那位舉止彬彬有禮者，以及與他同行的溫和者，一同向我喊道：帶路吧，導師！我們懇求你，快些；我們請求與你交談的時間。

title.en: The Forest of the Suicides
title.zh: 自殺者之林

region.en: Seventh circle, wood of self-slayers
region.zh: 地獄第七環，自戕者之林

period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 13, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 13

summary.en: A thorn-forest of dusky foliage, thick with harpies who wail on the branches — for the self-destroyers are turned to plants, to be plucked at judgment and never wear again their own flesh. Dante breaks a twig and blood runs down as the trunk cries 'Why pluck'st thou me? Men once were we, that now are rooted here.' Pier della Vigna, Frederick's double-keyed secretary, tells his fall from honour to slanderous disgrace; and from among the trees, where harpies feed, the ghosts of hanged men come running.
summary.zh: 陰鬱的荊棘之林，人面鷹身的哈耳庇埃在枝頭哀鳴——自戕者被化作草木，末日審判時方可復得己肉而永不復得。但丁折斷一根樹枝，血沿樹幹滴落，樹身喊道：「你為何折斷我？我們曾是世人，如今被植於此。」彼特羅·德拉·維尼亞——腓特烈雙鑰的重臣——自述由尊榮墜入讒言之辱；哈耳庇埃啄食的樹間，被吊者的幽靈奔竄而來。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the metamorphosis-punishment is Dante's most famous invention against self-destruction.

passages.text: Ere Nessus yet had reach'd the other bank, we enter'd on a forest, where no track of steps had worn a way. Not verdant there the foliage, but of dusky hue; not light the boughs and tapering, but with knares deform'd and matted thick: fruits there were none, but thorns instead, with venom fill'd. Here the brute Harpies make their nest, the same who from the Strophades the Trojan band drove with dire boding of their future woe. Broad are their pennons, of the human form their neck and count'nance, arm'd with talons keen the feet, and the huge belly fledge with wings. These sit and wail on the drear mystic wood.
passages.zh: 涅索斯尚未抵達對岸，我們便進入了一片森林，那裡沒有任何足跡踏出過道路。那裡的枝葉並非翠綠，而是暗沉的色澤；樹枝並非光潔細長，而是扭曲變形、盤結濃密：那裡沒有果實，只有荊棘，且充滿毒液。這裡是那殘暴的哈耳庇厄築巢之處，正是牠們從斯特洛法德斯群島趕走了特洛伊人眾，預示著他們未來的災禍。牠們的羽翼寬闊，頸項與面容呈人形，腳上長著銳利的爪，巨大的腹部覆滿羽毛。牠們棲息在這陰森神秘的樹林上哀號。

passages.text: Thereat a little stretching forth my hand, from a great wilding gather'd I a branch, and straight the trunk exclaim'd: Why pluck'st thou me? Then as the dark blood trickled down its side, these words it added: Wherefore tear'st me thus? Is there no touch of mercy in thy breast? Men once were we, that now are rooted here. Thy hand might well have spar'd us, had we been the souls of serpents. As a brand yet green, that burning at one end from the other sends a groaning sound, and hisses with the wind that forces out its way, so burst at once forth from the broken splinter words and blood.

I it was who held both keys to Frederick's heart, and turn'd, locking and unlocking, with so sweet a strength, that from his privy purpose, few did thrust me. Sleeping and waking I was still so true, that I was as it were another man, since I did trust to my integrity. But that foul envy, which but turns to evil her own most gracious temper, was the cause of all my ruin, infusing such a poison in the emperor's breast, that, drawn from state and honour, I did fall, and from the loftiest height. And then, with those disloyal thoughts, my temper, that was loath'd and hated, and did blush to be accounted vile, my breast did beat, and with a fatal blow upon a tree, my flesh fell from me: and now to the tree, by my own sentence, I have changed my body.

title.en: Ulysses' Last Voyage Beyond the Pillars
title.zh: 尤利西斯最後的航行

region.en: Eighth chasm of Hell, fire-cloaked spirits
region.zh: 地獄第八溝，火焰裹身的靈魂

period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 26, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 26

summary.en: In the eighth chasm a single flame, parted at the summit like a tongue, holds Ulysses and Diomede together — punished for the horse, Achilles' guile, and the Palladium. At Virgil's entreaty the greater horn rolls and speaks: leaving Circe, 'nor fondness for my son, nor reverence of my old father... could overcome in me the zeal I had t' explore the world, and search the ways of life, man's evil and his virtue' — past Hercules' pillars, 'O brothers!... ye were not form'd to live the life of brutes, but to follow virtue and knowledge', until the sea closed over them before the mountain of Purgatory.
summary.zh: 第八溝中一支頂端裂如舌頭的火舌，裹著尤利西斯與第奧墨得——馬計、阿基琉斯之詭與帕拉狄翁之罪的刑罰。維吉爾代求後，老火舌開口：辭別瑟西之後，「不為幼子之愛、老父之敬……能勝我探索世界、追尋人生善惡之志」——越過海力克士之柱，「兄弟們啊……你們生來不是為獸類之生，而是要追尋美德與知識」——直到煉獄山前海水合攏。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; Dante's invented ending of the Odyssey is among the most influential rewritings of Greek myth.

passages.text: The guide, who mark'd how I did gaze attentive, thus began: Within these ardours are the spirits, each swath'd in confining fire. He replied: Within Ulysses there and Diomede endure their penal tortures, thus to vengeance now together hasting, as erewhile to wrath. These in the flame with ceaseless groans deplore the ambush of the horse, that open'd wide a portal for that goodly seed to pass, which sow'd imperial Rome; nor less the guile lament they, whence of her Achilles reft Deidamia yet in death complains. And there is rued the stratagem, that Troy of her Palladium spoil'd.

Of the old flame forthwith the greater horn began to roll, murmuring, as a fire that labours with the wind, then to and fro wagging the top, as a tongue uttering sounds, threw out its voice, and spake: When I escap'd from Circe, who beyond a circling year had held me near Caieta, by her charms, ere thus Aeneas yet had nam'd the shore, nor fondness for my son, nor reverence of my old father, nor return of love, that should have crown'd Penelope with joy, could overcome in me the zeal I had t' explore the world, and search the ways of life, man's evil and his virtue. Forth I sail'd into the deep illimitable main, with but one bark, and the small faithful band that yet cleav'd to me.

Tardy with age were I and my companions, when we came to the strait pass, where Hercules ordain'd the bound'ries not to be o'erstepp'd by man. The walls of Seville to my right I left, on the other hand already Ceuta past. O brothers! I began, who to the west through perils without number now have reach'd, to this the short remaining vigil of your senses still be true, that ye may not, in the wheel of your own five glad senses, deny experience of the unpeopled world behind the sun. Consider of your origin: ye were not form'd to live the life of brutes, but to follow virtue and knowledge. Five times re-illum'd, as oft vanish'd, from beneath the moon, the light that had been ours, was spent, when the strait of the true sea-gate we enter'd.

Then of our tall mast we rear'd, we spread the sail, gave way, and travell'd the flood; and more and more to larboard we did turn. 'T was the end of night, the stars already far, that rose when we first parted from the sea, and their companions fled with such a flight of east wind; and ere then a mountain rose up, to us new made, as in the shapes of those that so far appear'd to us; we joy'd, but soon to mourning turn'd; for from the new land a whirlwind rose, and smote our ship; the waves, that follow'd, bore away her poop; and o'er our heads the bow, with both her men, and all our weight of lives, was cast; and thrice turn'd round with all the waters, at the fifth arose, and sank our vessel, and the sea clos'd over as it pleas'd another.

title.en: Count Ugolino's Tower of Famine
title.zh: 烏哥利諾伯爵的饑餓之塔

region.en: Ninth circle, frozen Cocytus, Pisa
region.zh: 地獄第九環，冰封科塞特斯（比薩）

period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 33, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 33

summary.en: In the ice of traitors, Count Ugolino gnaws the skull of Archbishop Ruggieri, who imprisoned him. His tale: locked with his sons in the Tower of Famine, he dreams the hunt that gored wolf and whelps, wakes to hear his boys weep for bread, and 'all stone I felt within' will not weep before them. 'Father, we should grieve far less, if thou wouldst eat of us' — and after days of silence, hunger does what grief could not. Pisa's shame is thundered in the comedy's most harrowing canto.
summary.zh: 叛徒之冰中，烏哥利諾伯爵啃咬囚他入塔的呂吉埃里主教之顱。他的故事：與諸子同鎖「饑餓之塔」，夢見狼與幼狼被獵犬咬傷，醒來聽孩子哭討麵包；「我心中如石，不肯在他們面前流淚」。「父親啊，你若吃了我們，我們的悲痛便會小得多」——靜默數日後，饑餓做了悲傷做不到的事。這是全詩最令人心碎的一章，比薩之恥被雷鳴般宣告。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the child deaths are within the poem's judgment frame and recounted with horror, not endorsed.

passages.text: His jaws uplifting from their fell repast, that sinner wip'd them on the hairs o' th' head, which he behind had mangled, then began: Thy will obeying, I call up afresh sorrow past cure, which but to think of wrings my heart, or ere I tell on't. Know I was on earth Count Ugolino, and th' Archbishop he Ruggieri. Why I neighbour him so close, now list. That through effect of his ill thoughts in him my trust reposing, I was ta'en and after murder'd, need is not I tell. What therefore thou canst not have heard, that is, how cruel was the murder, shalt thou hear, and know if he have wrong'd me.

When I awoke before the dawn, amid their sleep I heard my sons (for they were with me) weep and ask for bread. Right cruel art thou, if no pang thou feel at thinking what my heart foretold. Now had they waken'd; and the hour drew near when they were wont to bring us food; the mind of each misgave him through his dream, and I heard, at its outlet underneath lock'd up the horrible tower: whence uttering not a word I look'd upon the visage of my sons. I wept not: so all stone I felt within. They wept: and one, my little Anslem, cried: Thou lookest so! Father what ails thee? Yet I shed no tear, nor answer'd all that day nor the next night, until another sun came out upon the world.

When a faint beam had to our doleful prison made its way, and in four countenances I descry'd the image of my own, on either hand through agony I bit, and they who thought I did it through desire of feeding, rose o' th' sudden, and cried, Father, we should grieve far less, if thou wouldst eat of us: thou gav'st these weeds of miserable flesh we wear, and do thou strip them off from us again. Then, not to make them sadder, I kept down my spirit in stillness. That day and the next we all were silent. Ah, obdurate earth! Why open'dst not thy gates for us?

The fourth day came, and Gaddo at my feet fell outstretched. What more thou hast to ask, or wherefore have I strength? What more hast thou to ask, or why my tongue longer speak? We were four souls; I gave my life a prey to hunger and to grief, or e'en the sixth day's sun had reached its meridian height; my sons who perish'd in the tower, Pisa, had I not murdered them, thou knowest the story well: 'twas my own flesh they wanted. Then I, where I had been, still sought; and neither dead nor living, I or they knew more. And in my grief, that quiet sleepless grief, I did not move; but lay and rooted in the ice of my great sorrow.

title.en: The Three-Faced Lucifer in the Frozen Lake
title.zh: 冰湖中的三面魯西弗

region.en: Ninth circle, well of Cocytus, centre of the earth
region.zh: 地獄第九環，科塞特斯冰湖，大地中心

period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 34, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 34

summary.en: At the bottom of the universe Lucifer, 'the creature eminent in beauty once', stands fixed in ice — three faces, bat-like wings whose flapping freezes Cocytus with three winds, six eyes weeping bloody foam, and three mouths chewing Judas, Brutus, and Cassius. The geography is geometry's: the climbers emerge 'to see again the stars' on the far hemisphere, having crossed the center of the earth — for Hell was made when Heaven fled from Lucifer, 'the earth that sway'd him, he did raise from fear' of the sun.
summary.zh: 宇宙之底，昔日「容顏絕倫」的魯西弗倒嵌於冰中——三面、蝙蝠之翼（其撲動以三股風凍結科塞特斯）、六眼滴血淚，三口咀嚼猶大、布魯圖與卡修斯。地理即是幾何：二人穿過地心，「再度看見繁星」於另一半天球——因為當諸天從魯西弗遁逃時，地獄便在其落點生成了。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the frozen-Lucifer geography is Dante's own invention, not scriptural.

passages.text: The banners of Hell's Monarch do come forth towards us; therefore look, so spake my guide, if thou discern him. As, when breathes a cloud heavy and dense, or when the shades of night fall on our hemisphere, seems view'd from far a windmill, which the blast stirs briskly round, such was the fabric then methought I saw. Now came I (and with fear I bid my strain record the marvel) where the souls were all whelm'd underneath, transparent, as through glass pellucid the frail stem.

That emperor, who sways the realm of sorrow, at mid breast from th' ice stood forth. That creature, whose appearance was once most beauteous, as he is hideous now, and yet did dare to scowl upon his Maker, well from him may all our mis'ry flow. How passing strange it seem'd, when I did spy upon his head three faces: one in front of hue vermilion, th' other two with this midway each shoulder join'd and at the crest. Under each shot forth two mighty wings, enormous as became a bird so vast. No plumes had they, but were in texture like a bat, and these he flapp'd i' th' air, that from him issued still three winds, wherewith Cocytus to its depth was frozen. At six eyes he wept: the tears adown three chins distill'd with bloody foam.

At every mouth his teeth a sinner champ'd bruis'd as with pond'rous engine, so that three were in this guise tormented. That upper spirit, who hath worse punishment, so spake my guide, is Judas, he that hath his head within and plies the feet without. Of th' other two, whose heads are under, from the murky jaw who hangs, is Brutus: lo! how he doth writhe and speaks not! Th' other Cassius, that appears so large of limb. And noting how that Lucifer had three winds for the frozen river, they departed; till my guide, within the hollow cave whose floor already stank, that led us back to the fair world, set me upon the steep, and first himself descended the rough bank; I following his steps, we climbed, he first, I following his steps, till on our view the beautiful lights of heav'n dawn'd through a circular opening in the cave: thus issuing we again beheld the stars.

title.en: Virgil Departs: Come, Spouse, from Libanus
title.zh: 維吉爾離去：新婦，自黎巴嫩而來

region.en: Earthly Paradise atop Mount Purgatory
region.zh: 煉獄山頂的地上樂園

period: Divine Comedy: Purgatorio, canto 30, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Purgatorio canto 30

summary.en: At the top of Purgatory, where the thorn forest of the earthly Paradise blooms, Beatrice descends in a shower of white-veiled flowers 'beneath green mantle, rob'd in hue of living flame' — and Virgil, reason's guide, is gone: 'Virgil had bereav'd us of himself, Virgil, my best-lov'd father... nor all, our prime mother lost, avail'd to save my undew'd cheeks from blur of soiling tears.' Beatrice's rebuke opens the second half of the Comedy: 'Dante, weep not, that Virgil leaves thee... behooves thee feel the edge of other sword.'
summary.zh: 煉獄山頂的地上樂園中，貝雅特麗齊在白色花雨中降臨——「著綠色斗篷，披火焰之色」——而理性的導師維吉爾已離去：「維吉爾，我至愛的父親，捨我而去……縱大地之母盡失，也未能拭去我臉上的淚痕。」貝雅特麗齊的斥責開啟全詩下半：「但丁，莫為維吉爾之去而哭泣……你還須感到另一柄劍的鋒刃。」

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the classical guide replaced by the theological one is the Comedy's structural argument.

passages.text: Forthwith the saintly tribe, who in the van between the Gryphon and its radiance came, did turn them to the car, as to their rest: and one, as if commission'd from above, in holy chant thrice shorted forth aloud: Come, spouse, from Libanus! and all the rest took up the song. I have beheld, ere now, at break of day, the eastern clime all roseate, and the sky oppos'd, one deep and beautiful serene, and the sun's face so shaded, and with mists attemper'd at lids rising, that the eye long while endur'd the sight: thus in a cloud of flowers, that from those hands angelic rose, and down, within and outside of the car, fell showering, in white veil with olive wreath'd, a virgin in my view appear'd, beneath green mantle, rob'd in hue of living flame.

No sooner on my vision streaming, smote the heav'nly influence, which years past, and e'en in childhood, thrill'd me, than towards Virgil I turn'd me to leftward, panting, like a babe, that flees for refuge to his mother's breast, if aught have terrified or work'd him woe: and would have cried: There is no dram of blood, that doth not quiver in me. The old flame throws out clear tokens of reviving fire: but Virgil had bereav'd us of himself, Virgil, my best-lov'd father; Virgil, he to whom I gave me up for safety: nor, all, our prime mother lost, avail'd to save my undew'd cheeks from blur of soiling tears. Dante, weep not, that Virgil leaves thee: nay, weep thou not yet: behooves thee feel the edge of other sword, and thou shalt weep for that.

title.en: The Love That Moves the Sun and All the Stars
title.zh: 推動日月星辰之愛

region.en: Empyrean rose, the final vision
region.zh: 淨火天玫瑰，終局異象

period: Divine Comedy: Paradiso, canto 33, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Paradiso canto 33

summary.en: The Comedy's close: St Bernard prays to the Virgin — 'O virgin mother, daughter of thy Son... Here kneeleth one, who of all spirits hath review'd the state, from the world's lowest gap unto this height' — and Dante's sight, refined, passes into 'the ray authentical of sovran light', where 'in one volume clasp'd of love, whatever the universe unfolds' is seen: three orbs of triple hue, 'as rainbow is from rainbow.' The last line of the poem is the doctrine: 'But yet the will roll'd onward, like a wheel in even motion, by the Love impell'd, that moves the sun in heav'n and all the stars.'
summary.zh: 全詩收束：聖伯爾納向童貞女祈求——「童貞女母，聖子之女……此人閱盡靈界，自世界最低之淵至此至高之光」——但丁的目光被煉淨，進入「至聖之光的真實之射線」，其中「以愛裝訂成一冊，收錄宇宙所展開的一切」：三環三色，「如虹出自虹」。全詩末行即是教義：「然而意志卻如均勻轉動的車輪，由那推動太陽與群星之愛所驅。」

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the Marian intercession is doctrinal poetry, not scripture.

passages.text: O virgin mother, daughter of thy Son, created beings all in lowliness surpassing, as in height, above them all, term by th' eternal counsel pre-ordain'd, ennobler of thy nature, so advanc'd in thee, that its great Maker did not scorn, himself, in his own work enclos'd to dwell! For in thy womb rekindling shone the love reveal'd, whose genial influence makes now this flower to germin in eternal peace! Here kneeleth one, who of all spirits hath review'd the state, from the world's lowest gap unto this height. Suppliant to thee he kneels, imploring grace for virtue, yet more high to lift his ken toward the bliss supreme.

The eyes, that heav'n with love and awe regards, fix'd on the suitor, witness'd, how benign she looks on pious pray'rs: then fasten'd they on th' everlasting light, wherein no eye of creature, as may well be thought, so far can travel inward. I, meanwhile, who drew near to the limit, where all wishes end, the ardour of my wish (for so behooved), ended within me. Bare me into the ray authentical of sovran light. Thenceforward, what I saw, was not for words to speak, nor memory's self to stand against such outrage on her skill.

O grace! unenvying of thy boon! that gav'st boldness to fix so earnestly my ken on th' everlasting splendour, that I look'd, while sight was unconsum'd, and, in that depth, saw in one volume clasp'd of love, whatever the universe unfolds; all properties of substance and of accident, beheld, compounded, yet one individual light the whole. In that abyss of radiance, clear and lofty, seem'd methought, three orbs of triple hue clipt in one bound: and, from another, one reflected seem'd, as rainbow is from rainbow: and the third seem'd fire, breath'd equally from both. Here vigour fail'd the tow'ring fantasy: but yet the will roll'd onward, like a wheel in even motion, by the Love impell'd, that moves the sun in heav'n and all the stars.

title.en: Better to Reign in Hell: The Consult of Pandemonium
title.zh: 寧在地獄為王：萬魔殿的密議

region.en: Pandemonium, Hell's council hall (vision-setting)
region.zh: 萬魔殿，地獄議事堂（異象之境）

period: Paradise Lost, books I-II, 1667

source.work: Paradise Lost, John Milton, books I-II

summary.en: The fallen host wakes on the burning lake; Satan rallies them with the epic's most quoted defiance — 'All is not lost—the unconquerable will... to wage by force or guile eternal war' — while Mammon's legions quarry the gold of Hell to raise Pandemonium. In council, Moloch calls for open war, Belial cringes, Mammon argues for Hell as a kingdom, and Beelzebub delivers Satan's own scheme: the new world of Man. The catalogue of fallen angels and the founding of the infernal commonwealth follow.
summary.zh: 墮落者在火湖上醒來；撒但以全詩最著名的抗辯召集他們——「尚未全失——那不屈的意志……以武力或詭計進行永恆的戰爭」——瑪門的兵團開採地獄之金築起萬魔殿。密議中，摩洛主戰，彼列怯懦，瑪門主張以地獄為國，別西卜代陳撒但之計：新造的人間世界。墮天使的名錄與地獄邦國的創立隨之鋪展。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary-religious imagination; the infernal parliament is Milton's epic invention, shaped by 17th-century politics.

passages.text: All is not lost—the unconquerable will, and study of revenge, immortal hate, and courage never to submit or yield: and what is else not to be overcome? That glory never shall his wrath or might extort from me. To bow and sue for grace with suppliant knee, and deify his power who, from the terror of this arm, so late doubted his empire—that were low indeed. Since, through experience of this great event, in arms not worse, in foresight much advanced, we may with more successful hope resolve to wage by force or guile eternal war, irreconcilable to our grand Foe, who now triumphs, and in th' excess of joy sole reigning holds the tyranny of Heaven. So spake th' apostate Angel, though in pain, vaunting aloud, but racked with deep despair.

There stood a hill not far, whose grisly top belched fire and rolling smoke; the rest entire shone with a glossy scurf—undoubted sign that in his womb was hid metallic ore, the work of sulphur. Thither, winged with speed, a numerous brigade hastened: as when bands of pioneers, with spade and pickaxe armed, forerun the royal camp, to trench a field, or cast a rampart. Mammon led them on—Mammon, the least erected Spirit that fell from Heaven; for even in Heaven his looks and thoughts were always downward bent, admiring more the riches of heaven's pavement, trodden gold, than aught divine or holy else enjoyed in vision beatific.

The Fiend looked up and knew his mounted scale aloft: nor more; but fled murmuring, and with him fled the shades of night. Meanwhile, Satan, on the burning lake, thus to his legions: Peace is despaired; for who can think submission? War, then, war open or understood, must be resolved. He spake; and, to confirm his words, outflew millions of flaming swords, drawn from the thighs of mighty Cherubim; the sudden blaze far round illumined Hell. Highly they raged against the Highest, and fierce with grasped arms clashed on their sounding shields the din of war, hurling defiance toward the vault of Heaven.

title.en: Sin and Death Build the Bridge over Chaos
title.zh: 罪與死在混沌之上築橋

region.en: Chaos, between Hell and the new world (vision-setting)
region.zh: 混沌，地獄與新世界之間（異象之境）

period: Paradise Lost, book II, 1667

source.work: Paradise Lost, John Milton, book II

summary.en: Satan, himself the bridge, 'on the broad circumference hung on his shoulders like the moon' — wings like sails, beaming like a comet — threads the howling vagary of Chaos by sign and star. As he passes, Sin and Death, left behind in Hell, feel their works begin: the sovran of Hell builds his own road, a vast and long bridge 'wonderous to the sight' of ninefold gates and three-fold stairway, along which Sin and Death march to work the ruin the Fiend's rebellion will open. The bridge is the epic's cosmic geometry of Fall.
summary.zh: 撒但自身即是橋——「如滿月懸掛於肩後」——翅膀如帆，光芒如彗星，穿過混沌的呼號而前行。他一過，留在地獄的罪與死便覺其事業開始；地獄君王為自己築就長橋，奇觀巍然，而罪與死沿橋而行，去成就叛者所開啟的毀壞。這座橋是全詩墮落的宇宙幾何。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary-religious imagination; Sin-Death personifications are Milton's invention.

passages.text: He scarce had ceased when the superior Fiend was moving toward the shore; his ponderous shield, ethereal temper, massy, large, and round, behind him cast. The broad circumference hung on his shoulders like the moon, whose orb through optic glass the Tuscan artist views at evening from the top of Fesole, or in Valdarno, to descry new lands, rivers or mountains in her spotty globe. His spear, to equal which the tallest pine hewn on Norwegian hills, to be the mast of some great admiral, were but a wand, he walked with, to support uneasy steps over the burning marle, not like those steps on Heaven's azure; the hostile dread of his departure made them bow to the seas.

title.en: Eve Plucks the Fruit: Earth Felt the Wound
title.zh: 夏娃摘果：大地感到創傷

region.en: Tree in the midst of Eden
region.zh: 伊甸園中央之樹

period: Paradise Lost, book IX, 1667

source.work: Paradise Lost, John Milton, book IX

summary.en: Milton's epic turns 'from truculent and satirick brawls' to tragedy: the serpent reasons Eve into the fruit — 'greedily she ingorged without restraint, and knew not eating death' — and 'Earth felt the wound; and Nature from her seat, sighing through all her works, gave signs of woe, that all was lost.' Adam's love-lament follows — 'How art thou lost!... flesh of flesh, bone of my bone thou art' — and he chooses to fall with her. The tradition's great retelling of the fall, set into the doctrine of original sin.
summary.zh: 史詩由刀劍與嘲諷轉入悲劇：蛇以言辭說動夏娃——「她貪婪地盡情吞嚥，不知吃下的乃是死亡」——「大地感到創傷；自然自其寶座，於萬物之中歎息，顯出哀兆：一切都失落了。」隨後是亞當的哀歌——「你怎麼失落了！……你是骨中之骨，肉中之肉」——他選擇與她同墮。這是原罪教義最偉大的重述。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary-religious imagination; the fall narrative retold for the doctrine of original sin.

passages.text: No more of talk where God or Angel guest with Man, as with his friend, familiar us'd, to sit indulgent, and with him partake rural repast; permitting him the while venial discourse unblam'd. I now must change those notes to tragick; foul distrust, and breach disloyal on the part of Man, revolt, and disobedience: on the part of Heaven now alienated, distance and distaste, anger and just rebuke, and judgement given, that brought into this world a world of woe, sin and her shadow Death, and Misery death's harbinger.

So saying, her rash hand in evil hour forth reaching to the fruit, she plucked, she eat! Earth felt the wound; and Nature from her seat, sighing through all her works, gave signs of woe, that all was lost. Back to the thicket slunk the guilty Serpent; and well might; for Eve, intent now wholly on her taste, nought else regarded; such delight till then, as seemed, in fruit she never tasted, whether true or fancied so, through expectation high of knowledge; not was Godhead from her thought. Greedily she ingorged without restraint, and knew not eating death.

O fairest of Creation, last and best of all God's works, Creature in whom excelled whatever can to sight or thought be formed, holy, divine, good, amiable, or sweet! How art thou lost! how on a sudden lost, defaced, deflowered, and now to death devote! Rather, how hast thou yielded to transgress the strict forbiddance, how to violate the sacred fruit forbidden! Some cursed fraud of enemy hath beguiled thee, yet unknown, and me with thee hath ruined; for with thee certain my resolution is to die: how can I live without thee! how forego thy sweet converse, and love so dearly joined, to live again in these wild woods forlorn!

title.en: The World Was All Before Them: Expulsion from Eden
title.zh: 全世界在他們面前：逐出伊甸

region.en: East gate of Eden
region.zh: 伊甸東門

period: Paradise Lost, book XII, 1667

source.work: Paradise Lost, John Milton, book XII

summary.en: The archangel Michael leads the exiled pair up a mount of vision, shows them the history of the world to come, and girds their loins for exile — 'the world was all before them, where to choose their place of rest, and Providence their guide: they, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, through Eden took their solitary way.' The last eight lines of the epic made the homeless pair the West's emblem of mortality borne by providence.
summary.zh: 天使長米迦勒引被逐的二人登異象之山，展示未來世界史，並束其腰以備流亡——「全世界都在他們面前，可供選擇棲身之所，而天意是他們的嚮導：他們手牽著手，以緩慢的漫遊腳步，走過伊甸，踏上了他們孤寂的路。」史詩的最後八行，使這對無家夫婦成為西方「以天意承載必死之身」的象徵。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary-religious imagination; the exile close is among the most quoted endings in English poetry.

passages.text: The world was all before them, where to choose their place of rest, and Providence their guide: they, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, through Eden took their solitary way. The archangel Michael leads the exiled pair up a mount of vision, shows them the history of the world to come, and girds their loins for exile — 'the world was all before them, where to choose their place of rest, and Providence their guide: they, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, through Eden took their solitary way.' The last eight lines of the epic made the homeless pair the West's emblem of mortality borne by providence.

title.en: Paradise Regained: The Tempter Foiled in All His Wiles
title.zh: 復樂園：試探者詭計盡破

region.en: Wilderness and temple pinnacle (vision-setting)
region.zh: 曠野與聖殿殿頂（異象之境）

period: Paradise Regained, 1671

source.work: Paradise Regained, John Milton, book I and IV

summary.en: Milton's brief epic answers Paradise Lost: 'I, who erewhile the happy Garden sung by one man's disobedience lost, now sing Recovered Paradise to all mankind, by one man's firm obedience fully tried through all temptation, and the Tempter foiled in all his wiles.' The Satan of the wilderness trial, once foiled, still returns 'as a swarm of flies in vintage-time'; at the temple's pinnacle he dares the leap; offered the world for one worship — 'the abominable terms, impious condition' — the Son answers with the first commandment, 'Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and only Him shalt serve.'
summary.zh: 彌爾頓的短史詩回應《失樂園》：「我先前歌詠因一人悖逆而失落的樂園，如今歌詠萬人重得的樂園——靠一人的堅定順服，受盡試煉，試探者詭計盡破、被擊退。」曠野受試的撒但屢敗屢返，「如釀酒季的蒼蠅群」；於殿頂之上他竟敢誘其一躍；以萬國榮華換一拜——「可憎的條款，不虔的條件」——聖子以第一誡作答：「當拜主你的神，單要事奉祂。」

sensitivity.note: Christian literary-religious imagination; the inversion of the fall by obedience is Milton's theological structure.

passages.text: I, who erewhile the happy Garden sung by one man's disobedience lost, now sing Recovered Paradise to all mankind, by one man's firm obedience fully tried through all temptation, and the Tempter foiled in all his wiles, defeated and repulsed, and Eden raised in the waste Wilderness. Now had the great Proclaimer, with a voice more awful than the sound of trumpet, cried Repentance, and Heaven's kingdom nigh at hand to all baptized. To his great baptism flocked with awe the regions round, and with them came from Nazareth the son of Joseph deemed to the flood Jordan—came as then obscure, unmarked, unknown.

Whom thus our Saviour answered with disdain:— I never liked thy talk, thy offers less; now both abhor, since thou hast dared to utter the abominable terms, impious condition. But I endure the time, till which expired thou hast permission on me. It is written, the first of all commandments, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and only Him shalt serve. And dar'st thou to the Son of God propound to worship thee, accursed? now more accursed for this attempt, bolder than that on Eve, and more blasphemous; which expect to rue. The kingdoms of the world to thee were given! Permitted rather, and by thee usurped.

So Satan, whom repulse upon repulse met ever, and to shameful silence brought, yet gives not o'er, though desperate of success, and his vain importunity pursues. Or as a swarm of flies in vintage-time, about the wine-press where sweet must is poured, beat off, returns as oft with humming sound; or surging waves against a solid rock, though all to shivers dashed, the assault renew, vain battery! and in froth or bubbles end.

title.en: St George and the Dragon of Silene
title.zh: 聖佐治與西勒尼的龍

region.en: City of Silene, Libya (legendary pin)
region.zh: 利比亞西勒尼城（傳說定位）

period: The Golden Legend, compiled c. 1260 (Caxton trans., ed. Ellis, 1900)

source.work: The Golden Legend, The Life of S. George (Caxton, 1483)

summary.en: The Golden Legend's most famous episode: a pond-dragon poisons the country until children are drawn by lot, and the king's own daughter is led out as a bride for the beast; George, armed and garnished with the sign of the cross, spears and throws it down, binds it with the princess's girdle so it follows 'as it had been a meek beast', and the dragon is slain only after fifteen thousand are baptized. The canonical dragon-slayer myth of the West, told here from the hagiography that fixed its shape.
summary.zh: 《黃金傳說》最著名的一章：池中毒龍為害全境，抽籤獻童男童女，連國王之女也被裝扮如新娘送與獸；聖佐治畫十字記號、提槍刺龍並擊倒之，以公主腰帶縛龍，使其「如馴良之獸」相隨；待一萬五千人受洗後方斬龍首。西方屠龍英雄神話的原型，定型於此部聖徒傳。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition of high devotion (St George); the dragon tale is told as the tradition's own legend, with the apocryphal status the Legend itself admits noted.

passages.text: S. George was a knight and born in Cappadocia. On a time he came in to the province of Libya, to a city which is said Silene. And by this city was a stagne or a pond like a sea, wherein was a dragon which envenomed all the country. And on a time the people were assembled for to slay him, and when they saw him they fled. And when he came nigh the city he venomed the people with his breath, and therefore the people of the city gave to him every day two sheep for to feed him, because he should do no harm to the people, and when the sheep failed there was taken a man and a sheep. Then was an ordinance made in the town that there should be taken the children and young people of them of the town by lot. So it happed that many of them of the town were then delivered, insomuch that the lot fell upon the king's daughter.

When she was there S. George passed by, and when he saw the lady he demanded the lady what she made there and she said: Go ye your way fair young man, that ye perish not also. Then said he: Tell to me what have ye and why weep ye, and doubt ye of nothing. Then said S. George: Fair daughter, doubt ye no thing hereof for I shall help thee in the name of Jesu Christ. Thus as they spake together the dragon appeared and came running to them, and S. George was upon his horse, and drew out his sword and garnished him with the sign of the cross, and rode hardily against the dragon which came towards him, and smote him with his spear and hurt him sore and threw him to the ground. And after said to the maid: Deliver to me your girdle, and bind it about the neck of the dragon and be not afeard. When she had done so the dragon followed her as it had been a meek beast and debonair.

Then she led him into the city, and the people fled by mountains and valleys, and said: Alas! alas! we shall be all dead. Then S. George said to them: Ne doubt ye no thing, without more, believe ye in God, Jesu Christ, and do ye to be baptized and I shall slay the dragon. Then the king was baptized and all his people, and S. George slew the dragon and smote off his head, and commanded that he should be thrown in the fields, and they took four carts with oxen that drew him out of the city.
