The king built a town near the lake and served the elephant and his mother continually; when the mother died and her obsequies were performed, five hundred sages came to dwell at the monastery he founded there, the king made a stone image of the Bodhisatta and paid it great honor, and to this day the folk of all India gather yearly for the Elephant Festival. Of that time, Ānanda was the king, Mahāmāyā the she-elephant, and the Master the elephant that fed his mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 455 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Pāniya-Jātaka (No Sin Is Small)
title.zh: 水飲本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Villages of Kasi and the city of Benares
region.zh: 迦尸諸村與波羅奈城

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: Five householders of Kasi each stumble into one small sin—a stolen draught of a friend's water, a covetous glance at another's wife, a lie told to robbers, a permitted slaughter-feast, a permitted drinking festival—and each, seized with remorse on self-examination, develops insight on the spot and becomes a Silent Buddha. Standing at the king's gate they declare their sins in verse, and the king, sickened by desire, renounces his throne.
summary.zh: 迦尸五位居士各犯一微罪——偷飲友人之水、貪視他妻、對盜賊說謊、准許殺生祭、准許飲酒節——各自省察生慚，當下修得神通，成為獨覺佛。五人於王門以偈自陳罪由，王聞之厭離諸欲，捨王位出家。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master assembled Brethren who at midnight indulged in thoughts of sin, and told them there is no such thing as a petty sin—wise men of old, before the Buddha came, subdued their sins and attained the knowledge of a Silent Buddha. Of old in a village of Kāsi two friends went afield with drinking vessels, and one, thirsty, husbanded his own water and drank from his friend's pot. At evening, examining his day, he remembered the stolen draught and cried, "If this thirst grows upon me it will bring me to some evil birth; I will subdue my sin." Making that stolen water the subject of his meditation, he gradually acquired supernatural insight and attained the knowledge of a Silent Buddha, while his astonished friend watched the marks of a layman vanish, yellow robes wrap about him, and the figure rise poised in mid-air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 459 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: In like manner a land-owner who looked with desire on another man's beautiful wife thought, "This desire, if it increases, will cast me into some evil birth," developed supernatural insight, attained the knowledge of a Silent Buddha, and flew to the Nandamūla cave. A father and son journeying together had agreed to deny each other to the robbers posted at the forest edge—a premeditated lie—and the son, resting after the escape, remembered the lie, repented, and became a Silent Buddha before his father's eyes. A zemindar who had laid an interdict on slaughter yet told the crowd at the spirits'-offering to slay deer and swine as aforetime saw the heaps of fish and flesh and thought, "All these creatures have been slain because of my word alone," and even for that trifle felt remorse till insight arose; and another zemindar who permitted the time-honoured drinking festival, and saw legs broken and crowns cracked in the brawls, thought, "If I had not permitted this, they would not have suffered this misery," and he too won Pacceka-Buddhahood. Five Silent Buddhas thus gathered.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 459 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some time after, the five Silent Buddhas alighted at the gate of Benares seeking alms; the delighted king invited them into his palace, served them, and asked what cause had moved men of their age to leave the world. Each answered in verse: "The water-draught of my own friend, although a friend, I stole: loathing the sin which I had done, I afterwards was fain to leave the world, an eremite, lest I should sin again"—so the first; the second the lustful glance, the third the lie to the thieves, the fourth the slaughter-feast, the fifth the drinking-bout, each with the same refrain. The king bestowed robes and medicines and let them go; ever after he loathed the pleasures of sense, would not speak to women, sat staring at a white wall till he fell into a trance, and recited his loathing of desire in verse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 459 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: His chief queen, hearing him through the door, praised the joy of sweet desire in answer, but the king replied that desire is worse than whetted swords, knives driven in the heart, a pit of live coals, or poison. Gathering his courtiers, he rose into the air before their wailing multitude, delivered a discourse, went along the path of the wind to the furthest Himalaya, and in a delightsome spot built a hermitage, where he lived the sage's life until, at the end of his days, he was destined for the world of Brahma. Of that time the queen was Rahula's mother and the Master was the king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 459 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Yuvañjaya-Jātaka (The Dewdrops on the Grass)
title.zh: 優闍那本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Ramma city (the Benares of this birth) and the Himalaya
region.zh: 藍摩城（此世之波羅奈）與雪山

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: The viceroy Yuvañjaya, riding to the park, sees dewdrops strung like pearls on every grass blade at dawn and gone by evening, and knows that the life of beings is fashioned like dew on the grass. Over his parents' pleading he renounces the throne of Benares, and his youngest brother follows him to the Himalaya hermitage; the Master tells this to show that the Great Renunciation was not made once only.
summary.zh: 儲君優闍那晨遊御苑，見露珠如珠串綴滿草尖，日昇即消，遂悟眾生之命如草上露。不顧父母泣勸，捨波羅奈王位出家，幼弟亦隨之入雪山；佛陀以此示其出家非止一世。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Brethren in the Hall of Truth praised the Buddha's Great Renunciation—how a delicately nurtured kshatriya, who might have been a universal monarch with a thousand sons, perceived the bane of desires at midnight and rode away on Kanthaka. "This is not the first time," said the Master, "that the Tathāgata has made the Great Renunciation." Of old a king named Sabbadatta reigned in Ramma city with a thousand sons, and to his eldest, Yuvañjaya, he gave the viceroyalty. Early one morning the prince drove in splendor to the park and saw dewdrops hanging like strings of pearls on tree-tops, grass-tips, branch-ends and spiders' webs. "What is this, friend charioteer?" "Dew, my lord, that falls in the cold weather." In the evening, returning, he could not see one of them, and the charioteer told him they melted as the sun rose higher.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 460 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince was distressed: "The life of us living beings is fashioned like dew-drops on the grass. I must be rid of the oppression of disease, old age and death; I must take leave of my parents and renounce the world." So because of the dewdrops he saw the three modes of existence as a blazing fire, and asked his father's leave in the Hall of Judgement. The king offered him anything rather than the homeless life; the prince answered that nothing was lacking to him, but he sought a refuge where old age makes no attack, and warned that if he lingered he might become a prey to age intoxicated with lusts. His mother, told the news, came swiftly in her golden litter and begged him to stay; he answered, "Like as the dew upon the grass, when the sun rises hot, so is the life of mortal men: O mother, stay me not!" And the king, unable to refuse, gave his consent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 460 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: His youngest brother Yudhiṭṭhila greeted his father and asked leave to follow the religious life, and the king consented to both. The queen wept that Ramma would be empty—the eldest of a thousand sons, like gold to look upon, has left the world the yellow robe to don—and cried "Make haste, and bless thee!" to the departing prince. The Bodhisatta first bade his parents farewell, then took his brother and went out of the city, sending back the great multitude, and the two built a hermitage in a delightsome spot of the Himalaya. There they embraced the holy sage's life, cultivated the transcendent rapture of meditation, lived on the fruits and roots of the forest all their lives long, and were destined for the world of Brahma. Of that time the father and mother were of the present king's family, Ānanda was Yudhiṭṭhila, and the Master was Yuvañjaya himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 460 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Daśaratha-Jātaka (The Rama Story)
title.zh: 十車王本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Benares and a Himalaya hermitage (symbolic pin for the forest)
region.zh: 波羅奈與雪山隱居處（森林為象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: The Buddhist Ramayana: king Daśaratha's second queen demands the throne for her son Bharata, so Rāma-paṇḍita, his brother Lakkhaṇa and their sister Sītā withdraw to the forest until the king's death. When Bharata comes to bring them home, Rāma neither weeps nor wails, and teaches his kinsmen the doctrine of impermanence; for three years his straw slippers rule Benares from the throne, clapping together whenever a judgment is unjust, before Rāma returns to reign sixteen thousand years.
summary.zh: 佛教版羅摩衍那：十車王后妃為其子婆羅多求王位，羅摩賢者與弟吉祥、妹悉多遁入林中。父王死後，婆羅多往迎，羅摩不哭不慟，為親屬說無常法；三年間其草鞋代掌國政，判案不公則鞋自相擊；後羅摩還都，治世一萬六千年。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Buddhist Jataka sharing characters with the Hindu Ramayana (Dasaratha, Rama, Sita, Bharata)—though here Sita is Rama's sister, not his wife; retold freely as living-tradition scripture; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this to a landowner crushed by sorrow for his dead father: wise men of old who knew the eight worldly conditions felt no grief even at a father's death. Of old a great king, Dasaratha, reigned righteously in Benares; by his eldest queen he had two sons and a daughter—Rama-pandita, Rama the Wise, Prince Lakkhana, and the Lady Sita. When the queen died the king set another in her place, and she bore a son, Bharata. When the boy was seven the queen claimed the promised boon and demanded the kingdom for her son; the king snapped his fingers at her—his other two sons shone like blazing fires. Fearing she might use forged letters or bribes to have his sons murdered, he summoned them: go to a neighbouring kingdom or the woodland, and when my body is burnt return and inherit the kingdom. The soothsayers gave him twelve years more, and the sons promised to return at the twelfth year; the Lady Sita said she too would go with her brothers, and the three departed to a hermitage in the Himalaya, where the younger two gathered wild fruit and fed Rama-pandita as a father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 461 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: King Daśaratha pined after his sons and died in the ninth year; when his obsequies were done the queen ordered the umbrella raised over Bharata, but the courtiers refused—"the lords of the umbrella are dwelling in the forest." So Bharata took the five emblems of royalty and a complete army to fetch Rāma-paṇḍita back, and coming to the hermitage found him seated at the door, unmoved, like a figure of fine gold. Bharata told all that had happened, fell at his feet with his courtiers, and burst into weeping; but Rāma neither sorrowed nor wept, and no emotion stirred in him. When Lakkhaṇa and Sītā returned with wild fruit, the wise brother considered that the young ones' hearts might break at a sudden blow, and made them stand in the pond before telling them, stanza by stanza, that King Daśaratha's life was at an end. They fainted thrice and were carried out of the water, and all sat weeping together—yet Rāma did not grieve.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 461 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asked by what power he grieved not, Rāma-paṇḍita explained in verse the impermanence of things: when man can never keep a thing, though loudly he may cry, why should a wise intelligence torment itself thereby? Young and old, fool and sage, rich and poor—one end is sure: each man among them dies. As the ripened fruit fears its fall, so mortals fear death; the fool grows thin and pale with weeping and cannot bring the dead to life; as a blazing house is put out with water, the wise scatter their grief like cotton before the wind. One mortal dies, and straightway ties of kindred are born to another; the strong man, skilled in the sacred text and keen in contemplating this world and the next, is not vexed by any grief, however great. Hearing this discourse the company lost all their grief, and Bharata begged Rāma to take the kingdom of Benares; but Rāma would keep his father's command, and for the three years remaining he gave his brother his straw slippers: "These shall do it."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 461 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: For three years the slippers ruled the kingdom; the courtiers placed them on the royal throne when they judged a cause, and if the cause were decided wrongly the slippers beat upon each other—at that sign the case was examined again; when the decision was right, the slippers lay quiet. When the three years were over Rāma came out of the forest, and his brothers, making Sītā the queen consort, performed the ceremonial sprinkling and gave him the kingdom. Standing in a magnificent chariot he entered Benares in solemn procession, mounted the great terrace of his splendid palace Sucandaka, and reigned there in righteousness sixteen thousand years, then went to swell the hosts of heaven. The Master identified the Birth: king Suddhodana was Daśaratha, Mahāmāyā the mother, Rāhula's mother was Sītā, Ānanda was Bharata, and he himself was Rāma-paṇḍita.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 461 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Suppāraka-Jātaka (The Blind Sea Captain)
title.zh: 善導船長本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: Seaport of Bharukaccha and the marvellous far seas
region.zh: 婆留醯遮查海港與諸奇海

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: Suppāraka, blind from salt water yet master of all seamanship, leads seven hundred merchants through a chain of marvel seas, netting diamonds, gold, silver, emeralds and coral while hiding their names to curb their greed. Driven toward the VALābhāmukha sea whence no ship returns, he performs an Act of Truth—he has never knowingly taken a life—and the ship flies home in a single day, leaping over eleven hundred cubits to the mariner's door.
summary.zh: 善導尊者雖盲於海鹽，而盡通航海之術，率七百商人歷諸奇海，以漁網暗取金銀珠寶珊瑚而不言其名以抑貪心。船入無回路之婆羅菟海，乃以真實語誓願救船——誓畢，船一日還鄉，躍過一千一百肘而至其門。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Brethren praised the Buddha's matchless wisdom, and the Master said that even when his knowledge was immature he was wise—blind though he was, he knew by the signs of the ocean what jewels lay hidden there. Of old a king named Bharu reigned over the seaport of Bharukaccha, and the Bodhisatta was born to the family of a master mariner there, amiable and golden-brown; by sixteen he had mastered the whole art of seamanship, and with him aboard no ship ever came to harm. In time the salt water destroyed both his eyes, so he entered the king's service as valuer of elephants, horses, pearls and gems. Feeling all over a state elephant, he named it deformed behind from a fall at birth; a state horse lacking its dam's milk; a chariot made of a hollow tree; a royal rug with a rat-hole—each judgment proved true, yet the king paid him only eight pieces a time, and Suppāraka, judging his king a barber's brat, went home to the seaport.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 463 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Merchants fitting out a ship could find no skipper better than the blind wise man, and pressed him till he consented. For seven days all went well; then an unseasonable wind carried the vessel four months over a primeval ocean until she reached the Khuramāla Sea, where fish with razor-like snouts dived and rose. "Merchants come from Bharukaccha, seeking riches to purvey—this is Khuramālī ocean," he answered. In that sea diamonds lie; but knowing that if he told them they would sink the ship in greed, he lowered a net as if to catch fish, hauled up a store of diamonds, cast the worthless cargo overboard, and said nothing. So they passed the Aggimāla sea blazing like a bonfire, where he netted gold; the milky Dadhimāla sea, where he netted silver; the kusa-grass-green Kusamālī sea, where he netted emeralds; and the reed-like Nalamālī sea, where he netted coral.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 463 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they came to the Valabhamukha Sea, where the waters are sucked away and rise on every side in sheer precipices, a wave standing like a wall with a roar to burst the ear and break the heart. "Once a ship gets there she will sink and go to destruction," said the Great Being, and seven hundred souls aboard cried out like those burning in the lowest hell. "Except me no other can save them; I will save them by an Act of Truth." He had them bathe him in scented water, put new garments on him, and set a full bowl in his hands at the ship's prow, and there performed the Act of Truth: "Since I can myself remember, since intelligence first grew, not one life of living creature have I taken, that I knew—may this ship return to safety if my solemn words are true!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 463 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: Four months they had voyaged in far regions; now, as though endued with supernatural power, the ship returned in a single day to Bharukaccha, and even crossed the dry land, leaping over a space of eleven hundred cubits to rest before the mariner's door. Supparaka divided the treasure among the merchants—"this is enough for you: voyage on the sea no more"—discoursed to them, and after a life of giving went to swell the hosts of heaven. The Master was the wise Supparaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 463 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: Phandana-Jātaka (The Lion and the Tree-Spirit)
title.zh: 樹神本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1897 (Francis & Neil)

region.en: A carpenter village outside Benares and the Himalaya woods
region.zh: 波羅奈城外木匠村與雪山林地

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 3 (trans. Francis & Neil, 1897)

summary.en: A lion lying under a palāsa tree is struck by a falling branch and, blaming the tree-deity, vows to tear the tree out root and branch. Meeting a carpenter seeking wheel-wood, he helpfully recommends the palāsa; but the tree-spirit, disguised as a woodman, persuades the carpenter that a wheel rimmed with a black lion's neck-skin is strongest—so the carpenter kills the lion, fells the tree, and both destroyer and destroyed perish together.
summary.zh: 黑獅臥波羅樹下，為落枝所傷，遷怒樹神，誓將樹連根拔起。遇木匠尋製輪之木，獅獻計薦波羅木；樹神化為樵夫，教匠人以黑獅頸皮包輪緣最堅，匠人遂殺獅伐樹——相爭者同歸於盡。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this on the bank of the river Rohinī to kinsmen taken up with a family quarrel. Of old, when Brahmadatta was king of Benares, there stood without the city a village of carpenters, among them a brahmin carpenter who gained his living bringing wood from the forest and making carts. In the Himalaya region stood a great palāsa tree, at whose root a black lion used to lie when hunting. One day a wind smote the tree, a dry branch fell on the lion's shoulder, and the pained beast leapt up in fear; finding no pursuer, he decided that the tree-deity could not away with his lying there, and in unseasonable anger struck the tree, crying that in a few days he would tear it out root and branch and chop it into chipmeal, and away he went in search of a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 475 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The brahmin carpenter had come that very neighbourhood in a waggon with two or three men to get wood for his trade, and was searching with adze and hatchet when the lion, hoping to see the back of his enemy, stood under the tree and hailed him in verse: what tree is it you want, O man with the axe? Amazed that a beast could talk like a man, the wright asked what wood made good cart-wheels, and the lion gladly answered, "Not sal, acacia, not mare's-ear, much less a shrub is good; there is a tree they call palāsa, and there's your best wheel-wood," and described its drooping branches so the man might know it, promising it would do for spoke, felloe, pole or any part of a cart. Joyful, the lion moved aside, and the wright began to fell the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 475 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tree-deity thought, "I never dropped anything on that beast; he fell in a rage out of season, and now he is for destroying my home, and I too shall be destroyed. I must find some way of destroying his majesty." Taking the shape of a woodman, the spirit came up and asked what the man would do with the tree; told it was for a cart-wheel on a black lion's advice, the spirit praised the plan but counseled more: flay the skin from a black lion's neck, a strip four fingers wide, and bind it round the outer edge of the wheel like a sheath of iron—then the wheel will be very strong and you will gain a great deal. "But where can I get the skin of a black lion?" "How stupid you are! Go and find the lion who told you of this tree, bring him here, and while he suspects nothing and points out where to cut, wait till he sticks out his jaw, smite him with your sharpest axe, kill him, take the skin, and fell the tree at your leisure."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 475 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The delighted carpenter killed the lion, cut down the tree, and went his way. "Thus palasa tree contends with beast, and beast with tree contends; so each with mutual dispute to death the other sends"—and so among men, where feud or quarrel arises, men cut capers peacock-wise; learn peace with all men, said the Master, and the quarrelling kinsmen were reconciled. Of that time the Master was the deity who lived in that wood and saw the whole business.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 475 (Francis & Neil 1897); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wise Matanga, Outcast Ascetic (Matanga Jataka, no. 497)
title.zh: 摩登伽賤種聖者本生（第四百九十七）

period: Jataka no. 497, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Benares and the kingdom of Mejjha, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈與彌闍國（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A Candala-born ascetic is beaten for defiling a rich girl's eyes, wins her as his wife, and stages a false descent from the moon as Great Brahma; her proud son Mandavya later reviles the same sage at an alms-hall, is twisted by city goblins, healed by the sage's rice-leavings, and outcasted with the other brahmins - while the kingdom whose king kills the sage is annihilated by hot ashes.
summary.zh: 賤種出身的聖者摩登伽因「不祥」被商人女眷僕從毆打，後娶得此女，假扮大梵天自月輪降世；其子曼達耶於施捨場辱罵聖者，被城中鬼神扭頸，賴聖者剩飯得癒，卻與眾婆羅門同被逐出種姓——而後殺害聖者的彌闍國被天神降下熱灰燼滅國。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this tale of king Udena, who had once broken a basket of red ants over a meditating elder. Long before, in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a Candala's son named Matanga. When the merchant's daughter Dittha-mangalika caught sight of him at the city gate she cried that she had seen an ill omen, washed her eyes with scented water, and her crowd beat the innocent man senseless. Matanga resolved never to move until he had her, and lay at her father's door for seven days until the girl was given to him. He kept her honourably, then left for the forest and in seven days mastered the eight attainments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Matanga Jataka (no. 497) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: He returned as the Great Brahma: Dittha-mangalika was coached to say her husband had gone to Brahma's heaven and would return at the full moon breaking the moon's disk. On that night the sage blazed through the sky, thrice circled Benares, descended, and touched her navel, leaving her with child and a prophecy that kings would pay tribute at her feet. Her son Mandavya grew rich, feeding sixteen thousand brahmins daily. When the ragged sage stood at the gate, Mandavya reviled him as a vile outcast and bade his servants kill him; the sage rose into the air - reviling a sage, he warned, avails as much as swallowing blazing fire - and the city deities, avenging him, twisted Mandavya's neck backwards and left the brahmins writhing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Matanga Jataka (no. 497) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: His mother fetched the sage's rice-leavings as an elixir: Mandavya rose cured and ashamed, and the sixteen thousand brahmins, having tasted a Candala's leavings, were put out of caste and moved to the king of Mejjha. Matanga next humbled the proud ascetic Jatimanta: his dropped tooth-sticks floated upstream into Jatimanta's hair, and when the ascetic cursed him to die with a bursting head, Matanga held the sun from rising until Jatimanta was dragged to him with a lump of clay on his head and plunged into the river. Later, men of Mejjha killed the sage for his alms-food; the deities rained hot ashes and wiped that kingdom from the earth. Udena was Mandavya, the Master said, and I was the wise Matanga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Matanga Jataka (no. 497) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: King Sivi Gives His Eyes (Sivi Jataka, no. 499)
title.zh: 屍毘王施眼本生（第四百九十九）

period: Jataka no. 499, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Aritthapura, kingdom of Sivi, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 屍毘國阿利提城（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Sivi, unsatisfied with six hundred thousand pieces a day in alms, vows to give part of his very self; Sakka tests him as a blind brahmin asking for an eye, the surgeon removes one and then the other, and by an Act of Truth on the worth of every suitor Sivi's eyes regrow as eyes of Truth that see a hundred leagues.
summary.zh: 屍毘王日施六十萬錢猶感不足，誓以身體所有施人；帝釋化作盲婆羅門索眼，御醫先後剜其二目，王無悔意；因誓願諦實，雙目重生為「諦實之眼」，能透山越牆遠觀百由旬。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: King Sivi of Aritthapura kept the ten royal virtues and gave six hundred thousand pieces daily at six alms-halls. Sitting on his throne on a full-moon day he decided that outside things no longer satisfied him: if a suitor asked his heart he would cut it out as one lifts a water-lily from a lake; if his flesh, he would carve it off; if his blood, he would fill a bowl with it; and if any demanded his eyes, he would pluck them out as one draws the pith from a palm-trunk. Bathed and adorned, he rode to the alms-hall to meet whatever came.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sivi Jataka (no. 499) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sakka, king of the gods, resolved to test the vow and took the shape of an old blind brahmin on a mound, stretching out his hand. The courtiers wept and offered pearls, coral, chariots and elephants instead; the king answered that a man who swears to give and then withholds puts his own neck in a snare. The surgeon Sivaka protested, then loosed the right eye with burning powders, severing the hanging ball; blood stained the royal robes. Gazing with his remaining eye, the king set the eyeball in the brahmin's socket, where it fixed like a blue lotus in bloom - and then, thrilled by the joy of the gift, he gave the second eye also.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sivi Jataka (no. 499) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Blind, Sivi handed his kingdom to his courtiers and withdrew to the park as an ascetic; Sakka's marble throne grew hot, and he came down to offer any boon. The king asked only death - for he was blind. Sakka bade him make an Act of Truth upon his gift. Whoever comes to ask of me, the king declared, he is dear to my heart: and one eye grew in the empty socket, then the other - eyes neither natural nor divine, but eyes of Truth Absolute that see a hundred leagues through rock and wall. Restored, the king preached to all Sivi: never eat food without giving something away. Ananda was the surgeon, Anuruddha was Sakka, and I was King Sivi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Sivi Jataka (no. 499) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Rohanta the Golden Deer King (Rohanta-miga Jataka, no. 501)
title.zh: 金鹿王本生（第五百零一）

period: Jataka no. 501, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Himalaya, Lake Rohanta (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山羅訶塔湖（象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Rohanta, golden king of eighty thousand deer, supports his blind parents in the Himalaya; snared at the drinking-place, he stays mute until his herd is safe, and his brother and sister refuse to abandon him though he begs them to flee; the softened hunter frees him, and with golden hairs as token teaches the Law in the queen's name to satisfy her dream-craving.
summary.zh: 金鹿王羅訶塔率八萬鹿群居喜馬拉雅，奉養失明雙親；於飲水處被獵人羅網所縛，先忍不發聲以免群鹿驚散，弟妹寧死不離；獵人動憫放生，鹿王贈金毛，教其代為說法以滿王后夢中求聽金鹿說法之願。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: When Brahmadatta ruled in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a golden stag in the Himalaya named Rohanta, king of eighty thousand deer, with a golden brother Citta-miga and golden sister Sutana; all three served their aged blind parents beside Lake Rohanta. A dying hunter told his son of the golden deer, and when Queen Khema dreamed of a gold-coloured stag preaching the Law with a voice like a golden bell, she woke crying for it. Feigning a woman's craving, she threatened to die without hearing such a stag, and the king sent the hunter's son with money to snare him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Rohanta-miga Jataka (no. 501) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The snare was set at the drinking-place. Caught at the pole's end, the Great Being stood feigning to drink until all eighty thousand had drunk and withdrawn; only then did he jerk at the noose - once till the skin split, twice till the flesh, thrice till the tendon - and raise the cry of capture. His brother Citta refused three times to flee: I am ready to lay down my life, I will not leave thee here. The doe Sutana ran a little way in fear, then returned to die beside him. The hunter came up with his spear, guessed they were born of one womb, and heard Citta plead: slay him and you slay all five, for he supports his blind parents; grant him life and you bestow life on us all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Rohanta-miga Jataka (no. 501) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hunter cut the thong, washed the blood away, and by his love and the Bodhisatta's perfection the wound closed without a mark. Learning the queen's craving was the cause, the stag bade him stroke his back - the hand came away covered with golden hairs - and taught him ten stanzas on the holy life to preach in his stead. The hunter recited them on a golden throne; the queen's craving was satisfied, the king heaped rewards on him, and the man chose instead to become an ascetic in the Himalaya. Channa was the huntsman and Sariputta the king; I was myself the royal stag Rohanta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Rohanta-miga Jataka (no. 501) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Campeyya-Jātaka (The Serpent King's Vow)
title.zh: 詹波龍王本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Campa river between Anga and Magadha, and the naga world beneath
region.zh: 鴦伽與摩竭陀間之瞻波河及龍界

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A poor man, dazzled by the glory of the serpent king Campeyya, longs for that splendour and is reborn in the naga palace—then, loathing the reptile shape, keeps the fast-day vows on an ant-heap by the road, yielding his body to any who want it. A snake-charmer seizes and tortures him for a month's profit; his consort Sumana, warned by three signs, follows, and king Uggasena buys the serpent's freedom, visits the jewelled naga world, and asks why one so glorious would be a hermit.
summary.zh: 貧者慕詹波龍王榮耀，感生龍宮；旋厭蛇身，於路旁蟻垤持齋布薩，自捨其身任人取用。弄蛇婆羅門捕而虐之月餘以牟利；其妻須摩那依三兆知之，訴於空中；鄔伽 Sena 王以金贖之，並遊龍界，問其何捨殊榮而為苦行者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master praised certain lay Brethren who had taken the fast-day vows, telling how wise men of old renounced even a Serpent King's glory to keep them. Of old the river Campa ran betwixt Anga and Magadha, where the serpent king Campeyya reigned in a jewelled palace under the water. King Magadha, defeated in battle, rode his charger into the flooded stream, and the serpent king took him to his throne and comforted him: by the serpent's power Magadha slew his rival and ruled both realms, paying yearly tribute at a jewelled pavilion, while all beheld his glory. A poor man going down with the crowd coveted that splendour, and dying was reborn seven days later on the dead king's couch. Ashamed of the reptile shape his merit had won, he put it off and ruled the serpents; but the serpent maidens again broke his fast-day vows, till he resolved to keep them among men: on fast days he lay coiled on an ant-heap by the high road, saying, "Those who desire my skin or any part of me, let them take it; or if any would have me a dancing snake, let them make me so."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 506 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Villagers built a pavilion over him and worshipped him as a serpent king, and women craved sons by his aid. His consort Sumana, fearing the world of men, asked by what sign she should learn of danger, and he led her to a lucky pond: "If any one strike me, the water will become turbid. If a roc bird carry me off, the water will disappear. If a snake-charmer seize me, the water will turn to the colour of blood." Then a young brahmin of Benares, schooled at Taxila in the charm that commands all things of sense, caught him on his way home: the charm pierced his ears like burning splinters, yet the serpent shut his eyes and hooded his head lest his poison destroy the man and break his virtue. Spat upon and blained, squeezed with a goat's-foot staff, his teeth broken, dragged by a cord through his nostrils, he bore the torment and never glanced at his tormentor, lying month after month in a basket, dancing for money in village after village, refusing frogs that none might be killed for his sake, and food, that he might not die in the basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 506 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: In a month the charmer came to Benares, and before the multitude at the palace court made the Great Being dance, while thousands waved kerchiefs and jewels showered about him. That day Sumana looked at the pond and saw the water red as blood; she traced his path, learned all in the frontier village, and came to Benares, where above the palace court in the air she stood lamenting. The serpent, ashamed, crept into his basket; the king, seeing the radiant shape in the sky, asked what she was. "No goddess I, nor Titaness, nor human, mighty king—a female of the serpent kind, come for a certain thing." He might burn the town to cinders, she said, but loves the holy way; caught on a holy day at the four-ways keeping his vows, he begs freedom. The king offered gold, a hundred kine, a village, jewelled earrings and thrones; the charmer wanted no gifts—the deed itself would be meritorious—and released the serpent, who shed his shape and stood a young man magnificently arrayed, swearing by wind-moving-mountains and sea-running-dry that he could never lie; and the king, believing, out of gratitude swore never to return ill for good.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 506 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Eager to visit the serpent's world, the king came with his army, and the Great Being made visible a wall of seven precious things, adorning all the approach; in Campeyya's halls, lit like the ruddy sun with a thousand perfumes and celestial harps, the king feasted seven days on divine food. On his fair seat he asked why one so glorious left such magnificence to lie on an ant-heap and keep the fast-day vows. "Not for life or sons or pelf do I wrestle with myself; 'tis my craving, if I can, to be born again as Man." "How does our world surpass thine?" "Comes control and cleansing when one is in the world of men, only there: once man, I'll never see nor birth nor death again." The king vowed henceforth to do manifold virtuous deeds; the Serpent King offered treasure without count—gold untold, pearls five thousand loads—to build houses of gold and enrich Benares, sending it loaded in hundreds of carts; from that time, they say, the ground was all golden throughout India. Devadatta was the snake-charmer, Rāhula's mother was Sumana, Sāriputta was Uggasena, and the Master was Campeyya, King of the Snakes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 506 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Hatthipāla-Jātaka (The Renunciation That Emptied Benares)
title.zh: 養象者本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and the Ganges bank hermitage
region.zh: 波羅奈與恆河岸精舍

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Four god-sons, promised to a childless chaplain by a bullied tree-deity, are named for elephant-, horse-, cow- and goat-herds and raised in those trades to keep them from the religious life. Yet Hatthipāla, offered the kingdom, refuses it—'death comes in youth as in age'—and renounces; one by one his brothers, the chaplain, the chaplain's wife, the king (taught by his queen's vulture parable), and the queen follow, until Benares stands empty and Sakka must build a hermitage thirty-six leagues long for the multitudes.
summary.zh: 樹神受迫而賜婆羅門四子，皆天神託生，取名養象、養馬、養牛、養羊，寄養各行以防出家。然長子 Hatthipāla 拒受王位，言「少年亦會死」，遂出家；諸弟、婆羅門夫婦、王（受王后禿鷹喻啟發）相繼棄俗，波羅奈城為之一空，帝釋遂為之營建三十六由旬精舍。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of the Renunciation, that it was not the first time he had made it. Of old, in Benares, king Esukārī and his chaplain, both childless and fast friends, bargained: if a son was born in the chaplain's house he should be lord of the kingdom, but if the king had a son he should be master of the chaplain's wealth. Meeting outside the south gate a wretched woman with seven hale sons begotten through prayer to the banyan tree, the chaplain for six days threatened to have the deity cut down and chopped piecemeal if no son was granted the king. The tree-goddess sought the Four Great Kings, the goblin war-lords, and at last Sakka, who found four meritorious god-sons—once weavers of Benares who had shared their winnings five ways—about to descend from the Heaven of the Thirty-three; they consented on their own terms: born in the chaplain's family, not the royal house, and renouncing the world while yet young. On the seventh day the goddess cleft the trunk and promised not one son but four, all to the chaplain, though they would never live in a worldly household.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 509 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The eldest, Hatthipāla, Elephant Driver, was entrusted to elephant-keepers to hinder his renouncing; Assapāla, the Groom, grew up among horse-keepers; Gopāla, the Cowherd, among cattle-breeders; Ajapāla, the Goatherd, among goat-herds. All ascetics were banished from the kingdom. When Hatthipāla was sixteen, king and chaplain, fearing royal splendour's confusions, disguised themselves as ascetics and went begging to his door; the lad welcomed them with delight, offering seats and water, till the chaplain revealed his purpose—to sprinkle him king if he saw him without renouncing. "Oh, my father, I want no royalty; I will renounce the world." "First learn the Vedas, get you wealth and wife and sons... sweet is the wood to live in then." "Truth comes not by the Vedas nor by gold; nor getting sons will keep from getting old; from sense there is release, as wise men know; in the next birth we reap as now we sow." And to the king's blessing—"may they see a hundred years of health in store for thee"—the prince answered that no man has a covenant with old age, and that as a ferryman's boat is left at the further shore, so mortals tend to sickness, old age and death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 509 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Hatthipāla departed to the Ganges bank with a league-long company, to wait for his brothers and all Benares. Then the test was repeated: Assapāla refused the umbrella his brother had spewed out—"pleasures of sense are but morass and mire"—and followed; Gopāla, like a man who has found his lost cow's track, said "never put off till the morrow what should be done to-day," and followed; Ajapāla, youngest, said death comes in youth as in age and none bears a mark of it, and followed. Then the chaplain, "a sonless man is a disbranched tree," led out sixty thousand brahmins; and the king, greedy for the chaplain's treasure, was taught by his queen a parable: she heaped dog's-flesh ringed with a snare, and the wise vultures, too heavy to rise, disgorged and flew free, while the fools that ate on were caught. "A brahmin vomits out his lusts, and wilt thou eat the same? He who eats a vomit, sire, deserves the deepest blame." Repenting, the king left his sovranty; the queen opened the storehouses and engraved on a golden plate where the treasure lay; and the whole city emptied itself, shops standing open, none turning to look.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 509 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The company grew till it covered thirty leagues; Sakka, perceiving what was afoot, ordered Vissakamma to build on the Ganges bank a hermitage six-and-thirty leagues long and fifteen broad, with leaf-huts, pallets, wells and fruit-trees, everything necessary for the religious, and to banish all hideous sounds and hateful beasts from the place. Hatthipāla entered by a footpath, took the ascetic's dress, and admitted the rest to the Brotherhood, setting apart huts for women with young boys, for old women, for the childless, and for the men. A certain king, hearing there was no king in Benares, came and was admitted with his band; six other kings joined them—these seven kings renounced their wealth—and Hatthipāla's teaching, quelling each arising thought of lust, saved the multitude from hell, from animal birth, from the ghost world and from Titan birth, two-thirds of them passing to the Brahma world. Of that time, king Suddhodana was Esukārī, Mahāmāyā his queen, Kassapa the chaplain, Sāriputta was Hatthipāla, Moggallāna was Gopāla, and the Master was Hatthipāla himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 509 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: The Prince of the Iron House (Ayoghara Jataka, no. 510)
title.zh: 鐵室太子本生（第五百一十）

period: Jataka no. 510, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Benares, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A jealous co-wife's prayer turns her into an ogress who devours two newborn princes; the third is born and raised for sixteen years in an iron house; paraded for his coronation, the prince counts womb and prison as two hells, refuses the kingdom in a torrent of stanzas on death, and walks out - with his father, court and the whole city following him to the hermitage Sakka has built.
summary.zh: 妒妻咒願成羅剎，連吞二位新生王子；第三子於鐵室中降生並被囚養十六年；及至登基出巡，太子自省：十月處母胎如糞獄，十六年居鐵室如牢獄，縱脫羅剎之手仍不免老死——遂連篇偈頌堅辭王位出走，父王、臣民舉城相隨，入帝釋所造精舍出家。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: A barren co-wife of the Benares royal house prayed in anger to devour her rival's offspring, and was reborn a goblin. When the queen bore her first son the goblin snatched him before her eyes and crunched him like an onion; a second child met the same fate. When the Bodhisatta was conceived the king summoned all the smiths of the realm and built a house wholly of iron, pillars and all, lit continually with lamps; there the queen bore a marked prince, named Ayoghara-kumara, the Prince of the Iron House, while the ogress perished seeking the water of Vessavana to drink.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Ayoghara Jataka (no. 510) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: At sixteen the king resolved to set the kingdom on him, and the prince, decked for coronation, made his circuit of the decorated city and asked the courtiers what fault was his that he had been caged so long. None, they said; a goblin devoured your brothers, and the iron house saved your life. He pondered: ten months in my mother's womb were as the Hell of Dung, sixteen years in this prison as the Ussada hell; and though I have escaped the goblin I have not escaped old age and death. In twenty-four stanzas he declined the throne - no warlike prowess stays death, no juggler's trick cozens it, no serpent's venom or physician's skill - and asked his father's leave for the religious life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Ayoghara Jataka (no. 510) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king refused. Then, as a mad elephant bursts his steel chains and a young lion breaks out of a golden cage, the prince burst his carnal desires, saluted his parents, and departed; his father cried that he wanted no kingdom and went with him, and the queen, the courtiers and every soul in Benares left their houses behind and followed - a crowd twelve leagues long - into the hermitage Sakka had caused to be built. The king's parents were that royal pair, and I was myself the Wise Ayoghara.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Ayoghara Jataka (no. 510) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: The King's Debt to the Man-Ogre (Jayaddisa Jataka, no. 513)
title.zh: 勝武王償羅剎債本生（第五百一十三）

period: Jataka no. 513, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Kingdom of Kampilla, Northern Panchala, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北般闍羅劍浮沙國（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A queen's rival became an ogress and devoured two princes but reared the third on human flesh; generations later that man-eater waylays King Jayaddisa, who buys a day's grace to pay a brahmin, and the crown prince Alinasattu goes in his father's place, wins the ogre's reverence by his fearlessness, proves him the king's long-lost uncle, and converts him to the ascetic life.
summary.zh: 王后情敵墮為羅剎，吞食二位王子，卻將第三子當獸撫養、以人肉為食；多年後此人形羅剎攔路擒獲勝武王，王以須償婆羅門偈金為由乞一日之期；太子勝軍代父赴約，無畏供身，感化羅剎，並查明其實為王之失散長兄，勸其出家。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: A queen's rival in the harem prayed to devour her offspring and became an ogress. Twice she seized and crunched the newborn prince; the third time guards turned her away before she could eat, and the child, suckling at her breast out of ignorance, kindled a mother's love: she hid him in a rock-cave of the cemetery and fed him on human flesh until, losing the magic root that masked his shape, he prowled the forest road as a man-eater. The fourth prince, born safe after her death, was called Jayaddisa, the Victor, and his son was Alinasattu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Jayaddisa Jataka (no. 513) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: King Jayaddisa, who had promised a brahmin four stanzas worth a hundred pieces each, was returning from the hunt with a slain antelope when the ogre leapt up crying: after seven days' fast, a mighty prey at last. The king offered him the venison and was refused; he offered nothing but truth - a promise made to a brahmin is still unpaid - and the ogre gave him till dawn. He paid Nanda the brahmin four thousand pieces, told his son, and set out to die; but Alinasattu would not have it: if you go I will follow you, and both alike will cease to be - and the king let the boy go in his place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Jayaddisa Jataka (no. 513) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: To the ogre the prince offered his own body freely: eat me and free my father, for death I do not fear - I have weighed birth and death in this world and the worlds to be. Sent to gather firewood for his own pyre, he returned with a blazing pile and bade the ogre stand no longer gaping but take and slay him; the ogre confessed that to eat one so truthful would burst his skull in seven pieces. The prince, noting that the creature's eyes were red and unwinking yet cast a shadow, declared him no ogre at all but his father's lost brother, proved it before a clairvoyant ascetic, and left him ordained in the forest while the king founded the town of Cullakammasadamma for the ascetics' support. The man-eater was Angulimala, and prince Alinasattu was myself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Jayaddisa Jataka (no. 513) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Chaddanta-Jātaka (The Six-Tusked Elephant King)
title.zh: 六牙象王本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Lake Chaddanta in the Himalaya (legendary); Benares
region.zh: 雪山六牙池（傳說之地）與波羅奈

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The white six-tusked elephant king Chaddanta, slighted by his lesser queen Cullasubhaddā twice—with dry twigs instead of flowers, and a seven-shoot lotus given to her rival—vows rebirth as a queen of Benares and sends a hunter to kill him. The hunter Sonuttara journeys seven years, seven months and seven days, shoots him with a poisoned arrow from a pit, and the dying Bodhisatta, seeing the robber's yellow robe and feeling no anger, saws off his own six-rayed tusks as a gift toward Omniscience; the queen who receives them dies of grief that very day.
summary.zh: 白六牙象王遭次妃以枯枝代花、七莖蓮予妒妃之辱，誓生為波羅奈王后，遣獵人殺己。獵人跋涉七年七月七日，伏坑以毒箭射之；象王見其黃衣而不怒，忍痛自鋸六色光芒之象牙以施，發願趨一切智。后接牙當日心碎而亡。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A female novice of Sāvatthī, hearing the Law, suddenly recalled a former existence: in the time of Chaddanta the elephant she had been one of his wives, and she had harboured a slight grudge and sent a hunter who killed him with a poisoned arrow; she laughed, then wept aloud, and the Master, smiling, told the assembly, "This young Sister wept, on recalling a sin she once committed against me." Of old, by lake Chaddanta in the Himalaya, girt with seven mountains and ringed with leagues of lilies and lotuses, dwelt eight thousand royal elephants; their chief, the Bodhisatta, was pure white with red feet and face, eighty-eight cubits high, with a trunk like a silver rope and tusks thirty cubits long that emitted six-coloured rays; he honoured the pacceka buddhas and lived in a golden cave with his two head queens, Cullasubhaddā and Mahāsubhaddā.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 514 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Striking a sāl tree in full flower as the herd disported itself, the king showered flowers and pollen on Mahāsubhaddā, who stood to leeward, but on Cullasubhaddā, to windward, dry twigs, dead leaves and red ants; and when, after the bathing of the herd, an elephant offered him a seven-shoot lotus, he took it in his trunk, sprinkled the pollen on his forehead, and presented it to Mahāsubhaddā. Twice his lesser queen conceived a grudge. Entertaining five hundred pacceka buddhas, she put up a prayer over her gift of wild fruit: may I be reborn a royal maiden of the Madda line, become chief queen of the king of Benares, and send a hunter with a poisoned arrow to slay this elephant and have a pair of his six-rayed tusks brought me. She took no food, pined away, died, and was born as the Madda king's daughter Subhaddā, married to the king of Benares and chief of his sixteen thousand wives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 514 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Recalling her former existences, she feigned sickness, and when the king promised all joys, she demanded that all the hunters of his three-hundred-league kingdom be assembled before she named her desire. Among the sixty thousand who came she spied Sonuttara, broad of foot, thick-bearded, scarred, once an enemy of the Great Being; from the topmost floor of the palace, hand stretched to the northern Himalayas, she described the seven mountains, the Golden Cliff, and the great banyan tree where the six-tusked white elephant dwelt with his herd of eight thousand, whose wrath would consume any man who saw them. Terrified, the hunter was reassured—her prayer to the pacceka buddhas would be fulfilled—and given a thousand pieces and a hogshead sack of provisions, leather ropes, elephant shoes and a parachute. Thrice sending back his retinues, he alone crossed eighteen wild regions, felled thickets, crossed morass and flood, and climbed mountain after mountain by grappling-iron, peg and rope, descending the last like a bird on his leather parachute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 514 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: After seven years, seven months and seven days the hunter dug a pit by the pool, and in false top-knot and yellow robes shot the king with a poisoned arrow. Mad with pain, the king had wellnigh slain him when a yellow robe met his eyes. Extinguishing his anger he asked why wounded: the queen of Kāsi, said the hunter, had dreamed of him and coveted his tusks. "Rich store of goodly tusks have I: 'tis at my life the wretch aims." He bade the hunter saw off his tusks before he died; the Great Being bent his body, let him climb his trunk, and guided the saw with his own trunk, cutting them off as it were sprouts. "I give them not because I value them not; the tusks of omniscience are a hundred thousand times dearer; may this deed win me Omniscience." By the tusks' magic the hunter reached Benares in seven days; his herd mourned him, and pacceka buddhas kept vigil at his pyre; and the queen, taking the six-rayed tusks on her fan, remembered her dear lord; her heart broke, and she died that day. The hunter is now Devadatta; the elephant was the Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 514 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Sambulā-Jātaka (The Devoted Wife and the Leper Prince)
title.zh: 賢妃本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and the forest hermitage
region.zh: 波羅奈與林中隱廬

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: When leprosy drives the viceroy Sotthisena into the forest to die, his radiant wife Sambulā refuses to leave him and nurses him daily. An ogre seizes her at the bathing pool; her lament heats Sakka's throne, and the god drives the ogre off with his thunderbolt and chains him to a far mountain. Slandered as unfaithful, Sambulā performs an Act of Truth and heals the leprosy; back on the throne Sotthisena neglects her until his father rebukes him, and the pair live happily after.
summary.zh: 癩病襲儲君須提慎那，遁入林中待死；其妻三木羅不棄，日日侍疾。浴池畔為食人夜叉所執，其哀慟熱帝釋座，神以金剛杵逐之，鎖於第三重山。遭疑不貞，乃以真實語誓願癒其病。還宮後王疏遠之，老王出家為僧訓子，夫婦和樂終老。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of queen Mallikā, the devoted wife—"not now only, but formerly too, she was a devoted wife." Of old king Brahmadatta had a son named Sotthisena, made viceroy, whose chief consort Sambulā was so radiant she seemed a lamp-flame shining in a sheltered spot. Leprosy appeared, the physicians failed, and the loathsome prince cried, "What good is my kingdom to me? I shall perish without a friend in the wilderness," and left his harem. Sambulā, though he made many attempts to stop her, refused to return: "I will watch over you, my lord, in the forest," and went out from the city with him. In a leaf hut by a well-watered spot she rose early, swept the hermitage, ground simples and anointed his sores, gathered wild fruit, washed him with powders and clay, bathed his feet, and lay down by his side; thus she watched over her lord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 519 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, bathing at a mountain cave, she lit the whole forest with the radiance of her person, and a goblin out hunting prey fell in love and questioned her from his hiding. She told him plainly: her lord lay sick in the forest, she tended him alone, and the venison in her basket was for him. "What good is this sick lord of thine to thee? No wife, but nurse is what he craves. I will thy husband be." She refused—he was worn and wretched, let the ogre woo some fairer dame—and when he threatened to eat her, seized her by the arm, she still deplored only that her dear lord's love should fall away. Then the abode of Sakka shook with the efficacy of her virtue, and the god came with all speed, thunderbolt in hand, and standing above the goblin threatened that his skull be riven into seven fragments if he touched her; the goblin let her go, and Sakka, thinking he would offend again, bound him with celestial chains and set him on the third mountain from thence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 519 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Escaped from the ogre, she fled to her hut in the moonlight, lamenting like a bird that finds its fledglings dead, hailing priests and brahmins, tigers and grasses, Night and Ganges and Himavat in her sorrow. Sotthisena, suspecting a lover, put her to the test; she declared she was seized by the ogre and saved by Sakka, but he answered that womenkind are too clever and their truth a rarity. "Though you do not believe me, by virtue of the truth I speak, I will heal you." Filling a pot of water and performing an Act of Truth—"May Truth for aye my shelter be, as I love no man more than thee"—she poured the water on his head, and the leprosy left him as copper rust is washed away in acid. They returned to Benares; the king raised the umbrella over his son and made Sambulā chief queen by sprinkling, then himself adopted the ascetic life in the park.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 519 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Sotthisena ignored her and took his pleasure with other women, and she grew thin and pale with jealousy till her veins stood out; to her father-in-law the ascetic she lamented that she no longer reigned in his affections. The old man rebuked his son: when you were crushed by leprosy and hid in the forest, she went with you and ministered to you, and by the power of truth healed your sickness, and now you do not even know the place of her sitting and uprising—an act of treachery to a friend like this is a sin. A loving wife is ever hard to find, he said; do thou, O king, to Sambulā be true. The king asked her pardon, conferred on her all power, and promised that he and the maidens would be obedient to her command; thenceforth the pair lived happily, and after a life of charity the ascetic passed to the heaven of Brahma. Sambulā of that time was queen Mallikā, Sotthisena the king of Kosala, and the ascetic father the Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 519 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: The Kingdom Where Everyone Cursed the King (Gandatindu Jataka, no. 520)
title.zh: 萬民詛咒昏君本生（第五百二十）

period: Jataka no. 520, composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; English translation by Robert Chalmers, 1901

region.en: Kingdom of Kampilla, Northern Panchala, India (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北般闍羅劍浮沙國（印度，象徵定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 5 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A tree deity - the Bodhisatta - admonishes the careless king Pancala in eleven verses, then guides the disguised king and chaplain through villages where a thorn-pierced elder, an old mother with unwed daughters, a ruined ploughman, a kicked milkman, children mourning a calf skinned for a scabbard, and even a frog eaten by crows all curse the king by name; chastened, the king rules righteously ever after.
summary.zh: 菩提薩埵化身丁多迦樹神，以十一偈諫誡怠政的般闍羅王；王與國師喬裝出巡，沿途聽聞老者足刺荊棘、老嫗之女無人可嫁、犁伕失牛、賣乳者被牛踢翻、童子哭祭被剝皮製鞘的小牛、乃至乾塘中青蛙被烏鴉啄食——無不指名咒罵國王；王乃懺悔，自此行正法治國，廣行布施。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); Jataka/moral material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: King Pancala ruled unrighteously in the kingdom of Kampilla: oppressed by taxation, his subjects took wives and children to the forest like wild beasts, fencing their empty houses with thorn branches and hiding all day. The Bodhisatta was then the divinity of a tinduka tree outside the city, honored yearly with an offering worth a thousand pieces; pitying his benefactor, he stood in mid-air at the king's bedhead one night, bright as the new-risen sun, and admonished him in eleven verses: zeal is the way to Nirvana, sloth leads to death; a slack king is no master of his realm, and the careless sink here to ruin and hereafter to hell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Gandatindu Jataka (no. 520) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Chastened, the king handed his kingdom to his ministers and went out with the chaplain disguised. In the first village an old man's foot was pierced by a thorn as he barred his house at dusk, and he cursed the king by name; the chaplain tried to excuse him, but the elder answered that by night they are prey to thieves and by day to the king's men, and lewd folk abound when evil kings bear sway. In the next village an old mother fallen from a bush cursed Brahmadatta because her two grown daughters lived unwed; a ploughman whose ox fell under the ploughshare cursed him; a milkman kicked by a vicious cow cursed him; children who saw a calf skinned for a sword-sheath while its mother roared and pined cursed him; and when the pair reached a dry tank where crows were striking frogs, the Bodhisatta put the curse into the frog's mouth too - and when the chaplain defended the king, the frog answered that the king, though people are oppressed, deems the priest's policy the best.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Gandatindu Jataka (no. 520) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king and his priest concluded that every creature down to the frogs in the forest cursed them, returned to the city, and ruled thenceforth righteously, devoting themselves to charity and other good works. The discourse was really preached to the king of Kosala; the divinity of the tinduka tree was myself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Gandatindu Jataka (no. 520) (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Ummadantī-Jātaka (The Beauty and the King's Trial)
title.zh: 鬱摩達女本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Aritthapura in the kingdom of the Sivis (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 濕毗國阿利陶城（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Ummadantī, of more than mortal beauty won by a half-robe given to a monk, is branded a witch by the dazed royal soothsayers and married to the commander Ahipāraka instead. At the Kattika festival she scatters flowers on the passing king, who loses his wits; Ahipāraka stages a hollow-tree oracle to spare him sin, and then, offering her as a free gift, refuses the king's relief until the king renounces the wrong—not for all the world would he do injustice—and so is cured of his infatuation.
summary.zh: 鬱摩達女因布施半衣與比丘而得絕世容貌；相士們見之失常，誣為妖婦，遂嫁統帥阿羅波羅迦。節慶之夜她向巡遊之王擲花，王遂神魂顛倒。統帥設空心樹神諭之計以護王免罪，並以妻相贈；王言「縱得全世，不行不義」，終斷痴念。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a backsliding Brother who, pierced with love's shafts for a woman seen on his alms round, wasted to a wild-deer leanness and gave up instruction and meditation. Of old, in Aritthapura in the kingdom of the Sivis, king Sivi made over his realm to his son, prince Sivi, who made his friend Ahipāraka commander-in-chief. In the same city dwelt the merchant Tiritavaccha, worth eighty crores, whose daughter Ummadantī was of more than mortal loveliness: all worldlings who beheld her were intoxicated as with strong drink. Sent for by the king to be tested by the fortune-tellers, she so unhinged the brahmins that some put their morsels on their heads and some threw them at the wall; furious, they told the king she was a witch, and she was not sent for—and she conceived a grudge, saying, "Should I ever see the king, I shall know what to do." Her father gave her to Ahipāraka, her husband's darling and delight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 527 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her beauty was the fruit of an old merit: once, a poor girl of Benares, laboring three years for a scarlet robe, met by the river a monk of Buddha Kassapa robbed of his garments and dressed in broken boughs; she tore her new robe in two and gave him half, then, seeing him blaze like the newly-risen sun, gave him the other half too, praying, "May I in some future existence be of such surpassing beauty that no one who sees me may have power to control himself, and no other woman be more beautiful." Born now in Aritthapura, at the Kattika festival her husband warned her not to show herself to the king; but when the king's chariot came first to their door in the moonlit procession, she stood at the window and threw flowers over him with all the charm of a sylph. The king, maddened with passion, failed even to recognise the house, asked his charioteer whose it was and whether the lady were unwed, and turning back from the festival lay on his couch chattering of Ummadantī: "I would be Ahipāraka one night or haply twain, and Ummadantī thus enjoyed, he might o'er Sivi reign."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 527 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Told that the king had gone only to his door, Ummadantī called him a pot-bellied fellow with huge teeth, and Ahipāraka saw that if the king did not get her he would die. "My duty is to restore him to life, if it can be done without sin on king or me." So he schooled a stout knave to sit within a hollow tree, a sacred shrine, and when the general made his offering and prayed to know why the king lay chattering, the knave delivered the lesson: your king is not sick but infatuated with your wife Ummadantī; if he gets her he will live, otherwise he will die. Repeating this as from the yakkha of the shrine, the servant secured the purpose, and Ahipāraka told the king the strange thing the yakkha had said. The king, shamed that his vileness was known to the very yakkhas, took his stand in righteousness—"Fallen from grace no godhead shall I win, and all the world will hear of my great sin"—and the two, in alternate stanzas, the general offering her as a free gift, the king pleading for his friend and his own honor, disputed the gift till dawn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 527 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: "Whoso shall wrong his neighbour nor repent, saying, 'See here a lord omnipotent,' will ne'er be found to live out half his days, and gods will view his conduct with dispraise," said the king. "I would not by an unjust act e'en heaven itself attain, no, not if, Ahipāraka, the whole world I should gain." Like the bull that leads the herd, so should the chief steer a direct course; father and chief and guardian of the land, he took his stand as champion of its rights, to his own will no more subservient: do righteously to parents, wife, children, friends, in war and travel, town and village, to brahmins and ascetics, to beasts and birds—thus heaven at last. When the king had thus been taught the law by his commander-in-chief, he got rid of his infatuation for Ummadantī. Of that time Ānanda was the charioteer Sunanda, Sāriputta was Ahipāraka, Uppalavaṇṇā was Ummadantī, and the Master was king Sivi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 527 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Saṃkicca-Jātaka (The Sage and the Parricide King)
title.zh: 僧祇叉本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares; Dayapassa park
region.zh: 波羅奈；達亞帕沙園

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Prince Brahmadatta murders his father for the throne despite his friend Saṃkicca's warnings; haunted like Ajātasattu, he calls for the friend who fled to the Himalaya. Fifty years later Saṃkicca returns with five hundred ascetics, and to the king who asks how transgressors fare after death he preaches the eight great hells, the parricide's torments, the river Vetoaraṇī—and then, opening the earth, shows the angel-worlds—and the king is comforted.
summary.zh: 婆羅多太子不聽摯友僧祇叉之諫，弒父篡位；如阿闍世王般為怖所纏，遣人尋友。五十年後，僧祇叉率五百仙人歸，為王說八大熱獄、弒親之苦、地獄溫泉之河，復開地示天界；王心得安。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka containing vivid depictions of hell; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this in Jivaka's mango grove concerning Ajātasattu, who at Devadatta's instigation had murdered his own father, and after Devadatta was swallowed by the earth at the gate of Jetavana lived in terror, finding no enjoyment in his royal splendour, till he went by night to the Tathāgata and his fears abated. "Not now only, but of old too, this man, after murdering his father, through me recovered his peace of mind." Of old, in Benares, prince Brahmadatta and the priest's son Saṃkicca grew up together in the palace, great friends, schooled at Taxila; the prince was made viceroy and the Bodhisatta lived with him. One day, beholding his father's glory, the viceroy thought, "If I shall wait for his death, I shall be an old man before I succeed to the crown. I will kill my father and make myself king," and told his friend. "Friend, the murder of a father is a serious matter. That way lies the road to hell. You must not do this deed," said the Bodhisatta, opposing him a third time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 530 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the prince's attendants fell in with the plot and devised the murder of the king, the Bodhisatta thought, "I will not consort with people like these," and without taking leave of father or mother escaped by a house-door and hid himself in the Himalaya, where he embraced the ascetic life and attained the powers of ecstatic meditation, living on roots and wild berries; many youths of good family were ordained by him. The prince put his father to death and enjoyed great glory for a very short time; then he was terror-stricken, lost his peace of mind, and was like one who had found his punishment in hell. Calling to mind the friend who had tried to stop him, he sang his praises through harem and court and longed for him: if he had been here, he would not have let me slay my father, and he would free me from this terror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 530 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: After fifty years in the Himalayas the Bodhisatta thought, "The king remembers me. I must go to him and teach him the Law and remove his fears," and with five hundred ascetics passed through the air to the garden called Dayapassa. Warned by the garden-keeper, the king doffed the five emblems of royal pomp—umbrella, turban, yak-tail fan, shoes and sword—and came on foot to greet the sage, recalling the converse of old days. Then, as occasion arose, he put his question: "How fare transgressors after death? Born to what state are they? I too have erred from righteousness." "Mark, sire, and understand: shouldst thou point out the road to one gone hopelessly astray, and he should follow thy advice, no thorns beset his way... Right is like the high road, wrong is but a bye-road; right to heaven aye wins its way, wrong to hell leads men astray."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 530 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Saṃkicca told of the hells: Sañjīva, Kāḷasutta, Roruva, Saṅghāta, the Great Avīci, with Tapana and Patāpana—eight major hells, and sixteen times more the minor Ussadas—four-square with fourfold doors, walled and domed with iron no flame may melt, where all who have outraged saints fall headlong and rise no more, their mangled frames piecemeal like fish on toast; seeking outlet on every side, baffled at every door by barring gods. The parricide is boiled in an iron cauldron till he peels, pierced with steel shafts, blinded and fed on filth, a hot iron ball between his jaws while vultures rend his tongue; the matricide is ploughed with iron shares and given his own blood to drink; adulterers hang on the iron silk-cotton trees of the river Vetoaraṇī, and slayers of beasts are driven into a briny flood. "Through virtue stored on earth of old the good to heaven attain," and opening the earth he showed the king the angel-worlds: "bear righteous sway throughout thy realm, my king, for justice done is merit won, nor e'er regret will bring." The king was comforted, and the Master identified the Birth: Ajātasattu was the king, and the sage Saṃkicca was himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 530 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Kusa-Jātaka (The Ugly Prince and the Radiant Bride)
title.zh: 菅草王子本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Kusāvatī in the Malla country and Sāgala in Madda (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 末羅國拘舍婆提城與摩達國娑伽羅城（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Granted by Sakka a wise but ugly son, king Okkāka's queen seeks a bride as lovely as the golden image her son himself has wrought—and finds Pabhāvatī, whose radiance lights a dark room. Hid from her by day, Kusa is discovered at a lotus-pool; she flees home, and he follows as a humble cook in her father's palace for seven months, until Sakka's ruse brings seven suitors with armies and her father threatens to hack her in seven pieces—whereupon she reveals the 'slave' as the lion-voiced king, who routs them all and marries off her seven sisters to the seven kings.
summary.zh: 天帝賜與智慧而貌醜之子菅草；其自鑄金像遍尋天下，終得容光可照暗室之婆薮跋提。因其例禁晝見，象糞馬糞戲之、騎象窺之、蓮池擒之，她終遁回母國。菅草化名入宮為庖丁七月；帝釋計使七王來求婚，父怒欲分尸七段遣之，她乃揭穿「賤役」實為獅吼之王。王大破七軍，以其七妹配七王，夫婦和樂。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka linked by commentators to Beauty-and-the-Beast tale-types; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a backsliding Brother smitten by a fair lady: through love of a woman, mighty sages of old lost their power and came to misery. Of old, in the Malla kingdom, king Okkāka's realm lacked an heir; dancing women were exposed in vain, and queen-consort Sīlavatī herself was exposed with religious sanction. Her virtue heated Sakka's throne; the god, disguised as an aged brahmin, took her hand before the jeering crowd, caused a hut to appear, and carried her to the heaven of the Thirty-three, where on the seventh day she knew him and asked a son. "Not merely one, lady: one wise but ugly, the other handsome but a fool; which first?" "The wise one." Sakka gave her kusa grass, a heavenly robe, sandal-wood, a coral-tree flower and a Kokanada lute, and bore her back to the king's couch; in ten months she bore a son named for the grass, Kusa, and later a second, Jayampati. Kusa, so wise that untaught he mastered every art, at sixteen was to receive the kingdom—but he had fashioned of gold a female image of matchless beauty, and vowed to wed only a woman like it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 531 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The councillors bore the image through India; everywhere the people admired the divine nymph, but nowhere could they match her to any daughter—till at Sāgala in Madda the humpbacked nurse, sent for water, struck the golden image, her runaway foster-child, on the cheek; finding it gold, she boasted her Pabhāvatī, eldest of the Madda king's seven daughters, worth a sixteenth part more. The envoys rejoiced, the marriage was contracted, and queen Sīlavatī made a family observance the condition: no wife might see her husband by daylight till she had conceived. So Kusa reigned with Pabhāvatī, meeting her only in the dark, lest his bride see his radiance. Yet he longed to see her, and his mother's devices told against her: in the elephant-stall he pelted her with dung, in the stable with dirt; when his handsome brother rode by she saw only the impertinent elephant-keeper—Kusa himself, betraying his joy with gesticulating hands; in the lotus-pool, hidden by a leaf, he seized her hand: "I am king Kusa." She cried, "A goblin is catching hold of me," swooned, and fled home to her father that day; and Kusa, too proud to hold her, let her go, vowing to win her back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 531 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her scorn had old roots: in a former birth, when his sister-in-law gave his cake to a paccekabuddha, he snatched it back in anger—hence his ugliness—and prayed that wherever she dwelt he might carry her off as bride. In sorrow he took a thousand pieces, his five weapons and his Kokanada lute, traveled a hundred leagues a day, and entered Sāgala as minstrel, then apprentice potter, basket-maker and gardener, each time making work for her hand, which she threw down in rage while her sisters laughed. As the king's cook he surpassed himself, and climbing to the princesses' dwellings was reviled by Pabhāvatī: "Kusa, for thee by day and night to bear this burden is not right; haste back to Kusāvatī; thy ugly form I loth to see." "Bound by thy beauty's spell, Pabhāvatī, my native land has little charm; Madda's fair realm is ever my delight, my crown resigned, to live in thy dear sight," he answered. The humpbacked slave, bribed with a golden necklace, praised him through thirteen stanzas—"Esteem him not by outward form or height, Pabhāvatī; great glory his, so do whate'er is pleasing in his sight"—till her mistress cowed her with threats of a cut tongue.
