At his word the earth bursts open on every side, and from the clefts arise countless myriads of Bodhisattvas with gold-coloured bodies and the thirty-two signs, each with a retinue like the sands of sixty Ganges rivers; they salute the two Tathagatas seated in the stupa, while fifty intermediate kalpas pass unnoticed, and Maitreya, baffled, asks whence this unheard-of multitude has come.
summary.zh: 他方菩薩請於佛滅後在此娑婆世界弘通法華，佛不許：我此娑婆自有菩薩眾，數如六十恆河沙。語畢，娑婆世界大地悉皆震裂，從地涌出無量千萬億菩薩，金色之身、三十二相，各攜眷屬，多者如六十恆河沙之數；漸次涌出，禮拜虛空中二佛並坐之多寶塔，經五十中劫而大眾如一瞬；彌勒菩薩惑然問佛：此無量菩薩從何所來？

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); scripture material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Out of the multitude of Bodhisattvas who had flocked from other worlds, some eight times equal to the sands of the river Ganges rose from the assembled circle and, stretching out their joined hands, asked leave to proclaim the Dharmaparyaya in this Saha-world after the extinction of the Lord. The Lord answered: Nay, young men of good family, why should you occupy yourselves with this task? I have here in this Saha-world thousands of Bodhisattvas equal to the sands of sixty Ganges rivers, who at the last period after my extinction shall keep, read and proclaim this Dharmaparyaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIV 'Issuing of Bodhisattvas from the Gaps of the Earth' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: No sooner had the Lord uttered these words than the Saha-world burst open on every side, and from within the clefts arose many hundred thousand myriads of kotis of Bodhisattvas with gold-coloured bodies and the thirty-two characteristic signs of a great man, who had been staying in the element of ether underneath this great earth, close to this Saha-world. Each of these Bodhisattvas had a train of thousands of Bodhisattvas similar to the sands of sixty Ganges rivers; there were those with a train equal to the sands of fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, ten, five, four, three, two Ganges rivers; those with a single follower; and those standing isolated — they cannot be numbered, counted or calculated, the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the gaps of the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: After they had successively emerged they went up to the stupa of precious substances which stood in the sky, where the Lord Prabhutaratna, the extinct Tathagata, was seated along with the Lord Sakyamuni on the throne; they saluted the feet of both Tathagatas and of the images of Tathagatas produced from the Lord Sakyamuni's body, circumambulated them, celebrated them with hymns, and kept themselves at a little distance with joined hands. While they were saluting, fifty intermediate kalpas in full rolled away, during which the Lord Sakyamuni and the four classes of the audience remained silent; then the Lord produced such an effect of magical power that the four classes fancied it had been no more than one afternoon. Then the four chiefest of that host — Vishesvaritra, Anantaviritra, Vimalakritaviritra and Supratishthitaviritra — asked whether the Lord was in health and the creatures docile; and Maitreya, with the eight hundred thousand myriads of Bodhisattvas like the sands of the Ganges, questioned the Lord in amazement: we never yet saw so great a host; whence have these Bodhisattvas come?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Physician and his Poisoned Sons (Lotus Sutra)
title.zh: 良醫與病子喻（法華經）

region.en: The Buddha's disclosure of his incalculably long lifetime, told as a family of sick children (symbolic pin — Ganges valley)
region.zh: 佛自宣久遠壽量，以病子之家為喻（象徵性定位——恆河流域）

period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884 (Kern ch. XV 'Duration of Life of the Tathagata'; Kumarajiva's ch. 16)

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: The Buddha announces that he attained enlightenment countless aeons ago and that his apparent extinction is a device: a skilled physician returns from a journey to find his many sons poisoned and rolling on the ground; those of right notions take his remedy, but the perverted refuse it, so he leaves again and lets word go out that he is dead. Bereft, the sons drink the medicine and are cured; the father returns. Even so, says the Buddha, I announce final extinction though I do not become finally extinct — lest beings, seeing me too often, should cease to prize the apparition of a Tathagata — and men of perverted minds worship relics without seeing that in this very place he continues preaching the law.
summary.zh: 佛自言：成佛已來無量無邊劫，所說示滅皆為教化眾生之權巧。譬如良醫離家，諸子誤飲毒藥，號呼輾轉；醫還，搗合良藥令服，中其心者即愈；心智錯亂者不肯服。醫父便設方便：告諸子言我老病死，棄之他國，遣使還報訃音；諸子聞父背寢，悲悼惶怖，遂肯服藥，毒病皆愈。醫父知子病醒，便還歸家相見。佛言：我亦如是，成佛已來無量劫，為度眾生故方便示現涅槃，而實不滅——眾生見我常在，便生憍恣，不肯勤求；故示滅度，使生戀慕。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); scripture material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved. Comparative parallel: the pretended death that saves belongs to the resurrection cluster of the wider corpus (the returned saviour wrongly believed dead).

passages.text: Let us suppose an analogous case, said the Buddha. There is some physician, learned, intelligent, prudent, clever in allaying all sorts of diseases, who has many sons, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred. The physician once being abroad, all his children incur a disease from poison or venom; overcome with grievous pains they lie rolling on the ground. Their father comes home at the time when his sons are suffering; some of them have perverted notions, others right notions, but all suffer the same pain. On seeing their father they cheerfully greet him: hail, dear father, that thou art come back in safety; now deliver us from our evil and let us live!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XV 'Duration of Life of the Tathagata' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The physician prepares a great remedy with the required colour, smell and taste, pounds it on a stone, and gives it to his sons: take this, and you shall soon be rid of the poison and be healthy. Those among the children who have right notions take it quickly and are soon totally delivered from their disease; but the sons with perverted notions do not take the remedy offered, because owing to the perverseness of their notions it does not please them in colour, smell nor taste. Then the physician reflects: these sons of mine have become perverted in their notions owing to the poison, since they do not take the remedy; therefore will I by some able device induce them to take it. He says to them: I am old, decrepit, advanced in years, and my term of life is near at hand; here have I prepared a great remedy for you — and skilfully betakes himself to another part of the country, letting his sick sons know that he has departed life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: They are extremely sorry and bewail him: so then he is dead, our father and protector, he who begat us, he so full of bounty! now are we left without a protector. Fully aware of their being orphans and having no refuge, they are plunged in sorrow, by which their perverted notions make room for right notions; they acknowledge that the remedy has the required colour, smell and taste, instantly take it, and are delivered from their evil. Then, on knowing that these sons are delivered, the physician shows himself again. In the same manner, says the Buddha, I have arrived at supreme perfect enlightenment since an immense incalculable number of aeons; but from time to time I display such able devices to the creatures with the view of educating them, without there being in that respect any falsehood on my part — for I see how the creatures are afflicted, but I do not show them my proper being; let them first have an aspiration to see me, then I will reveal to them the true law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XV (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Sada-paribhuta, the Bodhisattva who Never Disparaged (Lotus Sutra)
title.zh: 常不輕菩薩（法華經）

region.en: The world Mahasambhava in the aeon Vinirbhoga, under the Buddha Bhishmagarjitasvararaja (supernatural setting; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 威音王如來之世，大離車世界（超自然場景；象徵性定位）

period: Sanskrit sutra, c. 1st-2nd c. CE; Kern translation 1884 (Kern ch. XIX 'Sada-paribhuta'; Kumarajiva's ch. 20)

source.work: The Saddharma-Pundarīka; or, The Lotus of the True Law, trans. H. Kern (SBE 21, 1884)

summary.en: In the age when the counterfeit of the law was fading and proud monks oppressed its reign, there was a monk-Bodhisattva who taught nothing but one refrain: to every monk, nun and lay devotee he cried 'I do not contemn you, worthies! You deserve no contempt, for you all observe the course of duty of Bodhisattvas and are to become Tathagatas.' For years they abused him, threw clods and sticks, and nicknamed him Sada-paribhuta — 'always contemned.' At his death a voice from the sky expounded the Lotus to him; he gained the six perfections of the senses, vowed to live on, converted all who had reviled him — and the Buddha reveals that he was that bodhisattva himself, while the mockers are the five hundred monks, nuns and lay devotees of this very assembly, who had fallen to hell for their malignity but were ripened by him in the end.
summary.zh: 於威音王佛滅後、像法將盡、增上慢比丘橫行其時，有一比丘菩薩，不行讀誦，唯行一事：逢四眾則禮拜讚歎言：『我不敢輕於汝等，汝等皆行菩薩道，當得作佛。』眾人聞已，或以杖木瓦石擲之，避走而罵，因號之曰常不輕菩薩。臨命終時，於虛空中聞威音王佛廣說法華二十千萬億偈，得六根清淨，更增壽命，普為罵者說法，令住菩提。佛言：常不輕菩薩者，則我身是；爾時罵打彼者——今此會中五百菩薩、五百比丘尼、五百優婆塞是，彼以宿罵故，於墮惡道受苦，今得值佛，住不退轉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); scripture material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: After the complete extinction of the first of the Tathagatas called Bhishmagarjitasvararaja, when his true law had disappeared and the counterfeit of the true law was fading, when the reign of the law was being oppressed by proud monks, there was a monk, a Bodhisattva Mahasattva, called Sada-paribhuta. He was called so because he was in the habit of exclaiming to every monk or nun, male or female lay devotee, while approaching them: I do not contemn you, worthies; you deserve no contempt, for you all observe the course of duty of Bodhisattvas and are to become Tathagatas. That Bodhisattva at that time did not teach nor study; the only thing he did was, whenever he descried from afar a monk or nun or lay devotee, to approach and exclaim thus.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIX 'Sada-paribhuta' (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: But all were extremely irritated and angry at it, showed him their displeasure, abused and insulted him: why does he, unasked, declare that he feels no contempt for us? Just by so doing he shows a contempt for us; he renders himself contemptible by predicting our future destiny; we do not care for what is not true. Many years went on during which the Bodhisattva was being abused, but he was not angry at anybody, nor felt malignity; and to those who cast a clod or stick at him, he loudly exclaimed from afar: I do not contemn you. Those monks, nuns and lay devotees, always addressed in that phrase, gave him the nickname of Sada-paribhuta — both 'always contemned' and 'never contemned.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIX (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the end of his life the Bodhisattva happened to hear this Dharmaparyaya of the Lotus of the True Law: it was the Lord Bhishmagarjitasvararaja who expounded it in twenty times twenty hundred thousand myriads of stanzas, which the Bodhisattva heard from a voice in the sky as death drew near. On hearing that voice he grasped the Dharmaparyaya, obtained the perfection of sight, hearing, smell, taste, body and mind, made a vow to prolong his life for twenty hundred thousand myriads of years, and promulgated the Lotus to the four classes. And all those proud beings who had given him the nickname became his followers when they saw the strength of his sublime magic faculties; the Buddha declares: he who at that time was the Bodhisattva Sada-paribhuta was myself, and those who hooted at him are the five hundred Bodhisattvas headed by Bhadrapala, the five hundred nuns and the five hundred lay devotees of this very assembly, who, for their malignity, never saw a Tathagata for twenty hundred thousand myriads of aeons and suffered terrible pain in the great hell Avici — and thereafter were all brought by him to full ripeness for supreme perfect enlightenment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Saddharma-Pundarika, Kern ch. XIX (Kern 1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sage Asita's Prophecy to Suddhodana (Buddhacarita)
title.zh: 阿私陀仙人預言（佛所行讚）

region.en: The royal palace of Kapilavastu, city of the sage Kapila (modern Piprahwa, UP, India)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛王宮，仙人迦毘羅所居之城（今印度烏塔爾邦皮普拉赫瓦一帶）

period: Sanskrit kavya, c. 2nd c. CE (Book I by Asvaghosha); Cowell translation 1894 (SBE 49)

source.work: The Buddha-karita of Asvaghosha, trans. E. B. Cowell, 1894 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 49, Buddhist Mahayana Texts, Part I)

summary.en: Hearing a heavenly voice in the path of the sky that Suddhodana's son is born for the sake of supreme knowledge, the aged seer Asita — skilled in signs and penances — comes to the Sakya palace; beholding the babe with the wheel-marked foot and webbed fingers, he smiles and then bursts into tears. Alarmed, the king begs to know the danger; but Asita's grief is for himself: the child will leave the kingdom, attain the highest truth and become a sun of knowledge delivering the distressed world from the ocean of misery — and Asita, who has mastered all the stages of contemplation, is doomed to die before he can hear that law. He charges the king's young nephew, and departs through the air.
summary.zh: 仙人阿私陀於天路聞空中有聲：釋種之子將誕，為求無上知故。乃以神通至迦毘羅衛王宮；觀嬰兒足有輪相、指間縵網，微笑而隨即垂淚。王驚惶叩問：兒有夭折之厄乎？仙答：非也，慮在己身——此子當捨王國、樂出家，以精勤得最上真諦，為世界智慧之日，破除痴暗，以智慧之舟載度苦海眾生；而我壽將盡，不能聞其法，縱生最上天界亦是苦。遂囑其妹之子諦聽斯言，騰空而去。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Having learned by signs and through the power of his penances this birth of him who was to destroy all birth, the great seer Asita, in his thirst for the excellent Law, came to the palace of the Sakya king. Him, shining with the glory of sacred knowledge and ascetic observances, the king's own priest introduced into the royal palace with all due reverence; and Suddhodana, having duly honoured the sage with water for the feet and an arghya offering, invited him to speak. 'I am indeed fortunate, this my family is the object of high favour, that thou shouldst have come to visit me; be pleased to command what I should do, O benign one; I am thy disciple.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book I (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sage, thus invited, uttered his deep and solemn words, his large eyes opened wide with wonder: hear the motive of my coming and rejoice — a heavenly voice has been heard by me in the heavenly path, that thy son has been born for the sake of supreme knowledge; I am come with a longing to see the banner of the Sakya race, as if it were Indra's banner being set up. The king, his steps bewildered with joy, took the prince from his nurse's side and showed him to the holy ascetic; and the great seer beheld him with wonder — his foot marked with a wheel, his fingers and toes webbed, a circle of hair between his eyebrows, and signs of vigour like an elephant's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book I (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: But beholding the babe seated on his nurse's side like the boy Skanda by Devi, the sage stood with tears hanging on his eyelashes, sighing, looking up to heaven. The king, agitated for his son, asked in a broken voice: is the prince destined to a long life? surely he cannot be born for my sorrow! Knowing his fear, the sage answered: let not thy mind be disturbed, all I have said is true — my grief is for mine own disappointment; it is my time to depart, and this child is born who knows the means of destroying birth. He will leave his kingdom and shine as a sun of knowledge to destroy the darkness of illusion; the thirsty world will drink the stream of his Law, and he will proclaim the way of deliverance to the lost. Make no sorrow for him; it belongs rather to the pitiable world of beings who refuse to hear his Law. Since I have fallen short of hearing it, though I have mastered all the stages of contemplation, I count even dwelling in the highest heaven a misfortune. Then the sage departed by the way of the wind as he had come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book I (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Palace Lament: Kanthaka's Neigh and Yasodhara's Grief (Buddhacarita)
title.zh: 宮中哀慟：馬嘶與耶輸陀羅之慟（佛所行讚）

region.en: Kapilavastu, the royal palace, the morning after the prince's flight
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛王宮，王子夜遁翌晨

period: Sanskrit kavya, c. 2nd c. CE (Book VIII by Asvaghosha); Cowell translation 1894 (SBE 49)

source.work: The Buddha-karita of Asvaghosha, trans. E. B. Cowell, 1894 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 49, Buddhist Mahayana Texts, Part I)

summary.en: The charioteer Chandaka rides back the one-night road in eight days, leading the empty-saddled horse; the city bereft of the prince is a forest, and the crowds weep in the road accusing Chandaka, who answers that he and the householder's dress were abandoned together in the forest. Kanthaka enters the stable and neighs; the deceived women rush out in wild hope, then faint when they see the horse's empty back. Gautami falls like a golden plantain-tree; the women beat their breasts; and Yasodhara pours out her grief on the horse — three went away together and only two return — until the king recovers hope from the reading of the omens.
summary.zh: 車匿奉主命，一夜之路卻以八日返，牽空鞍之馬回城；城中失王子如曠野，眾人於道哭泣，責車匿竊王子；車匿答：非我棄主，乃主於林中將我與在家衣一併捨棄。健陟馬入廄嘶鳴，宮中婦女誤聞以為王子歸，狂喜奔出，見馬鞍空而昏絕。喬曇彌如失犢之母牛倒地；諸女捶胸慟哭；耶輸陀羅向馬致哀——三人同出，二人獨還——直至王觀其夢兆復生希望。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Meanwhile the attendant of the horse, in deep distress, when his unselfish master thus went into the forest, made every effort in the road to dissolve his load of sorrow, and yet not a tear dropped from him; but the road which by his lord's command he had traversed in one night with that horse, that same road he now travelled in eight days, pondering his lord's absence. And the horse Kanthaka, though he still went on bravely, flagged and had lost all spirit in his heart; and decked though he was with ornaments, he had lost all his beauty when bereft of his master. Slowly the two came back to the city called after Kapila, which seemed empty when deserted by that hero bent on the salvation of the world — like the sky bereft of the sun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book VIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The men of the city, hearing that they had returned without the pride of the Sakya race, shed tears in the road and followed Chandaka crying, 'Where is the king's son, the glory of his race and kingdom? He has been stolen away by thee.' He answered that he had not left the king's son; but that by him, in the uninhabited forest, he, weeping, and the dress of a householder were abandoned together. The women crowded to the rows of windows crying 'The prince has returned'; but having heard that his horse had an empty back, they closed the windows again and wailed aloud. Then Kanthaka, entering the royal stable with eyes full of tears, uttered a loud sound as if uttering his woe to the people; the birds and horses re-echoed it, and the people near the king's inner apartments, deceived by excessive joy, thought 'Since the horse Kanthaka neighs, the prince must be coming.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book VIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The women who were fainting with sorrow now rose in wild joy and rushed out of the palace full of hope like flickering lightnings from an autumn cloud — undressed, unkempt, their eyes dimmed by tears; but when they saw Chandaka standing helpless and the horse, the noble women wept with pale faces like cows abandoned by the bull. The king's principal queen Gautami fell bursting into tears on the ground with outstretched arms, like a golden plantain-tree with trembling leaves; others stood senseless as if painted, or watered their bosoms with their tears; the noble women beat their breasts with their lotus-like hands. Then Yasodhara spoke, her voice choking: 'Leaving me helplessly asleep in the night, whither, O Chandaka, is the desire of my heart gone? While three went away together, my mind trembles.' She rebuked the horse that carried away her treasure when all were asleep — and could not have done so had it but neighed once — till the king, by the signs he read, bade her cling to hope again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book VIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Bimbisara's Offer on Mount Pandava (Buddhacarita)
title.zh: 頻毘娑羅王磐陀山勸請（佛所行讚）

region.en: Mount Pandava near Rajagriha, capital of Magadha (modern Rajgir, Bihar)
region.zh: 摩揭陀國王舍城磐陀山（今印度比哈爾邦王舍城）

period: Sanskrit kavya, c. 2nd c. CE (Books X-XI by Asvaghosha); Cowell translation 1894 (SBE 49)

source.work: The Buddha-karita of Asvaghosha, trans. E. B. Cowell, 1894 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 49, Buddhist Mahayana Texts, Part I)

summary.en: The mendicant prince enters Rajagriha on his alms-round, and the whole city is stilled as at the presence of Religion embodied. King Srenya (Bimbisara), told that this is the youth the brahmans foretold would attain supreme wisdom or empire, climbs Mount Pandava to find him and offers half his kingdom, alliance in war, or the old career of pleasure and sacrifice. The bodhisattva praises the king's friendship but preaches the vanity of pleasures — even Indra's throne did not satisfy Mandhatri — declares his fear of worldly objects like serpents and thunderbolts, and says he goes that very day to the seer Arada. The king folds his hands and asks only: when thou hast accomplished all thou hast to do, show hereafter thy favour towards me.
summary.zh: 出家王子入王舍城乞食，闔城肅然，如見宗教化身。摩揭陀王頻毘娑羅聞婆羅門所預言者至，登山見之，願分半國、許以兵助，又以享受現樂、祭祀升天相勸。菩薩謝其友誼，而說欲樂之虛誑——曼陀陀那王得帝釋半座猶不饜——自言畏世間諸欲，如畏毒蛇雷電；今日即往阿羅邏仙人處。王合掌敬禮，唯求一諾：汝願成滿之日，當來度我。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Having crossed the Ganges with its speeding waves, the prince went to Rajagriha with its beautiful palaces and five hills. On seeing him, he who was going elsewhere stood still, and he who was standing followed him; those who wore gay-coloured dresses were ashamed, those who were talking fell to silence, and no one indulged in an improper thought, as at the presence of Religion herself embodied. King Srenya, the lord of the Magadhas, beheld the immense concourse from his palace and asked the reason; a man told him: this is the son of the king of the Sakyas, he who was foretold by the Brahmans — he will either attain supreme wisdom or the empire of the earth. The king sent a follower after the mendicant, who, having received alms, retired to eat in fitting manner and ascended the mountain Pandava.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book X (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king, deep in veneration, started himself to go thither with a modest retinue, and beheld the Bodhisattva resplendent as he sat on his hams with subdued senses — as if the mountain were moving and he himself were a peak thereof, like the moon rising from the top of a cloud. Drawing nigh and sitting down on the clean dark-blue rock, he spoke: I have a strong friendship with thy family, come down by inheritance and well proved. When I consider thy widespread race, thy fresh youth and thy conspicuous beauty, whence comes this resolve, set wholly on a mendicant's life and not on a kingdom? Thy limbs are worthy of red sandal-wood perfumes; this hand is fit to protect subjects, it deserves not to hold food given by another. If thou desirest not thy paternal kingdom, then at least accept forthwith one half of my kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Books X-XI (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Self-possessed and unchanged, the son of Suddhodana answered that the determination was prompted by pure generosity and friendship. I have experienced the fear of old age and death, he said, and fly to this path of religion in my desire for liberation; I am not so afraid of serpents or thunderbolts or flames as of these worldly objects. These transient pleasures are the robbers of our happiness; there is no calamity in the world like pleasures. Kings who have obtained all the earth wish to conquer the other side of the ocean; when Mandhatri had obtained the half of Sakra's throne, he was still unsatisfied; Nahusha fell, unsatisfied with pleasures. Who would trust worldly objects, which passed from Bali to Indra and back again? I go this very day to the seer Arada, who proclaims liberation — happiness be to thee, O king; guard the earth by the noble, and guard thy royal powers and thine own religion. The king, folding his hands, replied: when thou hast accomplished all that thou hast to do, show hereafter thy favour towards me. Having given his firm promise, the bodhisattva proceeded to the Vaivamtara hermitage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book XI (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Mara's Assault and Defeat at the Bodhi Tree (Buddhacarita)
title.zh: 魔軍攻擊與潰敗（佛所行讚）

region.en: The root of the asvattha (Bodhi) tree at Uruvela, on the Neranjara (modern Bodh Gaya)
region.zh: 優樓頻螺尼連禪河畔菩提樹下（今菩提伽耶）

period: Sanskrit kavya, c. 2nd c. CE (Book XIII by Asvaghosha); Cowell translation 1894 (SBE 49)

source.work: The Buddha-karita of Asvaghosha, trans. E. B. Cowell, 1894 (Sacred Books of the East vol. 49, Buddhist Mahayana Texts, Part I)

summary.en: The whole world rejoices as the sage sits resolved to win the highest knowledge, but Mara, the enemy of the good law, is afraid: if the sage overcomes him, his realm becomes empty. Armed with the flower-bow and the five infatuating arrows he had never spared even the lovers among birds, he assaults the seated saint, then summons his monstrous host — with the faces of boars, tigers and elephants, trunks, headless bodies and blazing hair — while the heavens fail to shine, the earth shakes and the oceans heave. Clubs are paralysed, hurled rocks hang in the sky, embers fall as lotus-petals, serpents stand charmed; the sage sits like a lion among oxen. An invisible voice warns Mara not to weary himself against this Meru of resolution; the flower-armed god flees vanquished, and the night gleams out like a spotless maiden as flowers fall from a clear sky.
summary.zh: 聖者端坐誓取無上智，世間歡慶；魔王懼其道場空虛，乃持花箭、五欲矢，勸誘不遂，即召魔軍——獸面獠牙、提頭無身、髮中出火——諸天失色、地動海翻。魔軍或擲石中懸、或降火成蓮、或蛇凝如咒縛；聖者如牛群中之師子，不動不驚。空中無形之聲告魔王：此志如須彌，不可撼也，宜斂瞋歸寂。花箭之神敗退；夜空如無垢少女，天雨眾花，皎潔清淨。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: When the great sage sat down there with his soul fully resolved to obtain the highest knowledge, the whole world rejoiced; but Mara, the enemy of the good law, was afraid. He whom they call in the world Kamadeva, the owner of various weapons, the flower-arrowed, the lord of the course of desire — it is he whom they also style Mara the enemy of liberation. His three sons Confusion, Gaiety and Pride, and his three daughters Lust, Delight and Thirst, asked the reason of his despondency; he answered: this sage, wearing the armour of resolution and having drawn the arrow of wisdom with the barb of truth, intends to conquer my realms. While he stands within my reach and his spiritual eyesight is not yet attained, I will assail him to break his vow, as the swollen might of a river assails a dam.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book XIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having seized his flower-made bow and his five infatuating arrows, he drew near to the root of the asvattha tree with his children, and addressed the calm seer preparing to cross the ocean of existence: 'Up, up, O thou Kshatriya, afraid of death! Follow thine own duty and abandon this law of liberation; that is a glorious path which has been followed by former leaders of men.' But when the Sakya saint, unheeding, did not change his posture, Mara discharged his arrow at him, setting his daughters and sons in front — the very arrow by which the god Sambhu was pierced with love for the daughter of the mountain. It was in vain: the arrow fell slack. Then Mara called to mind his own army, and his followers swarmed round wearing different forms and carrying arrows, trees, darts, clubs and swords — with the faces of boars, fishes, horses, tigers, bears and elephants, one-eyed, three-headed, with protruberant bellies, half-mutilated faces, yellow or smoke-coloured hair, clothed in leather or nothing at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book XIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the heavens ceased to shine, the earth shook, a wind of intense violence blew, and the oceans were agitated; but the great sage remained untroubled, like a lion seated in the midst of oxen. One demon lifted his club and his arm was instantly paralysed; those who lifted stones and trees could not throw them and fell themselves; a shower of live embers became a shower of red lotus-petals through his boundless charity; those who spat serpents found them unable to strike near him; an arrow set in a bow gleamed but did not issue forth. Then a being of invisible shape and pre-eminent glory addressed Mara from the heavens: fire might lose its heat, water its fluidity, earth its steadiness, but never will this sage abandon his resolution — pity the great physician who labours for the remedy of knowledge. Having seen the unshaken firmness of the saint, Mara departed dispirited and broken in purpose, and his host fled in all directions like a hostile army whose camp has been destroyed; the heavens shone out with the moon like a maiden with a smile, and a sweet-smelling shower of flowers fell down wet with dew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Buddhacarita, Book XIII (Cowell 1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Name Sarvarthasiddha and the Reading of the Thirty-Two Signs (Romantic Legend)
title.zh: 命名一切義成與三十二相之觀相（普曜經傳）

region.en: Kapilavastu, capital of the Sakyas (modern Piprahwa, UP, India)
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城，釋迦族之都（今印度烏塔爾邦皮普拉赫瓦一帶）

period: Chinese translation of a Sanskrit Lalitavistara-tradition text, c. 5th c. CE; Beal translation 1875

source.work: The Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, trans. Samuel Beal, 1875

summary.en: On the day of the babe's birth five hundred of everything came into being — Sakya princes and princesses, foals, white elephants, gardens and tribute-bearing embassies — and Suddhodana, seeing all things perfectly accomplished, names his son Sarvarthasiddha, 'perfect prosperity.' He then summons all the astrologers to cast the horoscope; reading the child against their sacred books, they declare him marked with the thirty-two signs of a great man: as a secular householder such a one becomes a universal monarch; as a religious recluse, a perfectly illuminated Tathagata — and they recite the signs one by one, from the level feet with the thousand-rayed circles to the netted fingers and the long arms.
summary.zh: 太子誕生之日，凡事五百同時而出——釋種五百王子、五百王女、駒馬、白象、林苑、進貢之使——淨飯王見諸事悉皆圓成，乃為太子命名曰一切義成（音薩婆達悉多）。隨後徵召國中相師占卜之士入宮觀相，參照其聖典，斷言：此兒具三十二相，大丈夫相；為在家者則為轉輪聖王，出家修道則為正遍知如來——相師乃一一數其瑞相：足下平滿、千輻輪相、指纖長、網縵指、臂長垂膝等。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: At this time there were five hundred Sakya princes born, of whom the Bodhisattva himself was by far the most illustrious; there were five hundred Sakya princesses born, of whom Yasodhara was chief; five hundred children born of the concubines, of whom Chandaka was chief; five hundred foals born of the royal white mares, of which Kantaka was chief; and five hundred white elephants appeared of themselves and went round the city. Five hundred lovely gardens appeared on each side of the city, five hundred merchant-men with gold, silver and precious stones arrived, and five hundred superb umbrellas and dishes of grain were sent as tribute by five hundred different princes — all with a view to conduce to the prosperity of the Bodhisattva.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. IX (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suddhodana, seeing that all these things were perfectly accomplished, thought with himself: what name shall I give my new-born child? — and reflected: since on the day of his birth all things were so perfectly accomplished, I will name him Sarvarthasiddha, 'perfect prosperity.' Then he opened his treasury and took a hundred lakhs of gold to offer to his child as he gave him the name, saying in a gatha: within the King's palace all things were entirely prosperous; therefore the young child's name shall be Sarvarthasiddha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. IX (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suddhodana then issued his commands that all the astrologers and fortune-tellers should repair to the palace to examine the child and cast his horoscope. The Brahmans with earnest purpose examined his appearance, comparing it with all that was explained in their sacred books, and addressed the king: what great fortune is yours! This child is indeed born a king of all that lives, for his body is marked by the thirty-two infallible signs of greatness; and of persons so marked there are two sorts — if secular, then universal monarchs; if religious, then perfectly illuminated Tathagatas. Asked to particularize, they recited the signs one by one: the sole of the foot perfectly level, with the thousand-rayed circles beneath; the fingers tapering and long; the heel round and smooth; the fingers and toes severally connected with a fine net-like membrane; the shoulders round as the king of stags; the hands, without stooping, reaching to the knees.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. IX (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

title.en: Devadatta's Wounded Goose and the Prince's Claim (Romantic Legend)
title.zh: 提婆達多射鵠與太子護生（普曜經傳）

region.en: The Kan-ku (diligent labour) garden at Kapilavastu, the princes' training ground
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛「勤學」苑，釋種王子習藝之地

period: Chinese translation of a Sanskrit Lalitavistara-tradition text, c. 5th c. CE; Beal translation 1875

source.work: The Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, trans. Samuel Beal, 1875

summary.en: At twelve the prince, self-taught and surpassing the masters, amuses himself in the garden shooting; his cousin Devadatta wings a passing goose with an arrow fixed in its feathers, and sends messengers to claim it. The prince draws the arrow, anoints the wound with oil and honey, and answers: if the bird were dead it would be yours; living, you have no title to it. When Devadatta insists that skill of shooting made it his, the prince summons the wise ancients of the Sakyas to judge; a deva of the Suddhavasa heaven, disguised as an old man, delivers the ruling: he who nourishes and cherishes is the owner; he who shoots and destroys is the loser and the disperser — and all the ancients confirm it. The prince adds his reason: he keeps the bird as a sign that hereafter, arrived at perfection, he will thus receive and protect all living creatures.
summary.zh: 太子十二歲，自學諸藝，勝於諸師；於苑中習射。其從弟提婆達多射飛鵠貫翼，遣使索之。太子拔箭，以油蜜塗創，答曰：若鳥已死，當還；鳥若生存，汝無所取。提婆達多言：我以射術得之。太子乃請釋種耆老斷之；淨居天化為老者而入眾中，判曰：養護者為主，射殺者為失——眾老皆許。太子自道其故：護此鵠者，示我來日成道時，當如是攝受救護一切眾生。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: Up to the time of his eighth year the Royal Prince grew up in the royal palace without any attention to study; but from his eighth year till his twelfth he was trained under the care of Visvamitra and Kshantadeva. Having completed twelve years and being perfectly acquainted with all the customary modes of enjoyment, it came to pass that he was visiting the Kan-ku garden, and amused himself by wandering in different directions, shooting with his bow and arrow at whatever he pleased, having separated himself from the other Sakya youths who were enjoying themselves in the several gardens. At this time a flock of wild geese, flying through the air, passed over the garden, on which the young man Devadatta, pointing his bow, shot one of them through the wing, leaving his arrow fixed in the feathers; the bird fell to the ground in the middle of the garden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Royal Prince, seeing the bird thus transfixed with the arrow and fallen to the ground, took it with both his hands, and sitting down with his knees crossed rested it in his lap; and with his own soft and glossy hand, smooth and pliable as the leaf of the plaintain, holding it with his left hand, with his right he drew forth the arrow and anointed the wound with oil and honey. At this time Devadatta sent messengers to the Prince: Devadatta has shot a goose which has fallen in your garden; send it to him without delay. The prince answered: if the bird were dead, it would be right I should return it forthwith; but if it is not dead, you have no title to it. Devadatta sent again: whether the bird be living or dead, it is mine; my skill it was that brought it down — on what ground do you delay to send it me?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Prince Royal answered: the reason I have taken possession of the bird is this, to signify that in time to come, when I have arrived at the condition of perfection to which I tend, I shall thus receive and protect all living creatures; but if you still say the bird belongs not to me, go and summon all the wise and ancient men of the Sakya tribe and let them decide the question on its merits. At this time a certain deva belonging to the Suddhavasa heaven assumed the appearance of an old man, entered the assembly of the Sakyas, and spoke thus: he who nourishes and cherishes is by right the keeper and owner; he who shoots and destroys is by his own act the loser and the disperser. At once all the ancient men of the Sakyas confirmed the words of the would-be clansman, saying: verily, verily, it is as this venerable one says, with respect to the difference between Devadatta and the Royal Prince.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tournament for Yasodhara and the Bow of Sinhahanu (Romantic Legend)
title.zh: 選妃競藝與祖父神弓（普曜經傳）

region.en: The place of tournament outside Kapilavastu, on the day of the Arrow Festival
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛城外競藝之場，射箭節之日

period: Chinese translation of a Sanskrit Lalitavistara-tradition text, c. 5th c. CE; Beal translation 1875

source.work: The Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, trans. Samuel Beal, 1875

summary.en: On the seventh day the Sakya youths go to the tournament, and the minister Mahanama proclaims that whoever wins the contest of skill and arms shall carry off his daughter Yasodhara as his prize. The prince sweeps the writing contest under the smiling umpire Visvamitra, then defeats the whole five hundred at figures under the master Arjuna, reciting the centenary scale of numeration and the atom-reckoning that runs to the sands of myriads of Ganges rivers. In the martial exercises he strings — without rising from his seat — the sacred bow of his grandfather Sinhahanu, which no Sakya can string, shoots through the iron target ten krosas off, pierces seven tala-trees and an iron boar into the ground to make the Arrow Well, and burns a sala-grove through seven water-jars, till all the youths surrender and the devas establish the Arrow Festival in heaven with the arrow Sakra has caught.
summary.zh: 競藝之日，大臣摩訶那摩立其女耶輸陀羅為彩：技勇之勝者得娶之。太子書藝勝五百釋種；算術上又敗算學大師阿耆那，能誦十進位數法與極微積聚之算，至恆河沙數。武藝之場，太子坐不離席即張其祖父師子頰供於天廟之神弓——釋種無能張者——射十由旬外鐵鼓，貫七多羅樹與鐵豬，箭入地成井（至今號箭井），又以燃箭貫七水甕而焚娑羅林；眾皆服輸。帝釋取其箭上天，諸天以此日為射箭節，至今為紀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: On the seventh day all the Sakya youths of the five hundred families, with Siddartha at their head, went forth from the city to the place of tournament. At this time the great minister Mahanama, having caused his daughter Yasodhara to be adorned with every choice ornament, made this proclamation respecting the victor: whoever the victor may be in this contest of skill and of arms, he shall carry off this my daughter as his prize. Suddhodana and all the old Sakya lords arrived at the jousting place with countless crowds of young men and women, desirous to see the prince and the Sakya youths contest for the prize. First they competed in writing, with Visvamitra as umpire, who smiled gently, knowing the prince's incomparable skill: whatever writing or books there be among men, in heaven, or among the Gandharvas, Asuras or Garudas, the prince is able thoroughly to understand them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XIII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came the art of figures, with the eminent master Arjuna as umpire. The prince proposed a sum that one Sakya youth copied down but could not do; then two, then three, till all the five hundred copied it down and failed; and when they proposed in turn, the prince solved every question without error. In astonishment Arjuna uttered his praise — surely we have found a master of figures, able even to count the drops of the ocean — and asked whether he could recite the numeration of figures above a lakh. The prince began: a hundred hundred thousand is a koti, a hundred kotis an ayuta — and so through the whole centenary scale, up to the enumeration that proceeds by the sands of one Ganges, or two, and by the sands of myriads of kotis of Ganges rivers; and to the atom-reckoning, in which seven minute atoms of dust make one mote, and so up to the measures of a yojana — a sum that made even the master confess himself in utter confusion of mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XIII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came the martial exercises. Ananda set an iron drum two krosas off as a target, Devadatta four, Nanda six, Mahanama eight, and Siddartha one of diamond-hardness ten krosas off; each struck his target in the midst, but could not go beyond. The prince bent the given bow till it broke, and asked for one fit for him, his grandfather Sinhahanu's bow, kept in a temple of the devas, which no Sakya could string. Brought to him, he strung it without rising from his seat and thrummed the string, a sound that filled the city with fear; then he shot through each target to the farthest, where his arrow disappeared in the distance. The assembled devas sang his future victory over Mara, Sorrow and Death, and showered flowers on him; and Sakra seized the arrow, wherefore the day of the Arrow Festival is observed among the devas to this time. Then he shot through seven tala-trees and an iron boar, his arrow entering the earth and making the spring called the Arrow Well; and with one sword-cut he felled seven trees. Every contest won, he rejoiced the heart of his father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XIII (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

title.en: Suddhodana's Seven Dreams and the Disguised Deva (Romantic Legend)
title.zh: 淨飯王七夢與化形梵士（普曜經傳）

region.en: The royal palace of Kapilavastu, on the night after the first omen
region.zh: 迦毘羅衛王宮，初見老相之夜

period: Chinese translation of a Sanskrit Lalitavistara-tradition text, c. 5th c. CE; Beal translation 1875

source.work: The Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, trans. Samuel Beal, 1875

summary.en: Having seen the prince turn home from the old man on the road, Suddhodana doubles the palace pleasures — and the devaputra T'so-Ping, still bent on ripening the bodhisattva's resolve, that very night sends the king seven dreams: an imperial banner carried out of the east gate by innumerable crowds, the prince in chariots passing the south and west gates, a jewelled discus flying through the north gate, the prince beating a great drum in the middle of the four highways, a tower from whose top he scatters jewels to the four quarters, and six men outside the city weeping and tearing their hair. The court brahmans cannot interpret them; but T'so-Ping, disguised as a brahman at the gate, reads each dream — the prince's renunciation, omniscience, fearlessness, the turning of the wheel, the drum of preaching heard through the heavens, the scattering of the gems of the Good Law, and the discomfiture of the six heretical teachers — then vanishes; and the king, misreading the comfort, resolves only to multiply the enticements of the palace.
summary.zh: 王聞太子歸而問故，倍增宮中之樂。時化樂天子時時欲成太子出家之志，是夜以神力使王得七夢：無數人眾擎天帝幡出東門；太子乘象車出南門；乘四馬車出西門；寶珠飛空出北門；太子於四衢擊大鼓；太子登高樓散寶珠四方；六人於城外拔髮號泣。朝中相師不能解。化樂天子化為梵士立於門，自言能解王夢；乃一一解之：太子將捨俗出家；證一切智十力；得四無畏；轉法輪；法音上徹梵天；散法寶於四方；伏六師外道。言畢忽然不見；王聞之，愈增宮中聲色，欲以繫太子之志。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Buddhism); the Buddha-biography material is freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: It came to pass that the Devaputra T'so-Ping, still desiring to cause the prince to arrive at a resolution to become a religious recluse, by the exercise of his spiritual power on that very night caused Suddhodana to dream seven different dreams. As soon as the king had retired to his couch and fallen asleep, he dreamt that he saw a great imperial banner like that of Indra, around which were gathered innumerable crowds of people, who, lifting it and holding it up, proceeded to carry it through Kapilavastu and finally went from the city by the Eastern gate. The second dream was that he saw the prince riding in a royal chariot drawn by great elephants, passing through the Southern gate; the third, that the prince seated in a magnificent four-horsed chariot proceeded through the Western gate; the fourth, that a magnificently jewelled discus flew through the air and proceeded through the Northern gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XV (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fifth dream was that he saw the prince sitting in the middle of the four great highways of Kapilavastu, holding in his hand a large mace and smiting therewith a large drum. The sixth was that he saw in the midst of Kapilavastu a high tower, on the top of which the Royal Prince was seated, scattering towards the four quarters of heaven countless jewels of every kind, which were gathered by the innumerable concourse of living creatures; and the seventh, that he beheld outside the city, not very far off, six men who raised their voices and wailed greatly, and with their hands plucked out the hair of their heads and flung it by handfuls on the ground. Suddhodana, awaking and recalling the visions, was greatly troubled, his hair standing erect and his limbs trembling; and he bade his ministers recite the dreams in the morning, and summoned all the Brahmans, interpreters of dreams, in the kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XV (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

passages.text: The wise Brahmans could make nothing of them: we never before have heard such dreams, they said. At this T'so-Ping assumed the appearance of a Brahman arrayed in the skin of the black deer, and standing at the gate of the palace cried out: I am able fully to interpret the dreams of Suddhodana and to satisfy all his doubts. Brought into the presence, he read each dream in turn: the banner carried from the city signifies that the prince will soon give up his present condition and, surrounded by devas, become a recluse; the elephants' car, his omniscience and the ten powers; the jewelled discus, his turning of the wheel of the perfect Law; the drum, that the sound of his preaching shall extend through the heavens of Brahma; the scattered jewels, his dispersal of the gems of the Good Law; the six weeping men, the distress of the six heretical teachers whom the prince shall discomfit. Then he said: your heart should be filled with joy, for these dreams are most felicitous — and suddenly disappeared, and was no more seen. The king thereupon resolved to multiply still further the palace enticements, hoping to prevent his going forth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Romantic Legend of Sakya Buddha, ch. XV (Beal 1875); not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Visits of the Buddha to Lanka (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 佛陀三訪錫蘭：彌訶央根那、龍洲與迦藍尼耶

region.en: Kelaniya (Kalyani), Sri Lanka — site of the third visit
region.zh: 錫蘭迦藍尼耶（今凱拉尼亞，第三次巡禮之地）

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, ch. 1

summary.en: In the ninth month after his awakening the Buddha flies to Lanka, where his doctrine is destined to shine, and terrifies the whole yakkha nation with storm and darkness until they grant him their island; he preaches and leaves a hair relic at Mahiyangana. Two later visits settle a war between naga kings over a jewel throne and reward the naga Maniakkhika of Kalyani with a promised return; footprints at Sumanakuta and meditations at Anuradhapura consecrate the sacred places of the future Sinhala Buddhist world.
summary.zh: 佛成正覺九月，乘空巡錫蘭，以風雨黑暗懾服夜叉大會，受其島而說法，彌訶央根那留髮舍利；五年後再至龍洲，止龍王叔姪寶座之爭；八年後應龍王摩尼阿奇迦之請至迦藍尼耶，留足跡於聖山，錫蘭遂為佛法所許之地。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); freely retold, no ritual secrecy. Note: the promised-land frame of the visits is used in modern Sinhala Buddhist historiography — handled descriptively.

passages.text: Nine months after his awakening, the Buddha knew that Lanka, though filled with yakkhas, was the place where his doctrine should shine in glory. He went to the delightful Mahanaga garden, the customary meeting-place of the yakkhas, where the whole nation had gathered, and hovering in the air above their heads he struck terror into them with rain, storm-wind and darkness. When the terrified yakkhas begged to be released from fear, he demanded a place where he might sit, and they surrendered their whole island to him. Spreading his rug of skin on the ground, he made it burn with flame; daunted by the heat, the yakkhas crowded to its border, and the Saviour brought a whole island, Giridipa, close beside them for them to settle on, then returned it to its place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 1 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The deva Mahasumana of Sumanakuta, who had already entered the path, asked for something to worship, and the Buddha, passing his hand over his head, gave him a handful of his blue-black hair. The deva enshrined it in a golden urn on a mound of many-coloured gems at the spot where the Master had sat. After the Buddha died, the arahant Sarabhu brought the Conqueror's collar-bone from the funeral pyre and laid it in the same cetiya, raising the stupa to twelve cubits; Uddhaculabhaya later raised it to thirty, and Dutthagamani, even while warring with the Damilas, built over it a mantle-cetiya of eighty cubits. Then the Buddha returned to Uruvela, the island having been made a fit dwelling for men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 1 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the fifth year of his buddhahood the Buddha saw that a war threatened between the naga kings Mahodara and Culodara, uncle and nephew, over a jewel throne inherited from an ancestor, and he went to Nagadipa to prevent it. The deva Samiddhisumana carried a rajayatana tree from Jetavana to shade him like a parasol. Hovering above the battlefield, the Master first spread dread darkness over the nargas and then brought back the light; comforted, they bowed at his feet, heard the doctrine of concord, and gladly gave up the throne. Eighty kotis of snake-spirits took the refuges and the precepts. Maniakkhika of Kalyani, an uncle of the combatants who had first heard the doctrine on the first visit, begged the Master to come again to his own country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 1 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the eighth year, at Maniakkhika's invitation, the Buddha came with five hundred bhikkhus to the Kalyani country and took his seat under a gem-decked canopy on the spot where the Kalyani-cetiya would later stand. After preaching, he left the plain traces of his footprints on Sumanakuta, spent the day there, and went on to Dighavapi, where he sat in meditation to consecrate the ground for a future cetiya. He likewise meditated at the future Mahamegha-vanarama, on the spot where the great Bodhi-tree would be planted, where the Great Thupa and the Thuparama would rise, and at the future Silacetiya, then returned to Jetavana. Thus the island, thrice visited, came to high honour among the faithful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 1 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Vijaya's Exile and the Conquest of Lanka (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 維闍耶流放與登陸錫蘭

region.en: Tambapanni, north-west coast of Sri Lanka (landing of Vijaya)
region.zh: 錫蘭西北海岸銅掌城（維闍耶登陸之地）

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, chs. 6-7

summary.en: Born of the princess who wed a lion, the turbulent prince Vijaya is exiled from India with seven hundred followers and lands at Tambapanni on the very day the Buddha passes into nibbana. Charged by the dying Buddha to protect him, Sakka hands the island's guardianship to a god who wards Vijaya's men with sacred water and thread; the yakkhini Kuveni devours the followers, is spared by the prince, and betrays her own folk so that he may rule. Vijaya marries a Pandya princess sent from Madura, banishes Kuveni, founds Tambapanni, and gives the Sihala people their name.
summary.zh: 獅子公主之後裔維闍耶，因暴行被逐出印度，率七百人於佛陀涅槃之日登陸銅掌。佛臨終託帝釋護之，神以聖水聖線護其眾；夜叉女鳩逸尼吞其部眾，被王擒而立誓，遂背其族使王得地。維闍耶後娶南印度般度王之女，棄鳩逸尼，建銅掌城，僧訶羅人之名由此而起。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); retold freely. Note: the Vijaya episode is the founding legend of the Sinhala people and is invoked in modern Sinhala nationalism — handled descriptively here.
sensitivity.zh: 活傳統之聖典（上座部佛教），可自由講述；維闍耶傳說為僧訶羅民族之建族傳說，見用於現代民族主義，此處僅作描述。

passages.text: A Vanga princess, prophesied to wed the king of beasts, fled into the Lala country and was carried off by a lion, by whom she bore twins: Sihabahu, lion-armed, and Sihasivali. When Sihabahu was sixteen he lifted the rock that sealed his father's cave and led his mother and sister away; later, offered a reward, he slew the lion that ravaged the border villages and was crowned king of the Vangas in his grandfather's place, though he passed the crown to his mother's husband and founded Sihapura in his own land, marrying his sister. Sihasivali bore him sixteen pairs of twin sons; the eldest, Vijaya, was of violent conduct, and when his father thrice rebuked him in vain the angry people demanded his death. The king instead had Vijaya and his seven hundred followers shaven over half the head and set out on ships.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 6 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The separate companies landed on separate shores — the children on Naggadipa, the women on Mahiladipaka — while Vijaya touched at Supparaka and then, the day the Tathagata lay down between the twin sala-trees, at the region of Tambapanni in Lanka. Dying, the Buddha charged Sakka to protect the exile and his followers, for his religion would be established in Lanka; Sakka handed the guardianship to a deva of lotus colour, who sat in the guise of a wandering ascetic, sprinkled Vijaya's men with water from his vessel and wound protecting threads about their hands. A yakkhini came in the form of a bitch, and a follower who chased her found her mistress Kuveni spinning at the foot of a tree beside a pond.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 7 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: "Stay! thou art my prey," Kuveni cried, but the magic thread bound the man against her, and she hurled him and then all seven hundred, one by one, into a chasm. Vijaya, armed with the five weapons, followed and caught the yakkhini by the hair with a noose at her neck: "Slave, give me back my men, or I slay thee." To save her life she swore to give him a kingdom and do him a woman's service, and fetched his men alive. Reassured by a portion of the meal, she took the lovely form of a sixteen-year-old maiden and became his spouse on a canopied bed under a tree. In the night, music and singing rose: in the yakkha city of Sirisavatthu a wedding was held, and Kuveni, fearing the yakkhas would kill her for bringing men into the island, promised to make her lord king — if he slew them all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 7 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Since the yakkhas were invisible, Kuveni cried out where they stood, and wherever her cry sounded Vijaya struck, his weapon falling by her magic upon their bodies; all the yakkhas were slain. Vijaya clothed himself in the garments of the yakkha-king, founded the city of Tambapanni — so named because his weary followers, resting their hands on the ground, reddened their palms with the red earth — and his ministers built villages about it: Anuradhagama by the Kadamba river, Upatissagama on the Gambhira. But Vijaya refused consecration until a maiden of noble house could be consecrated queen beside him, so ministers went by ship to Madura in the Pandya country and brought back the king's daughter with a hundred maidens, craftsmen and a thousand families of the eighteen guilds. Vijaya then put Kuveni away with her two children, was consecrated in solemn festival, and reigned in righteousness over all Lanka thirty-eight years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 7 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Wilhelm Geiger, The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, London: Pali Text Society 1912 (public domain)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE LION-KING AND THE EXILE. The Mahavamsa opens the Sinhala royal genealogy with a scandal: a princess of the Vanga (Bengal) royal house, prophesied at birth to be united with the king of beasts, flees a caravan and is carried on the lion's back to his cave, where she bears twins — Sihabahu ('lion-arm'), whose hands and feet are formed like a lion's, and Sihasivali. At sixteen Sihabahu escapes, and later, for a reward of three thousand gold pieces, slays the lion that now ravages the villages — his own father, whose tenderness turns aside the arrows until wrath lets the third fly. Crowned in his grandfather's stead, he founds Sihapura and marries his sister; sixteen pairs of twin sons follow, the eldest named Vijaya. Vijaya is 'of evil conduct' and his followers like him; when the people cry for his death, king Sihabahu has the prince and his seven hundred shaved over half the head — the mark of the unfree — and put aboard ships, men, women and children in separate vessels. They land separately: the children on Naggadipa, the women on Mahiladipaka, and Vijaya at Tambapanni, on the very day the Tathagata passed into nibbana.

MIDDLE: THE DYING BUDDHA'S CHARGE AND THE YAKKHINI. The chronicle welds colonisation to Buddha's deathbed: lying between the twin sala-trees, the Buddha tells Sakka that Vijaya is come to Lanka and that his religion will be established there — 'carefully protect him and Lanka.' Sakka delegates to the lotus-coloured god (identified by the commentator with Vishnu), who appears as an ascetic, sprinkles the men with water and winds charm-threads about their hands. A yakkhini in the shape of a bitch leads a follower to Kuveni (Kuvanna), spinning at a tree like a woman-hermit. 'Stay! thou art my prey' — but the sacred thread holds; she hurls all seven hundred into a chasm. Vijaya, suspecting the truth, seizes her with a noose and sword, and she buys her life with a kingdom, a wife's service, and an oath. Feeding his men on rice from ships of traders she had devoured, she assumes the form of a sixteen-year-old beauty and lies with him in a tented bed. Then comes the deeper betrayal: music from Sirisavatthu, the yakkha city, where a wedding is held; Kuveni, who fears the yakkhas will kill her for her part in bringing men, offers her lord the kingship if he destroys them — 'wheresoever they may be, I will utter cries, and where thou shalt hear that sound, strike!' All the yakkhas fall; Vijaya dons the yakkha-king's garments. He founds Tambapanni (the name from the red hands of his men on the red earth), and the followers of the lion-slayer Sihabahu are called Sihala — the etymological charter of the Sinhala people.

END: QUEEN FROM MADURA, THE BANISHED WIFE. Vijaya will not be consecrated without a consort of noble house, so an embassy sails to Madura in the Pandya south and returns with the Pandu king's daughter, a hundred maidens for the ministers, craftsmen, elephants, and a thousand families of the eighteen guilds — a charter for the island's craftsmen and society. Kuveni, who bore Vijaya a son and a daughter, is put away: 'men are ever in fear of superhuman beings.' She begs for a thousand pieces as an offering, then departs for Lankapura with the children; the yakkhas, taking her for a spy, kill her with a single blow. Her uncle warns the children to flee; they escape to Sumanakuta (Adam's Peak) and, brother and sister wed together, their descendants are the Pulindas — identified by tradition with the Vedda hunter-folk of the island's interior. Vijaya, 'having forsaken his former evil way of life, ruled over all Lanka in peace and righteousness' for thirty-eight years, sending annually to his father-in-law a shell-pearl worth two hundred thousand.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the founding legend of the Sinhala people (Sihala from the lion-slayer), the ethno-religious charter of the island (a land promised by the dying Buddha, emptied of its demonic inhabitants and settled under Buddhist protection), a charter of caste and craft (the eighteen guilds, the ministers' villages that become Anuradhapura's axis), and the origin of the island's aboriginal people (Kuveni's children). The yakkha-slaying is the ritual aition of Sinhala sovereignty: settlement follows purification.

RECEPTION. In modern Sri Lanka the Vijaya story is not a quaint tale: school histories, commemorative pageantry, and nationalist rhetoric have cast Vijaya as the first national hero and the landing of 483 BCE as the founding of the nation, while Tamil and scholarly counter-readings stress the story's dependence on Tamil marriage alliances and its literary artifice. The record states the chronicle's account; it does not endorse the charter as history.
narrative.zh:
開端：獅子王與流放。僧訶羅王統開篇即離奇：芬伽國公主宿命與獸王相配，逃亡中為獅所負，產雙生子——獅臂僧訶巴呼與僧訶悉婆利。十六歲之子肩負母妹出窟；後因賞金弒獅（其父，三箭為慈所折，怒而第三箭入體），代祖父為王，卻讓位於母之夫，自立獅子城，娶妹為后；生十六對雙生子，長曰維闍耶。維闍耶行惡，民怒求誅；王乃半剃其髮（示失自由），與七百徒眾分置船上流放，童子登那伽島，婦女登摩訶羅島，維闍耶於佛陀涅槃之日登銅掌。

中段：佛之遺命與夜叉女。佛於雙娑羅樹間臨終囑帝釋：維闍耶至蘭卡，吾法當立於彼——善護之。帝釋轉託青蓮色之神（論者謂毘紐天），神化為行者，以聖水灘其眾，結聖線護之。夜叉女化母犬引人至樹下紡線之鳩逸尼；『汝乃吾獵物』——聖線制之，她將七百人一一擲入深窟。維闍耶以五兵擒之，她以王國、妻職與誓言換命，並取出所吞商船之米食其眾；化十六歲少女為王妻。更深之背叛：夜叉城吉祥住婚禮之夜樂起，鳩逸尼懼族誅己，許以王位換盡殺夜叉——『我發聲處，即擊之』。眾夜叉盡滅，維闍耶服夜叉王衣，建銅掌城（因眾人手染紅土而名）；獅子城之徒遂稱僧訶羅——民族得名之憲章。

結局：馬都拉王后與見棄之妻。維闍耶必得貴族女為后方肯受灌頂，使臣航海至南印度馬都拉，迎般度王之女、百女、工匠與十八行會千家——工藝與社會之憲章。鳩逸尼育一子一女而被遣：『人恆畏超自然者』。她攜子往蘭卡城，夜叉眾疑其為諜，一拳斃之；其舅令二子速逃，兄妹相婚，其後裔即浦林陀人（傳為吠陀獵民之祖）。維闍耶改邪歸正，正法治國三十八年。

功能：僧訶羅建族傳說（獅子城得名）；島嶼之宗教憲章（佛許之地、夜叉淨空、聖護殖民）；行會工匠之憲章；及島上原住民之起源（鳩逸尼之子女）。夜叉之滅為王權之儀式起因：淨土而後定居。

接受史：現代斯里蘭卡中，維闍耶非閒談故事——教科書、紀念慶典與民族主義論述奉之為首位民族英雄，泰米爾與學術反讀則強調其對泰米爾聯姻之依賴與文學建構。本紀錄僅陳述編年史所述，不以憲章為史實背書。

functions: Founding legend of the Sinhala people (Sihala named from the lion-slayer Sihabahu)
Ethno-religious charter: Lanka promised to the Buddha's religion on his deathbed and settled under divine protection
Aition of settlement: the island purified by the destruction of the yakkhas before consecration
Charter of society and craft: the eighteen guilds and the Pandya marriage alliance with South India
Origin of the island's aboriginal Vedda people from Kuveni's banished children

variants.name: Dipavamsa (4th c. CE chronicle)
variants.text_tradition: The earlier Pali chronicle, Dipavamsa chs. 3-5
variants.summary: A shorter, cruder version of the lion ancestry and Vijaya's landing, without the detailed Kuveni dialogue; the Mahavamsa's polished narrative is an expansion of the same tradition.

variants.name: Later Sinhalese recension
variants.text_tradition: Geiger's printed Appendix A (Sinhalese recension divergent readings, Mahavamsa ch. 7 vv. 26-84)
variants.summary: The later Sinhalese recension gives divergent and fuller episodes around the Kuveni affair, showing the story's growth in the island's own commentarial and vernacular tradition.

variants.name: Ramayana counter-tradition
variants.text_tradition: Valmiki, Ramayana; Hindu and Tamil memory of Ravana's Lanka
variants.summary: The great Hindu epic makes Lanka Ravana's demon-girt realm won by Rama; Sri Lankan Hindu tradition reads the island's heroic age through Ravana, a counter-charter to the Vijaya story, and modern comparisons pair the two 'conquests' of the same island.

primary_sources.work: Mahavamsa, chs. 6-7 (The Coming of Vijaya; The Consecrating of Vijaya)
primary_sources.citation: Pali chronicle attributed to Mahanama the thera, c. 5th-6th c. CE; Wilhelm Geiger (trans.), The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, London: Pali Text Society, 1912, pp. 51-61.

secondary_sources.work: Wilhelm Geiger, introduction and notes to the translation
secondary_sources.citation: Geiger 1912, Pali Text Society — critical apparatus on the Sinhalese recension and the relationship to the Dipavamsa.

secondary_sources.work: R. A. L. H. Gunawardana, 'The People of the Lion'
secondary_sources.citation: Gunawardana 1979, in Ethnicity and Social Change in Sri Lanka / Sri Lanka Journal of the Humanities — analysis of the Sihala identity construction in the chronicles.

secondary_sources.work: Steven Kemper, The Presence of the Past
secondary_sources.citation: Kemper 1991, Notre Dame: University of Notre Dame Press — chronicles, politics and culture in Sinhala life; how Vijaya and Dutthagamani are used in modern political memory.

Sacred Texts — Mahavamsa English translation (Geiger), chs. 6-7 cross-check

sensitivity_guidance: The Mahavamsa is scripture-adjacent history for Theravada Buddhists and its Vijaya episode is actively used in modern Sinhala nationalism (from Anagarika Dharmapala to present-day politics), including claims that the island was promised to the Sinhala Buddhists. Retell the narrative descriptively; do not present the charter as historical fact; note Tamil and Vedda counter-memories (Kuveni as wronged first lady, her children as the aboriginal people).

title.en: Kuveni the Yakkhini, Betrayed (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 鳩逸尼夜叉女之被棄與死

region.en: Lankapura and Sirisavatthu, the yakkha city (north-west Sri Lanka; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 夜叉城吉祥住與蘭卡城（錫蘭西北，象徵性定位）

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, chs. 7-8

summary.en: The yakkhini Kuveni, who won Vijaya his kingdom and bore him a son and a daughter, is put away when a Pandya princess arrives: men, Vijaya says, are ever in fear of superhuman beings. Returning to the yakkha city of Lankapura, she is slain as a spy by a single blow; her uncle warns the two children, who flee to Sumanakuta and become ancestors of the Pulindas. The chronicle then turns to the marriage of Vijaya's successor Panduvasudeva with the golden maiden Bhaddakaccana of the Sakya line.
summary.zh: 夜叉女鳩逸尼為維闍耶奪國育子，然南印度般度公主既至，王謂『人恆畏超自然者』而棄之。她歸蘭卡城，夜叉眾疑其為諜，一拳斃之；其舅令二子速逃至聖山，兄妹相婚，後裔為浦林陀人。編年史隨即記維闍耶之繼承者頻陀娑由釋迦族迎金姑娘跋陀迦遮那為后之事。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); retold freely. Note: Kuveni figures in modern Sri Lankan literature and feminist re-reading as the wronged first lady of the island — handled descriptively.

passages.text: Kuveni had served Vijaya faithfully: she had given him the yakkhas' kingdom, done him a woman's service, and borne him a son and a daughter. But when the Pandya princess arrived at Mahatittha with her train, Vijaya said to the yakkhini: 'Go thou now, dear one, leaving the two children behind; men are ever in fear of superhuman beings.' Seized with fear of the yakkhas herself, she besought him again and again; he promised a thousand pieces for an offering to her, and at last she took her two children and departed for Lankapura, fearing what evil might come of it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 7 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: She set the children down outside the yakkha city and went in alone. The yakkhas recognized her at once, took her in their terror for a spy of the men who now dwelt in the island, and great was the stir among them; one who was violent killed the yakkhini with a single blow of his fist. Her mother's brother, a yakkha, came out and found the children: 'Here has your mother been slain, and they will slay you also if they see you; therefore flee swiftly!' Fleeing with speed they came to Sumanakuta. When the brother grew up he took his sister to wife, and multiplying with sons and daughters they dwelt, with the king's leave, in the mountain region; from these are sprung the Pulindas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 7 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Vijaya died with no heir, and for a year the ministers ruled from Upatissagama awaiting the prince. In Sihapura his brother Sumitta sent his youngest son Panduvasudeva, who came in the disguise of mendicant monks with thirty-two sons of ministers and landed at the mouth of the Mahakandara river. A soothsayer had foretold the prince's coming and that one sprung of his house would establish the religion of the Buddha in Lanka. Panduvasudeva, lacking a consort, was not yet consecrated; so when the golden maiden Bhaddakaccana — youngest daughter of the Sakya Pandu, fair as a woman of gold, wooed by seven kings — was placed by her father on a ship with thirty-two women-friends, she too landed robed as a nun, was recognized by a minister who had heard the soothsayer's word, and was consecrated queen; her companions were given to the prince's followers, and the monarch lived happily.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 8 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Asoka Receives the Great Bodhi-tree Branch (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 阿育王奉迎大菩提樹枝

region.en: Pataliputta (Patna, Bihar, India) — Asoka's capital and the Bodhi-tree of Pupphapura
region.zh: 摩揭陀華氏城（今印度巴特那，菩提樹枝分離之地）

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, ch. 18

summary.en: At the request of Devanampiyatissa's envoy Arittha, Asoka agrees to send the south branch of the great Bodhi-tree to Lanka with his daughter Sanghamitta. The god Vissakamma moulds a golden vase in a moment; the branch severs itself along a line the king draws with red arsenic, puts out a net of a hundred roots, and stands in the vase while the earth quakes and six-coloured rays fill the universe; rising into the air it remains seven days invisible in the region of snow.
summary.zh: 提沙王遣臣阿利陀至華氏城請聖菩提樹枝與僧伽蜜多；阿育王從摩訶目犍連子帝須之議應允。毘首羯磨神倏造金甕；王以硃砂金筆畫線，南枝自斷，下垂百根，立於甕中，地震而六色光芒遍照；樹枝乘甕升空，隱於雪山七日。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); retold freely; the Bodhi-tree remains an actively worshipped relic of the tradition.

passages.text: Remembering the thera's word, king Devanampiyatissa entrusted his nephew, the minister Arittha, with the mission: 'Canst thou go to Dhammasoka to bring hither the great Bodhi-tree and the theri Sanghamitta?' 'I can, if I may receive ordination on my return,' Arittha answered, and sailed from Jambukola, reaching Pupphapura on the very day of his departure by the thera's power. In Lanka meanwhile the queen Anula, with five hundred maidens and five hundred women of the harem, took the ten precepts and waited in a nunnery for the theri. Asoka grieved at parting with his daughter, but Moggaliputta-Tissa, asked whether the tree should be sent, answered that it should, and related the five great resolutions the Buddha had formed for the island.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 18 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king cleared and adorned the seven-yojana road to the great Bodhi-tree. Vissakamma, appearing in the guise of a goldsmith, moulded in a single moment a golden vase nine cubits around and five deep. With his fourfold army, a thousand theras and more than a thousand anointed princes, Asoka went to the tree, which gleamed with flags and garlands; he consecrated the great Bodhi-tree as king of his realm, walked around it three times keeping it on his right, and drew with red arsenic a line about the south bough: 'So truly as the great Bodhi-tree shall go hence to the isle of Lanka, shall this fair south branch, severed of itself, take its place in this golden vase.' The branch severed itself, floated above the vase, and put down ten strong roots and, from further lines, a net of a hundred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 18 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: With a hundred roots the tree set itself in the fragrant earth of the vase — a stem of ten cubits, five branches, a thousand twigs. The earth quaked; instruments sounded of themselves among gods and men; six-coloured rays went forth from fruits and leaves and made the whole universe shine; and rising into the air with the vase the great Bodhi-tree stayed seven days invisible in the region of snow. When the week ended, clouds and rays entered the tree again and it was displayed to the people; Asoka consecrated it twice more with kingship, kept it in a beautiful hall by a great sala-tree, and when new shoots appeared all at once on the seventeenth day he rejoiced and appointed a festival of offerings. So the adoration of the great Bodhi-tree opened the hearts of gods and men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 18 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Asoka's Conversion and the Third Council (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 阿育王歸信與第三次結集

region.en: Pataliputta (Patna, Bihar, India) — Asoka's capital and the Asokarama
region.zh: 摩揭陀華氏城（今印度巴特那，阿育伽藍所在）

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, ch. 5

summary.en: Candasoka, the wicked Asoka, slays his ninety-nine brothers and wins Jambudipa; the chronicle traces his cruelty and his generosity back to a former life as a honey-giver. The orphan novice Nigrodha, son of the murdered prince Sumana, preaches the Appamadavagga to him and wins the empire's faith; when a misguided minister beheads theras who refuse the uposatha with heretics, the king fetches Moggaliputta-Tissa, and the Third Council purifies the order, expelling sixty thousand and compiling the true doctrine.
summary.zh: 黑阿育弒九十九兄而得贍部洲；經中溯其行於前世施蜜之業者。被誅王子之孤沙彌尼瞿多為王說精進品，王歸信三寶；後有迷妄之臣欲強僧作布薩而斬上座，王遂迎摩訶目犍連子帝須，行第三次結集：逐六萬邪眾，出迦他颯度婆羅，正法得淨。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); retold freely. Note: the chronicle's Aśoka differs from the remorseful Aśoka of the Rock Edicts (the Kalinga war tradition) — a comparison, not a conflation.

passages.text: After the nine Nandas, the brahman Canakka anointed Candagutta over all Jambudipa; his son Bindusara had a hundred and one sons, and Asoka, high above them all in valour and wondrous powers, slew his ninety-nine brothers and won the undivided sovereignty, consecrating himself at Pataliputta four years later. The chronicle knows him as Candasoka, the wicked Asoka, for his evil deeds. Yet it traces his destiny to a former life: three brothers traded in honey; one gave a paccekabuddha a bowl of honey flowing over, and wished for the undivided rule of Jambudipa with his command reaching a yojana up and down; his brothers' grudging words and the maid who pointed out the honey-store ripened in their several fates. Asoka was the honey-giver.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 5 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The novice Nigrodha, son of prince Sumana whom Asoka had slain, whose widowed mother had been sheltered by a tree-god in a candala village, came calm and staid along the street, and the king felt kindly toward him. Bidden to a fitting seat, the youth approached the royal throne under the white canopy and sat upon it; the king rejoiced that he had honoured one of the highest rank according to his rank, fed him from his own plate, and heard from him the Appamadavagga on unwearying zeal. Won to the doctrine, Asoka gave eight perpetual supplies of food, which the novice allotted to his master and the community; next day the king confirmed the monks in the refuges and precepts, and ever after bestowed alms on sixty thousand bhikkhus, setting aside the false teachers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 5 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: As heretics in yellow robes crowded into the enriched order for revenue's sake, the bhikkhus could no longer hold the uposatha and pavaranа ceremonies; a minister sent to enforce the king's command struck off the heads of several theras who would not hold the festival with heretics, and only the king's brother's swift presence ended the slaughter. Troubled Asoka was told there was a bhikkhu able to befriend religion: the thera Tissa, son of Moggali, who dwelt alone on the Ahoganga mountain. Fetched at last by ship on the Ganges — the king wading knee-deep and giving his right hand to be taken as a pupil's — the thera wrought an earthquake bounded to a single yojana, taught him that no guilt results without evil intent, and recited the Tittira-jataka to comfort him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 5 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asoka then assembled the whole brotherhood behind a curtain and questioned each confession in turn: 'What did the Blessed One teach?' The adherents of the Sassata and other doctrines were expelled — sixty thousand in all; the rightly believing answered that he teaches the Vibhajja-doctrine, and the king was glad and named Moggaliputta guardian of the order.
