The thera chose a thousand learned bhikkhus gifted with the six powers and compiled the true dhamma in the Asokarama, even as Mahakassapa and Yasa had done; in the midst of the council he set forth the Kathavatthu, refuting the other doctrines, and in nine months the council ended, the earth shaking in applause. Asoka's son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta, ordained in the sixth year of his reign, were the lights that would carry the doctrine to Lanka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 5 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Mahinda Comes to Lanka and Riddles the King (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 摩哂陀降臨與芒果之問

region.en: Missaka mountain (Mihintale), near Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka
region.zh: 錫蘭彌思迦山（今米欣特萊，阿耨羅陀補羅之東）

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, chs. 13-14

summary.en: Mahinda, son of Asoka and twelve years a monk, waits until Devanampiyatissa is consecrated king, then rises through the air with four theras, the novice Sumana and the layman Bhanduka, and alights on the Sila-peak of Missaka. A deva in the form of an elk-stag leads the hunting king to him; the mango-tree riddle proves the king shrewd, the discourse on the elephant's footprint converts him and forty thousand men; the doctrine is announced over all Lanka and preached first to the women of the palace and the townspeople.
summary.zh: 阿育王子摩哂陀出家十二年，待提沙王灌頂既畢，與四上座、沙彌蘇摩那及在家弟子般圖迦乘空而至，落於彌思迦山石峰。山神化麋鹿引獵王至；芒果之問顯王機敏，象跡喻小經度王與四萬人歸依；法音遍聞全島，后妃萬民次第聞法得果。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); retold freely. The mango riddle (ch. 14) remains a set-piece of Sri Lankan Buddhist memory of Mihintale.

passages.text: The great thera Mahinda, charged by his teacher Moggaliputta and the brotherhood to convert the island of Lanka, pondered the fitting time: the old king Mutasiva's son must first become king. He visited his kinsfolk at Vedisa, where his mother Devi dwelt, and the deva Indra urged him on: 'Set forth to convert Lanka; by the Sambuddha hast thou been foretold for this.' On the uposatha-day of the month Jettha he rose into the air from the Vedisagiri vihara with the four theras, the miraculously gifted novice Sumana, and the lay-disciple Bhanduka — that they might be known for human beings — and alighted on the Sila-peak of Missaka mountain, on the fair tableland of Ambatthala, extolled by the gods of Lanka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 13 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: King Devanampiyatissa, who had held a water festival in the capital, went hunting on Missaka with forty thousand men. The deva of the mountain, wishing to show him the theras, took the form of an elk-stag; the king would not shoot the heedless creature but twanged his bowstring, and the stag fled toward the mountain and vanished. Terrified at the sight of the thera seated there, the king was calmed by the words: 'Samanas are we, O great king, disciples of the King of Truth; from compassion toward thee are we come hither from Jambudipa.' To test him the thera asked subtle questions about a mango-tree: are there other mangoes, other trees, anything beside kinsfolk and strangers? 'There is yet myself, sir.' 'Thou hast a shrewd wit, O ruler of men!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 14 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The thera then preached the discourse on the simile of the elephant's footprint, and the king with his forty thousand men took the refuges. Knowing the theras ate only at the proper time, the king left them on the mountain; Bhanduka was ordained on the spot and became arahant in that very moment. At the king's morning meal by the rock-basin the novice Sumana, bidden to announce the time of preaching, made the summons heard by his miraculous power over the whole of Tambapanni, and the call, echoed by earth-gods, rose to Brahma's heaven; countless devas gathered, and the thera preached to them. The next day the theras, refusing the waggon, flew to the east of the city, where the Pathamacetiya marks their descent, and were led in with honour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 14 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the palace the king himself served the theras rice-soup and foods, then sent for queen Anula, consort of the sub-king Mahanaga, with five hundred women. The thera preached the Petavatthu, the Vimanavatthu and the Sacca-samyutta, and the women attained the first stage of sanctification. The townspeople, crowning at the palace gates, were shown the theras in the cleansed hall of the state-elephant, where the eminent preacher discoursed on the Devaduta-suttanta; a thousand hearers attained the first stage. So the peerless thera, preaching the true doctrine in the speech of the island, brought to pass the descent of the faith into Lanka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 14 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bodhi-tree Crosses the Sea to Lanka (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 僧伽蜜多航海運菩提樹

region.en: Jambukola harbour to Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka (the tree's landing and planting)
region.zh: 自瞻波醯迦港至阿耨羅陀補羅大雲林園（錫蘭）

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, ch. 19

summary.en: Asoka loads the great Bodhi-tree on a ship of the Ganges with Sanghamitta, eleven nuns, and escorts drawn from every family and craft of his realm, wading neck-deep in the water to set it aboard. On the voyage the waves are stilled for a yojana around; the nagas try to win the tree by magic and are terrified by Sanghamitta in the form of a griffin, then worship it a week in the realm of serpents. The tree lands at Jambukola, is borne in fourteen days of festival procession to Anuradhapura, rises eighty cubits into the air in six-coloured rays, and is planted in the Mahamegha grove, whence thirty-two saplings and forty saplings from its fruits spread through the island.
summary.zh: 阿育王以船載大菩提樹於恒河，僧伽蜜多率十一比丘尼與諸族姓工藝之眾護送，王入水至頸奉樹登船。海中波平一由旬，龍欲以幻取樹，僧伽蜜多化為金翅鳥懾之，龍眾乃奉樹七日。樹至瞻波港，十四日慶典迎入阿耨羅陀補羅，升空八十肘，六色光芒照徹，植於大雲林園；枝果復生八樹與三十二樹，遍佈全島。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); retold freely. The Sri Maha Bodhi at Anuradhapura, descended from this tree in the chronicle's account, is an actively worshipped shrine.

passages.text: Asoka appointed escorts from the royal families, from ministers, brahmans, traders, cowherds, from the hyena and sparrowhawk clans, from weavers, potters and all the handicrafts, from the nagas and the yakkhas, giving them eight golden and eight silver vessels to water the tree. He brought the great Bodhi-tree to a ship on the Ganges with the theri Sanghamitta and eleven bhikkhunis, and Arittha's company; wading into the river till it reached his neck, the king set the tree down on the ship in seemly wise and stood on the shore with folded hands, weeping as it vanished from his sight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 19 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The ship fared forth into the sea, and for a yojana around the waves were stilled; lotus-flowers of five colours blossomed all around and music resounded in the air. The nagas practised their magic to win the great Bodhi-tree, but Sanghamitta, who had reached the last goal of the supernormal powers, took the form of a griffin and terrified the great snakes. They brought the tree to the realm of the serpents, worshipped it for a week by bestowing on it the kingship of the nagas, then set it again upon the ship; and on that same day the great Bodhi-tree arrived in Lanka at Jambukola.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 19 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Devanampiyatissa, forewarned by the novice Sumana, had made ready the whole highroad from the north gate to Jambukola; standing on the shore he saw the tree coming by the theri's power, and uttering an exulting cry he waded neck-deep into the sea. With sixteen nobles he took the tree upon his head, set it in a pavilion, worshipped it with the kingship of Lanka, and entrusted his government to the sixteen while he himself took the duties of a doorkeeper. Three days of ceremonies followed; on the tenth day the tree was placed on a car, and on the fourteenth, amid white sand, flowers and pennons, it entered Anuradhapura by the north gate and was brought to the Mahamegha garden, the place consecrated by four Buddhas, where the former Bodhi-trees had stood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 19 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Scarcely had the king loosed his hold when the tree rose eighty cubits into the air, floating and sending forth six-coloured rays that spread over the island to the Brahma-world until sunset; ten thousand persons, filled with faith, attained arahantship there. At sunset it came down and stood firm under the constellation Rohini; the roots closed over the vase and the earth quaked. A faultless fruit fell from the east branch, and eight saplings four cubits high sprang up before all eyes: one was planted at Jambukola, others at Tivakka's village, the Thuparama, the Issarasamanarama, the Court of the First cetiya, the Cetiya-mountain, Kajaragama and Candanagama; thirty-two more, from four later fruits, were set in a circle at a yojana's distance. Queen Anula's company received ordination from Sanghamitta, Arittha from the thera, and in the nunnery called Hatthalhaka the great theri dwelt; the mast, rudder and helm of the ship were set up in three buildings there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 19 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Dutthagamani and Elara: The Single Combat (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 杜多迦摩尼與伊羅羅之單騎決戰

region.en: South gate of Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka — where Elara fell
region.zh: 錫蘭阿耨羅陀補羅南門（伊羅羅陣亡之地）

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, chs. 22-25

summary.en: The prince Gamani, reborn of a pious novice, lies curled on his bed because the Damilas hold the land beyond the Mahaganga; his father's rebuke earns him a woman's ornament and the name Dutthagamani, the angry Gamani. Reconciled to his brother Tissa through the bhikkhus, he campaigns north with a relic in his spear and five hundred monks at his side, storms Vijitanagara with the elephant Kandula, and at the south gate of Anuradhapura fells the Tamil king Elara — whom he then honours with funeral rites and a monument before which princes still silence their music. Arahants comfort his midnight grief: only one and a half human beings have been slain by him.
summary.zh: 王子伽摩尼因提沙王國之外為泰米爾人所據，蜷臥不起；父怒賜女飾，遂號都他伽摩尼（怒伽摩尼）。經僧和解兄弟之鬥後，矛奉舍利，五百比丘隨行，先破維提城，繼於阿耨羅陀補羅南門與泰米爾王伊羅羅單騎決戰殺之；為之葬祭立碑，至今諸王經此息樂。阿羅漢夜慰其悔：所殺者唯『一又二分之一人』。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); retold freely. Note: the Dutthagamani-Elara story is actively used as a charter in modern Sinhala nationalism and was invoked in the civil-war era; this record reports the chronicle's account and its modern reception descriptively, without endorsing either.
sensitivity.zh: 活傳統之聖典（上座部佛教），可自由講述。杜多迦摩尼與伊羅羅故事見用作現代僧訶羅民族主義之憲章，內戰時期亦被引用；本紀錄僅作描述，不為任何一方背書。

passages.text: The chronicle inserts the Dutthagamani epic with the words: 'When he had slain Elara, Dutthagamani became king — to show clearly how this came to pass.' The pious novice of Kotapabbata, courted by the childless queen Viharadevi to be her son, died and entered her womb on the homeward journey; her cravings — a honeycomb a usabha long, the water that had cleansed the sword of Elara's first warrior, garlands from Anuradhapura's lotus-marshes — were read by the soothsayers: 'Her son, when he has vanquished the Damilas and built up a united kingdom, will make the doctrine to shine forth brightly.' The boy Gamani was born amid seven ships of gems, and the elephant Kandula came of his merit. At the rice-giving festival the brothers took the first two portions with joy; but at the third — 'Never will we fight with the Damilas' — Gamani flung away the morsel, went to his bed, and lay with hands and feet drawn in: 'Over there beyond the Ganga are the Damilas, here on this side is the Gotha-ocean; how can I lie with outstretched limbs?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 22 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Gamani announced that he would make war upon the Damilas, his father forbade him: 'The region on this side of the river is enough.' Gamani sent him a woman's ornament: 'If my father were a man he would not speak thus.' The enraged king answered: 'Make a golden chain; with that will I bind him.' So the son fled to Malaya and was named Dutthagamani, the angry Gamani. After the father's death he made war on his own brother Tissa at Culaanganiyapitthi and was driven to flight; starving by the ford, he set aside portions for the brotherhood, and the thera Gotama, hearing the meal proclaimed with his heavenly ear, sent a bowl through the air so that king and mare were fed. The bhikkhus made a mountain between the armies, and when Tissa fled into a vihara the monks bore him out on a bed as a dead bhikkhu while the king let him go: 'To tear away anything with violence from the guardian genii of our house is not my custom.' Later Tissa, brought by the thera Godhagatta with five hundred bhikkhus, made his peace, and the king sat with him in the midst of the brotherhood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 24 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Dutthagamani had a relic set in his spear — a royal standard carried before the host — and marched with five hundred bhikkhus the brotherhood gave him as penance: 'The sight of bhikkhus is blessing and protection for us.' He overpowered the Damila captains one by one along the river and destroyed Vijitanagara after four months' siege: the elephant Kandula, scorched by molten pitch, was shamed back into the breach by Gothaimbara's rebuke — 'Here is no sura-draught for thee' — and crashed the iron gate, while the ten heroes each broke the walls by his own strength, refusing to follow the elephant's path. When it was said he knew not his own army and slew his own people, he made a solemn declaration: 'Not for the joy of sovereignty is this toil of mine; my striving has been ever to establish the doctrine of the Sambuddha. And even as this is truth may the armour on the body of my soldiers take the colour of fire.' And it came to pass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 25 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Elara's champion Dighajantu scattered the decoy bodies of troops in the great battle by the tank, and fell to Siranimila's spear. Dutthagamani then proclaimed with beat of drum: 'None but myself shall slay Elara.' Near the south gate of Anuradhapura the two kings fought on their elephants; Elara's dart was evaded, Kandula pierced the other elephant, and the Tamil king fell there with his elephant. The victor united Lanka under one rule, then beat the drum and summoned the people from a yojana around to celebrate the funeral rites for Elara: he burned the body on the spot where it fell and built a monument and ordained worship — and even to this day the princes of Lanka, when they draw near to this place, silence their music. Bhalluka's counter-invasion fell to Phussadeva's arrow through the mouth; and when the king rested on his palace terrace, remembering the destruction of millions, eight arahants flew down from Piyangudipa: 'From this deed arises no hindrance in thy way to heaven. Only one and a half human beings have been slain by thee — the rest were unbelievers, not more to be esteemed than beasts.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 25 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

canonical_translation: Wilhelm Geiger, The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, London: Pali Text Society 1912 (public domain)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE CURLED-UP PRINCE. Chapter 22 opens with the Birth of Prince Gamani, told as a rebirth story: a pious novice of Kotapabbata who had served the brotherhood all his life, when dying was asked by queen Viharadevi — wife of Kakavannatissa, king of Rohana — to become her son, and entered her womb as she journeyed home. Her pregnancy cravings (a honeycomb as a pillow, twelve thousand bhikkhus fed before she ate of it; the water that had washed the sword of Elara's first warrior; unfaded lotuses from Anuradhapura's marshes) prompt the soothsayers' prophecy: her son will vanquish the Damilas, unite the kingdom, and make the doctrine shine. Gamani ('to the village') is born amid seven shiploads of gems and the arrival of the elephant Kandula. At the first-rice festival, and again in a three-portion test, the brothers accept every portion except the one eaten 'with the thought: never will we fight with the Damilas' — Tissa dashes his away; Gamani flings his morsel, goes to his bed and lies with limbs drawn in. 'Why dost thou not lie easily, my son?' — 'Over there beyond the Ganga are the Damilas; here on this side is the Gotha-ocean; how can I lie with outstretched limbs?' The king keeps silence.

MIDDLE: THE ANGRY GAMANI AND THE BROTHERS' WAR. Repeating his resolve, Gamani is forbidden by his father to cross the river; he sends back a woman's ornament — 'if my father were a man he would not speak thus' — and the king threatens to bind him with a golden chain, 'for else he cannot be protected.' The prince flees to Malaya and earns the name Dutthagamani, 'the angry Gamani.' On the father's death the brothers fight at Culaanganiyapitthi; Dutthagamani flees, starving, and stops to feed the brotherhood — a bowl flies through the air from the thera Gotama of Piyangudipa, feeding king, minister and mare alike. The bhikkhus raise a mountain between the armies to part them; later, Tissa sheltered in a vihara is carried out on a bed by monks disguised as a funeral, and the pursuing king lets him pass: 'Tissa, upon the head of the guardian genii of our house art thou carried forth; to tear away anything with violence from the guardian genii of our house is not my custom.' Reconciliation comes through the thera Godhagatta-Tissa, who brings Tissa to the king; the king seats his brother in the midst of the brotherhood, and sends him off to direct the harvest — the sinhala phrase meaning the campaign's preparations.

THE WAR AGAINST ELARA. In chapter 25 the king has a relic placed in his spear as a standard, marches with the brotherhood's gift of five hundred ascetics ('the sight of bhikkhus is blessing and protection for us'), and cuts through the Damila captains down the river. The fortress Vijitanagara falls after four months: Kandula, bathed in molten pitch and shamed by Gothaimbara's rebuke, shatters the iron gate; Nandhimitta breaks the wall by his arm; each hero refuses the other's path. Asked about his slaughter, the king performs a truth-act: 'Not for the joy of sovereignty is this toil of mine; my striving has been ever to establish the doctrine of the Sambuddha. And even as this is truth may the armour on the body of my soldiers take the colour of fire' — and it does. At Anuradhapura, Elara's host under Dighajantu scatters the decoy regiments before falling to Siranimila. Dutthagamani beats the drum: 'None but myself shall slay Elara.' At the south gate the two kings fight from their elephants; Elara's dart misses, Kandula's tusks pierce the rival elephant, and Elara falls with him.

END: THE FUNERAL OF THE FALLEN KING AND THE MONKS' ABSOLUTION. United ruler of Lanka, Dutthagamani summons the people from a yojana around and celebrates the funeral rites for Elara: the body is burned where it fell, a monument is built there, and worship is ordained — 'even to this day the princes of Lanka, when they draw near to this place, are wont to silence their music because of this worship.' The hero's nephew Bhalluka lands with sixty thousand men and, mocking at the gate, is shot through the mouth by Phussadeva, who then cuts off his own ear-lobe for having grazed the king's ear-ring in the flight of the arrow. That night the victorious king, resting on his terrace, 'knew no joy, remembering that thereby was wrought the destruction of millions.' Eight arahants fly down from Piyangudipa to comfort him: 'From this deed arises no hindrance in thy way to heaven. Only one and a half human beings have been slain by thee: the one had come unto the refuges, the other had taken the five precepts. Unbelievers and men of evil life were the rest, not more to be esteemed than beasts.' A remembered pebble — pepper eaten in the pod without a share for the brotherhood — becomes the scruple that turns him to building: the Maricavatti-vihara as penance, the Lohapasada, and the Great Thupa, where chapter 32 finds him dying and reborn in the Tusita-heaven as Metteyya's first disciple.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative is the charter of Sinhala Buddhist sacred kingship: a king whose legitimacy is monastic (fed by theras, protected by monks' mountains, comforted by arahants), whose war is fought 'for the doctrine', and whose enemies' deaths are weighed in a karmic calculus that notoriously discounts unbelievers. It is the nation-myth of the unification of the island under one Sinhala Buddhist rule, with Elara memorialized as a just enemy — a rare note of honor to the fallen. It is also, in modern reception, the most politically charged text of the corpus: from Anagarika Dharmapala's writings through the civil-war rhetoric of the 1980s-2000s, Dutthagamani has been invoked as the model of the righteous warrior-king defending Buddhism against 'invaders', and the chronicle's karmic absolution has been quoted to justify violence. The record reports the narrative and its history of use; it does not endorse the ideology.
narrative.zh:
開端：蜷臥之王。第二十二章以轉生故事開篇：拘陀跋陀寺之篤行沙彌，畢生事僧，臨終受羅訶那王迦迦梵那提沙之后維訶羅提毗所請，入其胎為子。孕中渴求（蜜脾為枕、先饌一萬二千比丘、飲洗伊羅羅首將之劍之水、取阿耨羅陀補羅蓮沼之花），相師斷言：其子破泰米爾人、合一王國、令法光耀。伽摩尼生時七船寶石並至，聖象坎杜羅亦因其福而來。初飯之節與三份之試中，兄弟受前二份；至第三份——『永與泰米爾人無戰』——提沙擲之，伽摩尼亦擲而歸榻，蜷臥不伸：『恒河之外皆泰米爾，此海之內方吾土，安得舒肢而臥？』王聞而默然。

中段：怒伽摩尼與兄弟之戰。伽摩尼請伐泰米爾，父禁之：『河之此岸足矣。』子返贈女飾：『父若丈夫，必不出此言。』王怒答：『鑄金鏈以縛之。』子遂遁於山地，得號都他伽摩尼（怒伽摩尼）。父崩，兄弟戰於初蘭伽尼耶；都他伽摩尼敗走，飢而分食供僧——皮央古提島之喬答摩長老以天耳聞唱食時，遣鉢凌空而至，王、臣與馬皆得食。僧眾於兩軍之間化山以隔；後提沙匿寺中，僧抬之若扶死僧而出，王不阻：『汝出於我家護法神之首上；強奪護法神之物非吾俗。』終由喬陀伽陀長老攜提沙來和，王於僧中與弟同坐，遣之督農——實為伐泰米爾之備。

伐伊羅羅之戰。第二十五章：王以聖矛奉舍利為軍旗，受五百隨行比丘（『見比丘者福而護也』），沿河逐一破泰米爾諸將。維提城圍四月而破：坎杜羅中熔鉛，經哥陀伊姆巴拉之斥——『此非汝飲酒之時』——復振，碎鐵門；南提彌陀以臂破牆，十勇士各以己力不循象徑。或譏其誤殺己軍，王行實語誓：『吾之勞非為王位之樂；吾之奮鬥常在令佛法人揚。若此為實，願吾士卒甲冑作火色。』果如其言。阿耨羅陀補羅之戰，伊羅羅之驍將提姜贊圖散其疑兵，卒斃於南提彌陀矛下。都他伽摩尼擊鼓宣令：『唯吾得殺伊羅羅。』南門之下，二王象戰；伊羅羅之鏢落空，坎杜羅之牙貫其象，泰米爾王與象俱仆。

結局：戰死之王之葬與僧之赦。都他伽摩尼合蘭卡為一，擊鼓召一由旬內之民為伊羅羅行葬禮：焚其屍於陣亡之地，建紀念之碑，命人祀之——『至今蘭卡諸王過此輒息樂』。其姪跋婁迦率六萬人登陸反撲，於門前辱王，為弗薩提婆之箭貫口而斃；弗薩提婆自削耳垂以彰過。是夜王於露臺回望戰功，『心無所樂，念及所殺百萬生靈』。八阿羅漢自皮央古提島凌空而至：『此業不障汝生天之路。王所殺者唯一人半——一已歸依，一受五戒；餘皆不信惡行之人，不足比於畜生。』胡椒入食不供僧之失，化為建寺贖罪之念：償罪建蜜利沙伐帝寺，繼建銅宮與大塔；第三十二章見王臨終，生兜率天，為彌勒首徒。

功能：僧訶羅佛教聖王之憲章（王權合法性出自僧團：長老飼王、僧山隔軍、羅漢慰心；戰爭『為法』而行；不信者之死按業之算術折減）。亦是全島統一於僧訶羅佛教政權之民族神話，伊羅羅得葬祀為敬敵之特例。然於現代接受中，此為全書最政治化之文本：自達摩波羅至內戰年代，都他迦摩尼屢被引為『護法戰王』之典範，其業之赦說亦被引以飾暴力。本紀錄陳述敘事及其使用史，不為該意識形態背書。

functions: Charter of Sinhala Buddhist sacred kingship: royal legitimacy mediated by the sangha (theras feed the king, monks part the armies, arahants absolve him)
Warrior-monk ideology: the war against the Damilas is framed as service to the doctrine, sealed by a truth-act
Nation-myth of the unification of Lanka under one Sinhala Buddhist rule
Honour to the fallen enemy: the funeral rites and monument for Elara, before which princes silence their music
Modern political charter: Dutthagamani invoked in Sinhala nationalism (Dharmapala to the civil-war era) as the model righteous warrior-king — reported, not endorsed

variants.name: Dipavamsa
variants.text_tradition: The earlier Pali chronicle, Dipavamsa chs. 18-19
variants.summary: A compressed account of the same campaign and victory, without the elaborate epic insertions (the rebirth omen, the curled-up boy, the monks' absolution) that the Mahavamsa develops.

variants.name: Sinhalese recension and Tika expansions
variants.text_tradition: Geiger's Appendix A; the Mahavamsa commentary (Tika)
variants.summary: The Sinhalese recension and the commentary add omen and dialogue detail, and the Kambodian Mahavamsa versifies several of the battle scenes — evidence of the story's continued growth in monastic tradition.

variants.name: Tamil counter-memory of Elara
variants.text_tradition: Tamil literary and oral tradition; modern Sri Lankan historiography
variants.summary: Tamil tradition and much modern scholarship remember Elara (Ezhu) as a just and wise ruler of Anuradhapura whose monument commanded respect from all; the same story is thus read either as liberation of the land or as conquest of a good king — the hinge on which Sinhala-Tamil readings of the chronicle diverge.

primary_sources.work: Mahavamsa, chs. 22, 24-25 (The Birth of Prince Gamani; The War of the Two Brothers; The Victory of Dutthagamani)
primary_sources.citation: Pali chronicle attributed to Mahanama the thera, c. 5th-6th c. CE; Wilhelm Geiger (trans.), The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, London: Pali Text Society, 1912, pp. 146-178.

secondary_sources.work: Steven Kemper, The Presence of the Past: Chronicles, Politics, and Culture in Sinhala Life
secondary_sources.citation: Kemper 1991, Notre Dame: University of Notre Dame Press — how the chronicle, and Dutthagamani above all, are used in modern Sinhala political memory.

secondary_sources.work: R. A. L. H. Gunawardana, 'The People of the Lion'
secondary_sources.citation: Gunawardana 1979, in Ethnicity and Social Change in Sri Lanka / Sri Lanka Journal of the Humanities — the historical construction of the Sihala identity in the chronicles.

secondary_sources.work: John Rogers, on the cultural politics of Sinhala Buddhist nationalism
secondary_sources.citation: Rogers 1987 (Journal of Asian Studies) — the political mobilisation of the chronicle tradition in the modern period.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive — Geiger 1912 translation of the Mahavamsa (source text read)
Sacred Texts — Mahavamsa English translation (Geiger), chs. 22-25 cross-check

sensitivity_guidance: The Dutthagamani-Elara episode is the most politically charged story in the Sinhala chronicle tradition: it has been mobilised from Anagarika Dharmapala through the 1980s-2000s civil-war era as a charter for Sinhala Buddhist rule over the island, and the chronicle's claim that unbelievers slain in battle are 'not more to be esteemed than beasts' has been quoted in nationalist apologetics. Present the narrative as the chronicle's own account; flag the karmic absolution passage explicitly as a monastic argument; note the Tamil counter-memory of Elara as a just king; do not use the story to support or refute any modern political claim.

title.en: The Building of the Great Thupa and the Sand of the Master-builders (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 大塔奠基與匠師沙量之奇

region.en: Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka — the site of the Mahathupa (Ruwanweli dagaba)
region.zh: 錫蘭阿耨羅陀補羅大塔（今魯梵維利塔）故址

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, chs. 29-30

summary.en: Dutthagamani founds the Great Thupa on the full-moon of Vesakha: the ground dug seven cubits, crushed stone stamped by elephants with leather-bound feet, and layers of butter-clay, brick, cinnabar, iron net, Himalayan marumba, mountain-crystal, copper and silver laid in order. Brotherhoods from Rajagaha to Alexandria of the Yonas gather; the thera Siddhattha stays the too-vast plan lest the king die before it is done; the shrewd master-builder, possessed by Vissakamma, shows a water-bubble the shape of the dome and wins the day by sifting one ammana of sand a day so no grass shall grow on the cetiya — while the gods bring bricks nightly to the four gates.
summary.zh: 都他迦摩尼於衛塞月圓日奠基大塔：掘地七肘，碎石以革裹足之象踏實，次第敷奶油泥、磚、朱砂、鐵網、雪山泥、水晶、銅與銀。自王舍城至希臘人之亞歷山大城諸僧畢集；悉達長老止王過大之制，恐塔未成而王先亡；巧匠為毘首羯磨神所附，以水面浮泡示塔形，一日篩沙一亞摩那——不使草生塔上；諸神夜夜運磚至四門。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); retold freely. The Ruwanweli dagaba remains an actively worshipped shrine of Anuradhapura.

passages.text: On the full-moon day of Vesakha the king began the Great Thupa. He had the place dug to a depth of seven cubits, had round stones broken with hammers and stamped down by great elephants whose feet were bound with leather. Over the bed he spread the ever-moist butter-clay brought by gifted novices, then bricks, rough cement, cinnabar, a network of iron, sweet-scented marumba from the Himalaya, mountain-crystal, stones, and finally, bound with kapittha-resin and arsenic oil, sheets of copper eight inches thick and silver seven inches thick. He appointed a festival for the laying of the foundation-stone and adorned city and roads for the brotherhood and the people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 29 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the whole Buddhist world the brotherhood came: with eighty thousand bhikkhus the thera Indagutta from Rajagaha; twelve thousand from Isipatana; sixty thousand from Jetavana; eighteen thousand from Mahavana in Vesali; thirty thousand from Ghositarama in Kosambi; forty thousand from Dakkhinagiri in Ujjeni; a hundred and sixty thousand from the Asokarama in Pataliputta; two hundred and eighty thousand from Kasmira; four hundred and sixty thousand from Pallavabhogga; thirty thousand from Alasanda, city of the Yonas — and countless others. Those alone who had overcome the asavas are reckoned at ninety-six kotis. When the king stepped into the circle to trace the boundary with a silver staff roped to a golden post, the thera Siddhattha prevented him: so great a thupa would not be finished before the king's death and would be hard to repair; the king, from reverence, took a moderate space, laid eight splendid bricks, and at the offering of jasmine-flowers an earthquake came to pass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 29 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king called the five hundred master-builders. One promised a waggon-load of sand a day, and the king rejected him — the cetiya would be a heap of sand overgrown with grass — down through halvings until one offered to pound the sand in a mortar, sift and crush it, and use a single ammana a day. At that moment Vissakamma entered into him; filling his hand with water he let a drop fall on the surface, and where a great bubble rose like a half-globe of crystal, he said: 'Thus will I make it.' The king, consenting, loaded him with gifts. pondering by night how bricks might come without burdening the people, the king was answered: the gods brought night after night to the four gates as many bricks as sufficed for a day; and work was paid, not pressed, at every gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 30 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wages and wonder ran together: bhikkhus, wishing to share the merit, smuggled clay and bricks among the workmen, and the king honoured them rather than expose them. When the three terraces for flower-offerings sank nine times beneath the bricks laid upon them, the brotherhood explained that theras of miraculous power had made them sink so the thupa should not sink of itself. Two novices brought six fat-coloured stones, eighty cubits each, bright as the sun, from the Northern Kurus for the relic-chamber, four disposed as a chest, one as a lid. In the chamber the king set a jewel Bodhi-tree with silver stem and golden fruits, a golden Buddha-image with Brahma, Sakka, Pancasikha and Mara's train about it, and thrones to the eight regions; and two women who had laboured for hire on the thupa, reborn in the heaven of the thirty-three, came back at night in radiance to worship the work their merit had raised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 30 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Relic-dona Enshrined and Dutthagamani's Death (Mahavamsa)
title.zh: 聖髑奉安與王崩生兜率天

region.en: Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka — the Mahathupa's relic-chamber
region.zh: 錫蘭阿耨羅陀補羅大塔藏髑室

period: Pali chronicle, composed c. 5th-6th c. CE (attrib. Mahanama); Geiger translation 1912

source.work: The Mahavamsa; or, The Great Chronicle of Ceylon, trans. Wilhelm Geiger, 1912, chs. 31-32

summary.en: The brotherhood charges the sixteen-year-old arahant Sonuttara to fetch the relic-dona destined for the Great Thupa, guarded in the naga king's realm under Mount Manjerika; the nagas swallow the urn and coil about Sineru, but the thera stretches an arm down the serpent's throat and takes the relics. Enshrined on the full-moon of Asalha, the relics rise into the air, assume the Buddha's form and work the twin miracle, and twelve kotis of gods and men attain arahantship. The dying Dutthagamani, reckoning his merits, chooses the Tusita-heaven of the future Buddha Metteyya, is reborn there in celestial form, and drives thrice around the Great Thupa.
summary.zh: 僧團命十六歲羅漢蘇努陀羅往龍王國取定於大塔之聖髑甕；龍姪吞甕繞須彌山三百由旬，長老伸臂入蛇喉取之。髑於頞沙荼月圓奉安，升空化佛身，現雙神變，十二俱胝天人得阿羅漢果。臨終之都他迦摩尼數其功德，擇未來佛彌勒之兜率天而終，天身現世，繞大塔三匝。

sensitivity.note: Canonical chronicle of a living tradition (Theravada Buddhism); retold freely. Relic worship and the Metteyya prophecy remain living practices of the tradition.

passages.text: The relic-chamber finished, the king summoned the brotherhood: 'To-morrow I will enshrine the relics.' The bhikkhus charged the novice Sonuttara, sixteen years old and gifted with the six powers, with the task, and told him the relics' history: of the eight donas of the Buddha's bodily relics, the one enshrined at Ramagama by the Koliyas was destined for the Great Thupa of Lanka; the thupa by the Ganges had been washed away, and the urn, floating to the ocean, had been taken by the naga king Kalanava to his palace at Manjerika and adored there under strong guard. Sonuttara plunged into the earth and stood before the naga king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 31 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The naga king, fearing force, signed to his nephew, who swallowed the urn and went to the foot of Mount Sineru, coiled there in a ring three hundred yojanas long, belching smoke and fire among a thousand heads, while nagas and devas gathered to watch the combat. 'If thou shalt see the relics, take them and go,' the uncle promised thrice; and the thera, standing on that spot, created a long slender arm, stretched it straight down the nephew's throat, drew out the urn and cried 'Stay, naga!' as he plunged into the earth and rose in his cell. All the nagas lamented that they were betrayed; from compassion the brotherhood left them a few of the relics, and they brought treasure offerings rejoicing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 31 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sakka came with the gods bearing a jewelled throne and a golden casket; Brahma held the parasol, the yak-tail whisk and the fan, the four great kings their swords, thirty-two celestial maidens their lamps, and the twenty-eight yakkha-chieftains stood guard against evil yakkhas. The king, bearing the casket on his head under the white parasol, thrice consecrated the relics with the kingship of Lanka, and ascending the thupa laid them in the chamber. The casket rose of itself seven talantas into the air, opened, and the relics, taking the form of the Buddha gleaming with the thirty-two signs, wrought the twin miracle of fire and water, as the Master had done under the Gandamba-tree; twelve kotis of devas and men attained arahantship at the sight. The relics lay at last on the precious couch in the shape of the Master on his deathbed; the earth quaked, and for a week the whole island's people, borne to the spot at one moment by Indagutta's power, adored the relics and returned to their houses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 31 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Before the plaster-work was done the king fell mortally ill, and his brother Tissa covered the unfinished cetiya with painted white cloths. Carried on a palanquin to see the Great Thupa, Dutthagamani lay between the stupa and the splendid Lohapasada, in the midst of ninety-six kotis of bhikkhus, and bade the scribe read aloud the book of his meritorious deeds: ninety-nine viharas, nineteen kotis on the Maricavatti-vihara, thirty kotis on the Lohapasada, a thousand kotis on the Great Thupa — 'but only the two gifts I gave in adversity, without care for my life, gladden my heart.' Six celestial cars arrived from six heavens to carry him; he stayed them till he heard the dhamma, then asked which heaven was fairest, and was told: 'The city of the Tusitas, where the compassionate Bodhisatta Metteyya awaits his Buddhahood.' Casting a glance at the Great Thupa he closed his eyes and died, and was seen reborn in celestial form in the Tusita car, driving thrice around the Great Thupa before he passed into the Tusita-heaven — first disciple, the chronicle prophesies, of the sublime Metteyya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahavamsa, ch. 32 (Geiger 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Anansi Swaps Himself for Tiger
title.zh: 蜘蛛人換虎頂罪

region.en: Dry River and Mandeville, Jamaica (symbolic pin: Mandeville)
region.zh: 牙買加乾河與曼德維爾（象徵定位：曼德維爾）

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921 from named tellers; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories', Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society vol. XVII (1924), tale 2 'Tiger as Substitute' (told by William Forbes of Dry River and George Parkes of Mandeville)

summary.en: Anansi tricks a king's two daughters into tying him up over a boiling pot, then swaps the trap for Tiger and escapes; and when caught raiding a field of gub-gub peas he forges a reading from a scrap envelope — 'tie Anansi and let him go when his belly is full' — gets bound instead of caught, then scares the watchman loose by claiming sorcerer's power and finally foists a red-hot iron on Lion by pleading that he never learned to hold a knife and fork.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人以國王之女設局反被困火鍋之上，趁虎經過把刑位換給老虎逃走；又闖入豆田偷豆，偽造信箋教守者『縛蜘蛛、腹飽即放』，屢屢脫身，終以『天生不會持刀叉』的哭訴騙獅子替他綁上火刑位，自己安然遁去。

sensitivity.note: Social amusement tale (Anansi cycle), collected from named Jamaican storytellers; living oral tradition, tales freely shared in public storytelling. Cross-ref: yoruba-ijapa trickster tales (motif family).

passages.text: Anansi courted a king's two daughters and made fools of them, and they caught and bound him and went off to gather wood for a fire under a great kettle of water. While the sisters were gone, Tiger came along. 'Lawd! Brar Tiger, I get into trouble here!' cried Anansi. 'For what?' asked Tiger. 'The king's daughters want to live with me and have tied me here.' Tiger, disgusted, said, 'You fool — untie me and tie me in your place!' Anansi tied Tiger fast and hid himself at a grass-root. When the girls returned and threw down their firewood, the younger cried, 'Sister! the little uncle we tied has turned into a big uncle!' They built the fire, dashed ladles of boiling water over the bound prisoner, and he jumped until the rope popped, tumbling down on the very grass-root where Anansi hid. Anansi laughed, 'Tissin, tissin, tissin!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, Jamaica Anansi Stories, tale 2a 'The King's Two Daughters' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: A man planted a great field of gub-gub peas and set an illiterate watchman over them; the crop grew lovely and everybody passing admired it. Anansi begged peas and was refused, so he picked up an old envelope, presented it to the watchman, and read it for him: 'The master says — tie Mr. Anansi at the fattest part of the peas, and when his belly is full, let him go.' The watchman did so. Back came the master, furious that no letter had ever been sent; the next day Anansi read the same trick again, but this time the watchman would not free him. Anansi spat threats — 'If you don't let me go, I'll spit on the ground and you'll rot!' — and the frightened watchman untied him, paying Anansi a sorcerer's respect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 2b 'The Gub-gub Peas' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the master caught Anansi, carried him to his yard, and bound him beneath a tree, heating a big iron in the fire. As the iron glowed, Lion came by and asked why Anansi was tied. Anansi wept that since the day he was born he had never held a knife and fork, and now the people demanded he should. 'You worthless man!' said Lion. 'I can hold it.' Lion freed him and took his place at the post; when the master came out he found Lion there, drew the red-hot iron from the fire, and shoved it into Lion's ear. Lion plunged, popped the rope, galloped into the bush, and stood panting under the very tree where Anansi watched — who, trembling, shook the leaves until Lion saw him and called him down. Anansi shouted to the household, 'See the man you were looking for!' and Lion galloped away forever, living wild in the bush, while Anansi went free.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 2b, closing episode (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Tiger Made to Prove He Is Anansi's Father's Riding-Horse
title.zh: 老虎被證明是蜘蛛人父親的坐騎

region.en: Dry River, Cock-pit country, Jamaica (symbolic pin: Maroon Town area)
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地乾河（象徵定位：馬倫鎮一帶）

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 3 'Tiger as Riding-horse' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: When Tiger is courting a fine young miss, Anansi tells the household that Tiger was his father's old riding-horse. Rather than duel the slander, Tiger insists Anansi ride him to the miss's yard as proof — and Anansi builds up saddle, bridle, horsewhip and double spurs step by innocent step, then gallops Tiger through the gate, calling him his father's old horse before the assembled household, and sings 'Poor Tiger dead and gone' as the shamed bully bolts for the woods.
summary.zh: 老虎正追求年輕姑娘，蜘蛛人竟對主人一家說虎是他父親的舊坐騎。老虎為自清，堅持讓蜘蛛人騎到姑娘家門前作證；蜘蛛人卻一步步『天真』地添上鞍、轡、馬鞭與雙刺馬釘，衝門而入高呼『父親的舊馬到了』，眾人嘩然，羞憤的老虎竄入山林，蜘蛛人唱著『可憐的老虎死了』揚長而去。

sensitivity.note: Social amusement tale (Anansi cycle). Note: the story records (and lauds) trickery; the 1924 transcription preserves 1920s vernacular stereotyping of the tellers themselves, avoided here.

passages.text: Tiger, walking to a fine yard to court one of the young misses, heard through the household the word that Anansi had put about: Tiger was Anansi's father's old riding-horse. Furious, Tiger summoned Anansi before the misses to retract it. Anansi sighed that he could not walk at all. 'If I have to carry you on my back, I will carry you,' snapped Tiger. So Anansi fetched a saddle — only to steady his weak feet, he said — a bridle to catch himself when he fell, a horsewhip to fan away flies, and two pairs of spurs, each innocent item explained with a stammer as Tiger, impatient, told him to put the things on and come on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, Jamaica Anansi Stories, tale 3 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Close to the yard Anansi clapped in the spurs, snapped the whip, and made Tiger gallop through the gate before the whole household. 'Carry him into the stable, sah!' Anansi announced. 'I make you to know what Anansi said is true to the fact — you are my father's old riding-horse.' Tiger bolted for the woods in shame while Anansi sang after him, 'Poor Tiger dead and gone!', to the tune the storyteller hummed as Si-lay-na, and the girls were left to decide who, that day, had truly proven anything.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 3, closing (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Tiger Swallows the Family: Anansi in the House-top
title.zh: 虎吞家人：蜘蛛人躲上屋頂

region.en: Maroon Town, Cook-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 5c 'In the House-top' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Sponging off Mr. Goolin day after day, Anansi is set up by Tiger, who lies disguised as a big barrow in the common: Anansi shoulders his prize, brags aloud, and is shaken onto the beard of Tiger beneath. He flees home shouting mis-heard commands — 'shut the back door, open the front door' — and the family takes refuge on the roof, where Anansi saves himself by shoving his hungry children one by one down into Tiger's mouth, then his wife (dangling from his sewn trousers), then tricks the tiger into piling soft trash for his landing and escapes into the rubbish where no one has found him since.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人日日榨取古林先生，老虎化身巨豬伏於公共地設伏；蜘蛛人肩負『戰利品』得意自誇，卻被搖落撞在虎鬚上。他逃回家高喊聽岔的口令，全家躲上屋頂；他為自保把飢餓的孩子一個個推進虎口，又推出吊在褲腳上的妻子；最後哄虎鋪堆軟垃圾作落地之處，趁虎翻尋不見而遁入垃圾堆——至今蜘蛛人仍藏身於碎瓦隙縫之中。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; contains slapstick family-peril comedy, transcribed with the teller's own framing. Paraphrase renders vernacular to standard English.

passages.text: Mr. Goolin had paid Anansi a hundred pounds to make his wife talk, and Anansi lived off the payment, coming to the yard daily for money. When Goolin wearied of him, Tiger offered to stop the nuisance: he turned himself into a big barrow and lay down in the common. Anansi arrived with his rope, 'caught' the barrow, hoisted it across his shoulders, and boasted to himself as he went, 'Ha! if I weren't cunnie, I wouldn't get this big barrow today.' He saw a long beard dropping over his face: it was Tiger, who began to shake him. 'O Brar Tiger, no shake! no shake!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 5c (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Anansi ran for his house, hollering 'Shet de back do', open de front do'!' — which his wife kept mis-hearing as orders to wash the pot and put on dinner. She got all the children up on the roof as Anansi set Tiger down and flew up after them. When each child in turn cried out hungry on the roof, Anansi shoved it down to Tiger, who swallowed it — six children gone, one after another. Anansi slept; his wife, foreseeing her turn, sewed the hem of her frock to the foot of his trousers with needle and thread. When she cried hungry and he shoved her down, her frock-tail caught on his trousers and hauled her back — until she cried hungry again, was shoved again, and Tiger swallowed Mrs. Anansi too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 5c, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Alone on the house-top, Anansi got hungry himself. 'Brar Tiger,' he called, 'you know what you do? I am a man so fat that if I drop on the bare earth I will mash up — so if you want me to eat me, cut a whole heap of dry trash.' Tiger heaped up the soft rubbish, and Anansi called 'Catch, catch, coming down!' as he let himself fall into it. Tiger searched the trash hard and never found Anansi until today — which is why, the storyteller said, Anansi still lives in the crevices. 'Jack man dora, choose none!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 5c, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Anansi's Belly Is White
title.zh: 蜘蛛人白肚之由

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 6 'Tiger's Breakfast' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Anansi dines at Tiger's house daily but feeds his host noise-signals that mean 'do not come'. Tiger repays the trick with a real breakfast and a fatal tip: reach into a lying cow for the tripe. Anansi tries it, the frightened cow clamps his arm, bolts downhill dragging him over the stones — and that, the tellers say, is why Anansi's belly is white to this day.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人日日在虎家吃早飯，卻用『有聲來吃、無聲莫來』的信號把老虎支開。老虎識破後以真早飯回敬，並給他一條『妙計』：把手伸入臥牛肚中取內臟。蜘蛛人依計而行，受驚的牛夾緊他的手，狂奔下山拖他跌過碎石——這便是蜘蛛人肚腹至今雪白的緣故。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale (origin of the spider's white belly). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Every day Anansi ate breakfast at Tiger's house, then said, 'Brar Tiger, tomorrow you must come to my house; but when you hear me making noise, come — that time breakfast is on; but if I stay still, you must not come at all.' When Tiger arrived, Anansi's meal was already eaten: 'Brar Tiger, you foot short!' And when Tiger objected that no noise had been made, Anansi said, just so — a man making noise cannot eat. The next day, shamed, he gave Tiger a little breakfast and taught him the table game: when I say 'Nyammy nyammy nyammy', you must say 'Nyam a wha' eat'. Anansi stayed eating everything, and Tiger never got one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, Jamaica Anansi Stories, tale 6 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tiger studied his revenge and served Anansi a generous meaty breakfast, letting the question slip: 'You know how I come by this meat? When I see a cow lie down, I run my hand inside the cow and hold the tripe — so I am never out of meat.' Anansi hurried away and tried it himself. The frightened cow on the hillside turned her head down to the lowland; Anansi cried, 'Do, Brar Cow, don't shut up my hand!' — but the cow clamped the hand the tighter and galloped right down the hill, dragging him over the stones. That, said Richard Morgan of Santa Cruz, is the reason you see Anansi's belly white.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 6, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Eggs and Scorpions
title.zh: 鳥蛋與蠍子

region.en: Dry River, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地乾河

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 7 'Eggs and Scorpions' (told by William Forbes)

summary.en: Anansi and the firefly Blinkie go egg-hunting with a rigged split: Anansi answers the big bird's cry, Blinkie the little bird's — so Anansi carries all the big eggs, and the offended firefly flies off with the light, leaving the spider alone in the dark wood. Hungry Anansi trades phantom eggs for Tiger's sheep-dinner, then steals the sheep itself in the night while Tiger, tipped off by Anansi's feigned crying, is only bitten by the scorpions he had set around his own eggs.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人與螢火蟲進林覓鳥蛋，卻事先安排：大鳥喚時他答『要大蛋』，小鳥喚時讓螢火蟲答——於是大蛋盡歸蜘蛛人。螢火蟲負氣帶走燈光，棄他於黑暗林中。飢餓的蜘蛛人以虛幻之蛋換得虎家的烤羊大餐，夜裡又偷走羊群；老虎反被自己佈下的蠍子螫傷，只聽蜘蛛人假哭家小作掩護。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; Blinkie the firefly is a Jamaican folk figure. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Blinkie and Anansi went into the wood to hunt bird eggs. Anansi made the bargain: when the little bird cries 'Who wants little egg?', Blinkie is to answer; when the big bird cries 'Who wants big egg?', Anansi answers 'Me want big egg!' In the night, with all the big eggs gathered and none for Blinkie, the firefly got vexed, left Anansi in the bush, and flew away with the light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 7 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the dark Anansi came to Tiger's house, where a sheep stood in the yard. 'Brar Tiger, if you give me dinner to eat tonight, I give you all the eggs,' he bargained. Tiger agreed, went to the sheep, and cried, 'Lay out, lay out, sheep!' — and out spread roast fowl, roast duck, and all sorts of things, which Anansi got at. Then he wanted to sleep at Tiger's house; and Tiger, suspicious, set scorpions around the eggs. When Anansi reached in and was bitten, he hollered 'Aye-e-e!' and answered Tiger's question with a tale of crying wife and children — and while Tiger went to bed believing it, Anansi thieved the sheep clean away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 7, closing (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bone-hole
title.zh: 骨洞

region.en: Dry River, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地乾河

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 8 'Tiger's Bone-hole' (told by William Forbes)

summary.en: Tiger boils a great pot of meat and keeps a hole where he throws the bones. Anansi creeps in with wife and three children to eat from the pot; when Tiger comes, the family hides in the bone-hole, and each thrown bone bruises one of them. Anansi keeps his brood hushed until the last bone cracks his own head — then all holler together in the hole, the terrified Tiger bolts from his own house, and the spider family eats his meat and runs him out of it.
summary.zh: 老虎煮好一大鍋肉，另掘『骨洞』丟骨頭。蜘蛛人帶妻小三口潛入鍋邊偷吃；老虎回來，一家五口躲入骨洞，每根擲入的骨頭都砸中一人。蜘蛛人喝令全體噤聲，直到最後一根骨頭砸中自己的頭——於是全家在洞中齊聲大喊，老虎大駭棄屋而逃，蜘蛛人家便吃光他的肉，把他趕出了自家屋子。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale, comic-creepy horror pattern. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Tiger had a big pot of meat, boiled it, left it, and kept a bone-hole where he threw what he finished. Anansi took his wife and three children and said the five of them would go to the house and get into the pot and eat the meat; when they heard Tiger coming, the five of them went into the hole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 8 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tiger came and said, 'Not a creature has eaten this meat but Brar Nansi!' — then began to eat. The first bone he threw into the hole knocked one of the children; as the child started to holler, Anansi said, 'Shut your mouth, sir, don't cry!' Another bone, another child knocked — 'Shut your mouth, sir!' Then the last child, then the mother, each bruised and each hushed, until the final bone knocked Anansi in the head. 'Let us all holler now in the hole!' they cried together — 'Yee! yee-e-e!' — and Tiger, terrified by the chorus in his bone-hole, ran and left his house; Anansi and wife and children came out, took all the meat, and ran him out of his house on account of that bone-hole.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 8, closing (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Top Take Off, Catch in the Middle, Lick Clean
title.zh: 削去頂、抓中間、舔乾淨

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 9 'The Christening' (told by Charles Wright, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Anansi and Tiger find a keg of butter and hide it in the bushes. Week by week Anansi claims a christening letter, returning each time to eat the keg down — the babies, he says, are named 'Top take off', 'Catch in the middle', and 'Lick clean'. At last he leads the exhausted Tiger on a long walk to the hiding place, puts him to sleep, scrapes the keg bare, wipes butter on Tiger's mouth and tail, and shrieks from a tall tree that Tiger has eaten the butter till it melts.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人與老虎尋得一桶牛油藏於叢中。此後每逢一週，蜘蛛人便稱收到受洗請柬外出一次，回來時桶中的牛油已見底——孩子們的名字分別是『削去頂』『抓中間』『舔乾淨』。最後他拖著疲憊的老虎走遍諸地方至藏桶處，哄其入睡，刮盡桶底，在虎嘴虎尾抹上牛油，再爬上高樹大喊：老虎把牛油吃到融化了！

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; frame-story pun on christening names. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Tiger both found one keg of butter. Anansi said to Tiger, 'Let us hide it in the bushes.' Some days after, Anansi said he had received a letter for a christening; when he returned, Tiger asked the name of the child. 'The name is Top take off.' Another week, another christening letter — the child's name, Catch in the middle. The last week, another christening — the name, Lick clean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 9 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Anansi said, 'Tiger, let us go look for this keg of butter.' He carried Tiger walking all over the place until he was tired; and when they nearly reached the hiding place, Anansi proposed a sleep. While Tiger slept, Anansi went to the keg, scraped as much butter as he could with a bit of stick, wiped a little on Tiger's mouth and a little at his tail, climbed a tall tree, and made a wonderful alarm that Tiger had eaten the butter until it melted — leaving the thief's accomplice, buttered, to take the blame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 9, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Eating Tiger's Guts: the Tell-tale Child and the Monkeys' Song
title.zh: 食虎臟：漏嘴的孩子與猴群之歌

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains and Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山與西摩蘭博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 10 'Eating Tiger's Guts' (a, Simeon Falconer; b, Henry Spence)

summary.en: Under the pretence of washing, Anansi trick Tiger into dipping his head in the river, steals his insides, boils them, and lives to hear that Tiger is dead. At his own mock wake he auditions each child's crying — until the youngest, the tell-tale, chanted the truth about 'the guts pupa brought last night', and is locked up. In the second telling Anansi teaches the monkeys to sing 'This time we eat Tiger gut down' as the rightful owner approaches; Tiger, hearing his own fate sung, kills the chorus — and the monkey he catches blames the song on the spider who taught it only yesterday.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人假意『洗頭』騙虎低頭入水，竊其內臟交妻燉煮，次日聞虎已死。他在假喪禮上逐一試聽孩子的哭腔，最小的漏嘴孩子卻唱出『昨夜爸爸拿回的虎臟』真相，被鎖了起來。另一版本：蜘蛛人教猴群見虎便唱『這回我們吃了虎臟』，虎聞歌大怒誅盡猴群，抓到的一隻卻供出——教歌的正是昨日的蜘蛛人。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale (cannibal-comic episode common in the cycle); recorded as folk narrative.

passages.text: Brer Tiger and Brer Anansi went to the river-side, and Anansi said, 'Brer Tiger, take out your inside and wash it out.' Tiger did so. 'Now dip your head in the water and wash it good' — and the moment Tiger's head went under, Anansi took up the inside and ran away with it to his wife Tacoomah to boil. Next morning he heard that Tiger was dead, and he called all the children to rehearse how they would cry at the funeral. Each said, 'Tita Tiger dead!' — but the last child said, 'Same something pupa brought here last night for Ma Tacoomah to boil — Tita Tiger gut.' Anansi locked that tell-tale child up; but the neighbors heard its crying and let it out to the funeral, and when Anansi saw it coming he ran away and took the house-top, and since then he has never come down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 10a 'The Tell-tale' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In another telling the two were bathing together. Anansi told Tiger, 'Meanwhile bathing, take out your tripe!' — and, coming out first, ate Tiger's tripe, telling him that whoever wanted to know how his tripe went must go down to Monkey town. Anansi got there ahead of him and taught the monkeys a song to sing whenever they saw Tiger coming: 'Dis time, we eat Tiger gut down!' So when Tiger arrived and heard them all singing, he killed off the monkeys — and, catching one, heard it protest that it was Anansi who had come down and taught them the song only yesterday.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 10b 'The Monkeys' Song' (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Throwing Away Knives
title.zh: 丟刀計

region.en: Mandeville and Dry River, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾與乾河

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 11 'Throwing Away Knives' (a, Benjamin Collins; b, William Forbes)

summary.en: A two-act swindle: Anansi loudly throws away a hidden object, goads Tiger into discarding his real knife, then alone can cut the pineapple — 'no man without a knife can eat pine'. In the paired telling he persuades Sheep to leave his spoon behind at the first breakfast-house, then sends him trudging back for it while Anansi eats the meals at every stop.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人高聲丟出暗藏之物，慫恿老虎也真的丟掉刀，隨後獨自持刀吃菠蘿——『沒刀的人吃不了菠蘿』。另一版本中，他哄綿羊在第一家把湯匙留下，再催他回去取匙，自己卻把一路上每頓飯吃光。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale, food-swindle type. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Once Brer Tiger and Brer Anansi were going along. Anansi said, 'Brer Tiger, I am going to throw away my knife, and when you see me throw away mine, you must throw away yours too.' Anansi took something and threw it away; Tiger took his knife and threw it away. When they reached the field to eat pineapple, Brer Nansi had his knife and was eating pine, and Brer Tiger got none. 'Brer Tiger, no man without a knife can eat pine!' said Anansi, cutting himself another slice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 11a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired telling, Anansi and Mr. Sheep set out walking over the country, each carrying a spoon. At the first house that gave breakfast, Anansi said, 'Mr. Sheep, leave your spoon here — don't carry it.' At the second he asked where the spoon was; told to fetch it, Sheep trudged back while Anansi ate off the breakfast. At the third, dinner came and went the same way — leave it, go back for it, come back to an empty table — and Mr. Sheep could not get anything to eat that day at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 11b (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Grace Before Meat: Clap Your Hands and Thank the Lord
title.zh: 飯前感恩：擊掌謝主

region.en: St. Ann's Bay and Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖安灣與西摩蘭博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 12 'Grace Before Meat' (a, Samuel Christie; b, Henry Spence)

summary.en: Traveling with Monkey, Anansi hoards his 'one and a half cunnies' and gets his friend's long tail lowered into a pit to rescue Tiger — climbing a tree while Tiger pounces on the helper. To free Monkey from Tiger's jaws, Anansi coaches the tiger to clap his two hands in joy, crying 'I get Monkey!' — and the primate drops free between the opened arms. In the paired hunting tale, Tiger's catch of a wild goat is lost forever when Anansi teaches him to tuck the goat under his arm and knock hands at the sky, saying 'Thank the Lord!'
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人與猴子同行，自誇『一份半機智』，卻哄猴子的長尾伸入深坑救虎，自己爬上樹看虎撲食恩人。為救猴，他教虎欣喜若狂地擊掌高呼『抓到猴子了』，猴子便從張開的臂間脫身。獵篇裡，老虎捕得山羊，蜘蛛人教他將羊夾在腋下朝天擊掌喊『感謝上主』——山羊一去不回。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; the 'grace before meat' frame satirizes ritual gestures, noted here as folk satire, not religion.

passages.text: Anansi and Monkey were traveling together, two good friends. 'Brer Monkey, how much cunnie do you have?' asked Anansi. 'Plenty, plenty!' said Monkey. Anansi allowed he had only one and a half — he kept the one for himself and gave his friend the half. Travbling on, they saw Tiger in one deep hole. Anansi said, 'You have plenty cunnie and a long tail; send down your tail into the hole and help Brer Tiger!' While Monkey sent down his tail, Anansi climbed a tree. Tiger came out of the hole, laid hold on Monkey — 'I nyam you today!' — and Anansi laughed on the tree while Monkey was in a fix, not knowing how to get away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 12a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the tree Anansi called down to Tiger: 'You have caught Monkey and you are going to eat him? Do like me, now — open your two hands and clap with joy and say, I get Monkey!' The moment Tiger opened his two hands to clap, Monkey got free, and Tiger ran after him while Anansi made his way down from the tree and went home. In the paired tale, Tiger out hunting caught a wild goat where Anansi caught nothing; Anansi taught him that next time he must put the goat under his arm and knock hands at the top, saying 'Thank the Lord!' Tiger did so, the goat got away and was gone — and the two lost their meat that day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tales 12a-b (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Day-time Trouble
title.zh: 白日之禍

region.en: Claremont, St. Ann, and Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖安克萊爾蒙特與曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 13 'Day-time Trouble' (a, Susan Watkins; b, Moses Hendricks)

summary.en: Rabbit begs Anansi to be shown 'day-time trouble'. Anansi kills a cub from Tiger's nest, puts the meat in a basket, and has Rabbit hand-deliver it to the tiger father before bolting up a tree: Tiger grabs at Rabbit, who dives into a stone-hole, and when Tiger sends for long-necked Reindeer to dig him out, Anansi slips Rabbit a razor — the decapitated digger terrifies the crowd, and Rabbit learns that day-time trouble, once seen, is never to be asked for again. In the paired telling Rat murders two of four cubs he believes Anansi killed, and carries the dead ones out before Tiger while Anansi's pair come out alive.
summary.zh: 兔子求蜘蛛人讓他見識『白日之禍』。蜘蛛人從虎巢殺死一隻幼虎，把肉裝籃，令兔子親手送到虎父面前便逃；虎撲兔子，兔子鑽入石洞；虎召長頸的馴鹿前來挖掘，蜘蛛人暗塞剃刀——馴鹿落頭而亡，圍觀者四散奔逃。兔子出洞後，蜘蛛人告誡：白日之禍，見過一次，終生莫再求看。另一版：老鼠誤信蜘蛛人所言，殺死四隻虎崽中的兩隻，捧屍迎虎；蜘蛛人的兩隻卻活著出籃。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; the 'day-time trouble' is a Jamaican idiom of dreadful revelation. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Brar Anansi and Brar Rabbit went for a walk, and Rabbit asked Anansi to show him 'day-time trouble'. Going on, Anansi saw Tiger's den with a lot of young Tigers in it, took one out, killed it, and gave Rabbit a basket with a piece of the meat to carry for the Tiger's father, walking him along to Tiger's house and telling Brar Rabbit to hand Tiger the basket. Anansi ran; Tiger caught at Rabbit to kill him, but he got away. Anansi ran up a tree — 'Run, Brar Rabbit, run! run for stone-hole!' — and passed him a razor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 13a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tiger raised a lot of men to get Rabbit out of the hole and sent for Reindeer, who had a long neck to put his head down and dig. But Anansi had told Rabbit that when Reindeer put his head down in the hole, he must take the razor and cut it off. A crowd gathered to see Reindeer take Rabbit out of the hole; instead, the Reindeer's head was taken off, he dropped dead, and the whole crowd ran away with fright. After Rabbit came out, Brar Nansi said to him: 'Brar Rabbit, so day-time trouble stays. So, as long as you live, never ask anybody to show it to you again!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 13a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired version, Rat and Anansi came across Tiger's four children. 'Two for me, two for you!' said Anansi, taking up a cub and making the motion of killing it — but putting it alive in his basket. Rat, thinking the cubs dead, killed his own two and carried them in his basket. Meeting Tiger on the home path, Anansi said, 'I saw your babies crying hungry, I took them up to meet you — I carry two, Brer Rat two.' Tiger lay down to nurse them: out of Anansi's basket came one cub alive; out of Rat's, one dead. Tiger sprang at Rat, who ran along the side of a wall until Anansi's cry — 'remember stone-hole!' — saved him, and Tiger, wheeling to revenge himself on Anansi, found the spider under the dry trash where, ever since, Anansi is always found under dry rubbish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 13b 'Rat and Anansi' (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: New Names: Che-che-bun-da
title.zh: 新名字：琪琪本達

region.en: St. Ann's Bay, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖安灣

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 14 'New Names' (told by Samuel Christie, St. Ann's Bay)

summary.en: Four friends — Anansi, Tiger, Tacoomah, Parrot — bargain that each will take a new name and eat his own mother if she speaks the old one. Anansi engineers the deaths of the other three mothers and then, night after night, drills his own mother in the syllables of 'Che-che-bun-da'. The singing procession arrives; the mothers of his friends are eaten, but Anansi's mother calls out the new name and her life is saved — a bargain Anansi made, the teller says, to feast on the others and save his own.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人、老虎、塔庫馬與鸚鵡四友立約：各取新名，若母親喚出舊名便吃掉母親。蜘蛛人設局令三友之母喪命，又夜夜操練母親記誦『琪琪本達』四字。遊行唱名之夜，三母被食，唯蜘蛛人之母喊出新名保住性命——這正是蜘蛛人與人立約的算計：飽食他人，獨全己母。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale built on a naming taboo (ATU-type name-custom tale); dark comedy, transcribed from named tellers. The covenant-wordplay motif links to Yoruba hidden-name tales (cross_ref: yoruba tradition, motif family only).

passages.text: There were four friends: Anansi, Tiger, Tacoomah and Parrot. Going for a journey, Anansi bargained that the four must change their names, and when they came home each must go to his mother's house — and if his mother called him the old name, he must eat his mother. The new names: Anansi was Che-che-bun-da; Parrot, Green-corn-ero; Tiger, Yellow-prissenda; Tacoomah, Tacoomah-vengeance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 14 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Tacoomah's house Anansi announced the name Tacoomah-vengeance; the mother, not understanding, said, 'Look, my child Tacoomah comes!' — and they killed and ate Tacoomah's mother. At Tiger's mother's, the same; at Parrot's, the same. But every night Anansi cried an excuse and slipped to his own mother's house: 'Mother, if you call me Anansi, they will kill you! You must call me Che-che-bun-da' — repeating it over and over that she might not forget.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 14, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The night came, the party singing along the road: 'Anansi name a Che-che-bun-da, cherry-senda, Yellow-prissenda; Parrot name a Green-corn-ero; Tiger name a Yellow-prissenda; Tacoomah name Tacoomah-vengeance...' As Anansi's mother saw the singers coming, she called, 'Look, my child Che-che-bun-da!' — the new name, and her life was saved. Anansi had made the bargain to feast on the others and save his mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 14, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Long-shirt and the Goat's Beard
title.zh: 長衫與山羊之鬚

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 15 'Long-shirt' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: At a dance in a land where everyone is naked but the one-legged head-man, whose long shirt can talk, Anansi the fiddler plays the crowd to sleep and swaps his old shirt for the magic one — which calls out its own whereabouts. Anansi offloads the enchanted shirt onto Ram-goat in a fresh swap; the head-man's wooden leg stumbles on the goat's single exposed horn, the crowd digs Ram-goat out, drenches him in dirty slops, and leaves him for dead — and the goat, wringing every garment but forgetting his beard, has carried its offensive smell ever since.
summary.zh: 眾人皆裸的國度裡，唯獨裝木腿的頭人穿會說話的長衫。蜘蛛人拉琴使滿場入睡，偷換長衫——衫卻自己喊出下落。蜘蛛人轉手把法衫換給山羊；頭人木腿絆上山羊露出的獨角，群眾掘出山羊，以穢水澆透棄之為屍。山羊擰淨衣物卻忘了擰鬚——山羊一身腥臊之味，便是由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale with etiological ending (goat's smell). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi, Tacoomah and Tiger made a dance — Anansi fiddler, Tacoomah drummer, Tiger tambourine man — and traveled till they came to a country where all the people were naked, except the head-man, who wore a long shirt and had a wooden leg. They invited all the people to the dance; they played until everyone fell asleep, and Anansi stole the head-man's good shirt, putting his own old one on the sleeper. The man woke, missed his shirt — and this shirt could talk. 'Long-shirt, whe' you den?' he called, and the shirt answered, 'Brar Nansi have me on-o!' The chase began; Anansi, frightened, met Brar Ram-goat and swapped: a new shirt for the old. The head-man called; Long-shirt answered, 'Brar Ram-goat have me on now-o!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 15 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ram-goat ran until he was exhausted, dug a hole, and buried himself — leaving one horn outside without knowing it. The head-man's wooden leg could not go fast; he bucked the leg on the projecting horn, fell, and rose thinking it a stump. He cut and cut until he saw blood — 'Look! come now-o, dirtee have blood!' The crowd dug the goat out, took off the long shirt, put on his own old one, and drenched him with all the dirty slops. They left him for dead; then Ram-goat got up, wrung the dirty clothes, wrung every slop from them — but never remembered to wring his beard. Jack man dora! That is the reason the goat has such an offensive smell until this day: he didn't remember to wring his beard!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 15, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Shut Up in the Pot: 'I Got Them Now'
title.zh: 鍋中封人：『這回我可逮住你們了』

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 16 'Shut Up in the Pot' (told by Simeon Falconer, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: In a famine year Anansi weeps to his friends that his family has not eaten bread for days — while his wife's dinner bell rings in the next room. Tiger and Tacoomah, shamed, feed him; Anansi then stages a sorcerer's trick: he enters a boiling pot, is shut in, knocks from within, and emerges alive. Ordered to copy the feat, the two friends are sealed in the pot under a heavy stone while Anansi piles the fire — and as they cook, he tunes up his fiddle: 'I got them now! Them think they got me, but I got them now!'
summary.zh: 饑年之中，蜘蛛人向朋友哭訴家人多日無糧，隔壁卻傳來妻子開飯的呼聲。老虎與塔庫馬羞愧之下拿食物來喂；蜘蛛人隨即上演法術：入沸鍋、加蓋、敲鍋、活著出鍋。兩友奉命效仿，被封入鍋中壓上重石；蜘蛛人加大爐火，一邊聽鍋，一邊調弦唱道：『這回我可逮住你們了！你們以為逮住了我，其實是我逮住了你們！』

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale (boiling-pot duel type); dark comedy from a hard-times frame. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a very hard time; no food could they get at all, so Anansi's family was well fed in secret. When Brer Tiger and Brer Tacoomah came to see him, he told them that for three or four days his wife and children had not eaten bread. They went home to send him food — and only dodged behind the house to hear his wife call, 'Here! dinner ready!' Back they knocked at the door; the wife opened it, Anansi slunk out of the house, ashamed, and the two friends were given some of the food to eat, and it was all fresh beef.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 16 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: They came back to Anansi, who said, 'I will get the beef, but whatever I tell you to do, you must be sure to do it.' He put a big pot of water on the fire, got into the boiling pot himself, had them shut him up in it, knocked on the pot, and was let out alive. Then he told Brer Tiger he must get in the pot — Tacoomah alongside — shut them up, put a heavy weight on the pot top, went outside, and told his wife to shove up the fire, bigger and bigger. When he came back and found them properly cooked, and they were going to eat now, he was tuning up his fiddle: 'I got them now! I got them now! Them think they got me, but I got them now!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 16, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Anansi and Brother Dead: the Silent Host
title.zh: 蜘蛛人與死神兄弟：沉默的主人

region.en: Whitehall, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地懷特霍爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 27a 'Brother Dead's Wife' (told by Grace Doran, Whitehall)

summary.en: In the wood Anansi finds a silent man drying meat on a barbecue and, receiving no answers to any question, helps himself to breakfast, pot, and meat — then leaves his daughter Sindy as 'servant' for the host. When the spider returns and finds only a ringed finger among the drying meat, he ties the silent Brother Dead's long hair to the trees, piles trash on the braids, and sets fire to them; the freed ghost looses his bow and arrow after him, and Anansi, standing on his house-top telling his children to jump down into Brother Dead's open hands, drops last into the dirt himself — which is why Anansi lives in the dirt.
summary.zh: 林中蜘蛛人遇沉默晾肉之人，問而不答，便自取早飯、鍋與肉，還留女兒辛迪作『僕』。再訪時乾肉間只見一截戴戒指的手指；蜘蛛人把死神兄弟的長髮縛上樹，堆碎柴於辮上點火。解縛的鬼魂張弓追射；蜘蛛人立在屋頂命孩子們一個個跳進死神張開的手中，自己最後一跳落進塵土——蜘蛛人從此住在塵土裡。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale with 'Brother Dead' (duppy) figure; told as entertainment at wake-nights, not restricted material.

passages.text: Anansi walked till he came into a wood where a man had a barbecue, plenty of meat drying. 'Hi, Brar! how you do?' — no answer. 'Brar, you have plenty meat and want someone to stay with you?' — no answer. 'Brar, give me a little breakfast?' — no answer. So Anansi went up on the barbecue, took the meat, asked for the pot, put it on, cooked, packed his bag, and said, 'Tomorrow I come back, and I see you need a servant, and I going to bring one of me daughter.' The daughter, Sindy, was left to cook for the silent host.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 27a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next visit, Brother Dead sat combing his long hair over his face, holding bow and arrow, and said not one word; Anansi went up on the barbecue and found his daughter's finger with a ring on it among the meat. 'I make you speak today!' He took the Dead man's hair, tied one long plait here, one there, two plaits behind to the trees; then piled dry trash and lit fire to the head. The plaits burned off, the Dead shook his head free, took up his bow and arrow and ran after Anansi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 27a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Anansi ran up to his house: 'Wife and pickney, go up aloft, Brar Dead dah come!' Brother Dead came in and sat waiting, hands open. 'Pupa, me hungry!' cried the children. 'Brar Dead, open your hand, pickney a come!' — six children went into the open hands, one after another. Then Mrs. Anansi cried out, 'Brar Dead, open your hand, me a come!' — and Anansi dropped now, dropped in the dirt. From that time you see Anansi live in the dirt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 27a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Brother Dead and the Brindle Puppy
title.zh: 死神兄弟與斑紋小狗

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 28 'Brother Dead and the Brindle Puppy' (told by Charles Roe, Maroon Town)

summary.en: The old witch Brother Dead never speaks to anyone — to speak is to die — and spends his days shooting wild animals and drying them uneaten. Anansi robs his meat-bag twice; on the second visit he coaches the brindle puppy: when Brother Dead sings his hunting-song and people drop dead, throw green bush on them. The witch tracks Anansi by blood on his arrow-points, sings the old medicine-song — 'Anansi ma shway...' — catches him, skewers him through the ears, and burns him to dust.
summary.zh: 老巫死神兄弟從不與人言語——開口即死——終日射殺野獸晾乾而不食。蜘蛛人兩次竊肉；第二次他密授斑紋小狗：若死神唱歌令人倒斃，便將青草擲於屍上救活。死神以箭血循跡追蹤，唱起古咒之歌『Anansi ma shway……』，擒住蜘蛛人，以弓貫其雙耳，堆火焚為灰燼。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; 'Brother Dead' is a duppy/witch figure of wake-night entertainment. Song transcribed phonetically in source; paraphrase given.

passages.text: There was an old witch called Brar Dead, who never talked to anybody — if he talked to anybody, he would be dead. He only made bows all day and set them to catch all wild animals, and when he caught them he put them over the fire and dried them, but never ate them. Mr. Anansi went there one day, said, 'Brar Dead, give me some of your meat now,' got no answer for his pains, went in and took a whole bagful of the dried meat and started to eat it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 28 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brother Dead had a brindle puppy.
