Thus, they outstrip all competitors, over the unstirred dust, out of sight!"

The Prince was greatly pleased and smiled. ... "Have you not heard," said Hsü Wu Kuei, "of the outlaw of Yüeh? After several days' absence from his State, he was glad to meet any one he had known there. After a month, he was glad to meet any one he had even seen there. And after a year, he was glad to meet any one who was in any way like to his fellow-countrymen. ... Long it is, I ween, since his Highness has heard the voice of a pure man at his side!"

title.en: The Divine Teacher Boy Who Governed the Empire as He Kept His Horses (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 黃帝襄城之野遇牧馬小童（莊子）

region.en: The wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng, beyond the known world (symbolic pin: Xiangcheng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 襄城之野（象徵定位：河南襄城）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor rides to seek the Tao upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain with six sage companions, and all seven lose their way in the wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng. A boy grazing horses tells them where the mountain is and where the TAO abides — and how to govern the empire: just the same as I look after my horses. See that no harm comes to the horses, that is all! The Emperor prostrates himself before the boy, addressing him as Divine Teacher.
summary.zh: 黃帝將見大隗乎具茨之山——七聖皆迷，無所問塗；適遇牧馬童子。小童曰：夫為天下者，亦奚以異乎牧馬者哉？亦去其害馬者而已矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the seven-sages-lose-the-way myth and the Divine-Teacher boy. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When the Yellow Emperor went to see TAO upon the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain, Fang Ming was his charioteer, Ch'ang Yü sat on his right, Chang Jo and Hsi P'êng were his outriders, and K'un Hun and Hua Chi brought up the rear. On reaching the wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng, these seven Sages lost their way and there was no one of whom to ask the road. By and by, they fell in with a boy who was grazing horses, and asked him, saying, "Do you know the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain?" "I do," replied the boy. "And can you tell us," continued the Sages, "where TAO abides?" "I can," replied the boy.

"This is a strange lad," cried the Yellow Emperor. "Not only does he know where the Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain is, but also where TAO abides! Come tell me, pray, how would you govern the empire?" "I should govern the empire," said the boy, "just the same as I look after my horses. What else should I do? "When I was a little boy and used to live within the points of the compass, my eyes got dim of sight. An old man advised me to mount the chariot of the sun and visit the wilds of Hsiang-ch'êng. My sight is now much better, and I continue to dwell without the points of the compass. I should govern the empire in just the same way. What else should I do?"

The boy declined to answer, but on being again urged, cried out, "What difference is there between governing the empire and looking after horses? See that no harm comes to the horses, that is all!" Thereupon the Emperor prostrated himself before the boy; and addressing him as Divine Teacher, took his leave.

title.en: Lu Chü's Two Lutes and the Twenty-Five Jangled Strings (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 魯遽調瑟，二十五弦皆動（莊子）

region.en: The hall and adjoining room (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 堂與室之瑟（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: A disciple of Lu Chü boasts he can do without fire in winter and make ice in summer; Lu Chü answers by tuning two lutes, one in the hall and one in the adjoining room, so that the struck note sounds in both — then, changing one string out of the octave, he strikes it and all the twenty-five strings jangle together. There was sound as before, but the influence of the key-note was gone.
summary.zh: 魯遽曰：是直以陽召陽，以陰召陰——於是乎為之調瑟；廢一於堂，廢一於室；鼓宮宮動，鼓角角動。於是乎為之改調，一於宮宮，五音不比，二十五弦皆動。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Thereupon he tuned two lutes, and placed one in the hall and the other in the adjoining room. And when he struck the Kung note on one, the Kung note on the other sounded; when he struck the chio note on one, the chio note on the other sounded. This because they were both tuned to the same pitch. But if he changed the interval of one string, so that it no longer kept its place in the octave, and then struck it, the result was that all the twenty-five strings jangled together. There was sound as before, but the influence of the key-note was gone. Is this your case?"

title.en: The Stone-Mason and the Scab No Thicker Than a Fly's Wing (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 匠石斲郢人之鼻堊（莊子）

region.en: Ying, capital of Ch'u (Jingzhou, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 郢都（今湖北荊州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: At Hui Tzŭ's grave, Chuang Tzŭ recalls the man of Ying whose nose bore a scab no thicker than a fly's wing: the stone-mason chipped it off with his adze while the patient sat unmoved, the nose uninjured. Summoned by the prince of Sung to try the same, the stone-mason answers that his material has long since perished — and I too, ever since he perished, have been without my material, having no one with whom I can speak.
summary.zh: 郢人堊漫其鼻端若蠅翼，使匠石斲之；匠石運斤成風，聽而斲之，盡堊而鼻不傷。臣嘗能之矣，雖然，臣之質死久矣！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ was once attending a funeral, when he passed by the grave of Hui Tzŭ. Turning to his attendants, he said, "A man of Ying who had his nose covered with a hard scab, no thicker than a fly's wing, sent for a stone-mason to chip it off. The stone-mason plied his adze with great dexterity while the patient sat still and let him chip. When the scab was all off, the nose was found to be uninjured, the man of Ying never having moved a muscle.

When Yüan, prince of Sung, heard of this, he summoned the stone-mason and said, 'Try to do the same for me.' "'I used to be able to do it Sire,' replied the stone-mason, 'but my material has long since perished.' "And I too, ever since he perished, have been without my material, having no one with whom I can speak."

title.en: Kuan Chung's Deathbed Advice: It Must Be Hsi P'êng (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 管仲有病，屬國於隰朋（莊子）

region.en: The Ch'i court (Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 齊廷（今山東臨淄）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Dying Kuan Chung refuses Duke Huan's choice of Pao Yü — pure, incorruptible, he will not associate with those unlike himself — and names instead Hsi P'êng, who forgets the authority of those above him, grieves over those not the peers of himself, and hears not the things in the State he should not hear. There is no alternative; it must be Hsi P'êng.
summary.zh: 管仲有病，公曰：鮑叔牙可乎？管仲曰：不可——其為人也，潔廉善士也，其於不己若者不比之。其於國也，有不聞也；其於家也，有不見也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Kuan Chung being at the point of death, Duke Huan went to see him. "You are ill, venerable Sir," said the Duke, "really ill. You had better say to whom, in the event of your getting worse, I am to entrust the administration of the State." "Whom does your Highness wish to choose?" enquired Kuan Chung. "Will Pao Yü do?" asked the Duke. "He will not," said Kuan Chung. "He is pure, incorruptible, and good. With those who are not like himself, he will not associate. And if he has once heard of a man's wrong-doing, he never forgets it. If you employ him in the administration of the empire, he will get to loggerheads with his prince and to sixes and sevens with the people.

"There is no alternative," replied Kuan Chung; "it must be Hsi P'êng. He is a man who forgets the authority of those above him, and makes those below him forget his. Ashamed that he is not the peer of the Yellow Emperor, he grieves over those who are not the peers of himself. To share one's virtue with others is called true wisdom. To share one's wealth with others is reckoned meritorious. To exhibit superior merit is not the way to win men's hearts. To exhibit inferior merit is the way. There are things in the State he does not hear; there are things in the family he does not see. There is no alternative; it must be Hsi P'êng."

title.en: The Showing-Off Monkey of Monkey Mountain (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 吳王狙猴之技（莊子）

region.en: Monkey Mountain of Wu (symbolic pin: Zhenjiang, Jiangsu, China)
region.zh: 吳之猨山（象徵定位：江蘇鎮江）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The monkeys of Monkey Mountain flee from the prince of Wu's shooting-party — except one which flaunts its skill and catches the flying arrow in its hand, to be killed by the guards' cloud of arrows. Beware! says the prince: do not flaunt your superiority in the faces of others. Yen Pu I goes home and studies under Tung Wu, and in three years his praise is in everybody's mouth.
summary.zh: 吳王浮於江，登乎狙之山；眾狙見之，恂然棄而逃——有一狙焉，見巧乎王；王射之，敏給搏捷矢。王命相者趨射，狙執死。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The prince of Wu took a boat and went to the Monkey Mountain, which he ascended. When the monkeys saw him, they fled in terror and hid themselves in the thicket. One of them, however, disported himself carelessly, as though showing off its skill before the prince. The prince took a shot at it; but the monkey, with great rapidity, seized the flying arrow with its hand. Then the prince bade his guards try, the result being that the monkey was killed.

Thereupon the prince turned to his friend Yen Pu I, and said, "That monkey flaunted its skill and its dexterity in my face. Therefore it has come to this pass. Beware! Do not flaunt your superiority in the faces of others." Yen Pu I went home, and put himself under the tuition of Tung Wu, with a view to get rid of such superiority. He put aside all that gave him pleasure and avoided gaining reputation. And in three years his praise was in everybody's mouth.

title.en: Chiu Fang Yin Examines the Eight Sons (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子綦八子，九方歅相之（莊子）

region.en: The father's hall (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 父之堂（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Tzŭ Chi summons the physiognomist Chiu Fang Yin to examine his eight sons; K'un will be the fortunate one — he will eat at the table of a prince — and the father weeps, for every uncanny effect must be preceded by some uncanny cause. Shortly afterwards K'un is captured by brigands, his feet cut off, and sold as door-keeper to Duke Chü — with meat to his dinner for the rest of his life.
summary.zh: 子綦有子八人，屬諸九方歅：楣也，必與國君同食以終其身。俄而楣到於燕，盜得之於道，刖而鬻之於齊——適為渠公之街，然食肉終身。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tzŭ Chi had eight sons. He ranged them before him, and summoning Chiu Fang Yin, said to him, "Examine my sons physiognomically, and tell me which will be the fortunate one." "K'un," replied Chiu Fang Yin, "will be the fortunate one." "In what sense?" asked the father, beaming with delight. "K'un," said Chiu Fang Yin, "will eat at the table of a prince, and so end his days." Thereupon Tzŭ Chi burst into tears and said, "What has my son done that this should be his fate?"

"My sons and I do but roam through the universe. With them I seek the joys of heaven; with them I seek the fruits of earth. With them I engage in no business; with them I concoct no plots; with them I attempt nothing out-of-the-way. ... Every uncanny effect must be preceded by some uncanny cause. Alas! my sons and I have done nothing. It must be the will of God. Therefore I weep."

Shortly afterwards, when K'un was on his way to the Yen State, he was captured by brigands. To sell him as he was, would be no easy matter. To sell him without his feet would be easy enough. So they cut off his feet and sold him into the Ch'i State, where he became door-keeper to Duke Chü and had meat to his dinner for the rest of his life.

title.en: Hsü Yu Runs Away from Yao (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 嚙缺遇許由，遁堯（莊子）

region.en: The hermit's path (symbolic pin: Jishan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 隱者之塗（象徵定位：河南箕山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Asked where he is going, Hsü Yu answers: away from Yao — who thinks of nothing but charity, and will become a laughing-stock of the world until future ages eat one another. Love and profit are born of charity and duty to one's neighbour; those who ignore them are few, those who make capital out of them are many.
summary.zh: 齧缺遇許由曰：子將奚之？曰：將逃堯——夫堯畜畜然仁，吾恐其為天下笑；後世其人與人相食與！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yeh Ch'üeh meeting Hsü Yu, said to him, "Where are you going?" "Away from Yao!" replied the latter. "What do you mean?" asked Yeh Ch'üeh. "Yao," said Hsü Yu, "thinks of nothing but charity. I fear he will become a laughing-stock to the world, and that in future ages men will eat one another.

"There is no difficulty in winning the people. Love them and they will draw near. Profit them and they will come up. Praise them and they will vie with one another. But introduce something they dislike, and they will be gone. ... Love and profit are born of charity and duty to one's neighbour. Those who ignore charity and duty to one's neighbour are few; those who make capital out of them are many. ... Yao knows that good men benefit the empire. But he does not know that they injure it. Only those on a higher level than good men know this."

title.en: The Two Kingdoms on the Snail's Horns (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 蝸角觸蠻之爭（莊子）

region.en: The Liang court (Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 梁廷（今河南開封）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: On a snail's left horn there is a kingdom called Aggression and on its right horn another called Violence, constantly fighting for territory — corpses by the thousands, pursuers away for fifteen days. Descend from boundless space to a kingdom with fixed boundaries, and in it is Wei, in Wei the city of Liang, and in Liang a prince — in what does he differ from Violence? Whew! cried the prince. Then Hui Tzŭ's tube-note: Yao and Shun, compared with Tai Chin Jen, are but whssh.
summary.zh: 有國於蝸之左角者曰觸氏，有國於蝸之右角者曰蠻氏；時相與爭地而戰，伏尸數萬——君之與蠻氏，亦猶是也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the snail-horn kingdoms are Zhuangzi's most-cited satire on war. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Prince Hui of Wei had made a treaty with prince Wei of Ch'i, which the latter broke. Thereupon prince Hui was wroth, and was about to send a man to assassinate him. When Hui Tzŭ heard of the ministers' war-plans, he introduced Tai Chin Jen to the prince. "There is a creature called a snail," said Tai Chin Jen. "Does your Highness know what I mean?" "I do," replied the prince. "There is a kingdom on its left horn," continued Tai Chin Jen, "ruled over by Aggression, and another on its right horn, ruled over by Violence. These two rulers are constantly fighting for territory. In such cases, corpses lie about by thousands, and one party will pursue the other for fifteen days before returning."

"Sire," replied Tai Chin Jen, "I beg you to regard it as fact. Does your Highness recognise any limit to space?" "None," said the prince, "It is boundless." "When, therefore, the mind descends from the contemplation of boundless space to the contemplation of a kingdom with fixed boundaries, that kingdom must seem to be of dimensions infinitesimally small?" "Of course," replied the prince. "Well then," said Tai Chin Jen, "in a kingdom with fixed boundaries there is the Wei State. In the Wei State there is the city of Liang. In the city of Liang there is a prince. In what does that prince differ from Violence?" "There is no difference," said the prince.

Thereupon Tai Chin Jen took his leave, and the prince remained in a state of mental perturbation, as though he had lost something. When Tai Chin Jen had gone, Hui Tzŭ presented himself, and the prince said, "Our friend is truly a great man. Sages are not his equal." "If you blow through a tube," replied Hui Tzŭ, "the result will be a note. If you blow through the hole in a sword-hilt, the result will be simply whssh. Yao and Shun have been belauded by mankind; yet compared with Tai Chin Jen they are but whssh."

title.en: The Sage Under a Menial's Garb on Mount I (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孔子之楚，舍於蟻丘之漿（莊子）

region.en: The wine-shop of Mount I, Ch'u (Yicheng, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 蟻丘之漿（象徵定位：湖北宜城）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: Stopping at a wayside wine-shop on Mount I, Confucius sees a servant climb onto the roof: a Sage under the garb of a menial, who has drowned himself on dry land — I think 'tis I Liao of Shih-nan. Sent to call him, Tzŭ Lu finds the house empty; the hidden one has scorned the toady's words.
summary.zh: 孔子之楚，舍於蟻丘之漿。其鄰有夫妻臣妾登極者——是陸沉者也。是其言也，猥以人乎！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Confucius went to Ch'u, he stopped at a restaurant on Mount I. The servant to a man and his wife who lived next door, got up on top of the house. "Whatever is he doing up there?" asked Tzŭ Lu. "He is a Sage," replied Confucius, "under the garb of a menial. He buries himself among the people. He effaces himself at the wayside. Fame, he has none; but his perseverance is inexhaustible. Though his mouth speaks, his heart speaks not. He has turned his back upon mankind, not caring to abide amongst them. He has drowned himself on dry land. I think 'tis I Liao of Shih-nan."

Tzŭ Lu asked to be allowed to go and call him; but Confucius stopped him, saying, "No. He knows that I know what he is. He knows that I have come to Ch'u to recommend him to the prince. And he looks on me as a toady. Under the circumstances, as he would scorn to hear the words of a toady, how much more would he scorn to see him in the flesh! How could you keep him?" Tzŭ Lu went to see, but the house was empty.

title.en: Poh Chü Asks Lao Tzŭ to Wander the World (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 柏據學於老聃，請遊天下（莊子）

region.en: Lao Tzŭ's retreat (symbolic pin: Ku county, Bozhou, Anhui, China)
region.zh: 老聃之居（象徵定位：安徽亳州苦縣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 24, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 24

summary.en: The disciple Poh Chü begs Lao Tzŭ to wander the world with him. The world is just as you see it here, replies the Sage. Poh Chü explains that he would begin in Ch'i, viewing the dead bodies of malefactors, pushing them to make them rise, crying to God and bemoaning their lot — for honour and disgrace were set up, and evil followed; wealth was accumulated, and contentions began.
summary.zh: 柏據曰：請之齊，見其辜，推而強之，解其朝服而幕之——噫嘻！夫子亦知古之所謂亂者乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Poh Chü was studying under Lao Tzŭ. "Let us go," said he, "and wander over the world." "No," replied Lao Tzŭ, "the world is just as you see it here." But as he again urged it, Lao Tzŭ said, "Where would you go to begin with?" "I would begin," answered Poh Chü, "by going to the Ch'i State. There I would view the dead bodies of their malefactors. I would push them to make them rise. I would take off my robes and cover them. I would cry to God and bemoan their lot, as follows:--'O sirs, O sirs, there was trouble upon earth, and you were the first to fall into it!'

"I would say, 'Perhaps you were robbers, or perhaps murderers?'... Honour and disgrace were set up, and evil followed. Wealth was accumulated, and contentions began. Now the evil which has been set up and the contentions which have accumulated, endlessly weary man's body and give him no rest. What escape is there from this?"

title.en: The Stone Coffin Under Sha-ch'iu: Duke Ling's Tomb Inscription (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 沙丘石槨銘（莊子）

region.en: Sha-ch'iu, the Wei burial ground (symbolic pin: Guangzong, Hebei, China)
region.zh: 沙丘（象徵定位：河北廣宗）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 25, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 25

summary.en: When Duke Ling died, divination showed it auspicious to bury him at Sha-ch'iu; digging several fathoms deep, the workmen found a stone coffin bearing the inscription: Posterity cannot be trusted. Duke Ling will seize this for his tomb. As a matter of fact, Duke Ling had been named Ling long before.
summary.zh: 靈公葬於沙丘而得石槨之銘：不馮其子，靈公奪而里之——靈公之為靈也久矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); tagged oracle-divination for the divinatory burial and prophetic inscription. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Confucius asked the historiographers Ta T'ao, Poh Ch'ang Ch'ien, and Hsi Wei, saying, "Duke Ling was fond of wine and given up to pleasure, and neglected the administration of his State. He spent his time in hunting, and did not cultivate the goodwill of the other feudal princes. How was it he came to be called Ling?" "The Duke," said Poh Ch'ang Ch'ien, "had three wives. He was having a bath together with them when Shih Ch'in, summoned by his Highness, entered the apartment. Thereupon the Duke covered himself and the ladies. So outrageously did he behave on the one hand, and yet so respectful was he towards a virtuous man. Hence he was called Ling."

"When the Duke died," said Hsi Wei, "divination showed that it would be inauspicious to bury him in the old family burying-ground, but auspicious to bury him at Sha-ch'iu. And upon digging a grave there, several fathoms deep, a stone coffin was found, which, being cleaned, yielded the following inscription:--Posterity cannot be trusted. Duke Ling will seize this for his tomb. As a matter of fact, Duke Ling had been named Ling long before. What should these two persons know about it?"

title.en: The Stickleback in the Cart-Rut (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 涸轍之鮒（莊子）

region.en: The road to the prince of Chien-ho (symbolic pin: Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 監河侯之途（象徵定位：河南開封）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: Poor Chuang Tzŭ borrows corn and is offered three hundred ounces of silver after the revenue is collected. He answers with the stickleback stranded in a cart-rut who begs a pint of water, and is promised the west river after a journey south to Wu and Yüeh: you might as well put me in a dried-fish shop at once.
summary.zh: 莊周家貧，往貸粟於監河侯。周顧視車轍中，有鮒魚焉——我，東海之波臣也；君豈有斗升之水而活我哉？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the dried cart-rut fish is a proverbial image of delayed relief. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chuang Tzŭ's family being poor, he went to borrow some corn from the prince of Chien-ho. "Yes," said the prince. "I am just about collecting the revenue of my fief, and will then lend you three hundred ounces of silver. Will that do?" At this Chuang Tzŭ flushed with anger and said, "Yesterday, as I was coming along, I heard a voice calling me. I looked round, and in the cart-rut I saw a stickleback. "'I am a denizen of the eastern ocean,' replied the stickleback. 'Pray, Sir, a pint of water to save my life.'

"'Yes,' said I. 'I am just going south to visit the princes of Wu and Yüeh. I will bring you some from the west river. Will that do?' "At this the stickleback flushed with anger and said, 'I am out of my element. I have nowhere to go. A pint of water would save me. But to talk to me like this,--you might as well put me in a dried-fish shop at once.'"

title.en: Jên Kung Tzŭ's Hook Baited with Fifty Oxen (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 任公子大鉤巨緇五十犗（莊子）

region.en: Kuei-chi and the eastern ocean (Shaoxing bay, Zhejiang, China)
region.zh: 會稽東海之上（今浙江紹興灣）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: Jên Kung Tzŭ baits a huge hook on a big line with fifty oxen, squats at Kuei-chi and casts into the eastern ocean; a year passes without a catch. Then a great fish swallows the bait, plunges, and shakes the deep with a noise like so many devils; and from Chih-ho eastwards and Ts'ang-wu northwards there was none but ate his fill of that fish.
summary.zh: 任公子為大鉤巨緇，五十犗以為餌，蹲乎會稽，投竿東海——已而大魚食之，牽巨鉤，鎅沒而下；白波若山。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Jên Kung Tzŭ got a huge hook on a big line, which he baited with fifty oxen. He squatted down at Kuei-chi, and cast into the eastern ocean. Every day he fished, but for a whole year he caught nothing. Then came a great fish which swallowed the bait, and dragging the huge hook dived down below. This way and that way it plunged about, erecting the dorsal fin. The white waves rolled mountain high. The great deep was shaken up. The noise was like that of so many devils, terrifying people for many miles around.

But when Jên Kung Tzŭ had secured his fish, he cut it up and salted it. And from Chih-ho eastwards, and from Ts'ang-wu northwards, there was none but ate his fill of that fish. Even among succeeding generations, gobemouches of the day recounted the marvellous tale. To take a rod and line, and go to a pool, and catch small fry is a very different thing from catching big fish.

title.en: Day Is Breaking: The Confucianists and the Mouth-Pearl (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 儒以詩禮發冢（莊子）

region.en: The tomb being opened (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 發冢之地（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: Some Confucianists open a grave in accordance with their Canons of Poetry and Rites; the master shouts 'Day is breaking,' and the apprentice reports a pearl in the mouth. Seizing the corpse's brow, they tap its cheeks with a metal hammer to make the jaws open gently and not injure the pearl — the satire: they quote the greenest corn that grows over graves even as they rob.
summary.zh: 儒以詩禮發冢——口中有珠。詩固言之曰：青青之麥，生於陵陂；生不布施，死何含珠為？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When some Confucianists were opening a grave in accordance with their Canons of Poetry and Rites, the master shouted out, "Day is breaking. How are you getting on with the work?" "Not got off the burial-clothes yet," answered an apprentice. "There is a pearl in the mouth."

So seizing the corpse's brow with one hand, and forcing down its chin with the other, these Confucianists proceed to tap its cheeks with a metal hammer, in order to make the jaws open gently and not injure the pearl!

title.en: Lao Lai Tzŭ Rebukes the Sorrowing Confucius (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 老萊子之弟子出薪遇仲尼（莊子）

region.en: The fuel-wood path of Ch'u (Jingmen, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 楚薪樵之塗（象徵定位：湖北荊門）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: A disciple of Lao Lai Tzŭ, gathering fuel, meets a long-bodied, short-legged, round-shouldered man sorrowing over mankind — Confucius himself. Lao Lai Tzŭ bids him get rid of his dogmatism, and asks whether the wounds of one generation being too much, you would take to yourself the sorrows of all time. Better than extolling Yao and cursing Chieh is oblivion of both.
summary.zh: 老萊子曰：丘！去汝躬矜與汝容知，斯為君子矣——不忍一世之傷，而鰲萬世之患。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: A disciple of Lao Lai Tzŭ while out gathering fuel, chanced to meet Confucius. On his return, he said, "There is a man over there with a long body and short legs, round shoulders and drooping ears. He looks as though he were sorrowing over mankind. I know not who he can be." "It is Confucius!" cried Lao Lai Tzŭ. "Bid him come hither."

When Confucius arrived, Lao Lai Tzŭ addressed him as follows:--"Ch'iu! Get rid of your dogmatism and your specious knowledge, and you will be really a superior man." ... "The wounds of one generation being too much," answered Lao Lai Tzŭ, "you would take to yourself the sorrows of all time. Are you not weary? Is your strength equal to the task? "Better than extolling Yao and cursing Chieh is oblivion of both, keeping one's praises to oneself."

title.en: Prince Yüan Dreams of the Divine Tortoise (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 宋元君夜半夢人被髮窺阿門（莊子）

region.en: The Sung court (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋宮（今河南商丘）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: Prince Yüan of Sung dreams that a man with dishevelled hair peeps through a side door: I am a marine messenger attached to the staff of the River God, and a fisherman named Yü Ch'ieh has caught me. The divine tortoise is slain for divination, and out of seventy-two omens not a single one proves false — wisdom has its limits; spirituality, that which it cannot reach.
summary.zh: 宋元君夢神龜——予，江河之靈也；漁者豫且得予。乃芻龜而卜，七十二鑽而無遺筴。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the River-God messenger dream is a landmark oracle-divination narrative. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Prince Yüan of Sung dreamed one night that a man with dishevelled hair peeped through a side door and said, "I have come from the waters of Tsai-lu. I am a marine messenger attached to the staff of the River God. A fisherman, named Yü Ch'ieh, has caught me." When the prince awaked, he referred his dream to the soothsayers, who said, "This is a divine tortoise."

Being told there was such a fisherman, the prince gave orders for his appearance at court. "I have netted a white tortoise," replied the fisherman, "five feet in semi-circumference." "Bring your tortoise," said the prince. But when it came, the prince could not make up his mind whether to kill it or keep it alive. Thus in doubt, he had recourse to divination, and received the following response: Slay the tortoise for purposes of divination and good fortune will result. So the tortoise was despatched. After which, out of seventy-two omens taken, not a single one proved false.

"A divine tortoise," said Confucius, "can appear to prince Yüan in a dream, yet it cannot escape the net of Yü Ch'ieh. Its wisdom can yield seventy-two faultless omens, yet it cannot escape the misery of being cut to pieces. Truly wisdom has its limits; spirituality, that which it cannot reach. In spite of the highest wisdom, there are countless snares to be avoided; If a fish has not to fear nets, there are always pelicans. Get rid of small wisdom, and great wisdom will shine upon you."

title.en: The Fish-Trap, the Rabbit-Snare, and Where to Find One to Converse With (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 得魚忘筌，得意忘言（莊子）

region.en: The dialogue's end (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 問答之末（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 26, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 26

summary.en: The raison d'être of a fish-trap is the fish; when the fish is caught, the trap may be ignored. The raison d'être of language is an idea to be expressed; when the idea is expressed, the language may be ignored. But where shall I find a man to ignore language, with whom I may be able to converse?
summary.zh: 筌者所以在魚，得魚而忘筌；言者所以在意，得意而忘言。吾安得忘言之人而與之言哉！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the fish-trap and rabbit-snare became the classic image for scripture as a means. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The raison d'être of a fish-trap is the fish. When the fish is caught, the trap may be ignored. The raison d'être of a rabbit-snare is the rabbit. When the rabbit is caught the snare may be ignored. The raison d'être of language is an idea to be expressed. When the idea is expressed, the language may be ignored. But where shall I find a man to ignore language, with whom I may be able to converse?

title.en: Shan Chüan Declines the Empire and Hides in the Mountains (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 舜讓天下於善卷（莊子）

region.en: Shan Chüan's farm in the wilds (symbolic pin: Songshan, Henan, China)
region.zh: 善卷之田（象徵定位：河南嵩山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Shun offers Shan Chüan the empire; he answers that he is a unit in the sum of the universe — fur in winter, grass-cloth in summer, ploughing in spring, rest in autumn — and declines, subsequently hiding himself among the mountains, nobody knew where.
summary.zh: 舜以天下讓善卷。善卷曰：余立於宇宙之中，冬日衣皮毛，夏日衣葛絺；春耕種，形足以勞動；秋收斂，身足以休食——逍遙於天地之間而心意自得。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Shun offered to resign the empire to Shan Chüan. Shan Chüan said, "I am a unit in the sum of the universe. In winter I wear fur clothes. In summer I wear grass-cloth. In spring I plough and sow, toiling with my body. In autumn I gather in the harvest, and devote myself to rest and enjoyment. At dawn I go to work; at sunset I leave off. Contented with my lot I pass through life with a light heart. Why then should I trouble myself with the empire? Ah, Sir, you do not know me." So he declined, and subsequently hid himself among the mountains, nobody knew where.

title.en: The Labourer of Shih Hu Goes Off to the Sea (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 舜以天下讓石戶之農（莊子）

region.en: The sea-coast of exile (symbolic pin: Qingdao, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 海上（象徵定位：山東青島）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Shun offers the empire to a friend, a labourer of Shih Hu. Sire, you exert yourself too much, says the labourer — the chief thing is to husband one's strength. Then husband and wife, bearing away their household gods and taking their children with them, went off to the sea and never came back.
summary.zh: 舜以天下讓其友石戶之農。石戶之農曰：捲捲乎后之為人，葆力之士也——於是夫負妻戴，攜子以入於海，終身不反也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Shun offered the empire to a friend, a labourer of Shih Hu. "Sire," said the latter, "you exert yourself too much. The chief thing is to husband one's strength;"--meaning that in point of real virtue Shun had not attained. Then, husband and wife, bearing away their household gods and taking their children with them, went off to the sea and never came back.

title.en: T'ai Wang Shan Fu Abandons Pin to the Savages (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 太王亶父居邠，讓地於狄（莊子）

region.en: Pin, and the new state at the foot of Mount Ch'i (Binxian/Qishan, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 邠地與岐山之下（今陝西彬州／岐山）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Attacked by savages who want his territory, T'ai Wang Shan Fu refuses to fight: to live with a man's elder brother and slay his younger brother I could not bear to do. He takes his staff and goes off, his people all following him, and they found a new State at the foot of Mount Ch'i.
summary.zh: 太王亶父居邠，狄人攻之；事之以皮帛而不受——與人之兄居而殺其弟，與人之父居而殺其子，吾不忍也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the migration-legend of the Chou royal ancestors, told by Zhuangzi. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When T'ai Wang Shan Fu was occupying Pin, he was attacked by savages. He offered them skins and silk, but they declined these. He offered them dogs and horses, but they declined these also. He then offered them pearls and jade, but these too they declined. What they wanted was the territory. "To live with a man's elder brother," said T'ai Wang Shan Fu, "and slay his younger brother; to live with a man's father and slay his son,--this I could not bear to do. Make shift to remain here. To be my subjects or the subjects of these savages, where is the difference?"

Thereupon he took his staff and went off. His people all followed him, and they founded a new State at the foot of Mount Ch'i. Now T'ai Wang Shan Fu undoubtedly had a proper respect for life. And those who have a proper respect for life, if rich and powerful, do not let that which should nourish injure the body.

title.en: Shou of Yüeh Smoked Out of the Hills (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 越王子搜逃乎丹穴（莊子）

region.en: Tan Hsüeh cave in Yüeh (Kuaiji, Zhejiang, China)
region.zh: 丹穴（今浙江會稽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Three successive princes of Yüeh have been murdered, so the heir Shou flees to the cave of Tan Hsüeh; the people smoke him out with moxa, have a royal carriage ready, and as he seizes the cord to mount he looks up to heaven and cries: Oh! ruling, ruling, could I not have been spared this?
summary.zh: 越人三世弒其君，王子搜患之，逃乎丹穴；越人薰之以艾——若敖之為君乎，不以國傷生。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In three successive cases the people of Yüeh had put their prince to death. Accordingly, Shou, the son of the last prince, was much alarmed, and fled to Tan Hsüeh, leaving the State of Yüeh without a ruler. Shou was at first nowhere to be found, but at length he was traced to Tan Hsüeh. He was, however, unwilling to come forth, so they smoked him out with moxa. They had a royal carriage ready for him; and as Shou seized the cord to mount the chariot, he looked up to heaven and cried, "Oh! ruling, ruling, could I not have been spared this?"

title.en: Yen Ho the Ox-Herd Vanishes Before the Messenger's Return (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 顏闔守陋閭，布衣帶索（莊子）

region.en: The hovel of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯之陋閭（今山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Hearing that Yen Ho has attained the TAO, the prince of Lu sends messengers with presents. I fear you have made a mistake, says the man in coarse grass clothes who tends oxen — go back and make sure. When they return there is no trace of Yen Ho, and the saying follows: the best part of TAO is for self-culture, the surplus for governing a State, and the dregs for governing the empire.
summary.zh: 顏闔將傅衛靈公太子——魯君聞顏闔得道之人也，使人以幣先焉；闔對曰：恐聽謬而遺使者罪——而顏闔已亡矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The prince of Lu, hearing that Yen Ho had attained to TAO, despatched messengers with presents to open communications. Yen Ho lived in a hovel. He wore clothes of coarse grass, and occupied himself in tending oxen. When the messengers arrived, Yen Ho went out to meet them; whereupon they enquired, "Is this where Yen Ho lives?" "This is Yen Ho's house," replied the latter. The messengers then produced the presents; but Yen Ho said, "I fear you have made a mistake. And as you might get into trouble, it would be as well to go back and make sure."

This the messengers accordingly did. When however they returned, there was no trace to be found of Yen Ho. Thus it is that men like Yen Ho hate wealth and power. Wherefore it has been said that the best part of TAO is for self-culture, the surplus for governing a State, and the dregs for governing the empire.

title.en: Lieh Tzŭ Declines the Prime Minister's Food (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 子陽遺粟，列子辭之（莊子）

region.en: The State of Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國（今河南鄭州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Poor Lieh Tzŭ, hungry-faced, is offered food by the prime minister Tzŭ Yang on the strength of what others said — and bows twice and declines. His wife beats her breast; but the men of Chêng presently rise in trouble and Tzŭ Yang is slain. His Excellency did not know me personally, answered Lieh Tzŭ: if men were to speak ill of me, he would also act upon it.
summary.zh: 子列子窮，容貌有飢色；客言之於鄭子陽。子列子笑謂其妻曰：君非自知我也，以人之言而遺我粟也——至於罪我者，又且以人之言。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Lieh Tzŭ was poor. His face wore a hungry look. A visitor one day mentioned this to Tzŭ Yang of Chêng, saying, "Lieh Tzŭ is a scholar who has attained to TAO. He lives in your Excellency's State, and yet he is poor. Can it be said that your Excellency does not love scholars?" Thereupon Tzŭ Yang gave orders that Lieh Tzŭ should be supplied with food. But when Lieh Tzŭ saw the messengers, he bowed twice and declined.

When the messengers had gone, and Lieh Tzŭ went within, his wife gazed at him, and beating her breast said, "I have heard that the wife and children of a man of TAO are happy and joyful. But see how hungry I am. His Excellency sent you food, and you would not take it. Is not this flying in the face of Providence?" "His Excellency did not know me personally," answered Lieh Tzŭ with a smile. "It was because of what others said about me that he sent me the food. If then men were to speak ill of me, he would also act upon it. For that reason I refused the food." Subsequently, there was trouble among the people of Chêng, and Tzŭ Yang was slain.

title.en: The Butcher Yüeh Refuses to Be Made a Minister (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 楚昭王屠羊說辭三旌（莊子）

region.en: The restored court of Ch'u (Jingzhou, Hubei, China)
region.zh: 楚復國之廷（今湖北荊州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: When Prince Chao of Ch'u lost his kingdom, his butcher Yüeh followed him into exile; on restoration Yüeh declines every reward — I recovered my office and salary, what need for further reward? — and refuses audience by the laws of Ch'u itself, until the prince orders him made a San Ching; and he still refuses, begging to go back to his butchery.
summary.zh: 楚昭王失國，屠羊說從；反國，將賞從者，及說——說曰：大王失國，說失屠羊；大王反國，說亦反屠羊。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Prince Chao of the Ch'u State lost his kingdom, he was followed into exile by his butcher, named Yüeh. On his restoration, as he was distributing rewards to those who had remained faithful to him, he came to the name of Yüeh. Yüeh, however, said, "When the prince lost his kingdom, I lost my butchery. Now that the prince has got back his kingdom, I have got back my butchery. I have recovered my office and salary. What need for further reward?"

When the prince heard this answer, he commanded Yüeh to be brought before him. But Yüeh said, "The laws of the Ch'u State require that a subject shall have deserved exceptionally well of his prince before being admitted to an audience. Now my wisdom was insufficient to preserve this kingdom, and my courage insufficient to destroy the invaders. When the Wu soldiers entered Ying, I feared for my life and fled. That was why I followed the prince. And if now the prince wishes to set law and custom aside and summon me to an audience, this is not my idea of proper behaviour on the part of the prince." ... "I must beg to decline. Let me go back to my butchery." And he adhered to his refusal.

title.en: Yüan Hsien's Mud Hut with a Jar-Mouth Window (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 原憲居魯，環堵之室（莊子）

region.en: The mud hut of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯之環堵（今山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Yüan Hsien dwells in Lu in a mud hut with grass-grown roof and a jar-mouth window closed by a wad of old clothes, sitting gravely there playing the guitar when Tzŭ Kung drives up in a fine chariot. Good gracious! cries Tzŭ Kung; whatever is the matter with you? I am merely poor, answers Yüan Hsien; I have nothing the matter with me.
summary.zh: 原憲居魯，環堵之室，茨以生草，蓬戶不完，桑以為樞而甕牖——上漏下濕，匡坐而弦歌。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yüan Hsien dwelt in Lu,--in a mud hut, with a grass-grown roof, an apology for a door, and two mulberry-trees for door-posts. The windows which lighted his two rooms were no bigger than the mouth of a jar, and were closed by a wad of old clothes. The hut leaked from above and was damp under foot; yet Yüan Hsien sat gravely there playing on the guitar. Tzŭ Kung came driving up in a fine chariot, in a white robe lined with purple; but the hood of the chariot was too big for the street.

"Good gracious!" cried Tzŭ Kung, "whatever is the matter with you?" "I have heard," replied Yüan Hsien, "that he who is without wealth is called poor, and that he who learns without being able to practise is said to have something the matter with him. Now I am merely poor; I have nothing the matter with me." Tzŭ Kung was much abashed at this reply; upon which Yüan Hsien smiling continued, "To try to thrust myself forward among men; to seek friendship in mutual flattery; to learn for the sake of others; to teach for my own sake; to use benevolence and duty to one's neighbour for evil ends; to make a great show with horses and carriages,--these things I cannot do."

title.en: Tsêng Tzŭ Sings the Sacrificial Odes in Threadbare Coat (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 曾子居衛，曳縱而歌商頌（莊子）

region.en: The State of Wei (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 衛國（今河南安陽一帶）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Tsêng Tzŭ in Wei wears a wadded coat with no outside cloth, hands horny hard, three days without fire; yet slipshod he sings the Sacrificial Odes of Shang, his voice filling the whole sky as though it had been some instrument of metal or stone. The Son of Heaven could not secure him as a minister; the feudal princes could not secure him as a friend.
summary.zh: 曾子居衛，縕袍無表，顏色腫噲，手足胼胝；三日不舉火，十年不製衣——正冠而纓絕，捉衿而肘見。曳縱而歌商頌，聲滿天地，若出金石。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tsêng Tzŭ lived in the Wei State. His wadded coat had no outside cloth. His face was bloated and rough. His hands and feet were horny hard. For three days he had had no fire; no new clothes for ten years. If he set his cap straight the tassel would come off. If he drew up his sleeve his elbow would poke through. If he pulled up his shoe, the heel would come off. Yet slipshod he sang the Sacrificial Odes of Shang, his voice filling the whole sky, as though it had been some instrument of metal or stone.

The Son of Heaven could not secure him as a minister. The feudal princes could not secure him as a friend. For he who nourishes his purpose becomes oblivious of his body. He who nourishes his body becomes oblivious of gain. And he who has attained TAO becomes oblivious of his mind.

title.en: Yen Hui Declines Official Life (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 孔子謂顏回：回何不仕？（莊子）

region.en: The hall of Lu (Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 魯之堂（今山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Confucius urges the poor and lowly Yen Hui into official life; Yen Hui declines — fifty acres beyond the walls for food, ten more for clothes, the lute for amusement, the study of the doctrines for happiness. Bravo! cries Confucius with beaming countenance: only now, that I have seen Yen Hui, am I conscious of the realisation of these words.
summary.zh: 孔子謂顏回曰：回！來！家貧居卑，胡不仕乎？顏回對曰：不愿仕——郭外有五十畝足以給飦粥；郭內十畝足以為絲麻。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "Come hither," said Confucius to Yen Hui. "Your family is poor, and your position lowly. Why not go into official life?" "I do not wish to," replied Yen Hui. "I have fifty acres of land beyond the city walls, which are enough to supply me with food. Ten more within the walls provide me with clothes. My lute gives me all the amusement I want; and the study of your doctrines keeps me happy enough. I do not desire to go into official life."

"Bravo! well said!" cried Confucius with beaming countenance. "I have heard say that those who are contented do not entangle themselves in the pursuit of gain. That those who have really obtained do not fear the contingency of loss. That those who devote themselves to cultivation of the inner man, though occupying no position, feel no shame. Thus indeed I have long preached. Only now, that I have seen Yen Hui, am I conscious of the realisation of these words."

title.en: Tzŭ Lu Dances with a Shield in the Starvation Camp (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 陳蔡之間，子路抗然執干而舞（莊子）

region.en: Between Ch'ên and Ts'ai (Zhoukou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 陳蔡之間（今河南周口一帶）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: Seven days without proper food between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, Confucius sings to his guitar; Tzŭ Lu and Tzŭ Kung grumble that whoever kills him is to be held guiltless. The superior man who succeeds in TAO has success, answers Confucius — it is the chill winter weather, it is frost, it is snow, which bring out the luxuriance of the pine and the fir. Tzŭ Lu hastily seizes a shield and dances to the music, and Tzŭ Kung owns he had no idea of the height of heaven and the depth of earth.
summary.zh: 孔子窮於陳蔡之間，七日不火食；藜羹不糝。子路曰：夫子逐於魯，削跡於衛——弦歌鼓琴未嘗絕音，豈君子之無恥也若此乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Confucius was caught between the Ch'êns and the Ts'ais, he went seven days without proper food. He ate soup of herbs, having no rice. He looked very much exhausted, yet he sat within playing his guitar and singing to it. Yen Hui was picking over the herbs, while Tzŭ Lu and Tzŭ Kung were talking together. One of them said, "Our Master has twice been driven out of Lu. They will have none of him in Wei. His tree was cut down in Sung. He got into trouble in Shang and Chou. And now he is surrounded by the Ch'êns and the Ts'ais. Whoever kills him is to be held guiltless. Whoever takes him prisoner is not to be interfered with. Yet all the time he goes on playing and singing without cease. Is this the right thing for a superior man to do?"

"The superior man who succeeds in TAO, has success. If he fails in TAO, he makes a failure. Now I, holding fast to the TAO of charity and duty towards one's neighbour, have fallen among the troubles of a disordered age. What failure is there in that? ... It is the chill winter weather, it is frost, it is snow, which bring out the luxuriance of the pine and the fir. I regard it as a positive blessing to be thus situated as I am." Thereupon he turned abruptly round and went on playing and singing. At this Tzŭ Lu hastily seized a shield and began dancing to the music, while Tzŭ Kung said, "I had no idea of the height of heaven and of the depth of earth."

title.en: Pien Sui and Wu Kuang Drown Themselves Rather Than Take T'ang's Throne (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 湯將伐桀，卞隨務光自投（莊子）

region.en: The rivers Chou and Lu (symbolic pin: Tongbai, Henan, China)
region.zh: 桐水盧水之濱（象徵定位：河南桐柏）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: T'ang consults the hermits Pien Sui and Wu Kuang about attacking Chieh — It is not a matter in which I can help you, say both — then attacks and vanquishes, and offers each in turn the empire. To depose a ruler is not to do one's duty to one's neighbour, answers Wu Kuang; to slay the people is not charity — and one after another they take a stone on their backs and jump into the river.
summary.zh: 湯遂伐桀，克之；因讓卞隨、務光——廢上非義也，而殺民非仁也。乃負石自沈於廬水。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When T'ang was about to attack Chieh, he went to consult with Pien Sui. "It is not a matter in which I can help you," said the latter. "Who can?" asked T'ang. "I do not know," replied Pien Sui. T'ang then went to consult with Wu Kuang. "It is not a matter in which I can help you," said the latter. "Who can?" asked T'ang. "I do not know," replied Wu Kuang. So T'ang took I Yin into his counsels. They attacked Chieh, and vanquished him.

Then T'ang offered to resign the empire in favour of Pien Sui. But Pien Sui declined, saying, "When your Majesty consulted with me about attacking Chieh, you evidently looked on me as a robber. Now that you have vanquished him, and you offer to resign in my favour, you evidently regard me as covetous. I was born indeed in a disordered age. But for a man without TAO to thus insult me twice, is more than I can endure." So he drowned himself in the river Chou.

Then T'ang offered to resign in favour of Wu Kuang, saying, "The wise plan, the brave execute, the good rest therein,--such was the TAO of the ancients. Why, Sir, should not you occupy the throne?" But Wu Kuang declined, saying, "To depose a ruler is not to do one's duty to one's neighbour. To slay the people is not charity. For others to suffer these wrongs, while I enjoy the profits, is not honest. I have heard say that one should not accept a wage unless earned in accordance with right; and that if the world is without TAO, one should not put foot upon its soil, still less rule over it! I can bear this no longer." Thereupon he took a stone on his back and jumped into the river Lu.

title.en: Poh I and Shu Ch'i Starve on Mount Shou-yang (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 伯夷叔齊餓於首陽（莊子）

region.en: Mount Shou-yang (Shouyangshan, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 首陽山（今山西永濟）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 28, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 28

summary.en: At the rise of the Chou dynasty the two scholars Poh I and Shu Ch'i go west to see men in possession of TAO, and are offered a treaty of emoluments sealed with blood and buried. Troops are mobilised to protect prestige; victims are slaughtered to give good faith to a treaty — the empire is now in darkness. They flee north to Mount Shou-yang, where they starve themselves to death.
summary.zh: 昔周之興，有士二人處於孤竹——虞暴亂以相誅，伐以要利——遂北至於首陽之山，遂餓死焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: At the rise of the Chou dynasty there were two scholars, named Po I and Shu Ch'i, who lived in Ku-tu. One of these said to the other, "I have heard that in the west there are men who are apparently in possession of TAO. Let us go and see them." When they arrived at Ch'i-yang, Wu Wang heard of their arrival and sent Shu Tan to enter into a treaty with them. They were to receive emoluments of the second degree and rank of the first degree. The treaty was to be sealed with blood and buried.

At this the two looked at each other and smiled. "Ah!" said one of them, "this is strange indeed. It is not what we call TAO. When Shên Nung ruled the empire, he worshipped God without asking for any reward. ... But now that the Chous, beholding the iniquities of the Yins, have taken upon themselves to govern, we have intrigues above and bribes below. Troops are mobilised to protect prestige. Victims are slaughtered to give good faith to a treaty. A show of virtue is made to amuse the masses. Fighting and slaughter are made the means of gain. Confusion has simply been exchanged for disorder.

"I have heard tell that the men of old, living in quiet times, never shirked their duties; but lighting upon troublous times, nothing could make them stay. The empire is now in darkness. The virtue of the Chous has faded. For the empire to be united under the Chous would be a disgrace to us. Better flee away and keep our actions pure." Accordingly, these two philosophers went north to Mount Shou-yang, where they subsequently starved themselves to death.

title.en: Robber Chê and the Liver Stew: The Harangue of the Great Brigand (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 盜跖怒斥孔子（莊子）

region.en: The robber-camp south of Mount T'ai (Shandong, China)
region.zh: 泰山之陽盜寨（今山東泰安南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 29, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 29

summary.en: With a band nine thousand strong, Robber Chê ravages the empire, and Confucius — charioteered by Yen Hui — goes to convert him, finding the brigand eating a dish of minced human liver. Chê's harangue turns every table: Yao and Shun got the empire, yet their descendants have not territory enough to insert an awl's point; you are the biggest thief I know of — if the world calls me Robber Chê, it most certainly ought to call you Robber Ch'iu. Confucius three times misses the reins, having cauterized himself without being ill and very nearly got into the tiger's mouth.
summary.zh: 孔子與柳下季為友；柳下季之弟名曰盜跖。孔子往見之，盜跖乃方休卒徒太山之陽，膾人肝而餔之——若以利惑其真而強反其情性，詩書發塚！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the spurious-but-canonical Robber Chê dialogue is Zhuangzi's great trickster-narrative. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Robber Chê had a band of followers nine thousand strong. He ravaged the whole empire, plundering the various nobles and breaking into people's houses. He drove off oxen and horses. He stole men's wives and daughters. Family ties put no limit to his greed. He had no respect for parents nor for brothers. He neglected the worship of his ancestors. Wherever he passed, the greater States flew to arms, the smaller ones to places of safety. All the people were sore distressed.

The latter had just encamped to the south of T'ai-shan, and was engaged in devouring a dish of minced human liver. Confucius alighted from his chariot, and advancing addressed the doorkeeper as follows:--"I am Confucius of the Lu State. I have heard of the high character of your captain." When Robber Chê heard who it was, he was furious. His eyes glared like stars. His hair raised his cap from his head as he cried out, "What! that crafty scoundrel Confucius of Lu? Go, tell him from me that he is a mere word-mongerer. That he talks nonsense about Wên Wang and Wu Wang. That what he says is mostly rhodomontade. That he consumes where he does not sow, and wears clothes he does not weave. That his lips patter and his tongue wags. Tell him that he deserves the worst, and that if he does not take himself off his liver shall be in my morning stew."

"Ch'iu! come here," cried Robber Chê in a great rage. "There is no State bigger than the empire. Yao and Shun both got this, yet their descendants have not territory enough to insert an awl's point. T'ang and Wu Wang both sat upon the Imperial throne, yet their posterity has been obliterated from the face of the earth. Was not this because of the very magnitude of the prize? ... And now you come forward preaching the old dogmas of Wên Wang and palming off sophistries without end, in order to teach future generations. You are the biggest thief I know of; and if the world calls me Robber Chê, it most certainly ought to call you Robber Ch'iu.

"Ch'iu! all your teachings are nothing to me. Begone! Go home! Say no more! Your doctrine is a random jargon, full of falsity and deceit. It can never preserve the original purity of man. Why discuss it further?" Confucius made two obeisances and hurriedly took his leave. On mounting his chariot, he three times missed hold of the reins. His eyes were so dazed that he could see nothing. His face was ashy pale. ... "He did," said Confucius. "I am a man who has cauterized himself without being ill. I hurried away to smooth the tiger's head and comb out his beard. And I very nearly got into the tiger's mouth."

title.en: Nest-Builders, the Provident, and the War Whose Blood Flowed a Hundred Li (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 有巢氏、知生氏與涿鹿之戰（莊子）

region.en: Chŏ-lu, the battlefield of the Yellow Emperor and Ch'ih Yu (Zhuolu, Hebei, China)
region.zh: 涿鹿之野（今河北涿鹿）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 29, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 29

summary.en: In Robber Chê's mouth, the great cultural myths are turned into an indictment: in olden times birds and animals outnumbered man and he built his domicile in trees — hence the name Nest-builders; the people did not know how to make clothes and warmed themselves by fire — hence the name Provident; in Shên Nung's days a man knew his mother but not his father and lived among the wild deer. Then the Yellow Emperor fought with Ch'ih Yu at Chŏ-lu, and blood flowed for a hundred li — ever since T'ang and Wu Wang we have had none other than disturbers of the peace.
summary.zh: 古者禽獸多而人民少，於是民皆巢居以避之；晝拾橡栗，暮棲木上，故命之曰有巢氏之民。古者民不知衣服——故命之曰知生之民。黃帝不能致德，與蚩尤戰於涿鹿之野，流血百里。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Robber Chê version of China's culture-hero sequence — Nest-builders, fire-warming providents, Shên Nung's age of perfect virtue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "I have also heard that in olden times the birds and animals outnumbered man, and that the latter was obliged to seek his safety by building his domicile in trees. By day he picked up acorns and chestnuts. At night he slept upon a branch. Hence the name Nest-builders.

"Of old, the people did not know how to make clothes. In summer they collected quantities of fuel, and in winter warmed themselves by fire. Hence the name Provident. "In the days of Shên Nung, they lay down without caring where they were and got up without caring whither they might go. A man knew his mother but not his father. He lived among the wild deer. He tilled the ground for food. He wove cloth to cover his body. He harboured no thought of injury to others. These were the glorious results of an age of perfect virtue. "The Yellow Emperor, however, could not attain to this virtue. He fought with Ch'ih Yu at Chŏ-lu, and blood flowed for a hundred li. Then came Yao and Shun with their crowd of ministers. Then T'ang who deposed his sovereign, and Wu Wang who slew Chou. After which time the strong took to oppressing the weak, the many to coercing the few. In fact, ever since T'ang and Wu Wang we have had none other than disturbers of the peace."

title.en: Chieh Tzŭ T'ui's Slice of Thigh and the Bridge-Assassin Wei Shêng (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 介子推割股，尾生抱柱（莊子）

region.en: The drowned assignation beneath the bridge (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 橋下之約（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 29, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 29

summary.en: Robber Chê's catalogue of the world's 'virtuous': Chieh Tzŭ T'ui cut a slice from his thigh to feed Wên Wang, then grasped a tree and was burnt to death; Wei Shêng made an assignation with a girl beneath a bridge, the water rose, he grasped a buttress and died; Poh I and Shu Ch'i died of starvation on Mount Shou-yang, their corpses deprived of burial — these four differed in no way from dogs and pigs going about begging to be slaughtered.
summary.zh: 介子推至忠也，自割其股以食文公；尾生與女子期於梁下——水至不去，抱梁柱而死。此四子者無異於磔犬流豕。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Among those whom the world calls virtuous were Poh I and Shu Ch'i. They declined the sovereignty of Ku-chu and died of starvation on Mount Shou-yang, their corpses deprived of burial. "Pao Chiao made a great show of virtue and abused the world in general. He grasped a tree and died. "Shên T'u Ti, when no heed was paid to his counsels, jumped into the river with a stone on his back and became food for fishes.

"Chieh Tzŭ T'ui was truly loyal. He cut a slice from his thigh to feed Wên Wang. Afterwards, when Wên Wang turned his back upon him, he retired in anger, and grasping a tree, was burnt to death. "Wei Shêng made an assignation with a girl beneath a bridge. The girl did not come, and the water rose. But Wei Shêng would not leave. He grasped a buttress and died. "These four differed in no way from dogs and pigs going about begging to be slaughtered. They all exaggerated reputation and disregarded death. They did not reflect upon their original nature and seek to preserve life into the old age allotted."

title.en: The Three Swords: Of the Son of Heaven, of the Princes, and of the People (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 說劍：天子之劍、諸侯之劍、庶人之劍（莊子）

region.en: The court of Wên Wang of Chao (Handan, Hebei, China)
region.zh: 趙文王之廷（今河北邯鄲）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 30, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 30

summary.en: Wên Wang of Chao loves sword-play, with three thousand swordsmen bouting yearly and a hundred killed; Chuang Tzŭ, engaged by the Heir Apparent, enters dressed as a fencer and offers three swords. The sword of the Son of Heaven — the stone wall of Yen-ch'i its point, the mountains of Ch'i its edge, enclosed in the four hordes, wrapped in the four seasons — cleaves the floating clouds above and cuts through the density of earth below; one flash and the princes of the empire submit.
summary.zh: 趙文王喜劍，劍士夾門三千餘人。莊子入殿門不趨——天子之劍：以燕谿石城為鋒，齊岱為鍔；包以四夷，裹以四時；上決浮雲，下絕地紀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Of old, Wên Wang of Chao loved sword-play. Swordsmen thronged his halls, to the number of three thousand and more. Day and night they had bouts before the prince. In the course of a year, a hundred or so would be killed or wounded. Yet the prince was never satisfied. Within three years, the State had begun to go to rack and ruin, and other princes to form designs upon it.

"What is the sword of the Son of Heaven?" asked the prince. "The stone wall of Yen-ch'i is its point," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "The mountains of Ch'i are its edge. Chin and Wei are its back. Chou and Sung are its hilt. Han and Wei are its sheath. It is enclosed in the four hordes of barbarians, wrapped in the four seasons, surrounded by the great ocean. It is made of the five elements. It is the arbiter of punishment and reward. It operates under the influence of the Yin and the Yang. In spring and summer it is at rest. In autumn and winter it moves abroad. Push it, it does not advance. Raise it, it does not go up. Lower it, it does not go down. Whirl it around, it does not change position. Above, it cleaves the floating clouds; below, it cuts through the density of earth. One flash of this blade, and the princes of the empire submit. Such is the sword of the Son of Heaven."

"The sword of the People," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "has dishevelled hair hanging over its temples. It wears a slouching cap with coarse tangled tassel, and a short-tailed coat. It glares with its eyes and talks in a fierce tone. When it engages in conflict, above, it cuts off head and neck; below, it smites liver and lungs. Such is the sword of the People. It is like a game-cock. One day, its life is cut short, and it is of no more use to the State. Now you, great prince, wield sovereign power, and yet you devote yourself to this sword of the People. I am truly ashamed of it." After this the prince did not quit his palace for three months, while the swordsmen, submitting to the new order of things, died in their own homes.

title.en: The Old Fisherman of the Apricot Altar (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 杏壇漁父（莊子）

region.en: The Apricot Altar in the Black Forest of Ch'u (Huaiyin, Jiangsu, China)
region.zh: 緇帷之林杏壇（象徵定位：江蘇淮陰）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 31, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 31

summary.en: Travelling in the Black Forest, Confucius rests at the Apricot Altar, playing and singing, until a snowy-bearded fisherman steps out of his boat and asks what the man is doing. The old man tells of the eight blemishes and four obstructions, and of the man who fled his shadow and died of running; the original purity is the perfection of truth unalloyed, given from God — ceremonial is the invention of man. Confucius waits until the ripples have smoothed down and the punt-pole's sound died away before he ventures to get up.
summary.zh: 孔子遊乎緇帷之林，休坐乎杏壇之上；弟子讀書，孔子絃歌鼓琴。漁父曰：真者，所以受於天也，自然不可易也——法天貴真，不拘於俗。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Apricot Altar of this chapter became the legendary site of Confucius's teaching. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Confucius, travelling in the Black Forest, rested awhile at Apricot Altar. His disciples sat down to their books, and he himself played upon the lute and sang. Half way through the song, an old fisherman stepped out of a boat and advanced towards them. His beard and eyebrows were snowy white. His hair hung loose, and he flapped his long sleeves as he walked over the foreshore. Reaching firm ground, he stood still, and with left hand on his knee and right hand to his ear, listened.

"There was once a man who was so afraid of his shadow and so disliked his own footsteps that he determined to run away from them. But the oftener he raised his feet the more footsteps he made, and though he ran very hard his shadow never left him. From this he inferred that he went too slowly, and ran as hard as he could without resting, the consequence being that his strength broke down and he died. He was not aware that by going into the shade he would have got rid of his shadow, and that by keeping still he would have put an end to his footsteps. Fool that he was!

"Our original purity," replied the fisherman, "is the perfection of truth unalloyed. Without this, we cannot influence others. Hence, those who weep to order, though they mourn, do not grieve. Those who assume anger, though violent, do not inspire awe. Those who affect friendship, though they smile, are not in unison. "Real mourning grieves in silence. Real anger awes without expression. Real friendship is unison without the aid of smiles. Our emotions are dependent upon the original purity within; and accordingly we hold the latter in esteem. "Ceremonial is the invention of man. Our original purity is given to us from God. It is as it is, and cannot be changed."

Thereupon he pushed off his boat, and disappeared among the reeds. Yen Yüan then brought up the chariot, and Tzŭ Lu offered the hand-cord to Confucius. But the latter paid no attention. He waited until the ripples on the water had smoothed down and the sound of the punt-pole had died away, before he ventured to get up. "Master, I have been in your service now for a long time, yet never did I see you treat any man like this. ... Yet before this old fisherman, leaning on his punt-pole, you cringe and bow and prostrate yourself twice before answering."

title.en: The Courtyard Full of Boots: Lieh Tzŭ's Relapse (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 列子反齊，門庭充盈（莊子）

region.en: The road to Ch'i and back (symbolic pin: Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 適齊之道（象徵定位：山東臨淄）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ turns back halfway to Ch'i in fear, for five out of ten restaurants would take no payment — conquer men's hearts by force of the external and trouble follows. Later his courtyard is filled with visitors' boots; the Master Poh Hun Wu Jen stands facing the north, cheek wrinkled on his staff, then departs without a word, crying: It is all over! Exerting influence unduly over others, you are by them influenced in turn.
summary.zh: 列子行食於十家，五家先逆——驚恐而返。居於鄙，人舍者將見之——見其客而歎曰：戶庭之閒，其人弗睹也！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Lieh Tzŭ went to Ch'i, half way there he turned round and came back. Falling in with Poh Hun Wu Jen, the latter said, "How is it you are so soon back again?" "I was afraid," replied Lieh Tzŭ. "Out of ten restaurants at which I ate," said Lieh Tzŭ, "five would take no payment. ... A restaurant keeper is one who lives by retailing soup. When his returns are counted up, his profit is but small, and his influence is next to nothing. But if such a man could act thus, how much more the ruler of a large State? ... That is what I was afraid of."

Shortly afterwards Poh Hun Wu Jen went to visit Lieh Tzŭ, and lo! his court-yard was filled with boots. Poh Hun Wu Jen stood there awhile, facing the north, his cheek all wrinkled by resting it on his staff. Then, without a word, he departed. Upon this being announced to Lieh Tzŭ, he seized his shoes and ran out barefoot. When he reached the outer gate, he called aloud, "Master! now that you have come, will you not give me medicine?" "It is all over!" cried Poh Hun Wu Jen. "I told you that the world would gather around you. It is not that you can make people gather around you. You cannot prevent them from doing so. Of what use would my instruction be? Exerting influence thus unduly over others, you are by them influenced in turn. You disturb your natural constitution, and are of no further account.

title.en: Huan's Suicide and the Dream of the Autumn Pine (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 鄭人緩也呻吟裘氏之地（莊子）

region.en: Ch'iu-shih, in the Chêng State (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 裘氏之地（今河南鄭州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Huan of Chêng graduates as a Confucianist in three years and sends his younger brother to study as a Mihist; when the father takes the Mihist's side, Huan commits suicide — and appears in a dream: It was I who caused your son to become a Mihist. Why give all the credit to him who is but as the fruit of an autumn pine? Verily God does not reward man for what he does, but for what he is.
summary.zh: 鄭人緩也呻吟裘氏之地，祗三年而緩為儒；其父以為墨者。緩於十年自殺；其父夢之曰：使而子為墨者，予也——秋柏之實者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was a man of the Chêng State, named Huan. He pursued his studies at a place called Ch'iu-shih. After three years only, he had graduated as a Confucianist; and like a river which fertilises its banks to a distance of nine li, so did his good influence reach into three families. He caused his younger brother to graduate as a Mihist. But inasmuch as in the question of Confucianism versus Mihism, the father took the side of the Mihist, at the end of ten years Huan committed suicide.

Then the father dreamed that Huan appeared to him and said, "It was I who caused your son to become a Mihist. Why give all the credit to him who is but as the fruit of an autumn pine?" Verily God does not reward man for what he does, but for what he is. ... Whereas a man who should regard his distinctive abilities as of his own making, without reference to his parents, would be like the man of Ch'i who dug a well and then wanted to keep others away from it.

title.en: Chu P'ing Man Learns to Slay Dragons (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 朱泙漫學屠龍於支離益（莊子）

region.en: The school of Chih Li I (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 支離益之門（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Chu P'ing Man spends a large patrimony learning under Chih Li I how to kill dragons. By the end of three years he is perfect — but there is no direction in which he can show his skill. TAO cannot be put into practice.
summary.zh: 朱泙漫學屠龍於支離益，單千金之家；三年技成，而無所用其巧。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the dragon-slaying vanity is proverbial. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chu P'ing Man spent a large patrimony in learning under Chih Li I how to kill dragons. By the end of three years he was perfect, but there was no direction in which he could show his skill. The true Sage regards certainties as uncertainties; therefore he is never up in arms.

title.en: Ts'ao Shang's Hundred Carriages and the Licker of Piles (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 曹商得車，舐痔之譏（莊子）

region.en: The court of Ch'in (Xianyang, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 秦廷（今陝西咸陽）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)
