source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Ts'ao Shang, the Sung envoy, returns from Ch'in with a hundred carriages and taunts the sandal-making Chuang Tzŭ. The physician who opens a boil gets one carriage; the man who licks his piles gets five — the more degrading the work, the greater the number of carriages. You, Sir, must have been attending to his piles to get so many carriages. Begone with you!
summary.zh: 宋人有曹商者，為宋王使秦；其往也，得車數乘；秦王有疾，舐痔者得車五乘——所治愈下，得車愈多。子豈治其痔邪？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: A man of the Sung State, named Ts'ao Shang, acted as political agent for the prince of Sung at the court of the Ch'in State. When he went thither, he had a few carriages; but the prince of Ch'in was so pleased with him that he added one hundred more. On his return to Sung, he visited Chuang Tzŭ and said, "As for living in poverty in a dirty hovel, earning a scanty subsistence by making sandals, with shrivelled face and yellow ears,--this I could not do. Interviewing a powerful ruler, with a retinue of a hundred carriages,--that is my forte."

"When the prince of Ch'in is sick," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "and he summons his physician to open a boil or cleanse an ulcer, the latter gets one carriage. The man who licks his piles gets five. The more degrading the work, the greater the number of carriages given. You, Sir, must have been attending to his piles to get so many carriages. Begone with you!"

title.en: The Pearl Under the Sleeping Dragon's Nose (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 驪龍頷下之珠（莊子）

region.en: Ho-Shang, the riverside hamlet (symbolic pin: Zhenjiang, Jiangsu, China)
region.zh: 河上之家（象徵定位：江蘇鎮江）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: A man presented with ten chariots by the prince of Sung puts on airs before Chuang Tzŭ, who tells of the poor plaiter of rushes whose son dived into the river and got a pearl worth a thousand ounces — from under the nose of the dragon, which must have been asleep. The prince of Sung is fiercer than a dragon: to get these chariots you must have caught him asleep, and when he wakes you will be ground to powder.
summary.zh: 河上有家貧恃緯蕭而食者；其子沒於淵，得千金之珠——必在九重之淵而驪龍頷下，子能得珠者，必遭其睡也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the black dragon's pearl became a classic image of perilous gain. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: A man who had been to see the prince of Sung and had been presented with ten chariots, was putting on airs in the presence of Chuang Tzŭ. "At Ho-Shang," said the latter, "there was a poor man who supported his family by plaiting rushes. One day his son dived into the river and got a pearl worth a thousand ounces of silver. The father bade him fetch a stone and smash it to pieces, explaining that he could only have got such a pearl very deep down from under the nose of the dragon, which must have been asleep. And he said he was afraid that when the dragon waked, the boy would have a poor chance.

"Now the State of Sung is deeper than a deep river, and the prince of Sung is fiercer than a dragon. To get these chariots, you must have caught him asleep. And when he wakes, you will be ground to powder."

title.en: The Sacrificial Ox Would Gladly Change Places with a Neglected Calf (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子釣於濮水，龜曳尾；犧牛之喻（莊子）

region.en: Some prince's court (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 聘使之廷（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Invited to enter a prince's service, Chuang Tzŭ replies to the envoy: Sir, have you ever noticed a sacrificial ox? It is bedecked with ribbons and fares sumptuously — but when it comes to be slaughtered for the temple, would it not gladly exchange places with some neglected calf?
summary.zh: 或聘於莊子；莊子應其使曰：子見夫犧牛乎？衣以文繡，食以芻菽——及其牽而入於太廟，雖欲為孤犢，其可得乎！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); quoted by Sima Qian in his biographical notice of Zhuangzi. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Some prince having invited Chuang Tzŭ to enter his service, Chuang Tzŭ said in reply to the envoy, "Sir, have you ever noticed a sacrificial ox? It is bedecked with ribbons and fares sumptuously. But when it comes to be slaughtered for the temple, would it not gladly exchange places with some neglected calf?"

title.en: Heaven and Earth for My Coffin: Chuang Tzŭ's Death-Bed (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子將死，以天地為棺槨（莊子）

region.en: The death-bed in Sung (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋之病榻（象徵定位：河南商丘）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: When Chuang Tzŭ was about to die, his disciples wished to give him a splendid funeral. With Heaven and Earth for my coffin and shell; with the sun, moon, and stars as my burial regalia; and with all creation to escort me to the grave, are not my funeral paraphernalia ready to hand? And when they fear the carrion kite: above ground I shall be food for kites; below I shall be food for mole-crickets and ants — why rob one to feed the other?
summary.zh: 莊子將死，弟子欲厚葬之。莊子曰：吾以天地為棺槨，以日月為連璧，星辰為珠璣，萬物為齎送——吾葬具豈不備邪？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the classic statement of the cosmic funeral. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Chuang Tzŭ was about to die, his disciples expressed a wish to give him a splendid funeral. But Chuang Tzŭ said, "With Heaven and Earth for my coffin and shell; with the sun, moon, and stars as my burial regalia; and with all creation to escort me to the grave,--are not my funeral paraphernalia ready to hand?"

"We fear," argued the disciples, "lest the carrion kite should eat the body of our Master"; to which Chuang Tzŭ replied, "Above ground I shall be food for kites; below I shall be food for mole-crickets and ants. Why rob one to feed the other? ... Those who trust to their senses become slaves to objective existences. Those alone who are guided by their intuitions find the true standard."

title.en: The Great Yü Drains the Flood: The Mihist Hero-Model (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 大禹治水：墨者之榜樣（莊子）

region.en: The nine divisions of the drained empire (symbolic pin: Yuzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 九洲通流之地（象徵定位：河南禹州）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 33, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 33

summary.en: Mih Tzŭ's followers take for their model the Great Yü, who drained off the flood of waters, causing rivers and streams to flow through the nine divisions of the empire — three hundred great rivers, three thousand branches, and streams without number. With his own hands he plied the bucket and dredger until his calves and shins had no hair left upon them; the wind bathed him, the rain combed him — and ages of Mihists wear short serge jackets and straw sandals, toil day and night, and make self-mortification their end and aim.
summary.zh: 昔者大禹湮洪水，疏九河，瀹濟漯而注諸海——腓無胈，脛無毛；沐甚雨，櫛疾風，置萬國。後世之墨者，多以裘褐為衣，以跂蹻為服，日夜不休，以自苦為極。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the Mihist retelling of Yü's flood-labour within Zhuangzi's survey chapter, cross-linked to the flood cluster. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Mih Tzŭ argued in favour of his system as follows:--Of old, the great Yü drained off the flood of waters, and caused rivers and streams to flow through the nine divisions of the empire and the parts adjacent thereto,--three hundred great rivers, three thousand branches, and streams without number. With his own hands he plied the bucket and dredger, in order to reduce confusion to uniformity, until his calves and shins had no hair left upon them. The wind bathed him, the rain combed him; but he marked out the nations of the world, and was in very truth a Sage.

And because he thus sacrificed himself to the commonwealth, ages of Mihists to come would also wear short serge jackets and straw sandals, and toil day and night without stopping, making self-mortification their end and aim, and say to themselves, "If we cannot do this, we do not follow the TAO of Yü, and are unworthy to be called Mihists."

title.en: Hui Tzŭ's Ten Paradoxes: Feathers in an Egg, a Nail with a Tail (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 惠施多方，其書五車（莊子）

region.en: The schools of Sung and Liang (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋梁之辯（象徵定位：河南商丘）

period: Zhuangzi ch. 33, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 33

summary.en: Chuang Tzŭ's survey of Hui Tzŭ, whose learning filled five carts: the sun at noon is the sun setting; southwards there is no limit and yet there is a limit; one can reach Yüeh to-day and yet be there before; the middle of the world is north of Yen and south of Yüeh; there are feathers in an egg; a nail has a tail; fire is not hot; wheels do not press down the ground; the shadow of a flying bird does not move — a great philosopher and very subtle dialectician.
summary.zh: 惠施多方，其書五車；歷物之意曰：至大無外，謂之大一；至小無內，謂之小一——卵有毛；雞三足；郢有天下；犬可以為羊；馬有卵；丁子有尾；火不熱；目不見。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: That the sun at noon is the sun setting. That when an animal is born, it dies. That the likeness of things partly unlike is called the lesser likeness of unlikes. That the likeness of things altogether unlike is called the greater likeness of unlikes. That southwards there is no limit, and yet there is a limit. That one can reach Yüeh to-day and yet be there before. That joined rings can be separated. That the middle of the world is north of Yen and south of Yüeh.

He said that there were feathers in an egg. That a fowl had three feet. That Ying was the world. That a dog could be a sheep. That a mare could lay eggs. That a nail has a tail. That fire is not hot. That mountains have mouths. That wheels do not press down the ground. That the eye does not see. That the finger does not touch. That the uttermost extreme is not the end. That a tortoise is longer than a snake. That a carpenter's square is not square. That compasses will not make a circle. That the shadow of a flying bird does not move. That there is a moment when a swiftly-flying arrow is neither moving nor at rest. That a dog is not a hound. That a bay horse and a dun cow are three.

title.en: The Tao That Can Be Trodden: The Nameless Beginning (Tao Te Ching 1)
title.zh: 道可道，非常道（道德經第一章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 1

summary.en: The opening cosmogony of the classic of the Way: the Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao; the Nameless is the origin of Heaven and Earth; the Named is the mother of all things — both secrets, doubly profound, the door from which issued the secret of the way of life.
summary.zh: 道可道，非常道；名可名，非常名。無名，天地之始；有名，萬物之母。玄之又玄，眾妙之門。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The Tao which can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao; the name which can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name. 2. (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of Heaven and Earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.

3. Always without desire we must be found, if its deep mystery we would sound; and if ever we are need desire, its outer fringe is all that we shall see. 4. Under these two aspects, it is really the same; but as development takes place, it receives the different designations. 5. Together we may call them the Mystery. 6. Where the Mystery is the deepest is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.

title.en: The Honoured Ancestor of All Things (Tao Te Ching 4)
title.zh: 吾不知誰之子，象帝之先（道德經第四章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 4

summary.en: The Tao is like the emptiness of a vessel, deep and unfathomable, as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things — I do not know whose son it is: it might appear to have been before God (the Lord of Heaven).
summary.zh: 道沖而用之，或不盈；淵兮似萬物之宗——吾不知誰之子，象帝之先。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel; and in our employment of it we must be on our guard against all fulness. How deep and unfathomable it is, as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things!

2. We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things; we should attemper our brightness, and bring ourselves into agreement with the obscurity of others. How pure and still the Tao is, as if it would ever so continue! 3. I do not know whose son it is. It might appear to have been before God.

title.en: Straw Dogs and the Bellows of Heaven and Earth (Tao Te Ching 5)
title.zh: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗（道德經第五章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 5

summary.en: Heaven and earth do not act from any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with — and the space between heaven and earth is like a bellows: 'tis emptied, yet it loses not its power; 'tis moved again, and sends forth air the more.
summary.zh: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗；聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗。天地之間，其猶橐籥乎——虛而不屈，動而愈出。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the straw dog (ch'u-kou) is the funeral-sacrifice image echoed in Zhuangzi's ch. 14. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with. The sages do not act from (any wish to be) benevolent; they deal with the people as the dogs of grass are dealt with.

2. May not the space between heaven and earth be compared to a bellows? 'Tis emptied, yet it loses not its power; 'Tis moved again, and sends forth air the more. Much speech to swift exhaustion lead we see; Your inner being guard, and keep it free.

title.en: The Valley Spirit Dies Not: The Mystery of the Female (Tao Te Ching 6)
title.zh: 谷神不死，是謂玄牝（道德經第六章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 6

summary.en: The valley spirit dies not, aye the same; the female mystery thus do we name. Its gate, from which at first they issued forth, is called the root from which grew heaven and earth.
summary.zh: 谷神不死，是謂玄牝；玄牝之門，是謂天地根。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the 'mysterious female' (hsüan-p'in) became a core inner-alchemy image. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The valley spirit dies not, aye the same; The female mystery thus do we name. Its gate, from which at first they issued forth, Is called the root from which grew heaven and earth. Long and unbroken does its power remain, Used gently, and without the touch of pain.

title.en: The Thirty Spokes and the Empty Nave (Tao Te Ching 11)
title.zh: 三十輻共一轂（道德經第十一章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 11

summary.en: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; clay is fashioned into vessels; doors and windows are cut out to form an apartment — but it is on the empty space that their use depends. What has positive existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for actual usefulness.
summary.zh: 三十輻共一轂，當其無，有車之用；埏埴以為器，當其無，有器之用——故有之以為利，無之以為用。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends. The door and windows are cut out (from the walls) to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space (within), that its use depends. Therefore, what has a (positive) existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for (actual) usefulness.

title.en: The Equable, the Inaudible, and the Subtle: The Form of the Formless (Tao Te Ching 14)
title.zh: 視之不見名曰夷（道德經第十四章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 14

summary.en: We look at it and do not see it, and name it the Equable; we listen and do not hear it, the Inaudible; we try to grasp it and do not get hold of it, the Subtle. These three blended obtain The One — we meet it and do not see its Front; we follow it and do not see its Back. When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, this is called unwinding the clue of Tao.
summary.zh: 視之不見名曰夷，聽之不聞名曰希，摶之不得名曰微——迎之不見其首，隨之不見其後；執古之道，以御今之有。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. We look at it, and we do not see it, and we name it 'the Equable.' We listen to it, and we do not hear it, and we name it 'the Inaudible.' We try to grasp it, and do not get hold of it, and we name it 'the Subtle.' With these three qualities, it cannot be made the subject of description; and hence we blend them together and obtain The One.

2. Its upper part is not bright, and its lower part is not obscure. Ceaseless in its action, it yet cannot be named, and then it again returns and becomes nothing. This is called the Form of the Formless, and the Semblance of the Invisible; this is called the Fleeting and Indeterminable.

3. We meet it and do not see its Front; we follow it, and do not see its Back. When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, and are able to know it as it was of old in the beginning, this is called (unwinding) the clue of Tao.

title.en: Return to the Root: The Unchanging Rule (Tao Te Ching 16)
title.zh: 致虛極，守靜篤（道德經第十六章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 16

summary.en: All things alike go through their processes of activity, and then we see them return to their original state; when things in the vegetable world have displayed their luxuriant growth, each of them returns to its root — the regular, unchanging rule whose knowledge is intelligence; he who is king-like goes on to be heaven-like, and possessed of the Tao he endures long.
summary.zh: 致虛極，守靜篤；萬物並作，吾以觀其復——夫物芸芸，各復歸其根；歸根曰靜，是謂復命。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree, and that of stillness guarded with unwearying vigour. All things alike go through their processes of activity, and (then) we see them return (to their original state). When things (in the vegetable world) have displayed their luxuriant growth, we see each of them return to its root. This returning to their root is what we call the state of stillness; and that stillness may be called a reporting that they have fulfilled their appointed end.

2. The report of that fulfilment is the regular, unchanging rule. To know that unchanging rule is to be intelligent; not to know it leads to wild movements and evil issues. The knowledge of that unchanging rule produces a (grand) capacity and forbearance, and that capacity and forbearance lead to a community (of feeling with all things). From this community of feeling comes a kingliness of character; and he who is king-like goes on to be heaven-like. In that likeness to heaven he possesses the Tao. Possessed of the Tao, he endures long; and to the end of his bodily life, is exempt from all danger of decay.

title.en: I Alone Am Different: Carried About as on the Sea (Tao Te Ching 20)
title.zh: 絕學無憂，眾人熙熙（道德經第二十章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 20

summary.en: The multitude look satisfied, as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring; I alone seem listless and still, like an infant which has not yet smiled, carried about as on the sea, drifting as if I had nowhere to rest — I alone am different from other men, but I value the nursing-mother, the Tao.
summary.zh: 眾人熙熙，如享太牢，如春登臺；我獨泊兮其未兆，如嬰兒之未孩——乘乘兮若無所歸。我獨異於人，而貴食母。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The multitude of men look satisfied and pleased; as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring. I alone seem listless and still, my desires having as yet given no indication of their presence. I am like an infant which has not yet smiled. I look dejected and forlorn, as if I had no home to go to.

Ordinary men look bright and intelligent, while I alone seem to be benighted. They look full of discrimination, while I alone am dull and confused. I seem to be carried about as on the sea, drifting as if I had nowhere to rest. All men have their spheres of action, while I alone seem dull and incapable, like a rude borderer. (Thus) I alone am different from other men, but I value the nursing-mother (the Tao).

title.en: The Grandest Forms of Active Force Come from the Tao (Tao Te Ching 21)
title.zh: 孔德之容，惟道是從（道德經第二十一章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 21

summary.en: The grandest forms of active force from Tao come, their only source — eluding sight, eluding touch, the forms of things all in it crouch; profound it is, dark and obscure; things' essences all there endure. Now it is so; 'twas so of old. Its name — what passes not away.
summary.zh: 孔德之容，惟道是從；道之為物，惟恍惟惚——窈兮冥兮，其中有精；其精甚真，其中有信。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The grandest forms of active force From Tao come, their only source. Who can of Tao the nature tell? Our sight it flies, our touch as well. Eluding sight, eluding touch, The forms of things all in it crouch; Eluding touch, eluding sight, There are their semblances, all right. Profound it is, dark and obscure; Things' essences all there endure. Those essences the truth enfold Of what, when seen, shall then be told. Now it is so; 'twas so of old. Its name--what passes not away; So, in their beautiful array, Things form and never know decay.

title.en: The Things Which from of Old Have Got the One (Tao Te Ching 39)
title.zh: 昔之得一者：天得一以清（道德經第三十九章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 39

summary.en: The things which from of old have got the One: heaven which by it is bright and pure, earth rendered firm and sure, spirits with powers by it supplied, valleys kept full throughout their void, all creatures which through it do live, princes and kings who from it get the model which to all they give. If heaven were not thus pure, it soon would rend.
summary.zh: 昔之得一者：天得一以清，地得一以寧，神得一以靈，谷得一以盈，萬物得一以生，侯王得一以為天下正——天無以清將恐裂。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are-- Heaven which by it is bright and pure; Earth rendered thereby firm and sure; Spirits with powers by it supplied; Valleys kept full throughout their void All creatures which through it do live Princes and kings who from it get The model which to all they give.

2. If heaven were not thus pure, it soon would rend; If earth were not thus sure, 'twould break and bend; Without these powers, the spirits soon would fail; If not so filled, the drought would parch each vale; Without that life, creatures would pass away; Princes and kings, without that moral sway, However grand and high, would all decay.

title.en: The Movement of the Tao by Contraries Proceeds (Tao Te Ching 40)
title.zh: 反者道之動（道德經第四十章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 40

summary.en: The movement of the Tao by contraries proceeds; and weakness marks the course of Tao's mighty deeds. All things under heaven sprang from It as existing (and named); that existence sprang from It as non-existent (and not named).
summary.zh: 反者道之動，弱者道之用；天下萬物生於有，有生於無。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The movement of the Tao By contraries proceeds; And weakness marks the course Of Tao's mighty deeds. 2. All things under heaven sprang from It as existing (and named); that existence sprang from It as non-existent (and not named).

title.en: The Three Ministers of Life and the Three Ministers of Death (Tao Te Ching 50)
title.zh: 出生入死，十有三（道德經第五十章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 50

summary.en: Men come forth and live; they enter again and die. Of every ten, three are ministers of life and three of death; three in every ten whose aim is to live but whose movements tend to the land of death — while he who is skilful in managing his life travels without having to shun rhinoceros or tiger, for there is in him no place of death.
summary.zh: 出生入死。生之徒十有三，死之徒十有三——陸行不遇兕虎，入軍不被甲兵；兕無所投其角，虎無所措其爪，兵無所容其刃。夫何故？以其無死地。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the 'no place of death' doctrine grounds later invulnerability claims. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: 1. Men come forth and live; they enter (again) and die. 2. Of every ten three are ministers of life (to themselves); and three are ministers of death. 3. There are also three in every ten whose aim is to live, but whose movements tend to the land (or place) of death. And for what reason? Because of their excessive endeavours to perpetuate life.

4. But I have heard that he who is skilful in managing the life entrusted to him for a time travels on the land without having to shun rhinoceros or tiger, and enters a host without having to avoid buff coat or sharp weapon. The rhinoceros finds no place in him into which to thrust its horn, nor the tiger a place in which to fix its claws, nor the weapon a place to admit its point. And for what reason? Because there is in him no place of death.

title.en: The Mother of All Under the Sky (Tao Te Ching 52)
title.zh: 天下有母，可以為天下母（道德經第五十二章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 52

summary.en: The Tao which originated all under the sky is to be considered as the mother of them all; when one knows that he is his mother's child, and proceeds to guard the qualities of the mother that belong to him, to the end of his life he will be free from all peril.
summary.zh: 天下有母，以為天下母；既得其母，以知其子——沒身不殆。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. (The Tao) which originated all under the sky is to be considered as the mother of them all. 2. When the mother is found, we know what her children should be. When one knows that he is his mother's child, and proceeds to guard (the qualities of) the mother that belong to him, to the end of his life he will be free from all peril.

3. Let him keep his mouth closed, and shut up the portals (of his nostrils), and all his life he will be exempt from laborious exertion. Let him keep his mouth open, and (spend his breath) in the promotion of his affairs, and all his life there will be no safety for him. 4. The perception of what is small is (the secret of) clear-sightedness; the guarding of what is soft and tender is (the secret of) strength.

title.en: Nothing Softer Than Water Attacks the Strong (Tao Te Ching 78)
title.zh: 天下莫柔弱於水（道德經第七十八章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 78

summary.en: There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it — he who accepts his state's reproach is hailed therefore its altars' lord; words that are strictly true seem to be paradoxical.
summary.zh: 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者莫之能勝——受國之垢，是為社稷主；受國不祥，是為天下王。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it;--for there is nothing (so effectual) for which it can be changed.

2. Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice. 3. Therefore a sage has said, 'He who accepts his state's reproach, Is hailed therefore its altars' lord; To him who bears men's direful woes They all the name of King accord.' 4. Words that are strictly true seem to be paradoxical.

title.en: The Creative Principle Which Is Itself Uncreated (Liezi)
title.zh: 有生不生，有化不化（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: Lieh Tzŭ's plot of ground in Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國圃田（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ repeats Hu Ch'iu Tzŭ-lin's teaching: there is a Creative Principle which is itself uncreated, a Principle of Change which is itself unchanging; the Uncreated is able to create life, the Unchanging to effect change — self-engendered and self-evolved, it would be a mistake to call it by any one of its names.
summary.zh: 有生不生，有化不化；不生者能生生，不化者能化化——自生自化，自形自色。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Taishang zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There is a Creative Principle which is itself uncreated; there is a Principle of Change which is itself unchanging. The Uncreated is able to create life; the Unchanging is able to effect change. That which is produced cannot but continue producing; that which is evolved cannot but continue evolving. Hence there is constant production and constant evolution. The law of constant production and of constant evolution at no time ceases to operate. So is it with the Yin and the Yang, so is it with the Four Seasons.

That, then, which engenders all things is itself unengendered; that by which all things are evolved is itself untouched by evolution. Self-engendered and self-evolved, it has in itself the elements of substance, appearance, wisdom, strength, dispersion and cessation. Yet it would be a mistake to call it by any one of these names.

title.en: Heaven and Earth Engendered Out of Nothing (Liezi)
title.zh: 天地安從生：渾淪與清濁（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The Great Change before substance (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 太易之初（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: The Liezi's great cosmogonic sequence: the Great Change, the Great Origin, the Great Beginning, the Great Primordial Simplicity — until substance, form, and essential qualities still blended together is called Chaos. Then the purer and lighter elements, tending upwards, made the Heavens; the grosser and heavier, tending downwards, made the Earth; and substance, harmoniously proportioned, became Man.
summary.zh: 太易、太初、太始、太素——形質混而不離，謂之渾淪；清輕者上為天，重濁者下為地，沖和氣者為人。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; a priority Creation & Cosmology narrative — the tai-chi sequence that later Cosmological Daoism systematised. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The inspired men of old regarded the Yin and the Yang as the cause of the sum total of Heaven and Earth. But that which has substance is engendered from that which is devoid of substance; out of what then were Heaven and Earth engendered? They were engendered out of nothing, and came into existence of themselves.

Hence we say, there is a great Principle of Change, a great Origin, a great Beginning, a great Primordial Simplicity. In the great Change substance is not yet manifest. In the great Origin lies the beginning of substance. In the great Beginning, lies the beginning of material form. In the great Simplicity lies the beginning of essential qualities.

When substance, form and essential qualities are still indistinguishably blended together it is called Chaos. Chaos means that all things are chaotically intermixed and not yet separated from one another. The purer and lighter elements, tending upwards, made the Heavens; the grosser and heavier elements, tending downwards, made the Earth. Substance, harmoniously proportioned, became Man; and, Heaven and Earth containing thus a spiritual element, all things were evolved and produced.

title.en: Why the Dead Are Called 'Men Who Have Returned' (Liezi)
title.zh: 鬼者，歸也（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: Lieh Tzŭ's plot of ground in Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國圃田（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: The spiritual element in man is allotted by Heaven, the corporeal frame by Earth; when the spirit parts from the body each returns to its proper place — that is why disembodied spirits are called kuei, which means 'returning,' returning to their true dwelling-place. And the Yellow Emperor said: If my spirit returns through the gates whence it came, where does the Ego continue to exist?
summary.zh: 精神者天之分，骨骸者地之分——精神離形，各歸其真，故謂之鬼；鬼，歸也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the kuei=returning etymology is the aition of the Chinese word for ghost. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The spiritual element in man is allotted to him by Heaven, his corporeal frame by Earth. The part that belongs to Heaven is ethereal and dispersive, the part that belongs to Earth is dense and tending to conglomeration. When the spirit parts from the body, each of these elements returns to its proper place. That is why disembodied spirits are called kuei, which means "returning," that is, returning to their true dwelling-place.

The Yellow Emperor said: "If my spirit returns through the gates whence it came, and my bones go back to the source from which they sprang, where does the Ego continue to exist?" Between his birth and his latter end, man passes through four chief stages of development:--infancy, adolescence, old age and death. In infancy, the vital force is concentrated, the will is simple, and the general harmony of the system is perfect. ... In death, he comes to his rest, and returns to the Absolute.

title.en: The Old Man in Deerskin Who Was Happy Three Ways (Liezi)
title.zh: 泰山之叟，被裘擊壤（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The wilds of Mount T'ai (Shandong, China)
region.zh: 泰山之野（今山東泰安）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Over Mount T'ai Confucius finds an aged man in a deerskin girded with rope, singing as he plays on a lute — happy for three grounds: it has fallen to his lot to be a man, the noblest of God's creations; to be a male; and to have walked the earth for ninety years. Poverty is the normal lot of the scholar, death the appointed end for all human beings.
summary.zh: 孔子遊於泰山，見裘公聲然操琴——天生萬物，唯人為貴；既得為人，是一樂也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Confucius was travelling once over Mount T'ai when he caught sight of an aged man roaming in the wilds. He was clothed in a deerskin, girded with a rope, and was singing as he played on a lute. "My friend," said Confucius, "what is it that makes you so happy?" The old man replied: "I have a great deal to make me happy. God created all things, and of all His creations man is the noblest. It has fallen to my lot to be a man: that is my first ground for happiness. Then, there is a distinction between male and female, the former being rated more highly than the latter. Therefore it is better to be a male; and since I am one, I have a second ground for happiness.

Furthermore, some are born who never behold the sun or the moon, and who never emerge from their swaddling-clothes. But I have already walked the earth for the space of ninety years. That is my third ground for happiness. Poverty is the normal lot of the scholar, death the appointed end for all human beings. Abiding in the normal state, and reaching at last the appointed end, what is there that should make me unhappy?" "What an excellent thing it is," cried Confucius, "to be able to find a source of consolation in oneself!"

title.en: Great Indeed Is Death: Tzŭ Kung Yearns for Rest (Liezi)
title.zh: 大哉死乎：子貢厭學（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The graves in the wilds (symbolic pin: Qufu, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 原野之墳（象徵定位：山東曲阜）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Tzŭ Kung, tired of philosophy, yearns for rest; Confucius points to all the graves, vaults, tombs, and funeral urns. Great indeed is Death! exclaims Tzŭ Kung — it gives rest to the noble-hearted and causes the base to cower. Men feel the joy of life, but do not realise its bitterness; they think of the evils of death, but not of the repose which it confers. And the dead are men who have returned.
summary.zh: 子貢倦於學，告仲尼曰：願有所息——大哉死乎！君子息焉，小人休焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Tzu Kung was tired of philosophy, and confided his feelings to Confucius, saying: "I yearn for rest." Confucius replied: "In life there is no rest." "Is rest, then, nowhere to be found?" "Oh, yes!" replied Confucius; "look at all the graves in the wilds, all the vaults, all the tombs, all the funeral urns, and you may know where rest is to be found." "Great, indeed, is Death!" exclaimed Tzu Kung. "It gives rest to the noble-hearted, and causes the base to cower." "You are right," said Confucius. "Men feel the joy of life, but do not realise its bitterness. They feel the weariness of old age, but not its peacefulness. They think of the evils of death, but not of the repose which it confers."

The ancients spoke of the dead as kuei-jen (men who have returned). But if the dead are men who have returned, the living are men on a journey. Those who are on a journey and think not of returning have cut themselves off from their home. Should any one man cut himself off from his home, he would incur universal reprobation. But all mankind being homeless, there is none to see the error.

title.en: The Man Who Feared the Sky Would Fall (Liezi)
title.zh: 杞人憂天（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The State of Ch'i (Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 杞國（今河南杞縣）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: A man of Ch'i is so afraid the universe will collapse and fall to pieces that he can neither sleep nor eat. Heaven is only an accumulation of ether, says his enlightener; the sun, moon and stars are bright lights within that mass; the earth is an agglomeration of matter filling the four corners of space — why be afraid? And Ch'ang Lu Tzŭ laughs at both: Heaven and earth must of necessity pass away, but neither will revert to destruction apart from the other.
summary.zh: 杞國有人憂天地崩墜，身亡所寄，廢寢食者——天，積氣耳；亡處亡氣。地，積塊耳；充塞四虛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the 'worry of Ch'i' (Ch'i-jen yu-t'ien) became a proverb for needless alarm. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: There was once a man in the Ch'i State who was so afraid the universe would collapse and fall to pieces, leaving his body without a lodgment, that he could neither sleep nor eat. Another man, pitying his distress, went to enlighten him. "Heaven," he said, "is nothing more than an accumulation of ether, and there is no place where ether is not. Processes of contraction and expansion, inspiration and expiration are continually taking place up in the heavens. Why then should you be afraid of a collapse?" "It is true that Heaven is an accumulation of ether; but the sun, the moon, and the stars -- will they not fall down upon us?" "Sun, moon and stars are likewise only bright lights within this mass of ether. Even supposing they were to fall, they could not possibly harm us by their impact."

"But what if the earth should fall to pieces?" "The earth," replied the other, "is merely an agglomeration of matter, which fills and blocks up the four corners of space. There is no part of it where matter is not. All day long there is constant treading and tramping on the surface of the earth. Why then should you be afraid of its falling to pieces?" Thereupon the man was relieved of his fears and rejoiced exceedingly. But Ch'ang Lu Tzu laughed at them both, saying: "Knowing these facts, who can say that they will never be destroyed? Heaven and earth must of necessity pass away, but neither will revert to destruction apart from the other. Who, having to face the day of disruption, would not be alarmed?"

The Master Lieh Tzu heard of the discussion, and smiling said: "He who maintains that Heaven and earth are destructible, and he who upholds the contrary, are both equally at fault. Whether they are destructible or not is something we can never know. The living and the dead, the going and the coming, know nothing of each other's state. Whether destruction awaits the world or no, why should I trouble my head about it?"

title.en: Mr. Kuo the Good Thief of Heaven and Earth (Liezi)
title.zh: 齊國國氏善為盜（列子天瑞篇）

region.en: The road from Sung to Ch'i (Shangqiu to Linzi, China)
region.zh: 宋適齊之道（商丘至臨淄）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book I (Cosmogony)

summary.en: Mr. Hsiang the poor man asks Mr. Kuo the rich for the secret of his prosperity: it is because I am a good thief — stealing the riches of Heaven and earth each in their season, the fertilising rain-water from the clouds, the natural products of mountain and meadow. The literal thief climbs walls and is stripped of all he has; Tung Kuo the learned explains that we are all thieves of the harmony of the Yin and Yang in order to keep alive.
summary.zh: 國氏曰：吾善為盜——盜天之時，盜陰陽之和，若耳目鼻口；向氏踰垣鑿室而盜，被殘而歸。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The latter travelled from Sung to Ch'i and asked the other for the secret of his prosperity. Mr. Kuo told him. "It is because I am a good thief," he said. "The first year I began to be a thief, I had just enough. The second year, I had ample. The third year, I reaped a great harvest. And, in course of time, I found myself the owner of whole villages and districts." Mr. Hsiang was overjoyed; he understood the word "thief" in its literal sense, but he did not understand the true way of becoming a thief. Accordingly, he climbed over walls and broke into houses, grabbing everything he could see or lay hands upon. But before very long his thefts brought him into trouble, and he was stripped even of what he had previously possessed.

Now let me put you on the right track. We all know that Heaven has its seasons, and that earth has its riches. Well, the things that I steal are the riches of Heaven and earth, each in their season -- the fertilising rain-water from the clouds, and the natural products of mountain and meadow-land. Thus I grow my grain and ripen my crops, build my walls and construct my tenements. From the dry land I steal winged and four-footed game, from the rivers I steal fish and turtles. There is nothing that I do not steal. For corn and grain, clay and wood, birds and beasts, fishes and turtles are all products of Nature. How can I claim them as mine?

title.en: Turtle's Escape from the Pot
title.zh: 龜脫鍋之計

region.en: Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加西摩蘭博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 41 'Turtle's Escape' (told by Henry Spence, Bog, Westmoreland)

summary.en: Caught for dinner, Turtle warns his cook that his fat will mash if the pot boils — so Anansi must lift him out at every bubble. A blow of the turtle's nose raises the water, Anansi sets him by the pan-side to cool, and the dinner slides back into the pond.
summary.zh: 龜被捕入鍋，先行告誡：水一沸，肥肉必爛，須隨時提起。龜以鼻息鼓水，蜘蛛人驚慌之下把他移到鍋邊『降溫』——晚餐便滑回了池塘。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Turtle fooled Anansi one day. Anansi went out and caught one turtle, quite glad of the turtle. When he got home, Turtle knew Anansi was going to eat him and said, 'Brar Anansi, you know me fat? When you put me on, as the water boils up you take me off, 'cause fat will mash.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 41 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: So when the water got warm, Turtle blew his nose to make the water boil up. Anansi got frightened, said the turtle would mash! So he laid him down at the pan-side to let the fat cool so he would not mash — and Turtle ran away into the pond. Anansi lost his dinner.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 41, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Fire Burns Out the Spider's House
title.zh: 火焚蛛宅

region.en: Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加西摩蘭博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 42 'Fire and Anansi' (told by Henry Spence, Bog, Westmoreland)

summary.en: Fire, unable to walk, requires a road of dry bush laid to his host's door. Anansi's wife, the Ground Dove, warns against the visit — he will burn the house and everyone in it — but the spider lays the trash anyway, and Fire, arriving in a great jump, burns Anansi, his house and everything except his wife.
summary.zh: 火不能行走，須沿乾柴鋪路來訪。蜘蛛人之妻地面鴿力勸莫邀——他必焚屋焚人——蜘蛛人不聽，照舊鋪柴；火到門前猛然一躍，焚蜘蛛人、焚其屋、焚盡一切，唯獨留下他的妻子。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; fire-as-personage tale linking to fire clusters. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Fire were good friends. Anansi came and saw Fire and they had dinner; then he invited Fire to come and see him. Fire told him he could not walk — from his house, Fire said, his host must lay a path of dry bush, and he would walk on top of the dry bush.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 42 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Anansi was married to Ground Dove, who told him no: he must not invite Fire, who would burn his house and burn him out. Anansi would not hear what his wife said and laid the trash on. Fire burned from his house, and when he came near Anansi's house he made a big jump, burned Anansi, burned his house, burned everything but his wife. Fire fooled Anansi!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 42, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Suit of Maggot-flies
title.zh: 蛆蠅裁成的衣裳

region.en: Lacovia, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加拉科維亞

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 43a 'Tailors and Fiddlers' (told by David Roach, Lacovia)

summary.en: At the ball the tailor Quit-quit's fiddle outdraws the spider's until Anansi's 'Me nyam-nyam taya' wins the girls. Quit-quit retorts that 'taya' is nothing; Anansi demands a suit of clothes that cannot be matched, and the tailor cuts it from maggot-flies — which, smelling the dinner meat at the ball's end, run off and leave the fiddler naked.
summary.zh: 舞會上裁縫的琴聲起初蓋過蜘蛛人，直到蜘蛛人奏出『我吃了肉泥』贏得姑娘們。布特布特反唇相譏；蜘蛛人便索要一套『無人能及』的衣裳，裁縫便以蛆蠅裁成——宴罷肉香一起，蛆蠅四散，琴師當眾裸身。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; fiddle-contest type. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Lizard went to a ball. Anansi was a fiddler, Lizard a tailor; Quit-quit was the fiddler's rival. Anansi played 'turn, turn, turn' and all the girls went round Brar Quit-quit; then Anansi played 'Me nyam-nyam taya!' — and it pleased the people, all the girls crowding round Brar Anansi. Brar Quit-quit said, 'Taya no somet'ing!' Anansi came in with his music — 'Me nyam de somet'ing! If taya no somet'ing, whe' are de somet'ing?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 43a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brar Anansi then said the tailor must make him a suit of clothes that could not be matched; Brar Quit-quit told him it must be made out of maggot-fly. After the ball they went to dinner — and when the maggot-flies smelled the meat, they ran off and left him naked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 43a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Spider Marries Monkey's Daughter
title.zh: 蜘蛛人娶猴家女

region.en: Newmarket, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加紐馬克特

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 44 'Spider Marries Monkey's Daughter' (told by May Ford, Newmarket)

summary.en: Monkey scorns Spider as too fast a suitor; Green-lizard's counter-plan is a guessing riddle — 'Miss Nennan-kennan-wid-a-turn-down-gown' — which only the spider, tipped off by the same lizard, can answer. Married with a baby in his arms, Anansi sings his own secret — 'A me cunnie mak me get yo' mama' — while the wife is at the pond; Monkey, arriving to hear it, grabs away the baby and kills Spider, and the baby drops dead from his hand. So never kill a spider: whatever you have in hand will surely break.
summary.zh: 猴嫌蜘蛛人太輕浮，綠蜥蜴獻策：以謎語婚試——『穿下垂裙的南南肯南小姐』——唯蜘蛛人得蜥蜴泄題而答中。婚後抱嬰獨守，蜘蛛人自鳴得意唱出機密：『全憑我機智娶到你媽』；猴子聞歌而至，奪嬰殺蛛，嬰兒亦墜地而死。故曰：莫殺蜘蛛——手中之物必隨之而碎。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale; hidden-name riddle marriage links to Yoruba hidden-name traditions (cross-ref motif family).

passages.text: Bredder Monkey had a daughter whom Bredder Spider wanted to marry. Monkey did not want Spider to marry his daughter, thinking him too fast and beneath him — he only kept Spider company because he found him useful. He jumped to Bredder Green-lizard: 'Fancy! Bredder Spider want to marry me daughter! I don't want to hurt his feelings, as he is useful to us, so help me to get out of it.' Green-lizard answered, 'I tell you a way, man. Call her Miss Nennan-kennan-wid-a-turn-down-gown, and whoever guesses her name marries her — for Bredder Spider never can guess that!' Then the lizard went direct and told Bredder Spider the name to say.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 44 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Monkey sent out word to all the gentlemen who wanted to marry his daughter to come and guess her name. Not one could tell it until Bredder Spider came and said, 'Miss Nennen-kennan-wid-a-turn-down-gown.' So Bredder Spider got the daughter and married her. When his wife had a baby, she left the pickney with Spider and went to the pond; and Spider, thinking her gone, started to sing, 'Hush, me pickney, hush me baby — a me cunnie mak me get yo' mama!' His wife turned back — 'What is that you sing?' — and he answered only, 'Hush, me pickney! Hush, me baby! It's a good t'ing marry yo' mama?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 44, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bredder Monkey had been coming to see him and heard what Bredder Spider was singing. 'So that is how you got my daughter!' — and he grabbed away the baby and killed Spider. And as he killed Spider, the pickney dropped out of his hand dead. So never kill a spider, as whatever you have in hand will be sure to break.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 44, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Chain of Victims
title.zh: 受害者之鏈

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 45 'The Chain of Victims' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Anansi borrows a dollar from Hog, Dog, Monkey, Tiger and Lion — each 'repayable tomorrow at twelve'. Next day the creditors arrive one by one, and the spider sends each successive guest into the back room with a warning to kill the one before: Hog kills nothing, Dog is sent after Hog, Monkey after Dog, Tiger after Monkey, and Lion finally kills Tiger. Anansi then calls Lion out to a deep hole by the kitchen 'to put on hot water', and the lion breaks his neck in it — leaving the spider alone with five creditors' bones to crack at night.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人向豬、狗、猴、虎、獅各借一元，約定『明日十二時來取』。翌日債主逐一登門，蜘蛛人卻把每位客人送進後屋，並囑其殺掉前一位；獅子終於殺了老虎。隨後蜘蛛人喚獅子到廚房邊深坑旁『燒熱水』——獅子墜坑折頸。蜘蛛人獨得五份『骨頭』，夜裡慢慢敲。

sensitivity.note: Anansi amusement tale (debt-chain / ogre-kill type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi saw Brar Hog and said, 'Brar Hog, lend me a dollar — tomorrow, twelve o'clock, come for it.' He saw Brar Dog and said the same; Brar Monkey, the same; Brar Tiger, the same; and Brar Lion, the same. Next day he heard a knock at the door — 'Me, Brar Hog' — and Hog came in and stayed talking until another knock.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 45 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Me, Brar Dog.' Anansi told Brar Hog to run into that room, for Dog was too bad — if he caught him he would kill him. When Dog came in they talked until Monkey knocked, and Anansi sent Dog into the room, telling him that when he went in he would see Brar Hog under the bed — kill him. Monkey and Anansi talked until Tiger knocked: 'Brar Monkey, run into that room and hide, or Tiger catch you!' When Brar Tiger came in they talked until Lion knocked, and Anansi sent Tiger in with the same instruction about Monkey.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 45, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: As Lion came in, Anansi told him: 'Look here! Plenty of meat. Brar Tiger gone in there; you are going to kill him!' Lion went in and killed Tiger. Meanwhile Anansi went out the kitchen door, dug a deep hole, and called, 'Brar Lion, run come here! We go put on little hot water to clean up those fellahs!' As Lion jumped out of the house, feeling so glad, and galloped to the kitchen, he got down into the hole and broke his neck. Anansi said, 'You brute! Look how much money I borrowed from you, and I have all your bones to crack tonight!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 45, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Tumble-bug Rolls in the Dung
title.zh: 推糞蟲何以滾糞

region.en: Dry River, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地乾河

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 46 'Why Tumble-bug Rolls in the Dung' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: The king offers his daughter to whoever brings a jar of money. Tumble-bug fills his jar with coin; Anansi fills his with cow- and horse-dung. At a wayside shop the two jars are swapped during a bread errand, and before the king Anansi's jar showers true silver while Tumble-bug's flings dung — 'Take it up, take it up, you nasty fellow, carry it out of the missis yard!' — which is why Tumble-bug rolls in filth to this day.
summary.zh: 國王懸賞：獻上一罐錢者可娶公主。推糞蟲罐中是錢，蜘蛛人罐中填牛馬之糞。途中兩罐在商店被調換；國王面前，蜘蛛人的罐子金幣嘩嘩傾瀉，推糞蟲的罐子滾出糞便——『撿起來！撿起來！你這骯髒的傢伙，把髒物帶出小姐的院子！』推糞蟲至今在穢物中打滾，便是由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a young lady, the king's daughter; her father said whoever came with a jar of money would get her to marry. Tumble-bug got a jar of money. Anansi got a jar and could get no money to put in it, so he got some cow dung and some horse dung and filled up the jar. As the two were going up to the young lady, they stopped at a shop, and the two jars favored one another. Anansi said, 'Brar Tumble-bug, let we go in the shop and get a drink' — and, sending him out for bread, took up Tumble-bug's jar and left his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 46 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Up in the king's yard Anansi said, 'Massa, must bring a clean sheet to throw the money out of the jar!' and he threw out money — wa-a-a-a-a! As Tumble-bug threw, he threw out horse-dung and cow-dung. Anansi said, 'Take it up, take it up, you nasty fellow, carry out the missis yard!' That is why you see Tumble-bug roll in filth until today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 46, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why John-crow Has a Bald Head
title.zh: 兀鷲何以禿頂

region.en: St. Ann's Bay and Bog, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖安灣與博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 47 'Why John-crow Has a Bald Head' (a, Margaret Brown, St. Anne's Bay)

summary.en: Anansi, nursing his grudge against John-crow for stealing his nests, invites the crow alone to a wedding feast — then stages a 'baptism' that uses nothing but boiling water: every guest dips his head into the copper. The scalded crow, in the paired dance version, receives a ladle of hot pop flung on his head for dancing too neatly — and no John-crow in this world has had a feather on his head since.
summary.zh: 兀鷲屢偷蛛巢，蜘蛛人懷恨在心。他獨邀兀鷲赴婚宴，宴後舉行『洗禮』——洗禮用的除了滾水別無他物：每位客人把頭浸入大銅鍋。另一版本：兀鷲舞步太過出色，蜘蛛人以滾粥一瓢潑頂，把那顆頭上的羽毛燒個精光——從此世間兀鷲再無一羽覆頂。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. The 'baptism' frame is folk-comic use of a church term. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi always had a grudge against John-crow: whenever he made his nest, the Crow flew on it and caught it up, and he could never keep a nest. So he said he was going to marry, and he was going to invite no one but Crow; and he had a big dinner, and no one was at the table but Crow. After the eating and drinking were done, he said he was going to have a baptism — but he did not baptize with anything but boiling water. After the water boiled, he took it off, ordered Crow to sit round the copper, and dipped every one's head into the water — and that is why Crow has a bald head today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 47a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired telling, Anansi and John-crow had a ball one night, and dinner was found for all the dancers. John-crow was a great stepper and could step better than Anansi; finding John-crow danced neater than he, Anansi got vexed. After the dinner, when the pop was hot, he told John-crow he must dance up to the pop — and just to be rid of John-crow that night, he took a ladle and dashed the hot pop right up on his head, and all John-crow's head stripped off. All the John-crows in this world never have had a feather on their heads since: Anansi burned them off with hot pop.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 47b 'The Dance' (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Dog Is Always Looking
title.zh: 狗為何總盯著人吃飯

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 48 'Why Dog Is Always Looking' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: Scouting land to rent, Anansi and Dog both fall for the same field. The spider boasts that his father once planted yams on that very spot — yams that bore 'big like me leg!' — and Dog, whose legs are worth more than thread, walks off to look round instead: which is why, when you are eating, a dog is sure to be looking at you.
summary.zh: 尋地租耕，蜘蛛人與狗同時相中一塊好地。蜘蛛人誇稱父親曾在彼處種薯，結的薯『大得像我這條腿』——而蜘蛛人的腿細如線。狗兒寧可去處處張望也不願與他合夥——所以如今你吃飯時，狗總在一旁盯著看。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi and Dog were friends. They wanted to go into cultivation, so both of them went out in search of good land to rent and came across a nice bit of land; Anansi fell in love with the spot, and Dog fell in love with the spot too. Anansi said to Dog he remembered when he was a little boy his father planted yams on that very spot — 'and the yams did bear.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 48 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Dog asked how big they bore. Anansi said, 'Brar Dog, they bear big — big like me leg!' (Anansi's leg is just like a thread.) Brar Dog said, 'Before I work and plant yam, and the yam not bigger than your leg, I sooner walk round and look!' That is the reason why, when you are eating, a dog is sure to be looking at you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 48, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Rocks at the River Are Covered with Moss
title.zh: 河石何以生苔

region.en: Bog, Westmoreland, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加西摩蘭博格

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 49 'Why Rocks at the River Are Covered with Moss' (told by Sarah Vassel, Bog, Westmoreland)

summary.en: Eating at the river-side, Anansi refuses a begging rock-stone a share of his meal — and when he tries to rise the stone holds him fast until a hidden passerby hauls him up, leaving half his skin on the stone: moss grows on the rocks at the river-side, and Anansi's skin grows there.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛人在河邊進食，乞食的岩石討不到一口，便在他起身時死死攥住他；藏在林中窺伺的路人最後將他拔起——蜘蛛人半張皮留在了石上：河邊的石頭上長苔，那是蜘蛛人的皮。

sensitivity.note: Etiological landscape tale (origin of river-stone moss). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Anansi was going out one day and stopped at the river-side eating. A rock-stone begged him, and he would not give it any. After he had eaten his fill and wanted to get up, the rock-stone held him and he could not get up — and began to bawl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 49 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: A man was coming past at the same time and asked, 'Bredder Anansi, who has been crying here?' Anansi said he did not know; the man went inside the bush and hid. Anansi hollered, and the man came out and caught him by his two hands and drew him right up — half of his skin left on the stone. Moss grows upon the rock-stones at the river-side: Anansi's skin grows there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 49, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Ground-dove Complains
title.zh: 地面鴿何以哀鳴

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924 print), tale 50 'Why Ground-dove Complains' (told by Simeon Falconer, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Tiger hires Dove to help watch his corn by night; Dove keeps the watch while Tiger sleeps — and by day destroys the corn himself. When Tiger, tipped to the scheme, dodges in the ground and catches the raiding gang, he slaps the traitor on the ears; the dove has been singing 'Me ears! me ears!' ever since.
summary.zh: 虎雇鴿子夜間守玉米；虎睡覺，鴿守夜——白天卻親自毀田。虎識破奸計，白日伏於地中擒獲劫掠的鴿群，摑其耳光；地面鴿自此哀唱『我的耳朵！我的耳朵！』至今。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Tiger was planting corn, and birds and everything were destroying the corn, so he got Dove to help him watch who was destroying it. After they sat up the whole night watching the corn, the next day Tiger went to sleep. Bredder Dove went back in the day and destroyed the corn himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 50 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: So the next day Tiger went in the day and dodged in the ground. Bredder Dove had a gang, and Tiger was slapping him on the ears as the gang was caught — and he sang out, 'Me ears! me ears! me ears!' And from that day to this the dove sings, 'Me ears!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 50, ending (2024); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Hog Is Always Grunting
title.zh: 豬為何總在哼哼

region.en: Harmony Hall, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加和諧堂

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 51 'Why Hog Is Always Grunting' (told by Norman Hilton, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: Bathing with Dog by the river-side, Hog takes off his mouth for the diving contest — and Dog, surfacing first, swims away with it. The mouthless hog surfaces grunting for his missing face, and has grunted ever since.
summary.zh: 豬與狗在河邊同浴，豬為比賽潛水卸下嘴巴；狗先冒頭，叼起豬嘴泅走。失去嘴的豬浮出水面，尋不著自己的嘴，只能哼哼作聲——豬的哼哼自那日起再未停過。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale (detachable-mouth motif). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Brar Hog and Brar Dog lived close by the river-side, and Brar Dog said to Brar Hog, 'Come! we get a bathe!' Brar Hog agreed, took off his mouth, and Brar Dog and Brar Hog jumped into the water. Brar Dog said, 'Come! let us see who can dive longer than the other.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 51 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two of them dived underneath the water. Brar Dog came up, jumped out of the water, took Brar Hog's mouth and went away with it. When Brar Hog came out of the water searching for his mouth and could not find it, he said, 'Humph! Brar Dog take a me mouth!' That is why Brar Hog is always grunting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 51, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Toad Croaks in the Wild Pine
title.zh: 蟾蜍何以在野松中呱呱

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 52 'Why Toad Croaks' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: The axe-magic bride contest — cut the cotton tree that fastens back its own chips — is won by Toad, who flings a pocketful of ashes at every flying chip until the tree falls. At the celebration 'washing', a great pot of boiling water is overturned over the stripped bridegroom-to-be, who jumps into the wild pine; every night to this day you hear him cry out, 'Kwoka soaka!'
summary.zh: 砍不斷自己復合的棉木樹——婚試之謎被蟾蜍破解：每有木屑飛回，他便撒一把懷中灰燼，砍倒大樹。慶功『淨身』時，一大鍋滾水被傾覆在剝光的準新郎身上；蟾蜍跳入野松，至今夜夜聽他哀叫『誇卡索卡！』

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale; axe-magic contest links to worldwide 'impossible task' cycle. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: One man had a daughter. He said, 'There is a cotton tree; the man who cuts down that cotton tree marries my daughter.' Every man went to cut it, and soon the cut chips fastened back, so they could not get the girl to marry. Toad said he would fell it. Toad filled his pocket with ashes, and every chop he chopped he flung the ashes upon the tree when the chips flew — and they could not fasten. So Toad did and did until he felled the cotton tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 52 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The master had a long barbecue and told him, 'Now you must go down there and strip yourself, and I will pour on the water to let you skin.' All this time a big pot of hot water was boiling on the fire; so they turned over the pot of hot water and said, 'Brar Toad, water come! Take your rubbing cloth.' And Toad jumped into the wild pine; up to this day, every night you hear him cry out, 'Kwoka soaka!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 52, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Woodpecker Bores Wood
title.zh: 啄木鳥為何啄木

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 53 'Why Woodpecker Bores Wood' (told by Samuel Wright, Maroon Town)

summary.en: A dying mother's wish to be buried in stone proves impossible: Woodpecker bores and bores and returns confessing failure, and lays her in wood instead — which is why the woodpecker bores the wood.
summary.zh: 垂死的母親願葬於石中；啄木鳥啄石不成，回來認罪，改葬母親於木中——啄木鳥啄木之習，便由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale with filial-piety frame. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a bird called Woodpecker who promised his mother to bury her in a stone, and went all about telling all his friends that he was going to bury his mother in a stone. The mother was poorly unto death, and he went to bore a stone — then turned back and said, 'Mother, I try the stone but I can't bore it. I'll bury you in a wood.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 53 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: And he bored the wood with his bill, working it wider and deeper day by day, until it was fit to receive her. After the death of his mother, he buried her in a wood, in the hole he had bored. That is the reason the woodpecker bores the wood, and bores it to this day, making the little round doors and windows of the dry trees for the dead of his kind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 53, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Crab Is Afraid after Dark
title.zh: 螃蟹何以夜間驚惶

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 54 'Why Crab Is Afraid after Dark' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Promised a head by God tomorrow, Crab sings and dances his gratitude all night until he muddies the water; God refuses him the head — 'if you get a head you will do worse' — and decrees he shall carry his head on his shoulders all the days of his life, trusting no shadow after dark lest he be picked up and thrown into someone's basket.
summary.zh: 螃蟹得神應許明日賜頭，歡歌狂舞至攪渾河水；神怒而拒賜——『得了頭你會更壞』——並判他終生以肩負首，入夜後不敢信任何影子，唯恐被人拾起扔進籃中。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Crab went to God to give him a head. God told him he must go back: 'Tomorrow come, I will give you a head.' After Crab was going home he rejoiced in himself, singing, 'Tank God, tomorrow God a'mighty gi' me head! Tank God, tomorrow God a'mighty gi' me head!' He danced until he muddied the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 54 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day he went to God a'mighty to get his head. God told him, 'Stop! Before you have gotten a head, you go and muddy the water; then if you get a head you will do worse. So you must carry your head upon your shoulder all the days of your life.' So when Crab was returning home, when he got to Orange Bay and stood there, he would not trust a shadow after dark, for he does not know when they will pick him up and throw him into a basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 54, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Why Mice Are No Bigger
title.zh: 老鼠何以不再長大

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 55 'Why Mice Are No Bigger' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Robin Mice-rat wants to 'turn big man'. The Saviour sets him the test of killing his oldest uncle; the first night he only strikes him, and the blabbing uncle — boasting of the temple-blow that would have finished him — shows the very spot to the disguised nephew, who returns and kills him there. The Saviour refuses promotion: 'You little bit of man, go kill your oldest uncle, then if I let you turn bigger you will do worse!' — and mice stay small.
summary.zh: 老鼠羅賓想『變成大人』。救主設考：去殺大伯。第一夜他只是打了一下；大伯事後炫耀『幸而只中此處』，指點太陽穴位置——化裝歸來的姪兒依言補上一擊，將他打死。救主拒其升格：『你這點小人，殺了大伯還想變大？只會更壞！』——老鼠便再未長大。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale with violent folkloric content, recorded as folk narrative. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There is a man named Robin Mice-rat going to his uncle's house. He and the uncle stayed in the dark the whole time; when he was going away, he said good-by, took a stick and struck his uncle. At this time he went to our Saviour and said he wanted to turn big man; the Saviour told him that if he wanted to turn big man he must go and kill his oldest uncle. So, as the uncle never died, he went back the next night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 55 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Talking with his uncle, he heard the account: 'That fellow Robin came here last night; when he was going away, he took a stick and struck me on the head. But if he had caught me here (pointing to the temple), the fellow would have got me.' So as the uncle showed him the place, when he got up he met his uncle at the said place and killed him stiff dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 55, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day he went to his Saviour to be turned into a big man. The Saviour said to him, 'You little bit of man, go kill your oldest uncle — then if I let you turn bigger, you will do worse!' So from that day, that is the reason you see mice don't grow bigger, to this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 55, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Rat's Wedding and the Burnt Rice
title.zh: 老鼠婚宴與焦飯

region.en: Harmony Hall, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地和諧堂

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 56 'Rat's Wedding' (told by Thomas Williams, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: At his own wedding feast Rat remembers the burnt rice he loves to scrape. Halfway home with his bride he invents a forgotten treasure, leaves her on the water-table, and sneaks to the kitchen — where the burnt-rice pot, disturbed, turns over and traps his head. Craping away in the dark, he is found, lifted, and killed by the cook's helpers: which is why there are so many widows in the world — their husbands died and left them.
summary.zh: 老鼠在自己的婚宴上惦記著愛刮的焦飯。半路撇下新娘，謊稱遺忘貴重之物，溜回廚房——焦飯鍋被碰翻，罩住了他的頭。黑暗中刮飯作響的鼠被廚娘逮個正著，一鍋抬起，當場斃命——世上寡婦之多，正因丈夫死了撇下她們。

sensitivity.note: Folk animal tale with comic ending. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Rat got married, and rice and peas were provided for the dinner. It was so richly cooked and so much that it got burnt. Rat remembered that the rice burnt in the pot, and Rat liked scrapping; while he was going home with his wife in the way, when he got part way he said to her, 'I forget something very valuable in the wedding house — have to go back for it!' She agreed, and he set the buggy out on the water-table and ran back to the wedding house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 56 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He never went in where everybody was merrying himself; he went to the kitchen. The pot with the burnt rice was leaning up by the side of the wall. He went to the pot, troubled it, and the pot, instead of rolling away, turned over and covered him underneath. When he found he could not come out he said, 'Chut! What about that? I wouldn't give a biscuit for a man who can't lose his night rest!' — and he began to scrape the burnt part, kur-ur-rup, krup, krup, krup.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 56, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: His wife was calling now, 'Mr. Rat! Mr. Rat!' — 'Me head fasten in pot-o!' — and he turned back scraping, scraping. The cook heard the noise, went out to the kitchen, found it was Rat underneath the pot, called out for help; they came out, lifted up the pot and killed him. That is why there are so many widows in the world — because their husbands died and left them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 56, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cock's Breakfast
title.zh: 公雞的早餐

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 57a 'Cock's Breakfast' (told by Richard Morgan, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Cockroach twice eats Cock's breakfast under the promise of a return meal with an Anansi-style noise-signal that never comes. Creeping back at last with his fiddle — 'Ring a ting ting, me know nigger fe nigger!' — he is heard inside a gourd, cornered, picked up and swallowed; and from that day not a cockroach walks into a fowl yard any more.
summary.zh: 蟑螂兩次吃掉公雞的早餐，又以『無聲即開飯』的暗號耍賴不還席。最後他拉琴潛返——『叮叮響，我知黑吃黑！』——卻在葫蘆中被聽破，被公雞堵住、拾起、吞下；自那天起，蟑螂再也不敢踏進雞院半步。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale (cockroach/fowl-yard proverb). Beckwith's source text contains period racial idiom in song; paraphrase avoids it.
