passages.text: One day Cockroach said to Cock, 'Brar Cock, get a little breakfast, so I will come and have breakfast with you.' Cock said yes. Cockroach came, Cockroach ate; when he had done, he said, 'Brar Cock, when you know my breakfast is ready, come.' — 'How must I know?' — 'I will give you a sign: when you hear me make noise, don't come; but when you hear me stay still in the yard, you must come.' When Cock went, he did not find Cockroach, and returned back to his yard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The second day Cockroach came and said, 'O Brar Cock! from the time I left you, pain all over my skin, so I went and lay down; but today you can come.' Cock did the same, went to the yard, did not find him, and returned back. When he got halfway, he heard in Cockroach's house — 'Ring a ting ting!' Cock took time, tiptoed along, and heard Cockroach inside a gourd. Cock took his bill and licked him at the gourd; Cockroach ran out, Cock picked him up and swallowed him. So from that day, not a cockroach walks into a fowl yard any more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Drum of Borrowed Skins
title.zh: 借皮製鼓

region.en: Harmony Hall, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加和諧堂

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 57c 'The Drum' (told by Mrs. Matilda Hall, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: Dog, Monkey, Tiger, Puss and Cockroach, hearing music everywhere at Christmas and having none, agree to cut little bits of their own skin to make a drum. Roach claims to have no skin, is driven from the company into a banana tree — and vows to be the first to play the finished drum. On Christmas eve the friends, three-quarters of a mile off at market, hear it sounding under Roach's feet; Puss finds him and kills him, and Puss has eaten Roach until this day.
summary.zh: 聖誕將至，狗、猴、虎、貓與蟑螂聽遍四方音樂而自己一無所有，遂約定各割少許皮來蒙鼓。蟑螂自稱『無皮』，被逐出夥伴、躲進芭蕉樹——卻揚言要第一個敲響此鼓。聖誕前夕，眾友在市集上三哩外便聽見鼓聲——是蟑螂以足擊鼓；貓尋聲而至殺之，貓吃蟑螂之習至今未改。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale (why cat eats cockroach). Skin-cutting frame is folkloric; no ritual instruction. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Once there were Dog, Monkey, Tiger, Puss and Cockroach. Christmas was coming and they heard music played all about, and they had none. They said, 'We have to make up to make a drum — how will we manage?' And they said, 'The only way is to cut a little of our skin to make a drum.' The Roach said, 'I have none' — so they drove him out of the company and he got into a banana tree to live; then he turned round to them and said, 'I first will play that drum!' — 'How will you get it to play?' they asked him, and he said, 'I first will play it!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57c (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: They fitted up the drum with the skins and hung it up to get cured. Christmas eve fell; going to the market to buy up all the things, about three quarters of a mile off they heard the drum playing — 'Biddy bwoy! who is playing our drum?' It was Roach, who had taken down the drum, put it between his feet and begun to play, singing his song. The Puss came and saw him and killed him, and Puss has eaten Roach until this day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 57c, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Hunter, Guinea-hen and Fish
title.zh: 獵人、珠雞與魚

region.en: Harmony Hall, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地和諧堂

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 58 'Hunter, Guinea-hen and Fish' (told by Thomas Williams, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: A hunter's clearing is also Guinea-hen's feeding ground, and the two unwitting strangers — one by day, one by night — keep thanking each other for the work. When harvest comes, Guinea-hen calls Fish with a trombone, trades a loan of her wing for his help, and harvests the field with him; at dawn she borrows the wings back 'to catch a butterfly' and sails away, leaving Fish in the furrow. The hunter finds the trembling borrower, is offered a song instead of death, carries the tub of water singing to the sea — and the Fish rides the first big wave home; which is why we always have to catch fish at sea.
summary.zh: 獵人墾的地恰是珠雞的食場——晝人夜禽，互不謀面，卻各自感謝『幫工』。收穫在即，珠雞以號角喚魚，借翼交易同往收穫；天亮前又借『捉蝴蝶』之名收回翅膀遠遁，拋下田中的魚。獵人擒住顫抖的借宿者，魚以歌換命，載歌載舞至海邊，乘巨浪而歸——所以我們總得到海裡才能捕到魚。

sensitivity.note: Etiological tale (why fish live at sea). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The Hunter was always hunting, and he met up with a splendid piece of rich land and thought to cultivate it, beginning the same day to cut bush. The piece of land was Guinea-hen's feeding ground; Guinea-hen comes out at night and does not walk in the day. 'Massa is good — he knows this is my feeding ground and begins to clean it, so I can get my pullings clear! Let me help myself,' and she made a little chopping herself too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old man came in the morning: 'Hi! thankful! I commenced work yesterday, and massa helped me!' — and did a little more. The third day he burned what he cut — 'Hi! thankful! massa burned the balance!' — and Guinea-hen came at night and gave thanks and cleaned up the balance of what the old man left. Then he planted peas and corn, and Guinea-hen came in the night and said, 'Massa is good! I don't need to plant any' — and began to eat what the old man planted. The old man came in the morning, saw the damage — 'Hi! what insect did this?' — and planted some more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: It went on until the peas began to ripen, about eight weeks. The old man said, 'Going to gather it in tomorrow.' Guinea-hen heard and went to the sea and called the Fish with her trombone: 'I planted a bit of corn and peas, getting ripe, and the old man is coming tomorrow; I want to gather it in tonight before he comes.' Fish accepted — but could neither walk nor fly; Guinea-hen lent her wing and they flew and dropped, and ran, till they came to the ground. 'Here is my own field; gather and eat as much as you like.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58, middle-b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When day commenced to light, Guinea-hen saw the old man coming and said it was a butterfly jumping about — 'Lend me your wings, I go catch it for you' — and sailed away quietly out of the field. The old man grumbled, picked what he could, and came to where the Fish was. 'O Fish! is it you who did this damage all this time?' — 'No, not I! Don't kill me and I will sing you some songs.' The old man liked music, put him in a tub of water to sing and dance; Fish said, 'Take me to the nearest sea-side you have.' The old man carried the tub on his head, dancing as the Fish sang, until a big wave came and the Fish aimed for it and went along with it. The old man stayed dancing, not knowing the Fish was gone; he ran home for hook and line and threw it into the sea to catch Fish — and that is why we always have to catch fish at sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 58, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Brer Rabbit and the Tar-pole
title.zh: 兔子哥哥與柏油樁

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 59a 'The Tar Baby' (told by Rennie Macfarlane, Mandeville)

summary.en: The classic sticky capture, Jamaican style: Fox's tar-pole ignores Rabbit's commands until fist, foot and head are fast. Offered the choice of burning, drowning, hanging or dashing over the bramble-patch, the captured rabbit begs for anything but the brambles — and the satisfied Fox hurls him there, to the freedom cheer of 'Oh, what a fool!'
summary.zh: 黏捉經典的牙買加版：福克斯的柏油樁不理兔子的喝令，直到拳、腳、頭逐一粘牢。火燒、溺斃、吊死、拋過荊棘叢——任選其一？被擒的兔子哀求『千萬別拋荊棘』；得意的福克斯便把他拋過荊棘叢——兔子落地歡呼：『哎呀，真是個蠢貨！』

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit tar-baby episode (Jamaican variant); cross-tradition cluster with Anansi tar-baby (Tale 21) and US plantation versions.

passages.text: When Brer Fox tried to catch Brer Rabbit, he could not catch him. He stuck up a tar-pole in his common, and when Brer Rabbit came and saw it, he said, 'Come out of Brer Fox's place, or I kick you!' And the tar-pole wouldn't come out. And he kicked it and his foot fastened. 'Let go foot, else I kick you with the other one!' — and he kicked it with the other one and the other foot fastened. And he boxed it and his hand fastened. 'Let go me, else I box you!' — he boxed it with the other hand and his hand fastened. 'Let it go, else I buck you!' — he bucked it and his head fastened. 'Let me go, else I bite you!' — and when he bit it, his mouth fastened, and he couldn't move or talk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Brer Fox said, 'Think I couldn't catch you! Burning you, and drowning you, and hanging you, and dashing you over the bramble — which one would you rather?' He said, 'Do anything you like, but don't dash me over that bramble!' And Brer Fox took him and dashed him over the bramble — and he said, 'Oh, what a fool!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Rabbit's Grace: Bless and Blind Us
title.zh: 兔子哥的禱文：賜福且致盲

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924 print), tale 59b 'Saying Grace' (told by Rennie Macfarlane, Mandeville)

summary.en: Captured again, Rabbit asks Fox for a pre-execution prayer — clasp your hands and repeat after me: 'O God, bless and blind us!' Fox, hearing only 'bless and help us', closes his eyes to say it devoutly; the rabbit runs away, and they never see him again.
summary.zh: 兔子再遭擒獲，請求臨刑前做個禱告——『合掌跟著我念：啊上帝，賜福且致盲於我們！』福克斯只聽成『賜福並庇佑』，虔誠閉眼誦念；兔子趁機逃走，從此再無人見過他。

sensitivity.note: Prayer-trick amusement tale; folk-comic use of prayer, not devotional material. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Brer Fox caught Brer Rabbit again, and was going to kill him. Brer Rabbit said, 'Do, Brer Fox — as you are going to kill me, have prayers.' And he said, 'Clasp your hands and say what I say: O God, bless and blind us!' But Brer Fox thought he said 'Bless and help us,' and he said it, eyes shut — and Rabbit ran away, and they never saw him again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59b (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Funeral That Wiggled
title.zh: 會動的葬禮

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 59c 'Pretending Dead' (told by Rennie Macfarlane, Mandeville)

summary.en: Bear comes to Rabbit's yard with news that Fox is dead and needs burying. Rabbit dresses for the funeral — bonpon hat, coatie, spectacles — sits in the rocking-chair and observes that folks who fall down dead always cock a foot in the air and say 'Pooh!' The corpse, taking direction, cocks its foot and says 'Pooh!' — and Rabbit goes away saying a man like that never died yet.
summary.zh: 熊來報喪：福克斯死了，須抬去埋葬。兔子盛裝赴喪——鐵罐高帽、外套、眼鏡——端坐搖椅批評道：『人死倒地，總該翹腳喊一聲噗！』屍體依言翹腳喊了一聲『噗！』——兔子拂袖而去：『你這樣的人，還沒死透呢！』

sensitivity.note: Feigned-death amusement tale (ATU 'pretend dead' cycle). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: When Brer Fox wanted to get Brer Rabbit again, he and Bear made up to catch him. Brer Bear went to Brer Rabbit's yard and told him that Brer Fox was dead and he must help to bury him, for he and Brer Fox were friends. When he got to Brer Fox's yard, he saw Brer Fox lying down. Brer Rabbit put on his bonpon hat and coatie and spectacles, sat up in a rocking-chair and said, 'I never see it so! What a style! What a funniness! I think that when folks fall down dead, they always cock up their foot in the air and make pooh!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59c (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Brer Fox cocked up his foot in the air and said, 'Pooh!' — and Brer Rabbit went away and said, 'A man like you never dead yet!' — for a dead man does not take instruction, and the corpse that takes it is only playing. He went home whistling, and the bear and the fox were left to bury nobody, the funeral breaking up over a wooden grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 59c, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Animal Race: Horse and Turtle
title.zh: 動物賽跑：馬與龜

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 60a 'The Animal Race: Horse and Turtle' (told by Alfred Williams, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Horse bets Turtle he will reach Kingston first; Turtle stations one of his children at every mile-post with the same travelling-song, the last at the Kingston wharf-house. All night Horse gallops, reining and spurring mile-post to mile-post, each one answering soft and sweet — until at the last post, riding into Kingston, he drops down dead.
summary.zh: 馬與龜賭賽先到京斯頓；龜在每個里程碑各埋伏一個孩子，同唱旅途之歌，最後一個守在碼頭倉房。馬整夜疾馳、勒韁加鞭，每一里程碑都『軟甜』應答——直到最後一站，衝進京斯頓的馬倒地而亡。

sensitivity.note: Hare/tortoise race cycle (ATU 275) in Jamaican form; family relay trick. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Horse bet Turtle that he would get to Kingston before him. Turtle bet him he would get to Kingston first, Brar Horse. Turtle took up one of his pickney and dropped them at every mile-post, and dropped the last one in at Kingston at the wharf-house, telling them they were going for a sack of salt. The night when they started, as Brar Horse caught up to the first mile-post he sang out in a harsh note — and Turtle answered quite yonder, soft and sweet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Horse said, 'Well! Brar Turtle gone!' Gallop, draw rein, and spur; as he got to the next mile-post he heard the same answer. Gallop and gallop till he got to the next mile-post, and the same song, and at every mile-post the answer soft and sweet from quite yonder — until, as Horse caught to that last mile-post going into Kingston, he dropped down dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Animal Race: Pigeon and Parrot
title.zh: 動物賽跑：鴿與鸚鵡

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 60b 'The Animal Race: Pigeon and Parrot' (told by Julia Gentle, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Courting the same girl — first into the house in the morning wins — slow-flying Parrot subcontracts a faster cousin: one goes ahead to sit in the tree by her door while the other follows Pigeon behind, answering every taunting call, until the Pigeon, believing Parrot has beaten him in the air, lands beaten outside a house where Parrot is already inside, married to the girl.
summary.zh: 二鳥同追一位姑娘——清早誰先進屋便嫁誰。慢飛的鸚鵡另雇一隻同族：一隻先去她門前樹上候著，一隻跟在鴿子身後應答挑釁之語，直到鴿子以為空中已敗，落在一座鸚鵡早已入內成婚的房子外面，只得留守門外。

sensitivity.note: Race-cycle variant. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Pigeon and Parrot were courting one girl, and she said whichever came first into the house in the morning she would marry. Parrot could not fly very fast; he made a bargain with another Parrot — one went before and left the other to follow Pigeon behind, and the first went near to the girl's house and sat down in a tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Pigeon called, 'Come on, me pretty Poll!' — and Parrot answered behind, 'Go on, me pretty Pigeon!' Pigeon sailed again and called again; Parrot answered again. When Pigeon nearly caught the house he called again in the same tune — and Parrot answered before him now. Pigeon said, 'Stop! all the while Parrot was behind; how has Parrot got before?' When Pigeon went to the house, Parrot was in the house; Pigeon had to stay outside, and Parrot married the girl.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 60b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Man Is Stronger
title.zh: 人是更強者

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 62 'Man Is Stronger' (told by Simeon Falconer, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Tiger boasts no one beats their strength; Lion knows there is a little something called 'Man'. The hunter misfires on his first reconnaissance — Tiger flattens a ram-goat, mistaking horns for guns, his belly-scar for a ram-rod, the scrotum for a shot-bag — but the true Man answers Tiger's challenge with a single shot, blood flying all through his body, and Lion gets his 'I told you' over the carcass.
summary.zh: 老虎自誇無人敵得過獅虎之力；獅子深知有個叫『人』的小東西更強。初探時，虎錯把公羊當人——角當槍、腹疤當槍栓、陰囊當彈袋——一掌拍倒。真的人只以一槍應答，血透全身；獅子對著虎屍說：『早跟你說過，如今信了吧！』

sensitivity.note: Animal tale on human supremacy (cf. woodland tradition parallels). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The Lion and the Tiger were very good friends. Tiger said, 'No one beats us in strength!' Lion said, 'No, my friend — somebody is stronger than we.' Tiger could not believe it; Lion said there was a little something called Man that was stronger. Tiger said he would have to find that something called Man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 62 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went hunting the Man and bucked up Mr. Ram-goat, asked if his name was Man — and whether the two things up here (the horns) were called gun, whether that long scar on his belly was called ram-rod, and whether that bag he had was called shot-bag. Goat said yes. Tiger walked up and licked him flat on the ground, and Goat hollered 'Wi-i! wi-i-i!' Tiger went back to Lion and said he had found something called Man and laid him dead with a single lick. Lion said, 'No, me friend! dat no Man — Man has two feet, and what you tell me has four legs.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 62, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went out again seeking Man, and a Hunter was out. Tiger saw him — 'Now this yah must be Man!' — and as he went up to the man, the Hunter was aiming for him with the gun. Tiger asked if his name was Man, and the Hunter drove at him with the gun. He ran back to Lion and could only say, 'I find Man, and him single answer — him answer me, blood fly all through me body!' — and he died. Lion said, 'I tell you; you no believe me; but you believe me now!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 62, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Yellow Emperor Dreams of the Kingdom of Hua-hsü (Liezi)
title.zh: 黃帝夢遊華胥國（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The kingdom of Hua-hsü, tens of thousands of miles away (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 華胥之國（夢中異域；象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: The Yellow Emperor, worn out by three months of fasting in heart after abandoning his schemes, dreams of the kingdom of Hua-hsü beyond the reach of ship or vehicle, where the people have no desires, feel neither joy in life nor abhorrence of death, and bestrode the air as though treading on solid earth. Waking on his throne, he knows the Perfect Way is not to be sought through the senses — and for twenty-eight years there was great orderliness in the Empire.
summary.zh: 黃帝晝寢而夢遊於華胥氏之國——其民無嗜慾，不知樂生，不知惡死；乘空如履實，寢虛若處牀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the Hua-hsü dream is the classic Taoist utopia-vision, tagged otherworld-voyage for the dream-journey cluster. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: For three months he abstained from personal intervention in government. Then he fell asleep in the daytime, and dreamed that he made a journey to the kingdom of Hua-hsü, situated I know not how many tens of thousands of miles distant from the Ch'i State. It was beyond the reach of ship or vehicle or any mortal foot. Only the soul could travel so far.

This kingdom was without head or ruler; it simply went on of itself. Its people were without desires or cravings; they simply followed their natural instincts. They felt neither joy in life nor abhorrence of death; thus they came to no untimely ends. They felt neither attachment to self nor indifference to others; thus they were exempt from love and hatred alike. They knew neither aversion from one course nor inclination to another; hence profit and loss existed not among them.

All were equally untouched by the emotions of love and sympathy, of jealousy and fear. Water had no power to drown them, nor fire to burn; cuts and blows caused them neither injury nor pain, scratching or tickling could not make them itch. They bestrode the air as though treading on solid earth; they were cradled in space as though resting in a bed. Clouds and mist obstructed not their vision, thunder-peals could not stun their ears, physical beauty disturbed not their hearts, mountains and valleys hindered not their steps. They moved about like gods.

When the Yellow Emperor awoke from his dream, he summoned his three Ministers and told them what he had seen. ... Now I know that the Perfect Way is not to be sought through the senses. This Way I know and hold within me, yet I cannot impart it to you. For twenty-eight years after this, there was great orderliness in the Empire, nearly equalling that in the kingdom of Hua-hsü.

title.en: Riding Home on the Wings of the Wind: Lieh Tzŭ's Nine Years (Liezi)
title.zh: 列子御風而行，九年之後（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: Nan-kuo, Lieh Tzŭ's home in Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 南郭（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ, having mastered the system of Lao Shang and Po Kao Tzŭ, rides home on the wings of the wind. His nine-year apprenticeship passes from silence about right and wrong, through the Master's smile, to the seat beside him, until his mind was frozen, his body in dissolution, and he was borne this way and that on the wind like dry chaff or leaves falling from a tree — I knew not whether the wind was riding on me or I on the wind.
summary.zh: 列子師老商子，友伯高子，進二子之道，乘風而歸——九年之後：心凝形釋，骨肉都融；不知風乘我邪？我乘風乎？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the wind-riding motif paralleled in Zhuangzi ch. 1 (skipped to avoid duplication with the chinese record). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Lieh Tzu had Lao Shang for his teacher, and Po Kao Tzu for his friend. When he had fully mastered the system of these two philosophers, he rode home again on the wings of the wind. At the end of nine years my mind gave free rein to its reflections, my mouth free passage to its speech. Of right and wrong, profit and loss, I had no knowledge, either as touching myself or others. I knew neither that the Master was my instructor, nor that the other man was my friend. Internal and External were blended into Unity. After that, there was no distinction between eye and ear, ear and nose, nose and mouth: all were the same. My mind was frozen, my body in dissolution, my flesh and bones all melted together.

I was wholly unconscious of what my body was resting on, or what was under my feet. I was borne this way and that on the wind, like dry chaff or leaves falling from a tree. In fact, I knew not whether the wind was riding on me or I on the wind.

title.en: Shang Ch'iu K'ai Walks Through Fire for the Pearl (Liezi)
title.zh: 商丘開下地投水赴火（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: Tzŭ Hua's hall in Chin (Taiyuan, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 晉國范氏之門（今山西太原）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: The starving old man Shang Ch'iu K'ai, jeered by a sorcerer's disciples, is tricked into leaping off a cliff — and is wafted down like a bird, not a bone hurt; into the river for the pearl — and comes up holding it; into a great fire — and returns with his garments unsoiled and his body unsinged. Secret I have none, he answers: my mind was simply One, and material objects thus offered no resistance.
summary.zh: 餓夫商丘開，為幻術之徒所弄；一躍而下，身若飛鳥；入水得珠，赴火不燎——吾心一也，外物不能梗。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; tagged faith-trial for the ordeal sequence (interpretive). Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: So, by way of a jest, they took the old man with them to the top of a cliff, and the word was passed round that whosoever dared to throw himself over would be rewarded with a hundred ounces of silver. There was an eager response, and Shang Ch'iu K'ai, in perfect good faith, was the first to leap over the edge. And lo! he was wafted down to earth like a bird on the wing, not a bone or muscle of his body being hurt. Mr. Fan's disciples, regarding this as a lucky chance, were merely surprised, but not yet moved to great wonder.

Then they pointed to a bend in the foaming river below, saying: "There is a precious pearl at the bottom of that river, which can be had for the diving." Shang Ch'iu K'ai again acted on their suggestion and plunged in. And when he came out, sure enough he held a pearl in his hand. Then, at last, the whole company began to suspect the truth, and Tzu Hua gave orders that an array of costly viands and silken raiment should be prepared; then suddenly a great fire was kindled round the pile. "If you can walk through the midst of these flames," he said, "you are welcome to keep what you can get of these embroidered stuffs." Without moving a muscle of his face, Shang Ch'iu K'ai walked straight into the fire, and came back again with his garments unsoiled and his body unsinged.

"Secret I have none," replied Shang Ch'iu K'ai. "Even in my own mind I have no clue as to the real cause. ... I knew not what part of space my body occupied, nor yet where danger lurked. My mind was simply One, and material objects thus offered no resistance. That is all. But now, having discovered that your disciples were deceiving me, my inner man is thrown into a state of doubt and perplexity, while outwardly my senses of sight and hearing re-assert themselves. When I reflect that I have just had a providential escape from being drowned and burned to death, my heart within me freezes with horror, and my limbs tremble with fear. I shall never again have the courage to go near water or fire."

title.en: The Tiger-Feeder Who Was Neither Antagonistic Nor Compliant (Liezi)
title.zh: 梁鴦養虎：不逆不順（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: King Hsüan's park-enclosure (symbolic pin: Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 周宣王之囿（象徵定位：陝西西安）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Liang Yang, skilled in the management of wild birds and beasts, feeds tigers and wolves, eagles and ospreys in King Hsüan's park without one clawing or biting another. His method: avoid giving live animals or whole carcasses, time their hunger and repletion, and be neither antagonistic nor compliant, so that the animals regard me as one of themselves.
summary.zh: 周宣王之牧正有役人梁鴦者，能養野禽獸——養虎之法：不逆其怒，不順其喜；虎可與遊者，必順其性也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; paralleled in Zhuangzi ch. 19 tiger-passage. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The Keeper of Animals under King Hsüan, of the Chou dynasty, had an assistant named Liang Yang, who was skilled in the management of wild birds and beasts. When he fed them in their park-enclosure, all the animals showed themselves tame and tractable, although they comprised tigers, wolves, eagles and ospreys. Male and female freely propagated their kind, and their numbers multiplied. The different species lived promiscuously together, yet they never clawed nor bit one another.

In feeding tigers, then, I avoid giving them either live animals or whole carcasses, lest in the former case the act of killing, in the latter the act of tearing them to pieces, should excite them to fury. Again, I time their periods of hunger and repletion, and I gain a full understanding of the causes of their anger. Tigers are of a different species from man, but, like him, they are docile with those who treat them kindly, though they will show fight when their lives are attacked.

Hence it is my aim to be neither antagonistic nor compliant, so that the animals regard me as one of themselves. Thus it happens that they walk about the park without regretting the tall forests and the broad marshes, and rest in the enclosure without yearning for the lonely mountains and the dark valleys. Such is the effect of using one's common sense.

title.en: The Sailor and the Sea-Gulls That Would Not Alight (Liezi)
title.zh: 海上之人好鷗鳥者（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The sea-shore (symbolic pin: Yantai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 海濱（象徵定位：山東煙臺）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: The sailor swam daily in the sea-gulls' midst, a hundred gulls and more flocking about him — until his father asked him to catch one or two for pets. The next day the gulls only wheeled about in the air and would not alight.
summary.zh: 海上之人有好漚鳥者，每旦之海上，從漚鳥遊；漚鳥之至者百住而不止。其父曰：吾聞漚鳥皆從汝遊，汝取來吾玩之。明日之海上，漚鳥舞而不下也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the 'birds dance but will not descend' (ou-wu-wu-hsia) became a proverb for self-conscious scheming. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: There was once a man, a sailor by profession, who was very fond of sea-gulls. Every morning he went into the sea and swam about in their midst, at which times a hundred gulls and more would constantly flock about him. One day his father said to him: "I am told that sea-gulls swim about with you in the water. I wish you would catch one or two for me to make pets of." On the following day, the sailor went down to the sea as usual, but lo! the gulls only wheeled about in the air and would not alight.

title.en: The Man Who Came Out of the Rock and Walked Through Fire (Liezi)
title.zh: 趙襄子率徒狩山中，石中生人（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The Central Mountains of Chao (Hengshan, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 趙之中山（象徵定位：山西恆山）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Hunting with a hundred thousand men in the Central Mountains, Chao Hsiang Tzŭ's party fire the forest, and a man appears, emerging from a rocky cliff to hover in the air amidst flames and smoke. What do you mean by rock? what do you mean by fire? he asks — I know nothing of them. Tzŭ Hsia tells Marquis Wên that the Master is able to do these things, but he is also able to refrain from doing them.
summary.zh: 趙襄子率徒十萬狩於中山，藉芿燔林——有一人從石壁中出，隨煙火上下，若無所傷。襄子曰：石？火？其人曰：不知也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; tagged faith-trial for the fire-ordeal. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chao Hsiang Tzu led out a company of a hundred thousand men to hunt in the Central Mountains. They dropped sparks in the undergrowth, which set fire to the whole forest, and the glow of the flames was visible for a hundred miles around. Suddenly a man appeared, emerging from a rocky cliff, and was seen to hover in the air amidst the flames and the smoke. Everybody took him for a disembodied spirit. When the fire had passed, he walked quietly out, and showed no trace of having been through the ordeal.

So the prince inquired what secret power it was that enabled him to dwell in rock and to walk through fire. "What do you mean by rock?" replied the man; "what do you mean by fire?" "What you just now came out of is rock; what you just now walked through fire." "I know nothing of them," replied the man.

"From what I have heard the Master say," replied Tzu Hsia, "the man who achieves harmony with Tao enters into close unison with external objects, and none of them has the power to harm or hinder him. Passing through solid metal or stone, walking in the midst of fire or on the surface of water— all these things become possible to him." ... "The Master," replied Tzu Hsia, "is able to do these things, but he is also able to refrain from doing them." Which answer hugely delighted the Marquis.

title.en: P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, and Shên Nung with Serpents' Bodies (Liezi)
title.zh: 庖犧氏女媧氏神農氏，蛇身人面（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The demi-gods of remote antiquity (symbolic pin: Tianshui, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 上古神人（象徵定位：甘肅天水）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: Outward form is no criterion: P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, Shên Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts — their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest; while Chieh and Chou, in all external respects like other men, had the minds of savage brutes.
summary.zh: 庖犧氏、女媧氏、神農氏、夏后氏，蛇身人面，牛首虎鼻——此有非人之狀，而有大聖之德。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the demi-god catalogue cross-linked to the chinese tradition's Nüwa records. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: P'ao Hsi, Nil Kua, Shen Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts. Thus, their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest. Chieh of the Hsia dynasty, Chou of the Yin, Huan of the Lu State, and Mu of the Ch'u State, were in all external respects, as facial appearance and possession of the seven channels of sense, like unto other men; yet they had the minds of savage brutes.

title.en: The Yellow Emperor's Beast-Army and K'uei's Musical Stone (Liezi)
title.zh: 黃帝熊羆貔貅貙虎前驅，夔擊石拊石（列子黃帝篇）

region.en: The field of P'an-ch'üan (Banquan, Hebei/Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 阪泉之野（今河北／山西阪泉）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book II (The Yellow Emperor)

summary.en: When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'üan, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, his ensign-bearers eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. And when K'uei tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound; the strains of the Shao on the flute brought the phœnix itself flying down to assist.
summary.zh: 黃帝與炎帝戰於阪泉之野，帥熊羆狼豹貙虎為前驅——堯使夔典樂，擊石拊石，百獸率舞；簫韶九成，鳳凰來儀。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the beast-army of the Yanhuang war, retold from Liezi. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'iian, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, while his ensign-bearers were eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. This was forcible impressment of animals into the service of man. The Emperor Yao entrusted K'uei with the regulation of music.

When the latter tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound of the music. When the strains of the Shao were heard on the flute, the phœnix itself flew down to assist. This was the attraction of animals by the power of music. In what, then, do the minds of birds and beasts differ from the minds of men?

title.en: Sarabha-miga-Jātaka (The Stag That Saved the King)
title.zh: 鹿王本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and the royal hunting forest
region.zh: 波羅奈與王家獵林

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: A hunting king, mocked by his courtiers for missing a stag, chases it alone into the forest and falls into a sixty-cubit pit; the stag he hunted hauls him out without a thought of malice and teaches him the Five Virtues. When Sakka tests the king by tempting him to shoot the stag that appears at his target, the king refuses—'this very stag saved me from hopeless woe'—and Sakka reveals himself and blesses his mercy.
summary.zh: 王獵鹿不中，為群臣所笑，遂單身逐鹿入林，墮六十肘深坑；所逐之鹿不念舊惡，援王出坑，並教以五戒。後帝釋化樹靈試王，誘其射鹿，王言「此鹿嘗救我於絕境」，堅拒之；帝釋現身讚其仁而賜福。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living Buddhist tradition; freely taught and retold; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this in the Hall of Truth to show Sāriputta's wisdom, after the miracle at Sāvatthī where a mango stone planted at the city gate grew before the crowd's eyes into a tree a hundred cubits tall; the quarrelsome sectarians were confounded, and the Teacher, ascending to the Heaven of the Thirty-three for the rains, returned by a stairway of gems, silver and gold at Sankassa, and there, by a ladder of graded questions, made known before all men and gods the greatness of the Captain of the Faith. "This is not the first time," said he, "that Sāriputta answered at large a question briefly put." Of old, when Brahmadatta was king of Benares, the Bodhisatta lived in the forest as a stag; the king delighted in hunting and reckoned no other man worthy of the name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 483 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day in the hunt the king declared that whoever let a deer pass should be punished, and the courtiers, posting him at the end of a path, drove a great covert toward him. Our stag was first to be put up; seeing men in an unbroken ring on every side, he saw his only chance where the king stood, and rushed at him with eyes dazzling like flung sand. The king shot and missed—the deer are clever to dodge arrows—and the stag, swift as the wind, broke through the circle. The courtiers made sport of their king without stint: "He has hit the ground!" Stung by their mockery, the king girded up his loins and chased the stag on foot, sword in hand, for three leagues. The stag sniffed the smell of water in a sixty-cubit pit hidden under weeds and swerved aside; the king went straight on and fell in. Hearing no footsteps, the stag turned, saw his peril, and pitied rather than hated him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 483 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: "Fear nothing, O king, for I will deliver you from your distress," cried the stag from the pit's edge, and with an effort as earnest as though he were saving his own beloved son he braced himself on the rock and hauled the king out of the deep pit, set him on his back, and carried him forth from the forest. There he admonished the king and established him in the Five Virtues; the king begged him to come to Benares and rule it, but the stag answered that he was one of the animals and wanted no kingdom—let the king keep the precepts he had taught, and teach them to his subjects. The king went home weeping to remember the stag's nobility, proclaimed by the drum of the Law that all the city should observe the five virtues, and at daybreak sat cross-legged and chanted his aspiration in six stanzas—"Hope on, O man, if thou be wise..." The chaplain, come thus early to enquire after the king's welfare, overheard the chant and deduced the whole adventure as clearly as a face in a polished mirror, and told it back to the astonished king, who gave him a rich present.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 483 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the king went into the park with the chaplain to shoot at a mark, and Sakka, perceiving how the king's virtue was filling heaven with new sons and daughters of the gods, resolved to try him. By his power he made the stag appear at the target, and entering the chaplain's body urged him: let fly the shaft, for the stag is meat for monarchs. "I am grateful for a service done, and therefore hold my hand from killing now," the king replied. Then Sakka threatened: kill it, a Titan, not a stag, and thou shalt be king of the gods; refuse, and thou and wife and children shall descend to death's cold river. "So be it," answered the king; "by my hand this stag shall not be slain. That very stag saved me from hopeless woe—how can I wish my benefactor dead?" Sakka left the chaplain's body and stood in the air in his own shape, blessing the true and faithful friend—"comfort with truth and goodness this domain, and thou shalt reign as Indra amid the gods"—then returned. Of that time Ananda was the king, Sariputta the chaplain, and the Master the stag.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 483 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Canda-Kinnara-Jātaka (The Kinnara Couple)
title.zh: 緊那羅本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Mountain of the Moon (Canda-pabbata) in the Himalaya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雪山月山（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The Bodhisatta, born a kinnara or woodland fairy, and his wife Canda live in loving song on the Mountain of the Moon. A king on a solitary hunting trip shoots the fairy out of lust for his wife; Canda curses the king, refuses his offer of queenship, and laments over her dying mate until her grief's power heats Sakka's throne, and the god, as a brahmin, heals the wound with heavenly water and bids the pair keep to their mountain.
summary.zh: 菩薩生為山林精靈緊那羅，與妻月女居月山，以歌相娛。王獨自狩獵，貪其妻之美，射傷緊那羅。月女咒詛王，拒其后位之誘，抱垂死之夫哀泣，悲慟之力熱帝釋座；帝釋化婆羅門以天水愈其傷，囑二神自此勿下山。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this in the palace of Rāhula's mother, praising her constancy: she had clothed herself in yellow at the news of his ordination, given up garlands, and refused the gifts of other kings. "Not now only, but even when born as an animal, she was faithful and mine alone." Of old, when Brahmadatta was king in Benares, the Great Being was born a fairy or kinnara in the Himalaya, and his wife was named Canda; the two dwelt together on a silver mountain called Canda-pabbata, the Mountain of the Moon. The king of Benares had committed his government to his ministers and gone alone into the Himalayas in yellow robes, armed with the five weapons. There the kinnaras came down for the hot season, crowned with flowers and clothed in flower-gauze, singing in honey voices.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 485 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: On a sandy spot white as a silver plate they spread a couch of flowers, and the fairy played upon a piece of bamboo and sang while Canda waved her soft hands and danced beside him, singing too. The king caught the sound, stole close, and stood watching from a hiding place; he fell in love with the female fairy and resolved to shoot the husband and live there with the wife. He shot the fairy Canda, who lamented in four stanzas as his blood flowed and his breath went—yet each stanza turned not on his own pain but on his yearning for her sorrow. Lying upon his couch of flowers he lost consciousness; the king stood where he was. Canda, rapt in her own delight, did not know he was wounded till she saw the blood oozing from the wound's mouth; then, unable to bear the pain of sorrow, she cried out loud, and the king came out and showed himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 485 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thinking him the brigand who had slain her husband, she fled trembling to the hill-top and denounced the king in five stanzas, praying that the woe that wrung her heart be repaid upon his mother and his wife, who would mourn her lord and son for this deed done for lust. "Weep not nor grieve: the woodland dark has blinded you, I ween; a royal house shall honour thee, and thou shalt be my queen," the king answered. "No! I will surely slay myself! thine I will never be, who slew my husband innocent and all for lust of me," she roared like a lion; and his passion left him, and he let her go to the Himalaya. Then she came down, embraced the Great Being, carried him to the hill-top, and laid his head on her lap, making her moan in twelve stanzas over every hill and glen and flower that would see her no more; and taunting the gods for leaving a righteous world ungoverned, she so wrought on them that Sakka's throne grew hot with the power of her pain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 485 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sakka, pondering, discovered the cause, and in the form of a brahmin approached with a water-pot and sprinkled the Great Being with water. On the instant the poison ceased to act, his colour returned, and he knew not so much as where the wound had been: the Great Being stood up quite well. Canda fell at the brahmin's feet and sang his praise for restoring her well-loved husband with the elixir of life; Sakka bade them go no more down from the Mountain of the Moon among the paths of men, and returned to his own place. And Canda said to her husband, "Why stay here in danger, my lord? come, let us go to the Mountain of the Moon, where the lovely rivers flow, all o'ergrown with flowers; there for ever, while the breeze whispers in a thousand trees, charm with talk the happy hours." The Master identified the Birth: Anuruddha was the king, Rāhula's mother was Canda, and the fairy was himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 485 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Dasabrahmana-Jātaka (The Ten Kinds of Brahmins)
title.zh: 十婆羅門本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Indapatta, capital of the Kuru kingdom, and Mount Nanda in the Himalaya (symbolic pin for the mountain)
region.zh: 俱盧國因陀羅波達城；雪山楠達山洞（山為象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Koravya's lavish almsgiving profits him nothing, for every recipient is wicked; his wise minister Vidhura catalogues ten kinds of men who are brahmins in name only—herb-sellers, bell-ringing servants, importunate beggars, wood-cutters, traders, cattle-dealers, sacrificers who slaughter, caravan guards, hunters, and scapegoats beneath the royal bed—and finds the only worthy recipients in five hundred Silent Buddhas of Mount Nanda, whom the king feasts for seven days.
summary.zh: 憍羅耶王廣行布施而無所得，蓋受者皆無德。賢臣毘提羅歷數十種徒有其名之婆羅門——賣藥者、鳴鈴僕役、強乞者、樵夫、商販、賣女者、殺生祭司、護商者、獵人、代王受垢者——並指唯有楠達山洞中五百獨覺佛堪受供養。王齋供七日，所施衣物隨之凌空而返。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this at Jetavana of a gift incomparable, given by the king of Kosala with discrimination to the holiest of the Brethren; "wise men of old, ere yet the Buddha had arisen, even they gave with discrimination." Of old, in the kingdom of Kuru and the city of Indapatta, reigned king Koravya, whose adviser in things temporal and spiritual was the wise Vidhura. The king's great almsgiving set all India in commotion, yet among all who received and enjoyed his gifts not one kept so much as the Five Virtues—all were wicked to a man—and the king's giving brought him no satisfaction. Desiring to give to the virtuous, he took counsel with Vidhura: seek me brahmins good, in whom much wisdom lies, men free from deeds of evil lust, that they may eat my food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 495 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: "'Tis hard to find such holy men," answered Vidhura, and in question and answer with the king he distinguished ten kinds who are brahmins in name only: some carry sacks of healing herbs, bathe, and recite magic spells—physician-like; some ring bells before the king and drive his chariot—servant-like; some with waterpot and crooked staff follow towns crying for gifts—importunate as tax-men; some, long-nailed and dirty, hew wood—mere hewers; some traffic in fruit and honey—merchants; some follow trade and sell their daughters in marriage—like Vessa; some as chaplains tell fortunes and slaughter many beasts at village invitations—like butchers; some stand armed with sword and shield before merchants' caravans—like bandits; some trap fish and hare in woodland huts—hunters; and some lie beneath the royal bed at the soma-sacrifice to catch the washing of the king's sins—like barbers. "These have no right to such a name: lost is their brahminhood," said the king to each in turn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 495 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: But there are brahmins, too, said Vidhura, men very wise and good, free from the deeds of evil lust, who eat one meal of rice and never touch strong drink—they dwell in the further Himalaya, in a cave of Mount Nanda. Then Vidhura bade the king proclaim through the city that all should adorn it, give alms, keep the holy-day vows, and pledge themselves to virtue; and himself, taking the vows, cast eight handfuls of flowers into the air, calling to mind the virtues of the Silent Buddhas: let the five hundred Pacceka Buddhas of the cave of Mount Nanda to-morrow partake of our food. The flowers fell upon them in their far dwelling; they understood, judged Vidhura no mean creature—one having the seed of a Buddha within him, to be a Buddha in this very cycle—and accepted the invitation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 495 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day they flew through the air from Lake Anotatta and descended in the royal courtyard; the king and Vidhura received their bowls, seated them on the terrace, gave them the gift-water, and served them with delightful food for seven days, presenting many gifts; on the seventh day he gave them all the requisites, and they gave thanks and flew back to their cave, the requisites going with them. Of that time Ananda was the king, and the wise Vidhura was the Master himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 495 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Haṃsa-Jātaka (The Golden Goose and the Faithful Friend)
title.zh: 天鵝本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and Mount Cittakūṭa (symbolic pin for the mountain)
region.zh: 波羅奈與質多羅山（山為象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Queen Khema dreams of hearing a Golden Goose preach the Law, and the king builds a lake to snare one; the goose-king Dhatarattha is caught, and his captain Sumukha, though free, returns to share his prisoner's fate, 'I'll not leave you... will either live or die.' The moved hunter frees and heals the royal bird, and the goose preaches all night to the king until the queen's craving is appeased, then flies home.
summary.zh: 吉祥王后夢聞金鵝說法，王遂鑿湖設網捕鵝。鵝王法螺賢落網，其部屬善友雖可脫身仍返相伴，誓同生共死。獵人感動，縱之療傷；鵝王入宮為王說法通宵，王后願足，雙鵝飛還山中。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this in the Bamboo Grove of Elder Ananda's renunciation of his life for the Teacher's sake—"not the first time." Of old, in Benares reigned a king named Bahuputtaka, Father of Many Sons, and his queen consort was Khema. The Great Being then dwelt on Mount Cittakūṭa, chief of ninety thousand wild geese, come to life as a golden goose. The queen dreamed a dream and told the king she had conceived a woman's craving to hear a Golden Goose discourse of the Law; told that such creatures lived on Cittakūṭa, the king made a lake which he called Khema, planted it with all manner of food-corn, had immunity proclaimed daily in the four quarters, and sent a hunter to catch the geese. In a snare set among the crops the Great Being was caught; the goose flock fled in three divisions, but Sumukha their chief captain, missing his king, came back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 502 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hanging in the noose, the goose-king tested his friend: "There go the birds, the ruddy geese, all overcome with fear: O golden-yellow Sumukha, depart! what want you here? ... Fly, noble bird! with prisoners no fellowship can be." "No, I'll not leave you, Royal Goose, when trouble draweth nigh: but stay I will, and by your side will either live or die," Sumukha answered, sitting on the mud. "'Twas but to put you to the test I bade you fly away," said the king of the geese. Up came the huntsman at top speed; Sumukha flew to meet him and declared the virtues of the royal bird, and the hunter's heart was softened. Asked how the birds, treading unfooted ways, had failed to spy the snare, the Great Being answered, "When life is coming to an end, and death's hour draws anigh, though you may close upon it come, nor trap nor snare you spy." Asked why, though free, he stayed with a prisoner, Sumukha said, "He is my comrade, friend, and king, dear as my life is he: forsake him—no, I never will, until death calls for me."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 502 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hunter thought that if he harmed such virtuous creatures the earth would gape and swallow him—what care he for the king's reward?—and set them free, drawing the royal bird from the stick, washing the blood from him, and setting the dislocated sinews, so that by the Great Being's perfections the foot became whole on the instant and not a mark showed. The goose-king chose rather to go to the town: the hunter would be rewarded, the queen's craving appeased, Sumukha's friendship made known, and by his wisdom he should receive the lake Khema as a free gift. So the hunter carried them on his carrying-pole to the king, who placed both geese on a golden perch, fed them with honey and fried grain, and held out his hands, praying them to speak of the Law. The goose catechised the king on his health, wealth, righteous rule, unblemished court, far-off foes, queen, and sons—"sons I have of fame, five score and one; tell them their duty: they'll not leave your good advice undone"—and then admonished him in five stanzas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 502 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: "He that puts off until too late the effort to do good, though nobly bred, with virtue dowered, yet sinks beneath the flood; his knowledge fades... as one moonblind at night sees all things swollen twice their size with his imperfect sight. Who sees the truth in falsity no wisdom gains at all, as on a rugged mountain-path the deer will often fall. If any strong courageous man loves virtue, follows right, though but a low-born churl, he burns like bonfires in the night. By using this similitude all wisdom's truths explain: cherish your sons till wise they grow, like seedlings in the rain." So the Great Being discoursed to the king the livelong night; the queen's craving was appeased, and by sunrise, having established the king in the virtues of kings and exhorted him to vigilance, the goose flew out of the northern window with Sumukha and away to Cittakūṭa. The Master identified the Birth: the huntsman was Channa, Sāriputta the king, Ānanda was Sumukha, and he himself was the Goose King.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 502 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Aḷambusā-Jātaka (The Nymph and the Young Ascetic)
title.zh: 阿蘭浮沙天女本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Himalaya hermitage and Indra's heaven (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 雪山精舍與天界（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The ascetic Isisinga, born of a doe that drank water mixed with a brahmin's seed, is warned by his dying father against women, yet the sheer power of his austerity so heats Sakka's throne that the god sends the nymph Aḷambusā to break his virtue. Her praise-song lures him to seize her in flight, and he lies lost in her arms three years; waking, he laments his broken vows, resumes his meditation, forgives her, and she begs a boon never to tempt a saint again.
summary.zh: 獨覺之子伊 西 行伽 乃母鹿飲仙人之水而孕所生；父臨終誡勿近女色，然其苦行威德熱帝釋座，神遣天女阿蘭浮沙誘之。天女讚歌相誘、佯逃相引，仙人執其髮而失定，沉眠其懷三年。醒後慟悔，重入禪定，赦其罪；天女求得「永不誘聖者」之願。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka paralleling the Rishyasringa episode of the Hindu Ramayana and the Barlaam-and-Josaphat tradition; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a Brother tempted to discontent by the wife of his unregenerate days—owing to her, said the Master, he once fell from mystic meditation and lay three years lost and distracted. Of old, in the reign of Brahmadatta in Benares, a doe ate grass and drank water mingled with a brahmin ascetic's seed, became enamoured, and bore him a man child, Isisinga, whom the ascetic reared with a father's affection, admitted to holy orders, and warned: "In this Himalaya country are women as fair as these flowers: they bring utter destruction on all that fall into their power." Soon after he was destined for the Brahma world; but the son, indulging in mystic meditation with all his senses mortified, became an ascetic so severe that the abode of Sakka was shaken, and Sakka, fearing to be displaced, searched the twenty-five millions of his handmaids for one equal to the task of breaking the saint's virtue, and found none but Aḷambusā.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 523 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: "Go, Temptress, ever dog his steps, for holy sage is he, and, seeking ever highest bliss, still triumphs over me," said Sakka; Aḷambusā asked why she alone of all the nymphs of Nandana, and feared the hell that waits on wrongs to saints, yet went at the god's behest. At break of day, before the sun was astir, she drew near to Isisinga as he swept out his cell. The ascetic questioned her—"Who art thou, like to lightning flash, or bright as morning star?"—and sang her praises from head to foot: slender waist, eyes like guñja berries, teeth like pearls, the triple line on her neck. While he spoke she was silent, and reading how disturbed his state of mind had grown, she answered, "Heaven bless thee, Kassapa, my friend, the time is past and gone for idle questions such as these—for are we not alone?—come let us in thy hermitage embracing haste to prove the thousand joys well known to all the votaries of love."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 523 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, with a woman's cunning, she made as if to run away; the ascetic cried "She is off," intercepted her with motion swift as air, and seized her by the hair. Just where he stood the lovely maid embraced him in her arms, and his virtue fell before the magic of her charms; in thought she flew to Indra's throne in Nandana afar, and the god sent a golden car with trappings spread. There the saint lay in her arms for many a long day: three years passed over his head as though it were a moment's space. At last he woke, saw the green trees and the cuckoo-crying groves, and wept bitterly: "I make no offering, raise no hymn; no sacrifice is here. Who can my tempter be, who by foul practice has overcome all sense of right in me, even as a ship with precious freight is swallowed in the sea?" Told that she was sent by king Sakka, he called to mind his father's warning—"Women are fair as lotus flower; beware, good youth, their subtle power"—and lamented that he had let his wise old father's words pass unheeded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 523 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: "Accursed be the life of old: henceforth I'll do as I am told; far better death itself to face, than be again in such a case." So he forsook sensual desire and entered upon mystic meditation; and Aḷambusā, seeing his steadfast power and courage return, became terrified and asked his forgiveness, kneeling to embrace his feet: "A mighty work I wrought, when heaven itself and gods of fame trembled with fear to hear thy name." "I pardon thee, fair lady; go, as thou wilt," he said, blessing the Thirty-three and her; and saluting him, she mounted the golden car and sped away like blazing torch or lightning flash. Sakka, glad at heart, cried "No boon can I deny," and Aḷambusā asked but this: "Let me ne'er tempt a saint again to violate his vow." Of that time the nymph was the Brother's former wife, Isisinga the backsliding Brother, and the great saint his father the Master himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 523 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Saṅkhapāla-Jātaka (The Serpent King's Fast)
title.zh: 海螺龍王本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Rajagaha in Magadha; river Kannapennā and the naga palace
region.zh: 摩竭陀王舍城；迦那奔那河與龍宮

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Prince Duyyodhana of Magadha, coveting the glory of the naga king Saṅkhapāla who visits his ascetic father, gives alms and keeps the holy days until reborn as a serpent king—then, finding the naga world no place for purity, keeps fast-days on an ant-heap, offering his body to all comers. Sixteen hunters stake and drag him; the landowner Āḷāra buys him free, is rewarded with a year in the naga palace, and returns to preach the vanity of desires to the king of Benares.
summary.zh: 摩竭陀王子睹龍王榮耀而生欣羨，廣行布施、持齋布薩，感生龍界為王；然悟龍身非清淨之地，遂於蟻垤持齋，自許其身任人取用。十六獵人戳刺拖曳；地主阿羅以牛與金贖之，獲龍宮一年之報，歸而向波羅奈王宣說欲之無常。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master, expressing approval of lay folk who kept holy days, told them that wise men of old gave up the great glory of the Naga world to observe those vows. Of old, a king of Magadha reigned in Rajagaha, and the Bodhisatta, born as prince Duyyodhana, was installed in the kingdom while his father took up the religious life in the park. Thrice daily the son visited the father, whose honor and profit thus grew so great that the old king could not even prepare for mystic meditation, and stole away without a word beyond the borders, to a hut by Mount Candaka at the bend of the river Kannapennā, where it issues from lake Saṅkhapāla. There the naga king Saṅkhapāla, issuing from the river with his company, would visit the ascetic and hear the Law. The son, seeking his father, came upon the serpent's departing magnificence and conceived a longing for the Naga world; ever after he kept the moral law and the holy days, gave alms at the four gates, and at his death was reborn in the Naga world as king Saṅkhapāla.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 524 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: In time he grew sick of that magnificence and longed to be born as a man, for dwelling in the Naga world his observance of the holy days was not a success and he deteriorated in morals. Leaving the Naga world he coiled round an ant-hill between the high road and a narrow path, resolved to keep the holy day, saying, "Let those that want my skin or want my skin and flesh, let them, I say, take it all," and lay there on the fourteenth and fifteenth of the half-month, returning to the palace on the first day of each fortnight. One day sixteen men of a neighboring village, hunting in vain for flesh, saw him and resolved to kill and eat the snake-king; fearing his size, they took stakes, and the Bodhisatta made his body big as a trough-shaped canoe, beautiful as a jasmine wreath, and tucked his head into his hood, resolved that when they struck him he would not open his eyes or regard them with anger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 524 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: They seized him by the tail, dragged him, wounded him in eight places with sharp stakes and thrust black bamboo sticks, thorns and all, into the open wounds; strung him by cords through eight piercings; and when his head drooped, pierced his nostrils with a slender stake and raised his head by a cord. Never once from the moment of the first wound did he open his eyes or look on them with anger. Then Āḷāra, a landowner of Mithila journeying with five hundred wagons, gave all sixteen an ox apiece, a handful of golden coins, garments, and ornaments for their wives, and so got them to release him. The Bodhisatta returned to the Naga palace, issued forth with a great retinue, took Āḷāra with him, and for a whole year satisfied him with heavenly delights, three hundred naga maidens serving, until Āḷāra asked instead for the requisites of the ascetic life and departed to the Himalaya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 524 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: In time the ascetic came to Benares and lodged in the king's park; charmed, the king asked why one of such noble presence had renounced earth's joys. Alara told him how on a trading venture he had met the captured snake, bought him with oxen and gold, and been led to a dwelling of gold and gems thronged with nymphs; and how the serpent-king, questioned, confessed that the mansion was owed to his own good actions as king Duyyodhana of Magadha—he supplied meat and drink religiously, and made his house an inn where sages refreshed themselves—and that he had suffered hurt on the holy days by no overmastering dread but in the cause of goodness, whose bounds like the seashore are never transgressed: "Nowhere but in the world of men, I ween, may purity and self-restraint be seen: if only once midst men I draw my breath, I'll put an end to further birth and death." The king vowed to perform all deeds of piety; the ascetic passed to the Brahma heaven, and the Master identified the Birth: the father-ascetic was Kassapa, the king of Benares was Ananda, Alara was Sariputta, and Sankhapala was himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 524 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Cūḷa-Sutasoma-Jātaka (The Grey Hair)
title.zh: 小蘇達沙摩本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Sudassana city (the Benares of that birth) and the Himalaya hermitage
region.zh: 須達沙城（彼世之波羅奈）與雪山精舍

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Sutasoma, whose face is glorious as the full moon, orders his barber to tell him when a grey hair appears—and on receiving that single grey hair renounces his vast kingdom over the wailing of his mother, father, seven hundred wives and his pregnant queen. He bribes the nurse to take his clinging seven-year-old son away, cuts his top-knot on the Palace of Flowers before the people, and leads a company covering twelve leagues to a hermitage built for him by Sakka's command.
summary.zh: 蘇達沙王面如滿月，命理髮師見白髮即告；得一莖白髮遂捨大國。母、父、七百妃與懷孕王后皆泣勸不果，並賄乳母抱走其七歲稚子；於花宮頂當眾斷髮髻，率十二由旬之眾往帝釋所命營建之精舍。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this concerning the perfect exercise of self-abnegation. Of old, what is now Benares was a city called Sudassana, and king Brahmadatta's chief consort bore the Bodhisatta, whose face was glorious as the full moon, so that he was named Somakumāra, and from his fondness for soma juice, Sutasoma. Educated at Taxila, he ruled a vast dominion with sixteen thousand wives, Candadevī at their head, and a numerous family. But he grew discontented with domestic life and told his barber, "When you see a grey hair on my head, you are to tell me." In time the barber, with golden tweezers, laid a grey hair in his hand. "My body is a prey to old age," cried the king, and descending from the terrace he seated himself on a throne before the people, summoned his eighty thousand councillors and sixty thousand brahmins, and announced, "A grey hair has appeared on my head; I am an old man, and you are to know that I am become an ascetic."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 525 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Each counsellor felt the arrow quiver in his heart: remember thy seven hundred wives, O king—what will become of them? "Their sorrows soon another will console, for they are young in years and fair to see; but I am bent upon a heavenly goal." His mother came in hot haste lamenting the day that hailed her mother of such a son; his father asked what Law led him to quit kingdom and home with old parents left alone; and he, for answer, showed them the Law and held his peace. His seven hundred wives threw themselves at his feet weeping that his heart must break or pity unknown; "My heart in sorrow may not break, though I feel pity for your pain, but holy orders I must take, that I may heavenly bliss attain." His queen consort, heavy with child and near her time, begged him stay till the babe was born; "The hour of thy delivery is nigh; until the babe is born, I'll stay with thee; then will I leave the royal imp and fly far from the world a holy monk to be."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 525 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: His elder son asked whom he must impiously slay for his mother's tears; but the younger, seven years old, comforted them both, and coming down from the tower clasped his father by the neck: "I too will hold thee by the hand, nor let thee go against our will." "This child is a source of danger to me," thought the Bodhisatta, and looking at the nurse, "Good nurse, behold this jewel ornament: this is yours: only take away the child, that he be not a hindrance to me." She took the bribe and led the boy away. His commander offered the subdued world; the rich merchant Kulavaddhana offered wealth beyond reckoning; his brother Somadatta begged to follow him into the hermit's cell, and was refused. "Like water through a sieve, our day so brief alas! fast slips away," the Great Being taught the weeping people, and then, on the topmost storey of the Palace of Flowers, cut off his top-knot with a sword and cried, "I am now nothing to you; choose ye a king of your own," casting turban and all into the crowd, who rolled on the ground in lamentation under the rising dust-cloud.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 525 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: A barber shaved his hair and beard; he fastened an earthen bowl on his shoulder, took the mendicant's staff, and stepped out into the street unrecognised; his wives found only the bundle of his adornments, and the city cried, "King Sutasoma, sad to tell, has left his throne for hermit cell, and, clad in yellow, goes his way like some lone elephant astray." The people followed him and the whole city emptied, until the company covered twelve leagues. Sakka ordered Vissakamma to build a hermitage thirty leagues long and five broad; the Great Being entered by the path, was first ordained, admitted the rest to orders until a space of thirty leagues was filled, and if any false thought arose in any mind he would come through the air and admonish them: "Call not to mind love's sports of yore... indulge without or stint or stay good will to men by night and day, so shall ye win the angel home." The saints abiding by his admonition were destined to the Brahma world; the elder son was Sariputta, the younger Rahula, prince Somadatta was Ananda, and king Sutasoma was the Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 525 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Nalinikā-Jātaka (The Princess in Ascetic's Dress)
title.zh: 天女誘仙本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Benares and the Himalaya hermitage
region.zh: 波羅奈與雪山精舍

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: Sakka stops the rain for three years to break the austere virtue of the young ascetic Isisinga, and tells the starving king of Benares that only his daughter Nalinikā can do it. Sent into the forest with ministers and elephants, the princess disguises herself as an ascetic youth playing with a ball that always returns to her hand, seduces the innocent boy, and slips away before his father returns; the rain falls that very day, and the father's rebuke restores his son's meditation.
summary.zh: 帝釋為破伊 西 行伽 少年仙人之淨行而止雨三年，語飢困之波羅奈王：唯王女娜律尼迦能成此事。公主隨眾入山，偽裝仙人少年，弄一手擲必回之球誘惑天真的小仙人，旋即遁去；當日雨降。父歸斥其為妖變所惑，其禪定復得。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this of a Brother tempted by the wife of his unregenerate days—of old it was owing to her that he fell from mystic meditation and was mightily destroyed. Of old, a brahmin of the North, trained in all the arts, became an ascetic in the Himalayas; exactly as in the Aḷambusā Birth a doe conceived by him and brought forth a son called Isisinga. His father admitted him to holy orders, had him instructed in the rites inducing mystic meditation, and the youth soon enjoyed the bliss of ecstasy, an ascetic of such severe austerity that the abode of Sakka was shaken. Sakka discovered the cause, and for three years stopped the rain over the kingdom of Kāsi: the country was scorched, no crops came to perfection, and the people gathered in the palace yard to reproach the king, who, though he took the moral vows and fasted, could bring down no rain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 526 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: At midnight Sakka stood in mid-air in the illuminated royal chamber and told the king that in the Himalaya dwelt the ascetic Isisinga, who constantly, when it began to rain, looked up at the sky in a rage, and so the rain ceased. "Should his virtue be broken down, it will rain." "But who is able to overcome his virtue?" "Your daughter, Sire, Nalinikā can do it." Though these were things not to be spoken of in words, the king, for the protection of his realm, talked with his daughter and sent her away with his ministers, elephants and footmen. Pitching camp at the frontier, they had the princess conveyed by foresters' paths to the edge of the hermitage; and while the Bodhisatta was gone into the forest for wild fruits, they surrounded the cloister, disguised the princess as an ascetic youth in a beautiful bark garment with all manner of ornaments, and sent her in playing with a painted ball tied to a string, while they stood on guard without.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 526 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Isisinga, seeing her come, was terrified and hid in his hut; but she played with her ball at the door, her lovely limbs exposed to his gaze, and when he broke forth asking what fruit of what tree this might be that however far 'tis tossed still returns again and never more is lost, she answered falsely of Mount Gandhamādana, whose trees bear such fruit. Believing her an ascetic, he offered seat and food; and being an ingenuous youth who had never seen a woman before, he was led to believe her extraordinary story, and through her seductions his virtue was overcome and his meditation broken off. When he asked by what road she had come, she described her hermit cot by the Kāusikī north of the Himalayan snows; but fearing his father's return, she planned her escape—"Alas! I fear I may no longer stay, but many a royal saint lives on the way: ask one of them to point you out the road"—and left the youth wistfully looking after her. That very day Sakka, delighted, caused rain to fall throughout the whole kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 526 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: But directly she had left, a fever seized the boy, and he lay groaning in his hut where his returning father found him. Then the boy poured out his lovesick lament over the fair youth—the smoothed dark hair, the curvéd rings at either ear, the voice softer than the cuckoo's—and begged to be told where this holy youth dwelt, or he would lie down and die at the door. The Great Being knew at once that through some woman his son had lost his virtue, and rebuked him: friendships exist and then they cease; just as a flood sweeps off the ripened corn, so will the power of virtue be overborne by such a meeting—"Demons there be that through the wide earth run in varied form disguised. Beware, my son!" The terrified youth thought, "She was a female yakkha, he says," and asked his father's pardon, promising never to leave the spot; his father comforted him and proclaimed the four Perfect States, and the son walked therein and once more developed mystic meditation. Of that time the wife of his unregenerate days was Nalinika, the backsliding Brother was Isisinga, and the Master was the father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 526 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Sonaka-Jātaka (The Crow on the Carcass)
title.zh: 蘇那迦本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Rajagaha, Benares royal park and palace
region.zh: 王舍城；波羅奈御苑與王宮

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: King Arindama forgets his friend Sonaka for forty years, singing his reward song through all Benares, while Sonaka, a withered sal-leaf falling before him, becomes a Silent Buddha. Fifty years on he teaches the reward-song's refrain to a wood-gathering boy, who sings it back before the king; led to the park, the king insults the shaven recluse and is rebuked, then hears the parable of the crow that feasted on a floating carcass until the Ganges swept it to the sea, and renounces his throne the same day.
summary.zh: 阿林達摩王四十年來遍唱「見我故友者賞千頂冠」之歌，而蘇那迦見落葉悟無常，已成獨覺佛。後教拾柴小兒續唱其歌詞；王循歌至御苑，斥剃髮行者為可憐蟲而遭反詰；聞「烏鴉食浮屍隨流至海」之喻，當日捨王位。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The Master told this concerning the Perfection of Renunciation: "not now only, but of old also the Tathāgata verily left the world and made the Great Renunciation." Of old, the Magadha king reigned in Rajagaha, and on the day the Bodhisatta was born to his chief queen as prince Arindama, a son was born to the royal chaplain and named young Sonaka. The two boys grew up alike as twins and studied at Taxila; wandering to Benares they lodged in the royal park, and at a brahmins' almsgiving the seats assigned them—white cloth for one, red woollen rug for the other—told Sonaka that that day his friend would be made king of Benares and would offer him the post of commander-in-chief. On the seventh day after the king's death the festal car stopped at the park gate for any worthy man to mount; the chaplain sprinkled the Bodhisatta king on the spot and led him into the city with a vast escort, and in the greatness of his glory the king forgot all about Sonaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 529 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: But when the king was gone, Sonaka sat again on the stone seat, and a withered leaf of a sal tree fell from its stalk in front of him. "Even as this leaf, so will my body fall into decay," he cried, and acquiring supernatural insight by reflecting on the impermanence of all things he attained that instant to the state of a Silent Buddha—his layman's marks vanishing, the ascetic's appearing—and set out for the cave of Nandamūla. The king, after forty years, remembered Sonaka, and offered a thousand pieces to whoever should see him with his own eyes and a hundred to whoever should hear of him, singing his aspiration: "A thousand crowns for one that sees my friend and playmate dear; a hundred lo! I give if one of Sonaka should hear." The song passed from mouth to mouth through harem, city and country till all sang it.
