Fifty years on, Sonaka, moved by the king's longing, came back through the air and taught the refrain to a seven-year-old boy gathering sticks in the park.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 529 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bathed and dressed in his best, the boy had a drum beaten through the city, and before all the people the king sang first and the boy—five tangled locks he wore—answered: "The thousand give to me who saw, who heard a hundred more: I'll tell thee news of Sonaka, thy playfellow of yore. Within this realm, in thine own park is many a big sal tree... and at their foot lo! Sonaka in meditation lies, filled with the Arhat's holy calm, when human passion dies." The king started in full force and found his friend at rest, passionless and saintly; but given up to evil passion, he insulted him without saluting: "His parents dead, with shaven head, clad in monk's robe I see, a wretched Brother in a trance, stretched here beneath this tree." "He is no wretched wight who in his every action, Sire, has aye attained to right; nay rather wretched those who right neglect and practise ill, for evil doer evil doom is destined to fulfil."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 529 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Proving himself king of Kasi, Arindama asked if the sage had met with anything deserving blame, and Sonaka told the eight blessings of the homeless monk; but the king cut him short: "I have no need of monkish blessings... how to gain both worlds at once, to me, I prithee, tell." Then came the parable: a foolish crow, seeing a vast carcass floating past on the Ganges' tide, boarded it for goodly store of food and stayed eating and drinking till the river swept him headlong to the sea, where the monster fish came ravening round and devoured him. "So thou and all that greedily pleasures of sense pursue are deemed as wise as was this crow, till ye all lusts eschew." "In pity once, nay even twice, utter the warning word, but keep not on repeating it like a slave before his lord"—and the sage vanished through the air. The king resolved, "To-morrow one may die, who knows? I'll be ordained to-day," gave his sixty thousand villages, elephants, horses, cars and maidens to his son Dighavu, and was destined for the Brahma world; of that time the son was young Rahula and the king the Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 529 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: Mahāsutasoma-Jātaka (The Ogre-King and the Four Verses)
title.zh: 大蘇達沙摩本生

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1901 (Chalmers)

region.en: Indapatta in the Kuru country and the man-eater's forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧國因陀羅波達與食人者之林（象徵性定位）

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 4 (trans. Chalmers, 1901)

summary.en: The king of Benares, given corpse-meat by his cook, conceives an incurable craving for human flesh, is exposed by his commander and banished, and becomes a man-eater who captures a hundred and one kings to sacrifice to the tree-nymph who healed his wound. Warned by that nymph, he seizes prince Sutasoma, his old teacher; released to hear four stanzas worth a hundred pieces each, Sutasoma returns under oath and wins four boons—life for the man-eater, the kings' lives, their release, and the end of cannibalism—till gods and men applaud the conversion.
summary.zh: 波羅奈王誤食人肉而生難遏之嗜，事發遭逐，成為食人魔王；為償樹神愈傷之願，捕一百零一王以祭。樹神勸其先擄舊師蘇達沙摩王子；釋之令聽四偈，王子誓言既立乃返，索四願——魔王長壽、諸王不死、各歸其國、戒食人肉——天人同聲喝采。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka containing cannibalism and vivid hell-threats; retold freely as scripture of a living tradition; no ritual secrecy involved.

passages.text: The Master told this concerning the Elder Angulimala, the blood-stained robber whom he converted without violence: "I also tamed him when I was living in a previous stage of existence." Of old, king Koravya reigned in Indapatta of the Kuru country, and the Bodhisatta was born his son, Sutasoma, sent with one hundred and one princes to the same world-famed teacher; Sutasoma, senior pupil, took prince Brahmadatta of Benares for his private pupil, and on parting bade them all keep the Uposatha vows and abstain from taking life on the new- and full-moon days. But the king of Benares never ate his rice meal without meat; when the palace dogs ate the meat kept for a fast-day, the cook, fearing death, served flesh cut from a corpse in the cemetery, and the king, thrilled to the seven thousand nerves of taste—human flesh had been his food as a yakkha in the birth before—commanded the cook to furnish it always: first from the prisons, then by a baited purse of a thousand pieces, then by murdering passers-by at the night-watches. Caught at last with his basket of flesh, the cook accused his master before commander-in-chief Kalahatthi, and the king confessed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 537 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: "Sire, do not this thing; eat not the flesh of men... if you do not cease from it, you will destroy both yourself and your realm." The commander told him of the monster fish Ananda, who tasted one of the fish that paid him court and then devoured his subjects until, madness and hunger driving him, he seized his own tail and was eaten piecemeal by the fish he had spared; but the king answered with his own examples—the lad who died for want of a third rose-apple, the brahmin's son ruined by a first taste of liquor, the gentleman who pined away crying for an Apsarā—and the golden geese who, eating the eggs, goslings and flesh of their own kin through a five-month rain, grew so feeble that the cave-spider sucked their blood one by one till their family was extinct. The citizens rose and would hear nothing: "Have him expelled from his kingdom." The king begged only his sword, his cooking vessel and his cook, and went into the forest, where he waylaid travellers, crying "Here am I, the man-eating robber!"—till he killed even the cook who failed him, and lived alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 537 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: A wealthy brahmin's caravan paid for convoy through the forest, yet the man-eater seized him from his white-oxen carriage and carried him off head downward, lamed by an acacia splinter. At the foot of his banyan tree he prayed the tree-nymph: heal my wound within seven days and I will sacrifice the blood and inwards of a hundred and one princes of all India. His wound healed, his old comrade of yakkha days taught him a spell of strength and wind-swift speed, and within seven days he found and captured a hundred and one kings, hanging them by cords through their pierced palms on the banyan tree. But Sutasoma he spared—"Sutasoma was my private teacher: let not India be altogether desolate"—and when he lit the fire and sat sharpening the stake, the tree-nymph, fearing the coming slaughter, sought the Four Great Kings and Sakka, who could not stop him but named the one who could: prince Sutasoma of Indapatta. Disguised as an ascetic, she let herself be chased three leagues, stood fast at the word "Stand!"—"I am standing; do you too try and stand"—revealed herself blazing in the sky, and counseled: bid him first bring Sutasoma, then offer his sacrifice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 537 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

passages.text: Learning by the stars when Sutasoma would bathe in the royal tank, the man-eater lurked in the water and took him from the midst of his army. "I weep not for myself or wife or child or realm," said the prince, "but for a promise: once to a brahmin I my word did plight; that word I fain would keep, and then, my honour saved, return to thee." "No man escaped from death returns to his foe," laughed the robber, till Sutasoma swore a kshatriya's oath and the man-eater let him go. Sutasoma heard the four stanzas the brahmin Nanda had brought from Kassapa Buddha, and went back with death written on his forehead. Awestruck, the man-eater begged to hear them, and offered a boon for each stanza; the prince chose: long life for the man-eater himself; the hundred kings not eaten; each king restored to his realm; and abstinence from human flesh. The ogre wept and yielded at last, bowing at the prince's feet and taking the five moral laws at his hands; the deities of earth roared applause, and the man-eater went with Sutasoma and loosed the kings. Of old the Master, as Sutasoma, tamed this man-eater.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 537 (Chalmers 1901); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tree-wife and the Spitting Trail
title.zh: 樹妻與唾沫之徑

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 67 'The Tree-wife' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: A childless hunter wishes a pretty Jessamy tree into a wife, clothes her, and lives with her until another man inveigles her away. Fleeing, she spits at every half-mile of the two-mile road; the abandoned husband sings the Maroon Koromanti death-song at each spitting-place, the spits answer him, and the trail of answers leads him to the door where he takes his wife home again.
summary.zh: 無子的獵人許願美麗的素馨樹化為妻子，為其穿衣、成家；後被他人誘拐。逃亡路上，她在兩哩間每半哩吐一口唾沫；被棄的丈夫在每一處唾沫地唱起馬倫人的科羅曼蒂喪歌，唾沫竟一一應聲——循聲而至，他把妻子領回了家。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale; the Koromanti death-song (Maroon burial song) is quoted in the source as sung at burials — noted here as cultural context, not reproduced verbatim.

passages.text: It was a man who had no wife and was a hunter-man; he hunted in the bush all day. One day he went into the bush and shot, and coming home he saw a pretty tree called Jessamy — 'O me biddy boy, that is a pretty tree!' He said, 'If this tree could turn a wife to me, I would like to be married to her!' And so it was: the tree turned a wife for him. The woman was naked; he left her at the spot, went home, got clothing for her, dressed her up nicely and carried her home to his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 67 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He and the woman stayed a long time, until one day he went out to the bush to shoot and slept out; another man came and inveigled his wife and took her away to his house. When the poor man came home from the bush the next day, he could not find his wife. The frightened woman, leaving one house for the next about two miles off, spat all the way until she got to the other man's house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 67, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The man was in a rage that he could not find his wife and did not know what to do. He sang the Koromanti death-song, the song always used by the Maroons at a burial — 'Jesta be-yo, eh, eh, eh, o! Jesta be-yo, a wi' die-o...' — and at every place where the woman spat, the spit answered him. He went and stood at each stopping-place of half a mile until the two miles were passed; and just as the woman heard the voice of the man, she stood at the door-mouth and saw that the man was coming. The man took his wife and carried her right back to the home yard. Jack man dora, choose none!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 67, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Sammy the Comferee Melted on the Iron Rod
title.zh: 康菲里小哥在鐵桿上熔盡

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 68 'Sammy the Comferee' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Sammy's stray arrow lands in Massa Jesus's yard; the wife detains the beautiful boy all day until rain soaks the Master's washing, and scolds her husband that Sammy is prettier than the Maker of him. Massa Jesus heats an iron rod red-hot and orders the boy to climb it; Sammy melts leg by leg, singing his farewell song — 'Ah, me Sammy de Con-fa-ri-a-e-ro, Gi-ra no, ah, in din ro' — and all the pretty men born into the world thereafter get some of his fat; the ugly ones get none.
summary.zh: 小哥的箭誤落耶穌先生院中；其妻扣留美少年整日，直到大雨淋濕晾曬的衣物，還向丈夫抱怨小哥比自己造物者更俊。耶穌先生把鐵桿燒得通紅，命其攀爬；小哥一節節熔化，唱著告別之歌——『啊，我是康菲里小哥，吉拉諾……』——此後世上所有俊美的男子都分得他的一點脂膏；醜陋者分毫不沾。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale with syncretic Christian frame ('Massa Jesus'); folk-comic use of scripture names, transcribed from named tellers.

passages.text: A woman had one son, a boy very unruly, who had nothing to do but fire bow and arrow all day. One day he fired the arrow and it dropped into Massa Jesus's yard. He went in to pick it up; Massa Jesus was gone out, but the wife was in the yard, and all the clothes were sunning out of doors. She detained the boy in the yard the whole day until the rain came and wet up all Massa Jesus's clothes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 68 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Massa Jesus came in wet, wanting dry clothes and finding none, he asked his wife what she had been doing all day. She answered that as Sammy the Comferee was in the house, that was why the clothes got wet — and when Massa Jesus pressed her, she replied that if he had been as pretty as Sammy the Comferee, she would have done more. 'I know I made Sammy the Comferee,' said Massa Jesus, 'and if Sammy the Comferee is prettier than me, I will see about it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 68, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Massa Jesus put up an iron rod, hot as fire, hot until it was red, and sent for Sammy the Comferee. He ordered the boy to climb the iron rod, and Sammy commenced to melt away, singing — 'Ah, me Sammy de Con-fa-ri-a-e-ro, Gi-ra no, ah, in din ro!' — he melted off to his leg, sang again, melted to his middle, to his hand, to his neck, and sang again until he melted off to nothing. When you look at the iron rod, a whole heap of fat is heaped up about it: all the pretty men that come into the world get some of Sammy the Comferee's fat, but the ugly ones don't get none of it. Jack man dory, me story done!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 68, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Grandy Beard-o and the Bull Who Didn't Care
title.zh: 大奶奶碧兒多與無畏的公牛

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 69a 'Grandy-Do-an'-Do' (told by Moses Hendricks, Mandeville)

summary.en: The rich witch Grandy Beard-o feeds no one who cannot name her. A hungry captive girl is sent for water past each separated pasture; cow, mule and horse fear to speak, but the mighty bull bawls the name aloud. Fed and freed, the girl inherits the estate when the old lady, tracking the telltale pasture by pasture, is tossed leg by leg, arm by arm, and finally by the neck into the air — which is why the land goes from hand to hand in legacy up to today.
summary.zh: 富有的女巫大奶奶碧兒多只餵能道出她名字的人。被扣的飢餓女孩穿過一座座隔離牧場去取水；牛、騾、馬皆不敢言，唯公牛大聲吼出其名。女孩吃飽獲釋；老太婆逐場追問洩密者，卻被公牛一次次拋向空中——先斷雙腿，再斷雙臂，最後斷頸——所以至今田產仍一代代易手相傳。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale (hidden-name witch type, ATU 500-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was an old woman, a witch, very wealthy, who lived quite to herself — plenty of stock, horses, cows, sheep, mules, each kind kept in a separate pasture. The old lady's name was Grandy Beard-o, but nobody knew that name. She wanted someone to sup with her, took home a little girl, prepared a meal — and said, 'Unless you tell me my name, I will not give you anything to eat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: She sent the girl out to fetch water through all the pastures, and the girl went along crying, being hungry. In the cow-pasture the cow asked what was the matter, and heard it — the old lady would give nothing to eat unless the girl could tell her name — but Cow was afraid to tell her. The mule wouldn't tell her; the horse wouldn't tell her. In the bull pasture, Bull said, 'Cho! when you go home, tell her her name, Grandy Beard-o' — Bull was a mighty man; he didn't care!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl hastened home glad to get food at last: 'Your name is Grandy Beard-o, ma'am.' The old lady, indignant, gave her a good feed, then started to find who told her — cow, horse: 'A ring ding ding, mamma, ring ding ding; no me tell.' In the bull pasture Bull confessed — 'Damme, me tell 'm!' She gripped the bull and tossed him in the air; he dropped unhurt. The bull tossed her now; she dropped, one leg broken. Toss for toss, her legs, then her arms broke, until the last toss the bull made — her neck broke. That was the end of her. The girl became mistress of all she possessed, and that is why the land goes from hand to hand in legacy up to today.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Grandy Do-an'-Do and the Singing Crab
title.zh: 大奶奶杜安杜與唱歌的螃蟹

region.en: Malvern, Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山莫爾文

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 69b (told by Julia Gentle, Malvern, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: A very bad woman sends her only daughter for river water with a name-riddle death-threat. The forgetful girl is returned empty twice; the second time the Crab tells her to sing the answer all the way home — 'Your name is Grandy-do-an-do' — and the maddened witch travels the pastures interrogating Cow, Sheep, Horse, Duck and Crab, machete in hand. The Crab owns the truth, sinks into his hole, and stays in the hole till now.
summary.zh: 惡婆遣獨女取水，以名字之謎相威脅。健忘的女孩兩度空手而回；第二次螃蟹教她一路唱回家——『你叫大奶奶杜安杜』。惡婆大怒，持彎刀遍訪牛、羊、馬、鴨、蟹追問洩密者；螃蟹認下實情，沉入洞中，至今仍在洞裡。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale, paired variant of the hidden-name cycle. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A very bad woman had only one daughter, and said, 'Go to the river for water, and when you come back, if you cannot tell my name, I will destroy you.' Going for water she saw Crab, who asked where she was going: 'Grandy sent me to the river for water and said when I come back, if I cannot tell his name, she will kill me.' The Crab told her, 'When you go, tell her that her name is Grandy Do-an-do.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she came back she had forgotten the name, and the old woman dashed away the water and sent her back. Going again, the Crab said, 'Sing it all the way!' So the girl went back singing, 'You name Grandy-do-an-do! You name Grandy-do-an-do!' The woman, mad when she heard it, traveled and met Cow — 'You Cow, did you tell the girl my name Grandy Do-an-do?' — 'No, no, me tell him so, you name Grandy Do-an-do!' Sheep said the same; Horse said the same; Duck said the same.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69b, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: She met Crab: 'You Crab, did you tell the girl my name Grandy Do-an-do?' — and Crab said, 'Yes, it is me who told him your name is Grandy Do-an-do!' She took the machete and chopped after the Crab, and Crab sank into the hole and stayed in the hole till now.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 69b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Jack and Harry: Four Kind Strangers and the Boy Who Ruins Them
title.zh: 傑克與哈利：四位恩人與敗事的孩子

region.en: Dry River, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地乾河

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 70 'Jack and Harry' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: In the cool morning the brothers beg coffee from an old man in the watch-house — Jack drinks the host's own cup and both flee. Hen, poor lady, and carencro each shelter them in turn; at each rescue Jack ruins it — popping the hen's wing, choking the lady, popping the carencro's wing — until the brothers knock themselves senseless, meet a land turtle, and Jack cuts off the head that Harry had called out of its shell.
summary.zh: 清早兄弟倆向守屋老人討咖啡——傑克卻把主人那杯也喝了，二人被追而逃。母雞、老婦、兀鷹先後施救；每次傑克都親手毀局——彈雞翅、掐老婦、彈鷹翅——直到二人摔得昏迷。醒來遇陸龜；哈利剛喚出其頭，傑克一刀斫下。

sensitivity.note: Folk tale (ungrateful-brother type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Jack and Harry were going out for a walk. The morning was cool, and they came to an old man in a watch-house. Harry said, 'Old Massa, beg you a little coffee if you have any.' He said, 'Yes, me pickney!' and gave Jack a cup of coffee and Harry a cup. The old man had not drunk his own coffee yet when Jack said, 'Harry, I gwine drink the old man's coffee.' Harry said no; Jack took the old man's coffee and drank it, and the old man took his stick after them and they ran.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 70 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Running, they saw a hen with some chickens. 'Do, me good hen, cover me with your wing!' — and she covered them like her own chicks; the old man came after, saw nothing, turned back. 'I gwine pop the hen wing,' said Jack, and popped it — the hen fluttered after them. They ran to a poor lady standing in the way, who covered them with her coat; Jack said, 'I gwine choke the old lady' — and as he choked her, she shook them out and ran after them. Then a carencro (crow) took them both up on its wing, flying right up into the sky — 'I gwine pop the carencro wing, mek him drop' — and as they dropped, they knocked themselves out of their senses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 70, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came to themselves, a land turtle was coming. Harry called to it kindly, and as it shoved out its head, Jack cut off the head with his knife — so the two boys, who had spoiled every kindness shown them on the road, ended the day by taking the one quiet stranger that offered no shelter and asking nothing back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 70, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Pea-fowl as Messenger
title.zh: 孔雀傳信

region.en: Maroon Town and Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮與聖克魯斯山

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 71 'Pea-fowl as Messenger' (a, Matilda Hall; b, Oliver D. Witter)

summary.en: Summoned to a lying-in, the midwife auditions the household for a messenger able to sing a man's name — cock, dog and puss fail; the pea-fowl, paid a quart of corn, flies miles singing 'You John Studee, for me master!' until the gambler hears his name from a house-top and rides home, hanging his gold chain on the bird's neck — which is why the peacock wears golden feathers there. In the paired tale the same errand ends in pecked baldness for Bra Peacock and a lump of gold for a head.
summary.zh: 產婦臨盆喚夫，接生婆逐一試鳥——雞、狗、貓皆不能名；孔雀受賄一夸脫玉米，飛行數哩高唱『約翰·斯圖迪，我主人在哪！』賭徒聞名歸家，把金鏈掛上鳥頸——孔雀頸上金羽由此而來。另一版本：同一差事卻以孔雀被啄禿頭、頭頂金塊收場。

sensitivity.note: Etiological bird tales. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The husband and wife were married people, and the husband a great gambler, never at home with the wife — until the wife was going to have a baby, and the ninth month came. They sent for the midwife; when she came there was no husband in. She wanted someone to go call the husband, John Studee. She called for the fowl, a cock: 'What will you say to call the husband?' The cock crew 'Ko ku ru ku-u-u!' — 'You won't do.' The dog said 'Hoo-oh!' — 'No, won't do.' Puss said 'Me-oo!' — 'Won't do.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 71a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then she called for the pea-fowl and provided a quart of corn, asking what he would say. Pea-fowl sang, 'You John Studee, you John Studee, fe me master John Studee! There's a pretty gal from Silo, there's a handsome gal from Silo, want the care of a new John bwoy — it almost deh!' — 'Yes, you'll do!' When the pea-fowl flew miles off and did not see the master, he took up the quart of corn and flew away; then he pitched on a house-top and sang his song again. The people said John Studee had been there but had just gone away — that great gambler! He flew another mile off and sang from another great house-top, and John Studee came: 'Who calls my name?' He took up the fowl, got the buggy in haste, took the gold chain from his neck and put it on the pea-fowl — the pea-fowl has the golden feathers round his neck on account of that chain. When the feather came home, the baby was born and named John Studee after him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 71a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired version, Miss Nancy's husband Contavio locked her up when he went to market. Hungry, she begged Sheep, then Billy-goat, to call him for a lump of gold — 'No, my dear, that will not do.' Then Bra Peacock flew right away until he saw Contavio, pecked him in his head and picked off all the feathers, and spurred him the whole way home until all Bra Peacock's spurs dropped off. When he got Contavio home, Miss Nancy flung the lump of gold on Bra Peacock's head — that is why the feathers on a peacock's head look like gold, why it has no spurs, and why a crow has no feathers on its head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 71b 'Contavio' (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Barking Puppy and the Phinney Man
title.zh: 吠叫的小狗與菲尼人

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 72 'The Barking Puppy' (told by Alfred Williams, Maroon Town)

summary.en: An old lady's nightly visitor is driven off by the barking puppy; she burns the dog in a big fire — and the ashes bark. Thrown into the river, they bark in the river; thrown into the sea, they hush. At last the gentleman comes in, draws a chair — 'So long I couldn't come on account of Dick and Dandy!' — says he is coming to marry her, sings back her own Phinney-man song, and tears her up to inch pieces: 'sometime shadow come back.'
summary.zh: 老婦的夜訪者屢被吠叫的小狗嚇退；她把狗燒了——灰燼卻仍吠。投入河中，河裡也吠；投入海中，方才安靜。紳士終於登門，拉椅而坐：『這麼久來不了，都是因為迪克和丹迪！』自稱要娶她，還回唱她的菲尼人之歌——隨後把她撕成碎片：影子，有時是會回來的。

sensitivity.note: Duppy-romance tale with violent ending, told as wake-night entertainment. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was an old lady living at home with one little puppy, and every night a gentleman came to pay her a visit; but the little puppy snapped and barked, and he had to turn back. The old lady caught the puppy and made up a big fire and burned the puppy. Next night the gentleman came back again, and the old lady sang her song — 'Heah, heah, Phinney man, heah, oh, heah, Phinney man; nobody heah, Phinney man, Dick and Dandy heah!' — and the ashes barked as the puppy. The old lady got up, took up the ashes and dashed them in the river, saying the gentleman was going to pay her a visit and could not, because the ashes barked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 72 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next night the gentleman came back again and hollered 'Hulloo!'; the old lady sang, and the puppy ashes barked in the river — and the gentleman would not come. The old lady took the river water and dashed it in the sea to hinder Dick and Dandy from barking. Next night the gentleman came back for the last time; the old lady raised up and sang her song while the gentleman danced, came in now, drew a chair and said, 'So long I couldn't come on account of Dick and Dandy!' — and said, 'I coming to marry you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 72, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old lady said yes, but did not know but a dog shadow had come — sometime a shadow comes back. She sang her song again, and the gentleman caught the old lady and tore her up to inch pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 72, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Singing Bird and the Well
title.zh: 會唱歌的小鳥與水井

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 73 'The Singing Bird' (a, Alfred Williams, Maroon Town)

summary.en: The waiting-boy Collin pitches his master into a well at the water-stop and drives home alone with the buggy, reporting visits and delays. A little bird in the tree by the house sings the crime to the mistress — 'Fine waiting boy, fine waiting boy, throw his master into a well' — a sensible person is called to interpret the whistling, the well is searched, the body found, and Collin is hanged.
summary.zh: 車伕科林在取水處把主人推入井中，獨自驅車回家，謊稱主人訪友未歸。屋前樹上的小鳥把罪行唱給女主人聽——『好車伕，好車伕，把主人拋進井裡』——請來通鳥語者解其哨音，井中尋得屍身，科林被處絞刑。

sensitivity.note: Murder-revelation ballad-tale (singing bone type, ATU 780). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A gentleman had his servant, and one day he said to the servant, 'Collin, go and look about the horse harness, my buggy.' Collin harnessed the master's horse and put it in the buggy; the master drove on till he got to a well and said he wanted some water. 'Massa, there is a well down before.' While the massa sat against the well-side, Collin pitched his master into the well, turned back, and went halfway home with the buggy; when he got home the missus asked where the master was, and Collin said he was going to pay a visit and coming tomorrow — the buggy going to meet him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 73a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Collin went the next day with the buggy; back at the house again, the missus asked once more where the master was — 'Gone to pay a visit, won't be back till tomorrow.' When Collin was gone, another servant in the yard said, 'Missus, hear what the little bird is singing?' The missus came to the doorway and listened, and heard the little bird whistling: 'Fine waiting boy, fine waiting boy — throw his master into a well! Collin, Collin, no ben see dat little bird upon tree so long?' She could not understand it, called a sensible person to interpret the bird, went and searched the well, found the master's body — and took Collin and hanged him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 73a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Miss Grace, My Fair Lady
title.zh: 葛蕾絲小姐，我的美人

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 74 'Two Sisters' (told by Margaret Morris, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Servant Miss Grace marries her mistress-sister's Busha and bears his baby; the jealous Miss Wheel lures her to pick peas by the sea-ball and shoves her in, taking the baby as her own. Nights on, the dead woman returns to the lying Busha's doorstep, and only the little dog answers her litany — hand me my baby, my bowl, my comb, my clo'es — until the neighbors' pail-of-milk-and-hot-water trap revives her in the sheet, her testimony is heard, and Miss Wheel goes down the hill-side in a barrel bound for the lime-kiln fire.
summary.zh: 女僕葛蕾絲嫁給姐姐侍奉的監工，生下一子；善妒的惠爾小姐誘她到海蝕洞邊摘豌豆，把她推入水中，抱走嬰兒據為己有。此後夜夜，亡魂回到昏睡的丈夫門前，只有小狗應她的連禱——把我的孩子、我的碗、我的梳子、我的衣裳拿來——直到鄰居以奶桶與滾水之計在白布下還魂；她道出真相，惠爾小姐被裝桶滾下坡，送入石灰窯的火中。

sensitivity.note: Murdered-sister revenant tale (ATU 780-linked 'Two Sisters' type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Two sisters stayed in a house. One sister was servant to a Busha (overseer) in one pen, and arranged for the Busha to marry the other sister — Miss Grace, my fair lady; the older sister, Lady Wheel, served her sister. The Busha went to his work and never came back till midnight. One day when he was out, Miss Wheel called Miss Grace to go pick peas; taking a basket and the baby — Miss Grace my fair lady's baby — they picked peas around the sea-ball, where Miss Wheel made Miss Grace take off her dress and shoved her into the hole. She picked up the peas, came home, washed her breast with water, took the baby for herself, and when night came, suckled it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 74 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Busha came home midnight and was given dinner, but never noticed his wife at all; three days he kept coming and never noticed. When he asked for the servant he was told she was sent out to the common and would soon come. Warned by a neighbor that harm had been done in his house — told not even to drink cold water in the house that night — the Busha lay down at midnight seeming to doze, but not asleep. There was a little dog called Doggie, and Dog saw when the dead woman came.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 74, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The gentleman heard every word; the lady said it was nothing, not wanting the Busha to hear. The last night, the neighbors put up a pail of milk and a pail of hot water at the doorway covered with a sheet; the dead woman came and called out the same litany, took the baby and put it to bed, stepped in the hot water, pitched into the milk covered with the white sheet, was taken out and wrapped up — and she looked up with her eyes fixed. 'What do you, me dear?' — 'My sister shoved me down in the ball. She called me to go pick peas and shoved me in there.' When the gentleman found out his wife had been dead, he took Miss Wheel, built a lime-kiln, shipped her into a barrel, pitched it down the hill-side and rolled it into the fire. Jack man dora!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 74, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Asoonah, the Big-Skinned Thing
title.zh: 阿蘇那：大皮怪

region.en: Mandeville, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 75 'Asoonah' (told by Philipp Brown, Mandeville)

summary.en: Asoonah, a big-skinned thing that sinks a whole yard, invades the house daily in the mother's absence, interrogating the children — where is your mother, where the pretty little one, where the house with the guinea corn, where's the mortar — until the father guns it down in the gully. The king offers three hundred pounds to name the monstrous skin brought to his gate; the little boy lifts it — 'Eh! no Asoonah 'kin?' — and everybody, frightened, comes right out, and the boy works again with plenty of clothes.
summary.zh: 大皮怪阿蘇那能陷沒整座院落，趁母親外出日日光臨，盤問孩子們——你母親何在、漂亮的小的何在、有玉米的房子何在、石臼何在——直到父親在溝壑中一槍擊斃。國王懸賞三百鎊辨認那張拖到王門前的巨皮；小男孩一舉——『咦！這不就是阿蘇那的皮？』——眾人嚇得四散，男孩得賞，穿新衣重操舊業。

sensitivity.note: Monster-slayer tale. 'Asoonah' is an unidentified large animal in Beckwith's cycle (cf. tale 75 note). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Asoonah is a big-skin thing; when it comes into your yard it will sink the whole place. One day the lady left her three children out and went to work; this Asoonah came in every day, and the children knew what time it was coming — and it asked the small one, 'Where is your mother?' — 'Gone a washing-day.' — 'Where is the pretty little one?' — 'Inside the room.' — 'Where the house with the guinea corn?' and it hollered, 'Where is the mortar?' — 'Inside the kitchen.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 75 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day when the mother came, the children said, 'Every day a big thing comes in here and can't tell what is what.' The mother said to the husband, 'You better stop and see what comes here in the daytime.' He got the gun and went up into the kitchen loft and sat; when he saw Asoonah come, it was so big he got frightened and dodged behind the door, but as it reached the gully he fired the gun and Asoonah fell down in the gully and broke its neck.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 75, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king heard about this Asoonah but couldn't tell what it was; he said anybody who could come in and tell what it was would get three hundred pounds. The little boy heard about it and was so torn up about it. The old lady keeping a jooty at the king's gate said, 'What way is Asoonah 'kin going to be brought in here today?' When the king asked everybody and nobody could tell, he called up the little boy; the boy went to take it up, and the king asked him if he knew what it was. He held it up like this and said, 'Eh! no Asoonah 'kin?' Everybody got frightened and came right out, and the king offered the boy three hundred pounds, gave him plenty of clothes, and got the boy to work again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 75, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Greedy Child at the Devil's Ford
title.zh: 貪心孩子與魔鬼渡口

region.en: Mandeville and Maroon Town, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加曼德維爾與馬倫鎮

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 76 'The Greedy Child' (a, George Barrett; b, Philipp Brown)

summary.en: The old ferryman takes breakfast from every child he carries but one — and drowns the refuser, singing up and down the rising water until the mother pays two pounds. In the paired Devil tale, the safe pass-phrase is 'no one go s'y, no two go s'y, no three go s'y, but it go s'y for him mamma' — and the greedy little sister, stuffing herself with the ferryman's plantain, repeats it wrong, is caught over the hill, carried to the river and killed; from that day the Devil's hair came off at the sea-side, and the sea got moss.
summary.zh: 老渡工向每個渡河的孩子討早飯，唯獨一個不給——他便淹死她，任水位隨歌聲一寸寸上漲，直到母親付兩鎊。魔鬼篇：通關口訣是『沒有一個過路、沒有兩個過路、沒有三個過路，只有他為媽媽過路』——貪嘴的小妹吃了渡口的芭蕉，把口訣念岔，被捉過山、拖到河邊殺害；從那天起，魔鬼在海邊掉了頭髮，海裡便生了苔。

sensitivity.note: Paired cautionary tales (river-toll and password types). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: The children were going to school, and every day the old man took them over the river. The old man asked some of them for breakfast; all the children gave him some but one. He appointed a day to come, and said he wanted something from her, and she would not give it. When she was coming back, the river came down; he took over the rest of the children and would not take over that one. The little boy sang, 'Mudder Galamo, I gwine dead today!' — and every time he sang, the water came up a little higher, while the mother was coming. The old man said, 'I must have two pounds'; she said all right, and took him over — and from that day he offered the old man breakfast every day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 76a 'Crossing the River' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Every night the Debbil went out; coming in he said, 'Wife, I scent fresh blood!' — 'No, me husband, no fresh blood here!' It was the wife's sisters who came looking for her. Every night when the Debbil was coming in, the wife knew and put the sister into a barrel. At daylight he went back over the river; the sister was given a plantain and told that when she reached the hill she would see the Debbil sitting right over it, and he would say, 'Go s'y (go your way), madame?' — and she must say, 'No one go s'y, no two go s'y, no three go s'y, but it go s'y for him mamma,' and the Debbil would let her pass.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 76b 'The Plantain' (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was a little small sister, and she was greedy. When the Debbil came in the night he smelled fresh blood; the wife denied it. At daylight the sister sent the little girl away and gave her a plantain; on the hill the Debbil said, 'Go s'y?' — and the little girl, so greedy now, said, 'No, go s'y for mamma, no one go s'y...' — and the Debbil caught her over the hill, carried her right over to the river and killed her. And from that day the Debbil's hair came off at the sea-side; and from that, the sea got moss.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 76b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Alimoty and Aliminty: the Swapped Frocks
title.zh: 阿莉莫蒂與阿莉明蒂：調換的衣裳

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 77 'Alimoty and Aliminty' (told by Julia Gentle, Santa Cruz Mountains)

summary.en: Jealous of the beloved niece Alimoty, the aunt contracts Lion to kill the girl in the red frock — and each night the frocks are swapped by the girls themselves, so Lion kills the aunt's own daughter, twice, until there are none. Sent to Lion's yard to be killed, Alimoty passes her dead mother's grave, drops the bottle of milk left there, and sings her fate — until the hunter Aliminty hears the voice, comes to the Lion's yard, and kills the Lion.
summary.zh: 嬸母妒忌人人喜愛的姪女阿莉莫蒂，約獅子誅殺穿紅裙者——女孩們夜夜自己調換衣裳，獅子兩次殺的都是嬸母的親生女兒，直至無女可殺。被送赴獅穴途中，阿莉莫蒂經過亡母墳前，失手跌落墓前留下的奶瓶，唱起自己的命運——獵人阿莉明蒂聞聲辨人，趕到獅穴誅獅。

sensitivity.note: Killed-through-swap tale (cruel stepmother type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: One day a lady had two daughters, but her sister had one; the sister's daughter was named Alimoty, and everybody loved Alimoty but nobody loved the lady's daughters. She went to the Lion and told him he must kill Alimoty for her. The Lion said she must put a red frock on Alimoty and a blue frock on her own daughter when they went to bed. After going to bed, the girl said, 'Cousin Alimoty, your red frock doesn't fit you; let us swap!' — and they swapped, and the Lion killed the lady's daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 77 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the lady told the Lion to kill Alimoty, whom everybody loved. 'Tonight you must sew the red frock on Alimoty and the blue frock on your daughter, and I come and kill her tonight.' When they went to bed they swapped again, and the Lion killed the lady's daughter — she had none now. The Lion said, 'Tomorrow send Alimoty to my yard; I will kill her.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 77, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Alimoty was going from the yard and her dead mother gave her a bottle of milk, which she dropped, and she ran off singing — 'Poor me, Alimoty, poor Alimoty, a me Dickie sahnie o-o, see me go long a wid two.' Aliminty was a hunter and heard the singing: 'That is Alimoty's voice!' He came to the Lion's yard and killed the Lion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 77, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: King Mu and the Sky-Palace of the Western Magician (Liezi)
title.zh: 周穆王西極化人，天上宮闕（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The magician's palace above the clouds (symbolic pin: Mount Tianshan, Xinjiang, China)
region.zh: 雲雨之上化人之宮（象徵定位：新疆天山）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: A magician from the far west, who could pass through fire and water and ride on thin air, treats King Mu of Chou to a flight up to his own palace of gold, silver, pearls and jade towering above clouds and rain — then to a region where neither sun nor moon could be seen. When the King begs to return, the magician gives him a shove, and he wakes on his throne with the wine still full of sediment: we were only wandering about in the spirit.
summary.zh: 周穆王時，西極之國有化人來，入水火，貫金石，乘虛不墜——王與之同遊；化人宮中，金銀珠玉之府；覺而坐其所坐之處，酒未清，肴未朒。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the King Mu flight is the classic Taoist otherworld-voyage, cross-linked to the chinese tradition's Mu Wang record. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: In the time of King Mu of Chou, there was a magician who came from a kingdom in the far west. He could pass through fire and water, penetrate metal and stone, overturn mountains and make rivers flow backwards, transplant whole towns and cities, ride on thin air without falling, encounter solid bodies without being obstructed. There was no end to the countless variety of changes and transformations which he could effect; and, besides changing the external form, he could also spirit away men's internal cares.

So the King clutched the magician's sleeve, and soared up with him higher and higher into the sky, until at last they stopped, and lo! they had reached the magician's own palace. This palace was built with beams of gold and silver, and incrusted with pearls and jade. It towered high above the region of clouds and rain, and the foundations whereon it rested were unknown. It appeared like a stupendous cloud-mass to the view. The King verily believed that he was in the Halls of Paradise, tenanted by God Himself, and that he was listening to the mighty music of the spheres.

When he awoke to consciousness, he found himself sitting on his throne just as before, with the selfsame attendants round him. He looked at the wine in front of him, and saw that it was still full of sediment; he looked at the viands, and found that they had not yet lost their freshness. ... "Your Majesty and I," replied the magician, "were only wandering about in the spirit, and, of course, our bodies never moved at all. What essential difference is there between that sky-palace we dwelt in and your Majesty's palace on earth, between the spaces we travelled through and your Majesty's own park?"

title.en: Life Is Really Illusion, Death Is Really Evolution (Liezi)
title.zh: 生者，假借也；死者，歸人也（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The venerable Yin Wen's inner apartment (symbolic pin: Qi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 尹文先生之室（象徵定位：齊，今山東）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: Lao Ch'êng Tzŭ studies magic under the venerable Yin Wen for three years; the old teacher quotes Lao Tzŭ's western journey: all that has the breath of life is mere Illusion — only one who knows that Life is really Illusion and Death is really Evolution can begin to learn magic from me. Returning home, Lao Ch'êng Tzŭ gains the power of appearing or disappearing at will but never makes public display of his art.
summary.zh: 老成子學幻於尹文先生——盡幻者之數——窮神知化，德之盛也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Long ago, when Lao Tzu was setting out on his journey to the West, he addressed me and said: 'All that has the breath of life, all that possesses bodily form, is mere Illusion. The point at which creation begins, the change effected by the Dual Principles -- these are called respectively Life and Death. That which underlies the manifold workings of Destiny is called Evolution; that which produces and transforms bodily substance is called Illusion. The Creator's ingenuity is mysterious, His operations secret and profound. In truth, He is inexhaustible and eternal.

Only one who knows that Life is really Illusion, and that Death is really Evolution, can begin to learn magic from me. You and I are both illusions. How are we, then, to make a study of the subject? ... Lao Ch'eng Tsu returned home, and for three months pondered deeply over the words of the Venerable Yin Wen. Subsequently, he had the power of appearing or disappearing at will; he could reverse the order of the four seasons, produce thunderstorms in winter and ice in summer, make flying things creep and creeping things fly. But to the end of his days he never made any public display of his art.

title.en: King by Night, Slave by Day (Liezi)
title.zh: 尹氏老役夫，晝為僕，夜為君（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: Mr. Yin's estate in Chou (symbolic pin: Luoyang, Henan, China)
region.zh: 周尹氏之莊（象徵定位：河南洛陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: The old servant of Mr. Yin, worked mercilessly all day, dreams every night that he is a king enthroned in authority — my happiness is beyond compare, so what have I to grumble at? Mr. Yin himself, full of worldly cares, dreams every night that he is another man's servant, until his friend explains the proper balance in human destiny.
summary.zh: 周之尹氏大治產，其下趣役者侵晨昏而弗息——役夫曰：吾晝為人僕，吾夜為人君；樂樂孰加焉？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was one old servant in particular whose physical strength had quite left him, yet his master worked him all the harder. All day long he was groaning as he went about his work, and when night came he was reeling with fatigue and would sleep like a log. His spirit was then free to wander at will, and every night he dreamt that he was a king, enthroned in authority over the multitude, and controlling the affairs of the whole State. He took his pleasure in palaces and belvederes, following his own fancy in everything, and his happiness was beyond compare.

In the daytime I am only a slave, it is true, and my misery cannot be gainsaid. But by night I am a king, and my happiness is beyond compare. So what have I to grumble at?" ... Every night he dreamt that he was another man's servant, running about on menial business of every description, and subjected to every possible kind of abuse and ill-treatment. ... "If at night you dream that you are a servant and exchange ease for affliction, that is only the proper balance in human destiny. What you want is that your dreams should be as pleasant as your waking moments. But that is beyond your power to compass."

title.en: The Wood-Cutter, the Dream-Deer, and the Magistrate (Liezi)
title.zh: 鄭人獲鹿，薪者夢鹿（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The fuel-wood path of Chêng (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄭國薪樵之塗（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: A wood-cutter kills a deer, hides it in a dry ditch, and forgets the spot — becoming convinced it was all a dream. A hearer finds the deer; his wife declares it must be his own dream that has come true. The wood-cutter, dreaming that night of the real hiding-place, recovers it, and the magistrate divides the deer between them: you began by really killing a deer, but wrongly thought it was a dream.
summary.zh: 鄭人有薪於野者，遇駭鹿，御而擊之，斃之；藏諸隍中——遽而失其處，遂以為夢。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the dream-deer lawsuit became the classic Chinese dream-paradox tale. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: A man was gathering fuel in the Cheng State when he fell in with a deer that had been startled from its usual haunts. He gave chase, and succeeded in killing it. He was overjoyed at his good luck; but, for fear of discovery, he hastily concealed the carcass in a dry ditch, and covered it up with brushwood. Afterwards, he forgot the spot where he had hidden the deer, and finally became convinced that the whole affair was only a dream. He told the story to people he met as he went along; and one of those who heard it, following the indications given, went and found the deer.

"Once upon a time," he said to his wife, "a wood-cutter dreamt that he had got a deer, but couldn't remember the place where he had put it. Now I have found the deer, so it appears that his dream was a true dream." "On the contrary," said his wife, "it is you who must have dreamt that you met a wood-cutter who had caught a deer. Here you have a deer, true enough. But where is the wood-cutter? It is evidently your dream that has come true."

So the next morning, in accordance with his dream, he went to seek him out in order to recover the deer. A quarrel ensued, and the matter was finally brought before the magistrate, who gave judgment in these terms: "You began by really killing a deer, but wrongly thought it was a dream. Then you really dreamt that you had got the deer, but wrongly took the dream to be a reality. ... Meanwhile, here is the deer itself in court, and you had better divide it between you." The question was referred to the Prime Minister: "If you want to distinguish between waking and dreaming, you would have to go back to the Yellow Emperor or Confucius. But both these sages are dead, and there is nobody now alive who can draw any such distinction."

title.en: Yang-li Hua-tzŭ's Blessed Amnesia (Liezi)
title.zh: 秦人逢氏子有忘疾，楊里華子（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The Sung State (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋國（今河南商丘）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: Yang-li Hua-tzŭ of Sung is afflicted in middle age by amnesia; fortune-tellers, wizards, and physicians all fail, until the learned professor from Lu shuts himself up seven days alone with the patient — whereupon the disease disappears. And Hua-tzŭ flies into a rage: preservation and destruction, gain and loss, sorrow and joy have begun to throw out their myriad tentacles to invade my peace — oh! if I could but recapture a short moment of that blessed oblivion!
summary.zh: 宋陽里華子，中年病忘——魯儒生能治之；既愈，大怒曰：曩吾忘也，蕩蕩然——今往事之是非，哀樂嗜欲得喪，相與繆刺之若此。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yang-li Hua-tzu, of the Sung State, was afflicted in middle age by the disease of amnesia. Anything he received in the morning he had forgotten by the evening; anything he gave away in the evening he had forgotten the next morning. Out-of-doors, he forgot to walk; indoors, he forgot to sit down. ... Fortune-tellers were summoned, but their divinations proved unsuccessful; wizards were sought out, but their exorcisms were ineffectual; physicians were called in, but their remedies were of no avail.

Then, one fine morning, the treatment came to an end, and, wonderful to relate, the disease of so many years' standing had entirely disappeared! No sooner had Hua-tzu regained his senses, however, than he flew into a great rage, drove his wife out of doors, beat his sons, and, snatching up a spear, hotly pursued the professor through the town. "Lately, when I was steeped in forgetfulness, my senses were so benumbed that I was quite unconscious of the existence of the outer world. But now I have been brought suddenly to a perception of the events of half a lifetime. Preservation and destruction, gain and loss, sorrow and joy, love and hate have begun to throw out their myriad tentacles to invade my peace. Oh! if I could but recapture a short moment of that blessed oblivion!"

title.en: The Old Man of Yen Who Wept for a Hoaxed Homeland (Liezi)
title.zh: 燕人生於燕，長於楚（列子周穆王篇）

region.en: The road from Ch'u to Yen (symbolic pin: Beijing, China)
region.zh: 楚適燕之塗（象徵定位：北京）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book III (Dreams)

summary.en: A man born in Yen and brought up in Ch'u returns to his native country in old age; his fellow-travellers hoax him through the Chin State — the capital of Yen! your village altar! your ancestors' tomb! — until he weeps aloud, then they laugh: this is only the Chin State. When he really does see the city and altars of Yen, his emotion is much less acute.
summary.zh: 燕人生於燕，長於楚，及老而還本國——過晉國，同行者誑之：此燕國之城、先人之廬、先人之壟——燕人大哭；眾人皆大笑。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was once a man who, though born in Yen, was brought up in Ch'u, and it was only in his old age that he returned to his native country. On the way thither, as they were passing through the Chin State, his fellow-travellers played a practical joke on him. They pointed to the city and said: "Here is the capital of the Yen State;" whereupon the old man flushed with excitement. Pointing out a certain shrine, they told him that it was his own village altar, and he heaved a deep sigh. They showed him a house, and said: "This is where your ancestors lived;" and the tears welled up in his eyes.

Finally, they brought him in front of a mound and said: "This is the tomb where your ancestors lie buried." The old man could control himself no longer, and wept aloud. But his fellow-travellers burst into roars of laughter. "We have been hoaxing you," they cried; "this is only the Chin State." Their victim was greatly mortified; and when they arrived at their journey's end, and he really did see before him the city and altars of Yen, with the actual abode and tombs of his ancestors, his emotion was much less acute.

title.en: Confucius and the True Sage in the West (Liezi)
title.zh: 西方之人有聖者焉（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: The court of the Shang minister (symbolic pin: Anyang, Henan, China)
region.zh: 商太宰之廷（象徵定位：河南安陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: A high official from Shang quizzes Confucius on the sages — the Three Kings, Five Emperors, Three Sovereigns — and gets the same 'I do not know that they were sages.' Confucius changes countenance: among the people of the West a true sage dwells — he governs not, yet there is no disorder; he speaks not, yet he is naturally trusted; so great and incomprehensible is he that the people can find no name to call him by.
summary.zh: 商太宰問於孔子：三王、五帝、三皇皆聖乎？孔子曰：西方之人有聖者焉——不治而不亂，不言而自信，不化而自行，蕩蕩乎民無能名焉。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the 'true sage in the West' passage later attracted the Jesuit reading as an allusion to Christ. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: A high official from Shang paid a visit to Confucius. "You are a sage, are you not?" he inquired. "A sage!" replied Confucius. "How could I venture to think so? I am only a man of extensive learning and moral culture." The Minister then asked: "Were the Three Kings sages?" "The Three Kings," replied Confucius, "were great in the exercise of wisdom and courage. I do not know, however, that they were sages." "What of the Five Emperors? Were they not sages?" "The Five Emperors excelled in the exercise of altruism and righteousness. I do not know that they were sages." "And the Three Sovereigns: surely they were sages?" "The Three Sovereigns excelled in the virtues that were suited to their age. But whether they were sages or no I really cannot say."

The expression of Confucius' countenance changed, and he replied after a pause: "Among the people of the West a true sage dwells. He governs not, yet there is no disorder. He speaks not, yet he is naturally trusted. He makes no reforms, yet right conduct is spontaneous and universal. So great and incomprehensible is he that the people can find no name to call him by. I suspect that this man is a sage, but whether in truth he is a sage or is not a sage I do not know." The Minister from Shang meditated awhile in silence. Then he said to himself: "Confucius is making a fool of me!"

title.en: The Repulsive-Looking Nan-kuo Tzŭ (Liezi)
title.zh: 南郭子貌陋而心虛（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: Nan-kuo, Lieh Tzŭ's neighbourhood (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 南郭（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: Nan-kuo Tzŭ, Lieh Tzŭ's next-door neighbour of twenty years with whom no visit passed, turns out to be a repulsive-looking creature who gazes blankly, body and soul seeming not to belong together — yet he fraternises with the hindmost row of disciples. He who has reached the stage of thought is silent; he who uses silence in lieu of speech really does speak.
summary.zh: 子列子學於壺丘子林——南郭子貌陋，形若槁木；迎見而語——見同者形骸之外，不以鏡之於形骸。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Nan-kuo Tzu was his next-door neighbour, but for twenty years no visit passed between them, and when they met in the street they made as though they had not seen each other. ... Accordingly, forty of the disciples went with him to call on Nan-kuo Tzu, who turned out to be a repulsive-looking creature. He made no show of receiving his guests, but only gazed blankly at Lieh Tzu. Body and soul seemed not to belong together, and to be unable to respond to the stimuli of the external world.

Their Master Lieh Tzu said to them: "He who has reached the stage of thought is silent. He who has attained to perfect knowledge is also silent. He who uses silence in lieu of speech really does speak. He who for knowledge substitutes blankness of mind really does know. Without words and speaking not, without knowledge and knowing not, he really speaks and really knows. Saying nothing and knowing nothing, there is in reality nothing that he does not say, nothing that he does not know."

title.en: Lung Shu's Hollow Square Inch of Heart (Liezi)
title.zh: 龍叔謂文摯：心有七孔（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: The physician's chamber (symbolic pin: Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 文摯之室（象徵定位：山東臨淄）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: Lung Shu tells the master of cunning arts that praise and disgrace, gain and loss, life and death, riches and poverty excite him nothing — what disease is this? Wen Chih, facing the light, sees that a good square inch of Lung Shu's heart is hollow, six of its orifices open and only the seventh blocked: you are mistaking for a disease that which is really divine enlightenment.
summary.zh: 龍叔謂文摯曰：吾疾——譽不以為榮，毀不以為辱；得而不喜，失而弗憂——文摯曰：見子之心矣，方寸之地虛矣；幾聖人也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: "I hold it no honour," said Lung Shu, "to be praised in my native village, nor do I consider it a disgrace to be decried in my native State. Gain excites in me no joy, and loss no sorrow. I look upon life in the same light as death, upon riches in the same light as poverty, upon my fellow-men as so many swine, and upon myself as I look upon my fellow-men. I dwell in my home as though it were a mere caravanserai, and regard my native district with no more feeling than I would a barbarian State. Afflicted as I am in these various ways, honours and rewards fail to rouse me, pains and penalties to overawe me, good or bad fortune to influence me, joy or grief to move me."

Wen Chih replied by asking Lung Shu to stand with his back to the light, while he himself faced the light and looked at him intently. "Ah!" said he after a while, "I see that a good square inch of your heart is hollow. You are within an ace of being a true sage. Six of the orifices in your heart are open and clear, and only the seventh is blocked up. This, however, is doubtless due to the fact that you are mistaking for a disease that which is really divine enlightenment. It is a case in which my shallow art is of no avail."

title.en: Teng Hsi's Herd of Swine and the Retort of the Vassals (Liezi)
title.zh: 鄧析難伯豐子，如犬彘乎（列子仲尼篇）

region.en: Tung-li, in the Chêng State (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 鄧里（今河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book IV (Confucius)

summary.en: Teng Hsi the sophist greets the vassals of Po Feng Tzu with the sneer that those who receive sustenance from others through inability to support themselves are in the category of dogs and swine. One of the company retorts: it is really we who may be said to employ the Government authorities — only when there is a combination of technical knowledge and power can co-operative service exist. Teng Hsi could think of nothing to say in reply.
summary.zh: 鄧析顧其徒曰：為若受——子不能自給，受養於人，犬豕之類也。伯豐子之從者曰：齊楚之處士多為工焉——吾實謂役使君之臣者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Teng Hsi then turned to Po Feng Tzu. "Are you acquainted with the true theory of Sustentation?" he inquired. "To receive sustenance from others, through inability to support oneself, places one in the category of dogs and swine. It is man's prerogative to give sustenance to other creatures, and to use them for his own purposes. That you and your fellows are provided with abundant food and comfortable clothing is due to the Government. Young and old, you herd together, and are penned up like cattle destined for the shambles: in what respect are you to be distinguished from dogs and swine?"

One of his company, disregarding the rules of precedence, stepped forward and said: "Has your Excellency never heard of the variety of craftsmen in Ch'i and Lu? Some are skilled potters and carpenters, others are clever workers in metal and leather; there are good musicians, trained scribes and accountants, military experts and men learned in the ritual of ancestor-worship. All kinds of craftsmanship are there fully represented. Now, if there were no division of ranks and duties, mutual co-operation would be impossible. ... It is really we who may be said to employ the Government authorities. Why then should you pity us?" Teng Hsi could think of nothing to say in reply.

title.en: T'ang Asks Hsia Ko Whether Things Existed in the Beginning (Liezi)
title.zh: 殷湯問於夏革：古初有物乎？（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The court of T'ang of Yin (Anyang, Henan, China)
region.zh: 殷湯之廷（今河南安陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: In the beginnings of antiquity, did individual things exist? asks T'ang of Yin. If things did not exist then, how could they be in existence now? replies Hsia Ko — to the beginning and end of things there is no precise limit; beginning may be end, and end may be beginning; but when it comes to something outside matter in space or anterior to events in time, our knowledge fails us.
summary.zh: 殷湯問於夏革曰：古初有物乎？夏革曰：古初無物，今惡得物——物之始終，初無極已；始或為終，終或為始。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; a priority Creation & Cosmology dialogue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: T'ANG of Yin questioned Hsia Ko, saying: "In the beginnings of antiquity, did individual things exist?" "If things did not exist then," replied Hsia Ko, "how could they be in existence now? Or will the men of future ages be right in denying the existence of things at the present time?" "Things in that case," pursued T'ang, "have no before nor after?" Hsia Ko replied: "To the beginning and end of things there is no precise limit. Beginning may be end, and end may be beginning. How can we conceive of any fixed period to either?

But when it comes to something outside matter in space, or anterior to events in time, our knowledge fails us." "Then, upwards and downwards and in every direction space is a finite quantity?" Ko replied: "I do not know." T'ang asked the question again with more insistence, and Ko said: "It may be that space is infinite, or it may be that it is limited. How can I tell? But beyond infinity there must again exist non-infinity, and within the unlimited again that which is not unlimited.

title.en: The Outer Shell That Encloses Heaven and Earth (Liezi)
title.zh: 四海之外，六合之外（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The lands beyond the Four Seas (symbolic pin: Yantai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 四海之外（象徵定位：山東煙臺）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: What is there beyond the Four Seas? Just what there is here in the province of Ch'i — Hsia Ko travelled east to Ying and west to Pin and found the inhabitants nowise different. The lesser is always enclosed by a greater without ever reaching an end: heaven and earth, which enclose the myriad objects, are themselves enclosed in some outer shell that is infinite and immeasurable.
summary.zh: 四海之外奚若？曰：猶齊州也——大猶含小，終無窮已；天地含物之體，亦自含於太虛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: T'ang continued his inquiries, saying: "What is there beyond the Four Seas?" Ko replied: "Just what there is here in the province of Ch'i." "How can you prove that?" asked T'ang. "When travelling eastwards," said Ko, "I came to the land of Ying, where the inhabitants were nowise different from those in this part of the country. I inquired about the countries east of Ying, and found that they, too, were similar to their neighbour. Travelling westwards, I came to Pin, where the inhabitants were similar to our own countrymen. ... That is how I know that the regions within the Four Seas, the Four Wildernesses and the Four Uttermost Ends of the Earth are nowise different from the country we ourselves inhabit.

Thus, the lesser is always enclosed by a greater, without ever reaching an end. Heaven and earth, which enclose the myriad objects of creation, are themselves enclosed in some outer shell. Enclosing heaven and earth and the myriad objects within them, this outer shell is infinite and immeasurable. How do we know but that there is some mightier universe in existence outside our own? That is a question to which we can give no answer.

title.en: Nü Kua's Five-Coloured Stones and Kung Kung's Snapped Pillar (Liezi)
title.zh: 女媧鍊五色石補天，共工觸不周山（列子湯問篇）

region.en: Mount Pu-chou and the leaning heavens (mythic NW; symbolic pin: Jiayuguan, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 不周山（神話西北；象徵定位：甘肅嘉峪關）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: Heaven and earth are themselves only material objects, and therefore imperfect: Nü Kua of old fashioned many-coloured blocks of stone to repair the defective parts, and cut off the legs of the Ao to support the four corners of the heavens. Later, Kung Kung fought with Chuan Hsü for the throne and blundering in his rage against Mount Pu-chou, snapped the pillar which connects Heaven and earth — that is why Heaven dips downwards to the north-west, and why all rivers roll to the south-east.
summary.zh: 天地亦物也——女媧氏鍊五色石以補其闕，斷鼇足以立四極；共工氏與顓頊爭為帝，怒而觸不周之山，折天柱，絕地維。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the Nü Kua repair-myth cross-linked to the chinese tradition's Huainanzi record of the same story. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Heaven and earth, then, are themselves only material objects, and therefore imperfect. Hence it is that Nii Kua of old fashioned many-coloured blocks of stone to repair the defective parts. He cut off the legs of the Ao and used them to support the four corners of the heavens.

Later on, Kung Kung fought with Chuan Hsu for the throne, and, blundering in his rage against Mount Pu-chou, he snapped the pillar which connects Heaven and earth. That is why Heaven dips downwards to the north-west, so that sun, moon and stars travel towards that quarter. The earth, on the other hand, is now not large enough to fill up the south-east, so that all rivers and streams roll in that direction.

title.en: The Exchange of Hearts Performed by Pien-ch'iao (Liezi)
title.zh: 扁鵲換心（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The clinic of the great physician (symbolic pin: Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 扁鵲之診（象徵定位：河南鄭州）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: Kung-hu of Lu and Ch'i-ying of Chao both fall ill and are cured by Pien-ch'iao — who then offers to grapple with each man's congenital disease: your mental powers are strong but your character is weak, says he to Kung-hu; his are weak while his character is strong. A potion of medicated wine throws them into a three-day death-like trance, and each man's heart is placed in the other's body — leading to a lawsuit between the two families.
summary.zh: 魯公扈趙齊嬰俱疾，扁鵲遂飲二人毒酒，迷死三日；剖胸探心，易而置之——辭而歸，則公扈反齊嬰之室。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the heart-exchange tale is a landmark of Chinese medical myth. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Pien-ch'iao turned to Kung-hu. "Your mental powers," he said, "are strong, but your character is weak. Hence, though fruitful in plans, you are lacking in decision. Ch'i-ying's mental powers, on the other hand, are weak, while his character is strong. Hence there is want of forethought, and he is placed at a disadvantage by the narrowness of his aim. Now, if I can effect an exchange of hearts between you, the good will be equally balanced in both."

So saying, Pien-ch'iao administered to each of them a potion of medicated wine, which threw them into a death-like trance lasting three days. Then, making an incision in their breasts, he took out each man's heart and placed it in the other's body, poulticing the wounds with herbs of marvellous efficacy. When the two men regained consciousness, they looked exactly the same as before; and, taking their leave, they returned home. Only it was Kung-hu who went to Ch'i-ying's house, where Ch'i-ying's wife and children naturally did not recognise him, while Ch'i-ying went to Kung-hu's house and was not recognised either. This led to a lawsuit between the two families, and Pien-ch'iao was called in as arbitrator. On his explaining how the matter stood, peace was once more restored.

title.en: The Three Magic Swords and the Blood-Feud That Could Not Kill (Liezi)
title.zh: 孔周三劍：含光、承影、宵練（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The house of K'ung Chou of Wei (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 衛孔周之家（象徵定位：河南安陽一帶）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: Lai Tan, whose body is slight but whose spirit is fierce, seeks the blood of Hei Luan and borrows one of K'ung Chou's three Yin-Emperor swords — Light-absorber, Shadow-container, Night-tempered. He cuts clean through Hei Luan's body in three places, but the victim is quite unconscious of it; the son laughs that he is merely motioning in a silly way with his hand — the improper use of divine weapons only leads to discomfiture.
summary.zh: 來丹請於衛孔周，得宵練之劍；三斬黑卵之頸——黑卵不覺；其子曰：汝以指揮吾手何也？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the sword allegory satirises the vendetta. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: This Hei Luan was the most ferocious character of his day, and in brute strength he was a match for a hundred men. His bones and sinews, skin and flesh were cast in superhuman mould. He would stretch out his neck to the blade or bare his breast to the arrow, but the sharp steel would bend or break, and his body show no scar from the impact.

"I have three swords," replied K'ung Chou, "but with none of them can you kill a man. You may choose which you like. First, however, let me describe their qualities. The first sword is called 'Light-absorber.' It is invisible to the eye, and when you swing it you cannot tell that there is anything there. Things struck by it retain an unbroken surface, and it will pass through a man's body without his knowing it. The second is called 'Shadow-container.' ... The third is called 'Night-tempered,' because in broad daylight you only see its shadow and not the brightness of its blade, while at night you see not the sword itself but the dazzling light which it emits.

Grasping his new weapon, Lai Tan now sought out his enemy, and found him lying in a drunken stupor at his window. He cut clean through his body in three places between the neck and the navel, but Hei Luan was quite unconscious of it. ... And happening to meet Hei Luan's son at the door, he struck at him three times with his sword. But it was like hitting the empty air. Hei Luan's son laughed and said: "Why are you motioning to me in that silly way with your hand?" Thus, the improper use of divine weapons only leads to discomfiture.

title.en: Effort and Destiny Argue the Case (Liezi)
title.zh: 力謂命曰：若之功奚若我哉（列子力命篇）

region.en: The debate between human striving and fate (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 力命之辯（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Effort claims power over length of life, success, rank, and wealth; Destiny answers with the catalogue of misallotments — P'êng Tsu's wisdom did not exceed Yao and Shun's, yet he lived eight hundred years; Yen Yüan's ability was not inferior, yet he died at thirty-two; Po I and Shu Ch'i starved at Shou-yang while Chi Shih waxed rich. When the way is straight, I push on; when it is crooked, I let be.
summary.zh: 力謂命曰：若之功奚若我哉？命曰：彭祖之智不出堯舜之上，而壽八百；顏淵之才不出眾人之下，而壽十八——窮聖而達逆，賤賢而貴愚。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: EFFORT said to Destiny: "Your achievements are not equal to mine." "Pray what do you achieve in the working of things," replied Destiny, "that you would compare yourself with me?" "Why," said Effort, "the length of man's life, his measure of success, his rank, and his wealth, are all things which I have the power to determine." To this, Destiny made reply: "P'êng Tsu's wisdom did not exceed that of Yao and Shun, yet he lived to the age of eight hundred. Yen Yüan's ability was not inferior to that of the average man, yet he died at the early age of thirty-two. The virtue of Confucius was not less than that of the feudal princes, yet he was reduced to sore straits between Ch'en and Ts'ai.

Chi Cha would not accept the overlordship of Wu, while T'ien Hêng usurped sole power in Ch'i. Po I and Shu Ch'i starved to death at Shou-yang, while Chi Shih waxed rich at Chan-ch'in. If these results were compassed by your efforts, how is it that you allotted long life to P'êng Tsu and an untimely death to Yen Yüan; that you awarded discomfiture to the sage and success to the impious, humiliation to the wise man and high honours to the fool, poverty to the good and wealth to the wicked?" ... "When the way is straight, I push on; when it is crooked, I let be. Old age and early death, failure and success, high rank and humble station, riches and poverty -- all these come naturally and of themselves. Of their ultimate causes, I am ignorant; how could it be otherwise?"

title.en: Chi Liang's Deathbed and the Three Doctors (Liezi)
title.zh: 季梁之疾，三醫並進（列子力命篇）

region.en: Yang Chu's friend's sick-room (symbolic pin: Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 楊朱友人病榻（象徵定位：河南開封）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Yang Chu chants to his weeping friend's sons that over his destiny man has no control.
