Three doctors diagnose in turn: the origin is traceable to disordered appetites — you are only one of the common ruck, says Chi Liang; it is incurable — you are a good doctor; lastly Dr. Lu: it was already fore-ordained in the mind of Providence when you were endowed with this bodily form at birth — you are a heaven-born physician indeed! Not long after, his illness disappeared of itself.
summary.zh: 楊朱歌曰：天其弗識，人胡能覺？——汝疾非由天，非由人，亦非鬼神；命之所制也。季梁曰：天醫也！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Yang Chu then chanted the following words: "How should men possess the knowledge which God Himself has not? Over his destiny man has no control, and can look for no help from God. You and I know this for truth, but our knowledge is not shared by sorcerers and quacks." The sons, however, did not understand, and finally called in three physicians, Dr. Chiao, Dr. Yü and Dr. Lu.

Lastly, Dr. Lu said: "Your illness is attributable neither to God, nor to man, nor to the agency of spirits. It was already fore-ordained in the mind of Providence when you were endowed with this bodily form at birth. What possible good can herbs and drugs do you?" "You are a heaven-born physician indeed!" cried Chi Liang; and he sent him away laden with presents. Not long after, his illness disappeared of itself.

title.en: Duke Ching Weeps on the Ox-Mountain and Yen Tzŭ Smiles (Liezi)
title.zh: 齊景公遊於牛山，北臨其國城而流涕（列子力命篇）

region.en: The Ox-mountain north of Linzi (Niushan, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 牛山（今山東臨淄南）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Duke Ching of Ch'i, gazing from the Ox-mountain at his lovely kingdom, weeps that some day he must die and leave it; two fawning ministers weep too. Yen Tzŭ smiles: if the worthy ruler were to remain in perpetual possession, Duke T'ai and Duke Huan would still be exercising their sway — condemned to a hard life on earth, you would have had no time for brooding over death. The Duke fines himself two cups of wine.
summary.zh: 齊景公遊於牛山，北臨其國城而流涕曰：美哉國乎！若何滂滂去此而死乎！晏子獨拊心大笑。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Duke Ching of Ch'i was travelling across the northern flank of the Ox-mountain in the direction of the capital. Gazing at the view before him, he burst into a flood of tears, exclaiming: "What a lovely scene! How verdant and luxuriantly wooded! To think that some day I must die and leave my kingdom, passing away like running water! If only there were no such thing as death, nothing should induce me to stir from this spot." Two of the Ministers in attendance on the Duke, taking their cue from him, also began to weep.

Yen Tzu replied: "If the worthy ruler were to remain in perpetual possession of his realm, Duke T'ai and Duke Huan would still be exercising their sway. If the bold ruler were to remain in perpetual possession, Duke Chuang and Duke Ling would still be ruling the land. But if all these rulers were now in possession, where would your Highness be? Why, standing in the furrowed fields, clad in coir cape and hat! ... And are you alone going to weep and lament over this order of things? That is unmanly. It was the sight of these two objects -- an unmanly prince and his fawning attendants -- that was affording me food for laughter just now."

title.en: Tung-men Wu Does Not Mourn His Son (Liezi)
title.zh: 魏有東門吳者，其子死而不憂（列子力命篇）

region.en: The State of Wei (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 魏國（今河南安陽一帶）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VI (Effort and Destiny)

summary.en: Tung-men Wu of Wei testifies no grief when his son dies. There was a time when I had no son, he answers his house-steward; during the whole period that elapsed before my son was born, I never had occasion to grieve. Now that my son is dead, I am only in the same condition as I was before I had a son — what reason have I, then, to mourn?
summary.zh: 魏有東門吳者，其子死而不憂。其室家曰：子之愛子，天下無有；今子死不憂，何也？東門吳曰：吾嘗無子，無子之時不憂。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; paralleled in Zhuangzi's drum-on-basin mourning scenes. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: There was once a man, Tung-men Wu of Wei, who when his son died testified no grief. His house-steward said to him: "The love you bore your son could hardly be equalled by that of any other parent. Why, then, do you not mourn for him now that he is dead?" "There was a time," replied Tung-men Wu, "when I had no son. During the whole period that elapsed before my son was born, I never had occasion to grieve. Now that my son is dead, I am only in the same condition as I was before I had a son. What reason have I, then, to mourn?"

title.en: Do You Know Why You Hit the Target? (Liezi)
title.zh: 列子學射中矣，請於關尹子（列子說符篇）

region.en: Kuan Yin Tzŭ's archery-ground (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 關尹子之射場（象徵定位：河南靈寶函谷關）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ learns archery and, able to hit the target, asks Kuan Yin Tzŭ's opinion. Do you know why you hit the target? No. Then you are not good enough yet. Three years of practice later: Yes, I do — hold that knowledge fast and do not let it slip.
summary.zh: 列子學射中矣，請於關尹子。尹子曰：子知子之所以中乎？對曰：弗知也——三年，又以報關尹子。曰：可矣，守而勿失也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Lieh Tzü learned archery and, when he was able to hit the target, he asked the opinion of Kuan Yin Tzü on his shooting. "Do you know why you hit the target?" said Kuan Yin Tzü. "No, I do not," was the reply. "Then you are not good enough yet," rejoined Kuan Yin Tzü. Lieh Tzü withdrew and practised for three years, after which he again presented himself. Kuan Yin Tzu asked, as before: "Do you know why you hit the target?" "Yes," said Lieh Tzü, "I do." "In that case, all is well. Hold that knowledge fast, and do not let it slip."

title.en: Three Years to Carve a Mulberry Leaf in Jade (Liezi)
title.zh: 宋人以玉為楮葉（列子說符篇）

region.en: The Sung court (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋宮（今河南商丘）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: A man of Sung carves a mulberry leaf out of jade for his prince; it takes three years, and imitates Nature so exquisitely that it cannot be distinguished from real leaves in a heap. Lieh Tzŭ hears of it: if it took the Creator three years to make a single leaf, there would be very few trees with leaves on them — the Sage will rely not so much on human science and skill as on the evolution of Tao.
summary.zh: 宋人有為其君以玉為楮葉者，三年而成；列子曰：使天地三年而成一葉，則物之有葉者寡矣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was once a man in Sung who carved a mulberry leaf out of jade for his prince. It took three years to complete, and it imitated Nature so exquisitely in its down, its glossiness, and its general configuration from tip to stem, that, if placed in a heap of real mulberry leaves, it could not be distinguished from them. This man was subsequently pensioned by the Sung State as a reward for his skill. Lieh Tzu, hearing of it, said: "If it took the Creator three years to make a single leaf, there would be very few trees with leaves on them. The Sage will rely not so much on human science and skill as on the evolution of Tao."

title.en: The Two Sons of Mr. Shih and Mr. Meng (Liezi)
title.zh: 魯施氏二子，孟氏同業（列子說符篇）

region.en: The courts of Ch'in and Wei (Xianyang and Anyang, China)
region.zh: 秦廷與衛廷（咸陽、安陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Mr. Shih's two sons, scholar and soldier, rise through Ch'i and Ch'u; his poor neighbour Mr. Meng's sons apply the same formula and come to grief — castrated in Ch'in, feet cut off in Wei. Success consists in hitting off the right moment, answers Mr. Shih; nothing in the ordering of this world is either at all times right or at all times wrong.
summary.zh: 魯施氏有二子，其一好學，其一好兵；孟氏同業而不同得——秦王宮刑之，衛侯刖之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Mr. Shih of Lu had two sons, one of whom was a scholar and the other a soldier. The former found in his accomplishments the means of ingratiating himself with the Marquis of Ch'i, who engaged him as tutor to the young princes. The other brother proceeded to Ch'u, and won favour with the King of that State by his military talents. The King was so well pleased that he installed him at the head of his troops. Thus both of them succeeded in enriching their family and shedding lustre on their kinsfolk.

The eldest son immediately set off for Ch'in, hoping that his moral culture would recommend him to the King of that State. But the King said: "At the present moment all the feudal princes are struggling to outbid one another in power, and the great essential is to keep up a large army. If I tried to govern my State on the lines of altruism and righteousness, ruin and annihilation would be the outcome." So saying, he had the unfortunate man castrated, and turned him away. The second son, meanwhile, had gone to Wei ... so, without more ado, he cut off his feet and sent him back to Lu.

Mr. Shih, however, said: "Success consists in hitting off the right moment, while missing it means failure. Your method was identical with ours, only the result was different. That is not due to any flaw in the action itself, but simply because it was not well timed. Nothing, in the ordering of this world, is either at all times right or at all times wrong. What formerly passed current may nowadays be rejected; what is now rejected may by and by come into use again."

title.en: The Duke's Laugh: the Silkworm-Tender and the Escorted Wife (Liezi)
title.zh: 晉文公將伐衛，公子鉏仰天而笑（列子說符篇）

region.en: The army of Chin on the march (Houma, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 晉師之途（今山西侯馬）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Duke Wên of Chin marches to attack the Duke of Wei; Tzŭ Ch'u throws his head back and laughs — recalling the neighbour who escorted his wife to her family and stopped to court a silkworm-tending woman, only to find his own wife receiving the attentions of an admirer. The Duke saw the point and turned home — before an invading force had already crossed his northern frontier.
summary.zh: 晉文公出，將伐衛；公子鉏仰天而笑——郊有蠶婦——見其妻之受非望之遇也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Duke Wen of Chin put an army into the field with the intention of attacking the Duke of Wei, whereat Tzŭ Ch'u threw his head back and laughed aloud. On being asked the reason of his behaviour, he replied: "I was thinking of the experience of a neighbour of mine, who was escorting his wife on a visit to her own family. On the way, he came across a woman tending silk worms, who attracted him greatly, and he fell into conversation with her. Happening to look up, what should he see but his own wife also receiving the attentions of an admirer! It was the recollection of this incident that made me laugh." The Duke saw the point, and forthwith turned home with his army. Before he got back, an invading force had already crossed his northern frontier!

title.en: Ch'i Yung, Who Could Tell a Robber by His Face (Liezi)
title.zh: 晉之郗雍能視盜（列子說符篇）

region.en: The robber-infested Chin State (Houma, Shanxi, China)
region.zh: 晉國盜藪（今山西侯馬）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: In the robber-infested Chin State, Ch'i Yung could tell a robber by his face and read his inmost thoughts; the Marquis delights in him — until the robbers band together and murder him. Wen Tzŭ of Chao has foretold it, quoting the Chou proverb: search not the ocean-depths for fish — and prescribes promoting the worthy to office instead; all the robbers flee to Ch'in.
summary.zh: 晉侯曰：吾有一人，逐盜而獲之。文子曰：以察伺盜，盜不盡矣——周諺有言：察見淵魚者不祥。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In the Chin State, which was infested with robbers, there lived a certain Ch'i Yung, who was able to tell a robber by his face; by examining the expression of his eyes he could read his inmost thoughts. The Marquis of Chin employed him in the inspection of hundreds and thousands of robbers, and he never missed a single one. The Marquis expressed his delight to Wen Tzu of Chao, saying: "I have a man who, single-handed, is ridding my whole State of robbers." Wen Tzu replied: "If your Highness relies on a detective for catching robbers, you will never get rid of them. And what is more, Ch'i Yung is certain sooner or later to meet with a violent end."

Meanwhile, a band of robbers were plotting together. "Ch'i Yung," they said, "is the enemy who is trying to exterminate us." So one day they stole upon him in a body and murdered him. ... "In Chou," replied Wen Tzu, "we have a proverb: 'Search not the ocean-depths for fish: calamity comes upon those who pry into hidden mysteries.' If you want to be quit of robbers, the best thing your Highness can do is to promote the worthy to office." The Marquis then appointed Sui Hui to be Prime Minister, and all the robbers fled to the Ch'in State.

title.en: Chiu-fang Kao and the Superlative Horse (Liezi)
title.zh: 秦穆公九方皋相馬（列子說符篇）

region.en: The court of Duke Mu of Ch'in (Xianyang, Shaanxi, China)
region.zh: 秦穆公之廷（今陝西咸陽）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Po Lo recommends the fuel-and-vegetable hawker Chiu-fang Kao, who returns after three months with a steed at Sha-ch'iu — a dun-coloured mare, he says, though it turns out a coal-black stallion. Much displeased, the Duke summons Po Lo, who heaves a sigh of satisfaction: what Kao keeps in view is the spiritual mechanism — in making sure of the essential, he forgets the homely details. When the horse arrived, it turned out indeed to be a superlative horse.
summary.zh: 秦穆公謂伯樂：子之年長矣——九方皋相馬：牝而驪——得其精而忘其粗，在其內而忘其外。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the judge-of-horses topos paralleled in Zhuangzi ch. 24. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: "You are now advanced in years. Is there any member of your family whom I could employ to look for horses in your stead?" Po Lo replied: "A good horse can be picked out by its general build and appearance. But the superlative horse -- one that raises no dust and leaves no tracks -- is something evanescent and fleeting, elusive as thin air. The talent of my sons lies on a lower plane altogether: they can tell a good horse when they see one, but they cannot tell a superlative horse. I have a friend, however, one Chiu-fang Kao, a hawker of fuel and vegetables, who in things appertaining to horses is nowise my inferior."

However, on some one being sent to fetch it, the animal turned out to be a coal-black stallion! Much displeased, the Duke sent for Po Lo. "That friend of yours," he said, "whom I commissioned to look for a horse, has made a nice mess of it. Why, he cannot even distinguish a beast's colour or sex!" Po Lo heaved a sigh of satisfaction. "Has he really got as far as that?" he cried. "Ah, then he is worth a thousand of me put together. What Kao keeps in view is the spiritual mechanism. In making sure of the essential, he forgets the homely details; intent on the inward qualities, he loses sight of the external. So clever a judge of horses is Kao, that he has it in him to judge something better than horses." When the horse arrived, it turned out indeed to be a superlative horse.

title.en: The Dead Rat Dropped by the Kite (Liezi)
title.zh: 白頷之鴞腐鼠（列子說符篇）

region.en: The rich man's balcony over the high road (symbolic pin: Kaifeng, Henan, China)
region.zh: 梁富人北宮之上（象徵定位：河南開封）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: A lucky throw of the dice evokes a burst of merriment from Mr. Yü's gambling party above the main road; precisely at that moment a kite sailing overhead drops the carcass of a rat among the young gallants below, who take it for an insult and exterminate every member of the family. Pride and extravagance lead to calamity and ruin in more ways than one.
summary.zh: 虞氏富樂無比——梁上有鴞，墮其腐鼠於中——虞氏之患以驕奢故也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: Mr. Yü was a wealthy man of the Liang State. It was his custom to have banquets served, to the accompaniment of music, in a high upper hall overlooking the main road; there he and his friends would sit drinking their wine and amusing themselves with bouts of gambling. One day, a party of young gallants happened to pass along the road. In the chamber above, play was going on as usual, and a lucky throw of the dice, which resulted in the capture of both fishes, evoked a loud burst of merriment from the players.

Precisely at that moment, it happened that a kite which was sailing overhead dropped the carcass of a rat in the midst of the company outside. The young men held an angry consultation on the spot: "This Mr. Yü has been enjoying his wealth for many a long day, and has always treated his neighbours in the most arrogant spirit. And now, although we have never offended him, he insults us with this dead rat. ... Let us summon up our utmost resolution, and combine with one accord to wipe him and his family out of existence!" The whole party signified their agreement, and when the evening of the appointed day had come, they collected, fully armed for the attack, and exterminated every member of the family.

title.en: The Honest Man Who Could Not Eat a Robber's Gruel (Liezi)
title.zh: 東方有士曰爰旌目，食於盜者（列子說符篇）

region.en: The hungered road of the east (symbolic pin: Linyi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 東方之塗（象徵定位：山東臨沂）

period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book VII (Causality)

summary.en: Yüan Ching Mu, overcome by hunger on the road, is fed with a bowl of rice-gruel by the robber Ch'iu of Hu-fu; after three mouthfuls he learns his benefactor's name, cries: I am an honest man and cannot eat your food — and clutches the ground with both hands, retching and coughing to bring it up again.
summary.zh: 爰旌目曰：嘻！汝非盜邪？胡為而食我？吾義不食子之食也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: In the east of China there was a man named Yuan Ching Mu, who set off on a journey but was overcome by hunger on the way. A certain robber from Hu-fu, of the name of Ch'iu, saw him lying there, and fetched a bowl of rice-gruel in order to feed him. After swallowing three mouthfuls, Yuan Ching Mu opened his eyes and murmured, "Who are you?" "I am a native of Hu-fu, and my name is Ch'iu." "Oh misery!" cried Yuan Ching Mu, "are not you the robber Ch'iu? What are you feeding me for? I am an honest man and cannot eat your food." So saying, he clutched the ground with both hands, and began retching and coughing in order to bring it up again.

title.en: Timbo Limbo: the Fish-husband
title.zh: 廷波林波：魚郎

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 78a 'Timbo Limbo' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Overworked Lydia, sent alone with a jug heavier than herself, is heard crying at the river by a Jack-fish, Timbo Limbo, who offers to help if she will be his wife; their song summons him each morning. The spying half-sibling betrays the secret, the father calls the fish out with the stolen song and shoots him, and a single scale flies two miles to fall on Lydia's breast. Learning the truth, she sings three times at the river — the water turns blood — and drowns herself where her husband's body was not.
summary.zh: 重役之下的莉迪亞獨負巨壺至河邊啜泣； Jack 魚廷波林波聞聲相助，許以婚約，並以歌相召。同父異母的妹妹窺探告密，父親用偷學的歌聲喚魚出水槍殺之；一片魚鱗飛行兩哩落在莉迪亞胸前。她知情後三次臨河而歌——河水化血——最後在丈夫不在的水中投河自盡。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale (fish-husband/animal-bridegroom type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A man had one daughter named Lydia. His wife died and he married another woman, who had children for the man and liked her own children more than the daughter-in-law — mostly it was the daughter-in-law she imposed the work on. She sent Lydia for water, giving her a big jug heavier than Lydia's weight, and would not send any of her own children to help Lydia up. When Lydia got to the river-side she was crying that the jug was too heavy and she could get no one to help her up; a Jack-fish in the river heard the lament, came up, and said that if she would be a wife to him he would help her up whenever she came to the river-side. Lydia consented, filled her jar, and the Jack-fish helped her up and she went to the yard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother-in-law pressed her about who had helped her up with the jar, and Lydia said she had no one. One morning she took up the jug and went to the river-side — the mother-in-law had sent one of her children to follow and watch who helped her up. Lydia had to sing to call the Jack-fish, whose name was Timbo Limbo: 'Timbo Limbo, same gal Lydia, Timbo Limbo o-o-o!' — and when the fish heard the voice of Lydia he came up to help her. The little child saw the Jack-fish, went home, and told her mother: 'Mamma, me sister Lydia does have a man-fish at the river-side to help her up.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At night the man was told; at daylight he had Lydia dressed and sent on to Montego Bay to buy pepper and skelion. He loaded his gun and went with the little girl to the river-side; the little girl sang the song three times, changing her voice, and the water went round so, and the Jack-fish came out — the father shot him. He stripped, jumped in, swam, took out the Jack-fish and carried him to the yard. As he began to scale the fish, one of the scales flew all the way, some two miles, and met Lydia and dropped at her breast; when she took it off she found it was a Timbo Limbo scale. She started crying, ran to the yard, took up her jar, went to the river and started her song — the Jack-fish didn't come up; she sang again, the water stayed steady; she sang again, the water turned blood. And when she found that Timbo Limbo was not in the water, Lydia took herself up and drowned herself right in the water. Jack man dory, choose none!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Fish, Fish, Fish, Pengeleng
title.zh: 魚啊魚啊，潘吉冷

region.en: Lacovia, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加拉科維亞

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 78b 'Fish fish fish' (told by Florence Thomlinson, Lacovia)

summary.en: One daughter goes to the river-side to worship a little fish with her song; the other daughter, sent instead the next day, copies the tune, catches the fish, and the family cooks it — saving a plate for the true friend, who refuses it and sings until all the fish rise and turn into one big fish she carries back to the river.
summary.zh: 一個女兒到河邊以歌敬奉小魚；次日被派去的另一個女兒照抄歌調，把魚捕回家烹食——還特意留一份給真正的朋友。她不吃，只是一路唱下去，直到所有的魚浮起、化為一條大魚，她把它捧回河中。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale; 'worship' of a fish is folkloric devotion within a tale, not ritual instruction. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: It was a mother and two daughters. One of the daughters went to the river-side to worship a little fish; she commenced to sing — 'Fish, fish, fish, fish, pengeleng; come on the river, pengeleng' — and the little fish came to her. She played, played, played, let go the fish, and the fish went back into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she went back home her mother quarreled that she had waited back so long; the next day she would not send her back to the river but sent the other daughter, who sang the same song she had heard her sister sing. She caught the fish and brought it home; they cooked the fish for dinner and saved some for the other daughter. When she came she would not eat it, for she knew it was the said fish; she began to sing 'Fish fish fish fish, pengeleng!' — and the other sister said, 'Tank God, me no eat de fish!' The mother said, 'Tank God, me no eat de fish!' She went on singing until all the fish came up and turned into one big fish, and she took it and put it back in the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78b, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Dear Old Juna
title.zh: 親愛的老茹娜

region.en: Claremont, St. Ann, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖安克萊爾蒙特

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 78c 'Dear Old Juna' (told by Richard Pottinger, Claremont, St. Ann)

summary.en: A girl betrothed to both a man and a fish cooks breakfast for each at ten o'clock, carrying a waiter of food to the river and singing Juna up: 'You mother run, you father forsake you, you don't know you deh!' — 'Kai, kai, Juna, me know you!' The jealous lover borrows the song, shoots the fish at breakfast, dresses and serves it, and everyone eats — until the girl finds out whose body it was, and drops dead at the instant.
summary.zh: 同時許身於人與魚的姑娘，每天十點為兩位『未婚夫』各備早飯，托盤送至河邊，唱喚茹娜出水——『你母親跑了，你父親棄了你，你還不知道自己在此！』——『嗨，嗨，茹娜，我認得你！』妒火中燒的未婚夫借得歌調，在早餐時一槍斃魚，烹而饗客——待姑娘認出盤中是誰，當場倒斃。

sensitivity.note: Animal-bridegroom tragedy type. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A man and a woman had but one daughter who was their pet. The girl was engaged to a fish, and to another young man too; generally at ten o'clock she cooked breakfast for the both. The man at home ate; then she took a waiter with the fish's breakfast to the river. When she went to the river she had to sing a song that the fish might come out: 'Dear old Juna, dear old Juna, oona a da vina sa... You mother run, you father forsake you, you don't know you deh!' Fish came now, singing, 'Kai, kai, Juna, me know you!' — and the fish came out to have his breakfast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78c (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: It went on for several days, every day she sang the same and the fish gave the same reply. The young man thought of it now; one morning he went a little earlier with his gun, singing the same tune. The fish came out and sang the same tune as it generally did; the young man shot it, carried the fish home, dressed it, and everybody ate now — the gal and everybody. At the end of the eating she found out it was the said fish, and she dropped dead at the instant.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 78c, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Juggin Straw Blue and the Seven-Headed Witch
title.zh: 賈金·斯特勞·布魯與七頭巫師

region.en: Lacovia, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加拉科維亞

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 79 'Juggin Straw Blue' (told by David Roach, Lacovia)

summary.en: Helped with her water-tub by an Old Witch man and sworn to secrecy, the niece betrays her helper; the aunt locks her in an iron chest, but tears through the keyhole are licked up — 'after the fat is so sweet, what says the flesh!' — and the witch bursts the door. Marching her off with music in his knock-knees, he sings his menu — your head and lights for my dog, your liver for my supper — until her sweetheart's mother issues eight eggs against the witch's seven heads and seven eggs; an egg smashed buys a day of light and a head cut off, until the last head falls and the girl goes home to be married.
summary.zh: 女孩受老巫相助卻泄密；姨母把她鎖進鐵箱，淚水卻從鎖孔滴出被巫舔盡——『脂膏如此香甜，血肉又當如何！』——箱門迸裂。巫以膝響為樂，唱著菜單押行——頭與心肝喂狗、肝臟為晚餐——直到戀人之母授八枚雞蛋以破七頭七蛋之局：碎一蛋換一日天光、斫一首級；第七顆頭落地，女孩得救歸嫁。

sensitivity.note: Wonder tale (seven-headed ogre/egg-and-head duel type, ATU 302-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A woman had a daughter and a niece, and the niece was courting one Juggin Straw Blue. The aunt loved the daughter more and always wanted the niece to do more work. One day she sent the niece to the river with a big tub; the girl filled it and could not lift it. An Old Witch man was by the river-side; he helped her up and told her not to tell anybody who helped her. But when she went home the aunt pumped her until she told; the aunt knew the Old Witch man would come for her in the night, and locked her in an iron chest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 79 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Part of the night the Old Witch man came in search of the girl. She was crying in the iron chest, and the tears went through the keyhole; he wiped it and licked it and said, 'After the fat is so sweet, what says the flesh!' And he burst the door open and took her out. He traveled with the girl, knock-kneed, the sound of his knee like music; and he said to her, 'Your head and your lights are for my dog, and your liver is for my supper!' So the girl started a song — 'Why, why, why, my Juggin Straw Blue... this rotten stuff, this stinking stuff, then carry me down to gully True Blue, you'll see me no more.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 79, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the girl was courting Juggin Straw Blue, his mother was an Old Witch too. The courting boy's mother waked him up and gave him eight eggs — for the Old Witch man had seven heads and seven eggs, one egg for each head. The boy went after the Old Witch man and overtook him and mashed one of the eggs — and daylight came — and he cut off one of the heads. The Old Witch man mashed one of his eggs and night came back; the boy mashed the next one and daylight again; and so they went on, the boy mashing seven eggs and cutting off the Old Witch's seven heads, taking away his girl — and he went home with his girl and married.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 79, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Witch and the Grain of Peas
title.zh: 巫婆與一粒豌豆

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 80 'The Witch and the Grain of Peas' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: The witch mother-in-law counts her boiling peas grain by grain, finds one missing, and swears the thieving daughter-in-law at the river: eat my peas today and you will be drowned. The girl's death-song reaches her sweetheart William, who gathers four limes, four hen's eggs, four turkey's eggs and four marbles, meets the witch in battle at the river-side, kills her, and carries the girl home to marry.
summary.zh: 巫婆岳母逐粒清點鍋中豌豆，發現少了一粒，便押繼女到河邊發誓：今日吃我一粒豌豆，便溺斃於此。女孩的哀歌傳到戀人威廉耳中；他備齊四枚青檸、四枚雞蛋、四枚火雞蛋與四顆彈珠，在河邊與巫婆決戰，殺之，攜女歸家成婚。

sensitivity.note: Witch-execution wonder tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A man was first married to a woman and had one child with her. She died and he married another, and the girl had to call her mother-in-law — who did not like the daughter-in-law, who lived in a house by herself. One day the mother-in-law washed some peas, put them on the fire, and went away to her ground; the daughter-in-law came to the house to catch the daughter, louse and comb her hair. The mother-in-law, an Old Witch, knew the daughter-in-law had come to the house; the daughter said, 'Look here, sister, mamma put some peas on the fire — why don't you take one grain of the peas?' And she opened the pot and took out one grain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 80 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Old Witch woman knew the daughter-in-law had taken out one grain, she put up her hoe, came back from the ground, took down the pot, turned out all the peas in a bowl, and coupled every grain until she found one that had no match. 'Look here! Did your sister come today?' — 'No, never came today!' — 'Yes, don't control me, for I see at the grain that your sister came and took out one grain from the pot.' She swore her at the river to drown her because she took the peas: 'If you don't eat my peas today you won't be drowned, but if you eat my peas you will be drowned.' So the girl took up her song — 'Oh, me dearest mama, me mama... a ring down, peace, oh, a ring down...'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 80, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the said time the young girl had a sweetheart outside named William. William's mother heard the song on the river-side and sent word to the carpenter-shop that William's girl was singing quite mournful there. He went up a lime-tree and picked four limes, went to a fowl-nest and took four fowl-eggs, went to a turkey-nest and took four turkey-eggs, took four marbles, called the girl and put her before him; and William and the girl's mother-in-law came to a battle at the river-side, and William killed the woman. He put the girl before him, carried her home and married her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 80, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Bosen Corner: the Egg Test
title.zh: 波森角：考蛋之局

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 81 'Bosen Corner' (told by Martha Roe, Maroon Town)

summary.en: On the road to Old Witch country the kind daughter-in-law greets the so-so head and crossed feet, is fed from one bone and four grains of rice, scratches the witch's back to blood without a word, and hugs the old cat sent in her place. Told to take the little eggs that cry 'don't take me' and break one at each of four crossroads, she finds a common, a drove of stock, a gentleman in a buggy, and a prince who marries her. The greedy own daughter, sent the same road, mocks the bugaboos, flings out the cat, and smashes the big eggs that cry 'take me' — snakes, insects, and a tearing Old Witch man kill her in the road.
summary.zh: 善良的媳婦一路向『孤頭』『交叉腳』問好，吃一骨四米之宴，為巫婆抓背抓到流血而不言，還抱起替代老嫗的老貓。聽囑取那喊『別拿我』的小蛋，在四個十字路口逐一打破——得一片牧場、一群牛羊、一位馬車紳士、一位提親王子。貪心的親生女走同一條路，譏笑鬼怪、摔貓出門、專取喊『拿我』的大蛋——蛇、蟲與撕裂人的老巫把她在路中殺死。

sensitivity.note: Two-sisters witch-road tale (Frau Holle type). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A woman had two daughters: one her own child, one her daughter-in-law, whom she did not use well. The place where they went for water was a bad place, Old Witch country, called Bosen Corner. One day she sent the daughter-in-law for water. Going along, she saw a so-so (only) head in the road and put her hand on her belly to make a kind howdy. Further on she saw two feet crossed in the road — 'Howdy, papa.' — 'Gal, where you going?' — 'Mamma sent me to Bosen Corner for water.' — 'Go on, gal; good before and bad behind.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 81 (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: She went on to a little hut where one old lady sat — 'Come in here; late night going to take you.' The Old Witch picked up a piece of bone from the dung-heap, chopped it up in the pot with four grains of rice, and boiled the pot full of meat and rice for the girl's dinner. When she had eaten, the old lady called her to scratch her back; as the girl's hand scratched, the back picked all the skin off her hand till it bled — 'What is the matter with your hand?' — 'Nothing, ma'am.' When she sat down, the old lady went out of the door and came in an old cat, which the girl hugged up and coaxed and was so kind to; then she slept and got up to go away in the morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 81, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old lady told her to go round the house and see some fowl-eggs: the eggs that cry 'Take me! take me!' are big eggs, she must not take them; the small eggs that say 'Don't take me!' she must take four. At the first crossroad she mashed one and saw into a big pretty common; at the second, the common packed up with cows, goats, sheep and everything a gentleman possesses; at the third, a pretty young gentleman came out into a buggy; at the fourth she mashed the last egg and found the gentleman was a prince, and he married her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 81, middle-b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The daughter-in-law came with her husband and drove into the yard, and the mother-in-law, expecting the Old Witch had killed the girl, sent her own daughter to Bosen Corner for water too. The girl mocked as she went — 'Ay-e-e! from me born I never see so-so head yet!' — was told 'Go long, gal! better day before,' ate the same bone-and-rice dinner, turned a puss and flung the begging cat out the door, had her hands cut scratching, and in the morning took four of the big eggs. First crossroad: a whole heap of snakes; second: a whole lot of insects; at the last crossroad she mashed one and saw a big Old Witch man, who tore her up and killed her stiff dead in the road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 81, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Dogs: Blum-blum, Sinde, Dido
title.zh: 三犬記：布倫布倫、辛德、狄多

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 82a 'Boy and Witch Woman' (told by Thomas White, Maroon Town)

summary.en: Begging fire from the Old Witch's kitchen, the witch-born William watches her knock children out of her own skin and beats her test — 'Boy, you just as good as me!' — by catching fire in rotten wood without her fire-stick. Marked for revenge, he wins the packey-knock courtship, is nearly razor-murdered in the night by his grumbling dogs Blum-blum, Sinde and Dido, leaves a boiling-blood basin as alarm with his deaf mother, and is stranded atop an apple-tree while the witch knocks out forty axe-men to fell it — until the basin boils over, the chained dogs come flying, and destroy the axe-men and the witch, whose scattered pieces are the cowitch weed of the whole earth.
summary.zh: 向老巫廚房討火時，巫種出身的威廉窺見她敲皮出子，又以朽木引火不取其火棒——『你這孩子，不比我差！』被記仇的巫以擲罐選婿之局選中；夜裡剃刀臨頸，三犬布倫布倫、辛德、狄多低吠破局。他留下沸血之盆為警報託付聾母；被誘上蘋果樹時，巫喚出四十斧手伐樹——盆血沸溢，鎖鏈掙斷，三犬騰空而至，誅斧手與老巫；撒遍大地的巫屍碎片，便是如今的毒漆草。

sensitivity.note: Witch-slayer wonder tale (animal-helper cycle, ATU 325-302-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Olden time it was a young man and his brother, bred up on a property penning cows. Every morning they wanted to pen, carrying their breakfast and their fire; one morning the food came but no fire. At twelve o'clock the smaller brother felt hungry and went to look for fire up a hillside where a smoke showed, and found a big open house, a lady in the open kitchen — an Old Witch. He was frightened and came back; then the bigger brother, William, went. He stopped behind a big dry stump and watched what the Old Witch did: she took a pot off the fire and dished out all the vessels right through, though no pickney was in the kitchen — only the Old Witch. She knocked on her side, pon-pon-pon, and all the children came out, twenty big men and small children, women and boy pickney; they sat and ate, smoked, and then she knocked again and all the children went up into her back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy called, 'Mawnin', Nana!' She was frightened, asked if he had been there long; he said he had only come up to beg for fire. 'Take fire, but don't take my fire-stick!' — and the boy turned back, broke a piece of rotten wood, held it against the steam of the fire and caught it alight. The Old Witch said, 'Boy, you just as good as me!' — 'No, Nana, I'm not so good!' William went down to the cow-pen, told his smaller brother not to make up fire but to pen the cows and go home quick quick — for this bigger brother was a witch himself and knew all about what would come after him; he went inside the house and fawned sick. In quick time the Old Witch was upon them, and said anyone who could knock the packey off her head she would take for a husband; the smaller brother flung and failed, and William, coming out sick, picked up a little trash and knocked it off — 'Yes, you is my husband!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the night, when William was in dead sleep, the Old Witch took a razor to cut his throat. William had three dogs — Blum-blum, Shade, and Dido — and when she took the razor, Blum-blum grumbled and the razor's mouth turned over; William woke. Twice more she rose, singing 'Sharpen me razor, sharpen me razor' — Sinde grumbled, then Dido grumbled, and the razor's mouth turned over. At daylight William and his wife went away into witch country, leaving a big white basin in the hall middle: as soon as it boiled up in blood, his mother must let go the three dogs. On the road the witch flung a marble to an apple-tree and begged William kindly to climb and pick the apple — 'Hah! I tell you I got you today! The place where you see me knock out pickney out of my skin, you will have to tell me today.' — 'Yes, I know about that long time, for it will be iron cut iron today!' — and the witch knocked out ten axe-men to fell the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82a, middle-b (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: William started his song — 'Blum-blum, Sinde, Dido...' — and the Old Witch sang hers — 'Chin, fallah, fallah...' When the tree was going to fall William said, 'Bear me up, me good tree! Many time me fader fell a green tree, leave a dry one.' The witch knocked out twenty axe-men, thirty axe-men; while William was in the tree, the white basin boiled up with blood, and his deaf mother, chattering with a neighbor all day, saw the blood stream slap on her frock, cut the chain of Blum-blum and Sinde — Dido cut his chain himself — and the three dogs galloped away. William, up the tree, only shook his hand, and the three dogs dropped; they waited until the Old Witch had forty axe-men round the tree, and in the height of the cutting destroyed every one of them and killed the Old Witch herself. William came down, took his machete and scattered the Old Witch over the whole earth — everywhere you go, that bad cowitch is nothing else than the pieces of the Old Witch. Jack man dory, choose now!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Lucy and Janet: Manners against the Witch
title.zh: 露西與珍奈：以禮克巫

region.en: Harmony Hall, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地和諧堂

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 2024)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 82b 'Lucy and Janet' (told by Martha Roe, Harmony Hall)

summary.en: Kind Lucy eats her school-road breakfast with the three escort dogs as with friends, and when the Old Witch man springs out to destroy her, the dogs run in and tear him up. Rude Janet, who quarrels at the escort's lateness and eats first before dividing the leftovers, calls the dogs harshly in her turn — and they will not come; the Old Witch kills the girl through her bad manners. 'Money won't take you round the island like civility.'
summary.zh: 溫良的露西與護送的三犬同桌共食如友；老巫竄出欲害她時，三犬撲上撕裂了他。粗魯的珍奈先責護送來遲，吃罷才分剩食，呼犬時聲色俱厲——犬不應命；老巫便因她的無禮殺了她。『錢財帶不動你環島，禮貌才行。』

sensitivity.note: Moral animal-helper tale. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: Once a woman had two daughters, Lucy and Janet, sent far to school. There was an Old Witch living along the road, and she had three dogs — Dick, Dandy, and Bellamo. In August, Lucy was going home to spend time with her mamma, and the mother had to send the three dogs to carry her home, all her breakfast for her and the dogs put together. Lucy was kind; when she came to her breakfast, she and the three dogs ate together, never considering them as dogs but as friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82b (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she came halfway, the three dogs stopped back and one big Old Witch man came out to destroy Lucy; the dogs had left her quite behind, and she called them: 'Yah! Bellamo, Dick and Dandy, yah! Bellamo, yo!' The three dogs ran in and tore up the Old Witch and killed him. Every time Lucy came, the three dogs guided her to her mamma to spend August, and carried her back to her school-missus's place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82b, middle (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Christmas Janet went. The dogs came to carry her home, and when they came she said, 'I wonder what you all doing so long!' and began to quarrel; when she got to eat breakfast, she ate her breakfast first, then divided what was left to give the dogs. As she started on, the dogs fell back the same as usual; when the Old Witch man came out, she called the dogs harshly — and the dogs would not come. The Old Witch killed that girl through her bad manners. So you find plenty of young people who don't have manners: money won't take you round the island like civility.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 82b, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Man-Snake as Bridegroom
title.zh: 蛇郎君

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 1924

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 85 'Man-Snake as Bridegroom' (a, Richard Morgan; b, Matilda Hall)

summary.en: A pick-and-choose girl accepts a coal-black pretty man who eats nothing but raw eggs and borrows the whole wedding outfit. On the road he sheds the borrowed finery piece by piece, walks her into a cave, turns a yellow snake, and sings 'a handsome man will kill you' over her rescue-song until the neglected brother Collin — in the bush shooting birds — hears his name, shoots the snake-head at her nose, and saves a sister who never counted him before.
summary.zh: 挑挑剔剔的姑娘看中一位烏黑俊郎——只生吞生蛋、婚禮行頭全靠借。歸途他一路脫下借來的衣飾，把她帶進洞穴，化作黃蛇，邊唱『俊郎者殺你』邊聽她呼救；被冷落的弟弟科林在林中打鳥聞名趕至，一槍擊中抵近鼻尖的蛇頭，救下從前從不把他放在眼裡的姐姐。

sensitivity.note: Animal-bridegroom cycle (ATU 425-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a woman to court. Every man came to court her and she said she did not want him, until one day she saw a coal-black man, a pretty man. 'O mother, this is my courtier!' She took the man; at breakfast and dinner he did not eat, only sucked a couple of raw eggs. She had a brother named Collin whom she did not count. 'Sister, the man you are going to marry is a snake.' — 'Boy, you ever hear snake can turn man?' — 'All right! The day you are married, I will be in the bush shooting my bird.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 85a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the wedding day, when the marrying was over, the man took his wife, all his wedding garments borrowed; going home, everywhere he went, all those things he borrowed he shed off one by one till at the last house he took off the last piece — the Bogie! He walked with his wife into the wood and to a cave, put her down to sit, turned a yellow snake, sat in his wife's lap with his head pointed to her nose to suck her blood and kill her. The woman sang, 'Collin now, Collin now, fe me li'l brudder callin' come o!' — and the Snake said, 'Urn hum, hum he; a handsome man you want, a handsome man will kill you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 85a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Collin said, 'Wonder who is singing my name in this middle wood?' and walked fast with his gun. When he came to the cave the snake's head was just going to touch the woman's nose; Collin shot him with the gun and took out his sister — and she never counted her brother till her brother saved her life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 85a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired version the well-pleased parents marry the Yellow Snake to their daughter, and halfway home he drops trousers, shirt and jacket, goes into a hole, puts out his head, lays hold of his wife's leg and swallows to the hip — 'Worra worra, me wi' swallow yo', swallow yo' till yo' mamma can't find yo'!' — while the girl sings for her hunter-brothers, Harry, Tom and John, who hear her crying, kill the Snake, and take the sister away: 'Pick and choose isn't good; if you weren't pick and choose, you wouldn't have married the Yellow Snake that was going to kill you now.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 85a-2 'The Rescue (2)' (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Girls Who Married the Devil
title.zh: 嫁給魔鬼的兩姐妹

region.en: Dry River, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加雞窩地乾河

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 86a 'The Devil-husband' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: The despised yawzy little brother turns cockroach and rides in the boat when the Devil carries his sisters home. Warned by the house-maid — 'He is Devil!' — the maid sets them loose each day by throwing out bags of corn, rice and barley for the talkative cock, who sings 'Massa handsome wife gone!' as the girls catch the boat; the Devil returns stamping 'John Studee!' to turn the boat back — until the last bag empties just in time, and only the little cockroach-brother's cunning saves them from the Devil.
summary.zh: 遭嫌棄的癬病弟弟化作蟑螂藏入小船，隨魔鬼把兩位姐姐載回家。女僕警告『他是魔鬼！』，並每日傾出成袋玉米、大米與大麥喂那隻多話的公雞；雞唱『主人俊美的妻子走了！』姑娘們便得以登船；魔鬼聞聲跺腳喚船『約翰·斯圖迪！』——直到最後一袋見底，船才及時離岸；若非蟑螂弟弟的機巧，魔鬼早已把她們害了。

sensitivity.note: Devil-husband escape tale (ATU 311-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There were two sisters who had a yawzy brother whom the sisters did not care about; they were fatherless and motherless. A man came to court the two sisters to carry them away, took them into the boat to carry home, and the little yawzy boy turned a cockroach and got into the boat. When they got home the house-maid told the two girls, 'What you follow this man come here now for? He is Devil!' The Devil told the house-maid she must feed them well, and the little boy came out of the boat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86a (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The house-maid said she would send them home in the boat, threw out a bag of corn for the big cock in the yard, saying that when he ate it done the boat would catch home. The cock commenced to eat — 'Hock kaluck kum ka turn swallow!' — knocking his wing bap-bap, then crowing, 'Ko ko re ko! Massa handsome wife gone!' Devil did not hear him; the cock crowed again and Devil heard now, and came singing 'Zin-ge-lay, wid dem run come, wid dem jump come, wid dem walk fas'!' The boat's name was John Studee; as he ran into the yard he stamped his foot and said 'John Studee!' — and the boat turned right back with the two girls and the little boy; as they most came, the little boy turned cockroach again and went in the garden, and the Devil didn't see him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86a, middle (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the Devil put the two girls up again; the maid threw out a bag of corn and a bag of rice — the same thing happened. The last day she threw out a bag of corn, a bag of rice and a bag of barley, and after the cock ate off the three bags, the time the girls caught home, leaving the boat at the shore-side, the cock clapped his wing — 'Plop plop! Massa handsome wife gone!' As the Devil heard, him came singing his song, stamped his foot and said 'John Studee-e!' — but the boat turned right back home; and if it wasn't for that little yawzy boy, the Devil would have killed them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86a, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Snake-husband and His Borrowed Collars
title.zh: 蛇郎與借來的領圈

region.en: Lacovia, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加拉科維亞

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 1924)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 86b 'The Snake-husband' (told by Emilina Dodd, Lacovia)

summary.en: On the drive home the finely dressed suitor must hand back collar, jacket and everything, one borrowed piece at a time, until he shows himself plain as a snake. He locks his bride up to kill her when he finds the 'bump'; the mother-in-law frees her with a barrel of wheat and a barrel of corn bought from the talkative cock — 'I don't care a damn, I will nyam and talk!' — and though the snake recaptures her once, the second barrelful buys the escape, and the snake beats the mother-in-law dead for it.
summary.zh: 歸途中，衣冠楚楚的求婚者須把領圈、外套一樣樣歸還，直到現出蛇身。他把新娘鎖起待誅，只待尋得『凸物』；岳母以成桶麥子玉米賄賂多嘴公雞——『管他呢，我邊吃邊唱！』——救出媳婦。蛇一度追回她，第二桶又換得脫身；蛇遂將岳母打死。

sensitivity.note: Animal-bridegroom variant. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A woman had a daughter, oftentimes engaged and never married, saying the gentlemen were not to her sort — until one day she saw a well-dressed gentleman who came and proposed. She had a brother who was an Old Witch, and he told her that man was a snake; she said the man was too well-dressed to be a snake, but the brother went home with them under the carriage as a lizard. The first place, as he was going on, somebody asked, 'Mr. Snake, I beg you give me my collar' — then, 'Mr. Snake, I beg you give me my jacket' — and so on until he showed himself plain as a snake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86b (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they got home he locked her up, wanting to kill her, but could not kill her without the thing called 'bump', and went out in the yard looking for it. The mother-in-law said, 'Me daughter, the man you married is going to kill you, because he is a bad man and he married a wife already and killed her, and he is going to kill you too. I would let you go, but he has one cock, and he is so chat!' So she threw out a barrel of wheat and a barrel of corn, and when the cock was picking it up he said, 'I don't care a damn, I will nyam and talk!' — and sang, 'Ko ko re kom on do! Girl gone, him no gone...' The snake came from the wood while the brother was taking her on the water and overtook her, took her home again and locked her in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86b, middle (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother-in-law threw out a double quantity of wheat and corn, and the cock ate all and sang again, 'Ko ko re kom on do! Girl gone, him no gone!' So when the snake came out from the wood he could not get her again, because she was near on land; he went back home and took a stick and licked the mother-in-law on the head and killed her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86b, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Bull as Bridegroom
title.zh: 公牛新郎

region.en: Santa Cruz Mountains, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加聖克魯斯山區

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 2024)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 87 'Bull as Bridegroom' (a, Richard Morgan; b, George Parkes; c, Florence Thomlinson)

summary.en: The stout suitor who skips breakfast for clean grass is a bull in his off hours, going and coming on his own song. At the wedding feast the toast is refused in favor of the little brother's song — 'See me, Nancy, a wind; think a me, Nancy, me come' — and the groom's hair and four feet grow in, the big bull bucks down the wedding house and gallops out of the story forever. In the paired versions a knee that rings like a bell betrays the debbil when a child sings his own play-song under the table, and Miles the field-hand, overheard mooing his murder-intent, is roped and poled at the ball by the men his victim's little brother summons.
summary.zh: 不吃早飯卻去啃嫩草的壯漢，閒時原是公牛，進退皆循自譜之歌。婚宴上弟弟不受敬酒，改唱其歌——『南茜看我，如風而來』——新郎毛髮四蹄齊長，公牛撞塌婚宴、揚蹄絕塵而去。另一版本：會響鈴的膝蓋出賣魔鬼，孩子在他桌下唱他自己的戲歌；田間的邁爾斯哼唱殺機被弟弟聽破，舞會上被眾人繩套棒逐。

sensitivity.note: Animal-bridegroom exposure cycle. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a woman with a daughter. One day in the yard she saw a man, a big stout man, who put courtship to her and she said yes. When the man came to the yard at breakfast time he did not eat, but always went away where clean grass was; she had a brother watching him all the time. When he went, the man began to sing, 'See me, Nancy, a wind; think a me, Nancy, me come' — and the man turned bull and ate his belly full of grass. When he had eaten he sang again, 'See me, Nancy, a wind; think a me, Nancy, me gone' — and turned the shape of a man back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 87a (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the wedding day the boy said, 'Sister, do you know what that man coming here is? That man is a bull.' — 'O boy, go away! Where you ever hear a cow can turn a living soul?' They came home from church, sat round the table, everybody giving toast, and they called upon the woman's brother to give a toast. 'I won't give toast, but I will sing.' The guests said they would like to hear the sing as much as the toast, so the little boy commenced: 'See me, Nancy, a wind; think a me, Nancy, me come' — the man began to bawl out and knock his head, calling out for a toast; the boy sang again — the hair of the cow grew, and the four feet — and the big bull began to jump and buck down all the people in the house, and he galloped and they never saw him any more again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 87a, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired version, the debbil dressed himself nicely to court a well-kept-up girl, and her witch-brother warned the mother he was the debbil — 'Go away, sah! what you know?' When the debbil walked, his knee sang like a ringing bell — 'Dirt i' room a yerry, double bing, double bing' — and if anybody else sang that song, the debbil's clothes dropped off, a horn grew on his head, and a tail grew out too. One night, while he talked in the house, the little boy underneath the table sang the song quietly; the debbil asked the mistress to stop the boy, who called it his little play-song — and the boy sang much louder, the debbil's knee sang very loud, the clothes dropped off and the tail and horns grew out. 'Didn't I tell you that man was a debbil, and you would not believe it!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 87b 'The Play-song' (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the third version, Miles courted Gracie and always sang for her — a song that Gracie was a fine girl but he was going to kill her — and she did not know he would kill her for true. Her little brother carried his breakfast to the field; before he got there Miles was not a man but a bull, turning man when he saw the boy coming. The boy told his sister, who called it nonsense until she followed and stayed far back and saw it was a bull eating grass, singing 'Me a Miles a moo, me Gracie is a fine girl, me Gracie me wi' kill her.' She raised a ball for the evening with men and ropes; when the little boy began the song, Miles demanded him turned out — but hoof and horn and tail began to grow, he got a big bull, and they tossed him and roped him and poled him and turned him out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 87c 'Gracie and Miles' (2024/1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Old Moody and Tep'y-tep'y: the Two Bulls
title.zh: 老穆迪與特比特比：雙牛記

region.en: Maroon Town, Cock-pit country, Jamaica
region.zh: 牙買加馬倫鎮雞窩地

period: Jamaican oral tradition; recorded 1919-1921; published 2024 (published 2024)

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 88 'The Two Bulls' (told by Alexander Foster, Maroon Town)

summary.en: In Garshen pen the great bull Old Moody allows no bull-calf to live — but heifers he nurses and licks fine. A cow climbs a high mountain to drop a bull calf, and the mother waits till he is a tremendous bull, teaching him to test his father's tracks at the river. At last he will not wait: 'Ma, I gwine go see me father!' — and the two bulls sing challenge and answer across the common before the fight, the old one tossing the son into the air, and the son lifting the old one higher.
summary.zh: 加申牧場的老穆迪不容任何公牛犢存活——母牛犢卻被他舔育得膘肥體壯。一頭母牛攀上高山產下公犢；母親等他長成巨牛，教他在河邊試踩父親的蹄印。終於他不肯再等：『媽，我要去見我父親！』——兩頭公牛隔著牧場以歌相對、以角相迎：老的把兒子拋上半空，兒子落地四蹄穩立；兒子再把老的拋得更高。

sensitivity.note: Father-son combat tale ( patriarchal-succession type); collected from named tellers.

passages.text: One time there was a bull ranging the common — the pen called Garshen pen. That bull would not allow a bull-calf to be born and raised in that pen barring out his one self; but every heifer born he nursed, went about licking them, nourishing them, making them grow fine. Until one time a cow, heavy, climbed up into a high mountain and had a calf — and when the calf was born he was a bull calf. The old bull they called Old Moody, and the young bull 'Tep'y-tep'y-today'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 88 (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother stayed until the calf grew a tremendous bull, and carried him down to the river to drink. Every time the father came to drink, he went away; when the son came, the son tried to put his foot in the father's track, and the bull mamma said to him, 'No, me son, the track no fit for you fader yet,' and carried him back a couple of days more. At twelve o'clock she carried him down again and he tried his foot for his father again — and now he felt to himself that he had become a man; he stood up in the same place and said, 'Must see me father today.' — 'Massy, me son, your pa is so cruel, there is a dread to carry son go!' He stood up and hollered, 'Ma, I gwine go! I gwine try to see me father!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 88, middle (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He raised a song — 'Santy Moody o, Tep'y-tep'y deh!' — and the old bull answered, 'Hum-um-m, what you say? Me just a go a brudder Dickey an' Sandy; Moody say me mustn't go.' Coming up the common to meet his father, all the young girls turned out for that gentleman, and he sang coming — and the old bull answered again. They met to fight now, and the old one tossed his son up into the air and he dropped on four feet; and the son lifted him up in the air now...
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 88, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Rabby in the Corn-Field
title.zh: 兔仔下玉米田

region.en: Andros and Green Turtle Cay, Bahamas (symbolic pin: Nassau)
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯與綠龜礁（象徵定位：拿騷）

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories', Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society vol. III (1895), story I 'B' Rabby in de Corn-Field'

summary.en: The Bahamian rabbit-hero reuses the Anansi letter-trick: fed on forged orders until the father catches on, he is bound, caged over six pots of boiling water — and talks his way out by presenting the execution as a royal wedding feast of boiled cow-heads, which Tiger demands to attend in his place, getting scalded instead. Escaping into a hollow pison-wood tree, Rabbit goads the scalded pursuer with a sharp stick and the feared 'hants', then escapes inside a rotten dead goat, whose corpse he blames for its own ruin with an accusing finger that no one dares point again.
summary.zh: 巴哈馬兔英雄沿用蜘蛛人的偽信計：飽食至東窗事發，被縛入籠、懸於六鍋滾水之上——卻把死刑說成王女婚宴的牛頭大菜，騙老虎替他受刑。逃入毒木空心，以利刺與『鬼怪』之名戲弄燙傷的追兵；最後鑽入腐爛死山羊腹中，把自家敗露歸罪於一根『指人爛背』的手指——自此無人再敢亂指。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian 'old story' (Rabby cycle, cousin of Anansi and Brer Rabbit); collected by Edwards 1889-1893 from named child tellers on Andros and Green Turtle Cay.

passages.text: So this day it was a man who had a big field of peas, corn and potatoes. The man did not use to go in the field — he sent his boy. This day B' Rabby came where the boy was and said, 'Boy, your pa says give me some peas, corn and potatoes,' and was let eat as much as he wanted. The next day he came back again with the same word; when the boy went home and asked, the man said he had not seen B' Rabby, and told the boy the next time Rabby came he must tie him and let him eat all he liked — but must not let him go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, Bahama Songs and Stories, story I (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day B' Rabby came with his order; the boy said, 'Let me tie you up first,' and Rabby agreed — all right, but when he was done eating he must be let go. When he was done eating and asked to be let go, the boy said no, and called his pa: 'Come, pa, got him today!' They caught B' Rabby, brought him up, put him in the iron cage; and they had six big pots of hot water standing by. B' Tiger came past and asked what was the matter. 'They got me in here to marry the Queen's daughter, and I don't want to marry her. See them six pots? They got them full of cow-heads for my wedding.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story I, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: B' Tiger said, 'Put me up! Take me up!' B' Rabby jumped up and fastened Tiger in. Rabby got away into a hollow pison-wood tree. The boy came out and said, 'Pa, there is a big one here!' The man came out with a big pot full of boiling water and swashed it on B' Tiger, who hollered 'It ain't me!' — 'Don't care if it ain't you, I going scald you.' Tiger gave one jump, knocked the cage all to pieces, and was gone; he came to the pison-wood tree where Rabby was, sat down right on the stump — and Rabby shoved a sharp, sharp stick right into him. 'My goody — hants here!' said Tiger. Rabby shoved the stick out and stuck him again: 'No, this ain't hants; B' Rabby here.' Tiger looked down in the hole and saw him — 'Never mind, you cause me to get scalded; I going catch you!' — but Rabby begged to be let out and got away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story I, ending (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: B' Rabby saw a dead goat in the road, stinking and rotten, its back rotting away; he got inside the dead goat. B' Tiger was coming fast, and Rabby groaned 'Huhn! huhn!' inside the goat. 'What is the matter, B' Goat?' — 'B' Rabby went past here just now; pointed his finger at me and all my back is rotting away.' B' Rabby went out of the dead goat. After that B' Rabby was fishing, with his finger bent; 'Mind, I going point!' — 'Do, B' Rabby, doan' point!' said Tiger, and so it was settled: no one dares point at another after that.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story I, tail (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Helephant and B' Vw'ale: the Rope Between Sea and Land
title.zh: 象與鯨：海陸之間的繩索

region.en: Andros, Bahamas (symbolic pin: shore line between pine-yard and ocean)
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯（象徵定位：松林與大洋之間的海岸線）

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story II 'B' Helephant and B' Vw'ale'

summary.en: The smallest creature on the beach bets the whale he can pull him ashore, and the elephant he can pull him to sea — then ties one rope around each neck with the instruction to pull when told, so that the two giants haul each other through surf and breakers until the rope breaks: the whale stays in the ocean, the elephant flees inland to the pine-yard, and the contest between sea and land is settled to this day.
summary.zh: 海灘上最小的生靈向鯨打賭能把他拉上岸，又向象打賭能把他拖入海——然後在兩位巨獸頸上各繫一繩，一聲令下各自使勁：兩位巨人在浪濤裡互拖不休，直到繩斷——鯨從此定居深海，象逃入內陸松林；海與陸之爭，就此定了界。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian 'old story'; tug-of-war type linking sea/land powers. Edwards notes the tale's kinship with Harris's Brer Rabbit versions.

passages.text: Now this day B' Rabby was walking along the shore. He saw B' Vw'ale and said, 'B' Vw'ale! I bet I could pull you on the shore!' — 'You can't!' — 'I bet you three thousand dollars!' — 'All right!' And Rabby went away. He met B' Helephant and said, 'B' Helephant, I bet you I could pull you in the sea!' — 'Me! There is not a man in the world can pull me in the sea!' — 'I'll try it tomorrow at twelve o'clock.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, Bahama Songs and Stories, story II (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He got a heap of rope. He tied one rope around B' Vw'ale's neck, and then one around B' Helephant's neck, and said, 'When you hear me say Set taut, you must set taut.' He said, 'Pull away!' When the Whale pulled, he pulled the Elephant into the surf of the sea — 'You think this little B' Rabby doing all of that!' When the Elephant pulled taut, he pulled the Vw'ale into the surf of the sea. The Vw'ale caught under one shelf of the rock, and the Helephant caught to one big tree; then the two of them pulled so heavy the rope broke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story II, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Vw'ale went into the ocean and the Helephant went away over in the pine-yard. That is why you see the Whale in the ocean today, and that is why you see the Elephant over in the pine bushes today — the rope between them never mended, and the shore keeps the line. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story II, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Rabby, B' Spider and B' Bouki: the Banana Dive
title.zh: 兔仔、蜘蛛與布基：潛水分蕉

region.en: Andros, Bahamas
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story III 'B' Rabby, B' Spider, an' B' Bouki'

summary.en: Coming home by boat with a bunch of bananas, the three agree the best diver keeps the most. Bouki and Rabby bring up four, two, six — but Spider floats, then demands the grapple-rope be tied to him so he can 'go down and get all'; he catches hold of them all on the bottom and cannot come up again, Rabby cuts the rope, and the judge blames the spider's own greed when his mother tries to jail the divers.
summary.zh: 三人泛舟攜蕉而歸，約定潛得最深者得最多。兔與布基依次撈起四根、兩根、六根——蜘蛛卻一入水便漂浮，只得哀求把錨繩縛在自己身上『好一次撈光』；他在水底抱住所有香蕉，再也浮不上來。兔一刀割繩；法官斷言：蛛死於己貪，罪不在潛者。

sensitivity.note: Bahamian 'old story'; spider's death by greed episode (note: in this tradition the spider-hero dies in the tale cycle, unlike the African Anansi). Collected by Edwards.

passages.text: B' Rabby, B' Spider and B' Bouki went in the field. As evening was coming they were coming home in the boat, and they had one bunch of bananas to share, and they did not know how to share it. B' Spider said to B' Rabby, 'Throw the bunch of bananas overboard, and then whoever could dive the mostest could have the mostest.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story III (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: They pulled off their clothes. B' Rabby had the first dive: down to the bottom he brought up four bananas. B' Bouki went down and brought up two. B' Spider, when he pitched overboard, floated. Rabby pitched overboard again and brought up six; Bouki brought up four; Spider pitched overboard again — and floated. 'You no tie the grapple to me and let me go down and get all!' — and he went down, caught hold of them all, and could not come up no more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story III, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: B' Rabby took his knife and cut away the rope, and they went home. When they were asked 'Where is B' Spider?' Rabby said, 'B' Spider had such a big eye; he wanted all the bananas and he couldn't dive. He did say, You no tie this grapple to me and let me get all.' Spider's mother said, 'If you don't go fetch him I put you in prison,' and they said they were not going; the woman carried them to prison, and B' Rabby put the woman in jail — and the judge said he could not put B' Rabby in prison for that, because it was B' Spider's fault.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story III, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Man, B' Rat and B' Tiger-Cat
title.zh: 人、鼠與虎貓

region.en: Andros, Bahamas
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story IV 'B' Man, B' Rat, an' B' Tiger-Cat'

summary.en: A rat spared from the trap repays the mercy from the road: cornered by the old tiger-cat whose three cubs he is carrying off, the hunter is coached into a suicide-chain — give the pigeons to the dog, eat the dog, let the cat eat you, let me eat the cat — and while the cat is studying the nonsense, the man's hand finds the gun and the shot answers. 'One good turn deserves another.'
summary.zh: 鼠自陷阱得赦， Road 邊報恩：獵人攜三隻虎貓幼崽被老母貓攔路索命，被救的鼠獻上自相殘食的連環計——鴿喂狗、你吃狗、貓吃你、我吃貓——虎貓正自思量胡言，獵人的手已摸到槍，一槍定局。『一報還一報。』

sensitivity.note: Gratitude-chain animal tale (grateful animal type). Collected by Edwards.

passages.text: Every time the rat used to go in the man's field eating his peas, potatoes and his corn; so now this day the man caught the rat and had him in the cage to kill him. The rat said, 'Do, B' Man, spare my life, I'll never come back any more!' — 'All right!' And he let the rat go; the rat went away over in the wood and never came back any more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story IV (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: This day the man went shooting pigeons, away over in the woods, and shot a big bunch; going back he saw three young tiger-cats and took all three. As soon as he made one step the old tiger-cat came after him growling: 'It is no good to put down my young ones, so you might as well keep them.' The tiger-cat was up in one tree ready to pitch on the man: 'You let the dog heat the pigeons; you heat the dog, and let me heat you.' — 'Talk fast, B' Man, talk fast!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story IV, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then that same rat that the man let go jumped out of the road: 'Yes, B' Man, do that — give the pigeons to the dog, you heat the dog, and let B' Tiger-cat heat you, and let me heat B' Tiger-cat!' The tiger-cat stood up studying what the rat said, and while it studied, the man went toward his gun, picked it up, fired, and shot B' Tiger-cat dead. Then B' Rat jumped up and said, 'One good turn deserves another! One good turn deserves another! One good turn deserves another!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story IV, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Bouki and B' Rabby: the Sheep That Walked Like a Lion
title.zh: 布基與兔仔：走如獅的羊

region.en: Andros, Bahamas
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story V 'B' Bouki an' B' Rabby'

summary.en: Raiding the Queen's pasture nightly, Rabby lifts the 'biggest sheep' — actually the lion posted at the flock's head — and palms it off on Bouki with an errand to the wood. Bouki discovers the beast walks like a lion, sings the warning, and gets his whole family onto the roof before the lion walks in through the door; child after child drops and is torn, until the husband, pointing silently down, loses his wife too, and survives the night alone on the roof because a lion cannot jump.
summary.zh: 兔仔夜襲王后牧場，抱起『最大的一隻羊』——實為守在羊群之首的獅子——以林中差事轉手布基。布基半路察覺『這東西走路像獅』，唱警全家上屋頂；獅穿門而入仰望屋頂，孩子們一個個撐不住墜下被撕，最後丈夫無言一指，妻子也墜；獅不能跳，他得以獨存屋頂至天明。

sensitivity.note: Dark trickster-transfer tale (Innocent wolf/hyena victim type, cf. Anansi-Tiger transfers in Jamaica). Collected by Edwards.

passages.text: It was B' Rabby; he used to go to the Queen's pasture every night and take the biggest sheep from the flock. So this night when he went, the Queen's servant had put a lion at the head of all the other sheep. B' Rabby was taking that to be a sheep, and carried him a little way in the road and said, 'Look here, this thing don't walk like sheep — this thing walks like lion!' And he called out for B' Bouki: 'B' Bouki, here, take this sheep. I got to go up there in the wood for the other one I got tied in the fence!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story V (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When B' Bouki got a little way he sang out, 'This thing don't walk like sheep — this thing walks like lion!' He hollered out to his wife and children, telling them all to get up on the roof of the house: 'The lion coming to tear you to pieces!' And when the lion got to the house, he walked in through the door and looked up at them all on the roof.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story V, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The smallest child said, 'Father and mother, I know you love me, but I can't hold out no longer!' — 'See lion here!' — and when the child dropped the lion tore her to pieces. The next one said, 'Father and mother, I know you love me, but my arms is tired!' — and when he dropped the lion tore him to pieces. The biggest one said the same and dropped and was torn to pieces. His wife said, 'I know you love me, and I love you too!' — the husband was so pitiful he could not talk, and just pointed his finger down to the lion, and his wife dropped. After he saw all of them were gone, he went up through the roof of the house and stayed there until the morning, and that is how he was saved: B' Lion couldn't jump, and he went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story V, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Baracouti and B' Man: the Shark Ferryman
title.zh: 梭魚與人：鯊魚渡夫

region.en: Andros, Bahamas (symbolic pin: shore crossing to the out-island field)
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯（象徵定位：往離島田地的渡口）

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 2024 (published 1895)

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story VI 'B' Baracouti an' B' Man'

summary.en: A field-worker rides the shark across to his plot four times, cutting him deeply each 'payment', until the shark waits at dusk for the return trip and holds a consultation undersea — Corb says cut him in two, Porpy says leave it to God, Baracouti says cut him to hell, and Rabby, drawing the shark inshore step by step with pretended deafness, advises the man jump ashore — and the shark commences to cry.
