summary.zh: 農人四次騎鯊渡海墾田，每次以『報酬』為名深割一刀；鯊忍至黃昏，遂在海底召開會審——石斑主張攔腰斬斷，鼠海豚勸其交由上天，梭魚主張斬入地獄；兔仔則以假裝耳背把鯊一步步引近岸石，末了勸那人：『跳上岸去！』——鯊魚哭了。

sensitivity.note: Ingratitude/underwater-counsel tale. Collected by Edwards.

passages.text: Once it was a man who had a field upon a different part of the shore. This day he wanted to go to his field; he met a shark and said, 'Please carry me across to my field!' — 'All right!' and the shark carried him across; when he got across he gave the shark a good cut. Coming out again from his field he met the shark again and begged one more crossing, and gave him a heavy cut again; the third day the same, with the promise of a fortune, and such a cut that the shark had to lay awake till he came out again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story VI (1895/2024); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sun was nearly down when the man came out and asked to be carried across again, promising to pay when he got across. The shark said, 'Get on my back.' The first fish the shark met was a Corb — 'B' Corb, you do man good and man do you harm; what must you do for him?' — 'Cut him in two!' Next was a Porpy — 'Leave it to God!' Next a Baracouti — 'Cut him to hell!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story VI, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The shark saw B' Rabby on the rocks: 'B' Rabby, you do man good and man do you harm — what must you do for him?' — 'Come in a little further; I ain't hear you!' — and the shark came in, and again, and again — 'I can't come no further else I get ashore!' — 'Why, let him jump ashore!' Before the shark could turn round to go with him, the man jumped ashore, and the shark commenced to cry. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story VI, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: The Loggerhead and the Conch
title.zh: 海龜與螺

region.en: Andros, Bahamas
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story VII 'B' Loggerhead and B' Conch'

summary.en: Racing for the King's daughter, the walking-beaten conch hires a stand of fellow conchs at every stake; the loggerhead greets each 'same' conch, stands talking while the racer slips ahead, and arrives at the palace to find the conch already there, married. The loggerhead took the sea for his dwelling place from that day.
summary.zh: 為娶公主而賽跑，步行必敗的螺在各處標樁僱下同族列隊；海龜每到一站便與『同一隻』螺寒暄，言談間真賽者早已前行——抵達王宮，螺已先至成婚。海龜自那天起便以海為家。

sensitivity.note: Hare-and-tortoise race variant (Edwards notes Aesop kinship). Collected by Edwards.

passages.text: They wanted the King's daughter. The King told the two to have a race — the one that beat the race was to have his daughter — and asked what sort of race they must have; he wanted to see who could walk the fastest out of two: the loggerhead and the conch. The conch knew the loggerhead could beat him walking, so the conch went and hired brother conchs and put them at the mark's stake, then went down to the river where the loggerhead was and told him he was all ready for the race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story VII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: They started off together. The first mark the loggerhead got to he met a conch there, taking it to be the one he had started off to race with, but standing talking; the one that went to race went ahead of the loggerhead. The loggerhead started from the place where the conch was, expecting it was the same conch; when he got to the next pole he met a conch again, still thinking it was the same conch. Standing there they small-talked, and whilst talking, the conch that had hired the other conchs had a chance to chat with him, then the conch had a chance to go his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story VII, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the loggerhead got to the King's palace, he met the conch ahead of him. The conch had beaten the race and got the King's daughter; and after that the loggerhead said he would take the sea for his dwelling place. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story VII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Eagle Lives North
title.zh: 鷹何以北棲

region.en: Green Turtle Cay, Bahamas (symbolic pin: cay shoreline)
region.zh: 巴哈馬綠龜礁（象徵定位：礁岸線）

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story VIII 'B' Crane-Crow, B' Parrot, an' B' Snake'

summary.en: A snake plagues the eagle's nesting tree until the babysitters — Crane-Crow and Parrot — call her down at the right moment and she kills it; but it has already eaten her young ones, and the bereaved mother departs north forever, to live on the northern side by Baltimore — which is why the eagle lives over there today and will not come to this side.
summary.zh: 毒蛇日日擾鷹巢，直到守巢的鶴鴉與鸚鵡及時呼喚鷹下樹誅蛇；但幼雛已被吃盡，喪子的母鷹永遠北去，棲於大海彼端的巴爾的摩一側——所以今日鷹在那邊居住，再不肯回到這一邊。

sensitivity.note: Etiological bird tale with local geography (Green Turtle Cay tells of Baltimore). Collected by Edwards.

passages.text: It was an eagle laying in a tree; after she had young ones, a snake used to plague the tree. Afterwards the eagle left B' Crane-Crow and B' Parrot to watch the young ones when the snake came to call; so when the snake came they called the eagle — 'Ma hoo eagle! The snake is coming!' — and she came, and killed the snake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story VIII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: She said, 'After he ate my young ones — therefore I'll go north, I'll live there all my life on the northern part, by Baltimore. No more to say: the snake had eaten my young ones.' That makes, so you see, the eagle live over there today; they won't come this side. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story VIII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Cricket and B' Helephant
title.zh: 蟋蟀與象

region.en: Andros, Bahamas
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story IX 'B' Cricket and B' Helephant'

summary.en: Challenged by the elephant — 'I bet I can mash you up' — the cricket answers that little man can make big man run, then proves it from inside the ear: the elephant bolts at the singing, every footfall a river, and Lion, boastful of strength, has his turn next; the cricket hops from ear to ear until Jack on the hill inherits the singing, the elephant drops dead of quivering, and a puff of wind ends the story.
summary.zh: 象誇口『我定把你踏成泥』；蟋蟀答『小者可令大者奔逃』，隨即鑽入象耳歌唱為證——象倉皇奔逃，步步如臨深河；自詡最強的獅子輪番受唱，蟋蟀在耳間跳來跳去；山坡上的傑克最後繼承了那支歌，象嚇得發抖倒斃，一陣風把故事吹散。

sensitivity.note: Small-defeats-big cycle (cf. man-is-stronger cluster). Collected by Edwards.

passages.text: It was a palm-oil tree where they used to go to feed. Every time B' Helephant used to go there he met B' Cricket: 'B' Cricket, I bet I can mash you up some of these days.' — 'B' Helephant, you can't mash me up, for it doesn't stand for the bigness of man: little man could make big man run.' — 'Go away, B' Cricket!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story IX (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: This day when B' Helephant came to the tree B' Cricket was there, and the elephant did not see him. He went into B' Helephant's ear-hole and got to singing, and B' Helephant put off running; everywhere he put his foot it was river. So he met B' Lion: 'B' Lion, man is more than me today; I am about the biggest beast in the forest and you are about the strongest, and still, if you were to hear what I heard today, it would make you run.' — 'Let him come, I'm a man for anything,' that was the word B' Lion said; and the cricket jumped out of the elephant's ear-hole and went into the Lion's ear-hole, and when the cricket sang out in the Lion's ear-hole, he and B' Helephant started together. The Lion tore up by the root a some iron-wood tree six times as big as a house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story IX, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they got there they met B' Jack standing on the hill: 'What you no running here about?' — 'B' Jack, man here today more than you and me and you two together!' — 'I'm the man to heat you and the man too!' So B' Cricket jumped out of the lion's ear-hole and went into B' Jack's own to tell him the bargain B' Helephant and he had under the palm-oil tree; so B' Helephant quivered so much he dropped down dead. 'My dear man, that was the harge (charge) what you and B' Cricket had.' — 'I tell you about a little man every day' — so a puff of wind came and ended this story. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story IX, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: De Big Worrum: the Fire-Swallowing Worm
title.zh: 大蟲：吞火之蟲

region.en: Andros, Bahamas
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story XI 'De Big Worrum' (Edwards notes African antecedents: Sotho, Kaffir)

summary.en: No fire in the house means raw potatoes, so the father sends one son and then the other to the smoke on the hill; each begs 'Dimme some fire!', is lured closer, and is swallowed down to meet the crowds of earlier swallowees inside. The father takes his gleaming lance to the worm with fire in its mouth, is swallowed slashing as he goes, cuts the worm right open — and all the people come out, and that was a big city right there.
summary.zh: 家無火只能生食；父親先後遣二子循山間炊煙討火，皆在『再近一點』的誘哄中被大蟲吞下，與先前被吞的眾人相會於腹中。父親提亮晃晃的長矛前往，邊被吞邊揮砍，將大蟲豁然剖開——腹中之人盡出，原地便成了一座大城。

sensitivity.note: Swallowing-monster tale of African descent (Edwards cites Sotho and Kaffir variants). Cross-tradition cluster: descent to the underworld, fire quest.

passages.text: So this day it was a man who had two sons, and they didn't have no fire; all they had to heat was raw potatoes. Now the man sent this boy to look for fire. He walked, and walked, and walked till he saw one smoke; when he got to the fire, the worrum was full of fire. The boy said, 'Dimme some fire!' — 'It is none; just do for me. Come in a little closer.' Soon as the boy went a little closer, when he went to reach the fire the worrum swallowed him down; the boy went down, right down inside the worrum till he stopped, and met a whole lot of people the worrum had swallowed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XI (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The man told the other son, 'I wonder where my son is gone?' — 'Pa, I going look for him.' He walked till he came to this big worrum that had the fire in his mouth. 'Dimme some fire!' — 'Keelie o' fire' (come and get fire) — 'Come a little closer.' — 'Time for Joe come' (time to go home) — and when the boy went to get the fire, the worrum swallowed him down; he went down till he met his brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XI, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now the man said, 'My two sons are gone, and I might as well go too.' He took his lance; it fairly glistened, it was so sharp. When he got where the worrum was with the fire in his mouth, the man said, 'Dimme some fire?' — 'You too do for me! Keelie o' fire' — and when the man went to get the fire, the worrum went to swallow him; the man took his lance, and as he was going down he cut the worrum, till he cut the worrum right open and all the people came — and that was a big city right there. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XI, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: B' Rabby and B' Tar-Baby
title.zh: 兔仔與柏油寶寶

region.en: Andros, Bahamas
region.zh: 巴哈馬安德羅斯

period: Bahamian oral tradition; collected 1889-1893; published 1895

source.work: Charles L. Edwards, 'Bahama Songs and Stories' (1895), story XII 'B' Rabby an' B' Tar-Baby'

summary.en: Rabby refuses to dig the well or cut the field — 'get it and drink it; get it and eat it' — and, while Lizard is decoyed into a trash-noise contest, dips the new well dry. The animals set the tar-baby in the road; fist, foot and head fasten in the classic sequence, and Rabby's sentence falls on the fresh-cut field: to be rolled in the cut cane-trash at midday sun.
summary.zh: 兔仔拒不掘井、拒不墾田——『渴了自己取來喝，餓了自己取來吃』——趁蜥蜴被誘入碎柴噪音賽，把新井汲個底朝天。眾獸在路心設下柏油寶寶；拳、腳、頭一一粘牢，兔仔被判在正午日頭下滾過新割的甘蔗田。

sensitivity.note: Tar-baby cycle (Bahamian variant); cross-tradition cluster with Jamaican and US plantation tar-baby episodes. Collected by Edwards.

passages.text: So this day B' Rabby, B' Bouki, B' Tiger, B' Lizard, B' Helephant, B' Goat, B' Sheep, B' Rat, B' Cricket — all the creatures of all kinds — said, 'B' Rabby, you going help dig the well?' — 'No!' — 'When you want water, how you going manage?' — 'Get it and drink it.' — 'B' Rabby, you going help cut field?' — 'No!' — 'When you are hungry, how you going manage?' — 'Get it and eat it.' So all of them went to work; they dug the well first, next they cut the field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: This day B' Rabby came, and they left B' Lizard home to mind the well. B' Rabby said, 'B' Lizard, you want to see who can make the mostest noise in the trash? You go in that big heap of trash there and I go in that over there' — and while the Lizard was making noise in the trash, B' Rabby dipped his bucket full of water. When B' Helephant and all the other animals came out of the field, the elephant demanded of Lizard how he let Rabby take the water; and Lizard, set on, told the company that Rabbit had drowned him in insults — the tale turned to the tar-baby that stood in the road, at which the fist, the foot and the head fastened one after the other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XII, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Caught fast on the tar-baby, B' Rabby was asked what was to be done with him; and the sentence that pleased the field-workers best was to roll him in the fresh-cut field at the heat of midday sun, in the cane-trash they had cut and he had refused to cut. E bo ban, my story's end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Edwards, story XII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Apaṇṇaka: The Two Merchants and the Truth
title.zh: 阿般那迦本生：兩商與真理

region.en: Benares, and the sixty-league Waterless Desert trade road
region.zh: 波羅奈城與六十由旬無水荒漠商道

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: When the Buddha's newly converted lay followers waver back to their old teachers, he tells of two caravan merchants: the fool who trusted a demon lost his water, his men and his life, while the wise merchant who held to the truth brought five hundred carts safely through a demon-haunted wilderness. The tale teaches that no refuge but the Buddha's is a true refuge.
summary.zh: 須達多長者的五百名弟子在佛陀離去後復歸外道。佛陀遂講述往昔兩位商隊首領的故事：愚商信妖言棄水，人畜俱亡於荒漠；智商堅守真理，識破妖計，五百車貨平安抵家。此本生示唯佛法僧三皈乃真歸依。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: At Jetavana the Treasurer Anathapindika brought five hundred friends who followed other schools to hear the Buddha. Converted, they took refuge with him; but when the Master went away to Rajagaha, they drifted back to their old doctrines. On his return the Buddha gently rebuked them: nothing in all the worlds equals the Buddha, the Truth and the Order, and those who seek refuge in these Three Gems are never reborn into states of suffering. To make the danger of a false refuge vivid, he told them a tale of two merchants, one fatuous and one wise.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 1 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Once at Benares two young merchants, each with five hundred carts, agreed to travel in succession through a wilderness that was both drought-stricken and demon-haunted. The foolish one, taking the road first, filled great jars with water and drove into the desert. At its middle a goblin, framed by magic into a lordly carriage drawn by white bulls, met him dripping wet, garlanded with lotuses, and swore that rain had fallen ahead and pools lay everywhere. Dazzled, the merchant broke his jars and threw away every drop of water, then pushed on till men and oxen sank down exhausted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 1 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: At nightfall the goblins came out of their city and slew the whole caravan, devoured the flesh and left the bones beside the untouched wares. When the Bodhisatta followed some six weeks later, the same goblin offered him the same tale; but the wise merchant halted his men and tested it: no rain-wind had reached them, no storm-cloud, no lightning, no thunder had been seen or heard within leagues. 'These are not men but goblins.' He pressed on, found the five hundred carts standing loaded and the skeletons strewn about, formed a laager, kept watch through the night, and in the morning loaded the choicest goods and reached his destination without losing a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 1 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Master linked the story to the lesson: in bygone days, said he, the opinionated perished in the demon wilderness, while those who clave to the truth escaped the demons' hands and came home again. Devadatta, he declared, had been the foolish young merchant, and he himself the wise one who was never deceived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 1 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Vannupatha: The Well in the Desert
title.zh: 荒漠本生：沙中掘井

region.en: A sandy wilderness sixty leagues across on the trade road out of Benares
region.zh: 波羅奈城外六十由旬的沙荒漠

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A Brother who had given up meditating in the forest is heartened by the memory of his own former birth: as caravan leader he alone kept heart when the desert-pilot overslept and the oxen wandered back to yesterday's camp, and his servant's resolute blows on a rock under the sand brought water to five hundred carts.
summary.zh: 有比丘於林間禪修無所成就，意欲還俗。佛陀以宿命事激勵之：往昔為商隊首領，嚮導睡著、牛車折返舊營、眾人絕望之際，唯他不棄；僕童奮力擊石，湧泉而救五百車人畜。比丘聞之重發精進，終證阿羅漢。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Once on the road out of Benares a caravan of five hundred carts came to a sandy wilderness so fine that men crossed it only by night, guided by the stars. Seven miles short of the far edge, the leader thought the night would see them through; he ordered the spare firewood and water thrown away to lighten the carts. But the desert-pilot, riding the front cart and watching the stars, fell asleep, and the oxen quietly turned and retraced their steps. At dawn the men found themselves at the previous day's camp, with wood and water gone, and every man flung himself beneath his cart in despair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 2 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Bodhisatta alone ranged to and fro in the cool of the morning until he found a clump of kusa grass. 'Water must lie beneath it,' he thought, and had a hole dug. At sixty cubits the spade struck rock and all lost heart; but he climbed down, laid his ear to the stone, and heard water running underneath. Calling a serving-lad, he said: 'If you give in, we all perish.' The lad struck the rock with an iron sledge; it split, and water rose in the hole as high as a palm-tree, so that everyone drank and bathed, the oxen were fed on chopped-up yokes and axles, and the caravan reached its destination to barter at four times the price.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 2 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Buddha told this to the faint-hearted Brother, and sang: untiring, deep they dug that sandy track till in the trodden way they found water; so let the sage, in perseverance strong, flag not nor tire until his heart finds peace. At the close of the lesson the Brother was established in Arahatship, the serving-lad of old having been himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 2 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Serivanija: The Hawker and the Golden Bowl
title.zh: 世利商本生：金缽

region.en: The city of Andhapura in the kingdom of Seri, across the river Telavaha (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 世利國特羅婆訶河彼岸的安陀城（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: Five aeons ago two hawkers of pots and pans met a ruined household that unknowingly owned a golden bowl. The greedy hawker scorned it as worthless; the Bodhisatta gave everything he had for it. The cheat, learning what he had thrown away, tracked his rival to the river and died there of rage and grief -- Devadatta's first grudge against the Bodhisatta.
summary.zh: 五劫之前，兩個賣鍋壺的行商遇見一戶破落人家。貪商以針刻驗知器為金，卻佯稱不值半錢棄之於地；菩薩則傾其所有換得金缽。貪商聞訊追至河邊，氣結吐血而死——此即提婆達多對菩薩結怨之始。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: In a decayed family of Andhapura only a girl and her grandmother survived of all its merchant wealth, working for hire; on their shelf lay the great golden bowl of former days, grimed with dirt, mistaken for common brass. The first hawker who came crying his wares was handed the bowl. He scratched it with a needle, knew it for gold, and, hoping to get it for nothing, cried that it was not worth half a farthing, flung it on the floor and left. The women were left with nothing to barter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 3 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Bodhisatta, the second hawker, entered the same street by agreement. Kindly spoken, he was called in and given the bowl. 'Mother, this bowl is worth a hundred thousand pieces; I have not its value with me.' The old woman marvelled that another's honesty should have turned the bowl to gold. He gave his whole stock of five hundred pieces and goods as much again, kept back only his scales, bag and eight coins, and hastened to the ferry.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 3 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The greedy hawker returned and learned what he had lost. Flinging away money and goods, he tore off his clothes, armed himself with the beam of his scales, and ran to the river-bank. The Bodhisatta was already mid-stream. Standing and gazing, the wretch's heart grew hot, blood gushed from his lips, and his heart cracked like sun-dried tank mud; through hatred of the Bodhisatta he perished on the spot. The Master told this to a Brother who had given up striving, and identified the Birth: Devadatta was the foolish hawker, and he himself the good one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 3 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Culaka-Setthi: The Merchant of the Dead Mouse
title.zh: 小長者本生：死鼠起家

region.en: Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: When the dull monk Little Wayman despairs of ever learning, the Buddha recalls a former life in which, from one dead mouse and a farthing, a beggar built trade upon trade for four months and rose to marry the Lord Treasurer's daughter -- while Little Wayman himself, taught by the Master, won insight from a soiled cloth and knowledge of all the scriptures in a single mealtime.
summary.zh: 愚鈍的小路比丘被兄長逐出僧團，將要還俗。佛陀親授一塊淨布令其誦念去垢，比丘觀布轉污而悟無常，一餐之間證阿羅漢並通曉一切經。佛陀又憶及往昔：乞士拾死鼠起家，四個月積財二十萬，終娶長者之女繼任財政大臣。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Little Wayman, the younger of two sons born to a runaway merchant's daughter, was admitted to the Order but proved such a dullard that in four months he could not learn a single stanza. His brother the Elder refused to include him in Jivaka's invitation and told him to leave the monastery. At daybreak, going out to renounce the robes, the lad met the Master, who seated him at his own perfumed chamber door and gave him a supernaturally clean cloth with the words 'Removal of impurity.' As Little Wayman handled the cloth it grew soiled, and he understood that this body itself had fouled it; realising impermanence, he won illumination.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 4 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Jivaka's house the Master had a servant summon 'him whose name is Little Wayman,' and the monk filled the mango-grove with a thousand replicas of himself, each unlike all the others. When the man seized the first who answered, all the others vanished, and the true Elder came to the meal, ranging through the whole of the sacred texts in his address of thanks like a young lion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 4 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Master told of a former birth. Treasurer Little of Benares, a wise man with a keen eye for omens, one day remarked by the roadside that any lad with his wits about him might start a business with a dead mouse. A beggar overheard him, sold the mouse to a tavern-keeper for a farthing, and with the farthing bought molasses and water for flower-gatherers, who paid him in flowers. He gathered fallen branches in the king's pleasaunce with bribes of molasses and sold the lot as firewood to the king's potter; he watered five hundred mowers at the city gate, cornered the grass market when a horse-dealer came to town, and bought a ship's cargo on credit with his signet ring, selling shares at a thousand pieces a head -- until he returned to Benares with two hundred thousand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 4 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Grateful, he laid a hundred thousand at Treasurer Little's feet, married his daughter, and succeeded him. 'It was through me,' said the Master, 'that Little Wayman has risen to great things in the Faith, as in times past to great things in wealth: I was the Lord High Treasurer, he my apt pupil.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 4 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Devadhamma: The Godlike Princes and the Water-Sprite
title.zh: 神法本生：水鬼問神法

region.en: A pool in the Himalayan forests (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅林間一池（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A boon rashly granted to a favourite queen forces two princes into exile, and their young brother goes with them. At a haunted pool a water-sprite devours everyone who cannot say what is truly godlike; only the eldest prince knows that the godlike are 'those who shrink from sin,' and his answer -- and his conduct -- win both brothers back and convert the demon.
summary.zh: 王后以舊願索王位，國王恐其加害二子，遣之入山，幼弟亦隨行。林中一池交與水鬼，凡下水而不能答『何為神法』者皆遭吞食。長兄菩薩以『離罪者為神』作答，且行其所知，水鬼悅服，歸還二弟，後隨菩薩入城，得定居所供養。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A king of Benares had two sons by his first queen and a third, Prince Sun, by a second wife. At the boy's birth the king had promised the queen any boon she would ask, and when the prince grew up she demanded the kingdom for him. Fearing what a scheming woman might do, the king sent his two elder sons into the Himalayas, bidding them return at his death; Prince Sun, hearing of it in the courtyard, followed his brothers of his own accord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 6 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the forest the eldest prince sent first Sun and then Moon down to a pool to drink and fetch water in a lotus-leaf. The pool had been granted by Vessavana to a water-sprite with leave to devour all who entered it, except those who knew what was truly godlike; he asked each prince the question, and each, answering 'the sun and moon' and 'the four quarters of heaven,' was seized and imprisoned below the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 6 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The eldest, missing them, tracked their footprints and girded on his sword. The sprite, in a forester's shape, urged him to bathe; the prince saw through him, and offered, unstained, to declare the godlike. Bathed, garlanded and seated on a splendid couch, he said: 'Those only are godlike who shrink from sin.' Pleased, the demon offered him one brother; the prince chose the youngest, for the boy's sake they had fled, and had he named him lost, no one would believe it. The demon cried that he not only knew but practised the godlike, and gave up both brothers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 6 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince then taught the sprite that his own past misdeeds had made him a flesh-eating demon, and warned him to renounce evil; he lived on under the prince's protection, and when the old king died, followed the Bodhisatta to Benares, where the prince reigned righteously and provided him a pleasant home with garlands and food.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 6 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Katthahari: 'Your Son Am I'
title.zh: 拾薪本生：空中認父

region.en: Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A king who trifled with a faggot-gatherer in his grove denies both the boy she bore him and the signet-ring he left as pledge. The mother appeals to Truth itself: if the child is his, may he stand in mid-air. The boy hangs cross-legged above the court declaring 'Your son am I,' and descends into no arms but his father's -- becoming King Faggot-Bearer in his turn.
summary.zh: 國王於林中悅一拾薪女，留指環為信。子既生，國王礙於廷議，否認父子，亦不認指環。其母祈以真諦：若此子果為王種，願其住於空中。童子結跏坐於半空，誦偈曰『我乃王之子』，千手齊伸而王獨接，後立為副王，母立為后。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Roaming his pleasaunce for fruits and flowers, the king of Benares came on a woman merrily singing as she picked up sticks, and loved her; the Bodhisatta was conceived then and there. He gave her his signet-ring: if she bore a girl she might spend it on the child's nurture, but if a boy, she must bring ring and child to him. When the boy could run about, other children's taunt of 'No-father' sent him asking who his father was; his mother showed him the ring and told him the king's own words.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 7 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: She brought the boy to the palace gate and announced them. Before all his court the king, knowing the truth but ashamed, denied the child; and when she held up the signet-ring, denied the ring as well. Then the woman said she had no witness left but Truth itself: 'If you be the father of my child, I pray that he may stay in mid-air; but if not, may he fall to earth and be killed.' Seizing the boy by the foot, she threw him into the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 7 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Cross-legged in the sky, the Bodhisatta repeated in sweet tones: 'Your son am I, great monarch; rear me, sire! The king rears others, but much more his child.' The king stretched out his hands crying, 'Come to me, my boy!' A thousand hands were stretched out besides, but the child descended into his father's arms alone, seated himself in the royal lap, and was made viceroy, his mother queen-consort. At his father's death he reigned as King Katthavahana, the Faggot-Bearer, and ruled righteously to the end of his days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 7 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Makhadeva: The Grey Hair
title.zh: 茂伽提婆本生：白髮之警

region.en: Mithila in the realm of Videha, and the Makhadeva mango-grove (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 毗提訶國彌薩羅城與彌薩羅芒果林（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: When his barber finds one grey hair among the raven locks of King Makhadeva -- a man with eighty-four thousand years still to reign -- the king sees the King of Death at his shoulder, hands his sovereignty to his son that very day, and spends eighty-four thousand years as a hermit in his own mango-grove before rebirth in Brahma's heaven.
summary.zh: 彌薩羅王茂伽提婆壽數尚餘八萬四千年，一日理髮師拔下一莖白髮置於掌中。王悚然如見死王臨頭，當日傳位於太子，入自家芒果林出家，修四梵住八萬四千年，命終生梵天；再世為尼彌王，復於同林出家。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: King Makhadeva of Mithila had spent eighty-four thousand years each as prince, as viceroy and as king, when he charged his barber to tell him whenever a grey hair should appear. Long afterwards the man found one, plucked it out with golden tongs, and laid it in the king's palm. At the sight the king was filled with dread, as though the King of Death stood over him or he were cooped in a hut of leaves: 'Foolish Makhadeva! grey hairs have come before you have rid yourself of depravities.' Sweat rolled from him and his raiment became intolerable.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 9 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He granted his barber a village worth a hundred thousand, summoned his eldest son, and said: 'I have had my fill of human joys; the time for my renunciation is come. Take the sovereignty; I will tread the ascetic's path in the Makhadeva mango-grove.' To his wondering ministers he repeated a stanza -- grey hairs are Death's own messengers -- and that same day went forth from the kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 9 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the grove he fostered the four Perfect States for eighty-four thousand years and died with insight unbroken, to be reborn in the Realm of Brahma. Thence he came again as King Nimi in Mithila, reunited his scattered family, and once more renounced the world for the same mango-grove and the same Brahma-heaven. The Master, whose Great Renunciation the Brethren had been praising, identified the Birth: Ananda was the barber, Rahula the son, and he himself King Makhadeva.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 9 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Nigrodha-miga: King Banyan Deer
title.zh: 尼拘律鹿王本生

region.en: Benares and the royal deer-park stocked by the king's huntsmen
region.zh: 波羅奈城與獵戶所驅之王苑鹿群

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: Two golden deer-kings agree that one deer shall die by turn, so none need be needlessly wounded. When the lot falls on a pregnant doe, King Banyan Deer lays his own head on the block in her place -- and by rising plea upon plea wins from the astonished king immunity for deer, four-footed beasts, birds and fishes alike.
summary.zh: 波羅奈王好獵，民人驅鹿入苑以供御膳。金鹿王與支提鹿王約定輪流就死，免鹿群遍體鱗傷。一日該死的是一隻懷孕母鹿，支提鹿王不允寬免；菩薩尼拘律鹿王代其就刑，臥於刑場。國王聞訊親至，鹿王連請，遂赦一切鹿、獸、鳥、魚之命。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The king of Benares was so fond of hunting that his exasperated subjects drove a whole forest of deer -- including two herds led by golden kings, Banyan Deer and Branch Deer -- into the royal park, sowed grass for them, and told his majesty to feed on them there. The king granted immunity to the two golden deer; the rest were shot at will until they grew weary and faint. To spare them useless wounds, Banyan Deer proposed to Branch that one deer a day, by turns from each herd, should go and lie with its neck on the block, and the cook take only that victim.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 12 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the lot fell on a pregnant doe of Branch's herd, who begged to be passed over until she had dropped her fawn. 'You must bear the consequences of your own fortune,' said Branch. She went to Banyan Deer, who answered 'Very well, you go away; I will see that the turn passes over you' -- and laid his own head on the block. The cook ran to the king, who mounted his chariot and came in haste: 'Did I not promise you your life?' 'Sire, a doe big with young prayed me to let her turn fall on another; as I could not pass the doom of one on to another, I have laid down my life for hers.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 12 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Never yet saw I, even among men, one so abounding in charity,' said the king. 'Arise! I spare you and her.' 'Though two be spared, what shall the rest do, O king of men?' 'Their lives too I spare.' 'Sire, only the deer in your park; what of the four-footed creatures?' 'Spared also.' 'What of the flocks of birds?' 'Spared.' 'What of the fishes in the water?' 'I spare their lives also.' Thus the Bodhisatta interceded for every kind of living thing, and established the king in the Five Commandments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 12 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the immune deer thereafter ate the crops, and the king would not revoke his promise, Banyan Deer forbade his herd to trespass, and taught the husbandmen to mark their fields with tied-up leaves -- a custom, says the story, that deer never broke. The Master identified the Birth: Devadatta was the Branch Deer, the nun was the doe, Prince Kassapa her fawn, Ananda the king, and he himself King Banyan Deer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 12 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Tipallattha-miga: The Stag Plays Dead
title.zh: 三墮鹿本生：詐死脫羅

region.en: The forests of Magadha about Rajagaha
region.zh: 摩揭陀國王舍城林間

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: Because the young Rahula, told to find his own lodging, slept without complaint in the Buddha's privy rather than displace any Brother, the Master tells how, as a young stag drilled by his uncle in six deer-ruses, he once lay in a snare feigning death so perfectly that even the blue-bottles swarmed on him -- and the hunter, loosing him to butcher him at leisure, gathered firewood and looked up to find the forest empty.
summary.zh: 羅睺羅因持戒謹嚴，被僧團逐出寮房而不訴苦，竟宿於佛廁。佛陀以此為教，講述往昔身為幼鹿：受舅父六詭之訓，落網後詐死——四蹄僵直、舌垂涎流、僅以一鼻孔呼吸，蒼蠅已集其身。獵師鬆縛，轉身拾薪，幼鹿一躍如雲散風馳，歸返母側。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: At Kosambi the Brethren, dreading to breach a new rule against sleeping in the company of novices, refused even house-room to the young Rahula; he went neither to his father the Buddha, nor to Sariputta his preceptor, nor to Moggallana his teacher, nor to Ananda his uncle, but took up his quarters in the Buddha's privy, glorious as a heavenly mansion, and bore the Brethren's tests with humble apology rather than say he had seen nothing. When the Master learned where he slept, his heart was moved, and he praised the lad's anxiety for the rules before the assembly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 16 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Not only now,' he said, 'has Rahula shewn such anxiety; even when born an animal he had it.' Once in Rajagaha of Magadha the Bodhisatta led a herd of deer, and his sister brought her son to him for instruction in the ruses of deer. Punctually the nephew came to be taught. One day, ranging the woods, he was caught in a snare, and the fleeing herd carried the news to his mother. 'Fear not,' said the uncle, 'your son has learned his lessons thoroughly,' and repeated a stanza: in all three postures your son is versed, he only breathes through his under-nostril as he lies couched, lifeless-seeming; six tricks he knows to cheat his foes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 16 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the snare the young stag did not struggle. He stretched his legs rigid, pawed up the ground, relieved himself, lolled his tongue, slavered over his body, swelled himself with drawn-in wind, turned up his eyes and breathed only through the lower nostril, until he lay like a corpse with crows settling and blue-bottles swarming. The hunter came up, smacked the stiff belly -- 'caught early this morning, he's going bad already' -- and, loosing the snare, turned aside to gather sticks for a fire. Up sprang the stag, and like a little cloud before a mighty wind was gone back to his mother. The Master identified the Birth: Rahula was the young stag, Uppalavanna his mother, and he himself the stag-uncle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 16 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Nalapana: The Monkeys Drink Through Reeds
title.zh: 蔗飲本生：蘆管飲水

region.en: The pool of Nalakapana in the Kosala country, by the village called Cane-drink
region.zh: 憍薩羅國那利迦波那池畔

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: An ogre lurks in a forest lake where every footprint leads down into the water and none come out. When he shows himself to demand the monkeys as his prey, the monkey-king answers that eighty thousand of them will drink through hollow canes without wetting a foot -- and by the power of a truth-act every cane around that lake became hollow, and so remains, to the end of the era.
summary.zh: 林中有水鬼盤踞湖畔，凡入水者皆遭吞食，湖邊足跡有下無上。猴王菩薩率八萬猴眾臨池不飲，靜待其來。水鬼現形索食，猴王言將以空心蔗管飲水，不濕一足。菩薩持誦十波羅蜜作真實語，吹管成空；並命環湖諸蔗盡成空管——此即本劫四大神跡之一。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When Brethren found their cane needle-cases hollow from top to bottom, the Master told them it was his own old ordinance. Once a water-ogre haunted a lake in a thick forest, devouring everyone who went down into the water; and the Bodhisatta, king of eighty thousand monkeys in that forest, had taught his subjects a rule: ask me first before you eat any fruit you have not eaten before, or drink of any water where you have not drunk before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 20 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day his troop, thirsty, found the lake -- and sat waiting for their king instead of drinking. When he came, he walked the bank and scrutinised the footprints: every track led down into the water and none came up again. 'Without doubt this is an ogre's haunt; you are quite right not to drink.' The ogre, cheated of his prey, rose out of the water in a horrible shape -- blue-bellied, white-faced, with red hands and feet -- and bade them go down and drink. 'We shall drink,' answered the Bodhisatta, 'yet not fall into your power: all eighty thousand of us will take a cane apiece and drink from your lake as easily as through the hollow stalk of a lotus.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 20 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He had a cane brought, called to mind the Ten Perfections, and made a solemn asseveration; the cane became hollow from end to end without a single knot. Then he made the tour of the lake and commanded: let all the canes growing here become hollow throughout. By the virtue of a Bodhisatta's saving goodness the command was fulfilled, and the canes of that lake are hollow to this day -- one of the four miracles, says the commentary, that endure through the whole Era. Seated along the bank, the eighty thousand monkeys drank through their canes at the same moment, and not one of them could the ogre get; he went off in a rage to his own habitation. The Master identified the Birth: Devadatta was the water-ogre, his disciples the monkeys, and he the resourceful monkey-king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 20 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Kukkura: The Dog's Judgment
title.zh: 犬本生：吐革雪冤

region.en: Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: When rain spoils the royal harness and the palace dogs gnaw it, the king orders every dog in the city killed. A wise cemetery-dog walks unharmed into the court, teaches the king that condemning the innocent while favourites go free is one of the four evil courses, and proves the true culprits by making the palace dogs vomit leather.
summary.zh: 雨夜浸濕御車革帶，宮中之犬囓之。國王聞奏大怒，令見犬即殺，城中犬群大遭屠戮。生為犬的菩薩率眾犬避居塚間，復孤身入城，伏於王座之下，諫王勿偏私——殺貧犬而宥良種，乃偏愛、瞋恚、愚癡、畏懼四惡道之行。國王依其計以酪拌草飼犬，群犬吐出革屑，冤情大白。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: After a day in the pleasaunce the king's chariot stood in the courtyard overnight; rain fell, the harness was soaked, and the king's own well-bred dogs came down and gnawed the straps and leather. Told that stray dogs had crept in, the enraged king ordered every dog seen to be killed. A great slaughter began, and the terrified dogs took refuge with the Bodhisatta, who had been born a dog and led several hundred of them in a great cemetery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 22 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'It must be the thoroughbred dogs inside the palace,' he reasoned, 'yet the guilty go free while the guiltless die.' Comforting his kinsfolk, he made his way alone into the city -- no hand raised stick or stone at him -- leapt under the very throne, and challenged the king: 'Do you know the dogs who actually did the mischief?' 'No.' 'Then it is not right to destroy every dog that is seen. And do your palace dogs escape death? Then this is no impartial doom of all dogs alike, but the slaughter of the poor.' He warned the king against the four evil courses of partiality, dislike, ignorance and fear, and taught that in trying cases a king should be as unbiassed as the beam of a balance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 22 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: To prove the culprits he asked for buttermilk and kusa grass, had the grass mashed into the curds, and made the dogs drink. Every dog vomited -- and brought up bits of leather. 'It is like a judgment of a Perfect Buddha himself!' cried the king, overjoyed, and did the Bodhisatta homage with the royal umbrella. The dog established him in the Five Commandments, and the king commanded that all creatures' lives should be safe, and that every dog from the Bodhisatta downwards should have constant food such as he ate himself; the Dog's Teaching endured for ten thousand years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 22 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Nandivisala: The Bull and the Hundred Carts
title.zh: 難提毘舍羅本生：百車之力

region.en: Takkasila in the Gandhara country
region.zh: 犍陀羅國呾叉始羅城

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A brahmin rears a marvellous bull on rice-gruel, and the bull, wishing to repay his nurture, bets a thousand pieces that he can draw a hundred loaded carts. Lost through one word of abuse -- 'pull, you rascal!' -- the wager is won back double when the brahmin learns to call him 'my fine fellow.'
summary.zh: 婆羅門得一小牛，以乳粥飯食精心餵養，名之難提毘舍羅（大喜）。牛長成，思報養育之恩，教主人與富商賭千金，稱能獨力拖曳百輛重車。首賭之際，婆羅門揚鞭罵曰『拉呀，你這賤畜』，牛憤而立定如四柱，賭注盡失。牛斥主人失言，令其再賭二千金，改稱『好夥計』，一拽而百車齊動。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: At Takkasila the Bodhisatta was born a bull, given as a tiny calf to a brahmin, who reared him like his own child on rice-gruel and rice and named him Nandivisala, Great-Joy. Grown mighty, the bull reflected that all India held no beast that could draw what he could, and told the brahmin: 'Go to some merchant rich in herds and wager a thousand pieces that your bull can draw a hundred loaded carts.' The merchant laughed but took the wager; a hundred carts were loaded with stones and gravel and leashed one behind another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 28 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The brahmin bathed Nandivisala, fed him perfumed rice, hung a garland on him, and seated himself on the pole. Flourishing his goad he shouted, 'Now then, you rascal! pull them along, you rascal!' 'I am not the rascal he calls me,' thought the bull, and planted his four feet like posts, budging not an inch. The merchant pocketed the thousand pieces, and the brahmin went home to lie on his bed in an agony of grief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 28 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Brahmin, in all the time I have lived in your house, have I ever broken a pot or made messes?' asked the bull, when he found his master weeping. 'Then why did you miscall me rascal? It is you who are to blame. Go and bet him two thousand -- only never call me rascal again.' Again the carts were leashed and the bull, very spruce and fine, harnessed to the leading cart with a smooth yoke-bar to keep it from skewing. 'Now then, my fine fellow! pull them along!' cried the brahmin, stroking his back; and with a single pull the bull hauled the whole string until the hindermost cart stood where the foremost had started. The merchant paid the two thousand, and the brahmin gained greatly by reason of the Bodhisatta.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 28 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Kulavaka: Prince Magha Becomes Sakka
title.zh: 枸吒迦本生：帝釋之因

region.en: The hamlet of Macala in Magadha, and the heaven of the Thirty-three (the heaven scenes are a symbolic pin)
region.zh: 摩揭陀國摩迦羅村與三十三天（天界部分為象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: Thirty villagers under the young brahmin Magha level the roads, dig tanks and build a hall, keep the Five Commandments, and survive a slander and the death-elephant; reborn together in the heaven of the Thirty-three, Magha as Sakka turns his victory-chariot back in full flight rather than crush the young Garulas -- and the Asuras, reading the wheel-marks, flee in terror of reinforcements.
summary.zh: 摩迦羅村三十家村民在菩薩（帝釋前身）率領下修路掘池、建堂設座，持五戒行善。村長誣其為盜，國王命象踐之，然群象見持戒者皆奔逃不前。國王遂賜村賜象。眾人命終同生三十三天。阿修羅來攻，帝釋兵敗乘金車遁走，途中不願輾斃林中迦樓羅幼雛，掉頭回車，阿修羅誤以為天軍來援，倉皇敗退。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: In the hamlet of Macala in Magadha the Bodhisatta was born as the young brahmin Magha. Finding the village square an uncomfortable scramble of standing-places, he made a comfortable spot for every man there, pulled down a pavilion to build a hall with benches and a jar of water, and led the thirty families of the village to keep the Five Commandments and work together: with razors and axes and clubs they rolled stones from the four highways, felled trees that would strike chariot-axles, made rough places smooth, built causeways and dug water-tanks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 31 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The village headman, who had grown rich on their drinks and fines, denounced the thirty men to the king as robbers. Without enquiry the king ordered them trampled by the elephant; but lead him as they might, the beast would not approach the men but fled trumpeting, and so did every elephant brought after. Searched for drugs, they were found to have none; asked for their spell, the Bodhisatta answered: 'We have no other spell than this -- not a man among the thirty destroys life, takes what is not given, misconducts himself, lies or drinks strong drink; we abound in lovingkindness, give alms, level the roads and dig tanks. This is our safeguard and our strength.' The king gave them the slanderer's wealth, the elephant, and the village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 31 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: They built a great hall at the meeting of the four highways, walled and gated, with fan-palms planted without and a pleasaunce and lotus-tank added by two of the four women of Magha's house; a third bought a share of the work with the gift of a ready-made pinnacle. At death all were reborn in the Realm of the Thirty-three, Magha as Sakka king of Devas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 31 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: There, when the Asuras he had cast down climbed back up Mount Sineru to war, Sakka fled worsted along the southern sky in his hundred-and-fifty-league chariot of victory -- until the fallen silk-cotton trees began to crush the young Garulas in their nests, and their heartrending cries stopped him. 'Let them not be troubled because of me; for empire's sake I will not destroy life. Rather will I give my life to the Asuras. Turn the car back!' At that very turning the Asuras, sure that reinforcements from other worlds were coming up, fled in terror to their realm below; a Palace of Victory rose through the riven earth, and fivefold guards were set against their return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 31 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Tittira: The Partridge, the Monkey and the Elephant
title.zh: 鶉本生：敬長之戒

region.en: A great banyan-tree on the slopes of the Himalayas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山麓大榕樹下（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: When Sariputta, chief of the disciples, is left all night without lodging by juniors who monopolised the cells, the Buddha ordains that seniority claims the best lodging, water and rice -- and tells of three animals at a banyan-tree who, asked which was eldest, found the partridge had known the tree from its seed and paid him all honour, winning heaven thereby.
summary.zh: 舍利弗在祇園僧舍被年少比丘搶佔而露宿樹下。佛陀藉此制定戒律：僧中長幼次第，年長者應得最好的臥具、水與飯食。並說往昔本生：榕樹下三獸——象、猿、鶉——互不敬讓，遂共議誰為年長。象言幼時此樹僅及腹，猿言幼時能摘其芽，鶉則言曾食其種而排出於此，故知此樹自其未生之始。二獸遂尊鶉為長，奉教持戒，命終同生天上。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: At Vesali the disciples of the Six, hurrying ahead of the Elders, monopolised every lodging, and Sariputta, the Captain of the Faith, passed the night at the foot of a tree near the Master's quarters. At dawn the Master heard his cough and, filled with anxiety for the truth -- if courtesy fails while he lives, what will it be when he is gone? -- assembled the Brethren. Asked who deserved the best lodging and water, some answered by birth, some by learning, some by ecstasy or sanctity; but the Master ruled that in his religion seniority claims respect of word and deed, salutation and all due service.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 37 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Even animals,' he said, 'once settled the question of seniority and honoured their elder.' Near a great banyan on the slopes of the Himalayas lived three friends without courtesy or order: a partridge, a monkey and an elephant. They agreed to find which was eldest. The elephant remembered the banyan as a bush over which he walked as a baby; the monkey, as a sapling whose topmost sprouts he could eat; but the partridge said he had once eaten the seeds of a great banyan elsewhere and voided them on this very spot -- he had known the tree from before it was born. 'Friend, you are the oldest; we will follow your counsels.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 37 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The partridge established them both in the Commandments and kept them himself; respectful and orderly, the three were reborn in heaven at life's close. 'The aims of these three are known as the Holiness of the Partridge,' said the Master, and ordained that no senior be ever again kept out of his lodging. Moggallana was the elephant, Sariputta the monkey, and he himself the sage partridge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 37 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Baka: The Crane and the Crab
title.zh: 泊迦本生：鷺與蟹

region.en: A lotus-pond in a forest haunt (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 林間蓮池（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A crane offers the fish of a shrinking pond to carry them one by one to a better pool, and eats every one at the foot of a tree. The last creature left, a crab, insists on gripping the crane's neck in transit, learns the truth over the heap of bones, and nips off the deceiver's head -- guile repaid by guile.
summary.zh: 夏日池水枯淺，魚群受窘。鷺佯裝好心，自薦逐隻銜魚往五色蓮花大池，實則棲於岸樹杈上啄食，魚群全數葬身樹下。最後池中僅餘一蟹。鷺欲以同法騙之，蟹卻要求以鉗夾其頸同行，途中識破詭計，逼鷺返回池邊，旋即剪斷其頸。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: By a lotus-pond stood a tree where the Bodhisatta lived as its tree-sprite. One summer the water sank low in a pond plentifully stocked with fish, and a crane sat down by the edge, deep in thought. Asked by the fish what he pondered, he offered to carry them one by one in his beak to a great pool covered with five kinds of lotuses. 'No crane ever thought for fish since the world began,' they said; but he proposed a trial, and a great one-eyed fish was sent to see the pool and returned full of its charms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 38 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Eager to go, the fish begged to be carried over. First the crane again took the big one-eyed fish -- but set him down in a fork of the Varana-tree on the bank and picked him clean, letting the bones fall at the tree's foot. Back at the pond he said, 'I've thrown him in; who's next?' -- and so took and ate the fish one by one till none were left. Only a crab remained, and the crane came for him too. 'How will you carry me?' 'In my beak.' 'Ah, but you might drop me; we crabs have a very tight grip -- let me hold your neck with my claws.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 38 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The unsuspecting crane consented, shewed the crab the pool, and made for the tree. 'The pool lies this way, nunky,' said the crab, 'but you are taking me the other way.' 'Very much your nunky dear am I! Just cast your eye on that heap of bones; as I ate up all those fish, so I will eat you.' 'It was through their own folly that those fish were eaten; but I shall not give you the chance. What I shall do is kill you: we will die together if need be.' And he gripped the crane's weazand as with smiths' pincers, till the bird, weeping and trembling, begged his life and set the crab down on the mud -- whereupon the crab nipped off his head as deftly as cutting a lotus stalk. The tree-fairy made the whole forest ring with the stanza: guile profits not the guileful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 38 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Vedabbha: The Treasure Charm
title.zh: 韋陀婆本生：咒雨珍寶

region.en: The road from Benares to the Ceti country, through the robbers' forest (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 波羅奈往逝地國道中盜林（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A self-willed brahmin holds a charm which, at a certain planetary conjunction, rains the Seven Things of Price from the sky. His pupil warns him not to use it; he uses it, two robber bands fight over the treasure until a thousand men lie dead, two survivors poison and stab each other -- and the charm's owner, who began it all, is cloven in two on the highway.
summary.zh: 婆羅門韋陀婆持有奇咒：行星會合之時誦咒仰天，七寶自天如雨而降。其弟子菩薩預警勿用；婆羅門為免贖金之苦，仍誦咒得寶。第二夥強盜劫寶殺之；兩夥強盜自相殘殺，千人殆盡；最後二人分贓，一欲毒殺、一欲刀殺，同歸於盡。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: In the days of Brahmadatta a brahmin of a village near Benares knew the charm called Vedabbha, precious beyond price: at a certain conjunction of the planets, if the charm were repeated with eyes lifted to the sky, gold, silver, pearl, coral, catseye, ruby and diamond would rain down from the heavens. Setting out with his pupil the Bodhisatta, he was taken in a forest by five hundred robbers called the Despatchers, who kept the teacher and sent the pupil to fetch the ransom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 48 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Today comes the great conjunction,' the pupil warned him as he left. 'Take heed lest, yielding to this mishap, you repeat the charm and call down the precious shower: calamity will befall both you and the robbers.' But at sunset, bound by his captors, the brahmin studied the rising moon, saw the conjunction at hand, and had himself bathed, perfumed and robed; then, eyes upturned, he repeated the charm, and the Things of Price poured from the sky. The robbers bundled up the treasure and marched off with him -- straight into a second band of five hundred robbers, who let the first band go, seized the brahmin, and demanded a shower too. 'It would be a year before the conjunction returns,' said he; whereat they clove him in two with a sword and flung his body on the road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 48 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hurrying after the first band, they killed every man of it; then split into two companies and fought each other down to two survivors, a thousand men destroyed by the treasure. One guarded the hoard with his sword while the other poisoned the supper-rice; each struck or was struck almost at the same moment, and both died. The pupil returned to find the severed body of his master and the strewn treasure, saw the whole story at a glance, burnt the corpse with wild flowers, and preached through the forest: 'Misguided effort leads to loss, not gain; thieves killed Vedabbha and themselves were slain.' Even the tree-fairies shouted applause.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 48 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Mahasialava: King Goodness Buried to the Neck
title.zh: 大吉之王本生：頸埋復國

region.en: Benares in Kasi, seized by the invading king of Kosala
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城，為憍薩羅王所襲

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A minister exiled for treachery in the harem proves to the king of Kosala that Benares is ruled by pure goodness: village-raiders may be caught and released with gifts. Invaded, King Goodness refuses to let his thousand warriors fight, and is buried alive to the neck -- yet escapes the jackals, enlists the help of two ogres, and wakes his usurper with the flat of his own sword.
summary.zh: 大臣因穢亂後宮被逐，投憍薩羅國，說動其王：波羅奈王大吉唯善，殺其民者反受贈而縱之，可不戰而取其國。三次試探皆然，憍薩羅王遂興兵入城。大吉王有千名勇士請戰，王皆不許——無為我一人而令眾生受苦。城破被擒，與千臣活埋於塚間，頸埋於土。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: King Goodness of Benares built six almonries, kept the Commandments and fast-days, and cherished his people with a father's love. When one of his ministers sinned in the harem, the king only banished him with his substance and family. The traitor entered the service of the king of Kosala and whispered that Benares was a honeycomb untainted by flies, its king mere feebleness. Testing the words, the king of Kosala sent three successive bands to massacre Benares border villages, then the city streets themselves; each band was caught, questioned, gently reproved, and sent away with presents.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 51 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Convinced at last, the king of Kosala marched on Benares. A thousand gallant warriors begged to meet the invader at the border; three times the king refused: 'None shall suffer because of me. Let those who covet kingdoms seize mine, if they will.' He opened the gates and sat in state on his throne with his thousand ministers. The captors were ordered to dig holes in the cemetery and bury the whole company alive up to the neck, for the jackals' nightly feast; yet so perfect was the king's discipline that not a minister disobeyed, and not one angry thought did the king himself harbour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 51 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: At midnight the jackals came. A great shout drove them off twice; the third time they judged their victims doomed and came boldly on, the leader making for the king. The king raised his throat as if to receive the bite -- and fastened his own teeth on the jackal's like a vice. Its howl frightened off the pack, and its frantic plunging loosened the earth; the king freed his hands, drew himself up, and dug out all his ministers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 51 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nearby two ogres were disputing over the division of a corpse. 'King Goodness is righteous; he will divide it for us.' They brought the body to the king, and by their magic supplied him with the scented bath, the robes, the perfumes and the dainty food laid out for the usurper. Having divided the corpse fairly, the king begged to be set in the usurper's own chamber; there he struck the sleeping tyrant with the flat of the state-sword. Waking, the usurper heard the whole story and swore friendship on the sword; next morning, before all his host, he begged pardon, restored the kingdom, and executed the slanderous traitor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 51 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Pancavudha: Prince Five-Weapons and the Ogre Hairy-Grip
title.zh: 五武器王子本生：毛手羅剎

region.en: A demon-haunted forest on the road from Takkasila to Benares (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 呾叉始羅至波羅奈道中魔林（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A prince prophesied to be peerless with five weapons finishes his schooling at Takkasila, is armed by his master, and walks straight into the ogre's forest. Every weapon sticks in the shaggy coat, then both fists, both feet and his head -- yet hanging there he is utterly fearless, for within him is the adamantine sword of knowledge; and the ogre, unable to eat so heroic a morsel, lets him go and is converted.
summary.zh: 王子出生之日，八百婆羅門觀其相，預言他將以五種武器威震全印度，遂名五武器王子。十六歲赴呾叉始羅就學，臨別師授五件武器。歸途經一魔林，人人勸阻，王子獅子般奮然獨入。羅剎毛手高如棕櫚，箭、劍、矛、棍皆黏其毛，徒手、雙腳、頭亦皆被纏住。王子懸於羅剎身上而無所畏懼，自稱腹中有金剛智慧之劍，羅剎食之必死。羅剎大恐，釋之並受五戒，被立為林中樹神。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: At his naming, eight hundred brahmins read in the infant's destiny that he should be famed and renowned for exploits with five weapons, peerless in all Jambudipa, and he was called Prince Five-Weapons. At sixteen he was sent to the world-famed teacher at Takkasila with a thousand pieces for his fee, mastered all that was taught, and received from his master, at parting, a set of five weapons. Armed with these, he set out for Benares.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 55 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Men at the forest edge warned him of the ogre Hairy-grip, who killed every traveller; bold as a lion, the prince pressed on and met the monster -- tall as a palm-tree, head like an arbour, eyes like bowls, tusks like turnips, beak of a hawk. Fifty poisoned arrows merely stuck in the shaggy coat and fell at the ogre's feet; the sword, the spear and the club stuck fast likewise. Then the prince, shouting his name, struck with his right fist, his left, both feet, and butted with his head -- and every member clave to the hide, so that he hung trapped in fivefold wise, yet undaunted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 55 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Why do you not fear death?' asked the astonished ogre. 'Each life has its destined death,' answered the prince. 'And within my body is a sword of adamant which you will never digest; it will mince your inwards, and my death will involve your own.' By this he meant the sword of knowledge. The ogre, thinking, 'This is a lion among men; not a morsel so big as a pea could I digest of such a hero,' let him go. The prince in turn taught him that his murderous rebirth as a flesh-eating ogre would carry him from darkness to darkness, and established the reformed monster as fairy of the forest with right to levy dues. Then he came armed and unhurt to Benares, and in later days ruled righteously as king. The Master identified the Birth: Angulimala was the ogre, and he himself Prince Five-Weapons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 55 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Andabhuta: The Blindfolded Lute-Player
title.zh: 阿檀浮陀本生：蒙眼彈琴

region.en: Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: To win at dice against a king whose lucky catch says all women are false, a chaplain rears a girl from birth behind seven gates and seven guards, and stakes everything on her excepted virtue. A hired scamp, smuggled in inside a flower-basket while dust-blinded guards are smothered, dances with the girl as she plays the lute for her blindfolded husband -- and cuffs him on the head.
summary.zh: 王與國師擲骰為戲，王每擲必唱吉語：女子多詐，故常勝。國師為破此咒，買一產婦所生之女，自幼幽閉於七層七門之宅，門設女衛，籃筐必檢。及女長成，國師對局加語唯我女除外，連連獲勝。王遣狡童設局：開香料店結識老嫗，詐稱其子，混入宅中藏於花籃；少女以布蒙夫之眼，借跳舞擊頭之戲令情人重擊國師。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: The king of Benares, playing dice with his chaplain, always won by singing his lucky catch -- that rivers wind by nature's law and all women work iniquity, given opportunity. Losing steadily, the chaplain resolved to raise a girl who had never seen another man: he found a poor woman about to be delivered, paid her to be confined in his house, and brought the child up under women's eyes alone in a seven-storied house with seven gateways, each guarded, every basket of sweepings searched. Only when she was grown did he challenge the king again, adding to the catch, 'always excepting my girl' -- and now it was the chaplain who won.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 62 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Suspecting the truth, the king hired a clever scamp, who opened a perfumery shop beside the chaplain's gate and waylaid the girl's single waiting-woman, falling at her feet and blubbering, 'O my mother!' while his confederates marvelled at the likeness. Laden with free flowers and perfumes, the old woman told her mistress of her son's mysterious malady: he was dying for love of the peerless beauty within. 'If you can smuggle him in here, you have my leave,' said the girl. The old woman filled a great flower-basket with dust from every corner and emptied it over each guard who tried to search her, until none dared; and the scamp was carried in inside the basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 62 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: After days of stolen delight, the scamp hid in the upper rooms, and the girl begged her husband to play the lute while she danced -- first blindfolding his handsome face with a thick cloth, she said, for shame. Blindfolded, the chaplain played on, and consented gaily to a playful blow on the head: which the hidden lover dealt so shrewdly that the brahmin's eyes were like to start out. 'It is a soft hand,' he marvelled, 'but it hits hard!' The scamp was carried out in the basket, told the king everything, and at the next sitting the chaplain -- still excepting his girl -- lost once more. 'You could not be certain of a woman even if you carried her inside you,' said the king, and repeated the stanza of the blindfolded lute-player.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 62 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Silavanaga: Good King Elephant and the Ungrateful Forester
title.zh: 吉象王本生：忘恩之報

region.en: The Himalayan forests (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 喜馬拉雅山林（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A white elephant-king, dwelling apart from his herd for its sin, rescues a lost forester of Benares, feasts him and carries him out of the forest. The man marks the trail, returns with a saw, and takes first both tusks, then the remaining ivory, then the stumps -- until the earth itself opens and swallows him down to hell.
summary.zh: 雪山白象王因象群有惡，獨居林中。一迷路樵夫遇救，象王以百果相待，負之出林，且囑勿洩居所。樵夫沿途默記山川，還城見象牙工坊，知活象牙價高，遂攜鋸而返。象王念其貧苦，許其鋸斷雙牙，並言此施乃為求一切智；牙售罄，樵夫再來索餘牙，再來索牙根，踐象鼻登象額，剜肉取根而去。大地不堪其惡，裂開深淵，地獄火焰捲之而入。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: In the Himalayas the Bodhisatta was born a white elephant, perfect in beauty, whom all the elephants of the mountains followed as their leader; but aware of sin in the herd, he dwelt apart in solitude, and the goodness of his life won him the name Good King Elephant. A forester of Benares, lost in that forest and weeping in fear of death, was found by the elephant, who stood still whenever the man ran and advanced only when he stood -- until the man understood the creature meant to help. Feasted on fruits for days, he was carried out on the elephant's back, marking every landmark, and set down on the high road with the charge: 'Tell no man of the place of my abode.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 72 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: In Benares the forester came to the ivory-workers' bazaar and learned that a living elephant's tusk was worth far more than a dead one's. Back he went with provisions and a sharp saw, whining that he could not make a living. 'Certainly; I will give you a whole tusk, if you have a saw to cut it off with,' said the Bodhisatta, and bowed his knees till he couched like an ox while both chief tusks were sawed away. 'Think not that I prize them not,' he said, taking them in his trunk; 'a thousand times dearer to me are the tusks of omniscience, and may my gift bring me omniscience.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 72 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the money was spent the man returned, begging for the rest of the ivory; then for the stumps themselves. 'So be it,' answered the elephant, and lay down as before; and the wretch, trampling on the silvered trunk and climbing on the snowy temples of the future Buddha, kicked the roots of the tusks clear of the flesh and sawed out the stumps. Scarce had he passed out of sight when the solid earth, unable to bear the burden of such wickedness, burst asunder, and flames from nethermost hell wrapped the ingrate round as in a shroud of doom and bore him away. The tree-fairy made the forest echo: 'Ingratitude lacks more, the more it gets.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 72 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Saccamkira: 'A Log Pays Better Salvage'
title.zh: 薩叉蜜羅本生：恩將仇報

region.en: The river below Benares, and a hermitage on its bend
region.zh: 波羅奈城河畔沙門草菴

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: A hermit saves a wicked prince from the flood together with a snake, a rat and a parrot; the three grateful beasts repay him with hoards and rice, while the king he saved has him flogged toward execution -- until the outraged crowd tears the tyrant down on his own elephant and crowns the hermit in his stead.
summary.zh: 惡王子河中遇溺，菩薩沙門連同蛇、鼠、鸚鵡一併救起。三獸感恩各以寶藏相贈，王子卻懷恨，登位後於遊行中拘捕沙門，欲於街頭鞭笞斬首。沙門沿途僅誦『拖木頭尚勝於救人』之偈，民眾聞其救駕之功，怒而弒王，擁沙門為王。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Fierce and cruel as a scotched snake, Prince Wicked of Benares was one day bathing in mid-stream when a storm burst and the flood swept him off, clinging to a tree-trunk and crying in fear of drowning. A rat reborn above a hoard of thirty crores and a snake reborn above a hoard of forty clambered aboard; a parrot from an uprooted silk-cotton tree alighted there also, and the four floated down together. A hermit on the bank, hearing the cries at midnight, plunged across the stream and hauled the log ashore, warmed the animals first and the prince after, and fed them in the same order -- which filled the prince with hatred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 73 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: At parting the snake promised forty crores to any who called 'Snake,' the rat thirty to any who called 'Rat,' and the parrot many waggon-loads of rice to any who called 'Parrot'; the prince promised the Four Requisites if the hermit would come to him when king -- while inwardly resolving to kill him. The hermit tested them all: the snake and the rat gave up their hoards, the parrot offered rice from the Himalaya marches. But when, dressed with care, he sought alms in the city, the king on his state elephant thought, 'Here comes that rascally hermit to quarter himself on me,' and ordered him bound, flogged at every street-corner, and beheaded outside the gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 73 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Under every blow the hermit only repeated his stanza: 'They knew the world, who framed this proverb true -- a log pays better salvage than some men.' The wise among the bystanders asked what service he had done the king, and, hearing the whole story, all classes with one accord cried 'Seize the tyrant!' and slew him on his elephant with arrows, stones and clubs. The crowd anointed the hermit king on the spot. Reigning righteously, he collected the seventy crores from snake and rat, housed them in a golden tube and a crystal casket, kept the parrot in a cage of gold, and fed all three daily in vessels of gold; and the four lived in harmony until their end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 73 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Illisa: The Miser and the Double
title.zh: 伊利沙本生：慳吝長者

region.en: Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 1 (trans. Robert Chalmers, 1895)

summary.en: The miser Illisa, worth eighty crores, breaks his family's tradition of bounty, burns down the almonry and drinks alone in a thicket. His father, reborn as Sakka, disguises himself as his son, flings the treasure to the city, and lets the wretched man be thrashed at every turn -- then reveals himself in mid-air and threatens the thunderbolt unless the almonry is rebuilt.
summary.zh: 慳吝長者伊利沙富有八十億，卻燒毀祖傳施捨堂、驅逐貧人，且怕人知，攜一瓶酒獨至河邊樹叢中獨酌。其父因布施而生忉利天為帝釋，見子悖行，化作其形入宮散財，城中人攜袋而至，取之立盡。真伊利沙歸來，被鄉民、僕役、守門人輪番毒打，求訴於王，王亦莫辨真偽。帝釋現空中自陳，並威嚇：不建施堂，必以雷霆擊死。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Illisa, Lord High Treasurer of Benares, was lame, crook-backed and squinting, worth eighty crores, and a miser whose house was like a pool haunted by demons: for seven generations his ancestors had been bountiful, but he burned down the almonry, drove the poor from his gates with blows, and neither gave his wealth away nor enjoyed it himself. One day, seized by a craving for drink, he grudged even a companion's share, sent a slave with a single penny for a jar of spirits, and crept to a remote thicket by the riverside to drink alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 78 (Chalmers 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: His father, in heaven as Sakka because of his lifetime's bounty, saw all this and resolved to convert his son. Descending in the exact shape of Illisa -- lame, hunched and squinting -- he told the king he wished to give his eighty crores to the royal treasury, and on being refused, cried 'Then I shall give it away to whom I will.'
