summary.en: In the world's first age men, beasts, fish and birds each choose a king; the birds pick the owl, and proclamation is made twice. On the third announcement a crow rises to object -- 'if this is his face in good humour, what when angry?' -- and flies off cawing his dissent, beginning the feud of crows and owls.
summary.zh: 初劫之時，人立王，獸立獅，魚立阿難，唯鳥無王。眾鳥集於磐石，選鴞為王，傳令三遍。第三遍時一鴉起而抗聲：『加冕之時尚作此態，震怒之時當如何？如芝麻撒於熱釜！』遂飛翔空中，連呼『吾不奉詔』。鴞起身追之，自此鴉鴞結仇。眾鳥改立金鵝為王。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When a Brother sweeping his cell found a basketful of crows' heads dropped from the trees by owls, the Brethren asked how long the crows and owls had been at enmity. 'Since the time of the first age of the world,' said the Master, and told an old-world tale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 270 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the first cycle of the world the people gathered and took for their king a man handsome, auspicious and commanding; the quadrupeds chose the Lion, and the fish of the ocean chose a fish called Ananda. Then all the birds in the Himalayas assembled upon a flat rock: 'Among men there is a king, and among the beasts, and the fish have one too; we should not live in anarchy. Fix on some one fit to be set in the king's place!' They searched about and chose the Owl, and a bird made proclamation three times that a vote would be taken on the matter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 270 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: After patiently hearing the announcement twice, on the third time up rose a Crow: 'Stay now! If that is what he looks like when he is being consecrated king, what will he look like when he is angry? If he only looks at us in anger, we shall be scattered like sesame seeds thrown on a hot plate. I do not want to make this fellow king!' Granted leave to speak his mind, he enlarged upon it: 'I like not, with all deference be it said, to have the Owl anointed as our head; look at his face! if this good humour be, what will he do when he looks angrily?' Then he flew up into the air, cawing 'I don't like it! I don't like it!' The Owl rose and pursued him; thenceforward those two nursed enmity one towards another. And the birds chose a golden Goose for their king and dispersed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 270 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Kurudhamma: The Righteousness of the Kurus
title.zh: 俱盧正法本生：求雨

region.en: Indapatta city in the Kuru kingdom, and drought-stricken Dantapura in Kalinga (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 俱盧國因陀羅巴陀城與迦陵伽但陀補羅城（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Drought-stricken Kalinga asks the righteous Kuru king for his state elephant; rain still fails, so the Kalinga king sends for the very Five Virtues themselves -- collected, scruple by scruple, from eleven lay figures who each fear the smallest stain, down to a courtesan whom Sakka himself tested. Written on a golden plate, the precepts bring rain to Kalinga at last.
summary.zh: 迦陵伽大旱，民人號泣。國王臥草蓆七日求雨不得。聞俱盧國行五戒故雨水時至，先求其寶象，得之而雨不至；復遣婆羅門求『俱盧正法』。王、母、王后、副王、國師、御者、車伕、富商、倉吏、守門人、妓女，皆以纖介之疑自陳其心——如誤踏蟹穴、誤以妹為婦等——眾人皆曰：『非意之罪，不入於帳。』逐一書於金版。國王習之，迦陵伽雨澤遂降。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: A Brother who could shoot a pebble through a wild goose's eye was rebuked by the Master, who told of the Kuru righteousness. Once Dhananjaya reigned at Indapatta in the Kuru kingdom, and the Bodhisatta his son, grown king, kept the ten royal duties and the Five Virtues -- as did queen-mother, queen-consort, viceroy, family priest, driver, courtier, charioteer, treasurer, master of the granaries, noble, porter, courtesan and slave-girl, every one. He built six almonries and daily distributed six hundred thousand pieces in alms, till all India was overspread by his bounty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 276 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: In Dantapura of Kalinga, King Kalinga's realm was afflicted: no rain fell, the crops failed, famine stalked the land, and three fears were ever present. Told that former monarchs lay seven days on a grass pallet after alms and vows, the king did so -- and still no rain. 'In Indapatta there is a state elephant, Anjana-vasabho the Black Bull,' said his court. 'The king there loves giving: were he but asked, he would give it without fail.' Eight brahmins went and hailed the Bodhisatta on the road to his almshouse; he examined the elephant three times round for any spot unadorned, besprinkled him with scented water, and made him over with his golden chain, driver and all -- 'a king's portion, worthy of a king.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 276 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: But although the elephant was come, no rain fell. 'Your king observes the Kuru righteousness,' said the brahmins on their return; 'our king is wishful himself to observe it: write it on a golden plate and bring it hither.' 'Indeed I did once observe it; but now I am in doubt about this very point. At the Kattika feast I shot a flower-wreathed arrow over the lake, and whether it fell upon some fish I know not; the doubt of life-taking makes a flaw in my virtue. But my mother keeps it well: get it from her.' So it went on: the queen-mother doubted her partiality in dividing sandal-wood and a golden neckband between her daughters-in-law; the queen at her lattice had looked with love upon the viceroy; the viceroy had let a crowd stand all night in the wet; the chaplain had coveted a sun-bright chariot; the driver's measuring-stick had perchance crushed a crab in its hole; the charioteer's goad had tired the steeds; the rich man had tied a handful of untithed rice; the granary-master's markers had perchance fallen on the measured heap; the porter had called a woodman's sister his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 276 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Each time the messengers answered: 'What is done without intent is not counted to the score. If you feel a scruple in so small a matter, what real transgression could you ever commit?' And from each they received the Five Virtues -- Slay not the living; take not what is not given; walk not evilly in lust; speak no lies; drink no strong drink. Last, the courtesan told how Sakka, in the shape of a youth, had given her a thousand pieces and never returned for three years, till she grew so poor she must apply to the Chief Justices for her old wage -- and how at the very moment her hand went out for another man's thousand, Sakka showed himself in his own shape, shining like the sun fresh risen, and filled her dwelling with jewels of seven kinds. 'Merely to hold out the hand is not a breach of virtue: that virtue of yours is the highest perfection!' Thus they bore the golden plate to Dantapura; the Kalinga king practised the Five Virtues, and in all the realm of Kalinga the rain fell, the three fears were allayed, and the land became prosperous and fertile.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 276 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Vaddhaki-sukara: The Carpenter's Boar
title.zh: 木匠豬本生：野豬陣

region.en: The forests and hills beyond Benares in the Kasi country
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城外山林

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Reared by carpenters and released into the forest, a tusked boar finds a paradise cave held in terror by one tiger. He arrays the herd in a lotus battle-order, lets the sham hermit's advice lure the tiger into a pit-trap, gores him, then fells the fig-tree under the fleeing hermit with one tusk-blow -- and is consecrated king of the boars on a chair of fig-wood.
summary.zh: 木匠所養之豬牙彎體壯，力能翻樹遞斧，恐為人食，縱之入山。得一石窟，水草豐美，然群豬皆瘦——晨有虎至，見者即被攫。木匠豬夜夜操練，布蓮花陣：母豬幼崽居中，戰豬環外；鑿圓坑陷阱。虎至，群豬不逃，虎作何狀，豬亦作何狀。虎回洞，偽沙門（分食虎祿者）譏其無勇，慫恿再往。虎撲，豬急閃身墮入圓坑之旁小洞，虎墮深坑，豬跳起以牙貫其股，傷其腎而斃之。偽沙門欲逃，爬上榕樹，母豬擔水、幼豬掘根、牙豬撞根，一擊樹倒，眾豬齧其骨。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: Carpenters settled near Benares found a young boar fallen in a pit and kept him; he grew big with curved tusks and well-mannered, turning trees over with his snout and fetching hatchet and adze, chisel and mallet, and pulling the measuring line by the end. Afraid someone might eat him, the carpenter let him go in the forest. The boar found a great cave in a mountain side, with plenty of bulbs and roots and fruits, and some hundreds of boars approached him: 'A nice place it certainly is, but dangerous -- there is a tiger comes in the morning, and every one he sees he seizes and carries off.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 283 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'One alone too many for all of you! I'll catch him, if you only do what I tell you.' At night he drilled the boars and prepared them for war, explaining that war is of three kinds, the lotus army, the wheel army, and the waggon army, and arraying them after the lotus pattern: the mothers and their suckling brood in the middle, then the sows without young, the little boars, the yearlings, the tusked, and the strong battle-boars by tens and twenties in serried ranks. Before his own position he had a round hole dug, and behind it a pit growing gradually deeper, shaped like a winnowing basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 283 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: At dawn the tiger came, stopped upon the plateau, and glared; and at a signal all the boars glared back. Whatever the tiger did, the boars did after him. 'They used to take to their heels as soon as they saw me -- now they stand up against me!' marvelled the tiger, and turned back to his lair. But the sham hermit who shared the tiger's prey mocked his empty paws and urged one roar and one leap; so the tiger plucked up courage and leapt upon the Carpenter's Boar. The boar dodged and dropped into the round hole; the tiger could not stop, but tumbled headlong into the jaws of the deeper pit; up jumped the boar, ran his tusk into the tiger's thighs, tore him about the kidneys and tossed him out of the pit crying, 'Here's your enemy for you!' They who came first had tiger to eat; those who came after went about sniffing at others' mouths, asking what tiger's flesh tasted like.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 283 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Still the boars were uneasy: 'the sham hermit can bring ten tigers more!' So they all set forth, found the man, chased him up a fig-tree, and the leader charged a great thick root with one blow like an axe -- 'twas enough to fell the tree to the ground, and the boars waiting below tore the hermit to pieces and gnawed the bones clean in a moment. Then they perched the Carpenter's Boar on the tree-trunk, filled the dead man's shell with water, and sprinkled him to consecrate him for their king, with a young sow for his Consort -- the origin, says the story, of the custom that a king at his crowning is set on a fine chair of fig-wood and sprinkled out of three shells.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 283 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Macch-uddana: The Fish Worth a Thousand
title.zh: 魚價本生：河神護財

region.en: The bank of the Ganges (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 恆河岸畔（象徵標記）

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: A thieving younger brother swaps a parcel of gravel for the family money and drops the 'gravel' overboard; the Ganges spirit, fattened on the merit of a meal-gift, has a fish swallow the parcel, sells it to the wronged brother for seven annas -- and even the Bodhisatta still sends the cheat his half.
summary.zh: 兄弟收債千枚歸途，兄臨眠以餘食擲河飼魚，功德歸於河神，河神神力增長。弟欲獨吞，以碎石包調換錢包。船至中流，弟佯跌，將『碎石包』墮水，實為錢包。河神令大口魚吞之。弟歸家啟包，唯見碎石，心如枯木。漁人獲魚，索價千枚七分，人人笑之；至菩薩門前只索七分。妻剖魚得錢。河神現身說明原委，並勸勿分與弟；菩薩仍遣人送五百枚與弟。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When Brahmadatta reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of a landed proprietor. At their father's death he and his young brother went to a village to arrange some business and were paid a thousand pieces of money. On the river-bank, waiting for the boat, they ate a meal out of a leaf-pottle, and the Bodhisatta threw what he left into the Ganges for the fishes, giving the merit to the river-spirit, who accepted it with gratification, and by the increase of her divine power became aware what had happened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 288 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The young brother was of a thievish nature, and wanted the money for himself: he packed a parcel of gravel to look like the parcel of money and put them both away. At mid-river he stumbled against the side of the boat and dropped overboard the parcel of gravel -- as he thought, but really the money. 'Brother, the money's overboard! What's to be done?' 'What can we do? What's gone is gone; never mind about it,' replied the other. But the river-spirit resolved to take care of his property, and by her power made a big-mouthed fish swallow the parcel. At home the cheat chuckled over his trick -- and undid the remaining parcel to find nothing but gravel; his heart dried up and he fell on his bed clutching the bedstead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 288 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some fishermen casting their nets took the fish by the spirit's power and carried it to town to sell. 'A thousand pieces and seven annas,' they asked, and everybody laughed; brought to the Bodhisatta's door, they let him have it for seven annas. His wife cut it open, and there was the parcel of money; he knew his mark. 'Who could believe the story, were he told, that fishes for a thousand should be sold?' he marvelled -- and at the moment the river-spirit hovered invisibly in the air: 'I am the Spirit of the Ganges. You gave the remains of your meal to the fishes and let me have the merit; therefore I have taken care of your property. There lies your brother, his heart dried up. There is no prosperity for the cheat: do not give it to him.' 'That is impossible,' said the Bodhisatta, and all the same sent the brother five hundred.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 288 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Supatta: The Crow Who Gave His Life
title.zh: 蘇波陀本生：烏鴉捨身

region.en: Benares in the Kasi country, and the crow-roosts hard by the city
region.zh: 迦尸國波羅奈城郊鴉群棲地

period: Composed c. 3rd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, Pali; Jataka translation 1895

source.work: The Jataka, ed. E. B. Cowell, vol. 2 (trans. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895)

summary.en: Queen Crow Softie craves a taste of the king's own cooking; Captain Prettybeak strikes the dinner-carrier's nose to make him drop the dishes, spends his life gladly for his king and queen -- and wins the white umbrella, the king's adhesion to the Crow-king's counsel, and daily food for eighty thousand crows.
summary.zh: 鴉王蘇波陀（美翅）統八萬烏鴉棲於波羅奈城郊。鴉后軟兒忽思王廚之食，思之欲死。隊長美喙自願捨身取食：令四鴉銜飯、四鴉銜魚侍奉王后，自撲膳夫，啄鼻塞口，飯盡落地。國王擒之，聞其捨身之由，嘆曰：『人尚不能為我捨生，烏鴉竟爾！』遂賜白傘。鴉以傘回敬，讚王后之美德。國王從其教，日煮大釜之飯以飼眾鴉，行善護生，其遺訓七百年猶存。

sensitivity.note: Canonical Jataka of a living tradition; retold freely; no ritual secrecy.

passages.text: When Brahmadatta was king in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a crow, and became chief of eighty thousand crows, Crow king Supatta, Fairwing, with his mate Suphassa, Softie, and his captain Sumukho, Prettybeak. Passing over the king's kitchen, Softie smelt the odour of a host of dishes of fish, uncovered a moment to cool, and longed for a taste; the next day she told her lord she must have some of the king's food, or die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 292 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: King Crow sat down to think, and Prettybeak asked if aught displeased him. 'Oh, that will be all right,' said the captain: 'stay where you are today, and I will fetch the meat.' He gathered the crows, posted them in companies to watch near the kitchen, and with eight champions sat on the kitchen roof: 'When the food is taken up, I will make the man drop the dishes -- and that is an end of me. Four of you must fill your mouths with the rice and four with the fish, and feed our royal pair; if they ask where I am, say I am coming.' The cook hung his dishes on a balance-pole and went towards the king's rooms; in the court the captain flew and settled on the carrier's chest, struck him with extended claws, pecked the end of his nose with his spear-point beak, and stopped up his jaws with his two feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 292 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king, walking on an upper floor, saw it all: 'Down with the dishes and catch the crow!' The man dropped the dishes and caught the crow tight; the crows ate all they wanted and carried off the rest as they had been told, till the craving of Softie was appeased. 'You have broken my servitor's nose and thrown away your life; what made you do such things?' asked the king. 'O great king, our king lives near Benares and I am captain of his forces. His wife conceived a great longing; at once I devoted my life; now I have sent her the food, and my desire is accomplished.' The king marvelled that a crow should sacrifice life for his king, gave him the white umbrella; and the crow saluted the king with the gift and praised the virtues of Fairwing. The king sent for him, heard his teaching, fed king and queen on the food he ate himself, and had a large measure of rice cooked daily for the crows; and the admonitions of Fairwing were remembered for seven hundred years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Jataka 292 (Rouse 1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Compair Lapin, the Elephant and the Whale
title.zh: 兔大哥、象與鯨

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA (symbolic pin: Lake Pontchartrain shore)
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地（象徵定位：龐恰特雷恩湖岸）

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 1895

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales', Memoirs of the American Folk-Lore Society vol. II (1895), tale I 'The Elephant and the Whale' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: The Louisiana rabbit trickster ties one rope to the elephant 'stuck cow' inland and one to the whale 'stuck cow' at sea, beats his drum, and sets the two titans hauling each other through mud and surf — then, when they compare notes, disguises himself as a poisoned fawn to beg both giants into revoking their bans: eat all the grass on land, drink all the water in the sea, and never miss him again.
summary.zh: 路易斯安那兔騙子編造『陷泥之牛』，把一根繩繫給陸上的象、一根繫給海中的鯨，鼓聲一響，兩位巨獸隔泥隔浪互拖不休。事敗之後，他假扮中毒的小鹿討得雙方撤禁——陸上牧草任食，海中清水任飲——二獸還叮嚀相遇者千萬手下留情。

sensitivity.note: Louisiana Creole animal tale; Fortier notes African origin of the elephant-whale motif. Cross-ref: afroatlantic-elephant-whale-tug (Bahamas, same cluster).

passages.text: Compair Bouki feared the giants would hear them listening, but Compair Lapin said he was more cunning than they, and would fix them. He went to get a very long and strong rope, hid his drum in the grass, and went to the elephant: 'Mister, you who are so good and so strong, render me a service; you would relieve me of a great trouble.' The elephant was glad to hear such a fine compliment and promised to help. 'I have a cow stuck in the mud on the coast; take this rope in your trunk, I shall tie it to the cow, and when you hear me beat the drum, pull hard on the rope, because the cow is stuck deep in the mud.' — 'All right,' said the elephant; 'I guarantee I shall pull the cow out, or the rope will break.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, Louisiana Folk-Tales, tale I (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Compair Lapin took the other end of the rope and ran towards the sea, paid a pretty compliment to the whale, and asked the same service about the cow stuck in a bayou in the woods. Compair Lapin's mouth was so honeyed that no one could refuse him anything. The whale took hold of the rope: 'When I shall hear the drum beat I shall pull.' — 'Begin pulling gently, and then more and more.' — 'You need not be afraid; I shall pull out the cow even if the Devil were holding her.' He beat his drum. The elephant pulled so hard the rope was like a bar of iron; the whale, on her side, pulled and pulled, and yet came nearer to the land, and when she saw that she was mounting on land she beat her tail furiously and plunged headlong into the sea — the shock dragged the elephant to the sea, who knelt with his front feet in the mud, twisted the rope round his trunk, and pulled the whale again to the shore. Each had been pulling the other, and neither had been pulling any cow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale I, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Lapin told me the same thing. I believe he is making fun of us.' — 'He must pay for that: I forbid him to eat a blade of grass on land because he laughed at us.' — 'And I will not allow him to drink a drop of water in the sea; we must watch for him, and the first one that sees him must not miss him.' Compair Lapin, who was listening, told Bouki it was time to leave; but he was not through with them yet. Soon he came by disguised in the skin of a little fawn dogs had killed, poisoned by Compair Lapin's curse for eating grass; the terrified elephant revoked his ban — tell Compair Lapin he is my best friend, let him eat all the grass he wants — and the fawn carried the same tale to the whale, who lifted her tail and asked Lapin to drink all the water he wanted and never be troubled again. 'You see I am smarter than they, and can fool them all the time,' said Lapin to Bouki.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale I, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Compair Lapin and the Earthworm: the Devil's Gift
title.zh: 兔大哥與蚯蚓：魔鬼的饋贈

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 1895

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale III 'Compair Lapin and the Earthworm' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: The helpless earthworm cries for strength and belongs to the Devil from the day of death; made suddenly huge, his hole deep as a well, he terrifies Compair Lapin — who has boasted he could beat the elephant and is scheduled to prove it. The rabbit sets up a duel between his two fears, coaching the worm to hide in the dust before the elephant's arrival, and the collision of giants settles both accounts at once.
summary.zh: 無助的蚯蚓哭求力量，從此死後歸於魔鬼；變得巨大、穴深如井，嚇壞了誇口能勝大象的兔大哥。兔仔設下二懼相鬥之局，教蚯蚓藏身塵土伏擊大象——兩強相撞，一筆帳兩頭清。

sensitivity.note: Louisiana Creole animal tale (devil's-bargain type). Collected by Fortier.

passages.text: It was a day in spring; the little birds were singing, the butterflies flying from one flower to another, and it seemed as if all the animals were rendering thanks to God for his kindness. A little earthworm was the only one crying and complaining — he was so small, had neither feet, nor hands, nor wings, and was obliged to remain in his hole; the little birds, the lizards, and even the ants troubled him and ate his little ones. If God would make him big and strong like other animals he would be contented, because he could defend himself; as it was, he was helpless in his hole. He cried and cried and said he would be glad if he belonged to the Devil — and hardly had he spoken when he saw the Devil at his side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale III (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Well, I heard all you said; tell me what you want; I shall grant it, and you will belong to me when you die.' — 'I want strength, to become big, big, and beat everybody who comes to trouble me.' — 'That is all right; let me go, in a short while you will be contented.' As soon as the Devil had gone, the worm found himself strong and big; his hole became large and as deep as a well, and he began to laugh and sing. At that very moment Lapin passed by and was terribly frightened: he ran until he could go no farther — 'Never was I more frightened; I shall never sleep again while that big earthworm remains in this country!' But he had boasted he could beat the elephant, and Bouki had told on him; so he set his two fears to fight each other, and hoped to get rid of both at the same time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale III, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went until he met the elephant, bowed politely, and let fall that another time he would come to try his strength — he thought he could beat him. 'You are a fool; go away, I don't want to harm you; I take pity on you.' But Lapin made him take the wager, and led the giant toward the worm's deep well of a hole, where the ground had been laid with a soft dust that could swallow a giant stepping wrong — and the elephant, thrown by the earthworm's ambush, never troubled the rabbit's boasting again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale III, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Compair Lapin and Compair l'Ours: the Crying Excuses
title.zh: 兔大哥與熊大哥：哭喪的藉口

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 1895

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale IV 'Compair Lapin and Compair l'Ours' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: Invited to help break corn before dinner, Lapin pricks up his long ears all day at 'calls from home' — a wife sickening, worsening, and at last 'all is finished' — while actually eating l'Ours's provisions house by house. The plank-test of guilt catches the thief vomiting in the sun, and the rabbit converts his own hanging into a rope-through-the-wall trick, crying loudly until the hangers think him dead — 'you see I am smarter than you, and I thank you for the good dinner I had at your house.'
summary.zh: 兔大哥受邀破玉米備宴，整天以『家中呼喚』豎起長耳——妻子病了、病重、終於『完了』——實則一戶戶吃空熊家的儲備。曬板驗賊計擒出日下嘔吐的真兇；兔仔卻把絞刑改成穿牆拉繩的戲法，哭聲由響至微，令行刑者以為人已斃氣——『我比你們機靈，謝謝你家那頓好飯。』

sensitivity.note: Louisiana Creole animal tale. Collected by Fortier.

passages.text: One day Compair l'Ours invited Compair Lapin and Compair Bouki to dine with him, telling them he had bought butter, cheese and biscuits — but before dinner they must come and help him break some corn for his horse. They accepted and went into the field before daybreak. At nine o'clock Compair Lapin pricked up his ears: 'I never saw anything so annoying as the people at my house; they are calling me and disturbing me in my work.' — 'I don't hear anything,' said Compair l'Ours. — 'It is because you and Bouki have such small ears. My ears are so long that I hear miles away.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale IV (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He went away and came back saying it was his wife who was beginning to be sick; he did the same thing three times during the day — at noon his wife was in the middle of her sickness, at three o'clock he came back very sad and said merely, 'All is finished.' The two pitied him, thinking his wife dead; instead, each time he had said he was going to his wife's house, he went to the house of Compair l'Ours and ate a little of his provisions — and when he said 'It is finished', he had finished eating all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale IV, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: At five o'clock the three friends left their work and went to the house of Compair l'Ours; all his provisions had disappeared, and he accused Lapin, who swore it was not he. 'I shall know right off: all three of us will lie down on that plank in the water in the sun, and the thief will surely be sick.' Lapin was not pleased to find it was the stage of a boat, where he could not get into l'Ours's shadow — no sooner were they down than he felt very sick in the water and sun and threw up all he had eaten. Caught, he proposed the merciful rope-through-the-wall hanging, crying while they pulled — until the cry grew so faint the hangers went to see the other side of the wall and found only the dust he was making, and his voice saying, 'You see I am smarter than you, and I thank you for the good dinner I had at your house.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale IV, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Buzzard Is Bald
title.zh: 兀鷲何以禿頂（路易斯安那版）

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 1895

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale VI 'Compair Lapin and Madame Carencro' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: The starving buzzard wife walls the fat rabbit into his oak-hole to eat 'the flesh on your bones' — and, thinking him smothered, unbricks the hole to climb in and claim her dinner. The rabbit makes one jump and gets out; days later, when Madame Carencro walks out with her newly hatched brood, he pours a tin pan of burning embers and hot ashes over them — thick feathers shake them off, but not before the head feathers burn to the skin: which is why the buzzards are bald, and never eat the bones of rabbits.
summary.zh: 飢餓的兀鷲太太用苔與磚把肥兔子封在橡樹洞裡，要吃『你骨頭上的肉』——聽不到動靜，以為兔子已悶死，便拆封下洞來收晚餐；兔子縱身一躍出洞而逃。數日後，她帶著剛出殼的孩子們散步經過，兔仔傾下一鐵盤炭火灰燼——厚羽抖得掉，頭頂的羽毛卻燒到了皮：兀鷲從此禿頂，也不再吃兔骨。

sensitivity.note: Etiological bird tale (parallel to Jamaican John-crow bald-head versions). Collected by Fortier.

passages.text: Once upon a time Madame Carencro was setting upon her nest on an oak-tree. Her husband was a good-for-nothing fellow and she was always starving. At the foot of the tree there was a big hole in which a rabbit dwelt; Compair Lapin was large and fat, and every time Madame Carencro saw him she wished to eat him. One day, while Compair Lapin was sleeping, she took some moss and bricks and closed the hole, so that he could not get out and would die of hunger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale VI (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Compair Lapin woke and found himself shut up he begged Madame Carencro to let him out, but she replied each time, 'I am hungry and I must eat the flesh on your bones.' When begging was useless he stopped speaking; and Madame Carencro, so glad she had caught Compair Lapin that she licked her lips at the good dinner, hearing no movement thought he was dead, smothered, and took away the moss and bricks. She began to go down the opening — and Compair Lapin made one jump and got out. 'You see, it is you who are caught, and not I.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale VI, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He ran to the house of one of his friends, afraid to go back to the oak-tree near Madame Carencro. Some days later, Madame Carencro — who had forgotten Compair Lapin — went to take a walk with her children, all just come out of their shells. Compair Lapin ran into the kitchen, took a large tin pan full of burning embers and hot ashes, and when the mother and brood passed near the gallery he threw down on them all he had in the pan, to burn them. But you know that buzzards have thick feathers except on the top of their heads; they shook off the embers and ashes, but not quickly enough to keep the feathers on their heads from burning down to the skin. This is why the buzzards are bald, and never eat the bones of rabbits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale VI, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Mr. Monkey, the Bridegroom
title.zh: 猴先生的新婚夜

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 1895

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale IX 'Mr. Monkey, the Bridegroom' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: A monkey in love with a beautiful girl dresses as a man and courts his way to a wedding; his best friend, jealous at the supper, sings the tune that makes all monkeys dance — and the bridegroom cannot help himself: he leaps about until the tail breaks loose and every guest sees what he is. The father beats him dreadfully; the friend runs off dancing and singing.
summary.zh: 戀上美麗姑娘的猴子男裝求婚，一路成婚；婚宴上妒火中燒的摯友唱起令猴群起舞的調子——新郎身不由己地跳起來，越跳越狂，尾巴破衣而出，滿堂賓客都看清了他的本相。岳父痛打一頓；搗亂的朋友載歌載舞而去。

sensitivity.note: Animal-bridegroom exposure tale (parallel to Beckwith's Monkey variants). Collected by Fortier.

passages.text: There was a monkey which fell in love with a beautiful young girl. He dressed as a man and went to call on her, and was so well received that one day he took his best friend with him to see his lady-love. The young girl's father asked Mr. Monkey's friend some questions about his daughter's lover; the friend said Mr. Monkey was good and rich, but there was a secret about him — which he would tell another day. Mr. Monkey was finally engaged to the young lady.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale IX (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the night of the wedding he invited his friend to the supper; the latter, jealous of Mr. Monkey, began at the end of the supper to sing — a song that made all monkeys dance. The bridegroom begged his friend to stop, beckoning him with his eyes; he continued, however, to sing, and all at once Mr. Monkey got up and began to dance. He jumped about so wildly that his tail came out of his clothes, and every one saw that he was a monkey. The father understood the secret and beat him dreadfully; his friend, however, ran off dancing and singing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale IX, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tortoise and the Flat Stone
title.zh: 龜與平石

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 2024 (published 1895)

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale X 'The Tortoise' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: Caged for the master's dinner party, the tortoise whistles, dances, and sings her way through the delighted child's escalations — open the cage, put me on the floor, take me to the bayou — and vanishes into the water with the lesson: 'Learn not to trust people whom you do not know.' The terrified boy substitutes a flat stone in the cage; the cook boils it, the master attacks it with every knife in the house and breaks the table, and to this day cannot understand how his tortoise was changed into a stone.
summary.zh: 被囚待宴的龜以口哨、舞步與歌聲一路哄騙欣喜的孩子——開籠、放地、帶到水塘邊——倏然沒水而逝，留下教訓：『莫輕信不相識之人。』孩子懼父，以平石代之入籠；廚娘煮之不爛，主人刀斧齊下、掀翻餐桌，龜巋然不動——至今他仍不明白自己的龜如何變成了一塊石頭。

sensitivity.note: Escape-by-flattery animal tale. Collected by Fortier.

passages.text: A gentleman living on the banks of a bayou caught a large tortoise and went to invite some friends to take dinner with him. His little boy, in his absence, went to the cage where the tortoise was, and the latter began to whistle. 'How well you whistle!' — 'Oh, that is nothing; open the cage and you will see.' The boy opened the cage, and the tortoise whistled better than ever; 'put me down on the floor and you will see' — and she danced and sang. 'How well you dance and sing!' — 'Put me on the bank of the bayou and you will see.' The boy took her to the bayou, and the tortoise danced and sang; all at once she disappeared in the water, and the boy began to cry. The tortoise rose in the middle of the bayou and said, 'Learn not to trust, hereafter, people whom you do not know.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale X (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy was afraid of his father and put a large flat stone into the cage. The cook, thinking it was the tortoise, put the stone into the kettle, and was astonished to see it remain hard so long; she called her master's attention to it. He ordered the tortoise to be put upon the table and took his table-knife to cut it — in vain; the carving-knife — in vain; the hatchet — in vain; the axe — he broke the dishes and the table, but the tortoise remained intact. He then saw it was a stone, and to this day he has not understood how his tortoise was changed into a stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale X, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Miss Mockingbird and the Fasting Suitors
title.zh: 嘲鶇小姐與絕食求婚者

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 1895

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale XIV 'Miss Mockingbird, Mr. Mockingbird, and Mr. Owl' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: The fasting contest decides the marriage — she on the ground, the suitors in the tree — and the mockingbird wins it by fraud, flying down for a kiss and a beakful of food at every descent. The honest Owl, singing weaker and weaker from hunger, is refused and finally slapped to the ground; he dies of hunger, and Mr. Mockingbird flies away with his bride.
summary.zh: 絕食之賽定婚約——她在樹下、求婚者在樹上——嘲鶇以詐取勝：每次俯衝『求吻』都討得一嘴吃食。誠實的貓頭鷹餓得歌聲愈來愈弱，屢遭拒絕，最後被一掌擊落，餓死樹下；嘲鶇先生便攜新娘飛走了。

sensitivity.note: Courtship-contest bird tale. Collected by Fortier.

passages.text: Once upon a time the Mockingbird and the Owl were courting Miss Mockingbird. She said to them, 'Well, I shall marry the one who remains the longer without eating. I shall remain under the tree and you upon it.' The mockingbird looked at his lady-love and flew down to her, singing his song; when he reached her, he did as if he wanted to kiss her, and she gave him some food which she had in her beak. Mr. Mockingbird flew back to his tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XIV (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Owl in his turn flew towards his lady-love and sang his own song; he wished to kiss Miss Mockingbird, but she turned her head aside and said, 'Go away; your wings hurt me.' The poor Owl had nothing to eat, while every day the mockingbird flew down and, kissing the young lady, got something to eat. The Owl came down also from the tree, but he was beginning to be very hungry, and his voice was very weak when he sang. Miss Mockingbird did not want to look at him or give him anything to eat, and he had to go back to his tree with an empty stomach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XIV, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mr. Mockingbird, on the contrary, grew more boastful every day and sang in a loud voice; the poor Owl was dying of hunger, and one could hardly hear his song. He tried to kiss Miss Mockingbird, but she said, 'Go away; your large wings hurt me,' and gave him a slap which threw him down. He was so weak from hunger that he died, and Mr. Mockingbird flew away with his bride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XIV, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: King Peacock
title.zh: 孔雀王

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 2024 (published 1895)

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale XVI 'King Peacock' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: The beauty who refuses every suitor is cursed by the scorned man in the golden carriage: within a year she will bear a daughter much, much prettier than herself — and when it comes true she locks the child away and orders the nurse to kill her. The nurse cannot; she gives three seeds and sends the girl to the well, one seed swallowed so she will not suffer — and the girl goes gladly, 'if my mother wants it so', to drown, and to whatever comes after.
summary.zh: 拒絕所有求婚者的美人，被金車中的憤然男子詛咒：一年之內將生下遠比自己美麗的女兒。詛咒應驗，她把女孩鎖進深屋，命奶媽行刑；奶媽下不了手，給她三粒種子送她去井邊——吞下一粒便不覺痛苦。女孩柔順地應允：『若母親要這樣，那就殺了我吧』——投井而去。

sensitivity.note: Fairy-tale (Marchen) with infanticide frame; collected by Fortier as Creole oral narrative.

passages.text: There was once a lady so pretty that she never wanted to marry; she found something to criticise in all the suitors — 'Oh, you are too ugly'; 'You are too small'; 'You have too large a mouth.' One day a fine man came, in a golden carriage drawn by eight horses, and asked the lady to marry him; she refused. He fell into a passion and told her that in one year she would have a daughter much, much prettier than herself; the lady sent him away with scorn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XVI (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: A year later she had a pretty little girl; seeing the child was so pretty, she shut her up in a room at the further end of the house with a nurse, who never allowed her to leave or even to look through the window. One day, while the old woman was sweeping the floor, she left the door open, and the young girl saw a large bird: 'Nurse, how do you call that bird which is so pretty?' — 'That is a peacock.' — 'If ever I marry, I want to marry King Peacock.' — 'May God hear you, my child.' That very day the mother called the nurse into a corner, drew from under her skirt a great knife, and said, 'I want you to kill my child; she has become prettier than I.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XVI, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The nurse began to cry and begged the lady to spare the child, but all in vain; that black heart could not be softened. When night came the nurse said to the girl, 'My poor child, I have to kill you; your mother wants you to die.' — 'Well, kill me, nurse, if my mother wants it to be so.' — 'No, I have not the heart to do any such thing, my little one. Here, take these three seeds; throw yourself in the well and drown yourself, but before jumping in, swallow one of these seeds and you will not suffer at all.' The girl thanked the nurse and went to drown herself; she walked until she arrived at a large well, and threw herself into it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XVI, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: The Singing Bones
title.zh: 會唱歌的骨頭

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 1895

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale XVII 'The Singing Bones' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: A good husband, a wicked wife, twenty-five children — and every dinner served boneless. Ten children go 'to grandmother's for the change of air', one a day, until the counting finds fifteen; at the threshold the great stone begins to sing — 'Our mother killed us, our father ate us; we are not in a coffin, we are not in the cemetery' — and the lifted bones tell all. He kills his wife, buries his children's bones in the cemetery, and never eats meat again, believing it would always be his children he was eating.
summary.zh: 善良的丈夫、邪惡的妻子、二十五個孩子——每餐的肉都不帶骨。孩子們一天一個『去外婆家換空氣』，直到點數只剩十五。門檻前的大石唱起歌來——『媽媽殺了我們，爸爸吃了我們；我們不在棺材裡，我們不在墓園裡』——掀開石板，白骨泣訴一切。他殺妻葬骨，從此終身不再食肉，唯恐吃的又是自己的孩子。

sensitivity.note: Singing-bone revenge tale (ATU 780 type) in Creole telling. Collected by Fortier.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived a man and a woman who had twenty-five children. They were very poor; the man was good, the woman was bad. Every day when the husband returned from his work the wife served his dinner, but always meat without bones. 'How is it that this meat has no bones?' — 'Because bones are heavy, and meat is cheaper without bones; they give more for the money.' The husband ate and said nothing; when asked why he did not eat meat, she answered that he had forgotten he had no teeth — and he said nothing more, because he was afraid to grieve his wife, who was as wicked as she was ugly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XVII (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When one has twenty-five children one cannot think of them all the time, and one does not see if one or two are missing. One day, after his dinner, the husband asked for his children; he counted them and found only fifteen. His wife answered that the others were at their grandmother's, and every day she would send one more for them to get a change of air — and that was true: every day there was one that was missing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XVII, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the husband was at the threshold of his house, in front of a large stone, thinking of his children and wanting to go and get them at their grandmother's, when he heard voices saying: 'Our mother killed us, our father ate us. We are not in a coffin, we are not in the cemetery.' At first he did not understand what it meant; but he raised the stone and saw a great quantity of bones, which began to sing again. He then understood it was the bones of his children, whom his wife had killed and whom he had eaten. He was so angry that he killed his wife, buried his children's bones in the cemetery, and stayed alone at his house — and from that time he never ate meat, because he believed it would always be his children that he would eat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XVII, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: The Little Finger: Manga's Story of the Middle Passage
title.zh: 小指頭：曼加的中段航道敘事

region.en: Louisiana plantation country, USA (symbolic pin: Mississippi River plantation)
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那種植園地帶（象徵定位：密西西比河種植園）

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 1895

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale XX 'The Little Finger' (told by a formerly enslaved woman about her grandmother Manga; English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: Told by a formerly enslaved narrator about her grandmother Manga: sold for a red handkerchief or a bottle of tafia, tied two by two to the ships, terrified that the captives boarding were to be drowned. Bought to nurse the beautiful boy Florimond, she loves him — and when the jealous stranger tries to buy her silence with threats of cutting her tongue and sewing her in a sack for the sea, she says nothing, all day long, though they torture her; only the little finger that escaped the sack keeps moving, as if to call someone.
summary.zh: 由一位曾為奴的敘述者講述祖母曼加的往事：以紅手帕或一瓶塔菲亞酒的價格被賣、兩兩相縛押上船，見同伴登船時只怕是要被沉海。被買去照料俊美的男孩弗洛里蒙，她傾心愛護；面對陌生人的威脅——割舌、縫入麻袋沉海——她整日受刑也不吐一字；唯有逃出麻袋的小指頭，至今彷彿仍在動，像在喚人。

sensitivity.note: First-person-descendant narrative of enslavement and the Middle Passage, recorded by Fortier from a named formerly enslaved teller; historical testimony framed as family legend, handled here with respect and without sensationalizing violence.

passages.text: Before we came here, poor devils, we were all free; we were not obliged to work for any master. It is the whites who came into our country, Africa, to get us: they stole some of us; they bought some of us from our fathers for a red handkerchief, for a bottle of tafia, or an old gun. When we went to war, those who were caught were sold to the whites who came to trade on the seacoast. We were led away tied together, two by two; and when we reached the seacoast like a herd of cattle — men, women, and children — we were exchanged, not for money, but for any kind of merchandise, and the whites put us into ships and brought us here. This is how we became slaves in America.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XX (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Manga, my grandmother, arrived at the seacoast, she saw a pretty little town with small houses, and many ships that seemed to be dancing on the sea — it was the wind, you know, blowing and shaking up the sea. My poor grandmother, who was young then, was afraid when she saw they were putting all the negroes on board the ships; she thought they were going to drown them in the sea. A white man came to her and bought her from her master, took her to his house, and told her in her own language: 'I bought you to take care of my little boy.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XX, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The little boy, Florimond, was so pretty — curly hair, blue eyes, white and rosy skin — that everybody adored him, and Manga loved him so much she would not have left him for anything in the world. When the master went away for gold-dust and elephants' teeth, a stranger came; Florimond would not look at him, and one day told his father he would tell on the stranger. 'Little black devil, if you ever open your mouth to say that here again, I will cut your tongue with my big knife, put you in a sack in my boat, and throw you into the sea for the fish to eat you.' Manga was so frightened she did not say a word, even when they tortured her all day — and the pretty little finger, which had escaped the sack, was moving as if it was making a sign to call some one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XX, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: John Green Peas and the Golden Goose
title.zh: 青豆約翰與金鵝

region.en: Louisiana bayou country, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那沼澤地

period: Louisiana Creole oral tradition; collected 1877-1888; published 1895

source.work: Alcee Fortier, 'Louisiana Folk-Tales' (1895), tale XXVI 'John Green Peas' (English translation by Mrs. M. L. T. Fortier)

summary.en: Asked by the king where to hide his chickens, his geese, and his gold, the old cabin-dweller John Green Peas cons each secret into the same hiding place — everything vanishes — and when the guards come he is ready with a fiddle-playing golden goose. Sold, exposed, sacked for the river, he talks his way out of the bag with a crying-fit about refusing the king's daughter, swaps himself for a lovesick shepherd, and sends the king diving into the river after a fortune in sheep and gold.
summary.zh: 國王接連請教藏雞、藏鵝、藏金之處，老約翰把每個秘密都導向同一個地點——於是雞鵝金幣一一消失；衛兵來捕時，他已備好一隻聞琴吐金的鵝。事敗被裝袋沉河，他卻以『不肯娶公主』的哭腔換來情癡牧羊人替死，自己牽羊而歸，並指點國王：河底還有金子——愚王跳水而亡。

sensitivity.note: Creole trickster-tale (grateful-animal/fortune-seeker type). Collected by Fortier.

passages.text: An old negro, called John Green Peas, lived in a cabin by the king's palace. As all the chickens of the king were being stolen he wanted to save his geese, and asked John to tell him where to put them; John was delighted, and the geese disappeared in the same way as the chickens. The king asked John to tell him where to put his money, and John told him to put his gold where he had put the geese — the gold disappeared also. The neighbors then convinced the king that John was the robber, and the king went with his guards to arrest the old man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XXVI (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: John knew what was going on, and placed on his table a goose with gold coin under its wings; when the king arrived, John showed him the goose and told him that whenever he needed money the goose would give him some, if he played on the fiddle. The king bought the goose; but when he saw how John had deceived him, he had him put into a bag to be thrown into the river. The men who were carrying the bag got drunk and left John for some time in the road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XXVI, middle (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He heard a shepherd coming with his flock, and began crying that he would not marry the king's daughter. The shepherd took John's place in the bag, in order to marry the king's daughter, and the old man went away with the sheep. The king met John, and the latter told him that he had found the sheep and the gold at the bottom of the river; the king threw himself into the river and was drowned. Poor simple king, to leave a palace to jump into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fortier, tale XXVI, ending (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Mr. Fox and Miss Goose
title.zh: 福克斯先生與鵝小姐

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA (symbolic pin: Putnam County)
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶（象徵定位：帕特南縣）

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-1881; published 1883

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus: Myths and Legends of the Old Plantation' (1883), tale I 'Mr. Fox and Miss Goose'

summary.en: Brer Rabbit, overhearing Brer Fox's plan to call on the washing goose, slips ahead with a friendly howdy and a warning: the fox is coming before day. Coach her to bundle the white folks' clothes on the bed, roost on the rafter, and let the grabber take the bundle — and when the fox seizes the 'goose' at first light, Mr. Dog sails out from under the house after him. The feud between fox and dog starts right there, and Brer Rabbit never disputes the credit.
summary.zh: 兔哥哥偷聽到福克斯要造訪洗衣的鵝小姐，便先一步登門問好、報信：天亮前狐狸就到。教她把白人的衣物捆好放床上、自己棲上房梁，讓來抓的人抓走那捆衣裳——天色微明狐狸搶『鵝』而逃，狗先生自屋下撲出窮追。狐狗之仇便由此結下；兔哥哥從不否認這份功勞。

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit cycle, told in the Uncle Remus frame by a named formerly enslaved raconteur; Harris collected from Georgia tellers 1879-1881. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: When Brer Fox heard that old Miss Goose was down there dabbling in suds and washing clothes, he licked his chops and allowed that some of these odd-come-shorts he was going to call and pay his respects. The minute he said that, Brer Rabbit knew something was up, and allowed to himself that he had better whirl in and have some fun while it was going on. By and by Brer Fox said he must be moving along toward home, and they both said good-bye — but Brer Rabbit slipped round and called on old Miss Goose, who was down at the spring washing, boiling, and battling clothes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, Nights with Uncle Remus, tale I (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Rabbit marched up and asked her howdy — she had just dropped her spectacles in the tub, she said, and would have taken him for that nasty, outrageous Brer Fox and scalded him with a pan of boiling suds. Being's how Sis Goose had fetched up Brer Fox's name, Brer Rabbit said he had something to tell her: 'He is coming, sho' — and when he come, it will be just before day.' Old Miss Goose wiped her hands on her apron and set her spectacles on her forehead, looking like she had trouble in her mind: 'Laws-a-massy! Suppose he come, Brer Rabbit — what I going do? And there is not a man about the house, no!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale I, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Rabbit shot one eye and said, 'Sis Goose, the time has come when you must roost high. You look like you got the dropsy, but don't mind that, because if you don't roost high, you are gone.' He told her to go home and tie up a bundle of the white folks' clothes, put them on the bed, and fly up on a rafter, and let Brer Fox grab the clothes and run off with them. She was much obliged, and that night she did as Brer Rabbit said, and sent word to Mr. Dog, who came down and said he would sort of sit up with her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale I, middle-b (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Just before day, here came Brer Fox creeping up; he pushed the door easy, the door opened, and he saw something white on the bed which he took for Miss Goose, and he grabbed it and ran. About that time Mr. Dog sailed out from under the house, and if Brer Fox had not dropped the clothes, he would have got caught. From that, word went round that Brer Fox had been trying to steal Miss Goose's clothes, and he came mighty nigh losing his standing at Miss Meadows's. To this day Brer Fox believes that Brer Rabbit was the occasion of Mr. Dog's being in the neighborhood that time of night, and Brer Rabbit does not dispute it — the bad feeling between Brer Fox and Mr. Dog started right there, and it has been going on until now they cannot get in smelling distance of one another without a row.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale I, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Brother Fox Catches Mr. Horse
title.zh: 福克斯捉馬記

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-1881; published 1883

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (1883), tale II 'Brother Fox Catches Mr. Horse'

summary.en: Fresh meat enough to last to the middle of next year: Brer Rabbit leads the vengeful Brer Fox to a big horse lying asleep in the pasture, and the quarrel over how to hold him down resolves into the rabbit's plan — tie yourself to the horse's tail, big man, and when he tries to get up, hold him down. One rap of the switch and the horse is up, the fox dangling in the air while Brer Rabbit skips round hollering 'Hold him down, Brer Fox! I'll stand out here and see fair play' — until a hind kick breaks loose and whirls the fox away, next door to killed.
summary.zh: 『夠你吃到明年年中的鮮肉』——兔哥哥把懷恨的福克斯領到牧場上酣睡的大馬跟前；『怎麼按住他』的爭執終歸兔仔的妙計：壯漢，把自己拴上馬尾，他一起身你就按住他。柳條一抽，馬兒躍起，福克斯懸空亂晃，兔仔繞圈高喊『按住他！我在這兒替你督戰』——直到後蹄一記把他踢得脫繩旋飛，險些喪命。

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit cycle. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: After Brer Fox got rested from keeping out of the way of Mr. Dog and caught up with his rations, he said to himself that he would slay old Brer Rabbit if it took him a month. Brer Rabbit got wind of this, and one day, while going along the road studying how to hold his hand with Brer Fox, he saw a great big Horse lying stretched out flat on his side in the pasture; he crept up to see if the Horse had died, and by and by saw the tail switch — so he knew he was not dead. Brer Rabbit loped back to the big road, and the first man he saw going by was Brer Fox, and he hollered, 'Brer Fox! Come back! I done find the place where you can lay in fresh meat enough to last you plum to the middle of next year!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale II (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Fox came galloping back, for it seemed like as good a time as any to nab Brer Rabbit — but before he got within nabbing distance, Brer Rabbit said the prize was a whole Horse lying down on the ground where they could catch him and tie him. When they got there, sure enough, there lay the Horse all stretched out in the sun, fast asleep; and Brer Fox and Brer Rabbit had a dispute about how they were going to fix the Horse so he could not get loose, until Brer Rabbit said the only plan he knew was for Brer Fox to get down there and let Rabbit tie him to the Horse's tail — for then, when the horse tried to get up, the fox could hold him down. 'If I was a big man like what you is, you might tie me to that Horse's tail — but being as I ain't, we better drop that idea if you are feared.' Brer Fox, jealous but bound to play biggity, agreed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale II, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Rabbit tied Brer Fox to the Horse's tail, hard and fast, stepped back with his hands akimbo and grinned: 'If ever they was a Horse caught, then we done caught this one. Look like we done put the bridle on the wrong end — but I lay Brer Fox has the strength to hold him.' With that he cut a long switch, stepped up, and hit the Horse a rap — pow! The Horse made one jump and landed on his feet, and there was Brer Fox dangling in the air while Brer Rabbit darted out of the way and hollered, 'Hold him down, Brer Fox! I'll stand out here and see fair play!' The Horse jumped and humped, ripped and reared, shook Brer Fox like a rag in the wind — 'Hold him down, Brer Fox! You got him now, sho'!' — until a hind kick fetched the fox a lick in the stomach, broke him loose, and sent him a-whirling; he was not exactly killed, honey, but he was the next door to it, and while he was getting well it came across his mind that Brer Rabbit had played another game on him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale II, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Brother Rabbit and the Little Girl
title.zh: 兔哥哥與小姑娘

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale III 'Brother Rabbit and the Little Girl'

summary.en: The garden-gate fraud: 'your pa says give me some greens' wins Rabbit a mess of collards day after day, until Mr. Man catches on, sets the trap, ties the thief with a fishing-line and goes for the little red cowhide. Left to the Little Girl's guard, Brer Rabbit sings — 'Mr. Mole, he hide in the groun'' — coughs his hoarseness, offers to dance instead, gets untied to do it, and dances clean out of the garden and home.
summary.zh: 『你爸爸叫拿點青菜』——兔哥哥天天憑此句進園飽餐，直到主人識破設伏，用釣線把賊捆牢、進屋取小紅皮鞭。看守的小姑娘被一支歌迷住——『鼴鼠先生藏在土裡』——兔仔咳稱嗓啞、改舞代唱、請她解繩；一解繩便舞出菜園、舞回家去。

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit cycle. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: One time, after Brer Rabbit had been tramping round hunting up some salad to make out his dinner with, he found himself in the neighborhood of Mr. Man's house, and near the garden-gate he saw the Little Girl playing round in the sand. When Brer Rabbit looked between the garden-palings and saw the collards, the asparagus-grass and the other garden truck growing there, it made his mouth water. He walked up to the Little Girl, pulled his roach, bowed, scraped his foot, and talked mighty nice and slick: 'Howdy, Little Gal — your pa says to tell you to open the garden-gate so Brer Rabbit can go in and get some truck.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale III (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: She jumped round, opened the gate, and Brer Rabbit hopped in, got a mess of greens, hopped out again, made a bow, and said he was much obliged. The next day he hid out until he saw the Little Girl come out to play, put up the same tale, and walked off with another mess of truck — and it kept on this way until Mr. Man began missing his greens, and kept on missing them, until he got to excusing everybody on the place of destroying them. Then the Little Girl said, 'My goodness, pa! You done told Mr. Rabbit to come and make me let him in the garden after some greens, and ain't he done come and ax me, and ain't I done gone and let him in?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale III, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mr. Man laughed and told the Little Girl that next time Mr. Rabbit came, she must turn him in and run fast and tell him — he had some business with that young chap that needed to be attended to. Sure enough, next morning here came Brer Rabbit after his allowance of greens; the Little Girl turned him in and ran up to the house hollering, and Mr. Man rushed out, grabbed up the fishing-line hanging on the back porch, caught Brer Rabbit tromping on the strawberry-bed, and tied him hard and fast: 'You done fooled me lots of times, but this time you are mine. I'm going to take you and gin you a larruping, and then I'm going to skin you and nail your hide on the stable door' — and he called to the Little Girl to watch Brer Rabbit while he went to fetch the little red cowhide.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale III, middle-b (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Rabbit was not saying nothing, but Mr. Man was not more than out the gate before he began to sing — and in those days Brer Rabbit was a singer, mon, and when he tuned up he made the other creatures hold their breath: 'The jay-bird hunts the sparrow-nest, the bee-martin sails all round; the squirrel, he hollers from the top of the tree, Mr. Mole, he stay in the ground; he hide and he stay till the dark drops down — Mr. Mole, he hide in the ground.' The Little Girl laughed and begged for more, but Brer Rabbit coughed and allowed he had a mighty bad hoarseness down in his windpipe somewhere; then he offered to dance instead — how could a man dance tied up this way? — and the Little Girl reached down and unloosed the fish-line. Brer Rabbit gathered up his feet under him and danced out of that garden, and he danced home: a man who has had Brer Rabbit's experience is not going to stay and let Mr. Man sacrifice him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale III, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: How Brother Fox Was Too Smart
title.zh: 聰明反被聰明誤

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale IV 'How Brother Fox Was Too Smart'

summary.en: Seeing how slick the play-dead trick worked for Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox copies it on Mr. Man's loaded market-waggon — laying down before the chickens, then before the pigs, then stretched out big enough to fill a two-bushel basket. Mr. Man stops, examines the third corpse with a horse-doctor's thoroughness, finds it warm and limber with no broken bones and no blood, and settles the diagnosis with one whack of the whip-handle behind the ears; the chicken-nabber scrambles to his feet and makes tracks.
summary.zh: 兔哥哥裝死之計見效，福克斯便在市場馬車前照搬——先攔雞車、再攔豬車、末了橫躺大得能填滿兩斗籃。主人下車驗『屍』如獸醫查病：耳溫、頸溫、肋骨完好、四肢靈便、無血無傷——診斷由鞭柄一記後腦定讞；偷雞賊翻身爬起，落荒而逃。

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit cycle (copycat-moral tale). Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: Old Brer Fox, when he saw how slick the trick worked with Brer Rabbit, said to himself that he believed he would try the same kind of game on some other man, and he kept on watching for his chance until, one day, he heard Mr. Man coming down the big road in a one-hoss waggon, carrying some chickens, some eggs, and some butter to town. Brer Fox heard him coming, and what did he do but go and lay down in the road in front of the waggon. Mr. Man drove along, clucking to the horse and humming to himself, and when they got most up to Brer Fox, the horse shied, Mr. Man hollered Whoa! and looked down: 'Heyo! There is the chap that has been nabbing up my chickens, and somebody has gone and shot off a gun at him — which I wish she had been two guns, that I does!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale IV (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mr. Man drove on and left Brer Fox lying there. Then Brer Fox got up, ran round through the woods, and laid down in front of Mr. Man again — 'Heyo! Here is the very chap that has been destroying my pigs. Somebody has gone and killed him, and I wish they had killed him a long time ago.' Mr. Man drove on, and the waggon-wheel came mighty nigh mashing Brer Fox's nose; but all the same, Brer Fox lit up, ran round ahead of Mr. Man, and lay down in the road all stretched out like he was big enough to fill a two-bushel basket, and looking like he was dead enough to be skint.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale IV, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mr. Man drove up and stopped, looked round for the cause of all these dead foxes, saw nothing, heard nothing, and studied a while; then he allowed he had better examine what kind of queer disease had got into the Brer Fox family. He lit down out of the waggon and felt of Brer Fox's ear — it felt right warm; felt of his neck — right warm; felt of him in the short ribs — sound; felt of his limbs — sound; turned him over, and, lo and behold, Brer Fox was right limber. 'Heyo! How come this? This chicken-nabber looks like he is dead, but there is not a bone broke, and I don't see no blood, neither do I feel no bruise; and more than that, he is warm and limber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale IV, ending (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Something wrong here, sho'! This pig-grabber might be dead, and then again he mightn't — but to make sure that he is, I'll just gin him a whack with my whip-handle!' And with that Mr. Man drew back and fetched Brer Fox a clip behind the ears — pow! — the lick came so hard and so quick that Brer Fox thought sure he was a goner; but before Mr. Man could draw back to fetch him another, Brer Fox scrambled to his feet and just made tracks away from there. That is what Brer Fox got for playing Mr. Smarty and copying after other folks — and that is just the way the whole Smarty family is going to come out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale IV, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wull-er-de-Wust: Brer Rabbit's Honey-and-Leaves Masquerade
title.zh: 『最兇最惡』：蜜與葉的假面

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-2021 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale V 'Brother Rabbit's Astonishing Prank'

summary.en: Ransacking Brer Bear's house while the family is out, Brer Rabbit is drowned in a spilled bucket of honey and rolls himself in leaves to clean off — a capering, swishy-swushy bogey that empties the settlement: Sis Cow bolts, the tolling girl flies, the shotes tear through the woods, Brer Bear tears down a fence-panel, and Kubs and Klibs skaddle through the bushes. Challenged by Brer Wolf in front of Brer Fox, the monster roars 'I'm de Wull-er-de-Wust, en youer de man I'm atter!' — and for a long time after, the gals at Miss Meadows's giggle about whether the Wull-er-de-Wust might drop in.
summary.zh: 趁熊家外出，兔哥哥搜屋時被倒翻的蜜桶澆了滿身，入林滾葉自救——一隻嘩嘩作響、蹦跳起伏的妖怪便出現在鄉間：母牛狂奔、放豬丫頭棄籃而逃、豬崽穿林亂竄、熊撞塌籬笆、雙胞胎捧帽狂奔。狼狐攔路喝問來者何人，妖怪跺腳咆哮：『我是最兇最惡的，你就是我找的傢伙！』——此後米多斯太太家的姑娘們一聽『妖怪』便咯咯直笑。

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit cycle. 'Wull-er-de-Wust' is likely a corruption of will-o'-the-wisp (Harris note). Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: One time he took a notion, old Brer Rabbit did, that he would pay Brer Bear a call — and no sooner did the notion strike him than he picked himself up and put out for Brer Bear's house, making his call while Brer Bear and his family were away from home. He sat down by the road and saw them go by — old Brer Bear and old Miss Bear, and their two twin-children, one named Kubs and the other Klibs. When Brer Rabbit saw this, he said to himself that he reckoned he better go see how Brer Bear was getting on, and off he put; and it was not long before he was ransacking the premises same like he was a sure-enough patroller. While he was going round peeping in here and poking in there, he got to fooling among the shelves, and a bucket of honey that Brer Bear had hid in the cupboard fell down and spilled on top of Brer Rabbit, and a little more and he would have been drowned — from head to heels that creature was covered with honey, so that he had to sit and let the natal sweetness drip out of his eyeballs before he could see his hand before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale V (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by a notion struck Brer Rabbit, and he tip-toed till he got into the woods, where he rolled in the leaves and trash to rub the honey off — he rolled, and the leaves stuck; he rolled again, and the leaves stuck again, until Brer Rabbit was the most outrageous-looking creature you ever set eyes on. He jumped round and tried to shake the leaves off, but they were not going to be shook off; he shook and he shivered, but the leaves stuck — and the capers that creature cut up out there in the woods by his own-alone self were scandalous. He looked exactly like one of these boogers that gets after bad children — if you had struck up along with him, you would have been mighty good and glad if you had got off with that.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale V, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: The first man Brer Rabbit came up with was old Sis Cow, and no sooner did she lay eyes on him than she hoisted her tail in the elements and put out like a pack of dogs was after her — which made Brer Rabbit laugh, because he knew that when an old settled woman like Sis Cow ran distracted in the broad open day-time, there must be something mighty queer about those leaves and that honey. The next man he met was a black girl tolling a whole passel of plantation shotes; when the girl saw Brer Rabbit come prancing along she flung down her basket of corn and fairly flew, and the shotes took through the woods with such a racket of running, snorting and squealing as was never heard in that settlement before or since. It kept on this way as long as Brer Rabbit met anybody — they just broke and ran like the Ole Boy was after them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale V, middle-b (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Rabbit paraded on down the road until here came Brer Bear and all his family; Brer Rabbit got crossways of the road and sidled toward them. Ole Miss Bear stood it as long as she could and then flung down her parasol and took a tree; Brer Rabbit jumped straight up in the air and gave himself a shake — and ole Brer Bear made a break, they tell me, and tore down a whole panel of fence getting away from there, while Kubs and Klibs took their hats in their hands and skaddled through the bushes same as a drove of horses. By and by here came Brer Fox and Brer Wolf fixing up a plan to nab Brer Rabbit, and they were so intent on their confab that they got right on him before they saw him — but gentlemen! when they caught a glimpse of him, they gave him all the room he wanted. Brer Wolf tried to show off, because he wanted to play big before Brer Fox, and stopped and asked Brer Rabbit who he was; Brer Rabbit jumped up and down in the middle of the road and hollered, 'I'm the Wull-er-de-Wust, and you are the man I'm after!' — and the way those creatures lit out from there was a caution. A long time after that, when Brer Rabbit showed himself laughing behind the stump, Miss Meadows heard about it, and the next time Brer Fox called, the gals giggled and asked him whether he was not afraid the Wull-er-de-Wust might drop in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale V, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Brother Rabbit Secures a Mansion
title.zh: 兔哥哥坐擁豪宅

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-2021 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale VI 'Brother Rabbit Secures a Mansion'

summary.en: The creatures go into cahoots to build a fine two-story house while Brer Rabbit — dizzy on scaffolds, palsied in the sun — walks round measuring and marking with a pencil behind his ear, doing nothing. He picks an upstairs room, moves in his gun, his brass cannon and his tub of scalding water, and when the builders come for their lodgings, the doors open on a hail of hot water and buckshot: the co-op house becomes a private mansion, and the co-builders scatter to their holes.
summary.zh: 眾獸合夥興建兩層樓房；兔哥哥自稱上架子頭暈、日曬抽風，卻拿著鉛筆在耳後轉來轉去、丈量標記——其實一事不做。房子落成，他選中樓上一間，偷偷搬進獵槍、銅炮與一大桶滾水；房客們前來投宿，迎門的是滾水與鉛彈——合夥樓成了私產，合建者各奔巢穴。

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit cycle. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: It turned out one time that a whole lot of the creatures took a notion that they would go in cahoots with building them a house. Ole Brer Bear was among them, and Brer Fox, and Brer Wolf, and Brer Coon, and Brer Possum — it seemed like plum down to ole Brer Mink was among them too; leastways, there was a whole passel of them, and they whirled in and built the house in less than no time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale VI (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Rabbit made like it made his head swim to climb up on the scaffold, and likewise he said it made him catch the palsy to work in the sun, but he got him a square, stuck a pencil behind his ear, and went round measuring and marking — measuring and marking — and he was so busy that the other creatures said to themselves he was doing a monstrous sight of work, and folks going along the big road said Brer Rabbit was doing more hard work than the whole kit and bilin of them. Yet all the time Brer Rabbit was doing nothing, and he might just as well have been lying off in the shade scratching the fleas off of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale VI (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: The other creatures built the house, and gentlemen! she was a fine one, too, mon — she would have been a fine one these days, let alone those days. She had upstairs and downstairs, and chimneys all round, and she had rooms for all the creatures that went into cahoots to help make it. Brer Rabbit picked out one of the upstairs rooms, and he got him a gun, and one of these here brass cannons, and put them in there when the other creatures were not looking, and then he got him a tub — and when the builders came to claim their lodging, the doors of the fine new house opened on scalding water and gun-fire, and the cahoots scattered to their several holes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale VI, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Brother Wolf Says Grace
title.zh: 狼哥哥謝恩

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XXVII 'Brother Wolf Says Grace'

summary.en: Caught in a trap with Brer Wolf's jaws closing, Brer Rabbit plays the etiquette-master: show your politeness, Brer Wolf — fold your hands under your chin, shut your eyes, and say grace — 'Bless us and blind us, and put us in the crack where the Ole Boy can't find us' — and before the blessing is finished, the wiggled-for rabbit lights on his feet and leaves a blue streak behind him.
summary.zh: 被狼咬住之際，兔哥哥扮起禮儀導師：『狼兄，展現你的教養——合掌於頷、閉目謝恩：願我們蒙福又致盲，藏進那老魔頭找不到的石縫』——祝禱未畢，兔仔一扭落地，身後只留一道藍煙。

sensitivity.note: Brer Rabbit cycle; grace-trick amusement tale. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: Caught with Brer Wolf closing in, Brer Rabbit asked how he could show his politeness: 'I want you to say grace, Brer Wolf, and say it quick, because I am getting mighty weak. Fold your hands under your chin, Brer Wolf, and shut your eyes, and say: Bless us and blind us, and put us in the crack where the Ole Boy can't find us. Say it quick, Brer Wolf, because I am failing mighty fast.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Wolf put up his hands and shot his eyes and began, 'Bless us and blind us' — but he did not get any farther: just as he took up his hands, Brer Rabbit fetched a wiggle, lit on his feet, and left a blue streak behind him. 'Oh, I just knew Brother Rabbit would get away!' the little boy declared; and Uncle Remus said that was right — put your dependence in Brer Rabbit and you won't be far out of the way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Spirits, Seen and Unseen: Daddy Jack's Ghost-Lore
title.zh: 顯形與隱形的靈：傑克老爹的鬼譚

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA (Daddy Jack, a Congo-born teller)
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園（講述者傑克老爹，剛果出生）

period: African-American oral tradition (Congo and Georgia tellers); collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XXVIII 'Spirits, Seen and Unseen'

summary.en: Congo-born Daddy Jack holds forth on the dead: children who laugh and talk to empty corners see ha'nts; a spirit called his name across the creek and his uncle walking backward by sundown proved it; and the Jack-me-Lantern — the dead man's ghost hunting the money that was stolen from him — can only be turned by turning your coat inside out, if you can get the sleeve turned. In the paired witch-lore, the old witch leaves her skin drying by the fire, finds it shrunk and stinking and no longer fits, and a black wolf lies in the yard by the fire's light.
summary.zh: 剛果出生的傑克老爹縱談鬼神：對著空角嬉笑自語的孩子，是見了鬼；溪對岸呼名的精靈，由日落倒行的叔父作證；『傑克燈』——被害者的亡靈持燈尋找被奪的錢財——唯把外套反穿方能退之。女巫篇：老巫離體而去的皮掛在火邊晾曬，尋回時已縮臭不合身；火光照見院中臥著一頭黑狼。

sensitivity.note: Ghost-lore and witch-lore discussion among named African-American tellers (Daddy Jack born in Africa; Aunt Tempy, Uncle Remus); transcribed 1879-1881.
