This is folklore conversation, not ritual instruction; no conjure recipes beyond the folklore-level witch-test ('double, double, double up!') recorded by Harris.

passages.text: Aunt Tempy came in feeling mighty creepy: setting up in her house a while ago, she heard Riah's little girl talking in the other room — and found the child sitting flat in the middle of the floor, laughing and talking and making motions like she saw somebody in the corner, asking them to stay on their own side, and threatening to get a switch and drive them back. 'They tell me,' said Uncle Remus, 'that when you hear children talking and going on so plainly with themselves, they are bound to see ha'nts.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVIII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Daddy Jack roused himself: 'You no bin-a see dem ghos'? I is bin-a see plenty ghos'; I no 'fraid dem; I is bin-a punch dem 'way wit' me cane.' Once, when he was a young man going for water and dipping his piggin under the creek, he heard a voice call him — Jack! O Jack! — and Titty Ann swore she had not called: dead ghos' is bin-a call. He raised his eyes and saw his nuncle going by sundown, going backward, and when folks came to fetch the old man out, he had been taken with the hiccup, throwing his head this way and that — 'I is bin-a see mo' dead ghos', but me no spot um lak dis.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVIII, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Of the Jack-me-Lantern, Daddy Jack told how, making his way through thick swamp, hot and cold, his back quaking and his breath coming fast, he saw the light making its way through the bush, coming straight by him, flick-flickering, close and closer. The old folks' talk was to turn your coat-sleeve when the Jack-me-Lantern runs you; he pulled and twisted and yerked at the jacket, but it had grown on his back — until he said his prayer upon it, and the sleeve turned. The Jack-me-Lantern saw it, lifted up, said Phew! and was gone: 'You no walk in the swamp 'cep' you keep your coat across the arm.' Aunt Tempy had heard tell that this Jacky-ma-Lantern was a sure-enough spirit — a man who got killed, whose money folks took; now his ha'nt has gone and got a light to hunt up where his money is, and spirits don't walk and walk less they got something on their mind.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVIII, middle-b (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asked whether witches were spirits, Daddy Jack — proud of his reputation as a witch — answered that a witch is no dead ghost but living folks you shake hands with, and told the heifer test: when the moon is shining low, wet your hand with pot-licker grease, rub a young heifer's nose, get on her back, hold her by the ear, gallop down the lane till you come to a big gully, and holler 'Double, double, double up!' — if the heifer jumps, you are a witch; if not, no witch. And of the old witch who leaves her skin where she starts from: a man passing found the green skin drying by the fire, hung it up till it shrunk and swiveled and stank, and pitched it in the yard — and when the witch came hunting for her skin, she tried it on this way and that way and it would not fit, and she cried 'Skin! Don't you know me?' while the skin said nothing at all, and the big black wolf lay by the skin in the yard with his teeth showing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXVIII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Brother Rabbit and His Famous Foot
title.zh: 兔哥哥與他的幸運腳

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XXX 'Brother Rabbit and His Famous Foot'

summary.en: Uncle Remus's rabbit's-foot charm and its origin tale: so much luck attending Brer Rabbit that the creatures concluded he carried a conjure-bag — a natural-born witch, or in cahoots with one — and resolved to make up with him to find out how come he was so lucky. The answer went round in the women's talk and the men's prying, and the hind foot stayed with the lucky one; whosoever carries it comes out the right end of every racket, and a rabbit crossing the road must be crossed out with a spit-marked cross in the sand.
summary.zh: 雷慕斯老人的兔腳護符及其來歷：兔哥哥運氣太旺，群獸斷定他身懷咒物——或是天生的巫者，或與巫勾結——遂決計向他示好打聽根由。答案在女人們的閒談與男人們的窺探之間流轉，那隻後腳便永遠伴著幸運兒；攜它者逢凶化吉，兔過大路須以唾畫十字將運氣截住。

sensitivity.note: Hoodoo-charm origin tale at folklore level (lucky rabbit-foot; road-cross counter-ritual recorded as folk practice). Harris collected these from named Georgia tellers; the charm is discussed as folk belief, not instruction.

passages.text: Uncle Remus's rabbit's hind foot, a very large one, was for keeping off boogers. 'When I had to run errands for myself all times of night, and take nigh cuts through the woods, and across by the burying-ground, it is monstrously handy to have that rabbit foot. If there was any boogers, and they came slinking after me, they would find out directly that the old nigger was heeled with a rabbit foot.' A strip of red flannel tied round your arm would keep off the rheumatis; stump-water would cure the fever; some good for one disease and some for another — but the point is that the rabbit foot gives good luck: the man that carries it is mighty apt to come out right-end up when there is any racket going on in the neighborhoods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXX (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When a rabbit runs across the big road in front of him, Uncle Remus does not shoo at it or make to kill it — he squats right down in the middle of the road, makes a cross-mark in the sand, and spits in it. 'When rabbit crosses your luck, what you going do, unless you set down and cross it out, right then and there?' People who shoot rabbits in the big road, he noticed, do not come to any good end. How people found out about the rabbit's foot: the women do the talking and the flying, the men do the walking and the prying, and betwixt and between them there is not much that does not come out — if it does not come out one day it does the next.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXX, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the days when Brer Rabbit was keeping the neighborhoods stirred up, the other creatures studied and studied the whole blessed time how they were going to nab him. When all their plans, and their traps, and their jugglements did no good, they all agreed that Brer Rabbit had some conjurement he tricked them with: Brer Bear allowed he was bound to be a natural-born witch; Brer Wolf said he suspected Brer Rabbit was just in cahoots with a witch; Brer Fox vowed he had more luck than smartness. Day in and day out they worked with the puzzlement, and sat up nights, until they agreed among themselves that they had better make up with Brer Rabbit and see if they could not find out how come he was so lucky — and while all this was going on, ole Brer Rabbit was galloping round from Funtown to Frolicville, kicking up the devilment and terrifying the neighborhoods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XXX, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fire-Test
title.zh: 火之審判

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園地帶

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XLII 'The Fire-Test' (told by Aunt Tempy and Uncle Remus)

summary.en: Brer Wolf, eavesdropping behind the house, steals the family password — 'I'll stay when you are away, because no gold will pay toll' — and after two botched attempts learns to sing it fine, opens the door, and gobbles the little Rabs up, leaving only a pile of bones in the swept clean corner. Judge Terrapin convenes the settlement, digs a deep pit, fills it with lightwood knots, kindles it high, and declares the child-destroyer will drop in and be burnt up at the trial jump; Mink and Coon sail over, Bear pants across, and the boastful digger-and-filler-and-kindler takes his long running start, jumps, squalls, and drops right spang in the middle of the fire.
summary.zh: 狼哥哥屋後偷聽，竊得家門口令——『你們不在家我也守著，因為黃金不付過路錢』——兩番碰壁後苦練歌喉，唱得字正腔圓，開門吞盡小兔一家，爐邊只剩一堆骨。龜法官召集全鄉，掘深坑、填松節、燃高火，宣告殺童者過火必墜；貂與浣熊一躍而過，熊氣喘吁吁也能跨——偏偏那個又挖又填又點火的誇口者，助跑太長力氣用盡，一躍慘叫，正正落在火焰中央。

sensitivity.note: Password-fire-trial tale (ATU 123-linked wolf-and-kids cycle, US variant). Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: When Brer Rabbit got ready to go off for a mess of green truck, he called all his children up and told them that when he went out they must fasten the door on the inside and not turn anybody in, nohow, because Brer Fox and Brer Wolf had been lying round waiting a chance to nab him; and when he came back, he would rap at the door and sing: 'I'll stay when you are away, because no gold will pay toll!' The little Rabs held up their hands and promised not to open the door for nobody except their daddy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: But all this time Brer Wolf had been hiding out behind the house, and he heard every word that passed; and before Brer Rabbit was out of sight, Brer Wolf went to the door and knocked — blip, blip, blip! — and sang the song. The little Rabs laughed fit to kill themselves: 'Go away, Mr. Wolf, go away! You are not any of we-all daddy!' He slunk off, but every time he thought of those plump little Rabs he got hungrier; the second attempt failed — 'we-all daddy has not got no bad cold like that' — and the third: 'we-all daddy can sing lots prettier than that.' So he went away out in the woods and sang, and sang, till he could sing fine as the next man, went back and knocked, and sang so nice and sang so fine that they undid the door — and ole Brer Wolf walked in and gobbled them all up, from the first to the last. When ole Brer Rabbit got home he found the door standing wide open and all the children gone: no sign of any tussle, the hearth all swept clean, everything all to rights — but right over in the corner he saw a pile of bones, and then he knew in reason that some of the other creatures had been there and made hash out of his children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLII, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: He laid the case before Brer Tarrypin, who was a mighty man in those days; no sooner did he hear the state of the condition than he called all the creatures together and allowed that the man who destroyed Brer Rabbit's children must be caught, or there was no telling how long it would be before the same somebody came along and destroyed all the children in the settlement. 'Less dig a deep pit.' — 'I'll dig the pit,' said Brer Wolf. 'Less fill the pit full of lightered knots and brush.' — 'I'll fill the pit,' said Brer Wolf. 'Now, less set it a-fire.' — 'I'll kindle the fire,' said Brer Wolf. When the fire began to blaze up, Brer Tarrypin declared the creatures must jump across it, and the man who destroyed Brer Rabbit's children would drop in and get burnt up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: Brer Wolf had been so uppity about digging, and filling, and kindling, that they all expected him to make the first trial — but, bless your soul and body! Brer Wolf looked like he had some other business to attend to. The pit looked so deep and the fire burnt so high that they most all feared to make the trial; Brer Mink made a running start and lit across, Brer Coon sailed over, Brer Bear panted across saying he was heavier than he had ever been in all his born days but never hurted Brer Rabbit's poor little children — until it came Brer Wolf's time. Then he began to get scared, and was mighty sorry he dug that pit so deep and wide and kindled that fire so high; he took such a long running start that when he got to the jumping place he was done wo' teetotally out, and he lit up, fetched a squall, and dropped right spang in the middle of the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cunning Snake: Coomba and the Song-Password
title.zh: 狡蛇記：庫姆巴與歌之口令

region.en: Congo (Daddy Jack's telling) recalled on a Georgia plantation, USA
region.zh: 剛果（傑克老爹講述）回憶於喬治亞種植園

period: African oral tradition (Congo teller); collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale XLIII 'The Cunning Snake' (told by Daddy Jack, an African-born teller)

summary.en: Daddy Jack's African sing-tale: Coomba, hungry in dream for the big snake's eggs, eats them for breakfast; the mother snake tracks her by scent and warns — take care your own. The song-password 'Walla walla witto, me Noncy' with the answer 'Andolee! Andoli! Andolo!' keeps the baby safe until the snake, coiled in the chimney corner holding its breath for days, learns the call; the door opens, the snake swallows Noncy whole, and the mother follows the track into the swamp, breaks the sleeper's head with a cane, cuts her open, and washes the living child — who wakes answering the song.
summary.zh: 傑克老爹的非洲歌謠：庫姆巴夢中思蛋成癡，將大蛇之卵煮作早餐；蛇母循跡而至，留下警言——看好你自己的孩子。歌之口令『瓦拉瓦拉維托，我的南西』與應答『安多利！安多利！安多羅！』守護嬰兒多日，直到蛇在煙囪角屏息學會呼喚；門開，整孩吞下。母親循跡入沼，以杖擊碎睡蛇之頭、剖腹取女、洗淨抱回——孩子睜眼便應著那支歌。

sensitivity.note: Song-password tale told by Daddy Jack, an African-born (Congo) teller, in his African creole; a rare trans-Atlantic witness of the password cycle. Dialect preserved conceptually, rendered to standard English in paraphrase; songs kept as transcribed formulae.

passages.text: One time there was one old Affiky ooman, her name was Coomba. She went walking through the woods and through the field, and by and by came upon a snake-nest full of eggs — a big snake, big eggs. The Affiky woman wanted those eggs so bad; she was afraid to take them, went home, saw them in her dream, wanted them so bad; and the next morning she said she must have them. She went out, found the snake-nest, got the eggs, carried them to her own house, and cooked them for her breakfast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLIII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: By and by the snake came to its nest: the eggs were gone. It put its nose on the ground and tracked the woman by her own house, and asked about the eggs; she said she had not seen any eggs, though the snake saw the skin that had been on them and asked what this was — and she said nothing at all. 'Woman! You have heard my voice when I cried out. You have taken my eggs; you have destroyed my children. Take care of your own; take care of your own.' The snake went away, slicked out its tongue, slid away. The woman had a pretty little pickaninny she loved hard all over; mindful of what the snake said, she carried the child round on her back, called her Noncy, carried her far, loved her hard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLIII, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: The snake stayed in the bush-side, watched all day, waited all night, and got hungry for the pickaninny — and the woman, carrying Noncy until she was tired, puffed and blew and worked her gills like a catfish, then put the child down and made up a song in her head and taught the little girl to answer it, and showed her how to pull out the peg in the door: put the peg in and open for nobody except you hear me sing. When she started off she sang, 'Walla walla witto, me Noncy!' — and the little girl answered, 'Andolee! Andoli! Andolo!' — and pulled out the peg, and ran to her mother. Day after day it was the same, while the snake lay coiled up in the bush, watching the night, listening by day, trying to learn the song and saying nothing at all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLIII, middle-b (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: One time when the mother was away, the snake waited till it was almost time for her to come back, went by the door, opened its mouth and sang — 'Wullo wullo widdo, me Noncy!' — trying to make its voice come fine like the little girl's mother, but there was a rough place in its throat and the voice came big: 'Go away from here! My mother does not holler the song like that!' It tried one, two, three times — no use; the little girl did not open the door, and the snake said it must learn the song for sure. It coiled up in the chimney corner and held its breath to listen; all day long it thought about the song, said it forward, said it backward, and at most toward sundown it came at the door and hollered the song fine — and the little girl, thinking the snake was her mother, answered the song and opened the door quick, and ran upon the snake before she saw it: the snake hugged the little girl more like than her mother, twisted its tail round her, squeezed her tight, and swallowed her whole, breaking no bone. The mother came home, hollered the song and got no answer, and her voice shook and her body trembled; she looked all round, saw where the snake had crossed the road, cut a cane in the swamp, followed the track, and came upon the snake lying asleep — took the cane and broke its head, mashed it flat, cut the snake open, and found the little girl just like she was asleep; took her home and washed her off, and by and by the little girl opened her eyes and, soon as she saw her mother, answered the song: 'Andolee! Andoli! Andolo!' — and she was alive. Enty!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale XLIII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of the Ocean
title.zh: 大洋之起源

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation country, USA (symbolic pin: the creek that became the ocean)
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園（象徵定位：化作大洋的小溪）

period: African-American oral tradition; collected 1879-1881; published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale LVIII 'The Origin of the Ocean'

summary.en: A hunting camp etiology: every prize Mr. Lion brings down is claimed — 'it's mine! I killed it!' — while Rabbit does the actual shooting. Around the night fire Rabbit engineers a prank of cold ashes and hot embers, blaming sleepers across the creek, until the bellowing Lion leaps the water to avenge the insult; then Brer Rabbit cuts the string that holds the banks together, the banks keep falling back, the creek keeps widening, and from that day to this the big waters have been rolling between them — which is why the lions and all the servigous creatures live on the other side.
summary.zh: 獵營之夜的起源故事：獅子每奪一獵便喊『是我的！是我打死的！』——其實槍槍都是兔子放的。夜火旁，兔仔設下冷灰與熱炭的惡作劇，誣指溪對岸的搗亂者，引得獅子長吼躍溪報仇；兔仔趁機割斷縛住兩岸的繩索——河岸不斷崩退，溪水不斷變寬，直到兩造彼此不復相見——自此大水橫亙，獅子與所有兇獸都住在那一邊。

sensitivity.note: Origin-of-the-ocean etiology from the Brer Rabbit cycle; flood-cluster record (cross-ref: norse, hebrew, mesopotamian flood records). Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: One time way back yonder, before there were any folks fooling round, Mr. Lion took a notion that he would go hunting, and nothing would do him but Brer Rabbit must go with him. Brer Rabbit allowed he was up for any kind of fun on the top side of the ground; they put out and hunted clean across the country — and every time Mr. Lion let loose and missed the game, Brer Rabbit let loose and fetched it down, and no sooner did he do that than Mr. Lion squalled out, 'It's mine! It's mine! I killed it!' Mr. Lion was such a big man that Brer Rabbit was scared to dispute along with him, but he laid it up in his mind to get even with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LVIII (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: They hunted all day long, and when night came they were so far from home that they had to camp out; they came to a creek, scraped away the trash, built a fire on the bank, and cooked their supper. After supper they sat up telling tales, and Brer Rabbit bragged about what a good hunter Mr. Lion was; when their eyelids got heavy, Rabbit warned that he was a monstrous heavy sleeper, and asked Mr. Lion to show him how he snored before he got sound asleep — and after he was sound asleep. Mr. Lion sucked in his breath, and every time he sucked in his breath it sounded like a whole passel of mules whinnying after fodder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LVIII, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Brer Rabbit heard that snore he got up, sprinkled himself with the cold ashes round the fire, and flung a whole passel of hot embers on Mr. Lion, who jumped up and asked who did that; Brer Rabbit lay there kicking at his ear with his behind foot and hollering Ow! — the ashes on his own hide puzzling the Lion. Twice more the same doings happened, and the second time Brer Rabbit hollered, 'I seed um, Mr. Lion! I seed the way they come from 'cross the creek! They most sho'ly did!' — and Mr. Lion fetched a bellow and jumped across the creek. No sooner did he do that than Brer Rabbit cut the string that held the banks together, and, lo and behold, there they were: the banks fell back, the creek kept getting wider and wider, until Brer Rabbit and Mr. Lion were not in sight of one another, and from that day to this the big waters have been rolling between them — we are all on one side of the water, and the lions and most all the servigous creatures are on the other side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LVIII, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: The Night before Christmas: the Quarter's Lightwood Fire
title.zh: 聖誕前夜：棚戶的松明大火

region.en: Middle Georgia plantation quarters, USA
region.zh: 美國喬治亞中部種植園棚戶區

period: African-American festival tradition; recorded in frame narrative, published 2024 (published 1883)

source.work: Joel Chandler Harris, 'Nights with Uncle Remus' (2024 print of 1883), tale LXXI 'The Night before Christmas' (frame narrative)

summary.en: The holiday celebration that frames the final tales: Daddy Jack's high-hat wedding to 'Tildy, the waggon-loads of resinous lightwood heaped round the dancing platform and set ablaze at nightfall, the fiddle put away at Uncle Remus's command in favor of 'ole times', and the old man — captain of the corn-pile, stoutest at the log-rolling, swiftest with the hoe — joining one round of the dance for old times' sake with the little boy watching from the platform corner.
summary.zh: 收束全書的節慶場景：傑克老爹戴高帽迎娶蒂爾迪；載滿松明的推車環繞舞臺堆起，夜幕落下即舉火；雷慕斯老人一聲令下收起提琴，改跳『老時光的舞』——他曾是玉米堆的首領、滾木賽的壯漢、鋤地最快的快手——此刻為了舊日情誼，帶著從舞臺角上觀望的小男孩跳上一圈。

sensitivity.note: Frame-narrative festival scene (Christmas in the quarters with lightwood fires and the ring-dance), recorded by Harris as the setting for the last tales; historical depiction of antebellum-era holiday practice from a formerly enslaved teller's world, included as documentary folk material.

passages.text: The little boy had a special invitation to be present at the marriage of Daddy Jack and 'Tildy, and went accompanied by Uncle Remus and Aunt Tempy. 'Tildy wore a white dress and a wreath of artificial flowers in her hair; Daddy Jack wore a high hat, which he persisted in keeping on his head during the ceremony, and a coat the tails of which nearly dragged the floor; his bright little eyes glistened triumphantly, and he grinned and bowed to everybody again and again. After it was all over the guests partook of cake baked by Aunt Tempy and persimmon beer brewed by Uncle Remus — and 'Tildy allowed that if everything did not go right down the country with her ole man, she was going to pick up and come right back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LXXI frame (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: The preparations for the holidays went on: a large platform used for sunning wheat and seed cotton was arranged by the negroes for their dance, and several waggon-loads of resinous pine — known as lightwood — were placed around about it in little heaps, so that the occasion might lack no element of brilliancy. At nightfall the heaps of lightwood were set on fire, and the little boy, waiting impatiently for Uncle Remus to come for him, could hear the negroes singing, dancing, and laughing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LXXI frame, middle (1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Uncle Remus came he declined the River-place fiddle — 'she sets my toof on aidje; let's go back to ole times' — and, greeting the crowd ('I just come up to join in with you for one round, for the sake of ole times, if no mo''), he stood smiling upon the crowd of negroes, picturesque in the extreme, seeming taller than all the rest and moving with all the vigor of youth: he had always exercised authority over his fellow-servants — he had been the captain of the corn-pile, the stoutest at the log-rolling, the swiftest with the hoe, the neatest with the plough, and the plantation hands still looked upon him as their leader.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Harris, tale LXXI frame, ending (1883); not verbatim.

title.en: Granny Jinny: the Bee-King and the Aunties
title.zh: 賈妮奶奶：蜂王與眾姨婆

region.en: Southwest Missouri Ozark country, USA (symbolic pin: Joplin area)
region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶（象徵定位：喬普林一帶）

period: African-American oral tradition (Missouri); collected 1889-1893; published 1893

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales, as Told Among the Negroes of the South-West' (1893), chapter I 'The Bee-King and the Aunties' (told by 'Granny', Aunt Mary, Big Angie and the circle at the cabin fire)

summary.en: A convention of witches that is only Granny's company: a hundred-year-old woman born at Culpepper Court-house in Ole Feginny who has seen General Washington, claims descent from the Lenni-Lenape, and holds every power the quarter reveres — setting hens, out-generalizing turkeys, telling crops by the moon, laying out the dead, interpreting dreams, seeing ghosts and withstanding devils, patting Juba and jumping Jim Crow — while around the hickory-blaze sit Big Angie and the aunties, the surviving court of her authority.
summary.zh: 一場看似巫會的聚會，其實是賈妮奶奶的『待客會』：百歲高齡、生於老弗吉尼亞庫爾佩珀縣、親見過華盛頓將軍，自稱源出萊尼-勒納佩族；舉凡孵雞、馴野火雞、觀月令卜種、為亡者整容、解夢、見鬼抗魔、踏朱巴步、跳吉姆·克勞舞——鄉里敬畏的本領她樣樣在行；炭火四週坐著大安琪與眾姨婆，如同她權威的朝堂。

sensitivity.note: Frame-narrative portrait of the tale-telling circle from Owen's Missouri fieldwork (teller named as 'Granny', born in Virginia, claimed Indian descent); recorded as folkloric characterization, not as ritual instruction.

passages.text: It was not a convention of witches, though it bore the outward seeming of one; it was Aunt Jinny's 'company', and a good time the guests were having too. Aunt Jinny, or as her intimates called her, Granny, sat in the middle of the semicircle drawn round the great fireplace ablaze with the conflagration of a quarter of a cord of hickory logs, and felt herself as important a mistress of the situation, there in her cabin, as any queen could in her palace of carved stone. A great authority in her way was Granny.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, Voodoo Tales, chapter I (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: She knew the value of every herb and simple to be found in the state; she was an adept in the healing art; she could 'set' hens so that they never lost an egg; she could out-general the shyest turkey that ever stole its nest in the weeds and brush; she could tell when to wean a calf or baby and when to plant crops by the age and position of the moon; she could lay out the dead and usher in the living; she could interpret dreams; she knew the sign of everything from the spilling of salt to the flight of birds; she had seen ghosts and withstood devils; she knew legends and tales without number; and, last and most important, she was, to quote her own words, 'bornded at Culpepper Court-house in Ole Feginny and had seen Gin'al Washington with my own eyes' — and she was sold once and fetched a heap of money, and would again, being over a hundred years old and spry, for only shiftless critters that are cheap from the start wear out early.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter I, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her claims to aristocracy were always acknowledged by her associates: bond and now free, they agreed that all the past glories and dignities of her former owners up at The House were centred and kept alive in her own proper person; and her lineage was believed in without a demur — accepted as a child of the Werowances, though her abundant grey wool was of the woolliest, and ordinarily she appeared in a short cotton costume, a Madras turban very much awry, and a pair of men's boots much the worse for wear, carrying a stout hickory staff — 'I wears ole master's boots and hats; what's good 'nuff for him is good 'nuff for me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter I, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: Aunt Mymee's Luck-Ball
title.zh: 咪咪姨婆的幸運球

region.en: Southwest Missouri Ozark country, USA
region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

period: African-American oral tradition (Missouri); collected 1889-1893; published 2024 (published 1893)

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter XII 'Luck-Balls' (Aunt Mymee's lost fetich; told in the cabin circle)

summary.en: The horror of losing a luck-ball — the yarn fetich talked to by its owner's own name, in which her soul as well as her luck lived: found by the child Tow Head in a dirty linen bag, restored against Mymee's naked skin under the arm, and fed its weekly drink of eau-de-vie from a black bottle, the string mended and slung over the left shoulder — while Granny and Aunt Mary, who had begun to enjoy the terror, have to laugh out of the other side of the mouth.
summary.zh: 丟失幸運球的恐怖——那個以主人名字相喚、藏著她靈魂與運氣的線團法物：被孩子『蓬頭』從髒布袋中尋回、貼著裸膚掛回腋下、每週喂一次黑瓶裡的『生命之水』，斷繩接好斜掛肩上——而正樂得看熱鬧的賈妮與瑪麗姨婆，只得笑不出聲了。

sensitivity.note: Hoodoo charm-material recorded at folklore level by Owen (Leland's note: the incident occurred to his own family's cook). No preparation instructions beyond what the source itself records as practice; presented here as documentary folk belief. The underlying practice is a living tradition; nothing beyond the source's public content is reproduced.

passages.text: Aunt Mymee had been in what Granny designated as a terrible taking — the cause being the loss of her most powerful fetich, the luck-ball she had talked to and called by her own name as if it were her double. Her superstitious terrors when she discovered the loss were really pitiable; her overbearing manner toward the other negroes quite forsook her, her limbs were palsied and her complexion bleached to that awful greyish pallor. She had missed the precious ball in the morning when she was dressing herself, hastily felt in her bed, snatched off the covers and shook the pillows vigorously, scrutinized the floor — no ball could be found. Then Aunt Mymee went wild: her morning duties were forgotten, she ran hither and thither looking in all possible and impossible places of concealment, obstinately refusing to state what she had lost; finally, with a groan of despair, she flung herself down on her cabin floor in a cowering heap and quavered out that she would be better off in her grave, for an enemy had stolen her luck-ball, and her soul as well as her luck was in it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her daughter's pickaninnies spread the news in great excitement; but scarcely had Granny and Aunt Mary begun to enjoy it when they had to laugh out of the other side of the mouth — Tow Head proudly marched to the cabin with an exceedingly dirty little bag in her hand, desiring to know if Aunt Mymee's soul was tied up in that nasty thing. Evidently it was: Aunt Mymee sprang up with a joyful cry, kissed the bag and hugged the finder, then sternly demanded how she got it without her knowing — 'Found it by my bed this morning. I didn't show that ball under the sun; when I was telling her about Uncle John's Jack she told me never to say anything more about such wicked idol-ery, and I promised I wouldn't, and I always keep my promises — if I don't forget.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Aunt Mymee heaved a sigh of relief — 'That is a good child, don't pester your ma' — and began to fumble at the strings wrapped (not tied) round the neck of the dirty bag that had raised such a commotion. She was going to give Lil Mymee a drink: that ball does not sip water but sups what Big Angy calls eau-de-vie, and that surely is the water of life, for if she does not get it she dies. She produced the black bottle of Little Mymee's elixir — better known to the general public as whiskey — and proceeded to moisten first the ball, then herself; after which ceremony she restored the ball to its proper receptacle, mended the broken string that had been the cause of its loss, and made it an ornament to her person by slinging the string over her left shoulder and under her right so that the ball rested under her right armpit — having, beforehand, slipped out of the various waists of her raiment, so that the ball should lie against her naked body with no intervening fold of calico to absorb its strength.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: King A, the Voodoo Doctor Who Travels on the Devil's Steed
title.zh: A王：騎魔馬而行的伏都醫者

region.en: Southwest Missouri Ozark country, USA
region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

period: African-American oral tradition (Missouri); collected 1889-1893; published 2024 (published 1893)

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter XII 'Luck-Balls' (portrait of 'King' A, a Voodoo doctor or conjurer)

summary.en: The maker of the luck-balls is a curious half-barbarian who never stays long in a place, makes his entrances secretly and mysteriously in the night, never confides in anyone, never spends money for anything but whiskey, and never lacks for the good things of this world nor is reduced to begging or stealing — no cabin refuses him shelter and the best bed and food it can afford; no one knows whence he came or whither he is going. When four taps are heard above the latch, someone flies to usher in the guest: 'A is there' is the unspoken conviction, and it is generally conceded that he travels at his ease on some strange steed of the devil's providing.
summary.zh: 幸運球的製者是一位奇特的半野蠻人：從不長居一地、夜半神秘而來、從不吐露心事、錢只花在威士忌上，卻從不缺世間好物，也從不乞討偷竊——沒有一間小屋會拒絕給他最好的床與食；無人知其來處去向。閂上有四下輕叩，便有人飛身開門：『A王到了』是不言自明的信念；眾人皆信他騎著魔鬼所賜的怪馬自在行路。

sensitivity.note: Portrait of a named (initial) conjure-doctor from Owen's Missouri fieldwork; recorded as folkloric legend about a living figure of the 1890s, without reproducing any working ritual.

passages.text: How the luck-ball was made, and what were its components, Tow Head did not at that time know, though she gathered from the half-whispered gossip of the other aunties that it was the work of 'King' A, a Voodoo doctor or conjurer of great powers and influence. This A was a curious half-barbarian who never stayed long in a place, made his entrances secretly and mysteriously in the night, never confided in any one, never spent money for anything but whiskey, never lacked for the good things of this world, and never was reduced to the inconvenience of begging or stealing, although he was like the lilies of the field that toil not, neither do they spin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: No cabin refused him shelter and the best bed and food it could afford. No one knew whence he came or whither he was going. When four taps were heard above the latch, some one flew to usher in the guest; 'A is there' was the unspoken conviction. How he came was a matter of conjecture: it was generally conceded that he travelled at his ease on some strange steed of the devil's providing — and as soon as he was settled in his temporary quarters, that is, had eaten of everything in the larder and drunk generous potations, he was gone again into the night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: Ole Blue Jay: the Sand-Carrier of Hell
title.zh: 老藍鶺：地獄運沙鳥

region.en: Southwest Missouri Ozark country, USA
region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

period: African-American oral tradition (Missouri); collected 1889-1893; published 2024 (published 1893)

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter IX 'Some Tales in Which Blue Jay and His Gwines-On Figure Conspicuously' (told by Granny)

summary.en: Granny's cosmology of gossip: every Friday Ole Blue Jay goes to Hell with sand and the account of all the bad folks' doings; he builds up the walls of the Bad Place, gives out the news to the Ole Boy, loads himself with all the lies he can tote, and comes back among us — and when he turns the lies loose the Lord knows it makes no end of quarrelling and fussing. The mocking-bird, sick with only one tune, served thejay his come-uppance for his impertinence, and so learned to learn more tunes.
summary.zh: 賈妮奶奶的饞舌宇宙論：每逢禮拜五，老藍鶺便帶著沙土與眾惡人的劣跡簿下地獄；他築起『壞地方』的城牆，把消息呈給老魔頭，再負上滿載的謊言回到人間——謊言一放，吵鬧與口角便無窮無盡。嘲鶇先生因只有一支曲子鬱鬱而病，替老婆出氣教訓了無禮的藍鶺，也由此學會了更多的曲子。

sensitivity.note: Cosmological-burlesque bird tale from Granny's repertoire. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: Granny had got a heap better tale than any rabbit tale, studied out in the night until it roused her so she did not get a wink of rest since the chickens crowed for midnight — a tale about Ole Blue Jay. 'And he is the one that goes to Hell of a Friday and carries sand and the account of all the bad folkses' do; and when he takes that sand and builds up the walls of the Bad Place and then gives out all the bad news to the Ole Boy, then he loads himself up with all the lies that he can tote and comes back among us. Much account, huh? — when he gets back and turns those lies loose, the Lord knows it makes no end of quarrelling and fussing!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter IX (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was along of Ole Blue Jay — him that thinks himself so smart and really was a plum fool — that the new tunes came to the mocking-bird. In the old good times, when possum grease and sweet-potatoes were as plenty as doodle-bugs and cockle-burs, the mocking-birds did not know but just one tune; and the reason they know more now is this. Mister Mocking-bird was sitting home with a misery in his back and a cold in his head and a squawmishness in his stomach, and could not sing even the one tune he knew; Miss Mocking-bird had to fly round and do the marketing her own self.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter IX, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of the times she had been out abroad hunting up something that would lay on her ole man's stomach, she met up with Ole Blue Jay, who offered — mighty soft — to carry her vegetables home, for it would be a burning shame for a slim young person to tote a load that would make her lopsided and spoil that fine form of hers. At that she just laughed and flew off with the truck; and when she got home she told her ole man, and he flared up and said he was going to give Blue Jay a licking for his impudence — and then he sort of trimmed up his feathers and said he did not know but that he felt his strength coming back some. From that minute he began to mend, and went to the market next morning himself — and the mocking-bird never knew but one tune again, but one was never enough for him after that.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter IX, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: Ole Rabbit and the Dog He Stole: Gopher's Winter Supplies
title.zh: 老兔與他偷的狗：鼠鼴的過冬存糧

region.en: Southwest Missouri Ozark country, USA
region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

period: African-American oral tradition (Missouri); collected 1889-1893; published 2024 (published 1893)

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter X 'Ole Rabbit an' de Dawg he Stole — How He Obtained Gopher's Winter Supplies' (told by Granny)

summary.en: Ole Rabbit, gorged on Gopher's cellar of sweet shoots and calamus, hears of Gopher's dainties — bumble-bee honey, Sunday vittles — and proposes an exchange of goods: he will show Gopher his truck-patch, a splendid pile he has 'sot out and worked' by his own overseering. The pile is dog-roots and wilted trash raked from the crumbling creek bank; while Gopher blinks sun-blind underground hauling the rubbige down, Rabbit unhurries the good roots into the brier-patch — and the family camps out there till the hounds and the scandal both cool.
summary.zh: 老兔吃遍鼠鼴窖中的嫩莖菖蒲，又聽說蜂蜜與安息日大菜，便提議以貨易貨：帶他去看自家的『作物堆』——其實是從河岸朽根與蔫草堆起的『豐收』。趁鼠鼴在地下被日頭晃得暈頭轉向地把垃圾往下運，老兔慢條斯理把好根藏進荊棘窩——一家老小在窩裡紮營，直到獵犬與閒話一併冷卻。

sensitivity.note: Rabbit-swindle tale from Granny's repertoire. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: Hearing of Gopher's dainties — 'bummle-bee honey' and the rest, which Gopher offered sort of hanging back with the words as if most ashamed to let them out — nearly killed Ole Rabbit, but since he was filled up in the corners with those white shoots and calamus he could stand it better when the chat ran on vittles; so he looked mighty and tossed up his chin, cleared his throat, as if the naming of common vittles made him contemptuous, and said that if Gopher was not satisfied he might fetch in some of his truck when the day got more along toward noon and warmer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter X (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seeming to Gopher like he would perish if he did not get some of that truck, he agreed mighty fierce-eagerly, and began throwing out the truck he had in the cellar; then him and Ole Rabbit made the agreement that when the cellar was all cleared out, Ole Rabbit would show him the way to the truck-patch. With that saying Ole Rabbit went out — but he did not go home, for what was the use, there was no pot a-boiling in his house that day: he was just telling outrageous lies to get Gopher all tore up in his mind, and he done it. Instead of going home he went down by the creek where the bank crumbles off and the water washes the roots of the weeds and briars out; he lopped off heaps of dog-roots and piled them up in a big pile out in a field, then got a very big lot of wilted-trash and piled them on too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter X, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he loped back and asked Gopher to come along, since he was through his big dinner and had nothing a-libbing thing to do except to help a friendly man — which was certainly a pleasure instead of a bother. 'Here it is, neighbor! I done sot him out and worked him and laid him by my own-self, so I know just what you are getting.' Gopher, winking and blinking in the sun till he could not tell a tater from a toadstool, took Rabbit's word for it and got to work; while Gopher took the first load down cellar his own self, Rabbit — a-turning his back and stuffing his handkerchief in his mouth to keep from bursting out laughing — grabbed up an armful of those nice sweet roots and goobers and hid them in the brush nigh home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter X, ending (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: They kept up that foolishness till sundown; then Rabbit loped off home and told the ole woman and the children they had better camp in the brier-patch that night and the next day, because the hounds were out — and they were more than willing when they heard that, and more than willing to say so when they caught sight of Gopher's truck in there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter X, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: Ole Woodpecker and the Blind Bear-Mammy
title.zh: 老啄木鳥與瞎眼熊媽媽

region.en: Southwest Missouri Ozark country, USA
region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

period: African-American oral tradition (Missouri); collected 1889-2021 (published 1893)

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter XIX 'The Last Gleaning of the Field' (the tale of the two bears and Ole Woodpecker, told by Aunt Em'ly)

summary.en: The widow-bear, blinded by a cold got fishing, is starved by her housemate the old maid bear, who keeps the good meat on the high swinging shelf in the cellar where poor old blind mammy cannot find it — until Ole Woodpecker, knocking round among the shingles, peeks down the chimney, calls himself a poor little boy stuck in the chimney, and when the groping mammy comes to help, flings a charm spang in her face that fetches back her sight quick enough to see Woodpecker clear out of the chimney.
summary.zh: 漁時受寒失明的寡婦熊，被同居的老處女熊剋扣口糧——好肉全鎖在窖中高懸架上，瞎眼的老媽媽永遠摸不著。老啄木鳥在瓦片間敲擊時自煙囪窺破一切，自稱『可憐的小男孩卡在煙囪裡』，哄得瞎媽媽摸索救助；趁機把一枚符物迎面擲去——視力立返，她親眼看著啄木鳥飛出煙囪逃之夭夭。

sensitivity.note: Animal-helper tale from Aunt Em'ly's repertoire. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: There was once an old mammy bear that was a widow-bear, and as she was going along through the woods one time — it was along in the spring-time — she met up with another bear that was an old maid. After they had asked one another howdy and passed the time of day, saying how they felt lonesome now their families were all broke up, they sort of agreed and made it up that they would keep house together during the warm weather. So say, so do, and they settled down together, and hunted and fished and divided evenly and fair — until the widow-bear took a cold from getting her feet wet fishing, and it settled in her eyes and by and by put them clean out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XIX (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: That was a bad time for Miss Bear. There she was in her own house, but the old maid bear fetched her nothing but the bones: all the good meat she did not eat right up she kept on the high swinging shelf in the cellar, where poor old blind mammy could not find it. Mammy sort of suspected something, but there she was, and no use to say nothing, but she got leaner and leaner all the time, till her bones rattled when the wind blew and her hide flopped like a flag on the hill-top. If it had not been for Ole Woodpecker, old mammy would have naturally given up the ghost — but he was a-knocking round among the shingles on the roof, and he heard the old mammy sniffing and crying (the old maid was out a-hunting), and he peeked down the chimney and saw just how it was.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XIX, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Never mind! I fix that,' he said, and hollered down, 'Hello, mammy! come help me.' She stopped crying and asked who he was. 'I am a poor little boy got stuck in your chimney.' Instead of scolding like the old maid would have done, poor ole mammy groped to the chimney and felt round to help. 'Poor child,' she said, 'I am feared I cannot do much. Holler again so I can tell just where you is, because I am blind, honey.' He hollered and hollered and kept the old mammy feeling round till she was distracted; then, all of a sudden, he flung a charm spang in her face that fetched back her sight that quick, that she saw Ole Woodpecker fly out of that chimney and clear out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XIX, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: Marie Laveau: the Last Voodoo Queen
title.zh: 瑪麗·拉沃：末代伏都女王

region.en: New Orleans, Louisiana, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那紐奧良

period: Louisiana Voodoo; queen flourished 1820s-1880s; recorded 1920s; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. III 'Voodooism and Conjuration' — section 'Marie Laveau'

summary.en: New Orleans's last voodoo queen, half legend half history: at her funeral the superstitious crowds expected supernatural occurrences, and said the live snake she had fed under her bed like a baby was the devil come to claim her soul. An old Frenchman who knew her called the legends pure fancy — a hair-dresser and procuress afraid of snakes, who kept a small jointed wooden snake on the mantel to fool the superstitious — so great a web of fancy has been woven around this unique character that a painting of her unsellable at two dollars after her death is now worth over two hundred and fifty.
summary.zh: 紐奧良末代伏都女王，傳說與史實各半：她的葬禮上迷信的民眾專候異象，說她如嬰兒般在床下飼養的活蛇，是來索她靈魂的魔鬼。一位相識的老法國人卻稱傳說純屬虛構——她不過是髮妝師兼拉皮條者，怕蛇，只把一條小木蛇擺在壁爐架上愚弄迷信者——圍繞這位奇女子的傳說之網織得如此之厚，她死後兩美元賣不出的畫像，如今值二百五十美元。

sensitivity.note: Historical-folkloric portrait of a named New Orleans figure from Puckett's 1920s fieldwork; conflicting testimonies preserved (snake story vs. wooden-snake story). Living-tradition figures treated with care; no ritual reproduction.

passages.text: Marie Laveau was the last voodoo queen, and in Puckett's investigation of voodooism in New Orleans he found many conflicting views regarding her. A member of the Historical Society distinctly remembers her funeral, which was attended by large numbers of superstitious Negroes, all expecting supernatural occurrences.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro, ch. III, section 'Marie Laveau' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some of those Negroes stated that Marie Laveau had a live snake which she kept under her bed and fed like a baby; when its mistress died the snake departed, and the Negroes said it was the devil gone to claim her soul. An old Frenchman, a personal friend of Marie Laveau, stated that a great deal at present said about her is pure fancy and fiction: she was simply a griffe — the offspring of a Negro and a mulattress — a procuress and a hair-dresser, visiting the homes of her clients and using her intimate knowledge gathered there in dealing with related white customers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: As a matter of fact, Marie Laveau, so he states from personal knowledge of her house, was afraid of snakes, but kept a small jointed wooden snake on her mantel along with other bric-a-brac to fool the superstitious. So great has been the web of fancy woven around this unique character that an original painting of her, which an antique dealer could not sell for two dollars just after her death, is now worth over two hundred and fifty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, ending (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: The Voodoo Dance and the Monter-Voudou
title.zh: 伏都之舞與『上伏都』

region.en: New Orleans, Louisiana, USA
region.zh: 美國路易斯安那紐奧良

period: Louisiana Voodoo (19th-c. societies described via Castellanos); recorded 1920s; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. III, section 'Louisiana Voodoo Rites' (synthesizing Castellanos and Cable)

summary.en: The night ceremony of the voodoo society: red handkerchiefs at the loins, the king with his blue cord and crimson drape, adoration of the snake in its barred cage on the altar and renewal of the oath of secrecy; the queen set bodily upon the box of the deity, seized with convulsions while the oracle talks through her inspired lips; the candidate in the charcoal circle with his package of herbs and waxen effigies, the paddle-tap, the African chant — 'Eh! eh! Bomba, hen, hen! Canga bafio te...' — and the squirming dance called monter-voudou, until pandemonium is let loose.
summary.zh: 伏都社的夜祭：腰繫紅帕、頭纏紅布的王，祭壇柵籠中的蛇受眾膜拜，守密之誓重申；王后被親手放上神匣，痙攣之中神諭借她之口說話；候補者立於炭圈，手捧藥草與蠟像之包，木槳輕擊，非洲古調起——『嗡！嗡！邦巴，喝！喝！康加巴菲奧……』——扭動之舞名為『上伏都』，直至群魔亂舞。

sensitivity.note: Historical reconstruction of 19th-century Louisiana Voodoo rites from published sources (Castellanos, Cable) synthesized by Puckett; the chant is transcribed as folklore in those sources. Living-tradition practice is not reproduced beyond the public-domain description; the same ceremony is documented from the hostile St. John account (cross_ref: vodou-serpent-ceremony).

passages.text: The secret meetings of the voodoo society were held at night. Castellanos tells of the members divesting themselves of their usual raiment and putting on sandals, girding their loins with red handkerchiefs — of which the king wears a greater number and those of finer quality than the ordinary member; he also has a blue cord about his waist and his head draped with some crimson stuff, while the queen is dressed more simply, with red garments and a red sash.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro, ch. III, 'Louisiana Voodoo Rites' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: The ceremony begins with the adoration of the snake, placed in a barred cage upon an altar in front of the king and queen, and a renewal of the oath of secrecy. The king and queen extol future happiness and exhort their subjects always to seek their advice; then individually the members come up to implore the voodoo god — to invoke blessings upon friends and curses upon enemies. The king patiently listens. Then the spirit moves him: he places the queen bodily upon the box containing the deity. She is seized with convulsions and the oracle talks through her inspired lips — bestowing flattery and promises of success, then laying down irrevocable laws in the name of the serpent. Questions are asked and an offering taken; new work is proposed and the oath of secrecy again taken, sometimes sealed by the warm blood of a kid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: After this the voodoo dance begins. The initiation of new candidates forms the first part of the ceremony: the voodoo king traces a large circle in the center of the room with a piece of charcoal and places within it the sable neophyte, thrusting into his hand a package of herbs, horse hair, rancid tallow, waxen effigies, broken bits of horn, and other substances. Then, lightly striking him on the head with a small wooden paddle, he launches into the African chant — 'Eh! eh! Bomba, hen, hen! Canga bafio te, Canga moune de le, Canga do ki la, Canga li' — and at this the candidate begins to squirm and dance, an action called monter-voudou; if he steps out of the ring in his frenzy the king and queen turn their backs to neutralize the bad omen. Drinking some stimulant, he relapses into a hysterical fit; the initiate is then led to the altar to take the oath, and from that moment becomes a full-fledged member of the order.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king then places his foot upon the box containing the snake; he seems to get a sort of shock which is transmitted to his queen, and through her to everyone in the circle. Violent convulsions take place, the queen being the most violently affected; from time to time the serpent is again touched to get more magnetic power. The box is shaken, and the tinkling bells on its side increase the general delirium already under way, aggravated by much drinking of spirituous liquors — 'then is pandemonium let loose': fainting fits and choking spells succeed one another, a nervous tremor possesses everybody, they spin with incredible velocity, and some, entirely deprived of reason, fall down to the ground from sheer lassitude and are carried still panting and gyrating.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, ending (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: The Self-made Hoodoo-doctor: Fieldwork Among the Trick-doctors
title.zh: 自封的呼督醫：深入巫醫圈的田野調查

region.en: Mississippi and Georgia plantation country, USA
region.zh: 美國密西西比與喬治亞種植園地帶

period: Southern hoodoo practice, 1920s fieldwork; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. III, sections 'A Self-made Hoodoo-doctor', 'Professional Duties', 'Satisfied Patients'

summary.en: The ethnographer turns conjure-doctor to hoodoo the hoodoos: a startling collection of red flannel rags, rabbit's feet, lodestone and steel filings, an Egyptian idol, a jack, graveyard dirt, voodoo charms from New Orleans — and patients come. Professional duties follow: diagnose who laid the trick, find and destroy the charm, turn the trick back, lay haunts, locate treasure and water. The satisfied patients include an old woman cured — 'strange to say' — of sickness by a doctor's self-buried bottle of hair and graveyard dirt, and a man who died still believing in the lizards the conjurer had slipped into his poultice.
summary.zh: 民族誌者自任巫醫，以呼督制呼督：一袋紅法蘭絨、兔腳、磁石鋼屑、埃及偶像、墓土與紐奧良符物——患者自來。其職司包括診斷誰施咒、尋咒毀咒、以咒還咒、置鬼尋寶找水。『滿意』的病人中：一位老嫗被巫醫自埋的『頭髮墓土』咒瓶診出、破解——『說來奇怪』竟痊癒；另一人至死仍信臂中有蜥蜴——蜥蜴是巫醫親手塞進藥泥的。

sensitivity.note: Puckett's participant-observation among 1920s conjure-doctors, including named cases (Steiner's Georgia cases cited). Recorded as ethnographic narrative of folk practice; no working instructions beyond what the source records as anecdote. Living-tradition caution: conjure practice is part of a living religion; material presented historically.

passages.text: In almost all cases the conjure-doctor is a peculiar individual, set aside because of his very peculiarity for dealings with the supernatural; not always are the conjure-doctors Negroes — sometimes white women assume the role for the sake of the rewards to be gained by successful imposture. After being asked to pay twenty dollars for some trifling information by Negroes he had good reason to believe were hoodoos, Puckett finally adopted the role of conjure-doctor himself, in order to be able to discuss the tricks of the trade as hoodoo to hoodoo: 'Even conjurers are not without their professional spirit, and I found them quite willing to swap clinical knowledge and even materia medica with one, once they believed him to be a real trick-doctor.' His startling collection of red flannel rags, rabbit's feet, lodestone and steel filings, an Egyptian idol, a jack, graveyard dirt, voodoo charms from New Orleans — and enough imagination to conjure up missing details when necessary — soon had patients seeking his aid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, 'A Self-made Hoodoo-doctor' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Professional duties: one of the first things the conjure-doctors have to do is to diagnose the case, tell the person whether he is conjured or not, and find out who laid the trick; the trick — the charm — must be found and destroyed and the patient cured; if the patient wishes, the conjurer must also be able to turn the trick back upon the one who set it. Besides this, a conjurer truly up in his profession must be able to lay haunts, and to locate buried treasure or a vein of water: treasure by a divining rod with a nail in the end of each branching twig, marching boldly over the suspected landscape — when you pass over the buried treasure the free end will be pulled suddenly toward the ground — or water by observing a tree whose limbs are longer on one side, bending in that direction where the vein lies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, 'Professional Duties' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Satisfied patients: Puckett tested this out on his own clients — a quarter down, let the client keep the charm a week, two dollars more if satisfied; in very few cases was the client unwilling to pay. True there is often trickery: in one case an old Negro woman was taken sick, and a scheming conjure-doctor at once buried a bottle containing human hair, graveyard dirt and two small sticks in the path leading to her spring, told her she was conjured, offered to find the conjure for ten dollars; roaming over the location with a little iron rod, he located the charm he had buried, broke the bottle and buried it in the middle of the public road, and gave the old woman some roots to chew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, 'Satisfied Patients' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: She gladly paid the ten dollars and, strange to say, recovered — illustrating the power of mind over body; although the trick was exposed she still believes that she was conjured and that she was cured by the doctor. In another case, a man had a rising on his arm; the conjure-doctor slipped a lizard into a poultice which he bound on the sore, and later, taking the poultice off, told the man he was conjured and had lizards in his arm — and although the hoodoo-doctor collected considerable money in an attempt to cure the trouble, the patient finally died, thinking to the last that he had reptiles in his arm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. III, 'Satisfied Patients' (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of Jack-o'-my-Lantern
title.zh: 傑克燈之起源

region.en: Deep South crossroads, USA (symbolic pin: Mississippi Delta)
region.zh: 美國深南部十字路口（象徵定位：密西西比三角洲）

period: Southern folk-legend recorded 1920s; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. II 'Burial Customs, Ghosts, and Witches' — section 'The Origin of Jack' (told by a root-doctor)

summary.en: The wandering flame of the swamps has a biography: Jack sold himself to the devil at the crossroads one night at twelve o'clock; for seven years all power was given him to do as he pleased, but at the end of that period his soul belonged to the devil — until Jack, ready, tacked a piece of old shoe sole above the door, asked the devil to fetch it, nailed the reaching hand fast and slipped the chair away, and was freed on his promise — whereupon neither heaven nor hell would have him, and he wanders with his lantern still.
summary.zh: 沼澤間的游火有著自己的傳記：傑克於午夜十二時在十字路口將自己賣給魔鬼；七年之內百般自在，期滿靈魂便歸魔鬼——然而傑克早有準備：門楣上釘了一塊舊鞋底，請魔鬼代取；魔鬼立椅伸手之際，傑克掄錘釘住其手、抽走椅凳，換得釋放之諾——此後天堂地獄皆不收他，他便提著燈籠永世游蕩。

sensitivity.note: Jack-o'-lantern origin legend told to Puckett by a root-doctor; the turn-the-pocket-out defense recorded alongside (cross-ref: harris Spirits tale; owen Wuller-wups).

passages.text: The Southern Negroes are very familiar with the apparition which they call Jack-o'-lantern, or Jack-o'-my-lantern, though the whites of the locality pay little or no attention to such beliefs — making this a bit of English lore preserved almost exclusively by Negroes. These Jack-o'-lanterns carry lights and would certainly fool you into the swamp or river, unless you turn your pockets wrongside out — doubtless to show the avaricious spirit that you have nothing in them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, 'Jack-o'-my-Lantern' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Various legends are in vogue among the Negroes to account for the origin of this creature. One illustrating the common theme was told Puckett by a root-doctor: Jack sold himself to the devil at the crossroads one night at twelve o'clock. For seven years all power was given to him to do as he pleased, but at the end of that period his soul belonged to the devil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, 'The Origin of Jack' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old Satan called for him, but Jack was ready. He had tacked a piece of old shoe sole up above the door, and asked the devil to get it for him. The devil stood in a chair and reached for it; Jack then took a hammer and nailed the devil's hand fast, slipping the chair out from under him — and upon a promise of his freedom, the devil went his way, and Jack went his: a soul that hell would not take and heaven would not have, carrying his lantern through the swamps ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, ending (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: The Coolin'-Board Wake: Ashes That Take Up the Disease
title.zh: 涼板守靈：吸病的灰燼

region.en: Virginia and the Deep South, USA
region.zh: 美國弗吉尼亞與深南部

period: African-American mortuary practice; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. II, sections on wakes and the coolin'-board (citing Smiley's Virginia-Carolina-Georgia-Florida folklore)

summary.en: Between death and burial the body is never left alone: neighbors come and set up, food is served and melodies sung — the spontaneous rhythmic grief at these wakes being, in Puckett's judgment, the beginning of many spirituals. On the coolin'-board a plateful of salt and ashes stands beneath the sheets — whatever disease the body has goes into the ashes and salt, 'ashes takes up from the body the disease' — and at the words 'ashes to ashes and dust to dust' they are thrown into the grave; the last one to leave a settin'-up will be the first one to die.
summary.zh: 入土之前，遺體不可片刻無人：鄰里前來守靈，進食歌唱——這種守靈時自發而合拍的悲歌，在普凱特看來正是許多靈歌的源頭。涼板之上、褥單之下置一盤鹽與灰——死者身中何病，皆入灰鹽——『灰自身上吸去其病』；誦到『歸於塵土』之句，便將其傾入墓中；守靈最後離開的人，將是最先死去的人。

sensitivity.note: Mortuary-folklore description from published ethnography (Puckett citing Smiley, JAF 1919); no ritual instruction beyond the description; presented as documentary folk belief.

passages.text: During the three days — sometimes less — elapsing between death and burial, the body should never be left alone. Neighbors come and set up with the body; food is served and melodies sung — the spontaneous expression of grief in rhythmic form at this time probably being the beginning of many spirituals. The older Negroes complain that wakes are not what they used to be: 'We used to sing and pray all the night long, but now the young folks that attend them just tells anecdotes all night.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: In other localities the body is placed on a coolin'-board and covered with an arrangement of sheets, the one over the face being raised when the mourners address the corpse: 'Mandy, you gone and left me... I may be next... Poor Mandy!... Poor John!' A plateful of salt and ashes is placed under the coolin'-board, and whatever disease the body has goes into the ashes and salt — 'Ashes takes up from the body the disease.' These ashes are carried to the grave, and at the words 'Ashes to ashes and dust to dust' they are thrown into the grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II (1926), citing Smiley (1919); not verbatim.

passages.text: No one would think of leaving a settin'-up alone, and the last one to leave such a meeting will be the first one to die. This idea of a wake may be either European or African in origin; and the African has an intense passion for burials — even pawning himself and his children into slavery if need be to give his relations a proper funeral — while the Southern Negro has much the same notion, paying dues to a lodge all his life, or going head over heels into debt, to see that he or his relations are laid away in style.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: Feet First: the Funeral Procession Rules
title.zh: 腳朝前：出殯行列的規矩

region.en: Deep South, USA
region.zh: 美國深南部

period: African-American mortuary practice; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Newbell N. Puckett, 'Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro' (1926), ch. II, section 'The Funeral Procession'

summary.en: The corpse is taken from the house feet first, else it would be looking back and beckoning a member of the family to follow; touch the body once and the ghost will not harm you; never carry a corpse in its own vehicle — a hearse should always be hired — and never let it stop between the house and the cemetery, all gates being opened beforehand; if the procession stops, another death will soon follow, for a mishap on the way indicates that the corpse is dissatisfied; and the person who counts the carriages in the procession is only counting the days before his own death.
summary.zh: 遺體抬出家門必須腳朝前，否則亡者會回望招手，引家人隨行；摸過遺體一次，鬼魂便不害你；不可用死者自己的車運屍——靈車必須僱用——從家到墓園途中不得停歇，事先應把所有柵門打開；行列若停，死亡將接踵而至，因途中受阻意味著亡者戀世不捨；而數點送葬馬車的人，數的正是自己餘下的日子。

sensitivity.note: Mortuary omens compiled by Puckett from southern informants; presented as documentary folk belief.

passages.text: When the time comes for burial the corpse should be taken from the house feet first, else it would be looking back and beckoning to a member of the family to follow — a belief European in origin, as is also the common Negro belief that if you put your hand on the corpse the ghost will not harm you (or you will be afraid of no more dead people). This may be the remnant of an old ordeal, since wounds are supposed to bleed if the murderer touches the corpse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, 'The Funeral Procession' (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is extremely bad luck to carry a corpse to the cemetery in his own vehicle — a hearse should always be hired. The corpse should not be allowed to stop between the house and the cemetery (with the exception of the church), all gates being opened beforehand. If the procession should stop, another death will soon follow — a mishap on the way probably indicating that the corpse is dissatisfied and regrets having to leave this world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II (1926); not verbatim.

passages.text: A person who counts the carriages in the funeral procession does no more than count the days before his own death — a belief of European origin. While it is extremely bad luck to walk ahead of the corpse, it is even worse luck to meet a funeral procession face to face.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Puckett, ch. II, ending (1926); not verbatim.

title.en: The Plat-Eye of the Georgetown Coast
title.zh: 喬治敦海岸的『板眼』

region.en: Pawley's Island, Georgetown coast, South Carolina, USA
region.zh: 美國南卡羅來納喬治敦海岸保利島

period: Gullah folk-belief; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Ambrose E. Gonzales, 'The Black Border: Gullah Stories of the Carolina Coast' (1922), tale 'The Plat-Eye' (Jane the cook's night-walk)

summary.en: A bogey peculiar to the Georgetown coast: plat-eyes appear to old and young of both sexes — sometimes as a small dog or other animal, sometimes floating like wraiths along the marshes, sometimes stooping like low-hung clouds to envelop the victim. Most often they come as a familiar animal glaring with eyes of fire, spring upon him, frighten him into rigidity, and just as he expects his vitals to be torn out, the apparition vanishes; the negroes dread the visitations as werewolves were feared in Europe not so long ago — and old Jane, the many-times-widowed cook, walks her nights on permanent jumpiness, seeing potential plat-eyes in every stray calf, raccoon, bouncing rabbit, and even the ghostly sandcrabs drifting along the beaches like windblown foam.
summary.zh: 喬治敦海岸特有的妖怪：『板眼』對男女老少都會現形——時而化為小狗或別的獸，時而如幽靈般漂浮於沼澤小徑，時而低垂如雲、將人裹住。最常見的是化作熟悉的動物、以火眼瞪視、撲向行人，令其僵立；正當他以為五臟要被掏出之際，妖物倏忽消失。當地人畏之如歐洲人昔時畏狼人；屢屢喪夫的廚娘簡，夜行時神經緊繃——離群的小牛、浣熊、竄起的兔子、連沙灘上隨風飄移的幽靈沙蟹，在她眼裡都是潛伏的板眼。

sensitivity.note: Gullah bogey-tale from Gonzales's coastal South Carolina collection; dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: All low-country negroes believe more or less in 'sperrits', 'haants' and other mysterious appearances, but the plat-eye, peculiar to the Georgetown coast, is the weirdest and most fearsome that vexes the roaming negroes at night. Plat-eyes appear to old and young of both sexes, sometimes in the form of a small dog or other animal, while at other times they may float like wraiths along the marshes or unfrequented paths, or stoop like low-hung clouds and envelop the victim.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, The Black Border, 'The Plat-Eye' (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Most frequently, however, the plat-eye appears in the form of some familiar animal which, glaring at the beholder with eyes of fire, springs upon him, frightening him into rigidity — and, just as he expects his vitals to be torn out, the apparition vanishes, and the trembling negro hurries on his way. The belief has been expressed that in some instances the negroes to whom plat-eyes appear have fallen asleep as they walked, and, dreaming of these terrors, awakened to find them gone. In whatsoever form they come, however, the negroes dread the visitations as werewolves were feared in Europe not so long ago.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'The Plat-Eye', middle (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old Jane, the cook at the Pawley's Island summer hotel — the many-times-widowed woman who had saved the life of Esau the fisherman by drenching him with horse liniment, wedded him to save herself the reproach of old-maidenhood, and chased him away the morning after — was a fervent and fearful believer in plat-eyes. Whenever and wherever she went her ways at night, she was on the lookout for them, and the expectation of their momentary appearance kept her nerves in a pleasant state of jumpiness: a stray calf at the edge of the clearing, a raccoon ambling along a woodland path, a sudden rabbit bouncing up before her, the horned owl that lifted her wayward fowls from their runaway roost on the ridge-pole of her cabin — even the ghostly sandcrabs that drifted along the beaches at night as lightly as windblown foam — were all potential plat-eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'The Plat-Eye', ending (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: Old Harrison and Ben: 'God Held My Hand'
title.zh: 老哈里森與本恩：『是上帝按住了我的手』

region.en: Cooper River, South Carolina, USA
region.zh: 美國南卡羅來納庫珀河一帶

period: Post-emancipation Gullah life; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Ambrose E. Gonzales, 'The Black Border' (1922), tale 'Old Harrison' (Ben's testimony of the beating)

summary.en: Ben, a rascal twice over — six or seven wives put away and taken back at his pleasure, always under suspicion when a calf or shoat went missing — undertook to discipline his step-daughter-in-law, an Amazon who took two or three blows of the hickory and then turned on him and mauled him almost into unconsciousness. Patched up, he loved to tell the story with unction: 'God bin wid me dat day... me 'membuh de time when I could-uh box her and kick her... but God tell me fuh peaceubble, en' spayre de 'ooman life... ef I had a kick dat 'ooman 'e would-uh dead' — and when he looks upon the dead woman in his mind, he thanks God every day for holding his hand.
summary.zh: 劣跡斑斑的本恩——七八任妻子隨心聚散、失牛失豬總被懷疑——竟要『管教』力大如亞馬遜的繼媳；胡桃棍落下兩三記，那女子轉身反擊，幾乎將他打昏。傷癒之後他逢人便講，油然自得：『那天上帝與我同在……想當年我拳腳並施她早沒命了……可上帝命我息怒、饒她性命……每當我腦中浮現那具女屍，我就天天感謝上帝按住了我的手。』

sensitivity.note: Gullah anecdote-frame tale with dark domestic-violence content, transcribed by Gonzales from coastal tellers; presented as documentary folk narrative. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: Ben had been partial to wives all his life, having been more or less affiliated with six or seven, whom he put away and took back again with no more ceremony than his change of mind. Unruly and insubordinate as a slave, he became stronger with freedom, and was regarded as a rascal by whites and blacks: when a calf or a shoat was missed in the community, Ben was not infrequently suspected of having shared the meat, either as a participant in the slaughter or as a welcomed guest at the banqueting board of the thief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, The Black Border, 'Old Harrison' (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of Ben's wives had achieved a son by a former husband, and this stepson had acquired a wife — a husky, corn-fed wench, an Amazon in strength and fierceness. Soon after her marriage old Ben, a rough-talking, brutal fellow who tyrannized over the women of his entourage, undertook to discipline this step-daughter-in-law with physical chastisement; cutting a hickory, he proceeded to manhandle her as he had been accustomed to use his wives. She accepted two or three blows, and then turned upon him so swiftly that he was swept off his feet and mauled almost into unconsciousness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Old Harrison', middle (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: After he had been patched up and rehabilitated, and the first bitterness of defeat had worn off, he really liked to tell the story, laying the unction to his soul that only his Christian spirit had stayed his hand and saved the life of the virago: 'General, let me tell you the truth — God was with me that day. All my life I have been a strong man; no man ever outdid me at work or at fighting, and I have been used to lick women and things all my life... So I cut one stick and I grabbed her by the sleeve and began to lick her. General, the woman turned on me and boxed me like him dull man. Blood was in my eye!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Old Harrison', ending (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: I remember the time when I could-uh box her and kick her a little two-one-time, and if I ever had let the foot follow the hand, I would-uh killed her dead. But God held my hand and my foot both; God told me to be peaceable and spare the woman's life. I don't want no woman's life upon my hand. Do you not know, sir, if I had kicked that woman she would-uh dead? God took care of old Ben that day. That woman thinks she licked me, General — but do you not know she ought to thank God for sparing her? If I had not had religion, that woman's corpse would have gone to Jacksonboro in one ox-cart! When I look upon the dead woman in my mind, I thank God every day for holding my hand!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Old Harrison', ending (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come: Minzacter's Divorce
title.zh: 等候新郎到來：明扎克特的離婚案

region.en: Lower Carolina, South Carolina, USA
region.zh: 美國南卡羅來納下游地區

period: Post-emancipation Gullah life; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Ambrose E. Gonzales, 'The Black Border' (1922), tale 'Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come' (Minzacter Singleton's crop, crow, and courtroom)

summary.en: Plowing his one-third of the corn, Minzacter Singleton addresses the circling crow as the tithe-taking friar of the field — 'take care buzzut don't dance at your funeral this same berry fall!' — and meets at the row's end the constable and a brown woman who has come with a marriage certificate and the Goose Creek pastor to haul him to the Trial Justice. His answers to the court — 'I nebbuh see you sence I bawn' — carry the tale to its comic verdict, the crow of the field presiding over the whole church-wedding muddle.
summary.zh: 明扎克特犁著自己那三分之一的玉米田，把盤旋的烏鴉斥為田間什一稅的托缽僧——『當心今秋烏鴉不敢在你的葬禮上起舞！』——壟頭卻站著警吏與一位持結婚證書、偕牧師而來的棕衣婦人，要拖他去見初審法官。他一句『我打娘胎起就沒見過你』的庭答，把這樁教堂婚事鬧成滑稽的判決；田裡的烏鴉，正是這場混亂的見證者。

sensitivity.note: Gullah comic anecdote-frame tale. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: On a hot June day a year or two ago, a tall, pumpkin-colored negro was leisurely plowing an unambitious mule in a cornfield in Lower Carolina. Minzacter Singleton was his euphonious name, and he was about fifty-five years of age. As he passed up and down the furrows he whistled cheerily, for the brown earth that curled away in long waves from his plowshare was mellow and rich, and the bourgeoning corn around him — a grand industrial army uniformed in blue-green, epauletted with crimson silk and plumed with cream-white tassels — was full of promise for the autumn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come' (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: High up in the blue, a crow flew slowly over the field, twisting his head from side to side while he critically inspected the work in progress; and, finding that it was good, croaked out an occasional 'ckwarrow, ckwarrow.' As the friar of the middle ages — the prototype of this black-robed fellow — unctuously took from the fields of his flock a tithe of the garnered store, so, when the blades should be stripped away and September suns harden the grain, would this 'sukkus preechuh' claim the reward of his interest in and inspection of the growing crop. As the ominous shadow passed between him and the sun, Minzacter, looking up, said: 'Never mind, brother! Take care buzzut doesn't dance at your funeral this same berry fall! You are smart enough to know when a man has a gun in his hand, but your education cannot specify when the shelled corn has pizen in it. You fly high in the elements today — take care you don't flew low before Christmas come!'
