passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come', middle (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Upon reaching the end of his row, Minzacter found awaiting him the burly black constable of a neighboring Trial Justice, accompanied by a middle-aged brown woman: 'Mister Singleton, I thought you was a gentleman, but I come to find out you cannot specify as a gentleman, because you run away and left me over to Goose Creek, and gone and married Paul Jenkins's gramma just because she got four cow and I have not got no cow. You run away and left your lawfully lady, and I come to take you to the Trial Justice to throw you in Walterboro jail.' With apparent nonchalance Minzacter said: 'Go away, gal!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come', ending (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Who you call husbun'? I never see you since I was bawn. I has got no time for holding composition with every which-and-why woman that comes along the road. This corn has got to lay by.' Julia Singleton, the ecru claimant, left him with the threat that she would go home and fetch the marriage stipulation to prove that Minzacter was her lawful husband — and sure enough, on the day set for the preliminary examination, she appeared with not only the marriage certificate, but accompanied by her brother and the Rev. Sancho Middleton, the Goose Creek locus-pastor, who was alleged to have performed the ceremony.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come', ending (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lion Killer: Fat Negroes and Escaped Lions
title.zh: 獅殺手：胖黑奴與逃獅

region.en: Pon Pon district, South Carolina, USA
region.zh: 美國南卡羅來納蓬蓬區

period: Post-emancipation Gullah tale; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Ambrose E. Gonzales, 'The Black Border' (1922), tale 'The Lion Killer' (Joe's account of the escaped lion on the Cumbee)

summary.en: When the lion escaped from Orangeburg, he ran spang to the Sawlketchuh swamp and never stopped till he got to Lewisburg — for Massa's negroes are fat, fat as a soul, and the lion can smell a fat negro farther than a lean one. Locked in their houses all night with fires built so he cannot come down the chimney, the terrified people pray and bargain with the Lord — one promises never to steal Massa's rice again if He only takes the lion's jaw off him, every one confessing some light sin they are willing to throw away if their lives are spared — while the heavy sins they hold like a sheep holds a mule's tail till Gabriel blows his horn.
summary.zh: 獅子從奧蘭治堡逃出，直奔索爾凱丘沼澤，一路不停直到劉易斯堡——因為主人家的黑奴胖得很，獅子嗅胖奴比嗅瘦奴遠得多。眾人整夜閉戶、生火防它從煙囪下來，嚇得紛紛禱告交易——一個許諾只要上帝把獅口挪開便永不偷主人家的米，人人供認些『輕罪』願意拋卻換命——而『重罪』嘛，且像羊叼驢尾般握著，直等到加百列吹號、上帝親手取走。

sensitivity.note: Gullah humorous horror-tale from Gonzales's collection. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase; the period term 'fat negroes' is the teller's own framing, noted as such.

passages.text: When the lion got away out of the circus, he went spang from Orangeburg to the Sawlketchuh swamp and never stopped till he got to Lewisburg. Why should he stop at Lewisburg? Do you not know, sir, that Massa's negroes are fat — fat as a soul! The lion has sense enough to know a fat negro when he sees him, and he can smell a fat negro farther than he can smell a lean one — and Massa makes his negroes fat on heavier crops of rice and lettuce and things than all the other negroes on the Cumbee river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, The Black Border, 'The Lion Killer' (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as the lion got to Lewisburg he stopped, knowing his dinner was there, and his mouth began to run water. By and by in the nighttime his voice rolled in Massa's pineland, and all the negroes were terrified like a chicken terrified when the hawk's wing throws its shadow over them! They were afraid till they were foolish; they locked themselves in their houses all night, and, although it was the dead summertime, they made fires to burn so the lion could not come down the chimney.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'The Lion Killer', middle (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the lion could get no negroes to eat because they were all locked up, he went into the wood and met a cow and killed her for his dinner; and after he had eaten the three cows — 'Three cows! How can he eat three cows when he only killed one?' — 'He can eat them, sir; I don't know if he ate them dead. You ever see a lion? What does a Pon Pon negro know about a lion?' — he went back to the negro-house yard to see if he could get a chance to eat a negro. He walked up and down, thrashed his tail, gnashed his teeth, and hollered like a jackass and an alligator and a bull all at one time!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'The Lion Killer', ending (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: You could hear the negroes in their houses praying: every one of them promised Jesus to follow His word if He only spared their lives — one told Him that if He took the lion's jaw off him, he would never steal Massa's rice again — and every one told the Lord about some of those light sins which they were willing to throw away if their lives were spared. Light sins! Why did they not promise to throw away their heavy sins? 'No, man; they are not going to throw away their heavy sins — I don't know if the lion would crack their bones. In slavery time a negro begged his massa's pardon for stealing his fowl when he got caught, but when he killed a cow he never cracked his teeth... No, man; you hold your heavy sin like a sheep holds a mule's tail, till Gabriel blow his horn and the Lord take it off!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'The Lion Killer', ending (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: Shangó, Santa Bárbara: the Thunder God in Cuba
title.zh: 香戈與聖巴巴拉：古巴的雷神

region.en: Havana, Cuba
region.zh: 古巴哈瓦那

period: Cuban Lucumí religion; recorded c. 1902-1906; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Fernando Ortiz, 'Hampa afro-cubana: Los negros brujos' (1906), ch. on the orishas — 'Shangó equivale a Santa Bárbara' (brujo Bocó de Fendishe's courtroom defense)

summary.en: In Cuba as in Brazil, the assimilation of the orishas to the Catholic saints proceeds by function: Shangó, thunder-lord and famous warrior-king, is Santa Bárbara, patroness of thunder and lightning — 'Shangó is Santa Bárbara male', say the Cuban brujos, as the Brazilian ones do, making light of the difference of sex; perhaps the sword in the saint's hand helped. In both hemispheres Shangó is symbolized by a meteoric stone — the 'piedras del rayo' — and his idol is dressed in white linen with red stripes. Tried before the tribunal, the brujo Bocó de Fendishe defended himself skillfully: the altar in his house was dedicated to a Catholic divinity, Santa Bárbara — therefore he was not a brujo.
summary.zh: 在古巴與巴西，神祇與聖徒的同化依職能而行：香戈——雷電之主、昔日的戰國之王——即雷電主保聖女巴巴拉。古巴的巫者說『香戈是男身的巴巴拉』，巴西亦然，性別之異被一笑置之；聖女畫像中的佩劍或許也助了一臂。兩個半球上，香戈皆以隕石為象——巫者稱之『雷石』——其神偶身披紅條白麻。受審之時，巫者博科·德·芬迪舍機辯如流：家中祭壇奉的是天主教神巴巴拉，故而非巫。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era criminological source (Ortiz, 1906) using period criminalizing language ('brujos', 'fetichistas'); the syncretism itself is living Lucumí practice. Recorded here as archival description of syncretic equivalence, not as religious instruction; cross-ref: yoruba tradition records of Shango.

passages.text: In Cuba, as in Brazil — which demonstrates the logic with which the negroes assimilated their orishas to the Catholic saints — Shangó equals Santa Bárbara: both divinities are patronesses of thunder and lightning. At this point the religious identity of Catholics and African fetishists is absolute, and the latter recognized it without hesitation in one hemisphere and the other. Before the equality of the functions of Shangó and Santa Bárbara they made light of the difference of sex: 'Shangó is Santa Bárbara male,' say the brujos of Cuba, as those of Brazil do. Perhaps the circumstance that Santa Bárbara is frequently represented with a sword in her hand contributed to this — which may have seemed to the African fetishists another analogy with Shangó, who was on earth a famous king and warrior.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz, Hampa afro-cubana: Los negros brujos (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The brujo Bocó de Fendishe defended himself skillfully before the tribunal that condemned him, saying that the altar he had in his house was dedicated to a Catholic divinity, Santa Bárbara, and that, therefore, he was not a brujo. In Cuba and in Brazil Shangó is symbolized by a meteoric stone; the Afro-Cuban brujos commonly call them piedras del rayo — stones of the lightning. The idol of Shangó is a wooden figure dressed in white linen with red stripes — the colors of this orisha — and adorned with necklaces of beads of the same colors; the kind of mural crown it wears seems to be copied from that which Catholics attribute to Santa Bárbara in her images.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Ifá in Cuba: Sixteen Palm-Fruits of Divination
title.zh: 古巴的伊法：十六顆棕櫚果問未來

region.en: Havana, Cuba
region.zh: 古巴哈瓦那

period: Cuban Lucumí religion; recorded c. 1902-1906; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Fernando Ortiz, 'Los negros brujos' (1906), ch. on the orishas — Ifá, Odú, Opelú and the diviner's chain

summary.en: The last of the three great orishas is Ifá, the revealer of the hidden and patron of the relations of the sexes and of death — called also Bangó, god of the fruits of a certain palm, because sixteen of these fruits are employed to obtain the prognostics. In Bahía a kind of collar is used to deduce the auguries, and in Cuba too, where some call it, in Ortiz's judgment erroneously, Ifá of Osunda. Ifá has a companion: Odú, and a messenger: Opelú — and the oracle of the chain of palm-nuts answers questions the saints of the calendar could not, for the negroes found no professional saint among the Catholic list who could satisfy their desire to know the future.
summary.zh: 三大奧利沙之末是伊法——揭示隱秘之主、男女之事與死亡的護佑神——亦稱邦戈，某種棕櫚之果的神：因問卜需用十六顆此果。巴伊亞以一串念珠推算吉凶，古巴亦然（有人誤稱『奧松達的伊法』）。伊法有伴神奧杜、信使奧佩魯——棕櫚果鏈的神諭能回答聖曆中聖徒所不能者：因天主教諸聖之中，無一能滿足黑人求知未來的心願。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era description of Ifá divination material culture (16-palm-fruit chain); the deeper Odú corpus is living initiatory knowledge and is NOT reproduced. Cross-ref: yoruba Ifá records.

passages.text: The last of the three great orishas is called Ifá, who is the revealer of the hidden and the patron of the relations of the sexes and of death. He is also called Bangó — god of the fruits of a certain palm — because sixteen of these fruits are employed to obtain the prognostics. In Bahía a species of collar is used to deduce the auguries, and likewise in Cuba, where it is called, in Ortiz's judgment erroneously, by some Ifá of Osunda.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ifá has a companion: Odú, and a messenger: Opelú. Nina Rodrigues does not cite the Catholic saint assimilated to Ifá, and Ortiz could not discover it: probably the negroes did not find among the list of professional saints one that could satisfy their desires to know the future and the other hidden things — and so the oracle of the palm-fruit chain remained, in the diaspora as at home, the mouth of what is hidden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906), citing Nina Rodrigues; not verbatim.

title.en: Yemayá, Virgin of Regla: Goddess of the Springs and the Bay
title.zh: 葉瑪雅與雷格拉聖母：泉與港灣女神

region.en: Havana, Cuba (Regla, across the bay)
region.zh: 古巴哈瓦那（海灣對岸的雷格拉）

period: Cuban Lucumí religion; recorded c. 1902-1906; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Fernando Ortiz, 'Los negros brujos' (1906), ch. on the inferior orishas — Yemanyá and Virgen de Regla

summary.en: Among the inferior orishas, Yemanyá or Yemayá, born of Obatalá, is adored as goddess of the streams and the springs, and her fetich is a stone taken from them. In Brazil she is assimilated to Nossa Senhora das Candelárias; in Cuba, to the Virgen de Regla — surely, Ortiz reasons, because that Virgin is the patroness of sailors and is represented over the sea, that is, over the waters of the bay of Havana, on whose edge her sanctuary is raised.
summary.zh: 次級奧利沙中，葉瑪雅——奧巴塔拉所生——被尊為溪流與泉源女神，其法物是一枚取自泉石。巴西將她同化於燭台聖母；古巴則同化於雷格拉聖母——奧蒂斯推斷：蓋因聖母乃水手之主保，畫像立於海上——即哈瓦那灣的水面上，聖堂便築在灣畔。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era source (1906); syncretic equivalence recorded as archival fact. Cross-ref: yoruba Yemoja records.

passages.text: The inferior orishas are numerous. Inferior is Yemanyá or Yemayá, although born of Obatalá; she is adored as goddess of the streams and the springs, and her fetich is a stone proceeding from them. In Brazil she is assimilated to Nossa Senhora das Candelárias; in Cuba, to the Virgen de Regla — surely because this Virgin is the patroness of the sailors and is represented over the sea, that is to say, over the waters of the bay of Havana, on whose edge the sanctuary is raised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906), citing Nina Rodrigues; not verbatim.

title.en: Oshósi, San Jorge: the Archer Who Freezes the Majá
title.zh: 奧索西與聖喬治：定住巨蛇的獵手

region.en: Havana and Bahía (diaspora), symbolic pin Havana
region.zh: 哈瓦那與巴伊亞（僑居地），象徵定位哈瓦那

period: Cuban Lucumí religion; recorded c. 1902-1906; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Fernando Ortiz, 'Los negros brujos' (1906), ch. on the inferior orishas — Oshó-oshi, the majá, and San Jorge/San Huberto

summary.en: Oshó-oshi, born of Yemayá, is the god of hunters and walkers, symbolized by a human figure armed with a bow, or by the drawn bow holding an arrow — the weapon of his hunting expeditions. An anonymous chronicler records his invocation: when the brujos see a majá — the great Cuban boa — they cry three times 'Osó, osó, osó!' and the animal stands immobile; and they believe that when the serpent is a hundred years old (then they call it Yayá) it casts itself into the sea and becomes a new being that suffers much, cursing at its transformation whoever found it and did not kill it — a malediction greatly feared. In Bahía the hunters' god is Catholicized as San Jorge, mounted and lancing a dragon the negroes took for a snake; in Cuba he is San Alberto — perhaps they meant San Huberto.
summary.zh: 葉瑪雅所生的奧索西是獵人與行旅之神，象徵為持弓人像或引滿之弓——那是他狩獵遠征的武器。佚名記事者錄下其呼法：巫者見巨蛇『馬哈』，三呼『奧索！奧索！奧索！』，蛇便僵立不動；又傳百歲之蛇（彼時稱『亞亞』）投身入海化為受苦的新生，變形時必咒那遇之而不殺的人——此咒極受畏懼。巴伊亞獵神化為聖喬治——騎馬挺矛刺龍；古巴則稱聖阿爾韋托——或本是聖胡貝托。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era source; the Yayá-transformation legend recorded as folk narrative. Cross-ref: yoruba Oshosi records.

passages.text: Oshó-oshi, born of Yemanyá according to A. B. Ellis, is the god of the hunters and the walkers; he is symbolized by a human figure armed with a bow, and sometimes by the drawn bow holding an arrow — that is to say, by the weapon with which the god served himself in his hunting expeditions. Without doubt the bow and arrow to be seen in the frontispiece of the altar photographed by Ortiz is an invocation to Oshó-oshi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: An anonymous chronicler records the invocation: 'When the brujos see a majá, so that it may not do them harm they cry three times these words: Osó, osó, osó! and the animal remains immobile.' They believe that when the animal has completed a century of age — then they call it Yayá — it casts itself into the sea, transforming into a serpent (?) and in that new life suffering much, which is why every time a majá presents itself they try to kill it; for at the moment of its transformation it curses the one who found it and did not kill it — and this malediction is greatly feared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906), quoting an anonymous chronicler; not verbatim.

passages.text: In Bahía Oshó-oshi is Catholicized under the name of San Jorge, because that saint, in his images, is mounted on horseback and lancing a dragon which — the negroes, not knowing infernal monsters, must have thought — was hunting a snake, which must be the orisha Oshó-oshi. In Cuba they call him San Alberto, for what reason is unknown (perhaps they mean San Huberto, little pronounced in Cuba).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Ogún and Eshú: He Who Opens the Road
title.zh: 奧貢與埃舒：開路者

region.en: Havana and Bahía (diaspora), symbolic pin Havana
region.zh: 哈瓦那與巴伊亞（僑居地），象徵定位哈瓦那

period: Cuban and Bahian Yoruba-diaspora religion; recorded c. 1902-1906; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Fernando Ortiz, 'Los negros brujos' (1906), ch. on the inferior orishas — Ogún, Eshú and the iron fetiches

summary.en: Ogún, emanated also of Yemayá, brother of Shangó and Mars of the Yorubas, is worshipped in Cuba — sometimes confused with Eshú and with Oshúsi under the name Osunda. A negro told Nina Rodrigues, in a figure of speech, that 'Ogún is the one who opens the road for Eshú' — showing that Ogún and Eshú are two orishas, not one: Ogún benign though warlike, Eshú the malign one. Both are represented by iron fetiches, which facilitates the confusion that exists in Cuba too — and the Afro-Bahianos Catholicize Ogún under the name of San Antonio.
summary.zh: 奧貢——同出葉瑪雅、香戈之弟、約魯巴人的戰神——在古巴受供奉，時與埃舒及奧蘇西混同為『奧松達』。一位黑人對尼納·羅德里格斯打比方說：『奧貢是為埃舒開路的』——足見二者是兩位神：奧貢雜好戰而性善，埃舒則為惡神。二者皆以鐵質法物為象，故混淆亦生於古巴；巴伊亞的黑人則把奧貢化為聖安東尼。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era source (1906). The road-opening formula is recorded as speech, not ritual. Cross-ref: afroatlantic ogun character; yoruba Ogun records.

passages.text: Ogún, emanated also of Yemanyá according to A. B. Ellis, brother of Shangó as Bowen says, and Mars of the Yorubas, is worshipped in Cuba, confused at times with Eshú and with Oshúsi, being called also Osunda. The circumstance that Ogún is god of war and of struggle facilitates the confusion with Eshú, the malign divinity; his non-distinction from Oshúsi arises besides, without doubt, from the phonetic likeness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: A negro said to Nina Rodrigues, in a figure of speech, that 'Ogún is the one who opens the road for Eshú' — which also demonstrates that the orishas Ogún and Eshú are two. Moreover Ogún is represented by fetiches of iron, just as Eshú is, which facilitates the confusion, which in Cuba seems also to exist. The Afro-Bahianos Catholicize Ogún, adoring him under the name of San Antonio.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906), citing Nina Rodrigues; not verbatim.

title.en: The Skull Altar of Remedios: the 1904 Police Raid
title.zh: 雷梅迪奧斯頭骨祭壇：一九〇四年警查

region.en: Remedios, Villa Clara, Cuba
region.zh: 古比亞克拉拉省雷梅迪奧斯

period: Colonial-era police report of a conjure-society ceremony, 1904; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Fernando Ortiz, 'Los negros brujos' (1906), ch. of 'Noticias' — the Remedios Buenavista cemetery profanation and the raid on the house of M. C. (police commissioner's letter, 1904)

summary.en: The 1904 case that made Ortiz's book: the grave of a woman two days dead was found in the Buenavista cemetery with the head separated from the trunk; the peaceful town at once supposed the work of brujos. Months later, confidences revealed a meeting of reputed conjurers at the house of a pardo called M. C., 'president of a society of negro brujos'; the police commissioner waited half an hour for the drum that announced the ceremony, then assaulted the house, revolver in hand. On the altar, lit with candles, a cranium; around it jaws of others, spurs of birds, horns of animals, rosaries of human teeth, and a great wooden doll — 'the Messiah', the prisoners said, indicating the name of the person to be profaned to serve as idol for their beliefs.
summary.zh: 一九〇四年舉國轟動一案：布埃納維斯塔墓園中，一位死去兩日的婦人之墳被掘、頭顱與屍身分離；小鎮居民立疑為巫者所為。數月後線人揭出：蓬頭混血者M.C.家中有『黑巫者會』會議，警長候鼓聲半小時、持槍破門。燭光祭壇之上是一具頭骨，環列下顎、鳥距、獸角、人齒串珠，還有一具大木偶——被捕者稱之『彌賽亞』，指明下一位要被褻瀆為神像的亡者之名。

sensitivity.note: Archival police narrative (1904), preserved here as historical record of colonial criminalization of Afro-Cuban religion; the account is the state's framing of an alleged Palo/Nkisi ceremony, not the practitioners' self-understanding. Names redacted as in source; no ritual instruction reproduced.

passages.text: In the Buenavista cemetery, a rural barrio of Remedios, the sepulture of a lady deceased two days before had been violated and her cadaver profaned; the profanation consisted in separating the head from the trunk of the cadaver, and it impressed the peaceful inhabitants of the territory greatly — from the first moment it was supposed to be the work of brujos, of the many that unfortunately exist in the country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz, 'Noticias' ch. (1906), from the police commissioner's letter; not verbatim.

passages.text: Active efforts to discover the authors obtained nothing for some months; then, by confidences obtained, it became known that on the 23rd of September certain individuals stigmatized as brujos had met to hold a session in the house of a pardo named M. C., a subject regarded as president of a society of negro brujos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The commissioner waited half an hour more, and when he felt the tap of the drum announcing that the ceremony had begun, he assaulted the house with two guards, revolver in hand, surprising the negroes, who tried to flee and were immediately arrested — and there presented itself a repugnant spectacle. In the place of honor of an altar illuminated with candles there was seen a cranium, and around it, jaws of others, spurs of birds, horns of animals, rosaries of human teeth, and a great wooden doll which, according to the declaration of the detained, was the 'Messiah' that indicated the name of the person who was to be profaned to serve as idol for their beliefs. The ceremony consisted in this: the one who acted as president, dressed in a strange costume and a high cap, gave leaps and savage cries before the altar, and the rest of his companions, arranged in chorus, with lowered heads and arms thrown backward, in an attitude of praying. Occupied with the objects, the commissioner conducted the detained, all of the black race, to the city, putting them at the disposition of the court, which condemned them to six months of prison.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ortiz (1906), from the police commissioner's letter; not verbatim.

title.en: Yemanjá's Bursting Womb: the Birth of the Orishas in Brazil
title.zh: 葉瑪雅裂腹誕神：巴西的奧利沙譜系

region.en: Bahía, Brazil
region.zh: 巴西巴伊亞

period: Afro-Brazilian Nagô mythology; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (published 1905/1906), ch. on the Nagô religion — the Yemanjá genealogy of the orishas

summary.en: From the marriage of Obatalá the Sky with Odudua the Earth were born Aganjú, the firm land, and Yemanjá, the waters. Yemanjá married her brother and bore Orungan, the Air, the heights, the space between earth and heaven; he conceived incestuous love for his mother, seized her while the father was away, and violated her. Mad with horror, Yemanjá wrenched herself from her son's arms and fled; he pursued her, and just as his hand was about to fall she died — and her body grew monstrously, and from her monstrous breasts two rivers gushed forth that met and made a lagoon; and from her enormous belly that burst came Dadá, Shangó, Ogún, Olokun, Olochá, Ogé, Ochun, Obá, Okó, Ochosi, Ajé-Chaluga, Chankpanná, the Sun, and the Moon.
summary.zh: 天父奧巴塔拉與地母奧杜杜瓦結合，生下堅土阿甘茹與眾水葉瑪雅。葉瑪雅嫁兄而生奧倫甘——空氣、高天、天地之間的空間。奧倫甘對生母生出亂倫之愛，趁父親外出擄母行惡；葉瑪雅瘋狂掙脫狂逃，追者將及，她倒地而死——屍身暴長，雙乳湧出二河匯成湖；巨腹迸裂之處，誕下植物之神達達、雷神香戈、鐵神奧貢、海神奧洛昆、湖神奧洛夏、尼日河神、奧順河神、歐巴河神、農神、獵神、醫神、天花神、太陽與月亮——十五位神祇。

sensitivity.note: Nina Rodrigues records the Yemanjá genealogy as told by Bahian Nagô heads — he notes it was relatively recent and contested by some Candomblé elders (Ifá and Elegbá have no place in it). Presented as a recorded variant of the diaspora pantheon-genealogy. Cross-ref: yoruba creation records.

passages.text: From the consortium of Obatalá, the Sky, with Odudua, the Earth, were born two children: Aganjú, the firm land, and Yemanjá, the waters. Marrying her brother Aganjú, Yemanjá gave birth to Orungan — the Air, the heights, the space between the earth and the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues, Os Africanos no Brasil (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Orungan conceived an incestuous love for his mother, and taking advantage of the father's absence, seized her and violated her. Afflicted and delivered to violent despair, Yemanjá wrenched herself from the arms of her son, fled hallucinating, despising the infamous proposals for the continuation of the criminal love in secret. Orungan pursued her; but, close to laying hands on her, Yemanjá fell dead. Her body grows monstrously, and from her breasts, monstrous, two rivers are born which later unite, constituting a lagoon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the enormous belly that bursts are born: Dadá, goddess-or orishá of the vegetables; Shangó, god of thunder; Ogún, god of iron and war; Olokun, god of the sea; Olochá, goddess of the lakes; Ogé, goddess of the river Niger; Ochun, goddess of the river Ochun; Obá, goddess of the river Obá; Okó, orishá of agriculture; Ochosi, god of the hunters; Oké, god of the mountains; Ajé-Chaluga, god of health; Chankpanná, god of smallpox; Orun, the sun; and Ochú, the moon. It is to be believed that this legend is relatively recent and little spread among the Nagôs: our negroes who direct the Yoruba cult, even those recently in Africa, are entirely ignorant of it, and some contest it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Shangó and the Swallowed Charm
title.zh: 香戈吞符記

region.en: Bahía, Brazil (Nagô tellings)
region.zh: 巴西巴伊亞（納戈講述）

period: Afro-Brazilian Nagô mythology; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on the Nagô religion — the legend of Changó and the charm of Obatalá

summary.en: Changó, reigning in Ovó, was given by Obatalá a powerful charm which, swallowed, made him able to conquer all his enemies; he ate the greater part and gave the remainder to his wife Oyá to guard — who, in his absence, ate it too. The next day, in the council of ministers, when Changó's turn came to speak, he was transfigured, and flames came out of his mouth, dispersing the whole audience; the same happened to Oyá with her ladies. Certain now that he was an orishá, Changó stamped his foot on the ground, which opened and gave him passage with his three wives — only the end of the iron chain he carried in his hand remained outside the earth.
summary.zh: 香戈在奧沃為王，奧巴塔拉賜他一枚可勝萬敵的符咒；他吞下大半，餘者交妻歐雅保管——歐雅趁他不在也吃了。翌日朝會，輪到香戈啟口，他已形貌大變，口中噴火，滿朝盡散；歐雅與侍女亦然。香戈自知已成神，頓足於地，大地裂開，接他與三位妻子入地而去——只有他手中鐵鏈的一端留在了地面上。

sensitivity.note: Nagô legend recorded by Nina Rodrigues from Bahian tellers; variant of the Yoruba Shangó cycle. Cross-ref: yoruba Shango records.

passages.text: Changó would be, instead of being born of Yemanjá as in the preceding myth, a son of Obatalá, and began by reigning in Ovó, capital of Yoruba. One day Obatalá gave him a powerful charm which, when swallowed, made him capable of conquering all his enemies. Changó ate the greater part of the charm and gave the remainder to his wife Oyá to guard — who, in the absence of her husband, ate it too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues, Os Africanos no Brasil (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the next day, in the council of the ministers, Changó's turn came to speak, he was transfigured, and flames came out of his mouth, which dispersed the whole audience; the same happened to Oyá with her ladies. Certain that he was now an orishá, Changó beat with his foot on the ground, which opened and gave him passage with his three wives. But there remained outside the earth the extremity of an iron chain that he carried in his hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Shangó under the Earth: the End of the Iron Chain
title.zh: 地下的香戈：鐵鏈之端

region.en: Bahía, Brazil (Nagô tellings)
region.zh: 巴西巴伊亞（納戈講述）

period: Afro-Brazilian Nagô mythology; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on the Nagô religion — the variants of the death of Changó (Oyá's flight; the fisher Huisi; the hanged king and the chain)

summary.en: The variants of Changó's end chase one another: Oyá steals the charm, flees to her brother Olokun the sea, then to Olochá the lake, then hides with the fisher Huisi — who eats the stolen charm, becomes an orishá, and duels Changó with an uprooted tree against a canoe until the earth opens for the tired thunderer. In the euhemerized telling the missionaries circulate, Changó was the first king of Yoruba, deposed by the parrot-eggs and the message 'it is time to go sleep', who fled to the forests and hanged himself — and the mourners, going to find the corpse, found only a depression in the soil with the end of an iron chain: they nailed it to the ground, heard Changó speaking under the earth, built a little temple there, and knew that the king had not died but had turned orishá.
summary.zh: 香戈的結局諸版本互相追逐：歐雅竊符，先逃海兄奧洛昆、再逃湖姊奧洛夏，最後藏身漁夫懷西家中——懷西吞符成神，拔樹為兵與持舟作械的香戈決戰，力竭的雷神踏地遁走。教士們流傳的『人化神』版：香戈是約魯巴開國之王，因鸚鵡蛋之諭被廢，夜遁森林自縊；弔唁者尋屍不見，只見土窪中鐵鏈一端——釘鏈於地，聞地下有人言語，遂建小廟：王未死，已化為神。

sensitivity.note: Nagô variants recorded by Nina Rodrigues; the 'English missionary' euhemerization is attributed by the Bahian elders themselves to Protestant mission influence — preserved here as an internal debate about the god's historicity. Cross-ref: yoruba Shango records.

passages.text: A simple variant of the myth is that in which Oyá steals from her husband the remedy-charm. Terrified by the threats of Changó, Oyá went to take refuge in the palace of her brother Olokun, the sea. Accompanying unseen the sun that was setting, Changó went there; a violent fight was waged between Changó and Olokun, and in the meantime Oyá fled to the house of her sister Olochá, the lake. Changó pursued her, demolishing everything in his march, tearing up the trees by the roots and hurling them to great distances. Recognizing that her sister could not protect her, Oyá fled again and hid herself in the house of the fisher Huisi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Terrified, the fisher asked Oyá how he, a simple mortal, could fight with an orishá like Changó; Oyá made him eat of the stolen charm, and Huisi, transformed into an orishá, went out to meet Changó, brandishing a tree he had torn up by the roots — there was no other in the place. Changó brandished as weapon the canoe of Huisi and charged his adversary. The arms broke at the first encounter, and the orishás fought body to body; unable to conquer, and fearful of being conquered, Changó, who began to feel himself fatigued, beat with his foot on the ground, which opened and received him. During the fight Oyá fled to Lokoró, where the people erected a temple to her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another version, found in Bahía principally among the negroes who were under the direction of the English missionaries in Lagos, gives to Changó an entirely euhemeristic origin — which our negroes generally attribute to the protestant missionaries, interested in robbing Changó of his qualities of orishá. Changó had been the first king of Yoruba. Tyrant and cruel, the people did not wish to suffer him any more, and, according to the custom of the country, sent him the bowl with the eggs of the parrot and the traditional message: 'that he must already be too much fatigued with the labors of government, and it was time to go and sleep' — which meant the king's retiring to his apartments and letting himself be strangled by his wives. But Changó did not conform to the intimación and resisted; he was defeated and sought to flee to Tapa, the land of his mother. He abandoned the palace at night, followed only by a slave and one of his women, and entered the forests; the woman abandoned him too. Lost in the forest he wandered for days without eating; at last he ordered the slave to await him in a given place until he returned — and the slave, tired of waiting, went to look for him and found him a few steps off, hanged on a tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: By chance the slave could discover the way and carried the news to Oyá. Fearful of being held responsible for the death of Changó, the magnates went at once to seek the cadaver — but they no longer found it. Near the tree there was a depression in the soil from which came the extremity of an iron chain. They nailed the end to the ground and heard Changó speaking under the earth. Thus they convinced themselves that Changó had not died, but had transformed himself into an orishá; there they constructed a small temple, and around it, more...
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Odudua and the Hunter of Ado
title.zh: 奧杜杜瓦與阿多獵人

region.en: Bahía, Brazil (Nagô tellings of the Ado legend)
region.zh: 巴西巴伊亞（納戈講述的阿多傳說）

period: Afro-Brazilian Nagô mythology; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on the Nagô religion — Odudua and the great temple of Ado

summary.en: Thus must be understood some legends that celebrate the amorous adventures of Odudua, who from that time forward is Venus: the great temple of Odudua in Adó, fifteen miles north of Badagry, had this origin. In one of her hunting excursions through the forests, Odudua met one day a young hunter of such rare beauty that there instantly sprang up a violent passion in the ardent temperament of the orishá. They abandoned themselves easily in the same place to the satisfaction of that passion, and for some weeks enjoyed their delights in a hut the two had built. Sated at last, Odudua departed — but in grateful memory of that love so intense and so fleeting, she promised to constitute herself protectress of the mortals who should come to the place; and thither flowed at once all who sought divine protection there, and from the case the city took the name of Adó, which means lascivious man or woman.
summary.zh: 自此被視作維納斯的奧杜杜瓦，其情史傳說正解釋了阿多大廟之由來。一日林中狩獵，女神遇見俊美無雙的年輕獵人，熱烈的神性頓起狂愛；二人於原地搭棚相守數週。盡興之後奧杜杜瓦離去——然為記那濃烈卻短暫之愛，她允諾庇佑凡來此地之人；求神庇護者雲集，城因之得名『阿多』——意即放浪的男人或女人。

sensitivity.note: Nagô legend recorded by Nina Rodrigues (following Ellis's Yoruba material) from Bahian tradition. Cross-ref: yoruba Oduduwa records.

passages.text: Thus must be understood some legends in which are celebrated the amorous adventures of Odudua — for from here forward Odudua will be Venus. The great temple of Odudua in Adó, fifteen miles north of Badagry, had this origin. In one of her hunting excursions through the forests, Odudua met one day a young hunter of such rare beauty that there instantly sprang up a violent passion in the ardent temperament of the orishá. They abandoned themselves easily in the same place to the satisfaction of that passion of the moment, and for some weeks enjoyed their delights in a hut which the two had built.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues, Os Africanos no Brasil (1906); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sated at last, Odudua departed; but in grateful memory of that love so intense and so fleeting, she promised to constitute herself protectress of the mortals who should go there. There flowed at once all who sought in the place the divine protection, and from the case the city took the name of Adó, which means lascivious man or woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906), citing Ellis; not verbatim.

title.en: The Washing of the Bonfim: Senhor do Bonfim Is Obatalá
title.zh: 邦芬洗堂禮：邦芬主即奧巴塔拉

region.en: Bahía, Brazil (Igreja do Bonfim)
region.zh: 巴西巴伊亞邦芬教堂

period: Afro-Bahian religious practice; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on survivals — the washing of the church of the Bomfim

summary.en: A Yoruba or Nagô religious practice still alive in Brazil: the washing of the church of the Bomfim is, for the Africans, creole and mixed-blood followers of the sect, a living cult — for Senhor do Bomfim, the Lord of the Good End, is Obatalá himself. Nina Rodrigues sets it against the carnival clubs of Rio — survivals by tradition rather than belief — and against the Afro-Bahian carnival clubs in which both currents flow at once: the Embaixada Africana celebrating a remembered Africa of kings and courts, the Pandegos da Africa parading the enthralled Africa itself down the city streets.
summary.zh: 一項在巴西仍鮮活的約魯巴宗教實踐：邦芬洗堂禮——對非洲裔、克里奧爾與混血的教眾而言，這是活的祭拜，因為『善終之主』邦芬主，正是奧巴塔拉本人。羅德里格斯將它與里約的狂歡節會（僅存於傳統記憶）相對照，又與巴伊亞的非裔狂歡會並列——那裡兩種血脈同時奔流：非洲大使會追憶國王與宮廷，『非洲樂事會』則把被奴役的非洲本身抬上街頭。

sensitivity.note: Description of a living syncretic feast (Lavagem do Bonfim) from Nina Rodrigues's typology of survivals; cross-ref: yoruba Obatala records.

passages.text: The distinction Nina Rodrigues establishes is between manifestations of a belief, a practice, a custom or feast African, still alive among us, and the tradition or recollection of sentiments that only existed in activity among our seniors. The washing of the church of the Bomfim is, as he demonstrated, a Yoruba or Nagô religious practice — but it is a truly living cult, for, for the Africans, creole negroes and mixed-bloods of that sect, the Senhor do Bomfim is Obatalá himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues, Os Africanos no Brasil (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the contrary, the carnival clubs of the Cucumby, of Rio de Janeiro, described by Dr. Mello Moraes, are popular feasts that have passed entirely to the state of tradition: the choice and the preference of the theme still betray the Black Race, but other races can associate themselves with those feasts, seeing in it only the element of characterization which is the essence of Carnival.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: There are finally intermediate or transitional cases, in which the African usage participates at the same time in tradition and in an institution still alive among us — the case of the African carnival clubs of Bahia, where of late the Bahian carnival is reduced almost to African clubs organized by some Africans, creole negroes and mixed-bloods. In the constitution of these clubs the two distinct sentiments reveal themselves: in some, like the Embaixada Africana, the dominant idea of the most intelligent or better-adapted negroes is the celebration of a survival, of a tradition — the characters and the motif taken from the cultivated peoples of Africa, Egyptians, Abyssinians. In the others there is, on the part of the directors, sometimes the intention of reviving traditions; but their popular success consists in their being true African popular feasts: the theme is uncultivated Africa that came enslaved to Brazil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pandegos da Africa: King Labossi in His Shell
title.zh: 非洲樂事會：貝殼中的拉博西王

region.en: Bahía, Brazil (carnival streets)
region.zh: 巴西巴伊亞狂歡節街頭

period: Afro-Bahian carnival; recorded 1899; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on survivals — the Pandegos da Africa and the char of the Zambeze (Diario da Bahia, 16 Feb. 1899)

summary.en: The carnival car of the Pandegos da Africa 'represents the margin of the Zambeze, on whose bank, reclining in an immense shell, rests King Labossi, surrounded by his ministers Aua, Oman, Abato, the last bearing the standard of the club'; behind came a car with two members representing powerful personages of the king's court — Barborim, Roda; three cavaliers preceded the African charanga that came on foot, with their strident and impossible instruments. Then a car representing the hut of Pai Agen and his woman with the fetish-calabash, giving good luck to everything and everybody. A compact multitude of negroes and mixed-bloods, incorporated into it and accompanying it, singing the African songs, beating out their dances, hailing their idols or saints shown in the car of the fetish — one would say a colossal candomblé parading through the streets of the city; and in fact the felichist negroes thus avenged themselves of the intermittent impertinences of the police, exhibiting their feast in public.
summary.zh: 『非洲樂事會』的花車『再現贊比西河畔：拉博西王斜倚巨貝，由大臣阿瓦、奧曼、阿巴托環侍，末者高舉會旗』；後隨宮廷權貴之車，三位騎士先行，非洲樂班徒步相隨，奏著刺耳難名之樂；最後一車再現巫師阿真夫婦的茅屋與法力葫蘆——為萬物萬人賜福。黑奴與混血人群密匝匝地加入隊伍，唱非洲之歌、踏非洲之舞、向車中神偶歡呼——簡直是一場穿行街市的巨型康東布莱；巫俗信眾藉此向警察的刁難報復，把節慶公然抬上街頭。

sensitivity.note: Carnival-club description from contemporary Bahian press (Diario da Bahia, 1899) compiled by Nina Rodrigues; cross-ref: afroatlantic-bomfim-washing.

passages.text: In the Pandegos da Africa, the car, one diary describes, 'represents the margin of the Zambeze, on whose bank, reclining in an immense shell, rests the king Labossi, surrounded by his ministers Aua, Oman, Abato, the last bearing the standard of the club.' Behind came 'a car with two members representing powerful and influential personages of the court of the king — Barborim, Roda.' Three cavaliers preceded the African charanga that came on foot, with their strident and impossible instruments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906), quoting a Bahian diary; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, 'a car representing the hut of pai Agen and his woman with the caboré of fetish, to give good luck to everything and to everybody.' The success of this club was enormous: there was seen a compact multitude of negroes and mixed-bloods that had, so to speak, incorporated themselves into it and accompanied it singing the African songs, beating out their dances, and hailing the idols or saints that were shown to them in the car of the fetish. One would say a colossal candomblé parading through the streets of the city — and in fact the felichist negroes avenged themselves in this way of the intermittent impertinences of the police, exhibiting their feast in public.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: And it is not a small revenge after all — for, well counted, including all the bands that announce how many feasts of the outskirts exist, more than a dozen of these opportunities are organized annually. If this testimony of an eye-witness could be charged with partiality, it would be ratified by the unanimous transcription of the local press.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Gods of the Haitian Mountains: a Nursery Lesson in Mythology
title.zh: 海地群山之神：神話啟蒙課

region.en: Croix des Bouquets hills, Haiti
region.zh: 海地花束十字山丘

period: Haitian Vodou; recorded 1927-1929; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. I-III 'The Voodoo Rites' (Louis's theology lessons under the palms)

summary.en: Under the trees Louis taught the names and attributes of the many Voodoo gods: Papa Legba, guardian of the gates, the most benevolent; Damballa Oueddo, wisest and most powerful, whose symbol was the serpent; Loco, god of the forests; Agoue, god of the sea; Maîtresse Ezilee, who was the mild Blessed Virgin Mary; Ogoun Badagris, the bloody dreadful, 'One whose voice was thunder' — dozens of them, like a nursery lesson in Greek mythology, except that to Louis these were not myths, they were more real than he or the white visitor who sat listening.
summary.zh: 樹蔭下，路易教他眾多伏都神的名號與職司：守門最仁厚的雷格巴老爹；智慧至高、以蛇為象的丹巴拉·維多；森林之神洛科；海神阿古埃；即是溫柔聖母的埃稀麗女神；以及『聲如雷霆』的嗜血可怖者奧貢·巴達格里斯——神名以十計，如一堂希臘神話啟蒙課；只是在路易眼中，這些不是神話，而是比他、比那位白人聽者更真實的存在。

sensitivity.note: Seabrook's 1929 popular-ethnography, sensational in places but based on participant observation with named informants (Louis, Maman Celie, Papa Theodore); the loa theology here is teaching-level content, not initiatory knowledge. Living religion: nothing beyond the published record reproduced.

passages.text: Louis and Seabrook began to go wandering in the hills together and sitting under trees, where he would tell of the names and attributes of the many Voodoo gods: Papa Legba, guardian of the gates, who was the most benevolent; Damballa Oueddo, wisest and most powerful, whose symbol was the serpent; Loco, god of the forests; Agoue, god of the sea; Maîtresse Ezilee, who was the mild Blessed Virgin Mary; Ogoun Badagris, the bloody dreadful One whose voice was thunder.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. I (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: There were dozens of them, it seemed. It was like a nursery lesson in Greek mythology, except that to Louis these were not myths — they were more real than he or Seabrook. No need to catalogue all their names: most of them fell naturally into the record later. Perhaps before the book was ended a table of theological Voodoo statistics might be compiled, but it would not be as congenial a task as sitting with Louis under a palm tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, ch. I (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Good Friday: Damballa Bows His Hooded Head
title.zh: 受難日：丹巴拉低垂蛇首

region.en: Croix des Bouquets hills, Haiti
region.zh: 海地花束十字山丘

period: Haitian Vodou; recorded 1927-2029 (published 2029)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. II 'The Way Is Opened and Closed' (the Good Friday burial of the altars)

summary.en: The Christian flute that once piped first-communion hymns now piped pagan melodies to Legba and the serpent gods — and its first-communion papers lay with ancient thunderstones on a Voodoo altar. But late in a Holy Week Seabrook returned to see that same altar stripped of all its sacred objects, Christian and pagan together, laid as if dead in rows upon the ground, covered with palm fronds, to remain thus buried as Lord Jesus was until the Easter resurrection morn: during Golgotha's tragedy even the great Voodoo serpent-god Damballa must bow his hooded head — and with the half million Voodoo altars in Haiti, on each succeeding anniversary, it was the same.
summary.zh: 曾奏初領聖體聖歌的笛子，如今為雷格巴與蛇神吹起異教的曲子；初領聖禮的紙片，與遠古雷石同置於伏都祭壇之上。然而聖週將盡，主人再訪時只見同一祭壇已被剝空——基督徒與異教聖物一同橫陳如死者，覆以棕櫚枝，如主耶穌般安眠，直待復活節清晨：在各各他受難之日，連偉大的伏都蛇神丹巴拉也須低垂其蛇首——海地五十萬座伏都祭壇，年年如此。

sensitivity.note: Recorded description of syncretic Holy Week practice; living religion documented from the published 1929 account.

passages.text: Ye patient, pious, and mildly tolerant priests of Croix des Bouquets — would it have caused you pangs to know that the flute you once gave Louis from the goodness of your hearts, which your own consecrated hands taught him to play, was now piping pagan melodies to Legba, serpent gods, and peacocks; to know that his pretty first-communion papers, engraved in the shadow of Saint Sulpice and brought in Christian vessels across the seas, now lay with ancient thunderstones upon a Voodoo altar?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. II (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: If so, your pious pangs would have been in part assuaged could you have seen that selfsame altar as Seabrook chanced to return and see it long afterward, late in a Holy Week: all its sacred objects, Christian and pagan together, were stripped from it on the evening of Good Friday, laid as if dead in rows before it upon the ground and covered over with palm fronds, to remain thus buried as Lord Jesus was until the Easter resurrection morn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, ch. II (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: During Golgotha's tragedy, even the great Voodoo serpent-god Damballa must bow his hooded head. And with the half million Voodoo altars in Haiti, it was and has been, so Seabrook was told, on each succeeding anniversary the same. Here are deep matters, not easily to be dismissed by crying blasphemy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, ch. II (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: The Damballa Ritual March
title.zh: 丹巴拉儀仗行進

region.en: Cul-de-Sac plain, Haiti
region.zh: 海地庫爾德薩克平原

period: Haitian Vodou; recorded 1927-1929; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. on the ceremony — the Damballa ritual march (papaloi with asson, serpent flags, mamaloi in scarlet)

summary.en: The drums began a new, less deafening rhythm — the Damballa ritual march. The celebrants approached processionally, singing, from the mystery house: at the head the papaloi, blue-overalled, bare-footed, a surplice on his shoulders and a red turban on his head, waving before him the asson, a gourd-rattle wound round with snake-vertebrae; two young women at his right and left holding aloft, crossed above his head, two flags sewn with serpentine and cabalistic symbols in glittering metallic beads; a young man bearing aloft a sword on his upstretched palms; the mamaloi in a scarlet robe and feathered headdress revolving as she progressed in a sort of dervish dance; then two by two, a chorus of twenty or more women robed in white, chanting as they marched: 'Damballa Oueddo, nous p'vinid' — 'Oh, Serpent God, we come.'
summary.zh: 鼓聲轉入一段不再震耳的節奏——丹巴拉儀仗進行曲。祭眾自神秘之屋列隊而來，且行且歌：領頭的老祭司身著藍布工裝、赤足，肩披白衣、頭纏紅巾，搖動纏繞蛇脊的葫蘆鈴；左右二女高擎繡有蛇紋符號、金屬珠片閃光的雙旗，交叉於其頭上；一少年雙手平托長劍；猩紅袍、羽冠的女祭司旋轉如旋舞；其後二十餘白衣女子兩兩成列，白布纏頭，且行且唱：『丹巴拉·維多，我們來了。』

sensitivity.note: Seabrook's footnote is kept in spirit: the ceremony as described is a new formalized ritual grown from the earliest slave-days merging of African cults, not the unchanged African rite. Published description only; living practice not reproduced beyond it.

passages.text: The drums began a new, less deafening rhythm: it was the Damballa ritual march. The celebrants approached, processionally, singing, from the mystery house. At the head came the papaloi, an old man, blue-overalled, bare-footed, but with a surplice over his shoulders and a red turban on his head, waving before him the asson, a gourd-rattle wound round with snake-vertebrae. At his right and left, keeping pace with him, two young women held aloft, crossed above his head, two flags on which were serpentine and cabalistic symbols, sewn on with metallic, glittering beads.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Behind him marched a young man bearing aloft, horizontally on his upstretched palms, a sword; and next the mamaloi, a woman in a scarlet robe and feathered headdress, who revolved as she progressed in a sort of dervish dance; next came marching, two and two, a chorus of twenty or more women robed in white, with white cloths wound bandana-wise on their heads, and as they slowly marched they chanted: 'Damballa Oueddo, nous p'vinid' — which would be best translated, 'Oh, Serpent God, we come.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seabrook's own note records what the practitioners' caution would add: although Damballa, the ancient African serpent god, remains enthroned as its central figure, this Voodoo ceremony is not the old traditional ritual brought over from Africa, but rather a gradually formalized new ritual which sprang from the merging, in earliest slave days, of the African cults with the circumstances of the new world.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929), footnote paraphrased; not verbatim.

title.en: The Zombies of Hasco: Ti Joseph's Cane Gang, 1918
title.zh: 哈斯科的還魂屍：小約瑟夫的蔗田隊

region.en: Cul-de-Sac cane fields, Haiti
region.zh: 海地庫爾德薩克蔗田

period: Haitian legend, event of 1918; recorded 1927-1929; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. 'Black Sorcery' — the Hasco story told by Constant Polynice

summary.en: In the big cane season of 1918 the Haitian-American Sugar Company offered a bonus for new workers, and one morning old headman Ti Joseph of Colombier appeared leading a band of ragged creatures who shuffled behind him staring dumbly like people walking in a daze, making no reply when asked their names. They were poor unhappy zombies, Joseph and his wife Croyance had dragged them from their peaceful graves to slave for him in the sun — and everyone knows the zombies must never be permitted to taste salt or meat, so Croyance tended two pots, theirs flat, tasteless, and unseasoned.
summary.zh: 一九一八年蔗季，海地美糖公司懸賞招工；一天清晨，科隆比耶的老工頭小約瑟夫帶著一隊衣衫襤褸、目光呆滯如夢行者般的『工人』前來登記，問其姓名皆不應答。那不是活人，是可憐的還魂屍——約瑟夫與妻子克魯瓦昂絲把他們從安息的墳墓裡拖出，為其在烈日下作奴；眾所周知還魂屍絕不可沾鹽與肉，故克魯瓦昂絲另起一鍋，其食淡而無味。

sensitivity.note: The canonical modern zombie narrative (Seabrook 1929, event of 1918); presented as legend told by a named informant. The sensationalist frame of the source is noted; no recipes or practical details beyond the folklore.

passages.text: The spring of 1918 was a big cane season, and the factory, which had its own plantations, offered a bonus on the wages of new workers; soon heads of families and villages from the mountain and the plain came trailing their ragtag little armies — men, women, children trooping to the registration bureau and thence into the fields. One morning an old black headman, Ti Joseph of Colombier, appeared leading a band of ragged creatures who shuffled along behind him, staring dumbly, like people walking in a daze. As Joseph lined them up for registration they still stared, vacant-eyed like cattle, and made no reply when asked to give their names.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. 'Black Sorcery' (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Joseph said they were ignorant people from the slopes of Morne-au-Diable, a roadless mountain district near the Dominican border, who did not understand the creole of the plains; they were frightened, he said, by the din and smoke of the great factory, but under his direction they would work hard in the fields — and the farther they were sent away from the noise and bustle of the railroad yards, the better. Better indeed: for these were not living men and women but poor unhappy zombies whom Joseph and his wife Croyance had dragged from their peaceful graves to slave for him in the sun — and if by chance a brother or father of the dead should see and recognize them, Joseph knew that it would be a very bad affair for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they were assigned to distant fields beyond the crossroads, and camped there, keeping to themselves like any proper family or village group; but in the evening, when other little companies gathered each around its one big common pot of savory millet or plantains generously seasoned with dried fish and garlic, Croyance would tend two pots upon the fire — for as every one knows, the zombies must never be permitted to taste salt or meat. So the food prepared for them was tasteless and unseasoned; and as the zombies toiled day after day dumbly in the sun, Joseph sometimes beat them to make them move faster, but Croyance began to pity the poor dead creatures who should be at rest — and pitied them in the evenings when she dished out their flat, tasteless bouillie.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Salted Tablettes: the Zombies Remember Their Graves
title.zh: 加了鹽的花生糖：還魂屍歸墳

region.en: Cul-de-Sac cane fields and Morne-au-Diable, Haiti
region.zh: 海地庫爾德薩克蔗田與魔難山

period: Haitian legend, event of 1918; recorded 1927-1929; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. 'Black Sorcery' — the Fete-Dieu ending of the Hasco story

summary.en: On the day of the great feast Croyance, pitying her dead drudges once more, bought tablettes — 'not salted or seasoned, they are sweet, and can do no harm just this once.' But the baker had salted the pistache nuts before stirring them into the rapadou; and as the zombies tasted the salt, they knew that they were dead, made a dreadful outcry, arose, and turned their faces toward the mountain. No one dared to stop them, for they were corpses walking in the sunlight; and at their own village in the twilight they shuffled past fathers, wives, mothers who screamed and begged them to stay, up the path to the graveyard, and each before his own empty grave clawed the stones and earth to enter it again — and as their cold hands touched the earth of their own graves, they fell and lay there, rotting carrion.
summary.zh: 大節之日，克魯瓦昂絲再度憐憫這些亡者苦工，買來花生糖——『沒鹽沒料，是甜的，就這一次無妨』。誰知糖販在拌入糖漿前先給花生加了鹽；還魂屍一嘗到鹽，便知自己已死，發出可怖的哀號，起身轉向群山。無人敢攔——那是行走在日光下的屍體。薄暮時分，他們踏著碎步經過認出親人、哭喊挽留的村人，走上通往墓園的小徑，在各自空墳前刨掘石土欲入；冰冷的手觸到自家墳土的一刻，他們倒下，橫陳為腐肉。

sensitivity.note: Sequel of the Hasco narrative; the salt-taste rule is folklore-level. Source is Seabrook's popular-ethnography; the melodrama is his, the folk logic (salt releases the dead) is the tellers'.

passages.text: As Croyance sat with her savory dried herring and biscuit baked with salt and soda, and her provision of clairin in the tin cup by her side, she pitied the zombies who had worked so faithfully for Joseph in the cane fields and who now had nothing, while all the other groups around were feasting; and as she pitied them a woman passed, crying, 'Tablettes! Tablettes pistaches! Trois pour dix cobs!' — tablettes are a sort of candy, in shape and size like cookies, made of brown cane sugar, sometimes with pistaches, which in Haiti are peanuts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, The Magic Island, ch. 'Black Sorcery' (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: And Croyance thought, 'These tablettes are not salted or seasoned, they are sweet, and can do no harm to the zombies just this once.' So she untied the corner of her kerchief, took out a coin — a gourdon, the quarter of a gourde — and bought some of the tablettes, which she broke in halves and divided among the zombies, who began sucking and mumbling them in their mouths. But the baker of the tablettes had salted the pistache nuts before stirring them into the rapadou, and as the zombies tasted the salt, they knew that they were dead, and made a dreadful outcry, and arose and turned their faces toward the mountain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: No one dared to stop them, for they were corpses walking in the sunlight, and they themselves and all the people knew that they were corpses; and they disappeared toward the mountain. When later they drew near their own village on the slopes of Morne-au-Diable — these dead men and women walking single file in the twilight, with no soul leading them or daring to follow — the people of their village, holding their hamboche in the market-place, saw them drawing closer, and recognized among them fathers, brothers, wives and daughters whom they had buried months before. Most of them knew at once the truth, that these were zombies who had been dragged dead from their graves; but others hoped that a blessed miracle had taken place on this Fete Dieu, and rushed forward to take them in their arms and welcome them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the zombies shuffled through the market-place, recognizing neither father nor wife nor mother; and as they turned leftward up the path leading to the graveyard, a woman whose daughter was in the procession of the dead threw herself screaming before the girl's shuffling feet and begged her to stay — but the grave-cold feet of the daughter and the feet of the other dead shuffled over her and onward. As they approached the graveyard they began to shuffle faster and rushed among the graves, and each before his own empty grave began clawing at the stones and earth to enter it again; and as their cold hands touched the earth of their own graves, they fell and lay there, rotting carrion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Peasants Build Tombs: Polynice's Apology
title.zh: 為何農人築石墓：波利尼斯的辯白

region.en: Grande Source district, Haiti
region.zh: 海地大泉區

period: Haitian funerary practice; recorded 1927-1929; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: William B. Seabrook, 'The Magic Island' (1929), ch. 'Black Sorcery' (Constant Polynice on tombs, graves beside the road, and the night-watch with shotguns)

summary.en: Polynice, the rationalist friend, would not call it superstition: why do you suppose that even the poorest peasants, when they can, bury their dead beneath solid tombs of masonry? Why do they bury them so often in their own yards, close to the doorway? Why, so often, do you see a tomb set close beside a busy road where people are always passing? It is to assure the poor unhappy dead such protection as we can — and for his own brother, killed as everyone knew, he and Osmann kept four nights of watch in the peristyle with shotguns, until they were sure the body had begun to rot.
summary.zh: 理性友人波利尼斯不肯稱之迷信：為何連最窮的農人也要把亡者葬入堅固的石砌墓穴？為何常葬在自家院中、緊挨門口？為何墓塚總立於行人絡繹的大路旁？——這是為那些可憐而不幸的死者盡我們所能的保護。至於他那位死因眾人皆知的弟弟，他與奧斯曼在祭亭持獵槍守了四夜，直到確信屍身已開始腐爛為止。

sensitivity.note: Haitian funerary-protective practices described by a named informant; the watch described is a protective vigil, recorded as folkloric fact from the published source.

passages.text: The zombie, Polynice's neighbors said, is neither a ghost nor yet a person who has been raised like Lazarus from the dead: the zombie is a soulless human corpse, still dead, but taken from the grave and endowed by sorcery with a mechanical semblance of life — a dead body which is made to walk and act and move as if it were alive. People who have the power to do this go to a fresh grave, dig up the body before it has had time to rot, galvanize it into movement, and make of it a servant or slave, occasionally for the commission of some crime, more often simply as a drudge around the habitation or the farm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook, ch. 'Black Sorcery' (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seabrook asked Polynice to tell him something of the zombie superstition, that he might get at some idea of how it originated. His rational friend was deeply astonished, and put his hand in protest on his knee: 'Superstition? But I assure you that this of which you now speak is not a matter of superstition. Alas, these things — and other evil practices connected with the dead — exist. They exist to an extent that you whites do not dream of, though evidences are everywhere under your eyes.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Why do you suppose that even the poorest peasants, when they can, bury their dead beneath solid tombs of masonry? Why do they bury them so often in their own yards, close to the doorway? Why, so often, do you see a tomb or grave set close beside a busy road or footpath where people are always passing? It is to assure the poor unhappy dead such protection as we can.' He would take Seabrook in the morning to see the grave of his brother, killed as everyone knew: open space all round it, close beside the trail which everybody passes — and through four nights Polynice and Osmann had watched in the peristyle with shotguns, for at that time both his dead brother and he had bitter enemies, until they were sure the body had begun to rot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Seabrook (1929); not verbatim.

title.en: King and Queen of the Vaudoux: Moreau de Saint-Méry's Account
title.zh: 伏都之王與后：聖梅里的記述

region.en: Western Saint-Domingue (Haiti)
region.zh: 法屬聖多明各（今海地）西部

period: Recorded c. 1790 (Moreau de Saint-Méry); republished by St. John 1884

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, 'Hayti; or, The Black Republic' (1884), ch. V, reproducing Moreau de Saint-Méry's description of the Vaudoux (1790s)

summary.en: According to the Arada negroes, the true sectaries of the Vaudoux, the word signifies an all-powerful and supernatural being on whom depend all the events which take place in the world: the non-venomous serpent, through whose grand priest and high priestess — the King and Queen, or Master and Mistress, or the touching titles of Papa and Mama — all its knowledge of the past, the present and the future is communicated. The two delegates, chiefs for life of the great family of the Vaudoux, keep the serpent in its box upon the altar; petitioners bring their vows of eternal love or maledictions against a rival; the Queen, mounted on the sacred ark, is seized by the spirit and the oracle speaks by her mouth; and the offerings gathered in a covered hat pay the expenses of the meetings and give aid to absent or needy members — a secret society that functioned, in part, as a burial-and-relief fund.
summary.zh: 據真正的伏都教眾阿爾達黑人所言：『伏都』意即一位全能超凡之存在——無毒之蛇——世上諸事皆繫於它；其神諭只借大祭司與女大祭司之口而傳——人稱王與后、主與母、或親暱的爸爸媽媽。二位終身執掌伏都大家族，蛇靈伏於祭壇木匣之中；祈願者帶來永恆之愛的誓詞或詛咒情敵的惡語；王后立於神匣之上，神靈附體，神諭借其口而出；以蓋帽收下的獻金支付聚會開支，並接濟遠行或困乏的會友——這個秘密結社，實亦兼作互助與喪葬金會。

sensitivity.note: 18th-century colonial description (Moreau de Saint-Méry) reproduced through St. John's late-19th-century hostile framing. The society's relief-fund function is in the source text itself; the record preserves the balance between the source's sensationalism and its documentary detail. Living religion: liturgy not reproduced.

passages.text: According to the Arada negroes, who are the true sectaries of the Vaudoux in the colony, and maintain its principles and its rules, Vaudoux signifies an all-powerful and supernatural being, on whom depend all the events which take place in the world. This being is the non-venomous serpent, and it is under its auspices that all those assemble who profess this doctrine. Acquaintance with the past, knowledge of the present, prescience of the future, all appertain to this serpent, that only consents to communicate his power and prescribe his will through the organ of a grand priest, whom the sectaries select, and still more by that of the negress whom the love of the latter has raised to the rank of high priestess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, Hayti, ch. V, reproducing Moreau de Saint-Méry (1884/1790s); not verbatim.

passages.text: These two delegates, who declare themselves inspired by their god — or in whom the gift of inspiration is really manifested in the opinion of their followers — bear the pompous names of King and Queen, or the despotic ones of Master and Mistress, or the touching titles of Papa and Mama. They are during their whole life the chiefs of the great family of the Vaudoux, and they have a right to the unlimited respect of the sectaries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: A young one solicits eternal love, or she repeats the maledictions that hate dictates against a preferred rival; there is not a passion which does not give vent to its vow. At each of these invocations the King of the Vaudoux appears absorbed in thought; the spirit seizes him, and suddenly he takes hold of the box in which the serpent is confined, places it on the ground, and commands the Queen to get on it. As soon as the sacred ark is beneath her feet, the new Pythoness is filled by the spirit of their god; she trembles, all her body is in a state of convulsion, and the oracle speaks by her mouth — now she flatters and promises happiness, now she bursts into reproaches, dictating as decrees without appeal everything she is pleased to prescribe in the name of the serpent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: After the questions have received their answers, they form a circle and the serpent is again placed on the altar; his followers bring as tribute the objects they think most worthy, and that no jealous curiosity may raise a blush the offerings are placed in a covered hat. The King and Queen promise the offerings shall be accepted by their god. It is from this collection that the expenses of the meetings are paid, that aid is afforded to absent members, or to those present who may be in want, or to others from whom the society may expect something in favor of its glory or renown — and a fresh oath engages each one to be silent as to what has passed, sometimes sealed by the warm blood of a goat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Initiation Circle and the Monter-Vaudou in Old Saint-Domingue
title.zh: 聖多明各的入會圈與『上伏都』

region.en: Western Saint-Domingue (Haiti)
region.zh: 法屬聖多明各（今海地）西部

period: Recorded c. 1790 (Moreau de Saint-Méry); republished 1884

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, 'Hayti; or, The Black Republic' (1884), ch. V — the dance of the Vaudoux and the admission of new candidates

summary.en: The fete begins with the admission of the candidate: the King traces a large circle with some black substance and places the novice within it, a packet of herbs, horsehair, pieces of horn and other trifling objects in his hand; lightly touching his head with a wooden wand, he thunders forth an African song repeated in chorus around the circle — then the new member begins to tremble and to dance, which is called to practise Vaudoux. If excess of excitement makes him leave the circle the song stops, the King and Queen turn their backs to avert the evil omen; he re-enters, trembles, drinks, and arrives at so convulsive a state that the King stops him with a touch of the wand — and from that moment he belongs to the sect.
summary.zh: 慶典以收徒開場：王以黑物畫一大圈，置新會者於圈中，手捧藥草、馬鬃、獸角諸物；木杖輕點其頂，朗聲唱起非洲古調，圈眾應聲而和——於是新會者顫慄起舞，是謂『行伏都』。若狂喜過度而跨出圈外，歌聲立止，王與后背身轉向以避凶兆；其人回圈再顫、復飲，終至痙攣之境，王以杖點其頂止之——自那一刻起，他便屬於這個教團。

sensitivity.note: 18th-century colonial description; the same ceremony reappears in the 1904 Cuban record (cross_ref: afroatlantic-louisiana-voodoo-rites, afroatlantic-vaudoux-king-queen). Living religion: initiation liturgy not reproduced.

passages.text: After these ceremonies commences the dance of the Vaudoux. If there should be a new candidate, it is by his admission that the fete commences. The King of the Vaudoux, with some black substance, traces a large circle, and in this the novice is placed; and in his hand he puts a packet of herbs, horsehair, pieces of horn, and other trifling objects.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, Hayti, ch. V (1884/1790s); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then lightly touching him on the head with a slight wooden wand, he thunders forth an African song, which is repeated in chorus by those who stand around the circle; then the new member begins to tremble and to dance, which is called to practise Vaudoux. If, unhappily, excess of excitement makes him leave the circle, the song immediately ceases, the King and Queen turn their backs to avert the evil omen. The dancer recollects himself, re-enters the circle, again trembles, drinks, and arrives at length at so convulsive a state that the King orders him to stop by striking him lightly on the head with his wand. He is taken to the altar to swear, and from that moment he belongs to the sect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: This ceremony over, the King places his hand or his foot on the box in which the serpent is confined, and soon becomes agitated; this impression he communicates to the Queen, and from her it gains the whole circle, and every one commences certain movements in which the upper part of the body, the head and shoulders, appear to be dislocated — a nervous trembling seizes them all, which they appear unable to master. In reading this account, freely given from Moreau de Saint-Méry, St. John was struck how little change, except for the worse, had taken place during the last century.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The 1864 Trial and the Empty Graves
title.zh: 一八六四年審判與空墳之謎

region.en: Port-au-Prince, Haiti
region.zh: 海地太子港

period: Historical event of 1864, described in a hostile colonial account (St. John, 1884)

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, 'Hayti; or, The Black Republic' (1884), ch. V — the trial at which the author was present, and the disappearances after execution

summary.en: The eight convicts of the 1864 sorcery trial were executed in white robes on a market-day for solemnity — and the Vaudoux priests gave out that although the deity would permit the execution, he would only do it to prove his power by raising them all again from the dead. Piquets of troops were placed round the burial place to prevent the bodies being carried away in the night; but in the morning three of the graves were found empty — the bodies of the two priests and the priestess had disappeared; superstitious fear had probably unmanned the sentries, and as most of the troops belonged to the sect, they probably connived at rather than prevented the exhumation.
summary.zh: 一八六四年巫案八名死囚著白袍於集市之日處決——而伏都祭司放話：神雖允許行刑，卻要以此證其大能，將八人全數復活。當局以衛兵環守葬地防人夜掘；翌晨三座墳墓已空——兩位祭司與女祭司的遺體不翼而飛。或許是迷信之懼令哨兵不敢久留；而部隊多屬教團中人，與其說阻止了開棺，不如說暗中成全。

sensitivity.note: SENSITIVE: This record treats the 1864 Port-au-Prince 'Vaudoux' executions as historical event within a colonial-era source whose accusations of ritual murder were part of a polemic (St. John's chapter was widely republished as anti-Vodou propaganda). Modern scholarship reads these trial narratives skeptically as colonial sensationalism; the record preserves the documented elements (trial, executions, claim of resurrection, empty graves) without reproducing gore, and flags the source bias. This is not representative of Vodou, a living religion.

passages.text: The trial was held before a judge who conducted himself with dignity, and whose court heard testimony from a young girl witness — protected from the prisoners' intimidation by being placed with her back to them while she whispered her story to the judge — and from other witnesses, until the guilt of the prisoners was fully established. They were all found guilty of sorcery, torture, and murder, and condemned to death. The execution took place on Saturday, February 13, 1864, the authorities wisely selecting a market-day in order that the example might have the greater effect; the prisoners, men and women, were all clothed in white robes and white headdresses — the garments reserved for parricides — and were drawn in carts to the place of execution.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, Hayti, ch. V (1884); details of the alleged crimes deliberately summarized without gore; not verbatim.

passages.text: The troops and National Guard were summoned, for even the word rescue had been pronounced; the prisoners, tied in pairs, were placed in a line and faced by five soldiers to each pair. As usual the prisoners behaved with great courage, even the women standing up unflinchingly before their executioners.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Vaudoux priests gave out that although the deity would permit the execution, he would only do it to prove to his votaries his power by raising them all again from the dead. To prevent their bodies being carried away during the night — they had been buried near the place of execution — piquets of troops were placed round the spot; but in the morning three of the graves were found empty, and the bodies of the two priests and the priestess had disappeared. Superstitious fear had probably prevented the soldiers from staying where they had been posted, and as most of the troops belonged to the sect of the Vaudoux, they probably connived at, rather than prevented, the exhumation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: Bondye and the Grand Chemin: Haitian Vodou Cosmology
title.zh: 邦迪耶與大路：海地伏都宇宙論

region.en: Haiti (symbolic pin: Port-au-Prince)
region.zh: 海地（象徵定位：太子港）

period: Haitian Vodou, attested from 18th c.; synthesized from 20th-c. scholarship

source.work: Alfred Métraux, 'Voodoo in Haiti' (Paris 1958/New York 1959); Leslie G. Desmangles, 'The Faces of the Gods' (1992); Karen McCarthy Brown, 'Mama Lola' (1991)

license: Paraphrase summaries only; no liturgical text reproduced

summary.en: Bondye — 'Bon Dieu' — is the distant creator who set the world in motion and no longer mixes directly in human affairs; below him the lwa, the ancestral and cosmic powers, mediate every petition. Between the worlds runs the Grand Chemin, the great road by which the dead travel and the living send word — a crossroads cosmos in which Legba holds the gate, Baron guards the cemetery, and every ceremony is a journey mapped on the peristyle floor.
summary.zh: 邦迪耶——『善神』——是遙遠的創世者，推動世界之後便不再直接干預人事；其下的羅阿（祖靈與宇宙之力）代為轉達一切祈求。兩界之間奔流著『大路』——亡者行旅、生者傳訊之道；十字路口的宇宙裡，雷格巴司門，男爵守墓，每一場儀式都是畫在祭亭地面上的一次旅程。

sensitivity.note: Deep record built from published scholarly paraphrase only. Vodou is a living religion: initiatory liturgies and veve sequences are restricted and are NOT reproduced.

passages.text: In Haitian Vodou the creator, Bondye (from the French Bon Dieu, 'Good God'), stands at the apex of the cosmos — but as a distant one.
